The banquet room was large enough to commodate all of us, had an adequate sound system that everyone could hear clearly, and a catering kitchen that put out a Cornish hen plate that was tasty and attractive. The carrot cake dessert was a bit over the top, but no one was complaining about the buttercream icing.   Service was unabtrusive, but kept the meal moving and the water glasses full.   Can't speak to the rooms above, but this operation handled our bar association meeting quite well.

While the Shops At Liberty Place offer an architecturally interesting structure in a modern urban environment, and attracts people for both shopping and sightseeing the latest in city planning, it also likely represents a business model that will not succeed in the long run.    The suburban mall made its presence felt as a post World War II phenomenon that mirrored the rapid growth of the automobile industry and the closely aligned migration of a generation of city dwellers into the countryside, a/k/a Suburbia.  They were the successful way to provide the "stuff" of life away from the urban core.  They worked well for almost 50 years.  But, as with most things, they were overdone, and failed to adapt to the changing demographics and cultural evolution that they spawned.  Walk through most malls today and you see lots of empty space, failing stores, and a subculture of youth versus elderly hangouts.    First the malls disrupted Main Street.  Then the Walmarts and Costco's of the world, disrupted the malls.  But, the disassociation from the communities where the consumer lived ultimately started to alienate them.  People wanted to return to their Main Street where possible.  More began to appreciate the quality of city life, and returned to the urban centers to once again live and work in the same place.  The suburbs began to lose its charm for many, especially those without young children.    These reurbanified folk did not want to shop in malls along an inhuman highway, and certainly did not want to spend much time in a suburban style mall transplanted in the city.  The developers who thought otherwise, are wishing they had been smarter.  The retail franchisers and chain expanders were the last to catch on, but the growing list of failing stores and malls bear witness to this truth.    So it is with the Shops of Freedom Place.  Fundamentally, a suburban marketplace miscast as a modern upscale urban experience that it turned out not enough people really wanted.  A J. Crew in a Center City suburban style mall just does not attract enough customers.  Never will.   It is not that such a public space could never work.  It can, but it requires a total reconfiguration that demonstrates an understanding of what people really want.  What is that?  A return to the village life, or that of the old neighborhood, where people knew each other, and felt like part of a community - in the city.  More impersonal and monotonous shopping is not where we are headed.    How accomplish that?  Start by thinking in human scale.  Change part of the Liberty Place skyscrapers into condos and apartments for people to live.  Add a supermarket, cinema, child care, medical facility, and more greenery throughout the buildings.  Create a vertical village or neighborhood.  Where are the green grocer, the deli, the bakery, the corner tavern?   The central rotunda can still work as a gathering place for activities, but it should feel more like the gazebo in the middle of the public commons.    People want their cities to be state of the art, cutting edge, and full of energy and opportunity.  But, they also want to feel like it can take care of their needs and make them feel part of it, not overcome by it.  There are examples of this being done successful around the country and the planet.  Visit some of the new cities in Asia, and even some of the new age projects in New York, Seattle(JB) and San Francisco.    Bring it down to human scale, and they will come and thrive.

The was a reason why this BK was practically empty when I stopped in for a quick breakfast the other day.    The Biscuit for my sandwich was hard and too small to enclose its contents.  It appeared to be a tube biscuit that had been made earlier and left in the open air to dry out, and then microwaved just before sale.  It rehardened quickly and was a crumbly mess to eat.  Just not very good, despite the fact that the rest of the ingredients seemed fresh.    Given the competition across the street, it is difficult to see how this place survives. Maybe their burgers are better, but I won't be back to find out.

Despite the hour long wait on Friday night, J.B. Dawson's in the Flowers Mill Shopping Center was worth the wait.  Normally, I would see the waiting room crowd and listen to the hostess's lament of the wait time, and walk out immediately. For some reason, my intuition counseled patience, so I took the radio buzzer they handed me, and found three seats to settle in.    The  bar was packed with Friday Happy Hour folk getting their zip on, and the two HDTVs in the waiting area were soundlessly tuned to Disney Channel and ESPN.  No one seemed to be paying attention, and the peeps around me were all conversing or buried in their smartphones. The time passed quickly, and we were eventually led to a corner booth in the barroom.  Our server introduced herself, took drink orders and came back promptly to take our order.  We wanted to share the Baby Back Rib and Chicken Tender plate, while young man went with his standard Cheeseburger and Fries.    Dinner took a little while due to the packed house, but not so long as to become an issue.  When it arrived in the hands of a different server, we beheld a half rack of Baby Backs nicely browned and caramelized on top, and a larger pile of Tempura coated white meat Chicken, plus sides of Garlic Mashed Potatoes and Spiced Apples.  I began to salivate involuntarily as the aroma of the BBQ sauce hit me.  I hoped the first bite would be as seductive.    It was more than that.     The meat easily pulled from the bone.  The taste was very good, and the texture just chewy and tender enough to be completely satisfying.  Although there was very little meat left on the bones, I found myself sucking on them to capture every last bit of BBQ taste.  If anything, the Chicken Tenders were even better and a much bigger surprise.  They were big strips of never frozen chicken, breaded in a Tempura style, that were juicy, lightly crunchy and delicious.  The small mound of Mashed Taters were a nice complement to the more exciting pig and bird, but did a great job absorbing whatever sauce was stuck to the plate.  The Spiced Apple was yet another change of directly with its tartness and heat.    I did not see a smoker on the premises, nor smell it at work, but regardless of how the meal was prepared, the execution was high end and the experience very solidly worth a return visit.

My office neighbor and I went to lunch at La Vecchia Osteria this afternoon, after postponing our plans a few times due to busy schedules.  So glad we finally made it!  We were greeted warmly by the owner, Pasquale, and served by his beautiful daughter. The side room was bright with the winter sun streaming in the windows and making the golden amber room glow.  The corner table offered a little privacy, but it was not crowded today.  Small Antipasto with a mix of prosciutto, salami, hard cheeses, buffalo mozz.,  black and green olives to begin.  Fresh, crusty bread with olio and herb dip.  Grilled Branzino filleted after cooking, and just before bringing to the table.  Pure white tender with light extra virgin and lemon.  Perfect!  My friend had Chicken Breast in olive oil and capers, with a side of Vodka Rigatoni.  We stopped our chat while we savored our repast.    Conversation resumed with a slightly gazed countenance of satisfaction as we finished with coffee and sharing a homemade Cannoli that was so smooth, sweet, and creamy that we had to close our eyes to fully absorb the experience.    Oh well, another dinnerless night.  But, it was so worth it!

I am just getting into BBQ in a bigger way, so when I saw Christopher D's review of Oink Johnson's Southern BBQ along with the few others, I had a strong impulse to drive up county and find out for myself what this place had to offer. It was a gorgeous early September afternoon special made for a open window stereo blazing cruise in the rolling Bucks countryside. I was in a good mood.  Driving up 611 north of Doylestown with the GPS alerting me that I was at my destination, I still did not recognize it at first.  There is a small cabin on wheels sitting in the middle of the rocky parking lot, with a fruit stand on one side, and a puppy barn on the other.  That trailered shack was Oink's.  The front porch of the structure has two large BBQ grills, a large menu nailed to the wall.  Took a few seconds to get oriented, especially when this big fella with a white apron and big white mustache came over and looked down at me and said:  "What'll it be, young feller?"  "Well, sir. I can't decide 'tween the Pulled Pork and the Brisket. What do ya think?"  "They're both lip smackin' good, my man.  Can't go wrong with either."   Ok. I was hooked by ol' Oink's charm even before I made a choice.  This guy and the whole set up was right out of a Michener novel.  I was game to play my role.   Two of his buddies sat to the side of the shack under an old beer company umbrella watching this transaction.  I looked over to greet them with a reference to the weather, and they chawed back that maybe I should get one of both the pork and brisket. Nice upsell, gents.   I ordered the Pulled Pork Sandwich, BBQ Beans and Corn Bread.  Oink disappeared into the enclosed portion of the hut on wheels to make his magic.  He appeared a few minutes later with a large white paper wrapped package that seemed too big to be a Sammy.  I couldn't see what was in it, which was just slightly troubling, but this man had such an aura of confidence that I let it slide thinking I was probably missing the point of just knowing it would be great without a need for a visual.   This place is strictly take out, so although I would have preferred to enjoy my BBQ on site, I had to take with and drive back home to eat it.  No biggie.  Upon unwrapping the creation I found it was indeed a huge quantity of meat, but the roll had been saturated with pork and BBQ juices, and was too wet to eat. I ate the pork with a fork.  It was tender and juicy, yet the BBQ flavor was not very strong, and it was a bit salty for my palate. The Beans were richly dark brown, heavy with molasses and chunks of fat back bacon. Excellent. The Corn Bread in the form of a muffin was good, but not overly sweet nor moist.   If I could give a grade just for personality and appearance, Oink Johnson would be a 5 Star experience. But, as the Pulled Pork was not as good as others I have eaten, and the roll was a total loss, the food comes in at 2 Stars for me.  I will get back there eventually to try the ribs and brisket, but I am disappointed by the lack of "Zing" in the Pulled Pork.  Still, I recommend stopping in as the characters are wonderful, the locale very pretty farmland, and the food worth a sampling.

Just returned to Keystone to buy 4 new tires. They recommended Continentals, and I agreed with their assessment of their quality and ride.   On the way home, one of them blew out!  What?!  True.  I called and returned the next day for a replacement (They had to order it).  They apologized for the experience, although it was clearly a manufacturer's defect, and discounted it down to the cost of mounting and balancing (normally part of the quoted price). They handled the paperwork.   While this was not a fun time, but Keystone stood behind the product and satisfied me of their integrity. I did not have to ask for some consideration. They offered it straight up.   I did not mind the small cost of mounting the new tire in light of how well they handled the situation.   5 Stars if they had taken care of all of it.

If you are like me, and enjoy a small business success story served with whipped cream and strong coffee, the Old Croydon Café is just about as good as it gets.    I stopped in for the first time this week and took a stool at the counter.  From my vantage point I could look into the kitchen service window and see the heads of the cooks making magic out of eggs and pancake mix.  The old joint is on the north end of State Road, which I soon discovered could be used as a detour from Rt. 95, all the way to Center City.  Good to know!  The place is small, with 7 or 8 stools and an equal number of booths and tables.  I sat next to a house painter, lawn mower repair man, and a roofer.  The conversation was cordial and full of gallant repartee.  The owners worked front and back and kept the dishes coming along with the warm banter.  I really liked OCC even before my French Toast Deluxe arrived.  This was as downhome as this part of Pennsylvania gets.   When my breakfast arrived I beheld an oval plate framing a still life watercolor.  The 3 slices of well grilled and caramelized French Toast, topped with Fresh Whipped Cream and Blueberries, Strawberries, and Bananas, and finished with a lazy drizzle of Blueberry Sauce. (See Photo) The toast was hot, the cream cool, and the fruit cold and juicy.  The tastes and textures were fun and delicious.  It was one of those meals that I did not want to end.    Old Croydon Café has definitely made my very short list of favorite breakfast nooks.  I will return to explore the menu, and even come back for lunch when possible.    This place is a hidden treasure.

It pains me to remember the recently completed dinner at Taco Suave.  Such high expectations after reading the other reviews.  Such auspicious beginnings. Such a sudden and disappointing finale.  We walked in to this tiny strip mall corner restaurant. About a dozen tables with white table clothes.  I was thinking that in my experience, the hole in the wall Mexican joints were always the best.  At least, that had been true in Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and even SoCal.    We sat and ordered the Agua de Pina (Pineapple Water), which was a first and a pleasant drink of diluted pineapple juice whipped to a froth.  Really good! I was getting more excited as I imagined we had just discovered the Fountain of Youth drink right here in Warrington.  Then the homemade Chips and Fresh Salsa came out. Heavy crunchy mild oily sensation with a mild Mexi flavor, and a Tomato, Cilantro Salsa with a sweetness equal to the chili's heat.  Loved it.   Encouraged and feeling adventurous by the fun of the apps and drink, I went for the Pollo Dorado (Golden Fried Chicken), the most expensive item on the menu.  Visions of plump chicken breast with a wonderful fruity sauce danced in my head. My friends had a Burrito de Carne Asada, and a Taco con Queso.    What was placed before me was instead three over cooked deep fried drumsticks with an oil soaked brown coating that tasted primarily of salt.  My physical reaction to eating this was matched by the instantly deflated sense of gluttony so rudely assaulted and kicked to the curb.  I kept eating hoping for a secondary burst of flavor to save this.  It did not come. I passed around the chicken and the reaction was universal. Bad.   The Burrito de Carne Asada was large and full of bits of beef and cheese, but way too mild, and a bit too fatty.  It was left one third eaten.  The Taco con Queso presented well, but was practically tasteless.  We liberally added hot salsa to throw them life preservers, but we could not save them.  The dinner was a victim of drowning.   We will not be back.  I wish I had a different review to write about Taco Suave, but true to the Yelpers Creed, I cannot hide from the bitter taste of a disappointing meal.    Our server, Mirna, was great!

"Welcome to Nirvana," he said with a open faced smile that hinted that he had practiced this line many times as an owner of Nirvana Fusion.  He waited for his words to penetrate and for our reaction.    Magically, we were transported to the Himalayas in Nepal, where we would dine this night.  You see, the "fusion" in Nirvana Fusion comes from the fact that the owners and chef of this mountain house are from Nepal, where they are at the cross currents of north Indian and southwest Chinese culture.  Fusion comes naturally when you grow up in it.  Both cuisines roll over each other, mix and retreat with each human tide; leaving behind something that is both informed by their neighbors, and creative of a new reality where turmeric and curry meet chili and dragon fruit.  The similarities are undeniable.  The uniqueness, extraordinary.    The menu read differently than those of similarly named restaurants.  Extra time was needed to penetrate, and many questions had to be answered by our hosts.  We were curious.  They were patient.  We ultimately ordered the Chili Chicken (Dry) and Gobi Manchurian (Dry) appetizers, the Chicken Zafrani traditional Indian dish, and the Vegetable Hakka Noodles from the Indo/Chinese/Thai Fusion section, to try a cross section of their offerings.    Both the apps were spicy hot and looked surprising similar in deep red amber sauces.  The Chili Chicken tasted of both Chili and Tumeric in the thick sauce coating the small morsels of chicken.  It was very good and left our mouths burning without reaching numbness.  The Gobi (deep fried cauliflower) in another dark sauce with pieces of clumped spices sticking to everything, was excellent in that the vegetable flavor and texture remained although bathed in the heavy float.  The cross fertilization of cultures was most evident here.  The Chicken Zafrani was more straight forward North Indian with a softer curry infused with the sweetness of Almonds, Cashews and Saffron.  There were also Kashmiri Chilies in there, but they did not dominate.  Finally, the Hakka Noodles really seemed more a straight up Chinese dish very akin to a chunky Lo Mein.  Very nice.   Nirvana Fusion took me by surprise - a pleasant one.  It is definitely deserves returning for more adventures.    We weren't in Hatboro anymore, Toto.

The Blue Duck is a nice place to stop for brunch or lunch if you find yourself in the vicinity.  It has a reputation for offering "Center City" atmosphere, with "Northeast Philly" earthiness.  I guess that means you don't always have to run downtown to find a cool place to eat, or conversely, that Northeast Philly now has its own duck fat fries outlet.  Can I hear a, "Hallelujah!"?  We stopped in for a late lunch after an appointment with Homeland Security on Drummond Road nearby.  That is never a sparkling experience, and we all wanted something to wash away the bureaucratic dust that comes with dealing with the Feds. We ordered three of their signature burgers, and the Salt & Pepper Fries for the table.  Water all around. We waited about 20 minutes for our meals to arrive, all the while smelling the grilling beef in the open kitchen.  This was a very hot day, and the HVAC was struggling to maintain the right comfort level.  Even with the front door closed, the humidity in the house was noticeable.    The House Grind Burger, Pork Roll Burger and Beast of Northeast Burger arrived in the arms of our erstwhile server.  All looked great with Brioche-style rolls, and the individual toppings.  My Beast was a mix of Wild Boar and Beef, Smoked Gouda, Sweet Tomato Jam, Bacon and Crisp Sriracha Shoestring Onions.  Beautiful to behold.  First bite should have been awesome, but aside from the interesting flavor of the fixings, the "Medium" finish requested was in fact, "Well Done."  With the juice gone, I could not taste the difference in the meats, and found the burger less than hoped. The same was true for the House Grind, although for some reason the Pork Roll Burger came out "Medium Rare,"  and amply juiced.  The S & P Fries were good; hot, but not crisp.   It is always awkward to low rank a popular restaurant, but it was what it was.  Someone needs to pay more attention at the grill, as it is likely to have happened before.    Good luck with your new Center City enterprise.

I am about to give up on Frozen Yogurt joints.   Over the last year or more, I have not found a single one that offers a quality product that tastes as good as the equivalent ice cream.  While it is nice to save on calories (if that is really the case), tasteless extrusions just don't satisfy my need for something cold, creamy and sweet.    This Redberry, while small and clean, offers nothing better than the others.  The Traditional Vanilla and Peanut Butter choices were indistinguishable from each other.  Only the add ons had any taste.   What's the point?

I found myself hungry around noon in Doylestown today, and decided to check out Hickory Kitchen for an early lunch.   First impression was that this was an efficient, sunny, Main Street bistrot serving everything from soups to burgers to BBQ, with a large vegetarian option.  I almost went for the Special Bison Burger after having just had a Yelp discussion about buffalo burgers, but had eaten enough meat yesterday, and just didn't want more.  So, I went for the Grilled Veggie Quesadilla and home brewed Sweet Peach Iced Tea.  The chef and server got busy at the grill, and produced my meal in about 10 minutes. It came out on a small aluminum baking tray (clever), with Sour Cream, Salsa, and a bag of chips (?).   The Quesadilla was very good, and I could not finish it. It was full of chunky veggies and cheese.  The Iced Tea was fine, just lightly sweetened. Each table had three bottle rockets with three varieties of BBQ sauce - mustard, maple, and tomato based. I tried each of them on the quesadilla in place of the jar based salsa.  I liked them more than the salsa, and think HK is onto something as an alternative to the traditional accompaniment for Mexican dishes.  The mix of Mexi - BBQ could be a big hit (but, it is not Tex-Mex).  This review will likely be updated when I return to taste the BBQ options here. Most of the raves seem to be for the ribs, so I will get back for them.   All in all, a good first bite, but I can't say that I am drawn enough to return promptly that being a fan suggests.  A nice effort with potential.

When you're down in Bensalem around Neshaminy Mall, finding a good Chinese/Sushi restaurant can be a challenge.  The AMC 24 is a nice place to watch a movie, but the "dinner and" part of that is limited in the immediate vicinity unless you like highway-style fast/casual food.    Then there is Misto Diner, which I found courtesy of Yelp. As other reviewers said, the location on this site is off by about a mile.  It is further down Neshaminy Blvd after passing Bristol Road if coming from the rear of NM, in a small strip mall anchored by 7-11.  Keep going.  You will get there. It is worth the search, as the quality of the room and cuisine are considerably above the standard Chinese American shop.    White table clothes and red cloth napkins are a nice touch suggesting a bit of quality control in the product.  The owner family is present and in charge.  They bring care and pride to the effort.  Although I did not ask, our server seemed to be the father.  He had a Jackie Chan appearance; friendly, engaged, and humorous.  His bifocals tried to hide his bemused visage as we asked questions about the menu and the history of the joint.    We settled on Hot and Sour Soup, Chicken Broccoli in Garlic Sauce, and Shredded Pork Mei Fun.  The soup was a rich, thick, spicy mix.  We added a spoonful of Chili Oil to bring out more of the hot richness.  It was a nice improvement to an already good bowl of soup.  The Chicken dish was off menu as we asked for garlic sauce as opposed to the Hunan style base.  The meat was tender and very tasty.  The broccoli cut into small enough sprigs and excellently cooked.  The mei fun was also good, but not at the same level as the other dishes.  To be clear, Misto Diner is still a traditional Chinese American restaurant found in most suburban areas, but it is a very good one.  It should not be mistaken for an authentic Chinese restaurant found in more heavily Chinese populated parts of the region. But, if you find yourself in this neck of the woods this is a very good choice.  Too, they have no problem giving you an extra pot of tea if you want to wait there for your movie time.

Kelly's Kitchen is the actual name of this breakfast/lunch café sitting at the bottom of Bristol Road in Bensalem.  It has a nice counter with about a dozen spinners, and an equal number of tables, but the kitchen is in the back of the house so you can't see the meals being prepared, nor smell of the bacon on the grill.   The service is good with prompt offers of coffee refills and light banter to make you feel at home.  My Kelly's Irish Omelet was a three egger with Onions, Peppers and Cheddar alongside a huge pile of crispy Home Fries, and Rye Toast.  I thought the eggs could have been lighter in texture if mixed with a little water before cooking, and there wasn't a whole lot of the veggies inside the eggs.  It was a bit underwhelming for a House Special.  The potatoes and toast were both fine.  The absence of credit card acceptance is annoying in today's world, and retailers who choose not to make their customer's lives easier in this regard should be called to account.    While the room and service were fine, the food was not consistently exceptional, and the Cash Only policy shows a lack of true concern for its customers. Hard to get past A-OK.

It's a bit surprising to find a decent BBQ joint in a back room of the Best Western Motel on Street Road, Bensalem, Pa.  The place has almost zero atmosphere, no aroma of smoking meat, no beer spillage on the floor, and no one in boots nor large apron cutting the brisket.  There is only Julie, the matron of the house and jack of all serving trades, handling just about everything.  She bartends, takes food orders, serves everything that comes out of the kitchen, and then collects payment at the end of the night.  She makes it personal by asking everyone's first name, and remembering them throughout.   Don't let the environment deter you from coming in.  The grub is very good.  First, there are several beers on tap or bottles, although on this Sunday night they seemed to be out of most of the good crafties.  Still, my End of The World draft was pleasantly cold and refreshing at $4 for 10oz. Friends seemed to be downing Yards brew as quickly as it was poured.    My crew of three ordered Half BBQ Chicken (3 sides, corn bread, fries); Coffee Rubbed Brisket (3 sides, hush puppies, fries); and a third rack of St. Louis style Ribs (4 bones, 2 sides, fries).  There was a ton and a half of food.  And, it was all very good to amazing.  The Half Chicken came our golden skinned without a crack in the covering.  It was uber-moist and had a wonderful flavor.  It needed no accompanying sauce to kick it up a notch, as it was really an apex bird.  The Ribs were very good, but not the meatiest I have encountered.  The dry rub was very solid, but I found it needed a little liquid zing to get to my preferred taste level.  The table had 2 unmarked bottle rockets, one based in vinegar, the other, tomato.  Both okay, but not the strength of the cuisine.    The unexpected star of the show was the Brisket.  This cut of beef in normally dry in my experience, but this was not the case at Ben's.  Whether the coffee rub, or the time in the smoker, this thin sliced pound of nearly black carne was just so moist, tender and delicious.  The taste of brisket was very present, but the secret sauce brought out undertones and texture that truly opened our eyes.  Even the normal stringiness of the cut was an asset on the platter.  It made for more surface area to hold the smoke and rub.  Can't say that I actually tasted coffee, but that wasn't needed to find this dish remarkable.    There are a few downsides to eating at Ben's.  First, service was slow by definition.  Only one person doing everything.  She made a few mistakes on our orders, but nothing so egregious as to require markdowns.  Then, we were given plastic utensils to negotiate the load of food.  They simply were not up to the task of dealing with the meat and sides.  Broken fork prongs, snapped knives were a part of the night.  How much better to invest in real steel blades and spikes to control the contest.  As mentioned above, they seemed to be out of many of their listed brews.   Prices are fair for the menu and (lack of) atmosphere.    Put the smokers out in the parking lot for all to see, maintain your beer inventory, and provide customers with the tools to subdue the wild animals on our plates, and Ben (Franklin)'s could become a great BBQ mainstay in this area.

When all the other historic sites in Philadelphia were closed because of shut downs and furloughs coming from the nonsense in Washington, alone in staying proudly open was Carpenter's Hall, much as it has since its founding in 1770.    An excellent example of Georgian style architecture, it was built by the first trade union in the United States, The Carpenters' Company.  It was here that the American Revolution really began with the First Continental Congress in 1774, when delegates from 12 colonies (nee Georgia), met to decide how to respond to the mounting British oppression.  They voted to boycott all English goods, and to meet again the following year should this not be enough to solve the problem.  The rest, as we all know, is our history.    Ben Franklin opened his Library Company on the second floor.  The first and second National Bank of the United States used the first floor for several years before grander quarters were built nearby (and ultimately failed when challenged by Andrew Jackson years later).   The building is set back from Chestnut Street, and approaching it gives a perspective of how it much have felt to do so in the 18th Century on cobblestone, horse manure, oil lamp streets.  It has a modest nobility for a structure so old and prominent in our nation's struggles for freedom.  Its larger grander cousin, Independence Hall, soon overtook it as the symbol of this fight and the center of courageous political discourse on the path to nationhood, but Carpenters' Hall continued to play a significant role as a meeting house for rebels and spies, the Philosophical Society, hospital, and Franklin's Library.   In a time when the struggle to birth a nation was very real and daunting, and men had to seriously pledge their sacred honor and very lives to take a stand, it is a sad comparison to realize how far we have fallen as a country this very day. Those people knew the meaning of what they were doing, and went ahead bravely.    Where are those leaders today?    Carpenters' Hall awaits their awakening and offers a reminder of what true patriotism means.

For a place that specializes in one thing - salad - there is a disconnect between their mission and final product.    I have eaten here a few times over the years, and while nothing I have ordered/eaten has been bad, my impression was that the bowls were thrown together by rote with excessive inattention to detail.  Often the ingredients are just dropped into the salad bowl and left unmixed or given a perfunctory stir.  Separate piles of cheese, nuts, dried fruits, etc., left where they fall.  Sometimes, one of the elements is forgotten without awareness of the shortcoming.    When the pleasure of this experience comes in over $10 for lunch, it is difficult to think that value has been attained.  Asking for the dressing on the side to take charge of the finish is helpful, but when it becomes necessary to insure that I am dealing with a salad and not piles of vegetables as yet unrelated to each other, I feel like I am doing their jobs.   With so many other restaurants offering healthy creative fresh salads as part of a broader menu, there seems little reason to go to a place whose sole reason for existence is doing something that is ultimately inferior to the competition.  There is something inherently contradictory in a mass produced "custom made" salad.    That contradiction is manifest by what comes across the counter at Saladworks.

Comfortable Star$$$ in the Acme Shopping Center just south of Bordentown off Route 130.    Not a fan of their burnt approach to java, but sometimes it is the only option in the vicinity.  The Flat White was fine, but the prices are designed to make the stockholders happier than the customers.    This shop was well laid out with ample table and comfortable seating around.  No problem with the staff.  Everyone was in a good mood this mid-week late morning.  Several quiet conversations and solitary students around and about.

I found myself here for lunch and dinner one day last week due to a long court appearance.  I have no complaints about the kitchen, nor the service of Spice Thai Cuisine.   The space is all cool dark wood and deep red texture that took me far away from the courthouse for a peaceful interlude.  The young server was gracious, engaging and had a high watt smile that made ordering a pleasure.  I asked if this was truly a Thai house, and she assured me the owner and chef were legit.    For lunch I had the Hot Jungle Special at heat level 4 (out of 7).  The plate arrived loaded with fresh veggies and a mildly pepper/curry sauce that brought everything together nicely, but wasn't quite the inferno I was looking for.  Still, it was totally enjoyable, and I used it as a measure should I chose to return for another round.  That I returned for dinner was totally unexpected, unless you consider leaving a briefcase behind as an act of kismet.  I had to return that evening to get it, and while there decided to sit for dinner.   I supped on Pad Thai with Calamari and heat level 5. This was more like it!  The meal arrived in a large ceramic plate with a built in pedestal.  It looked beautiful.  The spice level was excellent, and the Calamari was fresh and scored in a crosshatch pattern to expose max surface area.  It was soft and pliant.  The overall experience was delicious. I took enough home for another dinner.  Spice Thai Cuisine is a very good restaurant, if not quite at the level of Aroi Thai or some of the other specialty houses in the area.  No doubt, it could reach that apex with a little more time and imagination.

Wandered in after court one morning, needing coffee and something, having skipped breakfast to get out the door early.  Lily's was sitting there, cute windows suggesting something different inside. Wooden floors, large chalk board menus, dessert displayed right where they can do the most damage to good intentions.  And, bagels that looked more like they were from a ring toss game with sesame seeds and onion flakes.  Had to have it! Fresh, chewy and flavorful.  Good coffee. Yes, and lemon bars that squeeze the salivaries into submission with a crunchy smooth sweet tartness.  I walked out thinking this was a cool place; well worth another try, and wishing Lily's was in Newtown.

Grand Opening of Chinese take out joint on South Broad Street, Trenton.    It has a postage stamp size dining area with only 2 tables for eating in, and 3 chairs for waiting on take away.  The space is still clean and the kitchen shiny, as it has been open little more than a week.    The menu is extensive and basically a traditional Chinese/American emporium.  Nothing authentic, but if you wanted really good Chinois you would not be parking your wheels on S. Broad in the first place.  My Orange Flavored Chicken was a load in the styro container they give to even those who eat in.  The chicken was fresh enough, and had not been deeply frozen.  The sauce was gloopy orange colored, although the taste of the citrus was weak, despite the orange peel in the mix.  The Fried Rice was a bright yellow from the dye used in the bullion stock that morning.  It had plenty of roast pork and veggies in it, but I did not see much (if any) egg scrambled into it.    The people here are Fuzhounese, the province just north of old Canton, and across the straits from Taiwan.  Their cuisine is similar to Cantonese, but has some other influences.  It tends toward less sweetness, but close enough to allow for success in the Chinese take out wars.    If you are interested, go soon while everything is new and clean.  The owners are there and take an interest in getting things right.  Just remember what you are dealing with, and you will not be disappointed.  PRO TIP - They don't serve hot tea!

Solid Chinese/American house in Lalor Plaza. 20 years at this nearly invisible location. Owners are friendly and hard working.  The shop could be cleaner and the supplies stored out of sight, but the grub is reliable, if not exceptional.   While it will not become a standby option, it is worth remembering it is there for that time when the yen for Egg Foo Young or Sweet & Sour Pork overcomes you.  Some specifics - My Wonton Soup with the lunch combo was low average.  While the broth was standard, the wontons had exceptionally thick skin which detracted from the overall enjoyment of the bowl.  The Egg Foo Young was better, with fresh veggies and a decent brown sauce.  I don't know if they make their own wontons, but these had a very familiar feel to them, suggesting mass production from an outside vendor.    While a dive, once accepted as such, the experience was fine.

I don't know why this Rite Aid was so difficult to find on Yelp*, but it finally showed up.  Drug stores today have morphed from the corner mom and pop shop into a semi - big box convenience store that also sells prescription medications along with food, drink, and photo services.  It must be working as these modern day behemoths are spreading like a bad cold (poor pun).    This one does a decent job getting my prescriptions out quickly, and the drive thru option is a nice touch for those unable to park a car or walk into the store.  The crew is friendly and helpful.  Too, I have been known to pick up a chocolate bar in the candy isle, and a birthday card in the excessively large greeting card isle.    I bow to modernity, although I miss the personal touch of the old fashioned Rexall (now a cool Starbucks here in Newtown).

Great Harvest Bread Company sits in the same large Village of Newtown Shopping Center where McCaffery's now is. On impulse I went in this morning to see what was available for breakfast.  The friendly assistant bakery/counter person told me the muffins were still in the oven, but they had very fresh Blueberry Cream Cheese Scones available.  She pointed to them and allowed me to come around the counter to have a closer look (and take a photo).    I don't know much about scones, except for eating them a few years ago when in England.  I remembered a hard, cookie-like outside and a textured chew.  These were quite different. They were the shape of scones, and soft through and through. No crunch. Much like a muffin in the shape of a scone. I liked it, the same as I would have enjoyed the muffin. Perhaps they were less sweet than their cousins.   The loaves of bread were tempting, and I will try some of them over time.  The coffee was good, the beans roasted locally.    Their wall menu suggests that their sandwiches are worth trying, as does the video attached to this Yelp listing.    I look forward to future visits and sampling more of what appears to be high end healthy bread and all things that can be created out of it.    Very happy to have them in Newtown.

How to account for the two entries for this wonderful blue bridge on Yelp?   From the Philadelphia side it is called the, "Benjamin Franklin Bridge."  The Jersey Strong side in Camden has named it the, "Ben Franklin Bridge."  Seems more reviews use Ben.   I guess Jersey has a more casual relationship with this Founding Father.  But, we must ask if Benjamin would have anything to say about the 19th Century propriety of calling this prodigious and glorious old boy, "Ben," as opposed to his given name?    I'll stick with Benjamin until he and I are formally introduced and get on a first name basis.
Unfortunately, Agabiti's Cafe has closed its doors at this location.  Word is they are looking for another place to open shop in the area. Good luck to them.

As a sister city gift from Tianjin, China to Philadelphia, the Friendship Gate was the first of its kind in the USA. Engineers and artisans from the old country designed and built it on 10th Street at the corner with Arch Street.  When freshly painted (as it last was in 2008), it is a beautiful reminder of the cultural ties between two grand cultures, one very old, and the other quite new.  It is an accurate representation of a Qing Dynasty city gate that would historically be placed in an opening in the wall surrounding a city, or an approach to a holy site.  There is also magic spread over the structure with the carvings, painting and Chinese proverbs placed on it.  So, with a little belief and a lot of imagination, you can feel the changing atmosphere when entering or exiting Chinatown through this portal.  That is part of the reason why being in Chinatown feels so far away from the rest of our urban world.   Chinatown has suffered at the hands of last century's urban planners, as first one piece (Ben Franklin Bridge), and then another (Vine Street Expressway), and yet another (Philadelphia Convention Center) cut away at the neighborhood.  What was once a 12 block enclave, is now only 7.  Gentrification north of Vine will only make matters worse as the value of real estate skyrockets, forcing old owners out as taxes raise and rents follow. Luckily, the Phillies were not able to build their new ballpark where originally desired just off 12th and Vine.   Although I usually approach Chinatown from the north (as the Mongols did), I try to make it a point to walk through Friendship Gate (driving under it does not provide the special spell).  Either before or after a great meal, haircut, or shopping adventure, a moment within its aura seems to lighten my load, and give a sense of connection with a 5,000 year old culture.   Walk under it next time your in town.  Tell us how it felt.

I found Kriscroix while cruising Yelp for a change of pace meal in the area. Yesterday, I finally had the time to go there for an early lunch after dropping son off at the mall for a Magic tournament (that's another story).   On first approach it is easy to miss this place on the end of a small strip on the south side of a particularly ugly stretch of Rt. 1 in Fairless Hills. The signage is small, and first glance is of a store that looks like a beer distributor, with many brew signs on the windows.  Don't be deterred.  Walk in, turn left, and you are in a 1970's dining room with comfortable blue leatherette booths, brass fitting, and wall to wall maritime memorabilia.  Very seaworthy!  I was fortunate to have Tracy as my server.  She was friendly, funny, and took time and pride to show me through the menu and make useful suggestions.  From the reviews I knew I was going to have good choices, but decided to go with the standard Fish and Chips for my first taste.  It was a nice size Cod Fillet, batter dipped in a light English style coating, and fried enough to slightly harden the batter into a shell that left the fish soft and tender.  No oily taste nor texture.  The French Fries were not house made, but still crispy and fresh tasting. It came with Tartar Sauce or Cocktail Sauce.  I did not ask for Malt Vinegar, but I suspect it was back in the kitchen.  A tin of Old Bay was also placed on the table for the fries. A side of Cole Slaw came along for the ride. It was mayo based, but also fresh and enjoyable.  All the while Tracy was refilling my coffee mug, and telling me more about the restaurant. The only thing missing was having the Fish and Chips served in a newspaper cone as done in England.   I don't normally do dessert, but Tracy asked if I wanted to hear what was available.  Ok. I was game to listen. She said a few options, and then got to the Fried Oreos and Fried Twinkies. What?!  I went for it.   A few minutes later out came a large white shallow bowl with four halves of Twinkies, apparently wrapped in a crepe-like blanket, covered in powdered sugar, and drizzled with raspberry sauce.  The Twinkie Cream was slightly oozing out and mixing with the white and red.    How did it taste?  Well, imagine the first time you ate a Twinkie as a kid; that soft, sweet, creamy surprise...Now, imagine it hot, with extra sugar, and a hint of raspberry stirring your palate... Taste it?   It was a fun dessert.    Kriscroix Restaurant. Highly Recommended for fish and fun.

Slate Bleu (Blue Slate) Restaurant is part of a very attractive adaptive reuse of an old brick 19th Century building in Doylestown.  For that alone, the structure is worth a close look. The architect gets 5 Stars for adaptation and execution.   The restaurant is Au Provence French style look and feel.  Dark wood tones, center floor bar, and a quiet sensibility with white tablecloths, benches along the walls, and simple chairs.  The bartender (owner?) serves as hostess and maître d., serving drinks to the tables after she makes them. A nice touch.  Our waitress was friendly, knowledgeable and unobtrusive.   The dinner menu is not extensive, but covers all the food groups.  The chef is creative and makes the effort to bring his best to his work.  We had the Green Salad, Bronzino with a Fruit Salsa Sauce, and for dessert shared a Pistachio Souffle.   The salad was basically a fresh spring mix, but with a dressing that tasted weak in combination with the greens.  The Bronzino (Mediterranean Sea Bass) was very well presented, light tasting with a tasty Mexican-esque fruit salsa combination piled high on the fillet. It was very enjoyable. It was a daily special @ $28 per. Finally, the Souffle was made from scratch and came with a gravy boat full of hot chocolate for pouring into its center.  While very light, fluffy and yummy, the $15. plus price was a chill to the digestion. (I knew in advance and decided to bite the silver bullet in favor of making my companion happy. You know how that is.)   So, although Slate Bleu is an attractively appointed French/Country space, and the cuisine is very good for the most part, there is a sticker shock that accompanies the experience.  While I would return, it will only be when I have a very special occasion. When a dinner for two comes in over the century mark without drinks, reservations about reservations are appropriate.

This is an excellent and honest auto repair shop.  Too bad Yelp thinks it is in Clifton Heights, when it is in fact in Newtown, Bucks County. Check the website to get the right information. Once you do, you will find a place you can absolutely trust with your car.  Five stars is not far off.
Sarcone's Deli is gone forever.   RIP Primo's has now taken its place. Good luck to Primo and its customers.

I am normally not a fan of prix-fix menus, as they tend to be too limiting of choice, and suggests a kitchen unable to handle more options.  But, when that standard menu comes in 7 courses with additional vegetarian alternatives, and is packed into a Bedouin's tent of a restaurant, complete with belly dancing, baklava and honey tea, I can make an exception.    This is multiplied many fold when your 40 closest friends are packed into a carpet clad room with barely enough room to sit down, and an ambient noise level loud enough to make talking to anyone but those right next to you impossible. Yet, with enough wine and North African music to alter consciousness, this becomes an all-consuming environment that transports you out of South Street and into the dark, mystic souk casbah of one of the ancient cities of Morocco.   Marrakesh takes finger food to the ultimate.  From cool salads, to roast chicken, cumin lamb and grilled beef, cous-cous with veggies, the only thing between your fingers and the searing meal is the thin pita used to pinch, lift and stuff in your face.  Failing that, be prepared for first degree burns.    The large metal serving trays kept coming with more food.  We all appreciated the concession to the use of towels to cover laps and wipe hands. Some of the braver souls accompanied our graceful dancer as she gyrated her hips, abdomen, shoulders and arms with cymbals ringing. Some of our folks really knew how to move.  Impressive.  Stepping back out onto Leithgow Alley after 4 hours within this transporter, it took a few moments to reorient myself to being back in Philadelphia after our wild ride.  Marrakesh is not just a restaurant, it is a magic carpet.

Apple Cleaners is located in Goodnoe Corner on Sycamore Street, Newtown.  In a previous incarnation an office supply store occupied this space very close to The Green Parrot.  I don't claim any special expertise when it comes to professional cleaners.  I just want my shirts and pants done well and ready when I come to claim them.  Apple has been keeping me satisfied for the time they have been here.  The customer service is friendly, and they can remove spots that are pointed out to them.  Oh, and they seldom return my dress shirts with broken buttons; one of my serious peeves.  I offer three stars because although I am quite happy with Apple, I am not sure that being a "Fan" or having an orgasm (Woohoo!) really expresses the more moderate emotional response I have to a clean shirt.

I have been buying my tires here for several years.  Great service and prices, and helpful suggestions for safety where the rubber meets the road. Call ahead for an appointment, or drive over, and they take care of you and your car.

The other reviews capture the essence of State Street Kitchen. The owner and creative force, Micha, is a work of art. This is HER place.  She knows everyone by first name, and genuinely makes you feel you are her best friend. You might be! The food is fresh, and tasty.  There are standard menu items found in any comfy neighborhood cafe, plus specials that show imagination.  Yes. There is a Korean twist to many dishes, and most of them work well.  The dining area is smallish, so come early or late or be prepared to wait.  You will find it worthwhile.  There are many locals there every day.  If you are one of them, you don't need to read this.  For everyone else, don't be put off that we know most of the people in there. It happens because of the food quality and creativity, and the warm personality of the owner.  Order something unique and off menu, and you might find it on the menu in the future and named after you.

It was good to be back in the old neighborhood again up along Baltimore Avenue in West Philly.  Things have changed around my old home at 48th and Balto, mostly for the better.  I was here a few months ago sampling the heat at Chili Szechuan, and this time I was back to meet up with Yelp friends at Mood Café, the Chaat & Lassi emporium on the point at 46th Street.  Lucky for me, they were delayed arriving, and I had an opportunity for a long talk with Hasan, the owner/chef/creative genius behind the concept and the counter that is Mood.  I got the $.50 tour, and an autobiography worthy of Horatio Alger.   While I had eaten Chaat (pronounced, "Chart") before, it had never been like this.  Hasan has taken what is basically a common street food in India and turned it into an adventure in eating.  It comes at you in several dimensions - taste, texture, hardness/softness, shape, spice, food group, color and surprise.  It sat before me the most colorful assortment of edibles imaginable.  I had the Salad Chaat with Chicken, but there was so much happening inside that take out container that the meat was forgotten in the exploration of what was going on with all the reds, yellows, stars, logs, crispies, noodles, dried fruit, nuts, fresh mango, greens, feta cheese, chili sauces, curry notes, etc.  It is difficult to describe all the hyperactivity in that bowl.  Imagine an Indian version of Trail Mix thrown into a salad rather than croutons. If he had tossed in some M & M's I would not have been shocked.  This baby was Buh-Buh-Buh-Bizzzeee!!!  And, bottom line, it was awesome. We tried each others dishes, and all were unique and captivating.   And, that does not even get into the Lassis.  More than 60 varieties of cool, creamy yogurty, sweetness.  Mine?  A Rose Lassi, complete with Rose Petals! Not just amazing, but fun!  If this wasn't enough, Hasan brought us samples of other Lassi combos in small cups to try.  This man knows how to seduce with great taste. Oh. And did I mention the Kheer and Rice Pudding he gave us at the end?   Over the Top!  As good as Mood Café is, it is a very small shop.  Four tables with bench seats along the wall and plastic stools for everyone else.  So, not the most comfortable arrangement.  It is geared as a take out place, with everything served in take out containers and plastic utensils.  I would be willing to pay more for comfort.    The sheer enjoyment of the event (yes, this was more than just a cool meal) kicks the experience into 5 Star territory.  In truth, there should be another category available on Yelp that addresses the euphoria and exclamations needed for certain special foodie moments.    Mood Café would reach that level of extreme amazed unadulterated satisfaction.   Yeowee!!!

"I saw a werewolf with a Chinese menu in his hand, Walking through the streets of SoHo in the rain. He was looking for a place called Lee How Fook's.  Gonna get a big dish of beef chow mein.  Aaooooooo Werewolves of London.  Aaooooooo.  Aaooooooo. Werewolves of London. Aaooooooo."  The historic truth is that the werewolf wasn't from SoHo, London, but Chinatown, Philadelphia.  Poetic license for a largely underappreciated songwriter and rock performer, Warren Zevon. He spent a lot of time in the city, especially in the early 1980s, when he was living with, and ultimately married to a well know radio DJ here. They lived on Rittenhouse Square for several years, before divorce drove him back to California.  If you were very fortunate, you saw his concert at the TLA on South Street, and had your musical life changed.   He really visited the small Cantonese restaurant on the corner of 11th and Spring Streets and used it for inspiration for the song, "Werewolves of London." Even the kitchen door in an alley off Spring Street, found its way into the lyrics, as the door you must not open unless you sought the fate of the, "Little old lady, got mutilated late last night..." It remains a scary place even today with decades of thick, black grease caked to the walls and pavement. Who knows what evil lurks in those sewer drains?!   So, I was there the other day after a haircut across the street. I had been singing his songs as I drove to Philly, and wanted to pay homage to the man and have some good Cantonese food.   The dining room was small, with no more than eight tables. It was well preserved in dark mahogany stained panels.  It was fairly clean and tidy for a joint in C.Town. We were the only customers on arrival, and took liberties to walk around a bit and take a few photos. Amazingly, not a thing memorializing Zevon. Maybe this third generation Asian kitchen doesn't know from American rock and roll. Warren would no doubt get a laugh out of that.   We ordered Salt Baked Squid, Orange Beef and Fish Hot Pot; more than enough for two of us, but plenty to bring home for the sons. They were all very good, if not best of breed. The squid was tender and mildly salty as expected.  The beef was plentiful with a good dark red amber sauce and sliced onion and green pepper. The fish arrived in a covered casserole still bubbling from the fire in the kitchen. Soft, moist and delicious. Each dish was $11.95. Credit cards accepted.   This was one of the better Cantonese meals eaten in C.Town, made more desirable by the ability to think about Warren Zevon sitting at the table in back, chowing down and noodling about a song that we are still singing long after his death.   Aaoooooooo!

Empress Garden is a small shop on N. 10th Street in Chinatown, Philly, that changed hands about a year ago.  The original owner (the "Empress"), was a sterling hostess and stunning beauty who ran her house efficiently and with admirable warmth.  The food had a Taiwanese and Indonesian orientation, but also had the standard American/Chinese dishes for those who preferred them.  Their fruit drinks were freshly squeezed, and it had a strong following.   I returned after an absence of a few years, and my first run with the new operation.  While the menu was basically the same as before, the actual plates coming from the kitchen seemed to have lost a bit of their edge.  We ordered Scallion Pancakes, Curry Chicken with Onions, Salt & Pepper Pork Chops, Orange Beef and Sautéed String Beans.  A lot for the three of us to consume, but we were looking forward to bring the balance home.    While the Scallion Pancakes were good, they are certainly returned to the norm, and were not as exceptional as remembered.  The Chicken dish had the right taste and fresh chicken, but the Onions were harder than desired, and thus tended to dominate the dish.  The S & P Pork Chops had been a wonderful platter in the past, but this day the breading and meat was over-deep fried, making it tougher in the bite, and less enjoyable in the chew.  Disappointing.  The Orange Beef was the best thing on our table, with a nice spicy, not overly gloopy, sauce.  It was fun to eat even with the orange peel in its soft non-burnt condition.  Finally, the Veggies were fine with a light Garlic finish.    The meal was satisfactory, but not what I hoped for based on recollection.  Empress Garden was now just another Chinatown restaurant with a fair kitchen and price, but nothing to make it outstanding.

The first thing I noticed in the shop was the great renovation done to this old wooden building on Newtown Creek.  The owner put love and attention into the atmosphere she wanted to create, as well as her business plan for all organic products, showing commitment to a successful business and a healthy planet.  Did I mention she cuts my hair very well?  I know such salons are primarily for women, but men should feel comfortable taking a seat there.  They also do a great job on my 12 year old son who is very particular about the bushel of hair on his head.

If you grew up with Dairy Queen as your special summer sweet treat, then this classic free standing shop on the south end of Morrisville will bring you back in time.  It has the iconic architecture of those build in the 1940's and 50's, before DQ became of burger joint that sold soft serve ice cream.    This is the place to bring the kids and grandparents on hot August nights, stand in line at the two small windows, peruse the now expansive menu, and walk away with your favorite vanilla or chocolate swirled cone, sundae, or Blizzard.  The look and taste is exactly as it was in the early days, and a wonderful trip down memory lane.    Don't worry about the sketchy neighborhood.  Stay alert, but know that you are "under the dome," and security of your childhood reveries.

If you know Trenton, and particularly the Hamilton Avenue/Trenton Central High School area, you know it has a small commercial zone with a bunch of divey restaurants, only a few of which would you think to visit. The oldies but goodies (Eddie's Donuts, Chuck's Chicken Wings, that great cheesecake place), are either long gone, or hanging on with other outlets out in the burbs.   But, along comes Halal Brothers, with its bright red, white and black logo, sparkling clean shop, friendly, accommodating ownership and outstanding Afghani menu, and all those preconceptions are thrown out the window. This place is inviting and its food is top notch delicious. I was there for lunch recently and almost fell in love.  At the counter I admitted to my first time there, and was offered a sample of their chicken and lemon chicken over rice. A minute later I was handed a small bowl of the two finished with white sauce and a touch of chili sauce. Diminutive, it was still beautifully presented and terrific. I sat down to eat it and tasted the panoply of flavors dancing on my tongue. Both the straight chicken and the lemony version were tender, moist and a mouth full of interesting exotic belly dancing.  From there I decided on their chicken salad - the same regular chicken morsels with a load of salad (lettuce, tomato, onion, cheese, white sauce and spicy red hot sauce) in a bowl. With a bottled drink, $7. Quite a deal! And, it was as great as the sample. With check in on Yelp, a free triangle of baklava joined the party. Mine had a cream filling, rather than the better known honey nut stuffing. It was also very good, like a Bavarian Cream donut made with philo rather than cake dough.   All I can say is that such surprises deserve return visits and five star reviews.

232 Corner Café (formerly Hogeland's) is a pleasant surprise.   When the former luncheonette closed last year due to the landlord's expectation that this space would be taken over by a medical provider outpatient clinic at substantially higher rents, those of us who knew and loved the old gal were sad and disappointed.  It appeared to be the end of an iconic local institution that had been around, while changing hands, for nearly half a century.  Progress to some.  Loss of culture to others.   The "best laid plans...sometimes go astray...", and when the plans for the medical facility shrunk to a smaller piece of the strip mall, this corner was not included.  All the fixtures remained intact, and a new business bloomed out of the ashes of the old. Ron now runs the operation, and at first blush, the new order of things feels much like the former enterprise.  The counter and tables are the same.  The grill and coffee brew where they sat before.  The menu has been updated, but the kitchen still puts out very good breakfasts (and lunches).    My French Toast was done right.  The standard two slices were dipped in an egg/vanilla/cinnamon mix, and grilled expertly with caramelized edges.  The taste was what I wanted, and I appreciated that the "small stack" was now the main size for the plate.  A melt of butter; and splash of syrup, and I was a happy man.  The New England Roast Bunn drip java was hot, fresh and repeatedly refilled by Ron as he entertained the troops.    232 Corner Café is a victory for the community.  Come on down and join in the celebration.  UPDATE - JULY 13, 2018: There are signs of change since the last time I was here for breakfast in 2016. They now use a generic food purveyor coffee rather than New England beans. Too, the quality of their Kaiser roll has declined to a soft unibread that lacks a crusty texture and is basically white bread stamped into the form of a roll.  Considering a downgrade to 3 stars.

It would seem that this supermarket is now part of the 1st Oriental Supermarket group that has a huge facility down at 6th and Washington in South Philly. Looks and feels the same. I think I also recognized some of the clerks and cashiers.   Anywho, this store carries almost everything you needed for a well stocked Asian kitchen. From butcher to fishmonger, soy sauce and vinegar, noodles from around the world, and even those secret ingredients needed for great dumplings, are right at hand. Vietnam, Thailand, Korea, Cambodia and China are all well represented. The green grocer department has fruit and veggies that often can only be found where they are grown in Asia. They even had a box of super fat green frogs for exotic eating or taking home as pets.   It was a pleasure to grab a grocery cart after a good dim sum brunch right next door and walk it off up and down the aisles.  The free parking replicates what they have down the city, but it sure makes life easier not to have to hunt and pay for a space for wheels.

Papillon Cafe in Goodnoe Corner, Newtown, PA, was a first for me. A French Kosher Organic Cafe in the heart of this 325 year old ville. It is a sign of the growing diversity in my home town, and it may actually make it, with something tasty for everyone. Even plenty for gluten frees.  This Sunday afternoon, only the owner was running the show. He had a perfect friendly personality, making me feel immediately welcome. His middle eastern accent with French lilt suggested the nature of the house. The shelf full of great looking pastries was one direction, the long list of crepes, another; and Paninis and onion soup, yet other possibilities. The weather frigid, I went for a hot tuna melt panini and coffee washdown.   The plate was served by the Le Monsieur, sporting the split sandwich on crisp and crumbly pressed baguette, and a pile of thin sliced pan fried potatoes with a garlicky white sauce drip. They were fine, if not inspired. Certainly, a solid contribution for lunch. The pomme frite were interesting - served cold. Rather than being the expected French fries, it became a very good cool potato salad side dish. Like it, even if unintended.  The java was also surprising. Although equipped for expresso drinks, all I wanted was something hot and strongly caffeinated. What I received was a corrugated paper cup that required no heat shielding cuff (clever). For the milk stir-in, I was handed the large stainless frothing pitcher full of cow juice, heated with the steam wand. I poured and stirred like a rookie barista. Great touch, and the Groundwork beans showed their strong roasted roots. Impressive.  I really liked Papillon, but it could use a little TLC. With only one person doing the entire operation, the details  got away from him. Someone bussing tables and sweeping up would eliminate crumbs on tables and floor and make the experience an unqualified pleasure.  3.5 STARS

BREAKFAST TAKE OUT REVIEW  We had an office meeting in Norristown, PA, this morning. Our office manager took our requests for breakfast and ordered everything from nearby Pauline's Deli. There were eight of us.  I asked for a sausage, egg and cheese sandwich on toasted English muffin.   When I arrived I sat at the conference table with an aluminum foil wrapped package before me. It was still warm. Upon opening, I quickly realized that I had a pork roll, egg and cheese on English, not what I had requested. This may not have been Pauline's doing, as I looked around and noticed my associate had a very similar sandwich, but with sausage. It was too late to make the exchange, as he was already happily half way through MY SANDWICH. For the sake of team building, I said nothing.  I am not a pork roll guy. Don't care for the taste, nor the texture. Still, I suffered through it, and drowned my disappointment in the hot coffee made in our office.   Better labeling might solve this kind of mix up, and a closer examination by the consumer would certainly be a benefit. I realize that it may not be fair to say Pauline messed this up, but I really didn't care for the sandwich. Hopefully, I'll get another chance at the next breakfast session, and be able to judge what I actually wanted.   YELP Suggestion - There should be a box to check for take out reviews. It isn't close to equivalent to evaluate a dining in experience with a take away bite. I quickly stop reading take out reviews as being irrelevant to the quality and enjoyability of the exact same meal eaten in these two divergent circumstances.

Thirty years ago when I first moved to Bucks County from Trenton, Aldo's was only All Star Pizza in the Village Shires Shopping Center.  A generation later it has expanded into a nice size full fledged Italian restaurant named after its founder.  This all happened gradually, and it seemed to reflect the overall growth of this area. Farms began to grow suburban housing developments. Those new folks needed local places to eat. Etc. The dinners were good, and we could walk there from home.    Stopped in for lunch the other day with my bud, Phil.  I guess I was in a rediscovery mood, as I had just visited Not Just Wings in the same center the weekend before.  We opted for a couple of plain slices for Phil, and an Eggplant Parmiagana Sandwich on a torpedo roll for me.    Phil knows from pizza (tomato pie) as he is from the Burg in Trenton.  I watched him hold each slice up to test their rigidity, and satisfied, devour them.  He smiled and said they were very good, but not like Papa used to make, or even his uncles DeLorenzo.    The Parm was large, crusty and sealed in melted Mozza.  It, too, was decent, especially the toasted roll which was a joy to eat.  The Eggplant itself was cut into long, thick pieces, and were still a bit firm to the bite.  I prefer them to be completely soft from being sautéed in light breading and olive oil before being torched in the pizza oven.  The Sauce was ok, but lacked a distinctive flavor.  I go for Eggplant Parm Sandys often, and this one passed the acceptable test, but did not stand out.  I would not rush back to have it again.    I may return for dinner in the near future, as they still evoke fond memories.  When I do, I will update this review.  But, for now, Aldo's for lunch is simply Okay. However, I may take a cue from Phil and stick with slices.

Definitely one of the best burger joints in Philadelphia, especially if price plays into your taste appreciation. What used to be a food truck operation has now taken root on West Girard Avenue (2800 Block). Although, small in stature, their burgers, cheesesteaks and roast pork sandwiches are worthy of being called, "Philly Prime." At less that $10 per, they offer a strong value compared to some of the expensive burger houses.   My Ponderosa Burger with grilled onions & mushrooms, Swiss, and fries inside the potato bun, topped with a drizzle of their secret steak sauce, was both a sight and delight.  Although slightly beyond my requested Medium finish, it remained juicy with a great taste profile from the added ingredients. The first bite told the tale.  It exploded in my mouth with so much forceful flavor, that some of it squirted out from my loosely closed lips. Glad I had grabbed enough napkins at the counter to deal with it.   My lovely companion sampled the Manayunk Roast Pork Sammy (pork loin topped with American, coleslaw, pickle and BBQ sauce).  She could barely finish half!  Too, their fries were copious, crisp and freshly cut.   Service, friendly and engaging. Order and pickup at the counter.   Excellence all around.

"Andale," means "Let's go," or "Hurry Up," en Espanol.   All I can say after my visit there earlier this week is, "Andale out of here!"  This local Chipotle wannabe seems to have lost some of its magic described in earlier reviews. What I discovered was a small make it as you like it shop in need of a thorough cleaning and responsible guiding hand.   Just standing at the order section of the assembly line it was easy to see that the kitchen was not regularly nor professionally cleaned daily. With so many open chaffing dishes in a warm room, the opportunity for bacterial surprises were everywhere. I considered leaving without eating, but I wasn't feeling hostile - just concerned that there was some risk eating there.   I decided to accept the risk, because the folks working there were pleasant and I wanted to avoid a scene in front of the other customers. Went with a chicken quesadilla to remove all those leafy choices from the meal.  Yelp had a check in bonus of a free soft drink with the solid options.  Those whistle wetters were from Jones Soda, the all natural sugar people. I had a choice of bright colors - Blue, Green, Red, Pink, etc. I selected the blue one that said it was blueberry lemonade soda. Neon blue. 100% sugar. Totally undrinkable for anyone who values their health. Left it at the trash deposit.  The quesadilla was okay, although the little chicken chunks had a mildly weird flavor from their marinade.  Sour cream? I don't know what that thin watery white liquid was, but it is doubtful it was dairy. Again, too fearful to indulge. Thanks to the Cholula Hot Sauce, I evoked some spicy taste from the grilled cheese and chick.   This is a once only experience. With so many really good Mexican or quasi-Mexican joints sprouting up in the area, Andale will likely be departing at the end of their lease.   Just not good, and far too dirty to avoid the health department for long.   Andale, Andale!

Our very personable waitperson described Jones as serving, "American Comfort Food."  Even before seeing the menu my mind was wandering about what that would mean to my Chinese friends experiencing local cuisine for just about the first time.  For me, a brownie and a glass of milk is comfort food, but for anyone lacking a database of experience, they might have some fairly wild ideas.    Turns out, they didn't have a clue and relied on me to order for them.  Okay. I was up for the challenge.  How about a good burger for the 19 year old, and a turkey club for his mother?  Handled.  I've been curious about the chicken & waffles craze, so when I saw it on the menu, I stopped reading.    We were all satisfied with our lunches.  The burger was a big hit with the young guy.  He believes burgers are the height of American culture.  He could be right.  Turkey is not well known in China, but the combination with bacon, lettuce, spicy mayo and tomato seemed to captivate my friend.  I moved quickly to remove the long wooden picks used to hold each quarter together, as she was unaccustomed to this shiv and nearly poked her eye out.    The fried chicken arrived as a breast/thigh combo with golden brown crispy coat.  It was good, but perhaps a little too salty.  The waffle was the better companion, done well on an iron and still steamy soft within with a hint of sweetness to counterbalance the NaCl on the bird.  As a lover of Southern Fried Chicken, I did not truly appreciate the passionate embrace of these two carb loads on one plate.  Call me old fashioned, but I will stick with waffles for breakfast and fried chicken for other meals; although I might be convinced to change my mind if someone poured pure maple syrup over both and allowed me this sticky indulgence.   Jones is a very nice facility with high ceilings, which make the brown sandstone columns around the house quite attractive and draw eyes upward, giving the sense of a mountain lodge in Red Rock, Sedona.    Made the saying of "Grace" seem totally appropriate.

As McDonald's go, this one on West Trenton Avenue in Morrisville, Pa., is in the format of a modern smaller footprint, with a drive through that wraps tightly around the building, forcing pedestrians to cross this lane of traffic. With all the young people who frequent these kid magnets, you would think they could find a safer design.  Alas, not.   I stopped in the other morning when traffic heading over the Delaware was so bad I decided to find a rest stop to wait for the clogged artery that is the Calhoun Street Bridge to pass its blockage.  Mickey's was right there, so I went in.  The place was clean and a little busy. Still, my order was taken promptly.  I had to wait a while for it to be filled as the staff seemed to lack any real organization for the counter.  The six people I saw all had their backs turned to the customers, and when any one of them was free and looked around to see us there, they carried out the next step in the process.  Three different people worked on my order.  I finally realized that what I was observing was the result of the heavy drive thru business which kept everyone's attention, and left those of us inside as forgotten players in their fast food game.  Efficient, perhaps, but not given to warm face to face.   My Sausage, Egg and Cheese Biscuit was smallish, and thrown together in such a way the top of the biscuit adhered to the cheese to one side of the sandwich, leaving the rest exposed.  It was wrapped and bagged that way, and made the eating a bit awkward. I guess if this product had gone to a drive away customer, by the time it was opened, they would be too far away to do anything but grumble.  Another casualty to the dominance of drive thru culture.   For me, I was just disappointed with the lack of care in the work product, and knew that I wasn't coming back for another round of being ignored.    Oh. The coffee was good.

This is a franchised large format Japanese Hibachi house that also offers sushi and a few "fusion" offerings from China and Thailand.  This style restaurant seems to be coming into fashion on the East Coast, although it is more played out on the Left Coast.   This one is apparently under new management, and they are attempting to make the facility more comfortable and attractive.  They have done a good job on the creature comforts, and the service is also attentive, except for the minor language difficulties in understanding each other through the Korean and South Jerzee accents.    I was the guest this night, and my hostess did all the ordering.  I opted for the sushi side of the joint, although the Hibachi room was more active and colorful, especially when they performed their volcano show with the ball of fire shooting into the air.  Luckily, we could see that from the safe distance on the far side of the room.    The Clear Soup was quite good as part of the dinner package.  The Sashimi platter (Deluxe?) was ample with a nice variety of well sliced fresh fish.  They all had good taste, but I would have preferred them slightly cooler.  I tasted all the offerings, but was not feeling compelled to finish them.  The Rolls (Sorry. The names were not disclosed to me) were okay, but not exciting.  Typical sushi rolls, but why the chef put cream cheese in it is beyond me.  Do they even have that in Japan?  This is not something I would consider ordering on my own.  Maybe this is what is popular in this part of South Jersey, or because it is close to Philly, cream cheese is a concession to local culture. Fish and cream cheese? No. Thank you!  I was happy to have dinner with a friend, and content to let her treat in return for something I handled for her.  Still, something more authentically Japanese would tempt me more than this Korean version of an Americanized Japanese Hibachi/Sushi store.  It just didn't hang together for me.

Miami Beach has its Big Pink diner-esque food forum. Furlong has its Back to the 50's; a pink edifice loaded with nostalgia for days gone by when the Victrola and AM radio were the only ways to listen to contemporary music.  This place is replete with black and whites of Elvis and Marilyn, and the lesser lights of the mid-20th Century.  It is a breakfast/lunch emporium with a dozen or so booths and the same number of tables.  The coffee comes fast and furious, delivered by black clad waitresses calling everybody, "honey," "doll," or "sugarcakes."  Ya' gotta' luv it!  The breakfasts are pretty good, with many fresh fruit specials added to pancakes, waffles and French toast. Still, nothing that makes me want to rush back for more.   Yu wan meat wid dat?

Shing Kee is one of the few Chinese houses on Washington Avenue.  It serves of Hong Kong/ Cantonese style dishes that are fairly authentic, very tasty, and at good prices.  It came highly recommended by my friends who work in the area, and rightly so.  Service was above average in that promptness and smiles were part of the interaction with the servers.  My only nit was that there were two large HDTVs on the walls that were both tuned to the same channel that no one was watching, although the Eagles preseason game was available.
