They just couldn't manage to change over to the game despite saying they would.  I just decided to finish quickly, and catch the game on the car radio.    The dinner was good aside from that annoyance. Scallion Pancakes were two deep and as wide as a large dinner plate.  Not too greasy, and enough green onion flavor.  The Pork Cutlets were large, well fried and very tasty is a good Garlic Sauce.  There was some bone left, but it was easy to pick them up and work the meat off.  I appreciated that they were a large size and non-oily.  The ubiquitous Broccoli Florets were ho-hum.   Shing Kee is a definite keeper, especially in light of the absence of many legit alternatives in the area.  It also is a good driving destination as they are in a shopping center with a decent parking lot.  While there, there are a couple of markets for grabbing your Asian ingredients for your adventures in Asian cooking.

Ariana's store front dining room may be long and narrow, but there is still plenty of room for a small intimate party with 40 friends, belly dancing, and all around carousing with interesting cuisine and effective service.   As with many such get togethers, the food takes a backseat to the festivities, but it refuses to be completely overlooked.  Our limited Prix fixe menu was part of the standard faire and was quite good across the board.  We all shared Aashak (dumplings) and Sambosa (Samosa), which while distinctly unique from what I was familiar with from a Chinese and Indian kitchen, were still quite good. Too, my Badendan Chalow (Chicken & Eggplant Curry) was tasty and the sauce worthy of all the excellent rice used to absorb every drop.    The entertainment was top notch and most of us got up to attempt to move our body parts in unison with our exotic dancer.  Impossible, but oh, so much fun.   I would def return to explore the menu of this house down at the bottom of Chestnut Street.

This stretch of Bustleton Avenue in Northeast Philadelphia is lined with one strip mall after another, and it is hard to tell them apart. Each has a few restaurants in them, but unless you know what you are looking for you are likely to become numb from their sameness and just keep driving. Taj India could unfortunately suffer than ignominious fate, but luckily is located right next door to the new Georgian Breads, and a street before the new Super Wawa.  It is worth finding.   This is a vegetarian house.  Their menu consists of six pages of mostly Kerala delights, with a little other North and South India thrown in to keep it interesting and popular. It was a perfect place to settle down after excellent foot massage right up the road at Lavendar Spa.    We shared these dishes: Sweet Corn Soup, Chili Pakoda, Kaju Curry, Vegetable Jalfrezi and Garlic Naan.  All were good to near excellent, except for the Masala Tea which was tasteless and disappointing. I love most forms of corn soup, and this was fairly standard. Sweet kernels with a light dusting of curry. Not sure if it came from a fresh ear of corn or a can, but it was still good.  The Chili Pakora was a nice surprise - Jalapeno peppers stuffed with mashed potato and spices, dipped in a heavy pakora breading and deep fried.  Very spicy and a strong nod to Indo-Mex cuisine.  The Kaju (cashew) Curry was a cool play on nuttiness in a mild, almost sweet pale orange curry.  Terrific. Perfect for sopping up with the Garlic Naan, which was more lightly tandoored than most I have eaten.  The texture was not heavy with oil nor garlic, despite its strong taste.  Very well done. Finally, the Veggie Jalfrezi provided a mix of mostly standard local green is a pleasant moderately heated curry.  We went with Level 5 on all dishes, except the Chili, and found it adequate for our tastes.  Regardless, some were hotter than others, but quite satisfactory across the board.    Service was friendly and efficient, and prices on the pleasant side of reasonable. $44 for all the above four dishes, naan and tea.  There are several decent Indian kitchens in this area, and Taj should be on your list when in the neighborhood and in the mood for quality vegetarian meals.

I confess to being a first generation Eagles fan, as I've lived in the Philadelphia area for only 30 years. That makes me a newbie. Still, it is long enough to understand the long, disillusioned wait become elated jubilation that folks who live and die Eagles football feel now that we have climbed to the mountain top and see the world from this new and pristine, exhilarating perspective. Dare I say we see the world through the eyes of a soaring eagle?   Hell, yeah!  We wander in the desert no longer. We have paid whatever penitence was due by our generations seeking the promised land. We have breached the palace walls and stand among the kings of football. The trials and tribulations, as painful and soul torturing as they were, have made us stronger.  We were the barbarians at the gate until Sunday night. Now, we are the new Eagles Empire, prepared to take our rightful place in the pantheon of football gods.   Move over Willie Joe. Move over Johnny U. Stand aside Terry B. Step to your left, Joe M. Make room Bart S. There's a new QB in town, and Nick F. be his name. Tommy B. be damned! We got this now. You want it back? Come and try!   We like the top of the mountain, and we are not about to give it back without a mighty battle.   The Great Eagles Nation arise! It is our turn to bask in the sunshine of a new day, and fly ever higher on the winds of Championship.

Rediscovering Bordentown, I stopped into Angie's Family Restaurant for breakfast last week to check it out.   True, there is something of a time vortex effect within its shop.  The colorful hand painted murals, lazy tables basking in the sun along the front windows, and the small counter with maybe a half dozen spinners, all combined to catch me off guard and drop me into somewhere in my youth, perhaps 1972 in Boulder, Colorado.    It may have played tricks with my mind, but it did not impact my taste buds.  My French Toast, Orange Juice and Coffee Special was fresh and tasty. The FT nicely cauterized by the hot grill to provide the light crunch I crave. My server wasn't Angie (I asked), but she and her mother had worked with Ms. A for many years and knew her to be a lovely person.    In fact, this joint is so square it's hip.  It suits its neighborhood in this transforming river town.  If Bonaparte was still here, he would be a regular.    Those fortunate enough to come often must call this place, "Angie's," as there is no need for the rest of the name.    Angie speaks for herself.  APRIL 2, 2015 UPDATE - Went with the Breakfast Special today; Kielbasi, Onion and Jalapeno Omelet @ $8.95, a bit pricey compared to the rest of the menu, but I liked the concept.  It included Home Fries, Toast and Coffee.  The Omelet was not as I imagined it.  Rather than chunks of fresh Kielbasi from the Polish deli, it was a thin sliced pink colored processed meat-food that had no resemblance in look, nor taste to the Polish Sausage.  Too, the Jalapenos were the pickled and sliced version, rather than fresh pepper cut and sautéed before being thrown into the mix.  Overall, a disappointment.  Stick with the tried and true regular menu options going forward.

Just visited Burns Auto Repair for the annual inspection and an oil change.    In at 8:00.  Out at 9:15.  Dave Burns, himself, drove me to my destination, and called when the work was done.   Still a complete 5 Star experience in automotive maintenance excellence.   Glad Yelp finally accepted that this shop is in Newtown, Bucks County, Pa.

Big Q BBQ sits out in front of H Mart and looks like a weird Sonic Drive In.   I've only sampled their wares once; buying a St. Louis Ribs dinner and Fried Chicken platter with sides of Chak & Meez and Baked Beans with Ends.  Waiting in the antechamber felt a bit odd because while there were plenty of people in gray shirts in the kitchen, I did not see anyone working with the food.  Too, as someone else mentioned, there was no odor of smoked meats, nor BBQ sauces, nor even of frying chicken.  It was almost as if the food was prepared elsewhere and shipped here for sale.  No smoker outside, either.   The food is really just okay. The Chicken was the better of the main offerings.  The breasts were large and juicy, although the breading would have shone off with more spice.  The Ribs were dense and coated in a thick ruddy sauce, but it seemed that there was insufficient liquidity to really impact the meat.  It made for a dry texture with underwhelming flavor.  Knife and fork were helpful in separating meat from bone, and when gnawing at them with dirty fingers they were not particularly tender, but good enough to be worth the effort.  I prefer a looser presentation with more gravy, but that is a matter of taste.    The sides were actually pretty good.  The Mac & Cheese was pretty much standard creamy fare, but the Beans were surprisingly hearty and well spiced.    No rush to go back to Big Q, as there are better fried chicken places close by, and while a bit of up country driving is needed to find more authentic homespun Q, I would sooner cruise the countryside in search of that holy grail (or rack).

TJ Smith's on Easton Road near the border between Doylestown and Warrington gives the feel of a western mountain lodge - all exposed wood and stone, high vaulted ceilings and beams.  The bar room where we ate was spacious on a weekday afternoon, and the service was friendly and informative.    We opted for their 4 beer sampler to go with their self-proclaimed famous burgers and a cheesesteak.  At $8.50 for the 3 oz. glasses, the price was about right, and the offerings of national brew was tasty and interesting, although 2 of them had a pumpkin component in honor of the season.  They were fine.    The burgers were large (8 oz.) with the appropriate fixings, although both of them came out beyond the medium finish requested, which, with an empty house was hard to understand other than inattentiveness at the grill. Their tastes were good, and the beef had not been frozen.  The cheesesteak was average and clearly not their forte.   Plenty of HDTVs everywhere for those who want sports stimulation while eating or drinking (this is a sports bar), but not so overwhelming as to be a distraction to conversation.    Attractive house.  With more attention to detail, it could be an exceptional stop in an otherwise nondescript strip of Bucks County.

Dos Amores (Two Loves) Mexican Cuisine is a strictly take out stall in the Village of Newtown Farmers Market. Along with the rest of the shops it is only open Thursday through Saturday, so there is only a small window for getting in/out with a good sampling of their south of the border offerings. Most are of the self contained variety, like enchiladas, quesadillas, empanadas and chile rellenos, that can be prepared in advance, kept cool and then heated at home in the microwave or oven. You can also eat in the market within the common dining area at the back of the store.   That is what I did. I ordered beef and chicken empanadas, and asked them to be heated for consumption in the market. That took all of 3 minutes. They were handed to me in a paper boat with small containers of salsa and sour cream. Other sides were available, but as it was my first dive into their delectables, I opted to forego any additions.   Both empanadas were very good. The dough was crisp and strong enough to stay together as I bit through them. The chicken and ground beef were both nicely spiced, and I was also able to pour more salsa inside through the bite hole, and keep it contained until next munch. The beef was cooked with more chili powder, and had a warmer profile than the chicken. Still, I enjoyed them both for their freshness and authenticity. Like everything else in this market, prices are high. You pay the same as if you were dining in a full service restaurant.   The atmosphere of the farmers market is entertaining with all the Amish/Mennonite vendors dressed in their traditional garb and speaking colloquially. That is certainly worth the premium paid, as it is the only place in town where there is a real cultural exchange. Admittedly, Dos Amores lacks the Pennsylvania Dutch accent, but their Spanish makes up for that.   I really should come here more often just to step away from modern times for a little while and enjoy all the interesting grub.

This Big Bear Natural Foods in Langhorne, Pa., is one of five shops in the Bucks/Mercer area providing a huge array of vitamins, minerals, supplements and organic/vegan foods to a grossly underserved segment of our community.  Family owned since 1971, it has deep roots and a loyal following.  While some question their choice of locations (both stores on Lincoln Highway - Rt. 1 - feel sketchy, there is little doubt that there was considerable savings in these spots as opposed to more upscale commercial zones.  So, if you want those healthful things that can't be found in supermarkets, and don't want to pay Whole Foods or GNC prices, then The Bear is the place to shop.  I am a semi-regular customer in the to Bucks stores.  My own focus is on quality vitamins and supplements like, Grape Seed Extract, Saw Palmetto, Ginseng, Co Q 10, and Vitamin B combos.  Over the past 20 + years I like to think they have helped keep me healthy and slowed the aging process.    There are only a few natural food stores within a 20 minute drive from home, and the majority of them are Big Bear outlets.  Luckily, they have everything I use in multiple brands and strengths.  The staff is knowledgeable and usually friendly.  I am comfortable with the treatment and satisfied with the results of my visits.  I have never sampled their juice bar, nor eaten their prepared food.  I prefer making my own fresh smoothies, and I live/work too far from their spots to make it for breakfast or lunch.    It's very good to have Big Bear around all this time.  Hope it has been worth it for them, too.

A convenient Star$$$$ for this part of the world, with access from both Street Road and Second Street Pike.  Its proximity to some of my favorite restaurants - Aroi Thai, Blue Sage and House of Pho - make it a perfect quick après dinner stop for hot brew on the way to the movies or home.    It is not the most attractive franchise unit in the area, but it serves a functional purpose.   Unlike a box of chocolates, you always know what you are going to get.

1911 Smoke House Barbeque sits on the red cobblestones that remains of Front Street, Trenton, NJ.  It is very close to the historic Trenton Barracks, where Washington surprised the Hessians on Christmas Day, and began the turn around in the fortunes of the American Revolution that ended with the United States of America.  As such, if you stop in for a drink and/or a meal, be sure to tip your glass to the memory of those heroes.  The bar/dining room is right as you walk in the door. It is small and cozy. In good weather there is a back patio that is a nice space to hang. We sat is a half booth close to the bar. Service was very friendly and informative.   We ordered brisket, pulled pork sandwich and a third of a rack of ribs dinner with baked beans and mixed veggies. Each was pretty good, but none outstanding. They all needed help from the table rockets of sauces. Of those, the Hickory and 1911 were the best. When squirted up, the meats were more tasty and entertaining. The ribs were partially over grilled so that half of the three were charred and carbonized to a hard shell. Gave my molars a crunchy workout. The beans had been sitting around too long and lacked moisture. The veggies we're ample, but bland.   While we liked the place, and that it is close to my office, we agreed that the Q was less than hoped for, and that we have had better recently at several places.  Maybe it was just an off night.

Some say it is better to look good than to taste good. For those few, Brown's Bakery in Dublin, PA, is for you.   A small shop with one community table, two deuces, and a tiny display case, there were beautiful pastries, donuts and cakes to see, but their tastiness was very much hit or miss. I was excited to finally visit, and although I was there shortly after noon, there was still ample choices available. I selected a half dozen donuts (old fashioned sour cream, glazed), coffeecake mini, brownie and sugar/cinnamon stick. The ten pieces came to $10 and change. Not unreasonable.   I was 30 minutes from home, and I drove expectantly delaying gratification until I could brew fresh coffee and relax over my sweet score. Upon opening the taped box I beheld the beauties until deciding which to eat first. The sour cream cake donut with the cracks coated in glaze came first. I bent and broke it in half to better fit into my mouth.   First bite was nice as the flavor of the icing and texture of the cake unveiled. Immediately thereafter I noticed that the foundational base was not completely fresh, but somewhat dry and becoming stale. Too, the flavor of the glaze was not what I anticipated, but a strange tone of sweetness unlike anything I had tasted. It wasn't bad, but it was less enjoyable than traditional dip. The same was true of the standard glaze siblings. Not completely at their peak, and the same weird flavor.   On the other hand, both the brownie and coffeecake were very good. The chocolate moist, rich semisweet and nicely chewy. The coffeecake chunky brown sugar, cinnamon and powdered sugar on top of a small rectangular pound cake base. Liked them alot.  What to make of this mixed box? Hard to timestamp a pastry or donut. But, it is necessary to inquire about the age of their wares in order to avoid the suboptimal components. I have never done that, still if aging products are for sale it is necessary to be alert to this and do your due diligence.

I am slowly warming up to Newtown Bagel Company.  Over the past year I have stopped in a few times due to its proximity to my office, and find that the continuously gracious management is winning me over.   The bagels have not changed, and I wish they would find out how to make the crust a little crunchy, but as I have eaten several I find them more acceptable.  They are always fresh and have a good chew once the crust is penetrated.  The coffee is still good.  Now, if they offered hot oatmeal on cold winter morning, I could become a real fan.   For now, the reality that I visit here about once a month indicates that I am satisfied with the overall experience, and should reflect my changing opinion with a third star.

Rosemary's Grill is deceptively large inside, but gives the impression of a traditional diner in a non-traditional structure.  It lacks a counter and stools, which would provide a whole lot more charm than the current environment, which although clean, is all earth tones and lavender and has a dreary feel to it.   I had to inquire about the Greek/Middle Eastern menu, as it was not provided with the main handout.  Too, said menu did not list the Gyro Pita, but required that it be asked for in order to know it was available.  I found that odd, except when I realized that most other things on the menu were more expensive that the gyro.  As I was there at lunchtime, the absence of the most popular dish in the reviews was dubious.  Oversight, or intentional subtle upsell?   The service was very good.  The Lamb Gyro was excellent with well grilled lamb slivers mixed with lettuce, onion, cucumber and yogurt dill sauce.  The pita was hot and the entire presentation attractive.  Even the frozen fries were okay.    While I will keep Rosemary's in mind when in the vicinity and in need of sustenance, it will not be a primary source for a Mediterranean style meal.  I have too many questions about the above issues, and there is too much strong competition nearby to put Rosemary on my speed dating list.

There may have been changes in ownership and management, but Italian Peoples Bakery on Butler Street in Trenton, NJ, continues to turn out great bread, pastries, cakes and deli sandwiches like they were partying in 1999.    I recently rediscovered this small shop on one-way Butler Street, where double and triple parking is a way of life.  Still found a spot for the wheels and walked into a doughy time machine.  The high glass display counters. Back shelves filled with donuts, loaves of many types, and great guttural Trentonese dialect, sent me back in time to when there were several awesome Italian bakeries in the Burg, and they competed with each other for quality dominance.  The last baker standing is the latest incarnation of IPB, for whatever might be missing, their bread remains classic and museum worthy.    The deli in back still offers wonderful sandwiches with the star of the show always the bread in which it is captured.  On two recent visits I found that the Home Roasted Turkey, Swiss, Lettuce and Mayo on Onion Roll, and the follow up Chicken Salad on small Torpedo Roll, to be delicious and priced for smiles.  Zaftig sandwiches like these for under $5, are too good to be true, unless the kitchen and ovens are trapped in the prior century.  Each creation was really two meals.  The wall of drink coolers provided substantial choice, and there was always budgetary room for one of their large cookies, cannoli, or even deep double fudge brownies.    Yes. You do have to navigate into the inner recesses of Chambersburg, and deal with all the one way streets, and the sudden loss of GPS signals.  But, once you're there and exploring this historic haven, you are in for a mighty treat.

Not sure the last time RJ's boiled and baked the bagels in the bins, but as I am eating one less than 30 minutes after purchase @ 1:00 pm on a Sunday, it is already approaching staleness. Too flat upon observation; a tough slice with a sharp serrated knife; tough crust with no crispness; and too dense at its heart.   Very ordinary.  Bagel Train is far superior to my taste.

Russell Gardens Center in Churchville, Bucks County, Pa., may not be the largest nursery garden plantation in the region, but in my estimation it is one of the best. I have been shopping here since moving to Bucks and starting a garden around the house (The enterprise is never done).  Originally, I was tipped off to its existence by a nurseryman friend who helped me with design and bare root tree planting.  He swore by Russell's for perennials and colorful annuals and shrubs that most other dealers either lacked, or only possessed in inferior quality.  As an example, twenty years ago I bought a small pot of Coreopsis, a hardy fern-like leafy base with yellow star flowers that bloom in late June/early July, and spread to fill any space they are in.  Yesterday, I returned to see what was new in this native American beauty.  Now, they are available in a few shades of red/orange, and most strikingly, in a red/yellow flower that is breathtaking in its simplicity and kinship to its elder cousin.  Love at first sight. It is now planted across the walkway from the original, and it is easy to imagine its growth over the coming years.    We purchased 3 other low growing, shade loving varieties to replace the old builder's grade junipers that had run their course.  Three Heuchera with rich dark maroon/gray foliage, two Veronica (Speedwell) that push up spikes of pale blue to indigo flowers in early June, and three low dark green/purple grasses that spread through their roots to cover bare soil and need little maintenance. They are all happily in place beneath the living room window.   Always more work to do.  Plans call for a redo of the west side foundation plantings.  Russell Gardens will get the call as we lay out our plans.  Their inventory, knowledge and understanding of gardens and gardeners, makes it the place I trust most with suggestions and products. Prices are about the same as the other shops.   Russell Gardens is why we dig in the earth.

Richman's Ice Cream on Bristol Emile Road in Levittown, Pa., is a local burger joint that emphasizes its ice cream, but does a bang up job on their beef pucks.  It has a 1960's feel to it, with indoor/outdoor dining and order/pickup windows. You order and the receipt has a number that will be called when your meal is ready.    We stopped in after shopping in the area for a late lunch.  We ordered their Original Burger (Double with cheese, onion, lettuce, tomato, mayo and a spicy chipotle-type sauce, on a bun), and a Southwest Burger (avocado, lettuce, tomato, cheese and extra spicy sauce).  The combo provides an ample load of fries and a large drink, so we ordered one combo to share those extras. At $14, it was a good deal.  The burgers were hand packed and loose enough to grill up well and retain that special grease that makes good burgers, great. They reminded of 5 Guys, but better in that they were not crushed in wrapping, and the sauces were nicely complimentary.  Liked them a lot.  Only negative was the quality of the roll, which was not strong enough to hold together after a few bites.  It became necessary to find the plastic forks so as to avoid having to pick up the pieces falling out of the sandwich with sticky fingers. A better roll (potato or Kaiser) would offer longer support for the weighty innards. The fries were well done (the way I like them), and the lemonade tart enough to quench two dry whistles.   We didn't get a chance to try the ice cream, as although we sat outside under blue sunny skies at first, by the time we were halfway through the meal, the skies had darkened, and it was raining pretty hard, forcing us inside, where it was crowded and difficult to move around.  Will try their 'scream next time.   All in all, a pleasant burgerlicious experience.

Many years since I last visited this IHOP at the intersection of North Olden Avenue Extension and Parkway Avenue, Ewing, NJ.  It looks about the same on the outside, but there has been a modest makeover within making the space appear brighter and renewed.  The greeting by the staff was legit friendly, and the care provided throughout breakfast was very good. One of the servers actually came over to me to compliment me on my watch.  That is a very rare occurrence.   I ordered the brioche French toast from the griddle menu.  At $6.99 is seemed reasonable.  The carafe of coffee was another $2.49 for a bottomless mug.  Still, getting out from a full breakfast for under $10, was appreciated.  Yet, there must have been a little communication problem with I did not catch until my food was served.  My very pleasant server came back to me after ordering to ask if I wanted blueberries or peaches with my breakfast.  I hadn't originally asked for that. Nothing was said about an up charge, and I thought it was something everyone was offered with this meal.  In fact, it wasn't.  The extra canned peaches, caramel-like syrup and dollop of whipped cream was another buck fifty.  No biggie, but I would have preferred to be told the complete deal.    The food itself was good, but too sweet with the syrup they drowned the bread with.  I have a lighter touch on breakfast syrup.    I would return, but be sure to be prepared for the attempt to upcharge for extras I really did not need.

Gibby's is another of the 1950's style ice cream houses that dot lower Bucks County.  It is all glass, stainless and jutting ascending red roofline, staffed by high school cuties that bring the innocence necessary for a complete summer childhood reverie.  It sits at the bottom of Veterans Highway, just south of New Falls Road in Levittown, PA., across from a long row of old strip commercial drive ups that help complete the sense that you are more than just an ice cream licker, but also a time traveler.    The Store carries mostly hard 'scream, with a nod to vanilla and chocolate soft serve. Given the lack of choice compared to its siblings in the area that offer at least a few more soft flavors, I went with Black Raspberry and Butter Pecan in a medium paper cup.  At $3.50, it was a steal, or more accurately, confirmation that I had entered 1976.    The only real issue here is that the creme glace was not as good as the other joints in the area.  Not sure who makes their brand, but it had a flat taste; nor was it as creamy and sweet as expected.  The Butter Pecan had fewer nutty implants, and lacked the mild saltiness of the pecan that so well offsets the usual sugar rush on the tongue.  The Black Raspberry had a mildly tart afterbite. Not bad, but had me wondering why it was there.    After the individual scoops melted and merged into each other, it was more enjoyable.  Still, not the heavy smooth happy zazz found in Jo-Jo's, nor the amazing cool creaminess of Dairy Delight.

Great Shanghai Chinese Restaurant in the Morrisville Plaza Shopping Center is another primarily take out shop that has been around for many years providing Chinese/American dishes to the neighborhood at affordable prices.  Although there are two tables in the house, the lack of heat in winter makes it obvious they don't expect (want) people to consume their products there.  So, when I ordered sesame chicken and hot/sour soup and indicated I would eat while the food was at its peak heat, they asked me twice if they understood me correctly.  They did, and pulled out a plastic orange tray to deliver the take away containers to me, along with cheap utensils.  They were kind enough to remove the staples used to close the styro lid, so that I could gain prompt access.    My lunch was pretty much okay.    The hot & sour soup was made without MSG, and had a good taste with ample tofu and veggies, and the right amount of vinegar.  The sesame chicken was not over breaded, and the meat could be tasted, and was not lost in the goop.  The quantity was plenty for a midday meal.  The fried rice had been made earlier, had the tint of the bouillon it had been cooked in, and had a fairly fresh texture of being prepared earlier in the day, not yesterday.    Overall, it was what was expected from this type of kitchen, and perhaps, slightly above average based on the soup and rice.    The price/quality ratio was just about right, but having to wear a coat while eating is inhospitable, and knocks it down from average to just below.

Royal Chef is much bigger inside than it appears from outside. There are actually ten tables for dining in, so it is more than just a takeout joint. I stopped in for a late lunch and ordered from the lunch menu (General Tso's Chicken, Fried Rice, Broccoli with a bowl of Wonton Soup).  The soup was actually the strongest part of the lunch. The chicken consume base was tasty, and the wontons, although somewhat thick skinned, actually had a decent flavor, too. The general's chicken was a large mound of amber glossed bird nuggets. About half of them were the right texture and taste, while the others were either too thickly skinned, or too crunchy to enjoy. Could not always taste the meat within. The fried rice was a large helping with adequate veggies to keep it interesting. Of course, the broccoli florets were there for decoration more than consumption.   The meal was just okay overall.  I appreciated that there was a dining room where I could sit and eat lunch.  It would have been even better if they used real plates and flatware, rather than styro and plastic, and a take out container for the soup.  Service was provided by the cashier who was attractive and pleasant to all customers.    The sign out front is worn and faded, and could use a little TLC to keep the shop from looking worse than it is. A little fresh paint and relettering would make China Chef a more upbeat place to chow down (no pun intended).

Dave Burns and his crew are highly reputable and spend the time necessary to find what is wrong with your vehicle and make the needed repairs after discussing it with you.  They have the integrity to tell you up front if they think they can't do the work as well as the dealer. How often have you had that happen? Well, Dave apologized that he thought he should pass on a particular problem I was having with my car, and recommended I take it to a dealer for the specialized treatment required.  I truly appreciated his honesty and directness.  For that and everything else he has done for me, Burns Auto Repair is deserving of 5 stars.  I still wish Yelp would get his location right. Newtown, Bucks County; not Clifton Heights.   Jeesh!

I have returned several times during the year for "a trim."  Both my son (now 13) and I enjoy the casual, yet well appointed atmosphere of Sycamore Salon.  It is nice to see more people working there, a sure sign of growing reputation and success.    It is well deserved.  If you want your hair and scalp treated with care, kindness and only organic products, your best choice in Newtown remains Sycamore Salon - The Organic Option.

When Sal DeForte's Ristorante was still in Chambersburg, Trenton, NJ., it was one of my favorite Italian haunts for a delicious and romantic dinner.  Dark woody tones, beautiful old bar, and aproned servers trained in the old ways.  It was a complete experience.   Time passes, and as with almost all the casas Italiana in that great neighborhood, they moved out to the burbs to follow the migratory paths of their customers.  Sal's landed in Ewing on Pennington Road.  It took me many years before I found my way back, but I finally made it this week for a business lunch with a client.   I expected it would only be a shadow of its former self, but I was wrong.  It wasn't a recreation of the Old World house, but about as good as a modern setting can be in attempting to capture the essence of the past. The atmosphere was still hushed, and the décor was both formal and comfortable at the same time. Cloth tablecloths, fresh flowers, large curtained windows all around, and servers in black gliding around the floor.  The menu was much as I remembered it. Fresh veal, chicken, pasta, soups and salads, served with roast potatoes and string beans. Side salad for every dish.  Lunch sized portions coming in around $8.95 per meal.    My chicken francaise was two fillets, egged, and pan fried with a touch wine and lemon.  Excellent!  My business associate's platter was a grilled salmon, that he devoured with relish. The bread basket had a nice sliced loaf of very fresh crusty acqua y farina.  Overall, just an exemplary midday meal that completely out distanced my expectations.   Would I return for another meal?  Without a doubt!    This lunch was so good it made me forget how much I missed the old Sal's.

Ray's Sub Shop on Pennington Road in Ewing, NJ mainly serves the college crowd from the College of New Jersey up the street from there. It is a small store with six tables and a substantial menu of sandwiches, wraps, subs, burgers, etc. There are several lunch specials available daily which make for an economical meal.  They use Dietz & Watson delicatessen smoked meats and cheeses, and pretty good hoagie rolls.   My honey turkey and swiss submarine was large and tasty, with plenty of meat, cheese, lettuce and tomato. I nixed the onions. I couldn't finish it.  No complaints. With a bottle of Stewart's, it came to about $8.  Good price.    The only downside happened when I went to the cashier in the rear of the store, and looked over at the small grill used to prepare the hot sandwiches and burgers.  It was very dirty, and actually left an unpleasant odor in that part of the joint. I would not be ordering anything that required time on that hot iron.  Too, the sole garbage container was overfull when I tried to put my trash in it.  Someone should be watching for that and replace the trash bags before this happens.    More attention to detail would go a long way.   2.5 Stars, because cleanliness is important.

This is a first time for me visiting a take out only Pizza Hut.  Walking in, there was a counter for ordering, and the long conveyor belt oven for baking the pies.  The three workers there seem primarily involved in the preparation of the food, although someone came out to either take a walk up  order, or to hand over the boxed food if ordered online.    We had ordered through the internet from the not totally user friendly Pizza Hut app.  I finally figured out how to get it done, and requested the large Traditional Pan Pizza with half Mushroom and half Italian Sausage be ready for us by 6:00.    When we arrived at 5:55, the pizza was busy baking and we were told it would be ready shortly.  It was.  We saw it emerge from the oven (see pic).  I had ordered the Fire Spice finish for the crust, so we watched as one of the assembly dudes painted on some oil around the circumference of the wheel and then sprinkled on crushed red pepper.  He then cut it up with a semi-circular blade, and slid it into its box.  The internet price was $7.99, which is very hard to beat.    How was it?  The deep dish values of a thicker crust were obvious, although it could have used more baking on the under carriage to make it more well done.  The topside was loaded with our requested shrooms and sausage, and well baked to a nice melt.  It would seem that a small oven adjustment to increase the heat on the bottom and reduce it on top would result in a better finished product, if that is possible.  Taste was decent, but due to the above heat distribution, its texture was a bit off, and the bottom crust not crisp enough.    Health code wise, it was apparent that no one was using latex gloves for the food prep.  That was a violation and a turn off.  There is plenty of better pizza in the area, not to mention across the mighty Delaware River.  This place will do in a pinch.

Way cool coffee house in the heart of Newtown.   Comfortable minimalist décor, with smaller and larger community tables that invite the private conversation and the long work session with excellent brew in hand.  Counter Culture beans and friendly skilled baristas/owners keeping their hands and hearts in their business.   My chai latte was excellent, served in a large dark blue ceramic cup and saucer.  My co-conspirator had a regular latte and almond biscotti, both of which he said he enjoyed. The casual atmosphere made for a good place to talk.    They seem to be developing bakery oriented snack offerings in addition to the Italian dipping sticks.  Cookies, brownies, bagels of varying stripes were under glass up front.  Tempting, but too close to dinner to indulge.    It is natural to compare The Coffee Room with Starbucks right down the street.  They are different in ambiance and selection of drinks and nosh.  Starbucks has more to eat and a larger drink menu on the wall, yet the coffee creations at The Corner Room seem higher quality, and certainly more tasty when comparing their respective javas straight up.  Here, there was no burnt taste so often associated with Mermaid coffee.    There is plenty of room for both joints in Newtown.    Welcome to the hood!

30th Street Station, the main railroad station in Philadelphia, and the 3rd busiest Amtrak station in its system, has been open since 1933.  It is on the National Registry of Historic Places for its size, Corinthian columns, art deco decoration, gold and red paint coffered ceiling, and several innovations in station design - pneumatic tube system and its over-train passenger functionality, which allowed people departing trains under the station to immediately ascend into the station and avoid the soot and smoke of the earlier version locomotives.  I read somewhere that at one time there was a mortuary in the building, chapel, hospital space, and enough room to land a small aircraft.  Can't imagine that.  It is a beautiful structure as many reviews so well describe.  For me, it is really a museum of American transportation culture that is fully interactive and functional.  In addition to serving the transit needs of millions of people a year on the East Coast, and westward to Chicago and beyond, it offers art (Angel of the Resurrection,1952, by Walker Hancock, and Spirit of Transportation bas wall relief, 1895, by Karl Bitten); and multiple choices of fast and casual cuisine to provide a small measure of comfort to weary travelers. It has found its way into several iconic movies; Blow Out (1981), Trading Places (1983), and Witness (1985).  Seems like it is time for another cinematic experience.    Along with its grander sibling up river, The Museum of Art, it offers spectacular examples of the vision of Philadelphia's City Mothers and Fathers over the past century.  In a city that was once the nation's largest, its capital, and the birthplace of our grand experiment in democracy, it is a living monument to that historic dream.   I was a daily user of 30th Street Station, commuting to/from Trenton for several years. I came to appreciate it as a way station; meeting and becoming friends with people I met every morning, and said "goodbye" to most nights. Drinking the same coffee and buying a newspaper before the digital revolution made paper obsolete. Life on a train for a few hours a day is another story, but having this terminus start and end each workday forged a personal relationship with this edifice.  Like any sibling it was not always a lovefest, but I knew it was doing its best to make my commute bearable, if not deeply existential.   But,you don't have to be going anywhere to enjoy a visit.

I'm not sure how they pack so many flavors into a thin coating of pastel icing, but Factory Donuts knows their secrets and does a great job keeping their signature roundies beautiful and sweetly refreshing. How will we Newtownians ever leave home now that these pristine creations are living among us?   When you get to select the combination flavors you want, watch freshly baked round white cakes exit the oven and begin their short journey on the conveyor belt where multiple workers customize them as requested and then box them in attractive cardboard, you are experiencing tantalizing delayed gratification until you get to your car and can break open the box and take that orgiastic first bite.   YEUWEEE! Instant sugar rush accented with both loud and subtle flavors.   Strawberry Lemonade, Blueberry Bake, French Toast, Bananas Foster...you get the picture. They taste even better than your imagination. And the underlying donut cake is a strong platform; mildly vanilla light white that taste good in their own right.   Certainly not inexpensive compared to other shops, but a perfect indulgence when you want to treat yourself well.   Bet you can't eat just one!

What is it about bridges?  Since childhood on the upper west side of Manhattan when I played underneath the George Washington Bridge, they have held a special fascination for me.  From ground level, the soaring towers and thick cables looked like a magical castle drawbridge. Even now I get an excited sensation every time I walk or drive over even the most modest crossing over a creek.    It is hard to believe that before 1926 when the Ben was opened there was only ferry service carrying people and commerce across the Delaware. Too, it is passing strange that it was not until 1956 that Big Ben Blue received its current name, and that it was the largest suspension bridge in the world for a while.    Yes. It can be maddening to deal with the traffic during rush hours, and the cost makes us wish for the return of ferries.  Still, when it lights up at night, or we cross it on a weekend and can look upstream or down, the sense of flight and the required leap of faith that the roadway will hold us on our passage to the other side, blend into a metaphor for life.     Someone once said, "Great cities have great bridges..."  I am sure Ben would agree.

When I finally got around to dealing with curtains for the French doors leading to the back porch, I had to admit I had no idea how to deal with them.  Way above my pay grade!    So, breaking it down into the elements I thought involved, I went first to a fabric store to find material for drapes.  Twenty overwhelming and mind numbing minutes later, I was defeated by the aisle upon aisle of material that could be used to make curtains.  No wonder it had taken so long for me to address this project.    Serendipity plays funny games, and if not for my tortured look as I approached a saleswoman at the measuring/cutting counter in the rear of this megastore, I might have never known of Marburn Curtains.  I asked this saintly person how I should approach buying fabric for curtains, and how find someone to actually measure and make them.  She looked at me as if I was not the first clueless guy to ask this dumb question.  It was like; "If you gotta ask, then you really don't want to know..."    She was right.  I was going about it entirely the wrong way.    Then, she told me a secret that lifted the dark clouds and pointed the way.   "Go to Marburn Curtains in Bensalem.  They have premade curtains in all styles and sizes.  They can help you out."    Thirty minutes later I walked into this throwback 20th Century warehouse/store that had more curtains hanging in the aisles than I could look at.  The shop was staffed by a crew of ladies whose life was curtains.  One took my hand and led me to the back of the store where the kind of curtains I described were displayed.  We were down to less than a hundred now, and the task seemed manageable.  I finally selected the two packs of 60 X 84 beautiful beige lined silk-like pieces, complete with grommet holes and the necessary hardware for installation.     All this and immense piece of mind for under $70.  What had been so daunting was reduced to a simple transaction.    Next step - installation.   (To be continued)

Located in the White House Building on South State Street, in the same location as Duck Sauce, Snacks by the Pound is the latest tenant to occupy the other corner space.  We wish them great success there!  I mention its neighbor because that is the way I first noticed this shop set back from the street.  I came out of Duck Sauce and walking on the covered front porch I noticed the new store and went in to have a look.    I didn't know that homemade chocolate would taste so good after a good spicy Asian meal, but it did!  In fact, I suggest that these owners talk to each other and start to cross market their goods.  A little chocolate delivered with the lunch or dinner bill would be a great touch (and better than the Andes Mints).  A discount coupon for a quality Chinese or Thai repast with the purchase of $10. worth of candy, would also be a hot commodity.  Maybe they are already doing that, but I did not see it. Come talk to me.  S/P is a veritable wonderland of sweets set in a well appointed comfortable setting. Made to look "country," it succeeds in taking you away from the world outside and dropping you into a childhood daydream.  Hard not to smile and salivate when looking at the enormity of the collection here, and reminiscing about those candies you craved as a kid.    Yes. It is a little decadent, but it is so innocent that no one will turn you in to the diet police.

Heng Fa Market on 10th Street in Chinatown is a relatively small shop specializing as a green grocer, butcher and fish monger. No canned goods here. Everything looked fresh and well maintained. Prices were better than the Asia basement store, and the crowded aisles we're ample proof.   There are only handheld baskets as there is no room for shopping carts. That limits how much you can buy in one visit unless you come with a team to help carry your take. There is constant bumping into folks, and the floor around the seafood department is always damp, so some caution is required. But, the jostling is worthwhile to secure the quality goods offered here. Just be sure to secure your wallet because there is more than one type of fishing going on.   We picked up meat, veggies and eggs ($3.50 for 3 doz. XLs!), paying much less than in the aforementioned dungeon. The cashier line runs up the vegetable aisle, so you can imagine the low level confusion going on.   Still, if you enjoy interacting with humanity the experience was almost enjoyable. Just glad we weren't running for a bus.

While I will always prefer the real French pastries found on every corner in even the smallest ville in France, at least this particular Paris Baguette has the touch and feel of a real old fashioned Boulanger. Wooden floors and display shelves, mural of the Tour Eifel, and decent cakes, breads, tarts and coffee, make this a pleasant stop and relaxation spot.  This is the third PB I have visited, and it is by far the most comfortable on a human scale.  The others have either been too big and cold (Edison), or too small and subterranean (Elkins Park).  This one does it well.   Glad they got it right this time.

I liked my breakfast at Hampton House Waffles & Eatery.   The dining room was nicer than expected, and service was outspokenly friendly and accommodating. I sat at the short counter where I was attended to by several people.  Coffee arrived promptly, and my order was taken with interest.  The server wanted to be sure that I knew what I was getting with the Gus' Special Omelet. He described in detail that it was a pancake type egg dish, with the home fries, as well as the feta, onions and green peppers inside the egg shell.  No problem. That was exactly what I wanted.   It arrived about ten minutes later, filling the entire plate from rim to rim.  The rye toast arrived a few moments later, lathered in butter. A few shakes of the pepper shaker and I was good to go.   It was a solid, filling meal.  Plenty of ingredients to load it up, with each element identifiable on the tongue. Maybe, a little more feta would have been helpful. The toast was also worthy of special recognition, as it was very hot from the toaster, and had a great crunch.   Next time, have to try the namesake waffles.

Zaika on Grant Avenue in Northeast Philly, is one of the best Pakistani/Indian restaurants I have ever had the pleasure of supping in.  I mean, there are some strong reviews from people I respect, but I didn't think I was about the experience a gastronomic wonder. Chef Mohammed has it going on!    Somewhat surprising that we were among the very few customers on a Sunday night, but no complaints. The house was recently renovated with a larger dining room, and a touch of class with comfortable seating and sparse, but attractive décor.  Our server, Nema, was excellent.  She knew the questions to ask to make sure we got what we wanted.  Correct level of spiciness, and the right dipping sauces for the dishes ordered. No ice for the water. When undecided about whether to go with garlic or chili naan, she had the ready solution of having the tandoor bake up a combo of the two.  Garlic chili naan, indeed, was a winner.   The rest was a cavalcade of wonderous dishes that expanded my understanding of what was truly possible in an IndoPak kitchen.  There were only three plates requested; a Samosa Chat app, Chicken Kashmiri and Bhaingan Bharta (eggplant). Each was uniquely distinct from similar plates in other restaurants, and each was outstandingly better.    The Chat was a deconstructed Samosa, with the crisp fried dough on the bottom of a mass of tender chickpeas, potatoes and spicy homemade Masala sauce.  It was ordered for medium heat.  Auspicious beginning!  It had a complex flavoring and texture that was similar to other samosas, but somehow better, with a subtle sweet undernote to the usual fritter-like taste.  Delightful.   The Chicken Kashmiri was ordered because of familiarity with this dish elsewhere; knowing it to be cream based and a lightly sweet alternative to all the curried heat coming from the other sources.  This version was that, but so much more.  Rather than just the combination of the heat from the cream sauce, the sweetness was supplied by raisins, pineapple and dried apricots.  A complete and unexpected surprise, that was in turn a mystery to be solved.  It took a while to figure out what those flavors/textures were.  But, when realization dawned, so did a big smile at the elegantly simple, yet creative genius at work.  Pineapple and apricot discovery was better than a game of charades. I loved this masterstroke.   The Bhaingan was not as wildly original, but an excellent mashed roast eggplant, green peas, onion, pepper and tomato mixed with traditional herbs and spices.  Ordered hot, it was a nice counterpoint to the cooler sweetness of the Kashmiri.   Last, but far from least, the Garlic Chili Naan, was a knockout bread sensation.  A bit oily, but the interplay of the two main ingredients so well seared to the surface of the naan, and the chewiness and absorption of the lightly crisped dough, made for great taste and the perfect utensil to pick up the sauces from each dish and slowly devour every last drop.     Yes. There was a Mango Lassi, too.  Best way to cool an overheated tongue is to bathe it in cool mangoed yogurt drink.    Zaika - The best meal I have had so far this year.

I totally get the cult of Federal Donuts; the lovechild of Zahav and Percy Street BBQ.    The old corner shop is in a warren of narrow old streets in Pennsport, and the space itself has a tiny charm that could easily be a time warp to the 18th Century.  Standing in line or waiting for an order creates a sense that time has slowed down, and even the dust in the sunbeams may have danced for our forefathers. The combination of Korean style double fried chicken and deep dive dough balls is a natural fit for preparation, but I am not yet comfortable eating both at the same seating. The double dose of fats challenges my guilt.   When we arrived mid-Saturday afternoon, all of the fancies were gone, but the 3 daily offerings were available.  Folks were gnawing on their chicken bones at the counter, blissful in their enjoyment.  We ordered a half doz mix of Vanilla Spice, Maple Brown Sugar and Strawberry Lavender to take with us on the drive home.  They were individually bagged while hot, and placed in a larger paper bag, and ultimately triple bagged in a plastic take out carrier.    Opening the package, the heat and moisture has made the paper sacks damp, but still held in plenty of the essence of the dough wheels. We tried a Vanilla Spice.  It was covered in sugar and cinnamon, cake-like, and uber sweet. The bite and chew was pleasant, but there was no crispness due to the water vapors.  Very tasty.  A very good donut.  Over the next day, the rest were devoured, and although the taste varied with content, the general experience was the same.  A nice round piece of cake with a hole in the middle.   Federal Donuts deserves another house call earlier in the day when the fancies are in stock, and again for a unique fried chicken experience, which seems as varied as the sweet fat tires.  After those ingestions, an update will be in order.   Until then, the consumed donuts themselves were not life altering, but were certain A-Okay!

All the reviews capture the rare beauty of the Wissahikon Valley, carved out by the creek by the same name over the past 125 million years.  It is an amazing work of nature so close to the urban Philadelphia center.    The only things I can add are from an historic and geologic perspective.  The reference to the hermit cave derives from a settlement of Christian end of days sect who lived primitively along the creek in the 19th Century. The ruins remain in some places.   If you love rocks, the Valley is a very special place as well.  Due to a fault line that runs nearby, the area has shifted significantly over the millennia. The rock we see today was once more than 10 miles below the surface. The tectonic plates lifted and convoluted the strata of rock with pressure and heat so great that the nature of the rock changed from a granite bedrock formation into a waving and blistered schist.  It can be seen everywhere along the creek.  The good news is that this geologic action created a treasure trove of crystals to be found with a little effort. Mica (clear to black), Garnet(ruby red to burnt orange), Tourmaline(black and brown), Kyanite(sky blue) and others minerals are everywhere.  So, it is a great place to go with a bucket, strainer, geo hammer and eye protection.   Be careful after rains, as the Wissahikon Creek becomes savage and swells to several times its normal flow for many hours after the storm passes.  While the scour it causes reveals more riches, it can also quickly take a life.  Don't go alone.   This is some of the finest 1,800 acres of park land you will see east of the Mississippi.

No. That wasn't George W. at the round table in the corner plotting his next move in the campaign to evict the British from the Original Thirteen.  Although the Inn named for his most daring plan feels like it might have been around to provide succor to our troops, it actually came later.  Still, if patriotic memories served with drink and sustenance are your thing, the Washington Crossing Inn will make you a very satisfied customer.  The place just feels so authentic and historically grounded that it is impossible not to have at least a moment of reflection about the birth of our nation fought and died for all around on this hallowed ground.    On a quiet Friday eve in August, when many were far away on vacation or at the shore, the WCI provides a nurturing and comfortable abode for a well made libation to accompany an equally crafted conversation.  We sat at the bar catching up on too infrequently overlapping lives, me enjoying a Padron Margarita Up No Salt.  It was tart, smooth and strong, without ice to dilute, nor salt to dry the lips.  It was so good I anticipated the second long before I was close to finishing the first.  The conversation became poignant, and my hunger asserted itself, so we agreed to move to a nearby hightop to enjoy a tavern meal as we imbibed and edged closer to the heart of our exchange.    My Tavern Burger was very good with Red Onion, Tomato, and Lettuce ensconced in a fresh Kaiser Roll.  It was dead-on medium as requested.  The accompanying French Fries (here France is still an ally to our cause), were plentifully crisp.  It was one of the better burgers I had eaten in the past year.  Together, the Rita and Burger were a perfect complement to unexpectedly meaningful evening.    For facilitating this exceptional moment in a wonderfully ambient historic environment, I genuinely felt this was as good as it gets.  Taken separately each element may have been less, but in its totality it was life affirmingly great!

This Dunkin Donuts on Bustleton Avenue in the far Northeast Philadelphia, is about average for this species of fried round dough outlets. Small footprint, but with a corner lounge with worn out leatherette sofa and easy chair, and slate accent wall.   Nice touches, but it comes down to the quality of their bread and butter - their coffee and sweet dough. In this they cannot complete with the new wave of cafes, bakeries and donut specialty houses that are working harder for my dollar. In the last two weeks I have tasted far better java, and munched on way more luxurious cakes and dough fry around town and the burbs, than sampled last night. Maybe a little more money, but the difference in quality is patent. Too, they don't sweep the floor around you while sitting down to enjoy their wares. No one likes dust and dirt flying around their food. No one wants to feel swept out.   DD. Too much of a no longer great thing. Becoming stale; much like day old donuts.

"Music gives Soul to the Universe, Wings to the Mind, Flight to the Imagination..."                                             Plato  So believes Joel Zazyczny, the founder idealist who created Cafe Soul in Doylestown, PA. Scientist, innovator, philanthropist, Joel operates this simple, yet attractive eatery, as a non-profit to work with the younger people of the community in support of music and STEM education programming and scholarships. For this alone he has my admiration and support; for actually pulling off a well functioning breakfast/lunch haven with good food, he has my loyalty.   Now fully vaccinated against Covid, I visited Cafe Soul for my first professionally made Brioche French Toast in over a year. Walking in, the space was open, clean and prepared for social separation. I sat at a booth in back where I could see the entire room. Soon, I was approached by the young man running the front end. He was friendly and deferential. I did the short stack FT, and a mug of their Ellis Coffee brew. The joe was fresh and strong as expected from Philadelphia's oldest caffeine roaster (since 1854).   The frenchie was well panned, with plenty of caramelized edges for melted butter and syrup to accumulate. The egg mix tasted of vanilla and cinnamon, just as I like it. But for the Stuckey containers of corn syrup sweetener, it was a strong reintroduction to a favorite and missed morning meal. If real maple syrup had been an option, I would have jumped at the chance for a near perfect indulgence.   Otherwise, a wonderful first breakfast out in the world again.

Ashni Kumar Guru is the master chef and personality behind Guru Indian Cuisine on Cambridge Lane in Newtown, Pa.  It is housed in the former Mexican/Guatemalan restaurant, Mamita's, and retains the colors and Latin feel.  It reminds of the Indo-Mex restaurants I ran into in Montreal; full blown spice assault with a Tequila chaser.   Chef Guru has a great feel for the elements of Indian cooking; mixing taste, texture and color with fresh ingredients to produce an array of very good to excellent plates that are as appealing to the eye, as to the tongue.  He makes a point of coming out to meet his customers to be sure they are satisfied and inquire about anything they might desire.  His visage tucked under a Philly's cap was a personal touch that is so often lacking in other restaurants.    We came in for Saturday buffet around 1:00.  The joint was empty but for us.  Surprising given the popularity of the place, but maybe not given it being the day after Christmas.  The spread was attractive, but fairly limited in options, with only a handful of offerings from all food groups.  It was enough to get an idea about the quality of the food, but not enough to really sample a broad cross section of the menu.  I am neglectful to record what we were eating, but the two chicken dishes were very good with wonderful creamy spiced tawny sauces, and the vegetable choices were tasty.  Fresh Naan brought hot to the table was a great approach to balancing the more mass produced buffet table with something prepared just for us.  As always, the Naan was a wonderful pinch and sponge to grab all the delicious sauces on the plate.  Contrarily, the Mango Lassi was watery and tasted of coming from a mix, rather than any approximation of fresh fruit.   I want to return to order off the menu to experience main courses prepared only for us, as something is always lost with a buffet.  After experiencing Guru's apex efforts I will be in a better position to fully appreciate the magic of his kitchen.  JANUARY 21, 2016 - The Bucks County Department of Health just cited Guru for 13 health code violations dealing with hand washing, proper cooling. All correctable, but stay informed about this by visiting the County website where the reports and follow up inspections are found.  FEBRUARY 23, 2016 -  Updated Inspection Report. Many violations corrected.

Riverside, NJ, is no longer the thriving Delaware River side town it was in the middle of the last century. Scott Avenue is still a wide expanse well designed for Independence and Veterans Day parades, but the storefronts on either side are now either boarded up or operating as low budget businesses working hard to survive in this dusty backwater now that its industrial base is gone. That is, except for the Golden River Restaurant.   Their building has been standing for over one hundred years, taking many forms from drug store to early age department store and appliance outlet. Since about 1992 it has been a restaurant, most recently in its present form as a breakfast/lunch emporium. I stopped in after court in Mt. Holly to see what they had going on.   It is a large room with booths and tables up front and an old lunch counter in back. It feels dated, yet comfortable - quietly fitting into the over the hill sensibility of Riverside itself. I took a stool at the counter and was immediately approached by a very friendly server offering Lacas Coffee and a menu. People were shorter a century ago, and I discovered that I could not fit my legs under the counter. I moved over to the end of the row where there was a bit more room due to warpage and a bent stool frame. Fit my 6' 4" fine there.   I ordered their Greek Omelette with rye toast, and suggested the chef put the home fries inside the egg case along with the onions, peppers, mushrooms, sausage, feta and whatever else was in there. In the meantime I sipped my joe and chatted with my counter lady and other customers. Everyone was talkative and willing to share their thoughts. Cool!   My breakfast was delicious and filling. The eggs were still wet enough to meld with its filling, allowing each element to speak in its own voice, yet harmonize perfectly together. It was definitely a case where the whole was greater than the sum of its parts. A splash of hot sauce completed the dish, adding a touch of heat to the rest of the opus. The rye had crunchy texture and sourness, exactly as I like. This was a strong candidate for omelette of the year.   As I departed the chef/owner met me at the door to ask after my satisfaction. He was pleased with my reply. Turns out that he had spent years in Trenton and knew many of the same restaurants and lawyers from the capital city where my office is located. A pleasant surprise.   I congratulated him on his success in Riverside, and reminded him that his employee at the counter deserved a raise.   Hope she gets it.

Maybe it's because I have visited China Café often enough over the past few years to be its Duke, or maybe it's the way the owner of this twenty plus year establishment smiles at me when she sees me walk in, but the food here seems to be getting better.    The joint still looks every day of its longevity in Lalor Plaza, and sorely needs a makeover that brightens it up and takes the storage out of the dining room, and it wouldn't be the worse thing in the world if Mr. Café trimmed his Confucian beard.  Nonetheless, some kind of magic is happening in the kitchen that is creating more distinct and enjoyable dishes from the lunch menu.    Today, the Hot & Sour Soup took me by surprise.  I told the Mrs. that I did not want MSG in it, and she assured me there would be none.  Sure enough, the small bowl arrived without the telltale sheen on the surface that denotes the presence of the food enhancer to which I am allergic. It was loaded with tofu, sprouts and other veggies, and had a great taste.  Next up was the Roast Pork Egg Foo Young.  It came out as two pancake omelets full of sliced pork, veggies, and covered in the ubiquitous brown sauce.  The eggs were not particularly oily and the sauce was hot without the aftertaste of sitting around too long.  Liked it a lot.   No one will mistake China Café for fine dining, but it seems to have found its equilibrium at a higher point than most other local wok shops.  The ingredients seemed fresher, and the attention to detail and timing of the elements more rigorous.  Given that I rarely give such houses more than an Okay grade, the upmark for this place is significant.    Whatever the reason, China Café has my appreciation, with sincere hope that it continues on this path.

The Golden Eagle Diner at the intersection of Route 13 and Bath Road, Bristol, PA, is an attractive renovated traditional roadside food emporium with extensive menu. On this Saturday morning it was bustling, and I sat at the small counter that serves as both a place to eat and their bar for drinks. As I supped on a morning omelette, the folks next to me sipped on Bloody Marys.    I ordered the Old Country Omelette (onion, green pepper, tomato, bacon, ham & sausage), side of home fries, rye toast) and Lacas perked coffee. It took a while for a server to notice me and begin service, but I was in no hurry. When she finally stopped by to help, she didn't hear me ask her to hold the ham. No biggie. But, it took her until I was almost completely finished with my meal to inquire how I was doing. I had already asked the floor manager for a caffeine refill, which he provided after bartending the first Bloody Mary.  Gratitude, my good man.   The only things missing on this weekend before Christmas were smiles on any of the faces working there. No one seemed happily employed, and they seemed incapable of offering even a glimpse of happiness to their customers for being there. They felt oppressed by something or someone. Though I deal with people's problems professionally, I didn't want to make theirs mine on my day off.   So, I ate quietly, sipped my coffee when it arrived and left when the mug was half full.

Crystal Diner (formerly Edgewater Queen) in Edgewater Park, NJ, is a small footprint roadside attraction on southbound Route 130. It looks recently renovated with stone and stainless fascade, and has a cozy if crowded ambiance. I sat down at the end of the counter and was immediately welcomed by a few of the staff hustling their platters and coffee pots.   The menu was a tour de force of traditional diner cuisine with several pages just for breakfast. I went with something small (I thought) before a more elaborate and expensive meal. The breakfast sandwich (sausage, egg & cheese on kaiser) seemed about right. I asked my server if they used quality rolls as opposed to the poor varieties found in some kitchens. She assured me theirs were good.   They weren't.  What arrived minutes later was a large plate, half of which was loaded with home fried potatoes, and a transected sandwich with long toothpicks holding the two halves together. I didn't mind that they used links rather than patties, even when they began to roll out of the sandwich. No biggie. However, the kaiser was a cheap imitation of an actual bakery product. It was crushed, lifeless and tasteless. What was worse were the home fries. They lacked flavor and were dry beyond redemption. Not even salt, pepper and hot sauce could salvage them. It was obvious that the kitchen didn't have a clue and that management was likely part of the conspiracy.   When was the last time anyone sampled their offerings to provide quality control? Not often enough.   It was a full house, so I expect I am whistling in the wind, but it is one and done for me.

Robert Morris, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, The Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, left his name to this old river burg, and even had his home, Summerseat, nearby. It was his plan to have the capital of the new United States established right here in Morrisville, PA. He was off target by about 25 miles, as the ultimate vote landed our first national city in Philadelphia. Still, Morris was nothing, if not ambitious for his adopted home town (He was born in England, and arrived here as a teenager).   How would he feel about having a tavern named after him?  He would probably have enjoyed the notoriety of being associated with a dive bar with smoking privileges, but lacking a kitchen for a meal, and even taps for the beer they serve. Bottles and cans only, folks. Yet, he probably would have supped and indulged his muses elsewhere, as the joint has seen better days, and is now far from its prime.  The crowd is friendly, if loud and in its cups. The suds are priced right, and the barkeeps a smiling, tolerate group.   My aluminum Bud Light (Philly Philly) edition, was $3. Hard to beat that coinage for a long cold one.   Still, I couldn't escape the sensation that old Robert M., for all his wealth and colonial political power, would have only visited this establishment when he didn't want to be seen by anyone who would recognize him. It is easy to understand why.

This Giant on West Trenton Avenue in Morrisville is the same size as its sisters in Lower Makefield and Langhorne (Newtown), and has more or less the same inventory, but it does feel more dark and dingy than those other stores.  When I shop there, the lack of adequate lighting makes it a bit oppressive to spend much time.  The absence of the smaller, modern, carts available elsewhere, makes it necessary to use the larger, older and rustier pushers that often have gimpy wheels.    While it wouldn't take much to upgrade this commercial space into a more pleasant facility, the company seems to have decided to leave it as it is.  Perhaps, their lease is coming to an end, or the revenue from this location does not justify the expenditure.  Regardless, aside from the convenience of stopping in here occasionally, I would avoid it and frequent the newer and easier to navigate markets just to the north for the same prices.

Very glad I went alone to check out Texas Roadhouse on Street Road, Bensalem, PA. The wait for a table would have been at least an hour given the size of the SRO crowd in the entranceway and milling by the front door. Solo I was able to find the solitary empty bar stool and jump right on without putting my name on a waiting list. This was a first experience with this outfit and I was amazed by the full house and amplitude of the noise.   What was going on here to make it so popular? I soon found out.  No fewer than 3 bartenders stopped by to introduce themselves within the first ten minutes, with the first taking my order for a Sam's Winter Ale pint and a Smokehouse Burger. They all called me by name and seemed genuinely interested in my satisfaction. Despite the full house, and arrival of a few couples now standing around the small square bar hoping for a double vacancy, I never felt rushed nor put upon for ordering a sandwich rather than a large slab of grilled beef and dinner.   And, the medium finish burger was exactly what I got. Half pounder. Hot pink core. Cheddar/American cheese blend. Tomato. Red onion. Mushroom. BBQ sauce. Sesame seed roll. Squirt of Heinz red and I was ready to dive in.   It was excellent. Juicy and textured with luscious profile as I cleaved through it exposing a cross section of the large sandwich. Its 5 inch height was too much for my jaw to expand around, so I ended up using knife and fork to get the job done. Definitely fair value at $12 and change. The tag along fries were not as good, and I left most of them behind.   Folks on either side of me were into their steaks, and seemed as content as me in their choices. Must admit that the aroma from all that sizzling meat was intoxicating.   Leaving the house about an hour later it was even more crowded and louder than when I arrived. I wend my way through the peeps into the open air. So many families waiting to be fed; content to wait as long as it took to partake of the kitchen fare. Now I understood why. For meat lovers this was paradise on a budget. A place they could afford to take their families, have a filling tasty meal, and not break the bank.   Del Frisco's it wasn't. Nor did anyone want it to be.

After visiting Parx Casino for the first time I wanted to grab a bite on site to satisfy my skipped dinner hunger and check out one of its food options. I saw Liberty Bell Gastropub right off the casino floor and walked in to see what was going on.   The bar was a large rectangle with plenty of open seats. I grabbed one after the hostess said I was free to do so. The space is attractively appointed with very high wood planked ceiling and large HDTVs all around. The bartenders were friendly and efficient. I asked for a menu and then saw the Happy Hour card standing on the bar near me. I realized that HH was from 9 to 11, and that I was right in the middle of it. It had more or less what I wanted (burger & beer) and nice discounts. I went with their Smokehouse Burger (gouda, bacon, BBQ sauce on brioche bun), side of mashed rather than fries, and a Victory Prime Pilsner. $7 savings made for a great and tasty deal.   The burger was the perfect medium finish requested, and the garlicy mashed potatoes a pleasant alternative to overworked fries. The Philly brewed Victory beer was a cold refreshing washdown. Also nice to have linen napkin and heavy grade flatware on hand.   All in all, Liberty Bell Gastropub could easily stand on its own as a high quality roadside stop. Of course, the gambling operation no doubt subsidizes the cost in order to keep people near the gaming tables. Still, it was a job well done.

I used to be a daily commuter through 30th Street Station when I lived in Center City and worked in Trenton, NJ. That was nearly 25 years ago when the station, though still beautiful in its faded glory, struggled to maintain its class and dignity in a city that had fallen on hard times. Walking through the grand center hall was like a stroll in an ancient temple paying homage to the greatness of a bygone age. (Please read my earlier review for a flavor of its history.)  These days the station has been refurbished and renewed beautifully. It has returned to its former grandeur and it could be said it is even better now than ever. The expanded food court is an example of this improvement across the board. The entire south side of the station houses a multitude of fast and fast casual eateries, cafes and bakeries that are as attractive to sit in as their products are tasty to eat and drink. It reminds of the amazing food court that was rebirthed at Union Station in Washington, DC, a few decades ago.   30th Street is now both a high functioning contemporary transportation center and a "Please Touch" museum in the heart of America's first capital city. It has become a destination for rail travellers, city dwellers and visitors far and wide.   Even parking has been streamlined and made safe and affordable. Picking up my son coming in from Latrobe on The Pennsylvanian, I was able to park across the street, take the walking bridge to the station using the smooth escalators, and be waiting for him at Track 7 as he emerged from the beneath the station platform, in just minutes.

It's about time to bestow the fifth star to Newtown Bagel. It is awarded for consistency of effort, sincere and friendly service, long term partnership with the community and excellence in breakfast sandwiches. Their success is shown by the opening of a second shop, Yardley Bagel Co. in Lower Makefield, which produces the same quality baked rounders as Newtown, in a more expansive and comfortable space. Can a third be far behind?   While I still have a small issue with the texture of the bagel skin which is softer (less crisp) than I prefer, I can't deny that the pliable nature when fresh from the oven creates a perfect platform for a hot steaming sandwich. My just eaten sausage, egg & cheese on untoasted onion bagel was wonderfully delicious from first bite through last. The chew blended ingredients well and gave full voice to the harmonics exploding in my mouth. Alas, my tastes have matured to appreciate the pleasure of the different texture. There is a place in life for more than one variety of bagel.   Bagel Wisdom attained by hard experience and exhaustive bagel research cannot be denied.

Unable to reach my regular dentist after several calls, it was time to find someone who was actually available for treatment. After Yelp search and word of mouth inquiries, I chose Smile Culture Dental in Levittown for necessary and emergent dental care.
