Their facility on Oxford Valley Road was bigger than expected, especially after being accustomed to a one man office prior to this visit. The waiting area was attractive, with comfortable seating, and a self serve coffee station for all visitors. The sign in process had a few pages to read and sign, but that was simple and the folks behind the counter were pleasant and efficient. After about a 15 minute wait, we were called into the working area, and walked down a long half-walled hallway with dental chairs on both sides. I think I saw five work stations for the three dentists in the practice. Dr. Patel introduced himself in his aquamarine scrubs. He was friendly and had no problem with answering questions and explaining what he was seeing and what he intended to do about it.   He worked with a dental assistant who knew her stuff and had a warm and empathetic personality. When we heard the diagnosis of a broken molar that required extraction, and that he was going to remove the tooth immediately with consent, he gave his patient time to absorb what was going to happen, ask questions, and think about it before seeking approval.  When that was forthcoming, an office/billing person came over with surgical consent form and billing information for signing. It was professionally done. Not high pressure in any way.   Dr. Patel had a steady hand and explained the procedure from anesthesia through means of extraction and post op expectations. He was patient and had an easy, yet knowledgeable manner. He described what he was seeing and doing in a play by play narrative that was simple and understandable. Twenty minutes later the offending tooth was in the grip of his extractor (pliers), and he was packing the vacated space with artificial bone to maintain spacing and have a base for future implant.   He provided prescriptions for antibiotic and pain management (if needed), and explained proper home care and next visit. The cost was fair, especially compared with dental offices closer to home (upscale communities have upscale dentists). They seem to have some flexibility in pricing and a program for regular visits and maintenance if desired. We deferred that decision pending the outcome of this experience.   For the moment, I am quite satisfied with how we were treated at Smile Culture Dental. Should anything change, I will be sure to let you know.

When the sign on the front door says, "DO NOT ENTER WITH HOODIE OR MASK...IF SO YOU ARE NOW TRESPASSING," you know there is a fundamental problem being expressed by management.  This isn't the best neighborhood in the Capital City, in fact, it is one of the worst. I wouldn't be found here at night, but for a quick lunch with parking right out front, and Trenton's finest stopping in for take out, I felt pretty safe as I dined on my Eggplant Parm Sandwich.    The loaf was fresh, mildly crunchy and had a good mild yeasty flavor.  The Eggplant had been sautéed in a frying pan with extra virgin olive oil before being finished in the pizza oven to melt the cheese and seal the final product.  It was a good sandwich, even if not the lunch of the gods.   Service was friendly, if a little jumpy.  Only four booths for eating in.  Same ownership for 23 years.    I guess they have seen the hood change during that time.  How many holdups before the sign went up?    No doubt, one was enough.

Completed in Montgomery County in 2015, Pennypack Trail is actually 16 miles long (5.4 mi. in Montco), and part of the much larger trail network in eastern PA. In fact, the section extending into Bucks County reaches the Delaware River and connects with the East Coast Greenway which runs 3,000 miles from Maine to Florida. So, if you want a long hike, you can have one.   The portion I was on yesterday was the border of Lorimer Park that was historically the railroad right of way since the 1860s, when first the Philadelphia Montgomery County Railroad Co., followed by the Philadelphia Newtown New York Railroad and finally the Newtown Branch of the Reading R&R used it to transport people and produce before highways took their place. SEPTA had it last and suspended commuter transportation (Fox Chase - Newtown Line) in 1983, and donated it to the Rails to Trails Project.   While we all love a scenic walk, it sure would be nice to have mass transit available to get us from our bedroom communities to the heart of the city more conveniently, and redevelop the termini and old stations along the route for small commerce, too. There should be a way to have both more green space and village like economies working in tandem to attract people. Vision and capital are all that are required.   Still, the Trail is a beautiful route for nature and scenic lovers as it is, and can be enjoyed in almost any weather. Walking along the heights above Pennypack Creek and watching the water course through the steep ravine cut out by erosion over eons of time, is remarkable. In the 18th and 19th Centuries many mills were busy using water wheels to grind flour, which was transported by the nearby rails to cities for further production and consumption. Some of those old structures are still there (mostly in ruins), and the stone houses built near to them were often maintained and are lived in today.   Hiking further, the Bethayres Swamp beckons, with Audubon designation as an IBA - Important Bird Area. The trail goes through the town of Bryn Athyn, where the original train station has been repurposed as the local post office. Just beyond that is the site of a major head-on train collision in 1921, that killed many passengers. Not all the trail is smooth for bike riding, nor easy strolling, but with effort, grit and good footwear, these places can be reached, explored and fancied.  The Pennypack Watershed is an ecological zone with long human history in the Philadelphia area. It is well worth sustaining and maintaining, even with reasonable respect for progress and our shared future.

There have been a stream of Indian restaurants at this location on Krewstown Road, just off Grant, but none of them have stuck until now. Me thinks the Mayura may break that trend and hang around for a long while. The dining room is colorful, the service is friendly, if not quite polished, and the menu is South Indian with an interesting list of vegetarian and non-vegetarian choices.   We went with appetizers of Veggies Samosas, Onion Bajhi; large bowls of Vegetable Korma and Chicken Masala, and a smaller plate of Indo Chinese Chili Chicken. A basket of Garlic Ginger Naan and supply of Basmati Rice completed the table. Of course, we ordered way too much, but after tasting everything, we were happy to bring the leftovers home.   The Samosas were golden fried and filled with mashed potatoes and green peas. Very good. The Onion Bajhi were basically dipped and deep fried in a light flour batter, made to be complemented by an excellent sweet/tart tamarind sauce. The Korma was a load of soft veggies in a dark tan cashew mild curry reduction. The Masala was darker and spicier, while the Chili Chicken was a decent rendition of the interaction between Chinese and Indian notions of inbred meals, not as crisp as found in Tibet, but leaning on Szechuan red chili with tumeric bite from south of the border. Each was a carousel of flavor and texture that deserved a trek in the high mountains between the two nations where life is hard , yet a grand adventure. We enjoyed it all. Oh, and the Naan was great with that hint of ginger mixed with garlic.   The only downside was the Mango Lassi, which was from a mix that was so thick that it could not be pulled through a straw, and required major dilution with water in order to get it down the gullet.   Otherwise, Mayura was all around a strong showing with only slight fraying around the edges.

State Street Kitchen is NO LONGER open Friday nights for dinner.    The menu leaned toward Korean cuisine, complete with stainless steel bowls, chop sticks, and special hot sauces to heat your pallet and warm the soul.  The crowd is quite different than who you see at breakfast and lunch.  It seems like many of Micha's friends come down to hang out with her.  They bring wine or harder stuff for all to share, and often pick up a mix of desserts to pass around.  Sort of like a pot luck.   This is a great direction for this small house.  With the right people working the kitchen, expanding to other nights would be a boon to nighttime State Street.

When you love Thanksgiving with family and friends, but not the kitchen work required to feed everyone, the best thing to do is find a restaurant where turkey and all the fixings are on the menu for a reasonable price, and visit those dearest to you after the feast, but just in time for dessert. This year the choice was the new Metro Diner in the spot where the Wells Fargo Bank used to be in the corner of Lincoln Plaza Shopping Center.   The place was a buzzing half full house, with full complement of cooks and service personnel putting the "fast" in Metro's fast casual dining. The Roasted Turkey Platter (3 large slices of white meat, blanched green beans, stuffing, mashed potatoes & gravy) were placed steaming hot before me five minutes after ordering. It was all very good, and the included slice of pumpkin pie with dollop of whipped cream, the perfect alternative to the DIY option. The $15 per person charge gives "lazy" a good name.   These guys were closing at 2 to give staff time with family.  We went on to visit friends after their dinners and celebrated all we had to be thankful for for the remainder of the day.

Read Whitney A. from Holland review (12/2/12), which mirrors my own.  The staff is very friendly and fast, the price is reasonable, and the coffee decent. All good things. But, the bagels are not close to being the right texture nor taste. They could be so much better with a little tinkering.  It's not that they are bad, it's just that they miss the target of being really satisfying.  With so many bagelphiles adrift at the loss of Bagel Junction, Newtown Bagel could become our Shangri-la, and garner our undying devotion and business with a few adjustments.

Came down to The Pines Tavern on Radcliffe Street in old Bristol Borough to celebrate mi cumpleanos the other night.  Yelp reviews were very positive, and it had been a while since I had anything more than a cup of great coffee (Calm Waters Coffee Roasters) in this old river city.   The bar/dining room is small, with square bar and perhaps ten to fifteen stools and equal number of tables.  The room is dark with several HDTVs for sport enthusiasts. The crowd was a mix of octogenarians  and middle aged folks, who all seemed to get along smashingly.  Drinks were very reasonably priced, and the custom beer list, while limited, had enough for us to be satisfied. Service was prompt and friendly with black T-shirted smiling servers always available to bring what you needed.    The kitchen feels mostly homegrown talent.  They know what they are doing, especially in the realm of American or ethno-American cuisine.  The plates are full to overflowing, while still being dusted with herb and sauce for that new-American high end look.  I came for the Meatloaf and was lucky enough to discover it was "Meatloaf Night."  Saved a buck or two.  The meal was very good, with Garlic Mashed and fresh Steamed String Beans.  Liked it a lot!   My companions ordered Lobster Mac and Cheese, which came in a low baking dish, topped with Bread Crumbs and melted Cheese.  It was tasty, but to my tongue, the cheese was too strong for the Lobster and hid much of its flavor.  The third entre, a Chicken/Shrimp Thai Curry with Brown Rice, was weaker, as we knew Thai food too well to find this imitation close enough to experience and expectations.  The curry was a little off as if they might not have had all the ingredients needed for authenticity.  Plenty of bird and shellfish.   We also ordered the Buffalo Cheesesteak & Fries app.  It was huge and plenty hot between the Buffalo Red Sauce and semi-melted Blue Cheese.  Our twenty year old inhaled most of this.  It was a big hit.   All in all, we enjoyed our evening at The Pines.  This is far more than your average neighborhood tavern.  A real effort has been made to polish the kitchen and bring in people who want more than just bar food.  In this they have succeeded, even if not perfectly.   We applaud the effort and love the atmosphere.   We will be back.

Keystone is still the reliable discount tire house on Street Road, Bensalem, Pa. They offer a broad inventory of competitive tires, and provide honest assessments of which is best for your car and driving style.    Just came down to replace two all season touring hard rubbers, and had several to choose from, and others that could be on site within 24 hours.  They suggested which would most likely suit my needs, and it was on the low end of the price range.  65,000 miles rode wear guarantee.  They also showed me where my existing tires were worn unevenly, and strongly recommended an alignment at my earliest opportunity.  They didn't push.  They just pointed out the problems I had been having and would continue to experience if this was not addressed.   I drove away with a new set of shoes and a far smoother ride.

Whoomzie's is named for an owner's mother's nickname, according to the counter person who made my onion bagel, butter & Swiss sandwich this morning. In all respects but the new name, this bagel house is unchanged from its days as Jersey Girl Cafe. There is a small lounge area with TV, table and loveseat, as well as a sunny dining area with seven tables. Orders are taken toward the rear of the shop.   My morning repast was good, although I found the bagel denser than I prefer. Still a good taste with fresh butter and cheese. It was a very decent chew. Having I Love Lucy reruns playing in the background made for a relaxing and reminiscing moment. Those gags never get old.   Oh, I just realized that something else has changed. They reversed the entry/exit doors to improve traffic flow within the store. Too, the door latch hardware still sticks without paying proper attention to turning the knob.

Bai Wei is the successor to Sakura Mandarin at the corner of 11th & Race in Chinatown, Philadelphia. Same ownership. Renovated and expanded dining room. Where the focus was formerly on excellent xiao long bao and other Shanghai delights, it has now expanded to include a strong taste of Szechuan and Hunan pepper and black bean hot dishes. I quite liked the old house, and returned late last week to see what the newly imagined kitchen held in store.  From our exploration of the two dishes we ordered, it would appear Bai Wei (many tastes) has it going on.  Their takes on crispy spicy chicken and cumin lamb dry pot were excellent. The chicken was loaded with red Szechuan peppers and small morsels of deep fried chicken. Enough to give our tongues a sincere capcesin workout and loosen our sinuses; stopping just short of bringing on tears. Completely addictive. The lamb, tender in a mix of chopped onion and more peppers and overwhelmed with a dusting of coarse cumin seed. Delicious. About as good as the best Szechuanese bowls I've found in the USA.  The only downside was the continuing attempt by the staff at up selling our order. We were repeatedly asked about appetizers, drinks and rice - even after we declined multiple times. Sure, they want more money per customer, but it became excessive and annoying.   But for that weird dynamic, we thoroughly enjoyed the meal. Just train your servers to accept the customer's wishes and you have a winner.

I have been on a fried chicken binge lately, and when in that frame of mind any source of crispy skinned plump breasted chicken can capture my attention. Popeye's is no exception.   So it was, as I drove over to Prince's to give it another try, that I saw the bright orange sign and building for the Popeye's on North Olden.  Impulse got the better of me and I made the hard left into their drive thru line.  I had difficulty deciphering the menu, so I just ordered a few pieces breasts and wings. Seems I had to order a side and a drink or they couldn't handle my order. It turned out to be cheaper if I did one of their combos rather than just individual pieces.   When I arrived home and opened the box I beheld a large breast and wing that were bigger than I had seen on most chickens. It had me wondering what they feed those birds. The coating was as bright orange as the box it came in, and deeply textured.  Perhaps, the cumin and chili in the Spicy option affected the presentation.   The meat was still moist and very tasty.  Each piece was much larger than what I had sampled at the other place the week before.  The chicken easily parted from the bone and my fingers pulled off most of what was edible.  The rest I worked over with a fork to get into all the bone crannies.   The side dish (coleslaw) was pedestrian, and the biscuit was fairly deflated by the time I  got to it.  So, the thing to do is order the combo, throw away the sides and biscuit and go to town on the chicken itself.    It may not be the same as what is available in those little chicken shacks on the side of the road in Virginia or North Carolina, but it will do nicely up in Jersey on a wintery night.

Is this the best Italian restaurant in Newtown? I think so.  Is it the best in Bucks?  I could make an argument for it, but the real point is that it is so good that people who love Italian should give it a try. Back in the day I returned to Trenton to satisfy my Napoli needs, but those days are gone, and we all must find alternatives closer to home.  Pasquale is the owner/chef/creative genius of Vecchia Osteria.  He takes great pride in his cuisine, and oversees the details between being on the floor checking on his customers and making everyone feel welcome.  He can be generous.  Complimentary glasses of wine and cannoli are not uncommon.  In between, the courses are excellent and each taste follows on upon the one before building into a crescendo of taste, texture, and subtle overlay.  Maestro, please continue.   Last week, VO was one of several local eateries to donate dishes a for large dinner in town.  They provided Chicken Cacciatore (white version), and Rigatoni Vodka, enough for 60 people.  The Chicken was dark meat with lots of Rosemary covering everything.  The meat and bone were easily parted, leaving a succulent light wine and vinegar sauce to bathe the dark chicken flavors.  It was superb.  The pasta was the larger rigatoni, which held the creamy tomato gravy in its grooves and ridges like they were born together.  It was a subtle tone so as not to compete with the more robust cacciatore.  Great combination.  I was sure to take some leftovers home to enjoy the next day, as Chicken Cacciatore becomes even more satisfying with age.   I have eaten in Pasquale's house several times, and always wondered why I waited so long to return.    It always exceeds my expectations.

Over the years living in and around Philadelphia I have come to love its Chinatown. No, it isn't as big and old as the one in Manhattan, nor as historic with twisted alleys as San Francisco's, but for being 175 years old it has its own gritty exotic charm with good restaurants, shops and second story businesses that keep this commercial center thriving. The original Chinese zone was much larger than the core 5 city blocks between Race and Arch, but the demands for land for the Ben Franklin Bridge, Convention Center, Vine Street Expressway, Round House, and Federal Detention Center, have carved up the neighborhood to what we see today. Luckily growth is happening to the north to Callowhill Street, and the south around Washington Street.   I am there once or twice a month to shop in the basement grocery for Chinese ingredients I can't find in the burbs, to get a haircut, and have lunch or dinner at one of the dozens of kitchens offering cuisine from all over China. If my sweet tooth is active, there are now bakeries, bubble tea and Thai ice cream shops galore.   The Friendship Gate on 10th Street is worth walking under to capture the magic carved and painted into it by artisans from Tianjin.   Parking is always an issue, so if you live in center city, walk or Uber over. Otherwise, be prepared to pay for space on the edges of C'town that add to the cost of an otherwise inexpensive experience.

What Happened to the Copa brand?  Back in the Day, when Copabanana was only down on South Street, I spent my Friday nights after Tai Chi classes at the Painted Bride hanging out with the motley crew at Copa, downing rip roaring 'ritas, and munching fabulous Burgers laden with Pepper Jack Cheese and sliced Jalapenos, with a basket of Spanish Flies fulfilling a post workout greasy comfort food attack, and exchanging stories of daring do.  So very Yin/Yang. I either sat at the bar, in the dining room, or upstairs in the cramped attic before it became a cooler than you microbar.   Cut to the recent past, and I finally had a couple of opportunities to hit this Copa on Spruce Street, just off Penn's Campus.  Looked great from the outside - loads of colors - and even suggested some happening things within. One stop at the bar for drinks and eats, and another at a small corner table, left me scratching my kep and wondering whether it was my faulty memory, or the joint's loss of verve, that left me feeling that I was in the wrong Copa.    Yes.  The drinks were still stiff (one was enough for me), but the grub had fallen off a cliff.  My beloved burger memory suffered a rude awakening when I bit into what looked to be the same TexMex heat burger of ancient lore.  What had been a juicy joy had evolved into the proverbial hockey puck.  Hard from over-grilling, well done from inattention, and spiced by over-aged now gray peppers from absent quality control and pride.   Not once, but on both occasions, I departed a saddened and wistful patron, yearning for the old days when a Copaburger meant joy on a bun.

Visiting this McDonald franchise on S. Oxford Valley Road in Fairless Hills, Pa., was the first time that the drive up experience took me by surprise.    First, the voice taking orders was amazingly pleasant.  She seemed to be into her job and sincerely asked how I was doing, and how she could help.  The repartee was longer than expected, and warm throughout.  She didn't seem fazed that I was ordering a small meal off the Cheapo menu, and that the items cost less than $4.    Second, this was the first fast food interaction where I was handed a separate plastic bag with napkins and straw.  Someone realized that cleanliness and ease of transfer were important.  So much better than finding those things stuffed into the bag, or worse, not provided at all.    These made for a positive impression of this Mickey D's, and would have led to a higher star rank had the actual Double Cheese Burger been hot off the grill.  Not even close.  Barely lukewarm.  McDonald's burgers are not good enough to be enjoyed at low temp.  Their components start separating and the taste/texture is disjointed.  But, if they ever get that part right, this shop would really stand out.

Not only does Khmer Kitchen do Cambodian cuisine well, but the entire experience is so authentic that by the time you finish eating and pay the very reasonable bill, you may believe that stepping into this corner shop has transported you to the steamy streets of Penom Penh.  The house has only space for six tables with six chairs, but they can be separated for smaller groups like was done for us. This is a family operation from chef to cashier, and it runs efficiently. The front of the house belongs to Tony, who has been the sole (soul) server, busser, furniture mover for the past five years, and he has it down to a graceful science. Impressive.  The kitchen isn't fast, sending out one dish at a time as it is finished rather than bringing everything at once, but that is the style in most of Asia. Yet, once they arrive at the table they demand attention. They are beautiful to behold and distinctively delicious.   We apped on fried calamari. Big pieces, deep fried but not oily, with a nice spicy red amber dipping sauce. Very good. The lemongrass chicken was a huge plate with celery, onion, green pepper and a hot curry lemongrass sauce. Excellent! Finally, we got to work on a pumpkin papaya vegetarian soup that offset the heat with a mild sweetness. Next time I promise to remember the Cambodian names of these wonderful dishes.   The cooking here is a close cousin to Thai and Viet style, but with a few other spices indigenous to that part of Southeast Asia, and a tip of the hat to India and Burma as well.   On this hot day the air conditioning was inadequate, and with the door open to help circulation the flies came in to enjoy their own meals. They were the only reason Khmer Kitchen did not make 5 Stars on this visit, although their buzzing did add to the authenticity.

Unofficial Yelp Events (UYEs) are always just about as good as a party among social media friends can be, and this was no exception.  The meet up at Tired Hands Fermentaria was my first opportunity to visit this well known brewery in Ardmore, Pa., and to sample its wares.  I've got to say that sitting at a table with about 20 peeps, surrounded by the acoustically challenged corrugated iron-roofed warehouse and close to the stainless steel fermenting tanks where the magic is done, made for a loud amplified afternoon. Yet, sitting with folks that I look forward to seeing, and the new ones that I am about to meet, made it bearable.   Arriving late, I was still in time to find a seat and order a Shamabalac mystical ale and a veggie Banh Mi wrap.  Our server was cool and competent, keeping everyone in suds and sustenance, while allowing us to maintain separate tabs.  Quite a trick that she handled with aplomb.   The drink was blond and had remarkable fruity notes.  Liked it, and ordered a couple more. The Vietnamese interpreted sandwich was hardly banh mi at all, given that it was in a wheat wrap rather than a French baguette.  True, the daikon, carrot, tofu and siriracha were present, but the concept was wrong.  Better to just called it Vietnamese inspired, and leave it at that. It was okay, but the image in my head was abandoned unfilled.   Truth be told, I am not a beer maven, although I enjoy it in small creative doses.  Bourbon is my downfall.  Still, I see what people like about Tired Hands, and brewery clubs in general.  The capacity crowd on this late Saturday afternoon, certainly did, too.

Mario's sits on East State Street Extension, west of the I-95 underpass; an area of Hamilton where I rarely go because it feels a bit isolated. Glad I put on my big boy pants and drove out there for lunch Friday afternoon, because it is a nice shop with everything made in house, and friendly folks.   I sat at one of the few booths, in sight of the HDTV showing Trump's inauguration with commentary. Ordered the eggplant parmesan sandwich, and pulled a Coke Zero from the cooler. Even got to read the complementary Trentonian rag that was on my table.   The hot sandwich was a foot long, cut in half, and loaded with thin slices of breadcrumb coated, olive oil pan sauteed, deep purple nightshade. It was topped with a layer of mozza and finally a thick chunky red gravy. It was so big, I decided to use knife and fork rather than attempt direct oral assault. It was delicious and filling. I should have asked for extra sauce on the side, because the eggplant overwhelmed the top dressing, and more dipping would have made the lunch even better. Not complaining. It was excellent. I chose to leave most of the roll aside so I could concentrate on the prize.   Will return for their pizza and tomato pie and revisit Mario's star power, without the political commentary.

TWO SLICE SPECIAL REVIEW ONLY  The price at $4.99 for two large slices of pizza and a soft drink was excellent.  The size of the slices was also more than expected. The service was friendly.  The room was small, with only two tables for those who want to eat their pizza just out of the oven when it is at its prime. So, this is basically a take out joint.   We wanted a quick bite to tide us over until dinner. A slice apiece and sharing the drink was our intention.   I requested that the reheat be "well done," in order to bring the ingredients back to life after sitting on display.   What we received were slices that were not hot in the center where the cheese was thickest. That was likely due to the excessive amount of cheese piled onto the pie, out of proportion to the tomato sauce which seemed sparingly used. The result was pizza that could not be picked up by the crust because it was too heavy on the topside.  The taste was weak because of the cheese/sauce imbalance, and perhaps the quality of the cheese and sauce themselves.  The crust would have been improved with a little salt added to the dough.    Not an impressive effort by Pizza Land.

I'm here to check out the new Wendy's breakfast menu that recently came online. They appear to be in direct competition with the morning offerings from McDonald's, Burger King and Chik Fil-A, at least in this neck of the Northeastern woods.   As an aside I will note that the facility looks recently refurbished, because the old complaints about a run down enterprise is no longer true. The place looks modern and clean (w the exception of the men's room, which is another story).   I went with a sausage, egg & cheese biscuit combo, which included roasted potato wedges and fresh brewed coffee. It was immediately noticed that their sausage and biscuit retain the signature square shape, but appear smaller than their opposite numbers at the other joints. Regardless, the taste and texture of the sandwich were on target, with flakey, buttery biscuit and good flavored patty. The taters were a solid contributor with pleasant crispness and seasoning. The coffee was brewed for me and it was good and strong. At under $6 for the meal, it was a decent value.   How does the sammy compare? Glad you asked.   To my tastebuds and eyesight, it was palpably smaller than Mickey's, but perhaps providing a better biscuit and sausage flavor. Not by much, but still winning by a nose. It is definitely a superior product to that sold by B. K, but fell short of the excellent sandwich prepared by Chik Fil-A. Those guys really have the right stuff from top to bottom when it comes to stuffed biscuits. They are both larger and far more enjoyable.   So, there you have it. If absolute dominance is what you strive for, Chik Fil-A is your go to. However, if you can't find one nearby, choose Wendy's, McD's or B.B. King in that order if you want to sing the Breakfast Blues.

The amazing thing about Take A Taste Café is its unexpected presence in the Team Toyota Service Center of Lincoln Highway (old Rt. 1), in Langhorne.  I saw the reviews and could not visualize what the joint was all about - perhaps, a little space between the Parts Department and the Waiting Area?   Wrong!  It is a fairly large, totally café-like experience in the back of the service building; right next to the large and comfortable waiting zone, and sharing wall space with the "Theater," (another surprising variant in this auto complex).  The refrigerated display has a load of deli materials, and the walls were large format black & white ceramic tiles.  The Dude running the show was all hatted-up and super friendly.  He must be accustomed to people wandering in and needing a short explanation about what was going on.  He gave me the nickel tour, and I ordered a Sausage, Egg & Cheese Sandwich on Croissant.    No sweat.  He called my name a few minutes later and I went to pick up his handiwork.  It was an excellent sandwich on a fresh decent French airy, flakey crescent roll.  Darn good! And, the coffee was free to all who eat there or simply wait patiently for their chariots to be ready.    Fresh ingredients all around. Scratch preparation.  Home baked bagels and other loaves.    I may never drive a Toyota or Scion, but I was impressed with the marketing savvy and foresight of the folks who put this place together.  Take A Taste is worth the search and discovery.    Who knows, offer a test drive along with breakfast, and they might move their floor plan up the scale.   How about a vape shop next to the theater?

232 Corner Café (formerly Hogeland's) is a pleasant surprise.   When the former luncheonette closed last year due to the landlord's expectation that this space would be taken over by a medical provider outpatient clinic at substantially higher rents, those of us who knew and loved the old gal were sad and disappointed.  It appeared to be the end of an iconic local institution that had been around, while changing hands, for nearly half a century.  Progress to some.  Loss of culture to others.   The "best laid plans...sometimes go astray...", and when the plans for the medical facility shrunk to a smaller piece of the strip mall, this corner was not included.  All the fixtures remained intact, and a new business bloomed out of the ashes of the old. Ron now runs the operation, and at first blush, the new order of things feels much like the former enterprise.  The counter and tables are the same.  The grill and coffee brew where they sat before.  The menu has been updated, but the kitchen still puts out very good breakfasts (and lunches).    My French Toast was done right.  The standard two slices were dipped in an egg/vanilla/cinnamon mix, and grilled expertly with caramelized edges.  The taste was what I wanted, and I appreciated that the "small stack" was now the main size for the plate.  A melt of butter; and splash of syrup, and I was a happy man.  The New England Roast Bunn drip java was hot, fresh and repeatedly refilled by Ron as he entertained the troops.    232 Corner Café is a victory for the community.  Come on down and join in the celebration.

Classic German American bakery in Bensalem, Bucks County.  This two store chain produces some of the best sweet dough around.  Their Cinnamon Rolls are big, light and covered in excellent icing.  Eat 'em while they're hot for maximum load mind blowing experience. They react well out of the microwave, too.  Butter Cake is more dense, moist and uber sweet for those of us who love a mouth full of Domino delight. Heat it up and it becomes sweet butter soup. The large cookie, brownie, cannoli trays looked great, but will await another day.   This shop is well lit, allowing we gawkers to have close up looks at all the amazing goodies.  The staff is friendly and seems to enjoy all the customers drooling over their wares.    The coffee isn't bad, either.

I just finished wolfing down a Falafel Pita, and want to try to capture the essence of this memorable experience.  I did clean my hands before touching the keyboard.    King of Falafel in the Newtown Farmers' Market is very close to the main entrance, requiring a right turn past the pretzel stand, and then it is right in front of you.  It offers all manner of Middle Eastern/Greek delicacies from Fresh Feta and Olives to Stuffed Grape Leaves and Baklava.  It is all very good.  Today, I wanted a Falafel Pita.  I quickly brought it back to my office to devour, as the dining area was crowded with the lunchers.    As I unwrapped the aluminum foil the aroma of hot chickpeas and tachina wafted over me.  My salivaries reacted immediately, and I had to swallow hard to regain control.  The first bite penetrated the warm pita, sliced through a falafel ball, and diced the lettuce easily.  The flavor of fresh ground chickpeas dominated the oral sensations, but the tachina sauce quickly caught up with its own sesame subtleties.  The mix was fresh and insisted I pay attention.  The falafel was well fried (not over done) with little oily taste and a hint of gentle sweetness, while the tachina took it all in a different, slightly sour direction.    It was great!  It took me back to the Souk in Jerusalem where I had first tried the varieties of things that could be stuffed onto a pita and rolled up as a twenty something student at Tel Aviv University.  My reverie ended, but as I went to toss away the recyclable remains, I noticed something else in the bag.  It was a single piece of Baklava thrown in as a final sweet ending by the owners. Nice surprise!   My lips are still sticky.  The philo dough, grounds nuts, and honey were a wonderful end to an enjoyable lunch break and time travel experience.    I will make new travel reservations soon as the Newtown Farmers' Market is only open 3 days a week.    All aboard!

The status of Duke must mean that I like the place enough to return more often than any other Yelper.  It has sought of snuck up on me that I have become Newtown Bagel Company royalty, but it does reflect reality.    I have grown accustomed to their bagels, and more particularly the warm friendly way they greet me and know what I want before I order it.  Yes. They are making a safe assumption for someone who is a creature of habit when it comes to bagels.    They informed me that they have a punch card and since acquiring it I have scored a couple of free cups of coffee.  Nice touch.   I have become a fan based on the above, and it is time for my reviews to reflect this.

The layout is the mirror image of The Home Depot I visit most often, but it only required a second to figure that out.  The orange aprons were friendly and helpful.  We found what we needed, and after reading a few of the labels, made a choice in remote garage openers (serious shit, I know!). After we got it home and read the fine print inside the packaging, I realized that my machines are antiques and several generations behind contemporary technology.  Seems 1993 was the cut off date for the latest radio frequency devices, while mine are a few years older.  How can such things that still work well be obsolete?   So, had to return it today to my local THD, and go with the Genie brand, which, after all, were the ones I installed originally.  Only they make the expensive key to maintain their own stuff.   Should have the code mastered soon, and have two functioning remote door openers to allow for ease of access and egress for both old and new(er) vehicles.   Now I know more than I ever wanted to know about remote garage door openers.    Ah, wisdom!

It seems that Pho Tan, the first and only Vietnamese pho house in Trenton, NJ, has been sold, and is now under new management.  "Pho Friendly," is a catchy name, and hopefully its positive personality carries with it both the good will of the old shop, and the high expectations of the new.    I stopped in yesterday on my way to visit a client at his home.  They are in the same neighborhood.  Driving by, I saw the new sign hanging over the storefront and was immediate both sad and curious.  Street parking can be a problem, but I found space right around the corner, walked back and went in.  Looked exactly the same as before (it was a Mexican resto before it went Asian).  The menu was identical.  There were new handwritten signs on the walls saying, " We Have Hoagies. $5."  I love the traditional Banh Mi sandwich, so I asked the woman who greeted me if they made them.  She pointed to the sign and nodded her head.    A keener mind might have thought to confirm that their hoagie was in fact the same as the Banh Mi.  I did not ask for clarification, and ordered a chicken version with the vision that it would be all dressed up in a French Baguette, with daikon, cilantro, jalapeno, etc.   Not exactly.   Rather, it was more of a chicken steak sandwich with a twist.  Plenty of sliced bird bathed in Hoisin Sauce, with medallions of cucumber, sautéed onions & green pepper, with some Sriracha mayo, in a poor quality hoagie roll that lacked any crispness or good texture.  No daikon, cilantro, jalapeno to be found.    Disappointing. It wasn't bad, but not what I was looking forward to.   I did not try the namesake pho, so it is possible they do that well enough to redeem themselves.  In truth, I should have been more alert to the fact that they now advertise themselves as offering Thai and Chinese food in addition to Viet.  I would venture a guess that the lovely proprietress who served me (and her husband) are Chinese, and are attempting a "fusion" house, but with Chinese culinary sensibilities.  That is not necessarily a bad thing, but it does require the customer to find out what they really do best. Obviously, it isn't Banh Mi.  2.5 Stars with a dose of disappointment.

Who'da thunk that the simple grilled cheese sandwich could morph into a 21 Century restaurant chain centered on this basic food group? Bread and cheese becomes delicious fast casual cuisine. Born in New York, the brainchild of a twenty something selling hot sammies from a window operation, it now extends as far west as Minnesota. The Newtown store is the second in PA; the first in King of Prussia Mall.   I caught it on its first day. It seemed the entire staff was on hand to help out. They wore black T's with the Melt Shop logo on the back, and ball caps similarly adorned. The place was crowded with assorted families and kids just out of Council Rock North's last week of school. The music system played on a rock loop that made for a very noisy atmosphere that was unnecessary given that it just interfered with conversation and made ordering a shouting contest.   Just turn off the sound system, please!   The food was very good. I went with the Maple Bacon Grilled Cheese (maple cured thick bacon, cheddar/American slices) within decent bread slices, and Shop Tots (tater tots sprinkled with grated cheese and mild spices). Plenty of chewy flavor inside the hot grilled pain, and well deep fried crisped tots. Liked them both alot. Drank a bottle of their signature water from GIVN, an outfit that brings clean H2O to communities in need.   Prices add up quickly, so if you want a shake with that, lunch reaches $15 in a hurry.   Melt Shop also does variations with fried chicken and burgers, both of which looked good on other tables. Will make it back to check them out. I'll give them a while to figure things out first.  Shout out to Davide, one of the managers, with whom I had an informative discussion about the store.

East Kensington Avenue is about the grittiest urban zone in Philadelphia. With early 20th Century elevated subway (the El) rumbling above the shadowed street below, it can be difficult to see any hope of renewal. Yet, a closer look shows seeds germinating in the cracks in the sidewalk.   The 3900 block has several Southeast Asian restaurants that are more than just surviving, but thriving in this unforgiving environment. Vietnamese, Lao, Chinese and Thai kitchens are turning out some of the best cuisine in the city. I drove down last weekend to explore some of the possibilities, and selected Vientiane Bistro as my starting point.   Right next door to the well known Cafe Pho Ga Thanh Thanh, the Bistro is nicely renovated with utilitarian metal furniture, plank floors and simple wall decorations. The aroma of lemongrass, ginger and garlic greeted me at the door, quickly followed by the attractive, friendly server pointing me to a deuce in front along the side wall. She returned with menu a moment later. She was unaware that there was also a lunch list and when I inquired, she confirmed with the owner that it was available as well. She retrieved one promptly. My Yelp research paid off, giving me a chance to sample a few smaller portions of more dishes; Lao style dim sum .  Coconut Soup, Veggie Spring Roll, Chicken Pad Kee Mao (Drunken Noodles) and Tamarind Wings appetizer, were soon being prepared by their talented chef. I was about to be entertained by a four act play.   The soup was mildly sweet, full of veggies and a nice place to start. Loved every slurp and picked up the bowl to drain every drop. The six Tamarind Wings were large, grilled and bathed in a dark rouge/amber thick tart glaze. After the soup, it presented a very different taste and texture. A lover of tamarind duck, this was a great counterpoint and subtle reminder of that favorite. The Spring Roll was the weak link, but with the sweet dipping sauce was more of a bridge to what came next. I asked for the Pad Kee Mao to be done "extra spicy." That was what I got. Each bite of the veggies, chicken and broad noodles ignited my lips, gums and tongue with a pleasant burn, that gradually increased as I worked my way down the large mound in the wide bowl. Never numbing, I felt as much as tasted every morsel. Special surprise at the bottom of the bowl, where all the oils and spices collected and covered the last few pieces of food. I knew I probably shouldn't, but I couldn't resist spooning all of that into my mouth.   Holy cow! It was a hot blast that brought tears to my eyes and blew out my sinuses. Tears of joy, I assure you. Should have asked for more napkins, but it all ended well.   The influence of Lao and Thai cuisine on each other is wonderful. The hybrid creates a flavor/texture profile that connects the delicacy of Thai sauces with the heavier heartiness of Lao cooking. That is a beautifully delicious thing and a place that I could live happily forever.

We weren't sure where to go for a good haircut/shaping for her thick black Chinese hair, but waiting longer for a visit home was finally off the table. She decided to walk around Chinatown and check out a few salons and talk with the cutters to see what they recommended. Our third stop was Famous Hair Salon on Cherry Street between 10th & 11th. Not sure how the decision was made, but she took a seat in front of the mirror and the manager/stylist went to work. I sat on a bench and nodded out.  She looked great and seemed very pleased with the result. Happy she. Happy me!   The prices were reasonable, although it is a cash only shop.

Hing Wah is a Chinese take out house on New Falls Road, Levittown, PA, that also has a couple of tables for those who prefer to eat in while the food is optimal. It is fairly representative of the genre, with a menu that you could have memorized from most others you have tried in life. Only significant difference was the friendliness of the owners, both of whom engaged in small talk with me both before and after the meal. Nice folks.  My lunch special consisted of wonton soup, pork fried rice and general tso's chicken. The consommé was standard chicken stock with two thick skinned wontons and fresh cut scallion greens. No pork or other floaties to be found. Still, it was unobjectionable, even if unimaginative. The fried rice was dyed dark yellow, but had enough veggies mixed in to keep it interesting. The general would have been satisfied as I was, with the quantity of the chicken morsels breaded and deep fried with a dark red amber goop slathered on top.  There were actual Szechuan red chili peppers within adding to the pleasurable heat encountered with each bite. The breading was reasonable and did not overwhelm the bird beneath.   For around $7 plus tax, lunch was decent and a reasonable value proposition. It fulfilled my weekly yen for typical Chinese/American grub.

I didn't expect to find a decent Chinese restaurant in a Street Road strip center in Bensalem, PA, but there it was. Hong Kong Star Noodle House is a traditional looking Asian dining room with mahogany stained furniture and considerable menu primarily of Cantonese cuisine, and a tip of the cap to Szechuan and Thai tastes. But, it calls itself a noodle house and that was what I was there for. I really like chow fun, and they say on their Yelp page that it is done very well in their kitchen. A bowl of Hot & Sour Soup was my introduction on this cool windy afternoon, to be followed by Beef Chow Fun.   First positive was the presentation of the soup. Rather than being served in a standard round bowl, it arrived in an oblong dish carried atop a white plate. It made it look voluminous with a rich ochre luster. It was full of mushrooms, strips of soft tofu and sprouts. The flavor was perfectly balanced between the vinegar and sesame oil. The textures mixed well between the crunchy sprouts, medium dense mushrooms and silky tofu. It was delectible.   Next came the semi broad noodles and brown sauce of the chow fun. The thin sliced beef was very tender and had been grilled expertly. The noodles, onion and sprouts were in good proportion and the brown sauce both mildly spicy as requested, yet still subtly sweet as per the original recipe. Liked it very much, but it was too much to finish, and I took the rest home for the family.   Service was prompt and friendly. My tea mug and water glass were refilled as needed by the woman who appeared to be a manager/owner of the establishment.   Hong Kong Star Noodle House impressed me with its close proximation of a old school Chinese restaurant and the quality of its kitchen. It was several rungs above what is normally found outside of Chinatown.

Core Creek Park is part of the Bucks County Parks system, and it is the largest county park in lower Bucks County.    It is a great place for families, joggers, dog owners, casual boaters, fisherpeople, and folks who just want a place to mellow-out in a pretty, natural setting.  It is very well landscaped, with trails, and a nice manmade lake from the flow of Core Creek.  There is even a leash-less dog park. You can rent a canoe or paddleboat by the hour or half day, or bring your own small craft (no motors) and buy a launch permit for a few bucks. Be forewarned that if you are over 6' you will have a problem fitting into the paddle boat and working the bicycle-like leg churners that power the craft.   In good weather, the park fills with large family gatherings for picnics.  There are acres of areas with large trees and green lawns for your selection.   While much smaller and more tame than Tyler State Park a few miles away, Core Creek Park is a very good facility for bringing people close to nature.  The more you visit and find your favorite spot away from others, the more you will return and make the park your back yard.

The Tacony neighborhood in East Philadelphia may never achieve toney status like East Passyunk or Northern Liberties, nor become gentrified like Fishtown or Callowhill, but being 8 miles from Center City also has benefits no longer shared with those better known enclaves. Up here, it is still possible to buy a townhouse for south of $100 grand, and catch the train to Suburban Station from Torresdale Septa stop. You can live among folks who have roots that go back generations, and fit in as a newbie welcomed to the hood. It is possible to find your pioneer spirit in the 21st.   And, when you explore a little, you can find places like Athenian Diner on Torresdale Avenue that has been slinging excellent hash & eggs for over 50 years at the same row house location. Walking in and taking a counter stool immediately alerts you that some things just never change. The breakfast dishes are excellent. The waitresses have been there since at least the turn of the century, and they make you feel right at home with their first smile and easy urban offhand manner. Yes. You can eat the atmosphere; it is that timeless.   I sat at the end of the counter across from the Bunn-O-Matic. My white mug of joe arrived quickly, and my request for milk over creamer was met with a short glass of moo juice just for me. Greek diner required a Greek breakfast, and the Greek Omelet seemed the only way to go. Tomato, onion, green pepper, & feta mixed with two eggs and a side of home fries, presented as beautifully to the eye as it was to the tastebuds. Rye toast with a touch of butter completed the ensemble. It was delicious. I love that salty tartness of feta blended with the more subtle savoriness of the onion/tomato mix. Even the potatoes fit in nicely, although I did leave some of them behind to save on calories. Didn't need nor miss that third egg, at all.   I parked on a side street to avoid the meters, and to build a walk into the experience. It was obvious that despite some economic development on this main street, that Tacony still had a long way to go before it became an upscale desirable address. In many ways, that truth made it all the more attractive.

Palo de Azucar Cafe (Sugar Stick Cafe) is the second coffee house at this location that was an old time Italian deli for over fifty years before changing hands. I was a customer of that antique urban store, and loved their breakfast sandwiches, especially the sausage, egg and cheese creation. The old grill in the back room turned out many a delicious meal.   So, when I saw that the new place had a morning menu including a SEC sammy, I know the temptation to explore that offering would be too great to let me stay away for long.   And, so it was. I walked in today after finding a parking spot open in front. The room looked the same as the first cafe, but with interesting artwork on the walls, and a very pleasant crew of baristas handling the preparations on the polished stainless Expresso maker. I asked for the sandwich and large coffee, and looked around while waiting for it to be completed. Clean and well maintained.   I watched as one of the women made my bagel sandwich on the small grills on the back shelf. Double meat. Double soft fried egg. Double cheese. She and I had a brief conversation about how Trenton had changed over the years (not all for the better, we agreed), but certainly with new life springing up in the shadows of this former "All American City." She constructed the layers of ingredients and nicely packaged it for my trip down the street to the office. That sticky decal with the cafe's logo was a very nice touch.   Saving the best for last, the sandwich was among the best desayunos I've had the pleasure to consume. It was loaded, and each bite an explosion of tastes and textures, as my teeth slices through it. Amazing how exponentially better doubling the contents made the dish. A bagel is leaky by design, but it wasn't so extrusive as to require extreme caution. Yes, my fingers were involved in picking up all that fell out. It was all too good to waste. The coffee was a medium roast that continues to hold its flavor without bitterness to this very moment.   At five minutes from the office, Palo de Azucar is too good to not become a regular morning stop. The sandwich so reminded me of the old guy cooking in the backroom, that it was almost like he was still around.   Great way to commemorate the great grandfather of the shop by allowing his spirit to shine through.

New King Wok is a pretty much average Chinois restaurant on Bensalem Road right next door to Bagelocity/Soup Kitchen. Nice to have the convenience of grabbing the necessities of life (bagels & fried rice) in one stop.   There are only four tables in the house, so it is primarily a takeaway joint, but I prefer to sit and eat while the wok burn is paramount. Folks are a husband wife team, with the old man at the stove and frau tickling the register keys. She is friendly and bilingual. As a first timer, I ordered the General Tso's Chicken lunch special, which came with choice of rice and egg roll or cold drink bottle. I asked for it extra spicy.   It arrived in take out regalia on a plastic tray; thin white fork on the side. The tso sauce was a beautiful red amber color that matched well with the hyper yellow of the fried rice. There were a few Szechuan peppers thrown in in answer to my request. It was thick, but had decent flavor. The chicken was over-breaded, making for unnecessary heaviness. Had it been thinner, it could have been a contender for a surprisingly good rendition. As it was, it was about average for the genre. I left most of the rice behind as it made too long before my arrival.   This wasn't a bad meal, but it could have been alot better given the apparent skill level in the kitchen.

No doubt, NJ Weedman and his Joint have a long and interesting story to tell, but that is best left for historians and devotees of the man.    Me?  I was just looking for a cup of coffee after exiting Trenton City Hall across the street.  And, I was successful.  The small shop with the brightly painted van out front was empty when I entered, but I heard rustling in the back, and soon enough Weedy's son came to see me to inquire of my desire.  When all I wished for was hot coffee, he easily obliged by pointing me to the coffee corner where self service was the order of the day.  What's more, he asked if I was a government worker. No. I'm in private practice, but thanks for asking.    Never mind, then.  You can have a free cup, too.  His father believed in hospitality and graciousness to all, and he was continuing that generous tradition.    Felt a little guilt not ordering anything else to put some gelt in his cashbox, but I didn't see anything within sight.    The coffee was very good (Jamaican Blue?), and stayed hot all day in my coach given our steaming weather.    My curiosity has the better of me.  I want to go back and learn the Weedman's story.  Next time, over lunch.

Pho Nam Giang (village) is the new Vietnamese kid on the block in southern Bucks County. It sits on Franklin Mills Drive, one of the access roads around the now "Philadelphia Mills." The room is spacious and utilitarian; comfortable and attractive in a Spartan kind of way.   I sat alone in the back corner to give myself and everyone else sufficient space to remove our masks and feel confident in this renewed COVID social environment. The room wasn't crowded, but there were enough customers to keep the staff busy. They were efficient and friendly. I ordered Chicken Lemongrass Dumpling Pho and the Roast Pork Banh Mi, and settled in and waited to be served, sipping a plastic glass of hot tea (orange pekoe?).  PHO - I liked the variety of noodle soup offered on the menu. The choices were much broader than just traditional spicy beef base and thin cuts of steak, tendon, meatballs, etc. The Chicken Lemongrass Dumplings were plentiful and very good, even though the lemongrass flavor was not pronounced. The complexity of the stock could have been more subtle as well, but with the addition of jalapeno slices, Thai basil and squeezed lime wedges, it was a solid enjoyable slurp. The nest of thin rice noodles beneath the surface were tender and held the broth well as I sucked them up through whistled lips.  BANH MI - Excellent sandwich on very good french demi baguette, stuffed with lots of roast pork, cucumber, carrot and daikon strips with sprigs of cilantro across the top. It was a solid bite and chew, made better with a light touch of combined sriracha and hoisin for extra punch and smooth smokey sweetness. Definitely, one of the better banh mi's I've enjoyed in the past few years in Philly.   Pho Nam Giang has a real chance to succeed if it maintains its standards and spends a little more time enriching its base beef and chicken stock. It uses quality ingredients and keeps its facility clean. There isn't much competition nearby, so with effort and good fortune their road is clear ahead.

If you are into old world bakery pastries like you used to munch when grannie took you shopping, then Eet Gud Bakery is the place that will fill your nostalgic sweet tooth.   Large format Danish, donuts, cakes, cookies and loaves of Euro-style breads overflow the display cases and back shelves.  The copious icing on the top only hints at the abundance of cream filling within.  Like Glazed Donuts?  Look no further.  Cream-filled sticks?  Glazed Sour Cream rounders?    This is your Shangri-La!  All this caloric glory provided courtesy of the women behind the counter who have been packing bags and boxes of these incredible delights for the past 40+ years.    Once you bite into their cruller or cherry-cheese Danish there is no going back.  The addiction is instantaneous and dream-evoking.    Go after a particular bad day when you need a sugar fix.  This place will do ya!

Just returned for another round of Chengdu Heat.   The Diced Chicken with Dry Hot Pepper was impeccable, with tender chicken coated in a hot spice dusting and lightly fried, all stirred with a variety of peppers. The more I ate the more comfortable my palate was with the heat.  We had a Fish Fillet dish on the Specials Menu.  It was likewise tender, moist, and more of a blast furnace due to the red sesame oils it was simmered in.  This one never cooled down.   If you are unaccustomed to unadulterated Szechuanese 5 alarm cuisine, this may not be your cup of tea. Han Dynasty doesn't approach this degree of conflagration. But, if you are into it, you will find your experience here quite fulfilling.  This guy is on fire!

F. W. Woolworth built a retail empire at the end of the 19th into the mid twentieth centuries, out of the "Five & Dime" store concept. In its heyday it had over 5,000 stores on 4 continents. One of those iconic enterprises was build on Haddon Avenue in downtown Collingswood, NJ. Today, the high tintype ceiling, wood plank floored space is where Sabrina's Cafe holds court. Walking in from the rear parking lot the room feels cavernous and a real blast from the past.   It sounded that way, too. Without acoustic softening from all the cheap clothing Woolworths used to sell, the crash and clang of scraping chairs, dozens of conversations, kitchen noise and background music, made for very discordant uncomfortable ambience. If they hung tapestries rather than blackboards, and placed sound panels strategically along the ceiling, Sabrina's would be a much more pleasant restaurant to visit and hang out. As it is, regardless of food quality it is not welcoming enough to be worth a return.  What about my breakfast last week? Well, it left a lot to be desired. My server was pleasant and efficient, but never brought the milk requested with their good coffee. She probably couldn't hear me. Their signature Challah thick cut french toast looked great, but the egg/sugar/cinnamon mix had not penetrated into the body of the slices, making it dry and tough chewing. There was sweetness baked into the bread, but even melted butter and poured syrup did not significantly reduce its lack of moisture within. I took half home thinking I might be able to salvage it in my kitchen, but by the next morning it had lost all freshness and couldn't be revived. RIP.   I wonder what good old Frank Winfield Woolworth would do about this situation? It was he and his brother Charles who added the lunch counters to their successful stores and made them a new part of American culture. They would no doubt figure out how to perfect the experience and make more money doing it right.

Solid new Casa Mexicana on Markley Street, right in front of El Primo Mercado and Cafe. Limited parking in front, with much more behind. Bright and colorful with a limited menu of their greatest hits. Friendly, efficient service from the lovely woman working the floor.   I ordered their Cemita Poblano Torta, a supersized fresh sesame seeded roll full of spicy ground beef, queso fresca, lettuce, red salsa, al pastor style. It was a huge work of edible art. Hot bites and I could only manage to consume half while sitting at a high top table. Took the rest home.   They did bring two bowls of red/green salsa to me, but the chips never arrived. On the other hand their horchata was a chill, refreshing and cinnamon flavored liter of strong slurp. At $2 for the "small" size, it was the bargain of the day.    Given a choice between this "Mexico City Woman" restaurant and El Primo about 100 feet away, I would go with El Primo based on more choices and stronger kitchen talent, although the former rice drink was more flavorful than the later.   Norristown and environs continues to impress with its broad array of comidas Latina Americanas.

Taranovas Pizza & Pasta sits in the same commercial strip as the PennDot Service Center, which is how I first noticed it as I waited for a new driver's license. Its dining room is a good size, as is the breadth of the menu, which covers all three daily meals.   I stopped in for an early dinner before an evening meeting, and was greeted by a friendly server who also vibed as a possible manager. The broad glass windows face directly west into the setting sun, casting a bronze glow over everything, as beautiful as it was blinding. Even lowering the thin verticals did little to reduce the glare. I ordered the standards - chicken parmagiana, linguini aglio olio and small side salad (balsamic).   There was plenty on the plate when I dug in. There were one and a half breasts, lightly breaded and pan fried in olive oil, covered in rich red gravy. It was crisp edged and a real palate pleaser. The pasta was a special request to change from more marinara. While plentiful in a large bowl of its own, the kitchen used pre-minced garlic rather than fresh sliced and sautéed bulb, making it nearly invisible and translucent, rather than the golden browned garlic I love in pasta. A bit of a disappointment. The small salad was fine, but using only one cherry tomato seemed rather retentive.   Overall, it was a satisfactory meal that would have scored better had there been a stronger effort on the linguini sauce and more generosity with the salad. Still, the chicken warmed the heart and I walked away with leftovers, so the negatives are muted.   3.5 STARS

Don Panchito's sits in a former banquet facility at the corner of Grant and Academy in Northeast Philadelphia. The dining room is fairly large with minimalist decor, especially in response to required Covid Protocol. So, the atmosphere feels more utilitarian, than ethnic, but that does not distract from the quality of the food put out by the kitchen.   I went with two appetizers; Esquites and Chicken Flautas. The first, a fresh sweet corn dish mixed with chipotle mayo, spices and crema. The kernals were plump and firm, making for an engaging cool salad-like dish that showed me a new way to enjoy corn off the cob. The Flautas were three homemade tortillas stuffed with excellent ground chicken, spices and cheese, cut in half and served in a star pattern, topped with crema and guacamole. This way, it became finger food, holding shape and contents from presentation to mouth. They were hot, crisp and delicious.   An interesting aspect of Don Panchito's is that it has a halal kitchen. Before going, I really couldn't imagine how that looked in reality. Turned out that many of the other customers there were in a party that was partially Muslim. They had a Call to Prayer in a corner of the dining room while I was there, complete with carpet for kneeling. I was impressed with the dedication to their faith and the obvious comfort they felt in observing their customs in that setting. Definitely unique for a Mexican grill!   And, I have to mention Sophia, my friendly server who was covering the whole floor alone. She never lost her cool despite handling both the solo me, and the twenty or so partiers who were only minutes ahead of me ordering their food. The kitchen was slammed, but everything kept moving smoothly, due in large part in Sophia's verve and grace.

Although I'm sure they had something else in mind in naming this Chinese fast food establishment at the corner of Castor Avenue and Unruh Street in Northeast Philly, that " Boom" can signify the other side of explosive pleasurable cuisine, and be something quite the contrary. Unfortunately, that was where our experience cratered.   We stopped in for late lunch around 3 when part of the menu shifted from lunch to dinner prices. As all ordering is done online even when sitting in the restaurant, it made for some confusion in both ordering and paying. To make matters worse, there were two menus - a paper menu on the tables and a very different online ordering menu, that were not well coordinated.   So, while we wanted and thought we ordered beef soup with dumplings; what we got was just poorly crafted dumplings with thick skin and low flavor. Disappointing. Beyond that, the Vietnamese style spring rolls @$3.95 for twins, was mostly cabbage within. Double whammy!  Finally, the beef sandwich was basically a soft scallion pancake rolled up with "meat" inside and a squirt of hoisin sauce for sweetener. While the best of the bunch, it left alot to be desired.   No doubt this Boom Buns is primarily a takeout joint, and customers are far away when they open the bag and see what they got (BOOM!) For those of us eating in house, the sound of deflated expectations created a rumbling crash in our stomachs (BOOM)!   Maybe the Xao Long Bao is the way to go here, but we'll never know, because a return visit is just not in the cards. There is too much competition in this growing Asian neighborhood for anyone to give Boom Buns a second try.   DOUBLE BOOM!!

Frank's Spaghetti House is an old time Italian restaurant on Castor Avenue in the Rhawnhurst section of Northeast Philly. You know you're there when you see the dark red painted storefront and large white/red sign inviting you to dine in or take out. They have been there so long that the prices seem of another age when paper money was backed by gold. It is a bit dated with Formica tables and stained wood benches for the wall booths, and a tight fit bar in the front corner.   Yes. It reminds of the set of an old Martin Scorcese movie. It's all part of the charm.   We were there for our Valentine's dinner and chose Frank's because we thought it might not be crowded. It wasn't, but had a bustle to it that kept the joint lively. We had a booth immediately on entering without reservation.   Our server was friendly, but not informal with us. She took our drink order (half carafe Chianti) and handed us menus. She returned with our hearty red vino, two glasses and basket of bread. Nice start with good crusty Italian loaf and aromatic wine with strong paisano flavor. We ordered Veal Scallopini and Chicken Marsala, with soup and veggie sides, and listened to a romantic serenade of Italian crooners.   The entrees were quite good, with special mention of the marsala which although thick cutlets, were tender with delicious white wine/butter/lemon/garlic reduction, and plenty of fresh mushrooms on top of penne. The Scallopini was thin, tender with rich savory red gravy. The sides were pedestrian with lifeless stringbeans and cool french fries. My cup of Chicken Noodle Soup was a pot bottom bowl of too salty bouillon. We weren't there for those little plates anyway. We did enjoy the Caprese Salad appetizer, with soft Buffalo mozza, basil and decent off season tomatoes.   With the wine and tip, we still walked out for under $60. So while a little inconsistent in execution, we were still very satisfied with the experience. It was the romantic and memorable celebration we hoped for.   3.5 STARS

The Newtown area has an embarrassment of riches when it comes to fresh, homemade ice cream.  At last count, there are at least four shops making their own cold creamies, and each has something special going for it. With February weather reaching 80 last week, climate change now makes ice cream an all year delight.   Uncle Dave's is located in the main store on Shady Brook Farm off Stony Brook Road and the Newtown Bypass. They offer an interesting selection of their ice cream with the ability to accessorize with sprinkles, fudge, caramel, etc. Prices are about right for the competition. Under $4 for the "Kids" size; $5 for the "Medium," and $7 for the "Large." In my experience, that Kids size with three scoops of up to three of your favorite flavors was enough. Don't let the description of "Kids" deter you from getting only what you can lick in one serving.   I went with two scoops of butter pecan and one scoop of the seasonal pumpkin. They were both creamy and tasted as they should. Not too sweet, not under-flavored. Both were pretty much what I expected. My friends and their young kids opted for more varieties, including cappuccino, strawberry and peanut butter with a side of peanut butter sauce.  They were all happy with their choices.   Was it the best ice cream in greater Newtown? That's a matter of personal preference.  But, given all the alternatives, it represented Dave's well.  Their offerings were more standard that some other parlors, so if exotic and romantic taste is your thing, you might find this place a little uninspired.  For you folks, OhWowCow in Wrightstown is the only way to go. Of course, it also costs more for premium.   Lick on!

Mad Hatter Cafe occupies the space formerly used by another morning/lunch house in Hatboro, PA. While small in size with only a few hightops and an loveseat, it is warm and welcoming due to the hard work of the owner, Barbara, who wears her heart on her sleeve and makes everyone feel like family.   I was looking for a good cuppa joe and a light early repast when this place jumped onto my Yelp screen. I parked across the street at a meter ($.25/hour), and crossed Main Street (York Road) to get to the door. I was the only customer when I arrived and had a few moments to chat with the proprietress as she expressod my Cafe Americano and walked back into the kitchen to put together my breakfast sammy on an everything bagel. Let me just say that I felt much compassion and sympathy for her as she spoke about her current circumstances. Stop by if you want to know more.  The coffee was excellent. Roasted by Valerio in Audobon, PA, it was rich, darkly volcanic soil based, and full of nutty and savory fruit tones. Probably should have purchased a bag of their Congo whole beans, but thought I might visit their roasterie and get it there I was so impressed. The sandwich (sausage, egg & Swiss) was also very good, but not as memorable as the java. They did harmonize well together, though.   I do hope all goes well for the family, and that Mad Hatter stays a magical place for superior coffee and a comfortable time out.

Found myself in Columbus, NJ, after a court appearance in Mt. Holly, the county seat of Burlington County.  This building is right in the center of town and looks to have been a bank in the past.  It is mostly takeout, but there are a few tables (mostly taken up by the owners' kids) for the brave souls who prefer to eat while the food is hot.    The Sesame Chicken was above average.  Although the amount was somewhat less than given in most other Chinois houses, the breading was not overly thick, and the sauce was actually pretty good.  The Fried Rice was full of pork, peas and a few other veggie pieces.  I liked the dish.   Most appreciated was the curtsy to hospitality provided by the real plate on which the meal sat.  It was a pleasant touch to get away from serving in-house customers as if they were taking lunch with them.  I don't like eating out of Styrofoam when seated in the restaurant.  The small extra cost of washing a few dishes is nothing compared to the sense that the other places really don't want you around.  The front of the house woman was friendly and engaging as she watched over her kids and the shop.    While Hong Kong Restaurant is still a Sino/American house with standard menu, their effort to provide a welcoming touch to their operation goes a long way.

Pat's Polish Deli surprised me.  Although small in size, the market is full of Polish delicacies from assorted kielbasa to homemade pierogi and snacks known only to those who have walked the old city streets of Bialystok and Gdansk.   I was there to check out their dining room, kitchen and breakfast/lunch menu on a gorgeous mid-June morning. I saw french toast on the list of offerings, and despite it not being polish toast, I was intrigued. Sometimes my curiosity gets me in trouble cuisine-wise, but this day it led me to a wonderful discovery. Pat's F.T. was all that, and about the best I had eaten in the past year.   My white oval plate arrived with two slices of average sized bread, dipped in egg slurry with vanilla extract, sugar/cinnamon mix and grilled expertly to reveal caramelized nooks and crannies, and then topped with sliced juicy kiwi and blueberries. A dusting of sugar/cinnamon finished the   presentation. It looked great, a sensibility only surpassed by it amazing taste.   First bite was was a five star riot. The combination of ingredients was both a textural and flavor banquet for the tongue and soul. How this was created in the tiny kitchen behind the dining room may never be fully discovered. It sent a shock wave through me and woke the deeper recesses of my brain. This dish was something very special. The cook explained that they were out of the expected strawberry and banana garnish, and that he worked with what he had. Kiwi was soft and sweet, while the blueberry, plump with exquisite pulp. It was a winner all the way around.  Although not my usual stamping ground, this stretch of Brownsville Road has a number of very good restaurants hidden in this older part of southern Bucks. It is now even more worthwhile to return to find out what other pleasant surprises come out of Pat's kitchen.

One of the largest grocery store chains in the region, Giant competes well with Acme for the merchandising middle ground between quality and price, but not in the same class as Wegman's, nor Whole Foods. Yet, it may have found the sweet spot that allows it to survive in hard times and modestly prosper in good. This outlet on DeKalb Pike in Blue Bell, PA, can stock your pantry, fridge and medicine cabinet with almost everything you need, even if not everything you yearn for.   We stopped in recently while in the area for hair styling, hoping to pick up a few things there rather than drive the 30 minutes back home and then stop at our local Giant, when we were hungrier and didn't feel like making that detour closer to dinner. Actually newer than our regular shop, and a touch larger, we discovered that its layout was different than we were used to, and thus slower to cruise through as we searched for our needs.   The space was clean, with special attention given to their extensive salad bar and back of the shop deli/bakery and the organic section of their their produce department.   Found what we needed in the personal care aisle and bakery, and slid through checkout in a minute. Considered grabbing a roast chicken, but there were not available at the moment. Will probably get that on the next visit to Costco.

This second generation pizza shop on Bristol Road, was a surprising find last week. Housed in one of the old strip commercial buildings, it has the benefit of low rents to keep their prices very reasonable, as well as recipes handed down from parents to kids that have stood the test of time as being what people love to eat when thinking traditional Italian-American cuisine. The walls of the dining room are full of old family photos in black and white that add to the ambiance of this vintage pizza parlor.  I settled into one of their three booths to await a single slice appetizer and 12" Mixed Sweet/Hot Sausage, Pepper & Onion Sammy. I could hear the kitchen folk chatting away and banging pans and oven doors as they prepared takeout orders along with mine.   The regular slice (well done) arrived first. It was a little heavy with cheese and dripping oil, but the first bite was still crisp with nicely charred undercarriage and very good red sauce. It was better than it looked. The sausage P&O likewise didn't look like a work of art, but when the sauce was dripped on top, it came alive with great flavor, texture and interplay amongst the ingredients and torpedo roll.
