The sausage mix demonstrated it may have been locally produced, from the freshness of the chew and subtlety of the flavors. In any event, it was an exceptional; a best of breed for me this year.   I hear the Sarappo family has another restaurant in Croydon, PA. It is now bookmarked for future exploration.

Father's Day Brunch @ Blue Sage Vegetarian Grille (everyone knows it as Blue Sage), was the epitome of a meal that makes a wonderful day nearly perfect.    While I have dined there several times over the years, it had fallen off my circuit at some point for no particular reason.  When my 12 year old wanted to take me out for a good meal for Father's Day, Blue Sage came to mind.  I called at 10:00 on Sunday morning and was fortunate to secure a table for 2:30 that afternoon.  By no stretch am I a vegetarian, but I do enjoy a tasty healthy meal at any time.    We arrived a couple of minutes late after canoeing in Tyler State Park ran a little long (that's another story), and were seated promptly.  The staff was friendly and knowledgeable. The brunch menu is a shorter version of the regular menu with several specials thrown in. It's a one from Page One and one from Page Two deal for $18., including organic coffee.    I ordered the Corn Johnnie Cakes with Berries and the Relleno.  The Cakes looked like four small dark pancakes topped with Strawberries and Blueberries.  It was pulled together with a Sweet Cream Butter whip that was just sweet enough, but did not interfere with the berry flavors, nor the hot corn cakes.  It was delicious.  The Relleno was a Red Pepper stuffed with mild melted cheese, beans, onions and red/orange cherry tomatoes.  It was finished with a tawny copper colored tangy sauce that made me glad I had a spoon so I could claim every drop.  I was completely satisfied.  My son had two different dishes of Sweet Rice Pudding balls and Mashed Potato Empanadas which he enjoyed. They were filled with red pepper pumpkin seed pesto mixed with the potato, and it came with Giant White Beans pickled, Gazpacho Sauce, and a Tomato - Avocado Salad. I know this because he only reluctantly allowed me to taste them.   This would have been a delectable meal on any day of the year.  That is culminated Father's Day for me makes it vastly more memorable.  I will be sure to consider Blue Sage on my list of "go to" places on special occasions.  It was a great place to complement a great day.

Even on Saturday morning, Rt. 73 in Marlton is a pain in the butt to drive, but at least it now has Bhan Thai as a worthy destination, making the traffic and crazies causing it, tolerable.   I hadn't eaten a good Thai meal in many months, and decided a few days before to get up early this weekend and cruise across the Burlington Bristol Bridge and down 295 to this well reviewed Vietnamese kitchen. Arriving just as it opened at 11:30, I walked into an empty dining room and was greeted by a friendly Asian woman who welcomed me and confirmed I could dine outside on their umbrellaed patio. Seemed like the safer way to go in this renewed age of raging Delta Covid.   I went with faves, Tom Kha Soup and Drunken Noodles (veggie), 'Thai Spicy'. They threw in a sushi orange ginger dressing salad, which was a surprise. The Tom Kha was excellent, with plenty of fresh mushrooms, sliced chicken, carrots, onion, coconut milk and lemongrass for kicks. Loved each and every slurp. The Drunken was a large plate with extra wide noodles and lots of colorful veggies.   It also came with plenty of cubed tofu pan sauteed to a near burnt finish. The heat was there, although not the conflagration desired. The taste of the overdone tofu while subtle, was enough to through the flavor of the dish slightly off. So, while it was still recognizable, it could have been much better with a more deft hand holding the pan.   Bhan Thai is a reasonable facsimile of a genuine attractive Thai restaurant, but candor requires referencing that better can be found in and around Philly, Central Jersey, and closer to home.   3.75 STARS.

This newest Trenton McDonald's is located on Chambers Street, catty corner from St. Francis Medical Center and across the street from Trenton Central High School.  Pretty good location.   It is one of the newer designed, small footprint stores, with wrap around, two lane, drive thru.  They really expect most of their business to stay outside.  They are friendly and efficient at what they do. But, if you are a pedestrian, be careful approaching the front door as there will be traffic bearing down on you, with drivers not necessarily paying attention to your presence.    The food is standard Mickey fare.  I am more fond of their breakfast sandwiches than the burgers.  I grabbed a sausage, egg & cheese biscuit and large coffee on my way to the office.  Priced at just over $5., it was a reasonable deal.  The meal was freshly made, with tender, buttery biscuit and still hot patty.  The coffee has been pretty good lately, and the one price of any size is a clever marketing tool.    Breakfast @ desk is not my favorite way to eat, but some days it can be like that.    Everything was satisfactory.

It is really nice to have expectations exceeded by a local slow/fast food shop. That was exactly what happened yesterday when we visited Curly's Comfort Food in Levittown, PA.   Why "slow/fast"? Because although Curly does cheesesteaks, burgers, chicken and all the accessories, which are typically considered fast food; it is so slammed with people ordering and waiting for their food that the first thing the ordertaker said to me was that there was a one hour wait for pickup. After ordering their Diablo Cheesesteak with fried onions, Firecracker Crisp Chicken Sandwich and standard Burger, she asked for my phone number to be able to alert me when the kitchen had prepared everything. Well, okay. We walked across the parking field to the H Mart for a little casual shopping in that well stocked Asian market.   All the reviews suggesting the Curly's cheesesteak is the best of breed in the region. That is no lie! My son opened a zoftig sesame seeded long torpedo roll with enough thin sliced beef, cheese, jalapenos, and onions to fill at least two regular sized 'steaks.' He cut off a two inch end of the massive creation for me to taste, and he still couldn't finish it. My small sampling left me wanting more. It was a perfect roll wrapped around a glorious mix of deliciously delivered ingredients, complete with raw onion and sliced tomato.   Simply stunning!   The Firecracker Chicken wasn't far behind. Breaded and deep fried, it was a large breast with strong spice content, mayo, lettuce and tomato. I felt sorry for the round Kaiser roll attempting to hold it all together. It really couldn't, so before I was half way through it, I grabbed a knife and fork to assist. It was also excellent, and an unspoken contender in the chicken sandwich wars being waged by the franchises. Watch out, Popeye's and Chik-Fil-A!   The burger was the simplest on the menu, but still a half pounder surrounded by a copious load of pretty good fries, in the same Kaiser roll, with the requested medium finish. Who ever heard of a takeout joint paying enough attention at the grill to deliver the right doneness? Curly did!   Sure, the bill for all this quantity and quality was in the mid $40s. As I paid with that 3% credit card surcharge, I hoped it would all be worthwhile. Truth is that it was worth every penny and perhaps more, although that surcharge is obnoxious, and they would be doing a civic service to eliminate that, as it discriminates against the majority of consumers who are part of our credit economy.  PRO TIP - You have to ask them to switch the Diablo Chicken Steak to a Beef version which was not on the paper menu. It costs a little more, but definitely the way to go.

The Stuff'd Bunz food trailer was set up outside the Newtown Brewery last weekend. The two women inside were constructing a variety of sliders (see menu photo) at $4 per. We ordered a Pulled Chicken composition and Philly Cheesesteak Sammy on the way out of the beer den after purchasing a 4-pack of home grown suds.   While the Belgian Tripel went of $23, the amazingly tasty sliders were boxed expertly for $8 for a deuce, prepared the way you want it. Ample sauces, peppers, onions, relishes and melty cheese to beat the band. When we arrived home five minutes later, we broke open the grub and brew at the kitchen table and went off devouring the solids and guzzling the liquids.   Really, the Stuff'd Bunz were terrific; plenty of flavors and textures to entertain the tastebuds, and leave you wanting more. Strong BBQ base under sours and sweets and crunchies, held together by something that reminded of a potato bun. Even the mock Cheesesteak was a big chew hoot and a half. Gooey cheese over finely chopped beef, with onion mixed in. Not the Prince of Steaks, but a damn good facsimile.   Washed all that down with the expensive amber ale, and we were sated, if not poorer for the experience. When Covid is defeated, I look forward to hanging out at the bar and enjoying the wonderful repast to the fullest. Until then, takeaway is the only safe way to go.

Thai Orchid of Blue Bell is a beautifully appointed Siamese restaurant on DeKalb Pike in the wonderfully named town of Blue Bell, PA. It is one of those places where the environment is so rich in southeast Asian colors, textures and artistry, that it is possible to eat the atmosphere. From woodcuts to tapestry the space is relaxed and mellow enough to have you believing you've stepped into a palace in Chiangmai.   I was there for late lunch after a meeting in Norristown. The shop sits in a strip center, the last door on the far right. Don't be put off by that or you'll miss all the magic. There was only one other customer dining when I arrived and was taken to a table on a raised platform that held most of the tables. The menu was full of Thai delights, and lunch combo specials that included soup, appetizer and main entree, for around $10 and change. That seemed the way to go to sample a few things and get more bang for the buck. I went with the Thai Ravioli Soup (wonton), Veggie Roll and Drunken Noodles.   Believe me, it was a huge amount of food. The soup was vegetable based broth with fancy goldfish wonton filled with ground shrimp and chicken. It had a mild sesame oil flavor and tasted fresh and pleasing. The roll was deep fried with a filling of mixed vegetables, glass noodles and a small dish of sweet & sour dipping sauce. It was good, but a tad over fried.   The drunken noodle was a large plate full of medium width noodles (not jumbo), loaded with chunky onions, bell peppers, green beans, fresh basil, thin sliced beef and moderately hot Thai spices. I asked for it to be very chilified, but it was still pretty tame. It seems that regardless of what you ask for on the heat scale, it is interpreted as only moderately spicy. How you actually get the "Very spicy yet Bearable," fire level is beyond me. Here, it cost them a star for failing to honor my clear direction.   Aside from the width of the noodles and the lack of burn, this was a very satisfying meal, and enough to keep me sated for the rest of the day. The decor and food together make Thai Orchid of Blue Bell a worthy stop for quality exotic cuisine. It would be even better if they paid closer attention to what was being requested.

Below average wings at best. Ours were cooked to order, but overstayed their welcome in the deep fryer making them dry and way more chewy than should be. More like chicken jerky. Too, the fries were limp and dying by the time the styro packaging was opened. At least the Fanta Orange was as expected.   Definitely a one and done experience. There are just too many quality wings available in almost every restaurant in  the country to be satisfied with such a poor effort.

A shiny new state of the art garage door opener is not my usual birthday present, but in this Age of Covid when remaining home has become a virtue, it will do until something sexier comes along. The Liftmaster Model 8835 is a thing of beauty after all.   My old Genie finally gave up the ghost last week. There are no parts in stock anymore, so the only option was full replacement. Amazing how little has really changed in the world of remote door lifters. True, this one uses a band drive rather than a chain, but those are still available. Yet new tech seemed the way to go, along with built in WiFi that allows door control from a long distance through a smart phone. So, for $525 I upgraded to the modern variant of the old standard. Could have had battery backup for a buck twenty five more, but since there was a manual override, that wasn't necessary.   Carl arrived right on time at 1:58 p.m. Exactly one hour later he was handing me the two remotes and explaining how the outside digital code pad worked. He was quick, focused and obviously had been installing these babies for a long time. He was also able to carry on a good dialogue all the while.   So, now I have a quiet half horse door lifter, complete with dual lights, WiFi, outside keypad, electric eye safety stop and two remotes. I feel a chill down my spine as the motor purrs and pulls the four panel door up and down.   That's more than most gifts do for me.

Franco's Tomato Pies on Main Street, Yardley, PA, has been around for a long while doing mostly take out pizzas from their small shop right next door to Bagel Train. There are only two booths in house, so they don't get much dine in business. Still, I was there around 2:30 in the afternoon earlier this week, and wanted carbs to help finish my long day into night schedule.   I asked if I could eat there, and they were totally accommodating. I ordered penne aglio olio with sautéed spinach in a lunch portion, and they knew what to do. After about 5 minutes I was called to the counter to pick up a side salad and bread basket. The greens were plentiful, with tomato wedges, iceberg, red onion, cukes and sliced carrots. Actually, took me by surprise. The four slices of Italian loaf were fresh and ready for dipping into balsamic vinaigrette and the garlicy broth to come at the bottom of the pasta bowl.   A few minutes later, the white soup bowl of pasta was on the counter calling my name. I walked over to get it, and enjoyed the hot garlic breath of the dish wafting into my face. Smelled so good. The taste was about right, too. Plenty of pencil points under a nice load of soft spinach. The garlic could have been more golden, but no biggie.  The only difficulty I confronted was the large pond of garlic water under the pasta. No matter how long I waited to allow the water to drain from each forkful, it was still dripping onto my shirt, pants and tie. I was careful, but all will be visiting the cleaners to get the stains out. My bad for not bringing a long bib.   The store needed a strong cleaning, too. The floor looked grimy from lack of care, and the kitchen area visible from the counter failed the visual inspection test. Looks like the boss doesn't stop in often enough.

Szechuan House remains one of my favorite Chinese restaurants in the Mercer/Bucks region. While it doesn't have everything nailed down in terms of consistency of flavor and presentation, it makes a strong statement for traditional Szechuan cuisine. They recently reopened after a lengthy renovation, and although the vibe is the same, it does appear cleaner on the dining room floor and likely in the kitchen, too.   While food from Chengdu and Chongqing is more common here these days than it was decades ago, it remains an acquired taste for most consumers with its heavy hot chili spice and oil content. It is nothing like the sweeter Cantonese offerings found in Chinese American joints across the continent. For me the shift to preferring the numbing black peppercorns and flaming small red chillies over General Tso and the rest, came from my prolonged exposure to the kitchen heat during eight years I spent working and exploring the Middle Kingdom, primarily in Szechuan and Yunnan provinces. For me, eating this style food brings me back to the adventurous days when I became acculturated to this cooking, and loved life there.   I would never say this is the best representation of Szechuanese cuisine in the western world, but it is damn good and satisfying. Yes, part of its attraction for me is reminiscing about the past, and they do need to use more peppercorns to capture the numbing elements of what I like most, but unless I want to travel to China to satisfy my yearnings, Szechuan House is about as good as it gets for the gestalt I seek.   PS. Yes, Philly has some very strong candidates - Han Dynasty, Chili Szechuan, Chengdu Famous, Four Rivers and Ermi, among the best - they are not appreciably superior to S.H., although I love them all.

I returned to Szechuan House, the hidden treasure of a restaurant found on Rt. 33 in Hamilton Township, Mercer County, New Jersey, for another mouth numbing meal last week.  The last time I was there I underwent a root canal the next day without need of additional anesthesia.  It was that good!   Yes. This is a joke, but you might not think it funny if you don't take the warning seriously. If you are thinking "Mexican" spicy, you are in for a rude awakening.  Szechuan spicy is an entirely different dimension of heat.  I love Jalapenos and Habaneros, and even Ghost Peppers, and you can pile them onto my Flautas without me blinking.  Put an equivalent amount of Szechuan peppercorns, hot chili oil, and those cute little red Chinese peppers into a dish, and your review goes from 5 Star to 5 Alarm.    I love it, but it is an acquired taste. As someone said about this style food, "Numb is a flavor."   Last week, I was surrounded by Dan Dan Noodles with Minced Pork and Chili Vinaigrette, Steamed Dumplings with Chili Vinaigrette, Amazing Eggplant (that's the name), and Hunan Beef.    The Dan Dan's were spaghetti diameter, and had a nice ground pork sauce with a mild spicy quotient.  Very tasty and a nice start to the meal. (4 Star/3 Alarm)  The Steamed Dumplings with Chili Vinaigrette was found in the Szechuan Delicacies part of the menu toward the back page.  Six fairly large, hand stuffed and pinched, with the red chili oil and vinegar for a bath. There was a pleasant sweetness that I experienced before the heat arrived. Not sure how that was done, but it played well on my tongue. (5 Star/4 Alarm)  The Amazing Eggplant came on a large plate piled with the thin Chinese Eggplant, in a brown, spicy sauce with a light meat base.  This was delicious and stole the show. Tender, medium heat, and addictive. (5 Star/3 Alarm)  Hunan Beef came with an equal supply of broccoli in a shining brown Hunanese sauce.  The beef was thin sliced and very tender.  The Chinese chilies swam in the sauce at the bottom of the serving bowl.  Solid choice, if not completely inspiring. (4 Star/ 3 Alarm).  This was a totally satisfying meal, reminding me of my Chengdu daze.  The 5 Alarm dishes were not selected this time as my friends were not accustomed to Szechuan cuisine, and they needed to be broken in slowly.  But, if you are ready for the HEAT, I suggest the Fish Fillet in Hot & Spicy Sauce, the Diced Rabbit with Szechuan Peppercorn Vinaigrette (a cold dish with serious hot), or the Beef in Hot & Spicy Sauce to begin your Vulcan adventure.

I seem to be going through a mini tuna obsession lately. For the past few weeks I have found myself searching for deli or sandwich shop that does chopped tuna the way I like it - with mayo, celery, light black pepper and finished with hot and sweet pickled peppers. I can go for years without even thinking of it, but every once in a while I just gotta have some.  Slack's Hoagie Shack is a regional chain in these parts. They have a large menu of everything that can be stuffed into a torpedo roll and eaten. They happen to do tuna particularly well. They seem to grind it, more than chop it, making for a smooth, plyably, dense consistency, that hangs together well in a sandwich, and accepts additional condiments easily. It is not overly moist, so it is not given to slipping out the back door, and keeps it's shape until bitten.   One hoagie is enough for two meals for me, as the standard length is about 12 inches. Their bread is pretty good, but mine may have been past its prime, as it seemed ein bissel dry. In the Trenton area, with so many Italian bakeries, this is almost inexcusable. Fix this, and 5 Stars await.  Service was excellent, with easy ordering by phone, and smiling takeout once at the shop. Facility was also immaculate.

Very glad to report that nothing much has changed at Bagel Delight since my last report. Still baking very good Bagels, providing friendly service & above average Java. The regulars appear to be the same, too. Understandable. If I lived in Lambertville I would be one of them.

Just added two new dishes to the excellent heat profile provided by Szechuan House.  The Chongqing Chicken is a first cousin to the Spicy Chicken Dry Pot Style I have had in the past. High burn with every crunchy morsel. Just below numb on the volcanic scale, perhaps not reaching conflagration due to the meager presence of Szechuan black peppercorns and reliance on red chillies to cover for their absence, but still excellent.   The Crispy Fish Fillets Sweet & Sour was a large deep platter full of lightly fried fish and loads of orangey thick sauce. More Cantonese, but a strong interpretation. Really liked it in the face of all the other flames.   The few other plates were good, but not worth taking up more space here in light of all the other fireball delights found in this still surprisingly authentic Chengdu palace.

I am not a lover of 20th Century Malls (dinosaurs), nor most particularly their anchor tenants (dead men walking).  Yet, I found myself in JC Penny in the Oxford Valley Mall recently to exchange shoes that had been purchased online, but arrived the wrong size.  While that might warrant a negative review on its own, the way the folks in the store handled the problem was worthy of praise.   We came to the shoe department hoping to find the exact shoe we wanted, but their inventory was rather limited.  When we explained to the manager who happened to be at the register what was going on, she promptly accepted our explanation and the shoes and was able to credit our card immediately.  Beyond that, she ordered the shoes we wanted directly at the register, for free delivery within three days.    Sure enough, UPS dropped off the right shoes to our front porch three days later.  They made us happy to have dealt with them.  Even though it would have been better had the right shoes arrived the first time, the way the fix was dealt with was friendly, apologetic and efficient.  And, they threw in an extra $5 discount for our troubles.   I may be the victim of low expectations, but I was pleased by the overall experience. Mistakes can be made by anyone.  It is how they are remedied that tells the tale.   This experience made me a fan of JC Penny.

Serious Chinese-style massage going on here.   The residuals of two herniated discs in my lumbar spine occasionally require hands on attention to release the pent up tension and pain that comes from living a regular life.  Lizhi Health Spa is operated in the Chinese tradition, with lots of heavy hands, forearms, elbows, and back walking if a "strong" massage is what you want.    I did, and they did.  I found myself breathing in unison with my masseuse's work, because the pressure was so intense at times, that inhaling was not an option.  Joints and tense muscles began to pop and relax as the effort continued.  Even my left shoulder, injured thirty years ago, began to unwind as a sharp elbow found its target.  After torso and limbs addressed this way, she returned to my arms and legs and began to stretch them beyond their normal range to increase their motion and reduce restrictions.  My legs were torqued as she leaned her body weight into it.  My lower back begrudgingly responded, and for the first time in years, the sense of tingling in my feet stopped for the rest of the day.    All in all, an impressive display of Tui-Na.  I ended up on the table for two hours, and each minute was intensely worth it.  At $100 for 120 minutes, the price was fair for all the heavy lifting this diminutive woman undertook.  She had surprising strength and excellent technique.  My tip was commensurate with her quality work.  Will certainly return as needed.    Cash Only.

Of the limited Chinese options in the Newtown area, this place is by far the worst.  Strictly take out unless you want to sit at one of the two odd sized tables covered with newspapers.  Several Guangzhou brothers operate this relocated tiny shop.  The kitchen is in full view, and it is not always pleasant to watch how the food prep is done.  As someone else suggested, this is a place to go only when all the alternatives are blown away by a storm.

When my last order of locally roasted coffee beans was about to run out, I looked around online for other bean purveyors to sample. Liberty City Roasters in Bristol, PA, jumped out with a website that exuded passion for their craft. Last Friday I ordered Yirgacheffe and Peruvian 8 oz. bags, drip grind, @ $8.95 per, plus a reasonable shipping charge. They were on my doorstep Saturday afternoon, and brewing in our autodrip Sunday morning. This was quite amazing for a small company, and I suspect that someone in management drove it over to us on his way home from work.   Gotta love that level of personal service!   We regularly buy fresh roasted beans, and have adapted our pantry to hold the coffee in our own containers for longer storage. We customize each by cutting and affixing the labels from the roaster to our jars when received so we always know what we are drinking and take pride in our handiwork.   I've now sipped mugs of both, and can report on my experience. Yirgacheffe is a smaller bean (a/k/a Peaberry), from south central Ethiopia in a micro region of the Sidamo area. The hot days/cool nights at 7,000 feet above sea level are perfect conditions for producing mellow java. This coffee is great in a light to medium roast. It is mildly acidic and gentle on the tongue. It taste clean with a flavor of berries, lemon and perhaps, sweet peanut. Some say a hint of coconut emerges under certain roasting, but I don't know about that. Still, this is my favorite coffee overall, and our beans are an excellent example from the birthplace of coffee.   These Peruvian beans are similarly expertly roasted to allow peak enjoyment of its java. Its juice is more acidic that the Yirgacheffe, and has a stronger taste, but remains smooth and soft on the pallet. It has a light flavor of  fig, cherry and maybe a touch of peach undertone. It was balanced and lithe. My first encounter was fun and memorable.   At $8.95 for 8oz, the price was reasonable and only a small premium over mass produced coffee, even those bagged variants with well known names that still roast by the ton, not small batch.   Very impressive first take.

Returned to Aldo's for dinner for the first time in more than a decade. At one time it had been a regular stop in my rotation when I lived right across Buck Road in Holland, PA. It was good to be back.   The menu offered a broad swatch of Italian cuisine, mostly of the red sauce variety, but with enough variation to keep it interesting. We went with the Calamari appetizer, and entrees of Veal Parmesan and Chicken Francais, both with sides of pasta, minestrone soup and side salad. We were quite happy with our meals.   They started off on an off note with a luke warm minestrone that had not been sufficiently reheated, nor tested. The early salad was satisfactory, if less than imaginative. Things improved from there. The Calamari was perfectly prepared with tender squid wrapped in a tasty bread crumb dredge and a thick marinara dipping sauce. The veal was delicious with two thin filets, breaded and pan fried in extra virgin just right to maximize its delicate texture and finished with melted mozza and more chunky red gravy. The three Francaised chicken breast medallions were pan sauteed in butter, lemon and white wine. They were fork cuttable and the interplay of the lemon and wine played tartly and smartly on the tongue. We used the crusty bread to sop up as much of the reduction as possible. My request for the pasta side bowl to be penne aglio olio rather than more tomato sauce was a good call because I loved the well browned garlic and black pepper mix.   Aldo still does a solid traditional Italian American dinner in an attractive dining room. It was nice to know that for the most part they hadn't lost their touch.

Standard Dunkin outlet, perhaps in need of some TLC to spruce it up. My evening stop for a jolt of joe and sweet round dough found  their front doors in need of hydraulic repair to keep them from crashing back behind me, and in need of a sweeping.   Service was fine. The coffee decent. The donuts forgettable.   Just back from Southern California where independent donut shops abound. I wonder why that niche market hasn't taken off here? That competition would be great and raise the donut bar to new creative sugary heights.

In between all the smoker shops and other degradation along Bridge Street in Morrisville, Pa., stands a pizza shop that belies its surroundings, while well disguised within it.    Anthony's IV Pizza & Pasta is sentry at its corner with Washington Street, and after decades of inattention to its own condition, still puts out good pizza and better Italian-styled sandwiches for those lucky enough to know it is there.  You may find the house a bit dirty in the corners, and in need of some love and care, but the kitchen knows what it is doing.    When I walked in the other night looking for a modest dinner, I was met with a warm smile and greeting from the woman behind the high cashier's counter.  I asked if they were still serving, and was advised I could sit anywhere and be served hot food until late into the night.  The menu was full of most of the usual suspects to be found in a Roman bistro, excepts perhaps for the first Specialty Pizza, the Mexican.  I asked about their Sausage, Pepper & Onion Sandwich and was told it was one of her favorites.  Good enough for me.  What seemed like 5 minutes later, out of the kitchen walked the chef holding a white ceramic plate with my dinner.  Fast!  First look was of a split Sweet Italian Sausage well grilled and a pile of Sautéed Onions and Green Peppers overflowing the rim of the torpedo roll.  They may have saved a few bucks on the bread, which was sort of non-descript, but the innards were hot, tasty and a very good representation of the genre.  No need for ketchup or other additional condiments.  This was a heavy hitter with strong accent.  I liked it a lot, although it would have been even better with Green Frying Peppers in place of the generic greens.    And, at a cost of under $6 for this creation, it made little dent in my wallet.    I will be back to try the pizza and other goodies at Anthony IV, as this place is close to the best pizza joint I have sampled in the Morrisville area.  Between the down/dirty ambiance, friendly service, and good food, it checks off most of my boxes.  So nice to be pleasantly surprised.

Barnes & Noble sits in a single building in the same shopping center as Home Depot, Dick's Sporting Goods and Petco. I think of it as a historic artifact from the days when paper and ink were required to publish and market books.  These days that is becoming much less so, and it will only be the public's love of books and the emotional connection with libraries and bookstores that will keep this cultural icon from becoming extinct.    I enjoy the sensations of being surrounded by knowledge, scholarship and tons of information.  It reminds of the libraries of Alexandria, Athens, Rome, Xian, London, New York, and all the other great repositories of our wisdom.  It moves me in a way that the internet does not and cannot.  I, for one, will join libraries, and visit bookstores like B & N to contribute to their survival.    Last night I attended a writers' group of about a dozen people who love written expression and are willing to read their work and accept criticism from other writers.  Very interesting experience. You just don't know what a person can create and write about.  Sometimes their appearance is completely opposite to what flows from their own hand.   Barnes & Noble is to be applauded for making comfortable space available for such groups to explore the written word.  Whether any of us will ever find our tomes populating the shelves of this store remains to be dreamed of.   Oh, yes...The Starbucks is much too small for the demand it generates, and the chairs, tables and other seating areas are insufficient for the volume of customers who come and like to hang out here for extended periods of time to socialize or dive into the stacks.

This review reflects only on the Xiao Long Bao, Beef Scallion Pancakes, Crispy Salted Chicken and Dam Dam (sic?) Noodles, all of which are on the Dim Sum Appetizers menu.    We chose Shanghai 1 specifically for their reputation for good XLB as described by many Yelpers.  The shop is another of those long narrow houses with tables running along the north wall all the way to the restroom.  It is attractive enough with artificial flowers on each table and modern wall hangings.  The service is fast and friendly, especially if Mandarin is spoken in the exchange.    We found the Soup Dumplings (XLB) to be very good.  The skin was thin, the soup hot and savory, and the ground pork filling, soft and tasty.  The table rocket with the dumpling vinegar was a great tool for squirting into the open pouch once the top knot was bitten off to suck out the broth.  We liked them so much, we ordered another bamboo steamer of 6 after finishing everything else.    The Beef Scallion Pancake was likewise very enjoyable.  I did not find it overly oily given it was fried in that scalding fluid, and the beef within was tender and brought to sweet life with the Hoisin Sauce in which it had been prepared.  The Crispy Salted Chicken was their take on the fried chicken craze.  The chicken was tender, but the breading a might over-fried to a too-dark brown.  The pieces were very small and included many droplets of plain dough without any meat within.  While the taste was okay, the overall impression was underwhelming.     Both the XLB and Pancakes were winners, while the Crispy Fried Chicken left something to be desired. I leave it to others to discuss the relative merits of the XLB created by the other shops known for this Shanghai delicacy, Dim Sum Garden and Sakura Mandarin.  If we had stopped with the first three dishes all would have been quite content.  Our son was still hungry and wanted some noodles.  He ordered the Dam Dam Noodles with Chili Sauce hoping to top off his meal with some spicy carbs.  At 19, he can afford to do that.  Unfortunately, he was disappointed with this dish.  He complained that it was tasteless and bland.  He left half of it in the bowl and declined to take the rest home. Perhaps, we should have known given the exotic spelling of the dish.    We will stick with the Xiao Long Bao and Scallion Pancakes on future visits.

From its straight ahead name, to its gimmicky "Club" orientation, to the free coffee, and its semi-secret spot along the Delaware River in New Hope, Pa., Fred's Breakfast has it going on!  It took me long enough to get there and check it out, but now that I've been, I have to say, I really like their style (or lack of it).    There are no signs out front announcing its presence, yet the place was full on this Saturday morning at 9 am.  The front door was locked for non-members, but everyone knew that the world was invited.  Just wait for someone to open the door and go in.  Put your first name on the legal pad in the foyer and wait for it to be called.  In the meantime, pour yourself a mug of hot coffee (on the house), and look around.  There's a bakery in the corner with good looking housemade goodies, and T Shirts for sale with their logo House Labrador Retriever.  Check out the wood burning stove, and look out the large windows at the Mighty Delaware and Lambertville, NJ across the narrow truss bridge.  Plenty to keep you entertained while you wait for one of the 31 stools around the large room to become available.  Even on this crowded morn, we had adjoining spinners in about 20 minutes.  That's just the first act.  The menu is pretty much standard morning fare, with the major exception that everything is made in house.  Very tempting to try old standards and see what Fred's does with them.  So, we ordered Scrambled Eggs & Corned Beef Hash, and a Ham, Egg & Cheese on English Muffin.  The second came with a side of Hash Browns.  This is more or less a French kitchen, where everything is prepared in front of you.  It is easy to watch the staff do its thing, from making pancake batter, to buttering the toast.  Everyone knows their job and there is constant movement and teamwork.  My Corned Beef Hash was far more colorful than the normal variants.  This one had multi-colored peppers sliced into the mix, along with onion, potato and the meat.  The freshness was outstanding, and the taste a delight to my taste buds.  The scrambled were nothing special, but with a splash of hot sauce they were fine.  The English muffin was supersized and full of nooks and crannies.  It held its contents well, despite the load of sliced grilled ham, fried egg and American cheese.  Strong flavor along with the crunch.  Thomas's could learn a thing or two about improving their product.  The hash browns were plentiful and well cooked, with enough dark nibs and tenderness to be a textural as well as a tasteful side.   The house closes at 11.  Plan accordingly.

This warehouse of a shoe store is to feet what The Home Depot is to home improvement. It offers more than you could possibly need to do the job, but intoxicates with choices. Depending on your interest, you can wander around either one mesmerized by all the possibilities.  I needed a pair of dress browns to wear with business suits. The far left wall had at least 50. Wing tip, two tone, light, medium or dark umber. Contrasting laces, loafers. Traditional or light weight. American, English or Italian. Get the picture?   Eenie, meenie, miinie, mo...  The psychology is to force abandonment of rational decisions and lead you to the conclusion that it makes sense to buy more than one pair to get you past indecisiveness. Don't worry. You are saving money, too.   I fought off the urge to splurge and went with Aldo wingtips. Good fit. The cashier approved.  Will need to find the right color shoe cream to keep them looking spiffy.   Very proud that I didn't succumb to the pressure to buy them all (Yet).

Stopped in to kill both time and hunger while waiting for an order to be ready at a nearby shop.   From the outside, it seemed to be a nice looking facility for dinner. As I drove around I noticed an older edifice behind the main building which looked like a simple pizza parlor with a soft ice cream window. I ordered a slice of their Margarita Pizza and Regular to get a sampling of both their standard and specialty pies.  The two plus a 12 oz. drink was under $6. Much less than I was used to paying farther north.    Unfortunately, the slices were overly oily and I had to let the olive juice run off onto the nice ceramic plate.  The tip of each slice folded when lifted, requiring my index finger to lift it up to get it into my mouth.  Thus, it failed my first test of a good slice - the ability to stand firm without wilting.  Next, the taste.  Aside from being very hot, the sauce and cheese were nondescript.  The bottom crust was not crisp despite the reheating, and the texture was not quite right.  The second prong of the pizza slice test was also a fail.  To compound the problem, I was not provided with utensils to use to hold and cut the slices; something required by the behavior of the soft wedges.   This area of Fairless Hills has a multitude of Tomato Pie stores.  I am surprised that Arosso's did not come close to competing with the best of them.

Le Viet is not your every day run of the mill traditional Vietnamese restaurant.  Its modern décor informs about the approach the kitchen takes to its menu.  It too, is modern and uniquely different from most of the other ethnic houses in this community.  If you want a break from Pho and Broken Rice (or even if you don't), but desire creativity and great distinctive flavor, this is your destination of choice.    I had read the reviews, but was still very pleasantly surprised by the attention to comfort and privacy afforded here.  Booths with high back benches separating us from our dining neighbors.  Dark woody tones with high ceilings and subdued lighting. Glass vases, mirrors behind the bar, and extended front wall to let an image of the city enter, but keep us hidden within.  A place for a date.   We ordered #s 9 and 70 - Pineapple Salad appetizer and Short Ribs roasted in a clay pot.  Both were exceptional.  The App came in a hollowed out half Pineapple, loaded with fresh Fruit, raw Calamari, spicy Shrimp, and assorted sidekick Veggies, all held together with a Lime and Pineapple Juice base with an assist from a good Fish Sauce. It was delicious. It wasn't Cerviche, but suggested that style.  When the solids were consumed, we asked for spoons so we could drink the sauce remaining in the bottom of the pineapple.  I could have had that for a cocktail if mixed with a little light rum.   The Short Ribs had been torched to a dark burn, so that everything else in the clay pot had been caramelized into a thick glazy gravy that was hot with a hint of sweet.  The meat was easily liberated from the bone and also captured that intense taste.  We loved it.    If there was a weakness it came from the bar that prepared the Mai Tai we requested.  I envisioned a Trader Vic's drink, full of orange, pineapple and lime juice, two rums, coconut liquor, and Grenadine.  Aside from a squirt of lime and a pour of Grenadine and Light Rum, the other ingredients were absent, making for a thin drink lacking its soul.  Next time, we skip the drinks.   Otherwise, this was a top notch meal.  It was a great alternative to the usual stops on Philly-Saigon-Hanoi dinner train.

Imli (Tamarind) Indian Kitchen sits on Passyunk Avenue just a few blocks north of Washington.  It is in one of the few strips along this diagonal thoroughfare that is not very commercially developed.  The upside is there is usually street parking to be found nearby.  The down, is that Imli does not benefit from being around other choices for potential customers.  It stands on its own, an excellent South Indian house that is very worth finding. If you live in the neighborhood you have the best of both worlds; the relative quietude of living in a gentrifying residential area, and a great place to walk to for a superior South Asian repast.  Lucky you!  Early Sunday evening there was only one couple dining when we entered.  First impressions were very favorable, with odd angles due to its placement on a narrow point of the star caused by transecting streets; dark wooden and slate hues on walls and floors offering a cool vibe to chill the heat coming from the curry kitchen, and large storefront windows on the urban world, made shade from mature street trees. Two young women approached with smiles and menus in hand, and invited us to sit anywhere. We selected the front corner table with a view of the streetscape without, and the whole room within.  These ladies were definitely sisters, and they admitted to kinship with the owners.    As firsttimers, we ordered a cross section of the offerings: Chicken 65 for an app; Began Bhurta (veggie curry dish), and Chicken Korma (mildly sweet and loudly hot at the same time). The house put down a plate with Papadum and two dipping sauces, which was a nice gesture. Garlic Naan, Mango Lassi and Chai completed the symphony. The "65" dish came out deep red and slightly crispy.  It was a delicious opening gambit. It was expertly grilled so the tops and edges were near-black, making it visually stunning.  The eggplant (Began Bhurta) came in a deep silver dish and thick curry sauce.  It mixed well with the Basmati Rice and was great for sopping with the Naan.  The Korma arrived in a yogurt/creamy/nutty champagne-colored curry with a nice amount of fresh cut chicken.  Everything was ordered, "hot," and was true to its word.  The lassi and chai helped to reduce the heat as needed, and allowed us to continue through to the end of the meal with calling the fire department.  The Garlic Naan was served flat on a wooden board rather than in a basket (nice touch), and the bowls of rice were more the enough to cover our main dishes.    I have not been to every other Indian kitchen in Philly, but of the many I have tried in the region, Imli is right up there with the best of them.  It offers a pleasing combination of cool atmosphere, warm, efficient service, and excellent cuisine. It may not be strictly South Indian (who cares), but it certainly knows how to create an unforgettable meal.    Try to get there soon.

Kasdon's Restaurant & Tavern on New Falls Road, Levittown, is one of many such places in this area of Lower Bucks County.  It has been around since the 1950's, and maintains the feel of a dark, knotty pine hall, with decent kitchen and fair prices on drinks.  There are HDTVs on every wall in the bar and dining room, so it is definitely a sports bar, too.    On a weeknight the rectangular bar has several couples sitting around having dinner and  drinks.  The dining area was lightly populated with a few families in booths or tables.  It was both a young and old crowd, but as it seemed to be smoke free, it wasn't conducive to the rowdy bunch often found across the street.    The beer on tap is limited to basic American suds, but that is not a problem for the folks here.  Yuengling Lager was about as exotic as it got.  Still, at a couple of bucks for a pint I wasn't complaining.  The same holds for the kitchen offerings.  Several pages of standard American fare, including pizza, burgers, sandwiches and a long list of diner-esque dishes.  My Patty Melt was decent, but served naked on the plate, without even chips or pickle.  At a price shy of $7., I certainly received what I paid for.    Kasdon's has been around for a while, and it shows in the décor and long term servers/tenders.  It is a relatively safe place for a few drinks, chow and conversation with the people at and within the bar.  Families are also welcome.    After a few stops at the lanes nearby, where the crowd can be loud and obnoxious (although with better grub), Kasdon's feels to be a safe harbor.

Is it the best diner in New Jersey, Land of Diner Enchantment? Maybe not, but it certainly has history and local color going for it. Oh, and a great breakfast if you fancy overflowing plates, unlimited coffee, and a Greek Omelet that is a wonder of the world.   What is it about feta cheese and eggs that moves me so?  Don't know, but when mixed with sausage, potato, onion, peppers, all wrapped up in an fresh egg case, they become an amazing sensory explosion.   Trenton may have seen better days (we have been waiting for its resurgence since it was "Americas Town" in the 60's), but Pat's carries on. Diners are only partially about the food, and the rest about the concept, design, and lustful loyalty they inspire.  Pat's is a worthy contender for the Urban Diner List on Yelp* (If there is one).  Give it a try.  Sit at the counter and watch professionals do their thing. Sit at a window and see a worldview that captures the past-its-prime city, the capital of the Garden State, remind you that... We Are Still Here.

The Big Easy used to be Maxine's back in the day.  In those wild and wooly days of yesteryear, I was bartending around the corner, and would sometimes stop in here on an off night or after hours for a few drinks and/or dances.  The layout looks the same - like the inside of a ship.  Two levels of seating in an oval dining room.  Large dance floor still holding down the main deck.    I stopped in for breakfast earlier this week.  The door was propped open and I wasn't certain they were doing morning business.  They were. I was greeted by a warm smiling young woman who walked me into the smaller barroom, where I chose a table close by the front windows.  They were still setting/cleaning up, but made me feel quite welcome.    This kitchen is Halal, so I ordered a Beef Bacon, Egg and Cheese on an Whole Wheat Roll.  As you can see from the photo, the sandwich was big and loaded.  I enjoyed every bite.  The coffee was fresh brewed after I asked for some, and it was very tasty. I think that was Chicory mixed in as a nod to Café du Monde in NOLA.    This is a great place for an early morning meeting or just a quiet solitary breakfast.  It was fun to be back in the old joint, and to see it was being so well cared for.    For downtown Trenton, this is a definite gem.

There are two entries for this supermarket, the other being, "McCaffery's Supermarket."   Same store. Same experience.   Slightly upscale compared to the nearest competition, Acme and Giant, but not up to the quality and gestalt of the Wegman's, Whole Foods, and Trader Joe's of the world. Have to wonder what would happen if one of those retailers came to Ntown, which has been discussed, but not yet evolved into a real plan.     This shop has the mandatory Starbucks, and a pretty good produce department.  The rest is the same as everyone else. Close your eyes and open them again, and you could be in any generic supermarket in the USA.  No better. No worse. At least you know where everything is.   Definitely, middle of the road grocery experience.

When you live in or near Washington Crossing, and it is not permitted to build a commercial area that would be large enough to contain a supermarket, what you are left with is Colonial Farms, a convenience store sized, high end deli.    Here, you pay for the convenience of not having to drive up to Newtown to shop.  And, it fits into the atmosphere in Wash X that it is a bedroom community for high wage earners who prefer their town just as it is.  To each his/her own.  Colonial Farms caters to this community and does a fairly good job of it.    The bakery usually has very good muffins and other sweet goodies.  The deli makes really good sandwiches and salads, and the rest of the store is stocked with the basics needed to prepare your next meal.  But, don't make the mistake of thinking this store is all you need on an every day basis.  It is too small and select for that.  For large shopping excursions you still need to find an Acme, or Whole Foods or Wegmans, etc., to get broader choice and better price.     Still, for that morning coffee and breakfast sandwich, or a quick stop for a much better than Wawa customized lunch, or just to buzz in for a European chocolate bar, Colonial Farms be the place.

It took me two tries to find the front door of Mauceri Pizza.  It has combined two storefronts.  The one to the right lets you in, while the door on the left is permanently closed on the dining room side of the establishment.  It is not immediately apparent that this is now one operation, so take this tip to find your way.  It is worth your while to come inside.   First glance, it still looks like an Italian pizza shop with a couple of pies on display, and large ovens toward the back.  It is rather hot in there on a humid Judy day, but the now-glass wall between the two rooms also insulates the strong air conditioning in the dining room.  As there was no one else eating when I arrived, I sought permission to enter and have lunch.  No problem.  Although a Salvadoran house, most there spoke English well enough to understand each other.  The room is rather large with ample tables for a nice dinner crowd.    The menu is a cross between Italian and Salvadoran cuisine.  All the usual suspects on the Roman side, and substantial offerings in Spanish, as well.  One of their specialties was Chili Rellenos, one of my favorite Central American dishes, and I went for it.  What followed was a parade of plates from Chips and Salsa, to Pickled Peppers, Tortillas, and a huge platter with the Rellenos, Rice and Salad.  The stuffed chili pepper covered in egg and drowned in spicy red sauce, was about the best I had ever eaten.  The stuffing seemed to be a combination of ground meat, cheese, onion and more pepper.  It was filling and delicious. I will never know how they expected one man to eat that much.  I barely touched the tortillas and the rice.  My cold Jicaima Juice was a rich dark cranberry color, sweet and refreshing.   The only question that arose was the actual price for my meal.  The hand out flyer listed the dish at $7., while the hard menu said it was $8.  I was charged $9. They should work on getting some consistency in pricing to avoid any chance someone might think they were trying to take advantage of a gringo.  Yet, even at the highest price, it was still a deal. I said nothing and let the confusion slide.   This piece of Liberty Street is attempting to come back to life after a rough couple of decades.  There are now a few restaurants and shops on the street and a new CVS down the block.  With a little luck, they will all do well.

As the old saying goes, " Anything worth doing is worth overdoing." This perfectly sums up Redberry in Village of Newtown Shopping Center.  There are many franchises out there, and all are about the same, with only slight differences in flavors, textures, and toppings.  Here, the flavors seem tamped down.  The Country Vanilla was weak, and the Pumpkin more like nutmeg and Cinnamon, than real pumpkin.  The toppings are all sugary and add too many calories to be healthy.   The environment is very bright and bare bones.  No comfortable place to sit other than plastic chairs and small tables. Take out is certainly the message here.  It would be interesting to compare the calories here with the real ice cream places nearby.  For my taste buds, and someone who loves yogurt, Redberry is an underwhelming experience, although my young son likes it . At approximately $5. per serving with toppings, it is not a cheap treat.

Once upon a time, there was a Jersey Diner on Olden Avenue called The Extension Diner.  It had good food, but was old and tired. A reviewer stopped in for breakfast once in a while on his way to court.  He loved the counter service, the humongous muffins displayed in front of him, and the bottomless cup of coffee from the Cecilware perk antique coffee maker.  When he semi-retired, and stopped visiting "The Ex," the diner was so sad, it decided to close its doors.   Two guys named Peter came along.  They saw the bathetic eatery and its promise.  They decided to buy it, modernize it, and reopen with a fresh face, new menu, and the old Cecilware coffee maker.    Eventually, the reviewer came out of retirement, strapped on his suit and long sword, and returned to slaying dragons.  Driving down Olden Avenue he beheld the new Two Peters Diner where the old Extension used to be, and stopped in to see what it was about.  Much to his amazement the new joint was beautiful.  Everything inside was new, spacious, bright and cheerful.  The maidens were just as friendly and courteous as he remembered; the Cecilware coffee just a wonderfully dark and rich.    Half the long counter was gone, replaced by a large cake/pie display.  Still, he found a spinner and slid onto it.  As in past ages the muffins were directly in front of him as if time had not moved them from their appointed place.  They were still very large, with pillow tops and trim paper bases.    Had to have one.  Cranberry it was.   Toasted, it was still soft with a moistness that bespoke freshness.  The texture was dense, compressing pleasantly when chewed, and slowly releasing its sweetness, and mild acidic cranberry charm.  It crumbled slightly on the plate, but was easily captured with the tines of the fork. With Cecil coffee, it was an ample breakfast.   Two Peters is a worthy successor to the old "Ex."  In many ways a vast improvement.  This knight errant will make it a regular stop on his quest to slay the firebreathers.

The reviews for The Firkin Tavern are like a blind man touching an elephant. Depending on what you touch you have a different impression. Is it a dive bar?  A sports bar? A college bar? An old man's bar? A beer bar?  A good happy hour bar?  A foodie bar?  The answers are simple. Yes.   Any really good hangout bar is all things to all people.  That's what makes them fun and special.  Whoever you are; whatever you do; whatever you want; regardless of time; The Firkin delivers.  It allows you to feel at home, and make it your own.  I've only been here a couple of times, once for lunch and another for happy hour after work, and although the experience of each visit was different, the constant was an upbeat vibe with friendly attractive staff, and drinks, menu and activities that were entertaining, tasty and fairly priced.  Most important - the crowd mixes well together.  Labels are unnecessary and soon forgotten. Just have fun.    The space is surprisingly large, and well placed mirrors make it seem even bigger.  The dark tones make it seem older than it is and adds to the atmospherics.  The bar is big enough for bellyups, and the bar menu is sufficiently diverse to make a few hours on a stool pass quickly.  Decent beer choices for the craft people, and those who are happy with their Buds.  The kitchen turns out interesting plates of nachos, flatbreads, sammys, burgers, soups, salads, and more.  Your tastebuds will be satisfied.   I have sampled several of the above while sitting at the bar at happy hour, and been pleasantly surprised.  Cheesesteak Nachos!? Are you kidding me?  Fun comfort food at its best.  Stuffed Chicken Sammy on a fresh roll with a load of mushrooms, cheese and honey mustard sauce - very good.  Burgers; thick and way above average.    Yeah! The Firkin Tavern is a sleeper and a keeper, regardless of what part of the elephant you touch.

So this is 21st Century bowling.  Amazing!  As a kid growing up in a big city, I first experienced bowling in a tiny, 8 lane facility on the second floor of an old factory that had been adaptively reused into a recreation zone.   There was a tire store downstairs, and a candy store on the corner.  Games were 3 for a buck, and shoe rental another two bits.  It was great fun for my buds and me.    Brunswick Zone is a different animal entirely.  Bowling is not even mentioned in the name nor signage.  Yet, there are 48 lanes here, and the distant thunder of ball striking pin is buffered by the sounds of laser tag, pool, large bar/restaurant, and arcade with pinball wizards running up the score.  It has become full menu fun.  The cost is higher for all these options, but really still a decent value.   I went down to Feasterville to pick up number one son from an afternoon/early evening of Brunswick Zone entertainment.  Walking through the sliding doors I felt like this was another Home Depot, Cabellas moment - a huge warehouse hanger of a building jammed with every group game imaginable.  Overwhelming sounds and lights. I was preparing to head for the large bar to wait until the young man emerged from laser tag or a final few frames of a bowling tournament, but found him quickly in front of the laser tag desk.    I hope he has another invite to go there to play so I can check everything out in more detail.  If not, I will have to take him there myself.    I hear my childhood calling.

I have returned to McC's a few times since my last review in January, 2013, and have noticed a general improvement in the offerings, marketing, and prices.  While still tending to the more expensive side compared to the competition, it is now possible to find items on sale of more than a nickel off the normal retail price, and the staff seems to have grown into their new surroundings in Newtown, and are more friendly, courteous and knowledgeable.    It is still not my first choice for groceries (have to go to Trader Joe's and Wegman's in Lawrenceville, New Jersey for that), but I am willing to visit here for the things the family needs without gritting my teeth with self loathing.  Still wish they carried Finlandia Swiss and a few other non-Boars Head deli products, but I am learning to live with that, as it seems the others supermarkets in Newtown have cut the same deal with that company.    Time for a raise.  Three Stars.
Sunday Brunch UYE Review -  Sorry folks. You'll have to read the other reviews of this Am-azie-ing brunch venue.  I need to take a nap first.

A wholesome piece of Americana right on State Street, Doylestown.  It feels like a luncheonette with small booths, tables, and a very friendly "Coach" handling the orders and register.  High school banners on the walls and a HDTV tuned to ESPN. Local kids working the grills.  Feels familiar and timeless.  The menu is on a digital board (a bit incongruously).  As soon as I saw the juxtaposition of two of my favorite words, "burger and jalapenos," I knew where I was heading.  Rather than the quarter pound puck I expected, it arrived in a red plastic basket as two small sliders about 3" high, cheese melted over the bottom bun, and the sauteed onion and green 'pena holding up the roof. I smiled at the surprise. Still, it is the first bite experience that matters here, and it was great! I was thinking, "Fat White Castle," but after the jaw clenched and released, I felt my mouth fill with the combination of flavors and textures, and knew I had to savor the moment.    Thank you for a pleasant surprise that makes a day.   Coach's took me by ambush.  I wasn't anticipating anything special here, but came away with a memory and wish to return soon.

This GNC has been in the Village of Newtown for 15 years.  It is a good place to pick up nutritional supplements to assist your healthy lifestyle remain that way.  While diet is a key determinant of health, sometimes an assist from a quality vitamin, mineral, or herbal mix can enhance the constitution.    For me, several health professionals, both traditional, allopathic and alternative have recommended Grape Seed Extract, Ginseng, Ginko Biloba and a good multi-vitamin be added on a daily basis. After more than 20 years of using them they seem to have made a difference.  Skeptics can doubt, but I am a believer.    GNC offers high end products, and when I don't want to boil herbs to make health teas, I use their supplements based on confidence that they are high quality and subject to decent quality control.  Sometimes the higher price disturbs me when I find another good manufacturer at better price (I do shop around), but absent that, GNC has my loyalty.

Old Style pizza joint with a broader menu to attract more diners into their cozy dining room.    Problem is that while the Tomato Pie and the other spinning disks are very good, the same cannot be said for the rest of the in house cuisine.  This was my first visit to Palermo's III after visiting the others in Hamilton and Bordentown.    The Tomato Pie is thin, crisp and nicely spiced here, but if forced to compare with its former siblings, it would come behind the Bordentown establishment for quality pies.  We also ordered a family sized Caesar Salad and Sautéed Spinach as a side dish to get in our veggies for the day.    The Salad was just okay with nice Romaine, Shaved Carrots, Onion and Croutons.  However, the dressing came in a small plastic container and was mass produced and lacking in true Caesar flavor (no anchovy taste).  The Spinach was definitely from the freezer and was a watery tasteless waste to eat.  Very disappointing, and not worth the $6, by half.   Lesson learned. Stick to the pizza and tomato pies, and leave the rest to those who don't know better.

McCaffery Supermarkets recently opened another store at the site of the former Genuardis Supermarket. They have upgraded it considerably, and it is a very pleasant environment for food shopping. However, the prices have gone up and they are not really competitive with the Acme in the same shopping area, nor the new Giant that replaced Clemens last year. I went through it a few months ago, and realized that all the things I normally purchase were more expensive there than the other two venues.  I don't go there any longer, as any of the specialty items they carry that are not in the others markets, can be found in abundance at Whole Foods with more variety and an even nicer experience.

Haley's Homemade Sandwiches sits way up Parkway Avenue on the way to Trenton-Mercer Airport.  It is a quick jump stop off Rt. 95.  I stopped in last week to check it out and pick up a sandwich to take to the office.    Walking in, the first impression is of many tables in front of a large kitchen work area.  People were enjoying their meals, and there was a busy take out trade.  Large refrigeration units were around for a "take your own drink" approach to service. The staff seemed mostly college folk.  They were friendly and attentive, if a bit sloppily garbed for the customer service end of the business.    I ordered a Chicken Salad with Swiss Sub on a Sesame Seed Torpedo.  It was prepared quickly and presented to me already wrapped in white paper and sealed with tape.  When I reached the office, I opened it up to see a nice sized hoagie with plenty of chicken salad, cheese, sweet hot peppers and lettuce.  This was two meals.  I immediately appreciated the cost factor.  The first bite told me the roll was good quality and fresh.  The chicken was also of very recent vintage with large chunks in light mayo.  The Swiss had a pleasing tart nuttiness, and the peppers added an element of caliente zest. All in all, a pretty good sandy.  Compared to an alternative like Primo's, Haley's was better to my taste.    Haley's won't be part of my regular lunch rotation due to location and comparatives.  However, I will have no hesitancy returning there when the mood strikes, and sample other savories from his menu.  The Cheesesteaks seemed to be popular when I was there, and the people eating there, quite comfortable.

Dredge Harbor sounds like the name of a Stephen King novel, all spooked out for sleepless nights.   It isn't. Rather, it is a small marina on the Jersey side of the Mighty Delaware in Delran, just south of Riverside. The entrance is a bit obscure, and there is a long driveway to be taken until reaching the water. Once the river is before you, hang a left past the huge hanger drydock, being careful to avoid the heavy forklift moving boats in and out. The cafe is the building on the right next to the ramp leading down to the docks. It is an active marina and it is easy to be distracted by the beautiful boats plying the water among the berths.  This experience is all about outdoor dining. While there is an inside dining area, it has little atmosphere compared to the wide open vistas up and down the river from the overhung patio.  We arrived shortly before 9 am, and were seated at a table within ten minutes.  Coffee flowed, and the menus consisted of traditional breakfast fare from top to bottom.  We opted for a fresh poured and ironed waffle with bacon and a sausage & feta omelet with the home fries thrown inside.  While we waited, we watched the power boats cruising the river and slowly moving around the marina.  It made for a very relaxed and dreamy morning.   This is one of those adventures where the surroundings trumped the food.  The meals were good, but not more.  My omelet was absolutely loaded with meat, cheese and potatoes, but the sausage links were dry from over-frying, and the eggs could have used a little water in mixing to make them light and fluffy.  The waffle was fine, but would have been so much better with a maple syrup option, rather than the Smucker's corn syrup cheap substitute.    Still, we really didn't mind the food quality as we mellowed in the moment on the water's edge.  They certainly have the business humming, and don't need to upgrade if they choose not to.  I would come back again regardless, because the environment was so pleasant.    "... Summer breeze makes me feel fine.  Blowing through the jasmine in my mind..."

Pleasant environment for a first lunch at Vietnam Restaurant on 11th Street.  Dark wood tones, extensive menu, and apparently, a good bar.    My lunch was simple; Pho Tai.  The bowl was smaller than at other VN locales, but tasty and well presented with a full plate of accessories (spouts, lime, jalapenos,basil leaves).  The flank steak was thin and lean.  The broth as doctored at the table, spicy and engaging.  The noodles, soft and of adequate volume.  At $6.95, it was exactly what I wanted for a light lunch.  The Vietnamese coffee was also very satisfying.    I need to visit a few more times and try more on the menu before coming to a final opinion on this pleasant fixture on the edge of Chinatown.

Another boring supermarket. They are mostly indistinguishable from each other.  Only the signs out front let you know where you are.   Lack of real competition makes Acme a dull boy.  Same holds true for Giant and McCaffery's. They would all be empty warehouses if Trader Joe's, Whole Foods or Wegman's came to town.    Don't we deserve better?

Breakfasted here this week while waiting for my court appearance. The location is very convenient to the courthouses, and unlike the hilltop, there is no parking issue down here.    The space is large and bright, and looks the same as most Paneras.  The service was fine, although the ordering and delivery take place at opposite ends of the long half wall that separates the work from dining areas.  There were plenty of free tables at 8:00 am and I was very comfortable occupying a booth by myself.    I had a basic breakfast of Quinoa Steel Cut Oatmeal, which came with sliced Strawberries, Walnut and Brown Sugar.  It was thick and tasty.  Glad it was a small bowl.  The Toasted Everything Bagel was fresh and held the Veggie Spread well.  With coffee, the meal was under $10.  No problem there.    I have visited enough Paneras around the country to know that while they all look the same, they do not all act the same.  The Doylestown facility did not seem to have any problem with attitude, nor accuracy, although other Yelpers seem to have had different experiences.    Given the overall quality of the experience and the ease of parking, this Panera gets my vote for the optimal breakfast on a busy morning in the downtown area.

As the nearest watering hole to my Newtown office, Black Horse is a great place for an after work happy hour stop.  I just walk over for an hour, have a beer, martini or margarita and a nibble of pretty good bar food specials, and make my way home.  It is also perfect for pre/post meeting meetings to prep/rehash the issue of the moment.  I usually find my buds upstairs in a cluster, but we have been known to find a corner downstairs to stand around in as we strategize or just blow off steam.    The alcohol is what swings this dark horse, but the kitchen does turn out some quality dishes.  The wings, dumplings, Mexi/Texi tapas, and even the burgers are done well, though their concepts may be different than you have experienced elsewhere.    Too, you gotta like the overall atmosphere of the old place.  The renovations have not detracted from the historical marker that this tavern has been over many many years.  After one drink it is easy to imagine the Continental Army marching down State Street on its way to Washington Crossing.  After two drinks you realize that there are Tory sympathizers in the bar.  After three, the Sons of Liberty are ready to throw them out into the street.    I have not actually sat down for a full dinner here.  No particular reason other than the circumstances of the day.  The prices are higher than my other favorite watering hole, The Clubhouse, but the differential can be explained by the ambiance and the targeted customers.    Depending on my mood, BHT can be exactly right, particularly if planning the next skirmish in the War of Independence.

Richard Thorton was the original owner of this historic structure on the corner of State and Centre in the heart of Newtown Borough. While he would be proud that his home still stands sentinel after more than 250 years, his allegiance now would be to the nation he witnessed being born and to the Black Horse Tavern that occupies the premises and warms his ghost as he sits at the bar after hours, enjoying the many tales his compatriots tell as the town sleeps.

This one is difficult.   Joey G runs this deli near my home.  My young son likes to ride his bike down the road to get a snack there.  He enjoys the sense of independence this engenders.  It is the only place within a safe distance.  Yet, when I went in for lunch or to pick up milk or eggs for home use, I became wary of the sanitation standards.  The milk was sold after the "sell by" date. There was deli food outside the refrigeration unit when not in use.  The floor behind the counter was not always clean.  Then, I read the Bucks County Department of Health Inspection Report from 11/13, and saw that there were other significant problems, like no hand washing sink, mouse droppings, old fly paper, open doors without screens, and no soap for washing.   These were all signs of failing quality control and lack of supervision.  Still, the food prepared there was decent to good.  And, Joe does a good job with his catering.  I have had many experiences with his victuals at business lunches, and never had any real issues with it.  In fact, his crab cakes are excellent.  The website informs that there are now 3 locations for Joey G.  I applaud his success, but suspect that he has not caught up with the extra personnel and training needed to manage a larger operation.  As Joe is a well known chef, it may behoove him to hire an experienced manager to run these shops, rather than attempt to handle everything himself or in family.    No one likes to see a promising food outlet struggle to maintain high standards.  It is too easy to lose customers who won't give it a second chance.  But, more importantly, no one should have to run the risks that attend to dirty facilities.  Because this deli is in our home court, we will no doubt return and check out the improvements.  If they straighten out, we will remain customers (and raise the rating).  If not, most will migrate out of Joey G's orbit and find more acceptable places to buy our meals, snacks and drinks.

Morrisville has a surprising number of luncheonette and deli places that turn out a broad variety of primarily breakfast and lunch dishes.  Always on the lookout for an easier way to get into Trenton on a weekday, the Morrisville-Trenton crossings are often the least trafficked.  On my way, I like to stop for breakfast when time permits, and hit the bridges around 8:45 when the flow of cars improves.   So, I recently found Ben's Delicatessen on Bridge Street just a hop, skip and jump from the Trenton Makes Bridge.  Parking is fairly easy with a side parking lot, and once inside the ordering/paying/take away system is very efficient.  They def have it down to a tight discipline.  The crowd is primarily dudes in work boots and company logo shirts, with a few local office or retail folks thrown in.  I was the only suit.   I ordered their 4 piece French Toast, thinking it would be two halved slices of bread at the ridic price of $3.95.  Wrong.  It was four full slices.  Pleasant surprise.  I stood near the short order grill and watched the spatula man work at hyper speed to get the orders out and moved down the conveyor line to the packer and cashier.  Luckily, I was not overly concerned with the fact that a large coil of pork sausage was its neighbor on the grill, sharing its oozing juices with my egg soaked bread.    When I finally took possession of my meal, it was tossed on a styro plate, and placed on a plastic tray for me to carry to a table.  Plastic utensils completed the composition.  The bottom of the plate was not flat, and as I tried to cut the toast with fork and knife, it would spin on the tray, making surgical precision impossible.  The cook clearly did not have a concern for creating a quality dish, as the toast had an eggy top with dry center, suggesting insufficient time in pre-grill soak and absorption.   It was low average at best.  The coffee was fine.    Given what I saw of the operation as I waited, I realized that breakfast sandwiches were the way to go here, and I will return to give one a try.  Clearly, Ben's is a beehive of activity in the morning, and has a loyal following.  For now, it deserves the benefit of the doubt that most of what they do is decent or better  NOVEMBER 12, 2014 - Returned today for another breakfast, and went with one of my favorites, Sausage, Egg & Cheese on a Kaiser Roll.  That and a large Coffee set me back only $3.99!  Amazing prices.   The sandwich was very good.  The Sausage Patty was at least 4" in diameter, the Egg Fried, and Cheese American, and the Roll fresh and nicely chewy.  I enjoyed every bite and finished with a satisfied stomach.  The Coffee was hot and pleasant tasting and I appreciated the milk option as opposed to only half & half or those mini moos flavor alternatives. I sat and enjoyed my early repast with several other guys preparing to start their days.    Although not intentionally so, Ben's does have a men's club feel to it, as the only women I see aside from those who work there, order take out and don't hang out with us fellas watching the news or ESPN.   I'll stop back again and try something else, and if as good as my sandwich today, be in the mood to move up the ranking to a brighter star.

My current addiction to fried chicken found me cruising around Morrisville looking for my fix.  Driving along Pennsylvania Avenue after crossing the river on the pay bridge, I spied US Fried Chicken in a strip behind La Villa Italian restaurant.  I pulled into the parking lot, and wove my way closer to their shop.   Walking up to their door I looked again at their overhead sign.  Did it mean United States Fried Chicken, or We Fry Chicken? My curiosity became more intense when I saw that the enterprise was run by a Korean couple. They were friendly, courteous, and as I was the only customer in there when I arrived, willing to do what it took to please me.    They didn't have much chicken in the heating bins, so I asked if they would be cooking up some more.  Yes. If I was willing to wait 15 minutes, they would put a load together for the deep fryer.  Are you kidding me? Only 15 for fresh fried chicken?  I would have waited 30 if need be.  So, I watched as they took the chicken from the refrigerator (not freezer), put in into a large aluminum bowl and poured in the flour/spice mix and stirred it up.  A small cloud of orange dust rose from the swirling.  I could smell the pepper and other secret ingredients when they reached me.  Hmmm...  Mister US brought the bowl over to the fryer and carefully lowered the breasts and wings into the gurgling oil one piece at a time, while Mrs. US put together the Fried Rice that came with my order.
