Other folks came in while I waited, and each was taken care of in turn.  The operation was smooth and they worked very well together as a team.    When the chicken was golden and tested for completion, my take away order was packaged and bagged.  It was heavy from the 2 breasts, 2 wings and the hefty load of rice.  Smelled great, and it remained hot until I started eating it at home.    The Breast was plump, moist and almost entirely edible with little bone.  The coating was crisp, crunchy, and had a very satisfying spiciness that was a little hot from whatever chili essence might be in the mix.  The wings were similarly plump and delicious.  The Fried Rice was surprisingly good.  It did not taste stale from sitting around, but was still in its early stages of existence.    For the moment, US Fried Chicken has caught my attention and appreciation.  My search for the Southern Fried Grail continues, but at least now I know where I can go to find a fine substitute for the ultimate Fried Chicken.

Young man wanted a haircut that was long in front and crew in back.  He is old enough to make such momentous decisions on his own, but needed a ride and paymaster. You get what I mean?   Great Clips in The Village of Newtown Shopping Center was open on Friday night and wasn't busy. They took him right away. I stood back and permitted the stylista and Young Man to negotiate alone. They reached accord and the clippers started buzzing and scissors started cutting.   Ten minutes later the job was done. YM was satisfied with the rad results, and I was pleased with the $15 prix.   He didn't look bad, and I can get used to the blond streaks (I hope).   The shop is in the midst of major renovation. Be careful where you step. It should look great when completed.

Lovely to look at, but impossible to love.   The setting alongside Lake Afton is as pretty as a postcard, but the 3 car parking lot is ridiculously inadequate. It makes a difficult traffic location that much worse, forcing people to focus on parking rather than driving.  Double and illegal parking happen every day, creating a dangerous condition. Amazing that the Yardley government permitted Star$$$ to do this.    The coffee is the same as everywhere else, which to me is poor to average for the basics, but decent if you fall prey to the insidious upsell pressure to go latte or capp in order to be able to imbibe the burnt tasting brew.   The facility is pleasant once inside, with windows facing Main Street or the lake. It is also a front row seat to the near miss accidents that routinely happen there.

Canal Street Grille sits on the corner of Afton Avenue, and the narrow service road that runs behind Main Street in Yardley Borough.  The entrance is in the back of the building and is oriented toward the canal, which can easily be seen through the window wall of the restaurant.    My first impression was that it was a busy place for lunch, and a very attractive dining room with all the glass bringing in natural light and a pleasant view - even when the world is snow covered.  The Greek/Mediterranean menu is diverse enough to satisfy most palates.  We ordered a Bowl of Chicken Orzo Soup, Chicken Gyro with Fries, and Spanakopita, while sitting at a deuce in the middle of the floor.  We did not feel crowded nor lacking privacy despite the nearly full house.    The Chicken Orzo Soup was a bit pricy @ $5. for a cup, but the taste was right on with a lemony aroma and flavor and chunks of white meat chicken and creamy stock.  The Gyro wrapped a warm pita around roasted chicken, tahini sauce, lettuce, and red onion.  Very good mix of texture and flavor and a satisfying meal.  The fries were good, but nothing exceptional.  The Spanakopita for lunch was an approximate 5 inch square of properly backed, philo flakey, feta melty, spinach garlicy tartness.  All quality ingredients.  The overall meal was completely enjoyable, and made me wonder why I hadn't eaten here before.   The price structure is such that it is hard to get out for less than about $12 per, so Canal Grille might not be your every day stop, yet it certainly presents itself as a classy mellow space to enjoy a special lunch with an important conversation.    Well done!  UPDATE. JUNE 13, 2017 - Returned to Canal Grille a few weeks ago with officemates for lunch. The place looks the same, which is to say, attractive with its airy lightness and windows facing the canal.  Menu was about the same. Still predominantly Greek. Service professional.  My Salate Trio, consisting of a sampling of Sesame Noodles, Pineapple Chicken Salad and  Greek Salad, was pretty on the plate, and tasty going down. Each unique in texture and flavor, and just enough to fill me without feeling stuffed.  The pita was also light and excellent at absorbing the nuances of each salad.    Still a superior lunch in the heart of Yardley, Pa.

You know you are in for a treat when the chef/owner comes to your table to discuss what you want for dinner.   Lucky for me, my dining buddy was a good friend of DeAnna.  When he mentioned to our server that he should ask her how she prepared a certain pasta dish, the next thing I knew she was standing next to us and embracing my friend.  See photo.  She asked me what I was looking for, and I gave a soft description of something I hoped sounded like Pasta Oglio Olio with Sautéed Spinach.  She smiled, offered me a job as relief bartender, and retreated to the kitchen without another word.  Pleasant suspense.    While we waited our Eggplant Marinade app arrived for sharing.  App?  It was enough for a meal in itself.  It was a delicious rendition of thin sliced Eggplant with a rich Red Sauce, and mild taste of Plum Tomato, Rosemary, and Balsamic Vinegar.  Tender, subtle, and nearly melt in my mouth.  Auspicious beginning.   When the pasta arrived in its two large white bowls it was not merely the pasta and green I envisioned.  Rather, it was a Star Shaped Profiled Pasta with a Garlic and Oil based sauce that also included the Spinach, Tomato, Green Beans, Crumbled Sweet Italian Sausage, Aged Cheese and maybe a few other things I did not recognize.    Oh, My!  The first bite launched me on a cruise down the Tiber River.  The pasta was soft but its super fresh state deconstructed upon chewing into its constituent elements.  I had seldom experienced pasta so delicate and complex.  The garlic was present, but not overbearing, allowing the Veggies, and Mellow Cheese to harmonize with the textured Sausage and still snappy Beans.  The Tomato provided a tart note.  It was visually stunning to match the celebration of eating.   DeAnna and staff took turns stopping by to see how we were doing. Even the bartender inquired. Quite remarkably, thank you.    We shared both dishes, and it was the reasonable thing to do given the volume of each.  The glutton in me had different ideas, but was contented to know it would be easy to return for more.

Super Wok?  This one table takeout joint is the opposite of "Super."  The floor is crammed with inventoried cases of soda and packaging, suggesting it has not been cleaned in forever.    I went with the quick Lunch Special @ under $6. The price would be right if only the taste followed suit. Everything came out in plastic or Styrofoam containers.  The Wonton Soup was salty (MSG), the wontons themselves, thick and tasteless.  The General Tso's Chicken had a dark tawny gloopy sauce that was neither spicy, nor subtly sweet; but in some no man's land in between that satisfied neither end of the spectrum expected for that dish.  The Fried Rice was the best part of the meal.  It was not cooked in dyed bullion, but had lots of chunky pork and veggies, and little flavor.  Almost decent.   The advertising declares that it is, "Szechuan, Hunan, Cantonese & Thai Style."  Actually, what they meant to say was that it is none of those.  Not a big mistake.  It is a mish mosh of indistinct tastes and textures, none of which begin to be authentic.  It is not possible to get anything Thai on the Lunch Special, Special Platters, House Specialties nor Combination Platters menus.  There is a "Thai Style" list, but after watching and listening to the kitchen action, I would not recommend going there.   Super Wok? Super Not!.

It really is Nutts to come so close to being great, but fall short due to small details that are so easily corrected.   Consider the circumstances.  ~ Great location on Rt. 29, Titusville, NJ; right along the old canal and the mighty Delware.  ~ Cozy countrified space, with the inside a Pocono cabin and the outside a Frenchtown café.  ~ Real pizza oven with a solid rep.  ~ Creamy ice cream way station for tow path riders and walkers.  ~ Diverse menu for 3 meals a day.  ~ Hot, black T-shirted staff.   So, when I went in this morning for an early 8 am breakfast, had my choice of tables, and my first mug of good coffee, ordering a Spanish Omelet with Home Fries and Rye Toast, this was the result: ~ Very good 3 egg omelet and La Chalula Hot Sauce to spice it up. ~ Yet, two salt shakers and no pepper on the table. ~ Wide cut wholesome toasted Rye Toast that was at best room temperature the moment it      reached the table.  ~ A large pile of Home Fries, nicely darkened from their time being grilled, that were now at    best soft and cool, rather than hot and crisp.   ~ $2.95 for bottomless coffee. $9.95 for the omelet.  Nearly $16.00 for this missed opportunity    for perfection.   It is Nutts to have all these self inflicted wounds detract from a near perfect setting, and a kitchen that comes so close to getting it right....  But, doesn't.

What happened?!  Pat's was always the place to go for a decent breakfast at budget prices.  Something is amiss.   Today's breakfast was still inexpensive, but the quality of the meal was really unacceptable.    I ordered one of the breakfast specials on the back of the breakfast menu. Two slices of French Toast, Bacon and Coffee @ $5.20.  This is what was served by the pleasantly attentive server:  ~ Yellow dyed bread with barely any egg absorbed into it, grilled and tasteless, but for the Smucker's packaged syrup that had to used completely as it continually disappeared into the thick slices.  No sugar added to induce caramelization. No vanilla added for flavor.    ~ The two bread slices stuck together on the plate edge to edge, as it must have grilled, with no effort by the kitchen to separate them for better cooking or more attractive display on the plate.   ~ Bacon deep fried rather than placed on the grill, so that it was tough to chew and tasted of the oil it cooked in.    ~ Decent coffee.   Maybe it was a mistake to order a breakfast special because management sees it as a loss leader and puts almost no effort into preparing it correctly, or it wants to discourage people ordering it a second time. Regardless, it was a major disappointment, and showed a true dismissiveness toward the patrons.   But for the fact that I have gone to Pat's over many years, I would not choose to return.  If I find myself there again, I will order a la carte and see what I get.

Perhaps I am showing my cultural blinders, but I never thought a successful business could be created out of the sale of olive oils and vinegars.  Seemed like a hobby more than an enterprise. Shows how much I know!  Still, I walked into Olive Oil Etcetera, perused the merchandise, and after stifling a disbelieving chuckle, allowed myself to find something to taste.  The little cubes of Italian bread made for a perfect sponge.  I tried a few olive oils infused with garlic and was impressed with the intensity of the herb and the smoothness of the oil base.  Finally, I went for something more wild and personally rewarding.  I found the Black Cherry Balsamic Vinegar...  As in the old standard, "Love Potion Number 9," "I held my nose; I closed my eyes; I took a drink..."   It was truly an amazing sensation. Tart over sweet cherry flavors dominated.  The vinegar offered a plush background ooze in which to savor the coating of my tongue.  It was great!  Yes. I purchased a small bottle that fit easily in my hand. It looked to be a magic potion.  But, when I kissed my lady down at 34th and Vine, I knew that Black Cherry Balsamic  Vinegar was Love Potion #9.  Got to go back for more!!!

Love the location in the heart of Newtown, and very happy they appear to be doing well.  However, this variably topped flatbread is just not pizza. Many love it and are fans or more. I have eaten there a dozen or more times and find it curious, interesting, and mostly satisfying as a healthy alternative meal. Still, when I want real pizza I do not think of Jules.  It does not satisfy me the way a true tomato pie does.  It lacks the cultural affect, the aroma, the bite and crunch, and finally, the taste of traditional Italian pizza.  Too, no one speaks Italian behind the counter.    These are part of the pizza experience that are every bit as important as the actual slice, folded and ready for the big first bite.   Cent Anni!

Pura Vida (Good Life) is a new Costa Rican casa y taberna on Cummings Avenue in old Chambersburg, Trenton, NJ.  A lot of effort has been put into refinishing the outside in stone, while retaining the mid-Twentieth Century dark wood tones of the long bar and dining areas.  The place feels cool and comforting, with HDTVs in every corner playing Latin music videos that most of the customers can sing along with.    My server, Arlene, was smoothly bilingual as she welcomed me and brought me a menu. A picture of grace and beauty.  The food offerings were diverse, but focused primarily on the native cuisine of this Central American nation.  I ordered the "Sandwich Pura Vida" with Chicken, and a fresh Bastida Mora (Raspberry shake).  When it arrived, it was in the form of a Panini, with scorch marks top and bottom, and compressed down with lettuce and tomato showing from the edges.    After squirting on a little mayo from the table rockets, I clamped down for a big bite.  The juicy contents were hot and flavorful, although the chicken was slightly overcooked and dry.  Still, the overall impression was of a zesty, filling torta, well worth the $7 tag.  The accompanying French Fries were crispy and nicely spiced.  The Raspberry frappe was cool, tart, delicious, and made from real berries (not a mix).    I enjoyed my visit to Pura Vida, and it was obvious that the other clientele felt the same, as most were there engaged in conversation long after their meals were done.  This resto joins a growing community of casas Latinas taking root in the capital city; each distinct, yet providing a broad palette of color and exotic rhythms to the streets of Trenton.

Brooklyn Bagels is an open and spacious shop just off County Line Road at the intersection with 2nd Street Pike at the border between Southampton and Huntingdon Valley. It offers a wide variety of traditional and more modern twists on the bagel genre.    The bagels are large.  They have the right mildly crunchy exterior, but an interior that is a little too dense for me. That just means that it is kneaded too long before boiling, removing the air pockets that create a lighter product.  Sometimes the only way to know if the density is wrong is to wait to see what happens in its digestion.  When I get indigestion and a lingering aftertaste, I know it was not quite right.   Still, they use extra large baked onion chips on their bagels, and apply them evenly on both sides. All good.    I am sure that these rounders hold up very well clamping down on a heavy sandwich, and they certainly have their fans.  But for me, a lighter chew is preferable.  In my bagel quest throughout Bucks County, Bagel Train in Yardley comes closest to my desired Golden Fleece.

Taormina's is a newish facility built in the parking area of the Mallard Shopping Center, Richboro.  First impression is very favorable, as it feels cozy and modern with comfortable table and chairs in a medium sized dining room.  The staff is friendly, attentive, and knowledgeable about the menu and specials.    This was our first visit, and came before basketball practice, so we had to eat light.  We limited ourselves to a Cheese Steak and Chicken Parm sandwiches.  The Cheese Steak was the better of the two.  Very tasty on a good Italian Roll.  The Chicken Parm was OK, but falling into the average range of similar fare in the area.  A really nice touch was the plate of Red Pepper and Onion in Olive Oil offered with the bread basket. The former fit perfectly on the later, and the taste was very pleasant, a vastly superior approach to the more traditional pats of butter (also in the basket), or herbed olive oil.    We agreed that we enjoyed our repast, and wanted to return to sample some of the dinners (Francaise, Marsala, aglio olio), pizza, and pizza rolls (never had these before, but have great reviews).    Look for updated review in the next few weeks.

Stopped in mid-afternoon last Saturday.  Really liked what they've done with the place.  The core bar and dining area remains untouched, but there is a large outdoor canvassed patio out back that really expands the possibilities.  This day, a band was tuning up for an early set while a cadre of heavy metal thunder Harleys chilled and waited.   The people working the bar and floor were cool and sweet and handled everyone with grace and humor.  The food (Burger and Roast Pork Sandwiches) were very good.  My Yeungling Draft was cold and thirst quenching.   Haven't met Ralphie yet, but the dude got something going on!   Will be back pronto. Left something with our pleasing server that I really want back.

I was cruising down Maple Avenue, Langhorne, in need for a caffeine break.  Up ahead was what looked to be a fairly new Dunkin Donuts. I parked, went in, and ordered hot java.   To my surprise, the coffee was above average for a DD, and the staff friendly and efficient. They must be hooked up to a good water company for the coffee to be that smooth.

First visit to Cantina Dos Segundos, and the impression was overall positive. Small tables line the sidewalk on a hot night in very late May. People engaged in talk and drink. Lots of smiles and glances.  Stepping inside, hit with a wave of sound from the multitude of conversations at the bar to the right, and dining area to the left.  The bar looks interesting and worth a sit when less crowded. A wall of tequila looks like an arcade game where balls are thrown to knock them down. That would be a shameful waste of great glass.  We were led to a deuce in the very back without a wait at 7:15. As recommended, I had a Blood Orange Margarita (rocks, no salt). The bartender in me marveled at its prompt delivery on a busy night, and the good taste slipping past my lips from the chilled glass. Chips and 2 salsas (Verde slightly better than the Rojo) arrived before we pushed in our chairs.  Generally, I prefer a chunkier salsa with some tropical fruit in it, but this wasn't bad. The chips were not all that tasty, nor textured, but went well with the thinness of the salsa.  The Poblano Chicken Chimichanga was very good, and surprisingly had thin sliced apples inside along with the expected pulled chicken, beans, rice and cheese. I tried the Yuca(sic) Fries, and they were quite good with a Chipotle Mayo dipping sauce rather than ketchup.   The Tilapia Tacos were also pretty good, but the fish could have been more flavorful to compete with the stronger accompaniment in the tortillas. Still, this is not a serious complaint, just a realization that Tilapia may be too mild to handle the heavy chilliness of the spices. Generally, Mexican style seafood is my favorite. (Reminds me of the time in Ensenada...) The waitstaff was friendly, helpful and efficient on a busy Friday night.   Only downside - Poor acoustics and way too noisy for talking.   Certainly come for happy hour and a zillion tequila options. Think twice if you want a romantic evening in a quiet corner.  This is not that place.

Chiarello's Food Market is an old-time Italian deli in a stand alone building on Hamilton Avenue in Hamilton, NJ.  The Trenton designation is more a product of historic postal zones, than a geopolitical demarcation.   It is very small inside, but has a surprisingly well provisioned deli area that takes up at least half the space.  The public area is crammed with pastas and bottled/canned goods to assist in preparing a complete meal.    While it seems certain that their lunch and catering efforts are the primary focus of the business, they are also open early in the morning and advertising breakfast options.  When I inquired about early day sandwiches (ie., Sausage, Egg & Cheese), I was advised that such nourishment was not available.  They did have a few bagels, muffins and pour-your-own java for my crowd.    I opted for a Bagel, Butter and Cheese with a small cuppa joe to go.  The bagel was clearly not from their oven and was not exactly fresh.  The taste was okay, but required extra chewing to get it down.  The coffee was that Law brand; clearly offered merely as a convenience without an attempt at truly good café.    Overall, Chiarello's is not a morning place, but I might return for one of their more auspicious sandwich creations.
Can't speak to the rest of the menu this cold and rainy Friday morning, but this place certainly has hot decent coffee at a great price ($1. for any size joe).   Service for the drive thru was fine.

This Acme in the Village of Newtown Shopping Center recently underwent a makeover to bring it into the 21 Century.  The two main improvements were the new beer aisle and Starbucks, both very near the right side entrance to the supermarket, just beyond the bakery.    These in house coffee shops are a version of the outlets found in airports around the world. A decent work area for the crew, with smaller units for pastries and light fare, and very limited displays for their branded coffee and accessories.   The mermaid has been here about six months and they are efficient in their operation.  One early evening this week it was well staffed with a friendly crew ready to serve.  The barista kept her poise as she mixed my Chai Latte. Never missed a beat in our repartee. The others were cleaning up in anticipation of closing within the hour.    Perhaps, because they see the same customers routinely, but this shop was far better in its customer service than the equivalent business in an airport.  They show that the opportunity to build relationships enhances the overall experience.  No doubt, for both parties.   Even this Starbucks-phobe found this captive distribution point enjoyable.  It even made their drinks taste better somehow.   Good job!

Getting back to basics, all I wanted was the original double patty Elevation Burger, straight up with ketchup, jalapenos, and hot pepper relish. No fries. No shake. No sweet drinks.   That was exactly what was delivered to my high top several minutes later. It came neatly wrapped in a plain brown paper sleeve. Upon opening, there was copious grease dripping from the wrapper. The chef must have added that after grilling, because the burger itself was no overly wet.   It tasted great. There must be something to that organic, hormone free, free range cattle from whence the beef puck comes. The texture was soft, and the flavor, excellent. Definitely a step above 5 Dudes, and on par with Shake Shack at a lower price point. Reminded of Burgatory, one of my faves in the Pittsburgh, PA area. Priced right at around $7 for the sandwich.   Fries started at $3.50, and shakes, $5. Add those and pretty soon you have an expensive lunch on your hands. Without, the burger justifies itself every time.

Jack's Cold Cuts & Catering (aka Jack's Deli) on Street Road in Bensalem, Pa., has been around for a while making fat sandwiches and catering local parties.  When we walked in around 8:30 one morning last week, they were busy stocking up on the provisions that had just been delivered by the bakery.  We were looking for breakfast, and Jack waved us to a booth with a smile as he carried a large tray of breads to their bin.    The coffee wasn't made yet, so we knew it would be fresh.  We ordered a couple of sandwiches (Sausage, Egg & Cheese on Kaiser, Pepper, Egg & Cheese on Croissant), and settled in to the sound of the staff getting ready for the day.  The place is old enough to need a little TLC, but it is bright and airy.    Our meals arrived in plastic baskets a few minutes later.  They were hot and melty, but not best of breed.  Run of the mill roll and croissant, and average innards.  Adequate, but not calculated to win any awards.  The coffee was on the same level.  Okay.    Jack's advertises that it is a "Jewish Style Deli."  Maybe.  It does have the smoked meats and East European breads and soups that identify that cuisine.  But, it has ample pork products for the rest of the customers.    Jack's seems like a place that is loved by people who have grown up on their dishes, but more objectively is happy to be quite average.

Zen Den Coffee Shop is sort of an alley operation, running out of a back door on the narrow Donaldson Street, between Oakland and State Streets, in Doylestown.  I first discovered it a few months ago when visiting my attorney who also has a rear entrance backing onto the semi-hidden shops in between the main streets and small pocket parking lots.  Finally stopped in yesterday to grab some Joe and have a look.    First impression was that the space is much larger than anticipated.  The floor plan is spread out in two rooms, with many comfortable spots to settle in on a sofa, or work at a table.  There is even room for a piano in the middle of the main room.  The work space is in a corner by the entrance, which might be a problem if crowded, but when I arrived shortly after 11, there was only one person ahead of me on line.  I liked the vibe with all the natural colors and clubby furniture.  The southern orientation allowed sunlight to filter in softly in winter, creating a warm glowing ambiance.  I got the "Zen" reference, but doubted there would be much opportunity to meditate or chant there.  Caffeine takes people in another direction.    I went with a Café Au Lait and Blueberry Muffin for my first try.  The price was under $5, so I immediately thought it compared favorably to the Star$$$ of the world, where the same would have been a few bucks more.  The taste of the coffee was okay, but nothing special.  Likewise, the muffin while fresh, had a commercial bakery quality to it. Certainly edible, but lacking a spark of organic energy.    I will return to obtain a more representative sampling of the goods @ ZD, but at first blush, it seems a nice place for coffee and conversation, but not necessarily the first place I would think of for outstanding coffee.    Nonna's is the place to go for that.

We were looking for a solid Polish restaurant to satisfy our craving for pierogis.  Alexander's Café was the nearest to our location, although not exactly in the neighborhood. We found it after a twisted course mapped by my GPS.  It sits below the train tracks on Park Avenue in Elkins Park, in a nicely renovated early 20th Century building.  Walking in, the impression was of exposed red brick walls and highly polished dark wood floors.    It didn't feel Polish, and after sitting at a white tableclothed table and perusing the menu, it clearly wasn't only that.  There were more Italian and American dishes offered, with only a small piece of the list for East European cuisine.  That the solitary server was Asian helped complete the comfortable, yet disjointed, gestalt of the house.   Still, we ordered a mixed plate of pierogis along side the Chicken Parmesan Special, and a bowl of Cream of Broccoli Leek Soup.  We wanted to share everything, and we were provided separate bowls and plates of each dish.  It was a very strong touch of class and customer accommodation (See Photos).   The Soup was silky smooth and steaming.  The leek announced itself dominant to the broccoli, which was the way I liked it.  Fresh toasted croutons floated on top.  They were well seasoned and lightly crunchy.  The Pierogis were potato/cheese, sauerkraut and beef in unusually soft dough dumpling shell.  Excellent with a sautéed onion and chive garnish. We had four apiece; just enough for a co-staring role with the Chicken.  The bird was fresh (never frozen), pan fried in olive oil and breaded lightly.  The red gravy was homemade with a mild spiciness. The mozza was very new, and melted easily, without covering the color and texture beneath.  Quite tasty.    The shop was short a server that night, and our man was forced into hard labor to keep up.  He never lost his poise, but the time between courses and receiving our check was longer than necessary due to his need to be in overdrive all evening. Not on him at all, and we showed our appreciation.  Still, management has responsibility to assure service is impeccable if they are to receive highest rank.    Alexander's Café is a good place for dinner on a cold night, as long as you understand that it is not completely a Polish house.  Street parking can be challenging.

All reviews are in the end subjective.  Sometimes all the variables are evaluated, but in other instances one aspect so dominates that the other pieces are minimized by comparison.  For me, when the atmosphere of a restaurant so overcomes me with a sense of comfort and well being that the food or service tends to fade quickly, I react emotionally and start to fall in love with the entire experience.  I can't help it. I'm a hopeless romantic.   So it was with Coffee Cup Café on Bellevue Avenue, just off one of the ugly parts of business Route 1. I had seen the place for years, but was never tempted to stop and frisk the joint until reading the Yelp reviews.  It seemed like a decent place for breakfast, so I set aside a morning when not too busy to stop in.    Stepping inside after parking on the street in front, I immediately felt the effect of time warping taking me to circa 1980.  An old counter with about 6 or 7 spinners, and large kitchen service window in the wall behind, and more classic coffee mugs hanging on the walls than I could count. There was a nice size dining room to the side, and another tiny one right in front of the building.  Everything white with blue trim.    Then Beth approached from behind the counter and asked if I wanted coffee.  "Yes, Mam," as I took in her vivacious eyes and well-tatted skin.  Well, all right!  This woman had a story to tell, and I hoped she would share it.  After mentioning this was my first visit, she gave me the history of Coffee Cup Café back through the early 1970's.  She was second generation ownership, and her son, Jesse, working the kitchen grill would be the third.  She was proud and loud, and she was a groove. She welcomed me to look around, and even step into the galley for a photo.   The food?  It was just fine.  Coffee hot and fresh.  Breakfast sandwich loaded on a Kaiser roll and able to fill my happy stomach.  I could have hung out there all morning. I felt like a friend and guest of the house.  Some places are just that way.  How many coffee mugs are found in Coffee Cup Café?    I'll never tell.

Sometimes the best part of the retail shopping experience is not what you buy, but the advice that you get.    This was born out last weekend when visiting the Jo-Ann Fabric and Craft Store that is located next to the Best Buy on Commerce Blvd in Fairless Hills, across the Oxford Valley Road from the shopping mall that bears that name.    In need of new drapes, but without a clue about how or where to buy them (excuse me for lacking domestication), my idea was to buy fabric and somehow make drapes.  Simple, right? How wrong I was.  Take that approach and you end up at Jo-Ann walking up and down aisles full of bolts of fabric, trying to decide what would look good in that room.  I just got a headache.  Before walking out, I made the smart move of asking the woman behind the fabric counter how to deal with the "drape thing."  She was wise in the ways of the world.  Smiling, she whispered so no one but me could hear her; "You don't buy them here unless you want to spend a lot and then hire someone to cut and sew them for you.  I suggest you go to another store not so far from here that specializes in premade window dressings of all types.  They have a large collection and have good prices."    Confirming the spelling of the other place, I thanked her for the exact assistance I needed, and walked back to my car to see if I could find it on Yelp.  I did. That review to come.   Solid advice for the uninitiated.  True customer service.

That's quite a lot of braggadocio for a tiny Chinese takeout shop on the bad side of Brunswick Avenue in Trenton, NJ. Actually, there is no good side in that part of town. Of course, it is just advertising; meaning that none of that name is true.   This chop shop is state of the art dumpy and depressing. The woman at the order station is friendly enough, but the kitchen help spends a lot of time staring out at the customers. Just a little weird. Whether eating in or taking away, the food is served in the same closed take out containers. Plastic and styro all the way. Chinese tea? Bring yours from home.   It's not that the grub is bad, it is about average for a joint that doesn't much care about you, and assumes you know nothing about Chinese/American food. The wonton soup, pork egg foo young and fried rice were recognizable by sight and taste. Yellow dye chicken stock, thick skinned dumplings, day old yellow chunky rice - just the way they taught them in mail order cooking school.    Edible, but forgettable.

Staples is a cornucopia of office supplies.   Much like Home Depot for home repairs, or Cabella's for all things outdoors, this warehouse provides multiple alternatives for anything you need to run your office, prepare your kids for school, and even large colorful tins of Danish butter cookies for your office kitchen.   While not always the most competitive in price compared to the catalogue and online outfits, when a shop like Staples is in your town, and you can eyeball and touch the things you need before you take them home or to the office, there is an obvious advantage to the consumer that makes the cost differential worthwhile.  It is the only place I buy my calendar for the new year, and I admit to being amazed and amused by the variety of paperclips available.   If there is a shortcoming (and the basis for not shouting, "Woohoo!") it is that the staffing is meager and there are seldom enough workers on the floor to help out finding things.    Still, I am very happy to have Staples in Newtown.

Christine's Restaurant is difficult to figure.   First blush, the space is warm and cozy in a clubby kind of way, with lots of dark wood tones, white tablecloths, and plenty of windows.  All good.  Then, the menu says it is an Italian shop, which is something of a surprise as it gives no hint of its ethnic orientation.  So what? If the food is good Italian I don't care if it looks like a rib joint.   Next, checking the menu, it offers breakfast until 1:00. The prime item is Eggs Benedict - not exactly created in Palermo.  The breakdown is in Sandwiches/Wraps; Burgers; Pasta; Salads, and Entrees.  The pasta is the only strong hint that maybe this is where their specialty resides, but I am thinking, "Pasta in this place?" I still didn't get that this was home base for the kitchen.  So, I had the Florentine Chicken Sandwich and a side of Classic Caesar Salad.    The wedgie was grilled chicken, garlic sauteed spinach, with a melted cheese over the top.  I think the menu said the cheese was pepper jack, which would have been better than the too mild provolone that dressed the other main ingredients.  Too, the roll it came out on was fresh, but not Italian crusty.  It was a little non-descript, and although it carried the sandwich, failed to really pull its weight.  I left most of it on the plate to concentrate on the spinach and chicken.  It was not worth the calories.    On the other hand, the Caesar was quite good, with crisp romaine, homecrunched croutons, and a decent creamy dressing.  It actually saved the day, as it more than complements the sandwich.  If anything, it was the other way around.    The whole experience was a little topsy turvy. The side became the star of the show, and the supposedly dominant aspect of the plate was left in partial obscurity.    The staff was friendly, informed and timely.    There seems to be an identity crisis at Christine's.  Once it finishes therapy I will gladly return to see what they decided to become.

I rarely get to this part of Levittown, but I had a date with Levittown Printing just down Haines Road and decided to look for a breakfast place where I could hang out until they opened.  Yelp led me to Violetwood Café, yet another of those quiet gardens hidden from plain sight in a strip commercial center that has seen far better days.  The café is brightly painted and staffed by a cadre of black T- shirted servers who have a very positive attitude about their restaurant and seem to enjoy their jobs.  I sat down in a booth toward the back and had a mug of coffee in front of me within a minute. It was fine. The menu had both the popular usual suspects for breakfast, plus a few permanent house specials as well as a daily black board.    My Sausage Scramble (I think that was it) was a large mountain of Egg, Italian Sweet Sausage, Onion, Peppers, topped with Provolone.  It was moist, and chunky and fun to eat.  The Rye Toast was a real loaf complete with Caraway Seeds.    Violetwood Café is a 4 Star performer, and could easily move up.

Mr. China in the Pennington Road Shopping Center, Trenton, NJ, actually surprised me with its cleanliness and decent lunch offerings. The space while primarily for takeout, also has eight booths for people like me who prefer to eat in in relative comfort when the food is hot.   Service was friendly and smiling.  The house mother took orders, worked the cash register and delivered my General Tso's Chicken to me.  It was actually on a ceramic plate, not a takeout container, a big plus. The meal was pretty good for a generic well known dish. There was ample chicken. The breading was not overly thick, and the sauce was freshly made with chili flakes noticeable in the dark amber covering. The fried rice was a weak point, as it was mass produced with a yellow dye and few veggies, meat or egg.    With a bottle of Snapple, it was a $7 deal.   It was A-OK!

DeLorenzo's Pizza sits in the corner of the old strip Fairview Shopping Center on Trenton Road, Fairless Hills, Pa.  As the saying goes, "...Nothing is less fair than living in the Hills..." The oldest part of the establishment where the cashier is, is tiny with 2 tables.  It has its old Bucks charm, but is certainly gritty round the edges.  Only one table was available for this solitary traveler, as the other was being used as the office by the owner/manager (who spoke with a pronounced Russian accent).    The staff was friendly and the young cooks seemed to know what they were doing.  The most unusual aspect for this pizza joint was that it lacked the display of all their pizza option, so prevalent in most shops these days.  No. They had only one regular pie behind the counter, and they were willing to put anything you wanted on top of it.  (Well, maybe not ANYTHING...) That was refreshingly old school. At least I knew they weren't in the habit of making a multitude of pizzas with various toppings just so customers could pick from among them, even if they had been sitting there all day.  I ordered one plain slice and a sweet Italian Sausage triangle.    They arrived well done as I wished.  The regular slice had a good crunch, but leaked a bit of oil when tilted.  The taste was good.  The Sausage slice had been thickly spread with crumbled meat, yet it held up well.  The taste was even better.  This snack with a small Coke came in under $5. I threw the change into the tip jar.    The other side of the house had a dim, but pleasant appearing dining room.  The patrons all had large plates of food before them.  Looked interesting.   If I return, I will sit over there so I can join the other diners, rather than watch the boss train the servers and pay his bills.

FireGirl Mexican Kitchen sits in a less than state of the art strip mall on Street Road in Bensalem, Pa.  Word is that in a past life it was also a Mexican joint called Tortilla Flats.  Someone has a talent for interesting names.   We stopped in on Sunday for a late lunch in the midst of shopping in the vicinity. The large room was brightly painted with unusual lighting fixtures and plenty of tables, low and high, for dining.  Ordered were taken at the back cashier stand by a friendly native who was happy to explain how their system worked, and to quickly agree that their Flautas were a good way to go.    They arrived at our high top about 10 minutes later.  Rather than the normal flute-like crunchy tubes stuffed with Chicken, Cheese, and Peppers, this version was more of a roll up or wrap. The three filled tortillas had been sliced amidship after deep fryin, and were still soft rather than rigid.  In the middle of the plastic basket were small containers of Guacomole, Salsa, Cheese Sauce and Sour Cream.  While we were waiting we located the Hot Sauce Bar against the rear side wall, and brought back several small cups of various blasters to try with our meal.  All were good, but the Spicy Peach Sauce was far and away our favorite due to its sweet/heat quotient.  Tasted great poured onto each Flauta and immediately consumed.    The order was enough for both of us.  The taste was fine, if not completely authentic.  It was definitely designed for the American palette, which is not a bad thing.  They know their audience.    I don't get to this part of Street Road often, but will be returning in a few weeks to pick up something ordered at the curtain shop next door.  If hungry when I arrive, I would not mind returning to FireGirl to see what else they have in the kitchen.

Freddie's Tavern on Railroad Avenue, Ewing, NJ, is an old line Italian house within a mansion across from the West Trenton Railroad Station. It has a large square bar with tables on the edges, and a couple of large dining rooms. The space is carpeted with heavy curtains, and gives off the sense of at one time being a club to bring business associates or family for traditional boot dining and entertainment. New ownership took over fairly recently, but the place looks the same as before, with the exception of live music in the bar a few nights a week.   We sat in the bar at a hightop, ordered two drafts (Sam Adams Winterbrew & Stella Artois), and pulled a large Nonna's Margharita Pie, Calamari and bowl of French Onion Soup from the thick menu. While there, the band started playing Eagles covers in the opposite corner of the room. They were pretty good for a Tuesday night, so we hung around longer than normal to catch a few extra tunes.   The grub was good for bar food. The squid was a touch over deep fried, but still tasted good with their excellent dipping red sauce. It included tentacles, always a plus. The soup was sealed in melted gruyere, had a strong beef stock and a load of soft sweet onions and saturated bread within. Enjoyable. The pizza was a decent rendition of the Italian flag - red sauce, white mozzarella and green basil - on a thin crisp crust. It was good, but not in the pantheon of amazing bar pies found around the capital area.  All in all, we were quite satisfied with our night at Freddy's, and agreed we would def return to satisfy our  need for Roman cuisine or burgers. For me, it was nice to be back in the bar I spend much time in during my younger days.   Felt just like old times with older people, including me.

Apparently, China Express has been at the corner of S. Olden Avenue and Liberty Street in Hamilton, NJ, for several years, but managed to eluded Yelp detection.  Those hidden days are over now, and it is time for this small primarily take out joint to come out of the shadows.    The house has a couple of booths and tables for those who prefer to dine in, but even the house sitters get their General Tso's in styro and plastic.  No concession to customers who actually eat what they cooked in front of them.    My lunch special was pretty much down the middle of what is generally offered in these places.  Massive amounts of pre-dyed yellow pork fried rice with small pieces of meat and veggies, along with heavily glooped chicken pieces; breaded, fried and doused in mostly sweet amber jacket.  Nothing new under this sun.   It was neither better nor worse than most of the others of this genre.  Edible, if not inspiring.  At under $6., plus the cost of a drink, it was what was expected.    Ownership is friendly and efficient, and they keep the house bright and clean.  Best part is the small parking lot right next door.

Wild Ginger III in the Logan Square Shopping Center, New Hope, has a great name and suggests a deep excursion into the jungles of Southeast Asia. The layout of the restaurant reinforced that sensibility with huge tropical fish tanks and beautiful blue, green and indigo neon lit walls and ceiling.   It is an auspicious beginning for a new guest, although the fishy smell permeating the room from both the tanks and sushi bar do detract from the gestalt somewhat. Unfortunately, that is not where the disappointment ends.   I was there for the Thai and Chinese offerings of its fusion menu. Tom Kar (lemongrass/coconut milk soup), Pad Kee Mao and Szechuan Beef were my choices. I planned to eat the first two in house and take the third home for later consumption by the family working until later that evening. I like spicy dishes unadulterated forward the western pallette, so I asked for the hottest rendition available. I wasn't kidding, but the kitchen didn't believe me.   The soup had plenty of fresh veggies and sweet coconut juice, but lacked the kick of lemongrass. It wasn't in the pot!  Rather than red chili infused broad drunken noodles in a super heated brown sauce, what I got was actually sweet to my tongue, without a hint of the desired fire. I had to send it back to be reworked. It returned, the same noodles, but with some chili sauce or ground Szechuan red peppers or paste mixed in. It wasn't integrated, but I spun it for a moment and it was acceptable. Shame, because the noodles, veggies and chicken were all tender and done well.   At home we dug into the Szechuan Beef over rice. Again, it looked great and properly wokked, but without a sign of red chili pepper. It was hot as requested, but the burn came from chili powder or paste thrown into the sauce that attached itself to the meat far more that the broccoli, onions and green peppers. Not bad, but clearly prepared by a kitchen lacking the right ingredients to actually produce a Szechuan dish correctly.   Disappointing.  Wild Ginger is a misnomer. "Mild Ginger," is closer to the truth. Another case of Asian confusion, not fusion.

Liberty Two Diner (Freedom to Dine) was a good place to stop for lunch on my way north on Rt. 130 in Bordentown, NJ.  It doesn't look like much at 50 mph, but at speeds slow enough to allow for a seat at the 10 spinner counter, it had everything necessary for a solid meal.  Friendly service, large menu, Cecilware coffee maker, and small bowl of soup with every sandwich.    The Navy Bean potage was surprisingly good, loaded with white beans and well-stewed veggies in a mild tomato base.  Liked it a lot.  Followed on by a Chicken Salad Sandwich on Rye toast, which was tasty and filling.  Perhaps, not as chunky as I prefer, but still fresh, cool, and plentiful.  The side of French Fries was way over the top, but the few I sampled were hot and crisp.  Beware opening the ketchup bottle (It discharges on its own).   All this, and change for $7., plus tip.    I'll be back.

The owners of Pin Wei Chinese Restaurant on S. Henderson Road, King of Prussia, PA, may be Taiwanese, but they have taken the time to understand and produce first quality Szechuanese cuisine in the heart of Montgomery County. They have mastered the mysteries of extremely spicy sauces and cooking techniques that create the unique numbing style that finds its source in the history of Chengdu and Chongqing, China.  There aren't many of these authentic houses around, and when one is found it automatically shoots to the top of the list of great dinner spots.  From the size of the crowd waiting for tables last night, the secret is out.   This was our first visit, after looking mostly in vain for a Szechuan chili joint that knew what it was doing.  There are a few in Philly, and a couple in nearby Jersey, but by and large, the art of flamethrower dishes is a lost art.  We were very happily impressed with Pin Wei.   We ordered more than we could finish in one sitting, so we would have enough to take home and enjoy a second time.  Our choices consisted of: Scallion Oil Cucumber as an appetizer, and entrees of Chicken Dry Chili Peppers, Lamb Dry Pot, Twice Cooked Fish, and Deep Fried Longhots.   In a word; FIRE!   The cucumbers were served cold and marinating in the clear scallion oil.  Crisp, cool, mildly hot and a great introduction.  The platters arrived as they were finished in the kitchen, not all at once, in the traditional Chinese custom.  The longhots arrived next.  They were beautiful to behold - like dark green snakes coiled on themselves waiting for someone to bite them to release their venom.  Awesome, as each chew released more toxin, burning the gums and walls of the mouth, and bringing tears to the eyes.  Eventually, the scald tempered, and the underlying flavor of these peppers emerged transcendent.   The chicken dry pepper was a sight to behold, with a huge amount of small red Szechuan chilies, garlic, ginger, onion and small pieces of breaded and twice deep fried chicken mixed throughout.  The chili powder on the morsels was a powerful, sinus clearing, blast.  With every wonderful crunch more capsaicin was released, bringing the mouth to near full numbness.  Got to love that feeling to appreciate its otherworldliness. The lamb dry pot arrived next, and we were thankful for a little relief from the conflagration.  The meat was tender with a gentle sweetness beneath the cumin and other stimulants.  Plenty of mushrooms to absorb the dark sauce at the bottom of the heated metal bowl.  Excellent.  Finally, the twice cooked fish arrived. There was a small glitch when after waiting a while, the wrong dish came to the table - twice cooked pork (belly), which looked good, but, alas, was not what we ordered. Ten more minutes to get the right platter.  It was terrific, saving best for last.  Fish fillets, slightly crisp, yet also soft within, with a dark sauce that hinted of vinegar in addition to the less dominant burning powders.  I had to ask our server what that unusual taste was, but he just smiled and demurred.  Inscrutable.   The secrets of Pin Wei were safe with him. After all, he was the owner, and he didn't want us trying to replicate his magic elixirs at home. He didn't want to be responsible for what might happen.  HOT Damn, people!   PRO TIP - How does Pin Wei compare with Han Dynasty in Old City?  Food wise, it is a very close call.  Both are excellent, and there is no point in picking one over the other based on the kitchen.  Where there is some separation is in the atmospherics.  Pin Wei is a small place compared to Chestnut Street.  The dining room is very crowded and thus quite loud.  It is a bit distracting. HanDynasty is in an old bank building, and although busy, possesses more nooks and crannies where it is possible to feel some level of  privacy, even in the crowd. The front of Pin Wei was packed with people waiting for tables, and we almost had to fight our way out after dinner. The bar area was SRO, while Han has a larger bar zone, which seldom feels overwhelmed with people.  It is obvious than the success of Pin Wei, is also its shortcoming.  It needs a much bigger space.  Whether it wants it or not is a separate question.

I really enjoy the adaptive reuse of old factories in the heart of the city. What Conshohocken Brewing @ Bridgeport (Norristown) has done with this old gal is impressive. In addition to a utilitarian black brick with exposed steel and large windows, these guys brew up some very tasty and interesting suds, and have a dynamite kitchen.  Three strikes and you win!   So, we stopped in on a rainy afternoon to celebrate a significant milestone (securing a driver's license), and found a table on the first floor.  The space had a long wall divider separating the bar from the dining area. There was a metal grate stairway to a second floor retreat that might have been a cool place to hang on a crowded, hoppy night.  We ordered a flight of four drafts, and a lunch of their Brussel sprout app., Fiesta Tacos, and Harvest Salad.  The beers were: Puddlers Row ESB, Burn Everything Rye Porter, Glazing Saddles, and Viking Funeral.  They were 4 ounce samples of their extensive custom brew list.  All were distinctly different, some more appealing to my palate than others.    The ESB had a strong hoppiness, while the Burn Everything, a dominant bitters flavor.  I enjoyed the Glazing Saddles (were there really local donuts in the fermentation?), and the Viking Funeral, which was extra dark with a honey chocolate taste.  Liked these last two a lot.   The food surprised me on the up side.  The Brussels were roasted with parmigiana  cheese and pork bellies.  The were scorched and delicious.  I've been trying to make these at home, but never as good as these dudes.  The tacos were loaded with corn, beans, tomato, lettuce, and some other things wrapped in warm tortillas.  Very good.  The salad was full of dried cranberries, walnuts, romaine, gorganzolla and more leafy stuff in an excellent vinaigrette.  More than I could consume.  We took half the salad and a few remaining sprouts home in a neat black box.   If I was more a beer man, this place although a distance from home, would be a regular stop on the pilsner trail. Make that bourbon and I could be convinced to ride the circuit and tempt the traffic demigods on the PA Pike between Bridgeport and Bucks frequently.  Still, I read that the burgers are exceptional, so at least one more visit is foreseeable.

Tutti Frutti is a frozen yogurt shop in the Oxford Valley Plaza; the same commercial center that holds Bone Fish Grill.  The set up is a bit strange.  Upon walking in, there were a couple of tables and a shelf on the wall with paper cups for the yogurt.  However, the actual handles for dispensing the cool sweetness were in the perpendicular wall and not visible from the entrance.  Beyond that lies the toppings bar and cashier.  The back of the store cannot see the front, nor the machines without cameras.  Def not designed for functionality, nor safety.  The Yogurt?  There were five or six double machines capable of independent pouring or a mix of the two.  I opted for the French Vanilla, Peanut Butter and Cookies & Cream, with room for some blackberries, mini-Reece's, and wet pecans.    Unfortunately, none of them had much taste.  The vanilla was completely invisible on the tongue.  The peanut butter was recognizable, but weak.  The cookies & cream offered a glimpse of chocolate cookie, but the cream was absent without leave.  Not sure how the store manages to mess up the recipes, or maybe that is what is expected.  Not nearly as good as just eating regular yogurt.    There are many excellent ice cream alternatives in this area (Dairy Delight, Jo-Jo's, even Friendly's, to name a few), that it makes little sense to seek out Tutti Frutti for dessert decadence.     "So Fresh"  "So Light"  "So Tasty" ?  Not So Much.

Taqueria Aguila (Eagle) is really two places in one.  First, it is La Mexicana grocery store, with a great bakery and other standard items for la cocina. Second, it is a taqueria, with hot kitchen on wheels in back grilling up excellent plates of pork, beef and chicken for a variety of menu items from tacos to tortas and full dinners. In fact, the whole operation is turned around, with entrance in the rear leading to the tienda, and a dozen or so tables in back (front) for dining in. There is table service, but most of the trade is cash and carry.   I figured this out recently when I arrived looking for dinner, read the sign on the front (back) door leading me to the rear of the building, where the entrada was, right next to a shiny stainless steel trailer cooking away and scenting the air with all manner of delicious aromas. While they don't have everything listed on their printed menu, they do have the tacos, burritos, quesadillas and various specials available. I was happy to go with two Tacos Al Pastor and fresh Watermelon juice. At $2.99 per taco, and $3.00 for  large glass of refreshing red bebida, I thought the price right, if the meal was up to snuff.  And, it was.   The double layered tortilla rolled taco had plenty of tasty pineapple infused grilled slivers of pork, onion, peppers and crema, with lime wedges and sliced radish as garnish. A little squirt of hot sauce, a dribble of red/green salsa, and I was good to go. They were excellent - hot, crisp and a glorious mouthful to chew with a smile. The watermelon (la sandia), was cool, sweet and so refreshing. Like eating right from the totally absorbed fruit and crushing it in my mouth. Hard not to smile and let some of that delight run down my chin.   Yes. This joint is a little divey, but that adds to its authenticity. Mixed furniture thrown together over somewhat unswept floors, just adds to the impression that for the moment you have entered Juarez or Mexicali, and departed the USA without your passport.   I felt great solidarity with our Mexican brethren last weekend. This was the fastest way to travel to their side and join them in common cause.

Bagel appreciation is very subjective.    One person's phantasm is another persons disappointment. So, it is important to keep that in mind when evaluating a rounder experience.   This became paramount when I stopped by Abington All Star Bagel on Rt. 611.  The shop was small and clean.  The staff, friendly and helpful.  The bagels in the display, real beauties.  I ordered my standard Onion Bagel with butter and Swiss, and took the bag to go.    Upon opening the white sack, and unfolding its wrappings, I beheld a large, lovely, heavily onion flaked top, which still carried the aroma of its freshness.  First bite confirmed its recent vintage, and also that it was quite dense and firmly chewy.  Many like this texture in their bagels, but I prefer a crunchier skin and light, airy innards.    This was not that, but I appreciated the quality of the product nonetheless.  While I would not seek out All Star for my frequent bagel fix, there are others who will find these dough tires the cat's meow.   Freedom of Choice!

La Chapinita is a Guatemalan house on Chambers Street, Trenton, NJ.  The space was the famous home of Papa's Tomato Pies, and the look is the same now as then, with the exception of Spanish signs and futbol games on the HDTVs.  The booths that once bore great tomato pies, are now primarily for Guatemaltecans to enjoy the superior comidas that come out of the new kitchen.    The place is clean, with Tiffany-style light fixtures descending from the ceiling, and a very friendly, bilingual staff ready to assist this first time customer.  The lunch menu is fairly comprehensive with variations of beef, chicken and pork used as primary ingredients in styles Asada, Empanizada, a la Mexicana and Encebollado. They also do the traditional Tostados, Quesadillas, Burritos, Tortillas and Tacos. I ordered the Pechuga Empanizada (Breaded Chicken Cutlet with Rice and Black Beans), and Jugos Naturales de Pina (Pineapple Juice). The plate came with Black Beans and White Rice.    It was very big for a lunch.  There were two large, thin breaded chicken breasts, lightly browned, with a wedge of lime for seasoning.  A couple of raw onion rings, slices of radish, and a pile of lettuce completed the performance.  I cut everything with my fork and enjoyed every bite.  All was tasty, complementary, and filling (I did not finish the rice).  The Pineapple Juice was cool and refreshing with a nice bite of just juiced pulpy fruit.    This was an excellent lunch in a comfortable setting.  At under $10 for everything (plus tip), I was very satisfied, and happy that another historic Italian house was now transformed into an equally qualified newcomer from Central America.   Buena Suerte!

Cryo Spa Natural Healing Center in the Holland Shopping Center, Holland, PA, is a holistic alternative health services center at the intersection of Holland and Buck Roads. It can be a little challenging to reach if coming down Buck Road, but with patience the traffic and red lights can be overcome.  It is well worth your effort to find your way there.   Although cryotherapy (exposing your body to extremely cold temperature for a short period of time to deal with autoimmune conditions through the release of endorphins and anti-inflammatory proteins) is the main attraction, I was there on a first visit for a full body massage to address lingering lower back issues. I was greeted promptly by the front desk person, who asked me to complete three pages of information regarding my medical history and reason for coming. Before I was finished, my masseuse Marla was introducing herself with warm smile and firm handshake.   Before starting the massage, I was also introduced to Lucy, the owner of the facility.  She offered to give me a quick tour.  She showed me the cryotherapy equipment, shiatsu and mediation rooms, and finally the massage chamber where Marla would attempt to loosen my lumbar/sacral spine and take my discomfort away.  The place is bigger than it looks from the outside, and Lucy was very knowledgeable about all the modalities offered.    When it was time to start my massage, Marla directed me to disrobe and get under the sheets on the table, face down on the headrest. She left the room while I did so. Upon returning, she asked a few questions about the strength of the massage desired (strong), and instructed me to tell her if I was experiencing pain (Don't worry. I don't deal with pain in silence.) She explained that she would be doing a combination of stretches, deep tissue, pressure point and Swedish techniques which she labeled as, "Sports Massage."    She was amazing.  Her hands intuitively found the discomfort in my back and legs, and dug, kneaded, lifted/stretched my joints, and actually moved the muscles, tendons and ligaments around to release their tension and help them find their proper place in my body alignment. She had incredible strength, and was able to lift each leg, pull it further upward, while manipulating the musculature and joints. All the while, we conversed quietly about how I was feeling, giving me directions to help her, and informing me about her experience in massage and healthcare.  Fascinating woman.  Excellent healer.   After my hour, I arose slowly.  I felt looser and longer.  More significantly, a sense of wellbeing and mild euphoria surrounded me. I was extremely relaxed and felt a limberness and flexibility that had been absent for a long while. I slept very well last night.   This morning, even as I write this review, my body feels like it is glowing. I know I will return to CryoSpa regularly to maintain and improve this sensation of health, strength and vitality.   Marla did great work. I also want to give the Shiatsu a try, and if brave enough, go into the cryospa itself to see what that can do.   Totally positive first impression.

When a comfort food restaurant is empty at 7:30 pm on a Sunday night, there is reason to think that perhaps that is saying something about the operation there. That was what we faced on a damp March night, but we were already inside, and as the old saying goes: "What the hey?!"   Turns out that with the smoker out front, and a good chef in the kitchen, the food was pretty good.  Only problem was the slightly weird attitude of management that wanted our business, but at the same time had a series of rules they felt compelled to enforce while we ordered. First, they were closing in 30 minutes, which meant we had to order quickly.  We could eat inside while they cleaned up.  Second, our sandwiches came with fries, but any other side order was an extra buck. I wanted baked beans. Okay, bud, but fork over the sawback. Third, a medium burger wasn't possible because the health code required everything be grilled to well done.  What if I didn't like an over cooked burger?  They couldn't help me officially, but they did ask the chef to take it off the heat while still pink.  He said he would with a wink.   Ultimately, the brisket sandwich was quite tasty, with a nice rub making a flavorful bark.  It might have benefited from another hour in the smoker to make the beef more tender, but it was decent as it was.  My Firehouse Burger was very good, with nicely sautéed/grilled onions and peppers.  Half pound of ground beef was truly pink at its core, and proved a challenge to consume despite its excellent juicy profile.  The baked beans were also solidly flavorful, but could have used a few chunks of burnt ends or pulled pork in the mix to max out the texture and provide more twang.   The dining room was small, but comfortable, with Texas collectibles hanging for ceiling and wall. I would return to try the ribs or another burger, but not before I visited other nearby grillmasters to check out their goods.  I wasn't blown away by Fat Jack's, but neither was I repelled by their chuck wagon grub.

Number One Chinese Restaurant sits in the 700 block of South Broad Street, Trenton, NJ.  To be kind, it is not exactly the sweetest spot in the capital city to find an eating house, let alone one that had been there for 26 years under the same ownership.  Still, there is a reason it has survived, and maybe even prospered over time.    There is room for eating in, even though the vast majority of customers order to take out. The man in charge is warm and humorous, and his very ancient looking Confucian beard has turned white. When I asked for his recommendation for lunch, he promptly said the Chicken in Garlic Sauce was the way to go.  Who was I to disagree?   The plate arrived about 10 minutes later.  It was styro, but at least it wasn't served in a to go box.  It was accompanied with brown rice, and an egg roll, and too thin napkins.  There were ample strips of chicken and plenty of pepper, onion, carrot, pea pod, mushroom, water chestnut and baby corn.  The garlic sauce was noticeable, but not overpowering.  I liked the dish.  Even the egg roll was tasty, without oily aftertaste.    While this was far from the best Chinese food I'd ever eaten, it was also far from the worst.  At $5.35 for the who shebang, plus another buck for a bottle of water, I thought it was a good deal.  It was also obvious that they don't feel the need to keep the joint sparkling.  It was pretty gritty.     As I paid and walked out, I understood how Number One had survived so long.  A smile and low price still goes a long way.

El Barrio Cantina y Tequila Bar is a 5 Star facility with a 3 Star kitchen.   It was a very pleasant surprise to walk into a large warehouse space with corrugated iron ceiling, long bar with attractively bottled backbar, and Dia Del Muerte personality.  Skulls everywhere.  Plenty of booths in the three dining areas to feel comfortable.  Acoustics were trouble, as every sound was amplified by all the hard and harmonic surfaces.  Pleasant service.   We ordered pretty standard fare.  A beef burrito for son. Chicken flautas for the old man.  Shrimp Molcajete for stepson.  Chips & salsa as forespice. Everything was okay, but not memorable.  The burrito was stuffed with mildly spiced shredded cow, cheese and peppers.  My son drowned it in the available salsa to bring up the burn.  He ate every last shred, but announced it wasn't very different than what he had recently at Taco Belch.  My fried chicken, cheese and spice stuffed flutes were fine. It was an appetizer, but enough for me last night. Crisp shell. Decent bird mix. The molcajete was basically their version of fajitas - served in a hot volcanic rock, with only six medium sized shrimp and a load of sautéed colorful peppers and onions.  Small sides of black beans, rice, guacamole and sour cream.  He wolfed down the crustaceans and played with the veggies before declaring himself full (bored).  At $15., it was more floor show, than gut filling meal.   We left agreeing that the joint had potential, but that the food wasn't its strength.  Too young to partake of the bar offerings, we suspected that all the tequila on display might offer a clue to where the magic lies in El Barrio Cantina & Tequila Bar.    Next time I'll come with grownups and sample their tequila flight and margaritas.

La Hacienda (Home), is a very colorful Mexican restaurant on Neshaminy Boulevard behind Neshaminy Mall.  As with similar spots, the furnishings are wood carved tables and chairs that are brightly painted to suggest an eating establishment South of the Border.  It is successful in creating that atmosphere, and the servers are friendly and attentive, while speaking in heavily accented (but totally understandable) English.  While quite stimulating, I admit to seldom eating in such loudly decorated places in Mexico, where even the high end places tend to be more sedate.  Still, it does make for an unusual and stimulating environment.  Ultimately, it all comes down to the food.  Eating solo, I could only taste what I ordered, and my fork had no place to wander into a companion's plate.  The ubiquitous Chips and Salsa were fine, although the Chips did not have an in house made taste.  The Salsa was of the thin variety, but sufficiently spicy to catch my enjoyable attention.     My main course was Chicken Adobe - a grilled pounded thin Chicken Breast covered with Grilled Japapenos, Onions, Mushrooms, and Melted White Cheese.  The rest of the large plate was covered in Refried Beans and Yellow Rice (see photo).  I rather liked the Chicken and savory toppings.  The grilling was flavorful and texturally pronounced, and the accompaniment was translucent and very complementary in spice tones.  The Refried Beans were loose enough to spread across the plate lowlands, and could have either been reduced in quantity or given more body.  The Rice was just okay, and a rather large portion.    This is certainly a decent place for a Mexican style meal, and I would return if hankering for Mexicano when in that part of the County.  Yet, given several of the other awesomely authentic and delicious meals I have had the pleasure to encounter recently in my travels nearby, where the joint was fairly plain, but the comidas outstanding, I would not choose La Hacienda when I want an exceptional 4 or 5 Star Mexican experience.

Café Ole in The Valley sits in the place where Brooklyn Bagels once resided just off Second Street Pike and Bustleton Pike in Southampton, PA. The space is fairly generic, with minimalist furniture, gray walls, pseudo wood floor and large colorful mural on the back wall. Their one refrigerated display has a lot of beautiful looking pastries, but I was there for breakfast. I found the register toward the rear, and the large wall menu behind the cashier/order taker. With fresh croissant available, I went for a brekkie sandwich of turkey sausage, egg and cheese, and a small mug of coffee.   The java arrived first and immediately woke me from my morning malaise. It was hot, strong and had a nice bite. It was roasted locally by some guy named Jay, who knows about beans. It was so flavorful I had to ask about it. Just wish I knew whether refills were free, because I would have jumped at the chance. Alas, no one stopped by to pour more, and given that I had already paid upfront for my meal, I didn't feel like testing the question. Still, it was the best part of the meal.   The sandwich came from the back kitchen, and due to lack of any odor or sound emanating from that area, I concluded that a microwave was used to meld together the sandwich. It was fine, but the croissant was somewhat flattened in preparation, and not as flaky as this roll should be. The flavors worked well together, but it was far from extraordinary.   Service was okay, with a new POS system and tactile screen for adding a tip (before being served, nor even seeing what you were getting), and fingering a signature to complete the credit card process. That transaction point might be reconsidered by management, as being asked for a tip at ordering seemed awkward, and likely guaranteed to generate smaller gratuities then when dealt with at the close of the meal.   That key lime pie looked tempting, so maybe a return visit is warranted. Wouldn't go back for the breakfast, except for the luscious coffee.

This Jahan Kabob is the sister ship to a joint by the same name on Oxford Valley Road in Langhorne.  Yeah! That's right. The place tucked into the corner of a craft beer store just behind the Super Wawa.  But, the similarity ends with the name.    Abdul the owner and chef remembered me from the other place and gave me a smile.  His daughter sat by the register taking orders and making friendlies with the customers.  While waiting in line and perusing the take out menu, I took a look around this brand new Afghani/Middle Eastern establishment.  The bright neon beckoned all who find Morrisville an interesting, if offbeat, destination.  The floors were covered with oriental rug runners giving the space a feel of ethnicity, and in the rear stood a low platform with 6 meditation pillows for the Believers who felt the demand to pray before dining.   Ah Salaam Ahlaikum, my brothers and sisters.   When I entered I had intended to pick up and go, but the vibe (and aroma) was so unusual, that I decided to find a table to enjoy my meal right there.  When I reached the front of the line I had not decided what I wanted.  I asked Kadrianne what she recommended.  Abdul heard me, and turned from the grill to answer, "Chicken Curry is what you want."   Obediently, I agreed. Sometimes, Kismet takes a hand.   He was totally right.  A few minutes later a plate full of thick yellow golden gravied Chicken chunks and a large pile of Long Grain "Dirty" Rice was placed before me. The flavors came through my nose first almost bringing me to tears. My tongue joined the festival a second later.  It is amazing how different curry tastes around the world, because this was neither Indian, nor Thai curry, but something in between.  Cooler and more subtle than it Indian brothers, and suggesting a tartness that its Thai cousins have mastered.  It was unique and savory; smooth and expressive.  The Rice was wonderfully mildly sweet in contradistinction to the Chicken. It seemed the obvious thing to do was mix them together.  That was a moment to remember as my oral senses rejoiced.   The green Afghani Tea was a good astringent between shoveling the delectables into my mouth.  The Sesame Cookie at the end of the meal, a kind token of appreciation.    The other reviews are on target in 5 Starring Jahan Kabob.  This is a special place that will get even better with time, and become a landmark helping put Morrisville back on the cuisinery map where it belongs.

This is another underheated, undercleaned, primarily takeout Chinese/American shop in the Capitol Plaza Center in Ewing, NJ. It is very cheap for those lunch combos with fried rice, and a buck more for an egg roll.   My General Tso's Chicken was okay, cut into smaller pieces and not too heavily breaded, with a decent amber sauce. On the other hand, the fried rice was a dark brown from the beef consommé in which it was made, and served hard and clumpy, with a minimum of veggies/sprouts. Had the taste of being prepared too long ago, and left sitting in the pot all day.   The woman working the counter was friendly, and brought lunch to me at the table with a smile. She trusted me enough to wait until I was finished to accept payment.   A mixed bag.   2.5 STARS.

Noodle Eighty-Eight (Lucky Noodles), is a surprising hybrid house in Souderton, PA. Nicely renovated residence, the dining rooms are simple, but well appointed for comfort and utilitarian style. We were there for Sunday lunch, although there was no special menu. The main attraction were the Xiao Long Bao, the Shanghai soup dumpling specialty that I had been Jones-ing for. We added mushroom filled spring rolls as a second appetizer, and General Tso's Chicken and Short Ribs as entrees.   In order of appearance the meal ran from excellent to ordinary.   The XLB were very good, with steaming tasty pork truffle oil bouillon and filling. The gingered vinegar was a nice complement to pour into the pouch once the top knot was bitten off and the mixed contents sucked out. Such a tactile fun experience.   The Spring Rolls were deep fried and stuffed with ground mushroom and sweet dipping sauce. They were crunchy, but the filling had little flavor nor interest. Wouldn't get this again.  The side greens salad was small, but had a pleasing sweet vinegar finish. It's unusual to get a salad in a Chinese house, and this was a tip of their chef's cap to their hybrid intentions. Far better than the ginger goop dressing on iceberg found in almost all sushi zones.   General Tso was the weak soldier this day. The pieces were large requiring cutting to consume (thus, the need for western flatware). The breading was thick and not at all crisp, and the old man had spent too much time being woked. It was dry and lacked any verve. Disappointing.  Luckily, the day was saved by the Short Rib dish. More western than Asian in presentation and taste, it was tender, juicy and packed a tangy punch from the excellently reduced sauce. It pulled off the bone easily. But for the baby bok choy, this reminded of a good pot roast or sauerbraten. Regardless, it was nearly perfect.    We made the drive from Newtown in 40 minutes on a rainy afternoon. Given the overall experience it is doubtful we would do it again. The dishes were inconsistent, but priced for perfection. Service was good, but without expected hot tea, nor rice. Also true about the parking situation. Not good unless you park across the road, around the corner or find one of the few that hug the building.   3.5 STARS

In order to apply for a Pennsylvania Driver Permit, not only do you need to show a social security card, but the form also has a portion for a doctor's physical and certification that the applicant is healthy enough to drive.  This is probably a good idea, but it does add to the time and expense of driving in the Commonwealth.  My family doctor was willing, but the available appointment was a week away and the office visit charge was not insignificant.    So, I decided to call Premier Urgent Care in Newtown to see if they could handle this type of service.  They could and they did.  We could walk in any time during business hours and the cost would be $45 (apparently, there are sometimes special discounts to $25).  We went in the following morning.  The facility was bright and clean.  The employees were all dressed in high end med uniforms, and efficient.  We registered after filling out a 2 page form, and were seen by a medical assistant promptly.
