She took us into an examination room, did the basis BP, pulse, height, weight, and eyesight measurements and tests, and then left us to wait for the doctor to finish the exam.    It took about 20 minutes for Dr. Ferguson to arrive.  She was friendly and communicated well.  We went over the pertinent details of why we were there, and she completed he portion of the physical with quick looks at eyes, ears and throat.  She was quite professional.    Apparently, my young driving applicant was deemed healthy enough to get behind the wheel of a motorized vehicle, and we were sent on our way.    Overall, the experience was satisfactory for this type of medical function.  No emergency to deal with.  Just routine physical examination.  While lacking the sense of confidence I have with my personal physician, such "hand holding" wasn't necessary for this job.  We were out in about 40 minutes and had what we needed.    I would certainly use Premier Urgent Care again for simple medical needs.  It is sort of like going to Wawa when you want coffee and a sandwich, and don't have time for the bigger deli/restaurant experience.

It's great to have a high end Napolitan pizza house in Newtown!  It's even better that the enterprise is owned by Pasquale and Anna, the proprietors of Osteria Vecchia, the excellent casa Italiana right down the street. This shop is for the daughter and son-in-law.  Thus, begin empires.   The building is on the site of the former Minuteman Press.  That old structure was taken down to the foundation, and a new Euro-Country Casual establishment arose.  Attention to detail is obvious, as the space is beautiful, with quality stone, wood, glass and a "just off the boat" wood burning hive oven covered in red glazed tile and contrasting white ceramic lettering that shouts, "Pasquale & Anna/Acqua e Farina!"    We were greeted by Sal, the maestro de la casa, who sat my son and I at the corner table where we could see the whole operation.  We ordered a Siciliana pie, and as we waited, other servers brought thin slices of red sauced bread, and a small plate of Brussel sprouts that were soft and delicious from their time swimming in olive oil and spices.  I was even offered a glass of red wine on the house. Very cool touch!  The pie arrived with steam shimmering above it, on a large white platter.  It was cut in quarters, and covered in mozza, afterburn peccorino and chunks of eggplant.  Truly, a work of art with the bubbled crust and scorched undercarriage.  The special deal with these ovens is that they hold extremely high heat, such that the raw pie is placed in the oven for less than three minutes, while baking everything quickly and capturing all the flavor of the ingredients before they burn off and escape. The result is a wonderfully textured and tasty crust that is flavored by the ingredients you choose.  It is all about the dough (thus, the name, Water & Flour), and secondarily about the toppings.  Quite different than the better known pizza experience provided by most joints.   So it was here. A beauty to behold, and a pleasure to consume.  Of course, there is a downside to this approach to baking.  While the crust is excellent, the more ingredients you put on top, the wetter the center of the pie will be on the plate, because it is not possible to fully cook the veggies and meats in such a short time, and as a result of the lack of evaporation in the oven, the finished product will be softer that normal, and the drip from the collected moisture under the hood will be noticeable, and require care to avoid making a mess.   The secret is to order a simple pie with minimal topside accessories, so that the crust, cheese and sauce have the maximum opportunity to vent off the moisture.  This provides a drier bottom and optimal crustiness.   Dining at Acqua & Farina is very different than eating at pizza parlors.  It is designed as a feast for the senses.  There are more moving parts, and the resulting cost enhancement is noticeable. There is a time when "two slices and a soda," is what you want, but there are also times when although you yearn for pizza, you want a more rousing experience.    At those moments, Acqua e Farina will be calling your name.

In evaluating Akiko Sushi it is difficult to separate its quality fish from the environment in which it is served, especially should you choose to eat in the cramped and dirty dining area of the Newtown Farmers' Market.  While it makes little difference for some of the other vendors' products in the too small building, sushi is an art form as well as a food product.  How it is prepared, presented and eaten makes a difference to the Zen experience that so enhances Sushi-Do.   It is like watching a master at work when the sharp knives flash, the sticky rice is molded into seaweed wraps, and out of the efficient motions of the chef emerges a work of art that you hate to disturb by eating.  It is quite a dilemma.  How much better it would be if you could sit along side a gurgling stream and listen to the songbirds as each morsel was praised before eating. (Sounds a bit like Oishi).   But, that isn't happening here, so the best you can do is take it home and devour it quickly to capture its fresh essence before it slips away, or just "damn the torpedoes," and find a couple of empty chairs and enjoy it while everyone around you jostles for a place to sit, or scrape their tables and chairs to get in or out.    If you have a Zen mind none of this will matter as you just shut it all out while you contemplate the exchange of energy from fish to you, and back again.

Family run grocery that grew with the population and moved out of Trenton to this location in the burbs to keep up with their customers.    A good idea before the hypermarkets began to dominate the landscape and put immense pressure on the little guys to match either price (impossible) or performance (customer service and specialty items).  This it could do for a while, but ultimately it was not a long term solution.  Today, it struggles along as a convenience stop for those in the area.    The selection is limited, and the prices are higher than most of the competition.  The family is older and the next generation has not picked up the baton.    At least it is clean and the staff friendly for the most part.   In time, it too will pass into history.

SweetBriar Ice Cream & Cafe in Ambler, PA, has been around for a while. Fourth generation, so they say in the menu. Farm to table, too. Cute county feel with fewer than a dozen tables within and an equal number out on the patio in front. Warm, friendly service with genuine willingness to refill your coffee mug as often as you like.   I had an hour to kill before my next appointment, and a hunger for breakfast that needed attention. The specials board had a few interesting possibilities, but fresh fruit on a battered waffle with whipped cream seemed a bit over the top. Simple well grilled french toast was what I wanted, and the server said was excellent there. Visions began to dance.   Java came hot and strong. Real milk in a small stainless pitcher hit the mark. All I needed was a great short stack to make my day.   Looked perfect on the white ceramic. Darkly golden with yellow bread between the burn marks. An olive oil bottle with long spout full of syrup to address the sweetening. Nice touch. Unfortunately, the inside of the slices was dry as if it had not been conjoined with the egg bowl for long enough before touching hot steel. No eggy vanilla taste. Okay, but with more TLC it could have been a real contender, rather than the dry toast it became.   I think this place can do it better when it tries harder.

If I went into Dulce Pizza with a blindfold on and only tasted their food without sight of its surroundings, it would definitely have another star after its name. Yet, blessed with sight, the worn and crumby surfaces and poor condition of the shopping center where it is located, impact my overall impression negatively and detract from what would otherwise be a surprisingly good meal.   My first choice for dinner was the place next door, but its kitchen closed at 3 and they were locking up shortly. I saw Dulce and headed over. It looked like any other pizzeria, with pies in the oven and a small dining room with tubular chairs with holes in the seats and crumbs from earlier meals still laying around. This joint would never be mistaken for clean. It somehow reflected the poorly maintained condition of the shopping center, which had some of the largest parking lot potholes imaginable. A few customers were sitting around manging, so I took a chance and asked for an eggplant parmesan dinner with side salad and pasta. I ordered and paid at the cashier and took a seat near the front window to await it's arrival. I wasn't feeling too enthused about what might be coming my way, but I had already paid, so I was committed.   The salad came first with balsamic, romaine, tomato, red onion, black olives, cukes and that little plastic tub of dark brown viniagrette. It was cool and fresh. Not great, but not bad. The main platter arrived next with a red sauce covered load of very thin sliced, breaded and sauteed melanzone. The gravy was chunky and seemed to shine in the natural light from the window. I lowered my head to get a wiff of the steaming sauce. Its crushed tomato, garlic and basil aroma forced me back in my chair from its powerful scent.   What?! Wait a second. Was there someone in the kitchen who knew from red sauce? Must have been because when I forked that first bite into my mouth, it completely took charge of my taste buds, squeezed them hard, and forced me to involuntarily mutter, "Damn!" It was that exceptional. The eggplant was soft and totally baked, without a hard spot to be found. It tasted like it might have been sauteed twice before reaching the oven.   Then I tried the penne aglio olio I had requested rather than spaghetti with more red. It was also very good with a surfeit of sliced garlic throughout and a pool of extra virgin in the bottom of the bowl keeping it hot and dripping. A dusting of black pepper, romano and dried parsley on top provided the finishing note. Also, way better than expected.   Of course they forgot the bread to complete my total confounding.   What to do when the grub is better than good, but the facility and surroundings cry out for some TLC?   Wear a blindfold and eat.

Cleanest Friendly's I've ever visited.   Like an oasis in the middle of Gloucester Premium Outlets, it provided shelter and sustenance when I had had enough shopping and just wanted to get off my feet and quell the emerging late afternoon hunger pangs from dodging lunch.    Friendly service, and a reasonably priced patty melt with waffle fries were exactly what I needed.  The surprise free sundae put a creamy smile on my face.   Sure. I've had better, but Being There was Everything this day!

The question of the decade is: When it comes to cheesesteak, is there a difference between using a traditional Italian long roll or stepping out with a round poppy seed kaiser?   Donkey's Place on Haddon Avenue in Camden, NJ, has been an iconoclast for a generation, daring to shape shift and challenge all comers to demonstrate that their creation is in any way inferior to the classic torpedo. Now that I sat at the bar, watched the sliced beef being grilled and consumed a whole sandwich 'wit' soft, translucent sauteed onions, I have an opinion.   And, it is that there IS a difference in taste and texture that is pronounced and obvious. First, the flavor of the bread is distinct in each. While the Italian roll has a sourdough light saltiness, the round boy is a bit sweet as white bread tends to be. Second, the meat/bread ratio is changed, with relatively more meat to roll at Donkey's. After all, there is less bread in the Kaiser than a foot long. Third, the thin sliced beef is never separated for grilling @ Donkey's, but allowed to cook in a thick pile and turned over so that only the top and bottom of the pack touch hot steel. The rest are heated through passage of the heat through the slices. In my case, it meant that the middle of the sandwich was tender and juicy, while the outer layers were mildly overcooked, tougher and chewier. Forth, the Donk adds spice to the pile of onions simmering on the stove, giving them a reddish orange tint and slight chili flavor. Never experienced that at my favorite joints in and around Philly.   Don't get me wrong, I really liked the sandwich and the overall dive bar essence of this place. Service was pretty and efficient, and I was given a bumper sticker to commemorate the visit. Still, I would be less than honest if I said I liked it just as much as Steve's Prince of Steaks. No. It wasn't as instantly addicting and scrumptious as that. It was a half step down from that pinnacle of steakdom.   Still, overall it was a very enjoyable lunch, with the atmosphere contributing mightily to the fun. I understand what Anthony Bourdain loved about it, but he didn't live cheesesteak his whole life.   Doubtless, I will be back for more.

First impressions of Trentini's Restaurant off South Clinton Avenue in Trenton, NJ, are very positive.  The dining room reminds of an adobe bright colored house in New Mexico, with semi-exposed timbers and ersatz red tile roof extending from the inner walls.   The staff is friendly and attractive and provide a solid table service.    A couple of the office guys went there for a pizza lunch the other day.  We ordered a 12 inch pie with sausage and eggplant for two of us.  It was prepared fresh for us, and took about 15 minutes to reach our table.  It looked quite good with the steam rising from the bubbling volcanic cheese surface.  The aroma was exquisite.   We knew that this was a Spanish (Ecuadorian) Italian shop, but the menu remained heavy oriented toward Italiano.  This may explain the over-reliance on cheese, rather than tomato sauce and spices to define the pie.  The abundance of melted mozza made the pizza top heavy, and impossible to pick up manually, without fold and spillage.  This is often the mistake of pizza makers unschooled in the ways of the tomato pie, where proper proportion among the main ingredients is critical to the success of the creation.    The taste was still good, but we both resorted to fork and knife in order to keep the various layers together.  It was one of those circumstances when less (cheese) is more satisfying.   While I likely will not order pizza again from Trentini's, the rest of their menu, and the quality of service will lead me back there eventually to sample their other offerings, both in pasta and almuertzo Americano del Sur.

Cheeseboro's Kitchen is a stand alone building on Pennington Road that does soul food and other American classics.  It is primarily a take away house, with only a few tables along the front window for those who want to eat right there.  Ordering is done at the cash register, and each meal is prepared individually. The finished dishes come out on the other side of the room in front of the pizza ovens left over by the previous tenant.    The good thing about this approach is that the meals are hot and fresh.  Only the side dishes were premade and chilled as they wait for you.  The down side of this "just in time" production is that when they get busy, the wait can be rather long for your meal to be completed and brought out of the kitchen.  While I was there, people were going outside to wait, or leaving all together to return when the food was ready.  Some customers call ahead, which while a good idea, just prolongs the wait for everyone.   The people working here, including management, are friendly and appear to be working hard to get the food out.  My questions were answered with a smile, even when I was showing my cultural ignorance about how certain things would be presented.  For example, a "sandwich" is not something between two slices of bread, but instead is a load of whatever you want on top of three slices of white bread.  You can make a sandwich of it yourself, but there is way more meat, fish, etc., than can fit within the confines of a manageable sandwich. Easier just to eat the food and as much of the loaf as you desire. Me? I skipped it all together in order to consume as much fish as possible.  Happy to be enlightened.   What about my whiting sandwich and side of macaroni salad (recommended)?  Six large fillets, light breading and flash deep fried, made for a delicious lunch.  I could only eat four of them. The macaroni side came in a plastic tub, mixed with copious mayo and bits of tuna.  Cool and great tasting. Again, more than this man could stuff down.    The only drawback to Cheeseboro's is the wait for the food to be prepared, and secondarily to the unused space in the store that could be put to use with more tables or perhaps, displays.  The meal, with the side and bottle of iced tea, came to around $12.  Quite reasonable for the quantity and quality of the offerings.  Now that I have a better idea what is going on, I will be back to try the rib sandwich, and perhaps, even their burgers, and more of their side dishes.

This is a tough one to call.   The premises of Three Monkeys Café is beautiful, both inside and out. A lot of thought and money was put into bringing the old saloon back to life. From tin-type ceiling tiles, through refinished wood floors, exceptional back bar, and zany monkey decorations throughout, the inner sanctum of this place is a pleasure to sit in and enjoy.  Great job!  The outer side patio/garden is likewise a wonderland.  Colorful, whimsical, tall treed, and full of monkey business.  On a spring, summer or autumn day or evening, it is no doubt an endearing space for a few drinks and semi-romantic meal.  Gotta love it!  The weak link is the kitchen.   We were there for breakfast after visiting the USCIS facility nearby. It wasn't quite warm enough to dine al fresco, so we sat at a corner table in the barroom, and were served by a friendly management person.  We were introduced to Douwe Egbert Coffee, a Dutch brand in operation since 1753.  One of their spinoffs developed a novel approach to mass produced coffee that liquefies it in concentrate, and brews on site and when ordered, so every cup is fresh and strong.  Mine had a mild chicory flavor.  I really liked it, although I would need a lot more sampling and comparison to fresh ground beans to know if it was as good as what I grind/brew at home. Still, it was a pleasant cuppa Joe.   The sausage, egg and cheese on seeded roll with side of home fries, were the main attractions.  They left me somewhat disappointed.  It was fine that they used cut up links rather than patties, and threw them in with a few scrambled eggs and slices of cheese.  It was very big, because the roll was from a cheesesteak sandwich; not a hard Kaiser.  But, it had not been grilled at all, and did not really work with the breakfast theme.  Too, the mix lacked spice, and would have benefited by being cooked with a pinch of salt, pepper, and maybe even a shake or two of Pecos Bill.  Finally, the potatoes looked great and greasy, but were completely cold.    A little quality control at the grill, and perhaps retaining a real chef to handle the preparation or at least to train the staff, would make a world of difference.  Three Monkeys has a ton of potential. It just needs to polish the brass and sand the wood trim (culinary-wise) to become a completely enthralling experience.    3.5 Stars

When my son was in his early years, we were members of the Academy of Natural Sciences on Logan Circle, Philadelphia.  Our membership entitled us to free entrance into the museum, and discount tickets to the special exhibits they always had coming in.  Too, we received some kind of courtesy from the gift shop.    It was well worth the drive from Bucks County to explore the dinosaur permanent exhibit, as well as the few interactive corners and events that were available throughout the three story hall.  Digging for dinosaur fossils, and touching live reptiles and small mammals, had a profound effect on his young mind, and very likely explains why he now excels in high school science and math.  He went from wanting to be a paleontologist when he grew up, to a geologist, once he discovered there was something beyond huge skeletons in the ground.    The diorama halls were persuasive in suggesting how various species lived in the wild, and had him imagining he was standing on the savannas of South Africa, watching wildebeests run in a panic from hunting lions. In truth, it wasn't just the kid having these thoughts. It brought that child out of his father, too.   We explored the butterfly exhibit before it became permanent, and the frog rooms while available. We watched the nature movies in the theater and encouraged each other to dream big when contemplating our planet and universe.    In truth, we were also members of the Museum of Natural History in Manhattan, and went there as often as possible. It was much bigger and better in many ways, but lacked the convenience and crowd management that made the Academy so accessible.  No "Night in the Museum," here, unless you were lucky enough to get a cub scout sleepover.    If you scored that, anything was possible.

John's Barber Shop is a place where only men need apply for a haircut.   It is hidden in the back basement behind State Street in Newtown Borough, and is best approached by driving into the State Store lot, circling that building, and when 3/4s of the way around the liquor store, hang a sharp right into a smaller lot.  The side door next to the lot is John's.    Knock three times and whisper you were sent by Joe, to get in.    Want a cigar or beer with your trim?  This is the place for you.  Want your hair styled a little?  Maybe not.   Perhaps, it is because I went to the old fashioned barber shops as a kid, where the barber dressed in a white coat, and had a thick leather strap attached to the riser chairs, and I was intimidated by the straight edge razor blades, buzzing electric shears, and sharp scissors; but watching my son get his haircut there makes me nervous.  Going to the barber was second only to going to the dentist in striking fear deep into my psyche.  As a result of that youthful stress, only women touch my head now (you know what I mean).  I don't mind paying to have my limited crop look as good as possible, not like I just went to the barber. I still remember the smell of the Trol Hair Pomenade, or Brylcream "little dab 'il do 'ya."   Yes. I did enjoy the payoff of a lollipop. Not sure if John offers that along with the whiskey.

Opened this place Saturday morning @ 9.  It was nice to have a head start on what was to be a full house at Full Moon.    Clayton, our host and server had his act together and brought all of us coffee as we perused the breakfast menu.  Various omelets for my family and friend, and French Toast for me.  While the conversation gathered momentum, the plates were brought out and laid before us.  Everything looked very good, although I only tasted the homemade Potato Chips, which were good.  My French Toast was off the mark, however. I had asked for it "crunchy," and was told it would be left on the grill longer to make it all well done.  What came out with the real Maple Syrup were a half dozen pieces of French Demi Loaf that were actually lukewarm at best, and far from the cauterized ends I requested.  I was surprised given the repartee at the ordering.  They had not been on the grill long enough, and had been off the grill too long before serving. Wrong on both sides.  Disappointing, but not wanting to poop on the party I ate everything and enjoyed the real Maple Syrup.   My mates were satisfied, and the gestalt of the room was pleasing.   Three out of four ain't bad.

Heard good things about Pho & Beyond in Willow Grove, and was happy to have the chance to try it out.    It is on the first floor of a newish commercial strip off Davisville Road.  Entry from front and rear.  The décor is simple/comfortable Asian.  The menu is fairly complete for Vietnamese cuisine, with everything from pho to com, banh mi, and even bun bo hue.  Service was friendly, if a little lagging.    While I admit to enjoying my Pho Ga (Chicken Noodle Soup), the taste of the Pho Tai (Beef Noodle Soup with Ribeye Steak), and the Bahn Mi  Mem Nurong with BBQ Pork patty, the entire experience was blown up by the realization that some part of my meal had been doused with MSG, leaving me with an allergic reaction that felt like a mild hangover, without the alcohol.    True. MSG is a traditional part of Vietnamese and other kitchens, used to cover up stale meats and "enhance" flavor.  I guess that is what they mean when they talk about, "...authentic Vietnamese cuisine based on family secret recipes, techniques, and skills..." on their website.   Sorry to say, one of your secret techniques is out.  You really should find a better way that doesn't make customers ill, or at least warn customers that MSG is used in the kitchen.  Clean bathrooms.

Redhouse Bagels sits underneath Johnny Apple's Restaurant on Buck Road, Holland, PA.  It is in what was the walkout basement.  Coming from the north, it is easy to miss as it is behind the massive building housing Johnny's.  Still, plenty of parking on the side near the creek.  It is worth finding.   Bagels preferences are very subjective, but to my buds, Redhouse does a very good rounder. When fresh and hot from the oven, they are richly textural and flavorful.  They seem to do only one large batch in the early morning, so if you get there late like I did, there is the chance you won't get what you really want.  I'm an onion bagel maven, but as they were all depleted, I grabbed the last everything bagel in the house. Butter and Swiss is my standard order, so that the taste of the bagel complements, rather than being overwhelmed by a heavier load. They did not skimp on the toppings, and the overall experience was very positive. While I prefer a crisper skin and soft innards, this one was more pliant, but still had wonderful flavor to compensate.  The egg bagel was likewise a pleasure to eat according to my beautiful companion.   The only downside aside from the lack of crunch, was that Redhouse is strictly takeout, with no place to sit and enjoy breakfast.  If I were them, I'd look into clearing some of the brush in the parking lot along the creek, and putting in a few tables and benches for people to enjoy watching the roiling water flow just off the nearby old mill race.  That would be a fantastic place to hang out with good bagel and cuppa joe.

Adrianne, the woman who runs Mommie Joe's told me that the tiny shop at the corner of South Broad and Division Streets in Trenton, NJ, had been slinging Haitian dishes for more than thirty years at that location.  How is it that I never saw it before last week after living and/or working in the TNJ for almost that long?  I guess I just wasn't ready for it.   After the cover of each heated chaffing dish was lifted for me to see what was cooking, I had no problem selecting a plate of Black Rice, Oxtail Stew and a couple of golden fried Platanos. The Black Rice was a first for me, but I have learned it is possible to buy it in the right markets.  It acted like the paler version I was accustomed to, with the taste of salt, pepper, garlic, and maybe a touch of something like turmeric or coriander, that only required the spooning of the Oxtail bone and amazing tawny rich sauce to make it explode with a flavor combination that was savory, smoky, meaty and mysterious.  With only plastic utensils to handle the chunkiness of the beef, I really had no choice but to get manual.  It would have been great if lunch had been served on a plate rather than in styro take out containers, but I understand that sometimes low budget is the only way to survive.    It became an unruly mess to pick up and gnaw at the tender ox still clinging to this matrix, but after a few seconds I forgot about the office I had to return to, and the white shirt and tie I was wearing, and just let such stolid convention go.  The only way to eat this was DIRTY.    The Plantain was thin and nicely breaded before frying.  It was still starchy, but the flavor was compelling.    Mommie Joe's certainly needs a clean up, and a better spacing of the tables that were all pushed together in front of the store, but there is no question of authenticity.  Adrianne even let me come behind the counter to have a better look at her dishes.  She was very confident that I would like what was on the menu.    She was right.

Minuteman Press on Sycamore Street, Newtown, PA, has been under new ownership for the past couple of years, and the change in management has definitely been good for business.   I stopped in last week to see if they could produce a professional sign for the law office I was opening in town. It was a slat sign to be mounted on a larger directory sign in the front yard of this old converted 19th Century house.  I spoke with Scott Woron, who quickly looked at the old signs and explained to me that it was a thin vinyl sheet over the wood base that would carry the print, and not directly onto the planks.  He said it would be easy to do, and the cost would be very reasonable.   I stopped back in today to pick up the signs.  They were ready and looked great! Cost less than the estimate I received from another sign company that specialized in only that one thing. Happy to save a few bucks and miles.    Now, I applied for the borough permit to put up the sign. Once that is secured and the office is inspected for the Use & Occupancy permit, I will have the signs put in place, and be open for business.   It was great to have it done correctly, on time, and at cost by the local Minuteman Press.   Local business scores again!

Pat's Pizza & Bistro on New Falls Road, Levittown, PA, is part of a family run Italian chain in Jersey, Delaware and Pennsylvania. This facility is fairly new with lots of stone, high ceilings and wooden tables and chairs. Small parking lot is a challenge. The menu is primarily pizza parlor style - pies, steak sandwiches, wraps, salads. There are only a few actual dinner options. Chicken parmesan and a few pastas with meatballs or sausage.   We went with the chicken parmesan, which came with a nice size salad and bowl of pasta, "Rustic" chicken cheesesteak, and their BBQ burger. Of the three dishes, the burger was actually the best. Juicy, substantial and tasting without freezer burn. The rustic roll was a good alternative to the standard torpedo, but the makings were a bit dry and needed more flavor from the onions and peppers. The chicken parmesan was okay, but heavily breaded. The salad was bigger than expected and enough to share. The homemade fettuccine aglio olio was was real al dente delight.   Pat's provides nice atmosphere, but the kitchen could be more consistent. It has its highs and lows. It is certainly worth a stop to check out when in the mood to be in the mood for Italian food.

I had my second sports massage with Marla Solarski yesterday at Cryo Spa in Holland, PA. It was in a different room, but still with Asian atmosphere and nice background music.   Once again, she asked a few questions about how I was feeling and where I was feeling it. She was most interested in how I had responded to the first massage two weeks before. In fact, my lower back, legs and shoulders responded well last time, and I was ready for another strong stretching and deep tissue therapeutic hour.   This time, except when I had to interact with her by resisting her pushing/pulling, I was more relaxed and was able to zone out and go somewhere within while she worked her magic. Marla dug deeper into my thighs which had absorbed the result of two herniated discs. Painful, but necessary to relieve stress and increase flexibility. Torquing my hips and legs to open space between my discs. Leaning her weight into my folded knees to help loosen the perpetual tightness in my lumbar spine.   The time passed quickly, but at its end I felt great, and almost intoxicated from the work done. The spa allowed me to sit in a quiet room for a few minutes until that sensation ended.   Slept like a baby last night.  PRO TIP - Marla actually works in several locations, just call her to find where is most convenient for you.

The name on the sign out front is, "Mauceri's Steak House."    While I didn't see any steak on the menu, this crossover Salvadoran/Italian shop seems to know what they are doing in the cocina.  On my first visit, I had the pleasure of sampling their Chili Rellenos from the Latin side of the menu.  They was very good.  This time, I went with the Italian Hot Dog because of my curiosity about how it would be different than all the others I have eaten around Trenton over the years.  Too, at $3.50, it was the best deal in the house.    I was impressed.  The standard frankfurter arrived at the bottom of an excellent half torpedo roll, and buried alive with a load of sautéed onion, pepper and potato.  More French fries on the side.  There was ketchup on the table, but no mustard.  I decided to go with the flow and doctor my sandwich with what was available.  So, I squirted from the red table rocket, and poured in most of the salsa that came with the chips.    The result: A hot and spicy creation that looked Italian, but tasted like the hybrid it really was.  The salsa gave it a real kick in the pants, and brought the best out of the sandwich.  I enjoyed every bite.   The Licuados Tamarindo was cool and a bit sweeter than I prefer, perhaps because it seemed to come premade, rather than made fresh in a blender.  Still, @ $3., I wasn't complaining.   Overall, a very happy face meal.

When many folks think about bars in Newtown they think pretentious crowds and overpriced drinks and meals. You know who you are, and what I am talking about. Truth is, you guys are not far off the mark.  "Those places" do have an attytood.   Perhaps, the lone exception is the Clubhouse Bar and Grill on lower East State Street. It is the outrider that serves the rest of us who prefer to drink our beer and eat bar food or pizza with a jukebox playing in the background, and the sound of billiard balls slamming into each other, or hanging outback on nice evenings, watching the sunset to the sound of acoustic guitar and local talent entertainers. All this at such a decent price. You will get change from your Twenty for a couple of beers and a light meal.   There are plenty of brew alternatives here, both bottle and draft, with 'make you' happy hour specials. The wings come out hot, spicy and delectable, and no one minds if the bones pile up high on the table. They also realize that your fingers are going to get a bit sticky and bring out a stack of heavy gauge napkins without being asked.  Ain't nothing dainty 'bout the Clubhouse.  I had the cheesesteak quesadilla app the other night, and I took a quarter of it home to feed my son. He was so pleased he wants to go with me next time. Ok, buster.  It was that good!  The Clubhouse is not perfect, but who cares? It is still the mellowest joint in Ntown, and the place everyone knows your name.  It's where you want to be.   February 2, 2014 - Went to their take out side today to pick up wings and beer for the Super Bowl. Called ahead. Everything ready in 30 minutes.  Quite an efficient operation.  Great wings. Enough beer choices to keep everyone happy.   Definitely use Clubhouse again for home events.  The wings were large and tasty.  Blue Moon, Boddington and Redd's Apple Ale.  Everyone was happy, except the Broncos.

Villa Rosa was a regular stop in my early years in Bucks County, but as Newtown evolved into a community with many good restaurants, the need to travel to Lower Makefield (not Yardley), became an unnecessary time expense.  Last night I was driving back from a meeting and found myself hungry and very near Villa Rosa, and decided to stop in and have something light.    I ordered an Eggplant Parm sandwich.  It arrived a few minutes later in the hands of a pleasant server.  Although the store was scheduled to close in 30 minutes I felt no pressure to eat quickly, and my server returned a few times to check on my satisfaction.  The meal itself was quite good.  The Eggplant was very thinly sliced and lightly sautéed in olive oil before placement in the Torpedo Roll for toasting in the oven.  It was not breaded and held up well with the Mozza and Red Gravy.  The Roll itself was crisped nicely before arrival.  I normally just eat the innards and have only a few bites of the bread, which is what I did this time.  It was as filling as I needed it to be.    Overall, I was satisfied with my repast, and will have no hesitancy to return next time in the area.  Besides, there are a few other decent food outlets in this commercial center, not the least of which is Indian Garden, an excellent curry house.

Dolce Carini Pizzeria hasn't been reviewed since 2008!?  Wonder why?  I have gone in for a late lunch pizza a couple of times in recent months just to see how the tomato pie was faring around Ntown. Someone has to keep watch of the state of slice around here. It may as well be me. N'cest pas?  No one there when I arrived around 2.  The shop was clean and orderly.  The crew in back was friendly and accommodating to my request for 2 slices and cold drink (lemonade). They came out of the reheat oven in about 3 minutes and I sprinkled on the crushed hot pepper as I walked to my table.  The price was right @ under $6. A full two bucks less than Marco's for the same deal.   How were the slices?  I forgot my scale, but they did seem smaller than a similar cut in the other places I often go, perhaps offsetting the economy of slice noted above.  Still, the crust was thin and crisp, and held the weight of the sauce and cheese well.  No folding nor dripping. Big plus. The taste is where the rubber meets the road, and to my buds the oral sensations were not quite right.  The sauce was a little salty, when I prefer a mild sweetness and basil-esque retort. The cheese had little flavor and did not play well with the sauce.   I am not saying that the pizza was bad, just that it wasn't a complete pleasure, nor did it stand tall next to the local competition.   It was just A - OK.

I had not been inside Giuseppe's Pizza since before my twelve year old was born.  That is a life time in pizza years.  After today's basketball game in Churchville, we stopped in for a few slices and drinks to assuage the pain of another close loss.   The pizza was as good as I remembered it.  Strong enough dough to hold its point proudly without folding like a dog's ear; minimal drip of oil from the face of the pie; and a serenely enjoyable first bite experience.  My son's first impression was equally positive.  His comment to the effect that it was not quite as good as Marco's in Newtown was well taken and subject to debate.  Regardless, Giuseppe's is in good company. We will need to explore the menu further by venturing into cheese steaks, parms, and pasta to consider moving up the star ranks.

Stopped in the other day for a late lunch.  This was a first visit since this pizza parlor changed hands, and it was immediately apparent that the entire shop had had a makeover. The kitchen was now in the back, and the dining room in front; a reversal of its original layout.  New walls and floors made the place feel more upscale than the old place. Nice use of stone, wood and paint.   We opted for cheesesteak and eggplant parm sandwiches.  Both came with fries. The steak was a full load of chopped beef mixed with onions and mushrooms on a lightly crusted roll.  Very good.  The eggplant was thin sliced, breaded, sautéed in olive oil, and then grilled again in the oven, after which it was dosed with their homemade gravy and mozza.  Again, very good. The rolls were notable for their crunch and pleasant taste. The fries were really unnecessary, and were the weakest part of the repast, as frozen crinkle cuts.    Reasonable prices.  Friendly service.   Will definitely return for the pizza and more menu items when in an Italian mood.

In my Trenton Days, Halo Farms and the Trenton Farmers' Market on Spruce Street were regular stops on my weekly provisioning list.  I loved the ability to buy fresh dairy products at everyday good prices, and to support a worthy institution.  It is great to know it survived without my business these many years.  When I stopped in again on a cold Sunday afternoon, it was like visiting an old friend.    The store looks basically the same, with bins for milk at ground level, open refrigeration units for ice cream, and wire shelves for bread, donuts and snacks.  It is still rather dark and dingy, but the fun of finding quality local products at below market prices is what is most important.    Yesterday I purchased 2% Milk @ $1.49/half gallon, and 3 pint cups of their private label ice cream @ "Buy 2, get one free @ $6." When the ice cream is comparable to the high end labels at twice or thrice the price, you have a great deal.  What flavors, you ask?  Tahitian Vanilla, Raspberry and Butter Pecan.    With snow still deep, and ice still creep, the actual tasting will wait for a warmer moment or a burning fireplace.

If you want to go "Back to the Future", then you must stop in to Dairy Delite on Woodbourne Road in Levittown.    It is one of those time warp places where if you step up to the window and order one of their great soft sweet thick ice cream flavors in a cone or cup, or a extra thick shake, you can actually feel the strands of time pulling you into a vortex that lands you somewhere around 1957.  Look in the mirror and you would swear the lines on your face are lighter, and the sparkle in your eyes brighter.  Return often enough and you realize that the real secret here is not just the old original recipe, but that it sits atop the Fountain of Youth, and mixes its ageless serum into every drop that flows from its ancient spouts.  Those beauties taking your order may look 18, but check their birth certificates, and you see they are really 78.  Powerful elixir that Vanilla Swirl!  While I wish they didn't use Styrofoam cups, there is no debate that the soft serve here is about as good as it gets.  The prices are ridiculous. The former "Cash Only" requirement not oppressive simply because credit cards weren't as prevalent 60 years ago.   If only the Dollar was still worth what is was Back in the Day.

Well, all right!  The new and improved Acme in The Village of Newtown requires a revisit to the old review. It is no longer the boring step sister box store of yesteryear. Now, not only has Starbucks taken up residence in the front of the store, but they have installed a beer and wine aisle and a small eating area near the deli department. Will the wonders never cease?!  Even service seems to have moved up a notch. More friendly faces and helpful hands. Better trained cashiers and help desk personnel. The salad bar is definitely cleaner and better stocked than before, too.   Yes. It is still an Acme and not a Wegmans, so let's keep perspective. Yet, the new Acme is far better than the old, and they deserve an "A" for effort. Prices are still very competitive for the area. They are really working to hold on to their old customers and attract new ones.   These days I find myself thinking of stopping in their Starbucks, or grabbing a six pack rather than making a separate run to the local beer outlet. Give them credit for opening my mind to their new possibilities.

Wandering around Northern Liberties gives the feeling of late 19th Century urban America, when each neighborhood had to be self contained to provide its residents with all the necessities of life. Somehow the benign neglect that has allowed a slow evolution of this cityscape has resulted in organic growth that is very appealing to those of us seeking a comfortable alternative to what is now high speed life hot wired into our existence.   While a place like Soy Cafe would never have been dreamed of in those early days, the new urban pioneers create a new version of what a hood should have.  The retail space feels old and timeless, while the actual business is anything but.  If smoothies and light fare with a veggie bias is what you seek, then Soy Cafe is your siren song.   Work your way through the multitude of fresh fruit and soy milk drinks, each more satisfying than the last.  If something solid is required, don't hesitate to try a wrap or sandwich or a noodle bowl.  Everything is fresh and prepared with love. Grab a table and watch the gentles and notso come and go.   Zen Peach or Grill Eggplant Wrap are the yin-yang of a satisfying meal.  Always a house made sweet by the register for après dinez vous..

Modern Shanghai dumpling and soup house on Cottman Avenue just off the Roosevelt Expressway in Northeast (Dong Bei) Philly. This is a growing Asian neighborhood that is slowly becoming a legitimate alternative to Chinatown (Center City) and Washington Avenue (South Philly) for your dining and shopping pleasure.   Clientele is primarily Chinese, as is the staff. Cantonese is understood more readily than Mandarin. The menu is bilingual, with major focus on the beef/pork soup food group. Plenty of dumpling options, too, from Xiao Long Bao to wok fried pork gaozi. I was there for the XLB, so ordered two steam baskets (12) of them and a large bowl of Magic Noodles 101 (beef and bones in savory broth with mix of mushrooms and black fungus).   The Shanghai created XLB were steamy and quite tasty with a touch of vinegar dropped in through the opened top knot for added flavor. Only downside was that the skin was so friable that the act of lifting them gently onto my spoon with the metal tongs cause them to tear, leaving a leaking dough sack to contend with. Every one of them tore open. Nimble handling to place them quickly into the spoon was the only way to salvage the contents. I managed to do that, but still had to suck some soup from the spoon each time.   The Magic Noodle bowl was okay, but I found gnawing  the beef bones to be messy and less than fun. The mushrooms were flavorful and I knew the fungus was good for health.   This was a very tactile meal. It was definitely a change of pace cultural experience that was as entertaining as it was nourishing.

TWO SLICE LUNCH REVIEW  Despite receiving the "well done" reheat as requested, I was less than satisfied with the quality of the pizza served up at Nina's on Bridgetown Pike, Feasterville-Trevose, PA.   Most significantly, the balance of cheese to red sauce was way off. There was a ton of low grade mozzarella releasing oil and dripping on the plate, and the mass of fromage on top made the undercarriage too weak to hold the weight, causing sag from the get go. Too, the sauce, such as it was, was overwhelmed by the copious cheese, so that the only available flavor on the tongue was of salt. Not pleasant.   Service was fine and efficient. The dining room was partially open for sit down dining, with chairs on top of tables elsewhere in the room.   I didn't sample anything else on the menu, but Nina's is a No-No if looking for decent tomato pie, at least of the reheated variety.

I just had the best sandwich I have eaten in recent memory.   Hidden in plain sight at the rear of El Primo Mercado, the Mexican grocery store on Markley Street, Norristown, PA, is a moderate sized dining room and kitchen that cooks up amazing, authentic, wholesome, heavy plates of terrific comida Mexicana. Take a walk on the wild side past the bakery and chilis aisle, around the canned goods and wall of packaged tortillas, and finally humbly by the multitude of Madre Maria statuary looking down from the high shelves, into the eating area. Pull out a chair at a small table and await the friendly bilingual servers to present the large menu and take your drink order from the homemade fruit drinks and rice horchata.   I picked the Torta Milanesa de Pollo (fried breaded chicken sandwich) thinking it was a good way to introduce myself to the chef's skills. What I got was a gigantic sandwich on fresh super roll, loaded with delicious thin chicken breast, spicy mayo, lettuce, soft queso fresca (string cheese) and avocado. I could only eat half, and brought the rest home, where my 19 year old son devoured it in seconds, uttering only a muffled "Wow, this IS good," as he came up for air.  It was the second best thing I had consumed this year, after the Greek dessert I ate last week in Princeton. Just amazing, and worth the hour long drive back to Norristown from Bucks County just to see what else this cocina can turn out as remarkable as that Torta.

The Grange Fair is a traditional country fair run annually at this site in Wrightstown, Pa. It has all the attributes you would expect from a cultural events that has run for more than a century.  Livestock displays and competitions, 4H halls full of pies, pickled foods, flower arrangements, and art, with colored ribbons for the winners.   In addition, you can buy a tractor, arrange for a home visit by a landscaper or stone mason, and indulge yourself in carney food to your heart's content. For the kids (in each of us), there is a ride area with enough spinning, dipping and diving to upset your stomach for a week. My advice, ride before you eat, or better yet, come twice, once to ride and another visit to eat. The food is what you expect from a greasy country joint. Burgers, Sausage, Franks, Pizza, Ice Cream, and Kettle Korn (my fave). There is usually a beer wagon around that pours out a local brew and leaves a wet trail of suds on the ground. Beware the drunken bees that congregate there. Man, would I love to have some of the Beer Honey that hive puts out!   Yes, there are a fair share of Carney barkers and hucksters to enjoy with vigilance, and the local politicians trying hard to find votes by giving out balloons to kids. But, you can ignore that degradation and enjoy everything else.   The place is crowded at night when the cooler air invites families to come out for a night of old fashioned entertainment.  There is something special about a country fair at night. But, if you prefer to avoid the bigger crowds, arriving in the afternoon allows you a clearer view, and the ability to park and walk through the tents and sheds at an easy pace, when everyone who works there has more time to pay attention to you.  Be sure to make time to come up here. The roads around it are jammed in the evening, so give yourself time to wait in line.  If you know the roads, it is easier to approach from the north or west. Take out your GPS or paper maps and figure out how to do that. You could save yourself an hour of more in the queue.    The Grange Fair is definitely a child memory maker, so be sure to start your kids early and allow them to carry on this wonderful All American tradition.

Better known as Anthony's IV Pizza & Pasta on Bridge Street in Morrisville, Pa., which has its own Yelp page and more reviews, this old line pizza joint may not look like much, but turns out pretty good Italian sandwiches and platters at last century prices.   Only street parking available, but in the evening, the avenues of Morrisville are pretty much open and you can pull up right in front or on the side street (Washington).  Friendly faces and adequate booth and table seating.    This is another of the Mexican/Italian deals, but don't let that deter you.  The food is good and you won't really notice any Spanish accent unless you order the Mexican Pizza.  My Sweet Sausage, Pepper & Onion Sandwich was as good as most you can get across the river in the capital of New Guernsey.

Cafe Madison Holland sits in the Pheasant Valley Center at the bottom of Buck Road where a Chinese restaurant used to be. They have done a great renovation to the space and turned it into an attractive, comfortable room full of photos of customers. There are about a half dozen tables and small 6/7 stool counter for lone travellers. I grabbed a spinner so as not to take up a table and be able to chat with the staff. Turned out that Dean the owner was in the house, and we ended up in a long conversation about the trials and tribulations of opening a food business in Northampton. Let's just say his experience was not a business friendly welcome.   Glad he saw it through, because he has created an excellent place for an Americana breakfast. It is warm and feels quickly like home. The menu is extensive for the morning and afternoon meals and prices are fair. I opted to sample their french toast and homemade sausage patty with coffee. At $8.75, it was a deal and a half!   The toast was expertly turned. Amply saturated with egg/sugar/vanilla mix, the bread was thin and the right texture to absorb to its core. The edges were nicely caramelized to a mild crisp. The sausage was a freeform patty with very good flavor. I was glad I asked my server to help me choose among the alternatives. She was dead on that I should go with it. I appreciated that while they didn't have maple syrup, they at least had Log Cabin, rather than those corn syrup sweeteners. Lastly, the coffee was a Bunn drip that was hot and strong.   I have a feeling that Madison Cafe Holland is going to be a big hit where there are few good choices for a decent breakfast and lunch. It isn't that far from Newtown nor Feasterville that it won't draw from those communities as well. It will help put this corner of Northampton Township back on the map, something that has been missing since the passing of the Mill Race Inn. With Two Ladies Bakery Cafe, Johnny Apples, and Salvo's Pizza and a few other restaurants nearby, it is beginning to be a worthy destination again.   I, for one, am very excited to see this happening.

COVID-19 TAKE OUT REVIEW  Spice Garden is a take away only Indian kitchen that focuses on Kerala style South Indian cuisine. It didn't have to change much of its operation to adjust to the pandemic. On the end of an old commercial strip near the bottom of Bustleton Avenue just a few blocks before Grant Avenue, it is designed to accept your phone order for pick up 30 - 40 minutes later. That was our plan after grocery shopping at the large Asian supermarket on St. Vincent's Street @ Roosevelt Avenue. We called from the parking lot, arriving about 15 minutes later because of light Memorial Day Weekend traffic.  Now, I've had much better curries, masalas and garlic naans than are offered at Spice Garden, but on the other hand there is a trade-off of larger quantities and cheaper prices than available at standard Hindi houses, although the online menu states that recent cost of ingredient increases necessitated higher prices. That's just reality given these harsh times, and we didn't object to absorbing a couple of more bucks.   Of course, by the time we reached home the blush was off the rose. Reheating was required to reanimated each dish. We found each was tasty and very well spiced. The two chicken plates led the way, with the Kerala Chicken Curry in a dark thick sauce and the Chicken Pepper Fry bone in and the hottest of the lot. It was a finger food delight. The Channa Masala was lighter cream colored mildly sweet veggie dish that was a good sop for the Garlic Naan. The other diced mixed veggie bowl was a strong counterpoint to the rest of the tongue challenging heat packed into the two plastic take home bags.  The only real downside to the experience was the cleanliness of the small anteroom when I waited for the food. There were several insulated containers sitting on the floor, each more schmutzidick than the other. Clearly used for moving cooked food, there was no way they would pass a health department inspection. They left me wondering about the condition of the kitchen on the other side of that swinging door.   I'll let you know if I experience any side effects from this meal, which appears to be enough for three dinners.

The third child of New Leaf Cuisine (Manayunk & Broomall being the elder siblings), Purple has replaced the ill fated Golden China at the Floral Vale location in Lower Makefield. While "Asian Fusion" is often just confusion, this house seems to actually know what it's doing when it comes to Sushi and Chinese food.   Their menu is a complex of decent sushi, "Street Food," noodles and Chinese dishes, all well done with a touch of creativity and lots of flavor. Prices reflect the talent in the kitchen, so even the dim sum small plates add up fast. As a first timer, and suspecting that Mandarin was the primary language, we opted for that part of the menu to sample.   Smart move.  Our four dishes were; Beef Chow Fun (traditional Cantonese broad noodles), Chicken with Dry Pepper (medium heat w jicama for cool crunch) from Chinese Kitchen - Entrees, Spicy Crispy Chicken (crunchy fried chicken Szechuan style) and Wok-fried Lemongrass Beef (hottest dish w Thai spice sensibilities). They were all very good, with tender sliced beef, white meat chicken and no skimping on the spices nor portions. Three of us supped to our hearts' content with leftovers for another day. Each made its own statement without redundancy. The kitchen was well trained in the mystic art of Asian sauces.   If the sushi and other Japanese pieces are on par with the mainland portion of the menu, Purple Leaf could well be worthy of that fifth star. As it is, it is a giant leap forward for the local Asian restaurant scene.

While KO Modern Korean Cuisine does a tasty new take on traditional dishes from the peninsula, you must keep in mind that they call themselves a fusion restaurant that covers Japanese, Thai and even a pinch of Chinese in their kitchen. If traditional is what you want, then this is not the place for you. Try Mirim or the cafe inside of H Mart on Woodbourne Road for the real McCoy. It is only fair to judge based on their stated intentions, not on what they do not claim to be.   To my tongue they do a very good job on creative contemporary Korean food. I thoroughly enjoyed the small plate KFC (Korean Fried Chicken) and BBQ Pork Belly Bao. The extra spicy wings were just that. Messy and delicious. The Buns a tempting pile of belly and greens atop a soft round pinchable white rice bun. Had I stopped there I would have been seeing multi stars.   The Sushi and Bento Dinner from the Japan side of the menu were a different matter. Our Rainbow Roll ordered for a sushi neophyte, was less than inspiring. It appeared lifeless on the platter, and tasted less than brand new. When sushi is truly fresh, it has an inner glow. This did not. Perhaps, the use of dyed pink ginger was a tell, but it was less than optimal. I would like to see what they do with Gimbap, the seaweed and rice street food that most closely resembles sushi. I suspect it would have been superior.   The Bento options chosen were teriyaki salmon,  Dynamite Chicken and a similar shrimp offering (tiny deep fried crustaceans in a gloopy sticky sweet sauce). Again, this Japanese combo plate missed the mark. The salmon was good, but slightly overcooked. The chicken was barely above room temperature, and the shrimp was lost in the heavy batter shell and thick clingy sauce. Just not what we expected from this kitchen.   We agreed we would try again, but focus only on the Korean possibilities. This night, fusion could only be interpreted as confusion.

Aptly named Jersey diner on Rt. 206, Mt. Holly, NJ.   The place appears clean and well maintained.  All the marble shines from polishing. The staff in black shirts and red ties look like a well oiled machine.  I sat at the counter for a late breakfast.  The service was friendly, but a little bit off.  I ordered a short stack of French Toast, with a side of Sausage and Coffee.  The Bunnomatic brew was good, and my request for milk rather than Mini-Moo was well met.  The egged bread was a thicker, egg based loaf with the consistency of Chollah, but not actually that species. It grilled up well with lots of caramelized edges and a huge capacity to soak of the Smucker's Syrup.  Wish they had a Maple Syrup alternative, but guess not. Glad it was only two slices, as they were big and filling.   The breakfast sausage was four links that seem to have been cooked in the deep fryer rather than on the grill or in a pan.  They were uber oily and had a strange taste, perhaps from whatever had been deep fried prior to my order.  I tried, but could only eat half with max effort. Not good.   I received my bill before I was finished from an escaping server who wished me a good day, but never offered a second mug of coffee.  I had to ask one of the other women behind the counter for more, and she sweetly obliged.  This small slight of courtesy set my attitude toward the place.  Plenty of potential, but lack of execution; especially in human interactive skills and short cuts taken to save time/money, but disrespect the paying public.   This is one Pandora's Box I will not be opening again.

TAKEOUT REVIEW  Curious about this primarily take away Italian fast casual shop in Levittown, PA, I drove down late last week to pick up a light family dinner. I ordered three sandwiches; roast pork, chicken cheesesteak and sweet sausage, onions and peppers.   They were packaged in white, rectangular cardboard boxes and each half wrapped in butcher paper before being placed in a plastic bag before handing to me through the drive thru window. About $17 for the three. Good deal. Problem was that the placement of the boxes in the bag was haphazard. Once home and removing them from the sack and putting them on our kitchen table, it was obvious the boxes were not bagged upright, but on their sides. As a result, their was leakage and the roast pork a sloppy mess.   I did my best to reconstruct the sammy, and placed all three in the oven for a quick reheat. They were still tasty, although the rolls were damp and not first quality. The roast pork was juicy, the sausage had nice texture and plenty of flavor. The steak 'wich was only so-so.   I try to avoid take out most of the time because so much is lost not eating food right after it is off the grill. Zio Gio was no different. If I lived nearby, it is good enough to be in the be in rotation for a pizza/sandwich stop. Given the distance, it is unlikely to happen. There are too many local restos deserving our business.

TWO SLICE LUNCH REVIEW  Independence Plaza on South Broad Street, Hamilton, has been a difficult place to attract customers since its development thirty years ago. But, there is a new pizza joint down there now that provides reason for renewed optimism.   LaLucci Pizza has been open a few months. I stopped in last week for a two slice and a soft drink (water) lunch. Like most pizza parlor these days, it has several prebaked pies on display for consideration and a grill for hot sandwiches. As a first timer, I wanted to try a basic slice and something higher end for comparison. There was a good looking Margherita sitting up front and a regular pie on the counter, both with a few triangles missing. I asked for one of each, and mentioned that I like my reheats well done.  The store manager brought them to me a few minutes later, steam still wafting off the Vulcan surface. They were a nice size. I sprinkled crushed hot pepper flakes on them and went to work. First bite brought a crunchy report from the firm undercarriage. Very nice! No droop. Slightly salty taste to the sauce and cheese. The regular slice was leaking oil onto the paper plate, but not enough to require a demerit. The red, white and green margherita had the same hard edge crust and the pleasant flavor of fresh basil enhancing the chunky tomato gravy.   Both were better than the average reheat jobs for the area, and deserving recognition.   Happy to oblige with 4 big ones!

Decent enough small diner on York Road in Warminster, PA, where breakfast was had this morning. My third post-vaccine meal in a restaurant as the world crawls out of its collective cave to taste life again.   The Vegetarian Omelet was a substantial plate load of 3 eggs, broccoli, onion, mushroom and spinach, with a shovel full of home fried potatoes for balance and good measure. Rye toast was a crunch and a half. Very filling, but required extra black pepper for taste on both the eggs and taters.   I was surprised and concerned that the server was not masked, when we were required to be, and the owner was covered as well. Even with two jabs I would have felt more secure had she considered the reality that she was in contact with everyone in the dining room and kitchen and close proximity with every customers' food.  There is something to be said for keeping up appearances, especially in a food service business.   Maybe management will see this review and reevaluate its policy on proper social distancing protocols even in the improving circumstance of an almost safe, nearly post Covid world.

I really enjoy adaptive reuse of old buildings that bring old and new sensibilities to the fore. When done well, they are both attractive and useful in ways unforeseen when the structure was first constructed, and bring new uses into old packages, calling the imagination of the new occupant forward in wonderment. The Johnson Hall Coffee House is a great example. It offers a shop unimagined in 1890 when it was build, yet as redesigned, it provides a functioning java house that could have existed at that time, but has emerged due to the evolving cultural affections of our modern day. It looks old, but isn't.   It is a  warm, light and airy high ceilinged first floor retail outlet for excellent coffee products and breakfast, brunch and lunch options. Although limited by the kitchen equipment available to prepare meals, it still provides enough variety to make a stop very worthwhile. I loved the large windows, dropped period lighting, white ceramic tile, wood plank floors, and the friendliness of the staff.   I ordered an egg and cheese breakfast sandwich on croissant, with mug o' joe. It came in at about $8, and while ordering was at the counter in back, the servers brought the sandwich to my table. They would be wise to advertise the coffee roaster more dominantly both in the store and online, as I am sure I was not the only one curious about who produced the quality beans. The croissant was not quite French boulangerie, but still large and tasty enough to be satisfying.   Still, the atmosphere here is the star of the show. It is a great place for both solitary and collective pleasures.

Khmer Grill is one of the small shops in the new Chinatown Square food court in the middle of Race Street between 10th and 11th.  It prepares and serves up a limited menu of Cambodian style BBQ wings, beef skewers, sausage and chicken hearts on gizzards on sticks. There are also a few sides of rice and papaya salad.  Prices reflect that they are operating indoors in a newly renovated building with commensurate overhead. Thus, they cannot compete with the open air food carts at FDR nor Mifflin Parks in South Philly, where the vendors pay a yearly licensing fee, rent or buy their small stands, and are otherwise free of fixed costs.  If you don't want to wait for warmer weather for your Cambodian BBQ fix, Khmer Grill is presently your cold weather friend.    The food is well marinaded and basted while on the fire.  The result is a pleasant tasting mildly tart/semi-sweet flavor on tender meats that retain their juices.  My sausage was plump and spurted with every firm bite.  The thin sliced beef was easily slipped from its impalement on the bamboo sticks.  Liked them both a lot.   With any luck, both Khmer Grill and Chinatown Square will be successful and lead the way to other such food malls that have been so successful in the larger Asian population centers in Flushing, NY, L.A., San Fran., and Toronto.  In the space formerly reserved for one restaurant, you can now have a multitude of street food options from around the world. Right. Not the same as a standard sit down meal, but it has its place when interesting light bite snacks are more what you are looking for.    For those fortunate enough to have sampled the real thing while travelling through Southeast Asia, Khmer Grill is authentic enough to bring back fond memories.

Maybe it was because I came in around 3 in the afternoon, but my experience at Indigrill in Ewing, NJ, was pretty lousy. Let me count the ways.  1. Although nearly empty of customers, there was trash on some tables, the floor and the shelves near the soda machine and trash receptacle.  2. The Bollywood dance music videos played extra loud and on a nonstop loop from the TV high on the dining room wall.   3. The food counterman was pleasant, but the choices he had to work with were fairly limited, with only chicken, lamb and beef and three sauces available.   4. When I sat at one of their high table stools and began to eat from the biodegradable bowl and plastic spork, I found the meats room temperature at best, the chicken stringy and the lamb low quality with fat and hard spit outs.  5. The sauces were likewise cool, although they did have the right taste.   6. Ultimately, there was more brown rice in the bottom of the bowl than all the other ingredients combined.   7. What? No naan?!   It just wasn't very good and not worth the calories ingested, nor the more than $10 price with the sugary drinks.   I am not a fan of Chipotle Mexican Grill for its lack of authenticity and the comparison to the multitude of excellent Latin American restaurant with high quality offerings that abound in Central Jersey. The same is true for assembly line Indian cuisine. With all the wonderful South Asian houses within a 10 mile radius of here, why would anyone choose this poor copy of that bountiful and varied colorfully spiced deeply curried food?   The answer to that eternal question? No one with a working pallette and taste buds would, unless they were on a student budget that allows them to be abused by this low end excuse for fast food.   This place is atrocious.

All good things come to an end, so when my 13 year old war horse Infiniti finally went to the junkyard in metal heaven, I was sad, but not really surprised. Over 200,000 miles is a long life. It didn't owe me anything, and I had beaten the crap out of it.  I began a search for a replacement by checking with Car Gurus, an internet site that had been successful for me in the past. I thought I wanted to stick with the Infiniti brand, but find something newer in a quality used car. Compared to Lexus there were amazingly few oldies but goodies around. That was precisely why I chose Infiniti to begin with. Just didn't want the most popular in school, but that hidden understated gem.   On the second search I found a newer M 35x with low mileage on the lot at Holman Infiniti over in Maple Shade, New Jersey, about 25 miles away.   I gave them a call to find out if it was still there, and spoke with Mario Pinardo in their sales department. He went out to check and came back enthusiastic about how good the vehicle looked - Pearl White with light leather interior. I expected him to try to sell it, but he seemed naturally excited by what he saw. I asked him to hold it for me until tomorrow. He said he could only do so until 11:00 AM Tuesday.   I was there at 10:00.   This M 35x was worth being excited about. Perfect body. Not a scratch, dent nor ding. Immaculate within, with beautiful wood trim, sleek and sexy front and back. Well detailed to a perfect glowing leather, wood and metal trim. The drive was strong, responsive, with throaty exhaust and acceleration that offered no apologies for being six cylinders, 3.5 liters, as opposed to the eight 4.5 L the old boy threw around. Better gas mileage, too. And, the price for all that was very reasonable, and made it nearly impossible to walk away from.   Yup! An hour later it was mine and I drove it home.  The experience at Holman was excellent from beginning to end. The dealership is large, but they kept everything at a comfortable human scale. Mario was great. He was genuine, engaged and led us through the process with precise guidance. Even the minutes with the finance manager were decent. I didn't mind that he was a Cowboys fan.

Comes a time when those small trees taking root in the gutters of my home had to be dealt with, my sons didn't want to do it and climbing 30 feet up and down a ladder was a fool's errand for me. Had to bite the bullet and look for someone with the equipment and ability to do the job and stop it from being an annual problem.   After doing research and connecting with both local handymen, contractors and those professional gutter protection companies, I came to the conclusion that the only way to have the work done right, with warranty and acceptable prices was to go with the guys who specialize in this business. I chose LeafFilter Gutter Protection, a franchise located in Sharon Hill, PA.   I contacted them through their website and had a call back the next day. We met at my home a few days later, when I met Dan, their sales representative. He had a routine to go through, but he was genuine and made honest eye contact. He measured the gutters and explained their process and materials to me. I liked him, and found their technology to make sense compared to the competition. They have their pricing technique like the other solicitors for this service, which is always a put off, but ultimately we worked something out that was good for me on price, including 12 month interest-free financing.   Their crew arrived a day later with all they needed to complete the job. They power cleaned the existing gutters, anchored them firmly into the fascia with long screws and new braces, and them installed their vinyl covers and micro screens into the covers' frames. They finished about 5 hours later, cleaned up their mess completely and spoke with me about what they had seen up there that might need attention in the future. I signed off on the work order and sent them on their way.   We are expecting heavy weather this week, so the new LeafFilter will get an early workout. Given how much trouble the gutters were in past storms, I am looking forward to seeing how well the system works, and beyond that putting aside the worry I have felt wondering whether the next heavy rain would completely overwhelm the old aluminum runnels and knock them to the ground.   If this works as expected, I will put this anxiety behind, and become a convert to LeafFilter. If it doesn't hold up as advertised and warranted, there will be an addendum to this review.   For now, 5 STARS and a lot of anticipation.

Just finished an excellent breakfast at Lancer's Diner in Horsham, PA. I sat at the counter with a couple of other dudes and engaged in interesting conversation with my neighbor to the left and the owner of the establishment, while I enjoyed a Veggie Omelet, Rye toast and Coffee.  The three egger filled the plate from rim to rim, and was loaded with broccoli, spinach, onion, tomato, mushrooms and the home fried potatoes, I requested be placed inside the omelet. A few splashes of Tobasco and I was hot to trot. Very filling, tasty and satisfying, with plenty of refills of my coffee mug.   Our discussions covered many issues of the day, including mask wearing for school children (some initial disagreement, but we found common ground), the U.S. Constitution (I received free copies from the owner, which he distributes to everyone), the CCP (Chinese Communist Party - all opposed) and illegal opioid black market sales by pharmaceutical companies (put the bastards in jail). We clearly came from different perspectives and had desperate sources of information, but reached some consensus due to our calm, respecting demeanor and good grub. It was the best exchange I have had with strangers in a long time.   For that alone a fifth star is awarded in appreciation.

Can't say I was impressed with this Iron Hill Brewery in Abington, PA.   While the Pumpkin Ale was tasty and refreshing, our menu choices were fair to middling at best. We ordered their Calamari appetizer, Asian Salmon Burger and Country Schnitzel as main courses. The Calamari was all small rings (no tentacles) and overly oily from deep frying. Our guess was that these little things came from a large bag of frozen seafood. Nice to have slivers of hot peppers mixed in, but the ranch dressing dip really didn't contribute to the experience.   My dining mate didn't offer a taste of the Asian Salmon after she took a bite and put it aside. "Too much garlic," she explained. Those fries were quite crisp and crunchified, however, and I had a free hand with them.   The pork fillet Schnitzel was good; nice breading, pan fried with chunky Andouille Sausage white gravy over top. We ended up sharing that after she turned aside her salmon. I found the cutlets to be better without the gravy, and was able to push most of it off the entree. The sides (fresh spinach sautéed in garlic and oil, and the mashed sweet potato) were very colorful and also tasty strong contributors. Fair to say this plate was our dinner's salvation.   The space felt somewhat worn out. I don't like carpeted dining rooms, as they tend to hide the accumulated dirt that collects in the fibers. This wall to wall definitely had been down too long.   This was my third Iron Hill in the past month. Overall, unless very new, these breweries just don't seem to maintain high class facilities and appear worse for wear compared to their competition.  Three STARS is as far as I can go.

I am a fan of any new business that takes on the challenge of a major competitor with better goods, warmer environment and sincere service.  That Pretty Bird Coffee is about 50 yards from the green mermaid makes these folks heroic. That they are truly outclassing them is the stuff of legend.   The space, although a small storefront, is well designed and cozy.  There are a few deuces, high communal tables and a counter for those desiring to maximize the experience by sipping in.  The staff is young and very friendly, with a few managers involved to keep everything flowing.  It was easy to engage in a pleasant conversation with them as I waited for my latte and strawberry donut (homemade). These guys are really making an effort to build their reputation and customer base.    My latte was very good. No need for sugar or other adulterants, as it was strong and flavorful on its own.  The donuts were an indulgence, but they were sitting in the work area just staring at me. Impossible to resist.  When I took my first bite, I learned it was a cake donut with an interesting sugar/cinnamon/strawberry sprinkle topping.  Very good, but impossible to eat without a trail of crystals.  Slightly tart, too.  Liked it, but doesn't challenge Yum Yum or Mary's in the gooey goodness department.    At $6.50 for the medium cup and the dunker, the price was okay.   Pretty Bird is a nice place for meetups, and small conversations.   Parking behind the building and in the adjacent lots.

Tommy is the new kid in town.   He took over the old pizza joint named, "Gabriella's," renovated it into a bigger, more attractive kitchen specializing in burgers, hot dogs, chicken, ice cream and shakes. Indoor and outdoor seating available. Plenty of parking in back. It feels a bit like an escapee from New Hope just a few miles up River Road.   I ordered a Cheeseburger Junior (4 oz., w cheddar, sauteed onions and ketchup), and standard Hot Dog (mustard, ketchup, sweet relish), and Vanilla Shake.
