The hot dog was very good with firm casing and nice garlic beef profile, in an excellent torpedo roll with capacity to hold everything without leakage or falling off the truck when tipped. Liked it alot. The burger was half consumed by family before I had a photo opportunity.   My portion was decent for a quarter pounder, with juicy chew and flavor from the blend of shortrib, chuck and sirloin used for the puck, and the semisweet onion. The only weak link was the bun which was saturated by grease from the sandwich and did not survive the experience intact due to sogginess. The shake was cool and thick, but began separating before I could drink it all. It seemed to be made from soft-serve and milk rather than real ice cream. Not worth the $5.99 tag.   The closest comparison among offerings in the fast casual burger universe is 5 Guys. Tommy's hot dogs are superior, their burgers very similar, but the shakes need work. Can't speak to the rest of the menu, but I wouldn't mind returning to find out.

Apparently, the Popeyes website had so much traffic recently as people went crazy looking for their new chicken sandwiches, that it broke down! What followed was the exhaustion of sandwich provisions nationally, resulting in millions of disappointed customers arriving at bright orange & red stores just to discover signs across the wall menu that said,   " WE'LL BE BACK!"   I was one of those people at their small shop in Levittown, PA. The line wasn't long, but the sense of delayed gratification was tangible. After all those YouTube vids of people sitting with stacks of regular and spicy mayo sammies wrapped in specially designed paper, and watching them munch them up, rolling their eyes in delight, and attempting to speak waxingly with mouths full, it was almost too much to bear.   So, I grudgingly went home with a 3 piece dinner to share, knowing I would have a hard time convincing anyone that I didn't eat them on the way.   Brilliant marketing, though! Always leave us wanting more.

Hidden in the front corner of H Mart in Levittown, PA, lies Manna Kitchen, a tiny Korean restaurant serving cuisine from the homeland and China at reasonable prices. There are only four tables, so takeout is the primary focus. I stopped in yesterday to check out their Korean Fried Chicken, which comes six pieces to the container for nine bucks and change.   To be transparent, we seemed to have a small miscommunication about exactly what I was getting. I asked for Korean Fried Chicken Wings, which I thought the friendly order taker agreed I could have. Instead, what I got were a few wings and a majority of thighs. Now, I like thighs, but they are not the same as wings in taste nor texture. So, when I arrived home my first impression was that I had received huge wings. First bite told the tale, and disappointed my taste buds. The crisp was there, as was the delicious ginger soy finish, but the taste of the dark meat chicken could not be mistaken.   I am willing to chalk this confusion up to poor ordering on my part, rather than intentional misdirection by the staff. I did enjoy them once I realized what I had, it's just that my expectations were left unmet. This accounts for the loss of a star. After all, meeting expectations is what satisfaction is all about, and thus, reviews reflect that reality.   Still, I will get back to Manna sooner or later to see what else is going on. I do hope for no more misunderstandings, and that the chef is wearing her mask at all times while handling food, which accounts for the second demerit.

This place is really two restaurants in one.   First, Chester's Fried Chicken is something of an institution in this part of Trenton.  It has been frying up Chet's secret recipe for several decades.  Recently, the original chicken shack has been taken over by Pakistanis and added an identity of Shan Halal Pakistani, Indian & Bengali Cuisine.  The Southern Fried Chicken is still produced, but now there is a full South Asian menu complete from Masalas and Kormas, to Curry, Gosht and Naan.    The owner and chef is a devout Muslim, meaning he is friendly, courteous, modest, and accommodating. He was patient with me as I figured out what was being offered in these otherwise widely desperate culinary approaches.  I had not experienced a Fried Chicken/Chicken Masala house before.  But, I was game.  I wasn't completely ready to mix the two in one meal, and did not want to siesta after eating, so opted to go with Chester's grub.  I ordered the Special that included a Breast, Wing, 2 Jo-Jos (potato wedges) and a Roll.  At $3.99, I thought I had stepped into a time warp.  Turned out that the Chicken was quite good.  The coating was light and pleasantly spiced, without the oiliness that so often comes as part of the dish.  It was crispy from the deep fryer, but the layer of breading was so thin compared to what is found in the name brand competitors, that I appreciated why Chester had been so successful.  The Jo-Jos were also coated and fried, but were still just a close variant to what everyone offers.  The Roll was wasted calories from a store bakery.    Next visit I will explore the rest of the menu and file an update.  For the moment, Chester's Fried Chicken moves to the head of the class for a well designed and executed icon of country American dishes.  I would certainly pick some up for a family dinner.  To get the freshest and best tasting chicken, I will call ahead and ask for a fresh order to be prepared.

Phi Vietnamese opened its doors three weeks ago in the Crossroads Shopping Center off Rt. 313 in Doylestown.  It is the first shop to offer primarily Vietnamese food in the area, and for that they are worthy of appreciation.  Welcome to the hood.  The store is nicely appointed with black tables and chairs and burnt orange painted walls.  Looks good.  The staff is mostly indigenous to VN, and are quite attentive to their customers.  The menu offers what would be expected from this ethnic kitchen - Pho, Broken Rice, Summer Rolls, etc., at price points that while higher than in their siblings in less upscale environs, reflect the rent structure of the area.  $10 may be more than we are accustomed to paying for a large bowl of noodle soup, but it is a fact of life that things cost more in better communities.    Son and I stopped in for Pho Ga (Chicken Pho) and Bun Bo Hue (Beef Noodle Soup from the former royal capital of Hue in Central VN).  Service was fast, although belied by slower delivery of the side plate of Thai Basil, Jalapeno Slices, Sprouts and Lime Wedges.  They also forget to bring the Hoisin and Sriracha Sauces for customization.  No biggie. I went to get them myself.   The Chicken Pho was basic, but a solid presentation. It was steaming hot, with enough sliced white meat to keep son satisfied.  The Bun Bo Hue was another matter.  The spicing was off.  When right, it has a balance of Lemongrass, Fermented Shrimp Sauce, Chili Pepper and Sugar, to represent the major spice groups.  When joined with the amply simmered Beef Broth, and loads of thin sliced steak and brisket, it becomes a powerful combination that attacks the eyes, nose and mouth at the same time.  It can literally take your breath away until you adjust to its flavors and begin to taste how great they are together.  Phi's version was unbalanced with weak Lemongrass presence, and no sweet undertone.  Too, the table lacked the Vietnamese Coriander that adds to the complexity.  While it was hot and possessed some kick, it could not duplicate the burst of flavors a true BBH puts out.    Phi Vietnamese is certainly good enough for a second visit and hopefully they will get their spice legs beneath them and start to BRING IT!  They shouldn't underestimate the sophistication of the local pallets, or they risk losing face to the suburban houses that can do it right, like House of Pho in Southampton and Pho Palace in Feasterville.

Number 1 Chinese Restaurant on Parkside Avenue, Ewing, NJ., is classified at the apex of an imaginary list of Chinese houses.  Only if you hold that list upside down will it come close to the top.   This is strictly a takeout and delivery joint with good reason. If you walk in as I did to order and pick up your own food, you will discovery that it is unkempt with a layer of grime throughout. Not a pleasant place to wait.  The menu and prices are about what you would expect for a low budget kitchen.  The lunch specials are all under seven bucks for a pile of stale fried rice and choice of soup or egg roll in addition to the main offering.    I found my orange chicken to be small pieces of clucker, thickly breaded and wok fried so that it was not always possible to discern the actual chicken within its cocoon. As indicated, the fried rice was at least a day old, underheated, clumpy and dyed with whatever bouillon they cooked it with. The sauce was thick and gloopy, but the flavor was not so bad.  The overall experience just left much to be desired.   The only saving grace was the egg roll, which was actually better than expected, with pork strips within in addition to cabbage and spouts.   Not the place I would return to unless it was the only game in town.

Jumbo's is the new business in the free standing building out in front of H Mart on Oxford Valley Road, Levittown, PA. It claims to fame are its fried chicken, wings, burgers and hot dogs. As I was a rookie there, and it was late lunch time, I decided to try a few things - Jumbo's fried chicken, two types of wings and my most secret curiosity, the hot dog.   I ordered the 4 piece Fried Chicken (white meat, no sides), Spicy Sweet and Hot Fire Wings and the Elote Hot Dog. The exchange took place at the walk up drive thru window with the friendly woman I took to be an owner/manager. Everything was prepared in about 20 minutes, and she brought a neat package out to me as I waited in the car.   In no particular order -   The Elote Hot Dog was very good. The beef sausage was firm, fresh and loaded with garlicy flavor in a quality bun. The Mexican corn had plenty of spice and interesting taste, that although wet did not harm the strength of the bun. The Elote drizzle over the top was a bit salty, but not enough to be a distraction. Love me a great frankfurter, and this was almost that.   The Fried Chicken had lost its crispness by the time it reached my kitchen table. Probably inevitable, but still not at its apex. The flavor of the fried surface was milder than I like, and it needed more zest. The chicken itself was tender, but the lack of spice in each chew made the overall experience less than hoped. It just wasn't memorable.   The wings were a medium size. The Spicy Sweet was a decent sauce that was more sweet than spicy. The Fire Hot was a rub finish that had the right amount of burn. They compared favorably with the equivalents at Buffalo Wild Wings according to our sons.  Will have to return for the burgers and tots, but until then, 3 Stars is where it's at.

While Gay Street in downtown West Chester, PA, is way cool, with outdoor cafes, taverns and breweries competing with pedestrians for sidewalk space, this Iron Hill Brewery & Restaurant seems a bit out of sync with its very popular competition. Perhaps because it is older than many, the overall impression is drab and worn.   We were a small group celebrating a new member of the firm. Staff put a few tables together for us, giving us complete command of the main dining room late in the afternoon. We ordered drinks and a few appetizers and smoozed for a couple of hours. We had good conversation as we consumed a plate of hummus/pita, sweet potato fries w dipping sauces and roasted Brussel sprouts in balsamic (?) dressing.   The drinks were fine, if unimaginative; the same being true for the food. We consumed everything with a couple rounds of booze, and had no complaints, but it could have been so much more to keep us interested in their dark auburn atmosphere.  This Iron Hill just felt tired compared to other of their siblings I have visited and enjoyed. They occupy a key corner in town and it was easy to imagine how much more interesting and inviting it could be. How about an outdoor presence like everyone else? How about better marking of the main entrance door? How about better lighting around the bar to accentuate the back bar display?  Just saying...

If "A-Okay" is interpreted as mediocre, Siam Cuisine Thai Restaurant III, fits the definition. Although, "Meh," is also appropriate in some regards. Simply, I expected more from this outpost of Southeast Asian dishes, especially after dining in the past at its sister restaurants in the area, and the fabulous Thai meal eaten a few months ago in Metuchen, NJ.   Here, although the atmosphere was comfortable, the service and quality of the food left much to be desired.   We ordered three soups; Coconut, Lemongrass and Vegetable.  While the flavor of the coconut soup was accurate, it and the other bowls were populated mostly by broccoli florets, carrot slices and nearly tasteless mushrooms. The lemongrass was mildly spicy hot despite our request that all our dishes be heavy on the chili and other condiments.  Sadly, the veggie offering was just a weak diluted consume with the same contents.  Disappointing.  The entrees were also a mixed bag.  The drunken noodles were plentiful, but not hot enough.  The stuffed chicken breast plate was decent, but would have been much superior with a more spicy stuffing. My salmon dish was a nice fillet, but slightly past its prime.  Again, that broccoli and carrot thing.  Service was slow, and perhaps the bottleneck in the kitchen explained the lack of any attempt to accommodate our requests for spicier food.  However, given that our dinner for four came to nearly $100 with a beer and a couple of non-alcoholic drinks, they could have either made a stronger effort, or let us know in advance that they were unable to satisfy our requests.   Regardless, given the other Thai houses in and around Bucks County, there is no reason to visit Siam Cuisine again anytime soon.  2.5 Stars

Rice & Curry Asian Bistro is a Thai/Asian fusion house on Limekiln Pike in Maple Glen, PA. Although I ate outside at a table under the overhang, I did go in looking to let someone know I was there. The dining room was attractive, and in a post-Covid world I would definitely chose to dine inside.   Their menu is divided between standard Thai dishes and Japanese sushi. There may be compromises with strict authenticity for the sake of broadening market appeal, but not so much that close familiarity is missing. In fact, my late lunch and the green curry takeout for family were quite good and definitely worthwhile. I, for one, understand the business decision to find a reasonable common denominator in ingredients and style, as long as the fundamental touch, feel and flavor of the food remains.   This, Curry & Rice succeeded in doing.   My Spicy Noodles (not "Drunken Noodles") were prepared with medium width rice pasta, rather than the traditional broader noodles, but the sauce was right on and plenty hot enough, with a strong variety of fresh veggies (carrot, string bean, onion, green/red pepper). So, while there was less surface area for the sauce to cling to, it wasn't really noticeable on the tongue, although there was less chew. They also decorated the bowl with an iceberg wedge, which seemed incongruous. Too, my Tom Kha Soup was excellent, with a pleasing hot/cool profile of lemongrass and coconut milk, with a large supply of shredded chicken and fresh mushrooms. I tipped the rim of the bowl to my lips to suck out every drop. My son liked his Green Curry takeout when he got to it hours later.   I appreciated their lunch menu provided somewhat smaller plates at commensurate prices. I was able to push away from the table feeling satisfied without being overfull.   That is always appreciated.

Devil's Acre Tavern is a very attractive reuse of an old roadhouse along Easton Road (Rt. 611), Plumsteadville, PA. It takes it name from the nearby Devil's Half Acre, originally a stone tavern built in the 18th Century close on the Delaware River that sold alcohol and other services to the river traffic navigating upstream and down in a time the the river was the primary means of transportation in this part of colonial America. In fact, they had no license to make nor sell alcohol, and the joint was a place where violence and shady characters abounded. Legend and history say there were many people killed there and buried in the backyard.   Perhaps, to lessen the reliance on that unsavory history, the name was chosen without the word "Half," but the connection is not lost on those aware of these facts. Still, it appears often enough in the menu and on the walls of the establishment to hint at the local lore.   Luckily, this house is totally legit. Ownership has created an attractive utilitarian space, German American in nature, with excellent cross section of Deutsch brews, quality cocktails, reasonable happy hour choices and a strong kitchen. We stopped in on Saturday afternoon at the start of HH, and thoroughly enjoyed the entire experience. After a little confusion with our new server about availability of happy hour and where to sit to capture those prices, everything was resolved quickly and we waited for delivery to our dining room table of Three Onion Soup, Dragon Wings and Pierogi of the Day apps/sides, and two DHA Burgers and a DHA Dog.   Everything was very good to terrific. My stepson wouldn't share his potage, so it must have been great. We all sampled the wings @$.50 per. They were not too big, but were amply meaty with a good sweet/hot glaze with sesame seeds sprinkled on top. The pierogi were the weak link. The dough was thick, too chewy and dominated the flavor of the seasoned veggies within. Ate one and took the rest home. Maybe sour cream would have helped.   The burgers were huge with double patties, bacon, lettuce, red onion, and their DHA sauce. Both were past the medium well finish requested, but there was still plenty of flavor and moisture. I loved the double dog with chopped red onion, dark mustard and well done bacon in a fresh crisp torpedo roll. Great taste and texture. @$5 HH price it was a star of the show.   Devil's Acre Tavern is a 35 minute drive from home, but when in the mood for German beer and cuisine it is well worth the trip. Tuesday Burger Night sounds like a winner, too.

WHOLE PIE PIZZA REVIEW -  Stopped at Giuseppe's for late lunch after a beautiful walk around at Morris Arboretum. It was about half way home. Perhaps with eyes bigger than stomach, we went with a large pie, half pepperoni, thinking a fresh baked pizza would be more satisfying than reheated slices and we could take the rest home.   It didn't quite work out as planned.   Upon delivery to our table by the friendly server, we noticed a small pool of oil sitting mid pie. We blotted up as much as we could, but it remained shiny with the excretions from the pepperoni and low grade mozza covering the crust.   The request for a "well done" finish to make the undercarriage as firm as possible wasn't honored, so each slice drooped down when lifted and continued to drip oil. The cheese layer was too thick to be supported, and there wasn't any balance with the sauce, which was a bit salty for our buds.   Just not a very strong effort. Made us rue our decision and wish we had gone with a couple of slices, or better yet, not stopped in at all.

Grapevine has been anchoring North State Street in Ntown for years, and Chuck takes his position as organic food and nutrient provided to the community very seriously.  If he doesn't have it, he will get it for you quickly. Amazing how much fits into his small shop.   My primary purposes for visiting are to buy the vitamins and supplements that generally can't be found in the supermarkets of the area in organic form.  Too, he now carries Lynn's Coffees, bean or ground, and local roast coffee tastes best to me.   Thinking globally and buying locally is important if we are to maintain Main Streets that are economically viable.  Thankfully, Grapevine is a pleasure to frequent, as  Chuck and his people are knowledgeable and super friendly. It just feels good when I walk into his shop and he calls out my name in greeting.  I don't get that kind of reception in big boxes.    One of the coolest things about Grapevine is that in Spring and Summer the storefront is one giant hanging flower garden shop.  The riot of colors from the solid wall of hanging petunias and other flora is overflowing in abundance.  It is hard to find the front door from the foliage around it.  But, so much fun searching for it.

The space was modern, yet comfortable. Black tables, wood-like floors.  A nice diner-esque counter. HD TV on the wall.  Menu full of creative alternatives in the pancake, French toast, waffle and omelet genres.    Perhaps I made a mistake in ordering a simple Short Stack of French Toast.  It seemed as soon as I gave the friendly server my order she was coming back with it already mixed, dipped, grilled and plated.  Olympic turn around time.   But, something went wrong.  The four wedges were not fully cooked.  The toast was mushy and not hot in its core. There was no crispy caramelization.  It had been rushed for no apparent reason other than inattention.  Time constraints did not permit returning it to the grill for a few extra minutes, so I ate what I could and took my leave.   With so many good reviews, mine is surely an outlier.  I will try again in a few weeks and see what I get.  But for now, I have certainly had much better French Toast at many places in the area.

CURBSIDE SERVICE COVID-19 REVIEW -  Bualoy is a Lao restaurant in Devon, PA. It was fairly near Knox Covered Bridge in Valley Forge Historic Park, and the right place to pick up a late lunch to take home.   We parked out front and were greeted by a friendly order taker who handed us a paper menu and made good suggestions in response to our inquiry about what they did best. The conversation led to ordering Homemade Laotian Sausage, Nam Khao Salad and spicy Drunken Noodles with Beef. Fifteen minutes later she returned with our neatly packed meal.   Arriving home 50 minutes later, the sausage was still warm, the salad cool and the drunkens, hot. We liked all three dishes. The sausage had the interesting flavor of lemongrass, cilantro, onion and ground veggies mixed with pork. It came with a small side of mashed chilli sauce which added a kick. The Nam Khao was cool and hot with special mention to the crushed peanuts that were fried with a mild sweetener that added unusual interest to the dish. The Drunken Noodles were wide rice pasta loaded with green pepper, onion, carrot and sprouts in a three star hot scale brown gravy. Delicious.   We can only imagine how much better our meal would have been had we been able to eat in restaurant when everything was right from the kitchen. Still, it was good enough to make a return visit when it is safe to enjoy a sit down right at the source.

The facility is very nice with dark wood tones and adequate spacing of tables.  The sushi area is to the side and kept very clean.  The service is adequate, if not overly warm or informative.  Definitely, a nice space to eat and socialize.  The Hibachi is not much to my liking, as whether beef, chicken, shrimp or lobster, they all taste almost the same coming off the grill due to the heavy dosing with soy sauce.  The flipping of food morsels from the spatula into the diners mouth is funny the first dozen or so times it is experienced, but gets old (and messy) after a while.  This is not the place I would chose to have a delicious steak, as it is far from a Ruth Chris, Capitol Grille, or Walensky's experience.    The rest of the menu is diverse and generally decent, but not outstanding enough to want to return more than sporadically.  The presentation is done well, and the staff is prompt if not overly engaging with the customers.   I have tried the Udon/Soba Noodles with Chicken or Beef and enjoyed them, although they were less spicy that I generally prefer.  The Bento Boxes and lunch are a solid meal with Shumai, Tempura Veggies, and Haru Maki or other light roll as accompaniment.   For me, Mt. Fuji is a good alternative place for local lunch or dinner, but I would not drive far out of my way for the opportunity.  Thus, 3 Stars.

The name on the Spring Menu breakfast was: "I Can't Believe They're Vegan Pancakes."   Well, now I know that was just a bit of clever marketing, because after eating the nearly tasteless, dry, syrup sponges, I now fully believe they WERE vegan, and in a word, "boring."  My high hopes were dashed by reality.   But, I forgive Turning Point for misleading me, because everything else about their new facility in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center, is first class. The room is sun filled, bright and airy, with high fanned ceilings, white walls, and copious amounts of glass, letting customers be part of any sunny day outside while they sup within. A definite country cottage vibe throughout. Service is uber friendly without being unctuous, and the $2.50 house brewed java comes with a insulted pitcher of coffee, mug, and small glass carafe of milk (upon request). More than enough for me.   I enjoyed sitting at the bar and watching the coffee operation in front of me, and the dining room activity through the backbar mirrors. The rest of the menu was appealing for both morning and afternoon meals, even if the prices reflected the cost of Newtown's newly discovered sophistication (falling into the category of be careful what you wish for).   Turning Point, like its sibling nearby, Harvest, is the new order of things around here. Along with all the other restaurants already there, and those being planned (Chipotle, Iron Hill, Starbucks, Melt Shop, etc.), they will either become a sought after destination for fast casual dining, or a place to be avoided because of inadequate parking, and too much sameness. There is already talk of the center becoming a food court.   It definitely feels like a gold rush around here, and it remains to be seen how deep and wide the rich vein goes. It will thrive for a while, but whether it becomes a permanent part of life or a ghost town, depends on changing tastes, the local economy and how well conceived the plans were at the start.

For a coffee lover there is nothing as satisfying as quality raw coffee beans, freshly roasted, ground and brewed by a favorite method to create the perfect cuppa joe. Once introduced to apex java brew there is just no going back to Maxwell House or Folgers.   There are a number of excellent local roasters that provide the materials to produce this great way to greet the day. Covered Bridge in Feasterville is now one of my favorites. Housed in a rear out building behind an industrial garage, they have established a small shop loaded with all the paraphernalia needed to reproduce your coffee at home, with heavy duty roaster in back that produces enough customized volume to keep their growing list of consumers satisfied within a few days of ordering. In our case, we ordered directly from their website on Friday night and received an email that our beans were ready for pickup Saturday morning. The "born on" date stamped on the back of the resealable brown bag was actually the previous Monday.    That's pretty darn fresh.   Ordered were Ethiopian Natural Kembata Grade 1 and The Bee's Knees Breakfast Blend (Ethiopia & Brasil). Over years of java drinking I learned that the valleys and mountainsides of Ethiopia grew the best coffee beans on the planet. Mild, yet richly textured taste, I am willing to hunt for and pay more for it, rather than settle for mass produced coffee from Columbia and the like. So, I opened that bag this morning and inhaled deeply.   Its powerful aroma was overwhelming.   I waited a moment to let that snort settle in. It was decadent, yet innocent. I decided on a pour over of an individual mug, rather than brewing a full pot. When the filtered water was boiling in the whistle teapot, I began to slowly pour it through the cone filter and grounds sitting in our glass mug top funnel.    The result was near euphoria. First sip of the jet black suspension was intense, steamy, perfectly delicious coffee, that disclosed its lithe muscular body and subtle undertones of cocoa, strawberry and orange as it played on my tongue. It was as interesting as a fine glass of wine, without the alcohol, but with a similar intoxicating affect.   At $15/lb., it isn't cheap, but given how deprived we have all been in this lockdown quarantine Year of Covid, a little decadence at home is likely a good thing.

I stopped in at Namaste Indian Bistro in the Davisville Center in Warrington, PA, yesterday to chow down on their weekend lunch buffet. The shop is deep and quite narrow, obviously carved out of an adjoining store to create another retail space. Maybe a dozen tables in front, with the food spread out on a table right outside the kitchen.   There was plenty to choose from made up of a mix of chicken, vegetarian and even a goat curry dish. Some were very freshly prepared, while others were past their prime from sitting out over a steam table, inevitable when dealing with buffets. Still everything I tasted was good to excellent, especially the veggie korma and custom made garlic naan. Appreciated all the beautiful yellows, reds and amber colors from all the sauces.   I enjoyed my meal. At $11.99 for AYCE, I thought it a very good deal.   Service was minimalist, but how much to expect when basically serving yourself? My water glass was refilled, the used plate removed from the table promptly and the naan brought out from the tandor oven when fully baked and steaming hot.   What's not to like?!

Ray's Café & Teahouse on North 9th Street on the eastern end of Chinatown, has been brewing incredible coffee since the mid-90s.  The ambiance is def Taiwanese old school, with Grace and son working the Hario syphon butane java makers with aplomb and verve.  The best locally roasted beans are used to make single cups of joe, that are delivered to the table on a small tray, with doily and excellent butter cookie aboard. Little spout of milk on the side.   The Ethiopian Yirgacheffe beans from Main Line Coffee Roasters, were freshly ground the moment before their boiling bath and syphoning through the beautiful glass system, producing a superb cuppa joe. Not to put too fine a point on it, but this was among the very best coffee I have ever enjoyed. To watch Grace make my cup from grinding through pouring, was to see an artist at work. Perfect temperature. Perfectly balanced acidity.  A pleasure to imbibe. Easy to become addicted.  The Hario equipment was lined up on her counter, and the butane burner emitted a cool blue flame that brought the filtered water to a boil and flushed it up the tube and down through the coffee against a cloth filter.  Pure alchemy!   Even the butter cookie with the colorful sprinkles was a winner. Hard and crisp, the way it should be.   Yes. At $5 a cup, this is not for the faint hearted. But, for coffee lovers and mavens, going to Ray's is a trip to the mountaintop to sit at the feet of the javamaster.

Lily is the heart and soul of the Chocolate Paradise over which she holds expert dominion. Her friendliness and genuine interest in her customers matches perfectly with the homemade candy she creates. She explains that she is a first generation American of Chinese heritage who worked in a law office before discovering her true calling as a chocolateer.   Her small shop in the Pheasant Valley Center on Buck Road, Holland, PA, feels a bit enchanted upon walking in. There is a wall of shelves holding most of the milk, semi sweet and dark chocolate offerings, seductively packaged and fairly priced. They grab your attention until Lily's voice calls you across the room to where she sits packaging her goods and overseeing the operation. She asks what you like, makes suggestions, and offers samples to help convince you to take a deep dive into her cacao universe.   Just follow her lead. She won't disappoint.   I purchased a box of peanut butter cups and buckeyes, and sampled sea salt caramel chocolate covered cashews (sultry), sriracha honey peanuts (mildly sweet with a chili bite), and a German waffle cookie (Stroopwafel) dipped in milk chocolate with caramel center(nice crisp base for the creamy brown blanket and that sticky caramel kick). The peanut butter was high quality (way better than Skippy), creamy smooth that melded wonderfully with the equally soft and sexy chocolate casing. Made me wonder how anyone introduced to these babies could ever go back to Reece's!? (Rhetorical question - They can't.)   Well, maybe for Halloween, but otherwise I'd rather go for Lily's best - eat fewer, but kvell so much more.   Lily's Chocolate Paradise is where to go for your chocolate fix. Yes. There other a few other custom chocolate shops around, but none with Lily's exceptional personality, nor at such affordablilty.   This is rich indulgence for the people!

This is an older version of Friendly's on West Trenton Avenue, Morrisville, Pa.  The dining area is long and narrow, with about twenty tables and booths. It is an attractive space in a 1960's kind of way; feeling like a joint your parents would have enjoyed in their teens.   Adrianna was a fine server;  friendly, prompt, attractive.  Her red hair worked for her. She took my order of a patty melt, and like a skilled salesperson, inquired if I wanted fries, or the ninety-nine cent upgrade to onion rings.  What the hey?! I splurged.  She also thought that I might qualify for the free sundae, and delicately broached the topic with diplomatic flair.  In fact, I did.  Everything tasted good on the way down.  The melt had the appropriate finish and a goodly amount of grease.  The rings were uber-crisp.  The black raspberry scoop with KitKat crumbles looked strange, but tasted fine.  In fact, when I walked out I was considering a three/four star review.  That was until I went to bed a few hours later.  By that time, my stomach was in distress, and I feared a sleepless regurgitative night.    It was a close call, but a handful of Tums quieted the restive beast, and I finally slept somewhere around 2 am.    I'm all for low budget burgers, but I suspect the raw beef may have spent too much time above health department temperature requirements before being slapped on the grill.  Besides, this meal came to almost $12, with grat.  At those prices, I don't want to deal with unpleasant consequences.

Surprisingly strong fried chicken down on South Broad Street by Popeye's.   The bright orange shop has been there for several years, but always seemed out of place as a drive through box in the middle of urbanity. My bad for not checking it out before now. Walked in on a very clean space staffed with friendlies and stocked with trays of golden brown clucker.   Their two piece lunch deal came with one side and a biscuit. Under $5 for a filling and tasty treat. I ordered the spicy version. While it wasn't too spicy, it was certainly hot and crisp. The inner meat in the breast burnt my fingers as I ripped it apart. Soft and juicy. Really liked it. Actually gave me two wings along with the breast. Coke machine offered a large variety of their soft drinks.   There is another excellent chicken shack further down Broad, so there is a choice of good stops to satisfy the bird lover in you.

Unfortunately, the first observation from my dealing with Pho & More in Montgomery Commons is that while it may be a Vietnamese house, it certainly is not a Thai kitchen. As I ordered from both ends of the menu, I found myself happy with the Roast Pork Banh Mi sandwich, but damned dissatisfied with the Lemongrass Coconut Soup (Tom Kha) and the Drunken Noodles (Pad Kee Mao).   Why? Because although both those dishes have lemongrass spice as the key ingredient, there was absolutely no lemongrass to be found in either the soup, nor the wide flat rice noodles. The soup tasted of watered down coconut milk, with ample chicken and mushrooms, but without the strong bite that lemongrass provides. Very poor effort.   And the Drunken Noodles were not hot and chewy at all, but really just Chinese Vegetable Chow Fun with a few leaves of Thai basil mixed in. I ordered it "very spicy," and the cashier dude repeated that request to me upon pickup. Yet, despite the reasonable quantity of noodles and veggies, it totally lacked the heat punch desired. Boring, semi-sweet fat noods without redeeming fire signature. Major disappointment.   If I had to guess, I would venture that there was not a Thai person in the kitchen, nor even a real authentic recipe for Bangkok cuisine in the house. If they don't have lemongrass in stock, they just aren't Thai, and shouldn't misrepresent their abilities. Yet, the Banh Mi was decent and I grant that someone may have trained in Ho Chi Minh City or Hanoi to perfect their pho stock.   Had I known the truth about this joint, I would have happily stayed in Vietnam, and travelled to Thailand another day. As it is, with dishonesty at their core, I will never return to find out what they are really good at.   Fooled me once, shame on you! Fool me twice; never happen!

While I am not an Applebee's regular customer, I do like this chain for consistently decent food (primarily salads and burgers), reasonably priced drinks and a well trained staff. This particular location on Street Road in Southampton, PA, does not deviate from the norm. It is a pleasant place to grab a beer and bite at the bar when traveling solo, or at a booth when with family. They don't take themselves too seriously. They recognize they are a roadhouse, provide sustenance without pretension and work to let customers have a good time, in a wholesome atmosphere.   There was a wait for tables in the lobby when I arrived, but almost no one at the bar. I inquired of a passing server if I could belly up there immediately, and she said, "no problem." I was alone, and saw no point to occupying a table when a bar stool suited my needs. Bartender Kate approached quickly to take my drink order. I asked about pumpkins, and she told me that River Horse had just delivered their Hipp-O-Lantern pumpkin ale. Perfect! I was sipping from their signature hippo snifter a moment later. She also handed me a menu. I quickly decided on the whiskey bacon burger, pink.   What I received was a half pounder with melted cheese, crisp bacon, lettuce, tomato and red onion. While beyond pink, it was still fresh and tasty with a sweetish bun. I needed knife and fork to disassemble the thick sandwich. The fries were nice and hot/crisp.   At about $11, it was a value investment in a filling and enjoyable meal. We all have certainly paid more for much less in the current burger wars.

I'm not sure how the words, "authentic" and "style" can be used in the same phrase to describe the legitimacy of anything produced far from the original source, as done by Manhattan Bagels. "Style" suggests it has a similarity to the original, but really isn't from the creative source; while, "authentic," is defined as being from the original hands. So, it really can't be both - except in the world of Madison Avenue false advertising.   Please excuse the discourse on meaning, but the truth is that regardless of name and slogans, these are decent bagels. While not quite as crisp as I like on the outside, the texture is lightly chewy with a pleasant mild maltiness within, and without skimping on the toasted onion flakes or veggie cream cheese. I would like them even if from Manhattan, Kansas.   Service was friendly and quick, and the House Blend coffee provided the requisite morning kick in the pants.   This franchise is well represented in these parts, so while not on my list of absolute favorite bagel houses, it is certainly worth a stop when the breakfast bird is hunting for its early worm. You shouldn't be disappointed.

Honey Baked Ham is the non-kosher name for a chain of primarily sandwich places where you can order a combination of sandwich, bread, drink, side and cookie for a prix fix.  You can also order a full ham. This one is in the Village of Newtown section anchored by the Pier 1 store.   The few times I have been there I have gone with Turkey Breast, Swiss Cheese with lettuce and mustard, Cole Slaw side, Snapple Ice Tea and a Peanut Butter Cookie. It comes in a cute box.  They taste good, if not outstanding.  The service has been friendly, but when I am there it seems the owner is there alone and doing all the work.  This makes for a feeling that he is rushing around, for which he has my sympathy.    I have also been a regular of another HBH in the Mercer Mall in Lawrenceville, New Jersey.  That shop seems better organized, and the food is somehow more enjoyable.   Still, when I need to eat at my desk or want to be in Tyler Park for an hour of nature, HBH offers a great solution.

Hospitals are never fun places to be. Even when just visiting a sense of dread overcomes us.   Yet, Thomas Jefferson University Hospital, and all its component parts, makes the experience as positive as possible for most of us.  From the valet service drivers through the Chief of Medicine everyone approaches people with humanity and an understanding of what is involved in going there.    I have been using TJUH for a long time for myself, my family, and friends.  I recommend it to everyone seeking world class medicine with a friendly face.  From Rothman, The Heart Institute, Cancer Center, and ER, the treatment is state of the art and first class.   Unfortunately, I have seen my share of medical centers in New York, and for my health and for those I love, Jefferson is where I find the best combination of care and caring.   Before you decide on anything serious it is wise to at least obtain a consultation with a Jeff doc.  You will be glad you did.

This is an old style Jersey diner before they started using steroids to make them bigger. The ambiance suits the architecture, and the staff is friendly and prompt.    I stopped in for a late lunch last week.  I was greeted with a warm engaging smile by Christine, who led me to my table, handed me the menu, and went over the specials.    I went with the Chicken Salad Wrap which came with a cup of Chicken Okra Soup and Fries.  The Soup was really good; making me wish I had a bowl of it.  Lots of chunky okra and chicken, with other veggies thrown in for good measure.  The Chicken Salad was wrapped tight with Lettuce, Tomato and Sweet Pepper.  I could only finish half, but it tasted freshly made.  Quite enjoyable, although I prefer my chicken salad chunkier.    I was most taken by the atmosphere here.  It captured the feel of an old time diner, and while I ate I was able to temporarily depart this contemporary mortal coil, and spend a few moments in a bygone era.  Although the interior is of recent vintage, they did an excellent job in maintaining its simplicity.   Will definitely return regularly.

After a dozen or more breakfast take out visits, I have become a fan of this Cosi in the Newtown Business Commons.  The staff now recognizes me, knows what I want, and meet me with my coffee poured.    I like the personal touch.   The oatmeal, square bagel, and hot coffee is my routine, and I am sticking to it.  Definitely deserving of an upgrade.   Thanks, Tina.

Aside from being the only DD I know that has converted floor space into a fire pit leather sofa lounge, there is nothing out of the ordinary in this shop.  The coffee is hot. The donuts sweet. The service so-so.  The lounge full of Russian 20 somethings.  If any of these appeal to you, this is the place for you. Me?  Not so much.

California Tortilla has good, fresh grub in a Mexican/Tex-Mex style.  The store is large and clean, and the staff seems into its mission.  My Chicken Quesadilla was loaded with Beans, Corn, Lettuce, Fresh Jalapenos, Monterrey Jack and plenty of Doodle Do.   The Tortilla was thin and crisp from heating on the grill as its ingredients were gathered and mixed and then sealed with the melting of the cheese.  It was very nice.    Their signature is the wall of hot sauces that you can select and pour into little plastic cups in any configuration and quantity you wish.  I went with the Bee Sting Honey/Habanero and Pineapple Pizzazz (I do love fruity salsas).  The Pineapple combo was deliciously hot and played well with the quesadilla.  The Bee Sting was exactly that.  Hot, piquant, and left me to drive home with semi-numb lips.  It was great!   So, while I normally prefer my Southwestern cuisine in divey bars in Tucson or Nuevo Laredo, or even in the transformed taverns of Trenton that are now all Latin eateries, California Tortilla offers a very tasty and entertaining alternative, especially if you don't like adventure as part of your dining experience.

Ristorante Aida is located in the Mallard Creek Shopping Center in Richboro, Pa.  It is a small shop run by a young family.  The husband does the cooking, while the wife works the floor and assists in the kitchen. Bambino has a corner to himself to play and watch TV.    If an earnest desire to please was paramount, Aida would be a 5 Star experience.  I have seldom seen a server express the sweet insecurity of both expressing how wonderful she believes the food to be, and at the same moment showing her deepest hope that the customer will agree with her.   Those eyes.  The bathos was as rich as the creamy White Wine Lemon Butter Sauce on my Scaloppine Di Pollo (Francoise). It was a very good dish.  Luckily, the two home baked rolls were big enough for me to rip them apart throughout the meal and soak up both the Olive Oil and the zesty yet silky sauce.  The large plate also held the side House Salad of Lettuce, Tomato, Onion, Olive Oil and Vinegar.    If I had had room, the house desserts looked very appealing sitting in the front display. Maybe next time. Aida is worth another look.

Went in for a late lunch last Saturday after a grocery haul at 1st Oriental down the street.  The floor plan looked like many other Vietnamese houses, with an open space occupied by long tables for group dining.  Turns out that I.S. BBQ is run by Chinese folk with a large menu covering several Asian food groups, as well as their signature Hot Pot/Smokeless BBQ grill in the middle of every table.  I wasn't hungry enough for an AYCE meat meal, so went with a few of the small plates - Spring Rolls, BBQ Beef & Lemongrass with Rice, and a bowl of Pho with Lean Steak and Meatballs.   Service was prompt, but made the mistake of bringing the main courses before the app.  No biggie, but knew someone wasn't being attentive. The Rolls were very good.  Crispy, mildly oily from cooking, but loaded with Pork, Shrimp and Cabbage filler. Nice side of White Radish. The accompanying thin sweet sauce was fine.  Likewise, the beef dish was plentiful and tasty.  The Rice was molded into a plateaued mound, and in great condition to absorb the mix of sauces on the plate.   The only real shortcoming was with the Pho.  While the broth was decent, the beef was way overcooked and tough to chew.  It had been pre-cooked, and not left to simmer in the soup to reach the right doneness in the bowl. Given all the raw meat available for the Hot Pot, the failure to simply slip a few slices into the bowl was incomprehensible.  Too, the accoutrement lacked Jalapeno slices to bring up the burn.  Disappointing.  While I might consider a return for the Hot Pot or BBQ, the attractiveness of the overall joint was significantly dampened by the Pho Phail.

This was a first visit to Lee's Café and Bistro at the corner of 5th and Washington in South Philly.  The green awnings are inviting in this otherwise standalone renovated old house that sits in front of the 1st Oriental Super Market on that same block.    It is not until you get to the front doors that you learn that the actual café is on the second floor, while the first is occupied by their café displays where you can get java and bakery goods to go, or bring upstairs.  The dining space is very clean for a restaurant in this area, and the furnishings a step above the utilitarian space found nearby in Pho Ha.  The walls are brightly painted and HDTVs hang from the walls.  The menu is fairly typical for a Saigon house, but the servers are definitely more friendly and engaging than in most other Vietnamese joints.    We ordered Summer Rolls, Pho Tai and BBQ Pork Banh Mi, and recognized quickly that the prices were higher here than in the rest of the neighborhood.  It must reflect the cost of the recent renovations.  We hoped that the quality of the kitchen was likewise reflected in the pricing.    This was not really the case.  The Summer Rolls were cool and fresh, with thin sliced shrimp attracting the most attention through the opaque skin, but also stuffed with Pork and Cabbage.  The Peanut Sauce was a bit on the thin side and lacked any ground peanuts to supplement the textural experience.  The Pho was only average in terms of the beef broth.  Plenty of Sprouts, Thai Basil, Jalapenos and Lime Wedges, and a veritable bird's nest of rice noodles beneath the surface, but lacking the subtleties of the finer pho venues.  In point of comparison, Pho Ha, right around the corner and visible from there has far superior slurp for the demanding consumer.    The Banh Mi was fine - fresh and crunchy with ample BBQ Pork, Daikon, Carrot, Mayo and Cilantro.  But, the roll it came in was neither baguette, nor Italian, but some crumbly hybrid that although fresh, lacked the body of the real contender.  It wasn't fun to bite through and chew.  And, the cost at nearly $8. was far in excess of strong alternatives found nearby for under $5.   So, net/net, Lee's is a nice place to hang out and grab a bite in relative comfort while looking out the second story windows, but if outstanding cuisine is what you came for, you might find yourself underwhelmed.  With so many exceptional Vietnamese shops in the immediate vicinity, I found myself thinking of them rather than enjoying where I was.

When a young and growing child runs through a pair of athletic shoes in a matter of months, the need for a fairly priced distribution point becomes a financial necessity.    So it is that Dick's Sporting Goods a big box store very near the Oxford Valley Mall comes into play.  It is in the rear of that warehouse of a retail outlet that all varieties of foot gear are displayed and available for purchase.  Where some of the smaller shops have a few designs in a few colors from a few manufacturers, Dick's offers the most of all.  Too, if paying attention to the flyers in the mail or email advertisements, it is possible to save substantially.  Size 12 Nike Air basketball shoes listed for sale at $85, were actually secured for $20 less with the help of those coupons and cards.  The cashier was very helpful in making sure we got the best possible price.    Knowing we will be back in about 90 days to replace the worn out Nikes with a new and likely larger pair, is a good incentive for both parties to maintain good relations.    See you then, Dick.

Olive Garden "Italian" Restaurant is one of those places designed for compromise.  In my case, it was a reasonable place to go with family given the limitations of each member.  My son loves cheese, but hates veggies, and said he was not very hungry.  His mother (my ex) is a vegetarian who loves the unlimited Salad and Breadstick deal offered by the chain.  Me?  I love Italian cuisine, but also want to keep the peace and make it through a Mother's Day dinner without stress.  Given all the variables, Olive Garden was the obvious choice.    Surprisingly, the wait was not long when we arrived around 7:30.  We were seated within 10 minutes and our server was on us quickly for our drink and app requests. They arrived promptly, along with the first bowl of Salad without olives nor croutons, but with extra Red Onion, Tomato and Cheese.  I didn't know the salad could be special ordered, but it was a good idea.  The veggies were freshly cut and the Oil and Vinegar dressing was decent.  The Bread Sticks were hot and a little crispy on the bottom, which I liked.    I was the only one having an actual dinner, having skipped lunch, and went with the new light Garlic Rosemary Chicken.  It arrived with two smallish chicken breasts well grilled, but without any grill marks, on a bed of Fresh Spinach, a few Caramelized Garlic Cloves (needed more), and a nice plop of Garlic Mashed Potatoes.  The Rosemary was not visible, but the chicken did taste of it.    Overall, I was satisfied with the meal, although the sauce was thin and a bit salty.  For a "light" meal it was filling.  At $13.99 it seemed a reasonable value.  Would I order the same dish again?  Probably not, as the trade off in flavor for the lack of calories was not a winning hand.  It could be that I am comparing my experiences in many more authentic Italian restos, but I did not feel excited by the meal.  It was adequate.     As no one complained and we were able to have a low key dinner, Olive Garden did its job, and met my decidedly selfish expectations.

The cheapest gas in this part of town and right on my way home at night.   Yes. It is a busy station due to price and location (Route 29 Northbound), but I find the service to be prompt and friendly.  I never go into the store, so can't comment on the coffee, snacks nor social propositioning.    If you're looking for quality gasoline and good prices, this is a good place to consider.

A breakfast meeting brought me to Cafe Chorba in the Morrisville Shopping Center, just across the Calhoun St. Bridge from Trenton, NJ.  The cafe is a little hard to find, tucked into the east side of the center. Don't give up if you don't see it right away, as it is worth your while to find it, and chow down. The environment is diner-like in terms of menu, but more like a luncheonette in ambiance. Very Americana, despite its Turkish name.  I had the french toast.  It was among the best FT I have had.  A slight crunch on the outside, and soft and totally cooked on the inside.  Thick sliced fresh bread makes for a very nice meal with good coffee.  My meeting partner had eggs over and scrapple.  She said the "meat" was well above average. I admit to never having tried it.  The cost for the 2 breakfasts with coffee, $12.  Friendly staff, and decent traditional breakfast, lunch and dinner menu.   I will definitely return when the opportunity presents itself.   Suggestion: Offer real maple syrup for french toast and pancakes.  That would add to the overall value proposition here.  Even if charging extra for it, it would upgrade the experience beyond the little packages of industrial syrup provided now.  Overall - Very pleased!

First a bit of housekeeping - Winckler's Ribs is hard to find.  It is located in a small space on Washington Street, immediately to the rear of Anthony's Pizza. It is north of Bridge Street and difficult to see until you are right on top of it. Look for the red awning. Your perseverance will be rewarded.  Walking in, I immediately met Mike Winckler, owner and rib chef extraordinaire.  He was sitting on the only seating available inside his shop; a small bench for take out customers (and resting top chefs) to chill while waiting for the next wave.  He looked up at me with a smile as I apologized for ending his moment of peace. He was wearing a white chef's pants, jacket and high hat.  As I was the only buyer I took the opportunity to talk with him and look around as he stood over the grill working my order of a half rack of ribs. The sizzle and smoke arose in energetic clouds as it was sucked up by the exhaust fans.  Some of it escaped to my nose where my brain immediately went into hyperdrive as the sauce molecules slammed into my sensory filters.    Oh My!  Involuntary salivation. Gulp.  I saw his shelf of hot sauces from around the world, and those cans of mysterious powders in shades of orange, red and yellow like you find in huge piles in old markets in India or Pakistan. Not curries, but something more esoteric. The ribs were now showing black streaks where the meat was completely cauterized and the sugars from the marinade and basting sauces were caramelizing into a crunchy sealant. As the final step, Mike poured the red amber finishing sauce over the ribs, turning them a glossy orange-red. Loved that tint.   He packed the finished ribs in an aluminum foil bottomed styro box, accompanied by a small cup of his Cole Slaw and a chunk of Corn Bread.  Afterwards, we watched the video commercial for his ribs through You Tube on his HDTV above a refrigerator.  It was fun and further built my anticipation.  I drove home excited.   This prelude would be meaningless unless his ribs backed up all this build up.    They did.  The meat willingly parted from the bone. The first bite was a surprise.  Rather than the sweet, tart BBQ explosion I expected, I was confronted with something more subtle.  The taste was complex; both mildly sweet and hot, with undertones of other spices I could not identify.  Nutmeg?  Something sort of nutty?  Not sure, but I loved it.  The texture of the meat remained intact. Softly chewy and sticky.  The glaze and shards of meat that were left on the bone were sucked off with relish.    The Cole Slaw was sweet.  The Corn Bread was really more like Corn Cake - moist and sweet.    I loved these ribs, although they were different than what I had eaten before.  It was obvious that a lot of thought, study and preparation went into their creation.    I will return, and may have found a buried treasure in the droning leftoverness of Morrisville, in the shadows of Trenton, alongside the mighty Delaware flow.

I haven't tried the Wings here, but if they are anything like from their other locations, they are fine.  I stopped in for a Fried Fish Sandwich the other day for late lunch.  The Fish was light and flakey, the breading thin with a mild taste.  Most important, the oil was clean, so there was not unwanted taste from anything that had been fried before.  For comparison, the fish at JC's Fish and Soul Food  farther down Nottingham is better.   The accompanying Fries were also okay.    I wouldn't rush back to Chuck's, but I wouldn't avoid it, either.

I knew something was up when I walked into Hogeland's Corner Grill and the counter was full but for the very last spinner.  Laughter and the strong hum of conversation was the tip off that this joint was the hang for an old crew.  The fact that a stranger had just entered did not change the pace of socializing.  I was just another friend they had never met before.  Welcome!  The space is small, with only 4 quads and a counter with room for 8. Cozy. An ancient 12" TV hung from the ceiling.  The Formica countertop, old wall signs, and attentive silverhairs bustling around, contributed to the sense of being in a 70's / 80's sitcom, Mel's Diner.  Happy to play my part.  Irma, Sherry, and Steve were right out of central casting, with white aprons, dual-fisted coffee pots, and very long spatulas. They were open and diligent, friendly and forthcoming about the history of what has been several incarnations of a coffee shop/luncheonette over the past 20-odd years.  You know that something special has happened when a former worker becomes an owner, and then after selling the business continues to work at the place she loves.  That speaks to the closeness of the people, and the magic that happens when they are together.    All of that would be only a quaint tale if the food slung was not worth the price of admission to the theater.  It certainly was.  From my front row seat I watched everything.  After ordering Coffee and French Toast, I saw the bread bathed in egg and placed on the grill.  Steve lovingly pushed it around to be sure the surface was touching metal, and then cut the 3 slices with his spatula.  He asked if I wanted Powdered Sugar and Cinnamon on it, and I liked the idea.  He sprinkled it on after plating the toast, and walked over to lay it in front of me.  A little butter, a squirt of syrup, and I was ready to go.    It was great!  I prefer my French Toast to possess a little crispy crunch from the hot grill caramelizing the egg/butter/bread intersection.  It had that, while remaining soft and fully egged within.  It has been a long time since I had that, and I was pleased.   The Coffee was very good and was refilled before I had gotten half way through. I liked that I was asked if I wanted a refill before the pour, so I could decide how much was needed to maintain the right coffee/milk balance.    All the while, I was drawn into various conversations with the other patrons at the counter, so by the time I was ready to pay the bill and go, people were asking when I would return to continue the banter.  Turns out, I knew one of the guys that came in after me, and after a short exchange of kindnesses, I said I would be back very soon.    Richboro is not exactly in my home zone, but for an experience like this, I will certainly make the trip when my mornings allow.  Hogeland's is on the short list of exceptional breakfast emporiums.  Hear tell that lunches are good, too.

It's hard to get excited about a car rental experience. Still, there are better and worse ones, and this interaction with Enterprise in Fairless Hills, Pa., was better than many.    My vehicle was in the body shop for repairs after a rear ender than left the rear bumper of my car looking like the loser of a boxing match.  These folks picked me up at the shop, drove me to their store to complete the necessary forms and had me on the road in less than 20 minutes.  They worked seamlessly with my auto insurance to arrange for coverage, leaving me with a small balance to pay for the reality that most car rentals cost more than $16 a day.    My Mazda 6 was decent, if not exceptional.  It was clean and handled well.  It was efficient on gas.  When I brought it back, they drove me to the body shop with a warm smile and interesting conversation.    No hesitation to use them again.
Two listings for this new smoothie shop. This one appears to be secondary. Try the other for tips and reviews.

Leave it to Yelp to uncover yet another gem in the rough.  In this case, the rough refers to the section of North Brunswick Avenue in Trenton where Pho Tan has staked its claim and hopes to mine Vietnamese gold out of its kitchen.  In the shadow of the former Helene Fuld Medical Center, this unassuming storefront houses an authentic menu that turns out very good VN cuisine.  The space shows signs of originally being a Mexican joint, but I have no problems with that.    The staff is very friendly (and cute), and the owner/chef is checking with his customers to be sure they are satisfied and to tell his story of this 3 month old enterprise.  The room fills up in the evening with compatriots, some of whom are obviously family.  They fill the air with Vietnamese jokes and deference to the seniors among them.  Very nice to be part of this culture for the evening.   I wanted to try the Banh Mi with Roast Pork, and a Small Bowl of Pho with Flank and Tendon.  At $4. the Baguette Sandwich was large and stuffed with the Pork, Cucumber, Cilantro, Carrot, and some kind of Mayo.  A squirt of Hoisin from the table rocket brought the combination to the right flavor quotient.  It was very good, although the Pork had some rough spots.  It was enjoyable.    The Pho was accompanied by a full plate of Basil, Lime, Sprouts, & Jalapeno Slices that helped the simmering broth attain full taste.  The heat of the soup slowly cooked the once rare Beef to a nice medium.  The Noodles at the bottom of the bowl were hidden beneath the Beef and condiments, and had to be raised with my chopsticks and flat bottom spoon.  Once thoroughly mixed, the full mastery of this creation came to the fore.  It was a mighty fine bowl of Pho, full of subtle flavors and textures that were a pleasure to uncover a layer at a time.  I could not finish it, and was glad I had not asked for the larger portion.    Pho Tan has great possibilities.  I need to try their Vietnamese Coffee and Summer Rolls to be sure it is as good as my first impressions.  It will not take long for me to return to sample those things and revisit my ranking.    Pho Tan could be very special.   Good luck to Mr. Tan and his family in this endeavor   SEPTEMBER 10, 2014 - Returned this evening for another run at Pho Tan, and went with the Pho Ga (Chicken) and Spring Rolls.  The Spring Rolls were deep fried and stuffed with ground spiced pork.  Aside from the oily skin, the app was tasty and filling.  The dipping sauce seemed a bit thin and less sweet/pungent than expected.  A little more potency and thickness would improve the final result.    The Pho Ga only came in the LARGE size, and I could not finish it.  The broth was new in that it did not taste like it had been simmering for a long time to bring out the spicy flavors.  I added a shot of Sriracha to bring it up a notch.  However, the Chicken Breast slices were fresh, thick and plentiful.  It was the most chicken I had ever had in my pho.  I prepped a small dish with a mix of Hoisin and  Sriracha to dip the chicken in before eating.  Tasted great!  All the other fixings were on the table, and I put most of them into the bowl.  Good quantity of noodles lurking in the bottom of the bowl.

The Café sits in the Pine Watson Shopping Plaza on North Pine just before the intersection with Maple Street in Langhorne Borough.  It is the star of an otherwise undistinguished row of shops and restos. The interior is bright and homey with  nice counters, tables and booths. The servers are friendly, courteous and have time for a short chat with all the customers.   The breakfast menu is traditional, and the coffee is Ellis through a Bunn-o-Matic. Strong, middle of the road brew.  I went with a short stack of French Toast along with the java.  It was made with Texas Toast and arrived nicely crusty with caramelized edges.  It would have been even better with real maple syrup, but then the price would have been much higher.    There are a high percentage of regulars here which adds to the attraction.  The repartee with the high energy behind the counter ladies is warm and clever.  I imagine that if this was closer to home or on my way to work, I, too, would be a regular guest.   As it is, I am a fan, and I will get here sporadically when I can.

Corner Bakery is brought to us by a company with HQ in Newtown, so I take pride in its roots, and wish them great success.   The ambiance is high ceilings and dark wood, with tables and booths spaced well to avoid the feeling of being too crowded when eating. Yet, there is an issue with traffic flow between the front doors and the counter.  The coffee is right in the central area and can get a little congested.  A redesign might help.   The food is all decent, if slightly more expensive than other places in the area. Sandwiches, soups, salads for lunch.  Oatmeal, bagels, muffins, omelets for breakfast.   A community room adds to the neighborhood flavor.  There are always meetings going on of various sizes, and it is really nice that these activities were taken into consideration.   Parking is an issue, as the undersized lot is shared with TD Bank.  Any time near lunch is an adventure in parking.  Be prepared to park and walk a couple of minutes. As Woody Allen might say after a poor parking performance, "It's all right.  We can take a taxi from here."  6.01.13 - Time for an upgrade to 4 Stars. This morning walked in for a meeting reserved for the Community Room. Apparently, whoever took down the info was NOT the manager, and they knew nothing about it. Grrr...But, the real manager and his staff jumped into action and prepared the catering we required for the 12 people and 2 hour meeting.  Everything else went smoothly.   For stepping up when it would have been easier to just shrug and give empty apologies, they took care of us with professionalism and a smile. Time to move into a better neighborhood, CBC.  Thanks!

Located in the Newtown Business Commons, Cosi offers breakfast, lunch and dinner for the businesses in the area, as well as the Homewood Suites Hotel down the street.The chain offers moderately upscale, fresh foods in a comfortable, modern environment.  We had two Cosis in Newtown, but one closed last year.  The food was consistent from both of them. Breakfast meetings are my primary reason for being there.  Their oatmeal, square bagels (freshly made), muffins, and coffee are very good.  The lunch salads, sandwiches and pizzas are fresh, creative and tasty.  Try the Signature Salad with grapes, dried cranberries, walnuts and blue cheese.  Breakfast comes in at about $7., and lunch, $10.  Certainly, not outrageous.  The staff is competent, if not always warm. Overall, a very good place to enjoy a local breakfast or lunch with friends and associates.

CrisPanino is a small tapas/sandwich house in a mini strip center on Parkway Avenue in Ewing, NJ.  It is clean, utilitarian and somewhat stylish with a "lounge" along the front window for those who prefer to recline while eating.  The menu is posted high on the wall and takes a bit of scouting to figure out what is going on.  Luckily, I was the only customer when I arrived, and the good gentleman behind the counter came around to explain the system to me.    I had read about the Flight of Empanadas - three delicately wrapped fillings surrounded by Argentine imported dough that fries up light, crisp, airy an very tasty.  The inside are Ham & Cheese, Pulled Pork, and fine textured Beef/Gravy thing; each in a distinctly shaped enclosure.  They were a curiosity and fun to eat, with interesting textures, but lacking in any signature flavors.  They were all bland, leaving the outer shell as the most memorable part of the dish.  Perhaps, that was the point.   The Crispy Fried Chicken Panino was beautifully presented on oversized Sour Dough, with strips of Fried Chicken, an Aioli based Mayo, Tomato, Lettuce and American Cheese.  It was a handful.  I liked the bite, chew and taste of this sandwich, but later that night found myself suffering heartburn, possibly from the mayo or some aspect of the sauces within each empanada.  As it was the last meal of the day, this meal was the likely culprit.   Nonetheless, the house is pleasantly open and airy, and the staff very helpful and friendly.  I appreciate its uniqueness.    Still, I have no strong desire to return for another taste, and that implies that I am not yet a fan, and can't reach 4 stars.

Sometime last year the AMC Group sold this to Regal and now it has been renamed accordingly. Otherwise, it is the same as it ever was, except for the need to go to a different website to buy advance tickets.    What has become obvious is that the cinema business has taken a page from the sports complex business model.  Your ticket may seem expensive, but only until you step up to the snack bar cashier to order the pop corn, candy, pizza, chicken fingers, soda pop, and other sundries.  Those prices quickly double or triple your price of admission.  Outrageous.   So, most people find a way to bring in food and drink surreptitiously to avoid being gouged.  No wonder ticket sales are down annually and the movie theaters chains are shedding underperforming assets in an attempt to find a profit.  It would seem that the better way to go is to get a liquor license and set up a decent kitchen and make "dinner and a movie," into a unique one stop experience.    Hopefully, a more creative approach will save this icon of American culture.  After all, there are some movies that just have to be enjoyed on a huge screen in a dark auditorium, with your arm around your babe's shoulders.

We walked in during a birthday party for a young child.  The store was loud with kiddos shouting and running around.  Not bad if you like that helter-skelter ambiance.  But, not the place to find a quiet corner and enjoy a fresh baked and salted mini pretzel or three.  So, we took advantage of their special of 12 minis for $5., and boogied out to the car to continue on to Philly and munch in the voiture.   The pretzels were fresh and okay, but far short of spectacular.  Chewy.  Salty. Carb City. Definitely needed a washdown to keep the pipes clear.    The hot dog pretzels did look interesting.

I've picked up food from JC Teriyaki two days in a row to try a few of their main dishes to see what was happening there.  I've eaten their Fried Chicken and Hibachi Chicken, along with sides of Lima Beans, Potato Salad, Corn Bread and the Cabbage/Carrots combo that comes with the Hibachi offerings.    JCT sits on Parkside Avenue just north of Olden Avenue Extension in a somewhat rundown retail strip center which also has a Chinese takeout joint and an Italian pizzeria. Nice to have options.   While I enjoyed the entertainment of watching these three guys preparing the food, the actual finished products were only average.  The Fried Chicken combo of breast and wing was nicely meaty and never frozen, however the coating did not have very much flavor compared to the standards we all know.  It lacked sufficient spices to really stand out.  The white meat was plump and juicy and would have really shined with the right flour mix.  The accompanying Potato Salad was nicely sweet, but the Lima Beans were supersized and mushy.  The Corn Bread was pretty good.   The Hibachi Chicken order was large and with the Veggies really weighed down the container.  It was cut into small strips and doused well with Hibachi Sauce throughout grilling.  It was interesting to see the American short order grill used for a Japanese dish.  I had not thought of that before, but it was cool to put those two cultural icons together. The chicken was tender and had a nice flavor.  The veggies of Steamed Cabbage and Carrots were a little boring; lacking much taste.    JC Teriyaki is a mixed bag.  I like the concept demonstrating the cross-cultural bonds between Southern American cooking and Japanese grilling, but had higher expectations for the actual results.  Perhaps, the pricing of the meals (quite low) interferes with the ability to really pull out the stops and make the meals memorable.   3.5 Stars is probably the right place to be here, but I want to encourage an upgrade in performance quality which won't happen without a little mild criticism.

The same shop as the former Food Castle, this north Indian restaurant offers a menu of both Indian and Chinese cuisine.  They are on opposite sides of the take out menu, and no Chinese dishes were available in the luncheon buffet.  I have heard a lot about the Indo-Sino kitchens, but have yet to actually try it.  It is not clear that New Moghul cooks that way, but when I was there only Indian dishes were displayed.    Arriving just before 2, there was only one other customer.  I perused the offerings and filled my large plate with Vegetable Samosa, Chicken Tandoori and Chicken Makhani, Paneer Makhani, Chana Masala, Vegetable Biriyani and Naan.  They were all good, but none outstanding.  Having two Makhani dishes seemed redundant, but the sauce was nice and creamy. The Tandoori Chicken was the freshest on the table, as a new tray of it was brought out while I was loading up.  It was tender and easily separated from the bone.  It was predominantly thighs and drums.  The Biriyani was a nice dark color and had a pleasant flavor.    What I am discovering is that if you want to have Indian buffet for lunch, it is better to arrive early and eat when all the dishes are just out of the kitchen.  I am a late luncher, and it seems that many of the tureens are not heated, and left in the open for a few hours.  Many offerings are past their prime, and less enjoyable.    I was satisfied with my meal at New Moghul, but I have had much better North or South Indian victuals recently, and this place is not up to that standard.  To be completely fair, I will have to return for dinner and see if that changes the story.  Still, if a resto is going to offer a buffet it should be a reflection of what is available if ordering off the menu.    By that guide, this place is only A-OK.

First the Big News!   Oishi is moving to another part of the Village of Newtown Shopping Center!  They will be taking over the space formerly occupied by Basil Leaf and Lee's Hoagie House in the portion of the Center that has McCaffery's Supermarket.  It will take several months for that to happen, but it received its conditional use approval from Newtown Township last week, so it will move forward.  The space where the restaurant currently resides will remain a restaurant under the same ownership, but with a different orientation.  You heard it here first.   The current Japanese, Thai, Korean success story is about to write a new chapter.  But, the old story is still a very good one.  They still present some of the best sushi, sashimi, and true Asian fusion in Bucks County and the surrounding area. I returned there yesterday for lunch for the second time since joining Yelp.  The ambiance remains hushed dark wood and stone tones that are very comforting and warm.  The activity of the white hats behind the sushi bar continues to offer the sights and sounds of sharp steel knives on  cool granite as the Zen of fish slicing and rice molding into seaweed wraps captures our attention and imagination.  Quite a show!  When the orders are sufficient to keep the fish ultra fresh, the production is razor fast and the taste sensational.  Me? I love the Crunchy Tuna, but I am happy with whatever is put in front of me.  The Wasabi and Ginger are also fresh, so the mix into the light soy sauce complement each other perfectly.    Yesterday, my companions and I were in the mood for soup and noodles.  Three had variations of soups with Udon, Tofu and Chicken.  All looked great in the asymmetric bowls (see photo), and my Pad Thai, while bathed in a slightly unusual peanut sauce, was still quite good, although I do prefer the versions offered by Duck Sauce and Aroi Thai.   We were all happy with our meals.   Why not 5 Stars?  The prices are a couple of bucks higher than the competition, and they did not bring tea to the table, nor inquire if we wanted any.  The staff was courteous, but not particularly friendly, nor forthcoming with answers to our questions, nor suggestions.  They seem to believe that they are working in the best place in Newtown for this cuisine, and perhaps there was a sniff of arrogance in their demeanor.  That attitude always starts at the top and is passed down to the staff.  Some carry it off well, but most do not.    Oishi is well named, but there is more to being a great restaurant than just having "delicious" food.

This adaptive reuse of the former NASA centrifuge where our astronauts were trained before heading for the Moon, is a model of excellence in concept, design and performance.  It is worth a look just to see the once state of the art space technology now sitting above your head in a large circular room, bathed in warm blues, reds and greens.  Where once science reigned supreme, now houses one of the most interesting and comfortable banquet halls imaginable.    That we just attended a wonderful event honoring terrific people who helped make our Council Rock School District one of the best in Pennsylvania, if not nationwide, is very nice, but that it was held in this amazing "space," makes the moment unforgettable.   Wonder what they could do with a great rock band here?
