A nice smallish 11th Street veggie joint with a comfortable vibe, friendly service, and an interesting menu.    I stopped in after an appointment nearby for a late lunch.  I was the sole customer and had my pick of tables and all the attention of the lovely proprietress.  I went with a Scallion Pancake and the Soft Noodles with Peanut Sauce.  The Pancake was hot and the heat waves off it had the aroma of spring onion. Crispy and tasty.  Very nice.  The Noodles were a large plate (see photo), way more than I could eat, but with a wonderful creamy sauce topped with slivers of Red and Green Pepper, Sprouts and sprinkled with Sesame Seeds.  Delicious.   I took half of it home, and my car smelled great the whole way.   The prices seem an issue here.  The apps and noodle dishes seemed fairly marked, and the "Homestyle" offerings @ $10.50 across the board were alright.  I did not go for the "Main Courses," but at $15.95 for all items there, it seemed too much given the overall feel of the place.  Not sure I would be drawn to that part of the menu given all the other less expensive things ahead of it.  There is also a 24 count "Lunch Special" menu that is worth a look @ $6.50.    Certainly a decent place for veggie lovers to fill up.   Aptly named.

I am in the minority on this one, but to me the name misrepresents the products and atmosphere of the 2 Paris Baguettes that I have visited.    While the shop here is smallish and in the basement of the H Mart building, it is clean and has good service.  Yet, the selection here is not as varied as in the plant in Edison, New Jersey, and the seating arrangements not as comfortable.    Most important is that while all the baked goods I have tried are fresh and soft, they bear no relation to the boulangerie found in its namesake, Paris, France.  There, the taste and texture of each of the pastries is unique, while here they are uniform and provide little differentiation.  Yes. They are all sweet and tender, but are not anything like a French bakery.  Perhaps, I was spoiled living in France and enjoying the pleasure of great croissant and other delights on a daily basis, but as "nice" as these offerings are, they do not approach the amazing flavors and surprises found on every corner in Paris.    Paris Baguette?  C'est nes pas vrai.

New kid in town...Smoothie King in the Village of Newtown South. Near Marcos and Wendy's.  Huge selection of combo fruit drinks with nutritional additives of choice. Three sizes: large, larger and largest.  I just tried something with Orange and Mango Juices, plus Banana and some secret ingredients.  First sip came on strong, and it continued to hold my attention all the way to the bottom.    The owners of this new shop are good local folk excited to be opening a business in Newtown.    We wish them every success.

I seem to be going to more movies now that my son is old enough to go with friends, but before he can drive himself there. I had not gone to many theaters until this year as it was easier to rent at home.  I am enjoying the big screen experience again.   This United Artists Theaters @ Oxford Valley Mall is a freestanding building on the outer ring of the property with plenty of parking, and a short walk to the food court across the parking field.  It is one of the slightly older generation of modern cinema multiplexes, built about 20 years ago with some refurbishments.  It is a pleasant place to watch a movie; bigger theaters, decent sound, but without IMAX at this time.    Saw Man of Steel last night with young son.  For a first week of a potential blockbuster on a Friday evening, the place was surprisingly underpopulated.  The seats are comfortable with drink holders, but not as spacious nor as comfy as @ Neshaminy Mall. The popcorn is not always fresh here, as they seem to only make it every few hours, rather than on a more ordered approach. That is a no-no as the popcorn available for home purchase these days is excellent, and this does not compare most of the time. I won't mention the prices.  My favorite movie venue is the old Newtown Theater, where I can easily imagine I am sitting in the dark sometime around 1960.  The seats are old and creaky, and the screen is not designed for HD, and the projection equipment is in need of replacement for 21st Century viewers; but it is still an awesome experience up in the balcony with girlfriend and chaperon.

On the corner of 13th & Snyder in South Philly, AmeriThai was a pleasant respite on a steamy late June afternoon. Although as colorful as a Thai temple with rusty orange hues and elephants abounding, sitting in a quiet corner with the air cooling only ourselves, it felt a chill oasis.   The menu offered plenty of choices from soup to noodles, curry to bigger game like chicken, pork, beef and duck. We order Chu Chee Duck and Crazy Noodles, with appetizer of Curry Puffs.   In reverse order; the Curry Puffs reminded of Indian Samosas -  Sweet and White Mashed Potato, Onion, Peas,  mixed in mild Curry powder, deep fried, with semi-sweet/spicy Chili Dipping Sauce in a small brass dish. Excellently golden. Crisp shell. Tasty innards. Tart sauce. Liked it a lot!  The Crazy (Drunken) Noodles with tender Sliced Beef was a load and a half with big Fat Noodles, Veggies, and hot spicies. Plenty of dry Chili Pepper flakes in the mix. So glad we had Thai Iced Tea to tamp down the flames.   Chu Chee Duck had wonderfully crisp skin, moist delicious meat and a pale orange cream curry sauce. This became slightly sloppy finger food, as every morsel was too good to miss and required close examination and tongue probing to suck it all off the bone.   There are many very good Thai houses in and around Philly, and AmeriThai is certainly one. It is a little frayed around the edges, but it fits well with the neighborhood. Others mentioned that the kitchen is inconsistent, but I don't know about that yet. What I know is that when they get it right, it is an excellent place for dinner.

Returned to Olive Garden with gift card in tow after an hiatus of almost 2 years.  The place is still crowded, and the wait for a table just as long on a weekday evening.  The menu looked to be about the same, with the exception of a Specials Menu that had been in place long enough to justify its own handout upon seating.  The prices appeared to be about the same as my last visit.  While I am not usually enamored of the chain ethnic shops, I admit that this most recent experience was of a higher quality than the last.  I didn't remember what I ordered last time, but it turned out I ordered it again.  I did not care for it according to my last review, but this time, the Garlic Rosemary Chicken on the "Lite" menu was actually pretty good.  The two breasts had been well-grilled, and the garlic clove sauce was not at all salty.  The mashed were very good.    My companions were in their first exposure to Olive Garden, and were also quite happy with their Stuffed Chicken Marsala.    Finally, the three-way split of the Apple Crustada dessert was also a good ending to a surprisingly decent Italian-esque meal. It was a very good version of apple pie a la modec complete with a drizzle of Caramel Sauce.  Given the improvement in quality, we would certainly welcome another gift card.    Keep up the good work!

It had been more than a year since my last visit to Marty's Place. Time flies!   I was driving by this morning after court, having skipped breakfast at home in order to get a jump on traffic going into the city.  I saw a new sign out front on a Bud Light white board that breakfast was now being served 7 days a week!    Hot diggity!  I parked out back and walked in to a mostly empty bar (2 customers who looked like they were regulars).  The bartender approached and we engaged about their breakfast menu.  It was pretty wide open if my desires had anything to do with eggs.  They did. I opted for a sausage, egg and cheese on Kaiser roll, and mug of java.  While it was being created in the kitchen I watched a show about exotic car auctions.  A Borgati opening at a cool million bucks was an eye opener.  Another black transport used by John Lennon around London was also put up and sold.  Pretty cool entertainment.   The sandwich was great!  Double patty, fried egg, American cheese and a fresh, quality roll, made for a tasty and fun meal.  The side of homefries was likewise excellent - hot, crisp and spicy with sautéed onions in the mix. Coffee, strong and kicking. The only shortcomings were the lack of a joe refill offering, and lack of utensils. Luckily, I had a spoon from the coffee, which was fine as a shovel.    Afterall, Marty's is still a wonderful corner dive.  It was made for comfort, not for speed, nor etiquette.

My fourth visit overall to Café Chorba, and the first in over 6 months.  It was nice to return to the friendly, comfy confines of this fine house.   This morning, I was the only patron at the counter and Marie was my attentive server. She was solicitous and informative, keeping my coffee mug full, and providing a glass of milk for the coffee rather than the ubiquitous tiny creamers.  I finally had the strength to move beyond the excellent French Toast and try something new.    Today I moved on to the Greek Omelet.  It was spectacular with a pile of crunchy edged Home Fries, and Rye Toast.  The 3 egg platter was loaded with peppers, onions, tomatoes, Italian sausage, and feta cheese. They blended together well on the tongue, and with a little black pepper on top was terrific.  The taters could not be finished as they occupied nearly half the large plate.  Still, they were the right combo of crunch and tender properly spiced with a hint of butter to sweeten the palate.   It was a huge and hugely successful breakfast complete with good service and lots of fresh coffee.    It is not hyperbole to say that Café Chorba is as good as it gets for breakfast in the area and beyond.   Time for an upgrade to 5 Stars.

Sport's Pizza is located at the end of Makefield Road, just before it reaches Woolston Avenue in Morrisville, Pa.  It is far off the street in a dated strip center behind a gas station. It is very easy to miss, as I did the first time through.  It is a small shop with 6 booths, and clearly deals primarily in take away.  They have a wall of pizza boxes at the ready.    I was there for a light meal to replace the dinner I was too late to prepare at home.  I saw a handwritten sign that they had chicken noodle soup as a special, which piqued my interest on a chilly night.  Walking in and chatting with the woman at the register, I learned that the Brooklyn Pie was a new item.  There were a couple of squares left in the display, and I went for the corner slice to maximize the crunchy crust.  I also asked for a bowl of the soup.  Both were under $5.    I like my tomato pie well done, and asked for that.  It arrived on paper plate before the soup (?), not as hot as it should have been, but still warm enough to satisfy my desire for a hot meal.  I don't understand why some places can't handle requests for well done (reheated) pizza, and insist that everyone wants it the same less than optimal temperature.  Still, I recognized that the crust was done decently, and the sauce/cheese ratio was fine.  Nice touch to see a sprig of basil.  I've had better.   The soup was another matter.  It was very hot (microwave reheat), with lots of chicken, veggies and a few noodles, in a nice mild bird bouillon. A shake of black pepper and I was in business.  I liked it a lot. Enough to remember to order it again when in the vicinity.   I enjoyed sitting down next to a poster of Allen Iverson.  I would love a real meal with him to talk about his election to the Basketball Hall of Fame and what an awesome basketball warrior he was.

Corner Bakery Café is still a comfortable place for breakfast, lunch or dinner, and seems to have settled into its skin in the time it has been open in the Village of Newtown.    I am partial to the Steel Cut Oatmeal breakfast, and the sandwiches available for lunch. The basic Tuna Salad Sandy is tasty and filling at a reasonable price.  The option between Carrot Sticks or Chips is a good one.  The Bakery choices are very good, if perhaps a little pricey for the size of each slice, muffin or bagel.  Coffee is above average.   However, as the current Duke of this domain I am at a loss to understand why I was asked not to take a photo of the display case with all its goodies.  I thought free advertising was always a good thing.  Especially on Yelp!

Marty's Place sits at the corner of Hamilton and Johnston Avenues in Hamilton, NJ.  It has been a corner neighborhood watering hole for at least the last 80 years, under several owners and in various disguises.    This most recent incarnation is a comfortable dive that it almost too cute for that distinction.  It is bright and airy for a small space, with lots of color, and well maintained barroom. The bartender working the afternoon shift when I stopped in for lunch was a lifelong local and took pride in his work.  The bar itself is the shape of a "Question Mark," with the open end toward Hamilton Avenue, and the tail toward the rear near the pool table.  It is in good shape given its age, although the stools could stand refurbishment.    The menu covers breakfast, lunch and dinner, with special attention to oversized omelets, burgers and other hot sandwiches.  My large Burger with Cheddar, Fried Onions and Jalapeno Slices was better than expected, although it was obviously a prepackaged frozen disk.  It was closer to well done than the medium requested, but I don't mind cutting the kitchen some slack given that the result was still tasty and I had no expectations that it would be a gastronomic delight.  It was a satisfying chew, and came with choice of sides, for $6.75.  Very good deal.  The conversation was pleasant throughout, and the folks coming in and out all seemed to know the barkeep and all exchanged upbeat repartee.    The suds were mostly American, with the usual suspects from abroad.  This is not a craft dispensary; nor should it be.    Overall, Marty's Place feels like a winner for a quick lunch and conversation.  Evenings might be more lively, but I appreciated the relative quiet of a mid afternoon break.

Dominick's has been the pizza standard bearer in Washington Crossing for decades, but I had not stopped to sample their pies for a very long time.  After a dinner at their sister ship in Richboro a few weeks ago, I was tempted to return here to see if the magic was carried from oven to oven.  I went in for lunch earlier this week to find out.  First thing I noticed was that the once smallish primarily take out pizza parlor had expanded considerably.  It how had a dining room and a bar!  The rear area was dressed up a la a street scene in Napoli and the side barroom designed for those desirous of libations and wide screen TV with their Italian meal.  This room felt a little unfinished as things were stored in plain sight, and the quality of the furnishings did not match the richer feel of the wooden and mirrored bar.    I ordered two slices of regular Tomato Pie and took my seat in the barroom to await the call to get them after reheating.  That call never came, so I walked back into the central area to inquire.  The slices in the oven had been forgotten and were now two charred triangles ready for dumping.  Honest apologies were forthcoming.  They put in two more slices and promptly called me when ready.    They held their points when lifted, and had a pleasing crunch to the last bite.  The sauce was mildly sweet as I prefer, and the mozza still white after the furnace indicating it had begun that morning as a fresh cheese.  Nice.  Thin ribbons of basil lay on top of both, adding another texture and taste dimension.    These were good slices, but far from the best I have had in the past year.  Yet, the price with a Snapple came to under $6., which was a good deal.    To be a fan, I have to feel a desire to return for more in a short time.  Short of that, it is fairest to say that the pie is decent, but not memorable enough for me to put it on the short list of favorite places, let alone the pizza pantheon of great pies.   By way of comparison, I found the Richboro location to be more comfortable, with better service and more compelling food.  This proved that carrying the same name and pedigree does not guarantee the same experience from place to place.

The Tai Nam, Ve Don (Rare Steak & Crispy Flank) was a perfect counterpoint to the biting cold running rampant in the streets of Chinatown last night.   The space on the corner of 10th and Arch is small, but well maintained. The service is efficient, if not overly friendly, nor chatty.  But, given that there was a large bowl of steaming funky pho placed before me about 2 minutes after ordering, they can afford to let their speed and excellent broth do the talking. I found it rich and subtle with plenty of time simmering in a huge pot in the kitchen.  The star anise played second violin to the beef stock's leading melody.  The noodles were submerged beneath the ample supply of thinly sliced rare and well done meats.  It was all I wanted.  Some nights are just a little strange, and it wasn't even a full moon.  On my walk over to Pho Cali I was stopped by a man who told a story so believable about having his tools and wallet lifted, that I gave him cab fare home.  On the way out of the café, I was stopped again.  This time by a woman who claimed to be an art student in Jersey. She just wanted to take photos of me while I made a crazy face.  I obliged, half thinking that I would find myself on Facebook looking like a madman.  The end of a promising career in public service.   I just rolled with it all.  As long as the pho was superlative, I could tolerate almost anything.  Dark streets. Cold winds. Bizarre interactions. Take your best shot.

I am still a breakfast regular, and an occasional lunch person here.  My Oatmeal, Squagel and Coffee still offer a good price for a good meal.  In fact, the cost seems to have gone down recently due to some combo they put into effect.    It is a convenient stop on my way to the office.  They recently moved the coffee out from behind the service counter and it is now pour your own.  This makes for a small jam, but it is manageable.   Every ten breakfasts/coffees gets a freebee if you have their card.   Good deal.

Time warp pizza parlor with several HD TVs to remind everyone that their prices may be incredibly cheap (a la 1980), but they are still state of the art video-wise.    The regular Pizza Slice has a strong firm crust that holds its point even when somewhat cooled (second slice).  There is a preference for cheese over tomato sauce, making this a pizza rather than a T. Pie.  The taste is good, but the dominance of the cheese makes it a heavier experience with a bit of oil drip, rather than the more subtle flavors that arise when the sauce takes priority with hints of plum tomato, basil, oregano, garlic and even sugar.    Not a bad place for a quick lunch with a throwback flair.  Even the local constabulary has been known to drop in for lunch.  Two slices of regular pizza and a medium fountain drink (iced tea) comes in at $5.  Hard to beat!  You may not get the sensations of some of the more famous pizza houses in the area (you know who they are), but neither are you being asked to pay a premium for the privilege of manging on a pie with pedigree.    Anthony's Pizza Palace is a fun dine down memory lane.  The large pies are at most $17., and the dinners top out at $12.95, complete with salad and bread.  There is a place in the world for decent cheap Italian grub.

This place is the Penn Dot Driver's Service Center these days, although the signage may not have kept up with the its common parlance. Regardless, this is where you go in this part of Bucks County for all things driver's license and auto registration related.  It sits at the bottom of Neshaminy Boulevard, just behind the mall.    It was time for my license renewal (with photo), and I also needed information about how to secure a license for someone from out of country applying for the first time.  The first was accomplished in less than 10 minutes just before 4:00 on a beautiful Spring afternoon.  The second took a bit longer, as I learned that in order to secure a license for a foreigner who is waiting for a Green Card, is to obtain a social security number first, and then have a doctor complete another form vouching that the applicant does not suffer from a seizure disorder.  Of course, these steps are easier said than done.   At least, we had already applied for a work permit as well as the Green Card, but how long we would have to wait for Homeland Security to process them was another matter entirely.    Can't blame one bureaucracy for the foibles of another, but being at their collective mercy left us with a sense of frustration and annoyance.  At least, these folks were friendly and capable of human interaction.  Same can't be said for DHS.

Crowded to near over capacity this New Year's Eve Day, but we managed a table, ordered, and were served within 15 minutes.    Everything (French Toast, Corned Beef Hash, and Sausage, Egg & Cheese Sandwich) were decent, solid breakfasts.  No complaints.    Service was as good as it could be given the cramped conditions.  Had to bring the bill to the cashier in the back for payment.  Unusual, but no big deal.   Aunt Judy's has its charm as a morning get together joint.  It is one of those places where who you know there is more important than what you eat.

What do you get when you mix a Vietnamese wife and chef, who spend many years in Cambodia, with a Chinese husband and entrepreneur?  Neon Phnom Penh Restaurant on 7th and Wolf in deep South Philly, and some very good unintentional fusion dishes from that golden triangle of spicy cuisine. This small corner house with eight tables and booths has a cozy feel, from the wall art and houseplants, down to the Buddha shrine sitting on the floor with oranges in supplication.   We ordered their spring rolls (3 for $5), beef with fat noodles, and beef lo mein. They were all good to very good, but the star of the show were the deep fried spring rolls that had a great rough texture and were filled with ground pork, veggies, sprouts and homemade sweet dipping sauce with peanuts chunks. They were nearly a meal by themselves.   The fat noodles were also quite delicious with plenty of tender sliced beef, Chinese broccoli, string beans, onions, peppers, scallions and a tasty brown sauce that melded everything together.  Liked this a lot. The lo mein was also good, but not at the level of the former dishes. It had an interesting, indefinable almost smoky flavor, with plenty of meat and greens, but not as scrumptious as everything else.   We ended up taking half of each of the mains home with us, and one of the rolls, for subsequent consumption by our son.  He devoured all this the same night, and claimed to like it all, while also questioning the ingredients of the lo mein and that somewhat odd taste.   Still, a worthy stop in the heart of Cambodiatown. Plenty of atmosphere, and a friendly family team that spent more time that normal chatting with us about their lives in Asia and Philly. Good people with an interesting story to tell.   Made for an entertaining and satisfying dining experience.

After a hiatus of a few years, I returned to Four Rivers for an early dinner late last week.  The first thing I noticed was how much cleaner the place looked, and the new furniture really helped the joint feel more respectable.  Nice job.  The servers were friendly and attentive; another plus.  The new (clean) menus had the traditional Szechuan style cuisine, plus a curtsy to the American palate with some of the usual neutered dishes to avoid mouth burn.  It was my good fortune to dine with a Chengdu friend and she went after the dishes with glee after questioning the waitperson for a few minutes about how the dishes were prepared.  Satisfied, she went to work: Duck & Seaweed Soup, Crystal Wonton in Hot Oil, Dan Dan Noodles with Minced Pork, Double Sautéed Pork Belly, Water Spinach & Garlic, and White Rice.    The soup was a first for me.  I like Duck, but was not sure how I felt about mixing seaweed into the broth.  Fear not.  It was really delicious.  The large serving bowl overflowed with meaty chunks of tender Duck that was easily sucked off the bone.  The brackish flavor of the seaweed somehow complemented the bird's taste, enhancing them both.  I had several small bowls of it throughout the meal.    The Dan Dan Noodles were served lukewarm in temperature, and insufficiently spicy for me.  I asked for a side dish of Hot Chili Oil, and once engaged with the pasta and Pork, it came alive.  My sidekick loved it.  The Crystal Wonton in Hot Oil presented a semi-diaphanous skin with a delicate tail in a rich red hot oily sauce.  It reminded me of the Butterfly Dumplings found in nighttime food carts that set up shop everywhere in Chengdu after sunset.  These little darlings were made by hand only minutes before boiling.   The Pork Belly was tender with plenty of Red and Green Peppers in the mix.  Good, but I have had better in town.  Finally, the Water Spinach was done the traditional way with a load of fresh sliced Garlic thrown in with the thin leafed variety of this veggie.   Prices were very good for the amount of food we had on the table.  About $50. including tip.  I would definitely return with little prompting, but would probably choose E Mei on Arch as my go to Szechuan/Chongqing style dinner in Chinatown.

The merger with Continental Airlines may have been good for United, but it has not been a blessing for its passengers. Where Continental offered excellent people up front and in the aisles, quality entertainment options with the self-programming movie and music system, and decent food on international flights, the "new and improved" version is anything but.  Gone are the useful menus; replaced by, "Chicken or fish," without further information.  Gone are the stopby's to see how you are doing.  Now, the flights are sterile.    It is obvious that problems with management are spilling into customer services. Even the introductory videos with Jeff Whomever seem bland and not designed to offer even a sincere gratitude for flying with them.  In fact, in the video on the plane to Beijing, he seemed gaunt and suffering a health problem.  Hope he hasn't been spending too much time inflight, because often after one of these 14 hour jobs, I feel just like he looks.

The best thing about this Starbucks on Main Street, Doylestown, is the front elevation from the street. It occupies a historic building that dominates a key intersection in the Borough.  Very attractive.   Sadly, that is where the positives end.  Inside, the layout is dreary. Dark on the brightest days, it feels like a morose ghost inhabits it, making for a sense of weariness. The coffee at all Star$$$ is universally bad, and it is no different here. It forces you to upgrade to an expensive alternative to regular coffee, a perverse upsell that seems to work everywhere. The pleasantness of the staff is helpful, but cannot overcome the down energy that is ever present.   Many better choices in town, perhaps why the shop was not overly busy while life on the streets around it was jumping.

My first visit to any Home Goods occurred yesterday when returning a gift.  After securing the store credit I walked around the space to see if I could find something of equal value while there to avoid the need for a return visit.   I couldn't, and walking around this downscale sibling of TJ Maxx was actually rather depressing.  Lots of junque. No real value.   Big brother has more useful things.  Luckily the store credit extends to all members of this retail family.

First impressions - Warm, rich, dark red...umbrella-high ceilings, and Buddha smiling quietly... waiting on the Pad Thai. And, it gets better from there. A deep red glow accents the atmosphere in Aroi Thai & Asian Bistro.  The service is timely, friendly, and efficient.  The lunch menu was still in play although I walked in at 3:02. Only one other table occupied, and a couple at the bar.  Snow starting to fall. It felt like a Dashell Hamett novel.  First visit and I went for the Pad Thai.  It was excellent!  Hot, attractively presented with cool sprouts, and lime to bring out the tamarind and peanut undertones. Impressive portion for a lunch.  Jasmin tea chaser.  Wonderful lunch. Is it as "good as it gets?"  I won't know until I go back for more...soon.  10.27.13 - Returned for the fourth time last night and was again totally impressed with the atmosphere, service and cuisine.  I have ordered off the menu and from the specials, and each dish has been unusually flavorful, interesting and satisfying.  Last night I had Singapore Laksa Curry Noodle, a thick rich Coconut Curry Soup, loaded with a variety of shellfish, chicken, tofu, whole egg and veggies.  The coconut curry was subtle, yet spicy enough to warrant some caution.  I could not finish.  At $12. I was pleased.  Along with Jasmine Tea, I was a sated and happy man.    I think 5 Stars is warranted for Aroi Thai & Asian Bistro.  Aside from some amazing places I have visited in Bangkok and Pattaya, this is as good as I have had in the USA.
Still a great morning wake up! Strong java. Well made breakfasts. Friendly, homey, service.
Very sad to learn that Hogeland's has closed its doors for the last time.  Its food, and the warm community atmosphere it created, will be sorely missed.

It is a small world when it comes to falafel in Newtown.  Choices are limited to the part time place in the Newtown Farmers' Market, and this new house on State Street in Newtown Borough.    WoF is new and it appears they are still on their shakedown cruise.  While the signature offering is quite good, the overall gestalt is one of disorganization and lack of attention to detail.   The menu on the wall over the register/order area is limited to a few dishes, with the only real variety coming from the sides offered along with a falafel or eggplant pita or platter.  My styro plate was full of Israeli Salad, Hummus and BabaG, and the sandwich stuffed with Cukes, Tachini Sauce, and more Hummus.  Everything was fresh, but despite being put through a toaster belt, the pita remained room temp and lacked the complementary texture and taste of one heated first on the grill.  Therein lies part of the problem, in that there is no grill back there for that purpose.    The staff is young and earnest, but seem to lack restaurant experience.  Management didn't notice that the trash receptacles were full and needed attention.    World of Falafel has an opportunity to be a successful Middle Eastern Café if a few small steps are taken to bring up quality control.  Too, good coffee options would add to the ambiance and reason for people to come in to this attractive little shop and sample the wares.

TWO SLICE REVIEW   Average pizza from this small shop in a rundown commercial 3 store strip on Pennington Road, Ewing, NJ.    The crusts are thin enough, and the red sauce has a mildly salty taste on the regular pie and a basil-sweet flavor on the other one I tried, that looks something like a tomato pie. Both held up their points when picked up from the exposed crust, but both also had oil drip and a somewhat soft slice center despite asking for the reheat to be well done.   They private label their soda, and I liked the pineapple pop.    There are three tables in house, so this is primarily a takeout joint.  However, reading the complaints from customers waiting for delivery, going there to eat their stuff seemed the better course.    It was just okay. Nothing more.

Piccolo Trattoria is a local success story, and it is well deserved.  Its growth to 3 shops is testament to the hard work and persistence of its creator.  While I have only frequented the Newtown location, I hear great things about Flowers Mill and Pennington.    Take out pizza is an almost weekly order for us.  Friday or Saturday night would not be complete with a regular or Brooklyn Pie and a Spring Mix Salad.  The kitchen is a factory operation which you can watch as you wait at the register to pick up your food.  It is a beehive.   The pizza is very good and the Brooklyn Pie an excellent version of Sicilian with semi-sweet sauce, basil leaves, and copious mozzarella.  The Spring Mix is loaded with Green Apple slices, Walnuts, Feta, and first class Balsamic. The times I have eaten in house, everything has been well presented, tasty, and in abundance.  Most of the menu is traditional Italian American fare, so if you have a more adventurous palate, you may want to try Vecchia Osteria., or travel a bit farther afield to Philly or NYC.   Otherwise, you can't go wrong with Piccolo.

Mamma Flora's Trattoria sits at the end of the Shop Rite Shopping Center at the corner of North Olden Avenue and Parkway Avenue in Ewing, NJ.  It is surprisingly attractive inside with mirrored walls and large dining areas.  Service was excellent, with friendly repartee and suggestions for first timers like me.    I chose the eggplant parm sandwich, which came with chips.  For two bucks more, I could have had a side salad.  Prices were right at $7.25 for this grinder.  I made a good selection, because the hot sammy arrived a few minutes later steaming from its visit to the oven to melt the cheese and crisp the good Italian torpedo roll.    The eggplant had been sliced very thin and sautéed in olive oil before making its way to the roll where the chef put the remaining pieces together.  I appreciated that the nightshade was so thin that it was easy to heat and remained fully tender. No breading to add unwanted calories; just ripe melanzane. The homemade red sauce was slightly sweet with a nice basil undertone. The mozzarella was also quality and did not sweat from the oven's heat.  The roll was crunchy and good tasting (although I only ate half of it).  This was a very good rendition, although next time I would ask for extra sauce on the side as there wasn't quite enough to fully mix with the base ingredients below.    Still, Momma Flora's was a pleasant surprise for a neighborhood osteria. I will definitely return to try the tomato pie and some of their dinner offerings.

Way down Rt.13 in Croydon, PA, lies a new casa Mexicana run by a young entrepreneurial college student. Although bare boned at present, the large dining room, with colorful mural and carved/painted tables & chairs, already has a kitchen turning out authentic south of the border cuisine.   Last night I enjoyed an order of tacos dorado - chicken and cheese stuffed /rolled flautas (flutes), chips and salsa and tamarindo drink for less than $10. The roll ups were hot and crunchy with a top load of shredded lettuce, tomato and fresh crema dressing. I poured on the salsa from the table munchies to turn up the heat. Enjoyed it very much. The drink was tasty and sweet (perhaps, too much so), but refreshing and an effective counterpoint to the chili burn.   Service was friendly, informative and provided by the owner of the enterprise. Her pride and smooth effort was visible and a pleasure to behold.   Will be back to see what she does with the place.

A good bagel if you like the dense variety with plenty a texture and chew.   Mine was certainly fresh that morning, with those super sized onion flakes sticking resolutely to its top, and big enough to retain some moisture within and provide more flavor than the smaller chips that crunch well but fall off too easily. This was my maiden voyage to Bagelocity/Soup King, although I had liked its name since driving by the store in a strip center on Bensalem Road a few years ago.   I went with my favorite combination breakfast bagel sandwich with butter and swiss (love the interplay of nutty swiss cheese and those onion flakes on my tongue). With coffee the price was under $4, compared to a couple of bucks more for the same thing at my local place in Yardley.   The shop has been around for a while, but is still comfortable and clean. The staff I dealt with were friendly and brought the bagel to my booth when ready. Although I prefer a lighter, more airy, less kneaded round, I would certainly return to Bagelocity, especially to check out their soups and try a few more bagels.

A new generation of "comfy casual" dining is sprouting around the nation, and its seeds have germinated in Mt. Holly.  Kitchen 87 has taken root and its flowers are blooming even in the depth of winter.  While most diners, luncheonettes and cafés are second or third generation owned and operated, or simply maintaining the status quo under new management, this creekside establishment is going in a new direction.  Young owners with fresh ideas and fine execution bring streetlife and adventurous palates to once bucolic Mt. Holly.    Don't get me wrong, I love the traditional places making good food and reminding me of home.  Yet, there is plenty of room for a joint using the same ingredients, but reconstructing the menu into something unique and totally enjoyable, while keeping the sense of hearth and home through their use of most of the same tools and kitchenware with which we are all familiar.  From the vantage point of a counter stool, a spin around shows a wall lined with booths, a bunch of tables mid-floor, and a swinging kitchen door through which very friendly and gregarious servers come and go.  They are obviously proud of what they are doing, and want to share their confidence and happiness at being part of this enterprise.  I had good conversations with two women who were interested in more than just light pleasantries.  They really wanted to know what I thought about their place, and a slice of my worldview.  I was pleased to share.    My breakfast was on par with everything else that was happening inside Kitchen 87.  I had the "Which Came First" Sandwich - Breaded Chicken Patty, Swiss, Fried Egg, on a Brioche Roll, with Home Fries on the side.  It was a hot, happy, delicious, mess.   Knife and fork were mandatory, as it was too big and slick to be handled.  Everything melded well together, with drippy egg running through everything and giving its blessing to the rest.  The taters were dark grilled and spiced just right.  I really enjoyed every bite, although I could not finish the side.  The Coffee was brewed strong and the pot returned to me several times.   In the mood for a great breakfast that challenges you preconceptions about what can be done with eggs, cheese, bread, meat and potatoes?    You are ready for Kitchen 87.

China Dragon on Jacksonville Road, Ivyland, PA, is a fairly standard Chinese American house wokking dishes for the American palate. Their menu reflects it is from the same cooking school as every other such restaurant around the USA. The space offers a few tables for eating in, but the majority of their business appears to be takeout. They also offer sushi, Japanese and Thai platters, but I would be cautious going there if you have much appreciation for real food from those countries.   I found that the egg foo young I ordered was actually pretty good compared to many others I have tried.  The two pancakes were flash fried in the wok steel, so that the outside was light and crisp, while the inside was soft, pliant and tasty.  The ubiquitous brown sauce was made to order, and was smooth, without lumpy flour balls. The fried rice on the other hand, was mass produced at an earlier time, and tasted it. Its texture was a bit dried out, and was dyed by the food coloring in the bouillon used to cook the rice.   The net of it all was a three star moment.

El Rey de Oros (The King of Diamonds) is another excellent Mexican/Salvadoran restaurant in the heart of Bucks County, PA. It sits in a small commercial strip on West Moreland Avenue, Hatboro; the last storefront, farthest from Blair Mill Road.   Once inside, you find about ten tables with the counter and kitchen in the back of the house. I was greeted warmly by one of the owners, who guided me to a corner table and handed me their menu. Most of the offerings were Mexican, with a few Salvadoran specialties. I selected the chili rellenos (stuffed chili) dinner, which included rice, beans and a basket of four hot tortillas.   It took a while for my meal to arrive, but when it did, I immediately saw how big the poblano pepper was, and was advised by la senora that the dish was made from scratch for me. I could taste the difference. The queso stuffing was plentiful; the egg wrap completely encased the pepper, and the red salsa on top was fresh and piquant. A totally delicious take on this standard. This was one of my favorite Mexican dishes taken to a new level of satisfaction. Yes. It was worth the wait.   I also appreciated the old school approach to the chips and salsa gracing my table gratis. In the new world where many restaurants now charge for this table snack, it was very nice to have them placed in front of me with just a smile. In that regard, the chips were served warm and crunchy. The salsa was placed on the table in plastic rockets for squirting into small black bowls. They were smooth versions of hot sauce, and at first I missed the chunks of tomato, pepper and onion. The taste was the same, it just lacked the thickness I normally associate with salsa. I'll give them a pass on that.   This King of Diamonds is a full house of Mexican/Salvadoran cuisine. Definitely, worth a stop on your visits south of the border.

TWO SLICE LUNCH REVIEW  The first time I stopped by Alforno's Pizza a few weeks ago it was closed without explanation. Finally returned to check it out yesterday.   The shop is one of those Mexican Italian hybrids. Mexican soaps on the telly, tacos on the menu next to standard Italian fare. There are quite a few in the area. They seemed to be doing some rehabbing in the kitchen because the walk-thru from the counter area was partially blocked by a refrigerator.   I liked that they only had one pizza in the display case, rather than the multitude laying around in most parlors. Pies were made to order at least that day. A good thing. Still, I only wanted a couple of plain slices so I did not request they make a new pie for me. I asked that mine be reheated well done so as to achieve max reanimation.   That was exactly what I got a few minutes later. Black singed edges where the cheese touched hot metal and a slight darkening of the surface from the oven dragon's breath. Well done well done.  I prefer crisp crust that can hold it's point when lifted from the outer edge. This test failed as the inner half collapsed under the moisture and weight of the topside cheese. Yet, the upper half was stronger and drier and held up well. Crunchy good with a nice flavor. In fact, that part of the pie was pretty good. The sauce was a little sweet and played well with the crust and cheese. Just wish that was so throughout.   A little rebalancing of the cheese distribution on the pietop might fix this problem and result in a totally delicious pizza.

A & S Pizza & Pasta at the bottom of Edgely Road, just off Route 13, Levittown, PA, is a small parlor dealing pies, slices, pasta and Italian sandwiches. It has been in one family for decades. While not the best of neighborhoods, and a bit frayed around the edges,  they do prepare very good and filling dishes.   We ordered standard cheesesteak and eggplant parmesan sandwiches to check out their basics. Both were very good, if not best of breed. They were loaded - one with a ton of chopped steak, onions and cheese, and the other with thin sliced, breaded and fried nightshade, red gravy and mozzarella, run through the oven to melt and crisp everything. They use excellent torpedo rolls that toast up well and had a good flavor.   While straight up steak houses like Steve's in the Northeast/Langhorne and Dalessandro's in Roxborough, are the class of the field for steaks, these guys do a credible job for a corner neighborhood  place. Aside from a kitchen that works eggplant without breading and has faith in its sauce and olive oil to provide enough mass and taste on their own, A&S is as good as the best of them.   It's good to have strong local choices at fair prices.

Step into history with a visit to Newtown Hardware House.  This impeccably maintained old fashioned hardware store is a museum of Americana in screws, nails, tools, plumbing, electrical supplies, and even Flexible Flyer sleds and snow shovels.   The amazing and virtuous Dave C., the owner of the NHH for many years recently sold it to a local family to keep the operation open, so head in to buy the light bulbs and faucets you need for your fix-it projects.  Bring your kids so they can experience a slice of America that is almost extinct. While in the area, visit the other shops on State Street to support the community and the businesses that keep Newtown, Newtown.

This Taco Bell sits at the Route 206/Broad Street circle in Hamilton, NJ. It is a small shop with wrap around drive thru and low use dining area. It has been there for a few years and maintains a clean fresh look. This was my first visit despite the fact that my former law office was less than a half mile away. I really like Mexican food and this area has a lot of excellent cocinas Mexicanas, so "The Belch" was never high on my list of bookmarks. Still, its day had finally come.  I went for a chicken quesadilla - something simple, well known by me, and not overloaded with cheese to ramp up unwanted calories. It arrived about ten minutes later in a paper and glassine bag on top of a tray. I pulled it from the bag and placed the four quandrants on top of it (no plate provided). It was very thin with a little cheese melted and hardening at the edges. It was very hot.   The taste and texture were fine, although not brimming with chicken. It could have been spicier throughout, but I found that all the chili powder was in only one piece of the pie. Not a major complaint, but how hard is it to spread the spice across the entire tortilla while on the grill?   Given how good the authentic Central American restaurants in the region are, Taco Bell will remain far down the list of choices, but at least their stuff is okay.

After three visits Pho & Café Viet Huong gives the impression of being a Vietnamese diner.  A broad menu and very reasonable prices, but nothing all that impressive coming from the kitchen.   Last night I tried the Chicken with Rice in Lemongrass Sauce.  It was described as being spicy, but wasn't.  The Chicken was overcooked and dry, and the Lemongrass flavor weak.  The only veggies were Green Peppers and Onions cut large.  The Rice was fine, but I did not use much for sopping up the sauce as it was just not worth the calories.    In the recent past, I have tried the Pho.  It was adequate, but not the rich broth and ample meat and noodles that can be had right next door or across the parking lot.  Too, the smoothies and bubble teas are not all made with fresh fruit, but come from a can.  They are cool and sweet, but don't taste lively.    Lastly, the Vietnamese Coffee (hot) was pretty good.    This is really a place to come if you want a filling meal that doesn't break the bank. Still, the word that keeps flashing for me is, "Uninspiring."

Wang's Garden in the Village Shires Shopping Center off Buck Road in Holland, PA, is a family run Chinese/American house that has been wokking and rolling menu standards for a generation at this location. Mama runs the front of the shop, while dad is master chef. Prices are on the lower end of reasonable, reflecting the rent paid over the years.   My roast pork egg foo young was two smallish pancakes, full of pork and veggies and melded together with two eggs.  The brown sauce seemed fresh, and the accompanying fried rice was also above average, with plenty of pork, peas, shoots and more egg. A pretty decent lunch platter. The weak link was the hot & sour soup, which lacked fresh mushrooms,  had little tofu, and was dominated by its vinegar. It seemed past its prime.    Service was friendly and accommodating. They offer hot tea at no extra charge, which was appreciated.

This is the same place as Original Dominick's Pizza Shoppe, and that page has more reviews.    My review is posted there, but for those who prefer one stop reviewing, here goes:  The place has expanded over the years and now boasts a nice back dining room, and a side barroom.  One is very nice, while the other could use some work in putting things out of sight and matching the bar with the furnishings.    My experience at a recent lunch was likely an anomaly, but the two slices of tomato pie I ordered were forgotten in the oven and ended up in the trash when I returned to check on them.  The two I did eat were pretty good, with chunky red sauce, fresh melted mozza and a little basil.  I had eaten at their shop in Richboro the week before, and found the pizza there slightly better.  Why? I don't know, but it seemed a bit thicker and saucier.  I did not have dinner in this place as I did in Richboro, but at some point I will return to try it.  I appreciate the success of a family business, and Dominick's is a story of humble beginnings becoming auspicious rewards.    Washington Crossing doesn't have many offerings, but Dom's has been holding the fort there for decades.

From high restaurant prices great things are expected.  No doubt, Macaroni is a high end Italian house just off Old Bustleton Avenue in Northeast Philly, with cool dim lighting, modern appointments, black and white service and outdoor pergola for al fresco drinks and dining. Atmosphere is hushed and romantic. Settling in comes with a full plate of hopeful excitement that a special moment is on the way.   And, it almost is.   Our sauteed long hot pepper table tapas was great, but the bread past its prime, and dry. The calamari fritti was excellent with perfect deep frying and plenty of sliced hot peppers. The chicken parmesan was hugh and delicious, while the cavatelli and crab used shellfish no longer fresh and sweet, but fishy like it was a day too old. Finally, the bronzino special was two whole fish fillets in skin that was soft and tender, but plated with a bland mushroom accompaniment and too mild tawny sauce that left the tongue wanting more flavor. At $37, it was a deep water disappointment.   Most of us work hard for our money and don't like giving it away for a mezza mezza meal. With as many ups and downs as experienced at Macaroni, someone needs to call them on their "emperor's new clothes" reality. If they want to be special and charge premium dollars for the privilege of a table, they need alot more consistency and a bit less pretension.

If you are fortunate enough to remember when drug stores were primarily pharmacies where the expertise of the pharmacist and the family doctor were responsible for the health of the community, then you can appreciate Bear Apothecary in Lambertville, NJ.   Walking in is a step back in time, but where it matters - customer/medicine accountability - it is completely up to date. Mort wears the long white coat from 1960, signifying his deep roots in patient care and his long distance perspective on the evolution of drugs and illness. The generations of families that have relied on that knowledge testify to the commitment made by the owners since its founding.   True, Bear is not a contemporary super-pharmacy, but, isn't that a good thing? I really don't care if I can buy snacks, drinks or books when I need a prescription filled for my kid. Knowing that the pharmacist has seen it all before, and staked his career on the wellness of my community is paramount. Such knowledge (and wisdom) cannot be duplicated.

Le Pain Quotidien (The Daily Bread) is a Belgian bakery/cafe at the corner of 8th & Walnut in Center City, Philadelphia. If that sounds like a familiar location, that's because it is. Until recently this was the home of Robbins 8th & Walnut, the famous diamond dealer. So, if a Yelp review says that the boulangerie now there is a "hidden gem," they may not know how right they are!   These folks have done a great job morphing that old jewelry store into a continental bistro. High ceiling, floor to ceiling windows overlooking the teeming street life of this hospital part of town, large communal table in the center floor, wood everywhere. The atmosphere is captivating. It was a perfect place to relax over good coffee and densely textured blueberry muffin while waiting for an appointment across the street at Penn Medicine.   I took a deuce against the wall facing Walnut. My small order arrived within a minute. The java came in in a pot for pouring into a wide mouth cup, the muffin on a flat white personal size tray. Cool that something as common as coffee and a nosh were reimagined to present in an interesting alternative. If that was Brussels style, I was all for it!   Service was fast and friendly. Those baguettes and demi-pain looked great and tempting enough to want to return for a sandwich to sample the crunchy crust of traditional French bread.   On the way out I stepped on the old ceramic tile floor that had anchored Robbins for decades and was left in place by the new business. It neatly tied the past with the present, honoring history while adding ambiance to today.

El Negro De Oro (Black Gold) is a new Ecuadorian restaurant at the corner of Sewall and S. Broad in Hamilton, New Jersey.  It is easy to find because it is painted the colors of its name and stands out in an otherwise drab urbanscape.  Street parking is required, but the side streets around there offer plenty of space for a short stroll to the entrada.   Walking in, the color combination grabs your attention immediately. Black and gold floors and walls.  The house has been open only three months and the atmosphere is clean and bright with a small counter near the kitchen entrance, and an area for entertainment off to the side.  They did a very good job turning a small grocery/deli into an attractive place to dine.    Service was warm and informative and we had no trouble understanding each other though all accents (including mine) were thick as homemade salsa.  The menu is bilingual which is very helpful.  I ordered the Special Lunch of the Day, Catfish/Yam Soup and Quarter Roast Chicken with Red Beans and Rice.  A couple of dishes of salsa tagged along, one a traditional Green Sauce, and the other a more unusual thick Yellow Grainy Sauce, which had an unusual flavor that mixed well with the chicken and rice. Think Adobo.    The Soup contained a tender chunk of Catfish, bone in and with skin.  It was very tasty.  The orange color of the soup base came from the Yams in which everything simmered for many hours.  There was some spice thrown in for good measure.  The sweetness of the tubers was the most obvious flavor, and cooking the fish in it was an excellent approach, as the mild white meat of the Catfish had nicely picked up the Yamminess from the stewing process.    The Chicken was smaller than the typical clucker found in most restaurants, and had the look of a Cornish Hen, although the taste was not gamey.  I was able to pull it apart with knife, fork and fingers and suck the meat off the bones.  Liked it a lot.  The White Rice absorbed the juices from the bird and Red Beans and was a good companion to the rest of the plate.    While eating, the owner/chef came out to check on my satisfaction.  I learned that his nickname was "Black Gold," and that he was also a trained Italian chef.  As if to prove this point, he came out with a piece of Tiramisu prepared in his kitchen.  While this is not my normal tea and crumpets, it was soft, rummy, creamy and sweet.  I suggest he consider adding a few of his best Italian dishes on the menu to broaden the appeal of his shop.  There are not many Ecuadorian/Italian places around here (or anywhere).    El Negro De Oro is another of the first rate Latin kitchens sprouting up in Trenton and Hamilton.  It is a variation of what we know as Mexi/Guat/Salvador/Puerto Rican/Dominican/Cuban restos, and well worth a visit.    The cuisine and the hospitality are the real deal.

Slice & Soft Drink Review  Walked in to Yordana II tonight for a light bite and went with a slice of regular pizza that was sitting under glass. The place was empty but for me at 7:15. It had about a half dozen booths along the inside wall.  It was a clean house, with three guys in the kitchen. Everyone was polite.   I asked that the reheat be "well done," to bring the wedge fully back to life. The young cashier took my $4 and handed me some change for the tip jar on the counter. I went to pour my drink and retreated to a booth to await my victuals.   It arrived a few minutes later in the hands of the chef. It was a smallish slice, but I wasn't starving. My standard for good pizza wants the point to stand firm when picked up by the crust. It demonstrates a well baked and strong chassis upon which the rest of the vehicle is built. This one collapsed on elevation. The weight of the cheese and the trapped moisture in the underbaked bottom made for a soggy base.   I folded it over longitudinally to hold it together, and a rivulet of oil rolled off onto the paper plate. Cheap cheese. When I could finally take the first bite, the triangle was hot enough to melt the surface and warm the undercarriage, but had not reached full reheat, let alone the heavier burn I requested. Also, the top was almost entirely cheese with a thin tasteless layer of sauce. Bad proportions.   This was not a good pizza for me. Everyone has a different preference for their pie, but when requests are not honored, the problem goes deeper than lack of real experience with a classic American comfort food. It is about listening and translating that request into the desired product. This just wasn't done.   Everything else on the menu may be great, but the pizza reheat was not.

Erwin's Country Kitchen is along the strip of Brownsville Road in Trevose that helps you understand what commercial development without zoning looks like. Ugly. So, don't be too discouraged as you drive down the street looking for 4059.  There it is on the south side of the street with the small white sign hanging high above the front door.  Rest assured that once you come inside you will be relieved to find yourself smack in the middle of 1959, greeted by a black and white poster of Marilyn Monroe and another of a more colorful James Dean.    Rebel Without A Cause.  But, this time warping is a good thing.  The spacious dining room relaxes and helps recollect a time when things were good in grandma's home.  The wait people were lovely and straight from central casting.  They were in perpetual motion, bringing fresh coffee and large white plates full of grub to the starving masses.  When I came in, a group of ladies were in a breakfast meeting, and it looked like they might have been there for several years.  They showed no inclination to leave, and remained after I departed.  I wondered about their agenda.    The deuce along the wall in the back space near the kitchen was a great place to watch the play unfolding.  The coffee came quickly in an odd mug, and with large half/half cupettes.  It was constantly refreshed before I reached the bottom, and it was not difficult to maintain the proper proportion of java to cream with small pours from the creamers.    I ordered the French Toast (as I usually do), and was asked for the first time in my life whether I wanted thick or thin sliced bread.  Astute question.  While the intuitive decision is to get more and go with the thick cut, I have the contrary opinion.  Too often the thicker Texas/Challah Style leaves the bread eggless in its heart, and thus dry.  I prefer the thinner option as it tends to be moist to the center, thoroughly cooked, and better carmelized on the surface.  Those burn points provide the crunch I desire.   When the plate arrived, it had six half slices of toast, well grilled, and heavily sprinkled with powdered sugar.  A small paper cup of butter allowed for a light application of lubricant and additional subtle flavoring.  The syrup came in an old spring load top pitcher, which I promptly lifted over the plate for a healthy pour.    The French Toast was quite good, but not attaining the pantheon of the gods. It needed another minute on the hot grill, and a drop of vanilla in the egg mix for soft  mellow unique sweetness.    I will return to see Erwin again.  The menu looked to hold other secrets worth exploring, and it is not every day that I can slip in and out of the 50's without getting the bends.

Oliver A Bistro sits in the middle of lively Farnsworth Avenue, Bordentown, NJ.  As such, it is one of the many culinary attractions that now predominate on this old main street along the mighty Delaware River.  On this beautiful Friday afternoon, the place to be is under a red umbrella on top of the red brick that are the sidewalks of this historic burg.  Failing that, the next best place to dine is in one of the large window wells on either side of the front door.  That is where I found myself, as all the outside tables were taken when I arrived.    What is a bit disconcerting about Oliver, is that the inside dining room is rather dark and uninteresting.  Just dark brown tables and chairs with dark carpet and some wall hangings.  No real color, lighting, nor energy.  I directed my attention out the large windows and onto the street on this sunny day, but felt the welling darkness over my shoulders.    My French Dip Burger with optional side Caesar Salad was very attractive visually, although the puck was a little beyond the medium finish requested.  The description of this opus was of Swiss & Havarti Cheese melt, with Bourbon Caramelized Onions, Sour Cream Horseradish Sauce, and a side cup of Oliver Au Jus.  All those parts were present, and contributed to a good tasting burger.  I have always enjoyed a horseradish alternative to ketchup on my sliders, and it was good to satisfy this long delayed gratification.  It all came together well, especially when I occasionally dipped the burger into the Au Jus and savored the implanted memory of roast beef done this way.  The Caesar side was fresh, green and mildly anchovied.  Liked it.   At $12 for a full plated lunch, I was satisfied with the value received.  Come in closer to medium with pink center, and I would easily bump this experience up a star.  For a full blown 5 Star rating, something has to be done to lighten the gloom of the dining room.

The Terminal Restaurant sits at the crossroads of Moreland and Davisville Roads in Willow Grove, Pa. While the name originally referred to the railroad station that was once close by, that stop has moved into history, and the sense of the house now is that it is more the terminus of two old generational trails.  Although renovated, it has the feel of an older way station that still carries its legacy and kitchen skills very well.    The customer base is interestingly diverse, but the common thread seems to be old time locals who know where to find good, cheap vittles, and who are loyal to their institutions.  Can't blame them.  There is something deep and authentic about this place; its cramped booths and tables, its classic servers, and its faithfulness to real American grub.  No brunch served here. No mimosas.  Just straight ahead, no apologies, grill'em-ups.   The coffee flowed strong and free.  Not the best, but we were not here for La Colombe. All we wanted was caffeinated washdown, and got it. The Country Omelet was a 2 egger loaded with taters and 'yons, with grilled sausage added for taste and texture. Delicious, with a side of toasted rye.  The home fries had crisp edges, but could have used more flavor.  So be it. There was also the option for grits. Maybe next time.   Really liked The Terminal Resto.  Next time I feel like taking a drive in the country and into the past, I might find myself terminating the excursion right here.

If your looking for a big breakfast 24/7, plus a full lunch and dinner menu, then Amy's Omelette House is singing your siren song.   312 varieties of omelet at last count, plus, pancakes, French toast, sandwiches, muffins, quesadillas, burritos, and enough coffee to drown your sorrows - all presented in a large but cozy converted diner at the intersection of Rt. 130 and High Street in Burlington City, NJ.  Those of us who remember when this was the old Burlington Diner find it all the more remarkable, because it took so long for the BD to finally die that most of us forgot there could be good food at that location.    And, good it is.  The signature omelets are 3 eggers full of whatever you want.  Wet or dry, potatoes in or out, the result is a belly busting, can't stop myself, corker of a meal. The service is right in line with the product; fresh and swaggering. I haven't made it past the omelets, French Toast, breakfast sandwiches and a Quesadilla, but all have been at the very least, very good.    PRO TIP - Try to sit in the old original boxcar dining room.  It is so well maintained it feels like you are chowing down in a museum.  It makes everything taste even better.

Spring Garden Restaurant at the corner of N. 4th and Spring Garden Street in Northern Liberties, Philly, is an old school urban diner. There is a dining area to one side and a ten stool counter overlooking the grill on the other. The menu is traditional Americana breakfast and lunch, with prices the remind of the earlier years of the century. Nice to have lower rents.   On arrival it was a full house, but for a couple of spinners. When none of the earlier people waiting for tables wanted them, we accepted with gratitude. Not sure about the tables, but we felt lucky to be able to watch the show from our orchestra seats.   Our black shirt server came over promptly for drink requests, and kept her poise and humor despite the beehive of activity around her. The Bunn-O-Matic java was average, but it did provide a buzz and washed down our meal, which we thoroughly enjoyed. My better half went with a beef sausage, egg and cheese on kaiser, while I asked for french toast and bacon. Both were very good. The sammy was a two egger on a fresh and tasty roll. The frenchie had a great vanilla/sugar/cinnamon egg mix that saturated the three bread slices to the core leading to strong texture and taste. The crisp caramelized edges were aces. Melted butter and Kraft syrup pour and I was a happy man. Maple syrup would have made this dish perfect.   All the while we watched the chef (he was so much more than a short order cook) move through the orders without wasted motion. Grasping eggs with one hand, cracking them into a stainless bowl, and whipping them with a fork with the other; then pouring them onto the hot steel while shaping and flipping them with spatchula, before sliding the finished omelet or over easys, smoothly onto a plate. He then quickly scraped away the residue on the grill into the trough while he moved the plate to the counter to be retrieved for serving.  His efficiency was astonishing. He was intense and focused, and when a server expressed impatience waiting for her order despite his masterly effort, he reminded her with rich irony that he only had two hands. Two?!  It looked like four from where we sat.   Can't ask for more than a solid breakfast and great floorshow. They should charge a premium for those counter seats.

Crestview Deli & Market has been under new ownership for about 10 months, so if you haven't been there lately, you might consider stopping in again to see if there are any changes.  The two women I met when I stopped in to pick up a sandwich for lunch were very pleasant and efficient in constructing a Boar's Head Turkey & Swiss on Rye.  They asked if I wanted anything more in the sandwich and happily added sweet peppers to the project.    The "market" part of the operation offers limited provisions for those in need of a few small items.  It reminded of a small old fashioned grocery in a rural area, where larger supermarkets are not readily available.  There were also shelves of snacks and a back wall lined with refrigerated drinks, which reinforced the impression of somewhat stepping back in time.  I enjoyed the nostalgic break.    Opening the foil wrapped sandwich at my desk, I beheld a nicely packed load of turkey and cheese with lettuce, mayo and the peppers.  The bread was fresh and had a nice rye and caraway taste.  I liked it.    There is a small sitting area in a corner of this deli that could be a nice place to sit and enjoy morning coffee and a made to order breakfast sandwich.    I intend to return to find out, and continue my conversation with the nice folks there.

Georgian Bread Cuisine on Bustleton Avenue in Northeast, Philly, is an excellent deli/restaurant specializing in the very interesting and tasty kitchen from this small nation in eastern Europe on the Black Sea. That these people thrived as a gateway to Asia for more than a thousand years is both an important historic fact and an exceptional cultural phenomenon that is a great benefit to everyone. After dinner there it was fascinating how their food captured elements of all the Silk Road traffic that brought the food from the far East and West through Tblisi and other ancient cities, leaving their diverse flavors and skills behind.   Everything we sampled reminded of dishes eaten in other cooking styles. The eggplant with walnuts, with its mildly bitter nightshade base and soft sweetness from the ground walnut hummus-like spread, took me to Middle Eastern and Greek houses. The adjaruli bread boat with its tender hot dough split open on top to expose a lake of molten cheese and raw egg, came right from an oven that looked similar to a tandor Indian oven, and easily reminded of an Italian calzone, only more cheesily delicious. Finally, the khinkali soup dumplings were larger versions of Shanghai xiao long bao, complete with steaming beef/pork consume and flavorful filling, and eaten by hand.   Whether it was Marco Polo or Ghengis Khan bringing these ideas on their travels or conquests, or anyone else along the way, this Georgian restaurant continues the culinary exchange between East and West, and is awesome food for both taste buds and anthropologists.

It was a cold, windy, city morn when we reached Washington Avenue, and I still hadn't had my first cup of java. I was trying to maintain my good mood, but it would be a losing battle without some caffeine soon.   Desperate times called for desperate measures.   I remembered there was this Bambu shop nearby, so I Yelped it and realized it was right across 6th Street from where we were. We walked over and found it in the inner corner of the shopping center. It was a small shop, with short red sofa, three cafe tables, and a few chairs along the window. The walls were covered in menus and photos of their signature Che fruity concoctions.   Colorful, but I needed something stronger and hotter. Farther down the drinks list was the coffee. I asked for Vietnamese coffee, hot. I normally drink it in VN cafes or after meals, so this was my first takeout.   It was exactly as expected. Strong, hot and sweetened by condensed milk. I missed the whole drip experience but it was great to be able to shop the market with java in hand.

Can't say that a woman's accessories boutique is a subject in my wheelhouse, but I know an attractive shop when I see one. More to the point, when they are having a sale on handbags and I can stock up for Valentine's Day on leather I think she will like, it is a very good day.   Lou Lou Boutique has shelves of sacks and over the shoulder book pockets, not to mention, costume jewelry and a few clothing racks, that make browsing an enjoyable indulgence.   With the half price stickers, buying two was easy, even with the cost of parking thrown in. The stop at Green Eggs Cafe may have been a little over the top, but added to the quality afternoon.

In the best tradition of Black Friday we stopped in at Tio Juan's for late lunch and a few inebriants to succour us after the retail battles of the day. Traffic getting there was like swimming against a riptide, but once parked and inside things slowed down nicely.  The entrance foyer was large and empty, but for a solitary women behind a counter who directed us to either the lounge or dining room. We chose to be closer to the bar, and found our way to a clean booth on the far side. No one in uniform noticed our arrival, as we sat for several minutes with staff walking by without capturing their attention. I finally flagged down a server, who brought us menus and said someone would be with us shortly. She was, and we ordered our first margarita and Modelo Negro while reading the menu.   We chose the Steak Fajitas and Fish Tacos del Mar from the Lunch Specials. Chips & Salsa were good and spicy. The steak was plentiful and nicely pink within, while well blackened without. The side of fixings - lettuce, salsa, crema fresca, onions and guacamole, and 4 hot tortillas, allowed for alot of handiwork. We both liked the platter.   The fish tacos were okay, but not what was ordered. They were not the del mar version, but the straight fish tacos.  Thus, they lacked the proper sauce, cilantro and avocado; but had an aioli cream and red cabbage finish. Not even the roasted corn relish described on the menu for this dish was present. This was the more disappointing given that our server had recommended the del mar, but didn't recognize that she didn't have it in her hands.   Honestly, it wasn't until I read the menu again online in preparation for this review that I realized what happened. Retroactive annoyance.   This was not a bad experience, but for this. While not authentic Mexican cuisine, it knows how to make what we gringos like. Too, the bar lubricated us well.

Battery Park sits along a stretch of the Delaware River shoreline, beginning at the bottom of Delaware Street in New Castle, and going southwestward for a little over a mile next to Gambacorta Marsh to where Army Creek enters the Delaware.  There are two dikes, one holding back the marsh and the other a former railroad spur line. There is little left of the original battery built to defend against French incursions before the Revolution, and later against the British. Too, the railroad that used to run from where the small white wooden ticket office now stands, all the way to Frenchtown, Maryland, is little more than an historic footnote.    Yet, what remains is a beautiful place to walk or bike along the water's edge and witness some amazing sunsets. There are the remains of the small harbor sticking their waterlogged lumber above the surface of the river in spots, and a few ice piers placed to keep ice from clogging the shipping lanes.    It is hard to imagine that New Castle is older than Philadelphia, and was the spot where William Penn first set foot in America to oversee his vast land grant from the king.  But, the harbor here is not very big, and Philadelphia soon became the major port for this region.  Commerce was not sufficient to sustain any significant long term economic growth, although for about 30 years the New Castle & Frenchtown Railroad (the first on the east coast), did help with transport between Philly and Baltimore, because going by boat between the two cities was difficult due to the topography of the Delmarva Peninsula.  Eventually, first canals, and later larger railroads and toll roads assumed the largest share of commercial transport, and New Castle became a literal backwater in time.   Yet, without that, Battery Park would likely have been overrun by industrialization and extensive shipping, and not become the lovely green space that natives and visitors enjoy today.

Debbie's Deli on Liberty Street in Hamilton, NJ, has been in business for thirty years in the same location.  The sandwich emporium is as small as your master bedroom closet, but managed to turn out excellent breakfasts and lunches within its miniscule confines.    It is a Boar's Head joint, but with the license to roast the turkey, ham and roast beef on its own when delivered there by this provider.  That extra touch of freshness and originality shows that it is trusted to do excellent work to maintain the brand, and that they succeed in doing so.  Impressive.  Today, I ordered a blackboard special - a cup of Potato Leek Soup, and a third of a Roast Turkey & Swiss Hoagie.  The price; $5.95.  While waiting, I spoke to "Debbie," who is really her former partner after she left the business many years ago.  He is proud of his shop, and it shows in the clean, cozy atmosphere, and the outstanding quality of his products.    The Potato Leek Soup was heavily chunked with spuds and leek in a rich, creamy base.  Delicious.  Obviously, made with love that very day.  The sandwich came on fresh, light Italian loaf.  The home baked gobbler was cool, tasty and a pleasure to consume, with a couple slices of Swiss nuttiness to complement the more savory turkey.  A delight.    If Debbie's gets too famous, it will have to move to larger quarters, as there is room for at most ten standing people in there.  Nice problem to have.  It is somewhat surprising that these guys haven't run into this situation before.    Street parking can be a challenge on the narrow one-way streets in that neighborhood. But, worth the effort.

Provecho (advantage/good fortune) Mexican Grill on Philmont Avenue, Huntingdon Valley, PA, is a decent cafe style Mexican restaurant with a nice vibe, friendly service and kitchen that turns out a limited menu of traditional  platas somewhat tempered for the American palette. It is colorful with large wall murals and a few nooks with comfortable chairs and small tables right out of the Salvation Army store.    We were there early on a Saturday night, grabbed one of those tables under a mural, and ordered their chicken soup, shrimp fajitas and chicken taquitos. The soup was excellent. Shredded white meat bird, chunky carrots and smaller pieces of onion, it had big flavor from simmering all day long. The fajitas had plenty of medium sized shrimp, well grilled and lightly spiced over slices of peppers and onions. Rice, beans, queso fresca, sour cream and a dollop of creamy guacamole completed the platter.   Even with complimentary salsa added (not gratis across the board?!) the flavor was muted, and not the blast of spices and textures expected. The large amount of rice was offset by its blandness, although the refried beans were tasty. The three taquitos were stuffed with chicken, cheese and pepper and topped with the same finish as the fajitas. They were crisply deep fried and looked great. The chicken was again under spiced and even the chipotle salsa was too weak to kick it up to tickle the tongue.   I have no problem with charging for chips and salsa, but add on cost for salsa (even homemade variations) is ahead of the curve of acceptable charges for accessories necessary for the fulfillment of the underlying dish. It's like charging for ketchup on your burger, or cream for your coffee. Never saw that in all my time in Mexico, nor in any of the dozens of very good Mexican houses around Montco. Perhaps, they need to do that to keep doors open, but it seemed ungenerous to these guests.

If you are someone who loves good soft serve ice cream, give C & C Dairyland a try.
