It doesn't look like much out on Bustleton Avenue in the far Northeast, Philadelphia; in fact I was looking for it the other night and drove right by it and had to turn around. Which is to say, even though it is one of those mid-20th Century flat roofed  all white ice cream stores, it tends to blend into the background. Still, it is worth the effort to slow down and take a few minutes out of your day to sample their sweet creamies.   They do vanilla soft serve the way it should be done - taking the time to be sure it is fully blended and chilled before dispensing through their antique equipment. The result is among the best softies I have had the pleasure to explore with my tongue. While Kohr's down the shore remains the gold standard, C & C is just a step behind. Their thing is to add toppings to every cone and dish going out the windows. In my case, it was smashed cherries, although the Jimmies and wet nuts also looked damn good.   The only downside is the harsh environment surrounding the building. There are no trees, bushes, umbrellas, picnic tables, overhangs, etc., to shelter customers from the blazing sun nor Saharan heat. The choice is to stand around and melt with the ice cream, sit in your car with the air conditioner going full bore, or to drive away and hope when you arrive home your prize hasn't leaked onto the floor. Makes the consumption less than it could be if even a small effort was made to provide some seating in the shade. On a hot and steamy late Sunday afternoon it was quite oppressive.  I guess we could bring a beach umbrella and set it up on the grass behind the shop, but then I would need a sandy beach to make it feel right - and I might as well go down the shore for a Kohr's.   3.5 Stars

Down towards the bottom of North Union Street in Lambertville, NJ, sits Thai Nida (Thai Daughter). It is a one room restaurant with exposed beam cathedral ceiling, orange wash walls and a few Buddhist hangings. The western exposure made for strong afternoon sunlight through the windows, so I moved to the other side of my table to cut down the glare.   The was a large party at one end of the room keeping the one server occupied most of the time, but she kept her cool and managed to help me and another couple with our orders. She had skills and pleasant disposition.   There was no lunch menu on Sunday, so I went with their Pad Kee Mao (veggie drunken noodles), which I have had an addiction to for the past few months. I love those wide rice noodles, hot spice and heavy brown sauce, and each of the versions I have tried were distinct from each other, despite the same ingredients. Some have been amazing, while others have not.   Today's were toward the bottom of the spectrum to date. The noodles were plentiful, but aside from the bell peppers, onion and basil that come standard with the dish, there were only a few slim carrot slices and broccoli  florets to represent the vegetable kingdom. Not a mushroom, sprout nor stringbean in the lot. The spicing was not what I expected, neither chili nor lemongrass, but more a salt, black and/or white ground pepper with something else I couldn't identify. It was barely okay, and far from my favorite.   It wasn't a great effort. Maybe they were saving the rest of the produce for that big party across the room.  2.5 STARS

Strictly a low budget primarily take out joint that dishes out the standard Chinese/American fare at low prices.  Nothing original here, except they do provide hot tea in a large heated pot for those who ask for it.  Many places are so stripped down that only cold drinks are offered with lunch specials, and the iconic Chinese tea is forgotten.    The room was chilly for eating in as I did, making it obvious they did not encourage people hanging around to eat on their one or two tables.  Health issues were also present, as I observed the chef breading chicken pieces with his bare hands before dropping them into the wok.  Hate to think where those digits may have been.    The taste of my Sesame Chicken with Fried Rice was okay, although the rice had been made earlier with a yellow dye chicken broth.  I didn't expect it to be made to order.  Same was true for the Wonton Soup.  Thick skins and unidentifiable meatish food within.  Bad texture. Worse taste.  I left most of that plastic container behind.    How much better it would be if these places provided real plates and flatware, rather than plastic containers and utensils, for those few who chose to eat there.  Being served as if ordering take out just seems dismissive of those customers.  It doesn't change the taste of anything, but sure makes for a "we don't care about you," attitude.

Gold Garden is a middle of the road Chinese/American shop in the Homestead Plaza II, in Columbus, NJ.  It has 5 tables for those choosing to eat in.  The front of the house is a large counter where the wife of this H & W team holds court with efficiency and a smile.  The menu is what you would expect.    My Sesame Chicken was served on a plate (rather than in Styrofoam), with Fried/White/Brown rice options, as well as soup or soda.  At $5.65 it was one of the better prices I have seen for this luncheon combo.  Taste-wise, it was okay, with a nice pile of chicken breaded, fried, and smothered in semi-sweet goo.  You know ... the way you have seen it a million times.  Plenty of rice made earlier in the day.    The plaza where it is located also has ice cream and cupcake stores right next door, for those seeking things from all the nutritious food groups.  Luckily, the cupcake shop is closed Monday and Tuesday.    Temptation is everywhere.

This review is for the lunch experience at Hong Kong Gourmet.   The 5 Star reviews caught my attention, so even though it was a longer drive to Richboro to get to the location in Crossroads Plaza, I thought it was worth the time.  Walking in, I viewed a nice dining room with the ubiquitous leatherette booths and industrial carpet, and it was bright and airy.  The house was empty at 1:45, not unusual for a late lunch. There were two women working the floor.  They seemed tired, but dutiful.  I was pointed to a booth near the front and handed a menu.    After perusing the multi-page document and seeing a fairly broad selection of dinner dishes that were appealing, I finally reached the "Lunch Special" page in the back.  Although there were 24 items listed with a price range between $5.50 and $8.95, most listings were of the, "chicken/pork/beef with veggies/nuts/garlic/lobster sauce and fried rice," variety.  Uninspired.  All the better dishes were in other parts of the menu at much higher price points (read; dinner prices).  This approach certainly made me feel that lunch was not important to this business, unless I was willing to eat dinner earlier in the day.    Okay.  I was there. I was put off.  I would play it out.  I ordered the General Tso's Chicken, which had a little red pepper icon next to it.  It came with Hot and Sour Soup, and Pork Fried Rice.  The soup was not bad. Plenty of tofu, sprouts, and slivers of pork. Not too much vinegar.  The Fried Rice was a pleasant surprise.  It was fresh with chunks of pork and a nice supply of veggies. However, the Chicken came in thinly breaded cubes and rectangles, was dry tasting, and the sauce was neither sweet nor spicy.  There was only a hint of flavor in the thin glurb. Pieces of Green Pepper were thrown on top of the chicken, and while it was fresh, it was monochromatic.  I get that they did not want to invest heavily in my lunch, but why not a little red and yellow bell peppers, too?    My read from the experience, which included non-smiling service and the delivery of my check while I was still eating, was that Hong Kong Gourmet does not want to do lunch, and is only open at those hours to catch the unwary. I deduced that the soup and rice were good because they were prepared in advance of dinner, not for the lunch crowd.  Their evening victuals may well be better, but after this exposure of disinterest, why would anyone want to give them another visit?    I certainly won't.

This is the second OwowCow I have customered.   It is housed in a former industrial space and the reuse is attractive, if rather basic.  Small public space with a few tables, and the expectation that most people will take their ice cream and leave.   Their flavors are exotic-sounding, and for the most part they succeed in producing the subtle tastes that are seldom found in ice cream parlors.  My "Regular" sized cup of Indonesian Vanilla and Banana Caramel was smooth, creamy and required some attention to appreciate the variations and their mixture on the tongue.   The sizes are smaller than the competition, and the prices a bit higher, at $5. for two small scoops of whatever flavors you choose. That may be a good thing, as it does suggest slowing down to enjoy the moment over piling on luscious calories.   The shop is across the parking lot from Big Bear Natural Foods, and people have been known to park there without hassle.

The Peter J. Camiel Travel Plaza is a smaller scale rest stop along the Pa turnpike.  While all the plazas are being redesigned and modernized for the new century, this one, while clean and efficient, and provisioned with the expected vendors from Starbucks to Roy Rogers and the ever-present Wawa like shop, this one lacks the comfort of the others on a busy day.  The lines tend to knot with each other.    Still, it generally does what is supposed to do; provide plumbing and victuals for the road weary traveler, and help them on their way to their ultimate destinations.    It is functional and an improvement over its predecessor.  Who was Peter J. Camiel?  A Philly politician of the Rizzo era who was prosecuted for corruption in office, convicted, and ultimately vindicated on appeal to the higher courts. As his legacy he had this rest stop named after him.

Now that I am spending more time at the USCIS building on 41st Street, and the immigration interviews and other proceedings start as early at 8:00 am, I need a place to cool my jets over coffee or breakfast while I wait to be heard. I learned long ago that it is better to arrive early and wait for court or other meetings, than to deal with heavier traffic later in the morning, and risk arriving late. Today, I asked one of the guards in the security area where to go for coffee until the public was allowed into the building at 7:30.  He was thoughtful and thorough, giving me a list of places within a few blocks.  When he mentioned the restaurant on Market Street that had a full breakfast menu, he showed more enthusiasm then for the others mentioned, so I took my clients there for morning repast.    Turned out that Hamilton Restaurant is an old school luncheonette, with long counter with spinners on one side, and tables on the other.  Kitchen in back. The offerings were plentiful, with both breakfast and lunch available during open hours.  We opted for a couple of omelets (w/ home fries), turkey sage sausage, egg & cheese on Kaiser roll, and a grilled blueberry muffin.  Ten minutes later we were served by a very friendly and considerate woman, who seemed to anticipate our needs.  That was unexpected and exceptional.   Our food was very good.  The omelets were stuffed to the gills with the cheesesteak and sausage fillings two of them wanted, while my sandwich was not overly large, but very tasty with the turkey sage sausage a surprise star of the show.  Very happy with that recommendation.  The muffin had a strong resemblance to Costco muffins, but there were no complaints. Coffee was strong and the request that one be half milk, well received and delivered.   This location is beyond the spreading influence of UPenn and Drexel.  That means that it is still an original joint that has not been gentrified yet.  The cozy neighborhood atmosphere was palpable, and the prices reflective of that.    Very happy to find a place where I can eat and be comfortable while waiting to go to work.

On a recent return visit I sampled their cronut and macaroons.   Both were pretty good.  Sweet, but not overly so.  Textured well, so that the pleasure came from a combination of senses.   While still not close to a Boulangerie Parisienne, at least it is a reasonable facsimile of one, especially for those with sweet teeth, who have never been to Paris.

Nary a leprechaun in the house, but The Irish Horne markets itself as an Irish Bar. It is entitled to call itself whatever it wants, but the reality here is that aside from a half dozen Emerald Isle menu items and Guinness on tap, this is a new sports bar in the heart of Richboro, PA, with a lot of suds on tap and no corned beef and cabbage.   It is attractive with large rectangular bar except where it runs into the rear wall, plenty of brew choices and large format menu with predominantly traditional bar food and a tip of the cap to those Irish like dishes. I asked for Magnar's Irish Cider and a Shepherds Pie (although their House Burger was equally tempting). I was still finding out about the brogue in the kitchen.   The Magnars was excellent. Cool, tart apple and easy going down. No kick. No bite. The Shepherds Pie arrived in a small cast iron oven ready dish, still too hot to touch, and a soup spoon. It was topped with mashed potatoes over a ground beef, gravy understrata. The taste was fine, but it fell short in the veggie department. There were few carrot/pea/corn participants, and those that were there seemed from a bag of frozen mixed vegetables.   Disappointing.   How much better it would have been with serious veggie chunks to add texture and interest to the experience. As they were, they were practically invisible on the tongue. Perhaps, a deeper dish would allow for this. At $13.50, the value proposition is just not compelling when the standard burger offers more meat and veggies than does the Pie, for $4 less. And comes with fries!   So, while The Irish Horne has many good attributes, it should make more of an effort to really be an Irish bar, and consider how to improve their signature kitchen offerings.

Rhodes Newtown Flower & Gift Shop on South State Street, is an old fashioned florist that packs a lot of petals and stems into a tiny space in historic Newtown Borough. House plants, beautiful flower arrangements,  gifts of all stripes are in every available nook and cranny, except for the narrow path left open to get around. In the heart of the retail area is an old refrigerated display case with the more delicate flora, mostly roses, lilies and orchids.   There in the back, on the top shelf I saw a bouquet of peach roses with baby's breath and lavender in a green glass vase. It drew me to it despite the red long stems shouting for attention. There was something about the soft understated elegance of these young opening buds that called me. After years of buying on line, I had forgotten how sensual it was to buy flowers with my eyes, nose and hands engaged. Intoxicating.   It was my own private party as a prelude to the extra satisfaction of carrying them out of the shop and walking down the street with them in hand. It was noticed by those on the sidewalk, and I could have sworn that the women looked at me a bit more attentively. Nice!   All these extra fun dimensions for slightly more than the price to point and click. Plus, a warm human being answering questions and making suggestions.  So glad I rediscovered the classic way to get ready for Valentine's Day! Surely, the special atmosphere in Rhodes had a lot to do with it.

Cattani Catering & Kitchen on Parkway Avenue, Ewing, NJ, is an exceptional Italian house with small dining room and five stool counter, turning out creative and delicious dishes for those lucky enough to know it is there.   I stopped in for a late lunch last week, grabbing a spinner overlooking the kitchen. Only one table was occupied by women in bonnets, although a few people came in to pick up take out orders. Sherry was running the floor, and cheerily brought me the clipboard menu along with a cool copper mule mug of water and lemon. Prices were on the high side, but given the description of the food and Sherry's enthusiasm for each of them, I accepted that this was a "budget be damned" moment. I ordered the chicken milanese sandwich with side salad. The order in, I then saw Ms. Cattani herself putting my meal together. She waved and said hello while cheffing for me.   Turns out she is basically a self taught uber foodie, who decided to open her open shop after working for other restaurants for several years. She is self taught and obviously a great student of her craft.   My lunch arrived on a thin wood plank. Minimalist, but strikingly presented. A feast for the eyes, and ultimately, the stomach. The chicken breast was pounded into a thin steak, lightly breaded in Italian crumbs and pan fried, with marinated peperonata, parmesan and aged balsamic drip on a crusty seeded "rustic" torpedo roll. It was delicious. No one off, this. Each element made a contribution to the overall work of art. I like milanese dishes, and even prepare them at home. Still, none are as interesting and tasty as this, and it was just a sandwich! What would it have been as a stand alone fully plated dinner? Don't know, but a week later I am still thinking of when to find out.   All the while, Sherry was seeing to the incoming phone orders and refilling my water mug during the gaps in the calls. Service was friendly and informative. I was well cared for.   This was a superior lunch from an unexpected source.   Surprise was perhaps the tastiest part of the dish.

Online car shopping is only as good as the people on the other end and the principles of the organization they represent. Luckily for me the new owner of the Willow Grove Infiniti dealership is the Faulkner Group. They know how to put the customer in as much comfort as possible when shopping for a new/used car. The process is what is important to me, so even if we don't come to terms I feel appreciated as a valuable customer and know they want my business, if at all possible.    They happened to have a mature Infiniti that suited me quite well. I found it through Car Gurus. The communication was prompt and unpressured when I inquired. We were able to arrange a visit to their dealership and a test drive for later in the week. I arrived. I was introduced. I test drove. We discussed the outlines of a deal. All cordial and relaxed.   Life can interfere with even car buying. As Mick J sang, "You can't always get what you want...but ... you just might get you get what you need." Despite legit price reduction, I decided on a different direction for several reasons.   Regardless, I felt good about Faulkner Infiniti of Willow Grove, and plan to return for service and when it is time to replace my aging M. Such a great car. They were right when they say theirs was a better vehicle than the other one I was interested in, but sometimes better isn't what's best under all the circumstances. This was so here.   Someone's going to be fist bumping.  Someone's going to be frustrated. I'll get something that I can use well for several years, and save a few grand by being prudent.   But, I'll be back soon for service on my M, and to keep an eye on what they have out on the lot.

Breakfast Nook is a small morning/afternoon luncheonette in the Borough of Riverton, NJ, right across Bannard Street from the Cinnaminson Light Rail Station very close by the Delaware River. It sits on the first floor of a warehouse-looking building, not normally a place I'd look for breakfast. Still, it is a bright and clean house with a dozen or so tables and counter service toward the rear.   I plopped down on a stool and settled in as a server welcomed me, brought me coffee, milk and a menu. I appreciated the fresh milk availability in lieu of mini moo. The specials board caught my attention with its offer of a sausage, egg and cheese on grilled rye sandwich (with home fries, $7).   It called my name.  It was a very good sammy. Crisp, grill toasted bread, with tasty patty, sharp cheddar and still lightly drippy fried egg. Just the way I like it. The home fries were copious, with dark nibs throughout, and just greasy enough for max flavor. Coffee wasn't memorable, but it was hot and bracing on a cool late November morn.   While looking around I saw three wooden plates on the wall, each with the name of a restaurant owned by this team. Kelly's Kitchen in Bensalem, PA, Dredge Harbor Cafe in Riverton and Breakfast Nook. I had now eaten in all three, and wondered if there was a prize for this accomplishment. Probably not, but there ought to be at least a cupcake in recognition.   Maybe they'll read this and let me know.

This was my first visit to Mexican Mariachi Grill and it won't be my last.    Sitting in a nondescript mini shopping strip across from the old GM plant, this joint is a bright and pleasant spot for lunch, and probably dinner.  Once inside it is a long, narrow space with a wall of tables on one side, and the kitchen prep area on the other.  The menu is simple with the usual suspect tacos, burritos, quesadillas and the like, but as soon as I saw they had grilled pork Tortas, I zoned in on that.    The Chips and Salsas are self-serve on top of the counter, with a choice of hot and hotter green/red dippers in small plastic containers.  The chips are extra thick and crunchy. The lunch special includes a drink, smooth Black Bean mash, and mildly spicy Rice with kernels of corn mixed in. Both, tasty and textural accompaniments.  The Torta arrived - an oversized fresh roll stuffed with Grilled Pork, Lettuce, Tomato, Melty Cheese, Hot Sauce, and Chipotle Mayo dressing, half-wrapped in foil to hold it together and allow for pick up without mess.  Under $7.  The chew was a robust mix of hot and cold, sweet and spicy, chewy and compliant; a very tasty and intriguing eat.  The only note of caution is when removing the foil to attack the rest of the sandwich, remember that the sauce inside can leak and drip, and even dampen the bread.  You don't want that causing a trip to the cleaners.   Otherwise, a totally satisfying experience that I am very likely to repeat.

Yordana's Pizza & Pasta on Emilie Road, Levittown, PA., is a very good find for a well prepared Italian meal.  Although dressed up like a pizza parlor on the outside, there is a comfortable dining room within, with large wall murals of Venice, and a menu that covers most of the traditional Roman dishes, plus a few custom designed in house.  To my pleasant surprise, everything we ordered was first rate.    We went with two chicken platters; Parmegano and Valentino, with side of pasta and nice sized green salad. Both consisted of three breast fillets. The Parmegano was olive oil pan sautéed bread crumb covered in thick chunky red sauce, with a mildly salty and basil flavor, covered with melted mozza. It was tender and filling. Our request that the pasta side be done Alfredo was granted, and after a shake or two of black pepper, it was excellent as a complement to the main course. Similarly, the Valentino was laid over with freshly cut mushrooms and steamed asparagus, and a light cream sauce. The veggies were still crisp, while the chicken cut easily with a fork. The white sauce was mellow and perfect for the combination of other flavors and textures. It was very different than the Alfredo sauce, showing the skill of the chef in preparing each separately as ordered. The aglio olio penne pasta in the side bowl was likewise delicious.  We were very impressed how each dish was so remarkably distinct and fun to eat.   Service was friendly and prompt, but also not fawning nor overdone. This was still Levittown, after all.   This is the second or third superior meal we have scored on Emilie Road, and it is unlikely to be the last.  It is so worth exploring this neighborhood, especially when it is obvious that there is no loss of quality along with the appreciated loss of expense.   Yordana's is worth the trip.

I feel healthier already!   A morning fast breaker of Blueberry Smoothie and Egg Salad Toast was all I needed to put the pep back in my step and have my digestive tract shouting, "Hip Hip Hooray!" Dubious? Don't knock it till you try it.  Never a lover of egg salad, I am game when told it is from neighboring chickens and mixed with goodness and a little vegan mayo. This work of art, spread atop excellent multi grain toast and garnished with greens and petunia petals, was likely the best of breed. It was delicious, while providing superlative flavor and crunchable texture. Just stupendous!   The suck down smoothie called "Blueberry Wake Up," was all that, too. It was richly blueberried, and blended with other ingredients (see menu photo) that were almost addictive. Semisweet, darkly indigo, thick and creamy, and loaded with energy, it was hard to take the straw out of my mouth. And, combined with the egg salad, made for a surprisingly memorable morning meal.   Service was friendly, informative, impeccable and attractive. The small shop full of magical foods and additives to help you live a more healthy and essential life. Just check out the wire egg basket. Those uber fresh hard shells were right from the nest, without even a stop for a bath.   I'm a believer.

While I'm not a Starbucks guy (too often burnt beans), this new drive thru sit down plant in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center is very cool. Laid back, smaller footprint, friendly accommodating baristas, and decent breakfast profile, make for a pleasant interlude. Panoramic view of the ever expanding choices coming online in this primary commercial zone in Newtown. Can see Melt Shop, Factory Donuts, Naked Chocolate, Oishi, Nothing Bundt Cakes from my small deuce in the window.   Here for a quick Saturday morning meeting, I enjoyed their oatmeal with blueberries, crannies, raisins and a touch of brown sugar (How come you dance so good?!). Perhaps, a little too much packaging for a health planet, but they do have choices. Even the Pike's Roast was more flavorful and less bitter than usual.   Meeting went well, so this $$$bucks could become a strong house for getting together in private conversation. There is enough ambient noise from the polished concrete floor, high metal ceiling and sound system to mask any but the loudest voice.

Apparently the sibling of 1st Oriental Supermarket on 6th Street in South Philly, with similar layout and the same products from live fish through Vietnamese noodles and Thai sauces. Yeah, it has an odor of over ripe fruit and spilled frog water, but that goes with the territory. While some find it offensive, it reminds me of the outdoor markets throughout Asia where the smells are part of the experience.   We had the good fortune of eating dim sum next door at China Gourmet before shopping. It was very good and a great opening act for the aisle cruising to come. Made for a complete excursion to the East.

Maryland Crab Seafood House is located in the former Extension Diner on Olden Avenue Extension, Ewing, NJ. It is the fish restaurant project undertaken by the proprietor of the Ewing Diner, a traditional Greek stainless palace nearby.   The space is nicely renovated, but retains the familiarity of its beginnings with marble lunch counter and enormous slices of dessert cakes, pies and puddings. The service folk looked vaguely like the old staff at The Extension, but as it was many years since my last visit, I wasn't sure if we were all just older versions of our previous selves. They were well schooled in taking care of customers and made certain I had all the water and oven heated rolls I wanted.  I walked in after 3 and was hungry enough for dinner after skipping lunch and an early breakfast. I saw Flounder Francais on the Specials Menu, and stopped reading. As a Francais Fanatic there was nothing more to consider. Let's see what these guys could do with a favorite dish.   The side Caesar Salad was big and fresh, but lacked anchovy based dressing. The small Dinner Rolls were excellent right from the oven with a tasty herb butter melting into them. The large plate with a bed of yellow rice under Flounder fillet dipped in egg and lightly sauteed in more butter, lemon and white wine was flakey and tender and seemed to have avoided freezer time.   Its only shortcoming was caused by my expectation that it would be an Italian or French style finish with a pan sautee browning and thin lemon wine butter reduction. Rather, it was a much heavier bright yellow Greek gravy that was more a thick Avgolemono soup, than the delicate tart complement to the flounder. It wasn't bad, but just not what I envisioned.  That will remind me to live in the moment and leave expectations behind where they can't influence what's yet to come.

This Denny's on Old Lincoln Highway (Business Rt. 1), Langhorne, PA, is an older, bigger version of "America's Diner." It has large windows facing its southern exposure, making for a warm seating area even on cold days. It was so bright at my booth that I had to close the shades to keep from sweating.   There were only four other tables occupied when I arrived. I was greeted promptly and escorted to my booth. Coffee and menu arrived moments later. I hadn't been inside a Denny's in years, and my memory of Country Fried Steak was dominant in my head. I ordered that. It included two eggs (scrambled wet), and rye toast, in addition to the unlimited java. Service was friendly and timely. I was approached every few minutes as to my satisfaction and needs. Never felt neglected.   My tastes have changed since the last time I had this breakfast in my early twenties. I remembered the crunch and meatiness of the steak, but had forgotten how heavily cloying the gravy was. I was able to remove a lot of it, but it was still a strong element of the meal, making for a salty and overly caloric feast. Still, the eggs were done perfectly, and their home fries were nicely crisp. With the three mugs of coffee I drank, it was a filling meal.   Not sure there will be a next time, as, obviously, I seldom have the urge for Denny's. Yet, it was a decent, if salty, breakfast. It briefly connected me to my earlier life, and alerted me to how my tastes have changed. If there were to be a next time, I would lean to the french toast or pancakes, which they offer in abundant varieties. Prices are still quite reasonable.

Just attended a private party in one of Piccolo Trattoria's side rooms in their Newtown store. It went very well.   We were about 20 people celebrating a successful election season in town. The victorious candidates, their families and the campaign team came together with our own wine and beer, and a pre-selected menu of three entree choices (chicken francaise, eggplant parmesan and grilled tilapia) side salad, penne vodka, bread and tomato based dipping sauce. We had two servers assigned to us who did a great job of keeping everything moving.   I split the chicken and eggplant with someone, and both were excellent. The egg/lemon/white wine reduction was tart and played well with the pan sauteed tender bird and was ample enough to allow sipping up with the fresh homemade bread. The eggplant was likewise thin sliced and pan fried before going into the oven to meld with the tomato sauce and mozzarella. Delicious.   With a few glasses of Cabernet Sauvignon, a final sweet bite of chocolate chip mini cannolli and friendly conversation about gearing up for a more successful 2020 presidential election, we were on our way out the door in two hours.   Hope we weren't too boisterous. We will need the other diners to support our people next year.

Zhang's China House has apparently been sold and under new ownership for several years already, but the new information has not been loaded onto Yelp until today.   Never made it to Zhang's, but at least it had a website with menu and a little history. The new folks don't know how useful it is for marketing to be on line here and present themselves to the most active restaurant people in the area.   Hope giving them a Yelp page helps.

I read the few reviews while waiting for my Turkey and Swiss Hoagie to be served in the back room dining area. I admit to feeling some restaurant remorse imagining what I was about to get with a Snapple for my $9. (hair sandwich with attitude played in my head).   Instead, I received a very decent fresh soft Hoagie roll stuffed with my selections, including copious hot and sweet peppers, and a nice smile and "enjoy your lunch," from my server. I enjoyed the sandwich, and put the trepidation to rest. Nothing wrong with the meal. I am not in downtown Trenton that often these days, but I would certainly consider adding City Deli Hoagie Shop to the list of alternatives along Willow Street.

Before I was ready to write a review, I needed a refresher on the geography and history of Uzbekistan, the Central Asian nation surrounded by other "stans;" its cities of Tashkent, Samarkand and Bukara, some of the Pearls along the Silk Road from Istanbul to Xian, China, made famous by the epic journeys of Marco Polo.  I had visited Tashkent on business some years ago, and remembered it as very old and mysterious; full of mosques and museums - and especially, gem markets where trade in rare colored crystals and semi-precious stones, kept me excited, curious and negotiating for days at a time.    And, the food was equally excellent.  So, when we decided on impulse to have dinner at Chaikhana on Bustleton Avenue last weekend, it was with a sense of remembered delicacies and dinners that went on for hours into the wee hours of the morning; with too much local alcohol and toasts to everything under the sun and moon.  This was one of those friction points between two cultures, where each was influenced by the other.  Here it meant people who looked Asian, but spoke Russian and various dialects.  A place where Buddha was said to have travelled, and Islam flourished.    This shop is not typical Philly.  It announces itself loudly by occupying a large house fronting the busy Bustleton, and having a large enclosed patio in front, wrapped in plastic to maintain temperature, and lit by tiny white lights encased in miniature trees on each table.  No reservation was required this Sunday night, as we were seated on the end of a large table big enough for six.  This porch was occupied by a few large parties celebrating happiness, which naturally took a lot of attention to service well.  We still had enough of our gracious server's help to understand the menu with wise suggestions as to the dishes to mix without going overboard.  Her suggestions were right on, as each plate was loaded with enough for two people, and ordering as we would in another restaurant would have been overkill here.  We started with mushroom soup and bread.  One order was enough for both of us, and it was served in two bowls.  It had several fungal varieties in a rich and savor base stock.  Maybe a tad oily, but very flavorful and excellent.  The round loaf of bread was a very pleasant surprise.  It had a thick and chewy texture, and both a salty and sweet flavor.  It was amazing.  A smear of butter, or a sponging of the soup or gravies, made it the perfect complement for whatever was eaten.    Two apps were also shared.  The Cheburek, a deep fried folded over dough filled with spicy ground beef, potato, onions and a few mysteries, was richly textured, smooth and delicious. The other escapes me at the moment, but it was round, plump and baked. Loved it.  Our main entre was a chicken and lamb kabob, both of which were cooked to their apex of tenderness and flavor, with onion slices on the side.  They were both wonderful, and again, enough for us to share.  We ate well while those around us celebrated to the max.  It was fun to watch and listen.    We were full before dessert, although very tempted by the cherry Vareniki and honey cake.    There was plenty left unexplored on this visit.  But, like Marco Polo, many more trips to this part of Uzbekistan are anticipated.

Just ordered a 16 piece fried chicken bucket from Chicken Holiday on Olden Avenue Extension in Ewing, NJ. After calling it in, I drove there on my way home, and arrived just as it was coming out of the pressure fryer. It looked dark bronze and the odor of the steam being released went right to my head, and made me feel a bit intoxicated.   Nothing wrong with that!  I watched as the cook removed the chicken and transferred it to an aluminum tray for safe travel. I counted the pieces with him, and think my package carried 17 total. I appreciated the extra generosity. He then wrapped the tray in foil, and tore open the top dome to allow the condensation to escape. In turn, that was placed in a heavy gauge brown paper sack, and again split open at the top for additional moisture release.   By the time I arrived home, I was nearly overcome by the aroma enveloping the car. I decided to sample a wing while still hot and wait for the family before consuming more. First bite encountered crisp skin, followed by warm white meat and a pleasant clean oil fried chicken flavor. I nibbled and sucked all the meat from them bones, and I selfishly considered grabbing a plump breast for a long moment.   Nah! It would be more fun to indulge with the fam. So, I waited.   An hour later we were sitting around the kitchen table with sides of homemade mashed potatoes and green salad as excellent complementary pieces to a very happy meal.   A star is missing because truth be told, the chicken was a tad overdone. A lighter golden copper finish would have made it perfect. Turns out that as much as I love the color bronze, it is past prime when it comes to fried chicken excellence. Still very good texture and taste, but with a subtle aftertaste that missed the mark.   In fried chicken, even a seconds can make a big difference.

Part of the Pennsylvania Community College System, Bucks County Community College has three campuses. The largest is the 200 acre preserve in Newtown, sitting at the edge of Tyler State Park. The Tyler Mansion anchors the northern edge of the campus, and provides some administrative office space to the school, as well as a facility for the many catered events that take place there. The park and the manse offer the institution an expanse and historic dignity seldom found in our new public schools of higher education.   The tuition is approximately $10,000 per year, but most students qualify for some financial aid, bringing the average expense closer to $7,200. So, it is a good deal compared to double that cost for other state schools in the Commonwealth. Many of my son's friends start at BCCC and transfer to a four year college after graduation, thus saving money in the interim so they can more easily afford reaching a complete university education.   Recently, I drove over to the school to receive my two Covid vaccinations (Pfizer). Bucks Department of Health had transformed the student center into a large injection site. With online registration and email reminders, it was a convenient and efficient place to take care of this important community health care responsibility. The staff was professional and humane, with easy directions to proceed through the process. No long lines. Little fuss. No muss.   I was impressed with how smoothly everything went, and how well the school cooperated with the county government and the thousands people who chose to visit the school to take care of their important business.

I've had this Chase credit card since 1985.  When the new card arrived to replace the expiring one, I dutifully made the required call to activate it.  Little did I know I would be entering the Bizarro world of "Verification."  My call was transferred to a human being because their system did not recognize me.  I was told that they did not have my Social Security number, nor anything else in their records to identify me!   What?!  Thirty years in the system and suddenly I did not exist.  They had issued the card originally with some required information. They no longer had it.  They had sent me the renewal, but had no way for me to use it.  I had become a digital phantom.   My deduction was that my identity had been dumped or lost in a security breach, and now to be sure I was not one of the bad guys, I had to justify my existence.  How, you ask?  By going to a bricks and mortar bank branch and introducing myself to a bank officer with some backup credentials.    The story has a happy (if time wasting) ending.  I went into this branch today and met with one of their suits.  He was very nice and sat me down in his cubicle to review the facts and call the Chase verification center.  A five minute conversation ensued with an exchange of information with HQ, which resulted in my identity being accepted, and the card useable.    For the humorous professionalism demonstrated by SB (shall remain nameless), and his cutting through the BS and bringing my identity back online, I am a true fan of this gentleman and the bank branch he represents.

This old pre-Revolutionary War building has been well restored into an excellent interactive museum of the colonial period of New Jersey history. Given how poorly the other landmarks have fared in this capital city, the condition of this one is all the more remarkable and very worthy of a visit or two by history buffs.  It was built in 1758 to house British soldiers during the French & Indian War. Colonists objected to being required to quarter Redcoats in their homes, as even at that time tension was high between people who identified as Jerseyites more than English subjects and resented the control the King had over their lives. The colonial government built five of these barracks around the colony, although this one in Trenton is the only survivor.  There were Hessians and a few British officers housed here in December, 1776, when General Washington crossed the Delaware River on Christmas Day eve and surprised the enemy with an early morning cannon barrage and brief fighting, leading to a rapid collapse of any defense and the surrender of Colonel Rall and his 1,200 men. There was more fighting to be done the following week at the Second Battle of Trenton (Assunpink Creek Bridge) on January 2, 1777, and the Battle of Princeton on the 3rd, but this quick victory set the tone for the success to come, and convinced the Continental Army, Continental Congress and the American colonists that this insurrection could be won and that George Washington was the man to do it. The barracks became an army hospital thereafter, and it was here that army physicians conducted the first inoculations of small pox to protect the troops from the deadly pox. This was the first attempt at inoculations anywhere in the modern world. In more recent times, the buildings were reduced to what remains today to make way for Front Street to reach the New Jersey Statehouse. What we see now was privately owned for a time and used for housing, until purchased by a few revolutionary war memorial groups who wanted to preserve and protect it for posterity.  These days it is a surprisingly excellent museum of the revolutionary period, restored authentically to look like active soldiers living quarters, with workers/guides dressed in appropriate period costume. It is very easy to imagine what it was like to be alive in those days, and to participate in such important historic events  Take a tour and see how amazing it all is (and was)!

Thai Chef & Noodle Fusion is located on a dreary strip of Rt. 1 (Lincoln Highway) in Penndel.  The effort to bring new life is taking shape with a few new restaurants in a two block area.  This place is one of its anchors, and is a pioneer there over several years.    The shop has a casual air, much more laid back and cozy than it appears from outside.  The tables on one side are separated by privacy screens made up of thin branches and curtains.  The outer wall has carved wooden folding screens that can be opened to extend for more separation.  Nice touch.  The staff is friendly, informative and prompt.  This is primarily a Thai house, although the name and menu offer alternatives in Japanese and Chinese cuisine.  I join the other reviewers in skepticism that "fusion" is a reality as opposed to a marketing gimmick.  I have only tried the Thai dishes as the owners and chef are Thai, and they come by this style honestly - they live it.   I had a lunch special which is a combination of a choice of cup of soup, app, and entre.  I chose the Tum Yom Soup, Moon Dumplings, and Drunken Noodles with Chicken.  The soup had the strong taste of lemongrass and mild chili with ample slices of chicken and veggies.  I enjoyed it.  The Moon Dumplings were a pleasant surprise.  While small and lightly fried, they were loaded with ground mushrooms and possessed a nice earthy flavor, and absorbed the hot chili oil/sauce well.  The Drunken Noodles were very good, with the right ratio of broad noodles to veggies and chicken and a decent sauce.  It was a little bland so I asked for chili flakes to liven it up.  I was brought a shaker of finely ground orange pepper that was a perfect complement to the dish and brought it to the heat level I wanted.  Some joints don't have the right spice and offer only Sriracha, which, while hot, does not blend well and distribute evenly over most foods.  Thai Chef had what was needed.    I can't comment on the "fusion" aspects, but I was very satisfied with my Thai lunch here.  I know that I look forward to more visits, and that makes me a fan.  August 10, 2014 - I have had dinner here a couple of times recently.  If anything, the dinners are superior to the lunch deals.  Last night I sampled their "Jungle King" and "Cashew".  The names themselves were unique. Both were nice portions of fresh veggies, tofu, chicken, with a nice mix of spices, including ginger and a sweetish curry, and large cashews on one.  An order of House Fried Rice rounded out the meal, while leaving enough to take home for today's lunch.    The vibe continues to relax and encourage lingering.  The fact that the owners are Thai helps bring the authenticity home.

Folcroft Diner sits on Chester Pike (Rt. 13) in the northern panhandle of the borough by that name in Delaware County, PA. Before the interstate was completed, it and Rt.1 were the primary roads north and south between Philly and Baltimore. Driving it last Friday on the way back from UDel to Bucks County due to jammed traffic on Rt. I 95, was an historic tour of yesteryear America when roadside attractions were often the best part of a family car trip to the intended destination.   Cruising north with son after school was declared closed for classes for the remainder of the spring semester, it was natural to reflect on the drive with my parents between New York and Washington when I was a student in D.C. Felt like an unfortunate right of passage to be experiencing this due to the curse of COVID-19.   The diner was the perfect stage for a lunch stop to stretch and grab a quick bite of Americana. A cup of New England Clam Chowder and Petty Melt (medium, fries, slaw & pickle slices), were the way to go. Our booth was comfy, our server friendly and attentive, and the space around us sufficient to allow us to feel socially distanced. We considered whether restaurants would remain open for sit down business in the days and weeks ahead. If this was to be a last meal in the Age of COVID-19, then we would soberly celebrate the moment and pray our angels protected us.   The chowder was thick creamy and loaded with diced clam. The cup was very filling and more than enough for a sample. The burger was a half pounder, finished as desired, bracketed by quality rye toast, melted Swiss and filled with sauteed onions and mushrooms. A long red squirt of Heinz Ketchup and I had a fun, satisfying meal. I could only down half, and took the rest home. Prices were surprisingly reasonable for the quality and quality of the plates served, almost like the menu was printed in the last century.   Maybe it was.

Al's Airport Inn has come a long way from its dive bar existence in the last quarter of the 20th Century. What was once a place only lone drinkers and cheaters could love, it has moved more uptown into a comfortable local bar with a pretty good kitchen. Son and I dropped in last night for dinner, and were duly impressed.   We ordered Al's wings and two burgers, along with draft Miller Lites (There isn't much in the way of crafties here). The wings were very good, and justify their reputation. Crisp, meaty, and spicy without being volcanic. At 10 for $10, reasonably priced. Happy hour provides a $2 discount. The burgers were freshly ground and shaped in house. Although we requested medium finish, they were both well done. That could be because the chef was doubling as a waiter and not attentive enough at the grill. Still, with a little more seasoning they could have been very good. Superior brioche style bun held together to the end.   Al's accepts credit cards now, which is a big deal in opening their market to more of the public. It did appear that they didn't have much experience with them, as the original bill was not returned with the credit card invoice for signing, making it impossible to compare for accuracy. Better practice to do so.   Overall, Al's is vastly improved over its past life. Haunted or not, it is no longer a dive bar, and is a nice place to hang out.  3.5 STARS

Sofra is a Turkish café on Bristol Pike in Levittown, Pa.  It doesn't look like much from the outside, with small stature in a rather unattractive part of Bucks County, but grab some courage and go inside.  Within, you will find a small dining room, with open floor space for entertainment.  Most important, the chef knows a thing or two about Istanbul cuisine.    Our Saturday jaunt to a commercial area nearby resulted in us stopping in to check out what was going on here.  We were greeted by a gentlemen I took to be an owner, owing to his general lack of social grace. Why else would he be handling guests?  Still, we sat to one side and were brought menus and cold water.  I am no maven when it comes to Turkish kitchens, but Middle Eastern chow I know something about from time spent in the eastern Mediterranean.    I was looking for lamb gyro as an introduction to the skill here, but it was not available for lunch.  So, I looked further and found Shepherd's Salad, Falafel and Grilled Lamb in Pita Sandwich as attractive alternatives.  All arrived about ten minutes later in the hands of our erstwhile host.  The Salad was a plentiful pile of Tomato, Cucumber, Black Olive, Red Onion and a nice Olive Oil based herbed dressing.  Very refreshing. The Falafel Plate was 5 nice sized balls of ground chickpea and herbs, deep fried to a medium brown finish, with a stainless bowl of Tahini Sauce in the middle.  Wedge Tomato and Lettuce garnish.  Liked it!  Finally, the Grilled Lamb wrapped tightly in pita and again in paper, was excellent, with a rich BBQ-like flavor and more lettuce, onion and a wonderful savory taste.  Star of the show.   We weren't asked if we wanted dessert or Turkish coffee (we did), but were handed the check as soon as we finished eating our mains.  I guess we weren't on the guest list, even being the only customers in the house.    Too bad, because Sofra has potential.

It has been a long while since I last visited an old world Wawa convenience store - the ones without gas stations attached. They are so busy building the latest version that when I walked in for a snack and coffee I thought I was in a Seven Eleven. It was that disconcerting.   Still, it had the snacks and it had plenty of coffee, so I got what I came for. Although, I regretted it later when the food purchased (1/4 Lb beef hot dog) was so processed that I suffered with heartburn all night long. Won't be looking for that again. The coffee was fine.   I don't actually use the gas pumps at Wawa, as they don't identify the refiner, nor distributor of the fuel, and thus there is no assurance of the quality of the gasoline, nor the additives that may/may not have been added. That being so, I would go to this chain more often if I didn't have to deal with the gas station aspect of the operation.   On the other hand, assure me of the content of the gas and list it's pedigree, and I would be more willing to take advantage of the convenience once in a while, especially when away from my local friendly businessman and neighbor traditional gas station.

Eleven of us showed up at 10:30 for a Dim Sum experience in Philadelphia Chinatown last Saturday.  I had selected Ocean City Restaurant on the north end of 9th Street from Yelp reviews.  A little out of the way. A lot more available tables than other similar banquet halls closer to the center of CTown.   We were met near the front door by the owner/manager, who at first thought there were only two of us.  He was gracious, even knowing we could not eat enough to make his day.  Then, we explained there were actually nine more right behind us.  His face registered the glint of happy surprise as he swiveled and pointed to the large round table in the front corner with exactly eleven chairs around it.  Now, he was very happy, and walked with us and set up the lazy Susan in the middle of the table as we all gathered 'round.  Maybe, we would help his bottom line.    Indeed, we did.  As the cart ladies approached, the titular hostess of this feast arose and began to order for everyone.  Nothing random here.  She pointed and placed, requested and demanded, served and bussed, and made sure everyone had an equal amount of every dish desired.  Truly, an amazing display of taking charge, and improving the experience.  She has a future in the hosting business.    If you check the photos, you will see that we sampled a large amount of what Ocean City had to offer.  Everything was good to exceptional for dim sum.  Special mention to the Minced Pork Congee, Tofu Skin with Veggies, and the Seafood Dumplings.  Tasty and fun.  We didn't try everything, but enjoyed what we had, with even the rookies fully engaged.  We left enough on the menu for another visit.    It always surprises me how much food you get at a dim sum, and for what a fair price.  Eleven of us (9 adults), gorged for under $150, and even brought a few things home.    Ocean City is a traditional seafood house that does a splendid Hong Kong style 'small plates'.  Can't speak to the regular menu, but they do dim sum the old fashioned way. Full floor show. Totally satisfied.  Keep it coming!

A few years ago I noticed that Mill Street, Bristol, PA, was experiencing a rebirth of vital commerce with many new stores, restaurants, cafes and even a classy bakery with a beautiful dining room and sugar coma inducing display of cookies, cakes, danish and donuts. That shop, Angelina's, was the subject of my breakfast explorations last week.   First impressions were tremendous. Everything was whitewashed and had a Victoriana vibe. There were a dozen or so tables, and counter/highchairs in the two window bays on either side of the front door. Further back, the baked goods sat shelved and lit like colorful jewels and crystals waiting to be bagged and consumed. So seductive.   I sat close by the front and checked the front of the two sided breakfast/lunch menu. I went with the "Thin French Toast," over the "Thick" alternative. I figured I was in a bakery, and it had to know about the proper approach to this traditional dish. Well, perhaps I was overconfident about that.   The first clue of what was to come was the delivery of the FT accessories - butter and Smuckers syrup. The spread was fine, but that amber colloidal suspension was all high fructose corn syrup, about the worst thing for a human body. Luckily when the plate arrived, the four pieces of bread were sprinkled with powdered sugar, so I could skip the drip. Regular sugar is a better choice than artificial or high fructose sweetener.  When the finished platter arrived it looked good. I spread the butter to melt on the surface and cut a small wedge. It was obvious that it had spent little time in the egg/sugar/cinnamon/vanilla extract mix. The outside was nicely grilled, but the inside was dry. It had not been dredged in the mixing bowl long enough to permit absorption, but put too quickly on the grill. The chef needs find a better recipe.   Oh, well. This wasn't going to be my best morning. *%It happens.   I'll be back to check out those georgeous pastries. I suspect that is where I should have begun this adventure.

It may not have the shelf space of the large Asian Markets in Flushing, nor the mystique of my favorite subterranean shop in Philly, but H Mart is only ten minutes from home and provides me with most of the Asian specialties I would otherwise get stuck on the Verrazano Bridge to reach, or be forced to pay ten bucks to park in Center City.    Returned last night to pick up Chinese Eggplant, Ginger Root, Assorted Frozen Dumplings, Hot Dumpling Sauce, Crispy Chili in Oil, and a big can of Wasabi Sweet Peas (Thailand), for meals and snacks over the next few weeks; while checking out the fresh fish, and other exotics, like an anthropologist enjoying a stroll through a museum.    I have yet to take a seat in the little café to taste what's going on there, but until I do, the rest of the store suits my needs perfectly.

The Olde Worlde Bakerye & Café has 30 foot ceilings and suggests an old villa in Tuscany, with faux stone and large bread racks showing their attractive wares.  It does seem a little out of place sitting on Smithville Road in Eastampton, NJ, but that does not detract from its pleasant scale.  Outdoor patio seating for nice days is a definite upgrade from the ordinary java joint.    I stopped in around 10 am for a light breakfast and coffee.  The large menu is suspended from the ceiling behind the cashiers.  Only brekkie sandwiches are available during the week, although a full brunch operation happens on weekends.  No sweat.  I wasn't looking or a big and hearty meal.  The unmistakable aroma of baked bread permeated the room, although they were not baking anything when I was there. The racks behind the counter were loaded to make a bread lover swoon.  All shapes and sizes demonstrated the artistry of the baker. Impressive.  My Sausage, Egg & Cheese on a Roll was okay, but not more. Their bread was fresh, but lacked the texture and yeastiness I expected from a homemade offering. The sausage patty was about the thinnest I have encountered, but still tasty.  The fried eggs and cheese were ample, and clearly cooked/melted on the grill.  At under $6 for the whole shebang I was ultimately satisfied with the value, if not the exuberance of the sandwich.   Maybe their brunches have more of a "Wow!" factor.

Smith's Ace Hardware is an extension of Yardville Supply, a serious regional provider of all home improvement merchandise, geared for the professional contractor set more than the general public. Their Ace ventures attempt to overcome that marketing disadvantage by fitting a niche between big box highway warehouses and mom & pop corner retail hardware shops.   In Newtown, they compete with the historic Newtown Hardware on State Street in the Borough, which has been in business for over one hundred years. So, the disparity between shopping old and shopping new could not be greater. Ace is larger and has superior inventory as a result, but lacks the community roots and hands on experience of the museum-like NHH. They don't really compete on price, because they are both more expensive than the big boxes.   So, whether you want to buy self piercing screws or replacement screens to patch the originals on your back porch, depends on your feeling about local vs. corporate enterprise. You wouldn't go to either if price was your primary focus, as Home Depot and Lowes are both cheaper. But, if keeping local businesses afloat is important to you, the choice is a closer call. This Ace is owned by a Jersey company and is limited to a small region in NJ and PA. It provides local jobs to help the economy. Yet, if you like a dose of true history when you are looking for small pieces to complete a home project, and love to rummage through old wooden drawers full of nails, screws, and electrical parts, Newtown Hardware has you covered.   The choice is yours.

Maybe if I hadn't just returned from a trip to southern Virginia where BBQ is a daily part of existence, I would have been more overcome with smoke ring lust for the meat factory that is Sweet Lucy's Smokehouse, but it was that travel into the near South that had me wanting more Q, and Lucy's was getting all the local accolades. It was the natural place to go.    The adaptive reuse of an old industrial brick and mortar was well done, and the layout of the plant was well conceived with nice "country" dining area, new bar with very good brew list, and an efficient order and table delivery system.  Yet, their efficiencies cut some corners that should have been left in place.    As first timers not knowing the lay of the land, the order and sit down process had to be explained, and the ability to have Q & A with someone about the menu important.  That was not really provided with pressure on the cashier to take orders as people stood before them and then accept payment.  It was hard to ask about the various options and receive comprehensive answers.  We ordered the BBQ Pulled Pork Platter, Half Rotisserie Chicken Platter and the Double the Fun (Ribs & Pulled Pork) Platter; all with Cornbread and a cross section of the many side dishes.  The prices were reasonable, and the wait not too long.  Going over to the bar in the dining room was easy enough, but required a second payment.  Unless you knew you would have room for desert and ordered with the entre, another queue-up was required.  Easier for the business, perhaps, but not for the customer.    Then, everything arrived in styro and plastic wrap - a turnoff for both comfort and ecological reasons.  Open your white foam package with someone sitting across from you, and the top of each was overlapping and in the way of the other.  Awkward.    There was plenty of meat and ample sides.  Yet, rather than using a confident dry rub in the smoker that would let the meat speak for itself, and allow a choice of saucy finishes, the plate arrived already covered in Kansas City style thick and somewhat salty/sour dark amber glaze. This one size fits all approach denied a choice of flavors that is so elemental to the full BBQ experience.  Personally, I prefer a sweet/tangy bite and chew that comes from a St. Louis, Memphis or even Carolina smokehouse, but there were no table rockets with these options, and I was unaware of any sauce alternatives as a newbie.  My Ribs were smoked well with pink ring, and it easily pulled off the bone.  Still, I would have been happier with a different sauce encasing the experience.  The Pulled Pork was soft and pleasantly chewy, but had a vinegar taste that was not my cup of tea.  Again, allow me to mix in what my tastebuds prefer, and I would have been a happier camper.    The sides were all pretty good without any of them being standouts.  On the other hand, the Cornbread was excellent.    Given the great beer choices and the generous portions, this could have been a full fledged BBQ riot with the ability to elect how I wanted the meal to cross my palette. I would gladly pay a bit more, or gorge a bit less, if given free choice (and be pleased with the meal arriving on a large swatch of paper rather than plastic).   So near, but yet so far.

Eagle Diner on Street Road, Warminster, PA, is a traditional Greek food emporium with broad multi-page menu covering all three meals, plus a significant salad bar. It is open 24/7.  The only thing missing is a counter with stools for those who prefer that old line dining experience, like me.   I stopped in for diner last weekend, hoping for a good meal for this solitary traveler. I had to wait about 15 minutes for a table, as the place was SRO when I arrived around 6 pm. A stool at a counter would have eliminated the wait, but I did not mind standing in the entrance area and observing all the scurry from the staff. It also gave me the chance to check out the cakes, pies and other bakery goods made on premises. Certainly did not hurt my appetite.   I was eventually shown to a table in the back, and handed the short novelette menu. So much food; so little time. I chose their meatloaf mini dinner, with mashed and cup of soup or salad bar. I grazed over the greens for a while and returned with a full plate of various salad components. It wasn't a stunningly broad spread, and a lot of it was processed and not fresh, but it still provided many colors and flavors that worked well on top of a lettuce base. Three bean salad, beets, red onion, macaroni and potato salad, baby spinach, pickled everything, cheesebread and 1,000 Island dressing, kept me munching while waiting for the mains.   When my entre arrived, I was confronted by two huge slices of baked/grilled beef loaf and a dish of white mashed, with brown gravy on the side. The meat was tender and tasty, but better with a jet of ketchup, than the brown sauce (a bit salty). The slices were about 1.5 inches thick. I couldn't finish the meal. Absolutely no room for the luscious looking desserts.  At a price around $10., the value was evident in every bite.   I'm told Eagle does a good job for breakfast, too. Next time I'm in the area that time of day, I'll stop in again to check it out.

If you remember your childhood ice cream experiences with wistful images of hanging out at the old shack where the sweetest, creamiest, drippiest, crispest cone crunch, brought the timeless taste of the best childhood memories dancing back to your tongue, then Jo-Jo's is your magic carpet ride. Homemade 'scream so potent and cooly fresh, that a single lick transports you to that first moment you tasted these awesome American flavors of life.   This 1950's summer pleasuredome is a full monty.  The whitewashed walls, the elbow lighting, the sliding windows for orders and pick up.  The young faces of high school kids with their first summer jobs.  The old, wizened eyes of the master ice cream maker; watching intently as the next generation of innocence both inside the shop and outside on the winding line, take their turn on the carousel.  The pristine ecstasy of your child's first taste; a drippy spot on her nose.    All this happens effortlessly at Jo-Jo's.  So glad I found it.   My Peanut Butter Vanilla and Salted Caramel Pretzel scoops were as good as I have eaten anywhere.  Richness in flavor, texture and human interaction. My tastebuds rejoiced.  I sat with my cup of joy and watched as everyone else "kvelled" with this luscious pleasure.    How great to be there on a warm mid-March evening, before the crowds of summer demand delayed gratification, and I can be the first on line.    Simple.  Sweet Life.

Riverfront Market is a glorified food court housed in a redeveloped brick and beam warehouse on the banks of the Christina River in Wilmington, DE. It was built under the auspices of the state funded Riverfront Development Corporation in the late 1990s. It is an interesting destination in a part of town that was weed filled lots and dilapidated buildings prior to the large investment of taxpayer funds. It is much better to reestablish a functional, economically viable commercial center than to leave it forgotten and abandoned.   The mix of dining choices comes from all locally owned food outlets of varying ethnicity, including, Mexican, Thai, Italian, cheesesteak and Korean green grocer. New kitchens are taking the place of those that have not survived. With hours from 6 to 6, it is primarily a lunch choice, with only the Mexican place open for business when I arrived at 4 on a Friday. The rest were already locked down, or being cleaned and straighten in preparation for the next day.   The building is historically attractive, a pleasant place to walk around or sit at the many tables around the retail space or the second story open balconies. I was the only customer in the house and had time to explore before and after eating my tacos carnitas. It was disappointing that they were unable to sustain their businesses the entire day, but the market has made it this far (with possible subsidies), and the city and state should assure that it can continue to attract people to this part of town.

Down at the bottom of Walton Road, Warwick Township, Bucks County, PA, lies perhaps the most enchanted spot in all of Pennsylvania. Ross Mill Farm has been a secret haven since originally started before the Revolutionary War in 1740.   The lane is narrow and full of dips and rough riding, but so very worth the effort to find, especially if you love adaptive reuse of an historic property turned into a rescue home and boarding facility exclusively for Vietnamese Pot Belly Pigs.   180+ residents live there now, either from broken homes or as paying customers, housed there because it is simply the best place on the planet for happy, healthy PBPs. The 30 acres are idyllic for humans, too, but the facilities are designed by the owner from the perspective of an intelligent animal that stands little more that 18 inches from the ground. To truly interact with the residents you really have to get down on your knees, because these cuties lack the ability to look up at you. So, the world is very short, but expansive at Ross Mill Farm. The green lawns and gardens are perfectly suited for a pig.   And, for people who love them.   This amazing patch of heaven on the Little Neshaminy Creek is as magic as you want it to be. I found it easy to get lost in the peaceful magic of the moment. Make a donation and help it last forever.

Hate to admit that after many years of attending court in the same complex, that I never noticed Sal's Pizzeria before this week.  So, after an afternoon session, and hungry from skipping lunch, I drove around to the front of this oldish commercial strip center and spied this TPie shop.    Upon entry, I was struck by the orange and yellow walls in the surprising large restaurant.  Although dated, it had a wholesome ambiance conducive to an Italian meal.  Given the hour, I went with a single slice of Traditional Pizza with Sweet Sausage, and a drink.    Good choice, as the slice was larger than average.  I asked for it "well done," and that was what I received.  Upon lifting off the large attractively orange plate, I was immediately impressed that despite its size and extra weight from the topside, the point held firm and high with nary a quiver.  First bite was a full blown crunch through cheese, sauce and meat; all of which were received warmly with pleasure in my mouth.  It was a very good slice of pizza, despite being reheated.    With this lunch coming in under $5. I was very satisfied with the experience, and will not be a stranger to Sal's.  The rest of the menu listed the usual suspects.  If done as well as their pies, I will become a regular customer when in Mt. Holly.

Golden Dragon at the corner of Liberty & Franklin, Trenton, NJ., looks like a new entry in the Chinese Take Out Wars.  The shop is cleaner than many, with room for four tables for those who prefer to eat in (like me).  The young family that runs the show seem to know what they're doing, with the wife at the counter taking orders and money, and hubby wok and rolling in the kitchen.  The third wheel, perhaps a brother, helps out and does deliveries.    The lunch specials are the standard pork, chicken and shrimp in a variety of overlapping goopy sauces.  The fried rice is made in one large batch and has the yellow dye of most other chicken broth based steamers.  Unlike many of the other houses, this one is full of chunks of pork, peas, onion and carrots.  It actually tasted good.  My Pork Egg Foo Young was two pancakes, crisped edges, and loaded with meat, veggies and spouts.  The brown sauce was decent and packaged separately to keep things firm and able to be used at will.  It was a decent version of this old time dish.    Service was as limited as you would expect a basic take away store to be.  No accommodation for customers wanting to eat at a table.  Everything packaged in styro and plastic, with thin fork and spoon to handle the mouth shovels.   Still, at under $6., with soup or soda, it was a good deal.     Nice quality for a take out joint, even if they don't really want you eating there.  Offer hot tea in addition to soda, and put the food on a real plate with better plasticware for those who eat in, and Golden Dragon could easily be a four star experience in take out cuisine.  UPDATE: MAY 3, 2017 -  Have to say that my second visit to Golden Dragon has put me in a generous mood about the quality of their food. Today I sampled their Hot & Sour Soup and General Tso's Chicken.    The soup was surprisingly good.  It contained fresh cut mushrooms floating on top, and two types of soft tofu beneath.  The vinegar quotient was just right, and with the other veggies within, was about the best Chinese take out hot & sour I can remember tasting. Sucked all of that plastic container's contents dry.  The Chicken was also mostly meat and less shell, with a nicely balance spicy/sweet dark brown topaz sauce. The fried rice was plentiful, and although mass produced, still granular and full of pork, pea, carrot, etc. chunks.    Overall, an impressive lunch from this far flung outpost of the Chinese Empire at the corner of Franklin and Liberty.    Do it again, and you could find yourself the recipient of a full forth star.  But, for now...  3.5 Stars, with a bullet!

Just the fact that there is a local place that does Southern style cuisine in the area means Southern Comforts will be a success as long as they don't screw up this opportunity. Stick to traditional recipes, offer generous helpings and keep price within reason, and it will take off once Covid restrictions are in the rearview.   If my first exposure to their kitchen is any indication, they are on their way. They need to open their dining room to customers, and the rest is baked in. We ordered their "Make Your Own" dinners of 1) Country Fried Steak, roasted carrots & baked beans, and 2) Crab Cakes, bread stuffing, gravy and candied yams; with slice of carrot cake as shared dessert. It was all pretty darned good, except for the carrot cake. Allow me to elaborate.   The fried steak was a thin prefab ground patty, nicely fried and drowned in that white gravy. Nice texture and taste, with the gravy not too heavy on the tongue. The sides were a well made complement. Same with the crab cake. Crisp edges with crumbly crab with a little breading to bind them together, but with a dominant crustacean taste. We didn't use those little packages or tartar sauce, as there was enough flavor without them. The yams were sweet, but the bread stuffing was a bit dry and was not resuscitated by the gravy. Yet skipping the stuffing left a still very enjoyable meal.   Word to the wise - Don't over sell a dessert that is past its prime. I was asked if I wanted dessert, and since it was brought to my attention, allowed myself to be upsold because I do love carrot cake as a general proposition. This wayward slice was the exception that proved the rule. It was smallish,  without much cake nor cream cheese icing. It was also noticeably dried out from too much shelf time. Definitely not the place to end a successful meal. It just wasn't worth the calories nor sugar kick. I don't mind being upsold when the product is worthwhile, but when it is a disappointment, it is self defeating.   Almost lost me there, but decided the rest of the meal was good enough to warrant partially overlooking that mistake.   3.5 STARS

Liv & Charlie Real Food on North Union Street, Lambertville, NJ, is a morning/afternoon shop serving healthy and tasty meals on treadle tabletops in this beautiful river city. The people are friendly and confident in the quality of their menu.  I stopped in last week for breakfast and totally enjoyed the experience. Their french toast made with fresh challah was excellent. The egg/vanilla/sugar/cinnamon mix soaked in well and the hot grill caramelized the edges just right. Most important, the house used pure maple syrup and cold butter to allow me to doctor the slices the way I like best. I sipped my strong coffee (with fresh whole milk) as the beurre melted and the syrup eddied and swirled on the plate.   It was delicious. I kept cutting the toast into smaller pieces to maximize absorbency and stretch out the pleasure.   It was a quiet morning with only one other table occupied. The music track was alternative rock that suited the atmosphere of the house.   Liv & Charlie know what they are doing.   5 Stars all the way!

Great pleasant surprise when I drove over to Penn Medicine's offices on Township Line Road in Lower Makefield, PA, for an x-ray and found Nick Roast Beef's food truck in their parking lot. It was already 1:30 and I hadn't had lunch. I knew I would be over as soon as I was finished with radiology. The fates continued to smile when the lab time put me back on the street in less than half an hour and Nick's was still there and open for business.   I walked over to their window and was met by the lovely, friendly server, who smiled for a photo before taking my roast pork sandwich order. Her assistant worked the grill and constructed my lunch with a pile of hot pork on a kaiser roll. It was handed to me in a paper boat with small tubs of pickled jalapeno slices and white horseradish. Napkins and other necessities were on the side table to the left; drinks in two portable coolers on the ground to the right.   I drove home and demolished the porker at my kitchen table. It was a thick, juicy mother. All pale tender thin moist sliced roaster, without a lick of fat nor dryness. It was awesome, although the roll was a few minutes past prime. The peppers and radish brought up the burn to a warm wet kiss all the way down.   I hope this is a regular stop for Nick's truck, because I could become a faithful customer.

Barry's Buns is another small shop in the Markets at Wayfare on Germantown Avenue, Chestnut Hill. They do all manner of bakery sweets that go well with coffee for breakfast, or any other time of day when you desire a tasty sugar fix.   When I was there on Saturday afternoon the market was packed with beer drinkers both inside and out. Perhaps because of that Barry's inventory was pretty much threadbare. All I saw were a few chunks of Crumb Cake, Jewish Apple Cake, and somethings that looked like fruit topped cupcakes. The woman working the counter was friendly and answered my questions about what was left and smoothly packed up my order of two Crumb Cakes into a white paper bag.   My sense was that as soon as her meagre stock was gone, so was she. If she had been willing to sell that apple cake by the wedge, rather than requiring the whole kubboodle go at once, I would have been happy to grab a handful. I love Jewish Apple Cake, but I didn't want the temptation of bringing it home in my car. I couldn't trust myself not to dive in and fist large handfuls into my mouth like the 8 year old kid lurking within would do.   I did more calmly sample a piece of the Crumb Cake on the way after stopping at Poppy's Cafe for hot coffee to wash it down. It was excellent - still moist, soft, sweet, with clumped brown sugar/cinnamon/butter embedded within like a happy toy in a Cracker Jack box.
