Clearly have to come here earlier in the day to have the most choice.

My son and I were looking for a light dinner and decided to try Greenstraw Smoothies on Sycamore Street, the main drag in Newtown, Bucks County.  It is a new place on the nicely redeveloped commercial district.    The menu consists of a long list of healthy drinks with fresh fruits and veggies, along with nutritional supplements to suit your particular need - Maca, Hemp protein, Flax Seed, Chia, Spirulina, Wheatgrass Juice, etc.  The foundation of the smoothies are cow milk alternatives like Almond or Coconut Milk, Yogurt, and Fruit Juices.  The combinations are surprisingly refreshing and tasty.    I ordered a Leo's Favorite, consisting of Almond Milk, Apple Juice, Banana, Peanut Butter, Strawberries, Raspberries, and Greens.  The resultant reddish blend was thick and smooth, but simply sucked through a straw (Yes. It was green). It was a pleasure to imbibe.  My son had The Mango Tree, with Coconut Milk, Mango Juice, Banana, Mango Pieces, Pineapple, and Greens.  The mix came out a ruddy greenish mash that was also quite good.  We both smiled on first drought, and sampled each others drinks.    I was definitely satisfied with my liquid dinner and was not hungry again last night. Young man needed a bit more sustenance after finishing his homework.    This is definitely a worthy spot for a healthy drink.  The prices are reasonable at $5.75 for the middle sized concoction, which was quite filling.   There is also fair trade coffee available, but that will wait for another day.   Good luck, Greenstraw.

We had a great La Villa Traditional Square Pizza here last week. I had forgotten how delicious their pies were. It was loaded with peppers, onions, mushrooms and sausage, and baked to a wonderful crispy crust(see photo). Service was also friendly and prompt. The black clad servers certainly kept a certain 21 year old family member entertained.   However, the app special Crab Cake was drenched in a cheesy white sauce that overwhelmed the titular star of the show to such an extent that the crabbiness of the crustacean was lost.  The big Greek Salad while plentiful lacked imagination and an impressive dressing.  I would not ask for either of those again.   But, in the end it is all about the pie.  La Villa's are vastly superior to any of its nearby competitors, and can stand their own with some of the best across the river in Jersey or Philly.   Happily, it is much closer in Morrisville, in a nicely appointed renovated Pizza Hut structure in the middle of a strip mall parking field off Pennsylvania Avenue.

I can't speak to the authenticity of their German cuisine, because I was just there for breakfast, but I certainly enjoyed what I had for my morning meal.   Sitting at the bar under the huge head of a taxidermy moose, with large steins high on a shelf, I was surprised by the extensive breakfast menu.  Tracy, the manager/server in the barroom, was cordial, but gave me time and space to decide what to eat, after bringing me a mug of coffee and side cordial glass of milk. Nice touch!   I went with their, "Mini Vacation in Paris." You guessed it - a short stack of french toast with two extra plump pork sausages. After doctoring everything with butter and Smucker's syrup, I went to work. It was all pretty good, with good flavor packed into the two slices of white, and extra pleasant taste emanating from the bangers. It would have been even better with maple syrup, but at a price under $8 for everything, I am not complaining.    Coffee was refilled without asking, and I was even given the TV remote to watch whatever I chose on the corner monitor. That was a first, and even though I preferred to catch up on my reading, I appreciated the generous offer.   If I find myself out that way again, I would def stop in to discover more of the morning possibilities. I bet Tracy has some stories to tell.

I've driven around the block on various occasions trying for a parking spot within hailing distance of Trenton Bagel Shop on South Broad Street in Trenton, just one block south of State Street.  Never found one and thus was never able to walk into the shop until last Friday when I was at the NJ Motor Vehicle Commission over on Stockton Street.  After our appeals hearing was over (successfully), I decided this was the best chance to get over there.  It was about a quarter mile away, but it was a nice day for a walk.   The store was larger than expected, with a big kitchen area and several tables around the perimeter.  The bagel selection was depleted at 10:30, but I ordered an Everything Bagel, Butter and Swiss and Java from the pleasant women behind the counter.  The $3.50 price for all this was a pleasant surprise.  Left the balance of my fin in the tip jar.    On first bite it was obvious that my bagel was no longer fresh from the oven, and had been around at least since early in the morning.  It wasn't bad, it just wasn't at its apex texture and taste.  Looking toward the rear of the space I tried to find evidence of baking on premises, but could neither see, hear nor smell anything like hot dough in the air.  Could well be that the bagels were created elsewhere and delivered.  Not a problem when the bread is fresh, but tends to staleness before a round hole baked only a few feet away.    The coffee was that "Law" company product.  Not the best brew for take out as it drifts into bitterness as it cools.    Glad I finally checked out Trenton Bagel, but given the difficulty of approaching the shop via auto, and the step below first quality of both its namesake and the Joe, there is no urge to return anytime soon.

I now know the downside of having a pizza parlor make pies for display purposes.  If you are unfortunate enough to come in for a late pizza slice lunch, you end up eating old pizza from the display, rather than anything remotely fresh.    I learned this lesson the hard way a few days ago, when I stopped in after 2:30 for a small repast to tide me over until dinner.  My Tomato Pie was sauce without cheese (In my world it is sauce over cheese). It was okay, but basically too acidic from sitting around for many hours.  Too, the plain slice while large, had an overworked crust that proved tough and chewy rather than crisp as a cracker.  Time had not been kind to it.  I liked the gentleman who prepared my slices in the oven and brought them to the table, and it was not his responsibility to make a new pie for me.  Still, there outta be a rule that says display pizzas are dumped after being out in the open for more than 2 or 3 hours, so they are not reheated beyond human tolerances.

If you enjoy narrow gauge vertical lift truss bridges from the early part of the 20th Century, the Burlington-Bristol Bridge is for you.  I cross it several times a month on my way to Mt. Holly, NJ from Bucks County, Pa, but I keep both hands on the wheel to be able to drive in the single lane across the Delaware River, and can't "check in" often on Yelp.  Take my word for this.    While true that the drive is challenging, it is also somewhat exhilarating.  From the apex the view up and down the Mighty Delaware is large. The waterfronts of historic Bristol and Burlington are in full sight.  Burlington Island to the north sits midstream with the ruins of a 19th Century amusement park slumbering in the shade, its once proud roller coaster a skeleton after a fire destroyed the park.  To the south the rust of other Industrial Age factories likewise lie in ruin, or continue to operate and belch waste out of decayed smokestacks.    The engineering involved in the design of the lift mechanisms was invented by the Romans, but is still the height of expertise two thousand years later.  Watching the megaton slabs of concrete lower from the twin towers, and cause the lift of the central roadway with pulleys and cable, is also an amazement.  If I wasn't in such a rush to get to court I might really marvel at this human feat.  As it is, it is a very cool way to be delayed by forces beyond my control.    If time is not an insurmountable issue, there are great places in both towns that gave their names to this span, where meal and drink can be secured in its very shadow.

Pretty much a standard Pennsylvania roadside diner down on Street Road, Bensalem. It is well maintained, has friendly professional staff, large menu and reasonable prices.   I stopped in for breakfast recently, and sat on a stool at the traditional counter. Coffee was immediately available from the Bunn-O-Matic, and my request for milk over creamer was met with a small glass of moo juice. The daily special omelette was described well, and server and I agreed quietly that ham, bacon and sausage was just too much meat for three eggs to handle. Opted instead for short stack french toast and java only. Lately, it seems I am not as hungry in the morning, which helps explain the increased bagginess of my pants.   The thick white load was good with adequate saturation of the egg/vanilla/sugar mix into the heart of both slices. The soft butter and Smuckers table syrup finished off the plate. It was all grilled well, but providing a pour of pure Grade B maple would have been so much more satisfying. I would pay a buck or two extra for that sweet smokiness soaked into my bread. The cuppa joe was decent and refilled frequently.   I departed $10 the poorer, including gratuity. Not bad for this part of Street Road, right down the street from Parx Casino.

As part of my discovery of the western burbs around Philly now that I find myself on the turnpike twice a month, I stopped in at Pho Thai Nam last weekend.   The space is brightly decorated from top to bottom.  This must be how a marriage between Thai and Vietnamese looks.  Glistening stars against a black night sky, and warm sunset tones from wall to wall.  Very attractive.  The only issue I have comes from their apparent success.  The place is excessively loud, making normal conversation across the table difficult.    But, who talks while slurping Pho?  I ordered the Steak and Brisket Pho (Pho Tai Chin), and it arrived promptly, a steaming large bowl of Beef Broth, Noodles, lots of thin sliced Beef, with a nice plate of Thai Basil, Bamboo Shoots, Jalapeno Slices, Lime Wedges, with Hoisin and Sriracha on the side to add zest where needed.    It was very good - rich, savory, subtle undertones and long untamed noodles waiting to uncoil like a nest of vipers.  I enjoyed every slurping spoonful and chopstick clasp of it.  The only reservation would be he $9.95 cost, which is a couple of bucks more than other places I frequent.  I guess you pay for the popularity, because the place was crowded.    While I wouldn't rush back to Pho Thai Nam as it was no better than similar places closer to home, and there are other highly recommended joints nearby, I certainly would not hesitate to return should someone desire the experience.

A mall is a mall is a mall.  While this is closest to home, I generally find malls to be sterile barns.  But, for the associated AMC theaters across the parking fields, a few restaurants in the circle around it, and many medical offices, I would likely never frequent the place.   It seems that malls are a 20th Century phenomenon whose time may have passed them by, unless they are reconceptualized and reconfigured to meet the more dynamic needs of families, and consumers.  A sense of community purpose is required that is both traditional and state of the art.   Until that happens most malls will continue to lose stores and visitors. Just as the horse and buggy were replaced by the automobile, and the urban core was redistributed to the burbs (and now contracting again), the mall will eventually evolve into a new kind of commercial center than includes everything the old village maintained, but wired into today.

Corner joint on Brownsville Road, Trevose, Pa., Peppe's Mexican Grill is a family run kitchen turning out good South of the Border plates. Owners appear bilingual, adding a splash of interest and authenticity to a shop that is full of local schoolgirls behind the counter.   The menu is small compared to the casas Latinas in the Hispanic community in Trenton where I normally indulge my love for this cuisine, but what they do, they do well. Our burritos (chicken & shrimp) were stuffed to the max, and the two young guys devouring them barely came up for air. My flautas de carnitas were nicely rolled, stuffed and grilled tortillas full of roast pork, chilies, cheese, with bright red salsa, avocado, shredded lettuce and drizzled crema on top. Looked and tasted good.   Although we ate in, the food was brought to us as if it was to go. Plastic plates and utensils, wrapped in foil, etc. I prefer to be treated like a dine in customer when electing to eat while the food is hot, and would pay a little more for the pleasure. Too, the environment would benefit from less throw away stuff.   I liked Peppe's, understood it's neighborhood, but it could make a few moves to be a lot better. They do make their own horchata, which is a great sign of the possibilities.

On the dreary stretch of Rt. 1 (Lincoln Highway) in Fairless Hills, Pa., sits a solitary Colonel Sanders, aka, KFC.   I have customered it a few times over the years.  Each time the parking lot was nearly empty, and the dining area bereft of fried chicken lovers.  Hitchcockian if pushed for a description, with an orange neon sign on the wall saying it was "Sunday dinner every night."  Yet, the actual meals were good, and the Honey BBQ wings way better than average due in part to their initial preparation as Buffalo Wings, then lathered with the thick sweet tang of the Honey BBQ recipe, giving the wings a hot sweet sallow flavor that can lead to compulsive eating disorders.  The Original Recipe Buckets are also quite good, especially for feeding teenage boys coming together for a party.  Thus, my reason for being there late last week, as I waited for the order to be packed and bagged.  I was surprised when the bucket of 20 pieces and box of 20 wings came in over $40., but nothing is too good for my now teenage son.    My car smelled of greasy BBQ on the ride home, and it tortured my saliva glands so much that I nearly pulled over to put one of those rusty red chicken wings in my mouth.  I overcame that impulse and made it home in 20 minutes. As soon as I entered the house, my son, his friends, and a couple of parents became transfixed at the aroma, and silently rose to follow me into the dining room.  Shades of Night of the Living Dead.   The entire batch was devoured in a half hour, and there were sated smiles all around. I am convinced that a chemical analysis of the chicken coating would turn up crack in the mix.  It was that good.   Have to be careful as this stuff is quickly addictive, but so damn yummy.

Solstice, the nouveau cuisine restaurant recently opened in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center, bring something attractive and creative to the fairly standard kitchens that are crowding into town recently. Its space is open and bright, with high ceilings and the feel of a summer home at the beach on a sunny summer day. Walking in for our reservation immediately shifted my attitude from just another dinner, to the possibility of something transformative. It was that beautiful and unexpected.   The staff was equal to the environment, and took great care of us from seating to, "Thanks for coming. Hope to see you again soon." Likewise, the menu offerings were seasonal, with many vegetarian oriented appetizers and entrees. The summer listings were a cross between colorful blends of meat and leaf, pasta and creative takes on traditional dishes. We went with Lobster Risotto, Filet (medium well), Braised Waygu Short Rib & Mashed, and Sweet Corn Ricotta Gnocchi. I also sampled the Cantelope Gazpacho to broaden our exposure to their kitchen.   The result was less than perfection, but strong enough to appreciate what the chef was trying to do to separate Solstice from the ragtag assortment of other houses in the neighborhood. Special merit to the Gazpacho, which was just a delicious cold soup on an extremely hot day. In fact, it was the best thing brought to our table.   The Risotto was visually stunning with the yellow rice base and orange lobster, but not the most tasty rendition available for these ingredients. Liked it. Didn't love it. The Filet was mild pink throughout as described by our server, yet somewhat thinner than anticipated and less flavorful than hoped. Admittedly, my stepson may have been influenced by the same cut he ordered last week at Rocco's, which knocked his socks off. This slab was certainly less overwhelming, but still decent. It just suffered by comparison.   The Short Rib was perfectly cooked and was again a stunning visual presentation. The sauce could have used more zip, as it had the texture/flavor of American roast beef, rather than accentuating the Waygu or the many Asian or citrus spices that could have made this dish sing. In the same way, the Gnocchi was tender and mixed very well with the veggies and shaved cheese, but had a excess of water at the bottom of the deep plate and was a bit salty. As you can tell, everything was good to excellent, but each left something to be desired.   There will be a next time, but our approach will be to treat Solstice as a tapas house. We will order several appetizers, rather than entrees, and enjoy tasting many more of their creative dishes. The Gazpacho was the best we tried, and the hummus and other small plates seemed to have potential as we scanned the other tables for reactions to the food. I suspect, without knowing, that this may be the way to go.

Moish & Itzy's and its predecessors have been serving me breakfast and an occasional dinner for almost 20 years.  However, I frequent there less over time for a variety of reasons.  When I found myself there last week for a breakfast meeting, I had a few moments to look around, read the menu closely, and get in touch with what I have liked about M & I.    The physical plant looks worn.  Walls dinged; molding dented and chipped; dirty carpets; same old floor plan. The menu is still huge, but unchanging.  The prices fail to reflect the economic realities of our times, nor the effort of other restaurants to offer  less expensive options.  Finally, I compared my memory of decent food with current fare.  That was basically the same from what I could tell.  Big BUT - when I ordered Matzoh Brie (Fried Matzoh) I was told they had no Matzoh!  Okay, but how is that possible in a Jewish style deli? I will skip the fun analogies.    I ordered the French Toast instead.  It was fine, but uninteresting.  That sort of sums up my current sense of this place.  It looks and feels basically the same, but after so much time in business, perhaps it should do something differently to keep people engaged in the environment.  I felt tired after leaving M & I, despite all the coffee.   Moish and Itzy felt tired, too.

Long Life Chinese Natural Herbs is a Chinese apothecary shop much like you will find in most Asian neighborhoods around the globe.  It has both packaged and loose herbs for most known (and many unknown to western culture) ailments.  The owner and employees are quite knowledgeable at understanding your symptoms and making informed suggestions for treatment.    I observed as several customers described their physical problems, were questioned by the herbalists, and finally reached a thoughtful solution.  Then, the chief lay sheets of clean paper on the counter and began to place various herbs, roots, and barks onto each of them in approximately equal amounts before wrapping each carefully, and placing them in separate bags; one for each dosage - usually a strong tea.  Fascinating!  I was there for fresh, sliced American Ginseng to help stimulate my energy level, and an herbal patch for a friend with Plantar's Fasciitis.  Securing both after enjoying the cultural display rarely seen outside of the Chinatown's of the USA, I left with confidence in my new elixirs.  This place seems to move substantial volume, and it is a safe bet that their products are fresher than those sometimes found in stores that sell a multitude of other things.

El Limon, the Mexican Cocina that has expanded locally to 16 shops, has always been a favorite of mine for comida Mexicana in the region. I have visited four or five locations over the years and always found them to be authentic, creative and down to earth in the atmosphere department - utilitarian without painted carved chair ostentation. They are good eats at good prices.   My recent visit to their new Bensalem store has me reconsidering my past impressions. Maybe they are growing too fast, or their supply lines are stretched too thin by coming into Bucks County from Montgomery, or COVID logistics have overwhelmed them, but the charming delicious gestalt of past exposure was not present in this place.   I ordered a Torta Milanese (thin breaded fried beef sandwich) and Horchata rice drink. I've had both before at their other locales. Overlooking for the moment that the servers forgot to set up my table with flatware, napkins or glass of water even after delivering my meal, the sammy itself was a shadow of its previous self. Less meat, less chipotle mayo, less avocado, and a kaiser roll from the discount day old shelf at the back of their bakery. It was soft, tasteless and dry. There was no way they used such inferior bread on any other visits; in fact in the past their rolls had stolen the show they were so good.   Not this time. It was a complete sad sack.   Clearly, quality control has taken a hit at El Limon Bensalem. They need to step up their training in customer service, and seriously reevaluate their bread purveyor.   At least the Horchata was quite good.

Zara's Food Cart although on wheels and with a hitch for getting on the road, is a permanent fixture of the Riggins gas station on Street Road, Bensalem, PA. Its lime green paint job makes it easy to see on the southbound side. The menu is limited to gyros and over rice options in lamb, chicken or beef Afghani style faire. From what I saw and tasted, its popularity is well founded.   My son turned me on to it on our way back from a day visiting Delaware, and just describing his experience there made us hungry to try it. So, we got off RT. 95 and cruised up Street Road a mile or so until we found it. About 4 parking spaces in proximity, but all we needed was one. The cart is tiny which explains the absence of room for refrigerated drinks. Only a small person could work in such tight conditions. Zara be that guy.  My lamb Gyro was excellent. A ton of well cut and grilled seasoned lamb, with lettuce, tomato, cucumber and garlicy white sauce, in a soft, thick pita, wrapped in sandwich paper and aluminum foil. It was still hot and delicious when we got home. My son's chicken and rice was similarly loaded. He couldn't wait and scarfed it down in the car.   Had Zara had room for vertical grills, shaved the meat off the spit, and set up a few picnic tables to permit dining on site, this would have been a full five star adventure. As it was it was pretty darn close.   This one is worth going back to.

As large government bureaucracies go, the local office of the Social Security Administration on Lincoln Highway (Rt. 1), Fairless Hills, Pa., is doing a pretty good job.    The appointment given my client to deal with a question of overpayment was easily secured over the phone, and when we arrived at the given hour, our wait was no more than 15 minutes.  That is fairly precise for an agency that deals with all sorts of issues and people in varying degrees of stress and ability to communicate.    The representative who met with us was professional and knowledgeable about what we were there to discuss.  We quickly reached the heart of the matter, reviewed the facts and alternative resolutions, and decided on the best course going forward.    Everyone was satisfied with the quality of the meeting, as well as its efficiency.  We left the building in under 45 minutes from when we entered.    It is difficult to rate government from a "fan" or "Woohoo" perspective as needed for higher ranking, but in this instance, the "A-Okay," is from the heart.

Arriving at 3:30, I learned Ban Bamboo closed for two hours on Saturday afternoon and reopened at 4. So, I had a little time to wander along Ridge Avenue and take in the beautiful Spring day and the local color. The street scene was active with outdoor seating at the brewery and many open doors allowing the kitchen aromas to waft out to we pedestrians. Definitely created the aura of being a neighborhood.   When BB's "Open" sign lit, I went in to discover a small dining area with lovely Buddha shrine front and center, and heavy southeast Asian decor all around. A cafe in Vientiane or Pattaya would look as good. I ordered Tom Kha Soup (veggie), Beef Satay, Red Curry (veggie), Drunken Noodles (chicken), and Kai Soi (beef), to go. It was 40 minutes to readiness, so I continued my exploration of the area while waiting, and thought about what I remembered about Lao and Thai cuisine.   While both are very regionalized so that there are many distinctions even in different parts of each country. Still, there are a few generalities that hold true. Where Thai uses coconut milk in many dishes making it sweet, often counterbalanced by the heat of chili peppers and bitterness of lemongrass; Lao kitchens lack coconuts, and use more lime and fermented fish sauces for flavor. Lao is a lot saltier than Thai.   So, it was easy to know which was which in my package. The Tom Kha Soup came on strong on sweetness from its coconut milk/galangal base, followed immediately by a lemongrass bite. It could have used more variety of veggies in the bowl, but the taste profile set off a riot in my mouth. The Red Curry was similar in sweetness, but lit a fire from the chili paste used to turn the color crimson. The veggies were still semi firm, adding to the texture, along with the bell pepper, bamboo shoots and Thai basil. The Beef Satay was lean meat with excellent BBQ type sauce, and on the sweeter side. Drunken Noodles were definitely from Thailand in flavor and plenty spicy from roasted chili sauce. Kai Soi, on the other hand, was more a hybrid, using thin sliced beef in a coconut milk broth, mixed with egg noodles, red onion, cabbage and lemon/lime juices. It reminded of Indian curry with its sweet/sour profile.   Although travel time neutralized the higher taste amplitudes to reduce the delicate intricacies that exited the kitchen, it was still a wonderfully entertaining meal that is well worth revisiting, along with this Ridge Avenue neighborhood.

This was my first visit to a Costco, and I was duly overwhelmed and even impressed. Our neighbor is a member and came along with the secret password and handshake.   These are mega warehouses where most things are offered in bulk, whether you actually need that much quantity or not. Clothing to HDTVs, tires to industrial strength pancake mix, and everything in between. At the end of almost every aisle, free samples of food being sold nearby; so if hungry, you can graze your way from appetizers to dessert, and add the savings from lunch (although I hear the hot dogs in the cafe are very good) to the overall value.  Even though my household isn't big enough to warrant purchasing on this scale, I found myself seduced by the sheer magnitude of the offerings. I soon took leave of my senses, disregarded the reality that we just couldn't eat all the food while it was fresh at the scale it was displayed, and began to think that the lower price would save money despite the fact that it would become outdated in the pantry.   What a perverse incentive!   Buy more than you need and convince yourself that the lower cost per unit is saving you money, when the exact opposite is true. Money is wasted getting marginally useful or taking flyers on stuff you really don't need or are unlikely to consume in a timely manner. The cupboard will be full of things you won't believe you were crazy enough to buy after the intoxication wears off. I don't know about you, but I spent way more than I do in a normal shopping trip, yet still found we needed to go to the local supermarket for all the things Costco didn't have. Knocked our budget out of whack.   Why? So I saved a little on a huge box of Cheerios that will take six months to finish; the last half of which will be stale. Or, for two years worth of ketchup, the last bottle of which will have separated and taste like crapchup by the time I open it.   But, I saved a buck over buying only when ready to use it. Right?!  Wrong!  The only way this works efficiently for consumers is to go after eating a big meal, skipping all the free samples, and being disciplined with a list of the things it makes sense to buy at Costco, and NOTHING ELSE. Wear blinders. Don't browse. Don't allow temptation to seduce.   Run in. Run out.   Otherwise, like the poor Ulysses, you will fall victim of the Siren sweetly singing, just like I did. Poor soul.  There must be a 12 step program.  Can't wait to go back.

I've been on a bit of a bagel kick recently, bringing me to Redhouse Bagels in the Salem Center, Bensalem, PA. It is a large, comfortable shop with Kids Playroom (currently closed due to Covid), fire pit with worn easy chairs around it, and large self-serve coffee station with several java options. The vibe was welcoming and service friendly.   I ordered an Onion Bagel with Veggie Cream Cheese, one of my standards. It was ready in minutes, packed neatly in a white paper sack. I drove home and dove in.   The dough wheel was regular size and there was enough spread for a balanced chew. First glance, the color of the bagel appeared pale white compared to others I have eaten in recent months. The toasted onion flakes were larger than most bagelries, and were only on the top crown, with none on the side nor bottom. Too, the texture was denser than I prefer, indicating more kneading than necessary for a lighter, airier center. All in all, it left the impression that this was really a plain bagel with onion flakes added later on. My guess is that they also bake with bleached flour, rather than unbleached, which provides more color and flavor.  The bagel was okay, but would have been so much better with more attention to right ingredients, technique, and finish. A bagel school refresher course would likely do the trick.

Ratchada is a district in Bangkok known for less bustle while very entertaining. This Thai/Laotian house takes its name and atmosphere from this more mellow part of a very intense big city.  It is apt, as when walking in off of S. 11th Street (a half block off Washington), you immediately feel a sense of decompression and culture shift from urban hubbub to Asian serenity.  The dark wood tones, silks, and wall art invite you to leave the outside world behind, and wade into a secret jasmine scented pool of tranquility.   Hyperbole? Perhaps. But, after the week I just finished, it felt so to me.   We were seated immediately and on time by Jib, the diminutive whirlwind who seemed to be everywhere at once.  She was graceful, smiling, communicative and clearly loved what she was doing.  The menu was quickly explained and we were given ample time to peruse and select.  Tom Yum Nam Khon (Creamy Lemongrass Soup) and Tom Kha (Coconut Soup) to begin.  Fried Calamari to appetize.  Ratchata Duck (a Chef Special) to share.    The soups were hot, spicy, loaded with veggies, and a great way to commence.  My taste buds were on alert to the complexity of each spoonful.  The Calamari had a beer batter that seemed a little off for the dish as it created a coating around the calamari rings that easily separated from the crustacean and made the eating a bit disjointed.  Still, it was very fresh and the Sriracha/sweet&sour peanut sauce was good enough to eat by itself. Nothing was left behind.  The star of the show was the Duck.  Its skin was crispy and the meat perfectly tender and moist.  The Mango/Tamarind mix that created the sauce that covered the bottom of the platter was simply exquisite.  So glad for the rice to absorb every drop after the duck was gone. Sweet/tart/creamy. There was ample sliced canard on the plate for two, and even a drumstick bone underneath for me to pick up and gnaw off the slim morsels.    This was a thoroughly enjoyable and memorable dinner.  It put me in an excellent frame of mind to such an extent that we decided to have their Thai Tea Ice Cream for dessert.  It too, was revelatory.  How many times have I had Thai Iced Tea and never considered taking it the next step?  So glad someone around here had done so.  I mite expensive at $6. for a big scoop, but a great way to end a wonderful meal.   Revisiting Ratchada is as desirable as it is inevitable.

Don't know what everyone else has been smoking, but this former corner diner cum Nino's Pizzarama doesn't make very good pies.   The place sits at the intersection of Chambers and Genesee Streets, a locale that is not designed to make you feel secure.  Through the large dirty windows pass the tempest tossed ravages of Trenton.  The dive is tiny with 5 tables, and floors, walls and windows that have not been washed in who knows how long.  I came in for a couple of slices, and was told by the counterman that the uncut pizza in front of him had just come out of the oven.    No reason to doubt him.  He tried to fit both slices on a single white paper plate, and when the point of one folded over and began to drip onto his counter, I asked for a second plate to hold both triangles.  He handed me the plate and I slid it under the drooping offender.  I sat down at a booth, sprinkled on the hot pepper flakes, and picked up the first slice.  It had not folded, and the undercarriage was actually thin and quite firm.  It held its point well until I snapped it off with one bite.    It was indeed hot.  The immediate taste was that of pizza - if a little salty from the cheese, and slick from the oil moistening the surface.  After putting it back on the plate, the oil began to run off the slice and onto the plate and ultimately the table when I picked it up again.  Too much poor quality cheese, and not enough of any quality sauce.  I could not taste it over the shouting of the fromage.    The second slice, cooler, was no better.  The original damage required a two handed pickup.  The fold where I bent it to be able to pick it up began to run a rivulet of oil, and dripped from the outer rim.  the oily saltiness was the dominant message.    Just not very good.  The young lads next to me said their cheesesteak was good, so maybe that is the way to go.  Straight pizza slices, certainly wasn't.

If you really like finding your way out of a maze, IKEA is your kind of fun store. One way in. One way out. Little signs with arrows point you in the right direction. A few unmarked shortcuts if your keen enough to find them.   It's not that their products aren't good; they are. It's not that their Swedish meatballs aren't excellent; they are. It's all about their concept of how people think and learn. To IKEA, customers are to be lead around through the entire warehouse regardless of what they need, and forced to pass through every department on two floors until finally reaching check out cashiers at the end of a long and boring stroll. Once you've begun, forget about going back to the beginning. The human undertow will just drag you down. Need a restroom? Good luck with that.   It helps if you are a zombie or dyed in the wool shopper when dealing with IKEA. If you don't particularly like the "Costco" warehouse experience, this place will wear you down. I mean, how many DIY furniture projects do you have in one lifetime? How often do you need to build shelves for your office? Not nearly enough to make this entertaining.   Yeah. We did buy a few glass water containers for around the house, and the prices were good. But, how much better it would have been to be directed to the location where they were shown, and be able to go right to them, than be required to go on safari to find them.   What a perverse trade-off.

The "New & Improved" Village @ Newtown is slowly getting up to speed and opening the many restaurants that suddenly find this community simply irresistibly. Chipotle Mexican Grill is the latest to have its grand opening in the new complex across from McCaffrey's Supermarket.   Luckily the parking lot was completed on time, too, so there is plenty of parking available for it now, and hopefully when the other five kitchens are open for business at the same time. Walking in, the room is smaller than anticipated, with several high communal tables for people to eat & run. It wasn't so busy when I was there around 3:30. The assembly line concept seemed efficient, but I was causing a slowdown by asking too many questions. I'm generally not a fan of this approach to dining, so I needed instruction on some of the basics. In the end, a carne asada burrito was delivered to me at the end of the line - stuffed with brown rice, pinto beans, carne asada, queso, avocado and a few other things. It was stuffed to the gills with sour cream on the side. I took it home somewhat concerned the whole thing would explode, it was packed so tight!   It was a tasty package with so many things going on that it all blended together in my mouth. Definitely a four napkin meal. I enjoyed it, although I could only finish half. As two meals the $11 tag seemed quite reasonable.   I can see what people like about Chipotle. It uses fresh ingredients, is basically healthy with a little self control, and you can fit it into a lunch hour. But, if authenticity in Mexican cuisine is paramount for you, this burrito was no where near as delicious as can be found in any good Casa Mexicana elsewhere in Bucks and Montgomery Counties, or across the river in Trenton.   I wish them success in Newtown.

Perhaps the most beautiful urban park in the USA, Fairmount captures both the historic grandeur of Philadelphia, as well as its awesome potential. And, of all the great buildings and events that have taken place there, the one most strategically placed and incredibly majestic vista is seen when standing on the Belmont Plateau overlooking Center City.   While living in the neighborhoods near the Art Museum (Brown St.), West Philly (UPenn) and in West Center City (25th & Delancey), I was always close enough to walk, bike or drive to the Plateau for a softball game, holiday picnic or sleigh ride in the snow. It remains my favorite single spot in the City to relax, breathe deep and capture the essence of what makes this town great.   Sure, it's the people, but looking down into its urban core gives a sense of human potential and unique possibilities.   In short, the view is inspirational.

This review addresses two subjects; the BK App and the new Ch'King Chicken Sandwich. While the first lacks intuitive feel and is frustratingly obtuse, the later is a damned good attempt to compete with all the other clucker on brioche buns coming to fast food franchises around the country.   The app offers many benefits not available to walk-in/drive-in customers. There are free Whoppers with first Ch'King purchases, discounted sides and drinks as "points" are accumulated, and surprise gifts with purchase on a regular basis. Today, it was vanilla soft-serve in a cone or cup when buying something of $3 or more price. So, there are pleasant upsides if you like the BK menu and can navigate the app.   Easier said then done.  I found that the special offers didn't always appear on the app from use to use. It wasn't obvious, therefore, which deals were present, and which expired. I found myself repeatedly returning to the opening page as I tried to work my way through the process. I ultimately got the ordering completed with what I wanted, but the time waste was a pain in the butt. If not for my curiosity and persistence, I would have deleted the app and driven to Popeye's instead.   Yet, it turned out that the new Ch'King standard chicken sandwich was very good (I left the free Whopper for my son to devour). The breast was plump, juicy, well breaded/fried, and all quite tasty. The brioche roll was fresh and held together to the last bite. The special sauce was the flavor of mild mayo,tartar, perhaps a bit of Sriracha, and the pickle slices pleasantly sour and crisp. The Sammy was so thick that my jaws couldn't open wide enough to fit it in for my incisors to clamp down,without squeezing it together and shimmying it back and forth to slowly gain necessary placement between my dents.   I chose onion rings over fries, and thought they were a decent alternative, although more calories.   This Ch'king falls just shy of the Popeye's version, but ahead of Chik Fil-A, Wendy's and McDonald's iterations in terms of taste, texture, composition and fun. Too, it is competitive with the smaller chicken shops like Lovebird, at a better price. For someone who prefers chicken to burgers as a protein source, this is clearly a reasonable and satisfying way to go.

To be honest, bubble tea is lost on me. I have tried it several times when thirsty walking around one Chinatown or another, but never really found it all that good. Usually too sweet, and those tapioca balls on the bottom were an unpleasant semi firm gooey tooth sticky choking hazard. I never understood the attraction.   So, when Hi Tea Bar opened on State Street in Newtown it was surprising, but not particularly interesting to me. Yet, I passed it every day and the urge to Yelp about it eventually drove my curiosity. Longer story short, I stopped in today to check it out.   Walking in (the front door opens outwards), the shop was narrow and deep with service area behind high wall on the right, and tables Covid-spaced along the left. It was a bit incongruous seeing only local high school girls behind the counter when all prior experience had been a totally Asian tone. I had a brief conversation with the cashier/order taker and sat down at an open table at the front window waiting for the Popcorn Chicken and Peach Green Tea to arrive. This would be my lunch today.   The tea got there first, followed by a handled plastic bag with the chicken inside with plastic fork and small container of spicy dipping sauce. Not exactly an environmentally neutral package. Similarly, the peach green tea was in plastic, but very tasty and refreshing. I think they mixed liquid fruit extract in with the green iced tea. I really liked it alot. The chicken was cut in small pieces, coated in breadcrumbs and deep fried. As I didn't smell anything cooking, I guessed it was premade and heated in a microwave. Not soft/crunchy like popcorn, but still texturally satisfying, with decent flavor  enhanced by the dipping sauce, I was enjoying an interesting snack.   Overall, a pretty good light meal and drink that differed greatly from standard American fare. Worthwhile even without the bubbles.   When Covid is over, Hi Tea Bar management will hopefully be less wasteful with materials, but continue to create enjoyable teas, smoothies and snacks that will have a permanent place in our local economy, right in the heart of town.

Bunn's Natural Foods on Street Road, Southampton, PA, is one of the original organic foods, vitamin and supplement outposts in Bucks County. If you're looking for some zinc to enhance immunity, or K2 to offset possible bone density loss due to the extra D2 taken in this Age of Covid, or just stocking up on healthy frozen food, Bunn's is your little slice of heaven.   The staff is very knowledgeable about their inventory and will gladly walk you to the part of the store where your needs are answered, and provide explanations for the available choices. I found them particularly useful while attempting to purchase the correct dosage of a mineral recommended in reading I had done on the subject of enhanced immunity, and learned that a low dose would be more effective than a higher one of one element due to side effects. Always good to know.  Bunn's does enough volume to carry their own label vitamins at a excellent discount to the national brands. They built a new center for their business several years ago, which while still small by comparison to other retail spots, is expansive enough to carry what most people want in a clean and friendly environment.   In a difficult economy where many of these small local shops are closing, Bunn's is surviving fairly well and will hopefully continue to do so.

Excellent bagel joint in Doylestown Borough. Small customer area, with room in back for ovens, preparation, storage and display case. The rounders have a crisp biting crust, while the inside has enough air pockets to keep it fairly light enough to allow the flavor of the topping (roast onion flakes) or whatever is added in the prep(butter & Swiss) to come through strongly.   I appreciate the bagel baker who knows not to knead the dough too long, which hardens the bread and makes it too dense. Too, here they are boiled and then baked in the right proportion to create the optimal bagel.   Having La Colombe and Ellis Coffee in house is also a big plus, as they are both top shelf Philadelphia roasters that have found success nationally and internationally.   These Borough guys are not fooling around. They give their customers quality bagels and first class java for a fair price. It wouldn't surprise me if their success was assured and they grew their enterprise as far as they wanted to take it.

While the tuna hoagie was prepared with the requested ingredients through Subway's app, the proportions weren't quite right, and as a result it was about the messiest sandwich I had consumed in several years.   Plenty of tuna, lettuce, tomato, green pepper, banana pepper, and sweet pepper hash loaded into their signature "footlong" roll, but also way too much squirt from the sweet onion sauce rocket, leaving the bread saturated and too weak to hold the entire package together. The result being a soggy, but tasty, mess, adding far too much sugar and unwanted calories to an otherwise simple creation. The flavor of the tuna was drowned out, and I had to find extra paper hand towels to keep the fallout under control.   The shop itself was exceptionally clean, and the counter person friendly as she completed my order after my arrival. She was generous with the accoutrements, and therein lay the problem. There was so much being stuffed into the torpedo that in wrapping up in waxed sandwich paper, I could see it starting to leak around the edges. Upon unwrapping at my desk, the excess moisture was escaping, and rivulets of sauce were flowing everywhere. With each bite food was evacuating out the back door, and my hands were getting drenched. The supply of thin non-absorbent napkins was quickly exhausted, and my fingers dripping and sticky.   Just not the kind of thing designed for a tidy working lunch. Yes, it tasted pretty good, but I had to wash my hands and face before touching anything else. If there is a next time, I will be better prepared, or better yet, get the superior Primo hoagies on the other side of town with that special sesame seeded roll.

Newtown has an embarrassment of creamy riches in the many home made ice cream joints in and near town. There is the new Goodnoe's on Sycamore Street, Zebra Striped Whale on State Street in the Borough, Owowcow up Rt. 413 in Wrightstown, and Sweet Pea Creams in the new Goodnoe's Corner (which stands on the holy ground of the original ice cream emporium of the same family name).  To my taste buds, Sweet Pea is decent, but the weakest entrant in the icecreamcapades.  I was there tonight with a group of kids from a local school after a 6th grade theater performance(that's another review).  I was lucky to have a Yelp deal for one free topping as a bonus.  Even with crushed peanut butter cups gracing a scoop of Burgundy Cherry Vanilla (or was it Bourgeoisie Cherry?) and Vanilla Pretzel Logic, the comparison of the local competition had me feeling a bit underwhelmed.  It is not that it was bad or unsavory.  It was only that it could not block out the memory of the others.  If a dish of glace is to achieve greatness it has to at least still the taste recordings of its near peers.  This Sweet Pea Creams could not do for me. It was somehow thinly sweeter and less engaging to the senses. Creamy, yes. Demanding complete attention, no.  We all have our favorites, and this place may be one of yours. I totally understand. But for me, I salivate most in anticipation of Goodnoes, followed by Owowcow, ZSW, and then Sweet Pea.  And, drooling in advance of a taste experience is what great ice cream is all about.

Yes. I've seen the Original Dominick's Pizza (Shoppe) in Richboro for many years, but never had the urge to stop in before the other night.  I regret my oversight.   In fact, Old Dom's is a very good restaurant hiding in disguise in the strip commercial development in the heart of Richboro.  What looks like a typical pizza parlor designed primarily for take out, is in fact a comfortable and attractive dining experience.  Just walk past the counter into the rear dining room, and be transported to a curbside café in Napoli.  Red tile roof, stucco walls, trellis, red checkered tablecloths, the smell of garlic and tomatoes. Yes, it is Disneyesque, but I can easily suspend my disbelief to allow the atmosphere to positively impact my dinner.    It was a quiet night and I had my choice of tables.  My server was attentive and did not mind answering my first timer questions.  I wanted pasta, and ordered Penne Aglio Olio with Sautéed Spinach.  It came with a side salad, but not just a small plate of iceberg and a few veggies.  A large bowl of fresh Romaine, Plum Tomatoes, Shaved Carrots, Red Onion, and Balsamic was placed in front of me.  It was almost enough to be a meal by itself.  It was very good, and I placed it to the side when the main course arrived, so I could enjoy them together.    The Penne was another large deep plate well mixed with Extra Virgin and Chopped Garlic.  The Spinach was fresh and sautéed whole leaf and piled nicely mid-plate.  Really well done.  All this for under $10.   I can see how Original Dominick's has expanded and thrived.  Good food and good value.   A powerful combo. No need to become the New Dom's.

In the Village Shires Shopping Center, Just Wingin' It has been around for a long time serving the needs of famished football television watchers for a generation.  As the name strongly suggests, Wings are what this place is all about, although they are making a strong effort to be diversified in their menu offerings.    Quesadillas, Ribs, Salads, Wraps, Burgers, Chicken Sandies, and Fries round out the growing comfort food menu.  They even have Pierogies. Super Bowl Sunday is their Christmas and New Years Day rolled into one.  They bemoan the end of the NFL season, as business slows down dramatically.  The owners and staff are very friendly, and make the place feel like the corner store.  The downside is that although there is a modern oven that allows grilling and baking in enclosed equipment, the wall of deep oil fryers tells you that the food is not the healthiest to eat, regardless of taste. The dozens of large plastic bottles full of sauces sitting on shelves and the floor also are somewhat disconcerting.    Still, they are very good at what they do.  The Wings are large, lightly coated and fried for a good, crunchy taste.  The Burgers are 10 oz. before cooking, and come out at the right finish with a large varieties of toppings. Mine was just medium, as requested, with Jalapenos, Onions, and Provolone. I think it is called the, "Philly Burger." The weak link was the bun, which could not handle the weight and juices from its companion.  It quickly became mushy and fell apart when attempting to pick it up at home.  Knife and fork were brought in to finish the job.  Probably, if eaten there this would not become and issue.  The Fries were very good, and reminded of 5 Guys, slid into a brown paper sack where the oils stains quickly appear.    It was a nice moment to return to Just Wingin' It after many years away.  The place looks nicer with new furnishings, and state of the art oven, and the food remains solid.  While I feel no compulsion to go back again soon, it is good to know they have succeeded, and they remain a popular place to satisfy the Wing Lust in all of us.

This Chick Fil A wannabe does a decent job of frying chicken strips into a reasonably good signature sandwich.  Fresh chicken, crisp breading, and not overly oily.    The fries are average, and the corn is sweet.   As good a choice as any if you find yourself needing sustenance while at Oxford Valley Mall.

Visiting a take out Chinese shop for an eat-in lunch is always a bit of a gamble.    You never know what you are going to confront the first time walking in.  Will it be a dive with your shoes sticking to the floor, and the food indigestible?  Or, will the place have a pleasant personality and tone with decent grub given its inherent limitations?    Very happy to report that China Wok is the later.    The small space is clean and bright, with the owners/operators equally so.  The menu is adequate for both lunch and dinner, but as I was here in the afternoon for a late lunch, I went with the lunch specials.  Orange Chicken, Fried Rice and a drink (water) for a very reasonable price.   Yes, it was served in its take out container, but in an interesting way.  It came on a tray with the take out menu opened fully to act like a placemat.  Pleasant alternative to just having the various folding boxes placed in front of me.  Too, the smile that accompanied the service was an unexpected bonus.  Could have used a spoon along with the skinny plastic fork, but why quibble?   The meal was on the high end for cheap Chinese walk away.  The Chicken was not heavily coated, and it appeared it had not been frozen for long, if at all.  It was soft and pliant without that freezer burn toughness so often present.  The sauce was properly piquant with slices of Orange Peel and Red Szechuan Chili throughout.  The Fried Rice was decent with small chunks of pork and veggies.   All in all, a surprisingly good meal.  While it would never be confused with fine dining, it was certainly substantial enough without the obvious pitfalls of fast Chinese, that it is worth another visit.

Reading through the more recent reviews of the Continental Tavern I had the impression that while most people liked the atmospherics, they were less enthused with the cuisine. While the two of us only had their "Best of Bucks" burgers, fries and soft drinks, we departed thinking we have had better elsewhere.

This is another of those Yelp doubles, that have more than one entry for the same business.  The other, Original Dominick's Pizza Shoppe, has a few more reviews.  The confusion lies in the addresses.  The number on the front door is 1045, the address for the "Pizza Shoppe" page.  1067 is given as the address for ODP, but that number is not on the door.    Until that is straightened out, just check out both pages for a full display of reviews, tips and photos.   Mange bien!

While the Banh Mi (BBQ Pork) was first rate, due especially to the French baguette loaf made in house with great texture, taste and crunch, the rest of the show leaves something to be desired.    We sampled the Egg Custard Tarts that came in packages of two and wrapped in plastic.  The result was that the crust was soft and soggy, while the custard filling seemed to be under baked.  The Durian and Jackfruit Smoothies seemed from a mix concentrate, and not based in fresh fruit which were available nearby in local supermarkets.  Overly sweet and sealed so the actual drink could not be viewed unless the plastic top was cut away. Once opened, the distinct rotten egg odor of the durian fruit wafted out.  At least it had been authentic when the concentrate was first prepared.   The biggest shock at Nam Son was how dirty it was inside.  A floor that hadn't been cleaned in a long time; car tires stored next to the drink display case, no gloves used in food preparation, reused woven wicker baskets that bore the stains of past meals.   Best of Philly Award in the category Banh Mi may be warranted, but it has some serious competition around town. Owner was friendly and engaging with customers, but he really should make an effort to upgrade hygiene in his shop.

Gyro Express is an Afghan gyro shop on the old pedestrian mall section of West State Street, Trenton, NJ.  It has a menu limited to about a dozen items all related to beef, lamb, chicken and falafel pita wraps or open platters with basic salads.  The primary owner is the face of the business, and he has a warm and polite persona. He is a great salesman.   I went with a combo plate of grilled chicken, beef and falafel, that included a small iceberg based salad and a bed of yellow rice. It was covered in a nice white dipping sauce and small side cups of a spicy green colloid that added a hot dimension to the meats.   The lunch was okay. There was ample protein, well grilled and tasty when mixed with the sauces and rice. Didn't see the spits that they may have been cooked on, and didn't smell that savory aroma that is so pleasantly addictive. I left most of the rice behind to avoid unwanted carbs, but enjoyed the small slices of meat and crushed falafel.   Gyro Express is a worthy option in the State Street food carnival, but not nearly the excellent Afghani delights found just across the Delaware in Morrisville, PA, where Afghan Kabob holds court in the Morrisville Shopping Center. Worth a long lunch hour walk over the Calhoun Street Bridge to sample ethnic dishes on a different order of magnitude.

When I walked in my first reaction was, "Wow! This looks way different than Cosi. Very colorful, light and airy, and lots of smiling faces behind the counter."    I had the Chicken Salad Pita Sandwich with a side of Grilled White Beans, which was really a thick bean soup.  Everything was fresh, if not totally original or outstanding in composition and taste.  It was very satisfying, and warrants a return visit to check out more items on the menu.  The manager came over to chat with us.  She was warm and engaging, and explained that part of the Zoes corporate culture was to contribute to the community.  She asked us to think of them when we needed donations of food for a good cause.  It seemed that it was too busy a place for meetings in a quiet corner, but the offer was well received here.   Zoes seems to be a very positive addition to Newtown's Sycamore Street core, and with the many alternative food outlets right there, it will help draw more people to the area when they are looking for a good meal in a great location.   Good luck, Zoe.

Didn't start off heading for Perfetto's Pizza, but when Chester's Halal Fried Chicken was closed for prayer Friday afternoon, I ended up across Lalor Street at this outwardly dumpy looking pizza joint.   I was wrong to judge a pizzeria by its cover.  Turns out that Perfetto's is bigger than it looks, with a dining room in back, counter service in front, and a comprehensive menu.    I sat down in the dining area (where it was warmer), alongside some of Trenton's finest.  I didn't want pizza, so ordered the lunch sized Penne with Broccoli, Garlic and Oil.  I asked for the garlic to be very well done.  The lunch came with choice of soup or salad, and a basket of home baked bread.    The platter arrived overflowing with Broccoli and Penne.  The Garlic was thin sliced, golden and ubiquitous. A little grated Romano and ground Pepper, and I was in business.  It tasted great!  The Salad with Balsamic was adequate, but not memorable, and the bread, while warm, was basically pizza dough shaped into a half loaf. It would have been better flat and covered with red gravy and cheese.    The service was friendly, bilingual, and perhaps a bit slow due to the dining room being out of sight of the front cashier and kitchen door.  Still, at $7.50 for a full meal with take home extras, I was pleased with finding Perfetto's.  Perfetto's was not perfect, but had its moments of grandeur.  MARCH 3, 2015 UPDATE: Returned today and had Cavatelli Spinach and a Bowl of Chicken Veggie Soup.  The Soup was loaded with soft Chicken, Onions, Celery and Carrots, and the Cavatelli was a full platter of well sautéed spinach with plenty of golden garlic.  Impressive lunch for $7.95!  UPDATE: MARCH 6, 3018 - Perfetto's is really making a statement now. The house was near capacity today @1:30. Far busier than last time I was here about two years ago. Still a better than average kitchen with a real bargain for lunch - almost a dinner size meal, now at $8.50. My penne aglio olio with broccoli was a heavy load, without skimp. Salad still needs an upgrade from iceberg, but otherwise, this joint is one of the best deals in town.

The New Madison Restaurant sits in an old strip of stores on Vets Highway in Levittown.  It is one of several around this part of Bucks County, developed to bring commercial opportunity and convenience to the new "suburbs" being created by Mr. Levitt.  As such it is living history.    Madison sits in the middle of all this 70 year old Americana.  Its interior is in the luncheonette style food dispensary, which adds to its authenticity and comfort.  It feels like you could easily sit down with your parents and grandparents at one of the booths for a $.75 meal.   Alone, I chose the old fashioned counter where I could alternate between eating, reading and chatting with the staff.  Here, that is a special pleasure because all the women were warm and attractive. Christine served me with a smile and friendly banter as sweet as the syrup on my French Toast.  Lori was equally engaging, and betrothed to Dean, the owner. I met him when he sat down at the counter to chat with another customer. Cool dude.  My breakfast was solid.  The coffee flowed freely, and the FT was made of "Texas Toast," well egged and grilled.  Even the Turkey Sausage was more than expected (4 links) and good tasting.  I asked for a drop of Vanilla in the egg mix, but there was none in the kitchen. Regardless, it still was very good.  Rumor has it that New Madison may have a sibling in Langhorne soon.  Stay tuned for an important announcement.    I am saving the 5th Star for credit card convenience.

This is the Shake Shack inside King of Prussia Mall, in the second floor food area.   I admit to being the last person on Earth to eat at Shake Shack, despite it's siren song of awesome burgers, fries and signature shakes. Now that I have finally had the pleasure of dining at this outlet in the fantabulous KoP Mall I can honestly say that I am happy to have the experience in my life, but really don't understand the halabaloo.   Aside from long lines and slick advertising, I found the burgers to be rather pedestrian (not that there is anything wrong with walking). A single puck sandwich seems to be 5 ounces of overcooked beef in a pretty good bun, lettuce, tomato and secret sauce. At most, a four biter. Just about every tavern in the Universe does a better one. My backyard grill puts theirs to shame. Most roadside joints have nothing to fear from this outfit.   True, the shakes are a kick in the pants, so maybe the burgers just accessorize the superior drink and are not designed to be the star of the show. If that is the intention, they have succeeded. The salted caramel shake far outshined it's burger cousin.   But, do I want to pay $6 for a small shake on a regular basis? No. I can do better at DQ on both counts, for far less money.   For me, Shake Shack is an exercise in hypnotic marketing, akin to the Emperor's New Clothes fairytale.   Caveat Emptor!

I've been to Tina's twice (not counting the visit to the bagel side of the building).  The first visit was to try their pizza.  I had a slice of Old Style Brooklyn Pie and one of Regular Pizza.    While the Brooklyn effort was excellent, with robust sauce, fresh basil and a lively crunchy crust, the Regular slice was just average.  Part of the problem was the while the oven time was sufficient for the thinner crust Brooklyn to be completely reheated, the standard pie had a thicker crust and it did not heat up to the proper temp, leaving the bite soft and thick, rather than firm and cracker firm.  That is just a matter of the kitchen knowing what the oven can do and how long it takes to do it.   My second visit last week went with the Italian Hot Dog on the recommendation of the server, (another Tina, I believe).  These creations were born in Trenton about a generation ago (the dearly departed Casino on Anderson St., and its sibling, Tony Goes).  This bambino was amazingly great!  It was loaded with Green Frying Peppers, and large, chunky Hash Brown Potatoes that were grilled to a nice brown firm edge.  Each bite sliced through the fresh Italian Torpedo, Crunchy Potato, Pepper, Red Pepper and finally the Frankfurter. Heinz Ketchup and French's Mustard were on the table.  It was so big, it could have been two meals. The lunch also came with a cup of soup (Chicken Noodle was homemade and tasty.)   With very good bagels, too, Tina's is a good destination for breakfast or lunch. They bring an extra ingredient to their menu - imagination.

Poppy's Pizzeria sits alone on a desolate stretch of Woods Lane, Langhorne, Pa. I didn't even know it was there for a dozen years until a detour took me past it recently.   It was Friday night - Pizza Night - so,what the heck?!  The layout was casual with three sections in the dining area. Tight booths and tables all around. HDTVs mounted high in the corners. We seated ourselves. Our server arrived quickly and introduced herself with menus in hand. We ordered a round pie half mushrooms, half sausage; a dozen Buffalo wings and cheesesteak calzone.   Everything was okay. The wings were hot from the hot sauce bath, but arrived looking overdone with several bones exposed and charred, but tasty. The pie had the right ingredients, if less than a full complement of shrooms and meat and lacking a crisp crust. The calzones was stuffed to the gills with steak, but could have used more onion and pepper within for added flavor. Took most of that home.   Poppy's has promise, and with a more skilled hand in the kitchen could find themselves in a more elevated zone.

One of my regular stops while in Tucson for the gem and stone extravaganza in late January every year is Miss Saigon (Yes. I've seen the play). It is another of the North Campbell Avenue string of pearl restaurants that I found and stuck with over many years.    The shop is comfortably designed with a relaxed Asian décor.  The staff is warm and usually prompt in that offhand attentive way we all know.  The menu is simple and everything I have tried has been solidly satisfying.    My choices tend to be the same each year, as I obviously can't get there often.  An order of Spring Rolls (Shrimp, Pork, Greens, Noodles in translucent Rice Paper), Mixed Wok Veggies with Tofu in Ginger Sauce, and one of several great Pho alternatives. My young son, as always the genuine food critic, came to love their Chicken Wings, Orange Chicken, and eventually, the Pho Ga. All these dishes have been enjoyable and strong enough to induce some loyalty.    Yes. I have eaten equally good Vietnamese cuisine elsewhere in the USA, but it is great to know I don't have to give anything away when I want some in Tucson.

To be honest, I planned to get dinner last night at the Moo Truck right next door, but discovered it was not there due to the illness of the owner.  Adriana's was sitting there, so I decided to check it out.    I was given a deuce close to the door by a friendly waitperson, followed promptly by the large menu.  As I was dining solo I was not in the mood for pizza, so I went for the Chicken Pannini with Spinach and Provalone, and Fries.    As I waited, I looked around and saw several families and a large group enjoying their time together.  The ambiance was warm, friendly, low buzz noisy, with the aroma of garlic, tomatoes and basil wafting the room.  Quite pleasant.    The Pannini arrived with a nice pile of crisp fries.  The Italian bread was nicely grilled with the pannini stripes well pronounced.  The Chicken was tender, if perhaps a bit too thick for the sandwich, causing pieces to fall out when picked up.  The Spinach was sauteed in garlic and a nice complement to the sandwich.  The cheese was fine, but lacked the sharpness that would have given the overall experience a bigger "bite."  Still, it was satisfying.    The Fries were standard, but crisp and a plus.   There seem to be mixed reviews about the pizza, but given that the pannini was pretty good, I will return with some help to work on a pizza.  My first impression was positive, but I could not escape the thought that with a little more attention to detail, Adriana's could jump to the next level of Italian osteria, and really make its mark in the area.

Aside from the dude hanging up without an answer when I called to see if The Sticky Wicket was open for lunch, the joint itself isn't a bad place for a dive bar with adequate kitchen.    Located in a desolate part of Trenton that at one time attempted to be a modern commercial area, it now is one of the few remaining tenants in Independence Square. The space is large, with an attached liquor store and a large rectangular bar with room to sit and have a meal.  The atmosphere is dark and wood paneled, giving the feeling that there are things in the corners you might not want to know about.  With a few hunting trophies on the walls, TSW could be a Western dive bar, as it has the feel of a large cabin.    I ordered a medium patty melt burger, fries and a cold Angry Orchard Apple Cider.  The prices were pretty good, with the food under $8., and the coldie at $5.50.  Good, friendly staff, and many regulars who seemed to know each other and kept the repartee moving along.  My patty melt was half medium as requested, but the other half was well done, no doubt from pushing it to the side of the grill to give it lower heat, but failing to turn it to keep the cooking balanced.  Although the menu claims the patties were never frozen, I have doubts about that given the crumbly nature of the finished puck.  It was an okay sandwich, but could have been much more given the copious fried onions, and melty cheese. I liked that it was on marble rye.    It is nice to know that Sticky Wicket is open and keeping busy.  It is a cool place to hang out over lunch.  If they served up a better burger I would become a fan.

On a warm Spring day there are few places that are better for sitting in the fresh air and watching the world go by than the veranda of Havana.  If it is approaching mid summer, it almost reminds of its namesake in Cuba.    When we stopped in for lunch yesterday after concluding our business in nearby Lahaska, we all marveled at the perfection of the moment.  Havana contributed to the occasion by providing drink and victuals to our liking, with friendly efficient service.  I split a Panini Cubano and Side Salad, both of which were very good.  The grilled sandy contained BBQ Pork, and Mild Cheese between the fresh large format bread.  The Side Salad was full of lively greens, reds, purples and yellows in a variety of shapes and a pleasantly spiced dressing.  The accompanying Fries were the thicker crunchy type, and not really necessary given the rest of the meal.    The other companions were also content, and we lingered a while, slowly finishing our drinks and conversations while we enjoyed the breeze created by the nearby Delaware River and the surrounding hills.    While I cannot speak to the nightside of Havana nor New Hope here, it is a wonderful spot for a leisurely lunch on a warm Friday afternoon in late May.

This was my third visit in so many months, and this time I ordered the Eggplant Parm Grinder (finished with a visit to the over to plasmatize everything).  It was great.  Thin sliced, sautéed, Eggplant, chunky Tomato Sauce, and fresh tasting Mozza on a large Italian Loaf; all brought to a sizzling climax with a brief visit to the pizza oven before serving.  For totally satisfying and delicious lunches, Tina gets 5 BIG ONES!

Established in 1919, this family owned/operated German style bakery sits in a small strip center between Easton and Davisville Roads in Willow Grove, Pa.  The Vietnamese restaurant, Pho & Beyond is right next door, and a convenient neighbor to have if dessert apres noodle soup is your sweet desire.    The space includes two storefronts, and is bright and cheery.  The staff dresses the part of bakers and assistants, with white coats and hats.  With all the goodies in displays, and glass walls permitting a look at the actual creation of the cookies, cakes, scones, petit fours, and cupcakes, Weinrich's is all about seduction and temptation.  In that it succeeds quite well.  It was next to impossible not to want to sample a little of everything in sight, especially when they offered me a petit four as a first timer.  That was small and delicious, and set everything that happened next into motion.    Just had a get a half dozen cupcakes (Raspberry Cream, Caramel Cream, and Lemon Cream), and the same number of the freshly baked and glazed donuts.  A small bag of scones were thrown in for good measure.    Everything was very good to excellent.  The cake bottoms were firm enough to hold the top load easily.  Each cupcake was injected with the cream of choice, right down to the bottom of the base. The icing was soft with subtle flavor, rather than the hard topping found in many shops.  The donuts were more the standard variety, with Red Velvet and Vanilla cake style, as well as traditional glazed and French Cruller alternatives.  All dipped in vanilla glaze icing, they were less enchanting as their texture, touch and taste were not so unique from the more mass produced options found elsewhere.  The scones were raisined, and had a mild sweetness.    There was far more in this shop than could be sampled or purchased in one visit.  I am not a bakery cookie guy, preferring home baked to almost anything that can be made in quantity, yet given what I've just tried, Weinrich's is certainly worth several returns to get hands and tongue into the rest of this cookie jar.

Zook's BBQ Barn is in the corner of the Newtown Farmers' Market, and operated by Amish folks in full dress and accents.  The market is only open Thursday thru Saturday, so plan accordingly.  The BBQ is excellent across the board.  From pork, chicken, and beef, through many vegetables, the most notable of which are the carrots, yams, and red potatoes.  As noted in the other reviews, the approach to BBQ is different than the better known rub cuisines of Texas, Memphis, North Carolina, etc.  Here the meat is smoked first until it is tender and falling off the bone.  Then it is mixed with a variety of delicious, tangy sauces and allowed to steep until the meat and sauce merge and something completely new is created.    I have purchased the whole chickens in the past, and they were very good. Perfect for a family dinner with a few of the original side dishes.  These days, I am more lunch oriented, and go for the pulled meat sandwiches and veggies.  The Pulled Pork is excellent, and the Pulled BBQ Ribs are so succulent I hate to swallow and lose the flavor orgy in my mouth.  Beware small bones.   The lunch special is one of the BBQ meats on a fresh roll and a side dish of your choice.  The prices run from $6 to $8 for the meal. You need to ask for napkins and a fork, as they are not routinely thrown into the bag.    All in all a great alternative for lunch, not to mention the overall curiosity of walking around the market and being tempted by everything else being offered by the vendors.   The only complaint is the general lack of cleanliness in the market. I guess that is why Zook's is called a "Barn."

Rosa's is tucked away in a tiny 4 store strip center just off North Campbell, and very easy to miss. But, it is worth finding.    The family run enterprise is a staple of Tucson, dishing out very good South of the Border plates at reasonable prices.  It is one of those few shops I always return to when in town for the gem show extravaganza in late January/early February.  There is usually a short wait for a table, as the space is small and a tight squeeze.    The food is decent, if not haute cuisine, and quite tasty and filling. A couple of margaritas or cervesas after a long day looking at hot rocks is the best way to begin the chill down.  The service can be erratic, but they make up for it with attitude and good humor.    One of the best things they have is a wall full of calendars for purchase with classic Mexican art the prime selling attraction.  I love hanging one on my office wall as a recollection of my time in Tucson, and Rosa's colorful hospitality.

In order to beat the morning traffic last week, I decided to spend the night at The Latham Hotel on 17th Street, and meet with visiting nephew, niece and baby-neph for breakfast the next day.    Brilliant, if I don't say so myself!  Everything from the online reservations, front desk, room, to valet parking was first rate.  I remembered being here maybe 15 years ago, when the place had slipped into a less than optimal condition, but the new version is just fine.    I loved my 5th floor corner room.  It was New York small, but clean and very comfortable.  My windows overlooked both 17th Street and the Philadelphia Baptist Church, whose spires filled up one window with an old-Europe sensibility.  I actually moved the HDTV out of the way so I could see it more clearly and take photos.  The bed was firm and I had way too many pillow choices.  Plenty of hot water and pressure in the morning rush times.    The only issue I had was with the parking.  While the valet is convenient, at $39 per night, it is expensive.  It would be better if upon reserving a room, the hotel provided detailed information on parking options (location, cost, in/out), and allowed the customer the ability to prepare in advance for using self parking down the street.  It might only save a fin or two, but having preferences honored is what good guest services is all about.    I would certainly stay at The Latham again.  This is a great spot in Center City, just off Rittenhouse Square, with plenty of streetlife for everyone's taste and habits.

Located in a rundown small strip commercial center where New York Camera is located on Bridgetown Pike, Happy Star Restaurant is at its root a take out joint with a couple of tables with ripped/torn chairs for the unfortunate few who opt to eat there.  I belong in that group, as I was returning from a meeting and wanted to have lunch before arriving at my office.    I ordered the General Tso's Chicken, as I often do the first time I dine at a Chinese shop.  Everything arrived quickly on a styro plate and with a plastic fork. Lovely.  Clearly they had no interest in making a dine in meal an even minimally pleasant experience.  At this they succeeded beyond measure.  The broken A/C on this hot afternoon just added to the overall ambiance of careless indifference.    The meal itself was pedestrian.  Chicken in a thick fried coating, but with a decent sauce with enough spice to know it was not just the same sweet sauce used on other dishes.
