The fried rice was yellow from the dyed chicken broth the rice was cooked in. One sprig of broccoli for contrasting color.  These folks had perfected the art of the cheap combo lunch.  No extra charge for churl.  Oh, and a can of soda - but extra for tea.   So,  there is no reason to return other than if I had masochistic tendencies.  As I do not, this place will soon be forgotten.  Written off on this site as unworthy of time, appetite, nor money.

Okay. Don't judge me harshly. It was late.  I was really hungry.  This Wendy's is close to my office.  I needed to get something quick to eat at my desk.  There it was.  Brash. Loud. Unrepentant. Singing its siren song. ("Come to me in your weakness and famishment...I will sustain you, at least for today...") I drove onto the drive thru line. Someone pulled in right behind me.  I could not get out if I wanted. I was trapped...or was I willingly caught?!  The big menu board was in front of me.  Seductively swaying in the cold rain, I was mesmerized.  I ordered, I paid. I picked it up at the next window.  I hoped no one I knew saw me. Back at the office, I took a bite of Dave's Single Special Combo with Cheese.  Better roll than I remembered.  Was that burger a tad more tasty?  A bit too salty.  Fries  lacking spine to hold straight, and bending like a willow branch in the wind. Also too much sodium chloride.   In a world in which Burger Culture has evolved several generations from Wendy's to Five Guys and Cheeburger Cheeburger, how can the poor little lass compete.   In truth, she probably can't, except in those moments of weakness when no other lover is around, and she offers her tiny hand with a vanilla frosty.

Stumbled upon Zeeno's the other day after a stop at Oxford Valley Mall to pick up something at Sears.  I just needed a snack to keep my hunger at bay.    I went it to find a brightly lit pizza joint with 8 to 10 tables along one wall, and the work area/cashier on the other.  Kitchen in the back.  It seemed fairly clean.  World Cup on the HD hanging from the wall.  I ordered two plain slices to test the water.    The chef came out of the kitchen to deliver my lunch.  The slices were smaller than normal, and the outer crust smooth rather than textured.  This was a cheese over sauce pie, where the sauce hides beneath the melted mozza.  This maintains the heat better than exposing the gravy, but also adds a lot of extra cheese to accomplish this approach.  I prefer a balance with less cheese so I can taste the sauce distinctly.  I would call this a Middle Eastern Pizza, rather than Italian.  Not bad, but not in the mainstream of East Coast tomato pie.    While it was not my favorite pizza, it was adequate for what it was.  The ingredients were fine; just not the style I like. The rest of the menu looked intriguing, especially if the kitchen was consistently eastern Mediterranean.  The gyro options might be the way to go here.

Great to have another Greek house in the area!   Greek Corner moved in about three months ago, and is still getting things settled.  Their menu is for breakfast, lunch and dinner, and offers cuisine from the Agean, as well as curtsies to the American palate with pizza and burgers.  They have not yet installed any spits for the roasting of the lamb-beef mix that goes in the traditional gyro, but grilling it on the griddle seems to do the trick quite nicely in the meantime.    The place is a former pizza parlor, and the basic elements remain unchanged.  Booths and tables along the walls and down the middle of the floor, counter and table service, and refrigeration units with drinks.  The women working there seem to be part of the family that owns the business.  They are friendly, and happy to see new customers.  They were willing to allow me to taste the Avolemono Soup to see if I liked it, without requiring the purchase of the large bowl.  That gesture won me over.  It was quite good, by the way, although thinner than the thick creamy version found at Mikonos in Ewing.    My Traditional Gyro Sandwich was a stuffed hot pita, full of nicely browned strips of lamb/beef mix, and a heavy Tzatziki Sauce, whose cool dillness played well with the hot spicy meat.  Shreds of lettuce were also wrapped inside.  The whole thing was delivered, held together tightly with thin paper, and a pile of French Fries finished the plate.  My request for a glass of cold water with lemon was replied to with a large pitcher full of ice and lime wedges.  Nice touch!   Greek Corner is only minutes from the office.  Very happy to have this lunch option so close at hand.

This is a Tale of Two Cities kind of review.   The shop sits on a concrete island on Business Rt. 1 in Penndel, Pa.  It's the kind of location where the only green you can see is the crabgrass in the cracks in the sidewalk. Not a pretty place.  Yet, the inner space is not bad - bright, lots of glass, and an open kitchen where you can see food being prepared if you care to do that in fast food joints.    The food we tried was schizophrenic.  The Western Burger (w/ A1 Sauce and large Onion Ring) was a frozen patty that was lifeless and too well done when it reached the table.  The crinkle cut fries were plentifully boring. Never do that again.  Yet, the Pressure Fried Chicken was another story all together.  The breasts were large and juicy.  The skin crisp and nicely spiced.  This seemed to be a clucker that had never been frozen.  It was among the best fried chicken I have had in the area during my recent obsession with this cuisine.    The menu is large, but it mostly revolved around deep fryer, pressure cooker and grill.  They do BBQ, Hoagies, Panini, Wraps, Soup and Salads.  Some of those choices looked pretty good as other folks wolfed them down.    The Tummy Yummies is a name that is cringeworthy, but they may just do enough things right to make it worth the occasional stop.

I have been here numerous times for meetings, but only spent the night here once.    The front desk is always efficient and friendly.  The staff working the meeting rooms know what they are doing.  The lounge areas is surprisingly comfortable at night if you don't want to spend all night in your room.  The rooms are adequate with most expected conveniences. Never had a problem with cleanliness or noise.  Comfortable beds and pillows.  Plenty of hot water.    The location just off Rt.95 is both good and bad.  It is easy to find, but not close to any services like restaurants.  You will need your vehicle to go into downtown Newtown or Yardley, but both are worth seeing and have plenty of good food options. A little further away are Trenton and Princeton.  A drive through Bucks County is always pleasant if you have the time.  Upriver are New Hope and Lambertville; both great stops for art and antique hunters.     It is certainly a viable reasonable alternative for travelers of all stripes.

The County Theater appears to be the only cinema in Bucks to show independent and limited distribution films.  For that it has my appreciation.  I certainly wish the Newtown Theater, the oldest in the country, had the same policy.  The digital projection is a big plus.   I was there last Sunday for a 4:00 pm show, and it was packed. Not an empty seat in the house! Applause to the members and others who take interest in this institution, as it makes it a  fine community resource.   If there is any downside (and I hesitate to mention it), it is that when crowded, the seats are a bit cramped, and not as comfortable as the "big house" theaters. Too, sometimes you get some attitude from the regulars who have their favorite seats, and refuse to move over to make room for another couple, forcing them to sit apart. Not much the theater can do about that.   Over all, a wonderful piece of Bucks cultural heritage alive and well today.

La Morena (The Brunette), sits on East Moreland Avenue just off the intersection with S. York Road in Hatboro, PA. It is a very small casa Mexicana, with about six tables with kitchen in the rear. It offers no parking, making for a difficult time for a vehicle if not familiar with this area. Apparently, there is an unmarked public lot across the street and down the block, but it is hard to see at night.   The menu is fairly much standard South of the Border fare, with somewhat higher than average prices, particularly in the dinner section. Service is provided by a very pleasant woman who I took to be La Morena, herself. She seems to be doing everything, including cooking, bussing, cleaning and greeting. There is one other person in the kitchen.   I ordered the chili relleno (stuffed pablano pepper) dinner, including rice, refried beans and side container of fairly fresh tortillas. The pepper was a fatty, with room for diced chicken in addition to the queso and crema. Decent red salsa poured over the top. It was good and filling, but not outstanding. Actually, the refried beans were the best part of the platter, with interesting flavor. I thought it should have been better for the $14 charge, especially since I had a similar dinner a few weeks before at a nearby Mexican restaurant for several dollars less, with much more compelling taste. The tortillas were clearly reheat jobs, as part of each was hot, while the rest was cold.   Given the dearth of parking, and the less than stellar performance of my dinner, the conglomerated experience was just okay. I think the kitchen is capable of better, but I may have missed the right selection to discover its greatness.

My orientation seems to have opened a portal to the West, and I have found myself driving through and around Wayne, Pa. recently.  Nice area. Last week I decided to slow down and smell the chili.  Found Ping Pong on my trusty Yelp mobile guide, and stopped in with son of mine for dinner.   First impressions were positive.  Clean, bright, colorful, smiling faces, pleasant aromas. We took a table along the wall and as I looked around I realized we were in a Chinese spice shop where the dishes would be measured in fire alarms.  My favorite cuisine, but not necessarily in my 13 year old's wheelhouse.  He loves Dumplings, so we went with an order of 6 fried.  I suggested we get Dan Dan Noodles so he could begin to appreciate the more gentle side of the firescale.  He was game for the Hunan Spicy Beef; a good, adventurous call.  I picked the Deep Fried Chicken with Dry Pepper, basically a spicy fried chicken dish he could assimilate.    All were very good to near excellent.  The Dumplings were perhaps the least interesting with a heavy dough shell, but well ground pork, and nice dipping sauce.  He actually left one behind.  The Dan Dan's were a big bowl full of thin noodles and a hearty pork sauce that completely covered the noodles beneath.  I had to add extra Sesame Oil to reach the desired heat, but my son was happy with them as delivered.  All gone!  The Spicy Hunan Beef was the best of the bunch - tender sliced beef in a mid-range Hunan brown sauce, Broccoli, Green and Red Chilis and a few other veggies.  Very good.  The Chicken was slightly hotter and quite tasty, but not the "chicken inferno" I had anticipated from other Szechuanese joints.  Still, just right for the initiat.    Service was timely and cordial.  The majority of the customers were Chinese, but no one seemed to mind two round eyes in their midst.  Besides, we both knew how to handle the chopsticks with aplomb.    All in all, an enjoyable repast, and one that I would certainly entertain returning to on one of my increasingly frequent trips west.    A very nice find, indeed!

Hard to beat a decent breakfast at half price.   I found their French Toast to be above average, although their coffee needs some work.    Still, when I can walk out of a restaurant after only paying 3 and a half bucks for a full plate and java, I am a happy man.   Saw a table card that said something about Tuesdays being "AYCE" Burger Days.    Very tempting.

For a small regional airport, Trenton-Mercer has a lot going for it.  First, it has contracts with Frontier and Allegiant airlines for service along the east coast and Florida, as well west to Chicago and Detroit. These are discount airlines, so if you fly light the fares will make you smile.   Second, although parking is no longer free, it is only $8 for 24 hours, in a secure lot right in front of the terminal. Park and walk right through TSA check, across the tarmac, up the stairs onto your plane. Try any of that at an international airport to the north or south.   Third, Enterprise, National, Avis and Budget have rental facilities here, and the rates are without all the extra airport fees and taxes. I have rented here twice when I needed a larger people mover for a day. Admittedly, I booked through Priceline and didn't have to deal with the rent a car games.   Fourth, the amenities are minimal, but it is a public place owned by the people of Mercer County. Think of it as a park with landing privileges. They didn't want their taxes used for first class lounges. It is seldom crowded, and the bar/restaurant Sky Lounge offers the basics for three meals and decent drink choice. You can snack and chill watching flights take off and land through the large window overlooking the runway. When was the last time you did that?   Fifth, flying lessons are available from private instructors with offices around the airport.   Sixth, living ten minutes from the terminal makes TTN part of the community, and too convenient to pass up.  Seventh, TTN has been in business since 1929, and the enterprises around the airport played an important role in WW II, and it is the home of many Fortune 500 private jets. Amelia Earhart even flew through here.   So, next time you consider flying from Trenton, maybe give yourself some extra time to explore the area. Several good bars and restos with a few minutes drive to help you on your journey.

I don't remember why Meglio's fell off my "Go To" list a few years ago, but when I drove by it last week I realized I had not been there in quite some time.  Maybe it was the new competition in Newtown that led me to other outlets for my pizza and cheesesteak fix. Maybe it was the sameness of the offerings.  Regardless, it was time for a return visit.   So, I went back for lunch a few days ago.  The space is about the same, with the wood oven on the left, and the dining room on the right.  The table layout remained the same with mostly deuces and quads around the room.  At 1, the place was buzzing.  A few business lunches, and some post-yoga cool downs.  The menu was all about pizza, cheesesteaks and salads at lunch, although the few dinner entres looked appealing.  The prices were surprisingly reasonable.  It was possible to get out for under $10 @ lunch, perhaps because the shop was in an older strip center and the rent is decent.   To ease my way back into their kitchen, I ordered a Chicken Cheesesteak with Fried Onions.  It arrived a few minutes later loaded with the prime ingredients.  The roll was soft, but fresh and pliant.  The amount of chicken in the sandy was enormous, and with the cheese and onions was a lot to eat.  The biggest pleasant surprise was how juicy it was.  It had been taken from the grill in time to avoid dryness, and the onions complemented the meat and cheese well.  I mentioned this to my lovely server, and she just smiled and said she had cooked it for me.  No reason to doubt her.   I won't let another half decade go by without returning for more dishes.  Pizza comes next.   However that turns out, I am definitely a fan of the Chicken Cheesesteak.

While the price of gasoline in Newtown seems to be higher than anywhere else in the surrounding area, the quality of the mechanics is also higher.   Steele's Gulf is a very good option should your car need repair.  They are fast, reliable, and have integrity with their work.

Had a thoroughly enjoyable lunch at the Farnsworth House yesterday.  The classic barroom was empty but for my companion and I, and we had the house and service to ourselves.    My French Onion Soup while in a smallish ceramic pot, was scalding hot, richly beefy stocked, thick with Onions, and sealed with a nutty Gruyere. The Pulled Pork Sandy was soft and mixed in a red BBQ Sauce that glazed the meat in its sticky pungence. There was a lot of it in that fresh roll which I opted to leave behind to shave a few calories off the meal.  Same with the large pile of French Fries that were good, but superfluous given the amply supply of Pork I was addressing.  My lunchmate didn't have any misgivings scooping them up and dipping them in her own excellent sauce covering the Veal A la Genoa she had ordered.    I tried a few and must admit they could put that combo on the menu as a side.   Spontaneous Poutine!   Farnsworth House is an Italian kitchen these days, and a good one at that.  In all the great things that are happening in Bordentown, Mr. Farnsworth still holds his own.    Even Bonaparte would find satisfaction here.

Nam Phuong was the last Empress of Vietnam.    Perhaps, it is fitting to name the queen of the Vietnamese houses after her.  She was born too late to enjoy her royalty for very long, and she was denied the privilege of living her life in her native land; dying in relative obscurity in France.    Her namesake is similar to her in some ways.  The restaurant is large and well run.  Chandeliers suggest a palatial guise, and the servers in black are disciplined, polite and respectful, as you would expect from a royal house. The menu is diverse to appeal to a variety of guests, and the kitchen is skilled in turning out top quality dishes that satisfy those invited to the Emperor's Table.   Even a solitary traveler such as I was treated with dignified homage. Though a busy night full of families and intriguing couples, I was given a nice table, plenty of time to decide my meal, and graceful delivery, checking on satisfaction, pickup and an offer to desire more before leaving.  I never felt rush by the staff, although the people waiting by the door might have been less patient.   My Pho with Round Steak and Tripe was excellent, with all fresh trimmings.  The broth was richly complex and a filling bowl at a very reasonable price.  The Summer Rolls were stuffed with fresh Shrimp and Ground Pork, and came with a very good Peanut Dipping Sauce.  As I ate I watched those around me enjoying all the things I wanted to try on my next visit.    I am not sure that the maxim that a Vietnamese restaurant filled with Vietnamese is a true indication of great food all the time, but it certainly was tonight.    Nam Phuong, where ever her spirit is now, would be pleased that her name is being so well cared for here in Philadelphia.

Levittown Kitchen sits at the end of a wasted commercial strip between New Falls and Emilie Roads in Levittown, PA. It is primarily a takeout Chinese shop that also makes sushi rolls and Thai noodles to widen it's appeal. There are only two tables in the front of the house, but an effort has been made to make the space attractive with a few Asian design elements.   I stopped in for a late lunch and grabbed a table after ordering Sesame Chicken at the counter from a dude wearing a backward baseball cap. The guys in the kitchen must have taken a sushi correspondence course, but skipped the class on proper costuming for fish slicers, because they lacked the proper headwear and aprons that create the sushi effect. So, try the Japanese menu at your own risk.   I prepared for the worst, but to my surprise the lunch was okay. There was ample bird cut small, with a better than expected amber goop atop average fried rice. It presented in a black plastic bowl, a step up from straight styro containers. No soup, nor drink included for the low $5.99 price. Never heard of hot tea either.   While there is no reason to rush back unless you lived in the neighborhood, Levittown Kitchen at least fairly represents the Chinese American genre dishes reasonably well. I would find more authentic cultural  skills for the other options.

I started visiting Charcoal when it was also, "Steaks and Things," about 30 years ago. In those days I lived on the Delaware River in Trenton, and came over to Yardley for an out of the way weekend breakfast/brunch.  It was a great place for a romantic wake up after a long night before.    Two massive floods and major grief later, a small riverside café has transformed into a full second story restaurant with an eastern wall of glass overlooking the river that when at peace is serenely beautiful, but when raised to anger is as dangerous as an angry rhino.  Sitting here today over a large white cup of java after an absence of more than a decade, I marveled at how light and airy this loft felt.  If you've spent time at the shore in a reverse living stilted home, you know the tree house sensation.  I was here for breakfast, and ordered the Brioche French Toast.  The room was not full, and I shared the space with various knots of people engaged in friendly conversation.  Being alone, I spoke with my server, Mary Anne, who was a natural salesperson for the establishment.  She updated me on ownership and changing cuisine, and even handed me a dinner menu to take with, hoping I would return to try some of the Small, Large, and Pasta Plates.    Although the environment and dinner menu are 5 Star worthy, the French Toast while good, exhibited a mistake often made by shops attempting the "Thick" approach to this dish.  The Brioche was generously sliced, but not left in the egg mix long enough to allow it to penetrate to the center, leaving the middle a bit dry.  Too, the grill was not hot enough to caramelize the surface nooks and crannies to give it the light crunchiness and moist center that separates the good French Toast from the great.    Looking around I noted some beautiful omelets and fresh fruit cups that hold promise. I will come back to check them out sometime soon.

International Noodles is the second incarnation of an Asian house at this location since the departure of the dearly missed, Siam Restaurant.  It appears to be operated by the same people who owned Basil Leaf and the recently replaced Asiana.    The ambiance is austere with simple tables spaced around the floor, and a grass thatch roof trim along the walls.  The hard finished floor made for a very clean appearance.  The staff the night we were there were local high school students, who were all pleasant, but somewhat lacking the comfortable personas of experienced servers.  They were fine.   The menu offers noodle based alternatives from the Pacific Rim.  Pho from Vietnam, Ramen and Udon from Japan, Pad Thai from Thailand,  spicy mein from China, and Mei Fun from Singapore, etc. We sampled the Udon with Tempura Shrimp & Veggies, and Pad Thai (Shrimp, Chicken).    The plates came out loaded with appropriately dressed Pad Thai noodles.  It looked good, and had a pleasant taste, although additional spice/heat was required to bring up the authentic flavor.  I found that while the noodles were plentiful and quite hot, the slices of chicken were room-temperature, a sign that they were prepared separately beforehand and not mixed in the wok with the sauce and noodles after they were removed from their boil. An oversight that is easily remedied with more attention to detail.    The Udon bowl was a decent representation of the Japanese soup; clear, mildly fishy, fat noodles and steaming.  Even better was the tempura that was surprisingly substantial alongside the soup.  The menu only mentioned shrimp tempura, but when the dish arrived, there were two large shrimp and several well prepared veggies, including, onion, carrots and broccoli.  Not the slightest bit oily and the star of the show.   Those who are spoiled by dining at the established restaurants specializing in these dishes both in the cities and some amazing local establishments, may find International Noodles a step below those benchmarks.  However, this place is a reasonable alternative when something closer to home, or more casual is desired.  Everything comes in around $11. per dish, so it may present some savings compared to the local competition.  JANUARY 28, 2016 - UPDATE:  This just in...The owners of International Noodles are not the same folks as the dearly departed Basil Leaf, nor Asiana.  New team in town!  The original "Danny" is now operating Lemongrass in Cherry Hill.

What can you say about the complete, in your face, sweet, gooey, dripping down your chin, jelly donut experience?  Great, right? If you go for that, and fresh hot glazed burn your tongue goodness, then this is the place for you, and everyone else with a sweet tooth. Forget the diet. Go get some!!!  PS.  Personal fave - glazed raspberry jelly filled. I see the light!

Westampton Family Diner sits at the outskirts of downtown Mt. Holly, standing sentry for all the traffic entering or leaving that historic burg.  In the middle of the last century it was about the only place to enjoy a sit down meal that wasn't grandma's house.  Those days have come and gone, and WFD has definitely seen its heyday pass it by.  Now, the center of town is coming back to life with new money and better ideas, while the old diner has yet to catch on to the new energy at the core of the city.    Really hope it can take its cues from the newer places nearby that are reinventing themselves and becoming pleasant and interesting joints for drinking and eating.  It would be a cultural shame to lose its place as the purveyor of huge plates of hash, flash and dash for the masses that it once was, and could be again with some new ideas.    When I was there earlier in the week for a quick breakfast, the first impression was of a place full of old folks both customers and staff.  It felt downright geriatric.  The countertop formica was worn and exhausted.  The equipment was several generations behind state of the art.  Dust and grime collected in the corners.  I felt a wave of fatigue overcome me before reaching the counter stool.  Coffee was required immediately.  Despite the aging optics, my simple breakfast of Coffee and toasted Corn Muffin was quite satisfying.  The java was hot and brewed with decent enough beans to alert my buds to an awakening.  The Muffin was homemade and the largest I had seen in many years.  Yes. It was fresh and very tasty.    Its location is across Rt. 541 from the court, and thus very convenient for my early arrival to beat traffic approach to work.  I will return on occasion, and hope that they can examine the new places opening up in town and adopt new style and menu to keep up with the changing tastes of the new age.

At $14 for a half dozen small cupcakes, these babies had better be the best of breed anywhere on the planet.   While they were enjoyable, they did fall short of the mark of being superlative.   First, they about half the size of a traditional cupcake, making the price twice as expensive as it first appeared.  $2.33 per is one thing, but when the equivalent of a store bought standard cupcake is more than $4.60, I have a problem with the expense.    The cake base was decent - moist, soft, and mildly tasting the way it was described.  It is a light cake, which is fine, but I prefer a denser bottom that holds more flavor.  The real star of the show was the icing/frosting on top of the crown.  It was thick, rich, creamy, sweet, and good enough to lick off and relish.  Regardless of the flavor, it came through loud and clear.  They approach addictiveness.    Overall, the experience was a mixed blessing.  While the flavors of the icing were fun and engaging, the cake bottoms were pleasant, but forgettable.  The cost being richer than the frosting threw the balance off for me, and left me in the middle of the road.

Now I remember why it is best to seek treatment at a world class teaching hospital, than to accept second best from suburban medical providers. They just know more and practice at the highest level of competence and integrity.   So, when I sought a second opinion before agreeing to a lithotripsy, I scheduled an appointment with Victor Carpiniello, M.D., on the 19th floor of Penn Medicine Washington Square, this week. Impressive offices and even more impressive people there, from reception through Dr. Carpiniello, and everyone in between. There was little wait to see the doctor after completing the standard forms/questionnaires.  He came into the examination room with a warm smile and years of experience. He knew what I was dealing with and the treatment options. If I wanted, he could take care of the condition later in the week on an outpatient surgical basis. I liked the way he talked to me, and his calm demeanor throughout.   We agreed to take care of business when suggested, but he wanted me to first have a cardiac clearance as a precaution because of my medical history. That was scheduled for two days later. Turned out, before undergoing general anesthesia for kidney stones, I would need a stress test (which I was due for anyway). That takes place tomorrow.   Given the unexpected twists and turns this situation has already taken, my decision to seek more information from a higher authority was the right one.  It is difficult to express the increased concern knowing the extra steps that are required to protect my health, while balanced by the sense of confidence and relief I also feel knowing I am in the best hands possible. No knock on my regular urologist who has tended to me for many years, but knowing I am being treated by a leading authority on these conditions; someone who is teaching other doctors how to do these procedures, offers a security blanket that makes going through all this much easier to accept, and sleep at night.   Will update this review as all the steps take place and I come out the other end.

Lucy's Café sits on the first floor of 240 W. State Street, Trenton, NJ, across the street from the State Museum/Library Complex and the Department of Education.  It is nothing fancy, but does have room for a lot of people for sit down breakfasts and lunches.  Furniture is vinyl and steel.    This morning I stopped in for breakfast for the first time.  There were only a few people there, and I was able to order directly from the cook.  I grabbed a small coffee and a table seat while waiting for the Sausage, Egg & Cheese Sandwich to be done.  When it was, the Korean owner of the shop called for me to pick it up and pay the $5 for everything.  Good price.  The sandwich was well made with a single patty, fried egg and American cheese on a fresh Kaiser roll.  A small side of home fries was included, and were nicely grilled with crisp edges.  A shake of black pepper and a squirt of ketchup and I retreated to my table to consume the beast.  The plate was Styrofoam and the fork, plastic.  Nothing fancy, but it was certainly substantial.    The taste was very good owing to decent ingredients, and a knowing hand at the grill.  Coffee was that Law brand; not the best, but strong enough to chase the morning fatigue away.    This stretch of West State Street is quiet in the summer when the legislature is out of session.  There is plenty of street parking available, making for easy in and out.  The parking meters eat quarters in 15 minute increments, so be prepared with enough to cover the time you plan to be inside.

Hong Luck is a traditional Chinese American restaurant on New Rogers Road, Levittown, PA. The same family has run the shop for over two decades. Bamboo screens and petrified blowfish are the most noticeable decor accents.   I was there for lunch earlier in the week on a first visit. My order was taken by the husband, although his wife was also out front at times. They were both friendly, if not loquacious. The menu was large, with a backpage of luncheon special combo plates. I went with the Hunan Beef, which included cup of soup (wonton) and pork fried rice.   In my experience, Hunan style is a spicy cuisine that gets it heat from a fermented black bean sauce and secondarily, Szechuan chili peppers. This dish had neither, but instead seemed to be overloaded with straight black/white pepper and salt. It made me thirsty instantly. Although the beef was thinly sliced and tender, the sauce made it difficult to enjoy. On the other hand the beef stock in the wonton soup was better than average, the dumpling not too thick skinned and the meat filling, decent. The fried rice was a bit on the hard side and had seen better days.   This isn't in my neighborhood, and it is doubtful I would return given my first taste impressions. Obviously, they have succeeded all this time without my involvement, and they will no doubt continue to do so hereafter.

Beautifully converted Lamberville, NJ mansion that offers three squares a day in a quiet, dignified house with plenty of space between the tables for intimate conversation surrounding very good victuals. All very late 19th Century.   I was there for midweek breakfast and walked in to a mostly empty restaurant.  There is an attractive marble counter with stools, but it was loaded with desserts and didn't seem the place designed to really eat. So, I walked to the next dining room, where there was one other table occupied, but so far across the room that I felt totally alone taking a smaller deuce along the opposite wall facing a window.    Each table in this room was rough cut from a larger tree trunk and finished with smooth top, but the edges left rough. Beautiful. I'd love one for home.   The menu is fairly small for the morning meal, and pricing is oriented toward higher end cafes, rather than more reasonable primarily breakfast joints. Still, my turkey sausage, fried egg and cheddar on an unusually attractive and tasty roll, reflected the gourmand focus.  Execution was superlative.  My server incorporated my choice for "lightly runny" eggs with aplomb. That is exactly what I got. Coffee from Counter Culture. Not sure why they don't use java from local roasters better than this North Carolina outfit given the trend toward local sourcing. Still, it was solid Joe, refilled gracefully as needed.   Nothing run of the mill about Café Galleria. If you're into morning romantic interludes, this is the place.

Hurricane Jack's Bar & Restaurant on New Falls Road, Levittown, PA, is one of many divey sports bars in this end of Bucks County. On a Saturday afternoon it was busy, but not a full house, with primarily men watching the Phillies as they chugged their beer and smoked their cigs between running conversations about the game. Friendly, welcoming crowd (I was wearing my Eagles Super Bowl cap), they allowed me to jump into their party.   I ordered a Sam Adams Seasonal and their Hurricane Special Burger (onions, hot pepps, provolone), medium. The ale was wet and refreshing; the sandwich large and tasty, despite the slippage into well done territory. Couldn't open my jaws wide enough to bite down on it, so I approached with knife and fork. Still juicy even with freezer time, and we'll worth the $6.95. Hurricane also does homemade potato chips as a side with the burgers. They were really good and well peppered, making the optional fries unnecessary. The surprise star in a supporting role.  I hung out for a while after I was done eating to watch the end of the game, and enjoy the regulars. Even with the multitude of similar inviting taverns around Levittown, Hurricane Jack's is a great low budget watering hole to chill.   Lots of choices are a good thing.

If a cozy country breakfast/brunch is your thing, then The Fancy Fig on Second Street Pike in Wrightstown, PA., is singing your song. Hidden in The Gathering, a small group of shops and offices in the heart of "downtown" Wrightstown, and cattycorner from Ralphie's Tavern at the intersection with Penn's Park Road, it may take a few minutes to find The Fig, but if you walk into what appears to be the inner courtyard, you will find it waiting there for you.   Stepping inside the first impression is of a bakery or small deli with kitchen behind the wall, and dining area off to the right. I was greeted by my server, who invited me to sit anywhere.  There was a group of guys (and two priests) sitting at the largest table, so I moved past them and took a small table against the rear window.  Auspicious to have my morning meal blessed by the local clergy. I was brought a small laminated menu and the first cup of their locally roasted coffee.    The java was joltingly strong and good, and I savored it as the chef put together my favorite breakfast sandwich. It arrived on a ciabatta roll, with egg and sausage links hanging over the edge. Didn't mind at all. They also offered a tiny square dish of fresh fruit, including one gigantic blackberry surrounded by watermelon and cantaloupe. It was all quite good. Fresh, locally sourced, and hot off the iron. Very good sammy!  The manager came over to inquire of my satisfaction. I gave her the right answer, and began a short conversation about the business and sources of their ingredients.  Most interestingly, the coffee beans were roasted in nearby New Jersey by a family member in the Joe business. "Crescent Moon" I think she said.  She suggested that the decaf was even better than the premium blend, so I requested a refill of that genre. She was right.  It had a more interesting flavor profile, but without the kick.    The view from the window of the interior court area was peaceful on this Indian Summer morn. It made for a perfect setting to start the day.  Open for a year, The Fancy Fig is a cool spot to enjoy your morning over quality coffee and a solid homemade breakfast.

Ali Baba is a Halal Afghani house on Bustleton in Northeast Philly. It is primarily take away, but there are a few tables if you prefer to eat your food hot from the grill.  We ordered a chicken veggie samosa as an app, and chicken kofta/beef tikka plate for the entre. Everything was to share. The time to prep the dinner was 20 minutes. No problem. We were enjoying the aromas and foot traffic coming in for take out.   Our meal arrived on time and looked great. Nicely grilled, with a load of long grain browned rice, a small side salad and piece of bread on a white plate. The samosa was larger than Indian style, and was more like a calzone.  Excellent. Everything else was very good. The beef was well spiced and the Korma was ground chicken with a pleasant savoriness. Couldn't finish the rice.   However, service was an issue. The food was served, but we were not given plates, nor silverware. We had to ask for each twice, as the server could not seem to remember what we needed. Same with our drinks. Had to return to the counter to request them from the owner/chef. Halfway through the meal the guy realized that we were using flimsy paper plates, and offered us real ones (If we wanted...). We declined, as we didn't want to play with our food at that point.   A Four Star meal with Two Star service.

TWO SLICE LUNCH REVIEW  Stopped in to Special Pizza City on Olden Avenue Extension in Ewing, NJ, today for a quick lunch on a beautiful day. Plenty of parking, but a surprisingly small footprint inside with tables crowded together requiring side sliding to reach those against the wall.   I asked for a regular slice and one Brooklyn square, well done. Order taken with a smile. Seven dollars and change. Looked good on the paper plates. Bigger than average.   The undercarriage of the plain slice was thick and held the topside firmly. First bite was a heavy crunch through a thick crust and formidable layer of cheese. Nice, but neither the crust, cheese, nor red sauce layer had much flavor. The balance of cheese and sauce was out of whack, with way too much yellow and too little red. Then, half way through the wedge, the molten cheese separated from the base and slid in a gooey mass on to the plate.  End of that mess.   The Brooklyn square was better, but not enough to save the overall experience​. It did not fall apart and had a somewhat better flavor profile, with fresher mozza and basil added on top.  Still, the taste was weaker than available in better Italian tomato pie parlors.   Trenton has some great pizza shops. This is not one of them.

I was thinking "Mykonos" as we drove to Mikonos Restaurant on Scotch Road in Ewing, NJ.  The Aegean island is a place I hung out for a while in an earlier life, drinking Gerovasilliou and Agiorgitiko to excess in the harbor side tabernas by day and surrendering to the liltingly haunting Bouzoukis by night.  I couldn't share my reveries, but I wondered how close to my recollections this Greek house by the same name would come to those wild Hellonic daze.    It wasn't fair to even entertain the possibility that there would be any similarity; after all, that was life in a mystic age long gone from this coil.  Still, it did serve to awaken something long dormant, and while this is the age of dark cynicism, the place had enough pictures on the walls and aromas wafting through the room to allow for a moment of silent appreciation. Wine saturated memories are sometimes enough.  The food was pretty good, too.    Our opening salvo of Avgo Lemono Soup was Star Dog Champion delicious. Creamy, Lemon bite, soft Chicken chunks, and Rice.  Our three spoons fought for each drop.    The follow up for two of us was the tour de force Liga Apo Ola for 2, a huge platter with ample Moussaka, Spanakopeta, Pastitsio, Dolmades, and maybe something else I have forgotten, served with a metal spatula to aid in distribution.  They were all exceptional, although the Stuffed Grape Leaves had more  dry rice filling than I recall from past experiences.  My guests had never eaten Greek cuisine before, and they were so impressed that they tried to duplicate the Lemon Soup at home the next day.    Our third member ordered a Chicken Souvlaki Platter.  It looked great (see photo), but my taste of the chicken surprised me with the strange toughness of the meat.  He gamely ate everything, but I could tell he was struggling with it.  A large slab of Moussaka from our plate was the least we could do to help him out.   But for that last bit of news, this was a 5 Star dinner.  We will return in due course for the Avgo Lemono and further exploration of the menu.  Those Gyros that went by looked amazing!

I finally made it to Felix's Caketeria on Christmas Eve and purchased a dozen of their unique creations to bring to the family celebration.    Walking in I was first impressed with the warm aromatic shop.  The display case is stocked with an amazing assortment of cupcakes and their bigger siblings that can be baked for weddings and other occasions. Everything was colorful and shining.  The staff was warm and professional and clearly proud of their work, as they should be.  I had no real idea which varieties to select, so I asked the charming woman behind the counter to do it for me, and she obliged.  She even offered to hand write a cheat sheet so I wouldn't forget what I had.   She alerted me that the shop was not "nut free."  Good catch as one of the young nephews has a serious peanut allergy.  The cupcakes were $3/ and $33/doz.  At first I was a bit taken aback by the price, but as I examined the products I realized that I would never do that much detail work for so little compensation.  So, I walked out with two plastic containers especially formed to hold 6 of those sweet babies each.    Now, I admit to not being a Cupcake kind of guy - if sweets are my undoing, they will be donuts and homemade cookies and pies.  So, while I marveled at the creative names and imagined the richness of the buttercream icing, I did not really know what to expect.  When I arrived in western Pennsylvania 5 hours later with my contribution to the dessert table I was surprised to watch the women in the family stop what they were doing and "kvell" over them.  They actually began to negotiate with each other over which delight they wanted, or were willing to share.  The other fresh-out-of-the-oven pumpkin and pecan pies, plates full of cookies, etc., were momentarily forgotten in their lust for these petite morsels of lathered dough in paper dresses.  Some were even taken aside and hidden in the cupboard; staking an absolute claim.    After sating ourselves over a great meal in the Allegheny Mountains, we finally reached dessert time.  The Oreo, Gingerbread Cheesecake, Chocolate Dirt, Tiramisu, and Lemon Drop sacrificed themselves first.  But, they were not devoured, but savored with each mini spoonful.  Eyes rolled and gasps of rapture escaped lips.  I selected a Carrot Cake plump tarte.  It was exactly like a great full size carrot cake with the creamiest, yet not overly sweet, icing imaginable.  Yes. I rubbed my fingers over the plate where it sat after ravishing its body to enjoy every molecule.  Mixed with fresh brew kaffe it was the perfect ending to a wonderful afternoon and meal in Westmoreland County.  For a few minutes the talk shifted from hunting to the more refined world of tiny cakes in tight skirts.    I did hear a few less than sterling comments on one or two of them, but nothing to seriously detract from an otherwise otherworldly experience.   Merry Christmas to all, especially those I have come to know and appreciate on Yelp.  Have a cupcake and reflect on all that is right in your lives.

Steele's Gulf and Steele Rick Service Station are the same place. Yelp should combine them.  This is an honest repair shop, with a family that has an excellent reputation for reliability and good communication with its customers.

The addiction has not improved, and if anything it has gotten worse.   Turns out, KK has a fundraising plan that allows the purchase of a larger quantity of their sinfully outrageous donuts to non-profits doing fundraising for their organizations at a nice discount. I guess that helps salve the gluttonous conscience when participating with your church or scout troops, but ordering most of the donuts for yourself.  The thought of someone else eating your donuts is just too much to bear.    May as well man-up and accept the fact that the crack they put in the donut fillings and glaze is overwhelming you, and that a stint in an in-patient addiction center is the only way to deal with this monster habit.    A hot cup of coffee to help wash them down is a solid second option.
See. RITE AID PHARMACY @ this location for reviews.

I don't like to date myself, but some of us remember the amazing burgers that downtown Trenton was famous for back in the day. Neon on Hanover Street, Tremont  Lounge on East State, The Famous also on East State closer to Montgomery.  These establishments' handmade patties and local Colonial Bakery rolls were the stuff of legend. Not even the original Rossi's in the Burg could hold a candle to these masterpieces, unless you valued immense size over eye rolling OMG juicy substance. (It was Neon that introduced me to horseradish to perfect a burger.)  Those vaunted halls have gone to Valhalla to feed the gods.  Lucky deities.   What generated these meat puck reveries was lunch today at Checkers, the dive bar/resto on S. Warren Street. The reviews spoke glowingly about the open grill kitchen and in hushed tones about the burgers. Would I be fortunate enough to séance with the burger-essence of yesteryear? The First Bite would tell the tale.  I took a big one and broke into a smile.  Excellent fresh ground beef, hand shaped, grilled to the desired medium finish, nicely sautéed sweet onion on top, well melted American cheese in between, and light local bakery roll holding it all together.  The taste was so pleasurable that I closed my eyes for a moment to savor it completely.  Just the right amount of grease to assure proper digestion.  The side red potato salad was homemade and without too much mayo.   While it wouldn't be fair to directly compare a Checker's Burger with those of its Trenton ancestors which have attained divine status, the fact that this experience brought those sainted heroes to mind is serious praise, indeed. Next time I'll request horseradish and see if the reality comes closer to the blessed memory.

Morrisville Plaza has been attempting a comeback for as long as I can remember. After the new bagel place failed last year it became a forlorn strip of despair on this end of Trenton Road. Since, a new cupcake shop, Pizza Hut and Fat Jack's BBQ have opened their doors. Three course meal just by walking to these nearby stores.   Yesterday, son and I visited FJB for early dinner around 5:45. The place was empty, but for a couple at one of the tables. All ordering is done at the cashier, where we were handed paper three fold menus to peruse. There were a limited number of choices between pork, beef and chicken in standard smokehouse styles. The ribs were much more expensive than other items, and were not visible nor smellable and thus hard to choose without some evidence of excellence to tempt us. As first timers, we went to their sandwiches as the way to sample their kitchen skills. The Notorious P.I.G. for the tennager and The Devil's Own Burger for the old man. Fries are the regular accompaniment, but I selected their BBQ beans for a buck upcharge.   We sat at a table along the wood planked wall. It had three bottle rockets with their various sauces, although no ketchup for the fries. The PIG had a load of bacon, pork belly and pulled pork with a drizzle of maple syrup and scoop of coleslaw between the jaws of a decent roll. Son squirted a mix of their magic sauces and dug in. He seemed content with his meal, although mentioning he liked the BBQ in Virginia better.   My burger was creative with all the varieties of hot peppers and sauce thrown on top of the puck, bacon, cheddar and frizzled onion. Liked it, but the ground beef tasted far from fresh, and more likely a freezer occupant for a while. It cuddah been a contender had the meat been spared the ice dungeon. The beans were tart and savory despite being watery.   There is better BBQ to be had in the area (Mission), and even in Morrisville (Winckler's), but Fat Jack will do if you don't feel like more time driving. Jack could pick up some pointers from these other places on how to enhance the quality of the overall smoked meat experience.

Sometimes, the sun shines a little brighter, and a public employee is so on the ball as to provide great information that saves time and restores faith in humankind.    It was time to renew my Pa. Drivers License; not the funnest task in a bureaucratic world.  I had already done the online work and received the document needed to submit to the PennDot office in order to qualify for a new photo license.  When I arrived at the Bensalem Service Center and beheld the multitudes waiting to be helped, I momentarily lost buoyancy.  How long would this take?    Luckily, I asked the security officer at the information desk about how to proceed.  She was in total command.  She asked if I knew where Fairless Hills was.  I did.  She advised that there was a Photo License Center on Oxford Valley Road, that had no waiting most of the time.  She estimated it would be at least 30 minutes before anyone would talk to me in Bensalem, and recommended I drive right over to Fairless and take care of business.    I did so.  It was on my way to work, and a great place to know about.  I was there in 15 minutes.  I was the only person in the storefront when I entered.  The photo person beckoned me to her.  I handed her the document.  She asked a few simple questions about organ donations.  She offered to take a second shot when the first made me look like a gorilla.  I was out in under 5 minutes.    Amazing!  That PennDot should be efficient enough to delegate photo license renewal to its own space, demonstrates planning beyond what most public bureaucracies are able to contemplate.  Thanks to everyone who made this possible, and who carried it off so smoothly.    You guys deserve a raise.

Dominick's Pizzeria is in the Anchor Crossing Center at the intersection of Rt. 413 and Windy Bush Road in Wrightstown, so don't be confused by the Newtown address shown in many places.   The entire center was eerily empty on a late Sunday in August. Only Dom's and Happy Panda were open for business. We stopped in for a light bite on the way to Doylestown's County Theater.  I couple of slices of regular pizza and an ice tea were inexpensive at under $5.50.  Friendly counterman. Clean shop.   The pizza came out of the reheat oven quickly and the cheese had nicely remelted. After sprinkling on crushed chili pepper flakes and allowing some excess oil to drip onto the paper plate the first slice was lifted, folder lengthwise, and brought to mouth. The slice held its form well, with firm crust reinforced by the vertical fold. First test passed.  The tip was hot and the bitten off tip was pleasantly crunchy.  Second test passed. After that, however, the grade began to slip.  The taste test was a weak result, as the sauce was bland and the cheese undistinguished.  It was pizza, but not a strong contender for top rank.   The second slice compounded the issue by failing to hold form after folding, and sagging in the middle before the tip could be bitten. But, for the chili flakes, the slice would have really left too much to be desired. With the added heat, it was adequate and filling, if uninspired.   Compared to the other alternatives in Newtown, just a few miles down the road, Dominick's pizza falls below Marcos and Newtown Pizza, and at approximately the same level as Dolce Carini Pizzeria.   I will return to sample other parts of the menu, but I am in no rush to do so.
There are two entries for this establishment for some reason.   Be sure to check them both to catch all the reviews.

I never noticed this tiny pizza parlor nestled at the end of a small strip center with only 4 shops, but my never ending search for the perfect tomato pie brought me here late last week as the clouds gathered beckoning rain.   Although small in stature, the menu is large with the usual suspects to be found in an Italianesque joint that has to move fast and be creative to complete in a universe full of larger predators. When I walked in, I was greeted by a short man (from central casting), wearing a backward baseball cap and speaking with a warm Spanish accent.  I asked if there were any slices of tomato pie available.  He apologized for not having any at the ready, but immediately offered to make a personal size TP for me if I had 10 minutes to wait.  Of course I did.   I watched as he retrieved an aluminum dough container, peeled out the slowing rising mass and slapped it onto his cool granite countertop.  Fingering, spreading, stretching, spinning, tossing it just enough to get it to the right size without over-manipulating it to toughen the finished product.  He laid out the mozza neatly around the disk, and then flicked globs of chunky tomato sauce on top like he was Michelangelo in his abstract period. Satisfied, he slid his wooden long handled pizza mover underneath, turned, and gently shook it off onto the hot oven floor.    About 8 minutes later he was walking toward my table with a steaming large plate on which sat my personal Tomato Pie.  It was beautiful and its heat wave struck my nose and eyes at the same instant, causing me to catch my breath and shed a small tear.    I picked up the first wedge and held it for a moment.  It was straight and true, never wavering nor bending under the weight of the topside.  The under carriage was beautifully scorched, but not burnt.  First bite was amazing. My teeth cut through the tomato and cheese and felt the heat on my upper palate. My lower jaw clamped down, closing mid slice on a crisp firm crackery crust.    Magnificent!  I had intended to eat half and bring home the rest, but it was so perfectly balanced between taste, texture and eye-rolling excellence, that I knew it would lose something essential if I did not eat the whole thing at that moment.  So, I did, and skipped dinner that night.   It's hard to tell if this experience could be duplicated, or if I had just stumbled into a apex moment that was beyond everyone's ability to recreate.  Regardless, this time was mine, and I offered thanks for having lived this one.

Wawa, the roadside rest stop version, named after the famous village in Pennsylvania of that name, has it all figured out.    Give people choice.  In coffee, sandwiches, snacks.  And, they will come.  Make all things reasonably good and competitively priced, and they will become loyal.    The newest shops take their cues from 21st Century design.  Large, airy, clean, with gasoline out front, and bathroom in the back. People like this feel and will find their way to them.  Just like Sheetz, Rutters, and major road service areas, they provide a more satisfying experience then the older, smaller, mini shop version of the late 20th C.   They don't offer the variety of a Starbucks or other national chain vendors, but their proprietary issue is decent, and saves a whole lot of shekels.   I can't say that I am a fan, but the concept and experience is growing on me.

OCI Bar & Grill is off the beaten path along Neshaminy Creek in Hulmeville, PA. I thought I was in the wrong place on a narrow winding road until I saw the actual building in front of me. It feels a little like Middle Earth, yet the joint is cozy and dim with a nice size bar and several TVs showing sports (The Preakness was on while we were there).   We were there for the "Make Your Own Burgers," and after settling in on a 4 stool hightop, we found the forms to be completed and the little golf pencils, and went to work. The process was to check off choice of meat, cheese, condiments and accompaniments (some free, some not), and the roll desired. Base price is $9.99, but with upgrades the price can jump a few bucks. Fresh cut fries are also available for an extra $2. I went with what I though was a patty melt (onions, spicy mayo and swiss cheese on Jewish rye), while son opted for sautéed shrooms and red peppers on brioche.    Although we both asked for a medium finish, the pucks were more medium well, without pink centers. Regardless, they were both juicy and delicious, with no sign of freezer life. Really very good. The only downside, and this could be on me for thinking the kitchen knew what the Jewish rye was for, was that what I got rather than a Patty Melt was a burger on plain, ungrilled bread. It just didn't work without a crisp bite to the rye from time on the hot steel.  I kicked the slices to the curb and ate everything else. Next time, I will specify the bread should be grilled. The fries came in a small deep fry stainless basket and were also quite good.   Despite those issues, OCI is a cool place to hang out. Prices are good, and once the kinks are worked out, the kitchen should turn out quality dishes. They are on the right track.

Mexican Taste sits in the Mallard Creek Shopping Center in Richboro, PA. It is a small shop with about a dozen tables and minimal decorations. This was an Italian restaurant before, and the pizza ovens can be seen through the kitchen service window.  We made reservations for Wednesday evening, although it wasn't necessary as the house was not crowded. Service was provided by a lovely attentive young woman who handled everything in the front of the store.   We ordered the following: chorizo shrimp burrito, ground beef enchilada, steak fajitas and chicken flautas (an appetizer on the menu, but big enough for a meal).  Other traditional Mexican dishes like tortas, sopas, homemade horatcha drink and fresh whole fish were not on the menu.  Given the relative lack of Latin American population in this part of Bucks County, it is understandable that they limit their offerings more to the American palate.   By way of full disclosure, I work in New Jersey where the presence of Central Americans is far greater and the number of ethnic restaurants reflects the larger customer base.  Thus, those kitchens serve primarily a Hispanic audience, and provide deeper possibilities for quality plates from the homeland.  It would not be fair to directly compare these very different food sources. At the same time, it is impossible to not be cognizant of the similarities and differences.    While all of found our meals to be decent, none of us thought they were outstanding. The steak for the fajitas was ample, but a bit dry from overcooking. The sauces on each of our dinners were not spicy enough, an unnecessary concession to the stereotype that Gringos don't like spicy food. Au contraire - we like it a lot, and appreciate the challenge. The flautas were big and stuffed well with shredded chicken and cheese, but they would have been improved if there was more chili in the mix.    Mexican taste is an okay introduction to Mexican food, but it could be so much more if they respected that their customers could handle the real deal, and the kitchen did not compromise on the true sabor Mexicana.   Just do it!

At the end of January, leaking into February, the largest gem, rock and mineral show in the world opens in Tucson.  It takes over the entire city, and very much like a gathering of gypsies it turns this high desert town into an amazing display of every of stone imaginable (and quite a few you never thought of).  For rock hounds this is the pilgrimage you yearn to make at least once in your life.    For those of us with businesses in gems and jewelry, it is nearly a "must go" if you want to see what is being taken out of the ground around the planet, and what very creative people are doing with them.  I have been on both ends of this experience, both buying and selling what I believed others would find attractive and workable.  My focus has been colored gems and stones (aquamarine, peridot, spinel, tourmaline, topaz, varieties of agate), while offering pieces that I found on buying trips to Mexico and Asia, both natural and antique.    It is a wonderful high to surround myself with these beauties of nature for a week, and allow their glow to filter into the mindspace where new ideas generate.  And, when not exploring the multitude of temporary shops set up in motels, or campgrounds around town, Tucson itself offers excellent diversions via great restaurants, parks, and hotels.  At first I went alone and rushed back after a few days, but seeing how extremely overwhelming the show was I began bringing my family to make a vacation of it.  It has become the place we most enjoy hanging out, especially when the winter drears on and on.

The first thing noticed entering Coffee House Too was how the people working there embrace your presence. From Josh the manager, to Channelle (#5) our server, right to the guy bussing the tables, everyone made a nearly superhuman effort to welcome us and show something of their personalities. Under some circumstances that could have felt cloying, but with these folk it was totally genuine and not overdone.   The dining area was up a narrow steep flight of stairs with the names of Philly neighborhoods written on the risers.  Good idea for keep our eyes where we were walking to avoid missteps.  The second story was bright with windows facing east, and yellow/gold painted walls all around. Lots of chachkas and potted plants. Channelle was to us in a blink, offering great coffee and mimosas/bloodies/orange juice.  The breakfast menu was a large page with their signature dishes - Hangover Sandwiches, Regular Breakfast Egg Sandies, Omelets, Waffles, etc. Even before ordering a Pastrami Omelet and Original Hangover creation, we received two homemade muffins compliments of the house.  Alcohol and bakery sweets gratis, just because...and, Josh stopped by to introduce himself and inquire where we were from and how we knew about CH2. Pleasant conversation.  I'm not a pastrami guy, but my companion sure loved the load of smoked beef, Swiss cheese and sautéed onions that filled her 3 egg plate.  My Original Breakfast Hangover Sandwich was a glorious monstrosity of 3 more eggs, garlic buttered sesame seed loaf, cheddar, sausage and their hash browns all in the mix.  Put hash browns inside my eggs and you know one of the keys to my soul.  With the first bite, my eyes involuntarily rolled to the back of my head, and I am told I emitted a low yowl. My inner wolf was free for a moment. Don't remember, but it was that good.  Don't think I bit anyone.  Doubtless, we will return to this or the other Coffee House Too in the near future.  We liked it a lot!

If you're looking for a large college oriented sports bar with lots of room, loud ambient noise, and a decent menu, Landmark Americana just may be what you are searching for. Right off the campus of The College of New Jersey in the new Campus Town commercial center, this place has room for hundreds in a boisterous barroom with rectangular bar, and slightly less obstreperous dining area.   I was there for a light bite supper while being entertained by the Saturday late afternoon/evening NFL playoff game.  In this place, the college basketball contest between Kansas and Iowa State was getting a lot more attention. I guess that's to be expected in a campus hangout with its own team.   I caught the end of the weekend happy hour, and grabbed a pint of Sam Adams Boston Lager for $3. I also ordered a bowl of Baked Onion Soup and their Brussel Sprouts app.  The soupe aux oignons was a small bowl with all the right ingredients, and melted gruyere all around the lip. It was pretty good, and most importantly, hot, on that cool rainy eve.  The choux de Bruxelles were halved, broiled and doused in a tart vinaigrette and bacon bits. There were a lot of them. Very tasty and an excellent choice, if I don't say so myself.   While my college days are mostly behind me (my son will be a freshman in September), I can still enjoy the high energy exuberance and animal spirits loose in the chamber. With an extended happy hour and better than average sports bar kitchen, this joint has a chance to succeed and see me again.

Ariana's Pizzeria & Italian Restaurant on Levittown Parkway is a basic pizza parlor with booths and tables that seems primarily to toss and bake tomato pies and related sandwiches, calzones, wraps, etc., that can be found in most red sauce establishments. They also have a short list of dinners and entrees that looked appealing on the menu.   We were all hungry and took the chance on the bigger (more expensive) meals, rather than the safer sandwich route. To some extent we regretted that decision. Each came with small side salad, heated torpedo rolls and butter, and a bed of pasta under the chicken offerings. Salad was fine. Bread hot and crusty, and spaghetti copious.   Problem was that while the marsala was decent with a nice load of fresh mushrooms in a sauce closely resembling what it should be, the Ricci and Abbruzzio chicken dishes were not quite right.  The Ricci lacked much flavor despite the load of sauce and melted mozza, and a corner of the pasta was much cooler than the rest of the platter, like it had been sitting too long far from the stove. A little red and black pepper in the mix while cooking would have made a big difference. The Abbruzzio with the large bore pasta looked great, but the chicken was overcooked and tough, and the sauce flavor, AWOL.  I was overall content with my dinner, but the fact that my family ate so little of their's reflected the reviews they would write if asked. We took the leftovers home to see with we could improve them with a little doctoring. Yet, at more than $15 per dish, we were unhappy with our choices and the abilities in the kitchen.   Teaches us to go out to eat hungry. Definitely clouded our judgment on how to attack the menu.   2.5 STARS

Second Street Bagels is under new management and working hard to up the quality of the rounders exiting their backroom oven. From my first bite this late September morning it seems they are succeeding.   I was fortunate enough to ask the owner where the bagels were made, and he was happy to take me on an impromptu tour of the operation. I followed him behind the counter and through the kitchen door. The large boiling pot was full of brine and the rack was full of aluminum trays with bagels just out of their bath and chilling before going into the oven for finishing. I knew that the boil helped set the crust's consistency, and that lye or sugar/molasses water were traditionally the elixir of choice, but didn't know that brine was an option.   It certainly worked to produce a excellent bagel. Thin crust. Nice bite. Pleasant mildly salty malty dense texture within. With sweet butter and nutty Swiss slices, it was an enjoyable bagel. Decent java, too.   Wish Second Street Bagels well with its new ownership team.

If mid-20th Century stainless steel railroad car diners are your thing, then Daddypops on York Road in Hatboro, PA, is a "must see" stop on your diner tour.  It sits on the main street in town, all shiny and bright over all these years. The granite counter is split by the kitchen entrance, with a half dozen spinners on each side, and creatively anchored at each elbow by an old barber's chair.  The outer wall is all booths and large windows. The joint oozes Americana charm.   The menu consists of one sheet, with breakfast on one side, and lunch on the other. Best to plan early meals, as the hours are only from 6:00 AM to 2:00 PM. I sat at the far left counter where I could see the entire dining area.  The two women working the floor were friendly, but respectful - no one called me, "Honey." They were efficient, and ever ready with a hot coffee pour. I sipped my java while awaiting the arrival of my french toast.   The three bisected thick slices of brioche were served on an oval plate that barely contained its load.  Side dish full of butter cups and Kraft syrup was close at hand for proper doctoring.  I could see that the bread had bathed in the egg/vanilla mix long enough to soak through to the core. The surface was nicely caramelized with enough crispy edges to provide the texture I like.  Allowing time for the butter to melt and run, and the syrup to absorb, I was quickly ready to dive in.    It was very good.    No dry spots.  No eggy extrusions. No scorch marks. Nothing fancy at this traditional meal hall. Just perfectly finished egg toast fry that was a pleasure to consume. Old fashioned, just like the house it was made in.

Most, if not all, TJ Maxx stores are the same.  Same layout. Same labels.  Same prices.  Same long wait at check out.    While I don't shop here for a fashion statement, they do provide a fair assortment of the basic necessities of haberdashery - primarily, dress shirts, socks and other garments that come packaged in multiples, at steep discounts off the MRP.  (Right, that is why they are also known as, "unmentionables.")  So, this warehouse appears to be smaller than others in the region, but the inventory seemed about the same.  If you have patience, and enjoy the sport of bargain hunting, this could be one of your stake out safaris.   Word of caution. Don't trust the sizes/prices posted on the store-attached tags.  They are often wrong.  Always check the garment directly to save the hassle of getting the wrong size and being forced to make returns.  After all, TJ Maxx is about saving money; not your convenience, nor fashion sense.   Caveat emptor!

PIZZA REVIEW:  Bacco Centro is a three store Italian chain in Bucks and Montgomery Counties specializing in fast casual pizza, salads, sandwiches and larger dishes in an attractive, comfortable environment. Their Richboro shop is the latest addition in the new commercial core of town on Second Street Pike. We stopped in for a late lunch after visiting Tanner's Farmers Market for our supply of fruits and veggies. Cat was our server.  The menu was interesting, but given the first time there and the hour of the day, we opted for their Brooklyn Pie with Meatballs, figuring we would have a small sample in house and take the rest home for the boys. As we waited, Cat brought us a small plate of cheese garlic bread. It was a pleasant forespice made from their pizza dough, but without plenty a garlicky pecorino.    The square Brooklyn arrived on a thin wood server and was settled on a wire basket stand mid table. It looked great in red, white, green and brown. First bite impression was crisp, firm and flavorful. Cut into twelve squares the edges were firm and easily held their weight without equivocation. The red sauce was nicely done with strong hints of garlic, basil and salt, counterbalanced by the basil and mozzarella. It was outstanding! The reheat job at home this evening was nearly as good according to the accounts by our sons.   Bacco deserves our pizza business given the paucity of quality tomato pie in Newtown (aside from Vince's). If their sandwiches and entrees are as good, they will have a long line of loyal customers.

If you enjoy throwback mid-twentieth century breakfasts and lunches, you really should give Sneddon's Luncheonette a visit. In the middle of Bridge Street in the Jersey Delaware River town of Lambertville, it is an excellent example of counter centered food service just as it was 70 years ago.  Formica countertop, a dozen spinners, open grill kitchen, and lovely ladies pouring joe and slinging hash up and down the line. Sneddon's is one of those places where you really can eat the atmosphere.   My morning stop to break my fast included several cups of hot java from the Bunn-O-Matic, and a short stack of french toast, served in tandem by two women who were straight from central casting. No extra charge for the charming small talk. There were three egg toast alternatives on the board, and I chose the standard white bread dipper, so to start with the basics and hopefully work my way up the list.    Gotta say, that the FT was the weakest element of the experience. I watched as the cook put the bread in a bowl of whipped egg and dropped them onto the hot steel.  He was multi-tasking and could have been more attentive to my space on the grill. What I received were two very eggy slices of Wonder Bread, where a lot of the egg was still on the surface, and had not completely absorbed into the center of the bread.  Given how thin they were, the absence of moist egg in the core was surprising (and a disappointment). It wasn't bad, and the melted butter and syrup certainly made the experience okay, but it could have been much more with a little more TLC in the preparation.   Still, I enjoyed the experience of finally getting to this institution.  Service was fun, the coffee was hot and ample, and the room itself like eating in a museum.  I was told the breakfast sandwiches and corn beef hash were stars, and will give them both a try on my next visit.

Golden One is a new Chinese American kitchen just behind Neshaminy Mall in the same center as DMV. It is a large room with well spaced tables and a fast takeaway operation. The menu is extensive and they do have a sushi guy slicing and wrapping seaweed.   My first impression was positive for a simple Egg Foo Young plate with Egg Roll, Wonton Soup and white rice. The base stock for the soup was chicken broth that was not too salty and had decent wonton/dumplings that were not thick skinned, nor with questionable meat filling. The egg roll was even better with adequate roast pork mixed with cabbage and a few greens. The EFY was two pancakes filled with more pork and veggies and a better than average brown sauce that seems to have been prepared just in time.   Overall, I liked this meal on their Combination menu for dinner. I particularly appreciated the absence of obligatory broccoli florets, which is way overdone by most Chinese restaurants.   The house being clean with friendly service was also a pleasant positive touch.   Yes. I grade these places on a curve.

I am not certain how many names this tiny end of strip Chinese house uses to attract attention, but, I drove by yesterday looking for Little Basil and found the awning in front of their shop was still shown as, "Levittown Kitchen." It had another name before that, but ownership may have changed. No doubt, however, that both listings are active on Yelp, despite the fact that they seem to be paying for advertising as Little Basil only.   Not that this approach to advertising changes anything about their cuisine. It is the same two table China house offering Thai options in addition to the traditional Sino/American fare. I liked their general's chicken and egg roll lunch deal. Better than some; not as good as others. Their sauce seemed to have been freshly made and not as heavily goopy as most.   I am interested to know whether using different names for their restaurant actually is good for either business. Can't fault them for trying something unusual.

Found in the Fareway Market on Germantown Avenue, Chestnut Hill, Poppy's Cafe is a cubbyhole of a shop dealing in good coffee and a few sweet cookie and sliced pound cake to keep their cash register ringing up sales.   The multigenerational family running the business is friendly and knowledgeable about their products, and seem to enjoy spreading their information to those customers who ask.   I chowed on a fresh chunk of vanilla iced pounder, washed down by a medium roast java lightened with milk. Very pleasant combo for the drive home.

Ateethi has nothing to do with mastication, although it may seem that way from its name. Rather, it is a hybrid North and South Indian kitchen in an old commercial strip at the corner of Grant Avenue and Krewstown Road in Northeast Philadelphia, very close by Bustleton.   It opens at 5:00 pm for dinner most days, so we found ourselves waiting for the flag to go up when we arrived a few minutes early in advance of scheduled foot massage nearby @6. Looking around we saw about twenty basic tables and metal framed chairs in a dimly lit room, with a large mural of the Taj Mahal on the back wall.  The orange tones and low wattage bulbs made for a rather dim perspective. But, our eyes adjusted and the menu became legible and was fairly extensive in its offerings.  Because there were Indo-Chinese dishes, we headed in that direction as it crossed many of our tastebud preferences, and it is not as readily available in most Indian shops.   Starting with Gobi Manchurian as an app, we received a long rectangular platter of cauliflower florets, onion and peppers in a heavy dark ruby chili sauce.  The veggies had a thin breading and had been fried enough to permit the outer shell to be somewhat crispy, while the heavy sauce held many spicy secrets that made our palettes shout for joy.  As entrees we had Chilli Chicken and their Baingan Bharta (mashed eggplant), and garlic naan to soak up every drop of sauce left on the plates. We discovered that the Manchurian sauce on the cauliflower was basically the same as the Chilli used with the chicken. Both were very good, but no need for both on the same night. Perhaps, they should use the same name to eliminate this confusion. The Bharta was extra hot, and delicious enough to make my nose run. Glad I had that extra napkin!  This was a very good and tasty Indian meal. Prices were good, too. We would definitely return to discover more about their offerings, especially the vegetarian options.  Services was informative and efficient, if not overly friendly.

The oldest movie theater in the USA, and a registered historic landmark and non-profit, the Newtown Theatre is a community treasure, playing current movies in an environment that brings you to the 1950's.   The physical layout is as old as this suggests, with a tiny ticket booth and refreshment area that would fit in your closet.
