Climb the narrow stairs to the balcony, and feel what it was like when your grandparents and great grandparents went on dates, and could only be alone in the dark with a chaperone between them. A great old place, well worth the trip.   PS. Check their website to see a photo in the snow in the New York Times. www.newtowntheatre.com.

$32 for a 50 minute foot massage, including hot herbal soak and upper body massage, is a good deal. Of course, alot of that depends on the quality of the work and comfort of the facilities.   Relax Foot Massage on Bustleton Avenue in the far Northeast Philly does a decent job on the tootsies in a dark room with large adjustable easy chairs, but not quite the same level of attention to detail on the arms, shoulders and back; making for a somewhat disjointed experience. I enjoyed the hot soak with Tibetan herbal salts, and found the poking, probing and stretching after that to be comprehensive and satisfying. Those were a full 30 minutes of occasional pain and moments of intense serenity.   The upper body work seemed more inconsistent, with varying pressure applied to the left and right appendages. My masseuse often didn't complete the application of force evenly on the muscles and ligaments - she would push down but not all the way, and rush to the next spot with adequate firmness at times, yet without the same degree of strength the next. I became very aware of what she was doing and it stopped me from really relaxing into that Zen zone where real healing takes place, and I cease being aware of where I am (not sleep, but close).   I liked the darkened room, which felt more private than the other place I often go where the big hall is light and a little noisy, but the overall skill of the Chinese men and women attendants higher than here.  Given the prices are the same, I will choose the healing hands over the shadow ambiance and continue with my long term spa until someplace better comes along.

Aside from the final battle of Yorktown, Virginia, where Lord Cornwallis surrendered the British Army to General Washington and marked the end of our colonization by the British Empire, the most important battles of the American Revolution were fought within 50 miles of this hollowed ground.  The two Battles of Trenton,  Battle of Princeton, and the crucial and tide turning Battle of Monmouth (NJ), determined whether we would be a failed rebellion or a new nation.   When the smoke cleared, our banner still waved.  But, this place was where Washington showed his desperate genius, preparing for a night river crossing ten miles north of where the Hessian garrison in Trenton lay; hoping for a surprise attack on Christmas morning.  It did not go off as planned.  His generals south of Trenton in Bristol, Pa., were unable to cross the icy river and abandoned their attack.  The river spirits attempted to swamp, drown, and freeze our soldiers with a sleet onslaught that almost completely blinded the Massachusetts boatmen who repeatedly forded the river carrying men, horses, cannon and supplies to the Jersey side, using 18 foot oars and iron tipped spike poles to row and push the Durham Boats across and back.  Somehow, where the others failed, Washington and his ragtag army succeeded.    The rest is now known as OUR history.     It does not take a huge imagination to feel that this moment is still with us when fully present in Washington Crossing.  Most prefer to join the crowds for the reenactment of the crossings, but for me the true essence of history is most strongly felt in quiet moments in the early dawn or at dusk, when it is only me and the River.  Standing still on a cold winter eve or morn, facing the Delaware and closing my eyes, I can feel the weight of the moment that lay on Washington's shoulders.  Sleet in his eyes and dripping from his hat, he had only his faith in providence and his grim determination to comfort him.  If he failed, the grand notion of a free nation died in these frozen waters.  If he succeeded, he hoped to fight another day.   It is in his success that we can acknowledge that our collective fate hung in the balance.

I remember the uproar when Applebees and another fast food shop were permitted to enter Newtown.  It was the beginning of the end to life as we knew it!   Not.  Applebees has taken its place as a well utilized restaurant in the Village of Newtown Shopping Center.  It follows the national formula and does not deviate beyond the mean.  It is busy for lunch, dinner and late night, and fits the need for a modestly priced option among all the high end restos in the area.    I don't go often, but I am glad it is there.  When I do, I stick with the ample fresh salads, and an occasional burger.  I sit at the bar when I dine alone, or one of the booths when with family.  I have not had a bad experience, nor ever felt it was misplaced here.    Go. Enjoy. Have a good time. This shop is locally owned by The Rose Group, and even if you prefer to avoid chains that expropriate your money out of the community, this particular franchise does not.  You can have a clear conscience.

Formerly the Carversville General Store and Post Office, the Kitchen is a beautiful reuse of this early 19th Century structure in the enchanted Village of Carversville, Solebury Township, PA. Although only 20 miles from home as the crow flies, the trip back in time is considerably further. With its aging stone and wood and surrounding pre & post revolutionary ambiance, this is a travel destination accessable only by fantasy and time machine. It lies in the heart of what makes Bucks County so magical.   Orders are taken at the cashier with options of fresh bakery goods, morning sandwiches and local roasted coffee from nearby Upper Black Eddy. You remember him, right?! Their Kenya mild roast was a superb blend that went down easy with a spot of milk. Kim worked the register and took ordered for the kitchen to fill. I went light with a fresh everything bagel and cream cheese to accompany the java. She delivered it to me at the small sitting shelve under the large paneled window. It was a decent bagel that allowed me to sit, munch and daydream about the days of Moses Doan and his clan of outlaws who lived in these parts as horse thieves and highwaymen at the time of the Revolution. Aside from the paved roads and iron horses, nothing much had changed.   Everyone was very friendly and eager to talk to this stranger about the timeless life in this hamlet. I was equally eager to listen. Never know when you may meet someone who will change your life.   This is just the place to pause and reflect on important things. Time and the creek passing through the center of this burg flow slowly and silently here, with an invitation to dive deep into its wellspring and avoid evanescence.

Seamless transition from Tea Talk to Tea Chat as the new ownership takes control.  Same friendly, attractive staff.  Same drinks and snacks.    This seems a good place to get your Boba On!  My Hot Green Bubble Tea tonight was nice company on the road back to Bucks.    Would certainly visit again, and perhaps discover what the story is with these pearls being sucked through oversized straws.

Meat. Meat. And, more meat.   This is heaven if home cooked roast beef, roast pork, meatballs, sausage sandwiches/platters in any combination (read, pepperoni), is your dietary preference.  If it's not, then you're plumb out of luck.    Sandy's is an unabashedly meaty place, in a dark tavern with HDTVs on every wall.  It sits in the middle of that small strip center out front of Oxford Valley Mall, facing Route 1.  The unique part of the experience here is that the meats are actually cooking and prepared for serving at the bar.  You can sit almost anywhere in the house and watch the steam table being opened and your order being set up in a torpedo roll or on a plate.  That's pretty cool.    They also give you a ton of meat with every dish.  Our roast pork sandwich was overflowing the loaf and spilling onto the plate.  The meatball sub had four nice sized spheres topped with a good tomato sauce.  Both were totally cooked into submissive tenderness, and had good taste.  The pork needed a little kicker if a more spicy finish was desired.  The meatballs were good just as they were.  The only real weakness was the quality of the roll.  They lacked any body and were quickly overcome by the moisture of the meat, turning soggy and difficult to handle fairly quickly.  The fork was invented for just such circumstances, and ours were put to good use.  The positive was that were ended up eating most of the meat without the bread, and saved those calories.   Used them up on the dark, cold, slow Guinness. Ahhh....perfect complement.   Sandy's is CASH ONLY, with a captive ATM on the premises.

This place took me by surprise.   Yeah. The reviews were pretty good, but a bagel joint on the ass-end of Hamilton Avenue?  I just wasn't sure anything amazing was possible.  Still, I found myself heading that way one morning this week, I was hungry, and Yelp Mobile alerted me that Bagel Stop was just ahead.    I didn't know if I would be able to sit down or the place was strictly take away.  That question was answered quickly when I opened the door and found myself in a tiny shop the size of my walk in closet.  Smelled very good.  Friendly faces all around.  Bagel bins in front of me singing their siren song.    I ordered my trusty Onion, Butter and Swiss, not toasted.  Four minutes later it was made, bagged and ready for payment.  Bagel and large coffee for under $4?! Surely you jest.    Sat in my car and opened the bag after taking a swig of java.  The bagel wasn't the biggest rounder I'd ever seen, but it had lots of Onion Flakes and a nice aroma.  First Bite Experience was amazing. The crust was firm, but giving.  The inner texture light and airy, allowing the onion/butter/Swiss mix to play its nutty sweet flavors on my palate.    This was an exemplary bagel.  Almost at the level of Bagel Train in Yardley.  It was so similar that I wondered if Bagel Train and Bagel Stop had a common ancestry.    A few more visits and I will know if I have discovered the holy grail of Jersey bagels.

BBQ Chicken PA is a Korean Fried chicken stall in the Assi Market, Welsh Road, North Wales. It is in the small food court on the right side of the warehouse-sized store. I was looking for a late lunch of double deep fried wings, plus some to take home to the family.   I thought I ordered enough with Secret Spicy sauce, but turned out the order taker put in the order for half my request, despite my double checking with him. That bleach job must have turned his brains blond in addition to his hair. Yet, maybe he was doing me a favor.  Eating the first one let me know that these guys were not the super crisp wings I've had elsewhere. Nope. These were slathered in the garnet red goop with good flavor, but the skin was not crunchy as anticipated. Plenty of meat in the bone, but lacking the corresponding bite.   Suddenly, the dude's inattentiveness was a small blessing as it cut my disappointment in half. Ten okay wings were better than twenty less than optimal pieces.   I'll be sure to thank him next time I'm in the neighborhood.

Huong Tram is easy to miss, hiding in plain sight in a small commercial building surrounded by high chain link fences that make it look like a construction zone. Consider yourself fortunate to find it, because this house under new management has a strong Vietnamese kitchen and is large enough to seat a lot of people.  The servers in green shirts are attentive and for the most part bilingual.  They seem to enjoy their jobs, which is a sign that ownership cares about them and the quality of their interactions with customers.    We stopped in after shopping down Washington Avenue, in need of some sustenance after stocking up on our Asian food supplies for the month.  We were in the mood for both Vietnamese and Chinese food, and found that they really did a good job on both.    We ordered Wonton Noodle Soup, their Deluxe Fried Rice, and Sweet & Sour Chicken.  A little from column A, and more from column B.  The soup had the excellent flavor of a long simmering beef based pho.  It was rich with mildly spiced undertones, thin sliced steak, and a load of vermicelli noodles and wontons.  The side plate of accessories was put to good use to bring the taste up even more.  It was such a large bowl, that we were given a second smaller one without asking.  It came in handy as I slurped heartily from the secondary pot. Didn't even need any Sriracha. If there was any weakness it was the wontons, that while delicate lacked much filling and thus, taste. This kept it from being nearly perfect.    The S/S Chicken was better than expected - crispy thin coating, tender white meat that did not have the texture of being frozen, and a thick tangy orange sauce, pineapple chunks and green peppers.  Liked it.  Finally, the House Deluxe Fried Rice was excellently made; moist and full of small caliber meats and veggies.  So good after too many Chinese take out mass produced fried rice sides.  This was the real deal.    Huong Tram is another superior entry into the Vietnamese world around Washington Avenue.  Will definitely be back to dive into their soup and com (broken rice) offerings. Their smoothies look great, too!

Pho Saigon in the 6800 block of Bustleton Avenue in the Great Northeast of Philadelphia is a very good pho and com house that can save those of us who live farther from Center City than this location many miles of travel down to Washington Avenue, South Philly.  Parking is just about as bad in this developing Chinese/Vietnamese neighborhood, but you are more likely to find a spot on the street with a little patience.   We took a table along the wall and appreciated the prompt service provided by staff.  Ordering pho tai nam (beef noodle soup with rare steak and flank), vermicelli with BBQ pork and summer rolls, we had more than we could finish for just slightly north of $20.    The pho had a nice broth base with plenty of thin sliced steak and flank. Plenty of good slurping, but on the way home I began to feel a little off, like there could have been some MSG in the pot to hasten the reduction process. I am mildly allergic to that, and began to feel lightheaded shortly after departing. That is my deal, and many do not have that reaction. Still, the bowl was loaded with noodles. The small bowl was enough, even though the larger vessel was only a buck more.  The pork dish was excellent, however, with the meat a deep dark amber from its time marinating in the BBQ sauce. It was chewy in a good way as it slowly released its smoky sweet flavor with mastication. Again, plenty of dry noodles in the bowl, along with shredded carrot and ground peanuts.  A little fish sauce splashed over the top, and we were in business. The summer rolls were nothing special, but were certainly fresh, with a good peanut dipping sauce.   I would return to Pho Saigon, but inquire about the MSG situation before ordering.   This neighborhood has potential.

Maybe I should have known better when I walked into Pasta On Time, and it was empty of customers. Or maybe, the awful acoustics of the walls and ceiling and loud TVs should have been a tip off that this may not have been the greatest place for a sit down meal. Regardless, I miss those cues, and ordered a full meal of chicken francais, pasta, salad and twist rolls for consumption on the premises.  It wasn't all bad, but neither was it possible to really enjoy it, given what was served. The salad was okay with balsamic vinaigrette, and it can be forgiven that they used iceberg rather than romaine. The FDA had advised throwing all romaine out until they determined that only lettuce from Central California was the source of dangerous leafies. And, the twisted rolls were also pretty good, although two small pieces seemed a little light in the generosity department.   No, the problem really began and ended with the chicken dish. While the three fillets were sautéed well, the sauce was from another planet. Rather than real lemon and white wine mixed with butter in proper proportion to make a delicious sauce, this combination seemed to use reconstituted lemon juice, no wine, and perhaps salted butter. The result was a awful tasting colloidal yellow soup with a strong bitter lemon flavor that sat on my tongue until I got home to brush my teeth free of it. Rather than savor the taste of my favorite Italian dish, I had to remove as much sauce as possible from the chicken, and avoid the spaghetti beneath all together.   Maybe a sandwich would have been the way to go, but some of the reviews say otherwise. What was clear, was that the kitchen didn't know how to make this meal, and followed a recipe that lacked any finesse, along with the absence of wine, lemon fruit and sweet butter.   It was a complete whiff.   "Pasta On Time," or, Pasta No Time?

Vault Brewing Co., as the name suggests, sits in a former bank on Main Street, Yardley, Pa.  It has been in operation for a while, and it really seems to have its act together when it comes to the art of brewing beer, and making interesting dishes in the kitchen.  It is often crowded at happy hour, but when I arrived for lunch with a friend, we had the entire vault room to ourselves, and the bar was not busy.  Sadly, because this was also a business lunch, we did not indulge in their golden liquids, but did enjoy their house made root beer.    Service was very good, with knowledgeable and affable dude, who gave us the time needed to chat as we perused their menu.  I ordered the chicken sandwich, although the pizza offerings were tempting. The meal was served on a wood plank with side salad and balsamic dressing. The sourdough bread was lightly toasted/grilled, and the chicken, cheese, aioli and lettuce held together well, and tasted great.  The side salad was mostly green with romaine, escarole, carrot slivers and vinegar. It was okay.  Overall, it was a solid, tasty lunch.  With the root beer and tip it came to $22 per person, which is rich for my blood for a midweek lunch.   Still, it was worthwhile to get inside Vault and appreciate how attractive it was in a dark wood, cloudy, kind of way. On this rainy afternoon, it exuded a quiet historic tone that was relaxing. It definitely calls for a return call, when there is time to enjoy their brewer's craft, and deconstruct one of their pizzas or other tapas.

Two Slices & Drink Review  Hidden Trenton, the underrated website that highlights the best of New Jersey's capital city, says that Jerry's Pizza has the best pie within the borders of this august urban jungle.  While this narrow focus eliminates all of the former greats that have moved out of town over the past decade, it is interesting to see what is considered today's best by another reputable source.  This website has led me to some excellent discoveries in the past.   Sitting in the 700 block of South Broad Street, admittedly not the most savory stretch of America even by day, Jerry's lights up the area with plenty of color and pictures of food covering their windows.  Within, the shop is small, with room for only 4 booths, and a narrow shelf and 3 bar stools along the opposite wall.  The pizza ovens sit behind a glass counter, with the kitchen beside it.  Everyone is bilingual here, although the menu is strictly Italian.    I checked out the pies on display and asked for slices of sausage and plain pizza.  I wanted them "well done," to bring them back to life - cheese bubbling and undercarriage scorched and firm.  That is exactly what I received.  The circumference was a very narrow band of exposed crust, while the rest was tomato sauce, cheese and crumbled pork sausage all around.  Big slices that emitted enough steam to fog my glasses and offer up an intoxicating aroma of garlic, tomato, basil and mozza.  A hearty shake of crushed red peppers and I was ready to chomp.    The first slice (sausage) held its point pretty well, despite the extra weight topside.  I was able to first bite without aid of a second hand.  The crust was thin and crisp with a mild yeastiness.  The sauce tended to the salty side (especially given the meat), and the overall BCS (bite/chew/swallow) was quite pleasant.  While I prefer a sweeter sauce, this one did not bother me.  The chef knew from tomato gravy.   The second slice had cooled a bit and needed a point lift to get into my mouth.  Not a real issue given how thin the crust was.  The overall taste and texture were also fine.    I have no reason to doubt that Jerry's (my namesake) makes the best pizza in Trenton.  It was solid.  Whether it can compete with the Tomato Pie royalty in the greater Trenton area, is a story (and review) for another day.  Jerry's is worth a visit.

I have seldom been at a big city airport that I enjoyed, so I have no need for harshness. For international flights I only use it when it is the cheapest of the alternatives by a substantial amount.  Terminal D (United) is no better or worse than others I have been forced to use.  Never expecting to have an airport experience any better than barely tolerable, Philly meets my expectations.   I will say that I just had the best shoeshine there. No brushes. Just soft damp rag and good wax.  Hope it lasts for a few weeks in China.

Stony Hill Kitchen is an immaculate breakfast lunch space in the Makefield Crossing Executive Center off Township Line Road, Lower Makefield, PA. Although the three buildings appear to have low occupancy these days, the cafeteria-like first floor space appears to be doing all right.   Ordering is by digital screens and credit/debit card. Food prep is behind the counter or from a large salad bar set up in the middle of the floor. Seems pretty efficient. I was aware of its existence from Yelp, as well as its previous incarnations. After visiting PennMed across the road, I decided to go over and see what was going on. First impressions were positive, so I ordered a Farmers Omelet (veggies, cheddar) home fries, sourdough toast and La Colombe Java. It came to around none bucks, picked up at the service counter and eaten at one of their free tables.   This was a 2 egger with adequate sauteed onions, mushrooms, roasted red pepper and melted cheese. One slice of buttered toast accompanied the main dish. The potatoes were undercooked, but not so hard as to challenge my molars. The coffee was the strongest entrant to the breakfast sweepstakes, as La Colombe usually is.   On a cooler day I would have been tempted to sit under the outdoor pergola to enjoy a more leisurely morning, but given the pre-thunderstorm forecast, I opted to remain inside in the sanitary surroundings. Too, given a choice I prefer less single use plastics than provided here. No deduction, but a word to the wise and ecologically sound.

Those of us who fondly remember La Gondola down on the corner of Anderson and Roebling, should sleep better knowing that the historic Italian house has now become Una Casa de Guatemala, Restaurante El Mariachi.   In fact, if you miss the old wall mural of the Venice Canals you can still see it there in all its glory.  I stopped in for lunch the other day on my way back to the office.  I parked a short distance away on Anderson Street, and enjoyed the stroll down memory lane to the side door.  Walking in, you might think this was still in the old hands.  Not that much has changed.  Then, I was approached by a lovely, hustling server doing double duty as the hostess, and rather than listening to a warm Italian accent, I heard the romanticism of Espanol.  It was a pleasant momentary adjustment.    The menu was full of taco, quesadilla and pupusa options.  Following the recommendations of another Yelper(Mark N.), I went with the Mixtas alternative so I could sample three varieties of the stuffed flat breads.  In addition, the heat of the day being so oppressive, I asked for a Licuado de Papaya con Agua (Papaya Smoothie w/ Water).  For $2, I should have ordered two.    The Pupusas were about 7 inches in diameter, and came out steaming on a plate also loaded with Pickled Shredded Cabbage/Carrot Combo,and three Salsas.  Each was nicely stuffed with meat, cheese, peppers, onions, and perhaps somethings I did not recognize.  They were well mashed within, and the textures of light pocket pupusa and the individual insides were subtle, but tasty fun.  They were also filling, and I could barely finish them.  The Salsas were Red, Green, and Mixed, each with their own piquancity.  The Licuado was fundamentally whipped Papaya and water.  It was very good and so refreshing on a 90-plus day.    The house had several table occupied when I was there, and everyone seemed to be enjoying themselves.  Although I was the only one there having to think about what to say in Spanish, the servers and other customers were very cool about the obvious Gringo in their midst.    The house is clean and bright, and a pleasure to visit.  Chambersburg may not be what it once was, but what it is becoming has promise to be something equally special.

Nadia Thai migrated from Lansdale to Willow Grove and hasn't looked back. Its shop offers solid Siam cuisine, while also being creative and adaptive to local taste.  Payne, owner and master of the front of the house, is enthusiastic and genuinely engaged in making the customer experience unique from greeting to stopping by to assure your satisfaction to salutation and inviting you back again.   My order of Wild Mushroom Coconut Soup and Hoi Tod (Oyster Pancake) was very enjoyable. The soup was especially sweet, hot and flavorful, although I am not certain all the nightshades listed on the menu were stirring in the bowl. I really liked it.  The Hoi Tod was topped with oysters, tapioca and shallots, the later two fried to a crisp. Nicely done. The sriracha based sauce held it all together with a strong bite. It was a thoughtful interpretation of the seafood pancake found in night markets throughout southeast Asia (admittedly at ten times the price, but who has time to fly over to Chiang Mai for a snack?).   Until I get there again, Nadia Thai will help keep those memories deliciously alive.   Oh...and the Yelp Check In bonus fried banana dessert will give your mouth a very happy ending.

Gallo Tropical (Tropical Rooster) is a Dominican/Mexican casa is in the heart of Hatboro,, PA, on York Street right at its intersection with Bayberry Road. Easy to find with metered parking all around (free Sunday). Walking in, it seemed like it wasn't ready for eat in business, but the gracious woman who greeted me advised I could indeed consume my meal on one of the few small tables or counter cleaned and ready for me. Great! I do prefer to eat when the dish is right from the oven.   I went with  Chicken Empanada as an appetizer, Chicken and Potato Flautas and large Jugo Tamarindo as a delicious health slurpdown. The Empanada was deep fried to a golden hue and loaded with mildly spiced shredded chicken. The outer shell was crispy, while the stuffing was tender and moist. Excellent! There were six fried wheat tortillas rolled up and full of either a chicken/cheese mix or pleasantly mashed potato. This was a first for me, but although I enjoyed the variety provided by the mashed, it wasn't as tasty and compelling as the traditional chicken flute.   The Tamarind was semisweet and very refreshing. A good offset to the spice of the other dishes.   There are several very good Dominican kitchens in Trenton, and Gallo Tropical compares well with them. In fact, there is a restaurant by the same name over there.  Wonder if they are related. Regardless, the Hatboro Rooster has a lot to crow about.

COVID-19 TAKEOUT REVIEW  These are the times that try our souls.  To grab a break from constant at home dining, at least two or three times a week we pick up takeout meals from either a place we haven't tried before, but has been bookmarked for a long time, or an old reliable that for some inexplicable reason had dropped out of the rotation. So it was with Primo Hoagies in the Glen Roc Center near Trenton-Mercer Airport in Ewing, NJ. Nothing like a premium submarine sandwich on a fresh sesame seeded torpedo roll to pleasure and comfort a weary heart. And, Primo, the former Italian deli out of Philly that is now an expansive regional franchise, knows how to bring that iconic satisfying experience home.   We ordered over the phone for curbside pickup and sent the 19 year old who is spending the rest of his college freshman year at home out to secure it. Ordering a Turkey Schwartzie (sliced roast turkey, Swiss, lettuce, tomato, sweet pepper relish and mayo),  Corned Beef Schwartzie, and traditional Roast Beef & Provo Hoagalone, at $10 per, we actually had enough for two meals after cutting them into quarters and mix/match sharing. Our separately purchased bag of uber crisp & spicy Herr's Jalapeno Potato Chips were the perfect counterpoint to the soft semi sweetness of the sandwiches.   And, an outstanding mention is demanded for the wonderful bread encapsulating the quality ingredients. Those babies were so delicious with sesame seeds generously spread atop each creation that I could easily have been happy with just them and a shmear of butter. So good!  As we sat devouring dinner at the kitchen table we were able to forget the seeming war zone coronavirus had turned out peaceful community into for a few minutes and talk of normal things like before this disease ended our innocence. In times such as these, we must fully appreciate such moments together.

Careful as you approach Sophia Bella on Street Road Southbound, as you will drive past their small parking lot curbcut before you know it, and be forced to drive around the block to get back to the entrance of this Italian kitchen in Bensalem, PA. Worse, you might decide to just drive on, and miss a straight up very good meal.   There are a few small dining areas in the building in addition to a large back kitchen and prepping/cashier zone up front. Attractively utilitarian, all. Room to stand and wait for your order without feeling cramped, as I was doing as my two hot sandwiches were working.   These were taken to go, so when I opened the brown bag at home, I found neatly packaged long torpedo sammies (Boardwalk Sweet Sausage, Pepper and Onion/Eggplant Parm) in separate recyclable styro containers. Naturally, the enclosed bread absorbed some condensation so they were no longer dry and a crunchy bite, but were still delicious. Quality Italian sausage complemented well with the sweet and savory sauteed veggies. Eggplant breaded lightly and pan fried in extra virgin before placed in the roll with mozza and tomato sauce on top, and baked in the pizza oven until all melted into a savory layered tasty ensemble.   I bought two to share, and everyone was happy, even the next day when reheated. Service was friendly and casual, and prices reminiscent of pre-pandemic days.   Pizza looked good, too, but will have to save comments until I return to sample a few.

TAKE AWAY REVIEW:  CC's Dairyland Soft Ice Cream is no more. In its place is Richman's Ice Cream & Burger, a sibling of the joint just off 5 Points on Bristol Emilie Road, Levittown, PA. The menu is identical, but the dining possibilities are much more limited. This location has no indoor dining area, but only round or picnic tables under too small umbrellas, that neither cast enough shade to protect from the sun, nor sufficient cover to hold the rain at bay. So, in a downpour or a drizzle the only real choices are to go home, eat in the car, or get wet.   I was handed a bag at the side window with a traditional burger (single patty, lettuce, onion, thousand island dressing, standard bun), hot dog (w mustard, ketchup, relish and hash on separated bun), fries and orange cream shake. All I can say is,  Never again.  By the time I was at the kitchen table 20 minutes later, this is what I retrieved from the sack: 1 hot dog so overloaded that with one bite it fell apart, spilling its contents on the floor. The bun had lost its stamina and become two soggy pieces of bread. The burger retained it's texture despite giving up its heat. The dressing and lettuce were lubricants, expelling contents with each cold bite. The fries had morphed into soggy pasty worms. Only the shake was a semblance of its former self and was pretty good, tasting like a creamcicle.  Lesson learned. Only hit up this Richman's on a nice day, and consume everything right on the premises to capture the promise that is an otherwise excellent burger joint. Although reading Jarrad R's review makes it seem eating there might not really solve the problem.

I didn't expect that I would be dealing five big ones for this cheesesteak, wings and burger joint in the Richboro Shopping Center. After all, this building had housed a few other restaurants over the past few years, none of them worthy of more than a passing taste test. Yet, D & M Philly Cheesesteaks and Wings, despite its longish and uninspired name, actually provided me with the best steak sandwich I have had in a while, and a very good burger, too.   The dining room is barebones, with half a dozen tables, and Philly sports teams logos on the walls. I was doing take out, so the clean room was noted, but not utilized. I discovered there was a discrepancy between the printed and online menus, because when I ordered their Three Pepper Steak sandwich and Special Burger that I had seen online, I was being given the right steak, but a different burger. This led to a discussion with the woman taking my order and the chef about what was said and what was heard. The chef was unaware of the online version of the menu, and had not heard of the Special Burger. They both apologized for the confusion. It worked out fine. A new burger was prepared as I wanted it, and the original burger was given to me as well, without charge. That's the right way to handle the situation, and I appreciated their easy willingness to make things right and treat me well.  So, when I broke open the styro package and unwrapped the burgers, I beheld three beautiful sandwiches. They used brioche style rolls that were rich and tasty, with excellent texture. The Three Pepper (hot, sweet and green) were mixed into a large load of chopped steak, along with onions and mushrooms.  It was excellent. I could only eat half. The Special Burger was a 6 ouncer, grilled to the requested medium finish, and topped with lettuce, tomato, American cheese and Thousand Island dressing. Although not the grass fed/open range beef, it was still juicy and delicious. The rolls really added to the experience with their subtle sweetness and ability to hold together under the stress of huge bites.   As a family with two sons who make cheesesteaks, burgers and wings a standard part of their diets, it was very good fortune to find this place not too far from home, that was so expert with a grill. No doubt, the wings will be sampled sooner than later, and D & M Philly Cheesesteaks and Wings will be toward the top of the list of places to go when that large itch must be scratched.   Just hope they come up with a shorter name for their family enterprise.  Isn't "D & M," enough?

Still love the colonial ambiance of the rear dining room and the tight squeeze of the front oval bar. The outdoor deck is also a cool place to hang out on a warm night. Yet, the kitchen remains inconsistent despite the more upscale menu and corresponding prices.   My son and I stopped in earlier this week to enjoy some time together before he returned to school. We had alot to talk about. We were given the table right beneath the large blackboard specials menu where they were advertising Steak Night. That moved the young man to order a New York Strip and frite, medium rare. Nice move. I went with one of their burgers with Gouda and "Million $$$ Bacon," medium, with garlic mashed rather than fries. Pineville at its best had always been a great burger house and I imagined our reunion after several years would be best served by honoring that memory.   It didn't quite work out that way this night.   While the steak looked and smelled awesome and kept my son entertained from first to last red juicy bite, my classic puck arrived far closer to well done than medium that not even liberally spread ketchup could revive, and the mashed tasted more of salt than garlic. I managed to eat half knowing it would be devoured when my son regained his appetite in the morning. Still, there was no denying my disappointment.   The dinner was saved by the spectacular homemade Rice Pudding (w whipped cream) that Pineville is also famous for. It hadn't lost any of its seductive taste - cool, chunky, mildly sweet with a nice cinnamon powdered finish. Served in a large coffee mug, it overran it's confines into the saucer beneath. We were careful to capture every last drop. Simply wonderful!   The night would have been five star if we began and ended with dessert, but the road to that perfection was paved with poor execution. Three estrellas is as far as I can go despite the blazing last act.

Great Jersey tomato pie comes to Levittown, PA.!   You don't need to love DeLorenzos pizza and T pie cousin stores originally from Trenton, NJ, to appreciate the arrival of those delicious creations on the western banks of the Delaware. In fact, it is even better if you never heard of them and discover this new pizza parlor on New Falls Road on your own.   When you do and wait the 30 to 60 minutes outside the entrance for a table to clear, and finally order a pie from a server in black and white, wait again to have it custom made just for you, and then climactically take your first bite, your will know this is something different than any slice you have had before.  The just right mix of flour, water and salt. The chunky tomato sauce with basil and a pinch of sugar. The high quality mozza that hides beneath the sauce that melts to a soft mellow. All this combined to offer a perfect chew that explodes on the palate like nothing you have experienced before from a "pizza."  Now, THAT is tomato pie! Not the upside down thing found in many joints. Not the pizza covered in heavy red gravy without any cheese. No. This is the real McCoy from Jersey that has finally arrived in Bucks to show pizza lovers how tomato pie is supposed to be done.   Bring beer or wine and mange bien!   You deserve it.  Happy Fourth of July, Yelpers!!!

This BK sits out on Nottingham Way next to China Express, part of the new commercial zone being developed at the old fairgrounds site. It is designed for drive around service, with a dangerous nod to in house dining. To walk in requires crossing the drive through lanes where most drivers aren't paying attention to pedestrians.   The drive up ordering system needs help because it is difficult for driver and ordertaker to understand each other. I could not hear what the young guy was saying to me, but it was apparent he didn't hear me well either. I repeated myself three or four times and hoped for the best. I was pleasantly surprised that I received what I asked for.   I ate at my desk. The breakfast croissant sandwich was small, but decent. The coffee just mediocre. Prices were very close to what is available at the many delis, cafes and morning taverns in the area, so unless time is at a premium, I prefer the other alternatives for higher quality and comfort.   Searching for a word to capture the experience, "uninspired," seems about right.

Akai Japanese Fusion is a Chinese owned/operated fresh fish house at the top of Mill Street, Bristol, PA. It replaced an old luncheonette, and has done a decent renovation to give it a darker ambient feel. Perhaps, too much narrow gauge siding and flooring, but don't blame them for saving money where they could.   The menu is long on sushi, sashimi and rolls, with a tip of the cap to Chinese and Thai cuisine. So, it's not really a fusion house, but wants to appeal to the fish phobes with a little something more palatable to them. Problem is, that seldom works, and those few offerings are poor relations to the primary actors. That appears to be the case here. More confusion than fusion.   So, I went with the salmon teriyaki bento box - 2 small pink fish fillets in a good sauce, 2 gyoza, 6 piece California roll and white rice. The salmon was pleasantly crunchy, the gaozi fried with a chicken filling, and ordinary Cali's. All reasonably satisfying, but nothing more spectacular. It would have been nice to be provided with enough ginger for all the roll nuggets, and more wasabi to mix with soy for dipping. Showed a lack of attention to detail that recommended against a return visit.   2.5 STARS

Quaker Steak & Lube is a fairly new extension of a grease joint in Middlesex County, NJ, that pumps out burgers, steak and steak sandwiches with brew wash down in a casual atmosphere. It sits where a former diner once operated. One can only hope that it has a better life expectancy.   I ordered one of their massive burgers that was dressed with thick bacon, interesting mayo, cheese on brioche roll. It was a half pounder, finished well despite my request for medium. It came with fries. Although I would have added a vanilla shake for a sweet, creamy luxury accompaniment, there was no way to order it online that I could find.   By the time I arrived home, much of the blush was off the rose. The burger though large, was a lukewarm mess with something falling out with each bite. Could have used a few more napkins. It was a decent bite and chew, but without any shining features to remember it by. Really in the same class as Red Robin and Cheeburger, but a step down from the Shake Shacks and Mooyahs of the world.   At about $13 for the sandwich and fries, it wasn't overpriced for the meal, but neither was it so outstanding as to find its way onto my Burger of the Year competition list.

Pizza Express on South Olden Avenue, Trenton, is one of several Spanish houses dressed up like pizzerias around the city.  Most of the menu looks and tastes Italian, but in the heart of the kitchen, hot Latin blood flows like the Rio Grande.  It is almost exclusively a take away shop, but there are two hightops for those few who prefer to eat while the food is at is apex of flavor and texture - right off the grill, or out of the oven.    Orders are taken across a high counter for defensive measures in the neighborhood.  The woman on the other side was pleasant and knowledgeable.  I asked about the best things on their Mexi-Rican list, and was given a few suggestions.  Well, maybe next time, but for now I was taken by the empanadas, of which I chose queso and papas (cheese & potato).    They arrived in their take out container, packaged neatly in a brown bag, stapled perfectly across the top.  I ripped it open and pulled out the styro box and little plastic cups of fresh, chunky salsa.  I dumped them on top of the two dough pockets.  They looked very nice together.  Still, it would have been nice if they gave me a fork or other utensil with which to consume my lunch.  Fingers would have to suffice.    Both were very good.  The cheese was melted and gooey, and the outer shell firm and crisp.  Same for the potato bag.  The contents were well mashed and spiced, with only small pieces of whole spud for a little texture.  Liked them both, and would certainly expand my horizons by sampling the other stuffings.    Should they see fit to serve their eat-in customers with a bit more hospitality, by throwing in real plates and functional flatware and even a few more tables and chairs to eat in house, Pizza Express could find itself in a fortunate cycle of improved ratings.  Right now, the priority is take out. Understandable, but the value of folks finding and sticking to your place is only enhanced when they can hang around to enjoy their grub.

The bagels were denser than I like, but otherwise Redhouse Bagels is a busy place on a rainy Saturday morning. Bakery in back, plenty of friendlies working the front of the house, and around ten tables for a sit down quick bite breakfast. My Onion Bagel, butter and Swiss sandwich was tasty with lots of baked onion flakes falling off with each bite. It was fine.  No, the turnoff came all at once when I took a visit to the men's room. There was a leak in the sink faucet that was causing black mold to grow at the base of the spigot and on the strainer over the drain. It looked like the condition had been active for a while. Given how toxic black mold is to some people it was shocking that it was allowed to remain without active professional intervention.   Please take care of this before someone becomes ill from it. If the Department of Health sees it, the shop will be shut down until it is returned to a safe condition.

MyThai Kitchen recently opened on Brownsville Road, Trevose, PA. It is in an old tiny strip with a narrow parking field right in front. Easy enough to get in, but a bit challenging when departing. Don't let that deter you, because once inside you enter a simple dining room with about a half dozen wood topped tables, and honest to goodness Thai dishes prepared with love and attention by folks who came naturally by their skills - they lived them from birth. No Thai pretenders here.  I was there for a late lunch, arriving just short of 3:00 to an empty house. I was greeted warmly by two women, one the chef and the other working the front room. They thanked me for coming, directed me to a table in the front corner and handed me their small double sided menu. I was in time for the lunch special. I ordered a small bowl of tom yum soup, drunken noodles with beef and an iced tea. I asked them to bring the heat.   The soup was strongly spiced with lemongrass and loaded with veggies, including fresh mushrooms. The first spoonful took my breath away, but I adjusted to the spicy boil and enjoyed it the rest of the way. I asked for high flames and that was what I got. I was pleased they did not make any "cultural adjustment" for a presumed western pallette. The noodles were broad and mixed with peppers and other multicolored vegetables. Thin slices of grilled beef finished the plate, along with an excellent opulent brown sauce. Loved all of it. The 10% grand opening discount was another nice touch (without asking).  Service was attentive and attractive from the orange apron woman. She stopped by often to see how I was doing and to answer my questions. On my way out I asked to take a photo to memorialize my visit. My wish was granted.   Take a look and tell me you wouldn't return as soon as possible for more authentic Thai cuisine!

DELIVERED LUNCH REVIEW :  Once a month I go to Norristown, PA, for an office meeting. Lunch is eaten in the conference room as we talk. It is routinely ordered from Rocco's the morning of the get together. The entire menu is in play. To date, I have gone with two of their salads and a hot eggplant Parmesan sandwich. The others around the table have sampled other things, with personal size pizza a standard option.   Now, it is not fair to rate take out or delivered meals the same way you do for those eaten in the restaurant. They can't be as good after packaging, cooling, crushing and sitting around for a while. (Yelp should consider a check off that makes this clear.) Still, this is part of the dining experience and should be part of learning about the vendor.   After these three experiences, I no longer order salads because I find them too past their prime upon consumption, even with the salad dressing applied just before eating. Just not very enjoyable. However, the grinder wrapped in foil and paper, although somewhat diminished in transport, retained its heat and flavor to a large extent. Yes, the torpedo roll had already lost its verve, but it kept its structural integrity, and was a solid handhold throughout the meal. The condensation as it cools has to go somewhere, and the bread is the only absorbing surface. It was a fair trade off for a tasty sammy, although I wouldn't say the same for the limp pizzas I have seen falling apart on the way to the bocca.   Obviously, I am not a delivery fan, but sometimes it is necessary. Rocco's does what it can to make everyone happy with what arrives from their shop. I suspect cold hoagies are the way to go, and I will order one next month, and report back to you.   Mangia bene!

Wing Wah Chinese Restaurant on New Falls Road, Levittown, PA, is a better than average Chinois Americain house. All takeout in response to Covid protocols, it has a decent kitchen if you are looking for something beyond the ordinary menu. Yet, it is far from perfect, and the actual Yelp score is closer to 3.5 Stars when taking all sampled dishes into consideration.   I really enjoyed the Beef with Hot Peppers. The meat was tender, the sauce nicely spiced (but, not to Szechuan heat levels), and the onion and carrot thin slices made for a pleasant blend of flavor and texture. The Orange Chicken was abundant, and about average for the genre. It was all white meat with orange peel in the dark brown saucy mix, which was appreciated so much more than some who use cheaper dark meat as a loss leader. Unfortunately, the Wonton Soup destroyed the overall evaluation, because it was hardly worth consuming. It was salty bouillon and thick skinned dumplings, with indescribable meat filling that almost took my appetite away.   So, avoid the soups that have probably been sitting around too long, and focus on their special dishes not usually found on the universal Chinese American menu.  There you may find a number of choices that demonstration the real skills in the Wing Wah wok.

Oaks Family Restaurant in Pipersville, PA, is a roadside café specializing in breakfast/brunch/lunch for the folks of upper Bucks County. It sits on Easton Road (Rt. 611) about ten miles north of Doylestown. It has a country vibe, with small counter with half dozen spinners, and a dining room to one side with about a dozen tables.   When I arrived earlier this week, the place was buzzing mostly with guys shooting the s*^t about local and current events. I found a stool at the end of the counter next to the cash register and plopped down for my morning meal. The servers were friendly and engaging; handing me a menu and taking my drink order promptly. Coffee with milk, por favor. I chose french toast based on the recommendation of the lady taking my order.  I won't hold that against her, but the egged fry bread left much to be desired. Although a thin sliced loaf, the center of the bread was dry because it had not been dipped long enough in the egg mix before frying. Too, I couldn't taste any vanilla or cinnamon, nor was there any caramelization of sugar from the hot steel. It seemed each slice had an egg skirt around it from where the mix had splashed down with the bread on the grill. I'm not a forensic chef, but there was evidence of lack of attentiveness in the kitchen. The result, a disappointing performance, and a lost opportunity to make a strong positive first impression.   The coffee was fine, and service, sterling. Still, when the star of the show doesn't come through for the audience, it is hard to give a standing ovation.  2.5 STARS

Nothing Bundt Cakes (Get it?) is a month old pastry shop in the Village of Newtown Shopping Center. It is in fact a franchise that deals in only one product - Bundt Cakes. Risky endeavor to rely on one thing to carry a business to profitability. To succeed, those cakes have got to be great.   And, they are.   World class cream cheese icing. Rich, moist cake full of plenty of flavor. A delicious meld in your mouth delight.   Our lemon cake was kept cool overnight in the fridge, and taken out this morning to sit at room temperature for two hours. It came in a large cake box and wrapped in plastic, which must be removed while still cold to avoid pulling the icing off at warmer temps. A small card with instructions is attached with a mini clothespin. Cute!  So, why not a perfect score? The store experience is a bit overdone. Before the door closes, a voice welcomes you to NBC, and directs you to the free samples. I had to look for the person talking to me who was behind the high counter. She took away my attention while scanning the shop, making me a little uncomfortable. I prefer a moment to orient myself before the friendly sales assault. Too, I did not relate to the scripted welcome. Better to allow the store to speak for itself, grab the imagination, and then offer a more natural approach by staff.   Also, if you look at the photos from the company, the top of each cake has a icing plug across the normal opening from the Bundt pan. Looks good. Our reality was no such cap over the hole, but just a deep well to the bottom of the cake. It was iced, like a snow covered vent from a volcano.   No mistake, our lemon Bundt was excellent. These babies are patently addictive.  A few adjustments and the experience could be completely unforgettable.

Andorra Ping Pong is the sibling restaurant to the Ping Pong Restaurant in Wayne, PA. It is similarly Szechuan oriented Chinese cuisine, but in a somewhat smaller footprint in the Andorra Shopping Center just off Henry Avenue very near to Wissakickon Valley Park, and just beyond Roxborough. It is family owned and operated, with husband running the kitchen, and wife, the front of the house.   We were there for a small celebration, and thoroughly enjoyed our time there. We ordered enough to be able to sample a cross section of their dishes, and had plenty to bring home for our sons. We went with: Deep Fried Chicken, Fish Fillet Dry Pot, Cumin Lamb and Hot Sauce Pig Intestine; all melded together with the help of an excellent Charles Krug cabernet (BYOB). Each entre was a full load. The chicken was crispy, yet still moist within. The fish fillets, tender with plenty of dry Szechuan red peppers, cauliflower, lotus root and cilantro. The cumin lamb was well covered in dry cumin leaf and accessorized with green pepper, onion and good sized long hots pieces, while the intestine skin was dark brown, surrounded by celery, peanuts, scallion and more of those small red heat devils from Chongqing. All tasty morsels.   If there was anything to talk about, it was the lack of numbing heat in any of the platters. A deep dive into the heart of each failed to discover any black peppercorn, nor star peppers - the two ingredients necessary for the development of numbing sweats.  When asked, we advised that they should bring the heat because we loved the sensation, yet it did not materialize. Spicy, yes. Numbing lips and tongue, no.   But, aside from that disappointment, the meal was filling, satisfying and most enjoyable. We will still return, and visit the sister ship before too long. Perhaps, we will bring our own extra burn, just in case the kitchen lacks those key ingredients when we arrive next time.

Samarkand is an ancient city in Uzbekistan in western Asia.  It sits astride the Silk Road that Marco Polo travelled on his journeys to the East.  It remains a beautiful and mysterious place with many old walls, narrow streets and amazing markets.  As a centuries old melting pot, it has created its own cultural reality; among the most interesting of which is food.  Taking from cuisine as far away as India, China and the Middle East, their kitchens at once remind you of each of those unique tastes, and at the same time something quite original.    A visit to Samarkand Restaurant is a much easier way to experience this exotic taste, than to make the overland caravan to this still isolated treasure.  Right in Bucks County the flavor and texture of Uzbeki dishes are available in a house with archways and desert murals that with a little imagination brings you right there. True, this is just the northern outpost of an ever expanding community of Soviet emigres who have settled in Northeast Philly, of which Uzbeks are but a part. Still, some would argue they are the most colorful and delicious. Leave that discussion for others while you take a trip to a terrific meal.   Our approach was to tapas the appetizers, including mushroom and white corn soup, samsa, cheburek and kutab, followed by lamb and salmon shish kebob.  We shared everything. Service was friendly and attractive in Russian accent.   Each element was very good to outstanding. Their use of dough to make all the apps was fascinating, as each was different and flavorful, depending on whether baked, deep fried or skillet heated. The lamb and salmon managed to be moist and well grilled at the same time. Excellent hands in the kitchen.   We finished lunch with their crepe dessert, stuffed with mildly sweet and sour cream, and drizzled with Nutella. It caused a nostalgia wave as sensory images of my grandmother's cheese blintzes danced in my head. Loved them!   Few of us have broad exposure to Uzbek cuisine, but I intend to spend more time exploring it, as it is quite unusual, fun and delicious.

I did Thai takeout at South Seas on York Road, Abington, PA, today, and gotta say I was somewhat disappointed. No issue negotiating the narrow driveway alongside the orange faced shop to reach the small parking lot in the rear, nor dealing with the staff inside picking up my order of Tom Kha Soup and Drunken Noodles (veggie). No, the problem was strictly the content of the food when I got home to consume it.  Neatly packed in leak proof containers and brown paper handled bag, it was fun to unload and helped build anticipation. The coconut soup had all the right ingredients and was as spicy as desired. Fresh mushrooms floating on top with carrot, string bean, broccoli, tofu and  chunks of ginger and long fibrous lemongrass lurking beneath the surface like gators in a muddy milky river.   Therein lay the problem. Love the bite of lemongrass and the tartness of ginger, but not when there is so much of it that it outweighs the edibles in the bowl. I tried chewing them to extract the flavor since there was so much of it, but the tough hard texture proved daunting, and I surrendered before putting a splinter in my gums or cracking a tooth.   Aside from that, the taste of the actual soup was good.   The Drunken was a large portion, but of middle width, rather than the broad rice pasta it is supposed to be. Narrower gauge means less surface area to hold the essential spicy sauce, and much less chew, which is key to the tactile experience of this dish. Too, the exact same veggies in the soup were in this melange, but not very much of them. The proportion of noodles to greens was off, with far too little of the crunchys, and way too heavy on the carbs, making the ensemble denser and drier than it should have been, without the joy of hot noodles glistening from the devilish sauce.  Thai Spicy, yes. Thai balanced, 'fraid not.   It just didn't work very well, and had me questioning who was cooking behind the Covid masks. Maybe that was why the shop looked like Chinese takeout, without any element of Siam decor. Nary a Buddha nor elephant in sight.   2.5 STARS

Seo Rabol, the Korean house on Old 2nd Street in the Olney section of Philadelphia, is one of the more established peninsula restaurants in the area. It is not far from the center of Seoultown on Cheltenham Avenue. They offer a full menu, but their specialty is BBQ grilled on the table.   We were not hungry enough to deal with the mandatory 2 order minimum (@$20 per), so opted for their rendition of seafood pancake and pork gui - letting them do the grilling in the kitchen and serve it ready to eat. The banchan arrived first in small square plates. The ten or so dishes were all very good and a tour de force of spicy flavors and textures from steamed egg to mackerel.   The pancake was frittata like, with plenty of shellfish within, and pan fried well enough to be firm, yet still tender. It was one of the better versions I have eaten. The gui was a large bowl full of pork strips grilled just right with an excellent spicy hot/sweet sauce. Much better than I could have done myself at the table, at less than half the cost. It was delicious and almost addictive. We couldn't finish either dish, so the remains were packed up for home consumption. We finished with complementary sweet ginger tea, which cleansed the pallet and was refreshing.  Throughout the meal the large HDTVs were tuned to the Winter Olympics in South Korea. National pride for sure, but no one really seemed to be watching. The table conversation was dominant across the large dining room, as it should be while enjoying a good meal with family and friends.   Service was efficient and cordial, but it certainly helped to have someone at the table speaking Korean.

Gianni's Pizza is a backdoor walkout Italian house on the bottom floor of an much larger and older building on Bustleton Pike in Richboro, Pa.  The fit out is smallish, and has the feel of a nicely finished basement.  The menu has the usual suspects of most pizza parlors, the service is friendly, and the prices amazingly low.    We sat in a booth in the newly painted dining area.  It was comfortable, if a bit tight.  We ordered the Old Fashioned Tomato Pie with Mushrooms and the Chicken Parm dinner, with the intention of sharing both.  No problem getting them served at the same time.  The dinner came with a house salad and pasta.  The greens were a basic romaine mix with a few red onion shavings, cherry tomatoes, cukes, and a standard balsamic.  It was cool and refreshing.    The Chicken Parm plate at $10.99 was what the cost implied.  Prefab chicken breast patties covered in sauce and mozza.  Not bad, but not all that tasty.  The side of penne with aglio olio was better, but needed more garlic to really announce itself.  The Tomato Pie had a thicker airy crust, perhaps to hold the weight of the too loose sauce topside. The wetness above caused the bottom layer to get soggy, and impossible to pick up without a tomato slide.  It was a situation where less would have been more.  Keep the sauce thicker and chunkier, and the moisture would not have been an issue.  In fact, we brought most of it home and re-baked it the next day, and produced the right texture and flavor.    This place has some nice things going for it with location, ambiance and service, but our sampling of the food suggested that perhaps in the attempt to keep prices low they sacrificed some of the finer points of Italian cooking.    There are better choices around if looking for good food from the boot.

State Road in Croydon, PA, is unlike the rest of the Delaware River shoreline in Bucks County. Obviously developed without zoning, it is an alternate universe with mishmosh of industrial, pizza shops, dive bars, and marshes across the gypsy wagon shack landscape. It is strange and unique to this area, and Smokerhead Barbeque fits right in.   It is the second BBQ joint in this small shed, half kitchen and half dining room. The owners have been doing truck catering for a while and took a chance on bricks and mortar. From the look and smell of things, it was a smart move. They do solid smoked meats in a variety of styles, and love rock & roll. Last night they had a live performer cranking out hits from the 70's thru 90's on his well travelled Gibson and accompanying soundtrack. Decent gravel baritone voice, too.   My third of a rack ribs were four fat boys done St. Louis way, with sweet tangy flavor and far more than I could eat. There were only two table rockets with North Carolina (mustard base) and Memphis (brown sugar and vinegar) squirts. The meat was smoked dry and the sauces were optional, yet very moist and tender within. Really well done if you prefer control over the finish served up to you rather than having the plate all slathered with basting juices. The pit beans were a mix of grains, tomato base and bacon for seasoning. Good, but a little dry.   Service was down home and friendly. There was cool comraderie between the chefs and floor staff, and some dancing and harmonizing when a favorite tune struck a fancy.   Beer cans in the cooler, too.   Thoroughly entertained with ribs to spare last Saturday night.

Made a return visit after an hiatus of almost 2 years, and was pleasantly surprised to find the house redecorated with more comfortable seating and brighter lights.   Accompanied by a teenager and his mom, I again realized that American fast burgers are very popular.  I tried one of their discount double burgers and fries, and found that while they were no match for Five Guys or that ilk, they were still decent and satisfying.  Watching the young guy wolf down his Double Baconator was eye opening. He was totally into it.  Oh, and the fries was ample and crispy.    Time for an upgrade.   No apologies!

The 5 Stars are not just for the style cut, but for the overall experience after stepping over the threshold of Artiva Salon.    First, I was in Chinatown, which always has a slightly exotic (if also decrepit) atmosphere, especially on those narrow side streets between the numbers. Second, the door was tricky to open, requiring a grasp of the latch and hard tug on the knob.  Third, once inside the space seems rather small, with a row of numbered doors along the wall.  Fourth, there is a lot of art on the walls, some quite good.  Finally, there is Ying, the proprietress of the salon and its creative force.  She has a staff of a few people providing massage in the tiny rooms behind the doors, as well as a space for shampooing and scalp massage after the haircut.    Ying has an interesting story to tell.  She began as a television reporter in China, and travelled extensively; somehow ending up in Philadelphia.  She has her art, and decided that cutting hair was a way to express her creativity and meet people.    Upon assuming the throne I was handed a page of photos of the backs of men's heads and asked which style I liked.  This was my first attempt at a cut outside of a strictly American barbershop or salon, and with my tricky locks I was apprehensive that she could do more than just a generic shaping.  She assured me she knew what she was doing.  In made no difference as I was already draped with no place to run.  Okay.  I wanted an adventure, and I was about to suffer the consequences, or so my imagination suggested.    Fear not!   Ying did a fine job while talking about many things.  Interestingly, she washed my hair after the cut, and massaged my scalp.  Very nice.  She knew how to handle this guy's longish wavies.  The damage?  $10 for the cut, wash and massage.  That is a deal and a half!   Next time, I will plan for a foot massage as part of the spa treatment.     Low budget? Definitely!  High entertainment and relaxation value?  No question!  I stepped back onto the dimming streets around 7:30, and headed over to Dim Sum Garden for a totally in character dinner.  But, that is another review.

The Temperance House has been in operation (off and on with a variety of owners) for over a century.  It consists of a restaurant, barroom, bed & breakfast. Since reopening earlier this year under new ownership, I have stopped in a few times for happy hour or later in the evening with friends and associates for after meeting meetings and socializing.    While I really did not like, "The Temp," before due to its heavy political personality, the new version is much more friendly to all invitees, and offers a few small back rooms for groups to get together with quality bar and kitchen service.  We were there last night for a couple of hours to catch up after last week's national elections (more commiseration, than celebration).  Our server was warm and efficient, and the food and drink were good and reasonably priced.    From our vantage point behind the barroom, we heard the live band playing in the bar, but not loud enough to interfere with conversation.  Entering and leaving, I spied several people I knew from around town, and we acknowledged each other with nod, smile or wave. They were all having a good time.    Now that the vibe is more welcoming, a check on their dinner menu is in order.  Hope it, too, is more warm and tasty than the dusty dryness of past party clubbiness.

Don't know New Mama Juana from Old Mama Juana, but what I do know is that this cafeteria style traditional Dominican casa de comidas cooks up a storm of excellent dishes.  Sitting at the corner of County Line and Newtown Roads in Warminster, PA, it has recently expanded into the neighboring storefront to add a utilitarian dining room in addition to the small original corner shop.   I stopped in when I couldn't find the Mexican place I was searching for, and decided to go in flying blind. Very glad I did, because while really nothing like Mexican food, it did have a strong resemblance to Puerto Rican cuisine with serious pork, chicken and beef options, and white/yellow/brown rice and well simmered beans. While it all looked appealing, I was most attracted to the rotisserie quartered chicken.    It was excellent. Its skin was dry and taunt, while the meat beneath was moist and pull-from-the-bone tender. The taste was subtle, but well spiced and easy to pull apart and devour. If you said it was like duck comfit, you wouldn't be wrong. The beans were also delicious, but not spicy, and the yellow rice mixed in for a tasty textured combination. Liked the meal a lot.   Service was friendly and attractive, and although ordered at the cashier, it was delivered to the table with a sonrisa grande by their Guatemaltecan assistant.   There were many other interesting possibilities that may tempt me to return. I saw tostones, empanadas, and platanos rellenos, that looked great.  I just can't eat that much, and much prefer eating at the source to carry out.   New Mama Juana is the name. Authentic Latin American island food is the game.

I generally leave New Hope for the New York weekenders and tourists to overpopulate, but sometimes on a Sunday night in the dead of winter the village empties and it is possible to find open tables for a quiet dinner that reminds of this ferrytown's historic beginnings. So it was this weekend past that we ventured into this picturesque river hamlet and found a nearly vacant The Dubliner on the Delaware Irish bar and kitchen on North Main Street. Parking was a breeze almost right in front, and the meter was was only needed until 9.   We chose a table overlooking the main drag along the front paned glassed wall. The street lights did their best to add a warm glow on a softly raining night. This 18th Century town somehow looked like the perfect set for a movie about the real revolutionary history that happened all along the river when the New Hope Ferry was the only way across the dangerous Delaware's current and icy flow. It was a wilder river then before a reliable bridge could be built.   Service was friendly, helpful and appropriate. We ordered a Guinness for an Irish brew novice and a Magnate Hard Pear Cider pour moi. Cool, tasty refreshing. From there, we ordered Shepherds Pie, Bangars & Mash, Crab Cake Sandwich and a fresh Cod Fillet with veggie accompaniment. They were all a big hit with the group, especially the first two. This house knows from mashed potatoes and does them quite well. The Shepherds Pie had plenty of ground beef, peas, carrots and brown gravy under the topside frilly  potato cover. Made me wish I had a flock of sheep so I could justify eating this substantial deep dish meal more often. It was fun and delicious.   The Irish sausage atop the same mashed came with a small dish of gravy, that when all mixed together made for another engaging and nearly addicting mouthful. I was permitted a taste and found it eye openingly exceptional. The Crab Cake was also good with far more crab than bread filler. The Cod was light but could have used a more flavorful finish to give it more spark.   We all agreed that our meals at The Dubliner were overall better than expected, and that a return visit would be an easy vote of assent. Those burgers looked great, too.   PS: This is the former Mother's Restaurant location, where I had been a semi regular at an earlier point in my life. I admit to approaching the heavy wood door with thoughts of those days and wondering if memories would haunt. Nope. Once inside the new energy of the joint took control and assured that this was a new day for this old haven and the ghosts that be were friendly.

Sedition is conduct that encourages acts of rebellion against the state. If a failure it is a serious crime; if successful, an act of revolutionary heroism. In times like these that try the souls of patriots, when it is difficult to differentiate between the criminals and the righteous, it is understandable that a subterranean public house would choose "Sedition" as its identity. No doubt the dark bricked, grottoed, underground tavern evokes an epoch when such weighty matters were discussed in hushed tones by serious people.   Chose a side or stand aside, but at least here you can do so with quality drinks and kitchen. We stopped in after visiting Penn Med a few blocks away. The basement felt cool in the dim light of reimagined industrial fixtures. We walked through coved rooms until taking a booth rather far from the bar. Yet, the friendly bartender found us with menus in hand. There were good beer choices, but having to return to see the medical staff after lunch, our libations were strictly water. We ordered the Philbano and Beer Braised Brisket sandwiches, and settled in.   Both were very good, as were the accompanying fries. The "Philly Cubano" was made up of smoked Berkshire pork butt, provolone, peach BBQ sauce and pickled long hots, all stuffed into a fresh Parker House roll. Simply put, it was a great pulled pork sammy. The combination of ingredients played well together and it was fun to identify the flavors as they announced themselves to the tongue.  First rate. The brisket was not quite as entertaining, but was tender and slathered in horseradish and coleslaw between the semi spheres of a brioche bun. Satisfying. Both were substantial enough to bring half home.   Whether you intend on sedition or will wait the next act out from the sidelines, be sure to enjoy life and stop in to Sedition for drinks and grub before deciding.

Lena's Deli on Main Street in Yardley, Pa., is a miniature charcuterie that is very attractive with outdoor patio seating in front, and sincerely and competent ownership/management in house.  Their thing is first rate deli lunches from soup through dessert, that are designed to be a step above the norm.    Generally, they succeed in that premise, but my experience exposed a few weaknesses in their execution.  I ordered their Turkey, Swiss, Sautéed Spinach and Roasted Red Pepper sandwich on Sesame Seeded Italian/French loaf.  Everything looked terrific being put together, and the anticipation excited my tastebuds.  I took it to my office for eating a few hours later.    When I opened the paper wrapping, I saw that the sandwich had not been fully enclosed in the aluminum foil sheet.  Because the bread was so wide and cut in half, most of it was not sealed, but open to the elements.  The result was a less than fresh bread and contents, that was already losing taste and crunch.  Still, it was a huge sandwich for the $10+ (with a side of slaw), and I could only eat half that day.  What I consumed still had a decent, and somewhat unusual flavor due to the more exotic ingredients.    I retrieved the balance from the refrigerator the next day.  Whatever the chemical process involved overnight, the spinach had become too bitter to eat.  I lifted the top side and scraped it and the peppers off.  The remainder of the day old was okay, but certainly had lost its lust for life.  There is always some degradation to a unfinished sandwich, and I don't hold Lena to account for that.  However, the bad taste of the greens, even with refrigeration, was a disappointment.    Spending more for an exceptional lunch is worthwhile, but when it can't survive to the next day, the value proposition is lacking.  Lesson learned.  Make sure it is properly packaged, and eat it as soon as served.  The first is a matter of quality control.  The second, of knowing true shelf life.

This Mario & Franks in Fieldsboro, NJ, is much smaller than number 4 in Trenton, but is nicely finished with a small, but comfy dining room.  Service is fine and prices on lunch specials are downright inexpensive.    So, when I saw a Chicken Parm Sandwich with Fries and Drink for $6.99, I was tempted.  Unfortunately, the excitement turned to disappointment once I dug in to the huge plate that was served.  Biggest hot sandwich I had seen in a long while.  At least a foot long, cut in half, and a pile of taters that took up the other half of the large square platter.   To my tongue, the chicken fillets had been frozen and deep fried, rather than pan sautéed, which is the right and tasty way to cook it.  Maybe cheaper to use frozen chicken and fry alongside the potatoes in a vat of common oil, but it sure kills the expectation that comes with ordering any parm dish.  Really did not taste good.   This was a shortcut to Never Never Land.

Right in the heart of the National Historic District on Delaware Street sits Jessop's Tavern. Some might say that it is also the true heart of Old New Castle, occupying a colonial building constructed in 1674, and operating as a bar/restaurant for at least the last 75 years. Jessop's is the perfect place to take a load off after exploring town, or as a way station just minutes of Rt. 95 south of Wilmington.    Reflecting the cultural mix of the early settlers, the offerings are from Sweden, The Netherlands, England, Belgium, and Revolutionary War Americana.  They have a large beer selection, with Belgians their claim to fame.  The kitchen is similarly oriented to traditional fare from those parts of the world.  As they say in their Mission Statement, they "serve history at Jessop's Tavern."    We stopped in for a late lunch last week after touring Rockwood Mansion, about 12 miles north. It was all dark woods and wenches in period dress.  A long bar along one wall, and tables against the other.  We ordered a dark Barbe ale and pear cider for drinks, and their, "Dutch Pastrami Reuben," and Swedish Meatloaf Sandwich.  Both were large, beautiful to behold, and solid tasty meals.  Every aspect was well designed from breads through sauces, although it was not apparent what the Dutch have to do with pastrami, but, they are entitled to a little poetic license.   Service was attentive and friendly. When a late afternoon cloudburst trapped us in the tavern just after we finished eating, they had no problem inviting us to stay as long as we liked, and offering us an umbrella to go to the car once the deluge passed.    Hear tell that they also have excellent ice cream available.    There will definitely be a next time.

I guess I did not do Yardley Pizza any favors by going to DeLorenzo's Tomato Pies last Saturday night. By my taste, DeLo's has one of the best pies I have eaten, and I have been a fan of theirs for more than 30 years. So, coming to Yardley Pizza for the next slices really puts them in a bad place.  Apologies before I go any further.  Anyway, the floor plan is quite nice. Bigger than expected inside, and comfortably casual with sufficient space between tables for a private conversation.  The staff is friendly and helpful.  Tuesday is Dollar Slice Day (I didn't know), so the price was right! The two plain slices I had were fairly typical of the American Pizzeria.
