Triangular cuts with decent, if thin, sauce and mass produced cheese.  A little oil on the surface, but not enough for a big drip.   Alas, the slices were quite ordinary in every respect. Nothing to sit up and take notice about, but certainly a better than average competent American slice of pizza.  The crust held up well, and did not droop under the weight of the toppings.  The bite held its crunch to the very last.  It was only the sauce and cheese that missed the mark.  Again, not bad, but not eye-opening.   As I said, DeLo's is a very difficult act to follow.

With friends from Changchun in tow, we came to Chinatown to do some shopping at Asia Market in preparation for some good home cooking, Dong Bei Chinese style.  But, realizing it wasn't wise to go food shopping on an empty stomach, we stopped in at M Kee for a late lunch.  This was a first visit for me, and I found the house to be cleaner and friendlier than most.  The menu was packed with rice and noodle dishes, wet and dry, and at prices that were very compatible with the desire to eat light.    My friends speak little English, but felt right at home chatting up the servers about the menu and how dishes were prepared.  Once satisfied, they went with Chicken Curry over Rice, Roast Pork and Wonton Noodle Soup (See Photos).   The Chicken arrived in a bright yellow almost creamy curry sauce, and a pleasantly mild flavor that only required a little tweaking with Sriracha to bring up the heat.  Tasty.  The Wonton Noodles Soup was more than I could finish, with a nest of thin noodles beneath the surface of the chicken consume.  The 4 or 5 Wontons were stuffed with ground Pork and Leek (maybe), and had goldfish tails for swimming in the hot broth.  Very nice.  Finally, the Roast Pork was excellent covered in a gleaming tawny finish.  There was a lot of it for under 7 bucks, and it was the star of the show.    It was easy to see why M Kee is so popular.  The quantity/quality/cost proposition is great here.  The three of us walked out with tip for under $20, totally sated and agreeing this was great down home victuals.  With prices this low, it almost doesn't pay to eat in my own kitchen.

Mamma Mia Trattoria sits in the Oxford Valley Mall campus, right across from Red Robin and in the shadow of Cheeburger x 2. It is part of the Carlucci restaurant empire, the local folks who brought us Mama Rosa's, Carlucci's, Carlucci's Express, this lovely place and a couple of kitchens in the old country. Word is that the old man was in the house just this morning checking on operations. His kids are starting to pick up their involvement as he starts to cut back. Sorry I missed him.   Of course, I didn't know any of this history until informed by our server after I asked about all the Carlucci photos on the walls. Had I known, I would have checked MMT out long ago. Now that I have, I won't be a stranger.   The house is casually attractive with two dining areas and a nice cozy feel. The menu is extensive and the kitchen visible along the western wall. We were here for a late lunch that would bypass dinner. We chose a personal size 12" white veggie pie and eggplant parmesan foot long sandwich/grinder to share.   Both were really good.  The pie was a beauty, with colorful components and a garlicky aroma. The crust was crisp, firm, yet airy. Good cheese veggie balance that did not let the fromage bog down the lightness desired. A sprinkle of crushed red pepper and we got down to business.   The melanzon was thin sliced, breaded and pan sauteed before being slid into a fresh Italian torpedo roll, top layered with mozza, splashed with chunky tomato gravy, and then placed in the pizza oven to finish it off with a melt and mild scorching of the roll edges. Great soft texture beneath the slight crustiness of the breading. Honest flavorful interplay between the elements.   If you already know the Carlucci experience at his other shops, MMT will not surprise you with it quality take on traditional Italian cuisine. They are similar, so like one, like all. If new to Carlucci World, this is an excellent place to begin your affair with his kitchens.

The Pineville Tavern is worth a try just for the historic structure and ambiance in the older rooms.  Someone once said you can't eat the atmosphere, but here it is possible to almost taste it.  The institution is worthy of respect. The latest changes have been both good and bad.  Read the other reviews to understand the complaints and disappointments. For me, this place has always been about beer, wings, burgers, and rice puddling.  The other stuff designed to attract a wider audience may not float everyone's boat.   Stick with what they do best, and you will leave happy and full.

When a family has been in the same business at the same location for 40 years, they must be doing something right.   Pizza Star is a traditional pizza parlor.  They do pizza, steaks and related goodies, and that is all. No pasta. No dinners. Nothing fancy. Just old style pie and sandwiches in a double wide storefront on Woerner Avenue, Levittown, PA.  If you know this commercial strip, you are aware it is not the most attractive bit of design and construction every created. Signage can't be seen from the main roads, and even the street seems more like an alleyway between New Falls Road and Emilie Road.   But, if you are in the mood for a throwback Italian experience, Pizza Star is the joint for you. Ordering is at the counter, and table service is provided by the kitchen staff. No waitresses here. Just find a table and settle in. The HDTV high on the front wall will keep you informed or entertained.   I went with their eggplant parmesan sub. There was only one size available - large, but the price was about the same as for a torpedo half the size. Hard to beat. When delivered to my seat, it looked great. Overloaded with melanzone - breaded thin slices, sautéed in olive oil and covered in mozza and their home brewed red sauce.  The roll was first rate, too; brought to highlife with the final bronzing in the oven.   Taste was very good, although the golden fried discs were perhaps a little too oily from their moment in the hot sun. Not a biggie, but it would have been near excellent had the oil been absorbed off before the sandwich was finished.   The Star is yet another strong find in this part of Lower Bucks. No doubt I will return to sample the steaks and pizza when I find myself hungry in this sector of the universe.

For a Bucks County vineyard, Crossing Vineyards is as good as it gets in terms of beautiful scenery, comfortable surroundings and quality of wines available for tasting and purchase. It reminds of the wineries in Napa and Sonoma with small acreage producing some of the best vintages. It is easy to relax , sample the wares and at least for a few moments be transported to the left coast.   This hacienda has been in the family for two generations, and the colonial home they live in looks the same as it did 200+ years ago (with better plumbing, electricity and fresh paint). Take a free tour of the grounds and production facilities, followed by a sit down on the patio in good weather to sip their award winning reds, whites and blushes.   The most engaging choice is the dark rouge and somewhat sweet and dusky Chocolate Cherry Truffle. The Viognier white, Cabernet and Merlot also merit consideration. While head on comparisons with California wines may not grade out well in every instance, they are competitive, and save the time and treasure of traveling west. Sometimes a pleasant afternoon is all you need to get away.   If you enjoy Crossing Vineyards it can be just the start of a magical mystery tour of the other Bucks County wineries that can make for a great weekend.

I think maybe I have grown tired of Five Guys Burgers & Fries.  This kind of experience used to be fun and unusual; a decent alternative to the traditional fast food slider & taters.  Not so much now.  The shtick is that you have a limited choice between a single or double (regular) burger, hot dog, and flies.  You can put almost anything you want on them from the list above the cashier.  That's cool, but when you have to repeat yourself three times to the order taker, and it still comes out wrong, it is a bit frustrating.  Then, there is the meal itself.  I asked for a regular (2 puck) burger with ketchup, fried onions and jalapenos, and a side of fries to share.  What I received was a crushed limp sesame sprinkled bun that could barely hold its load.  It managed to do so for the first bite, but the second clenching was too much torque and the burgers were expelled from the bun on a running river of ketchup and slick onions.  Looked like red mudslide.    Okay. So I finished the meat off with a fork and knife, as the bread had now expired.  I was surprised how lame the burger texture and taste were without the bun support.   Did I mention the fries were not in the bag?  Guess the cashier didn't hear that either, but by this time I was happy for the small favor of not having to pay more than the $27 shelled out for these disappointments of a bun.

This 12 table Thai restaurant on Easton Road, Abington, PA, is a lovely well appointed dining room, cozy enough to feel slightly enchanted, and authentic enough to leave you satisfied that you just got your money's worth of delicious northern Thai cuisine.   I was there for Saturday lunch. Finding their parking lot behind the building after cruising by the storefront, I walked in to a warm smile from the owner/server, who directed me to a deuce along the wall, a discreet distance from the two occupied tables. She went to the rear cashier area and returned moments later with a glass of water and the two menus available for dinner and lunch specials. She quietly explained the two lists and left me again to give me time to consider my choices.   I went with the afternoon combo - a small cup of coconut lemongrass soup (Tom Ka) veggied up with fresh mushroom on top, a bisected spring roll with dark orange dipping sauce, and a fairly large plate of Pad Kee Mao (Drunken Noodles). Liking spicy food, I opted for the "Thai Spicy" end of the heat spectrum. It did not disappoint. It added burn sufficient to make my tongue sweat and nose run, stopping just short of numbing my gums. Certainly no compromise for this western pallette. Loved every morsel of the thick noodles, chicken, green & red pepper, onion and green beans.   By the time I finished I was alone but for the pleasant owner. We talked for a few minutes about her business and our experience in Thailand. It was a genuine and interesting exchange, and an unexpectedly provocative dessert.

Finally made it to Dim Sum Garden.   Located mid-street on Race, it is a deep and narrow space with a step up half way back at the kitchen and mini-bar area.  One wall is slate, and the other smooth with the image of a huge dumpling adorning the wall.  That same design is emblazoned on the black T's worn by the wait staff.  I wouldn't mind wearing one of those.    Entering solo around 7:30, the tables were buzzing, but not SRO.  I was pointed to a deuce in the front window, and quickly choose to look inward rather than out toward the street.  If I was in a metaphorical mood that might mean something.  It seems natural to want to enjoy the floorshow.  The menu arrived promptly with a glass of water (cold, not hot), and a few minutes later the server returned to direct me through the offerings.  I knew I wanted the Xiao Long Bao (#1) because that what was most people raved about, but I also wanted a second dish - selecting Eggplant with Garlic Sauce as counterpoint.      Part of the schtick here is the servers offer to show you how to eat XLB.  For the uninitiated there is a learning curve and the risk of spraying scalding broth onto your neighbors, so there is some reason for caution.  Mild dexterity in the use of chopsticks and flat bottom spoon in tandem is required, but once mastered the manipulation becomes part of the fun.  Even life long experts can be seen chasing escaped dumplings across the table, so there is no fear of lost face.    I was surprised that the XLB were not as good as I expected.  Their dough was thicker than I have had in the famous Shanghai dumpling shops.  True, the pork filling was substantial and decent, and the steaming soup within pretty good, but they were disappointing nonetheless. Even the "Dumpling Sauce" on the tables was not quite right to my palate.  It used a vinegar that too strongly neutralized the flavor of the broth.  There was no ginger to mix with the vinegar. I had to mix the hot chili oil with the sauce on the plate to get to the heat I wanted to supplement the taste.  The second dish was good Eggplant with Garlic Sauce.  I asked for it "hot," and upon arrival it glistened from the oil it cooked in.  I liked it, but added still more chili to bring up the burn.    I will certainly return to Dim Sum Garden as there is much more coming out of the kitchen that looks interesting, and because so many of my friends love the place.  It calls itself, "Philly's Premier Authentic Shanghai Soup Dumpling Restaurant."  Who am I to question a marketing slogan, but if you say it, you should be able to back it up.    I don't think it did.

Not sure how Chickie's & Pete's is considered a café, as it seems much more like a dark and dingy sports bar with a huge collection of tap levers hanging from walls and exposed beams.  There seems to be plenty of suds to choose from, and the menu is adequate, especially if you like shellfish as your main course.    Problem here is that there are no side dishes with your meal.  Everything is a la carte, and the expense climbs rapidly.  If you want a beer with that, your tab will gouge you at least $15 for a sandwich lunch.    My Chicken Parm Sandwich was pretty good; deep fried and crispy outside, still soft and tasty inside.  The Tomato Sauce was mildly salty, but still a good blend.  Would have been even better if they figured out a way to give a small amount of Crab Fries with the platter, rather than charging another $7 for a full basket of taters.  The House Salad @ $10., was a large plate full of Romaine and some other veggies, and a reasonably good vinaigrette, but underwhelming at the price.   If you're into tired looking sports bars with ample brew (not necessarily craft-quality), and a menu that forces you to be very selective about the cost of your nosh, C & P is for you.  Otherwise, there are much better sports houses around with better food, drinks, atmosphere and prices.

Not the best bagel experience in the area, and not the worst.   The store is spacious enough for a number of tables and a long line waiting for service. Bins full of rounders appear smaller than my last Manhattan visit a few years ago (Clearly not real Manhattan Island bagels that are often larger than a saucer in diameter.) Still, my onion, butter and swiss had decent texture, loads of onion flakes and a good bite. Their coffee could stand a better bean roaster and more choices.   Service suffered from understaffing. There was one woman taking orders and working the griddle, making for a hectic burnout shift for her, and growing queue. When the owner/manager came out from the back, and put on plastic gloves, things got better, but he was not well trained in food prep, so the butter spread was uneven, and only a single slice of cheese was placed within - where a minimum of two is the normal allocation, and often more. Too, the transection did not completely separate the halves, so when one side was lifted, the other tagged along and fell apart.   I attributed that to having a bad morning.

If you love old school urban street corner restaurants, you are going to think you died and went to heaven when you step inside Pete's Clown House, at the corner of Frankfort Avenue and Pike Street, in the Port Richmond neighborhood of Philadelphia. It is a tight squeeze going through the front door and passing along the counter, but I found a spinner right there, and had the exalted pleasure of watching the action of the cooks, assistants and servers, as they danced around each other taking care of the hot steel grill and the crush of phone take out orders, while always finding time to chat with those around them with a quip and a smile.   This is definitely a greasy spoon dive, but in the best way possible. If you are entertained by fast hands and flying knives and spatulas, then there is no better theater in the City of Brotherly Love than a orchestra seat in the Clown House. You watch the action up close and personal, as take out orders are written directly on the white bags that will contain the food once cooked. No need for an order pad. And, if close enough to the grill, the occasional spattering of oil or home fries, or spitting bacon, will reach out to touch you gently, and remind you that there is no extra charge for the grease stains on your clothes. That iron is so full of food waiting to be off loaded onto plates or takeout boxes, that its amazing that the kitchen hasn't caught fire in the 66 years it has been slinging hash to the appreciative masses who have been scarfing their incredibly tasty dishes all this time.    "Delicious," is the right word for the food produced here. That grill is so well seasoned from decades of eggs, meats, potatoes, peppers and cooking oil, that it might be edible. The prices are cheap enough to be downright ridiculous. My sausage, egg and cheese sandwich on Kaiser roll, with a side of excellent home fries topped with sautéed onions and green peppers, all the hot java I could drink, came to less than $7.   ARE YOU KIDDING ME?!  So, I had an incredible breakfast, a month's worth of local color, and full bore entertainment from the totally engaging staff, non-stop for the half hour or so I was indulging myself. Although a rookie, I felt at home and one of the regulars. I really didn't want to leave, but I finished eating, and the next customer was waiting to take my stool.   Pete's Clown House - One of those places that defines what is so special about Philadelphia.   Definitely, a must see.

Gotta like the name given to this roadhouse on Street Road in Southampton, PA. Makes it sound like an offshoot of Iron Chef in heat. This is the third incarnation for this rear entranced bar and grill. It is attractive with vaulted ceilings, tall glass, and substantial rectangular bar. Plenty of wood and windows all around.   I liked my vantage point at the corner of the bar facing a kitchen door and HDTV. The beer taps were to my left. I appreciated being given samples of a couple of their brews when I seemed indecisive. I chose the Mango Cart, an obviously fruity beer that had a mildly sour mango flavor and beautiful yellow gold luster. Well worth the $6 pint.   My classic cheeseburger was okay, but missed on its requested endpoint, coming out well done rather than medium. Too, the ground beef crumbled as bitten, giving the impression that it may have been frozen for a while before hitting the hot steel. Perhaps that explains why pink centers weren't an option. It would have been fine as an $8 puck, but at $11, plus $2 for the homemade potato chip swap from fries, it was overpriced.  Service was friendly and prompt.   Plenty of sports available on the multitude of screens, and was fortunate to watch Tiger Woods win the Masters for the first time in thirteen years. Plainly, he had a far better day than I did. Wonder what was served in the clubhouse at Augusta on Sunday?

First visit to this Panera just off the campus of The College of New Jersey.   Walking in, the place was well kept with plenty of room to dine or simply order and take away. I approached the cashier while checking out their bakery products on the back wall and immediately in front of me behind glass. I went with an Everything Bagel, Chive/ Onion Spread and a thin Brownie that winked at me as I spoke with the cashier. Finally, a light roast java to wash it all down.   When I spread it all out on my desk, I learned that I would do the spreading. No sweat, knife included. The bagel was fresh, but the soft variety, rather than the crisp chew I prefer. Still, it was acceptable and I enjoyed it. The Brownie was likewise soft, but nicely chocolatey throughout. Half was covered with powdered sugar, giving it a sweet kick without overwhelming the basic premise of these brown squares. Finally, the Joe was hot and tasty from the light roast, which I often like more than the stronger heavier darker roasts.   Bottom line, this was a decent late morning snack for a busy day, and I won't hesitate to visit again next time I am near The College.

It is time to bump up the stars for Bagel Stop to 5 Big Ones! In fact, it is long passed time to do so. Please forgive my absent mindedness.   How do I know this is a supermax experience?   Because I find myself thinking about their excellent bagels even when I don't plan to be there that day, and excited when I know it is my destination. These babies have addicted me. They are my opioids.   The shop is still in the same location, and too small for tables and chairs. Yet, the master baker and his crew have perfected the onion bagel I prefer - firm skin, soft airy interior, and ample roasted onion flakes all around. When fresh from their ovens, they are plenty good enough to eat just as they come from the bin. If you time your visit just right, you can get them still warm from baking; nothing short of a completely memorable experience. Yet, even on the normal day when they have cooled and wait for your order in their bins, like puppies in the window of a pet store, they are simply a joy to consume with a heavy smear of favorite cream cheese (veggie, please!).   I stopped in today for my weekly fix, and picked up a bag full for the family this weekend. I figured it's time to share the bagel bounty with those I love.   They do muffins and breakfast sandwiches, too. They look zoftig, but I am more the purest, preferring my bagels the traditional way. Just slice, smear and get out of the way!

New Hope Star Diner is an old style roadhouse right out of the 1950s. So, it has that going for it. Too, the menu is as big as you could want. There is no shortage of choices.   When we drove down to Main Street, New Hope on Labor Day it was so crowded with masked and unmasked tourists that there was no social distancing. It wasn't safe to be there, so we drove back to the diner where there were many fewer customers and both indoor and outdoor seating. We wanted to sit outside, but the bees beat us to the shady tables. Rather than deal with those buzzing bandits, we went inside and we're shown to a corner table with lots of space around it. Staff was busy cleaning tables and floor when not serving food. We felt safe eating there.  Our patty melt (w fries, slaw) and Arizona Omelet (w home fries and coffee) were solid plates. My burger was not the medium requested, but it was otherwise tasty and filling. The 3 egger was too much to finish and was taken home. Service was friendly and prompt.   New Hope Star Diner is a 24/7 operation. It may not be the most popular restaurant in this upscale river town, but on a day when everything on the strip was overrun with people trying to escape the remains of Covid quarantine, it was great to have a place that provided both sustenance and safety from the horde.
An extra star for their community involvement is warranted.  Boy Scout Pancake Breakfast was a fundraising success.

Sitting in the strip commercial center at the corner of Columbus Boulevard and Washington Avenue, Pho Saigon is a typical looking large roomed pho house that gives the feeling of a cafeteria.  Service is friendly and efficient.  Apologies were sincere when advised that they were out of Bun Bo Hue before 8 pm.  I settled on another option (Pho Tai), and was very satisfied with that large bowl.  Superior broth, strong noodle mound properly cooked, and plenty of beef and accoutrements. Definitely on the high end of the satisfaction scale.  Yet, the Summer Rolls were a bit disappointing.  The Shrimp appeared to be sliced so thin that they could not be tasted along with the other ingredients.  That, and the cool skin of the wrap was too close to room temp, thus deprived of the coolness of the app.  The Peanut Sauce was adequate, but thinner than most.    The house was three quarters full this Saturday evening, and the HDTVs were showing college football games.    The Pho hit the spot, but everything else seemed a step below top quality, and exhausting the Bun Bo Hue so early was certainly a strategic blunder.    With all the other excellent options for Vietnamese cuisine in the area, there is no compulsion to return to Pho Saigon anytime soon.

Stopped in 30 minutes before the listed closing time.  A few customers remained, but the waiter who greeted me did not hesitate to seat me at a booth, and take my drink order. Mexican? Corona will do nicely, thank you.   The space was a rainbow of colored walls and furniture.  The carved wood backs of the dinner chairs were painted brightly, and the distressed wood tables felt like those I had sat at throughout the southwest and Mexico.  The atmosphere transported me out of Bucks and into Santa Fe, Tucson or maybe, Cancun.  It was an easy trip.   The chips and salsa arrived promptly and I had a quick taste. Hard and crisp shovels for spicy chunky sauce.  Satisfactory, but perhaps not the best I've had.  I was content to wait for the Chicken Flautas, which arrived with a light melted cheesy cover over three stuffed flutes.  Rice and Refried Beans on a separate plate worked well together. I poured the remaining salsa over the flautas to achieve max flavor, and dug in.    The tubes were full of large chunks of white meat chicken, beans, cheese, and a few sliced poblanos.  Everything was well cooked and placed in the oven to bring everything to melting temperature.  Very tasty and filling.  Totally enjoyable.   Why only 3 Stars?  Well, I had to ask for slices of lime for the Corona.  The Salsa was decent, but tasted ubiquitously the same as most store bought varieties, when a homemade approach might have offered something more uniquely their own.  The melted white cheese sauce was a bit too mild, and poured too freely over everything, where  more "kick" would have been more distinguishing.  These are not serious shortcomings, as the dish remained enjoyable. Still, to be fan-worthy or more, there should be something original or memorable about the experience.   I will definitely return to look for that special something, and when I find it, the stars will shine brightly.

Cheesesteak Review -  Dino's is primarily a take out pizza joint on Street Road in Warrington, PA. We wanted to eat while the food was prime, and opted to mange at one of the three tables in the front of the house. Son and I were in the mood for steak sandwiches, although the pizza looked appealing.   This Saturday night they had a three person operation in the kitchen, with Dino on the grill. The room was a bit chilly on an early December night, even with the little space heater. Still, hunger and strong aroma of the beef being chopped and tossed by the chef overcame any temporary discomfort.    The sandwiches were excellent. Fresh crusty rolls, huge load of grilled beef made in house and sliced just before touching hot steel to guarantee juiciness and surprisingly good flavor. A work of culinary art.   We congratulated Dino for hitting the cheesesteak sweet spot, and assured him we would return. Never too far to go for a great Philly steak sammy. And, if the pizza is as good, the beginning of a long delicious relationship.

Tabora Farm Market is primarily a bakery with a lot of home baked choices from cookies to fruit pies to my fave Jewish Apple Cake. There is a small changing offering of farm grown veggies and a deli counter in back if sandwiches and sides are your passion. It is all authentically rustic, and has seen better (cleaner) days. Prices are a bit ridiculous, with postage stamp lemon squares demanding $1.49 per. Expensive at half the price.   Yet, the donuts, apple cake and country grain bread are worthy, so the occasional indulgence is justifiable.   The best part may be the country road drive up county from Newtown on narrow two lane blacktop that twists and turns over hill and dale; even providing a romantic covered bridge or two to stop, walk through and admire.   Was a time not long ago when people reaching into bins to pick out pastries with bare hands would not have disturbed me in the least. Those days, like our innocence, are gone. Now, when I see a thoughtless sloven reach in touching several before grabbing his choice and then carrying it to the cashier, it makes me change direction to avoid his potential viral trail, and find something less compromised. A few signs with gentle reminders to "Keep Your Hands to Yourself," would go a long way.

Apparently, this is the latest incarnation of a series of Banh Mi shops at this location, as a quick YelpCheck shows this place has had several names over the years, while working with the same people and offering substantially the same menu.  As Robert Burns wrote so well, "A rose by any other name would smell as sweet."  And, so it is for this small store on S. 8th Street just off Washington.  The space is clean, with about 7 tables, and a warm staff that is attentive, yet unobtrusive.  I had plenty of time to peruse the double sided laminated menu, but I really knew what I wanted coming in.  The rep here is about authentic Vietnamese Sandwiches, Banh Mi, although they also provide Pho, Vermicelli and Broken Rice dishes, along with a long list of VN Coffee and other beverages.   The fresh ingredients are on display in the glass enclosed refrigerator that separated the customers from the food prep area.  The work on my meal was in plain view.  It arrived a few minutes after ordering on a white plate covered in sandwich paper.  The Baguette was fresh with crunchy crust and soft airy inners. The Grilled Pork was plentiful and cut into small pieces at the bottom of the sandwich valley.  Daikon Radish, Cucumber, Carrot, and Cilantro were piled on top and overflowing.    I took a bite to start the proceedings, and was met with each of the components as they lustily exploded in my mouth.  Really a great first bite!  I added a squirt of Hoisin and Sriracha to bring up the volume a bit and to experiment to see how they would change the experience.  The Banh Mi was fine as it was, but I can be excessive when it comes to flavor, so the addition of both more BBQ flavor and Chili heat was pleasing.   Café Tranh Truc also has a few HDTVs on the wall, so I was able to enjoy a rewatching of The Hurt Locker during dinner.    The entertainment was free.

INCOMPLETE  I have stopped at Priori's on three occasions when their sign says they are open for business over the past few months, and each time the shop was locked up tight without notice nor explanation. I even called while parked in front of the building, without answer.   This is a recommendation that you call before you go, so you don't waste time like I did.   Wishing them the best, whatever is going on.

Ben & Irv's Delicatessen began it's Jewish-style restaurant adventure in the Mt. Airy section of Philadelphia in 1955, and has remained in the same family as it expanded into the spreading diaspora of Montgomery and Bucks Counties, PA.  The house in Huntington Valley on County Line Road looks like most other dineresque large menu emporiums, with the important distinction that although not kosher in the kitchen, it still offers many ethnic dishes for Jewish tastebuds that easily remind we of that faith of our nanny's cooking. Matzo ball soup, potato pancakes, blintzes, pastrami, knishes, pumpernickel sandwiches, white fish salad, salami, borscht and my personal favorite, matzo brie.  Every once in a while it feels good to visit our heritage and taste our history.   Portions are huge, and the prices reflect that. It wouldn't be fair to compare B & I's quality to what I ate as a child, but I suspect that without a Yiddisha hand on the pots and pans in the kitchen, the intense flavor of memory cannot be duplicated. Still, my matzo brie was pretty good, and I was glad I asked the server to add sautéed onions to the mix. It arrived a huge platter of jumbled matzo pieces, egg and onion, scrambled to a semi-dry state.  My partners in crime seemed to enjoy their egg/potato/toast dishes, but spoke more of the quantity than the quality. I tasted a bit of everything. It was all very okay.   While I wouldn't rush back to Ben & Irv's, it is good to know it is there when I need a quick Jewish fix to connect me to my people via traditional comfort food.

Pho Viet HOA on Welsh Road, Willow Grove, sits in the middle of a modern strip center right next door to an Italian restaurant; one of the beautiful things about the melting pot we live in. Its modern utilitarian decor makes room for a dozen tables along both walls, with enough seating for social distancing in these Days of Covid. Service was prompt and efficient, with a suburban smile. The menu was primarily Vietnamese as would be expected, but also delved into a broader culinary universe found in neighboring Asian kitchens like Chinese and Thai style noodle dishes.   I ordered Veggie Fried Rolls as an appetizer, Wide Noodles with Veggies "Wet" in a light brown sauce, and two Banh Mi sandwiches, Grilled Beef and Pork (for family take out). I hesitated on their Pho based on the luke warm reviews from respected Yelpers and the price compared to favorite pho houses in the City, which were a few bucks less.   The four Veggie Rolls and dipping sauce were very good, crisp and full of real chopped veggies, and not just cabbage. The garnish of daikon and carrot were a nice touch. The large plate of fat noodles was supplied with ample broccoli, carrot, onion, mushroom and sprout, but lacking in spice. My mistake for not requesting lemongrass be added, but I squirted on Sriracha from the table rocket to compensate. Not precisely the flavor profile I hoped for, but decent enough to satisfy. I took half of that home.   The uncompromising winner were the Banh Mi consumed by the family later in the evening. They were both stuffed with excellent roast pork and beef, cucumber, daikon, carrot, cilantro and a tasty mix of hot/sweet sauces, all barely contained in fresh (if not exactly French), rolls. Baguettes would have been near perfection. Compared to what we ate the week before from another Vietnamese/Thai house, this was Blue Ribbon.   So, go for the Banh Mi for sure, perhaps not for their specials noodle list, while the jury is out on the Pho. I wouldn't hesitate to give it a try as long as the sammies were the primary focus.   P.S. The Banh Mi were eaten before photos could be secured. Apologies.

This Steve's Prince of Steaks is on Comly Road, just off northbound Roosevelt Boulevard, Somerton, PA, in the far Northeast of the city. If possible, it is even smaller than my regular Steve's on Rt. 1 in Langhorne. There are two windows within. One for ordering your sandwich, for which they have posted a long list of rules to follow to get what you want, and the other only for fries and drinks. Like the rest, the burden is on you to know what you're doing, or face the consternation of the staff and your fellow steak lovers. Not an enviable place to be.  I ordered two "cheesesteaks wit provolone," meaning I wanted two sandwiches with fried onions and provolone cheese. I like the Wiz, too, but preferred the extra mellowness offered by the hard white variation. It set me back $25+. Not unexpected, but I'd be lying if I didn't do a double clutch before paying the dude taking my business.   Normally, we would eat right along the walls at the Langhorne joint, but this shop was smaller and without short shelves and stools. We took them home to consume. These guys are fast and efficient, and it was fun to watch them work through the greasy glass window that separates kitchen from customers. It would have been a thoroughly enjoyable moment, but for Mr. Priss shouting not to take photos (after the last one).   Oh, me. Oh, my! Have to protect those state secrets.   At home, we added our own banana pepper rings to bring up the burn; the pickle bar being removed as a casualty of COVID. It was love at first bite. Great cross section of taste and texture as we incisored through the excellent torpedo roll, cheese and ribeye. My wife and I shared one sandwich, and left the other for her still growing son (6'3").   I have no dog in the fight between the chopped vs. solid slice approach to this Philly delicacy. I like them both ways, as long as the beef used is high quality. Steve's is among my faves, but with every pizza shop making their own version, we are really living in Cheesesteak Heaven around here. The worst one in the Philadelphia region is better than anything anywhere else.

One thing for sure - Water's Edge does Covid Protocol right!   Walking up the stairs to the main entrance you first see a large squirt bottle of hand sanitizer to clean hands before touching the door handle. In the lobby, your temperature is taken and then your driver's license scanned in case they need to notify the county health department to do contact tracing because they learn someone in your party developed Covid symptoms. Then they escort you to a bar stool or table properly distanced from the others. Everyone on staff is masked and gloved. As put to me; "We're dead serious about following protocol. We want to do everything required to keep our restaurant open and keep customers and staff safe."   Greatly appreciated!   So, we took a table outside on a chilly evening. Not only did we want fresh air to maximize safety, but we wanted to overlook the wide and muddy Bensalem Creek which the new owners had gone great lengths to accentuate with the tri-level deck between the banks of the creek and all glass back wall of the restaurant. On a warmer night in season, this would be almost idyllic.   A portable heater was wheeled over to us and sparked on overhead. It took the cold edge off the air, but didn't reach our legs, so we accepted that this would be a somewhat cold experience. Made the night more memorable.   We ordered the brussel sprout appetizer (smallish sprouts with bacon and parmesan mixed in), Tuscon Salmon (wild rice and asparagus), and the Five Alarm Burger w Fries (candied jalapeno slices, cheese, and an aioli spread on the brioche-style bun). They were all good, if not knock outs, but better than expected from a kitchen attached to what is fundamentally a sports pub with an excellent view.   Service was very gracious and attentive. I felt a bit guilty forcing the young woman to come outside to help us when she lacked any true winter wear. She didn't complain, nor even show she was frigid. I hoped a larger tip would provide evidence we appreciated her effort.   Will return with better weather for sure.

This Asian grocery, butcher, fishmonger, green grocer has been open right off Roosevelt Blvd @ St. Vincent Street for several years, having purchased the former 1st NE International Market in 2015. It is very similar to the supermarket at 6th and Washington in South Philly. It has just about everything you need for the complete Chinese kitchen, including pigs feet to fat green frogs, and dozens of vinegars and soy sauces for any dish imaginable.   True, the odor of fish on ice and tanks full of lobster and talapia can be pungent, but that is part of the experience and brings me back to the street markets all across Southeast Asia.   If you need it, they likely have it. If they don't have it, think twice whether it is really necessary.   Even found those Japanese versions of KitKat Bars in strawberry and green tea flavors!

The diversity of opinion on the Yardley Inn & Bar reflect that there is some inconsistency in the delivery of the product here.  Luckily for me, I caught it on a great night when everything came together as the creators must have envisioned it.    This was a business dinner for four.  As such, I had to be less obvious about my intention to write a review with my dinner mates, and kept my mobile phone in my pocket except for when the Tiers of Taste I ordered arrived.  Three plates placed vertically before me on a stainless steel frame that was tall enough to block my view of the person across the table.  We all exclaimed delightful surprise and I felt justified in taking a photo of this unexpected presentation.  That was just the beginning.   The Decoy red from Buckthorn was a great pick by Tom.  I am not a wine expert, but my palate is sensitive enough to know when it is being seduced by gentle tanins. Gotta get me a case of that!    The Marguerita Salad with Candied Walnuts, fresh Blue Cheese, and Tomato Vinaigrette was a cool sweet tart enjoyment.  My Tiers of Taste choices were Calamari with a Vinegar Pepper marinade/sauce, Pierogies and Stuffed Dates.  The squid was well fried, and the sauce was sweetly hot.  Pierogies with Onions and Sour Cream were softly pliant and offered a mild divergence from the stronger statement made by the calamari.  Finally, the Devils on Horseback (that's right), Chlorizo Stuffed into large Dates and Wrapped in Bacon, were a first that combined the luxurious flavor of excellent dates with finely ground Mexican Chorizo, girdled with well done Bacon.  I am not a bacon fan, but this was an exceptional experience.  It came together very well.  I was sated by this meal, and realized I had just come through a magic door that only a very extraordinary meal can open.    Winnie, Jeff and Tom all seemed quite satisfied, but because we were having a serious conversation while we ate, I could not bring myself to ask to taste their food.  But, the Crabcakes, Lemon Chicken and Berkshire Pork Tenderloin all disappeared with sounds of satisfaction.  As we walked out we all commented on the exceptionality of the dinner.    Yardley Inn sits at the bottom of Afton Avenue, directly across River Road from the Delaware River.  It has suffered repeated flooding, and now has an inflatable berm that can hold off all but the most ravaging floods.  Sure hope it works, even when patrons cannot reach it without a boat.  It is a sterling restaurant when the stars align and reflect deeply off the flowing river.   Last night I saw a constellation of 5 stars.

The old stable is now populated by diners enjoying the bucolic, high beamed ceiling, stone floors and exposed kitchen.  If outdoor dining in nice weather is your thing, you can be easily accommodated next to the boccie court and outdoor bar.   It seems I am there most often for special community events, and the layout works well for isolating small groups in places that do not overly interfere with the regular dinner patrons.  The food is family style Italian, meaning if there are more than 3 of you, many of the dishes come piled high and placed centrally on the table where everyone can partake.   The food has always been solid, both meats, fowl and pasta.  The service is much better than average, with black and whites hustling around to be sure everyone is getting what they expect in a timely and friendly, while professional manner.  The last event buffet consisted of Chicken Francaise, Vodka Rigatoni, Eggplant Rolatini, Grilled Veggies, Italian Bread.  All worth the price of admission.    Sure glad someone thinks enough of their guests to schedule a social/political event in such pleasant surroundings.

I should have been alerted to the possibility of issues when we walked in near 7 pm on a Sunday evening, and only a few tables were occupied and, none were Chinese.  Yet, I was with my Chengdu friend, and we wanted some authentic Szechuanese hot chow.  How could a place that calls itself, "Traditional Szechuan," and has pandas in their signs, not be prepared to satisfy a true native soul?    It wasn't.    Even while the owner sat with us and chatted away about home, the staff delivered our dishes in no particular order and spread them out across our table.  I guess he trusted the kitchen to do everything right, but in retrospect I would have preferred him sweating over the stove assuring that everything presented would make us happy.    The Dumplings in Chili Oil were large, but tasteless.  The Cold Sliced Beef in Hot Sauce, a delicacy at home, was over salted and gristly, rather than approaching the numbing spiciness desired.  The Fish Fillet with Dry Pepper was the best dish on the table, and the only one that we did not finish and agreed to take home.  The 3 Mushrooms Rice Cake Style was basically a mushroom consume poured over rice cakes prepared to sizzle.  It was decent, but nothing I would want a second time.  Water Spinach with Garlic was fine, but a bit too stemmy when the leaves are the tender delights.   Given the excellent Szechuan kitchens in the neighborhood (Emai, Four River, Spice-E), and those a little farther afield (Han Dynasty and Chili Szechuan), it is difficult to see how this place will survive.  As we were the last customers in the joint when we left at 8:30, its fate may already be sealed.

We just purchased a new Toro self-propelled lawn mower from Tanners on Rt. 532 in Newtown.  You may remember the location as the former Yamamoto's.   I walked in after our tired out mower's metal tube handle snapped from fatigue, and it became impossible to push it further.  The guys at Tanners showed me what they had to offer in a quiet, knowledgeable way.  They appreciated my frustration, and after asking appropriate questions to zero in on my lawn cutting requirements, directed me to a Toro.  There was a small rebate being offered by the manufacturer, to bring the cost in line with the big boxes out on Rt. 1.  I always prefer to buy locally, and keep the businesses in town open.  A small premium for that satisfaction is well worth it.   Tanners delivered the mower to my home yesterday, fully operational, with a full tank of gas, and road tested.  They took away my old mower, and we agreed that if they could repair it for under a certain amount they should do so, and my 12 year old would have a second machine for his budding lawn cutting business.  If not, they would give me a small trade in offset.  Fair deal.   When I arrived home my son ran out of the house with a big smile.  He had already cut two lawns with the new mower, and he was in love with his first machine.  We had a sharp cut lawn and a happy boy who had just gone through a right of passage.    All this and a new Toro ballcap, too.   Nothing better than that!

Sabrina's Pizza took me by surprise.  I mean, I knew it was there, but I never considered checking it out until very recently.    Now, I've had lunch there twice in one week, and it could easily become one of my regular stops for tomato pie or other midday meal.  Hamilton has dozens of decent small Italian joints that put out the standard fare, and it takes a lot of tasting to distinguish them from each other. Eventually, the better shops emerge above the rest and the circle of good restaurants finally closes.  If embarrassment of riches makes any sense for pizza parlors, this part of the world has it. That doesn't mean that other cities don't do it as well or maybe better (You know who you are). Still, I have come to appreciate the richness of the pizza/tomato pie tradition around here.   What about the food, you ask?  The Eggplant Parm Sandwich I had a few days ago was thin sliced, fine ground bread crumb coating and individually olive oil sautéed purple nightshade, placed in a fresh torpedo and topped with plenty of mozza cheese and a chunky tomato gravy.  Totally a knife and fork experience.  With an iced tea, it comes in at just under ten bucks.    Today's bar pie size Tomato Pie with Italian Sweet Sausage was even better.  It arrived in the hands of the owner/chef on a large ceramic plate, all steamy - a cloud of garlic infused vapors fogging my glasses and attacking my senses.  The crust was firm and crunchy, and even with the extra load of lumpy gravy and ground meat, managed to hold a firm point through most of the meal.  It was excellent and really tasted like it was made in Nonna's kitchen.    If there is anything to pic a nit about it would be that the pie might have been even better with a little less on top.  The tomato sauce was so chunky that it remained moist on the finished disk and as it cooled and released it water condensate, the remaining slices softened and weakened its ability to hold its load. There was actually a bit of water left over as the pie was consumed, and it lost its crunch.    Sometimes, less is more.

Best Buy has certainly gone through the trials and tribulations of all brick and mortar big boxes in this age of internet shopping, and it is really an open question whether it or any of its ilk will survive in their present form.  Nonetheless, there are some things that I still prefer to touch and feel before purchasing, and computers are one of them. I need to be sure I know what I am getting and can really do what I want with the equipment. ( I know I am showing my age here).   This BB is closest to home, and has become my showroom for the electronics I need. I find they have an adequate selection, knowledgeable staff, and the time to answer my questions.  Too, their financing can be reasonable when using their credit card, with zero interest if paid in full within 18 months. That can be handy on the larger business purchases.  For a while, I would only educate myself there, and then buy online.  I found that this did not work well for me and there was a level of disconnect caused by not having asked all the necessary questions, and then having to deal with the manufacturer's websites - usually a disaster.  So, I decided it was better to just go ahead and buy what I needed there once I had decided what that was.  It might cost a few sheckels more, but the total experience was more satisfactory.  I admit to also suffering minor guilt when BB went through bankruptcy/reorganization and came close to closing its doors permanently.    I thought of a world without a place where I could touch a product and talk to someone face to face who knew a lot more about it then I did, and whether I really wanted to contribute to that eventuality, even in a minimal way.  I decided to cast my vote (and spend my dollar) to maintain a retail market system that offered this alternative.  Somehow, it just seemed a more humane future.

For fast food franchised joints, Chick-fil-A does a very good breakfast sandwich.    My Sausage, Egg and Cheese Biscuit was far better than their equivalents at McD's or Burger K.  It is larger, fresher, tastier, and the biscuits themselves flakier and more buttery.    This was a drive thru order at this newish outlet.  They made a small mistake in my favor by throwing in a box of Taters at the bottom of the bag.  I didn't order them, but neither was I charged.  I wasn't aware of it until I arrived at my destination and saw what was in the bag.    Nice to come out on the high side of the transaction.  So often, these deals break the other way.

Chencha Y Chole is a very nice Mexican house at the corner of Broad and Cass in Trenton.  It has been open for several months and still has the "Grand Opening" signs hanging on the sides of the newly painted triangular building.  The odd angle of this intersection created an opportunity for the original architect and city planner to design a structure that fits snuggly in this narrow corner, thus adding interesting perspective to the establishment.  Inside is clean and bright and feels like a bit of sunny Mexico right here in River City.  The menu is diverse, and the plates leaving the open kitchen are equally colorful, and more importantly, very tasty.  I asked for my Hawaiian Torta with Grilled Chicken rather than jamon, and was easily accommodated.  The sandwich arrived loaded with bird, avocado, onion, lettuce, queso fresca ,fried pineapple, spicy mayo, and a few other unidentifiables that added to the overall finished product.  The toasted Roll made the entire package very enjoyable.  It came with good Fries.   Most surprisingly delicious was the homemade Tamarindo drink.  While I thought I was ordering a carbonated bottled of soda, in fact, I was getting something much better.  The Tamarind was cool, mildly sweet and tart, and so very refreshing.  It arrived in a large glass and was a mid-brown shade from the tree pods it was reduced from. Also, very high in antioxidants.  It is great to be so pleasantly overwhelmed.    Serendipity.  This is one of the best Mexican joints I have tried in the city.   4 Stars with a Bullet!

As a general principle I try to avoid big box stores because of the damage they do to the local economy of so many small towns across America.  Yet, there are times using them becomes necessary because the local shops are closed, or just don't have the universal inventory of HD.   Like most men I start to feel intoxicated when facing floor to ceiling tools, hardware, paint, lumber, you name it.  It is amazing what I can convince myself I need when walking up and down the aisles. You mean I don't already have a long handled hammer to extend my reach and leverage?  How can I live any longer without one? Gotta have it!  Right gents?  So, I found myself there yesterday with my son who needed two cans of spray paint for a 6th grade school project and had waited to mention it until after my Newtown Hardware House was closed for the night.  I felt the tug of the tidal wave sensation of all that great stuff.  After 10 minutes evaluating the Rust O Leum , more time picking up some light bulbs, and perusing that long handled blaster (all at good prices), we left the airplane hanger.    I was so drunk from hardware overload I had to let my son drive home.

Stopped in on my way to Winter Wine Fest in Skippack, otherwise I would seldom have a reason to be in Hatboro, although it is a cool place.  The man, himself, holds the fort @ Denny's Dogs.  It is a tiny shop in an old strip on Jacksonville Road.  Parking is limited and difficult to negotiate.  However, the Dogs are worth the effort.  You can get them as you like them, and fix 'em up with the extra relishes, peppers and table rockets full of mustard and ketchup.  They are all beef, and the rolls have good body and size to fit and hold the extra sauerkraut piled high on top.  When I was finished with my squirts and slices, I could still close the bun and bite into the creation without leakage.  That is a major plus, as there are no tables in the shop now, and I was relegated to eating in my car on this cold Saturday afternoon.  No fuss. No muss.   The only downsides are the aforementioned parking, lack of seating, and the use of styro packaging.  To save the planet, I would have been happier with a thick paper rollup, and paper towels rather than the thin napkins that require a handful to be effective.   Still, this is a frankfurter lovers' haven.  If you lust for one sometimes, a place like Denny's can be your port of entry to the Sea of Tranquility.   Go ahead.  You know you want one.

Actually in Wrightstown at 5 Points on Rt. 413.   Primarily a take out place, but there are a few tables if eating the food piping hot out of the kitchen is important (it should be).   The food is standard Americanized Chinese food. There must be one cookbook they all work out of, or a convention they all attend to get the same items on every menu around the continent. Still, Panda Garden is on the higher end of the quality spectrum even if the output is fairly much the ubiquitous fare we all know. I have had the Wonton Soup who's broth is above average; the various Chicken and Sauces, which are solid, but uninspired and sometimes overcooked; and the Noodle dishes and Foo Youngs, which are also acceptable. Just nothing to write home about unless you are having a very boring day and feel homesick.   If you find yourself in this part of Bucks County this choice is as good as you are going to find. It is an A - Okay option.

This Target is a great example of the old fashioned true department store, with a little of everything you need for daily existence.  Clothing, food, lighting, kitchenware, electronics, sports equipment, music, and automotive - all under one roof.  It may not have everything you want, but it generally has everything you need.    Heard that it is a good place to work, especially compared to the other Big Brother Big Box stores.    Not the highest quality, but not the lowest, either.    Even the snack/coffee area is offered as a convenience to their customers.    If you remember EJ Korvettes and other last century highway superstores, Target will make you feel a little nostalgic.

Capitol Restaurant, a/k/a Two Peters Diner, a/k/a The Extension Diner, has put a lot of effort into renovating this quasi-historic institution on North Olden Avenue (Extension).  It still has the look and feel of a Jersey diner, but with the added sheen of new lighting, a bar, and HDTVs around the house.  They still have a counter and appear to either bake or have access to beautiful pastries in the front display.  Glad they made the effort to come back after a stretch of bad luck.    I stopped in for breakfast after a short court appearance and took a spinner near the kitchen door.  My server was friendly, attractive, and training someone in the finer points of Jersey diner etiquette (You know, how and when to say, "Hun," "Doll," "Sweetheart," and, "You want fries with that.")  As a result I had excellent attention paid to my coffee cup and overall satisfaction.  I ordered the old reliable Sausage, Egg & Cheese on Kaiser breakfast sandwich, and was offered the choice of hash browns or fresh fruit on the side.  I went juicy.   My meal arrived on a large white plate, with the sandwich bisected and pinned together with long wooden spikes.  There were two pork sausage links, two scrambled eggs and a solitary slice of American cheese under the hood.  I should have asked about the meat, as I prefer patty to wurst in these creations.  Still, there was plenty of food, and everything was fresh and tasty (although the cheese was lost in the melee).  The roll was one of those white bread deals, where it is shaped like a roll, but tastes like plain white.  Maybe, if toasted it would have had more verve.  Due to the weight of the sausage and its slick skin, I soon discovered that every bite led to something slipping out the back door.  I switched from manual to fork and knife to control the losses, and keep them from landing in my lap.    I had three refills of my coffee and plenty of the milk I requested in a small stainless pitcher.  The java was pretty good.   All in all, a decent breakfast, but not the homerun I was hoping for.

Dealing with jewelers can be intimidating.  You seldom know what you are looking at, let alone a fair price for it, unless you are in the business.    Harry Merrill & Son, a third generation enterprise on South 8th Street in Jewelers' Row, does its best to make the experience of shopping and buying from them as informative and relaxing as possible (Let's face it, when spending a lot of money some anxiety is bound to creep in).  They are in no rush to sell you anything.  They ask plenty of questions to understand what you want, and are willing to show you many alternatives on the way to honing in on the bauble you seek. And, if they don't have exactly what you want, they can probably find it quickly and still make a good deal.   I have visited them a lot of late for a variety of reasons, and discovered that Rob Schwartz (Don't blame him for his predecessors choosing an Anglicized name for the family shop) is open and genuine; that his mother is still hard at work and has an amazing knowledge of the Philadelphia gem scene over many generations, and that the rest of his staff is well trained in people skills.  They make the jewelry purchase experience as transparent and no-pressure as possible.   Always comparison shop, but when you are ready to buy, be sure to visit Merrill.  You may find yourself wishing that you went there first.

I stopped into Euro Delights while visiting the various tasting rooms around Skippack on the Winter Wine Fest on a sunny, but cold Saturday afternoon in January.  There was a vineyard sharing its wares in a back room, but with the people two and three deep waiting for a pour, I knew the better move was to take a comfortable seat at a small window table away from the crowd, and to order one of Euro's exceptionally delicious bakery gem.    I settled in, but decided to walk into the retail section of the old converted home to se what was under glass.  One of the owners/sisters remembered me from the earlier visit, and introduced me to her partner in the biz. After a nice chat about their success and desire to expand, I selected a square of Washington Cake and Coffee to be brought to my table.    The cake was loaded with nicely spiced apples and a vanilla cake-like mix.  The texture was pleasantly chunky and mildly sweet with brown sugar and cinnamon accents.  The top was a Lemon Crème icing-one of my favorite flavors for pastry.  The overall impact was fun and totally satisfying.  I ate it as slowly as possible to stretch out my enjoyment. Luckily, the front dining room was not too crowded, and I did not feel rushed.    This stop at Euro Delights confirmed what I experienced the first time.  This is a fine bakery and café where the creativity of the baker and the warmth of the environment the proprietresses evoke mark Euro Delights as a one of a kind establishment where goodness translates directly to the taste buds.

One door closes and another opens...Such is the Circle of Life.  Giovanni's Custom Tailoring has opened in the space formerly occupied by its predecessor, Frank DeRito Men's Clothier.  Dino continues to tailor expertly and bring his warm, cosmopolitan charm and gifted abilities to the same location where he has worked for more than a decade.    I recently ordered a suit (S. Cohen of Montreal) and had Dino make the necessary fine tuning adjustments for my long arms and legs.  All done at a very reasonable price.  He is truly a master of the needle and thread, and knows before I do what will look good on me.    Hopefully, Giovanni's will carry the same quality clothing as Frank DeRito, and will likewise have the great sales when exceptional suits, jackets, coats, sweaters, shirts and ties can be purchased at prices not normally associated with high end Newtown.   At least, I can pray that happens.

I have a memory of being in this place about twenty years ago, and it looking very different back then.  I don't remember if it was McCool's or another name, but for sure it was a much darker and dingier dive in those days.  Today, there are large windows along the back wall letting in some light, and the bar has been moved to the inner wall to permit that to happen.  The place still has that old pub feel, all dark woods and lots of draft beer handles and liquor bottles on the back bar shelves.    Yes. Plenty of choices, and a decent menu, too.  When I stopped in around 1 for lunch before a meeting a few blocks away, there was only one other guy at the bar, and one table occupied.  Those people were gone before I finished, leaving me to have a good conversation with Heather, the bartender.  This is one of the benefits of late lunches. Miss the happy hour, but befriend the bartenders, and ask lots of questions.   Very cool that she has been there 13 years, joining the crew shortly after the old place was purchased by the current owners who made all the structure changes seen today.  Turns out the hosts are Greek and do a very good take on the tavern comfort foods coming out of the basement kitchen.  I'm told the new dumbwaiter was installed fairly recently, saving a load of stair climbing to serve customers.    I had a Summer Love draft and the house Macaroni and Cheese for a light meal.  The former was cool, mildly complex and easy going down, and the later, hot, cheesy and served in the same crockery as the French Onion Soup.  Although an app, it filled me amply, and left room for a coffee stop on my way to the meeting on Market St.    I was very happy with my short sojourn at McCool's.  In its quiet unassuming way, it is a nice haven from the street hustle, and in a similar vein, a pleasant alternative to the louder vanity stops that abound in Center City.    The reincarnation has gone very well.

Newtown Farmers' Market is an overcrowded, under-maintained, slightly tarnished version of the Amish markets in the Lancaster area.  They have proliferated to other locales around Bucks, but this was one of the first.  Honestly, it needs a refurbishment, as it gets dingier by the month.   Yet, there are a few stalls where the food product is original and tasty.  Barbie's Soft Pretzels is one of them.  They don't have a sign anywhere near the shop, but if you know your way around, it is right across from the sushi place near the main entrance.  Lately, I have become slightly addicted to their Jalapeno, Onion and Cheese Pretzel Dog.  They claim it to be a beef hot dog encased within a soft pretzel shell, with the Jalapeno Slices, Sautéed Onion and Melted Cheese all stuffed within the pretzel. The current price is $2.50 per, and it seems a good deal.  The pretzel is the same as you can get as a traditional twist, but the taste and texture are strongly influenced by the contents within.  Each bite comes at you with succeeding sensibilities of slightly salty pretzel, the garlicy dog, with a rush of jalapeno arriba, and finally the subtle cheese to finish each chomp/chew.  Damn enjoyable with each repetition.   Today, they had a special on Blueberry Shakes (in season), so why not?  I watched the young freulein put in two scoops of vanilla ice cream (they have their own supply right next to the Goodnoe case - they should work out a deal to use the local iconic brand), and then a copious amount of Blueberry mash.  She blended it for at least two minutes.  The taste was superlative with the straw constantly clogging with the sapphire blue berry slurry.  The best moment was when extra suction was applied to my end of the straw and the blockage finally gave way and exploded in my mouth.     In my munchies days, that would have blown my mind.   So, yes, I am a fan of Barbie's.  Yet, I wish they kept their stall cleaner.  As I stood and looked down into the lemonade machine, the clear sight of mold in the corners gave me pause.  It had not been cleaned well in ages.  Sigh...  I ate my lunch anyway, as I felt the obligation to post this review.

Pho Ha Saigon is located in an as yet not redeveloped part of South Philly on Oregon Avenue.  It is part of a small strip commercial center attached to the old Oregon Market.  This location is a satellite of the primary Vietnamese area on Washington Avenue, and it was a smart move to get to this place before the big money arrived to gentrify the neighborhood.    The house itself is very similar to most of the other Vietnamese kitchens, in that it has a large floor plan with basic amenities; designed more like a cafeteria than a comfortable hang around restaurant.  Tables and chairs are utilitarian and are appropriate for the speed service provided by the friendly staff.  The menu covers a broad cross section of VN cuisine, from Pho and Bun to Vermicelli and Broken Rice dishes.  Prices are reasonable in light of the probable rent on the property.  It is easy to get completely stuffed for less than $10.    While I normally start an exploration of a new Vietnamese house with a bowl of Pho, I broke out of the mold by ordering Broken Rice with Grilled Chicken for a lunch entre, and an app of Summer Rolls.  My companion went with a Vermicelli plate that included a sampling of Shrimp, Pork, Beef, Tofu, and a Fried Spring Roll.    Everything was good, but the most memorable pieces of our meals were the Grilled Pork and Shrimp, and the Spring Roll.  They were tasty and brought smiles to our faces.  The rest was decent, but no better than the fare offered by most other shops.  I found the butterflied Chicken Thigh to be a touch under marinated and undercooked.  Thus, the skin and thicker aspects of the meat were not right for consumption. A few more minutes on the grill would have solved this.  Copious squirts of Sriracha and Hoisin helped.    I will come back to try the soups which have received praise.

When Lynn's was open, and Leo was scooping out wisdom along with his personally roasted coffee beans, this shop had to be one of the best places in the region to pick up a bag of beans after discussing you tastes with the Man. It was from Leo I discovered Tanzanian Teaberry, and some of his own mystical blends.   Sadly, the storefront is now closed.  But, all is not lost.  The Grapevine on North State Street, just one block away now has Lynn's coffee for sale with many of the most popular varieties still in large burlap bags for sampling.  Chuck, the owner of Grapevine is more than happy to fill your order.  While his book of knowledge is quite different than Leo's, he has more than his share of great tales to tell.    By all means, buy your coffee here, and while you're at it, pick up some organic veggies, and your nutritional supplement needs.  Very cool store if you can find the front door behind the wall of hanging potted plants surrounding it.

Walking back through Skippack Village after Winetober Fest and a Brasserie 73 dinner, we came across a bakery café looking place in another old house on the main drag.  I wanted coffee to accompany us back home, and approached the front door to have a better look through the windows.  I saw a display case full of attractive pastries and wanted a closer look and sniff.   Turned out that Euro Delights is run by two sisters from Finland who have been here for many years, but still possess a delightful accent and a old world sense of comfort and taste.  The kitchen in the back is visible from the retail shop, and with the ovens just recently turned off for the evening, the aroma of cake and hot fruit and sugars wafted throughout.  Coffee alone would not be enough.   We shared a fresh miniature Apple Pie topped with Whipped Cream and a dusting of Cinnamon.  A personal pie scaled down to the size of a huge muffin.  Locally sourced ingredients made this an exceptional taste experience. The apple was sweet and surrounded by its juices. The brown sugar crumble on top was fun and firm to the bite.  The crust was excellent.  With the whipped cream adding a softness and subtle undertone, the entire desert was perfect.    With the rage over cupcakes in full bloom, it was only a matter of time before a creative baker would take it to the next level - personal sized pies. Maybe this is already being done, but it is new for me.   We ate alone in the dining area across the center hall from the shop.  It was full of small tables, colorful walls and curtains.  It felt like we had stepped into a time capsule as the décor was mid-nineteenth century.   Definitely worth a drive to Skippack for Brunch and Pie, or one of the other tempting delights under the Euro sign.  Euro Design has only been open for 5 weeks, but their future is bright if they keep producing wonderful pies and cakes.

Lola's Café is easy to walk passed without a second glance.  But, if you are fortunate enough to peer through the large storefront glass you will find a small utilitarian banh mi house that turns out a superior Vietnamese sandwich and a very good smoothie, too.    I walked in for a late lunch before my scheduled haircut around the corner looking for a good baguette based sandy made with skilled hands knowledgeable in the ways of Saigon fare.  I lucked out.    Lola is the young daughter of the owners of this shop.  The couple running the operation are very friendly and informative about their vision for the business and how they create their dishes.  I had the Roast Pork Banh Mi.  It came complete with in house baked pork roast sliced thin and amply placed in fresh French loaf.  The Daikon radish, Cucumber, Cilantro and Mayo were in there, too.  The bread was slighted warmed, and perhaps spread with a touch of butter or oil to bring up the flavor of the opus.    I learned that the roast pork starts as a raw ground meat that is mixed with spices and baked in the home oven for several hours before being sliced and used as the foundation for their sandwich.  It is not a "deli meat" at all, but done fresh by the owners as needed.    It was an excellent banh mi, perhaps the best I have sampled in Chinatown, and on par with those down around Washington in South Philly.  The Pineapple-Banana Smoothie was thick, cool and so refreshing. I walked around with it after lunch and was great on an above average mid October afternoon.  At $4 per BM and Smoothie, the prices were right!  Lola's is worth many return visits to see what else they do in the kitchen.    4 Stars with a Bullet!

This was my first visit to a Primo anywhere, and my initial impression is good.  This shop opened a few months ago, emerging from a fire that destroyed an earlier Italian deli/restaurant. "White" is the overall sense when walking in.  Everything appears clean, and the kitchen area is open for all to see, and everything appears orderly. The Hoagies come in three sizes, but the middle range, 9"er is the most popular and has the sesame seeds on top.  The others are "signature wheat rolls."  My first bite was of a Turkey Schwartzie, which is Sliced Turkey Breast, Swiss Cheese, Cole Slaw & Russian Dressing.  It was very good.  The sesame could be tasted immediately, followed quickly by the turkey, cole slaw, Swiss cheese, with the sweetness of the Russian Dressing acting like a final note of completion.   I thought I could handle the 9" for lunch, but I gave up at half time.  It was very filling.  So, it was really two lunches at a reasonable price.   The menu has lots of interesting options.  Reading the other reviews, I know I want to return to try the "Diablos," and Cutlet Combos.  ... All in good time, my friend. More stars to follow.

Walking out of Vince's Pizza after a less than stellar couple of slices, I needed something to take the bitter aftertaste of the sauce off my tongue. Imagine my relief to realize there was a bakery right next door. It was like finding an emergency rescue squad right next to a bad auto accident.    Cairo Cakes is a small shop.  There was a steady flow of customers as I waited, asked questions of the helpful man in white, and made my selections.  The display cases were full of cupcakes, and trays of various brownies and bars.  I jumped at the Lemon Bars, always a favorite.  The Chocolate Peanut Butter and something that tasted like German Chocolate filling with Toasted Coconut Shredded Wheat-like topping, also found their way into my box.  Finally, I picked up a couple of colorful cupcakes for my son to give his mom for a little treat on Mother's Day.    Everything I tasted was very good, if a little too dense for my palate.  The flavors were all strong and addicting, but they had a cloying stickiness that required a hot drink to clear from the tongue and teeth.  I would have preferred a lighter texture while maintaining the flavors, as can be found in many bakeries.    Still, this is a nice place to come for sweets in the area, and it certainly saved me from suffering the long term aftereffects of the lousy pizza put out next door.  I will return here when in the area and my sweet tooth needs attention.

I admit that I am a late convert to the value of a shop that specializes in olive oil and balsamic vinaigrette.  I never thought they offered enough of what shoppers wanted and would pay premium prices for.  I was wrong.   Tubby Olive has graced State Street in Newtown Borough for a few years, and has even opened another shop in Doylestown.  Walking in, the aroma of spices greets you, suggesting a casbah in Marrakesh or old Italian deli off Washington in Philly.  Large bottles and metal containers surround the room on shelves, everything labeled.  The staff is very friendly and informative, and takes pleasure in turning a customer on to new flavor sensations.    The garlic infused oils with secondary spices are amazingly subtle, and have your palette engaged as if drinking fine wine.  My fave are the fruity balsamics, especially the Black Cherry and Raspberry, which just surprise the taste buds with their soft sweet tartness.  On a fresh salad they are outstanding.   I inadvertently visited recently when hungry, and found myself dipping the offered bread repeatedly into one of the many samples and eating them until I was nearly full.  I am sure I was obvious, but no one complained nor hovered near to deter me.  That was one of the finest and unusual meals I have had in a long while.    After that, I had to buy some of what I had tasted, just so I didn't lose face.  It was well worth it, although at those prices I couldn't do it often.

This was going to be a one star review until management slightly redeemed itself at the end.   The story begins when I walked into this Modern Vac & Sew Center on Grant Avenue in Northeast Philly, in need of a power cord and foot petal for a Amazon purchased Singer machine that was delivered by the seller without those parts inside the box.  He didn't have them, and left me to my own devices to find where I could.  Good luck to me!  The folks here looked at the machine and said they would order the parts. They took a $20 deposit.  No sweat. A month later, no call from them, so I rang them up to inquire, and was told the parts had not arrived.  Seemed excessive, but what do I know from sewing machines?  In the meantime, I decided to make a second attempt to find what was needed, and realized there was a local sew and vac in town.  The good people there also checked the machine and thought they could help with securing what was needed.  I told them about the situation, and agreed to only see if they were available, without ordering until I had finished dealing with these guys.  Reasonable strategy.  Two weeks later, still no word, so, I went down to Grant Ave. again.  I asked for status, and the employee there could not tell me anything.  He looked around the shop, but found no parts, nor order for them.  I asked for my deposit back, but he declined to do so before talking to the boss about whether the parts had been special ordered and paid for in advance.  He promised he would call me in two days.  I wasn't happy about leaving without the money, but I calmed down and realized this dude was doing the best he could in these circumstances.   While I waited, I decided to buy the parts the hometown shop had located at a fair price. Intuition told me this place would not come through for me.    True to his word, the man at this store called to let me know I could have my deposit back.  He saved a star, and proved himself to be an honorable fella.  Can't say the same for ownership, who never saw the need to contact me about the status of the ordered parts, even after I called to ask about them. Not great customer service.   Can't read his mind, but he can read this review.

First bite at Casa Lupita was a little unusual.   I walked in for a late lunch and the large banquet/dining area looked like it was between weddings - all white tablecloths with pink bows and ribbons everywhere.
