But, to one side near the kitchen a few tables had been left aside for the day/evening crowd to use.  The only other person in the house at 2 was Alicia, the chef, server, manager, and Jacquelina of all trades.    She was Aces.  She took my order for Sopes de Pollo with Black Beans and Rice on the side, and disappeared into the kitchen to make my lunch.  It was only when I heard the rumbling in the kitchen and she finally emerged with a tray loaded down with my almuertzo and placed it before me that I realized what was going on. She played all the parts of this theatrical production.   Everything was very good.  The thick corn tortilla used as the base for the Sopes was freshly baked and was strong enough to hold the open face of the Chicken, Beans, Lettuce, Tomato and Grated Cheese that was piled onto each of the three 5 inch diameter disks.  The Mexican spices announced themselves in their splendid red and green, and two small dishes of Salsa waited patiently to be thrown into the flames.  So good.  The Black Beans and Golden Rice were ample, satisfying and filling.  My Mandarin Jarritos reminded my why it was my favorite carbonated drink - the fruit flavors always come through in a way that the Americano alternatives just do not.    While I consumed this excellent repast, Alicia sat at the next table and chatted with me about the shop and her life since coming here from Cuidad Mexico more than 20 years ago.  She was bright, charming, and had a confident air that was compelling. I thought she was the owner of this hall, but alas, only a very motivated employee.  Impressive, nonetheless.  Casa Lupita is 4 Stars with a bullet.  It may be the best of the Casas Mexicanas I have sampled to date.    It will be hard to keep me away.

The results on China Boys Chinese/American restaurant depends on whether you are there for take out or eat in.  As a take away joint the place gets passing grades for consistency, speed, and quantity/quality.  The same cannot be said for dining in, where although there are 6 tables, the space is unattractive, poorly maintained, and without effective air conditioning on a hot summer day.    The Wonton Soup I ordered with my lunch special was the same as in so many other houses of this ilk.  Chicken consume out of a can with thick skinned Wontons and some sort of meat-food within.  The Sesame Chicken was pretty average, but there was plenty for lunch.  The sauce while gloopy, still had the expected sweet taste that is used on almost all similar dishes.  The Fried Rice was made en mass in the morning (or the day before), and was dark from the beef stock it had absorbed, although it had a fair amount of veggies and pork chunks.   For me it was what I expected - unimaginative and strictly by the numbers cooking.  If you like this style then no harm coming here.  However, if you prefer something more authentically Chinese, one of the best places in Mercer County is right up Nottingham Way at Szechuan House.    These two places are as different as night and day.  What a difference a half mile makes.

Visiting Skippack Village for the first time to sample the local vineyards fare at Winetober Fest (Thank you for the tix, Yelp Philly), we finally had our fill and needed a place to get off our feet, and eat something.   After a few hours surrounded by fellow inebriants (have you ever been someplace where the entire ville is drunk?) we found Brasserie 73 in the center of town.  Even before walking in the door we passed a large patio out front. Had it been a warmer evening, that would have been our choice.  However, dining inside was an exceptionally pleasant experience.  The bar/dining room is large, with high ceilings, dark woods, and a definitely continental air. We had a corner table under the front windows where we could watch the winding down of the festival out on the street, while we admired the old world elegance within.    Service was good with a knowledgeable waiter and bustling staff.    The meal started off auspiciously with a very seasonal Pumpkin Bisque presented inside a locally grown pumpkin.  It was very nicely done with a creamy base and lots of veggies, sunflower seeds and bacon.  Really tasty!  The Salade du Maison was a spring mix with a light balsamic dressing.  Also decent.  We waited a bit longer than expected for the shared main course, Farfalle with Jumbo Shrimp, Tomato, Sundried and regular, Artichoke, Fennel, and Basil.  This dish was underwhelming given the ingredients, and what came before it.  It felt flat and lifeless.   I inquired of our wait person about the inconsistency in the quality of the dishes.  He was prepared for it.  He explained that the establishment had gone through 3 ownership changes over the past few years, which accounted for changes in philosophy and ability.  There was a Head Chef change a few weeks ago.  They now had a primo chef from Philadelphia who was still using the old menu, and creating specials to complement it.  The new menu was not yet ready, so we were caught in the middle of the changeover.  The bisque was his baby - creative, rich and savory.  The pasta was off the old menu, and lacked energy.  If you read the other reviews beginning several years ago, you can see the ups and downs of the evolution here.   The new menu will be installed by November 1, 2013.  I recommend everyone wait until after that date to come for a big meal or a party.  Before that, pay attention to the specials, as ordering off the old sheet will likely prove disappointing.   Still, a beautiful place to dine. Great wine list. Wonderful space. High prices.

While most of the bakery sweets are heavy, their icing is wonderful.  I have sampled many of their buns, cookies, bars, cakes, and they are all fun to eat.  My favorites are the Apple Cake which reminds me of the densely moist version my Yiddish grandmother made on most holidays, and the Lemon Bars which are equal parts tart and sweet with powdered sugar dusted on top, and a firm crunchy base.    Both are addicting and require self control to make them last.

Oregon Market appears to be the sibling of Vietnamese market in the Wing Phat Shopping Mall at 11th and Washington, although perhaps a bit cleaner and easier to navigate.  It is connected via the small inner space between stores to the Pho Ha Saigon restaurant, so it is convenient to shop and eat (or vice versa).    It always amazes me who much more variety of produce these Asian grocers have than the typical American supermarket.  Green leafies from peas, cabbage, lettuce, and every other form of vegetation are washed and bagged for consumption with any one of a score of sauces that go so well with the sautéed end product that is often just discarded in the West.  What's more significant is that it all tastes great fresh from the wok.    Quite an eye opener.  The fresh fish is ready for inspection and selection.  The boxes of live Blue Claws await their delectable demise.   If you wonder if there is MSG in your dishes in Chinatown, just walk down the spice aisle and choose from among several large cans and boxes of the white powder.  It is more prevalent than salt.    If you buy enough, when you go to the cashier you will be offered a free bottle or box of whatever they have in surplus that day.

Strictly take out with $10. minimum for credit card purchase.    The menu is extensive, both Chinese and Sushi, and the prices reflect the absence of tables and service expenses.  The front of the menu has a nice statement about healthy eating being their goal, and that the food is all natural, low calorie and how it is the, "only specialty take out serving authentic Chinese & Japanese in this area."   Maybe, but what they do not claim is that it is tasty or high quality cuisine.  Sadly, speaking only of the Chinese side of the menu, it is not.  The ingredients may have integrity, but the resultant dishes are ordinary and lacking in most redeeming qualities other than being filling. The food isn't bad, it just isn't very good.    I wouldn't attempt to compare it with the food produced in New York or Philly, but even by the rather pedestrian suburban standard, Lotus Garden hardly measures up to its peers.    It may offer gluten free dishes, but by the same token, it also offers tasteless ones.   Best to keep looking for a more satisfying fast Asian meal.

While the companionship of fellow Yelpers was 5 Star, and the overall ambiance of Luna Café nearly so, there is no escaping the fact that my brunch (and that of others) was delivered at the wrong temperature.    My pancakes, topped with fresh Blueberries, with a side a pure Maple Syrup, were no more than room temp. The dish would have been amazing if brought hot and steaming.  Apparently, the Blueberry Sauce and Maple Syrup were not heated before being poured over the pancakes, or placed on the table, and as a result cooled dramatically while awaiting transport by our server.  The ingredients were first rate, and even cooled had a wonderful taste.  Still, a cool pancake is not optimal for best experience.   I took the opportunity to talk with the chef to explain what had happened, and suggested the sauces and syrups be heated before use to be sure everything arrived ready for peak consumption.  He was gracious and appreciative for the information. I believe this oversight will be easily corrected.    Luna Café has a lot of promise.  It has history, charm, friendly service, and an interesting menu.  Fix the small glitches and it will take off.    I will return soon to find out if the stars ascend.

I have visited four BWWs around the country;  Chino Hills, CA., Flagstaff, AZ., Northeast Philly, and this one.  Not that this is a representative sample, but in my mind, this one is on the bottom of my list.  The distance between locations is matched by the yawning gap between this experience and the others.    The shop in Flag is large, clean, and a fun place to sit at the bar late into the night while drinking a broad selection of beer and well presented wings and burgers after a run to the Canyon.  Chino Hills has a different sensibility with a more Latin and Asian clientele, but just as much entertainment value and food quality.  Northeast Philly has none of the above, but a more tie off/working stiff/biker vibe, where you can still grab a stool and hang with the boys.  But, the former Don Pablos feels helter skelter.  Perhaps, the ghost of the former tenant haunts the room.  Still, the loudness of the music overlapping the glaring TV's , and a large step down in service and cuisine quality, make this a disjointed, cacophonous experiment.  Hard to converse, nor enjoy the subtle differentiation between the BBQ sauces. The burgers never come out Medium.  Well Done is the seeming only option.   While I wouldn't mind the "pay for the label" approach to BWW when the atmospherics are working well, when they don't, the price seems unwarranted and absurd.  As someone who has enjoyed the experience elsewhere, as well as a happy former stockholder, I suggest management get a grip on the quality control issues here, and bring the operation into line.    Otherwise, change the name to protect the franchise.  How about, "Bungalow Wild Winks?"

You can take home a par finished pie from Mom Mom's and finish the job in your oven, but if you prefer to let the real pizza oven handle it, just sit down at one of the deuce hightops and let the chef's hands do it. But, if you're not in the mood for tomato pie, Mom also does excellent homemade soup and fresh salads for the light diet crowd.   So, I went with a cup of roast chicken and rice soup and small salad with balsamic on the side. Both were very good, with the potage full of shredded bird and small grain white rice. The salad was big for a small, but brightly green and sprite. Eating in the small front of the shop was pleasant, as I was the only customer and could watch and chat with the proprietress as she worked. Although no longer in the store where the M. Night Shamalan movie, Signs, was shot, I still thought of the Mel Gibson scene where he too ate lunch in Mom's restaurant as he was discovering those crop circles in his fields.   It took me a long time to make it to the new Mom Mom's, but glad I finally did. Now that I have an office down State Street I will make it a point to visit with regularity.   Next time, the pizza!

No doubt the Trenton Pork Roll Festival could have been something special given the concept and all the vendors and bands that showed up. However, the word is that 2,000 people invited themselves for a 300 person party, and the logistics were just not capable of handling the scene.  Too, a massive thunderstorm in mid afternoon blew out the electricity, shutting down the bands, and dousing everyone and their pork roll sandwiches. The canopies were not able to control the deluge.    I was there for a few minutes in early evening after the last of the heavy downpour, but not post the straggling showers that seemed to hang over Trenton Social all day.  After standing in line and getting soaked, I decided discretion was the better part of valor, and beat a retreat to find a dry place for dinner.    Please try again next year, fellas.  You are on to something here.

So glad I finally made it here to sample the heat of Chili Szechuan.   My friends from Chengdu are living in New York for several months, and this was their first visit to Philadelphia. After showing them around the shut down historic sites in Old City (Carpenters' Hall was open), they wanted to see the Penn campus. They were hungry, and Chili Szechuan jumped to mind. Why not give them some home cooking?  They would tell me how authentic the cuisine was.  Driving up Baltimore Avenue for the first time since living at 48th and Baltimore back in the day, I was impressed with the changes on the street.  So much positive street life. And, right in the middle of the 4600 block sat Chili Szechuan.  Parking right across the street. We were in luck!  We started with Dumplings with Chili Oil and Dan Dan Noodles with Ground Pork. Both were as good as I have ever had. Spicy, succulent, and about 3 Alarm on the Volcano Scale.  We followed with Shredded Pork with Green Pepper (5 Alarm), Lotus Root with Pickled Garlic (3 Alarm) and BenBen Chicken (4 Alarm).  All varied as to heat, texture, and undertone. The BenBen is served cold and in skin.  All enjoyable.  But, I wanted to know what my friends thought of the dishes.   They devoured almost everything on the table covered with dishes. They are both small people, so I was amazed how they managed to eat more than I did.  Halfway through the meal they asked the waiter where the chef was from.  When he said, Chengdu, they said they were also from the city. A minute later he exited the kitchen and sat down with us to talk about home.  They switched from Mandarin to Chengduese (a subdialect of Szechuanese), and I was lost.  But, through their animated conversation I knew they were comparing notes about their lives here and in China. My friends clearly loved the food.  They exchanged business cards, and hoped to see each other again next time in Philadelphia.   As we walked out, and the owner/chef said goodbye again, my friends thanked him for the best meal they had eaten in the USA.  It was like being home in their own kitchen.  I took that to mean that they were very happy with the meal.   Seeing their enjoyment, and tasting the authenticity of the dishes, Chili Szechuan is as good as it gets for real Szechuan cuisine in this city.  Some might find the small confines of the shop more suitable for take out, and the single unisex bathroom a bit unpleasant, but if you are looking for the real deal in hot, spicy, numbing food, this is your Shangri-La.  10.27.13 - Ok. Here's the skinny on a comparison with Han Dynasty.  There really is none. While both have quality Szechuan style cuisine, the similarities stop there.  Han D is an upscale attractive forum for taking a date to an impressive dinner.  It is pricey and self aware of the experience it is creating.  Chili S could care less about that. It is in business for one reason - to turn out totally authentic hot numbing dishes that leave you in tears, and wondering when your tongue will come back online.  The atmosphere is basic Chengdu heat, as you find on every street and alley in the burgs of Szechuan Province.  It is small and unassuming.  There is only one bathroom.  You can hear the cooks arguing in the kitchen and the woks and pans banging on the stove.  But, if food is what you care about, and you are lucky enough to be with someone who really enjoys unpretentiousness and loves you for your own, then you can save a bundle tonight, and impress her next week with HanD. Both provide a REAL experience on the opposite ends of the lux scale.

Spice C (Noodles) is a solid choice if you feel the need for well drawn or cut handmade pasta from the Middle Kingdom.  They are all about made to order dishes that highlight the taste, texture and quality of freshly made soups that feature noodles as their base.  Dry dishes are also available, and there is the choice of "normal" or "Szechuan" style bowls if part of your zest for slurp includes a high capzasin quotient.   We opted for the normal large bowl of Beef Soup with Hand Drawn Noodles with Wonton, their version of Szechuan Spicy Chicken, and Chicken, Pork & Shrimp Spring Rolls.  All three dishes were very good.  The soup was robust with well prepared beef broth and a nest of noodles hidden beneath the tranquil surface.  The thin skinned Wontons floated like pale goldfish.  Each aspect contributed fully to the final product.  Wontons were light and chewy.  The noodles required patience to lift and separate into manageable lengths.   The Chicken plate was generously endowed with thin sliced meat that was cooked just enough to optimal tenderness, and approaching killer spice levels with a black bean chili sauce.  Plenty of veggies in the mix that had completely absorbed their surroundings.  So much pleasurable heat that we ordered another one to take home.  The Spring Rolls were loaded with filling and fried in clean cooking oil that had no leftover taste other than these ingredients.    Spice C is worth a visit (or two) if you are looking for a soup oriented meal with a Chengdu flair.

The Bagel Zone? Is that a veiled reference to The Twilight Zone?  I ask only because on a recent early morning visit there on my way to court in Mt. Holly, there were a group of men gathered there at pushed together tables that seemed like they were from another planet.  Men In Black kind of thing. They dispersed soon after I sat down with my bagel and coffee and opted to face them rather than the window behind me. Guess they didn't like the scrutiny.   Anyway, this was my first visit there, and although the staff was friendly and the prices rock bottom, the primary product was only average.  My Onion Bagel was richly sprinkled with Onion Flakes, but the texture of the bagel was more the consistency of dinner roll rather than a thick skin encasing a chewy but air-pocketed inner body. It was fresh and completely edible, but lacked the "bagelessence" I sought.   Coffee was decent, and with change from a Lincoln, the price was certainly right.

Trenton has become a haven for excellent Latin American cuisine. Guatelinda on Clinton Avenue is one such locale where you can find totally authentic dishes that help you forget for a few moments that you are in the heart of Jersey, and feel that you are on the avenidas de Antigua Guatemala while you dine on delicious plates of nearly homemade fare.    When I walked in around 2 in the afternoon last week, I was not only the only Gringo in the house; I was the only customer.  I asked the guys behind the counter if lunch was still being served.  They spoke not a word of Ingles, so I tried again in my mostly forgotten Espanol.  I was good enough to be understood, and after a few smiles and nods I picked a table and sat facing the front window with a view of the house around me.  The large menu offered Spanish and English descriptions, and even a few photos of the offerings.  The server was very friendly (and cute) and worked with me in her broken English to put together my lunch.    The platter of Tacos Guatemaltecos arrived loaded with three double tortilla soft folded wheat 'tillas full of well spiced grilled pork, onion, pepper, cilantro, and a few things I could not identify.  On top of the tacos were a half avocado, sliced radish, and a hot ghost pepper.  I doctored each with the accompaniments and went to work.  The combination was wonderful, with each part of the combo playing olfactory harmonics.  Hot, soft, crunchy, chewy, textured, smooth and cool - all in each bite.  It was great and fun to eat.   The JarritosTamarindo soda helped tamp down the overly hot spots.  Mexican pop is so much more flavorful than its northern counterparts.  It worked so well with its Guatemalan cousins.   There is a lot more on the menu I want to taste.  I will go back to this, as well as the two or three other very good shops in the area, to satisfy my lust for Central American food.  Don't let the streetscape outside deter you.  Guatelinda is the real deal.

The best way to experience the Battleship New Jersey is to arrange an overnight stay on the ship.  You sleep in a seaman's coffin-sized bunk in the bowels of the leviathan, eat in the original mess halls, climb and descend the steep stairs, and tour almost every aspect of the operations from the huge 16" gun turrets to the bridge where its captains directed naval warfare against enemies from World War II through Vietnam and Lebanon.   My son and I had this privilege when he was a cub scout a few years ago.  While he and his mates had no idea what this warship accomplished in its gloried history, and they were just having fun in an amazingly different reality, we dads who came along looked long and hard at the steel blue gray surrounding us.  We knew where this battle wagon had been since 1942; we listened to the number of engagements in which it had participated, the Presidents who had come aboard, and the death dealing it had dished out and absorbed in the cause of our freedom.  It was humbling and at the same time, prideful.   When they talk of, "Jersey Strong," this is what they really mean.  "Don't Tread on Me?"  That used to mean something. "Don't F**k With New Jersey," now, that still means exactly that. Asleep on the Camden Waterfront is the beast that helped turn the War in the Pacific into one of our greatest triumphs.   Visit this hero with your family and say, "Thank You!"

Shady Brook Farm has been an institution in the community for decades.  From a small farmers' market it has grown organically into a multifaceted event driven destination.  The family always comes up with new ideas to entertain on a grand scale. Our favorites are the Autumn Corn Field Maze, Pumpkin picking, and the Christmas Lights Night Drive.  All are done on a scale that let's you know it is not quite professionally polished, but done by the owners'/farmers' own hands.    Sadly, a large part of the Farm will cease to exist in the next year to become a medical facilities center.  The pumpkin field will be no more.    Be sure to visit Shady Brook Farm several times over the coming seasons, as the good times and culturally bucolic experiences will soon pass into history.

This is the TGI Fridays that is within the campus of Oxford Valley Mall, Langhorne (Middletown), Pa. It has the conventional layout of the older version of this national franchise, with a large bar and booths/tables all around.  The atmosphere is casual and bustling, and has the feel of the roadhouse it was meant to be.   We chose this spot as representative of contemporary popular American cuisine for our friends who had just arrived from Asia. They wanted something traditionally American.  What is better than nachos, burgers, salad, fried chicken and chicken/shrimp combos on top of pasta?    Don't answer that!   We had about a 10 minute wait for seating on a busy Saturday night.  Service was friendly and acceptably prompt given the crowd.  Our server was patient as we perused, translated and sought direction from our guests.  The youngest had no problem finding the fried chicken sandwich.  The mother and grandmother were slower in understanding meals without rice, but ultimately selected a traditional cheeseburger, and a grilled chicken pasta dish.  Of course, there was also the issue about western utensils vs. chopsticks, but we worked through that with the help of the large wooden spikes used to hold things together.  We natives moved more quickly to the salads, sliders and shrimp/chicken plates.   Everything was served together, and I watched as our friends took their first close up look at American food.  It was a cross between confusion and incredulousness. Big pieces. Nothing cut into small bite size morsels. Okay. They would just have to figure it out and dig in.  The rest of us went quickly to work on our Jack Sliders (very good), BBQ chicken salad (plentiful and tasty), chicken/shrimp combo (loved the shrimp, but left most of the chicken to take home). The fried chicken sandwich was devoured with relish.  So far. So good. Our second oldest guest just ate the fries around the burger.  She didn't seem to know where to begin.  I think she did not want to use her hands to pick up her food.  I asked if she would like to exchange a small slider for her half pounder, and she gratefully accepted.  She ate it with the spike holding the entire thing like a burger on a stick.  She liked it.  Her burger was pretty good, but a step below what I have sampled in places like Chilis or Applebees. It was not the medium finish requested, but far closer to well done. Granny was able to eat her pasta with the spike, but seemed tentative the whole way.  It wasn't the noodles she was accustomed to, but she was game.   All in all, it was a fairly good introduction to fast casual, something almost totally lacking in their part of Asia. They were impressed by the size of the crowd, and its diversity.    Welcome to America, sisters!  You aren't in homogenous Asia any more.  You'll love it once you figure it all out.

"We're not authentic...But, we keep it real..."   Amen, Brothers!  Real is what it is, and authentic is not required when the creativity and downright fun quotient is so high in what these dudes turn out.    We showed up Saturday afternoon when the place was nearly deserted and took a table in the corner nearest the bar.  The place was sunny and as colorful as a Chinese carnival.  Cues of Asian influences abounded, but did not carry the final impression, which was far more idiosyncratic.  Our server fit her part perfectly.  She was alert, funny, cool and ready to engage.    We were here for a quick stop before other errands.  We ordered only three small plates: Pork Soup Dumplings, Roast Pork Bao and Turnip Cake.  The Happy Buddha and Narragansett Beers were worthy companions.  Each dish was distinctive.  It suggested Chinese cuisine, while tasting quite different.  The Dumplings were tasty and fun.  Once the top knot was bitten off and the Miso Ramen Broth sucked out, the Ginger Vinegar was poured in through the vent, making the Pork Filling tart and a joy to eat.  It was a hybrid taste of slightly thick dumpling skin and Japanese infused innards.  Very nice.   The Roast Pork Bao was large and golden on top.  The consistency was right for a bun, but it also strongly suggested Kreplach to this Jewish palette. If my grandmother had been Chinese and Jewish, she might have created this masterwork.  It was like putting together a taste puzzle figuring out what this hollow doughball reminded of.  The Long Hots, Spinach and Provolone offered the possibility that someone's Italian aunt had a finger in this recipe.    Finally, the Turnip Cake was the biggest surprise.  It was made from Matzo Meal, Maple and Bonito, with a Fried Egg on top.  Again, my Polish/Jewish grandmother could not have done better.  It played with my tongue; teasing me to decide what it was all about.  It was delicious, but decided not Chinese.    "...a Willing Mind and a Willing Stomach,"   Yeah! You got that right.

I hadn't been inside Cross Keys Diner in at least a decade, but walking in it seemed like time stood still.  Everything looked and felt the same.    This had always been a community center where locals stopped in for a meal along with their neighbors and business associates to enjoy the home cooking and the hominess of the décor.  It still is.  I sat on a spinner directly in front of the kitchen entrance and was immediately serviced by all the workers who were picking up orders or refilling their coffee mugs.    The menu is diverse, but the real deal is in their breakfast specials.  I opted for the Thunder Cakes, made with a mix of fruit and nuts and a substantial pancake mix that made even the short stack (2 pancakes) more than I could manage.  The melted butter and house syrup absorbed into the coarse texture of the pancakes like water on parched land.  The taste was healthy and filling.  I added more syrup three times during the meal as it continued to disappear.  Yes. It was way sweet enough.    I couldn't finish the 2 cakes, and wondered how anyone could digest a full stack.  It did sit a little heavy in my stomach for a few hours, but not enough to reach a discomfort level.  I realized later in the day the true meaning of "Thunder."  No need to elaborate.  Cross Keys is still a meeting place that takes its cues from the 1980's, right down to the rock music of the era.  The staff is warm and enthusiastic. Definitely worth another round.

Royal Ashoka sits in a small commercial strip along Philmont Avenue in Northeast Philly.  If you are curious, go to their website for descriptions of their broad menu of north and south Indian delights, plus a nice video on top showing colorful veggies being tossed in a frying pan.    The house is well appointed with linen and silverware, although the ceiling recessed lighting needs improvement, as it casts shadows at odd angles over the tables. Lower, more subtle sconces would be a big help.  Service is great, and it is apparent management is knee deep in helping out, and takes pride in their efforts.    Our meal began with Ragada, a chaat variation with Potato Patties, Chickpeas, Yogurt, Mint and Tamarind.  It was delicious and the star of the show.  It was way more than expected, and it was hard to stop eating it to leave room for what was to come.  Gobi Manchurian was a battered and deep fried Cauliflower dish that comes from the mountainous area of North India, near the cultural borders with China.  It was reddish and spicy.  This dish was prepared with a heavy batter that coated the florets like you would find in a General Tso's dish in a Chinese  restaurant.  When I have had this before, there was no such batter, but the veggie was lightly breaded and exposed directly to the chili spice mix, holding a rich burning red and mildly crunchy finish.  The batter approach was not as good as the alternatives elsewhere.  Our last entre was Chicken Amwalla, a Mango Cream sauced Tikka.  This was a first taste of Mango in Indian food for me (other than Mango Lassis), and I liked its creamy fruitiness, and the curry mixed well with it.  The Chili Garlic Naan was great - fresh, hot and jalapeno/garlic richness.  Perfect sponge for sopping up the Amwalla sauce.    We were really stuffed by this point, and had decided to take the rest home, when our server approached with complimentary Rice Pudding.  Talk about max overload!  I took a small sample.  It was wonderfully creamy sweet.  They were kind enough to understand that we just couldn't finish it and packed it up with the rest of our leftovers.    Royal Asoka is very good.  Remove the drop ceiling and enhance the mood lighting, and it would be a more romantic destination.

I wandered on to High Street in Mt. Holly one morning earlier this week after getting out of court down the road.  I needed a jolt of Java, and Yelped to find Daily Grind at 48 High.    It is a small shop, but appointed as most local cafes are with old plush chairs and a few tables around the room.  The bar sits in the back with a wall of chalkboard listing all the creations they are capable of concocting.  About a half dozen regulars lazed in the morning sun pouring through the large storefront windows.  They all knew each other and exchanged small talk.   To honor the Thanksgiving Spirit, I opted for the special Pumpkin Latte. I hoped for a Cranberry Sauce Capa, but alas, they lacked the ingredients. It was fine; not overpoweringly pumpkined-out. It wasn't cheap at nearly $7, but I was willing to contribute to the success of the local economy in a small way.  There were some good looking muffins under glass on the counter, but I was not in need of the extra carbs.   High Street looked really good from my corner stool.  I saw two micro breweries on the block, and knew I would be back sometime soon later in the day to check them out.  So nice to see this main street of the county seat of Burlington County, NJ, coming back to life.

While BB&B offers almost everything you could possibly need in an American bathroom, bedroom or kitchen (other than large appliances), there is definitely a human scale problem.  With 30 foot ceilings and housewares stacked to that peak, walking through the narrow isles gives a sense of claustrophobia and strained neck.  Everyone is funneled through the counterclockwise flow of the warehouse, with side trips down tributaries to find the particular thing you need.    This feeling of being overwhelmed by the canyons and islands makes for an unpleasant experience.  It is true that the "one stop" nature of the store has benefits, and that the ability to examine multiple towel options, or alternate coffee making technologies, is educational.  Yet, the sheer verticality of the space is ever-present and unpleasant. Compare to Home Depot with similar floor to near- ceiling merchandise. There, the aisles are wider and there is a better proportional scale. There is no feeling that a towel slide could wipe you out.  Maybe their next gen factories will be more appealing.

Two Slice & Coke Review  I was hunting for a missed dinner nosh to spare me those overnight hunger pangs, and Fat Tony's appeared on my Yelp radar. Not many reviews, but you know what they say about 'any port in a storm'.   Fat T's sits in a small commercial strip right next to an excellent new member of the Morrisville restaurant community. Big window permitted full view of the house with only two deuces on the floor. Clearly a take out operation. But, I like my pizza well done and right out of the oven, so I sat down to await my first bite of Tonypie.   It wasn't what I hoped.   Although well done was requested, what I got were two slices without firm chassis that refused to lift off the paper plate when I elevated their crusty end. Saggy and limp. I had to pick up the laggard points and throw them over the thick end, making them more pizza roll, than pizza pie.   The sauce had promise, but if my slices can't salute when called to attention, they can't serve in my tomato pie army.

After a second stop in for a few more slices to find out if Gabriel's pies were as good as first impressions, I am very happy to report that they are even better than remembered!   Our Italian Sweet sausage and Fresh Mushroom reheaters were requested well done, and that super heated scorched bottom was just perfect. Rigid chassis. High point. Great crunching bite. Balanced sweet/salty sauce. Quality sausage and white thick slices shrooms.   Loved it so much I thought I was across the Delaware River in Jersey.   Gabriel come blow your horn.

Mugshot Diner in Fishtown, Philadelphia, is a classic urban diner, open 24/7 for the people of this north of Center City community.  We stopped in after a show at Punch Line comedy club the other night. Laughing so much made us hungry. We cruised around the block for parking and found a spot on our second pass on York Street. Thank you parking angels!  We sat in a booth along the front windows, where the hostess placed two menus and a specials laminated card. Our server came along promptly, introduced himself, and told us to let him know when we were ready to order.   At 10 it wasn't very busy. Decent music in the background. We ordered one of their burgers and eggplant parmesan on ciabatta, after our server warned us off other ideas. Gotta trust the guy. Both sandwiches were decent - the burger grilled to a juicy medium, and the eggplant tender with adequate red sauce and mozzarella. They weren't awesome, but neither was that expected for the place and price. We were satisfied with this late meal.   Mugshot has a sister house in Mt. Holly, NJ, where I have had several good breakfasts. If you like either one, your bound to like the other.

People are waking up to the fact that the world of coffee can be as complex as that of beer or wine. The region, altitude, shade, temperature, water, etc., all contribute to your cup of coffee. Small batch roasters are springing up all over the place to sell directly to the public at retail establishments and cafes, and through chains of distribution to local, regional and national outlets.   This is a business whose time has come.  Evermore Coffee Roasters on E. Union Street, Burlington, NJ has set up shop on the first floor of an old row house, and done a remarkable job renovating the space into an old century feeling comfortable house, with expresso machine up front, and a larger sitting room in back, with their roaster against the far wall.  Colors are soft gray/blue, and the windows let in a filtered light that provide a warm and dated ambiance commensurate with the age of the building.  Like the feeling here.   My cup of Congo pour over took a short while to brew, but when I picked it up at the counter, it was hot and steaming.  First sip announced a dark, mysterious roasted bean soup with a kick in the head sensibility. It took no prisoners.  Liked it a lot, even with its strong acidity. At $3.75 for a fairly small self-logoed cup, it was a bit cher for the quantity, but worth the experience. The offer of a refill at a reasonable charge (not to mention gratis), would have enhanced the value proposition. The near-lack of bakery goods or other light fare, had me packing up to move on quickly after finishing my drink.  The opportunity to enjoy any of these options would go a long way to establishing Evermore as a destination for the café crowd that often likes a little nosh with their bean wash.   Still, an interesting and caffeine-oriented stop on the back streets of Burlington is something to savor.    Street parking. Across from Brickwall Tavern.

The Benjamin Franklin Parkway (originally called the Fairmount Parkway until 1937) was designed as the centerpiece of the City Beautiful urban design movement of the late 19th Century.  Often compared to the Champs-Elysees in Paris because of its width and anchoring by key public monuments and edifices, in fact, it looks little like that famous roadway, but is truly an American take on European classical architecture and urban planning, talked about since the Civil War to signify a "model of an orderly, classical metropolis, crisscrossed by boulevards and dominated by stately groups of public buildings." And, true to that description, the buildings along its traverse from City Hall to the foot of the Art Museum, are what make this diagonal slash through Center City so dramatic, culturally worthwhile, and give the roadway its importance and stately beauty.    The emergence of these structures began in 1864 when the Cathedral of Peter and Paul was completed at 18th and Logan Square. Thereafter, in 1876 The Academy of Natural Sciences opened at 19th and the Parkway. In 1901 Philadelphia City Hall was finished.  Ground for the actual roadway was not broken until 1907, although plans for it had gone through several iterations until then - delayed by political considerations.  The final design was not approved until 1917, when actual construction commenced. The Swann Memorial Fountain in the middle of Logan Square started flowing in 1924. The Free Library main branch began lending books in 1927, and the first part of the Pennsylvania Museum (later renamed the Philadelphia Museum of Art) admitted its first visitors in 1928. Rodin Museum followed in 1929 at 22nd and the Parkway, and The Franklin Institute opened at its current location at 20th and the Parkway in 1934. Moore College of Art & Design moved to its campus on 20th Street in 1959; the Barnes Foundation in 2012 between 20th and 21st Streets. There are many other buildings along the Parkways length contributing to its overall grandeur.    Although Philadelphia is a city of neighborhoods, what gives this town its national and international identity (in addition to cheesesteaks and pretzels) are the Benjamin Franklin Parkway and all that is found along its length and breadth. From City Hall to the Art Museum, this space is where people meet for special events, from 4th of July concerts and fireworks, to the Papal visit and National Football League Draft.  It has a deserved reputation for a great party venue that has only improved with the new skyline in western Center City and the emergence of West Philly across the Schuylkill River as an educational and commercial center in view beyond the museum to the west.  It attracts pedestrians, bicyclists and motorists to survey its graceful imposing reality. It is a great place for people watching.  The addition of restaurants and cafes within a few blocks of the Parkway, make it also a cool place to find anything from a nosh to full dinner.    The only place better to capture the essence of the city is to get up to the Belmont Plateau on a late afternoon and take in the panorama of Center City from that vantage point. You can do both spots as part of one excursion, then come back; find a place to park, and explore the great collections and histories that populate the Parkway.

You have to really want to get to Mood Indian Restaurant because the approach is a challenge.   When 95 South was jammed south of Girard, I was able to jump off, zigzag my way to Spring Garden, make a left on N.4th, and start looking for my destination.  There it was, but at first view it seemed to be behind bars.  Fences and security everywhere.  Reminded of prison gates.  Quickly realized all that parking was for residents, and the street meters were the only nearby option.  At 12 minutes for .25 on a Saturday night, I fished out all my quarters and fed the hungry metal mouth. Then located the narrow opening in the fence and the walkway leading to the resto.  I hoped I had all the necessary credentials to get through customs.   The boss was squeegeeing his front windows as I walked up to the door.  I was impressed that he had not delegated the work, but took pride in his shop's appearance, knowing that first impressions are so important.  Stepping inside after confirming I had arrived with Ali, I was taken by the crispness of the white linen tablecloths and red napkins.  The space had high industrial ceilings, giving an open sensation.  I was shown to the table and sat down to await the arrival of my friends.  I was alone there at 6 pm; thinking that Indians/Pakistanis prefer late dinners.  I liked the vibe as I perused the menu and took in the details.    After V & M arrived, we ordered several dishes to get a cross section of the kitchen fare.  Samosa Chaat, Chicken Malabar for apps; Salmon Tandoori, Chicken Makhani, Baingan Bharta(Eggplant), a Bread Basket mix, and Basmati Rice as entrees.   Mango Lassi for me, and Sweet Lassi for M.   All were good to excellent. Most memorable were the Chicken Malabar which was grilled and breaded with Coconut, the Samosa Chaat, which had all the ingredients of a Samosa, but reformulated into an open dish full of Potato, Peas, various crunchy chips and spices. Additionally, the Baingan Bharta was very well done with a complementary heat/sweet texture, and the Makhani was tender in a Tomato base curry that was requested hot spiced and delivered fully.  The Salmon Tandoori was the most colorful dish (see photo), but the fish was a tad dry and the veggies and spices so overpoweringly good, that the mild taste of the Salmon was somewhat hidden by its pushy roommates.   All in all, a very good meal in a pleasant environment.  By the time we left around 8, the room was full, along with our stomachs.  We ended up taking a large portion home with us.    I will definitely return once they let me out on parole.

Recently returned to Buffalo Wild Wings Langhorne plant for a family Friday night.  While I didn't walk in with fond memories of my past visit, my son was in the mood for hot wings, and BWW certainly had plenty of those.    Truth be told, this experience was far improved.  The house was far from crowded.  All the other customers seemed to be families with teenage/early twenties boys who wanted the gorge on wings and watch sports on huge HDTVs.  We fit right in!    Service was better than remembered.  Our guy was over the top solicitous of our satisfaction; so much so that I jokingly asked him to calm down or he wouldn't make it through the night with his hyperactivity.  He was not so far gone as to not appreciate that I noticed he was working hard.  Even a small glitch in the cooking of the Alaskan Cod sandwich was handled with aplomb, with the house manager stopping by to apologize for the delay in bring the fillet to proper temperature.    Drinks were ample and fairly priced.  Can't object when a 12 oz. cocktail comes in at $6.50.    The chickens who sacrificed their flight for us came to us both Blazin and Thai Curry.  They were meaty, deep fried, and bathed in some impressive chili mix.  The former took the enamel off my teeth (much to the merriment of young man), while the latter had great south Asian flavor. Liked them both, but would never be challenged to eat a extra hot one again.  The fish sandwich on brioche roll was surprisingly decent, with the fish large enough to withstand the cooking process and still be crispy and tasty with aioli mayo and melted cheese.    Glad we decided to return to Buffalo Wild Wings on Rt. 1, Langhorne, Pa.  We enjoyed ourselves, and didn't feel the need to apologize to ourselves for going.    Improvements noted.

After many good to great Mexican and Central American meals in and around Trenton, Burritos is a bit tame for my taste.   What do I mean?  Well, the food is about as good as any average Casa Mexicana across the river, but the atmosphere is not from South of the Border.  It is rather staid.  The only Spanish I heard was from the television tuned to a futbol game.  I think I may have heard the friendly people behind the counter also habla algunas palabras. No music.  No Latin American art.  Neutral colors.  A dull environment.   Yet, my chicken flautas were pretty good, loaded with chicken and cheese, and deep fried to a dark brown ultra crisp finish, that defied the plastic fork and knife effort to cut through them.  I could crush them, but the utensils were too weak to actually do much work. I ended up using my hands. Burritos does a nice job loading up the top of the dish with guacamole, lettuce, tomato, corn, salsas, and almost anything else they have on the work space in front of them. This in addition to the rice and black beans that tag along as accompaniment.  I found the mango salsa to be quite tasty.  They put a ton of food on the plate, and dare you to finish it all.  I couldn't, but I was so full I did not want to think about taking the rest home.  The servers are cool, but way different that the crews that serve me in Trenton.  Those folks barely speak any Ingles, and work with primarily Spanish speakers, while here the folks appear bilingual and geared for the Yardley crowd.   Certainly better than Chipotle and Taco Belch, but not the full monty found across the river in the old Chambersburg part of Trenton City or Hamilton.

The Singer One sewing machine purchased through Amazon was a beaut, but came without power cord and foot pedal. A mistake to buy sight unseen. But, these parts shouldn't be too hard to find. Right? Thus began an unexpected adventure in sourcing spare parts in the arcane world of sewing machines.   The company didn't offer parts on their website, and recommended only their few dealers around the country. Too, they weren't pleased that their equipment appeared to have fallen off a truck somewhere to be scavenged for the missing parts. The old Philly warehouse shops dealt only in industrial strength sewing factory parts and couldn't help out, although they expressed understanding of this predicament.   Next stop was a small sew & vac store in Northeast Philly, who took a $20 deposit promising to order the pieces and notify when they came in. When called 6 weeks later to check on the status, they hadn't received them yet, but left the distinct impression they hadn't done anything but stuffed the $20 in their pocket. (A review of that enterprise is upcoming after I return to get back the cash.)  Two weeks ago I noticed a small shop in Newtown that handled vacuums and sewing machines. Looked to be a recent addition to the business community. What the heck?! I stopped in to inquire. Greeted by Sandor, the owner, I explained the situation as he listened patiently. He advised I bring in the machine and his expert mechanic would check it out. I dropped off the still boxed machina a few days later.   The following week Sandor called to say that he could order the new parts if I wished, or he could provide used cord and pedal already in his possession from another job. Sounded like a good idea, and yesterday I picked up the parts and happily paid his price. He actually dropped it a fin in support of the visit to the other dealer I was going to ask to refund the $20. He was sure, as I was, that those guys would have had the parts in hand if they had been ordered.   It was great to do business with an honest man who went out of his way to get something done out of the ordinary purchase and repair services he routinely offered.   Makes me wish I had gone to him before Amazon and experienced direct satisfaction.

Al Nahrain(Between the Rivers) is a Bagdadi restaurant just off Bustleton, and a block beyond Grant Avenue in Northeast Philly. It is attractive on the inside with a full wall mural of the old gates of Bagdad in pale blue with gold bulls, and an ornate ceiling with colorful inlaid tiles. There are only about a half dozen basic tables and a high perched centerpiece where the staff oversees operations.   The menu is fairly standard Middle Eastern/Mediterranean, with beef, lamb and chicken on skewers and vertical grills for shawarmas. House baked pitas are good and distinct from other nationalities, as they are thinner and better at scooping up the excellent hummus, parsley salad, and Moroccan Spicy that accompanies every meal as a forespice. We ordered the lentil soup, chicken shawarma plate, beef shawarma sandwich and okra. A basket of pita came along.    The soup was made with pale lentils and reminded of a thin split pea soup. It was very good. The sandwich was made with a long pocket pita stuffed with well herbed small chunks of marinated and grilled beef and topped with a nice vinegary tomato slurry. Very tasty. The only disappointment was the most expensive chicken shawarma.  While the flavoring was strong and savory, it was far too dried out. After a few attempted to chew it, we gave up. It seemed to have been overcooked to a point where is was becoming more like jerky. While I haven't been to Iraq, I have spent time in the Middle East (Egypt, Israel, Greece, Turkey), and never had to deal with that problem. The okra was in a heavy tomato based sauce, and tasted more like mushrooms than the mallow or firm lady finger texture anticipated.   Service was friendly and earnest. The young man was troubled that we did not like the chicken, but had no solution for it.   Given the overall imbalance of the meal, it is hard to grade it better than 3 Stars.

Nice country store feel for locally sourced ice cream studio.  Super friendly and informative people.  When I asked the difference between the Vanillas - Madagascar, Tahitian, and another exotic island label, I was told that the most "vanilla"-flavor was the Madagascar version, while the others were either too light in flavor or more of a marshmallow sentiment.  Went African Isle with a scoop of Blueberry Lemon.   Creamy texture, full blown taste bud involvement.   Instant smiles and satisfaction.    Clearly, a labor of love expressed in imaginative combinations and high quality execution, wrapped up in a easy to miss village ambiance shop.    The road sign is too small, so unless you know it's there, or have visited Carousel Gardens for other reasons, very easy to miss.    Worth finding.  NOTE 8.28.2013 - This ice cream just won a 10 Best In USA award from the Huffington Post.  Congratulations!

Okay!  I admit it.  The Home Depot has grown on me.  It still is a big box destroyer of family hardware stores, but now that so many of those mom & pop stores are gone, where are we to go for a choice of power tools, ladders, and expandable screws?   I found myself there this weekend as part of a home project to install curtains over a French door.  As all such jobs become, it was more than originally bargained for.  Now, that I had the actual drapes in hand, I discovered that my old electric drill was not in great shape after twenty years, and more importantly, that my handy step stool had been lost in divorce.    First stop - Power Tools.  I felt the rush of adrenaline upon seeing all the sleek steel packaged for a quick date.  Once one of the Home Depot dudes approached to assist, and he explained the difference between NiCad and Lithium batteries, I was the possessor of a new Ryobi power drill/driver, complete with battery pack and charger.  Sexy lime green and black.    Second stop - Ladders.  I am tall, but for working at over 7 feet to screw in curtain hardware, I needed help, and my old standby step stool had been purloined in a property settlement deal.  So, I checked a few here, and selected a GorillaLadders three step aluminum and rubber folding stepper for a great price, that I had to admit was much better (and safer) than the old one.    Third step - Get 'er done!  The Ryobi worked like a dream with variable speeds controlled by my trigger finger, and direction reversal with the push of a button.  I climbed up my new stairs and was able to complete the task with relative ease and speed.    Amazing what the right tools can accomplish in the hands of a rank and clumsy amateur.

South Warren Street in Trenton, NJ is one of the bright spots in downtown. It has a nice feel with cobblestone streets, mature street trees and several decent restaurants. Parking requires meter feeding or use of the garage at the corner of Lafayette Street. Rainbowtown Chinese Restaurant may be worth finding parking and going in for a bite.    The dining area is deep, with the cashier and buffet tables behind the counter. There is a full menu in addition to the $5.95 buffet. That is what I had when I went in a few minutes before 3:00.  Due to the lateness of the hour, the house owner suggested the buffet was the way to go as she would load up my plate with all I wanted. Plainly, I was a chance to sell the food rather than have to toss it before the dinner rush. Worked for me, as I sampled a half dozen dishes, rather than the regular two.  Everything was actually pretty good. The chicken did not taste of freezer burn, and the sauces were distinct. One of the offerings included sweet potato in the mix, which made for interesting texture and taste.  Even the Bourbon clucker, all dark meat, was okay. Of course, the fried rice was yellow dyed and dry at that time, but I didn't plan on eating much of it due to all the other options piled on my plate. They even had hot tea!   As far as Chinese American houses go, Rainbowtown was surprisingly ROYGBIV!   I would have no hesitation to return and work from their menu.

This was our first visit to The Irish Rover Station House in Langhorne, Pa, just across the street from the Septa train station (thus, the name). After being snowbound all day, we were looking forward to getting out for some grub, drinks and stimulation.   We sat at a hightop along the glass wall next to the patio. It was a peaceful scene with the patio covered in untouched snow, and the trains stopping at the little station house. It was a near perfect setting, but for the incredibly loud ambient noise in the dining room. There was a large party having a good time, but that didn't account for the poor acoustics that amplified sound from the bar and the entire space, and made normal conversation nearly impossible. After the big group left it was better, but still louder than comfortable.    They have a great beer list, with new specials every week. Impressive. They didn't have one of our first choices, but our server brought us two samples of similar beers he thought would satisfy. He was enterprising in this approach, and right that he had selected one that we liked and ordered. Nice job. In fact, he did a very good job with us all evening and we showed our appreciation.   We ordered the Emerald Potatoes app to start. Lovely to look at in a huge platter of homemade chips loaded up with cheese and scallion with large dolup of sour cream. This was a cousin to nachos or poutine, and pretty good. A little bacon bits or spicy ground beef in the mix would have made it exemplary.   The filet sandwich was tender and juicy on an excellent soft roll, sided with chips. Good. My two fish tacos were filled with a small breaded/fried frozen fish and aioli in soft tortillas. A small amount of salsa and shredded iceberg on the edge of the plate, and a small plastic cup of gaucamole. Multi colored tortilla chips filled half the plate. Not so good. For both dishes and the app there was no adjustment for the fact that we already had a large serving of chips in our meals and giving out more potato chips and corn chips was just overkill and boring. They were left behind.   We brought home two burgers for our teenage sons who could not join us for dinner. They both said they were mediocre.   Irish Rover seems more like a beer and wing sports bar, more than a full meal resto, with way better service than most. Reasonable prices.

It has been too long since I visited Barbie's for one of their exquisite pretzel dogs - all beef garlicy homemade weiner topped with jalapeño, sauteed onion and American cheese - all wrapped up in one of their freshly doughed, twisted, salted and baked pretzel skins.   Eat'em while they're hot for peak actualization.   Today their drink special was a Pumpkin Latte Shake. A good, cool, sweet gourdy slush that epitomizes Halloween. The small 6 ounce cup was $4.25, including a free hand twister.   Pennsylvania Dutch comfort food par excellence.

It may be true what the other Yelpers say about the quality of the breakfasts here, but as I was here for lunch I can't comment on the morning sustenance.   I can say that this looks to be a fairly recently renovated Jersey diner, very clean, friendly, and broadly diverse menu.  I sat at the small counter next to the hostess/manager as she was being mentored by the owner about ordering from purveyors.  He was calm, articulate, and seemed to appreciate his people.  Impressive.  Of course, the fact that he was dealing with a gorgeous employee may have had something to do with it.    My lunch was ordinary.  The Chicken Salad on Rye Toast was just okay.  The toasting seemed to have taken the life out of the bread, as it was overly dry and brittle.  The Chicken Salad was ample, but lacked much flavor.  The cup of Chicken Noodle Soup was a nice touch, but too salty.    Given the positive vibe of the place, I would certainly return for breakfast, but lunch, not so much.

Gotta love The Living Room Café on South 5th Street!   This corner breakfast/brunch nook is comfortable in its simplicity.  Expanded into the storefront next door, the dining area offers wooden tables and chairs along two walls and a little sofa and easy chair ensemble up front.  Big table toward the back for larger groups, or, as on the morning we were there, a place for a teacher to tutor her young student.  Wonderful human relations.  Cool back patio in the space between the two buildings.   The shop is run by Zack, who triples as host, cashier and chef.  He has everything covered with his engaging personality and obvious passion for his enterprise.  He brews the excellent coffee, takes orders, cooks and serves them with equal aplomb.  The impression after a few minutes settling in, is that you are visiting an old friend or first cousin who has welcomed you into his home.  Can't beat it!    The menu offers creative takes on American standards, and uses locally sources ingredients to the greatest extent possible.  Too, the names of the dishes pay homage to known personalities in the greater community.  Where to begin?  We opted for the Wake & Bake Burrito and Baked Cinnamon Apple French Toast.  Both were solid choices.  Baked eggs are used rather than fried, making for a drier and healthier meal.  Mixed with house salsa, black beans and sour cream, tightly wrapped and grilled in a tortilla, this breakfast burrito was a tasty substantial morning feast.    The French Toast used a light, thick cut slice of (apple?) bread, with Chinese flat bottomed spoons full of walnuts and shredded coconut, and a small pitcher of maple syrup, to apply as you see fit.  Very good idea, but for my full enjoyment, the bread itself lacked the coarse texture I prefer, as well as the caramelization that occurs when egg, sugar and hot iron meet on the grill, that crisps up the edges for added flavor and crunch (Perhaps, because frying on the grill is not their thing?).   Regardless, The Living Room Café is a cozy home to hang out in while eating your early day meal.  Def worth a visit or three.

Tony Luke's on Oregon Avenue close by the Sports Complex is as "Philly" as Philly gets.   Tucked in under the concrete and steel of elevated Rt. 95, it feels like a Lilliputian railroad car of a restaurant in the uber scale of its environment.  In winter the heavy plastic and aluminum walls are attached to keep the patrons warm.  I had the feeling of being in an ant farm next to the glass wall.  None of which detracted from my first time enjoyment of this iconic cheesesteak emporium.   Famished after skipping regular dinner to attend a way-to-long business meeting at a local hotel, I would have eaten just about anything.  Lucky for me, my pal suggested Tony Luke's.  We were there in minutes and I drove into the small parking lot next door.  The aroma of fresh (and stale) grease flooded my senses, squeezing my salivary glands, much like a vampire prepared for the first bite knowing it will bring strength and relief.  My mouth involuntarily hung open with jaws ready to clamp down on a great steak sandwich.  Melodies of Rocky Balboa rang in my head.    I had the Italian Special Steak with Sautéed Spinach.  It reached the take out window about 10 minutes later, tightly rolled up in white paper with Tony Luke's logo emblazoned across it.  We sat at one of the red tables, slit the tape and unwound the packaging.  First glance was of a long Italian torpedo roll, held shut by the former pressure, now free to open and display its steamy contents.  The brown of the steak; the dark green of the olive oil induced heavily garliced Spinach; the melted ooze of the Provolone - all combined to create an exquisite moment of anticipation.    The first chomp took in as much of the tip of the sandwich as my mouth could hold.  Garghhhh...womp.....grind....chew....swallow....Repeat. The bread was crusty and fresh, belying the following softness of the steak, cheese and spinach.  Texturally perfect! The sequence of the unfolding parts only overtaken by the totality of the whole.  Truly existential.   It was great, but to be completely honest, the Spinach was over salted with the garlic, and was too dominant a flavor on my palate.  Everything else was awesome, and the Birch Beer a smooth compensation for the sodium chloride load.    This is a Def place to return.  The overall gestalt is wonderfully and uniquely Philadelphia urban chic, as cool today as it was decades before.

Located in a nicely refurbished shop that previously had been a Chinese restaurant, Yardley Bagel Cafe in the Makefield Shopping Center, is a welcome addition to the area (Yardley is a more toney address, thus the name).  A corner space with windows on two sides, it is a comfortable place to bagel up with decent java and settle into a booth with friends or on a metal stool along a wooden shelf anchored to an exposed brick wall to do your daily reading. They really did a very good job creating a welcoming environment.   YBC does most everything bagel, with many choices of cream cheese, smoothies and sandwiches to match the multiple choice of well appointed rounders. A look at the bagel bins shows that these folks take pride in their product. They are plump and loaded with toppings so much so that the actual top crust cannot be seen beneath. The generosity is appreciated. The prices are competitive, and perhaps lower than the other bagels outlets in the area. My onion bagel, butter and swiss, with cuppa joe brought me change from my fiver.   My breakfast looked great with the layers exposed in cross section and little onion bits falling onto the plate with each lift and bite. While I prefer a crustier skin offset by a light and airy center, rather than the mono-textural bread presented here, the onion flakes were like savory poprocks that compensated a bit for that shortcoming.   Yardley Bagel Cafe won't replace Bagel Train (really in Yardley) for my favorite bagel in the area, but it is a cool place when hanging out is part of the experience.   Excellent job!

Peter Pan Diner is long gone.  Nottingham Diner lasted for about six weeks. The most recent incarnation at this old kitchen locale opened about a month ago as the White Horse Diner.  After dropping off a client at home apres court I decided to drop in for a late lunch and to see how the old gal looked.    This is one of the smaller Jersey diners, with a short counter of about six spinners, booths along the front wall, and a small dining room around the side.  Enough parking out back.  It looked like the new owners spent some shekels cleaning up the place.  Everything was spanking bright.  My server, Larissa, was, too.    There was plenty on the menu, but as a first timer, I went with the "Lunch Specials" list.  All the options were $6.99 with soup/salad, fries and a pickle.  At that price, they were cutting their margins to the bone.  I opted for their California Burger.    It arrived on a large platter.  The burger was housed in a shiny-topped egg bread roll, and a large slice of tomato, red onion and wad of iceberg under the hood.  The beef seemed fresh and came out hot. A shot of ketchup, and I was in business.  It held together very well under my onslaught.  Little escaped as I clamped down again and again with gizunta bites like a dinosauric carnivore. It all came together smashingly well.    While I didn't mistake this burger for fine dining, it was solid and enjoyable.  The fries were hot and crisp. The coleslaw, coleslaw.   That was more than enough to make me a happy fan.  Thinking about bringing the family for Thanksgiving dinner.

First & Ten Sports Pub doesn't look like much driving by this southwestern-looking one story brick house on Hamilton Avenue.  Aside from remembering that this joint has been a bar in many different disguises for years, I would not have bothered to slow down to catch the name on the sign out front.    But, I did, and looked it up on Yelp to see what the story was.  Reviews were mostly positive, with highlights on their wings and other bar food, while somewhat less than enthusiastic about the beer selection, despite being called a "Pub."  Walls with HDTVs for sports watching were also a clear part of the description.  What the hey?!  It looked worthy of a lunch drop in, so I found myself in their ill-maintained parking lot on a hot sunny sultry Wednesday afternoon.  It was dark inside despite several windows, and it took a few seconds for my eyes to adjust.    I saw a pretty large "U"-shaped bar, with room for near 20 barstools, two well stations for mixing drinks, and a beer pour stand with at least 10 handles.  From the look of them most were domestic labels, but a few made it across borders north and south.  Lots of HiDef screens up high tuned into the Olympics or local sports.  The walls were rough hewn pine panels, and the ceiling exposed painted beams with beer logos hanging from them.  This was, indeed, a dive bar dressed up for a sports crowd.  Nothing wrong with that at all.  In fact, it was pretty nice in a dingy beer drinking afternoon sort of way.  That was surely the intention of the half dozen other dudes who were trying to keep out of the sun.  Full sized pool table in the back looked like it had a few stories it could tell.  The bartender was working alone and seemed to know everyone, but me.  She approached to inquire, and brought my drink and menu with pace.    Not in the mood for wings & brew when I knew I had to return to the office, I opted for their Thin Crust Tomato, Mozza and Basil Pie Special @ $6.50.  I do love a good bar pie when the chef knows what she's doing.  It came out about 10 minutes later, and it was a beauty. Cracker thin crust. Slightly sweet sauce with fresh strips of Basil spread around atop the melted Mozza cheese, and sweet Cherry Tomatoes cut in half lengthwise spread strategically across the entire surface.  Very attractive.  How was the pie?  While not at the level of Jo Jo's, Ivy Tavern, nor Pete's, it was still a solid wheel with plenty of flavor and excellent crust.  I would not hesitate to have another along with a basket of Garlic Wings on my next visit.  Sufficient beer choices to keep me happy, although this is not a beer lovers paradise.  PRO TIP - Be careful driving around the building so as not to cause tire or alignment issues.  The back lot needs help.

If you have been cruising Mill Street over the past few decades you know that it has had better days, but also that a few brave urban pioneers have jumped into the breech and begun new businesses that seem to be taking root.  Calm Waters Coffee Roasters shows what dedication and imagination can do to turn around a main street in a struggling neighborhood.   The room is well renovated to feel about 1969, with exposed brick walls, sanded and polished narrow slat wood floors, and a tin panel-looking ceiling, that may not be authentic, but sure adds to the great ambiance here.    The coffee is roasted right in the middle of the house and served hot, fresh and new.  Guatemala seems to be the source of the beans, and the owner's TLC in producing a quality product is obvious.  The taste of the java is bright and subtle, and a pleasure to drink.  I will bring a bag home the next time I stop in before court.    They call themselves 'coffee roasters' for a reason.  That is what they are here to do.  Yet, they know people want to sit and enjoy their Cuppa Joe, and the room is well suited for a quiet conversation at one of the deuce tables.  Still, it is not yet a café as the offered accompaniments are not as good as the coffee at this point.  There is no grill for breakfast or lunch plates.  They provide instead a few pre-packaged bakery things like muffins, and a decent microwave oatmeal that they will heat and serve. There is a Panini press that toasts and stripes one at a time. How much better Calm Waters will be when they are able to install a short order kitchen for early breakfast, late brunch and midday lunch.    Regardless of what the future holds, the present is impressive enough (in a quiet way) to warrant high praise.    It has been too long since a Mill Street morning provided good reason to return.
Definitely time for an upgrade! I have become a fan. 4 Stars with a bullet.

The Fresh Works is a small family run chain of sandwich shops in and around Bucks County, specializing in cheesesteaks, wraps, burgers, and traditional deli fare. This shop in the Richboro Shopping Center has some new competition from the Super Wawa that opened up right up the street.  I wish them luck where they go head to head in the sammy department, but they do have the edge in seating, comfort and roots in the community.  The mini tuna hoagie (5") I had for lunch yesterday was decent.  Plenty of tuna, lettuce and tomato in a very good house baked torpedo roll.  Actually, the bread was the best part and worth return visits. The sandwich was served open face with tomato slices on top. It was a lot of lunch for $5, with added swiss.  Definitely, value there.   Reviews mention the steak sandwiches as being praiseworthy, but as a faithful devotee of Steve's Prince of Steaks, I may not discover what I might be missing. Still, it is good to have a solid choice in Richboro that does not require skipping a local business in favor of a large franchise.

Surprising good Chinese cuisine at this basement kitchen associated with the Asia Market on North 11th Street, Chinatown, Philadelphia. There may have been change of ownership and this is a first visit, but if the past owners were even better on the wok than these folks, then I missed something pretty special, because I was quite happy with what we ate this night.   Amazingly convenient if grocery shopping of Chinese ingredients is your reason for being there in the first place. Just go hungry, eat, and then shop.  Worked well for us. It is not too far fetched to think that if the Tasty kitchen runs out of something, they just walk a few feet into the supermarket and pick up what they needed. Symbiotic.   We ordered the wonton soup, salt baked squid and roast pork on rice. All were very good to excellent, despite the somewhat dank surroundings. The large bowl of soup was loaded with more than a dozen freshly handmade wontons with ground pork filling.  The beef consume was hot with a pleasant flavor.  Made for fun slurping. The squid was cut into fairly large pieces and coated with a light flour, salt and pepper breading.  It was tender and juicy. Especially enjoyed the scallion and sliced jalapenos the dish was mixed with.  The flavor/texture profile became quite animated on the palate. This was the star of the show.  The roast pork had a nice ruddy bark and was lean cut.  Not quite Ting Wong Restaurant level, but close enough. We ended up taking about half of the dry dishes home.    With all the wonderful alternatives on the street above, there is not that much reason to go subterranean for a solid meal, unless price motivates you highly. The numbers on the menu were very reasonable, and it is easy to imagine that Tasty Place does a large business with students and others on a budget.    You certainly get more than you paid for here.

After a second stop in for a few more slices to find out if Gabriel's pies were as good as first impressions, I am very happy to report that they are even better than remembered!   Our Italian Sweet sausage and Fresh Mushroom reheaters were requested well done, and that super heated scorched bottom was just perfect. Rigid chassis. High point. Great crunching bite. Balanced sweet/salty sauce. Quality sausage and white thick slices shrooms.   Loved it so much I thought I was in Jersey.   Gabriel come blow your horn.

Great reuse of a 19th Century firehouse in the heart of Norristown, now a museum and distillery for premium vodka, whiskey, gin, and special batches of other unique blends. Three story open barroom where once horse drawn firewagons were housed, with upper floor sleeping room for those once on duty and a rear space full of stainless steel distilling tanks and vats. Fascinating place I wish I had time to explore with a knowledgeable guide.  Maybe next time, but tonight we were there for a political fundraiser for a local county official seeking reelection. Judging by his choice of party venue, the open bar and the look of everyone present to support him and wish him success, he has a strong chance of re-election. Even the local congressman was there to wish him well.  With speeches and a good buffet (and that open bar) there was opportunity for limited sipping and light dining in the midst of the very loud din of conversation  between the soapboxing. The distillery itself remained background to an excellent soiree.   Will definitely return for more tasting and a tour.

This fairly new freestanding Dunkin' Donuts in the wilds of Eastampton, NJ, was empty when I arrived for a post court late breakfast and java. In my recent experience, the proliferation of DDs has diluted the quality and consistency of the signature products, so that the coffee is often harsh and undrinkable in some shops, and still quite good in others.  Same thing for donuts. Some have good ones. Some don't.  As everyone is trained the same way, it comes down to water quality and cultural familiarity with sweet rounders.  This joint was pretty good.  There was a small communications problem, but what I ultimately received (breakfast sandwich and joltin' joe) were both hot and tasty.    No complaints.  And, a nice facility with a large lounge area for those who want to get some work done, or take a comfortable nap - perhaps, both.

Salute Ristorante is another in the new and tasty options in the renaissance of Morrisville, Pa.  It sits on West Trenton Avenue, where Centre Fruit used to be and next to the venerable dive Morrisville Tavern.  Don't let the neighborhood deter you, because Salute is a very good Italian shop, with dark modern tones, and interesting menu.  I stopped in for lunch today after having it on my Bookmark list for about a year.    This is not a pizzeria by any stretch, in fact the only way you get a tomato pie is when it is offered as a special.  This place is all about a creative kitchen that spins out fresh and well considered dishes with panache. It is pricey for Morrisville, but the quality of the offerings made me forget that I was still in this struggling river town.  If they can do that, they are indeed, approaching magical.    Lunch included a small bowl of soup, and I chose the 16 Bean alternative.  It was a solid performer, although I confess to not counting the beans. They were well cooked and soft enough to show they were simmered a long time.  The elbow macaroni in the mix contributed to the interesting textures.  I could easily imagine a soup and salad return visit.   My eggplant parmesan sandwich became a platter upon request.  Didn't want all that bread, and my table had a large half loaf delivered up front with my water.  I was more than happy with a couple of its large sesame slices and a swipe of cool butter.  The plate was beautifully presented.  The chunky red sauce and white mozzarella covered the unbreaded thin slices of nightshade like an abstract painting framed by the square white ceramic.  Heavy silver toned utensils made short work of the cutting and lifting.  The taste was very nice, with the homemade sauce providing moral support to the veggie and cheese.
