It might have been a tad salty, but not enough to detract from the pleasure of eating.   Salute is a worthy addition to the growing (still nascent) restaurant scene in Morrisville.  I raise a glass of Sangiovese to your good fortune.

Ila Mae's Restaurant sits right off the intersection of Broad and Market in the heart of Trenton. Parking is next to impossible in this neighborhood, so be prepared to walk a few blocks if you want to chow down in a relatively undiscovered gem.    I stopped in on a cold, icy morning in February.  There were only a few people there and I settled in in the front dining room in front of the large HDTV sitting high on the opposite wall.  The furnishings were Spartan, but the space was clean and inviting. My server, David, handed me the large menu and I decided to have breakfast as it was still being offered.    I asked about their French Toast and their Breakfast Sandwiches.  David smiled.  He alerted me to the presence of their French Toast Sandwich - Short Stack with 2 Eggs and Beef or Turkey Sausage inside the well grilled bread.  No pork products here.  The meal arrived in about 15 minutes, and I realized that each meal was prepared separately by the chef/owner.  The two people ahead of me were served individually, and then mine was put together.  No problem. I was not in a rush to return to the inclement weather.   The French Toast was good on its own, but when combined with the spicy Beef Sausage and Scrambled Eggs it took on another identity which was tasty and fun to eat. The extra small pitcher of syrup came in handy to pour over the sausage when I opened the top of the creation.  Its strong flavor was nicely offset by the sweetness.  A sprinkle of black pepper on the eggs completed the effort.    This was a very good breakfast from atmosphere, through bottomless coffee mug, and everything in between.  Their lunch and dinner menu looks very interesting, and I hope to return to explore it in the near future.

Oh, Danny Boy....  Why so unassuming?  Why hidden in a forlorn strip of 20th Century retail excess?    Why aren't you sharing your gift with the entire Tomato Pie craving world?   The lights. The lights are calling...!  Your T. Pie is among the best I have sampled in my pizza-loving life.  It is in the local pantheon of greatness occupied only by a few other mozzarella souls - DeLo's, JoJo's, Ivy Tavern, Joey's, and a few others in the Mecca of the Pizza Universe, Brooklyn.   Micro thin crust firm enough to hold the topside without a quiver.  Sauce, chunky and mildly sweet with a hint of basil. Cheese hidden beneath with a gentle saltiness to balance the smiling acidity above.  Not a single drop of oil on the aluminum tray despite a spritz of pressed olive applied as the final touch before reaching the oven.  And, the sweet Italian sausage, home grown, and crumbled around the disk amply, with a wonderful aroma and fresh textured taste.    Though you labor in obscurity, Danny, your artistry is not lost on those who treasure the magic only a steamy right out of the oven slice of heaven can provide.

Sycamore Grill is good if you know what you want and don't overstay the best parts of the experience.    Especially in nice weather, the Back Deck offers a pleasant outdoor setting in the shade of the historic Sycamore Trees.  If you go for Happy Hour (4:30 - 6:30), and can find a seat on the deck, it is a very nice place to relax with a friendly conversation.  At other times, you have to go Monday thru Wednesday to avoid larger crowds that come on those evenings to listen to live music.  But, if tunes are what you like, you may enjoy that setting. Inside, the atmosphere is dark, cool and well appointed.  The Happy Hour menu is also decent.    Otherwise, the better time to go is at lunch.  The Burgers, Chicken Salad and Turkey Club Sandwiches are above average, and there are good Soups (Onion, New England Clam) and Salads (Wedge and Caesar) available at prices that while higher than many other places, are much more in line with a lunch budget than the dinners that seem pricey.  I have had the Combination Lunch - Bowl of French Onion and a Salad.  Tasty and filling.  The Burger Tuesday is also a fair deal - Your favorite Burger and Beer for $10.   The downside is that you have to know when to go.  If you prefer a more laid back moment, then you must be attentive to season, day and time.  If crowd and expense are not issues, than go anytime you wish and have a good time.

Hatboro Dish sits on York Road (Main Street) in Hatboro, PA.  It is a square room with black tables & chairs, but no counter.  It has the feel of a small café, without the emphasis on coffee.  Their breakfast menu is creative and offers a nice variety of morning choices.  I asked my very pleasant server which way to go - french toast or one of their skillets?  She unreservedly recommended the frenchie. Well, alright!  While waiting, I looked around the house. About one third full, with mostly locals who knew the staff well enough to have them sit a while to chat.  Nice vibe.  The coffee arrived in a thermos pitcher for unlimited refills, and the milk I requested, in a small stainless vessel.  It was decent java, but without pedigree. Nice to have all I wanted.  The main course was basically a thick cut cinnamon bread dipped in egg, and heated on the grill.  It was good, but because of its thickness, the egg did not penetrate deeply into the slices.  They were pretty dry, and the extra dose of their syrup (not maple) helped a bit, but, could not compensate for the lack of egg melding with the texture of the bread, which is what french toast is all about. So, it was okay, but not what it could have been given the excellent raw materials.   Too bad, because the Dish could have been a real contender.

The approach to Concerto Fusion takes you past a 60's era Dairy Queen, over old railroad tracks laid down when Fairless Works smelted steel by the megaton, and if you drive across the Delaware River from Trenton, on the girders of the famous "Trenton Makes" Bridge.  Quite a history lesson.   Then, you pull into the parking lot for Concerto and behold the façade of the side-facing entrance, all bright orange and red lanterns - like a cross between Miami Beach Ocean Drive and Lantern Festival in Xiamen. Pleasantly disconcerting cultural mix.  And, perhaps, that was the intention of the owners of this Asian fusion establishment, so neatly tucked away in a dark corner of Morrisville.  Get you slightly off-centered as you approach and enter their well appointed den, and prepare you for an experience both gastronomically and architecturally that is also designed to unbalance you.    The room is spacious with curved walls, flowing koi pond, mirrors and raised dining area.  The small bar sits in the middle of the room, almost invisible, yet with a half dozen stools for those who prefer cold liquid fusion.  Similarly, the sushi area is in a corner behind the entrance and bar wall, where a solitary chef moves silently and efficiently cutting, molding, wrapping and presenting his artistry.    We sat at a corner table closest to the sushi works and the kitchen, near enough to see what was going on, but not be a distraction.  The ambiance was of quiet confidence and appealing tones.  There was no doubt that a lot of thought had gone into the layout, and that the vision was carried out exceptionally well.  Even several years of operation and breaking in, while noticeable, had not detracted from the effect.     So, how was the food?  Glad you asked.   We appetized with the Hawaiian Tropical Roll (Eel, Avocado, Tobiko, Soy Wrap, lightly crusted Tempura and pleasing secret sauce). It arrived slightly warm with a mild crunch, and was a very enjoyable opening gambit.  Wasabi, Ginger and Soy discretely on the side of the plate. I would have preferred the naturally white ginger to the pink colored alternative, but that is a very small minus.   From there we selected from the Thai offerings: Pad Thai with Chicken and Pineapple Curry Fried Rice with Shrimp.  Both arrived on large round white plates in amounts beyond our capacities to consume.  They were good and satisfying, if not the best of breed that can be found in ethnic restos specializing in this cuisine. Nonetheless, we were happy to bring home the rest for another meal.  Most pleasingly, both had large quantities of nuts; whole cashews for the rice, and ground peanuts for the noodles, and plenty of shrimp and chicken, respectively.   Service was provided by our waiter who also was bartender this evening.  He kept busy, and was not the most engaging sort.  He seemed a bit ill at ease interacting with us.  No biggie.  Forgivable.   The only annoyance was the charge for hot tea.  Yes, quality tea is more expensive that the orange pekoe take out variety, but at $2.50 per green tea bag and a pot of hot water, it is off-putting.  That generates more profit than the bar. Makes it worthwhile to plan ahead and bring your own tea. Check. Your move.   Overall, while not the best sushi and Thai dishes in the world, everything we had was enjoyable.  The design elements within and without made it unusual and had the desired impact of slightly altering perception to be a unique environment much farther away from daily reality than a drive into Morrisville would suggest.

Aside from the historic appeal of old railroad cars, New Hope & Ivyland Railroad has nothing going for it. It is a very short run at a very slow speed for a very high price.  I hesitate to label it a tourist rip off for the unaware, but it comes close.    There are much better alternatives if your want a railroad experience.  If the train ride itself is your reason for going to New Hope, save the time and money and take the Light Rail from Trenton to Camden, or stops in between.  That is an actual passenger commute that rolls along the Delaware River for a while, and stations in some pleasant Jersey towns, like Burlington.  Last stop is the Camden Aquarium. If old railroads are your thing, make the day trip to Scranton, the old railroad capital of the USA. Plenty of museums and operational locomotives pulling plush Pullmans and a working roundhouse.   The NH & I experience will likely leave you feeling disenchanted.

Down to Earth Cafe in the Glenwood Center, Perkesie, Pa., is exactly that - a chillaxing joint where locally sourced creative breakfasts and lunches and excellent coffee induce comfort and good times.   We were looking for a colorful autumn drive up county on Saturday morning, with a nice destination as the goal. While the Bucks foliage had not peaked, Down to Earth certainly had. We walked in to a large room with heavily eurothaned wood slab tables, mix and match coffee mugs and huge blackboard with the daily specials. The shop wasn't crowded and we found a table across from the cashier, where orders are taken and paid for before pouring the coffee and settling in.   The first sip of the Speakeasy Roaster House Blend signaled we were in for something great. This Montgomery County company turns out amazing beans. I found myself working it over my tongue to identity it's subtleties like I would a glass of wine.  Superb!  I purchased a bag of ground for home.  My Breakfast Roll (Scrambled Eggs, Bacon, Green Pepper, Provolone and Jalapeño/Tomato Jam on fresh crunchy "Shad" roll ) was a mouthful of interesting flavor and fun. Really liked it. The Pork Roll and Cheese on Kaiser was solid, but nothing exceptional.   Service is personable, if slow. The delivery of the meals is a bit disorganized. The workers behind the counter seem to lose sight of the seated customers and are unaware of their needs. This is sometimes a problem with semi self serve plans.   Still, a superior breakfast and top notch java make Down to Earth Cafe a real find.  Antiques, smoothies and coffee mug club add to the feel of wholesome community displayed here.

Difficult to find office complex cafe in Yardley (actually, Lower Makefield), off Stony Hill Road. It is in the 790 Building which is in the middle of this corporate center. Signage is minimal. The easiest path is to walk around the right end of the building, locate the outdoor patio dining area, and enter through that door. Otherwise, you will be walking down long hallways without assurance you will reach your destination. Obviously, The Weekday Cafe (nice alliteration), is meant primarily for the folk who work in the complex, but if I owned the business, I would want to cast a larger net.   This is the third food operation at this location in about as many years, so they have their work cut out for them. Getting the word out beyond this small universe is critical.   And, while the attractive shop is diminutive, it is worth discovering. They do a decent breakfast with a limited menu and good coffee. Service is friendly and efficient. My "Early Riser" sausage, egg and cheese on toasted English muffin was solid and cost only $2.95. The java flowed hot and strong.   This morning, a few other office workers came in to pick up something to take to their desks, but not enough to make a success. Hopefully, their lunch trade carries them.  They do have two other similar locations in Ewing and Hamilton, NJ, that are larger and also require excellent tracking skills to find, but seem to be doing well.   As this Weekday Cafe is closest to home, I wish them good luck and smart advertising.

I needed to return my Dish Network "box," and the instructions received with a shipping container said that a UPS Store could handle the job, and that Dish would cover the cost.  So, I boxed it up with the remote, taped it closed, and drove over to the local UPS Store in the Summit Square Shopping Center in Langhorne, Pa.    I walked in around 5:30 pm.  The time sign said it was open until 6:30 pm.  I was the only one there, and I did not see an employee until I was near the counter in the rear of the shop.  At that point a woman came out from the back area to see what I wanted.  She saw the box and the telltale return shipping label.    "You want me to take that?"  "Yes, please. Can you handle this return to Dish?"   "We can."   "Great. Thank you."  I placed the box on the counter, and she grabbed it, slid it over the weighing scale, and pushed it to the side.     Not another word was exchanged between us.  No "thank you for your business, nor "have a good evening."  She seemed mildly put off that she had to do something without direct compensation from me.  I guess this project didn't deserve any courtesy.    I shouldn't complain unless the box doesn't arrive at its destination.  But, for all she knew, I planned to return tomorrow with a truck load of business for her.   Not!
Lotus Garden is no more. Drove by today and the sign was down and the shop was closed with a sign on the door.

The spinners at the counter are wobbly, and there is a photo of the marriage of JKF and Jackie O. on the wall, but Kitty's Luncheonette is as real as it gets for traditional breakfasts and lunches in this part of Philadelphia. They don't know from brunch, and they close before happy hour; so don't bookmark it for your weekend morning meal, nor try to stop in after work.  This is a 7 to 3:30 corner grill that had a few dozen thick scrapple slices frying to a dark brown while I drank their Ellis Coffee and awaited my first taste of their french toast.    The house has about a dozen tables in two rooms and eight spinning stools along the counter that overlooks the chef workspace.  It was about half full of neighborhood personalities who seemed to know each other as they were greeted by name.  The server, a lovely young woman who is Kitty's niece, took care of me, and filled me in on the history of the institution, open since 1952!   Yes. It looks its age, with family photos on the walls, and original floors, walls and stools.  Either you get the deeply rubbed in culture here, or you don't. With its gritty charm and surprisingly good food, it is easy to develop a crush on Kitty, and want to visit her often. She is as authentic as the day is long.  My three slices of thick egged toast were very good.  A little sweet from the vanilla and sugar in the mix, and a little crispy on the edges where the hot steel melted that sugar and left its hardened residue.  They know how to do FT here. $5.50 was a happy price. The java was strong and a little rough (bitter), but nothing to complain about. Again, her Joe is straight up Bunn-O-Matic.  No expresso options with Kitty.   Kitty's is very close to I-95, and an easy on/off if you want to stop before reaching Center City from the north. Not sure she could handle becoming a hit on the breakfast bookmark circuit, especially on weekends, so if you want to check her out, come on a weekday morning when the regular crowd is thinner.    But, if you like hard stop traditional breakfast without any frills, give this old girl a go.

Hua Kang Health Center is a first rate Chinese style massage spa sitting unexpectedly in the Marrazzo Shopping Center on Parkway Avenue in Ewing, NJ. It is bigger than most I have visited, with ten private rooms, each well appointed and very clean.    Their staff is well trained in traditional Chinese technique, plus Swedish and a little Shiatsu.  Lily, my masseuse, asked if I would like her to work deep tissue and walk on my back.  No problem.  She went from my shoulders to the soles of my feet like a dancer.  Very effective. With practically every step I felt/heard a snap, crackle and pop as she stretched me out.   Hot stones and steam towels alternated where I had the most discomfort, followed by her forearm and elbows probing the facets and pushing apart the disks in my spinal column.    It was an excellent, relaxing and therapeutic massage. I think I even fell asleep. At a buck a minute, it was a fair price.  After shoveling snow and feeling the sciatic stress, it was great to feel such prompt relief.    If they had a sauna or two, served fruit and hot tea, it would be just about perfect.

Just had a great breakfast at Bullard's American Cafe on Saturday morning. It took me by surprise that Warrington possessed what I enjoy most from a early day meal - old school charm, slightly worn yellow Formica counter, deeply involved husband and wife ownership with the former on the grill and later working the front of the house making customers feel like valued members of the family. And, let's not forget, exceptional food and warm friendly service.  We sat on a couple of spinners at the window end of the counter. Paige approached us with a bright smile, bobbed blond hair, and menus. She and the two other young women in black worked non-stop to keep up with the rush that seemed to follow us in and quickly filled up the booths, tables and stools. Luckily, we ordered ahead of the tidal wave, and received our platters in a few minutes.   I went with a short stack of french toast covered in strawberries, bananas and blueberries (red, white & blue). A smear of butter and pour of syrup (maple?) and I was a happy guy. The taste of the egg/vanilla mix saturated the bread and was grilled to optimum; cooked through and through with caramelized edges. Loved it!   Our other dish, Famished Farmer, was a special egg mix with potato, onion, ham and tomato, with a side of homefries; also solid and enjoyable. A black pepper shake or two brought up the flavor. We would ask for Tabasco next time to set it on fire. The homefries had great texture and taste.   We learned Bullard's offered dinner Thursday and Friday evenings. Meatloaf? Yes! Be seeing you again soon!

Legend tells of a mythologic Blue Moose that traveled the spiritland and Doan hills around New Hope and the north river highlands. From time immemorial it was the guardian that helped those hurt by natural, supernatural and even manmade acts, survive and repair their damaged bodies and souls.  Its gifts to all were amazing strength, nurturing support and a supply of local foodstuff to aid in recovery. It was also known for dexterity on the mandolin.  It seldom took sides. It was only there to observe and assist with sustenance and music.    Over the centuries Blue Moose has taken various forms animate and inanimate. An accomplished shape shifter, it appeared when the need was dire in a form acceptable in the current cultural milieu. It helped sustain our men during the Revolution, and helped build the longboats that made the Christmas eve crossing. Currently, it assumed the guise of a restaurant in a small old house on Mechanic Street in New Hope, Pa. Always brash, it has not bothered to hide its identity.   It sits in plain sight.  Café Blue Moose welcomes all to rest within its aging walls and taste its well honed victuals at any of its tables.   It was within these atmospherics that we arrived for an early dinner last Friday evening, climbed the stairs to the second floor and took control of the middle table overlooking the open space down to the front room.  Open paper umbrellas hung down gently spinning in the air currents.  Stars were painted on the exposed cathedral ceiling.  Period pieces on the walls completed the sense that we were encouraged to take leave of normalcy and enter the world of whimsy, where we could best appreciate the decompression from reality.  BYOB aided the transformation.   Our servers were lighthearted and sincere.  The menu a prix fixe affair allowing choices in any combination of Apps/Salad/Soups, Entrees, and Desserts that added up to 2 or 3.  Our choices were to share a Warm Goat Cheese Salad; Braised Short Ribs and Sautéed Salmon; and a Apple Crisp finale. The salad was a nice green plate with local leaves, Hazelnuts, sliced tart Green Apple and Dried Cherries in Balsamic Vinaigrette .  A round fried Goat Cheese ball was indeed hot, smooth, and subtle.  The parts played very well together and was a delight.    The Short Rib was already off bone having bathed a few hours in red wine and garlic.  The meat was sitting atop Garlic Mashed, and under a strong helping of Pickled Cabbage and Carrots.  The taste was mildly sweetly vinegar inspired, and completely pliant.  The Mashed and Rib sauces were blood brothers, bringing the best of both when combined.  Symbiotic to the max.  The Salmon was a reasonably sized steak on top of small grain White Rice Risotto.  It, too, had a pickled topside that tasted of onion/mango, but was likely something else.  It was finished well and easy to eat, although there with an unidentifiable aftertaste that was less enjoyable than the primary sensation.  A small nit in an otherwise inspired meal.    Finally, the Warm Apple Crisp was a fun crunchy a la mode mess with an oat/brown sugar crumble that was a joyful indulgence.    All the while, Blue Moose played his music in the background, completing a near-epic experience.  His mandolin put aside for a heavy bass line for rock melodies that soothed and awakened appreciation of meal and history.    As we stepped out into the snowfall and gathered our memories of what had just transpired, the sense that Big Blue was with us in deed and spirit was palpable.  We thanked him for his faithfulness and skilled metamorphosis into a shelter that was exactly what was needed in this age of doubt and cynicism.

La Casa di Lucia on the farthest end of Bustleton Avenue, in Northeast Philadelphia about a mile before reaching Bucks County, is another decent Italian restaurant slinging traditional dishes to the people of the nearby hoods. There is a big bar in the front of the house, and a small dining room behind it, with a larger banquet room to the side. It is clean and attractive. And, if you enjoy a cabaret feel with sultry smoky chanteuse, this house provides the entertainment several nights a week.   We were there for a light supper after strong foot massage, and La Casa di Lucia fit the bill. Plenty of choices, solid service and reasonable prices. This is the case in many such restaurants in this neck of the woods. We ordered a Caesar salad and large pizza, half mushrooms, half plain.  Both arrived within ten minutes.    It was a large salad with plenty of romaine, and good homemade dressing. We could even taste the anchovy paste. It was a strong accompaniment to the pizza. The pie was good, too, but not as crisp and balanced as I like, and as are available not very far away. Plenty of cheese (perhaps too much compared to the red sauce, garlic and basil elements).  The crust was still too moist making it impossible to pick up and hold its point. Had to fold it immediately to avoid a hot cheese slide onto the plate or lap. Taste was decent, but the texture needed a kick in the crotch to stiffen it up. Took half of it home for later consumption.   I would try La Casa di Lucia again to see what their dinners were about, but would pass on the tomato pie.

Fraternal Order of Police Lodge # 5 is the labor union for Philadelphia Police and Sheriffs Officers, providing a broad range of bargaining and social support services for officers both working and retired.   As part of their effort they have a nice size lounge for officers, families and friends at their Caroline Avenue facility.  Additionally, they have a large banquet hall available for rental to outside organizations.  It was in this capacity that I attended the Jefferson Dinner sponsored by the Bucks County Democratic Committee earlier this week.  The hall was spacious with high ceilings and chandeliers.  The food presented in buffet style was better than average for a mass feeding of about 300 people.  We are not talking haute cuisine, but solid Italian American fare with Chicken Francaise, Baked Ham, Roast Beef options, as well as tasty Pasta and nice Caesar Salad.  I ate well after listening to a few too many speeches from candidates in the up coming election. As this is not a political site, no need to discuss who and what was said.    If I had to organize a large event including dinner, drinks, dancing, and speaking in the Lower Bucks, Philadelphia region, I would certainly consider Lodge 5 as a good locale and forum.  I was very satisfied with the over ambiance of the place, as well as the food.    Too, when tired of the windbags, you can slip into the large lounge and take a seat at the long bar for a quick round or two, surrounded by Philly's Finest.  Nice to have a drink feeling secure.    Feel free to buy a round for the men and women in blue, and thank them for everything they do for us to keep us safe.

Patel Brothers is a family owned small chain of Indian grocery stores in New Jersey and Pennsylvania.  The operation in Bensalem, PA, on Street Road doesn't look like much on the outside located in a rather forlorn strip center, but once inside the vast array of produce, frozen and dry goods is fairly amazing.   For a first visit we were pleasantly surprised at the quantity and quality of the fresh produce.  We found it to be better priced than our regular supermarkets and very competitive with our local farmers' market.  We ended up stocking up on some very interesting south Asian veggies, especially hot peppers. Additionally, we picked up a few frozen items (garlic naan, veggie samosas) just to check them out, and some henna for natural hair color applications.  On our way out we marveled at the low cost of the five bags we hauled out of there.   The aisles were very well stocked, and it was possible to buy rice and flour in bulk.  There were many customers on Sunday morning and it was a bit crowded moving through the store, but this presented the opportunity to talk to some folks about their experience at Patel Brothers, as well as their recommendations for what to purchase.  Very useful.  Staff was ever present and helpful in finding what we sought.   This was a first visit to Patel Brothers and exposure to all the amazing possibilities present in a good Indian grocery.  Many return visits are likely.

If Korean Fried Chicken & Wings are your desire, then Chicko Tako in the Market at the Fareway in Chestnut Hill should be high in your list of destinations. Not only do you receive the benefits of excellent double fried cluckers in amazing sauces, but also the added bonus of being in a multiverse street fair community market that includes a brewery/pizza outlet, bakery, cafe, sushi shack, green grocer and butcher. So, you can cobble together the meal of your choice with ease without moving more than 100 feet in any direction, and dine in a common eating area shared by all. Delicious and impressive.   My 6 wing plate with sweet & spicy sauce took about 20 minutes to prepare. I was handed a buzzer to alert me when ready. In the meantime I secured a pint of pumpkin ale from Chestnut Hill Brewery as well as a seat at a long table with views overlooking an outdoor dining area. The place was crowded with folks doing more or less the same as me. When my buzzer started vibrating I asked the people next to me to watch my beer while I picked up the wings. They were happy to help me out.   The wings were on a beautiful rectangular ceramic plate on top of a tray. They glistened a dark red amber glow from the perfectly pitched sauce covering them. Three small pieces of celery and tiny cup of sour cream completed the meal. Exchanging the buzzer for the tray, I returned to my seat. The six wings were crunchy and meaty enough to sate me. The sauce was indeed both sweet and hot, and twisted my taste buds playfully. The cool, pungent ale was an excellent chaser, cutting through the heaviness of the sauce just enough to enjoy it again with each piece devoured.   Chiko Tako has both wings and half/whole cut up birds for sale, and they do primarily takeout from their stand in the market. The people there are friendly and efficient. They know they are a success, yet it has not gone to their heads.   Especially in combination with the other possibilities in the market, Chicko Tako is a great place for a street food snack.

Maybe it's the way I was introduced to BBQ that spoiled me for the suburban variant, but unless I can smell the meat in the smoker, and the piquant sauces bubbling in their vats, I feel somewhat deprived of the true experience.   As a city kid, BBQ was something the family enjoyed as we drove south or west and came across a roadside shack along a two land blacktop with a hand painted wood sign that said, "BBQ," or just had a picture of a pig painted on the corrugated tin roof.  So, going into a modern shopping center and entering a store for this most American meal just does not feel quite right. The space was dressed up to remind of those places, but aside from the flies buzzing my sandwich, it lacked true authenticity.  The lack of proper context detracted from the moment.   Still, my Pulled Pork Sammy was tasty and filling.  The Fries were too salty, but that is a matter of preference.  The meat was fully smoked; soft and pleasantly chewy.  The sauce was sweet and tart as I like it.  There were 3 table rockets with hot, hotter, and vinegar BBQ options.  They all were fine, if not unique. While the abundance of winged creatures at first annoyed as they Kamakazied my lunch, I soon began to find them amusing as the only commonality with my boyhood country experiences.   Yes. Most everything was Okay, but not addictive enough to draw me back on their own.

One of the nicer Asian markets in Philly proper, although there are very good H Marts out in the Northeast and Elkins Park.  The place is large, well lit, and stocked with all those things that have never been heard of by the Acmes and Giants of the world.  Need a regional chili sauce from Chongqing?  They have a variety of them.  Want thin noodles from Thailand?  Just ask for it.  Jonezing for sweet pea leaves for that special garlic recipe?  Yup.  It's there.  Need fresh fish for your father-in-law?  The red snapper is right off the boat.   The prices can be erratic, and sometimes the aisles are so overloaded with goods that two carts can't pass each other, but if that really bothers you, you probably never went to the markets in any town in Asia.  That's just the way it is.  Sell by dates important to you?  It may be better to just close your eyes.   Staff is very helpful and multilingual.  They even have a small apothecary to save you the trip to the herb shops in Chinatown.  Even had Wood Lock Oil.

Olden Avenue Deli has been sitting across the street from Coleman Kia Subaru for several decades...and it looks it.   The joint could use a makeover.  A coat of paint hides a multitude of sins. But, if you don't look too closely at the condition of the store, and just focus on the food that comes from behind the counter, you can almost imagine that you are in a cool old joint that really creates some first rate sandwiches for breakfast and lunch.  Management is very friendly and accommodating, and have time to chat and joke while they work.  The four or five tables make eating on site easy. Otherwise, takeout is the name of the game.  My homemade chicken salad sandwich on fresh rye bread was a strong contender for Lunch of the Week.  Moist, mayoed just enough. Piled with shredded lettuce and slices of tomato. My teeth cleaved through it, feeling each layer expose its secrets. Not an ounce of fat nor cartilage to be found. Along with the Calypso Southern Peach Lemonade, it was a very enjoyable and inexpensive lunch. Came in under $8, and I easily could have wrapped up half the Sammy for another snack.    Olden Avenue Deli also does breakfast.  I will be checking that out soon enough, but as sandwich places go, it should be on your list.  Just don't spend too much time looking behind the counter or at the outside trim, which definitely need work.

The old Post office in Main Street, Yardley, PA, is the size of a large closet. It still has a wall of copper coated post office boxes, and sells stamps and packaging materials. It is really only a substation to the main US Postal Service facility on West Trenton Road in Morrisville.   It retains it's charm and historical ambience, despite the fact that services are limited and parking can be an issue out front of in back.   If you find yourself in the Borough of Yardley for a medical visit, breakfast of early happy hour, it is worth a few minutes of your time to stop in to enjoy the atmosphere and pick up a few sheets of forever commemorative stamps.   It will have you thinking of the way your grandparents saw the world.

Almost everyone appreciates the cause of Mission BBQ,  support of our military and first responders. They are honored daily and even given premium parking right at the front door. But, what about the quality of the meats and sides offered in the kitchen?   From my point of view the ribs, brisket, sausage, chicken and the savory sides, are all good to very good, but as with most outlets in the northeast, not nearly as excellent as available in the American South and Southwest. We seem to lack the cultural history that creates the awesome smoked meats and heavily flavorful sauces found in every back road smokehouse from Virginia to Florida and Georgia to Texas. Still, Mission is not a bad substitute when time for a road trip is lacking.   I enjoyed the Baby Backs I sucked off the bone last weekend. The meat was tender, even if lacking crusty bark, smoke rings and thick, luscious sauces that are the true sign of authenticity. The Texas Twang and Tupelo Honey Heat were too thin to hold fast to the ribs, but remained at the bottom of the tray available for repeated dipping. My side choices of BBQ Beans and Cole Slaw were alright and completed the meal nicely. The corn bread was a small thin square, and somewhat dry, but sweet enough to remind me of what the real thing tasted like.   So, until I have time to visit my sister in Newport News, my former bro-lo in Charlotte or friends in Austin, Mission will have to do. The folks there are friendly enough to make it a positive experience.

Gentrification hasn't made it to N. 9th Street in the Callowhill neighborhood of Philadelphia. If it had, places like New Town Restaurant would be a roaring success spreading its Greek kitchen tentacles throughout the city like so many others who have become household names. Instead, New Town has scuffled along the past thirty years, one family turning out incredible breakfasts and lunches for those who live nearby or are fortunate enough to have found this hidden in plain sight tattered glory of a luncheonette.   Maria and Peter ("The best cook in Philadelphia."), are the front and back of the operation. She has the natural charm of your great aunt hostess, and he the stubbled smile and broad shoulders of a man who has been slinging hash for most of his life. The house looks like it was last renovated in the '90s, with Formica table tops and shiny plastic covered benches.  But, none of this would be worth imagining if the food exiting the kitchen wasn't equal to the narrative. Believe me, it is.   Our breakfast exceeded expectations. My veggie omelet with added feta and home fries thrown in the 3 egg mix was homemade excellent, with rye toast and bottomless coffee for under $9. My partner in crime went with their lamb gyro sandwich with Maria's famous tzatziki sauce. It was among the best seasoned grilled lamb and white sauce I've tasted. With tip everything was $20.   Yes, New Town Restaurant lacks pizzazz, nor any sexy millennial attractions. Developers may even tear it down when the next wave comes through, which would be a crying shame. But, what it has is all it needs. 24/7 authenticity, owners who have lived their lives within its walls for a generation, and real food that just doesn't quit.

The 800 block of South Broad Street, Trenton, NJ, has new life in the form of Finca Cafe, a Columbian coffee house standing where an old grocery store once did business. It is beautifully renovated with new floors and walls, but with well preserved tintype ceiling, painted black to fit into the overall tone of the shop.  There are small tables in the window wells in either side of the front door, a naugahyde love seat against the wall, and a few more deuces further back for those who prefer to drink their java right from the expresso machine before it cools. I chose a table facing front so to watch the world go by. I ordered a latte and panebouno, a fresh homemade cheese bread roll with excellent flavor and texture.   The beans were roasted at Calm Waters, Mill Street, Bristol. Obviously high quality beans, roasted perfectly by the good folks at Calm Waters, where I have had the pleasure of the joe on several occasions. The roll was delicately sweet with light cheese flavor. Liked it muchly.   It was very nice to see local residents with Columbian roots take control of their economic lives and become entrepreneurs in support of their families and community. They are proud of their success and happy to project their business acumen onto customers by extroverted behavior that made me feel very welcome. Their willingness to give the history of their enterprise and patiently answer questions, allowed their passion for their work shine through.   I expect to become a regular customer of Finca Cafe as it is less than a mile from my Trenton office. It will be a great place to meet clients and plan meetings with a small group.   May their coffee always be strong!

Newly renovated Men's Warehouse opened recently in Lincoln Plaza, Langhorne, PA, close by Oxford Valley Mall. We stopped in looking for a suit for my stepson, who had secured a promotion at work and wanted to upgrade his wardrobe with new threads.   Although the store is fairly large, the actual in store suit selection was meagre. Admittedly, the young man is tall and thin (6'3", 160 lbs.), but to have only two dark colored suits on the rack was disappointing to say the least. In fact, they had nothing in his size. Our salesperson did her best to make something work, by mixing and matching pants and jacket in one size larger to approximate his actual measurements. Ultimately, we were able to determine the right sizes, which then had to be ordered for shipping to our home.   Luckily, I know a guy good with needle and thread.   The shop seemed to have plenty of dress shirts and ties, as well as a reasonable supply of casual ware. Yet, they were bereft of more formal work clothes for the professionals in the crowd. Don't know if this is a decision by management based on actual marketing data, or just a supply chain issue, but given that this brand used to advertise to the well dressed male, it is hard to comprehend how far from that image Men's Warehouse has fallen. Perhaps, this is more evidence of new pandemic workplace realities, but some people still have to go to work and dress for success.   It would appear Men's Warehouse has decided that those people are not enough to carry the business as it once did. It is hard to justify another visit.   2.5 STARS

Malay Thai Kitchen is still operating with a temporary sign out front, but that doesn't mean they don't know how to run a first class Malaysian and Thai restaurant. That they certainly do very well.   It begins with the deep Asian décor of the dining room. Although simple, it has Shoji screens on the walls, and black & white photographs spread around that add to the cultural flavor.  It is a calming space, but for the out of place loud contempo western music blasting from the high speakers. How much better it would be with soft flute, strings and bells, to go with the Jasmine tea and delectable menu.   I ordered Basil Thai Noodles with chicken, at a 3/5 heat level. It arrived looking great on the white ceramic plate. The taste was excellent with plenty of Thai basil, peppers, onion, sprouts and chicken in addition to the broad noodles that offered plenty of surface area to hold the rich sauce. While I learned that the third heat level was more a one to my tongue, that did not detract from the wonderful taste. Really liked it a lot. I am sure they would have provided chili sauce if requested.   It was great to find another southeast Asian kitchen had arrived in southern Bucks County. It joins the rare few other pioneers who have staked a claim to broadening our cultural and culinary horizons. I will return for much more.    Congratulations on your recent launch, and great fortune in the future!

Johnny Apples sits at the bottom of Buck Road, just above the stream that runs through this valley into Neshaminy Creek.  It is a surprisingly large house, with bar and dining room running the front of the building, and a nice patio in the rear. It is casual and comfortable.  The beer list is relatively simple, and the menu offers traditional American fare.  We came in for dinner on Tuesday night when there were few people dining, and only two or three at the bar.  It was cool, and it felt great to get out of the suddenly oppressive heat enveloping southeastern Pennsylvania.   We ordered a cross section from their offerings.  Avocado burger with fries, blackened shrimp with mashed potatoes, and "The best meatloaf you've ever tasted," with taters and string beans. While all looked good upon arrival, none really lived up to our hopeful expectations. The burger was a previously frozen puck that was cooked beyond the medium requested, and lacked taste and texture.  The cheese and avocado registered, but the beef was not juicy, nor flavorful.  Their fries were the type with extra starch applied to make them crispy. They were not to our liking.  The six medium sized shrimp were grilled well and had good taste, but were not "blackened" with enough spice, nor exposed to mesquite coals to bring up the special blackened flavor.  They were well prepared without that, but  for $19 we looked forward to more. Finally, the "best" meatloaf, wasn't.  It was overly dense and baked far too long.  It was dry and burnt in part, making the pockmarked surface look like a rock sample from Mars.  The sauce was overly salty.  The potatoes and beans were fine.   Could be that we came at Johnny Apples the wrong way.  Perhaps, the apps alone with beer was the way to go.  Nice things have been said about their wings.  Regardless, we experienced a less than compelling meal that would deny a  good reason to return.

Stopped in this Wawa Deluxe to take advantage of their free coffee celebration today. It seemed busy for 3:00 on a Thursday afternoon, perhaps due to this special deal, or maybe they are always so popular. Plenty of nametagged staff working their takeout food operation, and others scurrying to keep everything stocked for customers.   The Cuban java was quite good, although somehow the Tanzanian African dispenser was empty despite all the attention being paid to this gratis offer. Too, their donut display was loaded and advertising a 6 for $3 bargain (I couldn't resist).   The store was clean and I was in and out in under 10 minutes. Parking was a breeze and the access through the side streets rather than the main street helped keep traffic moving smoothly and safely.   These Super Wawas are onto something. Providing a small discount on gasoline and standardized sandwiches, soups, snacks, drinks and solid coffee, in an attractive environment that keeps everyone moving quickly, is a great idea whose time has comes. Taking them off the turnpike and into the community is clearly better than just the convenience stores we have in most places now. The only thing we should worry about is the natural business inclination to demand too much of a good thing, thus creating a glut of copycat roadside service centers in the wrong places that compete for the same dollars.   I wouldn't mind having one near by, but not right next door.

What a terrific natural and historic resource Tyler State Park is! Looping trails traversing a hilly topography; good for hiking, biking, walking. Find the old homesteads in the park that reflect what this area looked like in 18th Century rural Pennsylvania, and occupied today by families renting them from Bucks County on long term leases.    Discover the beautifully rebuilt covered bridge over Neshaminy Creek, a great place for photos and dreams.  Rent a horse for a few hours.  Scramble up the foot trails along the narrow streams and get lost in time.  In July, find your own secret blackberry patch and pick your own, eating them and tasting their sweet essence.  Watch out for the thorns!    Rent a canoe and paddle upstream and out of sight of civilization.  Jump in the water and cool down.  Watch kids swing out over the flow from a rope tied to a high overhanging branch, and Geronimo into the water.  Walk along the creek bank and find an arrowhead among the river rock.    So much to do, so well utilized by we who know it.    Take a deep breath and appreciate the moment.

Nice Korean green grocery in the Morrisville Shopping Center on Old Trenton Road. Plenty to choose at prices better than the local supermarkets, but not as good as the true farmers' market at Tanners' Brothers in Richboro. Butcher and fishmonger, too.   Interesting oddities, too, like Polish kielbasa and German Milka chocolates.   Worth going to when a major veggie and fruit expedition is planned and you don't have time for Tanners' or the Bristol Amish Market.  Plenty to keep you curious, entertained and in the greens.

It's funny how so many people state their bagel bona fides by proximity to New York City. You know, "I'm from the City, so I know bagels..."   Sorry, I was born and raised there myself (Washington Heights), and I've had some great bagels in all 5 boroughs, but also sampled pretty bad ones in all corners of the Apple; often in the same neighborhood. True, soft water from old wooden water mains helps, but nothing takes the place of a great recipe and patience. So, the truth is there are awesome bagels to be had almost everywhere the proper ingredients and skills are present. That includes just about anywhere in the Eastern USA, and any bakery close to sea level.   So, not sorry.  The Bagel Cafe in Delran, NJ, is but one example. It looks innocuous enough in a bland Rt.130 North shopping center in the middle of Burlington County. But, it would be a mistake to pass on it out of a mistaken assumption that nothing exceptional could come out of an oven there.   Au contraire, Mon Frere.   That Onion Bagel overlain with Veggie Cream Cheese was a true delight. Its texture was perfect - firm crunch on the outside; airy light texture within. Mild sour flavor perhaps from the brief bath in boiling water with brine or lye to toughen its skin, yet not too much kneading to harden its tender heart. Piquant spread to pull the varied elements together.   True, I think I detected a soft Russian accent from the women behind the counter. That would give them an edge in understanding the cultural imperatives of a true bagel, but whatever their secret, their creation had me imagining old country roots in the villages outside Kiev.   Outstanding work, my friends!

This DD franchise approximates the mean of all Dunkins.    Decent Java, but too dependent on the water quality.  Bakery goods sweet and addicting.   Biggest issue is the location in the Lalor Plaza down at the bottom of Lalor Street, just off Rt. 129.  No problem during the day, but a bit sketchy after dusk.  But, this strip houses one of my secret lunch houses, Perfetto Pizza; so I find myself in this hood at least once a month.    Big plus - Bilingual staff!

El Limon - Norristown is another in the locally born chain of solid Mexican restaurants that seem to be expanding almost monthly. It is a smallish shop compared to most of the others, but the quality of the kitchen is just as high.   I stopped in after an office meeting nearby. I found it decorated with colorful tables and carved back wood chairs depicting the beauty of the traditional town square with church steeples, red tile roofs and flowering bourganvillas. The Muzac was a bit too loud for dining, but surely the staff enjoyed it throughout the day.  My lunch of their tacos dorado (golden fried tacos) was very interesting and tasty. Stuffed within the rolled "flutes" were mashed potatoes, grilled chicken, and cheese. The softness just behind the crunch was fun and unexpected. On top was the mix of lettuce, tomato and fresh crema found on every plate. The red salsa in the table rocket liberally applied brought it all together. Liked it alot.   It was fairly priced @ $8.50, and filling enough to skip dinner tonight.   Norristown has many Latin American restaurants to choose from. El Limon (The Lemon) is worthy of consideration for your pesos.

"You can take the boy out of the city, but you can't take the city out of the boy "   Very true. Perhaps this is why I always look forward to exploring Philly neighborhoods for cool places to eat. Today it was The New Olympia House on Castor Avenue that had my time and attention. A corner luncheonette that has been slinging hash for more than half a century, this little piece of Athens is well preserved, with long counter with about 10 spinners, booths behind that, and a large dining room behind the kitchen in this double wide row house neighborhood. The charm and cultural history were all in place, much as it has operated since 1960. I was very happy to have found the joint as I straddled the stool and was approached by the attractive server in black spandex pants.  The question at hand was - would the kitchen support the excited first impression, or no?   The answer was discovered soon enough. For this breakfast at least, the rude awakening was in the negative - my anticipation was better than the reality this day.   My french toast looked golden brown, and the old style syrup dispenser with slip down spring metal opening was way cool. However, the underside chassis had too much char, resulting in a burnt taste that required extra syrup to offset. That taste led me to think that the grill was not cleaned between orders, leaving burnt butter or other lubricant around to stick to the next food sizzling there. It also meant a lack of attention by the short order cook (not chef), and an attempt to hide the dark side from view. The three slices were ample, and had the decision been made to start afresh rather than hope I didn't notice, would have made me a true fan.  First impression dashed.   The Cecilware drip coffee was fine. I love those old contraptions. Yet, despite all the help behind the counter, no one saw that my small cup was bereft of coffee and needed refilling, until I asked. Hard to understand such inattentiveness when I was the only customer sitting there. Chalk it up to my invisibility, sometimes not the best superpower to practice while dining.   Still, I liked New Olympia House enough to regret this happenstance, and wish for a better experience. This could have been one of those true Philadelphia moments that only the city's profound indifference to perfection in the face of amazing potential, created the opportunity to transcend low expectations and truly hit the mark in miraculous laudation.   That moment must await a more hopeful day.

Trenton Farmer's Market is an institution from the time there were actually working (and profitable) farms around Mercer and Bucks Counties.  It has seen better days, but is still a great way to get the basic foodstuffs of life all in one place, at reasonable prices, and avoid the corporatism that is the supermarket industry nowadays.    If that wasn't enough of a reason to do your consuming here when possible, there are several other good ones - butchers, bakers, veggie mongers, deli delighters, and even candlestick makers who produce first rate digestibles and other things that you would be happy to eat and serve your family and friends.    Yesterday I stopped in to pick up fruit, veggies, chicken, a little BBQ, and sticky sweets, to tide me over through the coming Nor'easter.  The shops that were open in the afternoon were happy to have a late customer relieve them of some of their stock.  I found some good deals.   While in the neighborhood you can visit other great places to purchase food or just enjoy a good meal.  Halo Farms, Rozmaryn, and Pho Tan are just a few of the Yelpworthy destinations to consider.

Prince Fried Chicken protrudes from the 500 block of Hamilton Avenue, Trenton, NJ, due to the construction of a second story sunroom in front of the original small store.  While it likely does not satisfy the requirement of the ADA because of the steps needed to enter the shop, those who are able to climb will find the ascent well worthwhile.    Clearly, these dudes have thought about what people want to buy when they look for American fried chicken.  Boxes and buckets for sure.  Sandwiches, tenders and nuggets more than likely. Hamburgers for the chicken averse. Salads for the health conscious. Sweet desserts for absolutely everyone.  They have all this, and even more. Most importantly, they seem to do all of it quite well in their tiny space.    This is primarily a take out joint, with only a couple of stools along a shelf on one wall, so I knew that I would be eating at my desk.  That requires consideration of the grease and mess factor with all the paper in my work area. So, I ordered a fried chicken sandwich, rather than a box of chicken and sundries, and a single wing to discover the essence of the operation.  What I found was quite encouraging.  The sandwich contents were a plump, never frozen chicken breast, breaded lightly with a spicy flour coating that turned a golden brown with coaxing from the deep fryer.  A smear of mayo and a leaf of lettuce inside a soft sesame seed topped roll completed this simple creation.  First bite (always so important) reported the juicy freshness of the bird, as well as the interesting mildly hot jacket it was dressed in.  It was very good.  If only the roll had been stronger and able to hold up better, it would been remarkable. Still, I would definitely go back for more.  The wing, bagged expertly in a long narrow wax paper sleeve, was likewise tasty and properly cooked to its optimal moment.  It was easily pulled apart, and the meat removed by teeth and tongue.  Same spicy flavor.  If anything, I liked it more than the sandwich.    Conclusion: Prince Fried Chicken is really good.  A bucket for the family, along with a sampling of the large cookies, brownies and cheesecake, are in the offing for the near future.  Otherwise, I will just have to clear my desk before bringing in a box for my luncheon pleasure.

A1 Japanese Steakhouse sits in the strip center anchored by IHOP at the intersection of RT. 1 and Oxford Valley Road, Fairless Hills. It is one of the older sushi/hibachi houses, run by Chinese ownership and because of location and age, one of the less expensive operations. While the quality of the experience is a step down from the more modern Mt. Fuji, Sakura, Oishi, Arirang, etc., joints found throughout lower Bucks County, the difference is not so great as to make it unworthy of your dining out dollar, but is noticeable.   What do I mean? A1 is carpeted wall to wall. They doubtlessly hide the remains of years of food tossing by hibachi chefs entertaining customers with food flips aimed for your mouth. They would have to shampoo the floor weekly to keep the place with passing grade. They don't. With each grill housing its own grease trap, it is dubious that it is emptied and cleaned regularly. Yet, the health inspectors allow the business to remain open, so it is up to you to be vigilant.  Still, the food served looks and tastes good. Our salmon fillets (2 each) were fresh and presented well with sides of fried rice, mushroom soup (few in the small bowl) and grilled mixed veggies. Plenty to eat and even take home without ordering anything more. They even comp everyone 3 grilled shrimp. Nice touch. Their bar offers mostly national brand beers (Sam Adams Boston Lager) as well as some of those fancy ass fruity sweet things in hurricane glasses. So, if your policy on cleanliness is, "Don't ask, Don't Tell," you won't have a problem with A1.   One suggestion, salt free soy sauce for the chefs as they squirt and cook. Standard soy sauce tends to make everything have a similar taste, detracting from the natural flavors that should predominate.

The Gardenville Hotel has been standing guard on Durham Road for more than two and a half centuries, protecting travelers between Newtown and Easton from night terrors before, during and after the Revolution. In those days not every battle was in an open field, or behind trees or stone walls, but in the hearts of patriots and loyalists. It was in this very tavern that the debates about liberty and fidelity to the crown were argued, people took sides and made decisions that would effect their lives and the course of history. If you belly up to the bar today you may hear similar talk about status quo and change voiced with the same ferocity. It is good that some things never change much. The issues are as important today in their own way.  If you don't come for the history, be sure to come for the grub. It is very good. The kitchen knows what to do with meat. They have a smoker out back and a grill in house that does a job on brisket, prime rib, babybacks and steak that will satisfy the savage carnivore within. Our prime rib and brisket sandwiches were a load and a half of perfectly smoked and slathered beef, pretending to fit on a Kaiser roll. Each was enough for two meals. My side of baked beans came in a nice size dish that was about the best I'd ever tasted. Zangin' and twangin'!   You wouldn't think of Gardenville as a custom beer joint or martini bar, but they have enough choice to keep you satisfied. Between an IPA and citrus shandy, we were happy campers. The bar food is mostly fried, but there are plenty of quality options deeper in the menu and specials. Service is a pleasure with black and whites who enjoy their jobs.   Whether you live nearby or have to drive for a while, Gardenville Hotel is a worthwhile trip back in time.

Old school Wawa in the center of Main Street, Yardley Boro. Small parking lot in front. Larger one in back, but you may not know its there unless your local. Small footprint that still manages to provide most of the products and services of the latest supersized versions.   I was there to pick up a chicken salad hoagie before moving on to my next appointment. It had been a while since ordering with their touch screens and found the shear number of pages I had to endure to be somewhat daunting. How many screens just for mayo?!   Still, the sandwich was good with fresh chicken salad, but perhaps less so for the torpedo roll. Enjoyable, nonetheless.   Everyone there was well trained and friendly from front door welcome to cashier thank you for coming. Price was very appealing, with the customized sammy ten inch coming in at under $7.   Little wonder why almost everyone wants a Wawa near their town.

I don't know what it is, but gambling doesn't appeal to me. I understand the enjoyment some seem to have risking and most often losing their hard earned money, but I don't share the feeling. I also see that most lose what they come with, and would have been better off going bowling. But, I am not adverse to observing the mostly self-destructive behavior close up by sitting at a Blackjack table for a while and playing a few hands.   Some feel comfortable in a casino. I never have. Yet, Parx is very big and often so crowded that I feel invisible. That allows me to wander around close to the action, yet not be part of it. The occasional whoop from winning a big pot, or cry of angry frustration losing one are part of a tragi/comedy that plays out hundreds of times a day. The staff seems well trained to deal with the range of human emotions, and nothing gets out of control.   The best things are the number of food choices at reasonable prices. Happy hours are extensive and often late at night. It is possible to grab a drink and decent snack or dinner without handing over a $20 without change. If your not losing too much, Parx can be a decent date night, with live entertainment and lots of people watching.   Biggest negative - This is a smokers space. Anxiety increases the habit. The air system is not totally effective, so health is an issue. No doubt the employees are involved in risky behavior. Healthcare is not available to most workers unless they reached full time status, which is strictly formulated. You just can't afford to accept the exposure for very long.   Once a year is more than enough.   2,500 employees. That is a lot.

South Broad Street in Trenton, NJ, is always struggling with the birth pains of renewal. This capital city has had more false starts than a drunk runner waiting for the sound of the starter's pistol. Yet, there are signs of life springing up as a few pioneering entrepreneurs open shop amongst the crepitation of this down trodden burg. Look closely and you can find cafes, restaurants, and now an ice cream parlor flowering in the surrounding weeds.   Trenton Ice Cream Parlor opened recently in this part of South Trenton. It brings color and verve to this forlorn street, with a three table curbside deck and sidewalk cafe feel, new sign and lighting around the front steps, door and windows of this converted row house. Inside, is more of the same stimulation, with the addition of friendly servers and cashiers who are genuinely happy to see you.   The flavor choices are about a dozen, with Peanut Butter Swirl and Caramel Pretzel my choices in a three scoop cup. It's hard to explain the incongruity of finding creative flavors for cones, sundaes, and the like, where city grime has persisted for decades. Very happy that it is there, but somewhat disconcerting, nonetheless.   I sampled my ice cream as I drove home to Bucks. It was quite good, even if falling short of spectacular. It was creamy sweet with plenty of ribbons of peanut butter and chunks of pretzel, mixed in a solid vanilla and caramel base. The price for this "small" cup of three scoops - $3 and change. That's about half what I paid recently for a similar quantity across the river. Clearly, the rent in Trenton is a serious consideration for folks looking for a place to start a retail business.   My Trenton office is farther north in South Broad, but close enough to attract me when this viciously hot summer demands chill relief. Yes. I will be back.

Things are definitely looking up in Newtown, especially in terms of new eating establishments. Harvest Seasonal Grill & Wine Bar recently opened it's doors in the Village at Newtown.  It is an impressive and attractive house, with lots of stone and wood in a large room. It even has a three sided wall fireplace in the lobby, a large bar on the left, plenty of booths and tables, and al fresco dining under the extended overhang in front.   I was there for a business lunch this week without a reservation. No problem. At 1:00 pm we had a booth in under ten minutes. Service was bright and friendly, and it was obvious the staff was well school in the details of the menu.  First glance showed that prices were upscale, but so were the dishes described in the large format menu. With a little work it was easy to find a light healthy veggie lunch in the appetizer list and avoid the high end dishes farther in. For around $10 I enjoyed the hummus plate that included grapefruit slices, fresh dark green sweetpeas, scoop slices of carrot and zucchini, and triangles of warm pita. Very good. My associate ordered a quinoa type sandwich and side salad. She said it was also highly satisfying.   All in all, Harvest Grill is a new level of farm to table cuisine that brings up the standard for quality dishes in the community. There is a price to pay for it, but judging by the crowded midweek dining room, it is a price people are more than happy to absorb.   Such success does not come without some adjustments to the customary dining outlets in Newtown. They all have to step up their games to stay relevant in the local resto wars, or risk being left behind. On the other hand, the surge in new kitchens appearing in this quarter create serious parking problems that at some point may literally drive customers away as they tire of hunting for a spot to leave their wheels for a chance at a great meal.   For now, that is a good problem to have.

Barcelona Pizza is really a takeout shop with three booths for those foolish enough to prefer eating their food hot, like us. Folks are nice, but not very skilled in table service. The delivery people hang out behind the counter between packing their heat bags to make a drive. They weren't accustomed to having customers actually eating there, and we sort of felt in the way.   The food itself was average at best. My son ate his large chicken parm sandwich, but admitted to having had better. It was overly cheesed, out of balance with the red sauce and chicken pieces. The veggie calzone was enormous, and enough for four people. The crust was great, but there were far too many chunky greens and not enough tomato sauce to countervail. Too, we picked out several thick stalks of broccoli without any buds on them. Difficult to eat.   Finally, I ordered the Italian Sausage, Pepper & Onion Parm torpedo, but requested that the cheese be left off, and the sauce to be on the side. Apparently, this was a major challenge in the kitchen, because rather than a  nice length of sweet sausage, I received coin sized slices of the meat no doubt designed for pizza toppings long before the sandwich was created. It was mixed with the sauce in the roll despite my instructions. So, the sausage was dry and there was too much sauce for my taste. I guess the parmesan melted over everything would hide the ingredients, but when deconstructed, it just came out poor looking and a hodgepodge of other purposed food thrown together without the understanding of what an Italian sausage, pepper and onion sandwich was supposed to be.   Not even close.  Apparently, there wasn't an Italian in the house who could direct the kitchen staff, and the result was a poor imitation of what is basic cooking in a casa Italiano.   Come on, people!

This is strictly a 2 slices and a drink review.   Amato's on Trenton Road in Fairless Hills, is an attractive space for a neighborhood Italian meal.  On this Monday evening, it was bustling.  I found a deuce in the front window after looking at the pizza-on-display under glass at the front of the kitchen/cashier area.  It all looked good, but I was most attracted to the square cut Brooklyn and Amato Pies, and ordered one of each, "well done."    The point about "well done" reheated pizza is my attempt to awaken the previously baked pie's essence by making the cheese and sauce bubble again to bring out the original flavors.  There is little worse than a pie that has been sitting around for a while, and is only partially reanimated by inadequate oven exposure the second time around. If the oven master understands me, he knows that I don't mind a scorched undercarriage in my search for more taste.    A friendly server brought the hot squares to my table on a small aluminum pizza pan.  It looked good as the steam hit my glasses.  I asked for knife and fork because there was little crust to gasp and I didn't want to burn my digits.   First bite I realized that the crust had not been reheated sufficiently, while the topside was significantly hotter. The taste was okay, but the platform was soft and far from the more rigid structure I prefer.  The Tomato Sauce was dark thick red, and was nicely spiced.  As I looked around at the tables with fresh baked pies, I saw that those folks were able to lift their triangles without wilting, nor spillage.  They seemed quite happy with their food.  My wish is that all pizza parlors selling warmed over slices understand that those of us who can't handle a whole pie desire the same sensory experience as everyone else, and take the time to bring the fresh pizza "zing" to the rest of us.  I know it's a loss leader for many shops, but regardless of the price, failure to provide full participation only means they have a less than satisfied customer.

Remarkable.  Some Italian places are really just about pizza and sandwiches, with a nod to traditional dishes to attract people who want more than a couple of slices or a cheesesteak. Others, have talent in the kitchen, and can turn a beautiful platter, but don't really do assembly line tomato pie. It is much rarer to find a restaurant that does both very well while housed in a ordinary looking pizza parlor for the past 30 years. So it is with Paul's Penndel Pizza on old Route 1.   There was a steady line of pizza takeout orders on one side of the large room separated by half wall to create a cozy dining area on the other. Only two tables were occupied over here and the trifold menu didn't disclose all the hidden treasures possible in the kitchen. Photos on Yelp showed a good looking chicken francaise dish, but was it available?   Yes, it was! All I had to do was ask, and our attentive server Robyn made all the arrangements.   In addition to my request, we also chose chicken parmigiana and "Shrimp Our Way," a penne platter with lots of shrimp and a delicious pink sauce. Each dinner came with choice of soup or salad, and double bread baskets.   The francaise was incredible. Butter lemon sauce and perfectly pan sauteed egged medallions. Tender, light and pleasantly tart. The best rendition I have enjoyed in many years. The Our Way was likewise exceptional, with knock out pink sauce over a dozen or more crustaceans and quality pasta. The parmigiana was a heavy load with spaghetti and copious red gravy. Substantial and tasty but a step down from the other meals. The side salads were large, but mostly iceberg, detracting from the other ingredients and house balsamic. Finally, the Italian loaves were the weakest link, with little crust, texture nor flavor. They really would do themselves a favor by finding a better bakery.   The shortcomings were not enough to seriously detract from what was otherwise a fantastic and surprising dinner. Still, had they been eliminated, this could have been one of the best meals of the year. As it was, it was damn close.   4.5 STARS

If you are up and about very early, go to Cramer to get fresh donuts, muffins and scones.  Too, if you can order a cake for a special occasion, you will probably be quite satisfied. Otherwise, despite the charm of an old fashioned bakery, and the butternut aroma, the products are inconsistent, and pricey. The bread, bagels, rolls are not worth the trip. There are much stronger options for them only minutes away. To be a worthwhile destination everything must be good, available, and reasonably priced compared to the competition. Cramer is not quite all that.

The Mann Center for the Performing Arts (full moniker) opened in 1976 in West Fairmount Park.  It is one of the finest outdoor music venues in the USA, with room for about 14,000 people, both inside under the roof, and outside on the grass knoll.  There is no question that it brings life to this part of the city, especially at night, when the sound from a loud band or orchestra can be heard well into the surrounding streets of West Philly.   I was there the other night with my teenage son, who was attending his first concert. A right of passage from one generation to the next, I was transporting him to see/listen to Kid Cudi (Scott Ramon Seguro Mescudi), a rap, reggae, original actor and hipster, where I had previously gone to see Stevie Ray Vaughan, Roger Daltry and Robert Cray.  I was happy to be passing the baton. The venue hasn't changed much in the past 40 years.  It is still an awesome place to listen to music, and mix with like-minded heads.  The place was sold out and had the expected carnival atmosphere before, during and after the show.  There was enough haze generated to give everyone within a half mile a contact high.  Everyone inhaled.    The show was great.  Kid Cudi is a first rate musician and showman.  He played for about 90 minutes, despite coming on stage about an hour late.  His band was tight, and all the singers, lights and stagecraft contributed to a first rate experience. Wasn't sure I would like his style, but he was way better in person than listening to him on recordings or watching his videos. He had everyone moving and shouting for more.   Most of the main boulevards in the nearby park were closed to traffic, and it took a while to find our way to the parking area and the main entrance. There was a heavy police presence in the park just in case, but they did not interfere in any way with the happening.   At the end of the evening, my son and his friend were exhausted from all their singing and dancing, not to mention the inebriants in the air. They had a great time, and scored Kid Cudi T-shirts as memorabilia.   Just hope The Mann is around when my grandchildren are ready to boogie!

I really like the imagery Blue Ocean creates in my mind. Cool tropical island daylight. Fresh air. Clean water. Right off the boat fish for filleting into optimal sushi. Who wouldn't want sashimi or exotic rolls made from the best sealife available? Poetic license can be effective in selling a restaurant to consumers, but actual execution is what matters most.   This location is making a third attempt at Asian kitchen success. Yummy Sushi was here for several years before moving to the College of New Jersey neighborhood. Fame Dish arrived next, claiming to be an Asian fusion house, when in fact it was primarily Chinese with a wave to Thai, Japanese and Viet cuisine. It was gone in a year, because it was more confusion than actual fusion. Now Blue Ocean has taken over with the promise of sushi done right, plus a menu covering a lot of dishes from The Land of the Rising Sun.   First, it seems that management is Chinese, and that the sushi chef speaks Mandarin. So, sushi culture is not spoken as a first language. Still, the preparation and execution can excel with well trained hands and high quality ingredients. Second, it seems they are following the course of most such houses by duplicating the menu prescribed by graduates of Sushi University - limited high quality fish and lots of rolls with clever names; generic soy sauces, and gloopy ginger salad dressing. No creativity is possible with poor basic ingredients.   I ordered a spicy Salmon Roll and chicken katsu, to sample two aspects of the menu. The chicken came as a dinner with choice of soup or salad. Two deep fried spring rolls were brought to the table as a complement. Nice touch. The salad was all iceberg with a few carrot shavings. The dressing was that poor quality ginger mash. The lettuce hadn't been fully sliced, so a lot of it was still one piece and difficult to collect with only a pair of chopsticks. The 8 piece roll was okay, but not the freshest. Finally, the katsu was two thin cutlets, breaded and deep fried with a good dipping sauce. Sadly, it was cooked just beyond the point where it was juicy throughout. Liked the crunch, but not enough to want to eat all of it. At $17 it was a pretty big miss. The spring rolls were solid.   I hope Blue Ocean understands the issues and really wants theirs to be a first class sushi house. They can certainly make it so if they don't accept shortcuts and focus on quality across the board.   Wishing them insight and excellence.

LUNCH MENU ONLY REVIEW  Peking House on Makefield Road, Yardley (actually, Lower Makefield), Pa., sits in an older strip center that also houses RJ's Bagels and a couple of nail salons.  So, if you want to have some Chinese takeout while having a pedicure this is your special place.    Otherwise, the grub here is pretty standard fare for Chinese/American joints.  It relies on take away business, with only one table and service for eat ins in the same takeout containers.  They were able to boil water for hot tea, which so many these days just refuse to offer.  It was appreciated.  My lunch special was pork egg foo young, with fried rice and wonton soup.  The soup was the weakest link.  The dumplings were thick skinned and were filled with some meat thing that had little taste.  The broth was likewise, flavorless.  The pancakes were decent, with plenty of veggies and thin strips of pork.  The brown sauce was a bit too cool and had congealed in the plastic container. No Thanks!  The rice was made at some point in the past with a yellow dye  bouillon, but was too hard and past its prime.    There may be some better things on their menu for dinner, but as this isn't in my neighborhood, I am unlikely to find out.

Sometimes the condition of the shop tells the true story. No matter how good the food is, it is impossible to dismiss what is seen on the floor, in the corners or on the back of shelves around the retail space. So it was with Wicked Bagelz in Westampton, NJ.  This is the third iteration of a bagel breakfast/lunch joint at this location since I have been regularly attending court in nearby Mt. Holly (although all court business is now done online due to Covid-19). The predecessors had a problem maintaining operations, although each had reasonably decent round bread. I was sorry to see them close.   Wicked Bs has a cool name and a witchy Halloween decor. Manmade spiderwebs were draped over furniture, etc. The women working were friendly, and the bagels looked good in the bins behind the counter. I arrived late for breakfast and most of the choices were gone. I snagged an Everything Bagel with Veggie Spread. It was thick, round and boil/baked with a darker flour that added a rich flavor to the dough. It was very good.  But, as I waited I began to look around at all the decorations.
