My vision eventually reached the floor. I noticed it was dirtier than expected, like it hadn't been swept in days or longer*. I then saw that there was black crud along the molding at the base of the display cases, coffee station and tables. Plastic bottles of soft drink lay on the floor near their cooler, and hadn't been put into the fridge. It was obvious that no one was seriously cleaning the front of the house. I didn't want to see the situation behind the counter, nor the grill area.   I became more grossed out by the total slovenliness as I thought about it. No matter how tasty the bagel, the lack of concern for the health of their customers was offensive. With Covid-19 everywhere, such filth was just unacceptable and way beyond the pale.   One and done!  *Management sent me a message denying these conditions exist. Unfortunately, my observations were accurate. The black streaked moldy baseboards were a sad fact and hadn't been touched in a long time. There was no spill to report, and would have been if it existed.  Regardless, I understand defending your business, and I will visit again as suggested. If conditions have improved, I will amend the review, and thank you for being a responsible owner.

There are alot of great Mexican joints around Trenton these days, and Totopos up on Brunswick Avenue is one of them. True, it is tiny (2 tables inside and 2 more out front), and it is a dive (in the best sense of the word), but the skilled hands in la cocina tell a different tale.  When I parked on the street in front and walked in, a telenovela was playing on the HDTV high on the wall, and several people were working behind the counter. I approached to check their trifold menu and engaged the man who appeared to be the owner or manager. He was fluently bilingual making it easy to explain what was available and then how I wanted my Torta Milanesa de Pollo prepared.  I took a chair at one of the tables, and moments later my lunch was placed before me. It was an enormous sandwich on an oversized oblong roll, dressed in heavy foil at its waist and showing its internals at its edges. Just take a look at the photos. It was an amazing piece of working peoples culinary art.  I maneuvered my jaws for a first bite and attempted to compress the width of this monster to fit more in my mouth. I clamped down full force and cut through its many layers. The flavor of the breaded cutlet, spicy mayo, avocado, tomato, onion, queso and lettuce burst out and had a fiesta in my mouth complete with pinata. It was just an excellent sandwich. Eating half would have been enough for a satisfying meal, but I indulged and ate the whole thing right there.   Totopos has been in business for about three years. The family running it is from Oaxaca in southern Mexico. They give this corner of North Trenton another reason to visit along with some of the other great hidden kitchens in the neighborhood.  .

Please don't get me wrong. I love DeLorenzo's tomato pies, and have been amazed by them since moving to Trenton many years ago and discovering the Italian wonders of the Chambersburg neighborhood. I, like most of those fabulous Roman kitchens, have since left the city for greener lawns in the suburbs, but still returned to Hudson Street, and Robbinsville thereafter, just to continue our love affair with their thin crust tomato pies, that were the best I had ever eaten until that time.  They have since expanded into Bucks County, with their newest venture on Edgewood Road in Lower Makefield, PA. (No, it is not Yardley).  I couldn't wait to have the opportunity to visit their new digs. That finally happened yesterday on a Sunday evening. I had ordered by phone a few hours before to be certain they could handle my request given how busy their joint normally was on weekends. I was assured that my two large pies (one regular and one sausage) could be handled by the designated pick up time of 7:00 PM.    When I arrived, the smallish parking lot was overflowing, but I lucked into someone pulling out just as I pulled in.  Their store is all new construction alongside the Giant Shopping Center off Stony Hill Road. As expected, the waiting area was jammed with people waiting for tables.  I approached the very busy cashier, and when he had a second to look at me, gave him my name for the takeout order. He checked in the kitchen and relayed that my pies were not yet out of the oven.  Perfect! I would secure them at apex heat and transport them home while still baking inside.  I reflexively began to salivate at the thought of biting into the steaming chunky red gravy, mozzarella and thin cracker crust. Oh, Yeah!  The ten minute wait was fine with me. I used the time to take photos and watch all the happy customers. The aroma was timeless, and threw me into reveries of my earliest experience with DeLo's grand pies. I eventually paid the $35 for the two artisanal works of edible art, and drove home with visions of plum tomatoes and basil dancing in my head.   The sausage pie was just as amazing as I remembered. Local crumbled meat, fresh melted mozza, and mildly salty thin crust to complement the equally mildly sweet red sauce. The explosion in my mouth was a wonderful party with old friends. Unfortunately, the regular pie was overbaked, with too much crust burn and too little sauce filling the irregularly shaped base. I like some scorching as much as anyone, but this one was beyond that - complete carbon in too many places. This can happen when the kitchen staff is stretched to the max and doesn't watch each pie through the process. Chalk it up to a bad card in an otherwise sound hand.   DeLorenzo's is still about the best tomato pie in the area, especially on this side of the Delaware River.  Very glad to save the longish drive to Robbinsville, NJ,  although their cousin's shop in Levittown is just as good.

Mexico Lindo Restaurant sits on a rather forlorn strip of South Broad Street in Hamilton, a few blocks before you get to the Trenton line. Don't be deterred by the urban decay visible in the area, because once you walk inside this unassuming storefront you cross the border into Mexico.  Vibrant colors, a hodgepodge of odds and ends tables covered with more colors, a HD TV showing the latest soaps from Ciudad Juarez, and a hand painted mural of the Mexican Eagle grasping a Rattlesnake emblazed on the wall.  I was surprised I was not asked for my passport.  And, the food was very good, as there is an ever growing population of excellent Mexican, Guatemalan, Honduran, Salvadoran and even Puerto Rican shops in the vicinity - making for healthy competition.  My Torta Milanese de Pechuga was a fat boy sandwich on an oversized roll filled with Breaded Chicken Cutlet, Lettuce, Tomato, String Cheese, Mayo and a bit of Chipotle Sauce.  Delicious.  It was really too loaded to just pick up by hand and stuff into mouth.  Knife and fork were needed to get everything into my mouth collectively.  The accompanying Crinkle Cut Fries were also above average.  My most pleasant surprise was ordering the Jugo de Melon drink.  This was the water added version of a milk shake made from Watermelon, and it came served in the aluminum blender container.  It was totally refreshing.   My Spanish was just adequate for a few short conversations about the restaurant, and to permit me to compliment them on a terrific little joint.  The owner and his family came out to eat while I was there, and I made it clear the food was delicioso, and that I would revuelve pronto.

Cha's Seafood sits in on Pennington Avenue, Trenton, NJ, in a small "L" shaped shopping plaza where an old factory used to be.  It is very clean inside, with a large selection of breaded fillets and semi prepared shellfish, crabs and king crab legs in various sauces for purchase by the pound or in platters to take out.  The space is large enough for a few tables, but that is not their business model.    I stopped in for lunch this week around 1:30 pm, and I was just about the only customer there. I ordered a whiting lunch (3 fillets, fries, 2 slices of whole wheat, small cup of macaroni salad and a bottle of water for about $7.50, including tax.  The price was definitely right.   The fish was sliced thin and breaded in corn meal before bathing in the deep fryer.  I could only eat two of the fillets made into a sandwich, and left most of the fries behind.  They were okay, but far to many to eat in a balanced meal.     Strangely, they did not offer any mayo, tarter sauce, nor even ketchup with the take away lunch. Any of those would have added to the flavor of the fish and taters, which was sort of  plain as it was.  Next time, I will be sure to ask for those accessories.    Overall, just a decent, but unexciting monochromatic lunch.  Those pre-seasoned crabs and other shellfish did look pretty good.    Octavia did a good job taking care of me.  She was friendly and informative.

Aldo's Pizzarama on Bustleton Avenue in far Northeast Philadelphia has been at the same location for a couple of generations, and has the reputation for making the best pie in this part of the city. Perhaps, it has changed hands since those opinions were expressed, but it was not our experience when we stopped in for dinner over the weekend.   The guys behind the counter, although not busy, seemed unwilling to crack a smile or offer any service beyond taking our order and shouting out when the pizza or steak sandwich was ready, for us to pick up and deliver to ourselves. No silverware, no napkins, no courtesy offered.   My son liked the steak, but said it was not worth the drive to have it. The pizza looked great with crisped sausage slices and well done crust. The problem was the overuse of cheese out of proportion to the sauce. It was such a heavy layer that the undercarriage could not support the topside. Lifted from the outer edge left the center of the slice on the aluminum pan with its contents sliding off. The work involved in folding the slices allowed us to taste how salty the cheese and red sauce were. Just not a good pizza, despite the decent crust.   Won't be back.

I've been to a few Mission BBQ houses in the past years. While they could all be more consistent, their overall product tends to be good to excellent, and their "mission," highly worthy. So happens that the experience yesterday at this store was about the best I've had.   The place was almost empty at 3 in the afternoon. One or two tables occupied and a solitary customer at the register ordering a meal. We had plenty of attention from the friendly, dedicated staff. After ordering 8 oz of brisket for the spouse, I went with a combo of brisket, 2 ribs and sides of baked beans and Grandma's Mashed Sweet Potatoes.  Both came with a square of cornbread.   As you can see from the photos, the brisket was the blue ribbon winner. It was moist with plenty of dark brown bark. Both plain and wet it was a joy to eat. Great taste and texture. The ribs were pull off the bone tender and juicy, although not as dynamic as the beef this day. A shot of their Memphis sauce helped bring out the sleeping flavors. It was basically pulled pork without the effort of shredding. The beans were full of meat with a strong savory spicy base. Liked them a lot. The Grandma Sweets were over the top sugary, with a topping of melting brown sugar over already insulin inducing tawny tater. Not intended for diabetics, so be forewarned.   As we were finishing, the cashier who had originally seen us up front walked by with a whole tray of Freedom Fries for us to enjoy, on the house. Very generous gesture which we appreciated, but already stuffed, all we could do is take them home with the rest of the leftovers for later consumption.   We felt loved at Mission, and we reciprocated the affection for the staff and all first responders and military folk everywhere.

Very nice set up for this latest addition to the El Limon franchise in Bucks County. Radcliffe Street was already a great riverside lane in Bristol, but is even better with the presence of the small dining room (8 tables/booths) and cool outdoor curbside seating of this Mexican house. Definitely perfect for a still warm late September autumn night.   Really liked the Tacos Dorados with the combination of shredded chicken, mashed potato and spices, deep fried and topped with lettuce, tomato and queso blanco, and choice of red/green salsa from table rockets. Firm crunch, followed by smooth chew and blended flavors. Yet, @ 3 for $9., it seemed overpriced, as was the tempting and delicious Tres Leches dessert @$5.95. Good taste and texture, but I won't be that indulgent next time. The Horchata drink was cool and refreshing with the taste of vanilla and fresh cinnamon right down to the final suck through plastic straw.  Maybe I need to accept the pandemic inflation of late, but I still have optimism that prices will come down once the supply chain amps up and evens out. For now I appreciate the chance to get out and enjoy a meal beyond my own kitchen.

The key to understanding the Bagel & Bread House on Horsham Road is hidden in plain sight. The shop is quite small, and all you see are wire bins of bagels and a self serve coffee shelf, but not actual "bread" shown for sale. Nary a loaf in sight.   Why is that?   Best I can ascertain, at this business they are one and the same. A bagel is bread is true, but by that generalization, so are crackers and pita. Simplistic, but telling. While all bagels are bread, not all bread are bagels. Perhaps, by such gross definition, you don't focus on the doughy fact that you can make bread look like a bagel, but it may not actually be one. To my taste, this is what occurred here. These round wheels are perfect facsimiles of bagels, and look great. Still, by taste and texture they are not bagels. They are bagel-like bread creations that have neither the consistency, nor taste/texture of the real thing. It's not that they are bad, but more a surprising disappointment that upon first bite, reminds of sliced sourdough or rye, more than a properly boiled and baked traditional delicacy.   So, the best I can conclude is that at this establishment bagel and bread refer to the same thing. Problem is, there are no real crisp skinned, flavorful insides, light or dense, boiled and baked goodies here. Only bread in the form of bagels.   Some like them, but not worth the trip if real bagels are your preferred destination.

Pho Washington is the latest restaurant at this shopping center location at 6th and Washington. The menu is fairly limited to traditional street food of Vietnam - pho (noodle soup), com (broken rice dishes) and vermicelli (rice noodles bowls with choice of meat and greens). They also have a long list of beverages on the back page.   We stopped in before grocery shopping at 1st Asian Supermarket across 6th St. We ordered Pho Tai (beef broth w thin ribeye steak slices) and Vermicelli w Grilled Pork, Spring Roll and Shredded Lettuce (w thin sweet dipping sauce on the side). We started with Summer Rolls with thick ground peanut brown sauce.  Everything was good to very good, without any knockouts. The appetizer rolls were loaded with sliced shrimp and cabbage in a cool, sticky rice wrap. The sauce stuck to what it touched, so it really dominated the taste of the dish. The wrap was quite chewy. It was okay. The small bowl of pho was more than we could finish after adding all the sprouts, Thai basil, jalapeno and squeezed lime juice. The steak was plentiful and cooked well in the beef broth. While the beef stock was good, it needed more simmering with pot spices to attain the right degree of subtle richness. We squirted some sirracha from the table rocket to boost the flavor, which helped alot.   I liked the vermicelli plate the most. The pork was delicious with or without dipping in the accompanying sweet vinegar dip. It was tender and fully exposed with a few chews. The noodles were both warm and cool depending on where it was in the bowl in proximity to hot or cool food. Both temps were fine, and I found that pouring some of the sauce over everything enhanced the flavor of each element, but wasn't essential. I would definitely get that again, but probably go to Pho Ha across the parking lot for quality well cured pho.   Service was fine and prices reasonable for the overall experience.    The bakery next door looked like the right place to hang out over Vietnamese coffee with condensed milk and pastries. Next time for that!

Four Seasons Diner on Cottman Avenue, Northeast Philadelphia, is a traditional highway roadhouse in the semi-urban jungle that is this part of the great city. It is well maintained, with plenty of parking, classic lunch counter in back, and booths galore all around. They also have a lot of recessed colored lighting in the ceiling, which gives a somewhat funhouse quality to it all.   I stepped to the rear and was the only customer on a spinner. The menu is enormous for the morning meal, so it took a few minutes to go through it. In the meantime, I received my mugga joe and a side glass of milk, as requested. Ultimately, I went with their french toast and bacon combo for $7.95. Only these old joints that have paid off their construction loans can afford to offer such inexpensive vittles. Wish they also offered real maple syrup rather than the pre-packaged sweeteners. Still, with three large slices of bread and an equal number of well done bacon, I felt satiated without even touching the third slice of toast.   All the while, I had plenty of attention from the staff, who filled my mug repeatedly, and asked after my satisfaction. Had I been more gregarious, I no doubt would have had strong conversation with the ladies all morning. I preferred to stick to my reading.   This part of Philly has many diners to chose from. Glad I chose a decent one for today's brekkie. I passed several others on my way to the office, and will check them out in due course.

The drive down Woodhill Road, Upper Makefield, from Highland Road, is a perfect example of the beauty of Bucks County. Forests, farms, valleys, rolling hills. As you go east toward the Delaware River, you come upon Ely Farm and its multigenerational pork products agribusiness on the left. Its long drive framed by white picket fence escorts you to the large barn processing facility, small retail store, and the old farmstead under aging trees. It is a quite the bucolic vista, worthy of photograph, or at least a deep breath of appreciation.   Walking up to the shop we met several people waiting to pick up their freshly butchered deer. "Eat what you kill," has immediate meaning, as we saw a couple carrying out a large flat box full of neatly wrapped meat and a plastic bag holding a multi point antler rack deer head for mounting.   Not something you see every day.  The retail space is very small, with display cases showing many of their items for sale, access to walk-in refrigerators, and buzzing workers (mostly family) attending to the customers. It takes a few minutes for a first timer to figure out the process. We did, and ordered Seasoned Pork Chops, Hickory Smoked Kielbasa, Honey Bologna and Ground Beef. There was a lot more tempting us, but we had to start somewhere. Everything was made on site and looked great.   When we got home we quickly sampled the kielbasa and bologna. Both had rich taste and we're slightly addicting. I fried up thin slices of the bologna and scrambled in a couple of eggs, salt and pepper. Delicious! Will grill the chops later this week. Can't wait.  They are lean cut with thin edges of fat. Nothing will go to waste.   If the seasoned pork chops are as tender and tasty as they look and the smoked meats have proven to be, we will become regular Ely customers.

When another Chinese house was closed on Tuesday in Hatboro, we pulled out the trustee Yelp App and found Wing Lee Cuisine not far away in Horsham on Easton Road.  As the saying goes; "One door closes and another opens."  So it was last evening. We may never know what we were missing, because there is little chance we will return to Hatboro from Newtown for dinner, but we definitely discovered a very good Chinese restaurant about a mile away that is open seven days a week and serves good quality dishes with friendly service from ownership.    The room was well appointed, clean and attractive with white linen and heavy metal utensils in addition to available chopsticks.  We brought our own libations and were promptly given a table side ice bucket to hold the beer at arms length.  The menu was Chinese in front, and Japanese in back.  There were plenty of options from Cantonese, to Hunanese, to Szechuanese (although this was a light version of the kickin' spiciness we desired; lacking any Szechuan chili peppers or star peppercorns), and a page of fish platters. Regardless of that small disappointment, everything was well made with fresh ingredients, superior sauces, and nice presentations.    We asked for Hunanese Lamb, which was tender and spiced with black bean sauce.  Very good.  The Szechuan beef and the Szechuan Shrimp were both full plates with plenty of thin sliced beef and veggies, and large shrimp in a thick bright red gravy, but lacking in true Szechuan flavor.  We added some house chili sauce after the fact, which helped a bit, but could not approach the fire quotient of cooking with the authentic flamethrowers.  Finally, the eggplant in garlic sauce was good, although it seemed American rather than Chinese eggplant was used.    We enjoyed our meal (and birthday celebration).  The candle stuck in the cored/quartered orange and the singing of "Happy Birthday," were very thoughtful touches and appreciated.    This is one of the better suburban Chinese restaurants in this part of the world.  It makes up for lack of real Chengdu heat by the overall quality and skills apparent in their kitchen.  They would do themselves a favor by having the right spices above the stove for those who know what Szechuan food is supposed to taste like.  If they did, this place could be truly exceptional.

Chinatown Square on Race Street between 10th & 11th, is a nice attempt to bring Asian street food malls to Philly. It is a tiny version of these emporiums found on a grand scale in Flushing, NY, Toronto, and other major Chinese population centers. When done right in a large enough space, there are dozens of mini fast food outlets surrounding a central communal dining area where a group effort is required to scout for seats while the rest line up for the desired treats, and bring everything back to the demarked table. They are wildly successful.  It remains to be seen if Chinatown Square has the critical mass of enough choices balanced with adequate seating to make it. But, my first visit was fun and tasty, and will bring me back for more when in the mood for snacks reminiscent of all those delights experienced in travels through China, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. There, when the sun goes down, the streets fill with bicycle kitchens setting up curbside cafes to grill the delicacies you select from the table spread in front of you, and served on miniature tables and stools on the sidewalk. Such a kick!   The Cambodian sausage and BBQ beef on a stick from Khmer Grill were both greasily excellent. Tart/sweet marinade, just enough firing to cook everything without drying out, and timely delivery into a styro take out container, made for a delicious bite and chew.   The other counters serving buns, gyros, Thai ice cream, etc., were all busy with happy folk talking or eyeing their phones. There is even a karaoke bar upstairs.   Kudos to the developer who put this together. She is on to something that should be popular and lead to copycats all over Chinatown and the surrounding streets.   This is just the beginning.

This was my first visit to a Sonic Drive-In.  This one has been around on North Olden Avenue in Ewing for only a few years. The place has two rows of drive-in slots where you can enjoy their rollerskating, eat in the car, gimmick. With an outside temperature over 90 degrees, the better choice was to go inside and enjoy the air conditioning and stop polluting for a while.   The place was clean and bright with Sonic Radio playing background muzak, and LED HD displays showing their standard menu and specials. There was no one in there but me when I arrived at 1:30.  The young woman at the single cashier post was friendly and seemed to enjoy having a little customer contact rather than talking to people all day long through headphones.   The Carhop Classic for $3.99 was an irresistible deal.  Single burger loaded with cheese, mayo, mustard, ketchup, lettuce and tomato, it was a nice size. It came with a choice of onion rings, fries or tater tots.  I went with the later. The actual burger experience was pretty much average. Far from the best fast food burger I've ever had, but far from the worst, too.  Not all that much flavor, but the overall bitechew was okay.  At least it did not arrive crushed like at 5 Guys, nor cold as so often happens at the Burger Kings of the world. The price/quality proposition was decent given the special available on this combo.   Would I rush back? No. Would I avoid Sonic all together? No. Aside from the drive in cultural history, it is really no more than middle of the pack. If it was nearby when I was hungry, I would gladly chow down. Inside or out.

More Than Q on Klines Court in Lambertville, NJ, does a good turn for this river city across the mighty Delaware from New Hope, Pa.  It slow roasts ribs, brisket, pork and chicken to soft, pull-off-the-bone tenderness and rubs/bastes with quality dry and wet spices/sauces to produce a quality BBQ.  The house sits on this quiet backstreet, bracketed by Brian's and Di Napoli's, making for a tasty killers' row of excellent cuisine choices.  The interior space is designed for communal dining, so after ordering your food at the order window, look for seats along the long tables or wall counters, to await the call of your number at the pickup window.    You won't think you've been transported to Memphis or St. Louis, but for eastern Pennsylvania/western Jersey this is damn good. It is every bit as flavorful as the better known Lucy's, Mission, Ben's, Famous Dave's in Bucks, or Smoke-N-Grill and 1911 Smoke House in Jersey, to name just a few.   Our lunch of brisket and fried chicken sandwiches were loaded and delicious.  The beef was tender with a pleasant mildly spicy lasting taste.  My chicken was corn meal coated and fried just enough to leave the inner bird juicy. The aioli mayo and creamy coleslaw on top contributed nicely to the experience.  Side dishes of cornbread and baked beans were strong complementary textures and tastes - sweet cornbread was freshly baked, and the rich, savory beans were topped with pieces of burnt ends or pulled pork to enhance the chew.  Really got off on them beans!   Boylan's Soda (Grape) was a sweet washdown with all the tang.   While More Than Q is a small chain, it does have a local mom & pop feel to it.    Will def be back for the ribs.

This update is strictly for the breakfast this morning.  Their deli does prepare a limited breakfast menu, but unless you like microwaved eggs and sausage grilled between the cheeks of a pannini press, this might not be the place for you.  Absent a genuine grill they did a fairly good job on my sausage, egg and cheese sandy.  I do wonder if they clean that press before putting other breaded sandwiches inside.    While the taste and price were decent, I prefer the use of a grill to prepare my eggs and melt the cheese.  Although the coffee was okay and the ambiance very much "from the barn," I will likely not return for breakfast.   It remains a good place to buy farm fresh produce and enjoy the seasonal outdoor events.

PJ's Pancake House & Tavern is located on Bear Tavern Road in Ewing, NJ. It is north of Rt. 95 in a bucolic part of the township. If you have been around for a while, they renovated the old joint formerly known as The Silo Restaurant.   The house is western style, with wooden tables, chairs floor and a back room bar big enough for a large party. Gonna have to sell a lot of mimosas to make that work well for morning meal. Still, the place is very attractive, even if I was there just for breakfast.   I wanted a short stack of french toast, but that was not available. Three slices or tough luck. I ordered it, and waited for my first mugga joe. Service was friendly and there were plenty of servers on hand to handle the light customer presence at 8:30 am. The plate arrived with its cargo of well grilled and caramelized light loaf.  The kitchen did a good job with the egg, sugar, cinnamon and vanilla mix, which saturated the bread to its core. The edges and rises were nicely crunchified, and the application of butter and syrup made everything look terrific. The taste was very good, and even though I had asked for two slices, I found room for all three. The coffee was also strong, hot and kicky.   This was a superior breakfast.   I did find the $15 cost for my solitary breakfast to be excessive. Nearly $3 for the java, even if unlimited, caught me off guard. How much could I drink? Two mugs at most. $9 for the FT also felt like an extravagance which I am unlikely to repeat often. They would do well to offer a more affordable choice (short stack) if they want to bring in the masses.   I know PJ's is expanding rapidly right now, and just opened its fourth store in Kingston, NJ, but unless they want to be the hangout for only the rich and famous, they should find a few smaller/cheaper options.

The Pa Turnpike Commission has done a good job renovating the old service plazas along the roadway.  The Valley Forge stop is one of the smaller ones on the eastbound side.  It has only Starbucks and an A Plus Mini Mart for everything else.    It is clean and designed with high exposed beam ceilings and lots of glass to let in light.  Restrooms modern with waterless urinals and fast hand dry systems above the sinks.  It is certainly a big improvement over the old factory that was here.  But, it is still only a small oasis along a roadway that has had a difficult winter dealing with snow and vehicles trapped in bad conditions.    Hard to be a fan of something like a turnpike rest stop.  But, it is certainly A-OK.

Chestnut Hill Brewing Company had the foresight to be the anchor tenant in the Market at the Fareway on Germantown Avenue in the heart of Chestnut Hill. Already one of the most picturesque communities in greater Philadelphia, it has made itself a premier destination with the opening of the Market with the nano-brewery within. Now, it is possible to select from a broad variety of street food alternatives also housed within this adaptive reuse of an old warehouse, but also to wash it down with a decent beverage brewed on sight. They also have a pizza operation right there, with a Yelp deal that draws you a free pilsner with the purchase of one of their pies. These guys do everything right.   My choices: Korean Double Fried Chicken Wings from Chicko Tako and Pumpkin Ale from CHBC. Doesn't get much better than this!   The ale was rich with a nutmeg/allspice accent in a beautiful dark red amber liquid. Easy drinking, and a perfect washdown for the delicious wings with their crispy exterior under a thick gloopy sweet and spicy sauce. Cut through that like a hot knife through cool butter.  The brew tanks were visible to all, and the folks working the taps seemed to thoroughly enjoy their craft. At $6.50 a pint, it was hard to find anything to complain about. Even found a seat at a community table to enjoy my snack.   Kudos to Chestnut Hill Brewery for seeing the possibilities of producing and selling suds in this small market, and extra credit for the town council and mayor for letting it all happen to the betterment of the community.  The creative energy here was palpable and greatly appreciated.

There are many Mexican restaurants of the mom and pop variety throughout Montgomery and Bucks Counties specializing is home country cuisine primarily for their own compatriots who miss the wonderful flavors of home. Plates are loaded and prices tend to be low. In recent years a cultural crossover has emerged that offer similar dishes, perhaps somewhat less spicy that provide most if the flavor of Mexico, but for a more Norte Americano palate. Shops like El Limon have very successfully filled that space with folks who want something more authentic than Chipotle, but need English menus to participate in the experience.  El Sarape is a third kind of casa Mexicana. It brings an element of haute cuisine to the South of the Border Cocina, wrapped in a more high end atmosphere that transcends cultural bounds we are used to. This spacious house, with high ceilings, plenty of polished marble and dark stained wood, and brown ropes (cuerdos) hanging down from the rafters, calls for a reminder that an integral part of Mexican history was its involvement with Napoleon III, who was Emperor of the French Empire in the Eighteenth Century, where Mexico was its western outpost in America del Norte. The empire didn't survive, but its influence on Mexican food continues to this day. It involves excellent sauces, delicate recipes and Mexican looking dishes with French sounding names and haunting tastes. It is truly Mexican, but with a captivating twist.   This is where El Sarape stakes it claim, and it does an accurate rendition of this style of Mexican cooking. My Chile Relleno (stuffed pepper) was beautiful to behold in its sedate presentation. Neat, yet colorful. The same ingredients - poblano pepper, melted cheese, salsa verde, black beans and three tone rice - all on a white ceramic rectangular plate worthy of a more expensive restaurant. The flavor was full, yet more subtle than I've had in other places. The beans were moist without being dominated by lardiness often found in refried beans of all sorts. The rice was flaky, not clumpy. The twirled chip garnish atop the beans was a textural crispy counterpoint to the soft black semi mashed mound beneath.   I was there for late lunch and wasn't thinking dinner. I sat at the bar and received excellent service from the bartender as he prepare for the evening crowd. I would certainly return for dinner if in the area, although the drive from Bucks approaches 45 minutes, which may be beyond my hunger tolerant distance. Prices are higher than at the other great tiendas, but recognizing the different experience that awaits makes it worthwhile.

I've been on a bit of a diner kick of late, and this morning chose Cinnaminson Diner on northbound Rt. 130 in the town of that august name. It is not in a traditional Jersey stainless steel case, but still offers adequate booths and a small 5 stool counter for lone wolves like me.   After ordering the Country Steak Special (chicken fried steak, 2 eggs, home fries, rye toast & coffee), I settled in to watch the action on a busy Saturday morning. The staff seemed professional and appropriately friendly. They all wore cloth masks, with some carried beneath the nose, and thus useless. Same can be said of the customers waiting to be seated. Oh, well. It is hard to be constantly Covid vigilant.  Really liked my meal, however. The breaded/fried steak was smallish, but crisp and tasty. I asked for the sausage gravy on the side, because I wanted to limit the heavy calorics from that chunky white sauce. They brought out a small bowl of it, when all I needed was one spoonful. It was excellent, but less was more for me. The scrambled eggs were good with a few shakes of Tabasco, and the home fries were plentiful and nicely browned and crunchy. Java was strong and bracing, and I appreciated that my request for milk resulted in a small stainless pitcher of moo juice, rather than mass produced creamers. The joe was included in the cost of the meal; a nice touch too often forgotten in the 21st C.   This was the best of my recent diner experiences, and helped reaffirm my historic enjoyment of this meal style.

One door closes and another door opens...  This has been an article of faith for most of my life, proved to be true once again when the restaurant I had driven to Palmyra, NJ, to try their Thai kitchen was closed l, and I scrambled to find an nearby alternative. My trusty Yelp showed me Franco's Cafe was only about a quarter mile away up Cinnaminson Avenue.   Found it, parked in their side lot, and walked in.   Franco's is a Small Mexican casa, with half dozen tables, fairly standard menu and specials on a blackboard near the cashier. Daniella was my server. She was exceptionally friendly and said she was part of family ownership. Made sense, because she was totally engaged in keeping me in fresh brew coffee and whatever else I needed. As a first timer, I went with something basic - steak quesadilla.   It was excellent. Small strips of grilled beef, cheese and jalapeños, with small salad and sour cream, all crammed and flattened into a large tortilla cut in quarters. It was a healthy chew with just enough spice to keep my mouth fired up. The blackboard alerted to the presence of churros and ice cream as a special dessert. Love me some churros, and indulged.   They were hot, crisp and fresh; filled with a ring of caramel inside each fried strip of dough. Hot! So hot they deserved a warning, but the burn was extinguished by the Java accompaniment. Yup. Delicious, too!   There are full platter dinners available here, too. If you live in the area, it would be worth your effort to check them out along with their lunch and snack choices.   Franco's is a casual and tasty 5 Star experience.

Connecting Bridesburg, Philadelphia with Pennsauken, NJ, the Betsy Ross Bridge was opened to traffic over the mighty Delaware River in 1976. It moves vehicles well from one State to the other, helping commuters avoid heavy loads on Route I-95 during rush hour, or to simply bypass Center City density the rest of the day. I use it to travel from Bucks to Camden for court, and it saves me a bundle of time by circumnavigating the morning confusion at the Benjamin Franklin Bridge.   But, I admit to mixed emotions about using the Betsy because I know its construction history. The pilings on the Philly side are made up in large part of headstones from the Monument Cemetery that had interred people within it's hallowed grounds since 1839. Like its famous sister, Laurel Hill Cemetery, it was designed to reflect the sentiment of Pere Lachaise in Paris, France,  by being both a resting place for the dearly departed and a public park for the living. But, due to its relatively small size, once the 28,000 caskets were buried and there was no room for more, the maintenance fell off and the board of governors died or otherwise allowed the cemetery to fall into serious disrepair.   Temple University offered to buy it several times for use as a parking lot, but was rebuffed repeatedly.   Finally, the school saw its opportunity when the Betsy was being proposed. They again offered to buy it from the City if it would condemn it and seize by eminent domain. Philly agreed, and arranged to make the transfer if Temple would remove the bodies and headstones. This it did by notifying families of the deceased to retrieve the bodies and rebury them elsewhere. Only 8,000 were claimed, and the rest were transported to a mass unmarked grave in Lawnview Cemetery in Northeast. They then sold the granite and limestone markers to the bridge contractor who needed fill for the pilings upon which the upright supports would be anchored.   Thousands of headstones now lie underwater beneath the steel and can be seen sticking out at low tide.   So, when I cross dear old Betsy, I say a silent prayer for those whose lives were lived nearby and died only to be unceremoniously separated from their identities and dumped in a lost and unmarked grave, and their stone remembrances buried forever beneath the bridge.   "... Don't it always seem to go, that you don't know what you've got 'till it's gone. They paved paradise And put up a parking lot."  -Joni Mitchell, Big Yellow Taxi, Ladies of the Canyon, 1970

Maybe it was because I was there on a Wednesday evening, and the dining rooms were not crowded, mirroring the condition of the large buffet displays which were likewise limited in choice to few main courses, sides, breads and desserts, but there really wasn't much to enjoy about the dinner options that I had just paid in advance to consume, sight unseen. While $20 might have been reasonable for repeat visits to the buffet tables, that value proposition was shot to shit if the first rule of buffet dining was not accepted by the diner.   Be prepared to chow down in extremis, or the whole thing is a waste. Healthy dining this is not.   A half gone tray of meatloaf with choice of light/dark gravy, large pile of fried chicken as the only protein; a few macaroni/cheese elbows, Penni broccoli, mashed, stuffing and was that yams(?) as the heavy carb offerings, along with some nondescript bread; followed by copious amounts of jello, pudding, cookies, cheesecake squares and one last slice of dried out raspberry pie - all amounting to a heavy lugubrious carb centric plate. I neither wanted more after laboring through the first, nor would it have been wise for me to have attempted another helping.   Beside that, that raspberry pie lacked any berries, but was a purple sweet colloid held in dry tasteless crust, and thus, without redemption.   I just can't consume like that, nor was I really tempted to do so. But, I learned that my hunger is nothing compared to what the Golden Corral crowd is capable of.  Perhaps that explains why almost everyone there wore elastic waist sweatpants. They knew what they were there for, while I learned the hard way that it doesn't pay for people without that corpus and habitude to so indulge. We should know that the experience will be largely wasted on us.   Pass the Pepto, please!

Decent chicken salad sandwich, but the place is really dirty. Sat at a small table downstairs in their basement shop. The cracks in the red paint were black with grime and lack of strong cleanser for too long. Same for the floor and back shelves and undercounted storage space.   Need to do better and care more, even if never inspected by L & I.

Pat's Colonial Kitchen is exactly that - a first floor, cramped, cozy, warm, 18th Century breakfast and lunch place that suggests the way life was in 1813 in this community William Penn called his New Town.  If you enjoy living history, this is your place to chow down on pancakes, french toast, coffee, etc., for breakfast; and burgers, sandwiches, and salads for lunch, while imagining your horse and buggy are tied up to the hitching post outside.    Is it the best food you have ever had?  Some might say so, but that is only half the point of eating here.  Step into Pat's, and you step into real history.  The Revolutionary War was fought right outside on the street!  Geo. Washington really had his war council only one block away before deciding to cross the Delaware River and engage in the Battles of Trenton and Princeton.    Eat your breakfast and feel just as our forefathers did before we knew we had a country to call our own.   Judging by the far flung places the other reviewers call home, this is exactly what they came here for.

Village Pantry Deli sits on Bridgetown Pike, Trevose, PA., in the 1960s era commercial zone. It is a true mom & pop operation that specializes in fat hoagies and deli specials of the Eastern European variety. Prices are ridiculously low for 2021. So, if you're hungry and desiring a traditional stuffed sandwich, this is your huckleberry.   I stopped in and walked to the back of the shop where a large refrigerated display case was full of smoke meats and tubes of salami, bologna, ham and trays of homemade salads and cultural delicacies like pierogi and stuffed cabbage. I ordered a chicken salad sub, with lettuce, tomato and hot peppers on a long roll, and watched as it was made, wrapped and bagged. With Snapple and Herr's Jalapeno Chips, the cost was under $10. That was a deal and a half, and I didn't have to pay for the ton of old world atmosphere that came with.    As I waited, I looked around at all the accessories available. Awesome pound cakes, cookies, Cento pickles and sours, and a wall of cold drinks. Service was friendly, even for this stranger, and there were enough old-time regulars to make this place a hot stove center for local gossip. Very cool.  These neighborhood haunts remind of what America used to be when the first generations settled in and started life in the New World. Now, nearly a century later, they have generally aged well, although it has a hardscrabble feel to them with narrow streets, limited parking, and undersized stores and homes that are lovely, but feel somewhat dated.   Lucky for me, I love this sort of thing. It provides a getaway from the continual hassles of modern life and Covid anxiety. And, the sandwiches are great!

Tried the Korean BBQ Chicken Sandwich thinking it would have the crunchy skin of those excellent Korean wings in the form of a deep fried breast. Well, it wasn't that as it lacked the texture, but the chicken itself was plump and a big chew. Similarly, the family enjoyed the Chipotle Melt, Nashville Hot and Mike's Hot Honey. All substantial. All entertaining with their various sauces.   But, it became obvious that despite the overall quality of the sandwiches, they were wildly overpriced at $10 apiece including tax. They were smaller that Popeye's at nearly twice the cost. Given the comparison, Popeye, or even Chick-fil-A, are better.   Beyond the merits, I found myself in a situation with a small sign on the door that said they would be closing at 7 temporarily. That was fine, but their website didn't alert the public to that fact, nor did Yelp nor Google. Besides, it was only 6:40, so why were the grills shut off leaving no burgers, no fries and no salad? In fact, they were out of everything but chicken, so I ordered four different sandwiches hoping my peeps would understand why they weren't getting what they wanted.   I guess if you're plum out of supplies it's time to stop the grill, but it doesn't do much for the disappointment in the belly.
There are 89 other reviews under, "Yardley Inn Restaurant and Bar."  If you find yourself looking at only these two reviews, you are in the wrong place.

I was looking for a place where I could have both a foot massage and get some body work for my aching back. H A Foot Spa on Bridgetown Pike, Feasterville, advertised that combination for a 90 minute session at a reasonable price. Website photos showed a room with large recliners used for leaning back with feet in a bucket of herbed hot water, so it seemed they knew what to do.   Well, not exactly.   My private room was well appointed, and the masseuse pleasant, but she wasn't very skilled in Chinese massage. I asked for a strong technique, but she couldn't do it. Little pushing, digging nor probing with hands, elbows nor forearms. Little stretching of my limbs. On the other hand she did use hot rocks on my shoulders and lumbar, and hot towels after oiling my back and legs. It wasn't bad, but more strength as requested would have been better.   The bigger problem was that I must have misunderstood what they meant by combo foot and body work. Many past experiences provided 30 minutes off the table and in a recliner with foot bath and heavy hands on feet. Disappointed that never happened. In place of a real foot spa exercise, I remained on the table and was given a weak massage for about 20 minutes. A real foot massage is strong, digging and often a little painful. This was far from that. This felt more like going through the motions.   I will return to my regular foot spa down on Bustleton Avenue next time. They only offer chair massage as part of the hour, but they are expert in what they do.

Place One on Bristol Pike, Bensalem, PA, is one of those "fusion" houses, offering their take on Chinese and Thai cuisine. I love both styles of cooking, but seldom find them in the same place. Most are in reality operated by Chinese trying to broaden their appeal by imitating their neighbors in South East Asia.  Usually, these efforts fail due to the inability to deeply understand the roots of the secondary culture, or the unwillingness to stock the kitchen with the expensive spices required to do the dishes right.  The result is more often confusion, than fusion.  So it is with Place One.   One look around the semi-crowded dining room was a hint to what was to come.  The only Chinese, let alone Asian customers, were at our table.  We were looking for quality Chinese food that would save us the trip to Philly, and were willing to explore something off the Thai menu.  There were plenty of options on the list, all somewhat descriptive; with little red peppers indicating what was spicy.  We ordered an app of Thai calamari with dipping sauce, and entrees of their Double Wonder (beef & chicken in the chef's special sauce), Pineapple Shrimp Curry, and Coconut Shrimp Special. The first and third dishes had those little red peppers or the word, "spicy" attached to them.    The calamari wasn't bad. Tender chunks of squid, a bit too heavily breaded, and deep fried.  Decent dipping sauce. No real complaints. It was downhill from there.   The Double Wonder had a meager amount of beef sliced small, and more chicken, in a mildly spicy brown sauce.  Green and red pepper slices, good variety of mushrooms, but not enough flavor, and certainly not a wonder. Still, it was the best of the three.  The coconut shrimp had about a half dozen large shrimp, the same green and red peppers, pineapple chunks and not the faintest taste of coconut.  It was just uber sweet, with hints of mango and pineapple.  Can't believe they used canned pineapple on a white board special.  How hard is it to buy and cut up a few real ones?  The word, "spicy" was next to the name of the dish, yet there was nothing hot about it. No sign of chili pepper. It was just unabashedly sugary.  Finally, the pineapple shrimp curry was a Thai noodle dish.  It was awful. The noodles were mush, there was no curry taste, and then there were those canned pineapples, green and red peppers again.   Doesn't anyone in the kitchen do quality control? No coconut in a coconut dish. No curry in a curry plate. No spice in a spicy platter.  Canned pineapple in a pineapple dish.  Red and green peppers everywhere.   What a disappointment.  Place One. Star One.

BurgerIM is bastardized Hebrew for the word, "Burgers", "IM" being the suffix used for the plural. The company began selling franchises in 2008 after a successful launch in Israel a few years earlier. At one point eleven years ago, it was the fastest growing company in the stock market, with amazing earnings.  Unfortunately, the annual reports were determined to be fraudulent. The CEO fled the country ahead of the SEC charging him with security violations and criminal conduct. Confronted by all that, and lack of logistical support, most franchisees lost their investments and closed their doors. Those few shops that remain are survivors struggling to make ends meet. This is true for the BurgerIM in Warrington, PA.   Glad I made it while it was in business, because their business model is different than most fast casual joints. Their approach is the sale of multiple burgers in designer boxes, with more choice than most. Rather than just beef pucks and chicken fillets, they offer lamb and salmon alternatives, all customizable to taste. Too, they have excellent wings and a few potato choices as well as good onion rings and shakes.  I used GrubHub to score a family box which included 8 burgers (4 Angus standards, 4 Spanish spicy), 6 Sweet/Hot Chili Wings, rings and fries. These are 3 oz burgers, but with trimmings, one sandwich and a couple of wings, were enough for a decent meal. This was about 4-6 meals depending on appetite, and the cost was $49. Kept my family with two still growing young men sated last night, with leftovers.   The curbside pickup worked well. Didn't get inside to check out the atmosphere. Honestly, I liked the wings more than the burgers, but they were still tasty enough to be satisfying. I imagine everything would be better right from the grill, but with Covid, it's just not worth the risk of hanging around inside.   Still, the franchise has suffered due to the misdeeds of earlier management, so I hope these folks are around past social distancing and can demonstrate their worthiness thereafter.

A few visits to Dr. Rosenman has satisfied me that he is a good physician with excellent human interactive skills.  Beyond the thorough examination from scalp to toes, he diagnoses quickly and all the while keeps a warm banter going to help keep me at ease.  The provides running commentary on what he is looking at, and while still in the examining room records his office notes on what he has observed and talked with me about, so I can understand more fully what he is thinking, and provide time for questions.    When he saw something that he was not definite about, he asked me to return in a month to allow him a second look for changes.  As a precautionary measure he took a tiny sample for biopsy.  Nothing to worry about.    The office itself is clean, if a little dated.  The staff appears to be all women, some busier than others.  Still, I was in and out promptly, and not required to wait more than 10 minutes before he saw me both times.  The payment desk is efficient, and the billings have been reasonable and understandable.    See you again in a few years, doc.  Thanks a lot.

Crash serendipity led me to DP Autobody after my M45 was rear ended last month on my way home from work.  Actually, the guy who hit me recommended I go there because his family knew them, and would give me (him) a better price.  I got three estimates, and I found that DP was the lowest. Too, the owner, Dave Miller, had a great personal touch with me as a customer, and I immediately had a sense of trust with him.    So we went through the insurance formalities and car rental nuisances, but in the end, when the car was returned to me, I had a brand new looking chariot.  The dings and scrapes were gone, and the paint job was impeccable.    I was so satisfied that I decided to have to car detailed there in a few weeks.  I will update the review after that.    It is so nice to have a totally satisfying experience when it comes to auto repairs.  DP is now my only autobody shop.

Found my way to El Chapin for lunch yesterday.  It is located toward the bottom of Cass Street in Trenton, between the prison and Arm & Hammer Field.  It is not really on Lamberton Street, although it is possible there was once a door on that side of the building.   "El Chapin," is slang for a Guatemalan, so although the menu has a certain Mexican flair, this is a house that specializes in cuisine from its southern neighbor.  And, it is very good.  The lady of the house was taking orders and cooking when I went in.  The menu is rather extensive and it took a while for me to decide what I wanted - everything was bilingually displayed with many photos.  Mamita was patient and when I finally selected the Chile Relleno she smiled and said it was one of the best dishes in the house. I bet she says that for whatever people want.    But, she was right that it was special.  About ten minutes later, out came a large green Poblano Chili Pepper stuffed with spicy shredded Pork, Peas, Onion, Cheese, and a few things I could not define, all wrapped in a thin Egg Omelet.  Black Beans, Yellow Rice and a small Green Salad completed the platter.  It was delicioso. Every element of the dish could be tasted and the combination was a full pleasure to devour.  I also had a glass of Horchata, the Rice Milk and Cinnamon drink that is a national treasure.  As friend Marlyn describes, it tastes like liquid rice pudding.  When cold, I find it fun, tasty and thirst quenching.    As with almost all the Latin shops in Trenton, they were once Italian joints or corner bars that had seen the neighborhoods change and adapt to the influx of new residents.  Unlike most, however, El Chapin has somehow removed the old rustiness of these places and made it feel fresh and energetic.  It was very comfortable to sit in one of its booths and watch people coming and going.    While I have favored all the Mexican, Guatemalan, Salvadoran and Puerto Rican restaurants that I have sampled to date, I found El Chapin to be about the best of the lot.    Thanks for a great lunch, Mamita.

When it comes to pizza, loyalty to a geographic region's tomato pie comes close to fanaticism. It is completely understandable that raging debates about whether Brooklyn or Pittsburgh or Trenton or Philly or some little shop on the wild streets of South Boston make the best pie.  But, the wise peacemakers among us know the secret - they are all the best if you love them. So much better to put aside parochial claims of superiority and just eat them all! Even the worst is so much better than what those poor souls have to accept as pizza in Colorado or some other state with altitude.   Just mange and enjoy. Let your oralgasms carry you away...  Newtown Pizza makes a decent pizza, but it will never be mistaken for an escapee from Napoli nor Roma, let alone Brooklyn Heights nor Chambersburg. Yet, walking by the display counter with all the attractive pies can set your glands a-squeezing, and the Trenton Pie is very aesthetically pleasing to the eye and tongue.  The crust holds the weight of the toppings firmly, perhaps because it is a bit thicker than Romana, and the ingredients are top shelf.  Still, the overall taste sensation is not the transcendent experience of  my favorite pizza shrines. Nonetheless, it is a standup slice worthy of consumption.   The Eggplant Parm is not always prime, as I have found it to be tough chewing at times.  The same goes for the steak sandwiches.  Mostly a good fill, but occasionally a little under or over grilled.  Just enough to keep you guessing.   Friendly ownership, staff and crew, and a good citizen in the community.    As offered at the top, to each his/her own when it comes to pizza. For those of us who love Ntown Pizza, the world is your oyster. Chow down close to home.  For the others of us who have different pizza needs, we know where to go to satisfy them, both near and far.  8.27.13 I just had a couple of great slices of Newtown Pizza's Margarita Pie. Really excellent. I like a slightly charred crust because it tends to be crunchy and supportive of the weight above it.  This one was, with a mildly sweet sauce and fresh mozza, doctored with a light dusting of hot chili pepper flakes. Take a look at the photo.  It was as good as it looks.   Keep it up fellas and cinco estrellas could be close at hand.

By now, Isaac Newtown's is one of the old places in a very old town. It's gotta be at least twenty years sitting back in the parking lot along Newtown Creek.    Go for the incredible beer on tap or bottles, burgers, Caesar salads, quiche and calzone, but most of the rest of the menu is not as good as what they do best. Prices are decent, if a $10. burger does not scandalize you.   The facility has charm and worn ambiance and the floor plan is comfortable and uncrowded.  The upstairs dining area is where they generally seat families, but with booths you can only hear the kids, and it does not get unpleasant. The best seat in the house is at or near the bar, and that room gets crowded Friday - Sunday nights. Still, you will find many knowledgeable beer lovers hanging out, so you can have a seminar about hops along with your Belgian or local craft brew.   The bathrooms are in the basement, down a steep flight of stairs.  They can be a challenge after a few, and I have never been able to escape the sensation of descending into Dante's lair.    Still, a good local pub with a long beer list and decent bar food. The dinners, not so much.

Viet Kitchen is operated by the same folks who had the earlier International Smokeless BBQ. The new place looks about the same. Now, they offer all day breakfast, pho and com dishes, as well as tabletop grilling for later in the day.   Our disappointment stemmed from the pho ga (chicken noodle soup). Although there was plenty of bird in the pot, the underlying broth was weak. It lacked body and flavor, and clearly had not been allowed to simmer and mature over time. Worse, about 20 minutes after first slurps, I began to feel symptoms of MSG poisoning. Difficulty breathing, heaviness in the chest and mild headache. Their attempt at a flavor shortcut was an utter fail.   The fried chicken (thigh and partial breast) was okay, but not worth the struggle with the pho.

A Little Dragon sits in the same part of the Makefield Shopping Center as India Garden, but casts a much smaller shadow.  It does a good job with its American Chinese menu, and the price range is competitive with its peers in the area.  The floor plan has about a dozen comfortable booths.  The TV hung high on the back wall was showing CCTV News, the English language station in the PRC, for those of us who wanted to catch up on what was happening there with a pronounced nationalistic accent.   I had a basic lunch deal.  Wonton Soup, General's Chicken, Egg Roll and Fried Rice, which came in at $8.50 with tax.  The soup was based in chicken consume out of a can, and was a bit salty.  The wontons had a thicker skin, but the filling had a better taste and consistency than other places.  The egg roll was 95% cabbage, but there were traces of pork and shrimp.  The General was in full uniform and filled the oval plate completely with the fried rice covering most of it.  The sauce was nicely spiced, rather than the often overly-sweet variant often found in this dish.  The rice was loaded with pork and veggies.    I was a little surprised that A Little Dragon made the effort to provided above average Americanized Chinois. While it will never be confused with authentic cuisine that can be found in Philly or The City, it at least knows what it is, and does a good job of it without apology.    By now, Chinese/American is becoming its own distinct cuisine.  It may never be as purely satisfying as the real deal, but if you have a taste for it, this is a decent place to express it.

Jahan Kabob & Grill takes a bit of getting used to.   As a first-timer, I approached the shop looking for a door to the restaurant, and realized that it really wasn't a separate dining room, but a part of the larger well endowed beer store.  The kitchen is on one wall, and the tables for eating are along the front sharing floor plan with the beer display aisles.  There is a small opening in the kitchen's partition for placing orders, and then the long wait for preparation and service.  On a post snow winter night it is not the most comfortable place to dine. Live and learn.   The food, however, has promise.  Based on a Yelp suggestion we had the Spicy Chicken Cheesesteak, along with the Samosa app, the Banjan Eggplant side, and the Garden Salad. The Samosas were flat philo dough filled with very tasty Potato, Pea, Onion, and Pepper stuffing. They were very good.  The Spicy Chicken Cheesesteak came on a quality roll, and had an unusual taste that I thoroughly enjoyed. The spice was one that I did not recognize, and added the proper complement of heat. The accompanying fries were ordinary. If the meal had stopped there we would have been approaching a 5 star culinary experience. But, the Garden Salad was rather limited and bland, and we picked through it.  The Banjan Eggplant was sopping in its cooking oil, and although the taste with the Potato and Pepper was decent, the oiliness was too much and dominated the texture and overall experience. The Naan was cold, likely a misplacement of a heated bread, but tough and almost stale-tasting.   The reality of having beer buyers roaming the premises in close proximity to our table was not a big deal, but was noticeable and constant.  The slow service was understandable because there were only 2 people working the kitchen, and one was taking orders, packing the take out, and serving our meal. She was very nice and was aware of the problems. A third pair of hands would have been helpful to them, but the beer side of the operation did not seem to have anything to do with the restaurant, and they were not assisting each other.  Management might want to consider hiring someone who can help out on both ends.   Jahan is better utilized as a take out joint.  The custom beer operation is very interesting, and next time I would spend the time waiting for the food to go by selecting some exotic brews to bring home to accompany the Afghani victuals.  The Samosas and Cheesesteaks are worth another bite, and the menu may hide a few other worthy offerings.   It is not the place to bring a date for a romantic evening, unless looking at beer while noshing on comfort food is your thing.

Another of the Super Wawa gas station/convenience stores that seem to have sprung up almost overnight in this part of South Jersey.    The gasoline prices are competitive, but you never know who the real producer/distributor is for any of them.  So, it likely isn't wise to use it too often.  The convenience store takes its cues from the Sheetz, A Plus, Quik Cheks and turnpike service centers of the world. Every kind of sugar and quick energy drink is available.  In this case, the deli actually is capable to turning out decent sandwiches and soups.    I am not a fan of these places, but understand their efficacy.  They serve their purpose, and even offer reasonably good java.

Cattycorner from Pete's Steakhouse Tavern, Jeppy's is as small as Pete's is big.   It is primarily a take out joint with only a couple of tables in the closet sized space for guys like me who work near by, but don't want to eat at their desks.  I met the owner/manager who was friendly and had no problem fixing me up after 3:00 with their 2 Slice and a Drink Special at $4.95.    The pie was okay, but could have been more if it had spent enough time back in the oven to totally reheat the triangles to the original temperature, rather than removing them when only lukewarm.  The flavor was right, but the crust texture was soft and doughy from failure to bring the crust to the near molten state required to make it firm and crunchy.  As this seems to be endemic to many places, it may be my job to ask for a "well done" slice so they are left to burn a bit longer.    Otherwise, Jeppy's is a cool little place.  Much like the Little Engine That Could, Jeppy's sits across from Big Boy Pete's and with all its glare and attitude, repeating over and over, "I think I can. I think I can..."   Until it becomes, "I know I can. I know I can...."

Hong Kong Pearl is a mixed bag.  The facility is dark and dreary at high noon, giving the sensation of being in a 1940's movie.  Yet, the service is prompt and attentive, somewhat anomalous for a Chinese house.  The main courses are well prepared, with some attention to detail, but it takes a few shortcuts that diminish the overall quality of the meal.  The broth for the Wonton Soup is chokingly salty and a brownish tint that suggests use of bouillon with prepackaged salt, dye and possibly MSG to cut costs.  In a similar manner, the Fried Rice arrives artificially colored a dark tawny cast from its mass production earlier in the day. Both soup and rice are vastly inferior to the prime attraction, but as they are served with practically every meal, the overall result is "mixed."    On the other hand, the General Tso's Chicken was quite good in the context of a suburban Americanized Chinese shop.  It used chicken that had not been frozen long, if at all, a pleasant coating, and a sauce that used correct spices to attain the right sweet/hot spot that makes for a happy General. It even had whole chili peppers in the dish.  That was a big positive.   While I would not rush back to Hong Kong Pearl, it was certainly a decent place for lunch.  If they would eliminate the problems with the soup and rice, and attempt to make them the right way - with a long simmering stock and just in time fried rice, it could be an exceptional experience for this part of the world.

This is a human-free parking garage.   It puts a premium on following instructions as there is no one around to answer questions most of the time.  Everything is completely automated, from drive in through drive out.  Similar to a car wash, your vehicle is driven onto a moving platform or track and from that point on, everything happens robotically. Your car is pushed left or right to align it with the entrance to the storage area.  It is then lifted off the ground much like a garage lift, and then transported inside the vertical parking structure until you return to pick it up.    It is critical to take everything you need with you, most importantly your keys.  Turn off the engine.  Use the same credit/debit card to extract your car as used upon entry. Go to the other side of the building for retrieval.  Failure to recall the proper card could result in a long wait until someone arrives to deal with this screw up.  Reading the other reviews it is easy to see how it would be very frustrating to have to wait.    The evening cost is $14 for the night if in after 5.  Not a bad deal.

I know it's just me.   The folks at Berryssimo put a ton of money and effort into making their fro/yo shop unique from all the other build-your-own softee empororiums.  The back wall where the yogurt is dispensed in various flavors is made of gray slate stone. Very attractive.  The front of the space is a little sitting area overlooking State Street through wall to wall, ceiling to floor, windows.  Nice.  And, the staff is warm, pleasant and helpful (Thanks, Sophie).    Yet, where the yogurt meets the mouth, I find the same experience as in the other less well appointed stores.  Regardless of the sign on the machine and the small picture attached to same designating the flavor that will extrude when the handle is lifted, the actual experience is the same - looks good, feels good, but does not taste so good.  I sampled the Tahitian Vanilla, Very Berry, and Cookies & Cream, and added some Blackberry and Reece Cup toppings.    The texture was smooth and creamy and the toppings were rich and full, but the taste of the yogurt was practically non-existent.  I tried to sample them one at a time despite being in one cup.  A weak response to each of them, with the Berry being the strongest.  Just not worth the nearly $8 I paid for it.  Compared to the ice cream available very close by, the yogurt seems an empty vessel.    For my decadent sweet tooth, I want to be overwhelmed with pleasure; luxuriate in the smooth creaminess, close my eyes when the aromatic sweetness assaults my tongue and shoots to the brain.  None of this happens with Berryssimo, nor most other fro/yo joints.    I must be immune to that experience for some reason with super chilled yogurt.  I see that others are very satisfied.  I wish I was, too.

Hiding in plain sight within the H Mart in Levittown is a small Korean restaurant, accessible to shoppers to eat in or take out.  They also do catering.  The primary orientation is Korean cuisine, but Chinese offerings are also available.    The menu takes the form of large format photos above the ordering window.  They are labeled bi-lingually.  The staff is friendly and conscientious.  The food is quite good.   Today, we ordered Mandoo Kook, a Korean Beef Soup loaded with Veggies, Rice Cake and Egg.  It came with Fried Dumplings and Pickled Relish and Cabbage on the side.  It was richly savory and complex.  Additionally, we had Jeyuk Dupbap.  As we all know, that is Spicy Marinated Pork on top of Steamed Rice, and a small Lettuce Salad.  Very enjoyable and filling.    While this corner of H Mart would never be mistaken for haute cuisine nor fashionable comfort, it does offer a richly sustainable meal and rock bottom prices.  Definitely worth arriving hungry and eating here before working the aisles for a full shopping experience.

Circle Deli is the nearest food outlet to my office, and we order take out for eating in from there a few times a week. They deliver timely sandwiches, soups, wraps, and a plentitude of snacks neatly packaged and with a smile.   I prefer to eat later in the day and have stopped off there occasionally to order my own custom lunch.  They are willing to make anything off menu that they have the ingredients for, and do it well.  They are super efficient and friendly as a hard working husband and wife team.    What is really amazing is how much stuff they can cram into a small space and not seem cluttered and claustrophobic.   Generally, I am not a deli lunch kind of guy, as I prefer to have a more relaxing meal than sitting at my desk.  But, at crunch time, Circle Deli is a convenient and worthy alternative.   I am a fan.

The soups and sandwiches are fresh and well made.   It is fun to watch the crew make a sandwich as they have a discipline/routine to it that is very zen, although they may not know it.  It is a very local place, and it helps to know Becky or her people to feel at home there. I can understand some of the pejorative reviews from new customers, because they are not known and the young workers are not always people persons.  Still, the product is good, and the prices reasonable.  Bottom line - I enjoy the walk from my office for a take out lunch on nice days, knowing I will return with a tasty sandwich along with the stroll through historic Newtown.  PS. Becky's Deli now has 2 outdoor tables on nice days.

While I generally like Red Robin Gourmet Burgers for the consistency of the food in all locations, I find that this particular restaurant being very close to Sesame Place has a noise level just on the other side of comfortable.  Given the choice I prefer the newer facility close by Neshaminy Mall, which although smaller, is more modern and offers a cozier roadhouse feel.  Too, perhaps because of so many kids eating grilled cheese sandwiches, the signature burgers often are not finished to the desired degree, and present in less than tantalizing form.  Last time I was here my server did not ask how I wanted my burger done. I volunteered that I like it medium, but it came out well done anyway.  Maybe that was why I wasn't asked.  I also was not offered the endless fries that are so heavily advertised.   The burgers are okay in both places and the fries still better than average. The shakes are a bit underwhelming compared to their competition at Cheeburger Cheeburger, Nifty Fifty, and Jakes Wayback. Better to stick with the alternatives like bottomless limeaid or iced tea, where you can hydrate without the sugar rush, and even share the drink if one of you gets water.    It is likely better to come to this shop after Sesame Place is closed for the season, and some quality control is reasserted.  This place is a gold mine usually filled to capacity. Sometimes that success goes to the bottom line, but gets lost in the kitchen and on the floor.   See you in the winter.

"...Pulled into Plumsteadville, I was feelin' about half passed dead. Just need some place where I can lay my head. Say, sister, can you tell me where a man might find a bed?  She just grinned, shook her head. 'No,' was all she said..." (With apologies to Bob Dylan)  It may have been the heat of a near-100 degree day, or maybe the high humidity that seemed to choke the breath out of every living being, but here I was in Plumsteadville feeling slightly desert crazed and in need of hydration and restoration.  The Inn materialized in front of me, a shimmering apparition.  Real or not, I was stopping in for a drink and lunch.    Perhaps, it was my gaunt appearance when I walked into the barroom, but it seemed no one saw me as I sat down on a corner stool.  I allowed the dim coolness to resuscitate me.  Finally, a bartender saw me there and came over to see what, "...it'll be."    "Summer Shandy and a Bison Burger, medium, please."  "I didn't see you come in, stranger.  How long you been sittin' there?"   "Since breakfast, but I blend in."  My wink let her off the hook.  From then on the service was first rate from all the black & white servers, complete with sides of small talk and Potato Salad.   The Summer Shandy hit my thirsty spot dead center.  It was difficult not to just gulp it down it felt/tasted so good.  That squirt of lemon in the beer was an elixir.   My Bison Burger Special came out closer to medium rare, but I was pleased with it, as it was full on juicy and a deep rose color.  The pile of Shaved Onion, Cheese, and BBQ Sauce on Brioche Roll made for an excellent sandwich.  Knife and fork was the only way to go, and allowed me to pay attention to every morsel.  It was quite good.  The scoop of Potato Salad was a cool change from fries.    If not for the fact that I had a ways to go before the day was over, I might have lingered over a second or third drink, and become friends with the attractive keepers.  I had to face the withering heat regardless of my wish to avoid it.  Luckily, there was an ice cream barn right in the parking lot that was about it receive my dessert business.  More on that in another review.    The lunch had an epic feel to it due to the surrounding circumstance, but based on the food alone I feel no urgency to visit again.  It was a solid meal, but it would have attained higher rank if the bar folk had been initially more attentive as they busied themselves with prep work for the evening crowd.  The invisibility may have been part of the existential void I felt coming in, but they played their part in extending that sense longer than necessary.    Still, a worthy stop on the stagecoach line between Easton and Philadelphia.

East China Restaurant in the Giant Shopping Center in Morrisville, Pa., may have been in operation for a long time...and, it shows.    First impression upon entry is of a large buffet table (empty at night), torn carpet, dim lighting, and a desperate need of a makeover.  The temperature is lower than comfortable as demonstrated by the hostess/owner wearing her coat as she seats and serves.  This may be primarily a take out joint, but the large dining area belays that, and a few of the other reviews reflect dining in experiences.    My light bite dinner of Wonton Soup (I ordered Hot & Sour Soup, but what the hey...?!), and Fried Dumplings was average.  Chicken Broth with standard yellow dye, thick wonton skins and a meat filling that was lacking taste.  Same for the Dumplings, with the exception of the dipping sauce which I doctored with chili sauce requested for flavor.    East China feels and looks rundown and in need of a bright facelift.  The owners seem content to do the minimum required to keep the doors open without real concern for customer satisfaction nor comfort.    There are better Chinese/American houses nearby more deserving of your appetite.

Cool Blue.  Overhead river meandering.  Clear Mushroom Soup clarifying.   Captain Roll (Spicy Crunchy Tuna, Crabmeat, Salmon, Eel & Avocado) drizzled with Chef's Special Sauce), visual, tasty pleasure.   Hot and grainy Green Tea.   Great way to reach the end of the day.

Three generations of donuts have been baked and served from this Colmar, Pa. location.  It isn't an accident that they are considered among the best sweet rounders in this quadrant of the Universe.
