And, now that the Great Pumpkin has arrived, Yum Yum is baking its amazing orange squash variant in many forms.  They are all great!  While we went in just for a small sample with coffee, the counterperson advised us that buying 6 would cost the same as 5, we were easily persuaded to go with the half doz and bring home whatever we didn't consume on premises.  A couple of Pumpkin Sugar Cinnamons, a pair of classic Glazed, and a deuce of Honey Dipped, and a coupla small Joes, and we retreated to a corner table to dive in.    Each was excellent, but the Pumpkin stood out as large, authentically pumpkin tasting, and cake style.  Fresh and delicious.  The Glazed and Honey Dipped were less distinguishable from the competition, but still a sweet sticky mess.    These guys do donuts right!  How many made it home?  Just two survived the initial onslaught.

Pho 75 on Adams Avenue does only one thing, but it does it very well. Beef Pho in all its variations still makes for a fairly limited menu, but on the other hand makes for easy choices.  Round Eye, Tendon, Tripe, etc., are all there in either a regular or large size.  Their bowls are smaller than in other shops, but still big enough to completely fill your belly with very good beef broth, rice noodles, onion and a load of selected cow parts, to which you can add fresh Thai Basil, Sprouts, Jalapeno slices, and Lemon(not lime) Squeeze.    If Beef Pho is your yen, then you will be quite content here, because the steaming bowls flow quickly from the kitchen, and are very tasty and filling.  Just be sure you are not looking for a full course meal, because that won't happen.  No apps. No com (rice). No Binh Mi. No sweets. No Pho Ga.  They do offer coffee and a few other drinks.   So, what's the problem? The restaurant has little atmosphere; tables and heavy stackable chairs without the semblance of comfort.  The service is efficient with no effort to interact with the customers beyond perfunctory order taking and fast delivery. The place is a bit worn out and could use some TLC.  Most significantly, it is CASH ONLY, with a little ATM sitting near to the cashier.  For a business with five outlets in the region, that is another indication of lack of concern for the patron. Certainly they have the roots in the community and relationships with financial institutions to be able to offer a credit card option.    Bottom Line - While the pho is quite good, if restricted in options, the surrounding elements within make Pho 75 a less than desirable destination for my Vietnamese fix.  There are too many nicer, friendlier, more comforting joints, to make this place "go to."

It has been a long time since I was in the Gray's Ferry neighborhood, and it was good to be back.  I had heard rumors about a Thai house that was opened at 25th & Christian serving up good and relatively authentic Thai cuisine out of a small storefront.  So, after a great massage @ V&V over at 11th and Washington, I headed west and found Thai Square sitting right on the corner.    Parking can be an issue in these parts, but I was lucky to find a spot behind the restaurant on one of those super narrow backstreets. Parallel parking requires the front tire to go over the opposite curb to get the right angle for backing. Lucky my city skills had not abandoned me and I slid the chariot right into the space like a pro. So, I was feeling pretty good even before walking in.   The dining room was small, but clean, with the entire southern wall in glass overlooking a simple but attractive outdoor seating area.  The Madame moved toward us with a warm welcoming smile.  Handing us the menus, she suggested the specials and asked for our drink order.  The Ginger Tea she brought us a few moments later was excellent, with a nice ginger bite and honey background.  Our water was complemented by a small dish of squeezed lime juice and a small spoon.  Another great notion that brought the agua to life.  That was a first for me. Much better infused that a mere wedgely squeeze.   We were on a roll and the anticipation of what was to come grew.  While the Calamari was a small disappointment in that all the rings were large and coated in a hard jacket rather than a softer finish, the dipping sauce was good enough to demand we finish it with a spoon after the squid was gone.   Then we received our Tamarind Duck and Shrimp Pad Thai.    The Duck was nearly perfect.  Crisp skin.  Fully cooked and tender meat.  Tamarind Sauce that was sweetly tart and mild citrus finish, in a sultry dark red amber demi-glaze.  It was so good, I stuck my finger in it to suck it off. This was a treasure too special to waste a drop.   The Pad Thai was also very good; a full plate complemented with ground Peanut and fresh Sprouts.  It was a strong straight man to the wild machinations of the Duck.    This was one of those meals that I didn't want to end.  I strung it out as long as possible with rice to absorb all the outrageous moisture on the platter, and another glass of water with lime to carry it all the way down.    Yes. I took the rest home to savor tonight.  4.5 Stars with a Bullet!

Stella's Pizza has been at this location on Scotch Road for more than 30 years, but this was my first visit.    The impression is of an old style pizzeria with a side dining area.  When I arrived for a late lunch, Stella herself was sitting there having lunch and chatting with a customer.  I ordered an Eggplant Parm sandwich after seeing another sandwich order come out of the kitchen on a great looking torpedo roll.  It arrived at my table a few minutes later, nicely toasted and so inviting.  The bread comes from Italian Peoples' Bakery, and has that signature crispy crunch that is the beginning of a satisfying meal.  The eggplant was thin sliced, finely breaded and pan fried with minimal oil residue.  The tomato sauce was lightly salty, adding to the very positive overall experience.  All good.  While the facility could use an updating, the quality of the food is very good, and the prices a throwback to about 1990.  $6.50 for a 9" hot hoagie sandwich seems like an incredible deal, especially given the quality of the product.  It is easy to enjoy stepping back in time to an earlier day when a family operated restaurant meant the family was everywhere in the shop; cooking, cleaning, hosting, and just hanging out on breaks to talk with people.  I love the coziness that creates.    None of this would work if the food was not good, but it is.  So, it will be easy to return to try the other offerings, especially the pizza, and learn more about Stella, her family, and the history of a typical old fashioned family resto.

Man, has Mill Street come back to life!  I had not been down by the Delaware River for several years and was very pleasantly surprised by the return of vibrancy around there.  Kelch House was recommended by a local businessman we were visiting, and he was right on with his suggestion. The five of us had a variety of things on the menu, and all of us were happy with our choices.   I had the Apple and Feta Salad, consisting of Granny Smith slices, Romaine, Candied Walnuts, and a good amount of fresh Feta Cheese.  The Balsamic was a nice taste to wrap it all together. A good meal @ $9.  Looking at my mates I observed various stages of gluttony displayed over a Cheesesteak and French Onion Soup.  Someone mentioned the Fries were excellent.     The facility is dressed in colonial attire, with large windows bringing in wonderful light. The view of the river from our table was great on this autumn day.   Definitely worth a special visit to return to both Kelch House and Bristol.   Well done, City!

Stopped in recently about a half hour before closing on a weeknight.  Although not at all crowded, the warm brick/old wood ambiance mixed well with the several customers hanging on into the night.  The exposed brick and long bar anchored the room, while the wooden tables and chairs offered the sense of an Old City establishment that could have existed at any time since the late 18th Century.  In fact, the foundation was that old.  Walking in from cobblestone streets completed the impression that Prime Stache doubled as a time machine.   I sat briefly at the bar waiting for my companion to arrive for a late business discussion.  No pressure to order a drink after explaining my purpose, and the bartendress was friendly and attractive.  I had a chance to settle in and look around.  I liked everything I saw.  The bar menu looked appealing, and as a former barkeep I appreciated the fresh fruit and infusion jars resting around the work area.  I was tempted, but knew I needed a clear head.  Still, I have a strong desire to try something creative next time I come.    My contraparty arrived and we moved to a table.  She was hungry and ordered Turkey Sliders.  An app of Sweet Sautéed Carrots arrived first.  They were small and thin and obviously a local produce.  Nice snappy sweetness.  We discussed our businesses while awaiting the main course, and switched to questions that we could answer for each other while she enjoyed the mini burgers.  Really wish I was more hungry, but observing her face as she ate was a clear indication of high enjoyment.  I continued to sip away as our comfort level with the space and each other grew into a more detailed and tangential discussion.    We ended up closing the place.  All the other chairs were up on their tables when we finally walked out.    Prime Stache is known as an American Bistro.  The quality of the environment, drinks, and the food, makes it something more than that. While the word, "Stache," suggests both a Golden Age of American history, as well as a slightly out of date image for a modern resto, it successfully sets itself apart by a consistency of atmos, service, and product that liberate from the constraints of time and place, and bring you into a timelessness that is compelling.    I am excited about returning here again, and that makes me a fan.

My first time back here since joining Yelp*.  New Plum Tree is a Chinese/Thai restaurant in name, but it is fundamentally Chinese American cuisine with a Thai menu thrown in for good measure.  Neither are really outstanding, but both are competently prepared for the local palate.  I tend toward the Thai side of the street and have tried several dishes from noodle (Pad Thai) through Curries (Like the Green Curry dishes better than the Red).    Today I stopped in just after 12, which is early for me, but I was coming back from Philly, and decided to sit down rather than pick something up to eat at my office.  I had a veggie plate primarily of Eggplant mixed with Green and Red Pepper, Carrots, Peas, and Basil Leaves.  It had a mildly spicy brown sauce that also suggested some Ginger Root in the mélange.  It was good, and felt to be a healthier alternative without meat.    What can I say?  It was Okay. I am not rushing back, but neither will I avoid it.   My fortune: "If it seems fates are against you today, they probably are."  Thanks. I already knew that!  Learn Chinese:" A moment" = Yi hui er.  Yes. Time waits for no one. (Especially, bad fortune cookie makers.)

This is strictly a two slice and a Coke review.  Maybe it is just the luck of the draw that I walked into Aquilone's Cucina in the H Mart strip center only a few days after having one of the best Tomato Pies in my life over in Jersey.  Or, maybe it was because that unique experience fostered my desire to duplicate it in a new place.  Regardless, I was hungry and decided to eat something before going shopping in H Mart on an empty stomach.   Aquilone's is a fairly large joint with room enough for close to 100 people.  The colors are predominantly yellow and brown, and on a rainy day seemed to mirror the overcast darkness all around.  I ordered a slice of regular pizza and one with Italian Sweet Sausage and asked them to be reheated long enough to be well done.    When they arrived on a large plate (so much nicer than being handed pizza on paper plates), they looked good and heat was rising off of them.  I wasn't provided with utensils, and when I attempted to pick up the first slice, it immediately drooped over from the weight of the cheese and the fact that the center of the crust was not really very hot.  Too, oil dripped off suggesting that the crust was in fact somewhat soggy.    The taste was fairly good, but it was obvious these pies had been on display for a while, and had lost their life force. The same was true for the Sausage slice.  Quality meat, yet the cheese and sauce needed more refreshing than a turn in the oven could provide.   Perhaps, I should know better than to go for a late two slice lunch when the available pies have been around too long.  But, I did not want to ask for a new pie to be made, and there are shops that routinely put together new pizzas for the by the slice crowd every few hours so their wares don't lose their verve.    Nice folks. Good service.  But, these slices were past their prime.

All malls are dinosaurs waiting for extinction.   Neshaminy is no different.  Aside from the entertainment value of the AMC theaters, there is little to recommend it.  After ruining Main Streets around the world with large parking fields and lots of meaningless choices, they are now suffering the same fate.   People are "Malled Out!"   We want something more integrated into our communities; part of our social fabric, not something standing alone and uninvolved.  The next generation will be synthetic villages.  Smaller shopping markets clustered together and surrounded by neighborhoods, schools, parks, hospitals,  employment opportunities, and good roads leading to the rebirthed urban centers.  It is called by many names, New Urbanism, Post-Modern Cities, Back to the Future, etc. But, it is definitely coming.   There are examples of this next utopian model around the world, and if you find one be sure to investigate.    I, for one, am excited for the chance to return to a future full of the elements that made earlier societies function efficiently, while adapting the best that technology and science have to offer.
The outpatient radiology department works well.  Can't speak to other departments or services, but there is no problem going to St. Mary for xrays, catscans, petscans or MRIs as an outpatient.

This is one of the new versions of the old theme that is Dunkin Donuts.  The space is larger, brighter, cleaner than most of its siblings, with one end of the shop furnished with easy chairs and small tables to encourage hanging out.    The coffee is average DD brew. The staff is efficient. The baked goods looked all shiny and glazed, but I did not try one this visit.    Maybe next time.

When it comes to coffee there are three main ingredients: 1. the coffee, 2. the water, and 3. the maker. At Dunkin Donuts the constant is the coffee.  The makers are all trained in the same methods and everything comes packaged for ease of use.  That makes the quality of the water the primary variable.  For some reason, the coffee at this DD tastes different (in a bad way). It is harsh and leaves a bitter aftertaste.  It must be the water, because the nearest other DD in Lower Makefield near the Hampton Inn does not have this problem, but they are serviced by a different water company. Elementary, my dear Watson...

Only in America!  Here we have a "New York Bagel" shop run by Arabic speaking guys, who seem to know how to "make the donuts..."   I was impressed.    The crew of Ewing's Finest who were there ahead of me seemed to know a good morning stop.  I felt incredibly safe.  But, the parking lot was like a DMZ.

Worst pizza so far in my exploration of the tomato pie universe in the Trenton/Hamilton area.    Although visions of The Godfather played in my head, this is a very different branch of the Corleone family.  This is a tiny shop, with only 4 deuce tables within.  Take out or delivery is the business model here. That would be fine if the product made eating slightly "delivery aged" pie worthwhile.  I ate two plain slices right off a pie out of the oven, but my participation did not match my anticipation of the meal.   The slices came out on overlapping white paper plates.  I shook dried pepper onto them, made the fold in the crust to aid in pick up, and lifted.  The point immediately sagged as the underlying crust foundation was not firm enough to hold it.  As it flopped back to the plate, an inordinate amount of oil began to flow off the surface and onto the plate and table.  Not a good sign.  The visual was of a lot of cheese with little tomato sauce showing.  My first bites confirmed that this was more like a double cheese pie without much sauce.  The cheese was mildly salty.  The lack of gravy suggested that there would be no subtle basil flavor, which I prefer.  Such was the case.    After struggling with the chewiness of the excessive cheese, the lack of a balancing rich sauce with proper herbs, and a veritable drizzle of oil from both front and rear of the slices, I already knew this was not going to be my pizza place.  If the straight ahead plain slices could not pass muster, I wasn't going to try anything more complex.    One nice positive - the zepps (fried dough dusted with powdered sugar) were amazingly good!  A bag of three came free with any purchase.

Tan May Chinese Restaurant sits in the Shop Rite center just off Pennington Road in Ewing, NJ. While primarily a take out joint, there are six tables for sitting in, and for the owner's kids to hang out on during summer vacation. Nice to see the family together.  My lunch special was actually better than expected. The egg Foo Young was made with fresh ingredients and the ubiquitous brown sauce lighter and more flavorful than in most chop shops. Even the fried rice, though that prefab yellow cast, was at least tender and full of finely cut veggies.  Prices were ridiculously low (under $7), and there was a choice of soup, egg roll or bottled drink included. No extra charge for my Snapple.  While the place could be cleaner, and the mess in the hallway leading to the restroom organized and stored out of sight, the food makes it worthy of regular, if infrequent, visits.

If you don't have time to make the trip to Istanbul, Damascus, Beirut, Amman, Jerusalem, or any other Middle Eastern city, the next best thing could be a stop at Tulip Hookah Café in Langhorne, Pa.  Once inside, you are transported from Bucks County to a much more exotic locale.    Have imagination. Will travel.   Find a comfortable spot to sit or recline and order a variety of Shisha (Flavored Tobacco) from the servers.  They will return with a beautiful glass water pipe (Hookah) and your smoking preferences.  Sit, smoke and talk as long as you wish.  This is a old custom in that part of the world.  Pass the pipe's mouthpiece tipped hose around, and taste the flavors of Turkey, or many other Arab/Muslim-centric countries.    Tulip also offers snacks and non-alcoholic beverages, and live music entertainment several nights a week (check website or call ahead).  The $10. cover charge gives you license to stay all night.    When I resided in that part of the world I would often find a soft carpet and pillows to relax on the floor and watch the hookah's smoke drift and dance toward the ceiling. Sometimes there was music and song.  I would ask for a small cup of the local thick coffee, pour in a ton of sugar, and sip the caffeine alternating with a long draw on the pipe.  The visions were astounding. When feeling flush, I asked for flavored brandy to replace the water in the pipe, so I could completely experience the transition from hookah/coffee house to Bedouin's tent in a secret desert oasis.  Visions of Scheherazade, Princess of Persia and storyteller of the 1001 Tales of the Arabian Nights, await...

Tonight I went in for a light meal while waiting for my son to finish a Magic tournament at Oxford Valley Mall. I just couldn't bring myself to go to its food court, so I drove down Oxford Valley Road and remembered Jahan Kabob.   While the craft beer retail outlet dominates, this time, I was able to order a Falafel Pita and Rice, and sit with my excellent meal and ignore the rest.  The food was wonderful. The Falafel was fresh and moist even after deep frying.  The Pita was warm and pliant.  The Lettuce, Onions and Tahini Sauce was all perfect complements.  The Long Grain Basmati-like Rice was prepared with a rich spiciness that was very soft and tasty.  I usually don't enjoy rice as anything more than a sponge to sop up sauce.  This rice was exceptionally moist and flavorful.  It was a great side.  Clearly, this place has knock out cuisine inside a rather incongruous setting of a craft beer store.  If it was in its own space, it would pack in the diners.    While it is not the place to bring a date, and is primarily a take out joint, the food taken out of this context is first rate, and really an amazing opportunity to sample Afghani kitchen craft.  The owner/chef is also a first class host and salesman for his food.   A bump to 4 Stars is the right move.

Northern Liberties now has a fair share of interesting and comfortable places to eat, drink and hang out over cups of good coffee.  One of the earliest pioneers that continues to pump out java and decent bakery snacks is Higher Grounds on North 3rd Street.  This converted row house draws a local crowd, as well as longstriders from farther south in Center City, and the occasional visitor from farther afield.  It is attractive in a Salvation Army Store furniture kind of way, with a lot of art, crafts, and a vast variety of tchotchkes to catch your attention.  It is cozy and worn, like an old couch or settee should be.    The caffeine options are decent, but by comparison to other jumpin' joe joints in the vicinity, not in the vanguard in terms of coffee quality, nor barista excellence. Our sampling of hot chai latte and cappuccino left us feeling like we had tasted better elsewhere recently.  Still, the lemon pound cake was tasty, and the ability to sit back and watch this part of the Universe go by was a pleasant timeout.  Just wish we were holding ceramic rather than paper cups to enhance to quality of the experience.   There are ever more coffee outlets in the expanding urbansphere, and they all try to outdo each other with service, product, and atmospherics. Higher Grounds has the advantage of being an early provider in this neck of the woods, but also the disadvantage of staking its claim before cafes became more popular and the customers more demanding.    If it was open to suggestion, a gentle makeover with heavy cleaning, fresh paint, and a competition to select the best available local roasted coffee, would raise the expectations here to better account for the changing java life in Philadelphia.  The old furniture is reminiscent of grandma's house, and should stay.

Francisco has opened a third restaurant in Bucks, and his second in Newtown (Florentinos on State Street is the other).  His "Little Mama" is Salvadoran and Mexican cuisine done with a flourish.  This is no Chipotle fast food experience, although the ingredients are equally fresh, but more creative and satisfying on the palate.   I was there for lunch, and limited myself to a few dishes, one Apperitivo (Guacamole Mamita), and Empanadas (hand made corn turnovers stuffed with chicken, spices and beans).  The Guac was excellent.  Smooth, cool, and so easy in the mouth.  The Empanada was crusty and flaky with just enough heat to keep the tongue on guard.  The chicken filling was chunky and soft. Really well done.   Bottom Line - a totally satisfying, if somewhat cher, Almuerzo.   A good place to go for a business lunch to impress your clients with your international panache.   Next time, the Hamburguesa Mexicana comes off the board and onto my plate. A burger with jalapenos, onions and hot pepper cheese with a side of yucca fries has got to be incredible.  10.01.2013  -  Returned today for lunch.  Had the Hamburguesa Mexicana as promised. It came out loaded with cheese, jalapenos, lettuce, tomato, and avocado and a perfect medium rare.  The bun appeared to be toasted baguette-style loaf and a good fit for the innards.  Liked it a lot.  Only downside were the Yucca Fries, which were too dry and bland.  Asked for ketchup to give it some life.   Still a 4 Star attraction, as everything was enjoyable, especially the Mexican environment, and wild colors.  Definitely got that right.

Enzo's Pizzeria on West Maple Avenue, Langhorne, PA, is in the same strip center as CVS and Hong Kong Cafe. It is a traditional American pizza parlor with full complement of pies, stromboli, steak sandwiches and standard pasta and chicken dinners. There are a half dozen booths in house, so most of their business is takeout. Service is friendly.   I stopped in to check it out with an early supper. I took a booth toward the back and ordered their Enzo's Eggplant Bonanza sandwich, an amalgam of breaded fried eggplant, sauteed spinach, roasted red peppers, melted sharp provolone and very tasty pesto mayonnaise.   It arrived on a paper plate is a puddle of oil and thin plastic utensils. Presentation is important, and these guys blew it royally. What would it take to serve a heavy leaky torpedo on something more substantial? That the mess wasn't noticed or they just didn't care shows lack of quality control and disrespect for customers.   The ironic part is that the sandwich was actually very good. The combination of flavors and textures, and especially the pesto mayonnaise on the crusty loaf and the mix of the eggplant and peppers we're well worth the price of $7.95.   If they had just thought about a better way of dealing with eat in customers they would have been starred up for creativity in the kitchen.   2.5 Stars

Trenton Coffee House & Roaster is the epitome of a "Hidden Gem."  Housed in a second story walkup in an old brick industrial building on Cass Street in Trenton, NJ, it has only been open a few weeks, and already has a following of locals and the feel of a 1980's urban loft that has been designed for a community party.    In fact, that is exactly what it is.  Abdul, the proprietor and coffee maven, explained that the space was shared with an East European social club that uses this room for its larger get - togethers. The plan is to move the operation downstairs in the near future, to allow for more room and ease of access, especially for those who are challenged by climbing a narrow flight of stairs.  Of course, the added elevation adds something to the ambiance of the sun drenched room; making it feel more private and cozy than a direct walk in off the street.  Yet, from what I learned about the philosophy behind the joint - its local punk rock/street life orientation - moving into an old barroom will not cause any real loss of spatial/emotive relationship.   As for the Java, it is very good, if house roasted, hand brewed Joe is your cup of tea.  Abdul makes each order as received from his personal stock of prepared beans.  He has overseen every aspect of preparation other than the actual growing of the coffee bushes.  His love and attention to his trade is patent, as he will tell you his coffee story and provide a play by play of how he is making your "pour over."    The cast of characters here on a weekday morning was unique and very authentic.  There were hushed conversations and people working with pad and pencil, while I looked around taking photos and listening to Abdul.  The large, "UNWANTED," sign above the barista area makes a strong statement, but I thought it best not to inquire about it yet.    Trenton Coffee House is the newest piece of the underground arts/music scene in this past its prime capitol city.  There are many urban pioneers about "Renton," that hold hope for the future of this decayed mini-opolis.  If you feel called to be a part of it, stop in for some Java and conversation, and pick up a schedule for the local bands.    It'll do you good.  UPDATE: DECEMBER 21, 2016 - Winter Soltice.   Trenton Coffee House made the move downstairs to its new space on the first floor. Corner door lets you right into the main room. Red & white walls. Gray wooden floor. Roaster behind the counter.   Same excellent java. Same Coolio vibes.  Morning light through the glass block windows gives it a soft glow that easily shifts within.

As the nearest pizza joint to my office, I really have not taken advantage of its prime location. After trying Jeppy's Brooklyn Pie that oversight will soon be corrected.   Today I dealt with the man himself. Affable to the nines. He recommended slices of the 'Brooklyn' sitting in display.  Agreeing, he hand selected the best two available and put them in the oven to reheat.  The mozza was homemade, and tasted it. Mildly salty and soft. The crust, airy and cracker firm and crisp. Really superior work.   This shop is in the first floor of a converted residence with apartment above. The restroom is back in the kitchen, requiring an escort. The WC itself is unusual, in that it shows its previous adaption for family living with full shower.   Given the surprising quality of this pizza, it is definitely deserving of an upgrade to 4 Stars. That they forgot my drink keeps it from attaining top rank.

I am a little confused by this new chicken shack on Race Street in Philly Chinatown.   Yes. It is cool the way it is an up the stairs second story shop. Its utilitarian set up with basic tables and chairs with little comfort shouts that this is a fast food joint that doesn't invite hanging around, although the wings are prepped as ordered and take 20 minutes to come out of the fryer. I am okay with all that. Yet, although called, "bbq chicken," all lower case, in fact there is no BBQ chicken there. It is all Korean-type double fried chicken wings and cold drinks, bubble teas, smoothies, etc. The wall menu has about 50 drink options, yet just 7 flavor finishes for their wings. Bird choices are wings, boneless wings or chicken sandwich. If I didn't know better, I'd think this was really another over saturated bubble tea house offering wings on the side (By comparison, Vivi around the corner is all about interesting drinks, and offers deep fried wings as a nosh, for a lot less money.).  Go figure.  What about the wings? Well, they were crispy enough, and the soy garlic and secret spicy sauces were pretty good. As others have said, the secret in the spicy was that it was more sweet than hot, although there was some warmth behind the sugar. I liked the soy garlic better, but as I slowed down after the initial rush to dive into them, I began to taste the underlying oil they were cooked in. Not so nice.   Soho has nothing to worry about from understated lower case 'bbq chicken'. It needs to decide what it really is and let everyone know.

Charming Garden is a typical Chinese American house that offers both Chinese and Sushi in the middle of a just-off-the-highway shopping plaza in Lower Makefield, Pa.  Calling this location Yardley is a marketing ploy, as it is not that riverside borough, but does have more name pizzazz that its actual address.    Stopped in for lunch after a run to Home Depot last Saturday.  It is a bright, clean room, with efficient service.  The servers keep busy anticipating the needs of customers, while the sushi chef stands and waits for an order.   My Hot & Sour Soup was good, and seemed freshly made without reliance on MSG.  The Veggie Chow Fun was a nice size plate for lunch.  The assortment of greens was not vast beyond carrots, onion, peas, broccoli and a few baby corns, but the brown sauce covered everything in a decent tasting goo.  The broad noodles held the flavors of everything around them well enough.  My bud asked for extra heat on his dish, but got it bland with a side dish of Szechuan Chili Sauce.  He said it was not as good that way and he preferred when the sauce was cooked with the other ingredients.   No real reason to return to Charming Garden unless I find myself hungry again when in the vicinity.

Called ahead to pick up a large pie for dinner. Half plain. Half sausage. This was my first visit to Red Star Pizza 3, and my impression was that it was attractive inside, with room to sit for dinner, and had a friendly efficient staff. The pizza was ready when I arrived, and I was back on the road in under five minutes.   Opening the box in my kitchen, it looked good and had a nice aroma. Pizza is always best eaten straight from the oven, and this one confirmed that axiom. Both slices had the right combo of sauce and cheese, but having cooled for a while, the crust was now weak and could not hold the topside weight. Still, the taste was there. The sausage crumble was strong.   We had a decent dinner from Red Star, and will get back there to mange in house as soon as possible.

This is a mini-DD that shares the building with another business, yet it has a small outdoor seating area in front of the shop if you really feel like hanging out and smelling the exhaust of the cars parked right next to you.   The coffee is what most of us expect from this ever expanding franchise.  Average coffee whose main attraction is its basic consistency across the nation.    Service here is fast and efficient, if not overly friendly nor engaging.    It is amazing how different each DD "makes the donuts," however, I did not have any here and cannot speak to their taste and quality.

International House of Pancakes (or burgers if you follow their latest campaign) is nothing if not consistent with their primary menu. The pancakes are good wherever you find the IHOP sign, the coffee always hot and served with a pitcher for refills. Breakfast is breakfast across their wide spread enterprise.   We stopped in after an appointment to grab a morning bite. The store was large and divided into sections. We were seated in the back room and approached by our server in less than a minute.   Coffee, please. And, that spicy omelet with avocado on top, while you're at it. Extra plate for sharing, too. Easily done. It arrived with second plate in a few minutes. Surprisingly good, especially the unexpected BBQ brisket sticking out both ends that added a savory chew to the otherwise soft melty dish. The three pancake side was more than enough to split after spreading on butter and a combination of table syrups. Glad we had only one platter, because we were challenged finishing it.   IHOP is an easy choice if a decent American breakfast is what you want. The jury is still out on the burgers.

Wish I didn't have to return to DP Auto Body less than a year since my previous visit, but as luck would have it, I had another rear ender.  Ugh!   Dave Miller has a great way with people.  He is able to make an unpleasant experience as comfortable as possible by his friendly demeanor, clear explanations, excellent shop, and fair prices.    And, yes.  If I need more work done in the future, I would return without hesitation.

What was once Patrick's Pizza and BelItalia Pizza, is now 7 Brothers Pizza.  Let's hope the third time is a charm!  This tiny shop in the 1300 block of South Broad Street, Trenton, NJ, has been washed and painted, and provided new furniture (all 3 tables), in the attempt to attract and keep customers who need Italian takeout in this south Trenton neighborhood.  The owner is from Ecuador.  He is expanding his restaurant business from his "2 Brothers" location in Ewing near the College of New Jersey.  He is friendly and loquacious, and readily engaged in conversation about his new enterprise (open only 3 weeks).  He explained that this part of the capital city was already loaded with good Latin American restaurants, but was light in the pizza/cheesesteak category.  He was hopeful of filling this void.   If my Chicken Cheesesteak was any example, he has a good chance to succeed.  Their lunch special of sandwich, fries and cold drink for $6.50 was certainly priced to please.  Served on a ceramic plate, rather than paper, the sandwich also contained sautéed Spinach and the Fried Onions he suggested.  It was nicely presented for in house consumption, which I appreciated given that often times the meal is in take away form regardless of intention to eat right there.  That's treating the customer right.  As with every place I've been this past week, the air conditioning was overwhelmed by the heat of the day, not to mention the ovens, so I ate with a light sweat beading on my brow and dampening my shirt.  That did not deter me from enjoying lunch, as sometimes it is nice to roll with the elements, just like in the good old days before universal AC.    The food was good and tasty.  The only suggestion would be to improve the quality of the rolls to have a crustier bite.  There are many bakeries around Trenton that make great bread.  It may be more expensive than the regional soft roll providers, but I would gladly pay a little extra for a Wonder Roll from Italian Peoples down on Butler Street.

Wissahickon Brewing Co. is a low key suds emporium on Schoolhouse Lane in East Falls just above Ridge Road. Beer is all they do, and they do it well. Their minimalist decor is open and comfortable enough for a young family with their infant to hang out easily. The brew room is large and open right behind the bar. They also have seating in the loading dock, and more tables outside if fresh air with your pilsner is your thing.  We ordered a flight of four, mixing their Raisin d'Etra, Whit and Koho IPAs and Belgian Kelpius Kove. They were all very good. I preferred the the two bookends, while DT relished the hoppier IPAs. There is no kitchen here so if you're wanting solids with fluids you have to order out from a local pizzeria.   The staff was friendly and happy to educate about their products. Ordering at the bar was required, but the room was clean and uncluttered with everyone, both customers and workers, helping out.   As we were leaving we were introduced to the Wissahickon brewmeister who was working on Saturday night. He invited us to a quick tour of his domain, which we graciously declined due to time constraints. We asked for a raincheck, which he graciously extended.  Until next time.

Over the years, this basement emporium has become my last resort for ingredients that just can't be found anywhere else in the City.  That special vinegar for dumplings, the fried chili in oil with black beans, and the narrow gauge rolling pin for making dumpling skins from scratch, all reside in Asia Supermarket.  But, you might need help finding all of them from the amazing employees who have the entire layout memorized.    Speaking Mandarin or Cantonese helps, but with a smile and small kowtow, they switch to English and will even guide you to where these treasures are found.

This is the most beautiful and serene space for foot massage I have experienced in the USA. The décor is cool and quiet, despite it being a simple large space without inner separating walls. 20 large reclining chairs in 3 rows.  All visible, yet private. Choice of herbal bath for your feet to soak in, while 20 minutes is spent on solid upper body massage.   Very restful, except when my foot master dug deep into certain points and looked to see my reaction. He knew the meridians, and was able to push chi.  Green tea leaves sink to the bottom of my cup as I slip away.

For some reason, I was sitting in this DD trying to check in on my mobile phone, and was told I was too far away!  I guess that depends on what dimension of reality you are measuring from. Or maybe, this is in one of those GPS warps, where the directions get lost due to cosmic interference.   Otherwise, nothing special going on here. The coffee is only Okay (bad water?), but I have noticed a deterioration of DD coffee quality at many shops over the past few years. They really need to standardize the water variable, because without good water, the coffee beans can do little.   My son's basketball team was celebrating the end of their season here last night. The boys seemed happy with the Baskin Robbins, but I saw a dish of strawberry ice cream that was so red, I wondered what red dye farm it had visited before being consumed.   Loved the company, but will live without their goods in the future.

Lambertville Trading Company on Bridge Street, Lambertville, NJ, is right next door to Sneddon's Luncheonette, so it is possible to have breakfast at the former, and a decent java jolt at the latter, and feel good about your exploration of this beautiful river city.   The shop itself is quite small.  There are a few seats in the window alcoves, and a couple of stools in the rear, but otherwise, this place is mostly takeout. It is all wood and glass displays from floor to ceiling, and it is somewhat captivating in its downright cuteness. It was brewing coffee before there was a Starbucks, and certainly deserves your affection and appreciation for that.  They also do a small bakery product retail to go with the joe.   Word is that they use Small World Coffee Roasters out of Princeton, but I could not vouch for that as there were plenty of other bags of beans behind the counter with other labels on them. My own decaf latte was a bit harsher than expected and slowly degraded to a bitter aftertaste by the time I reached the office. The chocolate chip cookie I scored for accompaniment was nearly as large as my hand and was nicely crisp.  The $1 Yelp discount upon checking in made it a pretty sweet deal.   LTC is still the best place in L'ville to buy your coffee for your walkabout. It continues to fit right in with all the other antique shops in town.

This will be a review in several chapters.   I just started looking for new wheels this weekend.  Three people in my family with new driving permits eager to be part of the great American right of passage. Where is the best place to see all the alternatives and drive a few of them on a private test track?    Reedman Toll Auto World in Langhorne, Pa.   They have a series of connected showrooms along Rt. 1, with everything from Chevy, Jaguar, and Ram to Subaru and almost everything in between. We were free to meander around without interference; get in and out of any car there, and generally kick the tires as much as we wanted; all without a single salesperson approaching us to push us toward business.  This atmosphere in the comfort of modern display was surprising and refreshing.  We were around so long that I began to think perhaps they accurately read us as people only at the beginning of their shopping adventure.    We ended up at the Subaru end of the complex.  We sat for a while in a Outback Limited (very nicely appointed with Walnut inserts in the dash and door), and a Legacy, Sube's "full size" sedan (similar, but felt smallish in the cockpit).  Finally, the sales manager walked over with a casual air and inquired about what we were looking for.  They were busy, and promised someone would get to us soon.    There was more inventory outside, so we exited and strolled along the two rows of Outbacks of various colors and accessories.  Mostly green and black, some leather/wood; some cloth/metal.  After about ten minutes, a young guy wearing a knit cap and sweatshirt came up to us.  He introduced himself as a "floater," who worked at their Chevy operation and who could sell any car on the lot.  He was relaxed and friendly and offered to get the key needed for a car we liked, so we could test drive it.  That accomplished, he drove us to the back lot where the test track was located.  We circled the quarter mile loop a few times.  Pleasant car to drive. Not exciting, but clearly solid and competent.  Turns out our salesguide was a long term employee of Reedman, but relatively new to sales.  He was a mellow fellow who made our time with him very light and easy.  We got into some more personal talk, and it turned out he was in the middle of a lawsuit, and I was able to answer some questions for him.  By the end of our hour or so together we had developed the beginning of trust in each other. Me, in his basic honesty and willingness to work to find the best deal possible on one or two cars I was interested in; and he, in my willingness to listen to his concerns about litigation anxiety with patience and advice.    We will have to wait to find out how this story continues. I intend to buy new wheels by the end of the month, and will give this good man the first chance to close a deal.  DECEMBER 11, 2016 - UPDATE : This story ends quicky. Despite the new connection I imagined with our salesperson, I never heard from him again with the workup he promised.   So be it. As with fish, there are many more cars around to shop, consider, test drive and purchase. It just won't be at Reedman-Toll.   No hard feelings.

While I wouldn't wager on the last time the Department of Licenses and Inspections walked down the stairs into Asia Supermarket, I might take your bet that we could find a completely esoteric noodle sauce, cookie, or tea previously believed to be extinct anywhere outside of China.  This place seems to have all that stuff, and more. The prices are cheap, the aisles narrow, and the shopping carts from a bygone era.    Still, if it is something you remember eating back home, or a cooking utensil unavailable in Sears, this is the place you may find it.  Go for that reason, or for the great sense of nostalgia emanating from every shelf and refrigeration unit.    It is not every day that you can be both a consumer and an anthropologist at the same moment.  The museum-like quality of some of the dark corners makes this a multi-dimensional experience. Stock up on your packaged, canned and bottled goods at good prices as you explore its inner recesses.   Don't forget to come up for air.

When rescheduling a driver's test at the Bensalem facility in Bucks County had a three month wait, I called the number on the scheduling letter, and was able to get a new date at the Norristown, Montgomery County, operation for three weeks later.  What a difference!    Not only that, but their tester was friendly and actually encouraged my new driver to take her time, and not worry.  He wanted her to succeed.  So different than the attitude in the other place, where it was obvious the man with the digital pad could care less.    Yes, there was a wait of about an hour until we were reached, but there was only this one guy doing all the testing, and he was as thorough as he was pleasant.  In the end, he gave a passing grade, and congratulated her on a job well done.  He took the time to express his appreciation for how well she had parallel parked (only 2 moves), and that she also needed to always be attentive to all the conditions around her.  Point well taken.   He escorted us to the right desk inside the center, and from there, a temporary license was issued in a matter of minutes. The permanent license would arrive by mail in about two weeks.   The rest was all celebration!   It is not often that a bureaucratic experience like a driving test can be called "humane," but that was the case yesterday in Norristown.  "Lee" was all that and more. He deserves an award and a big raise.

Excellent burgers on South 5th Street, just where Passyunk intersects with the 5. Design your own using the three computer stations, or go to the counter to talk with the people working there. Either way you get a standard double patty complemented any way you choose. If you don't want to think that much about it, the menu offers several great combinations that are bound to make you happy.   Just the right amount of grease, potato or pretzel roll, natural sugar carbonated beverages, Bassett ice cream based shakes, and fresh fruit smoothies, all surround the ultimate comfort food for your indulgence.   Prices that won't break the bank just off the hippest street in town.   If there is something to improve upon, it is that it appears that every burger is finished to well done regardless of how you request it. Still, they are so juicy I almost didn't notice.

The restaurant scene in Doylestown, PA is always changing, mostly for the better. I have eaten three times in the space now occupied by Sesame China Bistro, and with each change of hands has come an improvement in the dining experience. This Asian fusion house offers primarily Chinois/American dishes found in every takeout shop across the western world, yet they do it with a fresh approach that brings some modernity and better techniques to the wok style.    Yes, they do offer a Thai dish or two, and even a glimpse at ramen soup, but it would be a mistake to think that Chinese cuisine is not what they understand best. I was there for late lunch and was at the cashier to order General's Chicken, Hot & Sour Soup and hot tea.  My meal arrived about ten minutes later on a large white ceramic bowl for the General, and small dish with flat bottom spoon for the soup.  A small mound of white rice was provided as accompaniment.   The Hot & Sour was full of tofu, mushrooms, carrot slivers, sprouts and a little pork.  No MSG in sight (thank goodness).  They used a vinegar that I was not familiar with, changing the flavor just a bit to the sweeter side.  I liked it, but the traditional vinegar would have probably enhanced the enjoyment for me. The chicken was not heavily breaded before deep frying, a definite plus.  The deep tamarind-colored goop was perhaps also sweeter than expected, but then again, I did not request that it be spicy.  There were some small pieces of chili pepper in the mix, but not enough to reach the balance of sweet and spice that the General is known for. Still, I liked it, and saw that preparation was well presented.   I would return to Sesame Chinese Bistro if the opportunity presented itself, but don't consider it more than a pretty good Chinese/American house, where I would visit for lunch, but not for a dinner when a more authentic MIddle Kingdom and Szechuanese hot and numbing meal is my preference.

I get the excitement everyone has about Comfort Food and Kitchenette.  It is an amazing place for Morrisville, Pa., and if it is a sign of things to come, this town is in for a renaissance.  The space is open and light.  Exposed industrial ceilings.  Brightly colored walls. Open kitchen.  Lots of interesting chachkas. Friendly service.  Locally sourced and health oriented menu (where possible).   The Pickle Brined Fried Chicken Sandwich with homemade Potato Chips came on strong, with a large breast of chicken, dipped in heavy batter, and fried to a golden brown.  The bird was still juicy under its new skin, and the tomato, lettuce, mayo accompaniment was harmonic.  Too big for handling, I resorted to knife and fork to demolish it.  Crunchy and tasty.  If there is a criticism, it is in how the breading/batter used to coat the chicken turned into a hard shell, rather than attaching itself to the chicken.  Although it tasted good, it cracked with each cut and was eaten separately from the bird.  Admittedly, this was a deboned breast, and not designed for hand to hand combat.  Still, I prefer when the breading and meat hang together and allow them to be eaten simultaneously, without an outer jacket falling away from the chicken beneath.  It was tasty, nonetheless.  The Chips, while flavorful, were too fry-centric alongside the chicken for one plate.  Cut fruit would have been better for me.    Live and learn.   Will return for at least one more round from this kitchen.  There were a lot of happy faces and kvelling sounds all around, suggesting that I may have simply made the wrong choice in selecting fried chicken in such an avant garde coolio joint.

When my HVAC system died last year, I called around for estimates to replace the 25 year old dinosaur with a more state of the art apparatus. Not only was Christian less expensive for equivalent mechanicals, but they did not attempt to oversell me on a product that my home really could not benefit from, regardless of rebates or government programs.  Much appreciated.  They got the job done in one day, were neat and quiet, and gave me both a coupon for an additional discount and my first tune-up as part of the deal.  One year financing without interest was also a nice touch.    With all the heat and humidity this summer, I think of them almost daily as I cool down in my favorite chair with a tall glass of lemonade.    Thanks, Christian HVAC!

Genius.  A Dim Sum Sports Bar in Chinatown!  Who'd a thunk that a hybrid Asian oriented kitchen with a beer dominated sports bar would work?  I hadn't, but I am sure glad the guiding hands behind Bar-ly did.  This is a fun and original spot, and likely a theme that will be duplicated around the country.   A greatly enhanced environment after the former tenants, a 60 label beer menu, and enough wide screens to allow everyone their own view.  The food is decent, with choices from spring rolls to kimchee cheesesteaks, with Japanese, Korean Chinese, Vietnamese and American influences throughout the offerings.  I had the boiled dumplings and a burger. Both were good, but not best in breed. Checking on the other plates exiting the kitchen, everything looked attractive, and the patrons seemed to enjoy the victuals.   If I was strictly interested in a good meal, I might chose a different restaurant that was more sedate and allowed for whispered conversation.  However, if the idea is a fun and fluid afternoon of football with above average bar food, or a Thursday night of Flyers, Sixers, or Phillies, with friends and compatriots, this place is definitely on the short list of cool places to hang out and get loud.    Kudos to Bar-ly. They have created a unique environment that acknowledges and celebrates the cross fertilization of two amazing cultures.  Go for a visit and take it in.   Good times for all.

After exploring the canyons of The Home Depot, we walked out into the cold dark gray sky. We were a little hungry after all the hiking and saw this Burger King on the edge of this shopping zone on Bromley Road.   The store was nearly empty @ 3:00, and there was no wait to order. Whopper meal and a double cheeseburger from the value menu. Easy. Right? Except, our order taker thought we wanted a second meal when we only wanted the sandwich along with the Whopper meal. Small miscommunication that was fixed with managerial assistance after the register froze.   The burgers were typical of BK cuisine. Adequate fast food. The Freestyle sodie dispenser was still fun. So many choices at my fingertips. Absent were any condiments on this side of the counter. No ketchup pump. No salt or pepper. No plastic utensils. I'm sure they had their reasons.   This experience wouldn't have been particularly notable if I hadn't been to another BK two weeks before in Pa (Oxford Valley), where we were literally treated like fast-food royalty, in a shop that even has a fireplace lounge, and a real personal touch.  Spoiled us for future BK visits.

This is a review of Plain Pizza Slices served at lunch.  While the reheat did a good job firming/crisping the crust so that the point held up and provided a firm bite, the remainder of the experience was somewhat of a letdown.  The sauce was on the salty side, while I prefer a sweeter, more basil flavor tone.  The cheese was ample, but without much taste to contribute to overall dining pleasure.    Two slices and a soft drink came in under $7.00, but the same can be had a several other places for at least a buck less.   Reviews say that their cheesesteak is the way to go at Venezia, but when the standard tomato pie is so ordinary and uninspired, I would not elect to return to give something else a try.  There are too many better choices in the vicinity.   Venezia does not make the cut for a quality pizza slice.

Chiangmai is an attractive Thai house on Fayette Street in the heart of Conshohocken, PA.  It is part of a three restaurant local chain that have a good reputation for authentic Thai cuisine in a nice atmosphere.  My experience at lunch confirms that opinion.   I entered about 1:00 PM and was seated at a deuce at the front window. Cool view of a bustling Fayette Street.  The menu was presented by an attractive server who directed me to the specials page offering a prix fixe of soup, salad/app and entrée for $9.95.  Sounded good, but I knew I couldn't eat that much, so ordered the Vegetarian Drunken Noodles.   While waiting, I took in the décor of the dining room. It was simple, yet beautifully appointed with wall and ceiling hangings from home. Lots of color and texture. The staff was likewise adorned in native dress.  It wasn't difficult to remember my days relaxing in Chaingmai after business in Bangkok. Brought a secret smile to my face.   The large platter arrived quickly - a massive load of broad noodles, chopped broccoli, carrots, onions, sprouts and cubes of tofu in a moderately spicy sauce. Really flavorful and good mix of textures, shapes and colors. As beautiful as the sarong on the woman serving me.   Very much enjoyed my lunch, and would not hesitate to return here, or to the other restaurants in their portfolio.

MEETING ROOM SERVICES ONLY  We held a fundraiser in the Pheasant Room last night for about 70 people.  We provided all the food and drink, but the hotel management provided set up/clean up, ice and ice containers, and a "Can Do" attitude for all our requests. They were helpful, friendly and made sound suggestions.  They also assisted with creating the sound stage for our musical entertainment.   All for a very reasonable price.   As a result, the event was a smashing success.  Everyone was happy and well fed, even when during speech time when all the local pols made their pitches to Get Out the Vote. No one left early, and many remained to listen to our local musicians make merriment.   Homewood Suites is definitely a place to consider for your next meeting or event. The only downside is that it lacks a kitchen for serious catering, but once there you can have fun and even spend the night.

Yummy Sushi has moved to new quarters to be replaced by the literally translated, Fame Dish. At first blush the shop looks exactly the same with blond woods and small sushi bar in back. Staff wears light aquamarine and black. Service is efficient. The menu tips it's hat to Japanese (sushi), Thai (pad thai), and Singapore (noodles), but is operated in Mandarin and is primarily a Chinese house. It remains to be seen whether it can carry out it's multi cultural concept, but if the chef is serious about it, and the market demands it, it is possible.   My General's Chicken lunch was a mixed bag. The wonton soup was pretty bad. Canned consume with two thick skinned dumplings with little core, nor taste. Disappointing. On the other hand, the chicken was better than expected after the soup. White meat with a very good freshly made sauce that included a fair amount of Chinese red peppers per my request for heat. I asked for brown rice, but got white. Oh, well...  At $12 with tip, it was more expensive than most other chop chop houses in the area, and it should have been more consistent from soup to nuts. Yet, it did show promise and is worth another look to explore other options.

The choice was between Jack & Jill hard ice cream and vanilla/chocolate/orange soft serve. I went with a cup of orange vanilla swirl in styro. While waiting at the window of this renovated former fast food shell, I watched all the families sitting around enjoying a cool moment on a humid sticky evening in June.   I was more in the mood to drive home and spoon the melting combo in air conditioned comfort. Besides, I prefer drinking this elixer to licking it. I sampled it at red lights along the way.   Have to admit to being disappointed. The vanilla had little flavor and the orange while tasty, was also grainy like the orange powder had not been mixed enough to reach the smooth silkiness desired for soft serve.   There are many choices for ice cream in this part of the world, so I hope this was just a glitch in a normally high quality operation.

There is no doubt that the Tanner Brothers Store that sits at the intersection of Almshouse and Hatboro Roads in Warminster, Pa., could use an extreme makeover to improve the shopping cart traffic patterns, and modernize the check out, but if that were done it would likely sacrifice all that it has been and continues to be.  What's that?  Only a well used, still functional, farm stand for the farm run by the family of that name for generations.  There wasn't a fraction of the population nor vehicular traffic in those days.  It was about the only game in town for fresh produce, dairy and other kitchen necessities before the Acmes, Clemens, and other grocery chains started pushing north into Bucks County.  Seen it this light, it is actually an anthropology museum with daily changing interactive exhibits.   Compared to those modern markers, Tanner Bros does suffer in the amenities department, but makes up for it with generally fresher produce, cheaper eggs, and excellent handmade ice cream.  Sure, as a convenience and secondary marketing attraction, it offers national brands on its shelves, and those things are not as competitively priced.  But, when we plan well, we hit Tanner's first, and then make a run to Giant or its ilk for everything else.  Makes us feel good to shop locally, and spend a little time in the past.    It's great to have large bins full of yams, corn, melons, leeks, etc., to touch and choose.  And, after lugging it all back to the car, to take a few more minutes to appreciate (and slowly consume) a great Butter Pecan Sugar Cone while watching the cows that manufactured the milk for it, lazily chewing their cud in preparation for the next milking.

Valentino's is a small pizza joint in the strip center that included JC Teriyaki on Pennington Road in Ewing, NJ. It has four or five booths, but business is obviously primarily take out. I stopped in for lunch this week and found the place bright and friendly, if a tad disheveled. However, their pies on display looked very appealing, and I opted for two king size slices reheated to well done, and a Snapple.  At $6 and change, it was a good deal.   The slices were very thin, yet firm enough to hold their points high and proud, without a quiver nor bended knee.  It was crisp, hot, and tasty and had splashes of chunky sauce throughout that reminded of tomato pie, but was in fact still a pizza with plenty of cheese visible beneath the red blotches. A heavy shake of crushed red pepper, and the slices came to life.  They were very good, with little drip or drop.   In fact, this lunch was far better than anticipated, and was one of the better pizza surprises of the past year. I would certainly return for a fresh pie and to sample their cheesesteaks.    If they found time to clean up the house, and put away all the unfinished boxes and cases of soda sitting in the back, Valentino's could find itself a nice romantic table for two hole in the wall for those wanting a private conversation over cracker crisp crusty pizza.

If you look at a map showing the Delaware River boundary between Pennsylvania and New Jersey, you can see where the southbound river makes a sharp turn to the west, creating the 'neck' geographic feature of the Garden State and the elbow of Bucks County, PA. jutting into it's eastern neighbor. This part of the region is dominated by the ancient flood plains of the Delaware. Driving through feels more like the Louisiana bayous than the Northeastern states. There is alot more water than dry land in these parts, with narrow spits of land for roads and a few homes surrounded by lakes, ponds, marshes and of course, the Mighty Delaware.   The folks around here have resided in this water world for generations. They are a tight community. When they want to socialize, Darby O'Gill's is where they meet to talk, drink, eat, play and inebriate. Yeah. It felt a little strange walking in for the first time with everyone looking up and following my steps to the square bar in search of a stool. But, my Eagles ballcap and 6'4" smile gave me a pass for the moment, so they just stared and waited to see what happened.   The barkeep, Desiree, yanked me a pint of Yuengling Octoberfest, and asked to run my credit card before taking my food order. The lager was excellent.    "I don't know you, honey. Have to be sure you can handle this."   "No sweat. House rules are fine. Do what you gotta do."   She returned with a more relaxed countenance and handed my card back to me. The sound of conversation and football games on the TVs returned to the room. I ordered their Paddy Melt and sipped on the dark rusty ambered brew.   This joint was the diviest of taverns. Operated by Darby since 1998, and housed in a large building considerably older than that, it had been decades since it was cleaned thoroughly. The underflooring was exposed in many places and the knotty pine paneling was grease and beer splattered.   Almost Heaven. West Virginia.   The grilled sandwich was pretty good with loads of sauteed onions and crunchy rye holding a half pound of burger and melted swiss. The ketchup was watery, but what the hey? It tasted good and was filling with a shovel of fries for an extra buck.   I paid with a reasonable tip for Ms. D, and walked out into the cool bright late afternoon sunlight. The parking lot was as torn up as the barroom floor. There was a ragged trailer park out back that appeared to be in the same condition as everything else around there.   As I found my way out of this strange wet and desolate area, I was amazed that this place was part of contemporary Bucks County, and not a piece of land that time forgot.

This Dunkin is located at the intersection of Parkway Avenue and Pennington Road in Trenton, NJ.  It is fairly new and is well maintained.  There is a drive thru option. Plenty of parking if you want to go inside.   I walked in after lunch to grab an afternoon wakemeup.  The woman behind the counter was friendly and efficient. They had a surprisingly full rack of donut and muffin options for the time of day.  A few customers sat at one of the tables discussing business. Overall, the place was attractive, with everyone doing their job professionally.    The coffee was what you expect from this franchise.  Consistent. Strong. Not overly acidic. Not particularly flavorful. Fully capable of keeping me awake for my afternoon surge toward the five o'clock world.    Right down the middle.

Ten of us showed up at Ocean Harbor late Saturday morning for dim sum. Perhaps because it was mid-August, street parking was available on Race Street, so we only had to walk a block to reach this large, bright yellow painted, high ceilinged, dining hall. Had this been a wedding, we would have been the guests of honor, because we were seated up on the stage at the rear of the room.   Wish I knew the names of everything we sampled, but it came at us so fast and furious, with multiple carts constantly dropping off dishes, that I barely had time to photograph them before they were snapped up by our crew's chopsticks. Regardless, everything was surprisingly good.   No problem with service, either. The size of our group provided all the incentive necessary to get us plenty of attention.  That most of our party spoke Mandarin probably didn't hurt.   All we ate and drank came to $100. Great deal for the quantity and quality of food consumed.   We agreed that coming back again was very likely.

This location of Penn Medicine on Township Line Road in Lower Makefield, PA, is close to home, so when I needed a follow up X-ray this was the place to go. There are many Penn doctor offices there, but I was only interested in the Department of Radiology on the first floor.   Turned out that this office was very well run. I made the appointment online through mypennmed.com for the same afternoon. On arrival I signed in and was seen by the intake person within five minutes. After showing my photo ID and insurance card, I went to the waiting room until I was called for the x-ray. In less then ten minutes the technician walked into the waiting area, called my name, greeted me, escorted me to the changing area and handed me a gown needed for the picture. Once done, we went to the radiology room and took the shot.   I was dressed and out the door from beginning to end in no more than 25 minutes.   Everyone I dealt with was friendly, accommodating and totally professional. I love going to Philly for best medicine at Penn, but getting an x-ray at one of their satellites make so much sense, especially with the digital images going directly to my doctor for his review.  Will be talking to him soon.

On the hottest day of the summer it was nice to slip inside Triumph Brewing Company and enjoy the dim lights and heavy air conditioning. A few brave souls sat outside, but after standing in the humid 90 degree heat at The Garden of Reflection to commemorate 9.11, there was no way I wanted more of it.  Today, the sun won.   My first visit here in New Hope, and the facility was spacious with big bar on one side, and dining room on the other.  We sat is a dark corner to discuss business although part of my mind and all my heart was elsewhere.  Triumph is proud that it locally sources its provisions and is serious about sustainable agriculture.  Way cool!    I had a half sized Watermelon Salad consisting of red and yellow sweet melon with Watercress and a light dressing.  It was exactly right for today - cool, pleasantly refreshing.  I read on Yelp that the Calamari was good, so when the wait person suggested that or Grilled Chicken, Beef, or Shrimp on the salad, I jumped at the squid.  It was not on top of the salad, but in a separate plate because there was so much of it.  Tasted like good Calamari should - crisp without oiliness, nicely spiced to offset the innate mildness of the crustacean. I took most of it home.    Sorry to say, it was too early to try any of the beer, and the heat would have turned the day into an Albert Camus novel. So, will return again to explore that end of the menu.  A very nice place, adequate parking (metered), and better than average healthy food. Very satisfied, and plan on going back soon.  Good business meeting, too.

Located on what has become a dead end on Mill Creek Road just before reaching the old Delaware Canal, the inn that shares its name with the road feels like it knows that it is now at the end of the trail, and is depressed about it. While prices are downright cheap for food and drink, the house has a dark and dusty aura. It does have its attractions, with pool table and large rectangular bar with a few primarily domestic beer on tap. Too, it is a smokers tavern, and a haven for those who enjoy socializing with ques and tobacco. For me, a non-smoker, the atmosphere was challenging.   The menu is limited, with cheesesteaks, burgers and a few Italian specialties (meatballs galore). Seeing that, I went with their California Burger and fries to get a sample of what they should do well. Well, my hopes exceeded reality. Looking good on the plate with fresh, soft large bun, the puck itself was 8 ounces of previously frozen ground beef, with little flavor beyond what was provided by the cheese and red onions. My request for a medium finish was returned far closer to well done. The half order of fries was plentiful, but with starchy texture and no crispness. Just a disappointing effort.   Sitting at the bar, I received pleasant attention from the tender, who was kept busy all night pouring shots, drafts and cracking bottle caps. She moved quickly, and was clearly on top of her game.   The cigarettes forced me to depart soon after finishing my meal and Michelob Ultra. It is unlikely there is enough there to make a return visit.

Not much here unless you have a seat at one of the four tables on the patio or on the Septa train coming down the tracks. With a beautiful Saturday afternoon bringing out bikers from the nearby trail to rest and recharge, all the seats were occupied, so we could only take our latte and pour over back to the car and keep going.   No doubt an interesting use of the backroom of the bicycle shop and an attractive old stone building. The lone barista was kept busy and did a good job. Bakery products were almost exhausted. Coffee okay.   We had a nice drive home through a part of Conshohockon we had not seen before, but Riverbend is not a great place for a coffee stop under these circumstances.   The Cafe is a takeout shop right now with potential to be a lot more.

It is great to see a new food hospitality business open its doors in Trenton, NJ.   Studio B Bakery & Bistro operates in the space of prior galleries and restos that were not able to survive the vicissitudes of street life in Jersey's capital city.  Yet, this one feels like it has a chance to make it.  The space is utilitarian and simple, but comfortable.  They sell attractive bakery goods and offer breakfast and lunch that is traditional, yet creative in the use of ingredients and awareness of contemporary dietary concerns.  The staff dresses in black Ts, and is certainly friendly.    I walked in just after 1 in the afternoon, looking for lunch and a good review.  The menu was high on the wall behind the counter.  The Pecan Chicken Salad caught my attention, and when I inquired about the availability of sandwich or panini, was told that the only option was a brioche roll.  No problem. I like brioche.  It came (eventually) with a side of sweet potato fries. I requested hot green tea on a chilled rainy day.    What was not mentioned was that although the front of the house was not busy, the kitchen was slammed with a large project (never explained), and that I would likely have to wait more than 30 minutes to be served.  Luckily, I wasn't in a rush, and I spent the time productively reading.    When the plate was bought to me, it was quite attractive.  The chicken salad was curried, with a load of pecans, lettuce, red onion, on a standard looking hamburger roll (not brioche).  Again, no explanation for the change, nor apology.  Still, I liked the meal.  The chicken was tasty with a pleasant lasting flavor on the tongue.  The sweet potato fries were plentiful, crisp and a nice change of pace.    At the end, the owner came over and apologized for the delay. He seemed a decent, high energy and sincere guy.  A little better communication up front would have been appreciated along with a check in during the meal to see if I needed anything.  Not biggies, but just enough to warrant less than full throated endorsements, and a wait and see attitude for what I hope will be a major success on South Broad Street, within walking distance of my office.  UPDATE: MARCH 1, 2017 - I went in for breakfast this morning after court.  There were only a few other patrons around the house.  I sat at the counter and was promptly assisted by one of the two servers in black T's.  I ordered the Orleans Scamble, a three egger with sausage, onion, parsley, crisped shredded potato and cheese, and their chicory enhanced java.  The white plate arrived a few minutes later looking great with a dusting of parsley around the edges and the meal piled up in a line mid-plate.  A few shakes of Crystal Louisiana Hot Sauce and I was good to mange.  It was very good and quite filling. I appreciated the mix of flavors and textures, although a minute less on the grill for wetter eggs would have been my preference.  The coffee was hot and the chicory was a refreshing reminder of how joe is done in The Big Easy. Would have been even better if a refill had been offered.    Solid and enjoyable. Still a 4 Star experience, until those small niceties are mastered.

If truth in labeling is to have any credibility, then Szechuan East deserves low grades for honesty in the kitchen. While at one time it may have been truly a spicy Chinese hot pot, with red chilies and black peppercorns to adorn their dishes, somewhere along the line it ceased to be that place, and became quite something else.  If I had to guess, I'd surmise it changed ownership a few years ago, with the original Chengdu folks selling out to people from Zhejiang Province (near Shanghai), but continuing the popular name without the intention of maintaining a similar menu.  In truth, there was not a red nor black pepper in the house. Neither was their cumin, or other heat focused spices to impact the other ingredients.  The strongest element in the kitchen was Hunan black bean sauce, which while temperate on the tongue, does not approach the numbness required of a Szechuan wok.   The chef has his skills, and the platters delivered were okay for the most part, but it was a mighty disappointment when we came desiring a visit with the fire god, but came away with the less satisfying earth and water deities. When you drive 30 minutes to a remote outpost in Northeast Philly, with the expectation of one thing, and end up with something less satisfying, it is hard not to scowl at the misdirection of management. This was only complicated by the further misrepresentation on their website that they had a bar, when in fact, they no longer did.    Still, we did the best we could.  Lamb Hunan, Chicken & Walnuts, Yeh Yang Shrimp, Veggie Chow Fun and Cold Sesame Noodles.  Each was a large portion, visually appealing, and well made in their own right.  The black bean sauce on the lamb added some mild heat to the tender strips of baabaa.  The Shrimp was mildly crisp on the outside, with an adequate, yet semi-sweet finish. The Chow Fun was well done as it should be coming from a chef that was schooled in such things.  The walnuts were the best part of the chicken dish - nicely crunchy and honey dipped, as expected.  The cold noodles were forgettable, especially when we had been jonzen for DanDan.    The room itself is old school attractive with red leatherette booths.  The service was also fine. They seemed apologetic that we could not get what we wanted.    Maybe it doesn't make a difference to some what is really being cooked within.  It is also possible that in this backwater of western civilization, the milder, sweeter dishes are what is desired, and the house is just catering to the majority of their customers.  Still, a little heads up as to what was actually going on would be refreshingly more honest, and allow us to decide whether we are willing to accept their compromises.     We were not.

Still a fine place for lunch, particularly on an early Spring day when a walk from the office is a perfect respite from the workload of the moment.   On such days, and many others, Becky's is a fine destination for a fresh and tasty meal.

Chinese/American Lunch Special Review -   I didn't expect much reward when I stopped into King China on State Road, Croydon, PA, for lunch after getting new tires for my car a few days ago. Walking in, the shop appeared worn and in need of some TLC. The menu was a trifold handout and photos of their greatest hits high on the wall. I ordered egg foo young, which came with wonton soup and fried rice, for around $7.   Surprisingly, the meal was pretty good (for Americanized Chinois). The chicken stock was not overly salted, nor did it taste past its prime. The wontons were fairly thick skinned, but the filling was decent. The rice was likewise recently made and still granular without being clumpy and with plenty of veggies and bits of pork. Finally, the egg pancakes were light and loaded with bbq pork, sprouts, carrot and peas. The brown sauce was well made and plainly  prepared just for my order. Although the soup was served in a plastic pint container, the solids arrived on a nice heavy gauge plate.
