It would have been great had they offered wooden disposable chopsticks, rather than flimsy plastic utensils.   I enjoyed the lunch despite its expected shortcomings, but moreso for its small unexpected pleasures.

Philadelphia is a cool town.    It honors its own, even when they are mythological personalities like Rocky Balboa, the Hollywood heavyweight champion of the world back in the day.   Much like the movie character himself, his statue did not always have a permanent home.  He bounced between the top of the Art Museum steps, the old Spectrum, the Wells Fargo Center, and finally a cozy corner at the Art Museum, somewhat hidden by the grand stairway and tall trees.  The city couldn't decide if Rocky was just a local sports icon, or a full blown cultural and historic personality deserving of so much attention, so he was on the move depending on who was pulling the strings in City Hall.  Finally, the people of this great city spoke.  We didn't care if he was just a movie hero who never really lifted a finger in anger or self defense.  For decades Rocky and his alter ego, Sly Stallone, were the best things that happened to this burg since Ben Franklin flew his kite.   In so many ways Rocky Balboa is Philadelphia. Hardscrabble.  Historic. Italian Market narrow street kid, Independence Hall.  The Constitution.  Belmont Plateau. All images of greatness and deep cultural roots.  Rocky takes his place among the must-see attractions in the City of Brotherly Love.   It represents the everyman we all aspire to be.

The first review I wrote for this burgerdom disappeared from Yelp a few years ago for reasons unknown. When I stopped in recently with my son, I realized I hadn't replaced it. Out of sight. Out of mind.   This is the BK closest to Sesame Place in Middletown, Bucks County, PA. As such it draws heavily from family visits, and has attempted to make this operation a showplace. To a certain degree they have succeeded. There are inside/outside play areas for children, ordering stations that let you avoid human contact if you don't want to deal with high school students working their first jobs, and even partial table service where your tray it brought to you by the staff rather than waiting around in the lobby to be called. There is even a cozy fire pit zone that could be considered romantic by some. Mostly good things (except, my first job was in a burger joint and it was a great training experience, that I wish they continue). Given these amenities, you know that they have some good ideas, and makes you wonder why they don't do these tricks everywhere.   Still, there are some things that don't change. Like the quality of the meal prepared in the kitchen. You still have to deal with thin, too salty burgers, that have little flavor, fries that chill quickly and become dry and lifeless, and sugar loaded drinks that just are not good for you.   Bottom line - Comfort is a variable they are willing to enhance to impress the visiting public, but food service remains inferior to most of the new fast casual joints sprouting up across the country, with much better sandwiches and shakes for only a few bucks more.   In the race for a better burger, BK only seems to be falling further behind.

Zebra-Striped Whale, named after the children's book of the same name and authored by the owner of this pleasant ice cream café, is an Alice in Wonderland place to disconnect from the outside world and kick back for a while. Sitting on State Street in Newtown Borough, it is a center of activity most warm evenings.  It is necessary to make reservations for the bench out front - it is that popular.   The ice cream is very good, and the coffee is too.  The back of shop seating area is comfortable and eclectic; a great place for a small meeting like I had this afternoon.  It is quiet on a weekday afternoon, and no one comes back to ask if you need anything else. Walk up to the front counter if you want a refill or another scoop.    While ZSW is not my favorite ice cream emporium in Newtown's creamy rich population of chill zones, it does possess the best options if you like to mix your SCREAM on cold marble with Reece Cups or Mason Mints.  To my tongue, Goodnoe's and OwWowCow taste better, but our Zebra is a whale of a place for the kids after dinner or weekends, and for us business folk during the day.    Glad they are here and successful.

The 6800 block neighborhood of Bustleton Avenue, Northeast Philly, has been reborn as a satellite Asian center now that both Chinatown and Washington Avenue have maxed out with markets, restaurants, sundry shops and boutiques that are very popular and have little room for growth, and almost nothing for more parking.    This community has two dim sum houses.  We decided to try Jade Harbor first, and were able to park right behind the kitchen in the alley (please don't tell anyone else).  This Guangdong emporium has a few dining rooms on the first and second floors.  The tables in each are packed tight to squeeze in as many customers as possible, and the narrow trail from the rear kitchen to the front of the house is often clogged with people moving around to get to their seats or restrooms.  Actually, that is something of a good thing, as it forces the carts to navigate slowly or at full stop next to your table to allow a close inspection of the goodies, and to ask the women handling them for more information.    We were seated behind the entry door to one of the dining rooms.  Three chairs, but really room for only two.  At least we did not have to wait.  Hot tea arrived quickly, followed by the first of many cart visits.  We asked questions and snagged seven dishes from Shrimp Shumai and Beef Meatballs to Watercress Dumplings and Sticky Rice Balls with Lotus for dessert.  Everything was good to nearly best of breed.  Special mention for the Sticky Rice Pork Dumplings that were sweet on the outside and savory within.  They were a first for me.    As Bustleton is closer to home than a trip downtown, we will no doubt find our way back here with some regularity when the dim sum bug hits us.  That I was the only "foreigner" in a house full of Chinese families suggests that this place may actually be as authentic as the banquet halls on Race Street. Jade Harbor certainly seemed that way to me and my beautiful Chinese companion.   Will explore the other dim sum shop down the street and get back to you.

State Representative Candidate Forum  The Bucks County Free Library system has mixed reviews from library users, but last night they did the community a solid by providing a meeting room for the League of Women Voters State Representative Candidates Forum.  More chairs and a larger room would have been helpful, but the organization cannot be blamed for the substantial turnout to hear the two gentlemen answer questions submitted by the audience.    This is the way democracy is supposed to work.  If someone wants your vote and thinks they have the qualities needed to make an exceptional public servant, they must stand before us and let us see them with all their strengths and weaknesses.  Transparency in past experience and future policy positions are essential to intelligent decisions by the electorate.    What was most remarkable was how similar their answers were to most questions.  They both seemed so amenable to listening to each other, and working together whenever possible.    Oh, that this was really so!  Yet, this was all somewhat less than honest due to what was not addressed at all.  Each party they represent operates collectively.  The track record of the party in majority or minority is just as important as what an individual candidate believes.  After all, politicians don't work in a vacuum.  They take their positions according to what their leadership dictates.  The influence of a rookie representative (both would be new), is less than minimal, especially if plum committee assignments, reelection and promotion are desired.  Unfortunately, they were not questioned about the position of their party on the important issues, nor how they would deal with disagreements they had with leadership.  Without that information, it was too easy to say whatever they believed, without any grounding in reality.   Opportunity lost.    Still, in my view, one was clearly superior to the other in terms of intelligence, thoughtfulness, compassion and experience.  I know who has my vote.

There is no Stella!  I don't know how to break it to you gently, so I'll just come right out and say it. There is no Stella @ Stella's House Blend Cafe.   But, there is a Tiki (goddess) running the show, and she has the joint jumping. It was a capacity crowd at 10 am on Labor Day. The old 19th Century corner building in the heart of Sellersville, Pa, is as busy now as it ever was. The first floor occupied by this breakfast/lunch house has been brought back to life with TLC and a vision.  Have a good kitchen and they will come. They do, and they did.  I found a seat at the counter between two big fellas, and felt a moment of guilt being alone and able to skip the queue waiting for tables. It didn't last long. From my perch the kitchen was visible, and I could watch to servers at work. Teamwork!  My French Toast with Strawberries and Blueberries was made from multigrain bread as they were out of Texas Toast by the time I arrived.  No problem.  Done right, FT pleases me in almost any form.  This rendition was very good.  I also asked for the real Maple Syrup, a $1.50 extra, because there is little point to eating great FT with run of the mill pancake syrup.  The Maple enhances, while the sweet corn syrup used by Log Cabin and the like, diminishes the flavor of the dish.    The plate arrived loaded with bread and berries.  Gorgeous!  The side of Bacon I requested well done, was precisely that.  Firm, crunchy and with a splash of Maple, a delicious complement to the main.  Everything tasted very fresh, and their local sourcing policy seemed to be working well.  Same with the java.  Local roaster makes awesome joe.  Strong. Savory. A touch of milk to take the edge off.    Stella's House Blend Café would seem to be about the coffee, but that would deny the strength of the menu, and the skill in the kitchen.  Just about everything about this joint is fun and affirming.    Hey, Tiki!  I really like what you've done with the place.  A wonderful place to end a beautiful September drive in the country.

Trenton, New Jersey, is the last of the state capitals to have a Starbucks.  After 400+ years of history, it has finally arrived.  And, from the look of the place, the Green Mermaid spared little expense in designing this java joint. It is large, bright and original.  Cut in a triangular shape at the corner of Front Street and South Warren Street, on the first floor of a State office building, the two outer walls are all glass, and both are lined with comfortable sitting areas for work and conversation.  The back walls are painted with colorful murals of famous cityscapes - including the famous Trenton Makes Bridge across the Mighty Delaware River to Pennsylvania.   The coffee is standard Starbucks (not my favorite), but there is something to be said for consistency.  Their reliable snacks are present, and the service is friendly, knowledgeable and efficient. Everyone gets "TO GO" cups, even those hanging out, to save on losses.   I enjoyed the fact that this beautiful facility was actually in this Sad Sack city, as much as I enjoyed my latte and slice of lemon pound cake.  I watched as people filtered in and out.  No one seemed to be taking the space for granted.  The gold balloons didn't let that happen.   I allowed myself a moment of pride and gratification for this city that has been down so long that Starbucks is a very big win. Let's hope it is the beginning of a renaissance that has been awaited since Washington surprised the Hessians on a cold Christmas morn.

As the name suggests, Peking Tokyo is a new Asian fusion house in the Pine Watson Shopping Center in the heart of downtown Langhorne, PA. In addition to Chinese and Japanese elements, Thai cuisine is given a nod with a few curry and noodle dishes. I was there for lunch, and as everyone working there were speaking Chinese only, I was most interested in that part of the menu.   I asked for their lunch specials General Tso's Chicken, extra heat, which came with a cup of soup (Wonton), small ginger dressed salad, and fried rice. I also had a mug of green tea (an extra charge, although not disclosed until the bill appeared).   Everything was okay, but the only thing that stood out was the quality fried rice. It was freshly made with a higher standard grain, veggies and no dye. The soup was beef consomme with thick skinned wontons and decent filling. The chicken was plentiful and encased in a thickish shell. The sauce was tart as requested, with a few Szechuan red peppers in the mix. Particularly tasty when the rice was tossed in. The salad was from their sushi offerings - a first for me for a Chinese lunch and a nice touch, although I am not a fan of that ubiquitous ginger dressing.  Service was fine, and the manager stopped by to check on my satisfaction. The sushi chef stood at his bar in uniform and at the ready.   Peking Tokyo (Bangkok) is a step ahead of its predecessors in variety and quality from this vantage point, and as a new business it is still on its shakedown cruise. Hope it maintains high standards and is successful. Langhorne Borough certainly deserves that.

The Groveland Grill on RT. 611 in Pipersville ,PA, is a small roadside kitchen specializing in breakfast and lunch. It sits in a small commercial strip and is easy to miss if driving at normal speeds. I actually had to turn around and go back to it as I went north and didn't spy it until I was passed the driveway into their parking lot.   The house is clean, with about ten tables and a counter with seven stools. The folks working there are very friendly, and welcomed this first timer with warm greetings. I took a seat at the counter across from the Bunn O Matic where Ellis coffee was being brewed. There was a dark blue ceramic mug with side stainless of milk in front of me in seconds, and a two page breakfast menu placed before me before I reached the counter. These people were on their game.   There was a list of omelettes, benedicts, pancakes/French toast, and combo platters, but I decided on a standard breakfast sandwich of sausage, egg and cheese on kaiser. The side of home fries with grilled pepper and onion bits was also too tempting to pass up.   The sammy was doubled up, making for a fat and filling meal in its own right. The taters were alright, but despite the flavor from the sauteed onion/pepper, the tubers themselves were a bit dry like they had been sitting on the corner of the grill too long. Maybe my arrival at 10:00 had some to do with that, but a word to the wise...  Loved the Ellis java, which was refilled as often as I desired.   Groveland Grill is definitely worth your breakfast attention.

Maybe the large "For Rent" sign next door was a symbol of what was to come, but I did not think of that on the way in.  I came down to Levittown to try Zhou's House based on Yelp reviews, and the fact that I eat Chinese food as often as I can and am always looking for alternative shops to try.   The space itself is nice.  It is bright, clean and comfortable.  The family operation is friendly enough and they take pride in maintaining a pleasant environment.  I stopped in for lunch around 2:00 and was the only customer.  As is my habit, the first time I visit a resto I order something standard off the menu that is available at every Chinese shop in the West for easy comparison.  This day it was General's Chicken, Fried Rice and an Egg Roll for $6.95.  All looked good when the large plate arrived at my table.  The colors, shapes and textures seemed right.  The aroma was nice.  Sadly, the positives ended with the atmospheric effects.  The Chicken was wrapped in a thick bready coating that hardened like a shell around a too small core of meat.  Not only could I not taste the chicken, but I could not even feel it in my mouth while chewing.  It was all bun/no beef.  The sauce was a thick goo, lacking in finesse and any heat quotient. All corn starch, little spice.  The Egg Roll tasted of stale cooking oil, and the Fried Rice was bland. Clearly, this was an empty dish designed to provide a full plate without substance at a lunch specials price. Feh!  It could be that the dinners at Zhou's are far better than the lunch menu, but I will never know.  Any restaurant willing to dish out the slop given me for lunch, is not one I would chance for dinner.

Thanks to all you Yelpers who pointed the way to House of Thai Cuisine on Cottman Avenue in the Mayfair section of Northeast Philly.  It really is a great find!  But, it did not seem that way when we first arrived on the scene.  Saturday night was the early celebration for St. Patrick's Day.  The streets were a sea of green -  drunken green. We had to weave our way around the crowded sidewalks, police corners, and pools of liquid whatever making for an obstacle course.  The block is not particularly attractive, and given the weirdness of the evening, I wondered how comfortable we would be once we entered the restaurant.  Would it be full of green curry?   Amazingly, once we opened the door and went inside the world became quiet.  We were the only ones in the house.  The space was beautiful - classy wood floor, linen tablecloths and nice lighting. We were greeted by the owner/manager, who was gracious and seemed oblivious to the crashing roar outside.  In his domain, he was in control.    The food was very good, too.  The Spicy Seafood Soup was loaded and tartly spiced.  My Vegetable Soup was full up with veg chunkies and Tofu, but could have been a bit hotter.  The Massaman Curry with Tofu and Sweet Potato was delicious, but surprisingly sweet.  My Drunken Noodles with Beef was simply great - a mountain of wide flat noodles, a ton of thin sliced beef, and a wonderful sauce.  I inhaled it. I did not even connect the fact that the roaring throng might be drawn to my inebriated pasta.   The room slowly filled up, and even a few carousers in emerald beads and hats came in to chill over a Thai meal.  The atmosphere was calming and their welcome by the boss directed their energies well.  No problems.   I really liked House of Thai Cuisine and put it in the class of my local favorite, Aroi Thai in Southampton.  When I want the distinctive urban charm of Mayfair, I will find myself there again.

Steve and Lisa Landolfi opened this café/deli only a few weeks ago in Yardleyville, the shopping niche on Afton Avenue in Yardley, Pa., For those of you who are not familiar with that name, it is where the Pink Daisy is located.    The space is nicely decorated in a modern sensibility, yet having red checkered tablecloths even for breakfast.  Like that touch.  Too, there is a fun black and white of a very young Frank Sinatra in a supposed mug shot pose for the Bergen County (NJ) Sheriffs Department.  The criminal charge - Seduction.     And seduction is what you get at Landolfi's.  Everything is clean and neat.  The coffee brew is very good, and Steve goes back into the kitchen to cook my breakfast, disappearing for several minutes while the smells and sounds of grilling Scrambled Eggs, Sausage and Home Fries emanate, and slowly prepare me for a home cooked morning meal.  Lisa delivers the large plate, piled high with Rye Toast and the other staples, placing it down in front of me with confidence.  There was no doubt in her mind that I would enjoy my breakfast. Hmmm...  She was right.  The Eggs were light and fluffy, while the 5 link sausages browned enough to provide a crunchy bite, yet soft enough inside to protect its soft mellow - spiced heart.  Best of all were the Home Fries.  Thin sliced and olive oil fried to a wonderful taste.  Still soft and full of flavor.  The Rye Toast handled the butter and played well with the rest of the plate.  A little Tabasco on the Eggs and I was in business.    Seduction by small bites.   There oughtta be a law...

One door closes and another door opens.   We were visiting the New Castle National Historic District when the choking heat and humidity finally crashed down on town in a major thunderstorm. We hung out in the local tavern as long as we could, but still hoped to catch a look at the beautiful courthouse in the center of the old city. We were late, as it closed at 4:30, but we did walk around the perimeter and grounds for a while.   Heading across Delaware Street, I noticed a sign pointing to a coffee house in a cobblestone alley. Trader's Cove's entrance was deep in that alley, and it also had "Secret Garden" behind the building that held the cafe. We went in to load up on caffeine before heading home.  Their expresso area was tiny with small display for pastry and miniscule kitchen behind that. We ordered chai latte and a cappuccino, with two small pastries (apple fritter and slice of apple walnut coffee cake). Once prepared we sat it the back room to drink and nosh.  Turned out that there was musical entertainment waiting for us. Two guys with acoustic guitars played and sang for us. Called themselves The Grantwriters, because they both had worked for non-profits and that was what they did. Their style was 50s - 70s soft rock, a la The Everly Brothers sound. Very pleasant.  An unexpected interlude, but appreciated. We listened for a while as the room filled with a group of elders who seemed to be having a meeting there. They needed more seats, so we exited, walked through the Magic Garden, and took our leave of New Castle.   In fact, from beginning to end the whole Delaware Day had been so magical.  PS. The java and cakes were good, too. Local roaster and baker. Nice find we might have missed if the courthouse was still open.

Robin Hood, the robbing hoodlum of Sherwood Forest, was known for taking from the rich and redistribution to the less fortunate. In many ways this diner-esque restaurant in Southampton, PA, is true to that calling. They turn out large, very good meals at excellent prices for their loyal customers. Open 24/7, it is an anchor of the community.   We stopped in for a Presidents' Day breakfast to relax on a Monday morning without work. The house was a bit more than half full and we we're quickly taken to a small table along the windowed wall. Coffee arrived with the requested milk, and we gave our order for a short stack of french toast, side of hash, and a standard scrambled, bacon, potatoes and whole wheat. It was all quite good.  The frenchies were constructed of large slices of texas toast with caramelized edges and pleasant vanilla flavor. Two slices were more than enough. The corned beef hash was likewise crispy with mellow savoriness. The packaged syrup took it down a notch, where real maple would have made it exceptional. The eggs were the right consistency - just north of soft, and the taters plentiful. We both commented on our enjoyment of the meals, and compared them to other recent experiences that we're not as good at more expensive locations.   Robin Hood was definitely one to remember.  PRO TIP - We were disappointed upon getting the bill and finding an extra charge for bacon when the menu indicated it was part of a breakfast special. Either we missed the fine print, or there wasn't any, that the special was not available on holidays like Presidents' Day. Not that it would have made a difference, but it would have been nice to be told this before settling on our order. Our server said she didn't know about it, and she was advised to add the charge by management. Foolish move. Now they have to see this addendum to an otherwise positive review.  Maybe they thought I could afford it, and they were the ones in need, so a little extra pinch was merely income redistribution. No. It was just bad business.

This was a first visit to Ponticelli's, and on walking in first impressions were positive. Small dining room a little worn around the edges, but a bucket of charm at the bottom of Haines Road, Levittown, PA. We were taken by the friendly service provided by one of the family of owners/operators, and decided to try their dinners rather than settle for their neon signed pizzas.   That turned out to be our mistake.   It began auspiciously with a wonderful bowl of cream of potato soup. It was the final drop, but smooth, chunky, perfectly spiced and as good as grandma used to make. It came along with oven heated buttered Italian roll, and decent side salad with balsamic dressing. Then came the entrees, chicken francaise and veal saltimbuca, both over fettuccine.   They looked beautiful in their oval platters - nicely pan grilled with white wine lemon reduction glistening and the veal wrapped in prosciutto and sauteed spinach. The skill in the kitchen was obvious and I began to salivate at what we were about to consume. Unfortunately, the kitchen had a very heavy hand with the salt, and our excitement turned to disappointment as the first bite landed on the tongue and recoiled at the harsh taste of excess sodium chloride.   For the first time in many years we returned the plates to the kitchen hoping it could fix the problem. The same food returned to us minutes later. The pasta had been washed to remove the saline sauce from the noodles. That helped. However, the chicken and veal had not been repaired, and were as inedibly salty as before. We tried a few bites and just couldn't do it. We advised our hostess and she removed the dishes for a second time. When she returned we agreed what we would pay for and what should be removed from the bill. It was fair and I went to the cashier to pay.   I was saddened when the elder gentleman behind the counter attempted to blame us for the problem rather than simple accept the house mistake. Yet, I understood his instinct to defend his people. No point in arguing. I reminded him that we had not raised our voices and stood before him honorably. These things happen. Best just to move on with apologies and reasonable resolution.   Strangely, I still liked the place and the family making it run. We might return for the highly regarded pizza, but anything with a sauce in a pan would remain off limits.

There is a simple reason almost all the reviews for The Dutch on S. 4th Street are 5 Star. They deserve every star they get!   I am not a regular part of the weekend breakfast/brunch scene in Philly, but given a reason to be in the Pennsport neighborhood early on a Saturday morning, I willing partake of this lovely cottage industry.  The small corner shop is bright and airy, even on an overcast day.  Pale and deeper blues offset the whitewashed walls, giving the feel of happiness and cleanliness.  There are two levels.  Dining room in the front of the house with around 10 small wood top tables, and a step up in the rear with a traditional counter and semi-open kitchen.  The owners are very hands on, supervising, serving, cashiering and hosting.  The "Double Wilkum" hex suits the personality of this place.   We walked in around 8:30 to a half full room.  We were shown to one of the small deuces toward the back of the dining area, and had a fresh large cup of java steaming my glasses in less than a minute.  The menu is short and sweet.  But, don't be misled by its list of offerings that look like any other hash house.  Hidden within the deceptively simply names are the creative energies of these "Dutchmen."    My Huevos Rancheros was not very South of the Border, but certainly tipped their sombrero in homage to the venerable dish.  Rather than tortillas, upon a base of Corn Meal Waffle were placed a shiny Sunny Side Up Egg, melted Cheese,  Fresh Tomato Salsa, Guacamole, Black Beans and well grilled and pressed thick cut Bacon; covered in mild Hollandaise.  Pretty as a picture on the plate, the assemblage had a great taste, if not overwhelmingly Mexi heat.  I never thought of corn and waffles in the same breath, but it worked like a charm.  It held all the component parts together, and sent the meal in an unexpected direction.    My companion's Ham & Eggs with 3 Over Easys, interestingly delicious Hash Browns, and thick sliced Marble Rye, was devoured with little offered to me to taste.  I did manage a couple of sly bites when she went to the WC, and understood why she was not in a particularly sharing mood.    This neighborhood is gentrifying, but still maintains its authentic South Philly personality.  On a less muggy day, sitting at the sidewalk tables would be a nice way to watch this part of the world go by.

East Front Café is the dream of two locals to have their own business, and at least one of them was able to walk away from the trials and tribulations of working for someone other than themselves.  In this, at least Sandy, the spirited face and personality of this breakfast/lunch house, has succeeded.  Layoffs come and go, but they were willing to take their assets and start something new.  Sandy may have been a nurse in a past life, but she is a full frontal restauranteur now.  She excels in her house personality role, and has no trouble picking up where ever needed.  Her husband, still on the force at Trenton PD, lives his dream through her.    Six years are long enough to settle in and dig deep roots in this downtown neighborhood.  They have a good thing going.  The dining area is small, but their takeaways are strong.  To keep things streamlined and efficient, customers order at the cashier in front of the kitchen from the many wallboards describing the menu.  Breakfast is a short list, but lunch has a lot to offer.  From salads to sandwiches; wraps to paninis, the ingredients are fresh each day, and the product well stuffed with food and love.  Take a seat or stand aside, and your meal will be delivered unto you.   Sandy recommended the Baja Wrap on Wrap Wednesday.  I accepted her challenge on spinach tortilla.  It arrived full of black beans, onion, pepper, lettuce, chicken and a mild chipotle sauce.  The package included soft drink and cookie or granola bar.  It was tasty and filled me completely.  Atmosphere was active and noisy, full of table conversation from engaged folk.    East Front Café is a keeper, with awesome personality and legit plates to satisfy the hungry beast within.

El Primo Plaza is a Mexican multi store that offers grocery, bakery and taqueria within its walls. Right now, it is the apex for south of the border cuisine in Bensalem, PA. A good indication of its authenticity is the near totally Mexican customers shopping and eating there. Walking around the packed space it was clear that this was a family destination, with cakes and cookies for those with sweet teeth, and a broad menu for the rest of us seeking a more balanced diet. It was truly impressive.  I was seated at a deuce facing the refrigerated display of sliced cakes, all with large strawberries or other fruit and colorful icing. Tempting, but I knew better than to start with dessert. So, I selected a plate of a large cheese stuffed poblano chile with yellow rice and beans, and small watermelon juice. Service was friendly and easily bilingual.   The meal was made with all fresh ingredients and was delicious. It was covered in a red sauce that tasted like it had been blended and spiced just before pouring. And, the watermelon juice was cool, sweet and so refreshing - like sipping through a straw right out of the melon.   All the while I watched little kids and their parents looking at all the sweets, buying them, and carrying them out in small boxes and bags for consumption at home, or in house dessert. Not really sure who was going to eat all I saw purchased, but next time I'm going to borrow my neighbor's kids and let them lead me around to those beautiful cakes and buy a few for me.   Going to El Primo Plaza is crossing the border without need of passport, nor dealing with DHS.

One of the reasons healthcare has become more expensive than ever is the way hospitals have become medical centers, and medical centers a place with hotel-like accommodations and amenities to comfort not only the patient, but their families and visitors, as well. Capital Health - Hopewell is but one beautiful example of the new breed in institutional medicine.   On a recent visit to a client I was overwhelmed by two things. First, the crowded parking lot that left drivers hunting for space both front and back of the buildings. Finally found a few near the emergency room entrance, but still far from the circular drive. Second, given this, how empty the actual hospital was. There were very few people in the lobby, gift shop, cafeteria and halls on this midweek morning. Maybe everyone was is surgery or the gym taking Zumba classes.   But, it was obvious that little expense was spared in the building materials, with wood and stone everywhere. The private room I saw was hard to differentiate from a three or four star hotel, with the exception of the absence of bathroom Jacuzzi. My friend was very comfortable, indeed. The staff seemed to be a full complement, with doctors, nurses, technicians, therapists, and orderlies scurrying to and from assignments.   This is what they mean by, "...progressive, quality patient care with significant investments in our exceptional physicians, nurses and staff, as well as advanced technology." It includes a Level II regional trauma center, stroke center, perinatal, Level III NICU and emergency mental health screening facilities, and the region's first Pediatric Emergency Department (including, autism-friendly pediatric E.R.). And, what would a state of the art medical center be without a neuroscience institute, comprehensive breast care and digestive health centers, Cancer Center, Heart & Vascular Institute, and orthopedic joint replacement "Center of Excellence?" There are numerous awards associated with these efforts, and to be sure, they all cost exorbitant amounts of money.   No doubt, we will all be glad everything is there in Hopewell if we need it some day.

Admittedly, being objective about funeral homes is a bridge too far.    When a good friend departed this mortal coil a few days ago at an age too young, it was just a matter of hours before his family arranged for his "launch" to take place here.  One door closes. Another opens. The soft breeze in the trees is the soul waving goodbye.   The chapel was no different than any contemporary synagogue.  It was quietly dignified and naturally had us reflecting on the passing of one life to the next dimension, and our own frail mortality.    Lots of oak. Family reading poems. Rabbinic eulogy spoken personally from the memories of family and friends.    The Mourner's Kaddish. A prayer for the living. Of the greatness of the knowing Breath. For Peace. That despite profound loss, the One is to be praised.   "... and the world will carry on..."

What used to be Dragon Restaurant, has been under new ownership for several years, and been renamed, "Dragon of Newtown." The new team has done a good job improving quality and consistency.   I have been a regular lunch customer since the changeover.  The combo meals as with most Chinese places offer a cup of soup, egg roll and entree with choice of rice and the ubiquitous broccoli sprigs in a price range from $6.95 to $7.95, including hot tea, hard noodles and duck sauce.  Service is prompt and courteous.  The owner is usually present to oversee operations, and she makes a point of checking with the diners.  This is typical Chinese-American cuisine, tending to the sweet Cantonese style most liked by western palates.  If you go for this kind of Chinese food, this is a good place.  If you are more adventurous, or know and like the dishes served in China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, or our bigger cities' Chinese communities, then this may not float your boat.  If you like the spicy Szechuan style, you will have to hunt further in my reviews to find one. My usual lunch: Hot and sour soup, egg roll, orange beef and rice.  Satisfying.   2.20.13 - After further review, and multiple lunches, an upgrade to 4 stars is warranted. I must be a fan to continue to return here for lunch on an almost weekly basis.  6.10.18 - The Dragon relocated to the old Meglio's site about a year ago. Smaller space, but same kitchen skills. Prices for lunch specials are now up to $8.50, likely reflecting moving, renovation and rental costs. Worth the increase for the far above average Chinese/ American house that is as prepared for you to grab a table as for picking up the well packaged take out.   Philamena continues to run a solid, tasty operation.

Bravo Pho has replaced the earlier Vietnamese restaurant at this location, and all I can say is, "Hallelujah!"   There is no comparison between the two enterprises. Bravo is the real deal, not just a reasonable facsimile for folks who don't know from authentic Viet cuisine. The menu is extensive, and the noodle soup (pho) and rice dishes (com) are excellent. The owners and chef are legit from Hanoi, and know their way around a Vietnamese kitchen. No excuses necessary!  I was in the mood for their version of wonton soup, which was basically pho broth with a large number of dumplings rather than noodles in the hot bath.  Same accoutrements (Thai basil, sprouts, jalapeno slices, lime wedge), and same great taste, but with beef/pork stuffed wontons. I thought it was a very good version of the classic.   Why not five star? Well, because I am spoiled by visiting Vietnam and eating incredible food in both the north and south of the country. The small houses in Philly and Ocean Grove, California are often excellent, and this one may yet transport me to the Mekong River as those do. When that happens there will be five stars shining above its door.   Bravo to Bravo for being as slurpin' good as it is!

Second Street Pike Grill is a nicely laid out dining room with the look of gray marble on walls and table tops. The menu is oriented around fruit smoothies, breakfast and lunch. When I walked in the other day around 8:45 AM, I was the solitary customer and was told to sit anywhere. I did so at a table close to the front window after picking up their bifold menu at the counter. There was a large board on the back wall listing the smoothie possibilities. Not for nothing, I wondered why there were no fruit, nor blenders in sight. Maybe not the best way to market their signature product.   So, I slid over to their more traditional breakfast options and Made My Own Sandwich of turkey bacon, cheddar and fried eggs on English muffin with side of home fries included. It arrived open faced about ten minutes later.   It was okay, but could have been better @ $9. The bacon was thick, but lacked crispness. The eggs were fried to near dryness, where a bit of runny would have better integrated the elements. The potatoes were mealy and lacked the firmness of quality chunky morning spuds. On the other hand, the house coffee was very good.   Service was friendly and informative. Access was fine throughout.   2 Street Pike Grill - Attractive with good ideas that fall short in execution. A more deft hand at the hot steel would help.

Schenk's Family Bakery on Veree Avenue in the Fox Chase neighborhood of Philadelphia, has been in the flour, water and yeast business since the early twentieth century when their first generation started baking in Germany before immigrating to Germantown  and opening their shop in 1938. Both the family and the bakery have moved around, but always remained Philly centric. Their recipes travelled well.  Today, their storefront is small and lined with glass display cases and shelved walls, all full of their classic cookies, doughnuts, cupcakes, custom iced cakes and amazing pound cake. My small sample of half dozen doughnuts (glazed, vanilla iced, cinnamon sugar and powdered sugar) were all fresh, lightly yeasty and full of sweet flavor. They were perfect for accompaniment with hot coffee.   The vanilla pound cake was dense, moist and was solidly superior to any commercial effort I have eaten. Better even than Starbucks, which has been on my pedestal for a long while. It would have been great heated with a scoop of ice cream, but stood unapologetically on its own. Why they loaded it up on three sides with copious amounts of white icing is a mystery. It was truly an amazing sugar coating, but unnecessary given the quality of what it covered. Diabetic overkill.   That shelf of large Eagles playoff cakes looked great and gave comfort that they would be the hit of any party or cold afternoon tailgate at the Linc. Unfortunately, the sweetness would not be enough to change the outcome of the game to come.

We had a very good dinner here last week while in town for haircut and walkabout.   The floor plan is spacious, with bamboo and other strong Asian cues.  The staff was friendly and able to answer a few of my more technical questions about the dishes.  The insights provided led me to try the Hue Style Noodle Soup.  Turns out, this potage uses Egg Noodles rather than rice, and has a red cast due to the ground up Spicy Red Peppers and Hoisin mixed into the Beef Broth.  Otherwise, the same Sprouts, Thai Basil, Jalapeno Slices, and Lime Wedges were available as desired. The taste slides up the heat scale and adds another dimension to the otherwise wonderful flavors of the traditional Pho.  A lot of sliced Steak in there, too.  Very satisfying.   The Shrimp & Pork Roll app was fresh and delish with a sweet peanut sauce for dipping.   Will definitely return to try more of the menu.  Very enjoyable experience at Vietnam Palace.

Met up with a friend the other night at Hot On D Spot, a Trinidadian Restaurant at the western end of Nottingham Way in Hamilton, tres close to Trenton.  Don't know about you, but I had never tried Trini cuisine before; and in fact while I knew that Trinidad was an island in the Caribbean, I knew little of its history and culture.  My loss.   Trinidad was settled by a mix of folks who really did not want to be there - African slaves and Indian indentured servants (almost slaves).  They mixed together into a very interesting and spicy society.  The food evolved into something that did not look or taste like either's home cooking.  It was sort of like Indian with similar breads and curry orientation, but with meat on the bone dishes that were of a different continent.    Regardless, the food was great. We had some Doubles - basically Chickpea and Potato mash with Curry in small round Naan-like soft breads.  Very tasty and definitely a cousin of Samosa.  Next I ordered Roti with Boneless Chicken, while my companion went with Roti and Goat.  Both had a side of the same mix of Chickpea and Potato found in the Double.  I thought the Chicken outshined the Goat.  It was tender and in small pieces long cooked in a spice pot.  The Goat was still on the bone.  It required more work to eat it, and to my palate, was darker and more gamey than I like.    The accompanying Roti was superb.  It was large and folded up on the plate, but as it was taken out and ripped apart to be used to pick up the meats and veggies, it had elasticity and a ground Chickpea and spice dusting on the inside that added taste and a curiously fine grit to the experience.  I could not finish it.    I hope to learn how to eat with one hand without using utensils and just pinching the food with the Roti.  It is much harder than it looks, especially if you try not to get your hand dirty.    The owners and staff were very friendly.  We engaged in a running conversation about the food and life in Trinidad.  Fascinating.  The house only has four tables and a fridge with cold drinks.  I stopped beforehand to pick up a six pack of Red Stripe to add to the festivities.   This one is a definite keeper.

Ironically, our plan was to walk over to 3rd & Chestnut after taking care of a few things in Chinatown.  The original destination was Han Dynasty in Old City so we could sample what was reputed to be among the best Szechuanese in Philly.    But, as John Lennon so cuttingly observed, "Life's what happens while you're busy making other plans..."  On our way down Arch we saw the sign for Szechuan Dim Sum Restaurant.  We had been looking forward to a brisk after rain walk, but on seeing this convenient alternative, we wordlessly took each other's hand, made a hard right and jaywalked directly to their front door. Not much traffic on this Saturday afternoon, or we might have been less impulsive.   We walked in to an almost empty house, with seven wood top tables and a mirrored wall.  There were two servers, also acting as hosts.  The young woman shepherded us to a table mid-shop, and dropped off two menus.  She asked what we wished to drink, and brought a nice aromatic hot black tea moments later.  The set up of fork, spoon and sticks was wrapped in a heavy paper nap with a rose printed on the right spot for the package to appear perfectly placed for casual elegance.  Nice touch.   The menu was bilingual so my companion had an easy time with descriptions and photo captions. She went quickly to the Spicy Crisp Intestine, and left the rest of the ordering to me.  Up for the challenge, I opted for the Szechuan Style Spicy Chicken (basically, salt/pepper dry pot chicken), and Spicy Eggplant in Garlic Sauce.  Wasn't in the mood for DanDan, Wonton, nor Mapo.    They arrived in that sequence, with about 5 minutes between each delivery.  All were very good to excellent.  The Intestine was thin cut, lightly fried, and loaded with Red Chili, Scallions, Celery and Peanuts.  Good heat, but not a conflagration, as I did not see any Szechuan Black Peppercorns in the mix; thus no anesthetic effect.  It took you to the edge of the fire, burned your eyelashes, but did not throw you in.    The Chicken dish was a variation of Salt/Pepper Dry Pot Style Chicken morsels, well dusted in a spicy ensemble, and flash fried twice so there was little oily residue.  Tender meat with more Red Chili, Peanuts, Scallions, and a sprinkling of Sesame Seed on top.  The heat quotient was perhaps a few degrees higher than the Intestines, with more spice during and after cooking.  Very tasty, but perhaps the weakest link in our dinner chain.    The biggest and best surprise was the Eggplant.  It was sliced into lengths of a four/five inches, skinned, and somehow wok-ked to give a mild crispiness.  How did they do that? It was a neat trick, and it was piled high on a deep dish that created an island surrounded by red, shining, heat vapored, sauce.  The heart of the nightshade remained soft and contained a hint of sweetness.  This combo tag team between the Red Chili flame and unexpected sugar underneath was delicious and fun.    We thoroughly enjoyed this repast.  If asked to compare with other hot houses in Ctown, it would fall somewhere just below Emei (across the street), on the same plane as Four Rivers and Spice C, and above Traditional Szechuan.  It really reminded me of the old Chili Szechuan on Baltimore Avenue, before it moved to larger digs and lost its edge.    Gotta say that this block of Arch Street has it going on!  Han Dynasty will just have to wait.

Farnsworth Avenue was all dress up for the Sidewalk Sale going on Friday afternoon.  Looked great!   I was in the mood to sample the Tomato Pie at Marcello's Restaurant & Tomato Pie, but as it was not offered by the slice, and the small pie was a glaring $16, I decided it would have to wait for another time when the cost was more in line with the occasion. It might be awesome, but it would have to knock my socks off.   So, I ordered the Eggplant Parm Sandwich with a two buck Side Salad (total cost: $10. plus tip).  It took a while for it to arrive, and I had ample time to look around the barroom where I sat.  Very attractive cross between Colonial and contempo styles.  The room was mostly full with leisurely diners enjoying this mid August afternoon.  The side patio was temporarily closed for construction, but it looked like it would be a nice place for a cooler evening al fresco dinner.    Maybe next time.    My meal arrived.  It looked great on the plate with toasted Italian loaf seared to melt and seal the Mozza and thin sliced Eggplant within.  There was more bread than veggie, and the diameter made it necessary to eat with knife and fork.  The Eggplant was well cooked; pleasantly soft and mixed well with the cheese and Tomato Sauce.  It is a matter of personal preference, but I prefer the double sautéed approach to Eggplant and the use of a light coating of spiced bread crumbs to give it more texture and flavor.  This dish was done in a single cooking style, and without the crumbs; thus, somewhat light on taste and interest.  There could have been more sauce as well, perhaps on the side, to provide more oomph.   Marcello's is a nicely appointed house, with attentive staff, and it clearly aspires to be a higher end Casa Italiana. In this it mostly succeeds.  But, I won't know for sure if it is all that until I take my first bite of its tomato pie.

COFFEE STOP REVIEW:  When the sign on the door of the nearby bagel shop said it was closed permanently, I looked for an alternative source for the caffeine fix I needed to account for my earlier than normal awakening to attend to a court matter in Mt. Holly, NJ. Luckily for me there was a Wawa right down the road.   It was an old version convenience store, sans gas pumps and large food preparation area. Still, it had 6 types of java and a fixings island. All this boy needed. The Guatemalan medium roast caught my attention, and I poured it into a 16 oz container with a milk lightener to taste.   I pulled in the first sip as I settled back in my car. Hot, strong and pleasantly robust, it was just what the doctor ordered. Had me humming and beating my fingers on the wheel in minutes. When I walked into the judge's Chambers I was fully equipped to handle whatever my adversary threw my way.

New China House down on Haines Road, Levittown, PA, is the successor to Zhang's, the mildly popular dine in/take out joint. The transfer of ownership took place three years ago, but this news wasn't shared with Yelp for some reason. Too bad, because it turns out that despite the divey appearance the Chinese American food is better than average. The place deserves some recognition.   The House is family run with wife up front and hubs in apron beating the wok. Strictly take out, I was told I could not eat my lunch on the one table on the floor. Okay, I'll leave. I can stand the rejection, but if you had permitted me a few minutes to eat, you would have heard me compliment your rendition of General Tso's Chicken as not being too breaded, with decent sauce, and appreciation for throwing in a few Szechuan peppers for the extra heat I requested.   Too, you would have heard me say that the wonton soup tasted fresh and that the wontons were fairly thin skinned and filled with decent ground beef/pork. Finally, that the pork fried rice had a natural color and good texture full of peas, carrots, onions and sprouts. Overall, a satisfactory lunch at a very reasonable price.  Just wish I had been there to let them know. Guess this review will have to do.

I have been fortunate not to know anyone inpatient at St. Mary Medical Center for many years, but I continue to come here periodically as part of my effort to maintain my health.  Their radiology department is still the nearest source of X-rays, CT Scans, MRI's, etc.    I was there again last week for a couple of scans requested by my family doctor.  The hospital itself has undergone a facelift over the past few years, and it shows.  The lobby is larger with more seating area, while the registration area is now out of sight.  The hall to radiology passes both a serenity garden with a glass wall for viewing, and the original cafeteria, which has always been a decent place for a bite.    I was in and out of the building in under an hour.  The check in was fast and courteous, and the lab technicians working with me were relaxed, yet professional.  They made the ordeal of passing through the CT Scanner as easy as possible, when required to remain still and hold your breath with arms overhead six times as the mobile bed slides through the huge spinning magnets.   Still; no harm, no foul.  I walked out into the waning spring day feeling better about taking care of myself.    St. Mary seems on top of its game for my purposes.

When Café Ole, right down the street from Downtown Deli had a sign on the window saying that it was closed and for sale, I looked up Warren Street and saw that the Deli was open for business this overly warm November morning.  I asked the folks working out front whether they were serving breakfast, and received an affirmative reply.    Say no more. Just point me to the coffee.    I settled into a table on the raised balcony/dining area and in short order a friendly woman approached to ask what I wanted to eat.  I didn't need a menu and I asked for a Sausage, Egg and Cheese Sandwich on a Kaiser Roll.  She nodded and said that particular item was, "...one of my specialties."    Well, all right!  And, she was right.  Her creation arrived a few minutes later.  The Eggs were Scrambled, rather than Fried, and I found that I liked the overall texture and taste better that way.  The Sausage Patty was slightly crunchy on the edges, which was unusual.  I couldn't tell if it was done purposely or not, but it was another surprising plus.  The Roll was fresh and chewy with a light yeastiness.  Nice.   The Coffee was some unknown brand to me, but went down hot and smooth.   Prices were lower than in the burgs, likely reflecting the lower rent paid in the core of this capitol city.  I made a mental note to keep Downtown Deli on the circuit for breakfast before court, and potentially, lunch, afterwards.

I have never seen a larger breakfast menu than at Cracker Barrel. It is all very traditional and Southern, with huge portions of everything. Prices reasonable, too. Yet, this is not the place to go if you want to avoid temptation to over indulge on very fattening dishes.  Simply unavoidable here.  Even the "healthy" oatmeal is loaded with sweet fruity things that sound good for you, but really are not. Too much sugar and processing with everything you eat.   However, if you feel like chowing down with country fried steak, biscuits and gravy, fat bacon, sausage ground from various animals, and lots of eggs, there are few places that can fulfill your fantasies like Cracker Barrel.  That, and a cute-to-death country store up front that is Americana gone to seed.  Where to look first?!   I was here for a business breakfast suggested by the other guy.  I was curious, because Cracker Barrel was new to me.  I've seen them around, but always thought it was more a gift shop than a restaurant. I was wrong. It is really both. I tried to order a simple breakfast sandwich on a biscuit, but was advised that was not on the menu because their biscuits were too small. Instead, I could have it on thick sourdough-like white bread, complete with eggs and cheese, but not with the meat on the bread.  It had to be a separate plated side.  Okay. Whatever. Do it your way. Surprise me.   What arrived was a large plate with oversized toasted bread, two fried eggs (medium hard), and a large dose of melty yellow Colby.  Two medium sized pork sausage patties were on a separate dish. I had to cut and assemble each forkful bite.  I didn't mind, but it was hard to believe the kitchen could not do this so that the pieces had time to meld together.  It was all decent and tasty.  The homefries mound which they brag about was also okay, but perhaps a bit to mashed and not as chunky as preferred.   The coffee was average, and flowed freely.    Can't say that I fell in love with Cracker Barrel, but I understood how that would be possible for people who like big breakfasts loaded with meat, eggs, cheese and/or pancake mix.  For me, it was just overload.

COFFEE STOP REVIEW:  Driving south on Route 130 (perhaps the ugliest road in New Jersey) on the way to court in Camden, I knew I needed a caffeine boost to compensate for my early start to the day. Up ahead I spied the golden arches on my side of the road and pulled in.   They had double drive thru lanes which seemed to be moving slowly for the cars in front of mine. When I reached the order kiosk I realized that the order taker was taking his time, repeating the order and asking if he had it right. Nothing wrong with that. I requested a small coffee with milk.   He asked me if I wanted to buy the milk to put in the coffee. What?! Apparently, this store only offered complimentary mini-moos for java, but milk was a luxury extra charge item. This surprised and annoyed me, and I wondered whether this dude had it right. Would McDonald's be that dumb as to refuse to open a house bottle of milk for such orders, or was this an untrained part timer gone rogue? My decision; two creamers, please. I wasn't going to pay for this bizarre policy.   Anyway, the coffee was a fine generic blend, hot and strong. It did its job, and I went about the rest of my day.

Kumo Asian Bistro is in reality a Chinese sushi joint in one of the many shopping centers along Bethlehem Pike in North Wales, Pa.  As such, they offer a nice facility with broad menu that is primarily rolls and cold fish, with minimum dishes from China and Thailand. Everything is decent, but nothing stands out as exceptional, requiring return visits, unless you are from the area.  It is very much a variation of the sushi theme, without high artistry. Still, service was fine, and I had no real quarrel with what we ate.   Meeting friends we were able to order extra dishes and sample everything placed before us. We ordered several apps, and two rolls (sorry, didn't catch the names).  We began with their "Sushi Pizza," a good tasting, if poorly named, mix that reminded of its Italian namesake only in its shape.  It was just as much "taco."  Crisp tortilla-like base with a pleasant load topside. Fun and enjoyable.  Their calamari was tempura style, which was not as good as the original in that it lacked good texture, and once cooled, returned to a too-chewy amorphousness.  The beef negiyaki was more interesting as a semi-spicy veggie combo wrapped in beef.  In truth, would not get either of those again. The two rolls ordered by our friends were fine offerings, one topped with eel.   This experience was more about our conversation than our meal, so the food was comparatively less important than what we were talking about. Still, the room and the platters were a good backdrop for us. We had room, space and time to relax and enjoy the moment. We never felt rushed, and our server engaged with us when appropriate.   Prices were reasonable given everything involved.  There are no doubt better sushi houses around, but this one was right for the occasion.

Two Slices & a Drink Review  The first thing you notice when approaching Mannino's Pizza is the pollution coming from the tobacco shop next door.  Heavy cigar smoke hangs in the air, making it an unpleasant challenge to go inside.  Public officials should not permit such uses near food establishments as is a negative and so unhealthy.   But, after getting inside, this Italian house is fairly typical of the genre.  Booths up front. Kitchen counter in the rear.  Dining room to one side.  Clean and pleasant.  I ordered a slice of Tomato Pie and another Regular with a soft drink.  The pizzaman behind the counter was friendly and understood with a nod when I asked for the reheat to be "well done."    That is what I received.  The slices were placed on a large plate (so much nicer than using paper), and were steaming nicely as I carried them to my table.  A peak at the undercarriage showed nice scorch marks from the oven, and the aroma of tomato, garlic and basil wafted pleasantly in my face.  The Tomato Pie was very good.  The crust held firm when picked up, and released a loud crunch when bitten.  In addition to the above ingredients, the sauce was mildly sweet, which I prefer.  A nice slice from beginning to end.  The Regular Slice was not quite as athletic.  Its point wilted when lifted from the crusty rim due to an excess of cheese that was too heavy for the underside to endure.  Folding the slice was a help, but it also provided a crease for the extra oil to run off onto the plate.  The sauce was okay, but overwhelmed by the cheese.  I prefer more balance between the two topsides.    Still, I was satisfied, if not ecstatic with my evening snack.  The place is comfortable and the staff is friendly and capable.    Just wish the dudes next door had better ventilation that didn't leave a cloud of Perdomo exhaust where non-smokers must inhale.

Croyden has its full share of divey bars and used-to-be-great taverns where a working person could belly up and grab a few mugs of frosty before heading home, or before bed.  Dog & Bull was one of those places in yesteryear, but is not THAT place any more.  That it is a way cool micro bar on the tracks next to the train station, is true, but what the owners have done with it brings it to another level of coziness and good grubbiness.   It is now a favorite watering hole for anyone looking for a cool place for a few drinks or a better than good lunch or dinner.  It is tiny.  But, they have a great number of crafts on draft, plus a menu that keeps you entertained.  So, even though I walked in thinking we would have a drink and conversation, we ended up sitting at a high top over dinner. The place is intriguing.   We both drank the hard Cherry Cider, a first for me, but likely not the last.  It was cool, mildly sweet, and oh, so, refreshing.  My Fried Chicken was done well with Mashed and lightly steamed String Beans.  It satisfied my recent addiction and it was interesting to see how different this dish could be from the standard KFC.  I did not taste my partners Salmon Wrap, but it was large and she stopped talking after she bit off the first chew.  Must have been good.   Before leaving, the live music began.  An acoustic set by a local artist whose first cover of a Neil Young classic was decent.  He was game, but playing at the back end of the barroom is not the best way to grab everyone's attention.  While his guitar and voice were amped, it was not so loud as to disturb anyone who wanted to continue conversing.  Nice touch.  I really like what they've done to the place, and will return for more of the cool atmosphere, good drinks, and well produced bar/comfort food.

Santangelo's Cafe is a down to earth example of creative adaptive reuse of old urban factories, this one in Norristown, PA. It is a tiny place with entry around the back of the large red brick structure, requiring attention to signs on the street directing where it is hidden. Plenty of parking back there.   This family run breakfast, brunch & lunch joint has been going for 15 years, and the siblings certainly know how to work together. They are friendly and justly proud of what they do in the community. I sat at the six stool counter overlooking the small kitchen. Although a curtain separates customer view from flying spatula, the sounds of breakfast making are easily heard and entertaining.   Coffee was decent, and my ask for milk over Mini Moos, graciously met. Unfortunately, it took too long to get a refill, as the curtain blocked the staff view of customers, and the floor person was obliviously attached to her phone. Yet, the short stack french toast was very good. Nice egg, vanilla and cinnamon mix for dipping, and good caramelization.   Overall, Santangelo's is a strong find on the post industrial streets of Norristown. A little polish on customer service would elevate this earnest cafe to a higher level to match the quality of its menu.

Take out only Chinese American shop on Lincoln Highway (Rt. 1), Levittown, PA. All the usual suspects, including General Tso's Chicken, my choice. The place needs a thorough cleaning, especially around the floor to near ceiling stack of soda cases around the cooler.   My combo included a heavy load of fried rice dyed dark brown from the bouillion in which it was cooked,  and a smallish egg roll that while crisp was 95% cabbage. The actual chicken was pretty good with the extra heat from a few Szechuan chilies I requested. The portion was impressive. I couldn't finish all that was stuffed into the plastic container.   Overall, if the main course is what matters most, 21 Chinese Kitchen did chicken well, with  respectable sauce. The rest of the meal was mostly empty filler, not worth consuming. If you figure out how to get just what you want without the other stuff, a satisfying meal is within your grasp.

I know Johnny G's Famous Pizza on Brownsville Road, Trevose, PA, is supposed to be all about tomato pie, steak sammies and other Italian goodies, but my first visit ended up being all about their burgers.   They said they were half pounders made from never frozen Angus beef, with assorted toppings and a side of fries for an extra buck fifty. Brioche style buns held them together and offered sturdy handholds for the heft of the large slider. I realized the risk from bypassing their signature dishes, but why all the menu space for burgers? Why the interesting combinations?   I had the answers when the large plate with Mighty Mike Burger was placed before me by the pleasant server in training. The roll top shined like it had been polished. The edge of the beef was thick, with a tip of bacon peaking out on top of melted swiss cheese. My request for medium finish was honored precisely.   And it was a great Burger! Hot, drip juicy, flavorful. Russian dressing adding a sweet creamy note. A joyful surprise first bite to last. Beautiful pink at heart, and true to its credo of never having seen the inside of a freezer.  Better than Guys, Shack, Smash, Robin and many others with catchy names; at about half the price.   How do they keep this joint a secret?!

Ting Wong on 10th Street in Chinatown is one of the old school houses specializing in Guangdong cuisine. The abundant evidence hangs in the front window where ruby roasted pork and duck are displayed on hooks as savory invitations to come inside with strong appetite.   The dining room looks nicer than I recall from my last visit sometime in the last decade. Newer furniture now graces the house, and maybe even renovated floors and lighting. The place is still packed on weekends with people young and old eating their fill of the excellent meat kitchen up front and/or the soup and noodle possibilities in back.   We had a bit of both. We ordered congee with ancient egg and beef chow fun from the latter and a plate of roast pork and duck over rice from the former. Everything was good to great. The congee was thick and loaded with black hard boiled egg, morsels of pork and chive on top. So much better tasting than it sounds! The pork and duck dish was almost all meat, perfectly roasted to a dark ruby bark and only the slightest fat for extra flavor. The chow fun was the weakest entre, as it seemed a touch overcooked without sufficient brown sauce to compensate. Still, the taste was there, it just needed more lubrication.   We liked our meal so much that we ordered half a duck and equal quantity of pork to take home. It was just as good tonight, two days later.   Ting Wong is a wonderful tradition in Philly Chinatown, with mostly great southeast China cuisine, great prices and a strong following. It is totally old fashioned. You would not want it any other way.

Covello's on South Broad Street, Trenton, has been at this location for thirty years. It's been at least twenty since the last time I walked in their front door. Now that I am working downtown again this old joint is back on my lunch rotation.   It hadn't changed that much. Still a big room with many booths and counter service along a front wall. Still the standard Italian pizzeria with pies, calzones, hot & cold sandwiches, salads, pasta and platters. I ordered an eggplant parmesan sandy and picked my booth to await its preparation and delivery.  It was very, very good.   Lightly breaded thin slices of nightshade, slightly crisp outside and soft within. Enough melted mozza to promote textural integrity, but not too much to swallow the intended star of the show. Fresh, basil sweet chunky sauce dolloped on top, and all of it housed in a really good Italian roll.  It was a foot long; cut in half. So much for $6.95!  I needed knife and fork to go after the heart of the sandwich, and then ate half the delicious bread toward the end, almost like dessert. Crusty, warm and flavored with everything it had held in its once molten valley.   So assuring that Covello's hasn't missed a beat in all these years.

What for decades had been a dilapidated ramshackle old corner at Langhorne-Yardley Road and Stony Hill Road has been nicely renovated into a small commercial complex with Edgewood Café anchoring the intersection.  The architect and builder did a very good job.  The property is now very attractive.   The Café feels both old and new.  Narrow plank wood floor and exposed beam high ceiling provide a light airiness, while the dark tones of the booths offer a sense of colonial times.  I sat at the counter with several other guys and had a nice overview of the operation.  The breakfast menu is two pages with an adequate variety of options and flexibility.  My wait person suggested that the fancy egg dishes were very good, but I opted for a full stack of French Toast and a mug of coffee.  A note said the toast could be made, "crunchy," so I asked about that.  Breading with crushed Captain Krunch. Maybe next time.   My breakfast arrived a few minutes later on a large oval plate, dusted with powdered sugar, and a small dish of butter on the side.  The syrup was brought up from under the counter, and had a thick pour.  Not maple, but decent.  The menu describes the dish as a "Texas" slice of bread.  Not sure as I did not measure it, but perhaps the extra width required more time in the egg bowl to assure full saturation, as the middle was slightly dry.  Not a serious shortcoming and easily corrected. My coffee mug was refilled thrice, and it was a good commercial blend from a Bunn drip.   One piece of advice I would offer is that the servers smile more.  They are helpful and efficient, but they put off a vibe that they are not comfortable in their jobs.  Perhaps, they are naturally shy young women, but learning to act like a wait person will improve their job approval, and tips. That is something management can talk to them about, and tell them to act more relaxed and try to have some fun while being professional.   PS. A sign at the back door/main entrance would be a big help for newcomers, as it is not obvious where the café is, nor how to enter from the parking lot.

This was my first visit to any Dollar Tree and I was surprised they could fill a supermarket sized store with so much cheap merchandise. I was sent there to pick up helium balloons for my son's Eagle badge court of honor the next day. Wasn't sure if 21 of those shiny boys would lift me off the ground or fit into my car, but I was going to find out.   Turned out that this Family Dollar was Balloon Central HQ. Right above the cash register were a few hundred already inflated stars and flags in a multitude of colors, with drawers along the back wall with dozens of additional choices. A large tank of helium with special nozzle to fit the mouth of the balloon stood at the ready.   The shop wasn't crowded and the young cashier had time to pull out the red, silver and blue ones already floating above her, and then retrieve the Stars and Stripes from inventory and fill them from the tank. They were truly a buck each, despite the amount of work required to prepare them for me. She was efficient and friendly throughout.   I managed to stuff all in my trunk and back seat without a loss, although that was all I saw in the rearview.   They looked great around the reception area after the ceremony today. Family Dollar made this piece of our day a pleasure to make happen, and would certainly use them again in a helium high voiced New York minute.

They've done a really nice renovation of the old Toll House, turning it into something useful and attractive again after decades of neglect. It will no doubt become a keystone of the new Village @ Newtown that Brixmor is developing.   We should hope that Nina understands Newtown history and its deep roots directly from William Penn's founding of his New Town in Bucks County, through its 88 years as the county seat, our central role during the Revolutionary War, and even the significant impact of anti-independence sentiment that tore the populis apart before final victory. In Newtown, it is ever more than selling ice cream. It is also about helping people see our story all around them. Nina's is in the unique position to do so with every lick.   So, yes. Their fresh, hot waffles taste great, and their proprietary ice cream recipes are sweet creamy delights, that measure well against the other milk churn outfits in town. Still, beyond the novelty, it will be known by how it contributes to the overall Newtown experience.   With so many new food outlets coming on line in their immediate vicinity, we can only hope that Nina has enough parking, that it survives the competition by taking full advantage of its special home, and that it calls on surrounding history as a big part of why it deserves our dollars.

Not a fan of the Chipotle approach to Mexican food, I was disappointed that the new Mariachi Grill in Campus Town on the edge of The College of New Jersey adopted that process. Their shops on Parkway in Ewing and Quakerbridge in Hamilton are the traditional full kitchen variety, and are pretty good representations of Mexican American cuisine. Although the "pick your ingredients" can be considered  the way to customize a taco or burrito, to me it seems more the way to limit the menu to only a few possibilities, while preparation of the elements in advance means you often secure overcooked and dried out parts. A look at all the choices on the steam table behind the counter, offered proof of theory. The steak, chicken and ground beef all seemed desiccated and lacking energy.   They were out of the al pastor (roast pork & pineapple), and the only remaining juicy-looking choice was the carnitas (BBQ pork). I went with that in their duo taco plate (rice, black beans, lettuce, tomato, lime, radish & pico). The double tortilla soft shell kept its poise throughout the meal, with minimal leakage. They were tasty and well spiced. The rice and beans were forgettable. At just under $9 with drink, the price was fair. I left belly full.   Still, I prefer other Mexican dishes like chili rellenos and flautas, not to mention fresh fish and fruit drinks,  much more than tacos, burritos and quesadillas, which all have the same contents with different packaging. Such variety was not on the menu there, although they are in their other tiendas.   If all you desire is basic Mexifast food, you can be satisfied at Mariachi. But, Mexican cuisine is far more diverse and delicious than portrayed here, and deserving of exploration and ravishing. There are plenty of those places across Trenton, Hamilton and Hightstown. Once seduced by those amazing spicy senoritas, it is difficult to really enjoy the Chipotle approach to South of the Border cooking.

Pop's Bagels sits in the shadow of Johnny Apple's in Holland, PA. It is a small shop with a few tables, counter and bagel bins along the walls. It is bright white, and on a sunny late September morning the room was very inviting. The folks working there were nearly as bright and cheerful. I ordered my customary onion bagel with butter and swiss, not toasted, and retreated to the side of the room to wait and watch.   Families came in for bags of rounders, and a few occupied the tables available. My coffee and bagel were called, and I grabbed and walked out again into the morning light. The parking lot is far larger than the store so there is never a shortage of spaces.   The bagel was fresh and pliant, with a mix of both savory (onion) and sweet (dough) flavors. The crust lacked any crispness and I couldn't differentiate between the skin and inner texture. Too, the meat of the bagel although light and chewy, lacked the air pockets found in traditional ones. Perhaps, more boiling or lye exposure would create that texture.   Many people prefer this style bagel, but it is not my desired finish.

Eddington House down on Hulmeville Road south of Street Road, Bensalem, PA, is a local bar with a decent kitchen and strong following. It is rustic with knotty pine barroom and dining area, and plenty of TVs for the sports contingent. Service is shared among all the floor people, who are collectively friendly and seem always on top of their game.   We ordered their signature Reuben on Rye and a Pepperjack Burger from their new large format menu. Sam Adams Winter draft and Coor's Light wet are whistles. $2.50 domestic drafts were greatly appreciated. We watched the Sixers take on the Hornets and end their losing streak by 8. (They really have to work on those turnovers!)   Both sammies were very good. The corned beef was sufficiently fatty to have plenty of taste, especially in the mix with melted swiss and Russian dressing pressed into toasted rye. The half pound slider had not been frozen and was served the requested medium finish, with Pepperjack adding some zing and straw onions a pleasant crunch. They had no problem subbing cole slaw for fries, although I sampled them on my beautiful companion's plate and they were crisp and nubby.   The only knock on the joint was the loudness of the bar, which circulated throughout due to poor acoustics. Made for challenging conversation at times. Aside from that Eddington House is a nice hangout for brew and bite in this part of Bucks County.   Quality, pricing and service are all right.

Pho & More 2 is a pleasant facility, nicely appointed to give it a clean open aire. The row of windows up front let in a lot of light for a bright, colorful sense that helps accent the casual semi-tropical feel of the place.  The service is equally light and friendly.    Having read here that the pho was not the strongest aspect of the house, we went in another direction.  We ordered Goi Cuon (Summer Rolls) as an app, with Pad Thai Shrimp and Com Thit Nuong (Broken Rice w/ BBQ Pork).  All were quite good. The Rolls were cool and crisp with a smooth Peanut Dipping Sauce.  The Pad Thai, while not the best ever, was a solid contributor with a good number of midsized shrimp and a mildly tangy sauce.  The Com dish offered a load of tasty Pork strips, Rice, and Pickled Veggies.  Each table had large bottles of Sriracha and Hoisin to use as needed to reach the desired personal taste of spice and heat.   We lingered after dinner to chat with our server about business and our time in Vietnam.  He was from HCMC and had been here only a year.  We were able to compare our experiences, and came away feeling very comfortable in his work home. Whatever may have been lacking in attaining haute cuisine status was compensated by the relaxed coziness of the shop and friendly interaction with the staff.    It is a place I can return for an easy meal when in the area to shop the Asian markets.

Stopped into JB Bakery after court the other day.  I had driven by many times, but never at a moment when I could check it out.
