This is a traditional bakery with wall to wall refrigerated display cases showing rainbows of cakes, donuts, cookies, as well as a coffee service station for those in need of java.  Everything looked great, and the young women working there were friendly and very helpful with making selections.    I ordered a half doz Glazed and Vanilla Iced Donuts for the office, and one Carrot Cake Cupcake for a home dessert.  None of them were as good as I had expected from just looking at them.  The donuts were a bit past their prime when I picked them up before noon.  Their edges were becoming hard, and the heart of the dough was no longer soft and fresh.  They were still pretty good, just not the stuff of deserving a ringing endorsement.    The Carrot Cake Cupcake was packaged well in a well designed plastic container, but I found the ample icing to be tasty, but lighter and less dense than true butter cream or cream cheese.  The actual cake was okay, but not the moist carroty base of a true carrot cake.  Again, it was decent, but far from great.   The coffee was brewed as I waited, and was fine.   Overall, this place is fun to explore, and perhaps there are other more delicious options within.  Still, I am a donut/cupcake person, and I would not rush back for more of them.

Ritz Diner at the intersection of Roosevelt Blvd and Rhawn, is a fairly typical roadside diner in Northeast Philadelphia. Its menu is likewise standard fare, with a full page of breakfast possibilities on the back. That's what I was there for, and it only took a minute to decide I wanted their Ritz Omelet (onion, green pepper, tomato and hot Italian sausage), with Rye Toast and bottomless mug of Java.   Service was very good and it was beautifully presented within minutes of ordering. First observation was that it looked to be a three egger with filling enough for a smaller shell. Its pants were too big for its body, as both ends were a couple inches of egg without anything within. It tasted fine although the heat from the sausage failed to materialize very often. It was still enough for me, especially with the well buttered toast and refills of coffee brought to me by my friendly server. So, I am not complaining, but only making an observation, and suggestion that if I was aware of this imbalance, others would be too, and perhaps adjustments should be made.   Didn't see much in the way of in-house bakery goods, nor a bar, nor even a traditional counter with spinners for the solitary traveler.    Adequate parking in front.

This is one of the Einstein Brothers Bagel franchises that has not been accurately identified on Yelp*.  As with all the other Einsteins I have customered, this one has in-house baked fresh bagels for any meal. The floor plan is large, the tables and high tops are not too close to each other, and in warm weather there is a small outdoor deck with a few tables.  There are more varieties of bagels than in most local shops, including those with jalapenos, cinnamon, asiago, pumpernickle, etc., along with the standards found almost everywhere.  The coffee is better than average, and its beans/ground are for sale. The staff is young, well trained and friendly.  This particular location often has seniors meeting at the large tables having a good time.  Perhaps, this is because there are a few assisted living facilities in the area, and this is a nice place to hang out as a mall walking alternative.  There are also doctors, nurses, lab techs stopping in on their way to/from the local hospital.  This is not my favorite bagel, as the outside is soft, not firm or almost crunchy, as I prefer them.  It is more like regular bread in a bagel shape.  Still, the freshness and customizing makes it acceptable when in need, or close by.   Many people enjoy bagel sandwiches, but I am not one of them.  Still, there are many options on the menu.  Their Bagel Dog (hot dog wrapped in a thin bagel skin) is pretty good.  Their daily soups are okay, and they have soup/sandwich combos at good prices.  Bottom Line - It is an OK place for a quick stop or sitting around for a while, but if a better bagel is what you need, a visit to Bagel Train in Yardley is your next stop.

This health food and nutrition shop has been located at the same location for decades. Walking into this converted residential bungalow, I was overwhelmed by the floor to ceiling shelving packed with everything from vitamins to dry goods to frozen foods. The store has aged well, and has become as much a cultural museum, as a retail outlet designed to assist in maintaining health.   We stopped in to purchase more supplements that had run out at home. A clerk who worked there approached with a welcoming smile and showed us where what we sought was resting on the highest shelf in the house. She climbed a stepstool to reach them. They had a sale going on, and the price was very fair. We bought two.   I loved the old wooden built-ins housing the drygoods, granolas and nut mixes. They would look great in our kitchen (alas). I could see how the claustrophobic might be challenged by the stuffed to the gills nature of this tiny store. But, for me, it was a cozy room that instant relaxed me and captured my curiosity.   Now that our usual health food shop has closed its doors, The Natural Foods Store may well become our regular stop for nutritional maintenance.

So, what's a "flexitarian?"   I didn't know either until I sat at the counter in the Silver Diner, and had it explained for me in their elaborate menu. Apparently, when health consciousness is a priority, local sourcing predominates and the offerings change with the seasons, you have created a flexitarian restaurant. So, although its stainless steel & glass shell suggests a traditional Jersey diner experience awaits, in fact nothing could be further from the truth. This is a new age epicurian delight on par with the Turning Points of the world, without the pretense and only some of the accompanying cost.   My Country Griddle breakfast (scrambled eggs, onion, green pepper, morning sausage, mushroom, potato and 2 tone melted cheddar) in a large bowl with fresh biscuit on top, was delicious and filling. The coffee was hot and strong, with a small pitcher of cold milk provided at my request (may have been from Amish cows). From my perch at the counter I could see into the kitchen where the white hats seemed to be having a good time.   Even if you don't know anything about flexitarian kitchens, you can find your way to a very pleasurable meal @ Silver Diner.   Nice going!

Typical Chinese kitchen in DeKalb Pike, Blue Bell, PA. All the usual menu suspects with long lunch specials list @$6.95, with rice, broccoli and soft drink. Soup and egg roll not included.   My General Tso's Chicken was served in house in a takeout container and flimsy white plastic fork. The flavor of the sauce had a little heat, but was otherwise unremarkable. Same for the fried rice and the florets. The only thing that stood out from the other Chinois/American hybrid houses was the outward charm and warm interaction provided by the friendly and solicitous owner, who was very happy to meet a new customer.   Decent takeout place, but not beyond the mean of all such restaurants. Good for a fast and cheap lunch. They had a stream of people coming in for pickup while I was there, most of whom seemed to have been there before.   Doubtful I will ever be in that group.

If mid 20th Century Archie & Veronica malt shops and Back to the Future big fin American road steel move your imagination, then Jem's Restaurant in East Norristown, PA, may be for you.   What from the outside looks like another shopping center fast food luncheonette constrained by its surroundings to be a boring food dealer, is in fact a real trip down memory lane. The joint is a museum of cultural artifacts from the early days of television, with large posters of Rebel Without a Cause, James Dean, and Seven Year Itch, Marilyn Monroe. Perhaps that's why the room was full with retirees and people over the age of 70 (except for those of us needing to eat and run). This place is the original greasy spoon, for all the right reasons.   The double "U" counter separated the kitchen from the dining room. My spinner faced the grill operated by two short order cooks who worked smoothly in tandem. I ordered coffee and Jem's Scramble with feta and rye toast. The full insulated carafe of java set in front of me was a nice touch. I listened to the repartee between customers and servers. It was familiar and entertaining. Most everyone seemed to be a regular.   I noted the pile of chunk cut red bliss potatoes and metal tray of bacon on the grill. I watched eggs, pancakes, french toast and breakfast sandwiches being cooked and constructed as spatulas flew. I also saw that the grill was not scaped clean between orders, allowing residue from everything grilled there to build up and become part of the next dish. No judgement. Then, my small Scramble arrived, steaming in my face and fogging my glasses. Smelled awesome and looked like a gently beckoning glistening syren.   It was delicious. The eggs held the sausage, onions, peppers and feta in a wet/warm embrace, allowing each forkful to hang together with all elements dancing on my tongue. There was also a hint of everything else that came before, making for a mysterious, yet very pleasant flavor.   Maybe that is the house secret to success, or just how it accidentally became an amazing greasy spoon. Intentional or not, Jem's has a full house every morning, and is definitely doing something right.

The first review did not take into account the real centrum of Isaac's - its beer.   As my awareness and taste for craft brews evolve I am developing a richer appreciation for Isaac's Bar and Newton's Natural Laws.  I have returned often enough to realize I have become a fan.    The choices are extensive and the additions well conceived.    4 Stars for what there is.  5 Stars for what it could become.  UPDATE: December 23, 3016 - Full House this Friday night before Christmas. 30 minute wait for a table not unreasonable. Nice booth for 6 upstairs. Service good given the crowd. Mad Elf in the house.  But, my Pickleback Burger arrived feeling neglected in the kitchen. More well done than the requested medium, and the deep fried Jamison pickles very dark brown and really burnt beyond enjoyable. Burger crumbled when forked, rather than holding firm as a never frozen puck would do. Disappointing effort by the no doubt busy grillmaster.

Adams Avenue in Northeast Philadelphia is a center for the Vietnamese community. The neighborhood is full of pho and com (noodle & rice) houses that are about as authentic as you can find on the East Coast. No, it is not yet as diverse as Garden Grove, CA, with little differentiation between southern and northern style cuisine, but what they do have, they do well by and large.   Pho Ha Saigon benefits from being a fairly new structure; well designed and spacious enough (in a post industrial sort of way) to attract and hold your attention, with a respectable and capable kitchen. The service staff is generally bilingual and large enough to stay on top of their work. Their HVAC is strong enough to suck the front doors closed and create a semi-vacuum between them, making prying them open to enter or exit a chore. Hopefully, that also means there is sufficient circulation to be sucking out any Covid suspended in the air.   I went with a smaller bowl of Pho Ga (Chicken Noodle Soup), Spring Rolls, and takeout for the family of Grilled Beef w Vermicelli, and Roast Pork/Beef Banh Mi). The bowl was still large enough for a few goldfish to swim comfortably. The chicken broth had very good flavor profile and there were plenty of accessories (Thai basil, sprouts, jalapeno slices, & lime wedge) to adapt to my tastebuds. The sliced breast meat was downright generous, and the under the surface nest of thin rice noodles, more than adequate.   While the Spring Rolls were generic, with standard sweet dipping sauce, the pho was a pleasure to slurp with flat spoon in one hand and chopsticks in the other. It filled me completely. I suppose the broth could have been somewhat deeper in secondary seasoning and simmer time, because I found myself suffering a mild case of MSG poisoning on the way home. I am allergic to it, and I should have warned them when ordering. Still, MSG really shouldn't even be in their kitchen. Chalk it up to my oversight. I won't remove a star, but reserve the right to let people know in case they are also sensitive to it.   That evening my family went after the Banh Mi and Vermicelli dish with gusto. The sandwiches were stuffed and had great taste with strong roll contributions. The Grilled Beef was succulent and in small thin sliced pieces. Delicious.   But for my bout with the food additive, I totally enjoyed my meal at Pho Ha Saigon, and will not hesitate to return with memo to self about inquiring about MSG.

This local Verizon Wireless shop recently opened, and it is likely they are still working out many kinks associated with any new operation.  Still, I found their willingness to fully engage the customer on the issues important to the phone/service buyer, ie., selecting a new phone, changing the SIM card from a foreign phone for use in the USA, selecting the right plan when five phones are involved, and working through all the set up requirements on the equipment (even in Chinese), was quite amazing. Props to Derek who went above and beyond the call in spending at least 90 minutes with us as we worked through these issues.  He never lost his cool, and remained open and inventive as one roadblock after another was deciphered and overcome.    This wireless phone business is not easy for most of us, and we all know that it has become increasing expensive with every passing year.  It is almost as if the next step in this industry is for private consultants to begin to offer analysis of need and service availability across the spectrum of alternatives and point us in the right direction, if not complete the transactions for us, and get paid by the phone companies for bringing customers to them.    Until that day arrives, it is fortunate we now have a local shop with knowledgeable and willing service folk who can at least provide that kind of insight for their own company's line of product and services.  We definitely felt that Derek was doing his best to listen to us, and respond with suitable alternatives.    These circumstances are never "Wahoo" moments.  But, I am certainly a true fan of the effort I saw today.

If this was just about the ice cream, the stars would be shining bright. The maple walnut, butter pecan and especially the apple pie flavors were very good. Left me wishing for more.   And, therein lies the problem. The pleasant service person inside the tiny take out window explained that the medium cup held three scoops of ice cream. If it did, I should have asked to see the size of the scoop, because what I received was far less than three standard scoops. Rather, there were at best half scoops of the nutty and quarter scoop of the apple pie. They were in the waxed cup to look like big scoops, but the reality was far less.   For the $$, there should be no skimping, and if they can't turn a profit without a thumb on the scale, perhaps they need to reevaluate their business model. The slight of hand trick just doesn't make folks want to return no matter how good the creamies are.   Reading the other reviews, the price was raised several times as being an obstacle to enjoyment. For me, it wasn't the cost, but the weight that was the issue. Perhaps, those amount to the same thing.   We work hard for the money, and don't want to be short sheeted regardless of how comfortable the bed may be.

Capital Health's new medical center in Hopewell, NJ, follows the trend in modern healthcare to merge the concepts of hospitals and hotels into a one stop shop for all medical needs, with a level of comfort and service that blurs the line between the two industries. Thinking of it as a hotel providing for health needs is probably accurate.   This is both good and bad. No one complains when a facility is clean, well staffed and meets the needs of everyone walking through the front door. The menu of services is extensive, with well trained professionals all around. Yet, the cost associated with these offerings can be excessive, and even with some insurance, beyond the financial means of most people. Those insurers have become more severe in their rejection of most invoices, realizing they are being asked to pay for a level of comfort for patients and visitors previously unavailable. What do you do when the hospital provides only private rooms and your carrier contracted with you to pay only a percentage of the semi-private rate? You hope you aren't admitted.   The level of specialization in each sub-discipline means a higher trained doctor is at your call, but while that is critical for some conditions, it is not for others. Still, the expense of over treatment is spread among all the patients without notice, nor consultation.   Part of this built in excess is due to how medical centers are developed, and the amazing tax advantages a health facility developer has over regular commercial work. The developer makes its money as the construction is done, while the management arm of the business can only expect pay as you go. Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers continually cut their portion of the bills to be paid, while the price tag on the service constantly goes higher. No wonder even the wealthy fear unanticipated medical expenses.   So, you have to hope the best medicine is available when needed, but also understand the cost of readiness and proximity may break your budget.

On a gentle rise over Peace Valley Park & Reservoir, Peace Valley Lavender Farm provides a splash of rich blue from its plantings on the slope. While the shop is closed due to Covid-19, it is possible to buy their wares from a price board listing all their lavender based products. More than just sachet, you can find lavender infused honey, lavender butter cookies, and lavender scone mixes for the DIY crowd.   Our purpose for being there was to check out the plants available for our garden. We are looking to add to our landscaping along our back fence, and a row of bushy sweet scented blue lavender would look and smell great for both us and our neighbors. There wasn't much to consider due to Coronavirus. But, at least we got an idea of how beautiful the dark blue variety would look in the ground or dried and hung around the house and offices.   It seemed that if we were patient, we could purchase the right seeds, dig the beds, plant, mulch and care for them from sprouting to crazy full mounds of wild in the wind sweet lavender.   And, Peace Valley Lavender Farm had everything we needed to get started.

Riverview Restaurant & Bar is the successor to Café Gallery on the river end of High Street, Burlington, NJ.  A lot of money and attention to detail went in to the makeover of the bar, although the dining rooms with the large windows facing the Delaware appear about the same. It remains a well appointed house designed for higher end dining and drinking in this historic river city.   I stopped in for an early breakfast last weekend.  Sitting at the bar, I appreciated the comfortable opulence of the thick dark stone bar top and the mirrored back bar holding a multitude of bottles of whiskey, tequila, brandy, and other libations. There was one other customer there waiting for a takeout order, and only a few tables occupied in the other room. 8:30 am was the perfect time to settle in and find out what the kitchen could do. The clipboard menu looked good, and I opted for their version of a croissant filled with sausage, egg and cheese, with the complementary side of home fried taters. Excellent strong java came first to further open my eyes to the coming day.   Service came directly from management, with an assist from an English-accented young woman, both of whom were friendly and willing to provide information about the operation opened less than one year. The meal was very good - everything fresh and cooked just for me. Thoroughly enjoyed it.  Special mention to the home fries, which were large chunks, well seasoned with taste and texture that had me devouring more than I should. The java seemed likewise freshly roasted, with a pleasant aftertaste that is often lost when the grounds age for a few days.   I will return for a romantic dinner sometime soon, to see how everything holds up after dark. But, as far as breakfasts go, Riverview really knows what it is doing.

The Trenton Train Station was a hub of my commute to Trenton when I lived in Philly, and after moving to Trenton, was just down the street from where I went to court every day of the workweek.  We had a joke that had the station and the cemetery across the street in the same sentence.  You can guess what it was. Something like going to Hell on Wheels...  Then New Jersey and the Feds put a ton of money into a complete renovation of the facility about 8 years ago.  The old, threatening edifice was transformed into a semi-modern "Transit Center."  Clean, secure, and a few fast food outlets to help you while away your time waiting for NJ Transit or Amtrak to pull in and get you onboard heading for points north or south. Parking nearby was also a vast improvement from the earlier "take your life in your hands" street or crumbled lot alternatives.    Now that the Hamilton Station has gotten busy and more difficult to use, and the Princeton Junction stop remains over exposed in bad weather and suffering from chronic parking shortage, Trenton has come back into play as a reasonable option.  Yes. It lacks the comfort of a suburban station, but us city bred folk can handle that, and like being that much closer to home.

Lahaska, Pa has a reputation for being overly touristy, especially in warmer weather. The label is earned by gitchy shops and bad traffic.  Yet, if you are able to rise early and cruise the rolling hills and farmers' fields of Bucks County and reach Chive Cafe before 9, there is a good chance of finding a table, or even an empty sun drenched front porch, and settle in for a excellent country breakfast.  Such was our good fortune on this picture perfect Saturday morning. Blue skies. White clouds. 75 degrees. Windows down. Windblown hair. Bob Seger tunes. We parked in back and walked in through the kitchen door, found our way to the front porch facing Rt. 202, and chose a deuce against the inner wall.   La Colombe joe arrived in large colorful mugs.  The small breakfast menu led us directly to their sandwiches. One based in lamb sausage for me, and in grilled ham for my beautiful companion. Fried egg. Melted cheese. Cut fruit and home fries (extra) completed the plates.   The "#3" sandwich stuffed into a toasted & buttered brioche-style roll; Lamb Sausage, Feta Cheese, Roasted Tomato, Grilled Onion and Fried Egg.  The meat appeared to be thinly sliced to provide more savory flavor.  All the parts played well together, but the Feta and Lamb were major elements, while the Egg, Onion and Tomato were minor scale.  Very tasty, especially when "animalizing" it by throwing the Home Fries into the fray and pressing down.   "#2" exchanged Country Ham, American Cheese and Herb Mayo for the strong parts of the above, and put them into a traditional Kaiser Roll.  Its statement was more reserved, but a solid chew and swallow.  The taters added some greasy zest.   There is more to the offerings at lunch and dinner.  Local sourcing is a priority.  The La Colombe coffee was strong and flowing freely.  If country atmosphere is part of your delight, Chive Café provides it is copious quantities.  Definitely worth another look later in the day.

Vic Sushi & Thai Cuisine is a small Asian house on Easton Road, Willow Grove. They have a split schedule with lunch until 2:30, when they close for a few hours to prepare for dinner at 5:30. I stopped in before the afternoon closure for a a plate of Thai noodles.   I asked for lad na with chicken. The dish derives from Laotian/Chinese cultural exchange, with thick rice noodles and heavy brown sauce into which is stir fried carrots, snow peas, onion and egg. It isn't necessarily spicy hot, but can be made that way by adding lemongrass or chili sauce available in Thai kitchens.   I guess the chef hadn't read the recipe, because what was delivered to me was something different. The noodles weren't thick and chewy, but of medium width and thickness. The sauce more a thin gruel than the heavy, clinging, noodle covering reduction it was intended to be. As a result, I was eating a drippy plate of lighter noodles and veggies, without the enjoyable chew and substantial flavor associated with the traditional dish. I had to request a spoon to deal with it. It wasn't awful, but a far cry from what it was supposed to be.   First impression of Vic's is that it is really just a sushitorium trying to distinguish itself from the competition by adding a Thai tail to an otherwise Japanese fish. While the sushi may be good, the Bangkok piece really doesn't work well.   One and done.

I guess you have to possess fond memories of Pollo Campero from your childhood or hometown to fully appreciate the specialness of this place.  It is a bright and happy place, and the food gets to your table quickly with a smiling face attached.  But, after taking a big bite out of their famous Chicken the party comes to an end rather quickly.   True, the chicken is fresh and juicy, and has a citrus and chili flavor going on to tickle the taste buds.  But, after that the experience is rather flat.  The side dishes are ordinary (beans, coleslaw, taters, etc.), and the drinks are generic except for the Horacha, which was too sweet and tasted like it was from a mix.   As fast chicken goes, this is a reasonable alternative to the Colonel or Popeye's, but not as good as a Bojangles or Cluck-U. There are other Guatemalan restaurants in Trenton that make great fried chicken in a much more unique and pleasant atmosphere.  If you have the time and sense of adventure, you should try them and compare.

I haven't updated this review since Dragon of Newtown moved to Swamp Road a few years ago.  The menu hasn't changed much, but the size of the restaurant has shrunk to fit in an appropriately smaller space retained from the years as Meglio's. It appears better organized and more tidy than before. Service remains friendly and attentive, and Philomena is still the empress overseeing the operation.   Although I am occasional there for dinner, lunch is my regular beat. Their combination specials are a few bucks higher than other Chinese houses, but by comparison the quality is higher than most. The wonton soup has a pleasant consomme base stock and the wontons are thin skinned and stuffed with a good ground pork filling. I normally request Orange Beef (fried rice, broccoli, comes with). The sauce is tart with slivers of orange peel, and appears to be made to order, rather than the time stamped heavy gloop offered elsewhere. Decent tea flows freely.   For a local dine in/take out, Dragon is a way better than average option among Chinese American kitchens. They are really making an effort to appeal to the pallette as well as the wallet.

Love Groucho or not, Duck Soup Cafe is a great place for breakfast and coffee. It is hard to find in Logan Square Shopping Center, but if you drive around back on the eastern side the rear door and sign are visible as the best way in.   Started 35 years ago by the same family running it now, the place has an easy Americana coziness and knotty pine charm that makes for a relaxing environment. The menu is similarly built on kitchen classics, with one side for morning victuals, and the reverse, lunch. I was the second customer when I walked in around 9:20. I liked the country vibe and took a table in the front corner under the windows and across from the cashier counter and kitchen entrance.  Their french toast was constructed from a thin cut croissant, and included fresh cool sweet butter to melt, real grade A dark maple syrup and two bacon slices. It was all very good, as was the bottomless coffee mug. Service was beautifully provided by Michelle, daughter of the owner/chef of the house. They both seemed to know all their customers, but me, and came out to greet everyone and catch up of the daily New Hope gossip.  One of the benefits of Logan Square is that it is not downtown in tourist centric New Hope. Rather, this is for the locals, with real quality and reasonable prices.

DJ Kitchen offers Szechuan cuisine on City Line Avenue, Philadelphia.   Well, sort of.   It has the red Szechuan peppers down in large quantities, and many other hot spices that bring the willing cognizant diner to the brink of tongue burning ecstasy. Yet, like most other Chengdu facsimiles around town, it stops short of the authentic 'flavor of numb' brought on by only the traditional black peppercorns and star peppers that grow in the hot humidity of the ancient Du plains in the plateau region of the central and western parts of the province.   Without the Numb, it just isn't true Szechuan. It is still quite good, with quality ingredients and plenty of meat, veggies, spices and sesame oils, but it isn't the Full Monty. The portions are substantial with leftovers for the boys at home.   We thoroughly enjoyed the Cumin Lamb and Long Hots with Beef. They were colorful with powerful aromas. The meat was tender while the peppers and onions, crisp. The red onion was particularly sweet in contradistinction to the growling bark of the green long hots. Both damn good. The only shortcoming beside the absence of numbing essence, was the saltiness of the Dry Pepper Crispy Chicken. It was an unnecessary distraction to an otherwise entertaining platter.   We enjoyed chatting with Ming, one of the owner/managers, who took time to explain some of the history of the restaurant. He and his partners have created an interesting haven for those seeking an alternative to the regular Chinese American grub, and although it doesn't travel all the way to to the numbing mountaintops, it does take us a long way up that winding spicy road.

Carlos Garcia seems to have a thriving pizzeria business with the recent opening of his fourth parlor in Morrisville, PA. They are all enumerated after his daughter, Camila. I haven't met her, but it is obvious her father takes great pride in her and the success of the enterprise.   The location is in a small strip center, replacing an earlier pizza/pasta joint that succumbed in the midst of COVID-19 last year (RIP). It is apparent that they have worked hard to freshen up the space with colorful wall murals and end to end cleaning. The people there are friendly and have skills, although the older dude folding boxes in front of the counter couldn't manage to make eye contact. Maybe a language problem.   So, I ordered by phone rather than GrubHub, to keep the money in their register rather than sharing with a third party. I went with a large pie, half sausage and penne aglio olio with spinach (which came with side salad and small loaf of oven fresh bread).   The pizza was good, with firm crust and scorch marks across the bottom. The slices held their point when lifted and folded for eating. As they cooled that rigidity waned and dog eared. The crumbled sweet sausage was plentiful, but a bit salty. The other half of the pie was plain, and probably would have been better with a tad less cheese, so the flavor of the tomato sauce and basil could shine through.   The pasta was not listed on the menu, and I suspected they didn't regularly indulge such preferences. Still, there was plenty of garlic and good taste. Having had the same dish at a different place last week that was over the top with whole fresh spinach leaves sauteed perfectly, this version was light on the finely chopped greens. I won't downgrade as the chef was doing me a favor and may not have had exactly what he needed for the optimal dish. I appreciated the effort.   Overall, quite decent for a neighborhood Casa Italiana Mexicana.   3.5 STARS

One door closes and another door opens.   We were in Mayfair to check out the Italian food at Emma's Cafe on Frankford Avenue, but when we learned it was booked up on Saturday night we decided to roll with it and pop in to the Aja Asian Fusion Restaurant right next door. The mental gear shift wasn't that difficult.   It had a big dining room and we were led to a booth against the wall in the middle of the room. It looked to be clean in the dim semi romantic light and our server was pleasantly efficient. Their menu made it clear that Aja was primarily a Chinese house with a cross section of sushi related dishes and a very few Thai choices, like pad thai and two curry options. My concern that it was more confusion than fusion was born out when we ordered the shrimp pad thai (only form it came in) and teriyaki salmon bento box with shumai and California rolls, with choice of miso soup or salad with ginger dressing.   The noodles were far too sweet and bereft of peanuts to have ever been touched by Thai hands, although there was alot of it on the plate. The grilled salmon was a very small steak, but had the right taste and texture. The miso was fine, but the shumai seemed a frozen, cheaply produced variety and the Cali roll was just okay, tasting mostly of avocado and seaweed. From what we saw at the sushi bar they didn't move enough fish to keep it all daily fresh. There was an awful lot being stored in plastic wrap.   Unless you're satisfied with generic sushi rolls that can mask the flavor/freshness of the fish, Aja Asian Fusion is better wokking up Chinese dishes for you. Leave the Japanese and Thai cuisine for more talented kitchens.   Once was enough.   Will make reservations for Emma's next time.

I had no idea when I decided to check out Basically Burgers in Doylestown that I would be entering a dilemma that required me to chose between fidelity to Yelp's creed of honest no-holds-barred reviews, and my understanding of the Golden Rule of treating people as I wish them to treat me.   My morality tale began as a walked the center of Doylestown Borough on an incredibly beautiful early August afternoon. Temperature 78; Carolina Blue sky; galleon clouds sailing their airy seas.  Perfect day.   My destination was Basically Burgers for a simple late lunch.  Yelp led me there, and I had every intention of ordering their best offering loaded with fried onions, jalapenos, and pickled sweet peppers. No cheese today to keep some semblance of austerity. Arriving, I noted the tables and chairs were bare bone, and a black and white mural on the wall that I took to be Doylestown. I wondered if Crayolas would be available to color between the lines. Given the high level activity on the street, I was a bit surprised that this joint was quiet and three quarters empty.  Hhhmmm....  The folks in front of me on line were four seniors who could not decide what they wanted. I took the opportunity to study the wall menu and figure out how to put together my slider sandwich.  Too complicated.  When my moment arrived, I was facing a kindly woman who took pity on my apparent ignorance and asked a few simple questions to lead me through the order process.   I sat at a small deuce near the front windows admiring the ant colony that Doylestown had become.  The old folks were double dating, and sat at a quad front and center in the main window, chatting about their Medicare. I felt an involuntary shiver run down my spine at the prospect of sitting there one day.   The burger arrived, delivered by the husband owner chef.  He slapped me on the shoulder as he walked back to the kitchen, with a, "..hope it's hot enough for ya;" referring to the chilis mounded on top of the double disks, and making a bed for them to sit on, as well.  I took a photo to memorialize my favorable first impression.   It is a shame when great expectations are dashed by poor execution.  This was it.  I asked for a medium burger, but received well done. Little juice left to mix with the pile of fixins, making the first bite experience (FBE) disappointingly dry and with no taste aside from the onion and peppers.  I moaned silently.  I took the ketchup table rocket and shot a long stream of thin red sauce all over the sandwich in an attempt to resuscitate it. Marginally successful, I ate the rest grimly.   The wife, cashier, waitress came by a few times to ask how I liked my food. She was so innocent and earnest. I smiled weakly. When I finished, I wrote the tip you see elsewhere on the website.   Now comes the dilemma.   On my way out of the bathroom I walked past the kitchen, where the chef caught my eye and asked again about the heat of the jalapenos.  I had no qualms with the peppers, so I honestly said they were fine, but I have a high tolerance for heat, and could have used more.  He pointed at another burger in front of him in a red plastic basket. "5 Alarm Burger, if you like 'em to roast your mouth." He listed all the hot ingredients and took out a bottle of his secret hot sauce. He would not let me touch it, but his sly smile told me that he was very proud of the nitro inside. I told him I would have to try it next time (Ugh. Conscience pang).   Then, he asked me if I was still hungry?  Well, I wasn't really, but where was he going with this line of questions.  "Yes. I could eat," as any good boy would say to his favorite BBQing uncle.  Next thing - he offered me the 5 Alarmer gratis because it was a misorder.    I was caught; hook, line and sinker. He was making a generous offer because he enjoyed our exchange.  Of course, I took it with a big smile and sat down to devour another double.  This one was actually pretty good.  Much tastier with all the chili varieties piled on, and the secret sauce torching my tongue. Still, too well done for me, but mine was not to complain in the face of unexpected acts of brotherhood and random kindness.   So, do I write the review I intended to draft after the first burger, or after the second?  Do I allow this real story to influence what I say about this eating experience?  Or, do I just lay it all out for you, and let you draw your own conclusions, and perhaps use it in your sermon next Sunday?

I always feel a bit out of my element when invited to a good steakhouse like Capital Grille in King of Prussia. Not a steak lover, I can appreciate the clubby atmosphere, the dark wood tones, and white jacketed servers always where they should be, attentively taking care of their beef obsessed customers. I even love the aroma of grilled sirloin and the menacing glitter of oversized serrated knives slicing through medium rare filet mignon. For me, the odor is the best part.   So, I ready my excuses for not joining in the carnivorial feast, yet always manage to find plenty of good things to enjoy on the menu outside of the main attraction. Nobody really minds that I am the guy who goes with calamari, wedge or Caesar salad and a tapas approach to the many veggie sides available. Give me interesting brussel sprouts, cauliflower or roast/mashed potato, and I go to town.   Capital Grille does everything well, and the servers are always on their game. The New England Clam Chowder, Wedge Salad and large plate of calamari (tentacles included) were all tasty and left me full even without the heavier meat load.   I mused as I worked through my choices, watching my office compadres cut bloody paths through their perfectly finished steaks and chops. I knew we were appreciated by the powers that be to be treated so well.

Coming back to Einstein after a hiatus of more than six months, it was shocking to see the changed conditions all around the shop. I never had strong attraction to their bagels, but the convenience and decent coffee was a sufficient draw to get me there sometimes.  This visit, while the staff was still friendly and helpful, it was impossible not to notice the amount of dirt all around.  The floors, counters, refrigerator, coffee urns, etc., all seemed to have been neglected.  I happened to see the back of a coffee sign sitting on the coffee counter, and it had not been cleaned in a long time.   These are signs of lax oversight and poor training. Either corrective steps are taken soon, or this EBB will slide into oblivion.   A downgrade is inevitable.  We have all experienced better than this.

It's great to see the effort being made to attract new ventures to the shopping centers on Trenton Road in Morrisville, PA. For too long this area has been struggling to attract customers. The best way to make a commercial zone less sketchy is to provide activities that can be enjoyed with the family. Good and entertaining food is part of the equation. Poke Ocean while not a home run, it a solid contributor with its sushi/poke/udon/teriyaki orientation. Three other food outlets are under construction as I write.   The floorplan looks alot like the previous BBQ joint that ran out of steam last year. It is just cleaned up a bit. Service is cordial and efficient with the right Asian flair. Lunch is served from 11 to 3, although there does not appear to be a poke list discounted for lunch, making the other parts of the afternoon offerings the more appealing. I asked for the salmon teriyaki lunch which included miso soup, iceberg ginger goop salad, white rice and a nice salmon filet over sauteed onion and carrot slivers. The amber sauce was quite good. Additionally, I received a complimentary fried veggie roll, which I liked.   The lunch was good, although I really don't get the attachment to the iceberg salad, found in every sushitorium in the country. It is all water with that thick orange ginger dressing. Without nutritional value, I would prefer a different option with a more interesting taste/texture profile. How about edamame?   3.5 STARS

For a state agency that deals heavily with the public, this PennDot Licensing and Photo Center does a pretty good job. It is certainly less crowded than the closest alternative in Bensalem, and the entire vibe ( such as it is), more relaxed.  We were in and out with a driver's test in under and hour, with time to go across the street to Ben & Irv's for breakfast. Sadly, the young man has to return to show more competence in parallel parking, but that gives us another opportunity for a good meal nearby.

This review is for the Raymour & Flannigan website, where we recently purchased a dining room set of a table and six chairs. The Langhorne store is the closest to home, but we did not shop in any of their warehouse sized facilities.   The experience was a breeze from start to finish. We saw a wood ensemble that we liked and the price was discounted for the coming Black Friday sales. We ordered it and arranged for delivery two days later. They called ahead in the appointed day, and arrived on time. The two guys were friendly and professional. They set everything up and took away all the packing materials. They were done in about 20 minutes and our dining room looks great. Everything was in perfect condition and makes the room pop. The chairs are wood and leather, quite heavy and surprisingly comfortable.   We easily qualified for their 12 month payment plan with no interest if paid in full on time, which made it all the more manageable.   This was my second purchase from R & F, and it won't be the last. They have eliminated the hassle of furniture buying and delivery delay, so that it works smooth as silk.

Two Slices and a Drink review only.   I came in around 3 on Sunday afternoon and asked for their 2 slices and a drink special, which is listed on the board for $4.99.  I requested the plain pizza I saw sitting in the display be served, "well done," so that it was heated enough to remelt the cheese and bring them back to life.    The pizza arrived hot enough, but also clearly past its prime.  Although the underside was firm and held its load well, it was approaching staleness. There should be a time limit for how long a pie can sit around before it is disposed of and replaced for the next customer.  Too, I am not fond of having my fingers burned from the hot oil dripping out the back of the slice when I fold it over in order to gain a stronger grasp.    Finally, I was charged $6 and change for the snack, clearly above the listed price.  Perhaps, I was there too late, or it was not available on weekends.  The sign should have so stated if that was so.    Clean shop. But, I have experienced better pizza by the slice.

I remember when Antonio's was just a good pizza joint on Trenton Avenue in Morrisville, Pa., just over the Calhoun Street Bridge from Trenton.  My fondest memory was eating there while waiting for oral argument in the New Jersey Supreme Court.  We won that case, so I always associate this restaurant with success.  Now, it is an "Italian Bistro," and has become an upscale stop for folks who like good Italian food but don't want to travel far to get it.    I sat in the base of the tower last Sunday night.  I had been jonezing for a good aglio olio, and the Café delivered.  My Cavatelli Siciliani came nicely plated in a deep soup bowl, complete with Sweet Italian Sausage, Broccoli Rabe, lots of browned Garlic and topped with Romano Cheese.  Although there was a fair amount of olive oil in water at the bottom of the dish, it did not diminish the full flavor of the ingredients.  I enjoyed it.    It came with a full loaf of in house baked bread, and a Green Salad with Balsamic.  The bread tasted like pizza dough (which it was), and was unnecessary calories.  The Salad was a fair mix of Lettuces, Tomato, Red Onion, Carrot.  Nothing creative, but a solid veggie accompaniment.    Service was fine with several servers in black stopping by regularly to refill my water glass and be sure I was satisfied.  Aside from it being a bit too cool for me in a T shirt, the experience was very good.   Coming at $15.99, the price was about right, but it would have been a true deal had it been a buck or two less.    Parking was not an issue Sunday night, but it is a small lot, which is likely trouble for a busy lunch hour or prime time dinner reservation.   Café Antonio is all grown up!

Cosmos on Trenton Road in Fairless Hills is a fairly big place, equally divided between restaurant and bar.  My time was spent in the watering hole, which has a large rectangular bar with a few dozen stools, and is surrounded by HDTVs high on the walls for a good view of whatever sportage is being shown.  The bartenders are friendly and knowledgeable, and very accustomed to people eating while they imbibe.    As it was my first visit, I opted for their Fire Apple beverage and a bowl of French Onion Soup.  Both were scalding in their own way.  The drink was a combination of Angry Orchard Hard Apple Cider and Fireball Whiskey.  Fireball is a cinnamon-based fermentation, and its flavor goes very well with the hard apple.  It was challenging to just sip it in its large beer glass, as the natural inclination was to take large gulps as I would for straight brew.  Alas, that was not a wise move, as the whiskey's bite clawed at my throat on first swallow, nearly causing me to cough.  A quick learner, I adjusted and thoroughly enjoyed the cool apple crispness with cinnamon kick the rest of the way.  And, yes, I was able to walk away when done.    Perhaps, the balance came from the very good bowl of L'Oignon Gratinee.  The beef broth was completely sealed by the melted Gruyere, and when opened with spoon, the steam rushed out like a volcanic vent.  Probing, I encountered a load of translucent onions, chunks of thick bread, and slightly oily-sheened beef broth.  It was tasty and savory, and played very well with the cool cinnamon appleness of the Fire Apple.  I had stumbled on a good combination of flavors, textures and temperatures.    The "cocktail" came in at $8.50, and the potage at about five bucks.  Definitely a nice place to hang out on a midweek evening while exploring both the bar and kitchen menus.   See ya soon!

One Up One Down Coffee is the new urban cafe on Cass Street, Trenton, that took the place of the previous occupant, the Trenton Coffee House. With a little spit and polish they have made the original Polish Falconer Club into an attractive reuse that is bright and comfortable, with lots of handworked wood bars and tables, block glass windows, and large coffee bean roaster where they control the production of excellent java.   In addition to a broad caffeinated menu, they sell a few pastries - cookies, scones and brownies, as well as carrying bags and sacks with their logo on them. You can tell they are really just getting started, but have a marketing plan in keeping with the hard edged neighborhood where they ply their trade. Trenton State Prison is right down the street, where hard time takes on an altogether new meaning.   I asked for Chai Latte, and it was handed to me minutes later in a large cup in saucer. It was well done and went down easy. They were kind enough to allow me to eat a bagel I had picked up earlier. I had intended to bring it to my office on South Broad, but when I drove by One Up One Down, I had a change of plans and wanted to take a little time on a chill Friday morning to enjoy a diversion.   Spontaneity completely made my day, even if I wore my mask in and out to honor Covid Protocol.

A party of seven can be a challenge for a popular and busy restaurant, especially when six of the guests have never eaten Italian food before.  Confusion, questions, blank stares.  But, when lucky enough to be handed off to a seasoned professional wait person, what might have been an eye-rolling chore, becomes an interesting and entertaining part of the evening.    So it was at Carlucci's Grill in the Lower Makefield shopping center that is anchored by Kohl's Department Store at the corner of Oxford Valley and Big Oak Roads.  I was given the responsibility of ordering for everyone, so after studying the menu I decided to stick with the classics, so everyone would discover what Italiano was all about for the most people.  Parmigianas for everyone, except for the more adventurous who opted for Carlucci's "Princess" finish to chicken and shrimp.  Standard sides of pasta with red sauce, except for the aglio olio linguini I preferred.    Gotta give kudos to our main man in black & white, and the kitchen.  The feast began with a puff bread with an olive oil garlic drip.  Never had that before, and it was very good fun to rip apart and devour.  The accompanying salads all had balsamic dressing, and were solid, if not exceptional.  We finally arrived at the entrees.  Large plates of veal, chicken and shrimp or eggplant, covered in red gravy and melted mozza or cream sauce (Princess), and sharing space with an ample load of al dente linguini, were placed before us.    We all fell silent as we dove in.  The veal was fine, thin sliced and sautéed before dosing in ample thick and chunky gravy, with just enough cheese cover to allow the dueling colors to swirl without sealing the meat within.  Nice chew, better swallow. The eggplant could have been more tender, probably due to the thickness of the slices and not enough time in the fry pan to really soften the large circumference of the purple beast.  Still, a credible job.  The pasta sides were average.   Carlucci's is BYOB, so we consumed Pinot Grigio and Corona in sufficient quantities to keep everyone lose and engaged.  Most importantly, we gave our guests something to talk about after returning to Asia.    This is what Marco Polo had in mind as he returned to Venice on the Silk Road with his first shipment of rice and noodles.  He could not have fully realized what he was starting.  The Carlucci's have certainly carried the traditions that evolved from the Court of the Great Kublai Khan to us in competent hands.

There is little doubt that Rocco's is the best restaurant currently in Newtown. This may change as there are new kitchens opening up almost weekly in the community, but right now, this steakhouse has it going on full bore.   I had dinner there with son and his girlfriend the other night. We sat in the glass enclosed porch that rings the first floor. The space is beautifully appointed in colonial style, and white table cloths and heavy stainless flatware. It is a pleasure to walk through the barroom and dining room to reach the porch. From that perch the Newtown bustle can be witnessed first hand. We were there to celebrate several occasions that had gone  unrecognized over the past 16 months due to Covid. We had much to be thankful for.   Son o'mine loves his steak, and his N.Y Strip done medium was beyond excellent in texture and robust flavor. He cut me a piece knowing that this was not my normal diet, but that I was open to experiencing superior dishes. Yes, it was amazing, and it was easy to understand his attraction. I had to concentrate to appreciate everything that was going on in my mouth as I chewed and savored. His girlfriend went with a medium filet. It wasn't as juicy as the strip by observation, but she was clearly loving every bite of her medium round thick slab of beef.   I went with the French Onion Soup and Prime Burger, knowing my diet couldn't handle a platter of solid beef. The soup qualified for possible the best of breed in a lifetime. It was rich, savory, onions, hearty beef stock, topped with french loaf under a thick layer of gruyere, seared to a near-blackened finish either in the oven or by blowtorch. The cheese had to be pierced to access the molten potage below, and to permit the superheated steam to escape. It was epic, and nearly a meal by itself.  Stupendous!   After all this, the burger was a bit of a disappointment. True, it was a combination of ground beef, short rib and brisket, topped with onion, tomato, lettuce and melted provolone, in a brioche bun. But, flavor-wise it was a situation where more is less. I didn't get off on the mix of beef. It just didn't taste like a high end burger. I like short rib and brisket at BBQ joints, but prefer them separately, where each of their distinct attributes can be appreciated, and not muddled together. So, it was disappointing after the star quality of everything else. The fries were standard crispers.   So, Rocco gets a less than perfect five stars here. Despite the burger, the rest of the experience was top notch, and the bar/dining area stunning In an understated way. On a less precipitous evening, eating outside would have been a legitimate option, but despite the umbrellas, we would have had to endure wet shoulders from the tropical storm brewing outside.   No wonder Rocco's is booked solid every night. It is truly a first class night on the town.

Another of the growing cadre of very good Mexican restaurants in and around Trenton.  This one, El Potrillo (The Colt) has taken over Marsilio's Kitchen on Roebling Avenue in the Burg.  It is amazing how Mexican rugs thrown over tables change the look and mood of one of the classic Italian houses.  One can only hope they can do something that is the Mexican equivalent of the great Chicken Cacciatore that its predecessor was known for.   The space is casual, but also clean and well organized.  The bar is no longer servicing alcohol, but in its place are fresh squeezed fruit/vegetable juices.  My large snifter of Carrot Juice was sweet and coolly refreshing.  The menu is diverse and provides just enough English to hint at what you will get.    My Torta Carnitas (slow cooked pork) was huge and enough for 2 meals.  The Roll was thin and nicely crunchy.  There was plenty of meat at the bottom and it was the base for the Lettuce, Avocado, Onion, Jalapeno, Fresh Cheese, Tomato and Spicy Mayo that all came wrapped neatly in paper.  I needed knife and fork to work my way through the half torta, taking the other piece home for another lunch.    The combination of fresh veggie juice ($4) and the torta ($8), may seem steep for this type of shop, but when you realize they are preparing two meals for you, the value proposition becomes outstanding.    El Portrillo asks if "You have tried the best Mexican food around?"   They are certainly entitled to their hyperbole, because it is among the best I have sampled in Trenton.

Frey's Deli & Pizza sits in a small strip center on northbound Lincoln Highway (Rt.1) in Penndel, PA. It is an unassuming place with a few tables, a big front window, and prep area in the back for pizza and takeout. There isn't much in the way of provisions in the refrigerated display case, but what they do have is either made inhouse or Dietz & Watson.   I asked about their tuna salad, and was advised it was prepared fresh that morning and a popular seller. Good enough for me, I went with a whole hoagie with lettuce, plus sweet/hot peppers.   Opened it back at the office. It was heavy in the wrap paper, and substantial upon opening. Not only was the tuna as good as advertised, but the roll had a nice crust and texture that was a pleasure to bite through. Quality sandwich all the way. Tasty, and not the least bit fishy. Just enough mayo to hold everything together and blend perfectly with all the ingredients. One of the better deli sammies of recent memory. Prices were good, too.   Only downside - there wasn't much to chose from in the drink department. Definitely would benefit from more selection for washdown. But, other than that, Frey's was a very pleasant surprise nosh.

Five Guys makes the best grease burgers!   Grilled on steel that is seldom cleaned during hours of operation, the beef sizzles until well done, when it is lifted off the heat and placed on a bun already prepared with whatever accessories you want. Whatever else they do to the body, they are incredibly tasty and provide excellent lubrication to the alimentary canal.   In addition, 5 Guys make great fries that far outclass their better known brothers. Their signature move is to toss extra fries in the brown paper bag after putting in the primary load carried in a paper cup. Excessive, but nicely so. Same goes for their shakes, which are also superior to the beef pucks. They are creamy, sweet cool ice cream splurges. Pricey, but the super caloric craving supercedes the doubtful overall nutritional value.   So, it is an upside down meal if you think about it, but certainly a ton of fun on a bun.   Unbeknownst to me, I had ordered online from the Five Guys on Lincoln Highway, but not the road running through Bucks County, A/K/A Route 1, but rather the one in Lancaster, PA., over 100 miles away. My bad. I wrongly assumed that their locations were in order of proximity to where I lived. Not so on their app, so the reference to Lincoln Highway led me astray. You know, I saw what I expected to see (Langhorne rather than the actual Lancaster) and impulsively jumped the gun.   This is where Five Guys superhero Tyler stepped in to save the day. When the shop didn't have my order, he asked to see my phone and immediately knew what had happened. Not for the first time, he explained. He immediately reordered everything on the register and comped the charges, knowing I had already paid their sister store. They could correct this internally.   Tyler's superpower - being supercool and knowing exactly what to do without making me feel like a bigger smacked ass than I already did. All this coolness made the enjoyment of my "special meal" almost a secondary consideration.   Almost, but not quite, as it was digestible proof that some classy teenagers are ready to rule the world.

Finally made it to Yardley Ice House, the back parking lot converted shed that puts out some excellent Italian Ices.    It sits behind Mil-Lee's Luv - In Diner off Main Street, Yardley, Pa.  You have to drive down the adjoining driveway to find it.  First impression upon parking, Oy. what a dismal place for an ice cream parlor.  That is soon forgotten upon walking inside.  The space is cute, in a claustrophobic way, but the folks are friendly and patient describing their options.    The Bordeaux Cherry/Vanilla Custard Gelato I had was quite good.  The ice was Black Cherry red with plenty of cherry chunks mixed in.  The taste was cold and true.  The Custard was even better.  Stand up curl.  Great creamy texture. Just the right vanilla flavor.  Very close in substance to Kohr's at the shore.  Nothing wrong with that.    The regular ice cream was not sampled, but I was very satisfied with this Gelato.  The question of the hour seems to be whether it compares favorably with Rita's?   To my buds, they are very close.  You can't go wrong with either selection, so it comes down to secondary preferences.  Do you mind consuming from franchises over stand alone family businesses?  Do plastic cups rank over paper containers?  Does your loyalty flow toward Pennsbury or Council Rock or Morrisville?   All important inquiries in the decision to choose your cool desserts.  But, I'll let you decide.    I'll take you anywhere you want to go.

This is the place New Jerseyans come to deal with the bureaucratic red tape that goes along with securing and maintaining the privilege of driving in the Garden State.  Licenses, Registrations, Titles, Suspensions, Renewals and Appeals, all take place somewhere in this large (formerly Sears) facility.    Parking is difficult despite all the government buildings in the area, and the lines for accomplishing anything seem to stand still for hours at a time.  Still, the employees do their best to address your problems, and there is seldom an outburst of frustration.    Yesterday, I represented someone who was to have his license suspended for two years due to some bad decisions several years ago. We appealed, and had a short hearing with a hearing officer to explain why this punishment would be an extreme hardship for him and his family.  We were successful in reducing the suspension to 6 months.  Still difficult, but much more manageable.    We all left satisfied.  I can't claim that is the result for everyone else who must venture into this giant labyrinth to deal with the autonomy of the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission, but the faces on those emerging from its dark doors attest that survival is assured.

The Borough Pub on Farragut Avenue, Bristol, PA, is a pleasant joint to stop for a beer or two, and a light bite if hungry. Although it is located on a fairly forlorn stretch of old Bristol Borough, the inside is a cozy knotty pine paneled long room with rectangular bar up front, and dining room/kitchen farther back. Prices are appropriate for the neighborhood, and there is a decent brewlist for those who enjoy a long draught of pilsner. They currently have a Yelp check in bonus of a domestic draft (not a crafty). I had a light beer with my meal.   Son and I stopped in for dinner recently for the first time, and were impressed. The space was well maintained, the staff friendly, chatty and accommodating; and the kitchen better than expected. I went with a small bowl of French Onion Soup and their "Pubrogies," a version of the popular Polish dough pockets stuffed with mashed potatoes, and covered in a nice mix of sautéed onions, green peppers and jalapeno, with a large dollop of sour cream on top of it all. Son with younger and larger appetite, ordered the Cheesesteak Spring Rolls and Honey Chipotle Pulled Pork (Chipotle sauced shredded pork with melted pepper jack, on a jalapeno cheddar brioche bun).   Everything was good to nearly great. The soup, perhaps the weakest link, had the right savoriness, but lacked the crusty bread and load of wine soaked onions of the original recipe from Les Halles. The "rogies," were tasty with a nice kick from the hot pepper, and balanced well against the inner mashed. The spring rolls were larger than anticipated, crisp and crammed with beef, cheese, onions and peppers. A kicky ketchup came along for the ride for dipping. The pulled pork was devoured by son (didn't offer me a bite) - always an indication that he was enthralled and unwilling to share. Glad he liked it so much.   Our server, Dawn, had a great attitude. Around just enough to keep everything refilled and moving, with a sense of humor and bonhomie.   Borough Pub is a place to relax, sip and chew in an atmosphere that is both family and sporty. It doesn't take itself too seriously, and as a result, it is a cool place to kick back and catch some sports and conversation with people you enjoy.

This is my third visit to a Manhattan Bagel store in the past few weeks. They all look basically the same, both in substance and cleanliness. Staff is friendly, helpful and efficient.   The bagels were all decent, but not in the pantheon of great New York style rounders. So, it is somewhat surprising that they use the name of the city that made bagels famous, because they fall far short of that standard. Yet, they are good enough to satisfy my breakfast hunger, even if not epic.   My onion bagel with veggie cream cheese was tasty and chewy, with a slightly crisp skin. The spread was ample, if not over the top generous. Their coffee was good, with a few alternatives between House Blend, Bold, fruity and decaf. Certainly, caffeinated to wake me up and keep me focused.   The only real issue worth noting was the inconsistent experience offered by the three shops visited in this area. They looked the same, and the cream cheese was enjoyable across the board, but the freshness and texture alternated between right on target with crisp outer surface and softer texture within; and a chew that suggested the bagel was not as fresh (although purchased and eaten an approximately the same time), and may have been from a batch made earlier in the day. When it comes to out of the oven bagels, even a few hours more exposed to the environment can mean an aging that is noticeable.   So it was with these samples. Today's was the least fresh, while smeared with the most cream cheese. Perhaps that was not an accident.

Einstein Bros. App Review -  I have returned to Einstein Bros Bagels after several years away, drawn in by their new app on mobile. Now that I have used it a half dozen times I have a few comments to offer: 1. The app is easy to use and attractively presented.  2. If using PayPal or credit card on the app, once you provide the account info, ordering is a breeze, and can be repeated with a few clicks.   3. Both curbside and walk-in pick up are available, but if ordering java, you have to go in and pour it yourself. They do put an empty 12 oz. paper cut and plastic top next to your bagged bagel, so there is a level of convenience if you don't mind walking to the self serve coffee shelf to take care of this.   4. Of course, their bagels haven't changed, so there is no magic in digitalizing the process. Still a soft finish, with a heavy dose of toppings all around. As I prefer a crunchy bite, these rounders will never make my hit parade. Nonetheless, the spreads are decent and the overall gestalt, satisfactory.   5. There are a few shortcomings in the bagel preparation which should be addressed. They don't cut the smeared bagel in half, as I remember they did when eating in. Too, there is no paper wrap around the bagel before placing in those small bagel sized envelopes. Thus, removing the bagel from its sack is a messy proposition. I never fail to get cream cheese on fingers in the process. Picking up and biting into these guys is a similar sticky problem.   So, while the app improves access to the bagels enough to warrant an additional star, other issues remain that continue to make their bagels problematic. Just don't forget to grab a few napkins before you leave, as the tiny bag is not big enough to slip them cleanly inside.

If you enjoy classic Italian cuisine with a touch of something more modern, set in an beautifully renovated house, La Strada is calling your name.   Its main dining room is a large round room that may have been a solarium in a past life, but has become a space large enough for a dozen or more tables amply spaced and fully windowed to permit the world outside to come in. As this is the older part of town, you can see 18rh and 19th Century buildings that remind of the pre and post revolutionary history of the area.   The menu has all the traditional dishes, some with a special flare away from what would be expected. For example, we ordered Calamari which came drizzled with a Thai Sweet Chili Sauce and Balsamic drip. All larger rings, it was a delicious surprise treat. Our Chicken Marsala and Francais were more classical, with two large breasts each atop Penne and wonderful reductions in Marsala Wine with fresh mushrooms and lightly dredged flour coat and  Lemon White Wine base, respectively. Tender enough to be cut with our forks.   Service was a bit slow, but not bad for a romantic Sunday night. We regretted not bringing our own bottle to this BYOB house.   Aside - All through the meal I had the feeling that this was a Roman room in the fine tradition of Trenton's Chambersburg neighborhood, which at one time had awesome Italian kitchens on every corner. They were classy and always full with locals manging to their hearts' content. Those days have turned to Spanish/Latino pleasures, but it's great to know that that Guilded Age can still be found if we look hard enough. In fact, the owners are from Trenton, and seemed pleasantly surprised to chat briefly about the old world, where I still have an office, and loads of memories.  La Strada is of that fine school.

Hawkeye's Country Tavern is a modern roadhouse on Route 113, Perkasie, PA. It has a decent, but limited beer list, and talented hands in the kitchen. The menu is primarily American classics, with a large sandwich page and multi component entrees for those desiring a bigger meal.   I sat in the step down barroom that felt like a basement with low ceiling and large rectangular bar. I didn't see the dining room. My server was prompt and friendly, bringing the draft Stella Artois to me in seconds. My plan was to have an early solo dinner while the family worked into the evening, and to bring home food for them so they had something interesting to eat when they arrived.  The chips & salsa table nosh was a nice touch.   I liked the homemade meatloaf dinner that came with mashed potatoes and fresh steamed zucchini. It was def a step up from a burger, with texture and flavor coming in part from the dark brown gravy on top. Washed it all down with the cold Stella.   I ordered the Brisket and Cuban Sandwiches and their Original Burger (grass fed locally w cheese, grilled onions and avocado) as takeout for the fam. Later that night I tasted the brisket on brioche and it was quite tender with a nice almost sweet BBQ bite. The Cuban disappeared without an offer from the stepson, while the burger was devoured by son after the rest of us went to bed. Told me he liked it, with special mention of the creamy avo adding interest when I saw him in the morning.   Overall, although labeled as a roadhouse tavern, Hawkeye's felt like a family restaurant (although I didn't see any kids). It did a very good job with the cuisine standards, and with a better curated brewery component and deeper whiskey shelf, it could attract a more rousing crowd and rock out.

As many reviews of Parkview Cafe explain, this place is difficult to find in the back of an industrial park off Horsham Road, and without a sign to let you know you are close. But, if you follow the GPS into the park, you will eventually see a green awning that lets you know you have arrived. Park the car, and walk along the walkway until you reach the front door.   Inside, you find a traditional looking luncheonette dining room with tables along a wall of windows, and a smaller room separated by a half wall from the main space. Everything is a simple comfort. The menu is limited to breakfast and lunch, and the morning I was there, one server for the operation, unless someone came out of the kitchen to assist with ordertaking and delivery. So, best to sit back and adjust to a slower pace.   I made my own omelet of three eggs, onion, pepper, tomato, feta cheese, and asked for it "country style," with the homefries inside the egg case. Twenty minutes and half a mug of coffee later, it was placed before me, with straight edges and two stacks of half moon rye toast alongside. The Valentina Mexican Hot Sauce splashed on top added a desirable bite.   Aside from being a tad bit dry in spots from overcooking on the hot steel, it was a good dish and quite filling. The buttered toast offset the spice, and the java washdown was satisfyingly bracing. A solid breakfast, but if I had been in a hurry, I would have found it almost unbearably slow. Because I wasn't, I can mention it without heavy markdown, and hope that a word to the wise is sufficient.   The only "Parkview" seen from the cafe is the vista of surrounding aluminum warehouses and light industrial structures with minimalist shrubery. Once I figured out that someone here had a deep sense of irony, I enjoyed the insight with a smile and tip of my cap to the desert dry humor.

Love the name. Love the notion of sourcing exclusively from a Pennsylvania Amish farm. Love the antibiotic/filler free birds resting easily in my belly. But, the actual experience of eating their Baja Chicken Sandwich, and the takeout confusion, not so much.   Lovebird just opened earlier this week, and making all the necessary adjustments as Bucks turns Yellow from Red (Covid-19 speaking), earns them some slack from this sensory deprived quarantine, but some things are still hard to ignore. I didn't mind that there was a communications gap between online ordering, paying, and the chaotic scene upon arrival at the small shop for pick-up. It was a bit tense as some customers came in to wait with their shirts pulled over their mouth and nose because they lacked required masks and recommended gloves and the business had none to offer. It was even okay to wait 30 minutes for my order to be ready, and watch a dozen teenagers scrambling to package the orders into brown bags and seem lost about how to construct a strong meal sack that wouldn't descend into a leaky mess at the bottom of the bag by the time it reached its destination.    That was annoying as the sandwich containers were removed with oil stains and partially deconstructed ingredients. Worst offender was the brussel sprouts side dish that tasted great in a black roast way, but whose oil cooking medium could not be contained and ran over everything in the bag. A class in solid trigonometry would have helped the unschooled packers.   Not sure what I expected from a $9 chicken sandwich, but I may have believed that it would compare well with the Chick-fil-A, Popeyes, Wendy's of the world which sold for a coupla bucks less. Aside from the warm fuzzies from knowing the chicken's impressive pedigree, the Bite & Chew left alot to be desired. Plump, yes. Crisp, no. Spicy, no. Hang together to the end, sort of. Of the local competition, Lovebird came in last.   Just not worth the high end pretense, especially for what they put you through to reach that conclusion.

The only Irish Sports Pub in Newtown, The Green Parrot, named for a 19th Century saloon of the same name that thrived at the other end of Sycamore Street and had a less savory reputation, has become the anchor of the new Goodnoe Corner commercial center that is the heart of Newtown Township.  If you want to catch World Cup action, this is the only local place to belly up to the bar and see it live at 6 in the morning.  It is also the centerpiece of all the street action fairs, shows and other events that occur in this fair burg.   If you enjoy loud bars with a couple of dozen HDTVs on the walls and winsome bartenders pouring your crafties, this be your place.  It has a rotating beer list that is bound to have something that appeals.  The kitchen is strong in the apps department, and grills up good burgers (starting at $10), but the dinners can be spotty, so for the price I tend to look elsewhere to sup.   Still, I am a fan for what The Green Parrot does well, and for its active role in the life of our community.  Plenty of parking behind the house, and on the street.  Entrances front and rear. Nice covered porch which works well for private parties.

After gorging @ Mood Café and wishing it had a lounge to push away from the table and offer time to digest, I realized the only alternative was a strong dose of caffeine if I was to make it home alert enough to dodge all the gaping potholes between West Philly and Bucks County.    Perhaps it was Devine Intervention, but as I turned the corner onto 47th Street, I saw the bright red neon of the Vietnam Café.  The image of a big glass of Vietnamese Coffee filled my head, giving me an immediate jolt of anticipation.  My parking angel was also accommodating; providing a space almost right in front of its door.  I uplifted a smile in gratitude.   Walking in, it was apparent that design and expense were put into the space.  It was very pleasant with many windows, attractive lighting, cozy tables, and a nice bar.  That was where I headed after advising the host/manager/owner that I was only interested in coffee.  The place was not crowded for a Saturday night, and there were a few empties at the bar.  The gracious gentleman did not skip a beat, and welcomed me to take a seat and he would see to the coffee.  Moments later, he was behind the bar, depositing my personal drip stainless steel press in front of me.  It sat on top of a thick cocktail glass with a half inch of Condensed Milk at the bottom.  I watched the dense brown colloid infuse the Milk, drip by drip.  I had time to take out my phone and check with Yelp about the place.  I learned that I had been in its sister ship, Vietnam on 11th  Street, in the past.  This made sense, given the attention to detail not often found in VN joints.  I also perused the menu, wishing I was hungry enough for a Banh Mi and a Com dish.    The coffee hit the spot and I decided to indulge with a Spring Roll to be a good sport.  It arrived precut and with a rich sweet/spicy sauce.  It was fried, a small surprise, but quite good.  I was in and out in about 45, deciding that I would definitely return for a full repast to show my appreciation for the graciousness extended, and the karmic smile bestowed.

Vinny G's sits at the corner of 4th & Broad in the lovely Delaware River town of Florence, NJ. For those of you who have never had the good fortune to visit this small burg in Burlington County, checking out its timeless charm is a great reason to make the trip, and Vinny's Bagel & Deli makes it even more worthwhile. This spot is one of the hidden places in the Garden State that will change your mind about the historic romanticism of Jersey.   Yes. The bagels are very good, too. They are large, fresh, light and covered in your condiment of choice. The skin isn't as crisp as I prefer, but from first bite to last chew, it was a tasty delight. My Onion rounder with Veggie Cream Cheese spread, washed down with their House Blend coffee was satisfying and tasted of the love they put into it.   Service was attentive and friendly. The woman who assisted me seemed genuinely happy to see me and had my bagel picked, sliced, smeared, wrapped, bagged and ready to go before I finished pouring my self-service java.   I drove to the office along the river enjoying the bucolic setting on a mid April Spring day, anticipating that first bite ecstasy awaiting me.   I was not disappointed.
