Although called Tom's Dim Sum, only a small portion of its menu deals with the small plate culture of China.  The first page offers the expected dumplings, shumai and a few cold options, but the majority of the kitchen deals with traditional big plate possibilities. Further, everything is ordered from the menu, rather than using carts and old ladies to bring all choices to the table for perusal and selection. The lack of a floor show is somewhat disappointing.   More importantly, the quality of the food was also less than stellar and consistent. We ordered a hot & sour soup, crystal shrimp shumai, pork buns and crab/pork xiao long bao(soup dumplings).   The soup was fine, with plenty of mushrooms, sprouts and a good vinegar base. The crystals were not. Looked shiny great on the plate, but tasted like they had been boiled in heavily salted water. Hot salty wet shrimp were unpleasant on my tongue, and not what was experienced in other houses. The pork buns were dry as if they had been sitting around for a while, although the ground pork filling was okay. The XLB had a decent broth within, but seemed sweeter than normal. Had to bite their top knots off and drop the table dumpling sauce into it to improve the savory flavor. There are much better soupies available in Chinatown.   Service was fine, and the dining room was clean.   Tom's is located on 11th Street under the covered portion created by the shopping mall. As our server explained when we asked, this is not really a dim sum restaurant despite the name. As such, it suffers from an identity crisis inherent in its business model. It offers a glimpse of dim sum without fully committing to the full monty experience.

Mayfair Diner on Frankford Avenue in Northeast Philly, is a classic stainless steel railroad car diner.  The front dining area has been well preserved, so if you are into these iconic food circuses, Mayfair is one you should consider for your collection.   We stopped in after a concert Saturday night.  The lights were on, and a few tables were occupied. Our server was efficient and gave us time to decide what we wanted as first timers. We ultimately ordered a patty melt, Buffalo chicken cheesesteak and hot Buffalo wings.  Everything came with a boatload of fries.    My rye burger was pretty good, with lots of sautéed onions on top of a half pounder encased in good rye bread.  The fries were okay, but not as crisp as I like. The cheesesteak was abundant with chopped chicken, onions, peppers and gravy boat of melted cheese. The roll was decent, too. I didn't try the wings, but my son scored them as average.   Eating in the dining car was a trip.  Although renovated, it still had the legit ambiance of a last century lunch wagon, with long counter and semi-swinging stools. It may date me, but I enjoyed this atmosphere even more than our meal.    There are several diners along Frankford Avenue, some bigger, others smaller.  Some may have better food, but none do the "Diner Experience" better than Mayfair.

The other reviewers are right.   This Lucky 7 Deli on Princeton Avenue, Lawrenceville, NJ, is more than it appears to be from the exterior. In addition to the expected convenience store, the operators have put in a small kitchen (grill) and dining area for folks who want to have a hot breakfast or lunch on the premises. It is all very basic, with industrial strength tables and chairs, but the cook seems to know what he is doing, and turns out decent grub.   My sausage, egg and cheese on kaiser roll, was a double egg and sausage patty job with a single slice of American. The roll wasn't so good and lacked texture and taste, but the runny fried eggs and meat offset that shortcoming. Too, they brew New England Coffee beans - a better than average large roaster/distributer.   While the joint lacks in the comfort department, my breakfast was delivered to the table by the manager/cashier with a smile, and the purpose of my visit was met satisfactorily. I wouldn't come here on a date, nor even a business meal, but a quick stop by is well within its parameters. They mention fried chicken on the outside sign, but didn't see any within to be able to evaluate its look and quality.   Maybe another time.

Where else but Philly can you find an authentic cheesesteak right down to the greasy last bite....in the airport? Eat at Joe's is that place in Terminal B. By the way, that isn't just the name of the joint, it's an order!

With an hour to wait before I was due back in court, I drove down High Street looking for a place to hang out over coffee.    I found that place with YelpHelp at the Mugshot Diner.  This is a corner establishment in the heart of downtown Mt. Holly.  It does not look like a traditional diner until you go inside.  Once the door closes behind you, all the cues are visible.  The counter with a half dozen high back stools; the booths along the walls, and the very friendly server slinging hash, Joe, and worldly wisdom to all who listen.  Of course, the mug shots are there, too.  Everyone from Frank Sinatra to Elvis hangs from the wall.  The multitude of bail bondsmen on the street close on the county courthouse explain why this name was chosen.    I ordered a Corn Muffin and Java and had time to talk with the waitperson, who happened to also be the owner of the business.  She was energetic and took pride explaining how she and her spouse had brought this business back to life after the original owner of the property had "bailed" on food here and taken the concept to Philly and other locales.  The café that had been here for a couple of years ultimately failed, and these good folk approached him about reincarnating the Mugshot.  The rest is current events.  My Corn Muffin was much better than average, remaining moist and mildly sweet even after grilling.  It was also larger than what I had sampled in other similar food outlets.  The coffee was strong and there was no hesitation when I asked to swap out the half and half for regular milk.    There are a few very good breakfast/lunch houses sprouting up in Mt. Holly lately, and Mugshot Diner is one of them.  I will be visiting again when I find myself with time on my hands in historic Mt. Holly.

When I came into Nifty Fifty's for the first time today my first impression was that the joint was almost empty at 2:30, and a far cry from the description of bedlam read in some reviews. Okay. That was a good thing, although I noticed the sign out front said something about being a "Family Fun Restaurant," with mini golf and an arcade. I hoped that that the victuals would still be as good as Yelped.   Clearly, NF's is more about the shakes and hand made soda concoctions than the burgers.  After all, you get a choice of more than 100 shake flavors, while the burgers menu is really rather small. Single, double or triple, with/without cheese, shrooms, onions, lettuce, mayo, etc.  Not even a jalapeno option.  The fries and onion rings sounded more exciting than the slider selections.   All this evidence became manifest shortly after I ordered the black cherry shake first, and then the single burger with, and mushrooms and fried (not sauteed) onions, and the onion rings.  The burger and rings came out in separate red plastic baskets, while the shake was overflowing its large aluminum container in which it was spun in the blender.  I looked at the feast before me.  Shake, rings, burger in that order of visual stimulation.  I grabbed a few extra napkins as the shake began to run down the sides of the container, leaving a path through the condensation.   The shake was just incredible.  Intense black cherry flavored, thick, sweet, creamy. I started to fade back to about 1954 (Yes. I was a kid then) and relived the wonder sensation of a DQ Blizzard.  A pleasure zone in my cortex was triggered and I silently convulsed with joy.  It was way to much for me, and I took half of it home.  The onion rings were extra large, and breaded with a mix of spices and bread crumbs that made the crunchy bites delicious.  The burger became an afterthought.  It was decent with adequate grease, diaphanous onions and canned shrooms, to satisfy my basic burger lust, but not up to the standards of 5 Guys, Jake's Wayback, nor In N Out. The single seemed smallish. The bun undistinguished, and the ketchup shot from an overused red plastic counter rocket. The bun collapsed under the oily weight of the topping and I had to retreat to a knife and fork.  Sure. I will go again.  The overall experience was fun and the meal had some major positives (the shake and rings), that overcame the rather lethargic effort at a good burger.  I obviously picked the right time to go, as I sat alone at the counter and had the friendly waitress to myself.  I enjoyed the meal in peace.

How many people love their jobs so much that they willingly pose for a Yelp photo without being asked twice?  Not so many.  But, at this Philly Soft Pretzel Factory, not only are the pretzels bagged while hot, but the workers there genuinely smile and have fun taking care of you.    We picked up 10 standard sized bowties, although we had the choice of minis, and singular chubby nubs.  During our interaction, they described how to use them as sandwich ends by slicing and even grilling before loading with our favorite contents.  Never thought to use them at home that way, but liked the idea.    I never believed a one item business would be successful in the long run, but these folks have been ongoing for more than ten years.  That is a hell of a lot of pretzels.

Now, you've heard 'bout 5 Guys. Had grease from Robin and Chee B.  Maybe even a sloppy Bobby or DQ.  But, you've never had a burger Till you've heard Buddy play the blues...  Beef ground fresh daily. Hand cut fries. Homemade sauces. Martin's Potato Bun. And, all the toppings and combos you can imagine, and then some...  The messiest burger I have enjoyed in a long time. First bite, and half the load of onions, shrooms, cheddar and Swiss slid out the back door onto my fries. Made them even better.   The mix of A-1, garlic mayo and ketchup was all over my fingers and running down my chin.   6 napkin job.  If this isn't burger heaven, it is at least an outpost along the way.

I just needed a caffeine boost to make it back to Pennsy and saw this DD on Broad Street.  It was dark and a little difficult to see the driving lanes in the parking lot.  Next thing I knew I was in the drive thru lane and couldn't get out!   I reached the order speaker, but did not understand the Hindi dialect being spoken.  I waited until it changed to English and ordered coffee and a round sweet.  Easy so far.  Of course, when I finally opened up the bag when I was back on the street, I had not been given what I ordered.    Ate it anyway. Not bad.  But, it does prove a point - Sometimes, a drive thru will not do.  There are some things that must be seen before being ordered.  For all I know, they gave me what they thought I wanted. Or maybe, it was just fate that brought me a Sour Cream Donut rather than the Glazed requested.    These things were meant to be a mystery.

Eat at Joe's...if ya know what's gud fo' ya.  You can almost forget that this is PHL when you ask for a breakfast sandwich or cheesesteak.  You can hear the sizzle, and smell the hot grease.  When the cook opens the torpedo roll and turns it upside down onto the innards of your sandwich, rather than scooping it up with the spatula and slapping it onto the bread, you almost believe you are at you corner pizza shop waiting on Carmine to drop it the wrapping paper and roll it up with tape.   Alas, that dream fades with the next announcement that your flight is overbooked and they need volunteers...But, maybe it is worth delaying your flight so you can enjoy another Eat at Joe's special?

Now that my office is in the area I have the opportunity to find and try a whole new world of food outlets.  One of my weekly staples is good pizza, and being so close to Trenton, tomato pie is practically on every corner.    Divine Pizza attracted me to its name as it was different than all the standard Tony's, DeLo's and other family named shops that abound.  Could be the name was Divino in the old world, but my first reaction was that they were trying to make a statement about their product being heavenly, or at least aspiring to be.  It's located in a mini strip commercial structure on Arena Drive with a Dairy Queen as the anchor tenant.  That was a good sign.  Built in dessert.    Walking in I noticed that this was a side by side orientation, with the dining room next to the kitchen/take out area, rather than front and back.  The dining area was not too big, and the tables had a nice black and wood top surface.  The menu was presented in a small bound book that covered everything for lunch and dinner.  Again, slightly different than most joints.  The radio was playing quiet rock; another pleasant distinction.    I went with the regular double slice of pie.  When it arrived a few minutes later I observed that the shape was almost equilateral, with narrow circumference  crust.  Picking up one it was quite firm, and held its point high without the hint of bowing.  First bite discovered a very firm undercarriage that demanded a purposeful clenching of the jaw to break through.  Very nice.  A peek under the hood showed the scorching of dough from a very hot oven.  The black streaks were just enough to demonstrate no fear of under baking, nor reheating.  It stood up to the challenge.    Finally, the chew and taste were purposeful and a little complex.  It was both salty and sweet, with the sweetness coming from the tomato and the saltiness from the crusty bottom.  They played very well together.    I liked this pizza much more than anticipated, and realized that there were many elements of the experience from the first moment that foreshadowed a good tomato pie.  Divine Pizza may not extend to the heavens, but it turned out a very enjoyable slice.  Given this introduction, I will certainly find my way back to see what else they can do that is better than expected.    Divine Pizza may yet be Dante's best work.

Mil-Lee's Luv-Inn Diner... It definitely feels like 1975 when you walk in to Mil-Lee's.  It is surprising spacious for occupying one half of an old Victorian mansion of Main Street, Yardley.  Looks like there is room for at least 60 people with many deuces around the room, and a few booths.  Brown and beige very pronounced neutral colors. The staff is warm and friendly, and promptly seat you and ask if you want something to drink.  The coffee arrives quickly while the large menu is perused.    My breakfast of french toast was good with powdered sugar and cinnamon, but did not seem to be the thick "Texas" style promised.  My partner in crime ordered eggs over, hash browns and well done scrapple, and her plate was overflowing.  The java kept coming, as did the smiling oversight of the waitpeople.  The crowd was mostly locals having meet ups with friends and associates.  One woman had a birthday, and the establishment provided a candled cupcake and announced to everyone that we should sing "Happy Birthday" to the honored guest.  We all joined in.  That was a first for any breakfast I have had - that kind of thing most often happens at a group lunch or dinner.  Great sense of community spirit.  The meals were solid and satisfy, if not particularly inspired, nor memorable for the cuisine.  The thing that makes the  experience special is the warmth emanating from the staff and customers.  After all, who calls their place a "Luv-Inn" in the 21st Century?    "...come on people now, get together, smile on your brothers, try to love one another right now!..." (with thanks and memories to Jesse Colin Young)  Come here for the timeless vibe of returning home, if not for the nostalgia of a good mom-cooked meal.  Mil-Lee's slogan : "Food From the Heart"

It looks like I waited too long to stop in to Cafe Ole. The signs on the front window indicate that the shop is closed and for sale.  If you know anyone interested in operating a "bistro" and cafe in wonderful downtown Trenton, have them check it out. Looks like I missed a cool place.

This rating is strictly in comparison to other 5 Guys Burgers and Fries I have sampled.   I think this is the 5th or 6th Cinco Hombres for me, and sadly, the worst of the bunch. The shop was practically empty when mi hijo y yo arrived around 6:30 pm on a Monday night.  That seemed peculiar at dinner time.  Nonetheless, we ordered our burgers; son a purist wanting only beef and cheese, and dad a single, no cheese, but with sautéed onions, mushrooms, and jalapeno slices.  We split an order of flies.    When the brown sack arrived it had the traditional oily blotches.  Unwrapping the aluminum foil packaging, I beheld a semi-crushed orphan baby of a burger, pinched and abused and looking for all the world like it required life support.  Whoever birthed this child needed a slap and handcuffs. But, realizing this was only a metaphor, I ate it after lifting its lid to slide ketchup on its head.  I know; I know. I should have done something.   It wasn't that they tasted that different then the other sliders from this chain, but that they came to us unloved, and unkempt.  Where was the care, poor child?    I could not figure out if this was standard for this location, or if we had somehow violated an unwritten rule about how much to order.  Perplexing.   Apparently, we were not the first to confront this odd phenomenon.  Looking around at all the empty tables clearly articulated that there was a problem.  I had just been too slow to grasp it.  Update 2.18.2014  Stopped in after a long night meet at the Crowne Plaza Hotel down Street Road.  First thing I noticed was that the entire kitchen crew was made up of women.  The second thing I noticed was that although they were busy on the grill, one chef shouted over to us to ask if we both wanted doubles, so she could throw them on while standing there, even before taking our official order.  That was a smart and efficient move.  Third thing was that the burger arrived neatly wrapped in aluminum foil, and when opened, the burger was in excellent condition. Forth thing, it tasted great with sautéed onion and jalapeno slices.    If something like this happens again, I will have to reevaluate my original impressions and review.  These women had it all over the male crew the first time I was here.    Gentlemen; get your stuff together!

Xi'an Sizzling Woks does its namesake food very well.  As others have commented, stick to their Chef Recommendation and House Special menu and you will have a unique and enjoyable meal.  The farther you wander from Xi'an, the more the cuisine slides toward the norm, and becomes like most other shops in the area.  Best to stay on the Silk Road from beginning to end.   My experience last week proves the point.  We ordered Dumpling in Chili Sauce (Szechuan), Xi'an Liang Pi (Cold Mild Spice Noodles), Biang Biang Noodles w/ Ginger Scallion Sauce (Rave), and Spicy Pot Flavor Fish Fillet (Surprise Star of the Show).   The Dumplings were the weak link in our meal.  The skin was thicker than in a true Szechuan house, and the ground pork while plentiful, did not exhibit much flavor.  The Chili Sauce was not nearly hot enough.  We were sorry we wasted stomach space on something so mediocre.    The Xi'an Liang Pi was a fettuccini width cold noodle bathed in a semi-hot sauce with Tofu, Shoots, and a few things I could not identify.  It was good and renewed our faith that the rest of the meal would be deliciously distinct.    We moved on to the Biang Biang Noodles in Ginger Scallion Sauce.  As you have already read everywhere on this page, these Biang Biang are Bangin!  Our server stirred the bowl for us to be sure the sauce coated as much of the pasta as possible.  These hand cut bad boys were longer than a foot, and required high end dexterity to lift them high enough to clear the pile in the dish, maneuver them over to the small plate and then work the chop sticks to your lips well enough to take hold of the noodle and suck it into your mouth. Slurpy mess, but well worth the effort, as these were terrific due to the play of ginger, scallion and cumin (I think) on the tongue.  Subtle heat that grew slowly, but never approach the scalding of a Szechuan chili dish.  The noodles were firm and chewy and filling.   We would have called the night a great success if we had stopped there, but the urge to try something more brought us to the Spicy Pot Fish Fillets.  These tender morsels of fluke were crisp on the raised texture of each fillet, and included veggies and mushrooms is a wonderful red/orange sauce that also packed a punch, but more gently than, say, Emai across the street.  I loved this dish, and will try the other variations with beef, chicken, lamb and pork intestine in the future.   Xi'an Sizzling Woks is a smallish shop with no more than a dozen tables.  Best to get there early or late to avoid a wait.  It represents the style and cooking of this very old city that was once the capital of a Chinese Dynasty, and is now an industrial and university town, exceedingly well. It is certainly worth a visit (both city and restaurant).  It could easily become a regular stop on my Chinatown cruise.

I stopped in after visiting the Jefferson Heart Institute and in need of sustenance after a fasting test earlier in the morning. This Au Bon Pain is conveniently at the corner of 10th and Chestnut.   The first thing I saw in the front window was their display of bakery sweets and bagels, and I didn't look much further.  I asked for a Everything Bagel Breakfast Sandwich and Coffee.  The staff was uber friendly and had no problem allowing me to switch from a plain bagel to an Everything Bagel.  I paid, took my receipt, and found a small table in back to wait for my name to be called.    The light crowd was predominantly hospital workers in the scrubs or wearing ID's around their necks.  Most were doing take out, but a few sat and talked with their associates, or fielded text or phone messages.  The flow was efficiently handled.  In about 5 minutes I had my food.  Reasonable wait.  The sandwich looked good (see photo) and had decent taste.  Its downfall was the texture.  The eggs were microwaved into a soft fluff.  I really prefer them cooked on a grill or in a pan for more flavor and chewability. The bagel while fresh, was likewise without the tougher exterior and softer insides, but was soft through and through.  Obviously, a bagel in name only.  Disappointing.  The meal was adequate, but not engaging.    I did not try any of their signature French-style breads, but they did look good. The critical piece is always the crustiness and right amount of salt in the dough.  If I find myself near an Au Bon Pain with an urge for bread, I will give them a try.  Otherwise, there are too many other interesting and tasty alternatives to consider ABP a contender for my breakfast short list.

If I am here often enough to be a Duke, I must be a fan!  Too, this morning I had the Raspberry Stuffed French Toast blackboard special.  Two slices of well dipped bread sandwiching homemade creamy Cream Cheese stuffing, and topped with in house Raspberry reduction topping.    Sweeeet & Tarrrt!  Filling enough for two meals.   Best thing I've eaten at Squirrels Nest.

The day the Gap arrived in Newtown I knew we had arrived.  When it expanded from the original small store on State Street and moved to the Village of Newtown, I wondered if it was possible to have too much Gap?  Apparently not. Both the large Gap and the Gap Body are successful.   If you like Gap gear this is an easy place to shop. Plenty of space. Good workers. Enough parking. Several eateries nearby when you need a break.

Golden Dawn was a disappointment on several levels.   First, sitting at the end of the counter it took overly long for someone to slip me a menu and offer me a cup of coffee.  I understand busy, but there were several staff people just walking around with their heads down.  Second, the French Toast I ordered, while thick as advertised, had not soaked long enough in the egg mix, and the center of each slice was dry.  This made for a less than enjoyable experience.  Just glad I went with a short stack.    Third, although I sat at the counter for at least 30 minutes as I waited and ate, no one came by with a pot of coffee and offered to refill my mug.  Again, servers all around trying their best to avoid eye contact with everybody.  They succeeded in making me feel invisible.   And, in making me feel an unwanted customer.    Have it your way.   Without me.

This review is only for the meeting facilities and first floor offerings of the Holiday Inn Philadelphia Stadium.   I have been here a couple of times over the years for larger meetings where people were coming in from around the country or region.  While the building is dated and can use refurbishing in the lobby and meeting rooms, the overall plant still functions fairly well.  This is a mid-range hotel designed for sports oriented guests to enjoy the professional teams coming in to play our guys.  It is far from state of the art, but serves its purpose.  If you want high end there are other places available nearby, and even better ones downtown.    So, accept it for what it is - a heads on beds, one day meeting center, where comfort, cuisine and pampering are low priorities.  And, if you need to stay a night or two and don't want to wander far afield, this place will do nicely.    Don't forget that there are fun entertainment venues, and Tony Luke's only minutes away.  Just ask the front desk or the bellman for recommendations.  They know where the action is.

Very nice place for our UYE last Friday night.  10 brave souls ventured out after a laborious week to enjoy each other's company and some good grub.  Karma was the choice of our up and coming unofficial social director, Sari (Another great job!).   The space was a little tight in the back of the house on a long table next to the lunch buffet table and hot plates, but with the glass of wine that came with our $20 three course dinner had us forgetting our surroundings as we caught up with our Yelphriends and new initiates.  True, that the cuisine is somewhat secondary to our passion for each other, but we are "foodies" to a greater or lesser degree, and we are aware of what we eat.    So, tonight had its good points and some of the other kind as well.  My Veggie Samosa was quite good with good mashed curried potatoes, peas and onion is a lightly fried dough with good tamarind dipping sauce.  One was enough for me.  My Chicken Xacuti had a nice coconut milk based sauce, but with somewhat dry overcooked Chicken.  The Naan/Garlic Naan were very thin, but tasty and capable of holding both the pinched main course and the superior Coconut Curry bath it came in.  The regrettable shock of the evening was tasting my buddy's Taj Mahal Indian Beer.  It was downright skunky, like it had been left in the heat for far too long and only chilled at the last minute.  Management took it off his check, but the damage to the  taste buds was not as easily mended.    Overall, a decent meal, but one that was not as good as many nearby Indian houses can provide, although our camaraderie made up for much of its shortcomings.

Very surprised that this Mickey D's does not show up on Yelp, although it has been open at this location for several years. It stands next door to the Broad Street Car Wash, so after a shine-on-line, I dropped in for a quickie before heading back to the office.   The shop is fairly small, but clean.  The counter staff was alert and efficient.  I tried a Double Jalapeno Burger on the Dollar Menu, and a Lemonade.    Surprisingly, the burger was decent (I know...compared to what?), with both sliced, pickled pepper and crispy, lightly dusted and fried bits of the hot green meanie.   It might be a few years before I hit another one of these places, but since the last time it was obvious they were trying to improve their offerings.    The $3.50 price for this small meal had me whistling a happy (meal) tune.

After trying the sushi, Yummy remains 3 Stars.    It is true as others say that the rolls are larger than in most fish houses.  By larger, I mean in circumference and in size of the component parts.  Yet, while the fish seemed fresh, they did not offer a pronounced flavor beyond the sauce that was drizzled on top and the Soy/Wasabi/Ginger accompaniments.    Too, the Wasabi was the mass produced green variety that most offer, and the Ginger was the artificially colored orange, rather than the actual white of natural Ginger.    It was adequate and fresh, but certainly far from best of breed that is available only a short distance away.    The family is very pleasant, and the hostess friendly and helpful. Her husband does the artistry, while the kids and grandmother sit nearby, making it feel somewhat like I was eating in their dining room.    Not bad, but not exceptional.  When convenience is the primary factor, it serves its purpose well.

Ota-Ya requires a bit of patience to find.  Sitting out back off Cambridge Lane in Newtown, it is easy to have never known that this place existed.  It is next door to Mamita's, the new Central American resto. If you don't know where that is, then you need to call ahead to speak with the very friendly owners who are accustomed to directing lost patrons.    If you are familiar with the current state of Sushi/Japanese houses; this is not that.  It is an older space, without the front row knifemen flashing blades nor rice shapers. All that creative stuff is done in the back (kitchen).  What you see is the finished product brought to you by management or an on-the-ball server who knows everything about the menu, and will tell you what she/he thinks is de rigor for lunch or dinner.  The floor plan is rather small for a contemporary restaurant, reflecting that Ota-Ya has been slicing fish for a long time without the need for floorshows.  The aura is dark, the tables and chairs old, and the overall atmospherics close and subdued.  Whispering comes naturally.  But, in exchange for being the anti-Oishi in Ntown you get the best sushi.  Fresh, creative, aesthetic and self-assured.  If you love old Zato-Ichi movies, this is your place.  The blind swordsman sits quietly while the nasty Samurais' steel slice each other up defending their noble's honor. Finally, when the dominant villian and his henchman are about to kill the last innocent, Zato-Ichi excuses himself meekly, unsheathes his short sword, and dispatches the baddies while holding a baby in his free hand.    "...so sorry for the disturbance, young prince..."  Have whatever you want here.  It is all very good.  If raw fish is not for you, there is plenty of excellent Tempura, Teriyaki, Udon, Bentos, and Salads.  The owners are happy to chat with you if they have time, and if not crowded feel free to ask for a refill of the Green Tea and sit a while.

It was very helpful to find a Mandarin speaking doctor in this part of Bucks County.  My Chinese guest's son was not feeling well and we needed medical attention from someone who could ask questions and understand his answers.  Dr. Ellen Kim was conscientious and made her patient feel at ease as she examined him and took notes on her laptop.  The blood work she ordered was appropriate and the results decisive in how to address the problem.    A big plus was the presence of Mercy Diagnostics in the same building.  They were able to take us promptly, draw the blood and get the results to Dr. Kim within a few days.   Visiting Wrightstown Family Medicine is also a worthwhile trip for the quality of the facility built to house them on Second Street Pike.  It is beautifully constructed and decorated to suggest an 18th Century farmhouse.    This medical practice and Dr. Kim are highly recommended.

Sub Maria's scores points just for its nameplay.    This now Korean deli is packed into a small corner storefront with floor to ceiling shelves and refrigeration that provide almost everything imaginable for a good Jersey lunch.  Superior loaves of fresh bread are the heart of any worthy sandwich, and Maria's uses an excellent bakery.  Light, mildly springy, just the right yeast aftertaste.  When loaded with well made Chicken Salad, Lettuce, Tomato and Sweet Pickled Peppers, it is a pleasure to indulge.   The back glass walled drink cases are full of the favorites, except for some of the more exotic international brands, like Jarritos.  But, you can't expect a joint this small to have everything.    The aisles inventory snacks and pre-packaged sweets to complete the meal.    Now, if they figured out a place to make fresh fruit smoothies, bubble teas, and real brownies, they would be a candidate for the Jersey Deli Hall of Fame.    As it is, Sub Maria's knows how to create an awesome Submaria...ine.   A little hard to find at the ass end of Nottingham Way, it is worth pulling out the GPS to enter this special emporium.    Parking lot out back.

First visit to Stadium Bar & Grill last Wednesday night while waiting for night class to let out.  I do remember this being Kris Krois, a deep blue seafood joint that I enjoyed a couple of times.  Times change.  Now we have a nice large rectangular bar with back dining room that pours national and local suds and an abbreviated short order menu for those so inclined.  Specials every night of the week.    This is a neighborhood bar looking for neighbors on this forlorn stretch of Rt. 1 in Fairless.  Only 5 people here when I walked in around 7:30 pm.  The friendly barkeep approached with a smile, and when I said this was my first time, she promptly gave me the quick tour of drinkables, and handed off their menus to examine.  My Sam Adams Winter Lager was perfect for a cold night, and had I been hungry, a few of the snacks looks appealing and very well priced.    The HDTVs were channeling plenty of sports, and the other guys were engaged in conversation about industrial cooking.  Apparently, they worked at different assisted living facilities, and had tales to tell.  I eavesdropped now and then, as one of the homes was in my town.  Good to know the inside poop.    My 45 minutes went fast. I paid and promised to return on a Monday for their wing night.  No one seemed to hear me, except the nice bartender, who said she would be waiting.    Cool!

I am a Bristol fan.   When I see something worth applauding on Mill Street I want a review with a marching band.  So, when Café Bombay came to my attention I had to visit ASAP.  Last night was the night. I drove down with two mystery munchers and entered just after 7 per our reservation.  We were the only patrons, which was a bit disconcerting, but we grabbed the table in front to have the best view of the world going by, and be farthest from the kitchen.  The turmeric in the air was so palpable that we all were sneezing within minutes.  At least we knew the Masala Sauce would be dynamic.   For apps, we order 1.5 orders of Veggie Samosa.  We were pleased that half orders (1 samosa) were viable, as we only were three, and wanted to save space for later. The Sams were excellent with soft potato and hard peas.  NIce.  Our entrees consisted of Kerala Chicken Curry, traditional dish; Chicken Xacutti, Roasted Coconut was the most noticeable spice;  and Navarathan Korma, veggies, cheese, nuts & herbs.  All the gravies were creamy and packed a punch.  Given that we had to find a common denominator of heat, the range chosen was between 6 and 8, and all tasted, "just right."  Additionally, we had Bombay Naan, a sweet version of the classic Indian Oven baked bread, with Almonds, Raisins, Ginger and Coconut; a perfect balance to the spicy heat coming from the main courses.  All these were first class.  The Mango Lassi while good, was undersized for the price of $3.50.  We were suggested to try a slice of Coconut Ice Cream Pie for dessert.  A first for me, it was pleasing like a cold Key Lime Pie, but a questionable purchase at $4.99.    Café Bombay is definitely worth another visit as the menu hides other treasures.  Still, in an attempt to learn the lesson here, I would skip the lassi and dessert, and stay with the variety of main courses and regional specialties listed on the menu.    One other oddity is that the online website menu does not list prices to permit changing market conditions.  That is a situation that should be easily remedied with a host changing the prices as necessary.

Seventh Heaven!  If they say it, it must be true.  Back in the Day downtown Trenton was a hotbed of cuisinery delights. So, it comes as a somewhat pathetic reality to acknowledge that there is at least one such institution there now.  Where once you could choose among very good Italian, Greek, Diner, Seafood, Soul Food, and even the hidden blues/jazz club within shouting distance of City Hall, today there are a plethora of dumps along the sad streets of T-town; and there is Settimo Cielo.   Born out of the ruins of an older restaurant, Settimo Cielo came into the world with the vision that this once proud city still held the potential for a classy well appointed joint that could kitchen up high quality Italian dishes.  Surrounded by State office buildings and concrete pill box garages, this oasis has been around long enough to prove the truth of that dream.    If they cook it right, they will come.  Went there for a business lunch the other day with two other attorneys who work in town.  They are semi-regulars, and were excited to bring me there for a sit down.  It was great to be able to walk there from their office near the County Courthouse.  Upon entry, the drab street was promptly left behind, and we entered a cool umber dining room complete with art and mirrors, tablecloths and shining silver.  The menu was presented, water poured, and specials announced within minutes.  Everyone had a Spanish accent, and that added to the intrigue of what was going on in the kitchen.    I have learned to eat light for a business lunch, so as to impress my companions with my lean approach to work.  No room for extra calories when preparing for battle.  The image seems to work.  My mates, not concerned with what I thought of them, went heavy with Pasta and a Creamy Vodka Sauce.  I heard there was a Spinach Salad Special complete with Pears and Apples, and went for that.   The Bread Basket offered decent baked dough, but perhaps not what exited the ovens of Italian Peoples or the belated Colonial.  Still, the crunch was satisfying.  My friends seemingly inhaled their thin pasta, while I navigated through an excellent fresh green Spinach Salad that included a touch of Blue Cheese and Walnuts.  It wasn't big, but it was tasty, and served the purpose of demonstrating my cross-pollinated Spartan/Epicurean style.    It was a satisfying lunch on several levels, not the least of which was the positive experience surrounding the food.   Settimo Cielo is certainly worth a return evening visit.

Bonjour Creperie Café is on the first floor of an office building at 790 Township Line Road in Lower Makefield, Pa. It seems to have been open a very short time as it is still bright and shiny.  Even the crepe cooker looks brand new.    Jean Pierre is the owner and crepemaster in this maison.  He dresses the part well, with black striped pants and white chef's jacket.  Even his very authentic French accent adds to the genuineness of the experience.  He greeted me with, "Bonjour," and seemed happy to have a short exchange in Francaise.    My breakfast Crepe of Bacon and Gruyere, topped with a smoky Vinaigrette drizzle was very good, and the accompanying Java was also a superior blend.  There is much more on the lunch and dessert menus, but they must wait for another time, when I don't have to run off to the office.    I hope Bonjour Creperie Café does well at this location.  This office complex does not offer any alternatives, and it is nice to have a quality vendor close at hand for the folks who work here. There is also an outdoor area for good weather dining.

Single Slice Review  I stopped into Tony's King of Pizza for a light bite after finishing an errand nearby.  The shop is fairly small, cozy and family run.   I just needed a little something to quell the hunger and get me to dinner a few hours off. A slice of pizza was the way to go, and visiting a new place always excited me. At the counter I saw one regular pie ready for reheating and consumption. I asked for a "well done" slice, and sat at a booth to wait.   It arrived in the hands of the young woman who had taken my order. Shy smile. A sprinkle of crushed chili pepper, and I was in business. It was as requested, with the extra heat remelting the cheese cover and running off onto the paper plate when I picked it up. Burnt fingers. A small puddle of oil.   The slice was unmanageable with all the leakage. This pizza just had too much cheese and was out of balance with the tomato sauce, which was lost in all the runny goo.   We're I to go there again, I would try the cheesesteak, or ask for a tomato pie with more tomato and less cheese.

With Philly off limits for the arrival of Pope Francis, I took the opportunity to explore a different part of the Universe and drove out to Telford for a taste of the Vietnam Café & Restaurant.  As the saying goes, "One door closes, and another opens..." And, so it was on Saturday night.    This family owned and operated Viet house has been at this location over ten years.  Upon approach it looks to be small and designed for take out, but on entry the large size of the dining area comes into view.  Plenty of room for dozens of people with tables off to the right.  Orders and most table service are provided by one gentleman who appears to be at least a manager of the shop, if not an owner.  His torn jeans approach to his job suggests the later.    We opted for Summer Rolls, Grilled Pork Banh Mi, and Chicken Fried Rice.  They were all very good.  The Rolls were stuffed with large Shrimp and ground Pork.  The Peanut Dipping Sauce was pretty much standard, but was the expected complement to this appetizer.  The Banh Mi was very good with fresh French Baguette, well-grilled and BBQed Pork, and ample sliced Cucumber, Carrots and Cilantro.  A squirt or two of Sriracha and the crunchy supple sandwich came to life.  Loved the bread.  The Fried Rice was really unnecessary, but it was a huge mound of freshly made White Rice full of Chicken and Veggies.  I would pass on this in the future.   The patrons here looked like the remains of the hippie literati with some curious couples thrown in the mix.  We fit right in!  Now that the Pope has departed, I will more likely return to Philly for my Vietnamese fix, but Vietnam Café & Restaurant was certainly as good as most of those I have tried around Washington Avenue.  Good to know it is there should the city fathers over react again to the coming of an international superstar.  With the Democratic Convention coming next summer, Telford could get another look.  PRO TIP - The Banh Mi is not on the menu.  They are found on the walls of the joint, and are available for the asking.   PRO TIP 2 - Pay your check at the register.

Apparently, Ginos was a Philly thing back in the day.  Now, its reincarnation attempts to recreate that experience for the 21st century burger palate.  Not having those memories, I am left to evaluate this Street Road stop in the present.   Burgers joints are going through a differentiation process.  The McD experience has evolved into a Red Robin/Cheeburger/Hooters high end burger place, and now, a middle rung on the ladder ala Five Guys/Nifty Fifty/Johnie Rockets.  Grease seems to be the special ingredient.  Not that I have anything against grease...it is the "secret sauce" of the burger biz.   Ginos falls into the space between McD and Five Guys.  It allows more self expression in what you want in the bun, and the fries are better than average.  The patty is free form and only 2 oz.  The bun is adequate and hold together better than the white bread variety found in many lesser establishments.  Whether you like this semi-customized approach comes down to whether you can accept that grease adds flavor and texture to the dining experience.  I think it does.  That, and some friendly service, brings me back for lunch when I am in the area.

Great first impressions!  The floor is well laid out with plenty of room in the front and back dining areas.  The space is tastefully decorated with Asian influences.  The takeout menu fits on one page, front and back, so it is not too complicated, even for a first time customer.  Appetizers run from spring rolls to fried egg rolls, dumplings and sugarcane wrapped ground shrimp.  We were there for the Pho, and had Pho Ga (chicken in steaming chicken broth with a heap of rice noodles).  The garnish of sprouts, basil leaves, jalapeno slices and lime, was fresh and added great textural flavors.  The Pho comes in two sizes, kids and regular.  The regular bowl is large enough for your pet goldfish (to swim in comfortably). Next time we intend to branch out into the sandwiches and grilled entrees, as they looked real good on the next table.   I have loved Vietnamese coffee since visiting Ho Chi Minh City, and it was exactly the same with condensed milk and personal size french press coffee drip at the table.  The fresh fruit smoothies looked tasty, too. Next time.  Bottom line - Maybe not quite the experience of a Pho cafe in Da Nang, or our bigger cities, but still authentic, flavorful and worth the trip.  Highly recommended.  2.20.13 - I have been back a few times and tried the Tea (personal teapot and wonderful teas), Sandwiches (BBQ Pork on authentic French Demi Baguette very tasty), and Mango Smoothie (creamy, fruity and so good going down).

We had a great fundraiser here at Rose Bank last night.   The tasting barn is a wonderful indoor venue for a party of 100 people or more. The high ceilings and exposed beams still smell of cedar, and the stone floor and windows help create a perfect ambiance for a fun evening.   Luckily for us, several of the best restaurants in Newtown pitched in with contributions of their popular dishes - La Stalla, Vecchia Osteria, Piccolo Trattoria, State Street Kitchen, Slack's Hoagie Shack, and Starbucks gave us more than enough food to keep us sated throughout the night. Kate Sotillie and Chuck Ball performed perfect accompanying music (she can really sing, and Chuck plays acoustic guitar with flash and style).  Kings of Leon! Fleetwood Mac! Adele! Come on people!!!  Yes, we did have a few obligatory comments offered by our County Commissioner, State Representative, and the "Two Tough Mother" candidates for Supervisor, but we did not allow the pols to take the air out of the huge room.    Every table had a bottle of red, blush and white to enjoy, and about a dozen more for given away as door prizes. What I tasted was pretty good, although I had to limit myself because I was the MC for the fete, and I did not want to embarrass myself.

It is time to revisit my past reviews of House of Pho, and update my impressions and ranking for this ever improving Vietnamese restaurant.    Returning for the first time in a few months, the first thing I noticed was the presence of booths along the front windows.  We sat there, and the additional privacy was felt immediately.  Great touch!  They also had moved the drink menu onto a table card for immediate perusal and quick ordering.  Smart move to save the time of waiting for the arrival of the menu.  We selected the Mango Smoothy and Coconut Tuoi, and had them at the table within minutes, and before we ordered the victuals. The Smoothie was sweet and creamy, just as I remembered it, and the Tuoi was a mild coconut infused water with thin Coconut shavings in the glass.  Mildly sweet and instantly refreshing.    We ordered the Spring Roll app, Grilled Shrimp with Lemongrass Sauce, and a small Pho Gai (Chicken).  The Spring Roll was cool, crisp and so fresh, with extra large Shrimp seen through the translucent skins.  The Peanut Sauce had a bit of a spicy kick and complemented the sweet crispness of the roll.  The Grilled Shrimp were smaller than in the Roll, but numerous, and arrived nestled in a lettuce leaf.  The Lemongrass Sauce was an interesting taste, less dominant that its Thai sibling, but well used with the shrimp.  It was subtle and I really appreciate the interplay with the light BBQness of the Shrimp. Finally, the soup was Pho-n-tastic; hot broth with large slivers of Chicken Breast and Noodles. The flavor was superb.  This is a clear broth as opposed to the sometimes tawny opaque smoky flavor offered by other pho joints.  Of course, it came with a side plate loaded with sprouts, basil leaves, jalapeno slices and wedge of lime. The bowl was so full when I finished preparing it I had to press down gently with my spoon to suppress the garnish and allow some soup into my spoon. A slightly bigger bowl with the same amount of ingredients might have been a good idea to avoid spillage. Totally satisfying.  We finished with VN Coffee and Green Tea, so we could sit for a while longer and talk while we continued to enjoy the evening created by House of Pho.  This establishment has become first class.  It need offer no apology to sister shops in nearby urban centers.  In fact, I recently returned from Garden Grove, California, the Vietnamese capital in the USA, where I sampled a few Vietnamese delights.  None were any better than House of Pho, and some were considerably worse.   5 Stars to House of Pho.  Great work, Fred and Victor!  OCTOBER 4, 2014 - The best places continue to evolve as they find their groove and have the courage to explore the outer limits.  House of Pho follows this tradition.  Their menu is broader as they are now offering special seafood dishes, no doubt putting a creative edge to a marketing survey to see where to go next.    The house remains clean and coolly inviting.  The staff seems to finally feel comfortable with the kitchen genius, and Fred and Victor reign serenely over their domain. Today's Jackfruit Smoothie was so good ($1. off) and my Com Thit Nuong tasty and full of Pork, Noodles and Spouts.  While I went in for the Pho, the alternatives overcame me, and I went with something new for me.    Still a 5 Star experience.  JANUARY 5, 2015 - Stopped in last night for a Pho dinner and decided to try the Spicy Hot Wings in their Signature Sauce.  They were hot, crisp, peppery, sweet, fat and delectable. A very good complement to the standard menu.   Keep it up, guys!

I have eaten lunch at Char Koon three times over the past two years, but never been there for dinner.  While the restaurant is family run, pleasantly appointed, and has a diverse menu covering Chinese, Thai and Japanese entries, including Sushi, the impression is that it is really a Chinese American joint that offers the other cuisines, but does not do a good job with them.  It all tastes "Chinese" and lacks the distinguishing flavors and uniqueness to be found in places that really understand the national dishes of the countries presented, and employees a kitchen that appreciates how the preparations differ.   I have tried the Pad Thai, General Tsao's  and other Chicken dishes, Soups, and egg rolls.  They are all decent, but can be found in better form elsewhere.  If you find yourself in Langhorne wanting Asian food, there are few alternatives.  You could do worse, but then again, it would probably be better to go across the parking lot to Brothers for pizza, and save your Asian urges for geographic areas with greater Chinese, Thai, Vietnamese, Japanese, or Korean populations.    The prices are very good for lunch ($6.00 - $8.00 for combo lunches including soup, rice and tea), and the quantities are large enough to fill you up.    It is difficult to get excited by Char Koon. Perhaps, their dinners are better.

Pho 75 on the 11th block of Washington Avenue in South Philly has about the best pho broth I have tasted around here.  It is rich and complex with subtle anise undertones that seem to shift in intensity from top to bottom of the bowl.  It is really quite amazing.  I ordered the Rib Eye Steak in a regular (small) bowl and had it steaming my glasses in under 5 minutes.  The side accoutrement of Thai Basil, Jalapeno slices, Lime wedge, and Spouts were all fresh and plentiful.  After using all I wanted, there was plenty remaining on the plate.  I pushed them aside to make room for the Sriracha and Hoisin Sauces into which l dip the beef for eating.    Maybe I am just a barbarian, but with broth this good it does not make a difference to me what meat goes into the bath, aside from its contribution to the flavor of the soup.  The wonder of the pho is all about the taste of the broth.  The most important thing is to be sure to finish every last drop in your bowl to reach and savor all of it.  Don't worry if you want to pick up the bowl and pour the contents down your gullet.    That's what everyone else is doing anyway!   CASH ONLY - Minus 1 star for lack of convenience.

I came here today with my Korean friend who operates a small restaurant in Newtown who needed to restock rice noodles, bowls and a few other things for the ethnic elements of her basically American shop.  This was my first visit, although she knew her way around from past experience here.    The supermarket is showing its age and lack of maintenance.  While large enough to inventory most of everything needed for an Asian home or resto, it has seen better days, and suffers by comparison to its competitors both nearby and in other Asian neighborhoods here and in Jersey or New York.  The fresh produce and frozen food sections are the highlight of the store, complete with those exotics and flavorfuls that are signature to such establishments.  The remainder of the aisles feel dark and dreary, but possess the required products unique to Asian stores.  The fish department in the back is large with plenty of whole fish on ice, and cut ups in refrigeration units. Plenty of staff to select, weigh, cut and package. However, the ice melts onto the floor, making for a slick foothold and slippery walk.  Yes. There is also the appearance of mold on the floor, bins, and walls.  Perhaps, not the safest place to spend time.    So, we were able to secure most of what we needed at good prices.  Yet, the check out was slow and bagging disorganized.  Right. Just like the old country.   There is also an in house restaurant that seemed popular, but we did not check it out, having filled up at Pho 75 less than an hour before.    This is not the place to make your primary market unless you don't have access to a better shopping experience.  Still, it has just about everything needed for an Asian kitchen at good prices.  It you don't mind the slovenliness, it is acceptable as the place you go to get the things you need while trying not to notice all the things that are wrong.

Bella Café is a new edition to the scene at the eastern end of New Falls Road in Levittown, Pa.  It remains an Italian house under new ownership and name.  They have an extensive breakfast menu for the early crowd, which I was there to take advantage of.  The place was clean and attractive in an old school way, and service was warm and efficient.    I was looking for French Toast, and Bela had a couple of choices.  Short or Tall Stack of Texas Toast styled egg fry, or the same in "Stuffed" versions with sweet cream cheese and fruit of choice toppings. Tempted, but I ask for the regular shorty.  A few minutes later, a large white round plate arrived with a nicely powdered sugar dusting of well grilled Pan Grille Francaise.   The egg had been mixed with vanilla, sugar and cinnamon long enough to absorb a lot of flavor, and left on the iron sufficiently to allow the edges and ridges in the bread to be caramelized.  The chef knew his stuff.  The thick toast looked great, especially after a melting of butter, and pour over of packaged Smucker's syrup.  The taste and texture were fine, and a nice reward for waking up early enough to indulge this morning.   I was the only customer today, which is unfortunate for all the folks who are missing a good wake up.  Even the coffee was fresh and strong.    If there was anything that kept Bella from ringing a fifth bell, it was the use of packaged corn syrup sweetener, rather than having a maple syrup option.  I would have gladly paid an extra sum for the chance to turn this French Toast into something magical with the addition of real maple grade B dark, to complement an otherwise excellent presentation.     Nice going!

I guess I'm not a Red Carpet kind of guy because unless it is very early or very late, I prefer just to sit with everyone else, plug in and drift away.  However, on those other occasions when travel and torture seem to become confused, even a less than optimal airport "club" can be the difference between tolerable abuse and downright grouchiness.    A free drink (or two), a passable snack, and a comfortable chair, can feel like an oasis in the desert.  Although PHL's United lounge is subpar, it can still save the day.  The staff overcompensates because they know what we are all dealing with.    Just wish they brought it some genuine cheesesteaks and Yingling to remind us of what can be so redeeming about Philly.

Squirrels Nest Café is a nugget of a find (not a gem) on West Bridge Street in Morrisville, Pa.  It has been there more than a decade after the owners of the Steaks, Eggs and Things on River Road in Yardley sold it to the folks who created Charcoal, and moved to the present digs in a more downscale part of town.    The house was bright with morning sun when I stepped inside for breakfast.  It was clean and homecoming attractive in a 1980's sort of way.  I liked its folksiness. The ladies of the day are still running it as they did the old place, making a space that feels like a cross between your kitchen and a country store.  Everyone knows everyone else, and most of the time I was at the counter the other stools were occupied by management and kitchen people chatting up a storm.  They seem to like each other.   Their Gemini Coffee Maker brews up good Joe, and the griddle turned out a nice full stack of French Toast for me.  The hot iron cauterized the surface of the egged bread quite well, creating the light crunch I prefer.  Amazing how many places can't get that right.    A little more attention to detail would garner this Squirrel's Nest another star.  Coming around with the coffee pot more often would be a big help, as would the timely placement of the bill in front of the patron for those who have someplace else to be.  Too, the use of an apostrophe where needed to demonstrate the possessive tense of the rodent so cutely displayed on the menu cover would really sharpen focus here.    I really liked it despite such nits, and will be back.

The return visit was even better than the first.  The Pho Tam Nam Gan, was absolutely crammed with thin sliced Roundeye Steak, Well Done Brisket and Soft Tendon, in addition to the nest of thin noodles, slivers of Onion and Scallion, plus the optional Sprouts, Thai Basil, Jalapeno and Fresh Squeezed Lime.  It was impossible to push down the flat bottom spoon to slurp the beef broth without causing spillage over the rim of the bowl.    Hot. Steamy. Meaty. Delicious.   (And not a hint of MSG.)

This Chicken Holiday has a few things going for it.    First, it turns out top of the line Fried Chicken, BBQ Ribs and Buffalo Wings.  Each order is individually prepared when it comes in, so nothing is sitting around waiting for an unfortunate to consume a less than prime meal.  I found the chicken to be moist with nicely spiced breaded and fried coating.  The Ribs were large, dark brown from the basting sauces, and nearly "fall of the bone" tender.  The BBQ taste was both sweet and tangy, just as it should be.  The Wings are larger than found in most outlets, but the hotness covers every nook and cranny.    I can't say that these items were the best I ever had, nor that they were as good as it gets.  Yet, given what is available in the area, they are all on the high end of taste and enjoyment, and for me, there is no need to look further afield to satisfy my Fried Chicken Addiction.   And, if you come on a Sunday afternoon you can enjoy an impromptu car show in the parking lot.  Folks are there from all over opening their hoods and hooking up their stereos to external speakers so everyone can check out their wheels to Deep Purple.

South Warren Street in Trenton is making an effort to get its act together.  It has always had the big trees and 19th Century architecture, but until the last few years, the storefronts were often empty or lacking in attractiveness.  Things have changed for the better, and it is now possible to walk down Warren and find several nice places to have a meal, drink, or even shop.    Sunrise Luncheonette is one of those urban pioneers.  It is a small shop with 7 or eight stools at the lunch counter, and about the same number of tables.  Décor is rather Spartan, but the management makes a real effort to make you feel welcome when walking in for breakfast before 8, while the surrounding state government drivers are yet to open.  I sat at the counter and watched as well known customers chatted with the counterman in friendly tones, swapping stories and jokes.  Coffee was served promptly, and was about average.  My Sausage, Egg and Cheese Sandwich on a Roll was also decent and tasty.  The convenience of location cannot be beat.  I enjoyed being able to park on the street without using a meter until 9 am, having a pleasant breakfast only 5 minutes from court, and getting out for under $6. Trenton is actually showing some gritty charm early in the morning, and I enjoyed being part of the wake up.  Sunrise's breakfasts should not be compared to suburban style diners where excess is the name of the game.  No. This is a cityscape locale, where the clientele tells a different story than heard out there.  Life is rougher downtown, and Sunrise Luncheonette reflects that reality.    If you get off on the difference, this can be a nice way to start the day.

Gold Fountain II Restaurant sits in the strip with McCaffery's Supermarket in Lower Makefield.  It has a nice facility, with more room than many other Chinese shops.  The tables are spaced far enough apart for some privacy.  The owners are pleasant and helpful.  The menu is the traditional Chinese American fare with little creativity beyond that. Still, if you like this style hybridized cuisine (and many do), this place is as good as the others in the area. For better, you would have to go to a city, or into Jersey to Shanghai Bun or Szechuan House, which are both more authentically Chinese.   We ordered an app of Fried Pork Dumplings, and they were good.  They may have been deep fried rather than pan fried, and the extra oil was noticeable but did not detract from the overall good taste.    The entres were from the Chef's Specials Menu; Sesame Chicken and Orange Beef. Both came with complementary bowls of soup.  The Hot and Sour Soup had too much vinegar for my taste, and was not so good. The Sesame Chicken was plentiful and the thick gooey sauce captured the big pieces of chicken like they were encased in amber.  The taste was what we expected, but some of the chicken seemed dry from overcooking or deep freezing.  The Orange Beef was better, with plenty of thin sliced and coated beef and a thinner sauce that allowed the texture of the beef to dominate. Both of us liked it better than the chicken.  Both presentations were surrounded by Broccoli Spears in the customary way.  So wish someone had a better concept of how to finish off garnishing multiple plates that did not demand broccoli on everything.  How much of that stuff can you eat?    Overall, Gold Fountain II was a run of the mill Chinois house, with the usual suspects on the menu.  As that is what most people want, there is no disappointment.  The quality is middle of the road; neither better nor worse than the local competition.    If I was asked to compare with its nearest competition, A Little Dragon, on the other side of this building, I would say that they are very similar, but based on what I have tried, the edge goes to the Dragon.

East Lincoln Highway, Langhorne, PA, is primarily noted as the location of the Reedman-Toll automobile dealership, the largest car outlet in the country. In its shadow are many smaller businesses, including this Friendly's restaurant. Obviously, it is well known, as when I arrived around 7 pm on a Sunday night, it was more than half full of customers chowing down on the traditional American cuisine and ice cream desserts for which this chain is known.   I was guided to a booth along the front wall by the hostess, and handed the laminated multi-paged menu. Their Sriracha Burger sounded interesting, and I went with it, medium. I was assured by my server that I would receive a pink finish from their never frozen ground beef.  She was right. Unlike many burger joints that promise the desired degree of grilling, but inevitably deliver only a well done puck, this kitchen did keep its word. I was given a medium burger that was lightly pink throughout. Gratitude.   The rest of the accompaniment - pepper jack cheese, bacon, onion straws, lettuce, tomato, sriracha mayo, on brioche bun - were all present and accounted for, although the "crispy" onion was soggy. The overall taste satisfied my burger craving for the week. At ten bucks it was priced beyond its actual value, but it was good to know that Friendly's was keeping up with the burger wars, where every food emporium had to offer a decent six ouncer to stay competitive.   It is safe to say that Friendly's keeps up with the other franchise Joneses in this universe. You can come here for a burger or other of their beef and chicken offerings, and leave sated. And, if in the mood, their ice cream makes for a very convenient and creamy end of meal.   Looks like Friendly's will be around for a while longer.   3.5 STARS

Quest Diagnostics has been operating in the Village of Newtown for several years, but has not yet made it to Yelp.  I go their as part of my routine health maintenance; getting blood and other lab work done prior to my annual physical examination.  It is convenient for those in the community, and the technicians do their jobs efficiently and with cordiality.  My arteries are difficult to find when blood is to be drawn, and the phlebotomists often have to go hunting with a thin, flexible needle before they locate a source for my fluids to flow into a vial.  While I don't have White Coat Syndrome, I make these folks work.    It is easier to get the lab work done before seeing the doctor, and the results are obtained faster, than having the doctor's office staff get the samples and then send them out to a lab for testing and analysis.    It is not really possible to be a fan of a place like this, let alone think that it is a great experience.  3 Stars will have to do.

Peng Yuan is a Hong Kong style cuisine restaurant located in the strip mall at 295 Buck Road.  It is in the same complex as Wild Wasabi and Ultimate Pizza, so this is a good place to head for some grub (See subsequent review of Ultimate Pizza, which received 1 star).   The floor plan of the dining area is small, with only 28 seats, plus a few for waiting for takeout.  The space could use a face lift, but it is clean, without feeling overcrowded.  Their luncheon menu is what you expect, but while I waited, Lisa, the owner, brought out a few gratis appetizers that were as good as they were unexpected.  They consisted of triangles of fried dough pockets with mashed potato and spice in one, and a soft cheese in the other.  Both were reminiscent of samosas.   I sampled the General Tso's Chicken, which was large chunks all white meat, lightly coated, then flash fried in a wok, with a tangy thick tart sauce.  Nice effort.  Additionally, the fried rice was plentiful and tasty.  Best was the hot and sour soup, which came out steaming, and full of pork, tofu, mushrooms and way better than average broth.  Most important for me, no MSG.  This was my first bite at Peng Yuan, and I will return for a second.  I need to try more to be able to count more stars.  Bottom Line - A very decent place for lunch, maybe dinner.

Lou Lou Burgers is a new house on Main Street, New Hope, PA. The inside dining room is small, but there are plenty of red umbrella-covered tables in the front yard to help out. It is run by college students, which keeps the energy level high to offset the laid back atmosphere in the woody dining room. It also means less than consistent service as sometimes they are more engaged with themselves than customers. No big deal, but you don't want to be that guy who gets impatient waiting for the bill with empty plates on the table.   My Firecracker Burger was a fresh ground half pound of round steak and brisket, finished to the requested medium on a decent bun. The taste was excellent, with a never frozen texture and true beef flavor. Liked it alot. The side of fries were likewise taters just moments before the drop into boiling oil. Crisp, lightly salted, with plenty of those little nibs to crunch.   Prices are reasonable @ between $6.50-7.50 per, but everything else costs, so it is hard to get out at less the ten bucks a person.   This is New Hope (No Hope), after all.

Bread Crumb is a nice old place just outside downtown Doylestown on Easton Road.  It sits in an older strip commercial zone and with lower rent can keep their menu costs down for the fixed income crowd, and those who enjoy a frugal breakfast on occasion.   The counter has room for about half dozen spinners, and the service from there is friendly and efficient.  The coffee was a good brew, and refills were offered several times as I sat and devoured the French Toast.  The Log Cabin syrup tasted like it might be a refill of an industrial strength brand, but the overall taste of the meal was okay, but not more.   The French Toast would have been improved with the additional of a little vanilla extract and sugar in the egg mix to bring up the flavor of the finished product and allow for the caramelization of the edges into a crispy bite.  Without them, the taste was a bit "eggy," and flat.    Still, the place has a certain sunshine charm that makes it a pleasant stop.

If you like street push cart hot dogs that can be found all over New York, you might really enjoy sampling a couple of "franks" at Russ Ayers Hot Dog Stand in Rt. 206 in Bordentown, NJ.    Although the push cart is now housed inside a hat box sized structure, they are still boiled in the stainless steel compartments that sit inside the old wooden external walls.  Even the wheels are still attached.  The menu is limited to a half dozen variety of toppings, and they are all slapped into basic white bread buns that can't hold the mustard, onions, relish and other options that the staff loads into them.    The environment is the best part of the Russ Ayers experience.  The small hut has about 6 stools at the small counter, but many outside tables for good weather noshing.  The drinks are simple soda fountain options or a few bottles in the standup refrigeration unit.    As a rookie, I ordered one of their basic dogs that came with mustard, onions, kraut and relish on top of the Hatfield pork/beef sausage.  The young cook worked very fast to open the top of the boil box, snag a hot dog, drop it into the bun she held in her other hand, and then slather and spread all the accessories is a blur of near-accurate preparation.  My other choice was a bacon and cheese dog (see photos).    They were both decent and fun to eat.  In chatting with the workers, I learned that Mr. Ayers was deceased for a couple of decades, but that when he passed, he left the business to his waitress.  She carried on the enterprise with the help of family until the present.  I also learned that they would be installing a milkshake machine soon to add to the festivities.  If done well, that would certainly help.    I could not help thinking how much more this joint could be with a little more imagination and investment in better provisions.  The Hatfield dogs had a cheap taste.  At $2.25 a dog it was obvious why they didn't have higher quality meat.  Still, I would gladly pay more for a kosher or all beef frankfurter that had better flavor.  Too, improving the buns and condiments would likewise make most people happier with the overall meal.  Finally, unless Mr. Ayers' Last Will & Testament strictly forbid using anything but boiled hot dogs, finding room for a grill as an alternative cooking source would broadly expand the possibilities.    As it is, Russ Ayers is fine enough for the uniqueness of the experience, as well as its unusual history.  Generations have stopped in for a few dogs and a coke.  So, it really doesn't need to change if it doesn't want to.  But, as a hot dog lover I would so appreciate having more available from this iconic never-franchised food classic.

This Burger King sits in the neighborhood of Sesame Place and Oxford Valley Mall.  As such, it is in a premier location to attract families and shoppers for a fast bite.  Anticipating this, BKHQ designed this shop with extra space, large kiddie room, and a multitude of dining areas with different looks and feels. They even put in a fireplace lounge for those in a romantic mood. It may be the nicest Burger King I have ever seen. Almost date-worthy.  My Whopper was as good as a Whopper can be, and still fell short of much of the competition. It was hot, but the large slices of onion were not. Mayo and lettuce caused slippage, and my fingers bore witness to the consequence. Fries were decent and there were plenty of carbonated beverages, while not the excessive choice of the new fangled sodie machines.   Service was amazingly efficient for a fast food operation, with servers walking my tray over to me beyond the counter. The space was very clean.   If BK figured out how to make a first rate burger, a joint like this would be a revelation.

Although Ginger Wok in the shopping center anchored by McCaffrey's Supermarket in Lower Makefield, PA, is oddly named given its decor and menu, it is an attractive modern Asian house with a dual identity. Operated by Chinese folk, it offers Japanese sushi and Chinese American standards in a room that feels much more oriented toward raw fish. A lot of money was spent on dark slate floors, white wavy walls, nautical wallpaper, and subtle lighting. No denying the place is beautiful. I was pleasantly surprised by how good it looked.   I was there to try their Chinese lunch menu, and was not disappointed. For $6.50, all the usual suspects were available with soup or eggroll and fried/white rice. While most deliver such deals in takeout packaging or cheapo plates, my meal arrived on a strong white sculpted platter and metal flatware. The black tea (+$1.50) came in a ceramic mug and with strong flavor.   The General's Chicken was well prepared (although a lighter coating would make it better), with a legit semi-hot amber sauce complete with small Szechuan chilies. The fried rice was copious, but could have been warmer. The wonton soup had a good light broth, with average wontons. Service was friendly and timely.   I walked out $10 lighter, but quite satisfied with my Friday afternoon meal.   PRO TIP - Walk to the back of the house to see the sushi bar and fish tanks, the second of which has a few Gar in the crystal tank. Exquisite fish.

It's not the largest beer distributor in Newtown. It's the ONLY beer distributor in Newtown. As such, it is a convenient place to pick up a few cases of Boddington, Flying Fish, or the King of Beers, for your next shindig or to get you through the week.   Yes. It still feels like a cool, damp warehouse, mainly because it is.  Floor to ceiling cardboard encasing a cool twenty-four is bound to make everything moist.   Don't forget to go next door to the State Store, a/k/a Ten Centre Wine and Spirits, to pick up your other alcohol requirements.  This one, two punch makes for convenience.  The big parking lot out front makes it hassle-free.   Drink responsibly. Party like a maniac.

When another Chinese restaurant was closed one night this week due to broken air conditioning, we turned again to my trusty Yelp app to find another Middle Kingdom kitchen in the vicinity. Henry's China Inn was right down Krewstown Road about a quarter mile, so we decided to give it a go.    Turns out that Henry no longer owns this house, but at 90 he can be forgiven for retiring and living the good life.  The current owners have been at it for several years, with husband chef working the wok, and wife hostess and service provider doing her social thing in the front of the house, along with a few other employees, who all seem to be content in their positions.   The menu is pretty much traditional Chinese-American fare, with lots of pork, chicken, shrimp and beef for combination with rice or noodles.  There is also a page of specials that allow the wokmaster to show off his talent.  We ordered three dishes, intending to bring home the remains for stepson who chose not to join us.  Salt & Pepper Shrimp, Orange Beef, and Eggplant in Garlic Sauce were our selections.  All were actually better than expected in terms of both quality and quantity.    There were about ten large shrimp very lightly breaded with enough salt and pepper to make it a fairly spicy dish.  It was cooked just enough to allow max taste, while leaving the crustacean juicy and fun to chew.  They were laid atop a mix of chopped green pepper and onion that supported the dominant flavor of the shrimp well.  Solid!  The orange beef was a full load, flash fried to a nice crunch, and drowned in a dark brown orange based semi-thick sauce.  We had requested it to be very spicy as the menu suggested was an option, but it arrived sweeter than we wished, and returned it to the kitchen for more chili to be blended in.  Second time was improved, but we still asked for a side dish of hot oil which we poured on top. That was the ticket. It would never be mistaken for Szechuan style, but it least it provided a pleasant burn on top of the Guandong sweetness.  Finally, the eggplant was very good and plentiful, and a nice counterbalance in both taste and texture.   We had a good conversation with Madame owner, and enjoyed the overall experience of our visit to Henry's.  We realized that it was difficult for a non-Szechuan kitchen to create the numbing flavor we were asking for, so we decided that going forward we would pack a jar of our favorite crispy chili in oil sauce when we went out for Chinese dinners, just in case we wanted to feel the burn, so we could doctor the dish to our specifications.    Henry's is a utilitarian space, designed for eating in without flourishes of heavy Chinese décor. Still, it was comfortable and clean.  We left very satisfied.   BYOB.

I've been conducting an informal tour of all the Mexican, Guatemalan, Salvadoran, Puerto Rican and other Central American restaurants that have sprung up in the Trenton-Hamilton area over the past few years, and generally replaced the Italian houses that came before them.  The transformation has been amazing, and after sampling lunch in more than half a dozen shops, I am impressed.
