City populations evolve over their lifetime as one ethnic group after another emigrate from somewhere else to a future in a new place.   So it is here, where the shift from southern Europe to South America has been steady and irreversible.  Of course, all this change is much easier to take whether you are part of the migration, or merely observing it from the comfort of your barstool or table for four, when the culture and cuisine are generally neutral to positive (no worse than what came before to the open mind and unbiased palate).   While I love Italian food (and even married into the tribe), I find myself thoroughly enjoying what has replaced it.  Las Casas Mexicanas are by and large, excelente.  This is very true of Taqueria El Mariachi on South Olden Avenue in Trenton, just west of Greenwood Avenue.    It was a rainy afternoon when I approached for lunch and found the adequate parking lot behind the row of buildings that house TEM. I was able to pull up directly behind their place and enter immediately through the back door. Barely a drop reached me, and the sketchiness of the street scene was minimized drastically by this direct access.  Walking by the kitchen, the staff smiled and directed me to the dining room, where they promptly followed me to my chosen table with menu and water glass.  The attractive waitperson spoke little English, but between my broken Spanish and her charming Spanglish, we got through introductions and my order of Flautas de Pollo (literally, Chicken Flutes).    When my plate arrived, it was covered over with Lettuce, Tomato, Onion, Avocado, Beans and Cheese.  The Flautas were buried beneath, almost invisible.  Cutting through the salad I uncovered four rolled corn tortillas stuffed and overflowing with a Chicken Cheese and Spice mix.  It was very well done. Delicious and fun to eat. Also, quite filling.  I ended up eating the stuffing out of two Flautas and leaving the flutes behind.  I also had a drink called, "Jamaica," which was a sweet fruity juice that I took to be Jicama and/or Pomegranate. All this, plus change for my $10.    The house has the same casual and divey atmosphere of most of the other Mexi and Guat spots I have tried so far.  The majority of the costumers were eating in their work clothes and were comfortable as if at home. I like this laid back setting.  I will continue my tour, but can easily recommend Taqueria El Mariachi for a good, filling and cheap Mexican meal.    PS.  This place is definitely Mexican.  It says so on the menu, and I asked my server (en Espanol) the nationality of the cuisine.

"It was the best of times. It was the worst of times."  - Charles Dickens, Tale of Two Cities.   With apologies to the master, my experience at Empire Szechuan resembles that opening line in the classic novel; in reverse.  We were just looking for a decent meal after excellent foot massage down Bustleton at Lavender Foot Spa.  I saw the sign and was curious without checking Yelp first.  Spontaneity can lead to wonderful discovery, or just bust your balls.  This was a strange hybrid of both.   Walking in, we quickly realized this was primarily a take out joint.  Two tables out front, with one occupied by the owner's sons playing computer games.  It was also chilly inside with everyone wearing jackets to keep the electric bill down.  I love Szechuanese cuisine and hoped the name on the sign reflected the product in the kitchen, when so many others simply do not.    We ordered at the counter. Apple ordering and pay system.  Reading the menu, it was obvious there was precious little Chengdu kitchen here.  Still, we agreed to ride it out and see what happened.  Orange Beef, Eggplant in Garlic Sauce, and Steamed Dumplings, were our desire.  We sat at the sole open table to wait, and hoped for the hot tea to warm us.    It arrived in a quart sized plastic soup container, with tea bags inside.  No teapot. No ceramic teacups.  Just styro cups. Free pour by bending the rim into a spout. Really?!  Before we could pour the tea,  our place settings were brought out.  Styro plates and skimpy plastic forks, with those take out packets of duck sauce, soy and mustard thrown on top.    Feeling so appreciated right there!    We poured the cha and waited for the next act to unfold.  This was either going to be a disaster, or outright conflagration, if their slovenliness continued.  We scored a pair of chopsticks, which were much sturdier than the malformed forks.  Then the moon broke through the brooding clouds.    The Eggplant dish arrived first.  It was a large amount of the veggie, with other colorful edibles mixed in.  This was way more than could fit in a Chinese take out box, and it glistened from the oily sauce that held it together.  We opened the rice box to shovel some on the plates as our base for eating, and sticked a few pieces of the purple nightshade on top.  We were guarded lest the load prove inedible.    We looked at each other in astonishment as the taste registered in our pleasure centered brains.  It was excellent!  Soft eggplant.  Appropriately cooked secondaries. Wonderful garlic sauce that was just prepared for our meal.  Yes. It was rather incongruous after the inauspicious start to the dinner, but one we gladly welcomed.    The Orange Beef arrived moments later.  Another huge pile of food, this time, dark brown spicy gloop on top of a motherload of nicely sliced beef, that had been wokked and rolled in a light batter and deep fried before returning to the stove for the final pouring of the Tso-like sauce.    Munch. Chew. Blooming, mouth expanding flavor of orange and chili, that had my eyes open wide in silent exclamation.  What the hey?!  This was even better than the eggplant.  The meat seemed fresh; not frozen, and again the sauce was prepared just for us.  It tasted as good as almost any orange beef I had ever eaten.  We agreed that we were enjoying an exceptional Chinese American meal, especially given the dive we were in, and the way the story began.  Quite frankly, we were blown away.  Maybe the secret of this place is to overlook the distain of the sons, and the stain of the environment, and just hunker down in the winter heatlessness of the house, knowing something those who only do take out and delivery never discover - that the food at Empire Szechuan is a slam bang winner for those who sit there and wait to eat right out of the wok. By the time it arrives to your home, the magic has disappeared.  Astounding!   We packed up the leftovers in anticipation of a second round of slammin' Chinois, suspecting it would not be anything like what we had just devoured.  We paid the twenty bucks or so, and walked out into the night slightly inebriated from this rags to riches saga.  PS. The dumplings sucked (not XLB), but we forgave them after this profane/sacred epiphany.

Shree Fusion Grill sits on Bridge Street, Morrisville, PA, in the only new building in that part of town.  It has a small dining room with about ten tables, as well as an outdoor seating area in good weather.  It is open for lunch between 11:30 - 3:30, and opens again for dinner at 5:30 until 9:30.    From reading the few reviews, it seemed that lunch specials were available at reasonable cost, but I learned upon asking that that deal is only for take out service. Disappointed, I inquired about smaller dishes on the menu for lunch.  The server informed me that they also made thalis, the famous Indian samplers that offer 8 to 10 different dishes in small stainless steel bowls, served on a tray with basmati rice, naan and papadam. At $10.99 it sounded interesting, so I went with the chicken thali.    It arrived about 15 minutes later, with a samosa, lentil soup, chicken tikka masala, eggplant (baingan bharta), potato and pea (aloo matar), chickpea and potato masala, plain yogurt, and honey rosewater gulab jamun, basmati rice, etc. It all looked good, and the heat level was enough to bring sweat and runny nose. Liked all of it, although it was a bit more than I could finish in one seating. The pitcher of lemon water came in handy.   Shree Fusion Grill is not haute Indian cuisine, but it is a solid kitchen in a casual setting. The menu tips its hat to "Manchurian" style Indo-Chinese plates, and also has French onion soup, wraps and burgers. Clearly trying to appeal to the broadest cross section of the community possible. It isn't Indian Garden, nor Guru, but they know their way around Indian spices and provides a very good meal for those looking for an alternative to the regular daily choices in the neighborhood.   PRO TIP - Plenty of parking in back, if you drive around the corner and follow the signs to Renaissance Center.

The Market at Styer Orchard is several things. First, it is a pretty good deli, making breakfast and lunch for people lucky enough to realize they have a kitchen and small dining area in the house. Second, it is a bakery producing excellent fruit pies, apple cider and other donuts, and a variety of other pastries and cookies.  Third, it is a gift shop with shiny Christmas objects, and all year round seasonal do-dads. A little too gitchy for me. But, if you come for the top two possibilities, the likelihood is you will leave happy.    I finally stopped in for breakfast earlier this week. At first, I could not find anyone who worked in the deli/kitchen part of the building.  I saw the deli case full of smoked meats and fresh salads, but no one to give my order to.  I saw women in the bakery taking pies in/out of their ovens, but they looked busy.  So, I briefly came around the deli counter and stepped into the back kitchen. Someone was back there, and when I called to her, she promptly came to me to apologize, and take my french toast order. Three slices of wheat bread and coffee, please.   I went to pour my java while waiting for the grillwork. There was limited selection, and it was clear that caffeine was not the priority around there. When I finally got a fresh cup and added milk it was really rather ordinary.  For $1.40 for the larger size, I really won't complain, other than to say a better bean would lead to happier customers. The Market was def not a café (But, it sure could be!).   My grilled egged bread was very good, however. Large slices of wheat loaf, dipped in a superior mix of egg, sugar and vanilla extract, that when kissing hot iron really caramelized the surface of the bread.  It had that light sweet crispness that I love in french toast. They fell short by only offering Smucker's syrup, rather than pure maple, but that would be expecting too much.   Given what's happening elsewhere in the vicinity with coffee and pleasant coffee houses, the potential at the Market @ Styer Orchard is tremendous.  They already have a superior bakery and deli, so they are way ahead of the game. Just bring in a coffee maven barista with the right equipment, redesign the floorplan a bit to make it more attractive and comfortable, and this joint would be jumping! I'm not talking slick, because you still want the current regulars to come in for their apple cider donuts and chicken salad sandwiches; but toned up enough to get the after workout and business breakfast crowd interested enough to make it a primary pit stop. Check out Be Well Bakery & Cafe in Huntington Valley to see what is possible.  This place is an undiscovered vein of gold waiting to be found by someone with a little imagination, capital, a touch of design skill and love of coffee.  Wish that person was me.

I've returned to Mil-Lee's a couple of times over the past year.  Have to say that the breakfasts have been consistently very good with overflowing plate and excellent friendly service.   The coffee has a nice bite.  The Sausage, Onion, Pepper Omelet I had today was tasty and filling. The accompanying Home Fries were too much to finish.    It is time to add the Luv-Inn to my short list of breakfast favorites on my way to court in Trenton.    I should have bounced to 4 Stars before this.

I love the name, "Wild Ginger."  It evokes images of spicy jungles with Jaguar eyes and Elephant tusks lurking in the deep canopy forests of northern Thailand.    This version of the two shop restaurant empire is not quite as wild as the name suggests, but does have its positive moments.  The Jamison store has dark red walls with black cut out images of exotic Asian women and the Eiffel Tower.  On a hot day it instantly cools the visitor with its permanent shade.    The menu works especially well at lunch, where the offerings on the Thai side are based on the main ingredient you chose - Tofu, Veggies, Chicken, Beef or Shrimp and range from $8 to $9 for the style you select.  I almost ordered the Pad Thai, but allowed myself to listen to my server telling me the Cashew Thai Style was just as good.  She was very pleasant, and she convinced me to try the nut approach.    First came the Tom Yam Soup, which was nicely spiced and steaming.  It was what I expected that soup to be.  Tart and sinus rattling. Nice. The main dish was very attractive with fresh Veggies (Pepper, Onion, Scallion, Carrot, Baby Corn, Cashews), and a light brown glazy sauce that made everything shine.  Looked great.  The taste was were the letdown occurred. While the menu described a mild sweetness, to my buds, there was little if any flavor. Freshness and quantity were not issues, but I truly wanted something bolder in line with my Thai-spectations.  Rather than ask for more sauce or something sweeter to add to the plate, I went the other way and asked for Sesame Oil and Chili Sauce to bring up the flames.    After dumping the small dish of spice and oil into it and mixing thoroughly, the flavor was much improved, and I enjoyed the meal the rest of the way.  It still wasn't authentically Thai, but it was reasonably good.   Turned out that Wild Ginger (II) was a "fusion" or hybrid kitchen, owned by someone other than Thais or Japanese.  Such 'con-fusion' houses usually don't work well as the concept doesn't exist in the "wild" of southeast Asia, and relies on the theory that no one here will recognize that this concoction approach lacks roots in any indigenous culture.    Wild Ginger gamely tries to offer a valid alternative, and the dishes are okay for what they are.  It's just that they fall short of being fully satisfying because of what they are not.

Unfortunately, Washington Crossing Coffee has departed the scene here at Capital Health. The area where it once resided is now just a seating area on the second floor of the medical center, with several high tops still in place where customers once sat. I was surprised how few people I saw inside the large building, especially considering how crowded the parking lots are all around the institution. Understandable how a small business couldn't survive in the absence of many people as potential customers and a cheap cafeteria on the lower level.   But, fear not.   Starbucks now has a micro stand inside Lori's Gift Shop on the first floor near the front door. It may not be as good as WCC, but give the youngster credit, it may ultimately succeed where the local mom and pop operation could not.   Time will tell.

First visit to a Quick Chek anywhere, and I was surprised how large this one was. It easily reminds of a rest stop along a turnpike or a Sheetz station anywhere in Pa.   They prepare hot dishes on request and have a long wall full of refrigeration units stocked with every American soft drink imaginable.    The coffee selection is broader than most 7/11s, and the adjoining snack section will remind you to take your insulin.    Fairly clean as such places go.  Good pricing, too.   I will stop into this and other Quick Cheks when the situation allows.

Two Slices & and Drink Lunch Review -  While the main Carlucci's Italian Restaurant sits around the bend in this shopping center, the primarily take out pizza joint is to the left of Shop Rite.  It is well appointed with nice enough furniture, although our table rocked so much I had to put my foot on its leg to hold it still.    The pies are ordered at the cashier/kitchen in the back.  There is a display of many of the pies for inspection.  I am not a fan of this approach as there is not "Sell By" time nor date to alert you how long they have been sitting around.  The more pies; the older they tend to be.   We ordered well done slices of the Cheesesteak Pizza, Old Fashioned Tomato Pie and Plain.  They were only Okay at best.  The Cheesesteak and T.P. were deep dish style, with light and airy crust, that tasted more like bread with toppings, than true pizza.  The Plain slice was more traditional.  It had a satisfactory taste, but had a leaky oil pan and no gasket.    This is not a tomato pie house I would return to as the samples tasted were not all that good. Probably better to walk over to the mothership for a full Italian meal.

Stopped in for an early lunch today at Xi'an Sizzling Woks, one of the three XSW sister shops in Philly.   They are known for this Biang Biang noodles and semi-spicy dishes.  Their sauces are excellent for sticking to the mein, and when you get the hand drawn pasta from their kitchen, you are in for a good time.   Two of us ordered the same thing (unusual for us); the cumin beef with noodles.  This was a single serving in a medium bowl.  It arrived with unseen noodles at the bottom of a pile of small strips of braised beef, green pepper and onion in a cumin based light sauce on top. Gentle mixing was required.  The noodles were not handmade, but a decent store bought variety.  The beef was tender with ample cumin powder and a little crushed cumin flakes, making for good flavor and a filling meal.   The third dish was a pita soaked lamb noodle soup, which I am told is a extra specialty of Shaanxi Province.  At $16 it should have been, but my spoonful did not impress my palette, despite the dent in the wallet. However, the one who ordered it seemed very pleased, so what do I know?!   Service was friendly and water/tea refills prompt.  It always helps to have Mandarin speakers in the party to get a little extra TLC from staff.  I'm not above taking advantage of that benefit.  This house is much larger than the shop on Race Street, but it also lacks the forced intimacy of sitting at tables placed on top of each other.  To each his own, but I remember Chinatown's version being somewhat better in kitchen quality and cultural (crowded) authenticity.

I don't often feel the need for a pedicure, but I admit that when my feet are beat and toe nails ragged, some TLC to the tootsies can be a true pleasure. So, after a particularly horrific week of office moving and presidential election poll working, I wandered through Morrisville one evening this week and found M & M Nail Bar Spa in the shopping plaza just off Trenton Road.    Even though it was 15 minutes to closing, and the front door was locked, the woman running the shop was happy to let me in and give me the full foot deal for $23.  Very much appreciated.  Hot soak, salts, scrub, clip, dig, sand, and massage, accompanied by my choice of alcoholic beverage, juice, tea or coffee.  Very cool way to mellow out.    Thirty minutes later my wheels felt like Fred Astaire's feet - Happy, light and content.  The glass of red wine may have had something to do with that.   Next time, how about a few apps?

Yummy Sushi has moved to newer digs just off the College of New Jersey campus, but their food hasn't changed along with it.   It had been a few years since last visit because I found everything I tried from pho to sushi rolls was average at best. Today I ordered their teriyaki salmon bento box, and must report that nothing has changed. The rolls are still on the thick side with far more rice wrap than contents. Made for an adequate chew, but lacking in much taste beyond the soy/wasabe/ginger additive. It was nice to see they were using white ginger.   If all the iceberg and cabbage were removed, there really wasn't much to the meal. Two small shumai, 2x4  grilled salmon with decent teriyaki BBQ sauce, and the six roll segments. Not complaining about the $12.95 tag, but a little more real food would have made for a better value.   Yummy is still a family place with Granny sitting in the corner and now teenage kids in the opposite corner yakking while serving customers. No problem with service otherwise.   There are still better choices nearby if higher quality dishes are your priority.

The original Jake's is here on Bustleton Pike in Richboro, PA. in a small strip center. The dining room/lunch counter is smaller than their house in Newtown, but with the addition of the extended barroom next door, the place feels more interesting. Also MaiTai brunches are always a strong addition.   I sat on a spinner and enjoyed the repartee with the ladies in black working the room. Time to chat and work on this rainy Columbus Day. They took turns serving menu, coffee and breakfast. Good teamwork. The java was from a Bunn-O-Matic; hot and strong.   The short stack french toast was good, with plenty of egg, vanilla and touch of sugar in the mix saturating to the center of each slice. Caramelized edges always please me, and I was not disappointed. Real maple syrup would have made this an almost perfect plate, but it is hard to offer that liquid amber elixir at these prices.   I sat in for a second mug of Joe to postpone walking out into the storm. I didn't mind extending my visit a little longer this wet day.

Mate's Inn on the grounds of the NJ Department of Corrections on Stuyversant Avenue, Trenton, is not an ordinary restaurant, and cannot be evaluated on the same standards.   This is a rehabilitation project by someone who took a brilliant idea and made it a reality. Teach skills that can be adapted in the community at large while serving the general public with a food experience that cannot be duplicated in the open market. Learning to be a chef, sou chef, and other professional kitchen worker, creates opportunities for employment not otherwise available to "guests of the State." While they serve time, they also learn to serve customers and cook up some very tasty dishes.    The Inn is on the campus of the DOC, in an old mansion converted into a restaurant on the first floor.  It is set up nicely, with plenty of tables in a large dining room.  Windows all around with views of the large facility.  Access is restricted, and everyone must show a photo ID in order to pass through the main gate.    Once inside, parking is easy, and walking into the building from the parking lot takes a minute. The menu offers five or six entrees, a few sides, soups and salads.  It is fairly constant for a few weeks before it changes again.  We chose the chicken wing special, Cajun pasta and the Italian hot dog (mine).  The other plates looked good, and my companions expressed satisfaction with their meals.  My hot dog was in fact 2 wieners, with a light topping of sautéed onions, green frying and sweet red peppers and roasted potatoes.  The bun was the only real disappointment, as it had no taste nor texture. They could use a better bread purveyor. The homemade carrot cake was highly touted, and was tasty with a nice cream cheese icing that could have been thicker, but had the right addictive flavor.   Otherwise, the service by the men in white chef's garb was very good, and the overall experience enriched by the reality that we were eating well and helping society writ large.  We were told of a BBQ the next day.  That was very tempting, but schedules did not permit such a rapid return visit.    Certainly, next time!

Royal Tavern on Passyunk Avenue, Bella Vista, Philadelphia, is a small dark gastropub made to look and feel turn of the 20th Century. It is shoehorned into a rowhouse footprint, with beautiful dark wood backbar, small dining area against the opposite wall and a step up space in back on the way to the restrooms. Kitchen in the basement.   "Dark," is the operative adjective here, because the lighting is so dim aside from a string of Christmas lights that even reading the menu, let alone eyeballing the meal, was a challenge. That's not necessarily a bad thing when the cocktails, beer and food are all first rate, and visuals only serve to support the party going on in your mouth. So it was @ Royal.  We started with a draft of Free Flow IPA, which had a refreshing grapefruit subtext, and a Fat Tire under glass. As Royal rookies, I went for their famous Angus burger (Gouda and whole Longhot Pepper being the most notable elements), and the special spicy shrimp tacos. Both were excellent, with the burger a perfect medium finish and hot to trot on the tongue, and the three tacos barely rollable with shrimp, lettuce, salsa and avocado loaded within. Damn good fries, too.   Of particular convenience to Washington Avenue and the Asian markets there that we came to stock up for upcoming Spring Festival. We just put all that stuff in the trunk and walked over to Royal. Made parking a non-issue.   Gotta do this more often!

The name says it all.  Uncle Mike's Homemade Ice Cream.  Tucked away in a small strip center on York Road, just off Street in Warminster, PA, with small blue sign above the store, it is a little hard to find as you drive by. But, I caught sight of a roadside flag as I approached, and was able to pull into the parking lot without problem.   The shop is bright white, with limited indoor and outdoor seating. Mike carries about 12 - 15 flavors at any given time. Only hard ice cream. No soft serve.  There are a combination of young and older kids working there who are friendly and efficient.   I ordered the two scoop medium size cup of butter pecan and peanut butter cookies & cream. They were large scoops and plenty for this lonesome traveler. It became obvious that Unca Mike really did mix his own flavors. Originally, the peanut butter cookies and cream had been two distinct flavors, but he must have been running low on the ingredients for both, and just threw them together to use them up. Necessity being the mother of invention, the result was the best of both worlds. Excellent peanut butter swirl and cookies and cream playing off each other like old friends who don't visit too often. So, in fact, I received 3 flavors within the two scoops.   No complaints.   They all were richly creamy and bursting with taste. Very good ice cream all around. At $4.50, it was a excellent deal.   This Uncle Mike knows from ice cream.
The Moo Truck is temporarily closed. Be sure to call before coming.

TAKE OUT REVIEW   I was looking forwarded to sampling the kitchen of Saigon Café, especially for a bowl of their bun bo hue and a bahn mi sandwich, but I failed to note that their hours were from 7 am to 6 pm. When I walked in at 6:55 pm, I was advised that the kitchen was closed and the doors would be locked in 5 minutes. My bad.   Luckily, one of the women working the counter took pity on me and offered to make a bahn mi for me to take out, as she had all the ingredients available, and nothing needed to be heated.  I could work with that. I thanked her and ordered a roast pork bahn mi with all the trimmings. I watched as she and a cohort put it together, wrapped it up, bagged it, and handed it over - all for $4. Couldn't beat the price.  I realized as I stood there that Pho 75 was right next door and I could bring my sandwich there and have it with a bowl of their excellent pho. That's exactly what I did. The guys there acted like they had seen this before and were fine with me spreading out my meal with some solids.   The beef noodle soup was awesome as always, and having the sandwich to eat with it made for a very nice meal.   The banh mi was very good, with plenty of daikon, carrot, tender pork and leafy cilantro. The only weakness was the roll itself, which lacked the crispness of a French style baguette, but was soft and too pliant. I guess at the end of the day, the bread had been around awhile and lost its crispy edge.   Aside from that I was satisfied, and plan to return to Saigon Café earlier next time so I can enjoy their menu more completely.

Divine Pizza has become a semi-regular lunch stop over the past year and a half.  Their pizza remains solid, but I have been impressed with the quality of their hot sandwiches.    From Eggplant Parm, to Italian Sweet Sausage, to Peppers and Onions, to Italian Hot Dogs, their plates are substantial, hearty and very tasty.  Their torpedo rolls are first rate, and are locally baked to produce crunchy skin and soft insides.    Definitely have become a strong fan.

In a strip center at the bottom of Bristol Road, Bensalem, PA, Taste Café is another of those Chinese/American joints catering to the sweet tooth of the American palette. The place is clean, with six tables for dining in, however, this is primarily a take out operation. Their menu has all the usual suspects from General Tso's to chow mein. My lunch consisted of orange chicken, fried rice and wonton soup.   In reverse order, the soup was served in a plastic takeout container even though I was eating there. I guess they don't have any bowls, because it seems wasteful and less than hospitable to serve and throw away those containers. Even with recycling, it seems incredibly inefficient. The taste was of a soup that had been in the pot too long, with thick skinned dumplings with little stuffing.   The main course came on a paper plate with the thinnest white plastic utensils imaginable. They could not cut the chicken without bending to the breaking point, and held little soup. I ended up picking up the soup and drinking it from the container. The chicken had the gloopy sauce thickly covering the deep fried breaded chicken morsels. Not an orange peel in sight, and flavor to match. It also seemed they might have been using old oil, as I developed stomach discomfort minutes after consuming it. The yellow dyed fried rice was okay, but also tasted of aging in the pot.   Not much going for Taste Café, except the average price for the lunch was under $9 with a bottle of water or soda.   No need to return.

Dacey's Pub (aka Dacey's Irish Pub) is a fascinating place.  The location is right out of a Kafka novel.  The railroad tracks across the street are a massive wall of gray trap rock and high fences.  Not a blade of grass grows, nor tree casts a shadow.  Viewing that while walking to the entrance can be oppressive and other worldly.    Yet, once inside I was enveloped in a dark mystique of long bar, high top tables, and rear kitchen window.  The rows of silently glistening bottles offer respite from the harsh glare outside. I slid onto a stool at the bar to await service and allowed the aura of the place to settle on me.  Felt good.  There's something going on at Dacey's, and I would figure it out.   The bartender came up to take my drink order and hand over a menu.  First timer, I needed a few minutes to reconnoiter the offerings. This was lunch so Redd's would have to do.  The special of the day was Guinness Fish and Chips @ $6.95.  Although I considered a burger, I was intrigued by what was "Guinness" about the meal.  Turns out, not much.  The basket was delivered with a nice load of chips (fries) and two frozen to deep fry breaded fish fillets, and a choice of tartar sauce and/or malt vinegar. I took both, as I sort of like my chips with tartar sauce over ketchup.  It did not seem that the fish had been dipped in Guinness before frying, which had been my expectation.  They were okay, but not more.  The chips were actually a bit dry.  So, I would not order that again.   Yet, the dudes at the table close by had saddled up to huge burgers and pints of suds, and were elbow deep in their meals and conversation.  That was the way to go, and will certainly be the next approach for me.  I felt like starting over and joining these guys, but thought better of it considering the time.    Walking back into the sunlight the prison escarpment across the road again stood a menacing presence.  I realized that Dacey's was the sentinel protecting the rest of us from whatever evils lurked behind that barbed wire, and the patrons and staff the soldiers on the wall.

Willow Grove Park Mall is not where I normally shop, but sometimes a little diversion pays unexpected dividends.  Generally, I find the latest incarnation of Macy's to be a shoppers hunting ground.  There are always sales, coupons, and additional discounts on lots of the merchandise, so at least in the clothing departments, it is possible to find quality pieces at surprisingly good prices.    This Macy's is laid out as the others in Oxford Valley or Quaker Bridge, but on this Saturday late morning/early afternoon, there were many fewer customers, and salespeople. Not sure what the story was, but I found what I needed, tried things on without interference from staff, and only found slight delay at cashiering on the way out.  It was almost like they were using an honor system.  Pick out what you want.  Try it on. Leave what you don't want. Pay for what you do.  Interact with Macy's only when you draw your credit card.  We trust you.   Saved about 60% off the original price, and left a happy man.

The mural on the wall shows the Sphinx and pyramids along the Nile in Egypt.  Then I heard one of the men behind the counter speaking something that sounded like Arabic. I realized I was in my first Egyptian pizza shop.  Why not?!  They certainly have a huge display of pies under glass for people to choose from.  Buffalo Shrimp, BBQ Beef, Cheesesteak, Chicken Parm, in addition to regular and mushroom standard oldies, to name but a few.  Their lunch deal is two slices and a large soft drink for $7.  I've seen that offer around town for less, but when you get the actual slices in front of you, and pick them up, it is obvious that the weight of each piece is equal to two in those other joints', so in fact you are getting half a pie for that price.  For those who value weight and max load for lunch, this is the place for you.    A traditionalist when it comes to tomato pie, I went for a slice of regular and mushroom.  The crust was thick and supportive of the topside.  With the first bite I knew that I had ordered far too much.  There was a thick layer of cheese atop the substantial base, which was more substance than I enjoy on pizza.  The flavor of the tomato sauce was drowned by the cheese, making for more of an open face grilled cheese experience, rather than a true pizza chew.  Fine if you like cheesy cheese pie, but not exactly what I was hoping for. I prefer a lighter experience where all the elements are apparent, and the topping an accent to the main attraction, as opposed to dominating it.    I knew I couldn't finish these heavyweights, so by command decision I ate half of each and left the balance behind.  Didn't feel called to take them home.    If you enjoy heavy pie, Purple Pizza is calling your name.  They certainly have a large selection of flavors. However, if you are more inclined to a lighter bite, and like a thinner crust and balanced top load, you may have to look elsewhere.   They also do fried chicken according to the sign out front, but I didn't get to try any on this visit.

There is a small table in the front of Belly Busters, but take out and delivery is really the only way to go for breakfast and lunch at this tiny roadside shack of a South American kitchen on old Rt. 13 (Bristol Pike) in Eddington, PA. We didn't know that until after we ordered, having cozied into the few chairs around that mesa and sipped their excellent coffee. I guess they took pity on us and allowed us to stay and eat our breakfasts. Or, maybe it was me taking pictures, asking questions and letting it slip that I would write a Yelp review about the experience, that changed their minds. Thank you.  We went with a breakfast special of doubled sausage, egg and cheese sammy and morning burrito. El senor worked the grill, while la senora was barista, cashier and hostess. Couldn't tell if the young guy making deliveries was family or not. Our grub was great and a good value. The biggest surprise was the new wing of the shop dedicated to java. It was a full blown Expresso operation born from the dozen years working at Starbucks before opening their own business, complete with bottled syrups for flavored lattes and capps.   We were fortunate to be able to hang out over breakfast and watch/listen to customers and staff interact. It was apparent that the family was proud of their success and showed appreciation to everyone who came in. Admittedly, Belly Busters is a bit of a dive, but only in the best way. The corners may be dusty, but the love and effort are tangible.

Huang's Garden is really a misnomer.   It may be Huang's, but it surely isn't a garden.    This Chinese house sits on the southern end of Farnsworth Avenue in Bordentown, NJ.  Where most of this main street has come to life in the past decade and now is attractive for strolling, eating and comfortable happy hours, this place is a throwback to when B'town was more or less a dump you wouldn't consider visiting unless you lived nearby.    My beginnings were not auspicious, as I parked at the front door, and immediately behind a exterminator's truck.  I asked the driver if he was about the treat the restaurant, or was coming in for lunch.  He appreciated my concern, and replied he was only doing an inspection as part of an ongoing service contract.  Glad they were on top of that.   I came in and sat down at one of 2 booths and 2 tables in the front end.  The space was cluttered and populated by three generations of the family running the operation.  Grandma and grandpa sat at a round table in front of an HDTV watching a Chinese station, while mom and dad worked the kitchen, and granddaughter came in and out doing what 10 year olds do.    I was sitting in their living room.  Gratitude for the invitation.    The menu was state of the art for 1990.  All the usual dishes.  So, I asked for the Sesame Chicken lunch special and a bowl of Wonton Soup for an extra 4 bits.  Let's see what was delivered.  The Wonton Soup was surprisingly good!  The 3 dumplings had a thin coat, and the ground Pork within was tasty.  The broth was unusual because it had a mild lemony flavor, which at first stopped me mid-chew, but ultimately was interesting and enjoyable.  Cool.    The Sesame Chicken was plentiful dark meat chicken that was textured as if it had not been frozen, with a very dark brown sauce that was not as gloopy as expected and nicely piquant.  Again, above average for the standard Sino American plate.  Finally, the Fried Rice while suspiciously uberdark brown, was full of chunkies, and tasted pretty good.    While I wouldn't make the trip to this tail end of Bordentown's main drag again for this, I was pleasantly surprised that the cuisine emanating from the kitchen was far better than the dining room atmospherics suggested.    Grandma was a gracious hostess and server as her hubby napped peacefully.  I left satisfied and appreciative of being adopted by this lovely family.

Hazy's is aptly named for the tobacco cloud atmosphere provided at this smoker's bar. Even with the Smokeaters working, the billows from Cigarman to my right blew by me horizontally, forcing me to hold my breath and push away from the bar until it passed.   Disgusting.   But, the friendly bartender saw my situation, frowned, and went to talk to the chimney to ask that he consider the other patrons. Cigarettes were one thing, but a fat stogie, quite another.   Aside from that annoyance, this was a pretty good bar. Bigger inside than expected, with two pool tables and a surprisingly good kitchen, and a large rectangular bar run by pleasant attractive woman who had everything under control. My sweet Italian sausage, pepper and onion sandwich was very good. Served with fries in a red plastic basket, the meat was still tender and juicy within the torpedo roll and tasted fresh.   I stopped in to see the Phillies and watched them implode in the 8th inning. Hazy's would be a natural hangout sports bar for me but for their smoking policy. They'd probably have more business, too.   I guess nicotine addicts deserve a place to go. Just doesn't work well for me.

Yelp should consider having a check off box for reviews that deal with take out/delivery or eat in experiences.  They are so often vastly different, that this information would be helpful.    ***  We decided to pick up a pizza from Uncle Charlie's on a Sunday afternoon after shopping in the area.  We walked in, realized that this was strictly a take away kitchen and decided on a regular pie we could bring home to devour.  Everyone behind the counter was pleasant, and it seemed to be a high school operation for local kids. No problem with that.  Everything smelled great all the way home, but after the 15 minute drive the pizza had lost its edge (quite literally).  The underflooring could not hold the topside weight, so every slice we attempted to lift from the box folded and left parts of the cheese behind, which quickly cooled to room temperature and was not enjoyable to eat.  The taste was no doubt impaired by this process, and though we knew it was still pizza, it really lacked much taste from the sauce and remaining cheese.  It just wasn't as good as eating pizza at its source.    Uncle Charlie must be aware of this as all they have it take out or delivery.  It really puts them at a disadvantage over restaurants that can have patrons eating there.  Maybe delivery is better if it is timely, but their vehicle holds the food in an insulated bag in the trunk.  Somehow, that image is not very appealing.   Seem like good folks, but their approach doesn't work for me.

Newest design for DD. Not surprised as it had to do something extraordinary to get into Upper Makefield. This shop has an inside lobby with doors on 2 sides to allow for circulation of customers. Too, it has a pleasant sitting area to one side complete with a lounge by the large front window.   The coffee is standard for a DD. Service is friendly and efficient.   Nice to have a morning hangout in the Crossing.

Very decent Vietnamese house in Mt. Laurel, NJ.  Man! This part of the world is all shopping centers and highways.  What happened to rural Moorestown and Mt. Laurel?  Well, at least they had the good sense to permit Pho Xinh to open their southeast Asian restaurant. It's not just Viet cuisine, as it also has offerings from Thailand.    My lunch was the Jasmin Grill, consisting of 2 very thin pork chops, grilled and barbequed, cuke and tomato side salad/garnish, and a cup of broken rice.  For another buck I also received a small fried spring roll.  Very good service, with everyone pitching in.    Taste was fine, especially after I mixed the Hoisin and Chili Sauces together for dipping the meat, and poured the thin spring roll sauce over the rice to add more flavor.    If I find myself in the area again, I will sit down for a bowl of Pho.   Not quite Washington Avenue, Philly, but strong for this neck of the woods.

The David Witchell Empire continues to grow in Newtown, Pa. His once solitary salon on State Street has expanded into several boutiques covering a variety of clothing styles and now, a home decor showcase in the former Allegheny Art Supply store. It is something very bright and shiny in the resolutely old school Newtown Borough.    I like it!   Walking around the surprisingly large space full of all those things I never knew I would find attractive, I was reminded of my recent visit to Southern California - San Diego, La Jolla, Laguna Beach and Long Beach. Those beautiful upscale Left Coast culture centers have such shops on every avenue and corner. They provide the texture of that ocean view mellow yellow lifestyle. (Yes. These tchotchkes can be found in New Hope and similar such venues, but the distance between New Town and Hope can be as great as that to So Cal).   Gala and Kellie were cool, leaving us to explore all the knickknacks and crannies with only light direction and inquiry. We picked up a few things (oversized mugs and a snowglobe Buddha), that we totally did not need, but enjoyed impulse purchasing.    So much cheaper than a return flight to Orange County, this whimsy shop.

Brought a dozen of these glamour babes to the office this week.  They were gone in under and hour.    Everyone wanted to know where they were from as they had not tasted such fresh, chewy, sweetly frosted doughnuts in an elephant's memory.  I only had a taste of two of them; the Blueberry and a Vanilla Frosted.  The former was mildly crisp on the outside, all fruit sweetness within.  The later had a fragile body, but a thickly poured sticky frosted coating.  Each was totally different than the other, as the frosted was soft with a delicious white coat, while the core was much like a well made glazed rounder that almost melts in your mouth.  The Blueberry was more cake-like, but totally infused with berryessence.   Mary's is located within the Bristol Amish Market on Green Lane, just off Rt. 13. This market is also worth a review, as it is large, bright and cleaner than the one I often visit in Newtown, Pa.    Only open Thursday - Saturday with the rest of the vendors there.  On Thursday morning around 7:30 am, there were few people in the building, and almost no line at Mary's.  Go later in the day, and you risk them being out of one or more of your favorites.  The Saturday mayhem may not be worth the trip.   I think I found its sweet spot.

River Cat is a smooth, soft footed feline. She prowls the rocky Delaware River shore by night, and sleeps in a sunny window ledge while the day is morning cool. She puts on an apron and works in her kitchen as humans arise and visit her for their early meal and cuppa java. An accommodating cat, she knows not to serve those mice captured during her dark hunt. She has learned amazing skills with people food, and shows them off daily at the whiskered cafe on the south end of Main Street in New Hope, PA. What once was a year round Christmas shop, is now a cool, exposed beam, clearstoried, glass walled mellow hangout for River Cat's friends and those wishing to become one.   I took a corner table facing the front patio with its black metal tables and red umbrellas. River Cat approached, blond hair clipped atop her head and menu, small pad and pen in paw. Her purring question about coffee rolled over me like a magic spell, slightly altering perception. I was no longer in a rush, with nothing but the moment influencing me. I watched her move away like the sure-footed chat blanc she was.   With coffee secured, I ordered an egg and swiss on ciabatta sandwich, and settled deeper into the chair to watch the morning evolve. Folks wandered in. Most seemed to know her and the crew, and exchanged pleasantries before sitting. This meow was popular.   My plate arrived with a cat's eye smile. It looked wonderful. Fresh roll with fried egg and melted cheese neatly packaged within. White and sweet potato mixed in a hill of home fries. Slice of honeydew, twist of orange and a strawberry as colorful garnish. Not too big. Not too small. Just the right size. Tasted great with a combination of flavors and textures to wake up the still sleepy beast within. With strong coffee washdown, it was a very enjoyable breakfast, and certainly the best of my week.   This River Cat should do great with the New Hope summer crowds, and offer the locals a pleasant place to break fasts and socialize in the off season. Let's hope success doesn't go to her river washed head, and she maintains the silky coated demeanor she shows in her opening days.   River Cat Cafe could be purr-fect.

While most American malls are slowly becoming dinosaurs of a past economic age, there are a very few defying the shift to a new urbanism that incorporates commercial centerism with residential and professional integration in close proximity, by going to the opposite extreme - supersizing the structure and filling it with ultra high end merchandise, and multiple choice cuisines, that create a sense of excessive exuberance that attracts the crowd with so much stimuli that it is irresistible.  Whether it will work long term is an unanswered question, but for now and the near future, it certainly seems to have traction that pulls on the senses as well as the wallet.   The new King of Prussia Mall, combining the old Court at King of Prussia and the KoP Mall of yesteryear, into one humongous bazaar, is really rather amazing. Its enormity dwarfs normal perception and invites you to visit a rather alien, yet very attractive, universe.  Hermes, Louis Vuitton, Bulgari, Cartier, meld with scores of other lesser known retailers (and some better known, as well), and a wide variety of food outlets that can please the most discriminating tongue and pallet. Bloomies, Macy's and Neiman Marcus are but three of the anchor department stores offering clothing and accessories right from designer showrooms and runways.  Henri Bendel, Jimmie Choo, Marmot, etc., are all there.  More than 450 shops in all.   So, go if you feeling like splurging. Go, if you just want to get out of the house and get a long walk done for the day. It is all rather overwhelming, like a giant circus wrapped in a vertical city, with enough to keep anyone occupied for as long as they feel the need to be so.   It will be interesting to see how long this concept works successfully, as it is a litmus test for the American commercial future.

Nonno's Italian Coffee Parlor is what a true café should be.    It is attractive to visit with its old wooden fixtures and furniture; it is truly artisanal in how it produces its signature drinks, both hot and cold; and offers creamy, colorful Gelato and bakery sweets to complete a wonderful experience.  It is no wonder that the place is packed from morning to night.  People know a great thing when they sit and taste it.   It really is that good!  But, there is a downside to success.  If you just want to stop in/take out a latte or capp, or even a small lemon gelato slurp, you may end up waiting as long as those people choosing to sip/dine in.  The service is often slow, making a quick business stop on the way to the office or a meeting, problematic.  They really need to figure out how to handle the crowds that love their stuff. The snaking line doesn't work when feeling rushed.  The other issue is the no credit card policy.  What's up with that?! Normally, that suggests a few financial problems that obstruct the acceptance practices of the offering banks.  The success of this venture suggests otherwise.  Cash flow does not appear to be the problem.  Offering an ATM in the back hall by the bathrooms is not really the image a Eurostyle café should be demonstrating.  This situation detracts from the customer service expected in quality establishments, and should be rectified.    But, man, the drinks are good. Makes the annoying sloth-like pace and cash only deal tolerable as long as I am not in a hurry.   To make 5 Star rank these things need to be fixed.

I am a regular visitor to Chinatown in Philadelphia. After eight plus years doing business in China, I need my Asian fix at least once a month. Whether a haircut at Artiva Salon, a subterranean grocery exploration, or a great meal at any of the scores of traditional regional kitchens, the gritty streets of C'town will find my footprints in the greasy dust.   Immigrants from Fuzhou and the old Canton arrive first starting 175 years ago. A laundry, then a few rice shops, and then a business association attracted more small family startups contributing to what was once a larger neighborhood. The increased density of a five square block area actually adds to the impression of walking through hutongs in Beijing or other large Chinese city. The Friendship Gate on 10th Street is authentic and carries the magic spells for success and happiness.   While true that the well to do residents have escaped west and north, leaving behind hourly workers, students and families that can't afford to move uptown, the community is still vibrant, evolving and exciting.   From creative bars and clubs to traditional restaurants with roast ducks and pig snouts in the windows to rolled ice cream and excellent teas and coffees, there is something for everyone on these gristled lanes.

Trejo Restaurant on Swede Street, just down a bit from the Montgomery County Courthouse, is a very good casa Mexicana in the heart of Norristown. It has about ten tables and a small kitchen in the back corner. The menu has a full monte of breakfast, lunch and dinner options. The people working there appear to be family and are likely ownership. They are friendly, hospitable and seem proud of their establishment.   It was late lunchtime, so a small Torta (sandwich) of thin sliced breaded beef caught my attention. When it arrived I knew that the adjective "small" was not really operative. This was a mega-sliced opus at least three inches thick, layered with beans, lettuce, avocado, tomato and spicy mayo, all held in a fresh roll with extra long toothpicks. The crisp fries were nice, but totally over the top unnecessary.   The torta was great. Too wide for my jaws to clench, I partially deconstructed it by removing a couple of layers of the tasty res empanada, and rebooting it to a manageable dimension. From there, every bite was a delicious combination of all the ingredients exploding in my mouth. At $10 I felt bad that I couldn't finish it. Still, it was one of the better authentic Mexican plates I have enjoyed in long while.   The good news is that my Norristown office is right down the street, so Trejo can become a regular stop when I am here for office meetings.

As Jersey delis go, Bob's Corner is a stud muffin!  It sits on the point (corner) of Delaware Avenue just west of Rt. 130, the first floor of a converted early 20th Century home.  Simple sign across the front steps, and small parking lot in back. There is barely room to turn around inside, but it is so well organized that it probably has everything you want for a solid take away breakfast and lunch.  The folks there are friendly and willing to chat while they do your bidding or take your cash.   I stopped in for a quick caffeine jolt.  I wasn't hungry, but the aroma from the grill, and the sweet temptations from the muffin/donut display sure had my attention. Immediate mental note to come back with some room in the belly. The java was tasty and fresh, and the small cup a buck and a quarter.  Hard to beat.    Roebling itself is a cool former company steel town that has had its own boom and bust cycle.  Now, it is a charming Delaware River burg that you have to have a reason to know about.  Mine? Mid morning cruise back to the office from Mt. Holly on an uber hot Friday in late July.   Would you be rushing back to work?

This was my second visit to a Panda Express, and true to it's corporate nature, it was consistent with my first experience. That is both a good thing and a bad thing.  Let's start with the positives. The facility was clean and bright, and constantly being mopped and wiped while I was there. They keep staff busy in visible ways. The service was friendly and expedient, if formulaic. I was offered a sample of a special chicken dish on a toothpick. Can't remember the taste, nor the name.   I ordered the two mains, one side option for $7.95. Veggie Lo Mein, Gung Pao Chicken, and Beijing Beef we're loaded onto my styro dish, which was place on to a plastic tray before being handed over.  I took a pass on their sweet waters.   All three were luke warm and past their prime. The taste was good, with strong spiciness on the gung pao, and crispy tangy sweetness on the beef, even though the latter's sauce was overly goopified from hanging around for a while. Really no better or worse than the versions found in traditional Chinese American shops, just not as hot. The noodles we're becoming al dente, but not beyond the pale.   Given a choice I would normally opt for the local momasan papasan joint over corporate mass produced dishes, but it is safe to say that the Panda is a reasonable alternative, especially if you come when the offerings are right out of the wok.  Even when approaching their sell by date, the taste is okay even if texture and temperature are not quite right.

17 Souls ...       Where were you when you learned of Nine Eleven?        Some things we can never forget.  Nor should we ever want to.        The Garden of Reflection is a work of love, loss and remembrance.  The families of those who perished in that horrific attack, along with some very talented and dedicated people, came together to create a one of a kind setting for the somber, yet uplifting, task of bringing us together to Reflect on and Remember what happened on that day.         We feel a shared emptiness in our hearts from the loss of loved ones many of us knew.  We appreciate the powerful yet gentle flow of the park-like design that guides us along its paths ever closer to its center, the twin fountains in a pool made of concrete, stone and reflections of trees and sky.  We count the trees planted around the low walls of concrete and glass with so many names...       This is a profoundly beautiful and haunting place. It echoes within, and calls out for love, peace, understanding, and never forget determination.  9.11.2013 - The Memorial Ceremony held here today was poignant and sad.  Finding and giving comfort was the message of the day from all the spiritual leaders asked to speak, pray, play music, and stand silently.  From the size of the crowd it is clear that we will always remember the national and personal losses we suffered that day 12 years ago.   Teach your children well.

My second visit to any Quick Chek, and I admit that their approach to Convenience Store is a nice upgrade over the traditional view of the genre.    They offer hot and cold customized food, an array of coffee and snack options, and a spacious floor plan that encourages you to walk around and check it out.  Too, the staff in both places I have visited is friendly and courteous to a very noticeable degree.    These places remind of modern rest stops found along the highways and byways of America.  Finding them on the streets of our cities is a bit of an amazement.   A very enjoyable one.

My first time to Indian Garden, a destination hidden in the shopping center on Stony Hill Road in Lower Makefield (we all know it is not really Yardley).  It is catercorner from the Giant Supermarket, and next door to Vesuvio Pizza.  Walking in the first impression is that the space is darkly lit, and in combination with the aroma of curry, cardamon, and other spices, feels a little like entering a bazaar on the subcontinent.  As the eyes adjust, white table clothes appear on small square and large round tables reflecting the dim recessed lighting and the illumination over the buffet tables. They are a little close together, requiring a bob and weave to access the back tables. Still, very engaging way to start the experience.  The staff in black and white with ties is super efficient and helpful.  I went with the buffet to be able to sample more than would be possible ordering off the menu, although another reviewer warned off doing this.  I tried : Vegetable Pakora (not hot enough, and thus a little oily), Chicken Tikka Masala (very good), Chicken Kadai (good and smokey flavored), Chicken Makhani (nice creamy tomato/ginger sauce), Vegetable Korma (was that frozen veggies in a good Korma?), Chana Saag (very enjoyable), Aloo Bhartha (love eggplant in all incarnations), Paneer Makhani (the cheese reminds of tofu, but decent), Naan (quite good, but wanted garlic), Mango Lassi (excellent), and mango pudding (really?). Ok. I won't have dinner tonight.  Total Cost: $12.50 Given the almost total absence of Indian food in the immediate area, Indian Garden is very good, and worth another trip.  Next time, I will order off the menu and see what shakes out.  Upgrades are definitely possible once the larger menu is penetrated and surrenders its secrets.  9.28.13 - Returned for another lunch buffet today with a few campaign people. The floor was not crowded when we arrived, but slowly filled after 1:00.  I think I was placed at the same table as my first visit. I love when that happens. Kismet. The food was as good as last time, and the Naan changed from Regular to Onion while we were there, and added to the sop up enjoyment of all the rich sauces mixing on the plate.  I was a bit distracted with conversation so did not commit to memory what I ate, but I thoroughly enjoyed the mix of flavors, textures, and basics.  3 Stars with a Bullet.  This place is going to move up soon.  11.11.16 UPDATE - Sometimes the best intentions to return to a restaurant soon to followup on good early impressions are swallowed by life taking you elsewhere. So it was with Indian Garden. Job changes, new food outlets, or just plain forgetfulness, play a hand. Still, I finally came back here last Friday night with family when we decided we hungered for local spice.   We were seated promptly without reservations at 6 by the smiling hostess. The large dining room was half empty on arrival, but filled quickly with some recognizable faces. Just beat the rush.   The three of us ordered Veggie Samosa and Chili Pakora apps. Both good, but the Pakora had a too thick fried coating over the pepper and filling. Reminded of a Relleno, but not as smoothly integrated. The Chicken Curry was fresh with a nice red mild heat. Our Lamb Korma had grilled baa-baa pieces in a smooth and almond sweet beige sauce, that was the star of the show. The third dish was a potato and eggplant combo with chunkiness and light spice finish without a pond around it. Their Basket of Naan completed our table.   Everything was solid, if not exceptional, with a tendency to underspice all their dishes, perhaps in tune with the palates of their clientele. Not a criticism, but an adjustment to reality. Yet, if a stronger  South Asian taste is what you seek, just ask for max heat, or try the local alternatives (Guru, Dream Spicy), where there is less accommodation to neighborhood preference for dilution.   Still, the quality of the meal was undeniable. A little fine tuning will achieve the heat quotient desired. Indian Garden is fan worthy.

Good things can happen even in the middle of a snowstorm, and I survived to write about it.   The drive from Carlisle to Bucks was getting worse by the mile as snow and then sleet fell and made road conditions difficult.  With the speed limit reduced to 45 MPH, and my head beginning to pound, it was time for a break.  I was thinking comfort food, but when I drove into Malvern and my first choice (Pho) was closed on this Sunday, I found Dixie Picnic just around the corner, and seeing good Yelp reviews, I went in.  It might not be my normal comfy meal, but it certainly was someone's, and I was about to find out who's.   The space was bright and cheerful even on a dank dark afternoon.  I arrived around 1:30, and they were closing at 2.  No sweat.  The owner welcomed me and told me to sit and relax.  He handed me the menu after explaining the general lay of the land with breakfasts, sandwiches, BBQ, and Box Lunches.  Everything done in house and from scratch.  Home brewed Iced Tea, too.    I went with the Georgia BBQ Pork Sandwich on a fresh roll.  It came with a choice of a side dish - Pasta Pesto, thank you. While I waited, I listened to the oral history of this Southern family and the old photos on the walls took meaning and personality.  Lunch arrived.    A huge heaping load of heavily sauced shredded pork that required a fork to consume because to pick up the sandwich was to risk a major lap spill.  It was that BIG. The first bite had me sucking in my breath as the deeply sweet and tangy mix attacked my tongue and olfactory center.  WOW!  This was going to required time and patience as I adjusted to its wonderful flavor.  It had just the right amount of vinegar to provide a sharp retort to the molasses-like thick sweetness.  It was soft and tender and an easy chew.  I found myself enjoying it immensely.  Meanwhile, the staff was beginning to close up, but I was assured that I could remain.  Good thing, because the other hot items were the Upcakes sitting seductively in the front display.    These were upside down cupcakes covered on all sides in thick creamy icing.  The variety of flavors had their own menu and were seasonal.  Here, while the cake base was homemade and excellent, the real story was unabashedly the multicolored toppings.  I decided on the Blood Orange Icing on Devil's Food Cake.    The icing was about a quarter inch think all around, save for the bottom (Actually, the top of this bottom's up creation). It was a soft cream, rather than a hard shell, and gave itself up freely.  While sweet, it was not overly so, and settled nicely on the tongue for a lasting taste sensation.  The chocolate cake was super moist and almost gooey.  I loved it.   Whoever thought this one up deserves a place in the Cupcake Hall of Fame.    Thanks to everyone associated with Dixie Picnic over the generations for your love of cooking and taking care of people.    You all certainly took great care of me, and introduced me to new possibilities in comfort food.   Gratitude and respect.

Yummy Sushi sits in an unconventional food court - a mid-sized strip center surrounded by Chinese, Pizzeria, Bagel joint, Hungarian, Italian and Sports Bar restaurants.  You can walk to all of them in under five minutes.  Very convenient if you have a diverse group that can't decide what to eat.    Although Yummy is ostensibly a raw fish house, I came strictly for the Pho, the Vietnamese Noodle Soup that is known as a wonderful comfort food.  And, it was so here.  The broth was rich and complex with the right spices and time spent simmering to unleash the subtle undertones.  The nest of rice noodles at the bottom of the large bowl was difficult to corral as they were very long and did not drop easily into the flat bottomed spoon.    They offer only one form of Pho here - Flank Steak and Meatballs. The Steak arrived medium/rare and continued to reach medium from the heat of the soup.  The Meatballs were sliced, but very dense, reminding me that "meatball" doesn't always mean Italian. The bowl already contained Sprouts and Basil Leaves when it landed on my table.  Only the Lime and Jalapeno slices were on the side.  Hoisin Sauce and Sriracha were delivered, but there was no dish to squirt them into.  I used the one the lime and jalapeno came in, and dipped the meat into both before eating.    I did also try the Fried Wontons (described as Pork Dumplings in the menu).  They were not very good, as they were over deep fried and had a burnt taste. The Duck Sauce that came with them was watery and lacking in flavor.    The Mama-san was very cordial to all the customers, although she spent a lot of time with those she knew best.  Her children were present, but did not disturb anyone.

I have returned three times since the review, and sampled their food each time.   Their burgers are very good.  Large patty cooked to the requested finish with loads of toppings and a steak knife piercing the sandwich like a dagger through the heart. Also ordered the cheesesteak sliders, which were basically cheesesteak encapsulated within a thin dough deep fried before presentation.  Also, good, but not the grabber that the burger was.   Beer selection is excellent for a neighborhood bar & grill, and the service remains friendly and courteous.   Work being done in the back to bring up the comfort of the dining area.  Too, the men's room is nice enough to be in someone's home.  Well done!

Philadelphia is known as a city of neighborhoods with good reason. There are many small enclaves with their own identity and distinct character with residents fiercely proud of where they come from. One of the best aspects of this street by street, hood by hood, awareness, especially from a Yelp perspective, is the presence of wonderful local shops, bars, and restaurants that maintain that sense of community every day of the week.    Tate's Good Food Restaurant on Torresdale Avenue, in this corner of the city that shares the name, is one such iconic luncheonette that serves both the gastronomic needs of the area, and supports the people with quality breakfasts and lunches and a place to gather and commune together (shoot the sh*t). It is replete with folks who have lived nearby for generations, and frequent this small institution regularly.  Yes. Everyone knows your name.   With this in mind, I stopped in for breakfast and took in the deep rooted atmosphere of this iconic establishment. I sat on a spinner along the counter, after checking out the tables on the opposite wall. A solo diner, I did not want to take up that much space, and after all, this was what a stool was for. Within seconds, I was called, "Babe," by one of the servers working the counter and floor, and, "Sweetie," by another, as she asked if I wanted coffee.    She replied when I asked if she was talking to me - "Whatever works, right, Babe?"  "That's cool. I just didn't want the other guys at the counter to get jealous."   With that, one of those old dudes looked over at me with a stern gaze, and retorted, "She WAS talking to me, but, I don't mind if you thought it was you."   Wink   I knew I was in the heart of Philly.   The menu was all about breakfast and lunch (they close around 2).  I went with the french toast, a side of corned beef hash and java. It arrived about 10 minutes later on an oval plate, with the hash on a second dish. I moved things around to get everything onto one before doctoring with butter and syrup.    The meal was filling and satisfying. Six slices well egged and grilled. No real caramelization, but very tasty nonetheless. The hash was excellent. Deep savory flavor, a little crunchy. A great match for the sweeter fry bread.  The Bunn-O-Matic brewed a strong industrial joe which was replenished as often as requested. A small glass of real milk per my wish to avoid the heavier half & half.   Tate's is another of those classic kitchens from a bygone era that have survived and even flourished.  It is as authentic today as it was in the last century.  It feels dated, but that is one of the two main reasons to come to a joint like this - For the wholesome hearty grub and to experience a living cultural museum.

Right down 17th Street from The Latham Hotel, I strolled down to Little Pete's one morning last week for an early breakfast while waiting for the rest of the family to get up and ready for the day.    A diner or luncheonette may be debated, but the atmosphere is mid-20th Century, and the tone is one of a dive.  That can be a very good thing if you like time travel with your eggs and coffee. I sat at the oblong counter and was promptly given a glass of water and a menu.  The coffee was poured a moment later.  My toasted Corn Muffin slid in front of me before turning the front page of the Inquirer.  Service in black with a sly smile seemed appropriate and I enjoyed the wonderment of my server's daily grind.    Before leaving, I looked around the counter at all the individuals sitting in their own worlds on their Ipads and smartphones.  I missed the banter than used to take place between waitperson and customer, and felt the loss of human interaction.  I put down my own technology and journal and exchanged a few pleasantries with the woman who had been refilling cups of Joe for decades.  She just needed a few interested ears to tell her tale.    So, next time you find yourself at Little Pete's try to be fully present and interact with this artifact of American history before it becomes extinct.

What a difference since my last visit.   I walked in around 2:45, just in time to catch the final few minutes for their lunch specials. I was the only customer. With my first breath inside I thought that the fish had taken over. The atmosphere smelled of piscean excess, like the air filter hadn't been cleaned in forever. Yes. They were a sushi joint and had two large tanks on the premises, but this was ridiculous. Fresh air, please.   I should have turned around and walked out, because it got worse from there. I sat down and ordered the sesame chicken, which came with fried rice and egg roll.   Whereas, last time the food was better than average for a Chinese American house, this time it was far worse. The breading was thicker than the meat within. Primarily cheaper, dark meat chicken was used, and it all was overcooked in deep frying, so that much of the pieces were overly hard, like encased in plaster rather than flour. It stuck in my teeth and tasted of old oil. The fried rice was aging poorly and the eggroll was mostly cabbage and more stale oil.   Really disappointing after a positive first impression several months ago. They must not being doing well, but without better effort and sense of smell, they won't have long to worry about it.

Cafe Lift on North 13th Street just south of Spring Garden, occupies the first floor of an old factory in this almost up and coming neighborhood south of core Center City. It's decor is all early 20th Century post industrial.  This has it's charm with high ceilings and exposed pipes and ducts, and large photos of the local buildings in black and white that are strong suggestions of it's history.   On Saturday morning it was packed with a 20 something crowd enjoying Rival Bros Coffee and a short, but tasty breakfast/lunch menu. Hard walls make for poor acoustics, and the din was several decibels above comfortable. But, everyone was friendly and dealing with the racket. Even the queue to the single restroom had cool people who understood the situation and willingly chatted with their line mates.  Our table wait was about 25 minutes, but we made it to a small deuce in the middle of the room, with people on either side. It was tight, but the ambient noise allowed for privacy. The menu was divided into brekkie and lunch on either side of the document. I went with the chicken salad wrap, and DT opted for their burger. Both we're good. The burger seemed hand packed which gave it a softer texture and more retained juices. I prefer a more chunky chicken salad, but had no negs about theirs. We were drinking the house java, which was hot and kicky, but served in small white cups that needed refilling after a couple of gulps. Larger joe vessels would have been more efficient for the staff and felt more generous to the customers.   Cafe Lift is a very interesting place to hang out. The room is really humming and the staff works hard to please. The harshness of the sound makes the experience not completely ideal, but that is overcome by the quality of the people and the kitchen, not to mention the enjoyment of just being in an old urban factory that has been so well repurposed.

Bobby O's Deli on Rozel Avenue just off 2nd Street Pike in Southampton, PA, is hard to find until you realize it is on this side street in a small strip center, without signage other than above the door. But, if you appreciate family owned and operated businesses that do things as they have for the past thirty years, it is well worth slowing down to find it.   We stopped in after taking the PennDot driving test nearby, in need of breakfast and coffee. Their all day breakfast sandwich sign in the window was most welcoming. No tables in the tiny shop, but a short wall shelf with four stools was all we needed. We each ordered a sandwich with variations of bacon, sausage and pork roll, egg and cheese on hard rolls. At $4.50 per, the price was right.   Daughter took our order at the cashier post, while Mom worked the grill and dad brought in new inventory. All their Sammies were very good, with special mention to the rolls which were fresh and excellent. Choice of cheese helped, too. Liked them alot.   If there was any shortfall, it was that the sausages seemed to be those precooked frozen jobs just reheated, rather than a fresh patty brought to life on hot steel. It would have been even better with the higher quality ingredient. Still, that is a minor nit in an otherwise high value morning meal.   May they have another 30 years!

What the heck is a Chalupa?  In Mexico it is a small boat or a food creation in Oaxaca and Puebla that molds masa dough (base ingredient of a tortilla) into the shape of a concave container, filled with pork, chicken, beef, peppers, onion and salsa, before deep frying. It looks like a cup or skiff, rather than a enlarged taco.  What I ordered at this Taco Bell arrived at my table looking much more like the big soft taco, than the smaller corn cup described on Wikipedia. So, the name is assumed via poetic license, and not the actual dish it is South of the Border.  Despite this misappropriated name, this version of a Chapula was still tasty and filling. I had the chicken filling, and found the package enjoyable to eat, if not the most authentic tasting Mexican food in the world. Really lacked serious spice quotient. The lunch special offered two of these babies, plus a soft ground beef taco thrown in for good measure. It was all far too much to eat in one sitting, unless gaining weight was a priority. I left half the second Chalupa and three quarters of the taco on the tray when I departed.   With all the excellent real Central American houses around these days, it is difficult to be excited by Taco Bell, which is a mere shadow of  good Mexican or Salvadoran food. Prices are low, but so is the dining experience.    Okay if hungry in the desert, but not close to what you can get if you really want the real deal.

A Happy Family is both the name of this Chinese/American shop and a description of the people who own and operate it.   I met both spouses during my lunch there yesterday.  The mister took my order and chatted with me, and the misses served my plate of egg foo young, egg roll and fried rice, with a smile and gratitude.  They have been in this location just off Brunswick Circle in Trenton, NJ for a few years, and seem to be making of go of it.    The store is long and narrow, with a small dining room in front, two middle rooms that appear to be used by the family, and a rear kitchen.  There is some distance between front and back, and they installed a bell for customers to use to catch their attention.  I used it to get them to come out and accept my payment.    The lunch was about par for the course in the metro area.  All the owners must have gone to the same restaurant school, because most of the wonton houses have identical menus, and tastes.  A Happy Family is no different, except that they deserve credit for making their fried rice without soup bouillon with dye to color the rice.  This pile of grain looked natural, and was nicely chunky.  The pancakes were full of veggies, wok fried, with a plastic cup of brown sauce on the side.  It was decent.  The egg roll was mostly cabbage with a few slivers of pork, but I didn't expect anything more.    They have a confusing menu because of the similarity of the lunch specials, and combo offerings.  Not clear what the differences are, except one costs less than $6, while the other comes in at $7.50.  Not a big deal either way, but I like to know what I am looking at when ordering.   A Happy Family is worth a visit if Chinois Americain is something you like. Your visit will do a lot to keep these folks pleased.

If old fashioned roadside luncheonettes are your thing, then Delran Coffee Shop is where you want to have your next breakfast or lunch.
