In the wilds of Delran (Delaware & Rancocas River/Creek merger nearby), this slophouse has been slinging hash and over-easy eggs, since your great grandfather was a youngun', and rode his bike with his buddies over for a greasy burger and fries.  There is a small counter for solo travelers like me, and a bunch of booths and tables for those who come with.  If this joint was any more authentic New Jersey, it would be one of Washington's stops during the Revolution in West Jersey.   The place has a timeless quality.  Although well maintained, it feels its age, and the life stories of all who have dined here over the decades.  It is totally country in a cool, off the beaten path, Jersey way.  From my perch at the counter, I was on top of the grill, and watched as the cooks cracked their eggs on it, poured pancake batter, and dropped their presses on the bacon and burgers.  More important to me, I watched my short stack of French Toast go from bread bag to egg mix bowl to grill, with care and expertise. I saw it plated and brought to me by the short order dude, with small cup of butter, and counter rocket of syrup.    When spread, melted and squirted, my breakfast looked great, and was caramelized on its edges, just the way I like.  The java was hot and free flowing, and the "honeys, and "dears," from the hard working server made me feel at home and appreciated.   Between this place and Grannies' Attic Café up the way, I have stumbled on two exceptional breakfast joints that both garnered 5 stars for just being awesome interesting tasty spots to stop for the first meal of the day.    And, they are both New Jersey thoroughbreds.

Home Place Restaurant sits in a rather forlorn older strip center on Bristol Road in Bensalem, PA.  This is the latest in a line of restaurants that have made a run at a successful kitchen at this location. It shares the strip with a Wawa, which offers indirect competition for coffee and breakfast sandwiches with its neighbor.   The house is pretty large with several dozen tables, a high display with desserts, and two HDTVs on the wall.  The furnishings are new utilitarian, but there is a dark carpet on the floor which is never a sanitary solution compared to a hard surface that can be swept, mopped and vacuumed clean. Service was friendly and attentive.  My small coffee mug was refilled twice without need to ask. Breakfast menu is larger than many restaurants, and although Home Place is not a traditional diner, and lacks a counter service, it did have a broad breakfast list with morning specials at very low prices.   I opted for their Greek omelet with special request to put the home fries inside, rather than on the plate.  That always adds substance to the eggs and allows the potatoes to integrate with the rest of the ingredients. Tastes better to me. The plate arrived ten minutes later looking quite good. The three eggs had been mixed with the feta cheese, onion, pepper and spuds, rather than left as a shell.  I prefer this approach, although it was no longer a true omelet. It was pretty good, but needed more than a shake of black pepper and salt to bring up the flavor. The feta, while salty, was not in sufficient abundance to offset the need for sodium chloride. The rye toast was lightly buttered and a good complement to the eggs. The coffee was strong and hot.  No serious complaints about Home Place. It was pretty much a decent breakfast, but lacking any WOW factor. The location and clientele do not permit prices necessary to do things to make the space and offerings more attractive and intriguing, yet does provide a substantial meal which should not be disregarded.

The United States Postal Service as embodied by the Post Office at 20 Terry Drive in Newtown has provided me and my business with a post office box address, mail and shipping services for several years.  I like having a face behind these services as it reassures that someone is taking personal and professional responsibility for making sure everything I send out gets to its destination, and that I receive everything that is sent to me.  Yes, FedEx and the others can do a lot of the same things, but there is something very American about having these guys and facilities in the community.    Let's hope they figure out a way to stay open and active as part of the American landscape.

The aptly named, "Moo," is a small burger shop on the south end of Main Street, New Hope, PA. What makes it unique is the use of locally sourced ingredients where possible in the construction of their sandwiches.  The beef, milk, ice cream (soft serve) are from the surrounding area, and they list their providers on a board next to the pick up window.  It is also staffed by locally sourced young folk, making for a very at home sensibility. There are three or four tables inside, with more counter space and stools along one wall.  More seating out front on the elevated patio overlooking the street.   We stopped in Sunday evening for a bite to satisfy our moderate hunger. Not looking for a big meal.  We ordered two Moo Burgers, one order of fries and a salted caramel shake.  That list cost us $22., which seemed a little on the high side, but perhaps not for New Hope. The dining room was more than half empty, so we took a table toward the rear, and waited to hear my name called.    The food was served on an aluminum tray.  The burgers were wrapped in paper with access on one end, and the fries were in a small cardboard barge. The shake was 7 ounces with a wide straw for better suction. The puck was medium to medium well, with lettuce, tomato, cheese and a "special" sauce.  Martin's Potato Rolls held the opus together.  They were very good, with a never frozen texture and fresh grilled flavor.  The rolls were strong enough to remain intact to the last bite. Always appreciated. The fries were also right out of the earth, with a short stop for washing and slicing. They were excellently crisp, with plenty of nubs for extra crunch. Finally, the shake was creamy, cool and sweet. Delicious, but perhaps an indulgence at $6 for a smallish plastic cup.    Overall, we liked Moo a lot, and would not hesitate to visit again when in a burger mood. Far superior to the casual fast food burgers proliferating around the nation.

Very nice to have a bakery café open in Chinatown late on a Saturday night.   The Vietnamese Coffee was very good.  The Dulces were varietal and fresh. And the service unhurried in a "have a long conversation" way.    Pleased to find a place to hang out for a while without high decibels, nor strutting nighthawks.    Table in the back. Stay as long as you like.

The last stop of my Farmers' Best, Kobawoo and H Mart Asian shopping day, H Mart falls somewhere in between the larger, well inventoried, but dirty FBM, and the smaller, well thought out aisles and cleanliness of KM.    This successful chain has expanded since 1982, and continues to offer well stocked fresh produce and a wide variety of Asian packaged frozen foods and groceries.  If I were to choose only one stop shopping, H Mart would be the best compromise.  Their prices are reasonable and you can find most of what you want for your exotic food requirements.  I have visited their locations in Levittown and Edison, and again, this one stands in between those two in terms of size, customer service and aisle access/comfort.    The most unique aspect of this shop is the space it shares with a decent food court for a sit down or take out dining experience, and the Paris Baguette bakery in the basement which provides a pleasant café experience pre or après purchasing your consumables.    Have you ever wondered how "H Mart" got its name?  I did, and went on its website to see if I could find out.  The "H" is the first letter of the phrase, "Han Ah Reum," meaning, "Arm full of groceries."  I leave it to the Korean readers to know if that is accurate.   But, the image works for me.

Market at the Fareway is the successor to the Chestnut Hill Farmers Market on Germantown Avenue, Philadelphia. It is owned/operated by the folks who brought you the Chestnut Hill Hotel, next door. It incorporates historic charm with contemporary cuisine alternatives, including the Chestnut Hill Brewing Company, for a fun and flavorful cultural experience in the heart of one of the most attractive neighborhoods in greater Philadephia (I hesitate to use the word, "quaint").  It still possesses the charm of the old farmers market, with butcher, baker and green grocer in house. But, in addition you can enjoy the pleasures of street food like Korean fried chicken, local microbrew beer, sweets straight out of the oven, pizza, and sushi, and more. There is a common dining area for those who prefer to eat while the food is at its apex taste.  Although there is a free parking lot behind the structure, it is often full, requiring a search of the streets surrounding the market. No doubt, the residential neighbors nearby find that annoying, to say the least. In fact, there is litigation going on between the owners of the market and the closest neighbors about the expansion of the operations to include an outdoor beer garden. An agreement between the previous owners and the concerned citizens was thought to deny this growth. The outcome remains to be seen at this time.  Certainly hope all sides can find a workable solution for this issue, as angry neighbors are never good for business, and overreaching businesses are seldom good for long term peace and prosperity in the neighborhood.  It would be a shame to lose the benefit of the new Market at the Fareway, for the sake of an effort to squeeze additional profits from an already successful venture. Why not allow for a certain number of outdoor days for the beer garden every year, and keep it closed the rest of the time? There is enough room inside for those who want to drink on site. And you can always buy some to take home. A special permit would be required from the ABC or State Police to allow for special events, but that seems manageable compared to fighting about this, and leaving it to a judge.  Should I return, I promise to eat and drink inside until this is resolved.

Hometown Deli in the Anchor Crossing Center doesn't look like much walking in. Small eating area to the left, a few rows of snacks and drinks coolers in the middle, and deli department to the left rear. It all seems a little worn. But, ordering a sandwich and taking possession of it quicky changed those first impressions.   My chicken salad on rye toast was delivered to my table by the deli chef. It was bigger than expected, and first bite opened my eyes in pleasant surprise. The chicken salad was chunky, creamy and had very fresh taste. Combined with a thick red tomato slice and dark green lettuce, inside real rye toast, it was very good and enjoyable. It was almost too much to finish.   Apparently, they do breakfast sandwiches just as good.   See you again soon, Hometown Deli.

Very nice facility in Bensalem, Pa. Dark tones. Square bar. Attractive, attentive service. Happy hour drink and apps menu at good prices. Outdoor patio for nice weather.   Food, however, is average to dull. Their Louie Burger looks great, but lacks fresh ground beef flavor and juiciness. Perhaps frozen. The sliders, same thing. Dry with little taste. Sauces don't bring them back to life. Their special bourbon wings were too wet. No crunch. Weak whiskey taste. Not fun to eat. Left most of them behind.   Looks like a meet up place for the after work crowd. That makes sense given the look of the place, location and happy hour discounts. But, certainly there are better places for burgers and wings.  2.5 Stars.

This is the laboratory collection location preferred by Parx Casino for prospective employees. After the initial interview at the casino, they hand over a large manila envelop with the proper Quest Diagnostics form for completion, signing, and to turn in to the Quest personnel for processing along with a urine sample.   It is not the most efficient operation, but they get you in and out as quickly as possible. There is a sign-in tablet for registering your presence, which seemed to work when we were there. The employees didn't have bubbling personalities, but they weren't rude, either. Just another day of handling blood and piss for them.   At the end, they keep the forms and samples, and send the results back to Parx within 24 hours in most cases.   If you've had illegal drugs in your system in the recent past, these tests will show them, and the job will be forfeit.

Hard Rock Café is an icon of the 20th Century.  It does feel dated and retro in the 21st.   I hadn't been in Philly's franchise for about twenty years, and it felt and looked the same as I remembered.  Guitars on the walls, TVs everywhere the guitars weren't.  A gift shop that remains the heart and soul of the establishment.  Overpriced? Check. Gitchy? Check. Mediocre food? Check.   My friends from Copenhagen really wanted to go so they could collect another Hard Rock T shirt. I remembered that their burgers were 'the thing.'  We went it to buy what they wanted first, and then grabbed a table for lunch.  The staff was professionally friendly.  The menu as expected.   $14 for a Legend Burger and $3.50 for a Lemonade (no refill offered) were strictly based on what they could charge, not on quality, but I guess you have to pay for the atmosphere.  The Burger was right on Medium, but crumbled when cut due to freezing.  It wasn't bad, but they would have done better hiring a crew from Five Guys to handle this chore. The Onion Ring on top was over-fried, as was everything on the Appetizer Mix Platter. The Wings were not good, the Chicken Fingers were dry and tasted of yesterday's oil. I stayed away from the Spinach Dip.   My friends are not foodies, and had no issue with the scene and grub.  This is what they were here to do.  Who was I to rain on their parade?

Another Benjamin Franklin first - the founding of the first hospital in the Original 13 - in 1751, Pennsylvania Hospital in the Society Hill section of Philadelphia, has been treating patients for a long time with quality medical care and innovation. The 534 bed facility at 8th & Pine, had the first surgical amphitheater in North America on the top floor of the Federalist style building; operating between 11 and 2 on sunny days, as when constructed there was still no electricity, and thus no lights bright enough for surgery.  The concept was that treatment was to be free of charge for all who sought medical care. Funding was accomplished by "matching grants" offered by the well to do members of Philadelphia society. First the land was donated, and then management volunteered their services. Collections were taken up to pay for the building of the structures. Franklin, Thomas Bond and the Stretch family, as leading citizens, were also the providers of most of the initial capital to get the project started. Ben's first contribution? 25 English pounds. Women were among the first students.  These days, it is nationally ranked in Adult Specialties of gynecology and orthopaedics, and also highly recognized for other specialties, including urology (the reason I was there). Its affiliation with the University of Pennsylvania Health System in 1997, added to its longevity and significance in the region.  The quality of care I received while there for day surgery was excellent. Everyone knew their roles, and clearly kept the patient's needs paramount. Every step was clearly explained, and I had conversations with everyone from the preparation team, to the anesthesiologist, nurses and my surgeon. There was plenty of attention in post op as well. I felt well cared for.   I was pleased with the decision to come to Pennsylvania Hospital for this procedure. Somehow, the 270 years in existence gave assurance that I was in very good hands.

Properly Fueled sits in the space of a former Japanese sushi house and although it has been beautifully renovated it still carries a quiet stillness in its light airiness that I found so comforting in the earlier incarnation. Whoever did the redesign must have felt it, too, because it remains fully present and even enhanced. Perhaps, this quality is given fuller expression now that it has been paired with wholesome natural locally sourced food.   The internal effect is likely similar, as my breakfast of a tartine made of goat cheese, sliced figs and honey on toasted sourdough, was delicious in it's simplicity. Crunchy, creamy, juicy and sweet - healthy. Their coffee from Small World in Princeton was served in a french press. Ready to be plunged (pressed) within minutes into a large white cup. It was strong, a bit gritty at the end and a total wake up.   Ownership works the kitchen and counter and are warm and gracious. They sure know what they are doing. Their fresh food combinations elegantly tease the senses.   No table service, but it is a short walk to pick up the cutting board tray.  You can feed me anytime.  Can't get those figs out of my mind.

This is definitely as good as it gets in this part of Bucks County, PA, when it comes to Salvadoran and Mexican cuisine. Without a critical mass of Central Americans nor Mexicans in the area, the kitchen knows they are cooking primarily for gringos, and not their countrymen. They keep the joint clean, are bilingual, and pay close attention to the spice tolerances of their customers. They also have adapted the new policy of skipping the chips & salsa as a complementary snack while you wait for your ordered dishes. If you want those crunchies and sauces, you are going to have to order them, and add it to your bill.   No problem. I don't need those extra calories, anyhow.   I ordered beef flautas and fresh guava drink. They were both excellent. The flutes were oven-crunchy and full of well grilled and shredded beef, spices and cheese. The more I chewed, the more the flavor enhanced my palate. Delicious, with lettuce, onion and white cheese drizzled on top. The guava was cool and refreshing. Reminds me of apple juice, but more sweetness, and a hint of sour behind the bright sugar rush.   Service was friendly and personable. Prices reasonable, coming in at just about $10 for my dinner, before tip. The room is a traditional colorful rendition of the restaurants found in the home countries. Even on a rainy evening, the dining room of La Corita Taco Shop shown bright.

The Dining Car is an old style stainless steel diner on Frankford Avenue, Northeast Philadelphia. It has a small private parking lot behind the structure, with much more space available in the Mealey Furniture lot next door. There is a dining room as well as a large counter for folks like me who are eating alone and enjoy watching their employees as they work.   The staff is friendly and efficient. I had menu in hand and a mugga joe before me within a minute of sitting down. Traditional diner fare, with a few things for which they are noted - chicken croquettes and Jewish apple cake - among them. It even had a moment of fame when it was the subject of Guy Fieri's Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives show on the Food Channel. Of course, Guy is all about spiked hair showmanship and excessive exuberance, and not necessarily honest assessment of the food he is mugging for. Here, his enjoyment was legitimately entertained by the urban nature of this part of town having its own stainless palace, but also likely uninformed by the other Philly Special joints in the same neighborhood that far outshine The Dining Car (The Clown House, for example).   I was there for a French Toast breakfast, although I was tempted to see what the fuss was all about with the apple cake. Doubt it was better than grandma's.   Still, I enjoyed my morning repast, even if not outstanding. Two slices of decent white loaf seemed a bit light if it wasn't a short stack. Although advertised with "maple syrup," I'm fairly certain that the sticky sweet colloidal liquid pouring out of the container on the counter was not from a maple tree. Tasted a lot more like a generic Mrs. Buttersworth. Still sweet. Still a decent companion to the fry bread. Just not Grade B Dark. The coffee was strong, hot and free flowing from the Bunn brewer.   The place was humming on Thursday morning. A definite community gathering spot.

Buckingham Valley Vineyards is another beautifully laid out small acreage winery specializing is the sweeter vintages of fruit and grape based fermentations. Like some of the others in the area it is second generation family run operation with the love and care given the vines obvious to any who stop in for a self guided tour and the tasting available throughout the year.   Although I prefer drier wines, I have sampled the bottles and casks here and found them to be pretty good, but not what I want to purchase for personal consumption. Still, a relaxing afternoon overlooking the long rows of arbors sipping peach and blackberry wines and heavier port like sipping liqueurs has a very mellowing effect on the soul.   Well worth a stop on the Bucks County winery tour.

Nate's Hot Bagels is the most forlorn shop in an exceedingly decrepit commercial center on Grant Avenue in Northeast Philadelphia. The large towering sign atop the storefront is bigger than the interior customer space, which is merely a small lobby big enough to turn around and to look at the bagel bins behind heavy Plexiglas protection. Lord knows, people up to no good can't get enough of these round dough mounds, and will go to dangerous extremes to get them. Business is conducted through a narrow space between the plexi and the locked door leading to what looks like a small bakery.  Cash only. Smallest order: half dozen for $5. Don't like it? Tough. Find another rounder house.   After I got passed the sense of walking into a 19th Century prison, I noticed the bagels looked pale compared to what I was accustomed to. Under baked? Perhaps, but I was there, and I wasn't going to walk out without a score. There was a buzzer button sitting atop the back of the cash register. I pushed it. It croaked out a notice to a man in back, who came up to take care of my wants. He was friendly enough, but didn't look like a baker. No flour in his hair. No poppy seeds stuck to his hands.   I asked for three onion and three everything bagels, and he went ahead and fetched them barehanded into a brown paper sack, and threw in a plastic bag for home storage in a refrigerator. My $20 returned the bag and $15 paper money. No taxes to account for here.   So, I tried an everything bagel when I got home, and had a toasted onion for breakfast this morning. They are denser than I normally like, but no question about freshness and full flavor. Definitely worth the gamble entering this mysterious shop.   Can't escape the sensation that there are more than bagels going on in Nate's, but as long as their signature products deliver on the promise of a decent bagel (and bialys), I can ignore everything else.

Pho Kitch'n on Ridge Pike, Eagleville, PA, is an Asian fusion restaurant with Vietnamese cuisine taking the lead and Thai/Chinese following close behind. It is in a free standing A frame building, with plenty of parking and nice size dining room.   I went with the namesake noodle soup with lean round steak and fatty flank. It was a large bowl for $8.95 and the stock was good with interesting and subtle flavors from long simmering, and a large knot of noodles beneath the surface.   Sadly, the side plate of accessories to add to the pho was disappointing, with withered Thai basil and dessicated lime wedge visible with a quick glance. Delivering them to the table was an act of disrespect and slovenliness that is impossible to dismiss as an oversight. The woman serving me certainly put the plate together in the kitchen, and just didn't give a damn, or worse.  Ironically, the pho itself was pretty good (even without the basil and lime), and would have garnered a higher score but for the passive aggressiveness served with the pho.   2 Stars

Not a bad place to stop for a cuppa joe on the way into Mt. Holly.    It's clean and the service is good.  Only 6 tables for those who want to hang for a few.  Definitely built for get and go, but lacking a drive thru window.    The seasonal Pumpkin Donut wasn't bad, either.

Not a bad place for a pie, but my experience with their Eggplant Parm Sandwich left something to be desired.   The slices of this nightshade were thick and not quite sautéed through and through, leaving parts of the meal somewhat harder than expected.  Too, they seem to have only been in the pan once after breading, rather than twice, before and after breadcrumbs were added.  When heated twice in hot olive oil the veggie is much softer and takes on the taste of the surrounding ingredients better.  No complaint with the gravy, cheese, nor roll. However, I would not order this again.   Nick's has the feel of a slice and cheesesteak joint.  It is small, but nicely appointed in a low key way.  The staff is fine, and anyone who has hands free behind the counter will bring out the platter when it is ready.    Lipton products, meaning that high corn fructose is a prime part of every bottle.  Not so good for health.  An upgrade in the drink cooler would be a big plus.

It has been many years since this joint was the Lemon Leaf (at least since 2014, if not earlier). Now, it is a Chinese takeout, with a menu half Chinese and half Thai, although the operation is totally Chinese. The waiting area has two tables if you prefer to eat your fried rice hot and not reheated. But, coming from a disappointment of a prematurely closed White Elephant a few miles away, I was still in the mood for Thai, and took a chance at the now named Asian Thai & Chinese Cuisine.   If there was a classification for "Dive Chinese Takeout," this would fit that description. Dirty all around and a kitchen that hadn't seen a clean mop or ounce of elbow grease in many a year (but, plenty of other grease abounded). Hunger drove me to suspend better judgement and plunge in with chicken pad thai.   It arrived in styro packing and thin plastic fork 10 minutes later. Ground peanuts atop a pile of medium width rice noodles, mixed with slivers of a few veggies , slices of white meat bird and light brown sauce. I asked for it spicy, so red chili powder was included, but not any heat from lemongrass.   The taste was nothing like pad thai, but some Chinese approximation of that dish using Chinese spices as substitutes for the real deal. Edible, but lacking authenticity. Satisfied my hunger, but approaching false advertising.   No need to return. Just hope White Elephant honors the hours on its door in the future.

Parx Beer Garden is a recent addition to the Parx Casino complex in Bensalem, PA. It is an indoor/outdoor facility with folding doors separating the large warehouse space from the attractive green garden area. This, it is much nicer in warm weather when the high walls are open and the fresh breeze is free to flow throughout.   There are many tables and a long bar capable of holding a couple of hundred guests. The draft beer list runs about two dozen, with an equal amount of bottled options. The bartenders are well trained in the art of cocktailcraft and chatter. Because the casino operates 24/7, it is possible to catch a late happy hour after 9:00 P. M. for a fair price on their decent bar food, brews and daily special drinks. Most folks seem to come and go between the gambling floor and the alcohol break in order to extend the evening and catch their breath from the honky tonk pace of money and chips changing hands. Problem is, the acoustics are poor, so between the sound drifting in from other parts of the expansive rooms, the sound system, large HDTVs, and general hubbub, it can be difficult to hear your friends.   Still, if your not expecting too much real entertainment, and are really there for poker and roulette, the Beer Garden is a nice place to clear your head, grab a bite and brew for a reasonable price, before heading back into the maelstrom.

Visited my first Playa Bowls the other day. This new tropical tan Jersey Shore original shop recently opened in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center, and the "Grand Opening" banner was still strung up over the front door. No question that if you like fresh fruit, smoothies, yogurt and granola, you have come to your little spot of heaven.   The large wall board menu is a bit daunting to read, but once I adjusted to the sound bombardment from the loudspeakers kicking out rock music several decibels above my comfort level, I settled on a Gogi Bowl consisting of sliced pineapple, banana, gogi berry, granola on a chill base of bright purple dragonfruit sorbet. I took a stool at a high plank table to await my name being called. The place was packed at 3:00 p.m., and it took about 10 minutes to hear my name shouted out above the crashing din.   I retrieved the midsized plastic bowl and spoon and returned to my seat. It looked great. The taste was of very fresh fruit, crunchy granola and cold, almost crystalized dragonfruit creamie. It was refreshing and fun.   All the while I took in the scene around me. Everyone was high school age. 90% female, and there was no doubt that I was the only one over 30. It was good that so many people my teenage son's age were hanging out healthy.   I just wish I didn't have to overcome the sound barrier, and I hope they recycle.

You would be forgiven if you approached the corner where Sabor Latino Bar & Restaurant is located, and decided not to park, nor go inside.  It is a particularly dreary intersection in the depths of Trenton, with a few boarded up houses, and war torn streets.  Yet, it you summoned the courage to open the door and walk in, you would thank yourself for bravery being well rewarded.    Sabor Latino (Latin Flavor) is a Dominican house with a kitchen familiar with the cuisine of Puerto Rico, Guatemala and Costa Rica.  The bar room also serves as the dining area, and the staff is friendly and attractively bilingual.  The broad menu offers lunch and dinner with prices below $10 and $16, respectively.  A few HDTVs on the walls broadcasting futbol en espanol, and gentlemen at the bar and high tops conducting business.    My server recommended the Pernil special, and I accepted her suggestion.  A few minutes later I was presented with a large plate of Roasted Pork, White Rice, Salad and a cup of Red Beans.  There was also a table rocket filled with a mix of spice and mayo for use on the greens.  The Pork was soft, juice and tender with a nice taste of mild BBQ sauce.  The skin took the fire well and it was crunchy to chew with a stronger flavor from the basting and flames.  The Rice and Beans were solid accompaniments.  The Salad was just some Iceberg and Tomato; not bad, but more of a garnish than a side dish.    I was checked on several times by my waitperson.  She clearly was concerned that I be satisfied with my meal and overall experience, and was pleasant in her relief that I enjoyed my lunch.    Sabor Latino is yet another of the strong effort coming from the Central American community in Trenton.  It may not yet have the well earned reputation that was Chambersburg for Italian joints in the last century, but this and the other casas are definitely on their way toward that recognition.

I wasn't sure what to expect when I found Tuscany Ristorante on Yelp. It was located on Rhawn Street in far Northeast Philadelphia, just off the Boulevard, an area not known for haute cuisine. But, we were not that far away and in the mood for an Italian dinner. My uncertainty mounted as I found the last parking spot right in front of the corner liquor store, and rolled up over the curb and sidewalk to park. The dudes out front gave me a glance, like, "What the F *** do you think your doing...?" I pulled my Eagles hat lower over my brow as I got out of the car and gave them a wink. Sometimes being 6'4" is enough for street corner respect or at least a pass. Or, maybe it was just the hat. They had less risky things to do on a Sunday night.   Anyway, we found our way inside the restaurant and were immediately taken by the white linen, heavy flatware, and polished marble floors. Okay. This wasn't a local pizza joint. These folks were serious about creating an atmosphere of opulence in the middle of this urban jungle. For the most part, they succeeded.   What was even more pronounced was the fine quality of the food coming from the kitchen. We ordered calamari, roast chicken and rice soup, chicken marsala, chicken francais, a side Caesar salad and house veggies - roasted potatoes and broccoli. One thing was better than the next.   The squid was nicely deep fried with excellent dipper. They were all rings, without tentacles, which gave the impression they were received that way from the purveyor rather than being sliced in house. Liked them, but would have been better if handled completely by the chef. The soup was excellent - creamy, flavorful with lots of chicken and rice. The Caesar and veggies came with dinner. Both were more than adequate, but small in size and just a solid complement to the stars of the show.   Tuscany knows from sauces. They did a masterful job on the marsala and francais reductions. The marsala had plenty of chunky fresh mushrooms in a dark marsala wine base. Very nice. The francais was heavy into lemon and white wine with light egg batter coating, in which the thin chicken fillets had been pan sautéed in extra virgin, amply caramelized and set afloat. One of the best things I have put in my mouth this year. Wowee!   Service was very good. Friendly and casual. Plenty of time between courses, and many stops to inquire of our satisfaction. Dessert looked tempting, but enough was enough. Most surprising was the pricing; reminiscent of the turn of the century.   Aside from the poor acoustics caused by all the hard surfaces, Tuscany Ristorante was a total win. We will definitely be back.

Pulled up to this Prince Fried Chicken after work one night last week.  The driveway is not on Olden Avenue, but on the side street next to the adjoining liquor store.  Miss that and you will have a job finding your way back here, especially after dark.  That being said, after trying their breasts and wings I will not likely be going back.  When I arrived home and sat down to eat my purchase, I found the coating to be overcooked and the meat a bit dry.  I had noticed that the chicken was a shade darker than richly golden, but as everything in the bin was the same color, I thought that would not be an issue.  It was, however.   The pieces were meaty and the prices very inexpensive.  If the chicken itself had been crunchy, spicy and moist, it would have been a big hit. It might have been a bad lot left in the fryer too long, or perhaps suffering freezer burn, but you only get one chance to make a first impression.    Given the alternative fried chicken shacks all around the area, I will keep searching for the perfect batch.

It has been a while since my last visit to any Ikea, and after spending two plus hours in their Conshohockon maze, I remember why I stopped shopping there.  Their warehouses are enormous, and there is so much stuff to look at that it can be overwhelming. But, the kicker comes when you have had enough browsing, decided not to purchase anything in order to consider the possibilities, and try to leave the premises.   It is then you realize that you are lost somewhere on the second floor and don't remember how you got to the office furniture area. The signs say the check-out and exit is "that way," but that just leads you through every other department in the hanger, past the cafeteria, down the only flight of stairs, and through a second maze on the first floor. The maps sparsely displayed look like a game of Candyland or Chutes and Ladders, with little dots meandering through every corner of the building. It was at least 10 minutes before I reached the cashiers and saw the exit doors beyond them. Someone with claustrophobia could easily panic before reaching fresh air.   Yes. I did see some desks, bookcases and lighting that might work well in the new office, but not as much as I had hoped. Prices were good, but I had the definite feeling that I would be settling for things based on limited choices, rather than true love of the furniture. And, by the time I made it out of the warehouse, I had little desire to go back in.   Make it easier to escape and I would have no problem going back in smaller doses to explore and find what I want. Absent that, why would anyone voluntarily submit themselves to such torture?

This Wendy's in the corner of Morrisville Plaza was renovated a few years ago, and has a nice look and feel.  It is a smaller shop, with minimalist décor, but clean and highly functional.  The hours are from 11:00 am to 2:00 am, although the hours presently on Yelp incorrectly state it closes at two in the afternoon.    It has a wrap around take out lane that requires drivers and pedestrians to be careful approaching the front door.  Very easy to ignore the vehicles coming from the left, or walkers in front of you while stowing a bag of nosh.  Service is fine at the counter.   There is no doubt that Wendy is attempting to up its game in order to compete with the fast casual burger crowd.  Most ingredients are fresh, and the new basic roll is an order of magnitude better than the old one.  It holds together throughout eating, and has a pleasant flavor.  The only remaining issue is the quality of the beef patty.  Its taste and texture appear the same as the old version, which is to say that it is somewhat mealy (frozen), and lacking any real verve in taste, and juiciness.  It still seems flat and uninspired.    So, the key to enjoyment is keeping the package together while consuming, with the fresh onion, lettuce and cheese can dominate the experience.  As a whole, the burger is just okay, although an improvement over its predecessor, it has a long road to travel until it can stand next to its cousins at Red Robin, Cheeburger, or even your local corner tavern.

Salvatore's Cucina is a new Italian house in the HMart shopping center in Levittown, PA. It is divided into two large rooms; one for lunches and light fare, and the other for more serious dining. This is reflected on their two menus.  The fancy one only lists the dinners. If you want a pizza, sandwich, panini or wrap, you have to ask for the second, smaller list.  As first time customers, that is what we requested. My approach to new places like this is to start with their basics and if satisfied, return for the high end expensive meals.    So, we ordered a chicken broccoli rabe panini, and a chicken, spinach sandwich on a 7" hoagie roll.  The place wasn't busy, so they allowed us to sit in the big boy room. Service was slow as a rainy Sunday afternoon in April, but we weren't in a rush.  They provided a basket of bread and an olive oil herbal mix for dipping. Enjoyed that.   Our lunches arrived looking quite nice on white ceramic plates. The panini was nicely grilled and came with a load of crisp fries. The smaller sandwich was less impressive, with a minimum of grilled chicken, sautéed spinach and two square slices of mozzarella melted over the top.  Son enjoyed half the panini and could not finish the second. We brought it home.  The chicken 'wich was just okay, with no effort to make it appealing or tasty. I guess we shouldn't expect much for the low price, but it was disappointing nonetheless.   We also ordered a small standard pizza with sausage to take home.  When we opened the box, it looked fine with plenty of chunky meat and red sauce.  We reheated it in the oven a few hours later, and found it to be a decent pie.  The sauce was a bit salty, but overall we liked it. Can't be too fussy about a reheat job. They are never as good as piping hot from the oven.   It was hard for us to get overly excited by Salvadore's.  It is certainly a place where you can stuff yourself at a good price, but the offerings we had were not the stuff of return visits. Yet, the large menu did have some tempting items in the pasta, marsala and francaise department. On another rainy day, we could find ourselves there again to check them out. Our server certainly encouraged us to come back and give them a try.

The Bristol Amish Market sits just off Route 13 at Green Lane, in Bristol, PA.  It is one of several such markets around Bucks County, and one of the newest and cleanest.    If you enjoy visiting Lancaster, PA, and the world of the Amish and Mennonites in Central Pennsylvania, you can have a small dose of that here, but without the traffic problems caused by the interaction of horse & buggy and combustion engines.  The people working here come by their dress honestly, from women's bonnets, to men's black hats and beards.  Everyone is friendly and somewhat shy.  Delightful!  The small shops within run the gamut from butcher to baker, and green grocer to donut maker.  Everything looks fresh and appealing.  Prices are not on the low end, however.  Compared to their sister market in Newtown, the Bristol Market is larger, cleaner, brighter, and easier to use.  If you go Thursday morning when they are just opening for the weekend, the space is lightly travelled, and it is easy to get in and out without lines.    As with most other Yelp reviewers, the highlight here is Mary's Gourmet Donut Shoppe, at the back of the warehouse.  She bakes up excellent fried dough; dipped in an assortment of ultra sweet and smooth topping and icing.  My poor blood sugar!  It sells both cake and light donuts, that spoil you away from Dunkin and the boys. Even the coffee is very good.  Unlike the other purveyors here, Mary's is not really Amish, and employs locals to run the shop.  They are willing to engage in conversation about their wares in much more detail than the Amish butcher baker ladies who only converse with customers beyond the business basics if faced with a determined interlocutor.   Just bought a dozen to bring to the office.  So hard not to rip open the box and dive in.  But, I was good, and allowed the staff to slice the tape sealing the box and savor the sticky moment.  Man, those Peanut Butter & Jellies were tempting!   They were gone before I could pour my coffee.

VITAMIN/SUPPLEMENT REVIEW ONLY  Visited the Carousel Gardens campus today, thinking Organnons Market might carry the things I needed in their vitamin supplement area. It was my first visit so I looked around the shop. Few customers on a Saturday afternoon, but the produce looked good and the canned goods were limited but interestingly esoteric. Nice selection of coffee, too.   Yet, they didn't have any of the three things I needed that are fairly standard in most health food stores. The worker was helpful, and apologized for not being able to help me out. No sweat. Drove down to Big Bear and found what I needed. Plus, they were selling Kicking Horse Coffee for $3 less per bag then Organnons.   Good to have a quality locally focused organic food outlet nearby, but given it's inherent inventory limitations and prices, it won't be a regular stop for our provisions.

Tre Fratelli was the first meal I had when moving to Bucks County many years ago.  It was decent then, and remains decent now.  The pizza, cheesesteaks, sandwiches and pasta are the way to go here.  The dinners are a step down from memorable, and not able to generate a strong desire to return for more.    Two of us had the Chicken Parm dinner, and our third, the Marsala.  The Parm's chicken breasts were large and cooked to the right point of nicely retained juiciness, but the Red Sauce was heavy and covered the entire bird so not even a pan fried edge could be seen for visual cuing. The Mozza melt was similarly overdone; making the plate about its toppings rather than complimenting the chicken.  The Marsala was overcooked and left less than tender medallions adrift in a dense brown wine redux that should have been lighter and more subtle.  Both dishes were edible, but less that we hoped.    The surprising upside were the sides that came with the meal.  Each of the three we ordered; the French Fries, Penne Oglio Olio, and Veggies arrived in large, family dinner sizes, and were totally enjoyable.  The taters were hot and crunchy, the veggies bright and lightly tossed with Olive Oil and Garlic, and the pasta, loaded with razor-thin Garlic Slices browned to gold like copper leaves in a mound of snow.  Al Dente and more fun to eat than the mains.    It happens that way sometimes.  Stick with the basics.

Chicco's Pizza on the corner of Brownsville Road and Philadelphia Avenue in Trevose, PA., is an attractive Italian house focused primarily on providing a solid lunch and dinner to the surrounding neighborhoods in the part of Bucks County.  It has a clean and bright dining room separated from the walkup/takeout part of the store. Their luncheon menu includes a plenty of torpedo based sandwiches made from quality ingredients that come to about $10 with tip. They also do pizza, but I did not try any this day.   My "South Philly Special," consisted of breaded/fried chicken breast, broccoli rabe and a ton of melted mozza on top of an oven toasted roll. There was also a heavy load of sautéed garlic in the mix, giving its dominating flavor to the greens. It was a large unfinishable sandwich, but tasty and made to order for me. In fact, the chef came out to tell me that it would take longer than usual to secure my meal because she was cooking up a fresh batch of rabe for me. It tasted it!   While this part of Bucks is not a regular haunt for me, I was in the area on business. So, if things go right, I could find myself back here to sample more of their menu, especially the tomato pies.

Sitting back off Bethlehem Pike a block from the top of Chestnut Hill @ Germantown Avenue, Thai Kuu is a small attractive Asian dining room. Buddhas and elephants adorn the walls and menus giving a serene atmosphere that augurs well for the meal to come. This establishment offers weekend lunch at a reasonable price, and I was there to check it out. Many similar houses eliminate the midday meal discount on weekends, and I appreciated that this one kept it in play.   I saw what I wanted and ordered Tom Ka Soup and Spicy Pad Kee Mao (aka Drunken Noodles). Service was provided by a gentleman I took to be an owner/manager. While efficient and cool, he also had an officiousness that was subtly off-putting. Maybe he objected to my black hoodie or my dining solo, but I wasn't going to allow his silent judgment interfere with my enjoyment. The food, on the other hand, could impact my take on the experience. At the end of my meal, that opinion was less than my first impressions.   The Tom Ka was pretty good with strong coconut flavor, a hint of lemongrass and fair amount of string bean, carrot, mushroom and broccoli. I lifted the square bowl to my lips to suck it all in. I anticipated the Pad Kee Mao would be hot and spicy from a chili pepper base sauce, and from the word "spicy" in the name on the menu. Not the case.   Instead, the word was used to label the sweetness of the middle width noodles and brown sauce, not its heat. An exceedingly small portion, its lack of traditional burn was disappointing; pointing to the conclusion that Thai Kuu was far more an Asian fusion kitchen than anything close to vibrant Siam fire.   It was all okay, but could have been so much more had they the courage of their culinary convictions.

La Cabana (The Cabin), certainly is not what the name suggests. It is far more than a cabin, but in actuality is a sparkling clean Latin American bakery, café and restaurant on Dayton Street in Trenton, NJ.  The casa recently opened and is totally renovated from the former occupant.  It is new from top to bottom.  The space is light and airy with a north facing wall of windows onto Dayton Street, and comfortable furniture and excellent service.    I stopped in for breakfast after court today to check it out.  I was given a paper menu and invited to sit anywhere.  I took a table toward the rear where I could see everything that was going on.  I went with strong Columbian coffee, and the La Cabana Omelet, which arrived stuffed with chorizo, peppers, cheese, onion, potato and topped with fresh pico de gallo.  There was also a basket of fresh sesame seeded bread and butter provided.    The meal was excellent.  Loved the egg dish.  It was steaming hot and melded together into a delectable hot mess.  Definitely a three egger. A few dashes of Tobasco and I was in business. The side of home fries were tender and nicely spiced, and really more than I could finish.  Nicholas stopped by several times to inquire as to my need for more coffee, and promptly took away the finished plates, while inviting me to remain as long as I wished.  Nice touch, as I was in no rush to leave this mellow, sunny place.    I was lucky enough to meet the new owner, who was in a business meeting at a nearby table.  As I prepared to leave, the gentleman with whom she spoke approached me to ask about my impressions of the operation.  He was there to develop a marketing plan for them.  I gave him my honest appraisal, and had a short chat with his lovely client. Clearly, she is serious about the success of this enterprise.  If she maintains this level of quality and professionalism, it is all but assured.   PS. Just a hint - Consider turning down the volume on the TV if no one appears to be watching it. Better soft music than talk shows, even in Spanish.

Tower Hill Brewery is a nano beer maker located in the Chalfont Village Shopping Center. Their equipment is easy to miss even though it is in the front of the shop by the door. Production is clearly limited to their own in house use unless they have other facilities elsewhere.   My pint of Himmel Hefeweizen was good, with smooth finish and mild banana flavor. I sat at the bar under two HDTVs, watching the Penn State - Iowa football game sipping, while the kitchen prepared the Loaded Pierogies I ordered.   Dinner arrived in a long handled white oven ready ceramic pan with four homemade potato and cheese perogies, topped with bacon bits and chopped scallion. A small cup of sour cream completed the presentation. The first bite was extremely hot and I needed my beer to extinguish the fire. Thereafter, with more caution, I worked my way through what was really more appetizer than an entree. The dough pockets were excellent. Creamy mashed and cheese with lightly onion flavor that went well with the bacon/scallion topping. These guys make great "rogies."   At $14 for four of these babies, I was paying a premium price for their quality. As good as they were, the value proposition was not right, and I left with the impression that they really were not worth having more than once. Still, Tower Hill Brewery does good suds and grub and is certainly a place to visit with thirst and appetite.

In the middle of a cold Saturday afternoon in Glenside Village just a few blocks from the famous Keswick Theater, Daryl's Pastries sits in a small aging storefront in the center of this attractive historic district. The shop was crammed with chest high display cases full of colorful cakes, cookies, pastries and my reason for being there - donuts. Perhaps six people could fit in front, and a half dozen more in the tiny cafe sitting area to the right side.   Service was friendly, if necessarily rushed due to lack of room. By my arrival, some choices were depleted, but I was able to score a box of traditional doughboys (glazed, chocolate glazed and apple crisp) and a cup of coffee for the drive back to Bucks to share with the family. Sadly, the old fashioned brownies I craved were not available.  I found all the samples to be enjoyably sweet and well textured. The skin was slightly crisp and the heart soft and tender as they should be. They went down smoothly with their coffee chaser. The family happily agreed.   Given the current popularity of customized donut shops offering multiple varieties made 'just in time' for the consumer, these badboys were somehow dated, but a pleasant reminder of how good rounders can be. Not every bakery needs to be Factory Donuts or other assembly line ultra expensive variant in order to create superlative timeless addictive floury confections.  Daryl knows from donuts.

I am not an expert on haunted hay rides, but I went along for the ride last night with my seventeen year old son and his two buds. At $36 per person, it was an expensive thrill, and if I had to cost it out, it came to about $10 a scare. Not really all that spooked out, but they are dealing with a mixed audience and what frightens me might cause coronaries in others. Yet, the monster in the Trump mask was so realistic I almost thought he was moonlighting.   The flatbed wagon held about a dozen people and the course went on for 20 minutes. There were plenty of ghouls and demons along the route and they never came out of character. The haunted house was very dark and foreboding, and the choreography was, again, well done. Plenty of screams.   There is a small snack area, but don't come to eat to avoid leaving it on the field.   The guys had a lot of fun and the two hours there went quickly. I probably won't do this again as the world is frightening enough without finding more ways to be scared s**tless!

Decent beer distributor in Richboro, PA.   Plenty of choice. Domestic, European, Mexican and some hard cider. I needed a case for an upcoming Spring Festival (Chinese New Year) dinner. In the absence of Tsingdao or other Asian brew, I opted for Modelo Especial, a very good Mexican lager with strong, yet balanced flavor.   The 24 count case cost $33 and change including tax. No bad, but not as reasonable as at my favorite alcohol warehouse in Jersey. Still, considering time and transportation, it was well worth it.   Happy New Year, Everybody!

It would probably be useful if Yelp separated dining in experiences from those of take out, as the issues are very different.  But, until it does, the combined reviews will continue to skew the results in a negative direction in most circumstances.  So it is for China Aston, a fairly nice small Chinese resto in Aston, Pa., although there is another unique issue that applies only to how this house is managed.    When we walked in the three of us planned to have one person have dinner because she was hungry before a long drive across the state. The other two of us wanted to sit with her and perhaps have an app or soup because we had eaten before meeting up with her nearby.  We discovered a sign on every table that said their was an $8 minimum to dine in, and a $5 min to take out.  That meant to us that we would not be served unless all of us ordered more than we wanted, or got unnecessary take out to keep them happy.  Inquiring of the owner/manager of our circumstances was met with a blank stare and repetition of the House Rules.    We didn't have time to look for another place to eat, and although wooden, we did not want to violate their demands.  So, I ordered some Orange Chicken and Pork Dumplings for Take Away, and one dish of Steamed Veggies and Rice for immediate consumption.  This satisfied the dowager, and we just grinned and bore it.    Turns out the Veggie dish while fresh and presented in a bamboo steamer, was bland and needed augmentation.  No Sesame Oil here, only some form of Chili Sauce.  When I returned home and went after the Chicken and Dumplings, I found very ordinary fare, with a thickish coating on the meat, and goopy mildly hot sauce at the bottom of the container.  The fried Dumplings were adequate, but not really hot enough to appreciate its apex taste and texture.  Everything was just meh.    The final choice of 2 stars comes from the complete absence of customer concern displayed by the house mother.  Rules were rules, and would not be bent or compromised for any reason.  In truth, this restaurant felt more like a school lunch program run by a cold and uncaring matriarch.    Maybe that's why the place was practically empty on a Monday evening.    Regardless, my shadow will not touch its door again.

Hulmeville Inn was a dive bar before the term gained currency in the 21st Century.    It sits at the crossroads of time, at the intersection of a stage depot between Trenton and Philadelphia in the 19th Century, and a cool and courageous crafty beer pour in the present day.    Sometimes it feels like they are shooting an episode of Duck Dynasty at the pool tables with all the beards on display.  Still, even a clean shaven face is welcome in this throwback bar.    The suds are amazing in their diversity from local to international, although the kitchen always seems a step behind in offerings and quality.  It is a fun place to go just to hang out and watch sports, or chalk up the old cue.  The prices can't be beat, and this is one of those places where they can sniff out pretension, so best to just be at your ease.    I don't get down to Hulmeville often, but when I do the Inn by that name is a worthy place to visit.   Walk in. Belly up. Buy a round. Shoot the sh*t.  Rack 'em up.  Break 'em. Set up shots for nightcaps. Head on home.  UPDATE. FEBRUARY 3, 2017   Came in tonight for dinner and beer. Here, we normally order food and drink at the bar, and bring the glass back to the hightops in the barroom to await the cook delivery of the plates. Their brew list comes on sheets of paper and a wall screen. There were at least 40 choices from around the world and as close as Bucks.   For drink we ordered Devils Double, a dark IPA, and Merry Monks. I guess we were feeling a little naughty and monastic at the same time. Both were strong mood setters. For nosh, we opted for a medium Firehouse Burger and their Boardwalk Cheesesteak.  We waited for our grub as the bar filled with Friday nighters. Nice, friendly crowd. Dates, friends, co-workers, fams. Bar Lady knew everyone's name and where they sat.   My burger was a half pound delight on a ciabatta roll, loaded with red onion, romaine and a perfect medium finish. Needed utensils to consume because my mouth just wasn't big enough (I know. Hard to believe.). The Boardwalk steakwich was HUGE, with finely chopped onions, peppers and roasted reds and a layer or American. The roll was great for holding the massive beefy pile and it's drippings, so if you desired less grease you only ate the top of the loaf. But, if you craved full force cardiac compromising taste, you chomped all of it. Freedom of Choice!   Hulmeville Inn has been tapping kegs for patriots for 200 years. You can feel it all around you, like a friendly ghost's embrace.   Hoist a few together.

Housed in the Riverfront Market on old Orange Street, Wilmington, La Taqueria is a food stall serving assembly line Mexican street food a la Qdoba or Chipotle. By the time I arrived around 4, most of the other shops were closed and the rest were cleaning up and getting ready to head home at the 6 PM closing time. In fact, I was the only customer in the house. I had the warehouse to myself.   I ordered their tacos carnitas with pinto beans and brown rice. I watched as the friendly preparer put my snack together, asking me to choose from each of the ingredient options as she moved down the steam table. She ended with the type of finishing sauce I wanted squirted on top. I went with the most spicy chipotle/chili pepper.   The tacos were good, if a bit drippy. The pork was tender and moist, and the overall big bite was tasty and filling. The rice and beans may have been on the steam table all day, so were past their prime - a bit dried out. Still, I was dining alone and had time to look around and appreciate the historic structure surrounding me. More on that in another review.

White Dotte Dairy Bar & Grill is an old school roadside attraction at the intersection of Rts. 38 & 206 in Vincentown, NJ. It produces good soft serve ice cream and an assortment of burgers, cheesesteaks and other  fast food that take your mind off the drive through pancake flat Burlington County.   I stopped by for breakfast earlier this week to find out what they were doing to be in business for 70 years. It is a small custom made railroad car like wooden structure with small counter and a few tables. Clearly their success relies on take out. Yet, I enjoyed my time on one of their stools at the green paisley lunch counter. The menu is All Americana standards. I asked about the french toast, and when the friendly server said she really liked it, I went with it.  I sipped their generic coffee while waiting for it to come off the grill in back.   The walls had pictures of the farmstead and family since inception. Curious about what "Dotte" meant, I asked whether it stood for someone named, "Dotty," or something else. I was surprised to learn that it had nothing to do with a person, but that "White Dotte" was the name of the chicken breed raised there. I googled that and found that the actual breed was Wynedotte,  an American egg layer developed in the 1880's to produce brown eggs. Beautiful bird, too. Very cool.  And, the french toast was very good. The mix had excellent proportions of vanilla, sugar and cinnamon, that completely saturated the three slices of their bread, and caramelized the edges. Surprisingly tasty.   White Dotte turned out to be much more than expected. Historic enterprise from one family. Cozy building. Esoteric name that added to the positive impression. Decent grub that made this a stop well worth repeating.   A chance to learn something unexpected and captivating.

Utsav ("Festival" in Sanscrit) is the latest Indian house at this location on Philmont Avenue near the border between Huntington Valley and Northeast Philadelphia. It serves Kerala style cuisine, and does a particularly good job with vegetarian dishes. The room is bright yellow, matching that shade of curry. We dined alone this Sunday evening, which hopefully is not a sign of their opportunity for success, because we were quite impressed with the quality of the food overall.   We ordered the Calamari Cochin appetizer, Chicken Amwalla, Vegetable Salan and Chili Garlin Naan. Pappadam was offered as a table nosh. Enjoyment scaled from decent for the squid, to excellent for the Veggie Salan, with the Amwalla falling in between. An explanation is required.  The calamari was the weakest link, and not the best way to start our exploration. It was dusted with a grainy flour similar to corn meal, which didn't really work texturally nor flavorably with the crustacean's own qualities. The onion, green pepper and garlic were sauteed in a heavy oil, which actually became the dominate taste. Just not pleasant when the squid should have been allowed to shine. Yet, the chunky, tender Amwalla was very pleasant with its mango mild curry mix. It was an indication of the playful possibilities in the kitchen. Likewise, the veggie salan was a surprising dish based in freshly cracked and poured coconut milk and yogurt sauce. The highlight of our dinner. The chili garlic naan was well baked and very tasty in its own right and as a handy scoop to capture the great sauces.   Service was friendly and informative. Prices reasonable and in a range that encouraged some experimentation.   Utsav takes it place among the very good Indian restaurants in the area. Be festive!

This was my first taste from an El Limon restaurant, and I have to say it was very good from atmosphere through loud post almuerzo belching.   We were the only patrons in the shop when we arrived on Friday afternoon around 2.  There were three women in the store, two sitting at a table in front who quickly stood and took us to a table and distributed menus. The third was in the open kitchen toward the back with a very large ladle stirring something is a mega-gallon pot on the stove.   The room is decorated a la Mexicana, with bright paint everywhere. Otherwise, the tables/chairs were utilitarian.  The two page menu offered lunch and dinner, with a little space for desert. I appreciated that there were sopas and tortas along with the standard burritos and tacos.   The refrigeration unit was full of Mexican sodas and homemade huaracha.  We stuck with water and lime, and ordered torta al pastor and tacos pescados. Somewhat surprising that there were no chips and salsa offered gratis for the table, but required a $4 charge. Never saw that in the many other shops I have dined in around the USA, nor even in the homeland. I guess that works for them.  Anyway, the meals were quite good. The tacos were full of lightly fried tilapia, onion, cilantro slung in hot tortillas.  Three were more than enough with sharing, especially with the accompanying rice and beans. The torta was even more engorged with pit fired strips of pork, tomato, cilantro and their own spicy mayonnaise, on a fresh large soft roll.  Delicioso!   El Limon does a nice balancing act between authentic Mexican fast food and the American palate. They understand their customers are from both worlds.   If they found a way to provide the chips and salsa in the traditional way, rather than to enhance their bottom line, this local chain would make my short list of favorite casas Mexicanas.

While I appreciate the difference between Joe Santucci's rectangular upside down pizza with mozzarella cheese baked under the dark red sauce, and traditional east coast round pies that put the cheese on top, I can't say that after picking it up to bring home that it is significantly better. I did like the somewhat thicker crust and pasty thick tomato sauce, but not more than the quality "Jersey" style pizza from joints like DeLorenzo's in Lower Makefield, or the Burg in Falls, to name a few others.   I guess being suckled on Brooklyn and Trenton slices spoiled me for other conceptions. I just like the thinner crusted, basil flavored, chunky tomato sauced, creations, with the secrets of the dough mixed with softer water that flavors the crust with subtle cracker-like tones and texture.   To my buds, the Trenton Pie is perfection, far superior to the upside down variation Philly is famous for. It's not that I don't enjoy this style once in a while, but given the choice, the ones from Trenton win every time.

Pulaski's Meat Products is a Polish butcher shop located in the Trenton Farmers Market on Spruce Street. It was drawing quite a crowd when we walked over to their high refrigerated display cases. No surprise when the huge selection of sausage was sighted. They had dozens of choices from pork, beef, lamb and combinations stuffed tightly into skins. There were kielbasi of every rank and order, even a cherry wood smoked variety that captured my attention.  Service was prompt, courteous and friendly from the folks in those long white aprons. We opted for a few grillers for the backyard, and one of the smaller cherry woods. Too, the sign said they carried "Homemade Pierogi," so I inquired about them, and was told to go over around the side of the displays to the wall units in the side hall leading to an exit. Found them. Selected the potato/onion stuffed dough. Grabbed two packages. Noticed that they were not homemade, unless they lived in Brooklyn. It all came to about $35.   Just a bit tony for the bad part of the capital city.   We noshed on the kielbasa on the drive home. Both varieties were very well made and had firm outer skin and tender filling. Sure they will be even better grilled or fried. That night we cooked up the Polish dumplings with a mix of fresh sauteed red onion, mushroom and red & yellow pepper as a topper. Very good after the boil/fry preparation, although I would have loved them more had the mashed potato been somewhat less dense. Enjoyed the combo, but it could have been spectacular with more attention to that detail.   The Trenton Farmers Market is still in operation after all these decades, and still attracting enough consumers with quality vendors willing to lend their credibility to make it all work.

Fitzwater Cafe on the South Philadelphia street by the same name appears to be a continental bistro style breakfast/ lunch maison with a creole flavor. In earlier incarnation it looks to have been an auto repair shop. It is a lot more gentrified today, with French, Louis XV paneled ceiling, long bar with mirrored back bar, and beautiful Provencal ceramic tile floor. The space is bright and airy with glass wall southern exposure. It is a beautiful setting for breakfast or brunch.   We stopped in after an early morning of medical attention and on our way down to Washington Avenue for grocery shopping. We ordered their breakfast burrito and morning andouille sausage, 3 egg and swiss Sammy on torpedo roll. Coffee (hot and strong) all around.   Both plates were enough for two meals apiece. The burrito had a great blend of meat, cheese and savory veggies. The Sammy was almost as good, but the hollowed out roll didn't have enough crunchy body to offset the oiliness of the andouille. Really needed a French rather than Italian case.   With everything premium priced to lead to a $30 breakfast with java, it was very good, but not the perfection implied by the cost. Still, Fitzwater Cafe is a winner for this corner of the City.

Solid 3.5 Star breakfast & lunch deli in the Glen Roc Shopping Center on Scotch Road in Ewing, NJ.    Décor is minimalist, with a few tables near the counter and kitchen and a second dining room to the right with ten more tables when the crowd arrives. The joint is clean and the service is friendly and efficient. Ordering is done at the cashier, and one of the staff brings the food to the table. There seems to be a group of regular alder cockers hanging out, but they are amusing and harmless.   My breakfast sausage, egg & cheese sandwich arrived with a small container of orange juice, a nice unexpected touch. The roll was better than average with a fresh firm crust and flakey innards. It was a good sammy with oozing American cheese and fried egg.  I would certainly have it again if nearby in the morning. The coffee was hot and middle of the road in strength.   Price was under $6 for food and beverage; a very attractive price.    If Deli-Licious Café had a bit more character and comfort, it could easily garner the fourth star.

This franchise recently expanded into this part of the world, and I finally found a convenient moment to check it out this week.  It is an attractive Chinese house; clean, organized and designed equally for eat in or takeout.  Yet, not an Asian in sight to speak to authenticity.  The options are set behind glass shielded steam tables, where the workers allow you to select from the number of different dishes offered, and spoon them onto a heavy cardboard plate with a side of white or fried rice.  As everything is prepared beforehand,  unless you arrive soon after wokking, the food cools and congeals to some extent, detracting from its overall taste and enjoyment. I went for orange chicken and Beijing beef with the fried rice.  Both had a good look with different shades of orange and red amber goopy sauce.  The taste of each was distinct, and I believe that if hot, they would have been a satisfying meal.  Unfortunately, that was not the case. Both were barely above room temperature when I sat down, and although I appreciated the flavor and textural potential, the heat issue really drove down my enjoyment.  I don't know how they can fix this problem. I don't like micro-reheats, and question whether they could successfully throw it back in a wok.    So, I give them credit for an interesting idea, and a tidy house, but just don't want past prime hanging around food as part of my diet.

I have a love/hate relationship with TJ Maxx. When I need to pick up a load of dress shirts and private garments they have always been a source for heavily discounted, recognizable brands that were perfect for the daily grind of my law career. With 30 suits in the wardrobe in heavy rotation, I needed that many shirts and twice as many ties to keep myself looking the part of a successful abogado. Why pay department store prices when the same garments were available at 80% off? On the other hand, so much rack space is full of junk and poor quality merchandise, that I hate walking in for anything beyond those few things I find useful.   Covid has changed all that with Zoom conferences and hearings where no one sees the suit beyond the headshot on the screen. Judges are no longer sanctioning lawyers for improper dress, as they leave their robes on the clothing tree in the corner of their chambers (if working from court at all). Professional life has become more casual, although I'd return to the old ways in a second if we could eliminate this virus and be fully safe in public again.   This visit I wasn't there for myself, but for my stepson who had received a promotion and had to upgrade his work garb to suit his position in management. We had purchased suits elsewhere, and now needed to supplement the basics with shirts and ties to complement them. While he was willing to buy everything in one place, I was compelled to teach him where to save money without sacrificing quality. When you can pick up seven name brand dress shirts for under $200 (list price more than twice as much), even he recognized what he could do with the money saved over a lifetime.   So, now he will be the best dressed manager on the casino floor. At 6' 4", he will stand out like a beacon of sartorial splendor. No one will ever know his new found secret to success.   And, I will have passed on a family value, and done my step parenting very well.

This is the same Ploy Siam that was in Robbinsville, NJ for several years. It relocated to reduce overhead from their former large restaurant. Same folks. Same kitchen. Same quality Thai cuisine. Just a much smaller storefront down in Burlington County.   I was there for a late lunch/early dinner last weekend. I recognized the 'mama san' from the original spot, and she confirmed the above information. We chatted briefly before she too my order for Tom Kha Soup and their Crazy Noodles (aka Drunken Noodles). The place is very basic with utilitarian tables and chairs and minimalist decorations. With three rows of tables in a narrow shop there was little room for Buddhas and elephants.   My meal was as good as I remembered. The Tom Kha was a deep bowl filled with veggies and medium spiced lemongrass and coconut milk broth. Delectible! It was hot enough to warm the gullet, but not so hot as to pucker the lips. Among the best of breed in recent memory. The noodles were Thai Spicy and loaded with more greens, onions, sliced chicken and a few shrimp. It did more fire damage than the soup, but by the time I was a quarter into it, I had adjusted to the flames and was having fun. Excellent brown sauce. Chewy broad rice noodles. The only momentary disappointment was the dearth of shrimp I had apparently paid extra for (without proper notice). Somehow a buck per was not what I anticipated. Yet, it was all tasty enough to be in a forgiving mood.   It was the Bhuddhist thing to do.   I was punished for my indulgence. Lesson learned.

Standard CVS drug store and food market in Newtown Borough. To my eyes they all look the same and really have little to offer other than prescription drugs. Everything else is predictable and overpriced.   I am surprised to see that the floor has industrial carpeting throughout, as it is difficult to clean. In a place frequented by sick people such flooring is not optimized for a healthy environment. I prefer hard surfaces that can be swept and washed often. Maybe this carpet is removable, but the question remains, how often?   The answer, not often enough.

Anthony's Pizza Town (& Cantina), has been at the same location on northbound Rt. 130 for a long time, and the passage of time has not been overly kind. The place looks like it did in 1990, with the same wall decorations and the same Anthony in his suave hat tossing dough and making conversation.  If you love Elvis and think he and Marilyn are the apex of American culture, this is your place.   The world may have changed, but the Anthony's pizza remains the same.  It is still crisp, with mildly sweet sauce, and a hint of garlic.  It is no longer at the top of the pizza food chain given the evolution of tomato pie over the decades, but it is still a solid and tasty option.  It just isn't the first place you think of when considering where to get your pizza fix.  In this part of the universe, Palermo's has that weighty distinction.    Pizza Town is now a Cash Only operation, although my memory tells me that this was not always the case.  It remains a place where you can have a beer with your pie, or even a brew without the slices.    The sign out front claims this is also a "cantina."  I didn't examine the menu closely, but offering a Mexi/Guat/Hondoran alternative along with the pizza, is a darn good idea!  It's already being done well by Castillo's on Clinton Avenue in C'Burg.

If you love simple and delicious Polish food, Pierogi Factory is singing your song.    This tiny four table restaurant is in the Shops at Red Lion on Bustleton Avenue, Northeast Philly.  The menu focuses on the staples: Pierogies, Stuffed Cabbage, Potato Pancakes, Kielbasa and a few other goodies.  Service is casual and sincere.    We ordered their Combo Dinners in order to sample as many of their dishes as possible.  Combo # 1 had two potato pancakes, 3 pierogis of choice (traditional potato and farmer's cheese), and 1 Golabki (stuffed cabbage), with a little container of sour cream ($9.95).  Every element was excellently prepared with taste as good as my grandmother used to make.  The other combo swapped out the potato pancakes for a nice length of smoked (grilled) kielbasa ($10.95).  Also, fantastic.    I was full, but not stuffed, when we finished eating.  We shared a piece of apple cake ($3.00).  It was not as good as granny's, as it lacked the moisture, density and large apple slices she used to fatten up her grandchildren.    Still, a very pleasant surprise on Bustleton. Will definitely visit here again.

Friends B & G is one of the better places to hang out if beer, sports and decent (not great) food are your priorities. When we arrived Friday around 9, the place was packed, but the good people at the bar were more than willing to move down and make room for us.  Love that kind of courtesy.  We had drinks and eventually a booth cleared and we were able to sit around and have a couple of apps that were ample for the 8 of us.  The Nachos Supreme were what you would expect - piled high with chips, cheese, chopped onions and peppers; and the Hot Wings pretty good when considering there were about 20 of them.  Good prices, too.  Our group often meets there after big events (like elections), and we always find space to celebrate.  We are hoping for a good reason to party next Tuesday night.    You are all invited.  See you there.

Same great big fat donuts as the other Yum Yum shops around.  Same good coffee.  Same very reasonable prices.  Same friendly service and pride in the baker's craft.   This one lacks a public restroom, meaning if that is one of the reasons for your stop here, you should consider visiting the Wawa Service Station across the street before you go.   Easier to indulge that way!

Bagelissimo is an Italian deli of a bagel shop, showing that cross cultural alternatives can work well. The shop in a fairly new strip center on Rt. 206 North, has a decent layout for eating in or taking out.
