They offer a fair variety of bagels, muffins and sandwiches, although the rounders are a bit denser than I prefer.   My onion bagel, butter and swiss had good flavor, plenty of dry onion flakes, and a lot of chewability. A few air pockets here and there would have brought it completely home for me.   Service was prompt and friendly. Prices about the best I have encountered recently. My sammy went for $2. I am sure the manager saw my double take. I dropped a buck in the tip basket out of appreciation for my wallet.

REHEATED SLICE COVID TAKEOUT REVIEW:  The constant problem with ordering pizza by the slice is that they require sufficient reheating in the oven to resuscitate it into edible condition. If not requested to be "well done," they are only partially revived, while the rest tastes dead or just lacking in energy.   The same is true here. Without knowing how long it had been sitting on the cooling rack, nor the heat of the oven, the time spent could have been enough to scorch the undercarriage and bubble up the cheese, but it didn't quite make it all the way back to life. As a result it was a mediocre slice. Decent crust, almost right sauce needing more basil, and thick cheese deposit in the center that wasn't quite the volcanic lava desired.   Not bad for noshing in the car on the way back to Bucks, but not the Jersey Strong hoped for.   Oh, and the shop really needs a deep cleaning. Where's the TLC?

TAKEOUT REVIEW  Can't speak to the cuisine served in the spacious but dark dining rooms, but the takeout seems like a separate operation going out the back door of Cena Ristorante in Bensalem, PA.   When I entered the front door, a server informed me that I should walk through the restaurant to the rear entrance to the patio, turn right, and go into the other door which was propped open. Once there I saw a counter with kitchen equipment behind it, and a couple dudes aproned up for food service. My personal sized pizza and cheese steak hoagie were already boxed and ready to head out the door.   Maybe using this Slice app would be acceptable. At least the food was ready as advertised.   Upon opening at the kitchen table, I beheld a 12" pie with heavy cheese, and lighter puddles of red sauce, mozza droppings and a scattering of green basil leaf. Looked sort of like a child's drawing of a clown face. The cheese steak hoagie was more handsome, with goodly amount of thin grilled beef mixed with cheese (provolone?), topped with lettuce, tomato and red onion. Liked it.  Taste was uneven. The pizza had too much cheese and not enough of anything else. Even still warm it was out of balance, with the crust its strongest attribute. The sandwich was good and hung together well in the torpedo.   Won't be rushing back for takeout, but the broader menu for in house dining might be worth a try aside from the tomato pie.

Nifty Fifty's is an authentic throwback burger and shake joint that epitomizes the Philly scene in the middle of the last century.  Loud, garish, neon-blitzed lighting, the whole 9.  It is diner-like with booths and counter service, and dedicated to the proposition that a great greasy burger, fries and sweet creamy shake are timeless icons that people never tire of.    They are quite right!  Our visit last Saturday night was met with a 30 minute queue for a booth.  The line moved along fast enough to hold our interest, and the aroma of hot grease was so overwhelming that we could not have walked out if we wanted to.  It is instantly addictive.  My companion for the evening was a new arrival to America, and this was her first exposure to old fashioned burger mania.    We were escorted to our table/booth and handed their bible (menu).  Rather than attempt to explain what this cultural event was all about, I just ordered the ever-popular Bacon Cheeseburger for her, and the Double Cheeseburger with Fried Onions & Mayo for me, along with a basket of traditional fries and a Black Raspberry Shake to share.    When everything arrived on the arms of our incredible server Destiny, I watched as my companions eyes widened as she took her first bite, munch and sip.  They said it all.  She was excited, happy and totally into the experience.  I was a half step behind her as I doctored my burger and the fries with ketchup.  The shake was creamy and cold in its aluminum mixing vessel.  It so nicely offset the crunchy saltiness of the ample fries, and the deeply satisfying juicy chewiness of the burger.    Nifty has perfected the formula for grease to such an extent that you crave it despite knowing it is not so good for you.  The soft bun absorbs much of what is not directly ingested, yet no thought is given to leaving it on the plate.  The fries have a similar subtle attribute that makes them very tasty, especially when there are small nubs in the bottom of the basket.  Love those babies.    Five Guys approaches Nifty's burgers for taste and texture, but lacks the overall ambiance of this iconic burger emporium.    I know there are other good things on the menu, but I have never made it passed the sliders.

If you know New York cheesecake, then you've already heard of Junior's.  Their restaurant in Times Square is a "must eat" destination when visiting the Big Apple.  Why?  Because since the passing of the dearly departed Ratner's in Manhattan, Junior's is left to carry the cheesecake torch.  It is super rich, creamy, sweet, and succulent.  It comes in a variety of flavors and sizes.  The wait for a table in any of their locations is legendary.    But, now, there is no wait at all if you come to their factory and outlet store in Burlington, NJ.  You can walk around and see what they have available, and walk out with a stack of sweet heaven.  The prices start at only $2 for a 6 inch plain cake.  That is sinfully glorious, because money ceases to be an object in the decision to buy.  There is no splurge at that price.    Nothing this good comes without a small reservation.  It is irrelevant to many, but the cakes in the outlet are slightly "irregular."  Some are lopsided; others have settlement cracks; a few have uneven swirls of strawberry or raspberry mixed in.  All these are rejected by quality control for the New York sites, but as a result, you can have a full cake here for less than the price of a single slice in the City.    True. Self control becomes an issue when something this decadent is available in large quantities, variations, and at impossibly cheap prices.  The addicts were lined up outside the door waiting for it to open.  They all made a beeline to the free samples and stuffed face until all the small paper cups were gone.  While they were buzzing there, I found the Raspberry Swirl 8 incher I was looking for, and made for the cashier.  That baby went for $11, and will feed my family for more than a week on rations.  The anticipation of that first smooth creamy bite sends shivers up my spine.   Who's the addict?

Francisco's Pizzeria is having a soft opening this week, and by the looks of things they know how to launch. They took over the former Cosi on Pheasant Run in the Newtown Business Commons, and have done a nice makeover with exposed brick wall, partially dropped ceiling for lighting and HVAC, and new pizza ovens in the open kitchen. The place looks good and the dining area is comfortable. The staff looks polished in their black T's.   We stopped in for a late lunch on Friday after finishing a list of chores. The menu offered most of the usual suspects found in Italo-American houses, with everything from salads to pizza to calzones to full dinner. We tried their buffalo chicken cheesesteak, fried chicken wrap and eggplant parmesan sandwich. All were good, although the steak Sammy and eggplant scored higher than the wrap. The torpedo rolls had good texture and taste, especially after being toasted in the oven to finish the job.   This is the closest restaurant to home, so it will get a strong workout from us, particularly if their pizza is top of the chart. Who knows? Perhaps my son who currently works at another Italian joint in town, will look into getting a job just 5 minutes away.

This Donkey Donuts is in the parking lot of Fieldcrest Center, Columbus, NJ. It has the latest style with smallish indoor sitting area and wrap around drive thru for those who don't have a moment to spare to get out of their cars and walk inside.   The coffee is pretty much standard DD, and the sweet dough fry what you expect from this outfit. Of course, the Christmas donuts are a pleasant diversion.   No problem with service, although I forgot that it was on me to pull out napkins and stuff them in the bag. Had some in the car anyway.  Maybe I've been spoiled by all the cafe/coffee house alternatives around these days, but I am finding the Donkey brew to be somewhat pedestrian. They really need to kick it up a notch if they want to succeed in the java wars.

Is it possible to be a fan or Wahoo for a shoe repair shop?   Existential inquiry, but one worth considering as long as your soul and sole relate well with each other. Mine always have.  The longer I walk, the deeper within I delve. Same for you?  Then, be sure to treat your feet well through well crafted footwear maintenance.   Newtown Shoe Repair sits in the middle of downtown Newtown Borough, in an undersized storefront shop, with walk up steps to the wood and glass doors.  Careful, if you open the door without the magic words, you are stepping into a time machine than has only one destination date - 1955.   The old machines, the smell of leather and wax, the shelves full of shoes and boots... Worth a visit, but of course the business owners would love you to take off your shoes and let them put on new heals and a shine.   It is a bit expensive for basic service - now $25. for almost any repair. So, as the other reviewer suggests, drop off your shoes and walk around Newtown for a great afternoon.  But, you might want to bring an extra pair of shoes...

Michael's is a roadside diner on Street Road, Bensalem, PA. It has a counter with spinner seats and a fairly large dining room. It serves three squares a day with professional servers who have been there for decades.   I stopped by for breakfast this week and took a stool facing the dessert cooler and ordered coffee with a Country Omelet, hash browns and rye toast. The java was industrial strength, as desired. The three egger was okay with an overload of green pepper along with onion and diced potatoes. The hash browns were a bit of overkill given their cousins in the eggs, and would have tasted better if they replaced the spuds inside the shell, as they had far more flavor and texture than those puny chunks used as filler. Overall, the opus was a tad dry, detracting from what might have been a contender had it been moister and had better balanced ingredients.   Liked the rye toast.   Service was fine. Access into the building was ADA compliant with ramp and wide front door. Didn't check the bathrooms.   Michael's was decent, but nothing to distinguish it from the other culinary attractions along this stretch of Street Road.

Perhaps it was just this particular Perkins, but it does seem that this franchise is a poor man's version of the ubiquitous IHOP. It was hard not to notice an immediate disappointment moving from the beautiful menu photos to the presentation on our plates. From proud to defeated, boisterously sensational to meekly fallen, the reality fell far from the mark.   Not that the french toast platter and quesadillas were without taste, but that they were not nearly as grand as advertised. The brioche thick slices absorbed the egg/sugar/vanilla mix, but not quite enough to overcome its dry core. The crisp bacon was not so, and the deflated quesadillas were so thinly filled as to believe the promised steak was little more than tender shoe leather.   True, the hall was crowded, the prices quite reasonable and the coffee topped off in a thermos pitcher on the table. Kenny's service was friendly, clever and accommodating, but could not overcome the the tools he was working with.   Perkins appeared to be an anchor of this Grant Avenue neighborhood in Northeast Philly. It should do something to assure that it does not contribute further to its distress.

Man!   You guys are so harsh on poor little DD here in Holland.  The three of you only gave it 1 Star apiece.    The coffee is standard for DD; no better, no worse.  The staff does seem disorganized and a bit comical how they step over each other and can't remember your order.   The donuts are never really good at any Dunkin, so nothing new there.    Yeah, I've had way better than everything on the board here. But, is it as bad as finding a mouse in your donut?  (Thus, the "Eek!")   I think not.

Authentic Polish/East European smoked meat emporium situated in the Trenton Farmers Market, with the touch and feel of butcher/deli of my childhood. The center of attention is the Kielbasi collection where you can order any combination of long red sausage you desire for slicing, grilling or mixing in a casserole. Also do their own stuffed cabbage quite well.   Not impressed with the pierogi which are no longer homemade, but trucked down from Brooklyn, and are thick skinned with too dry potato mash.   And, as with most of the outfits here, the prices are premium leaving little to the imagination. Definitely paying for the privilege of participating in a cultural event.

DiCarlo does itself a disservice by letting itself be called only a pizza joint. The "restaurant" is really the more important piece of the action at this small Italian kitchen in the Mallard Creek Shopping Center, Richboro. There is an extensive menu with some interesting dishes that cry for attention.   Very glad we went that way, rather than limiting ourselves to a couple of pies as suggested by the restricted name.   We ordered Chicken Francaise with Linguini, Veal Bruschetta with Broccoli, Carlos Junior with Linguini and a Chicken Parmigiana Sandwich. They were all huge portions, well designed and surprisingly tasty. The francaise was three large breast medallions in a decent butter, lemon, white wine sauce. It could have been more tender and penne would have worked better than the messy linguini. Still it was good, if not best of breed.  On the other hand, the veal was lightly breaded and pan fried before being topped with fresh chopped tomato bruschetta. It was delicious even if the broccoli had long tough stalks. The Junior was basically an Italian Sausage and Penne dish with a garlicky sauce. Good, but its name was the most creative part. Finally, the Chicken Parm sandwich was immense and very good.   Each dish was enough for at least two meals, so in combination with the reasonable prices, made for an economical family feast to celebrate surviving another week of Covid.   Because of the lack of attention to detail on a few of our choices, the actual score is 3.5 Stars, rounded up. Refine the francaise sauce a bit, pare down the broccoli to remove more tough stalk, use real Italian loaf for garlic bread, offer choice of pasta on phone orders; and this simple house could approach a five star takeout experience.

Gabby's Banh Mi is a Vietnamese sandwich shop on Main Street, Ambler, PA. It is on the first floor of an older building, giving it a subdued, dated, yet peaceful quality. It is run by a young family with infant in tow, which helps set the tone.   Their main offerings are the demi baguette sandwich with choice of protein and fixings, and pho with choice of meat in large bowl. I knew I couldn't consume both in one visit, so I opted for the Banh Mi with roast pork and all the accoutrement. A home brewed peach ice tea came along to assist with wash down.   The bread is the most important part of any sandwich, and this was no different. It was fresh, soft, mildly crusty, with sourdough flavor. I squirted extra hoisin into its matrix to enhance the sweet BBQ nature of the pork, and to complement the daikon, spicy mayo and cilantro. It was very good, leaving tiny crumbs behind on the table with each bite. The tea was likewise peachy keen, but could have been bigger than a 6 ounce glass for the price ($4.50).  In fact the nine bucks for the sammy seemed trop cher as well. I guess commercial rents in Ambler are on the way up. But, as South Philly is closer to me than Ambler, except when I have business in Norristown, I will most often continue to take such pleasures in the city when the mood strikes.   Otherwise, the bowl of ribeye pho on the next table looked damned inviting.

We waltzed into the Blue Danube just before 7 on a Saturday night during Christmas Week, and were immediately seated without rez at a very cozy table for two along a back wall that felt very private.  The layout of the restaurant reminds of many other old Chambersburg establishments that set up a kitchen in an old row house. While not in that part of Trenton, it is close enough to offer the same sensation. It was do doubt done in the 60's or 70's, and has all the charm you would expect from a deeply urban environment at a time when Trenton was still an All American City.  Sadly, those days are history.   The staff is friendly and helpful, and quickly understood that we were first-timers who needed a brief guided tour through the menu. Although my grandparents came from this part of the Old World, our being kosher kept us from sampling most of the better offerings from a Budapest or Viennese kitchen.  We ordered the Danube Sampler, consisting a Pierogies, Stuffed Cabbage, Sausage, and curly Noodles, all in their appropriate sauces.  As an appetizer it was a good introduction to several tastes we would not otherwise reach in one meal.  The star of the plate was the Stuffed Cabbage; tender cabbage and soft ground beef and pork mix with rice, with a mild sweetness that was most enjoyable.  The Pierogies were also soft with a potato/cheese filling and nice Sautéed Onion topping.  The special sausage was a very small piece, but that was just as well as the flavor was a bit odd to my tongue and would take some getting used to.    Our entrée was a shared Pork Schnitzel and Brown Sauce with a side of the same noodles.  It was quite good, but not particularly unique in any way.  The Brown Sauce was ladled on a bit heavy, perhaps diluting the taste of the breading and pork.   There was some confusion about our order, but our server handled it well, and we ended up with a free glass of wine to make up for it.  That was reasonable.    Bottom Line - We really enjoyed the atmosphere of Blue Danube, and the wait staff.  The food was good, but not great.  The standout was the Stuffed Cabbage, with the Pierogies a close second.  I would not rush back to try more things on the menu, but if someone suggested a good East European dinner, I would not hesitate to recommend a return visit.

Paying the check from breakfast on the way out, the owner/cashier ask why we were putting such a small tip on the credit card payment. After a second's hesitation born out of the discomfort of having to express criticism directly, I had to explain that the service we received at the counter from the server assigned to us was very bad. He wanted to know what I meant.  First, I mentioned that the guy sitting next to me was never served his meal and just walked out in hungry frustration. Then, I started on our experience. The milk I requested for my coffee took 20 minutes and a reminder to our waitress after she reappeared from her absence from the floor. Ten more minutes before our Greek Omelets arrived and a few more until she brought me silverware so I could eat. Beyond that, I was never offered a coffee refill, and she got the toast order wrong and had to return to the kitchen to redo it.   Although pleasant enough, she seemed not to see what was/was not in front of her, and unable to anticipate the sequence of providing and consuming a meal. For example, her response to our counter mate leaving in disgust was that she thought another server had given him his order and that he had eaten it. Yet, it never occurred to her that although she had taken his order, but not brought it out, that asking him about it would be the courteous thing to do; neither did she ever walk by him and realize that there was never any food in front of him - not even when she finally refilled his coffee.  Really inexplicable, and inexcusable.   It's not that the breakfast was bad. It was actually quite good, but the neglectfulness of this woman had gotten to us so much that we ate feeling miffed. It put a damper on our enjoyment, too, as we watched her continue with this behavior with other customers. By the time we were finished and ready to go we were again confronted by her being AWOL. When she appeared again several minutes later we asked for the check and a container for leftovers. She returned with the former, but forgot the later. We asked another server for that and she reached under the counter right in front of us and handed it over.   Maybe she was just having a bad day, but she certainly rained on our parade and made breakfast an ordeal. But, at least we ate, which is more than my neighbor could appreciate.   The owner seemed stunned by the story, and said he would straighten it out. Didn't offer us anything as compensation for our inconvenience, which would have been a good move, but at least he listened and believed.

Richboro Coffee is a new java house in the Mallard Creek Shopping Center in Richboro, Pa. It is on the small side with about a half dozen tables.  The front of the room has a shiny copper roaster where all their Ethiopian, Kenyan and Costa Rican beans are prepared for brewing or sale.   I sat down for a cup of their Ethiopian Sidamo, a muscular strong coffee that is great both straight up and with a little milk.  It is definitely a wake up call to the senses. The alternatives this day were a Kenya AA milder bean, or a Costa Rican decaf.  They can also be blended if desired.   Service was friendly and informative.  Josh, the owner's son, worked the new digital register for my credit card purchase and seemed proud to be part of this enterprise.  Michelle, poured the Joe into a glass cup with room for milk, and offered to bring it to the table for me. Not handicapped, I did that myself, but appreciated the gesture. First sip alerted my tongue that a strong brew was on the way. By the time I was ready to depart, the caffeine had reached the brain, and I felt the welcome surge of focus and energy that only the freshest darker roast can provide.   Exactly what I needed.   Prices are reasonable for a custom roast/brew operation, at $2.25 for a regular cup; slightly more for extra volume. There were a few folks working at the tables while I was there, thus no shortage of seats for those who wanted to sit and sip at this time of day.   Richboro Coffee joins other recently opened coffee houses in the area.  The coffee competes quite well with that from Newtown's Coffee Room and Yardley's Pretty Bird Café.  Each contributes in their own way to the upgrade of caffeine alternatives in the region, with Richboro seemingly with the best coffee, Newtown with the most comfort, and Yardley with the most variety on the menu. Fond of all of them.  Refills are a buck.

With a sign under the peak of the roof reading, "Circa 1734," you get the feeling that the Newportville Inn is pretty old. Approaching it as it sits on Lower Road running along Neshaminy Creek, it is easy to imagine it looked more or less the same 250 years ago when it was a pre-Revolutionary War weigh station between Philadelphia and Trenton. Historic lore mentions the likes of George Washington, John Adams, Alexander Hamilton and even Thomas Jefferson in the vicinity as they sought safe places to meet to plot the course of independence while the British Army occupied New York and threatened Philadelphia. This historic structure was there to offer room and board to the wayward revolutionists.   Aside from newer additions and the outdoor beer garden, the building is basically unchanged since back in the day. Sitting at the old bar in a small chamber with low beamed ceilings and deep well windows, time can seem to stand still. Yes, it could stand some renovation and deep cleaning, but not at the expense of lost charm and legendary significance. I enjoy such time warps on occasion.   Besides, the German menu and beer choices are hard to duplicate in the area. My Wartmeister Pilsner was cold, smooth and refreshing. The footlong wiener house special with potato salad and sauerkraut, a delectable authentic meal. Dining at the bar with Johnny Bartender working his magic, and the 76ers on the tube, was a very satisfying interlude. The hot potato salad was great, and the sliced apple in the sauerkraut a terrific idea, adding a touch of sweetness to the briney sourness.   While not a lover of all German cuisine, wurst and schnitzel I like, and Newportville specializes in them. Given how friendly everyone was to this stranger, I can see returning as the mood for a brat or breaded/fried chicken or pork schnitzel moves me.

Flip -N- Shakes is a 1960's-esque burger joint on 2nd Street Pike, Southampton, PA. It is a large room with tile floor and utilitarian furniture. Built for speed, not comfort. I was the sole customer when I walked in last weekend on a Saturday afternoon. I was mildly surprised by the lack of activity, but the staff was friendly, and answered by rookie questions with a smile.   I opted for the Chop House Burger (horseradish, darkly sautéed shrooms, steak sauce, dijon mustard, provolone and onion frizzle on a standard bun), and an apple pie shake. I asked for medium, but then I read that all burgers were served medium-well. At $6.59, the price was a little high for the product presented. Quarter pounder without fresh taste, and a ton of spicy additions that were enjoyable (love horseradish on my sliders), but somewhat contradictory on the tongue. The interplay with the steak sauce and dijon was not harmonic with the radish, and appeared to have been absorbed by the mushrooms so that the original earthiness from the cellar dwellers was lost. Not a bad sandwich, but I wasn't in love with it.   I had visions of a real slice of apple pie being placed in a blender with ice cream and milk to create the shake. Not exactly. There were a few small apple slices, and the cinnamon nutmeg flavor, but no crusty bits. The flavor was strong and sweet fun, but would have been completely off the hook with an actual slice of pie. It was comparable to a Shake Shack freeze at a better price, so no real demerits for the shortcut.   The Five Guys nearby makes a better burger (with double meat), while the shake was very good here. Flip City sound track is mostly classic rock, so the atmosphere is fine. These guys have some tough competition in the burger wars. I wish them well in finding the sweet spot that will distinguish themselves from the surrounding hordes.

Tony's Place Bar & Grill sits on Greeley Avenue, Ivyland, PA, across the street from the terminus of the New Hope & Ivyland Railroad.  It has an interesting history coming out of Philadelphia in the last century to set up shop in the wilds of Bucks County. The place is very attractive from the outside, with lots of slate and stone, and outdoor canvas covered patio to one side, and large bar/dining area within. Lots of HDTVs to establish its bona fides as a sports bar.   On a early Sunday evening in December it was about half full when I arrived around, but the crowd grew as it neared kickoff for the Eagles-Seahawks game.  This is definitely a good place to take in games with friends and family as the beer options are pretty good, and the kitchen cooks up a lot of comfort foods. Although high end steaks are also on the menu, I did not see any brought out. My pumpkin cider tasted like autumn and had a nice kick.    I was impressed with their Tomato Pie. Very thin cracker-like crust, mozza cheese under a nicely balanced sauce.  Similar to the pies found in New Jersey, and not the "upside down" thing that often is called TP, but is nothing like the real McCoy. So, congrats on getting it right.   Service was okay, but there were long stretches of time when no one stopped by to see how we were doing. Long wait for the check, too. The customers seemed to be mostly locals who were there for the games and party time, or to pick up a few pizzas to take home.

Kabobeesh is a Pakistani semi-fast casual house that serves very good South Asian cuisine on a budget. The atmosphere is utlilitarian, the service minimal, but the food excellent.   Following the sage guidance of Yelp friend Vinny B., we ordered the Resham Chicken Kabob, Lahori Chargha and the Chickpeas.  They were prepared in the kitchen and brought to us about 20 minutes later on styro plates, with a huge basket of naan.  All were very good to excellent.  The Resham was the ground chicken variety, heavily spiced and grilled over open file kabob-style. It came as a dinner, on a bed of basmati rice, small salad, and the order of chickpeas in a deep brown sauce.  The flavor was rich and rewarding. Wrapped in a torn piece of naan, or eaten straight up, it was a treat.  The chickpeas were likewise tender and richly tasteful as they mixed with the chicken in an adventurous combination.  The rice was pleasantly aromatic, although the salad was lost in the party of other dominant tastes.    The Chargha is a Pakistani version of roast chicken, well dosed in wonderful spices and in the oven long enough for the meat to easily pull off the bone. The strong flavor was unusual and captivating, requiring two hands to work the cut up parts to access all the chicken between the bones.  Luckily, we found the napkin stash and grabbed a few extras to keep the mess under control.  Really loved this dish.   The weakness of the experience was the general take out orientation of the business despite the many eat-in customers.  Styro plates and cups, plastic forks and knives, made for a less than fully enjoyable experience.  From both environmental, and personal comfort perspectives, the dinner could have been a complete home run with the availability of reusable dishes and flatware.  It might cost a little more, but respect for the planet and customers, would turn Kabobeesh into a full throated five-star evening.    It is still a very good place to go to get your Paki on.

This ten booth diner sits in the middle of a small commercial strip on Bethlehem Pike, Hatfield, PA. The bench I chose was lumpy and uncomfortable, but I found the high ground on the naugahyde, reviewed the substantial menu as I sipped their large mug of coffee. I went with the french toast, although my server had recommended the overburdened "He Man Special." Far too much for me, although I appreciated the sentiment. The long list of omelettes was likewise tempting, but my semisweet tooth got the better of me.   When the platter arrived ten minutes later, I beheld three thick slices of bread, yellow from the egg batter, and somewhat browned from its grill time. Unfortunately, as with many renditions of FT that use thicker breads, the egg/sugar/vanilla mix had not penetrated beyond the surface, leaving the center bland white and uninvolved in the frying. There was little caramelization to produce crisp edges, likely because the grill was not hot enough under the bread. This, along with table syrup lacking any flavor but sugary sweetness, made for a competent, but uninspired breakfast.   The free blueberry muffin presented upon payment was a very nice touch, that helped redeem the mediocrity of the morning meal.

Spice Rack on Knights Road, Bensalem, PA, is in a strip shopping center I had never visited before, called Bensalem Square. It is a small house with about a dozen tables, and courteous, efficient service and a rapid response kitchen.   Our order of a chaat appetizer (Sev Puri), spinach soup (Palak), chilli chicken and cheese curry (Mughlai Sahi Paneer), with garlic naan, arrived on time and as ordered.  Each had its strength and weaknesses, but overall was a good meal. The chaat was their take on traditional Indian street snacks, with a crisp cracker base, ground veggies and spiced crispies on top. Very good and fun to eat. The spinach soup was sort of a flat dark green broth with interesting flavor, but little body. I bit of cream would likely have really brought it to life. The chilli chicken (dry) was okay, but although said to be dry, was still fairly moist in a heavy goopy sauce. I have had this in several other Indo/Chinese fusion joints, where the chicken had a drier coated finish and a better texture/flavor profile. The paneer dish was rich and flavorful, and was the star of the show. We asked for it moderately spicy, and thought it hit the mark. Finally, the garlic naan was very good. Thinner and crisper than most I had eaten before. The mango lassi was a thick smoothie with crumbled cashews on top. A tad expensive, but a delicious suck.   Spice Rack is pretty far out of my way, so it is unlikely I will return. There are many better and more consistent Indian kitchens in and around Bucks County, so unless your in the hood, there are plenty of other choices.   Hidden? Yes.  Gem? Not really.

There he was. The famous Steve Stein came out from behind the long refrigerated display counter to greet me and apologize for having his staff request my photo ID and vaccination card before allowing me to enter the dining room to have breakfast.   I didn't mind. This was a new legal requirement for entry enforced by the City of Philadelphia by a fine of $2,000. Actually, I had no issue with the public safety needed to protect from Omicrom, but also saw how it could become rather draconian, while also damaging businesses forced to have customers move through a checkpoint in order to be served. It reminded me of military checkpoints I had to endure while traveling in the Middle East, but without guns and uniforms (at least for now?). Still, far from a pleasant prospect, and one I hoped wouldn't be necessary for long.   The facility is a classic Kosher style Jewish deli/restaurant, with 75% dedicated to smoked meat, fish, and a large variety of salads, knishes, bakery and many premade meals. There was also a large green grocery with beautiful veggies stacked high.   I ordered the Fried Matzo with extra Sautéed Onions mixed in. It arrived at my table the size of a large dinner plate. While not as crisp as my mother cooked in smaller patties, it was hot, steaming and delicious. A good shake of black pepper upped the spice level to where I liked it, along with the enhanced onion flavor requested at a $.50 up charge. I would certainly get that again.   I also brought home a few Onion Bagels (semi-dense and excellent when toasted), and a couple of Potato Knishes for later consumption. They were traditional and very similar to my childhood memories - light wrap that baked well and held their contents to the end. Loved them.   Not sure how often I'll go out to eat with these Covid regulations in place. They make the risk of exposure impossible to ignore.   We are, indeed, living in difficult and memorable times.  PS. The complimentary slice of Apple Cake was very good and greatly appreciated.

Housed in a former convenience store, Piazza's Bakery does all its work in their large workspace and ovens in the back room. A large tray of yeast glazed pretzel twist donuts was coming out, and I immediately pointed to it, saying, "I want some of those!"   Great choice, because they were terrific - light, airy, mildly yeasty and, oh, so, perfectly glazed. Very reminiscent of Crispy Kremes classics, but bigger. The brownies were just as impressive with a layer of chocolate icing above dense chewy choco base. Their croissants were also good, but not as flaky as a French boulangerie would create.   Their were plenty of cookies, fruit pies and customized celebratory cakes that looked great, but were beyond the limits of my sweet tooth. Didn't see much in the way of bread or rolls while there, but that could have been a question of timing.  Piazza's is worth another visit.

This Dairy Delite on Rt. 13 in Levittown is the twin of the ice cream stand on Woodbourne Road by the same name.    It is housed in a mid-twentieth century style all glass summer enhancing structure that is iconic for those of us who remember going to such places as children.  As was the custom then, it is staffed by lovely high schoolers who bring their innocence and enthusiasm to the job of ice cream dispensers.    When I got on the short line I saw the handmade sign for "Soft Peanut Butter," and allowed myself to be swayed by that suggestion.  No complaints, as the large cup of the dense, sweet, creamy, almost custard-like, soft serve was delicious to the last melted drop.   Under $4. for all that pleasure.  Maybe it still is 1970 at Dairy Delite!

Quite busy in the middle of Sunday, this Golden Dawn Diner in Burlington, NJ, is an institution in this part of South Central Jersey. It has been slinging hash for more than 50 years, specializing in breakfast, brunch and lunch, but with plenty of choices for dinner, too. Prices have gone higher with inflation pressure, but it is still on the lower end of cost as everything rises under the same economic realities.   I was there for a morning meal, and quickly ordered their Veggie Lover's Omelette, Hash Browns, Rye Toast and Coffee. The three egger was loaded with onion, green pepper, broccoli, snow pea, mushroom and tomato, with my ask for added feta cheese accepted with a smile from my amazingly attentive server. It was very good, with more variety of ingredients than usual. The potatoes were also a large score, with enough crisply browned surfaces to make me happy. The rye was buttered, yet remained crunchified to the end. The Java was was institutional Bunnomatic, but refilled so often I almost felt compelled to drink more just to keep my server feeling appreciated. She was very good, dropping off fresh napkins with each visit and making sure the requested glass of milk for the coffee was also replenished.   To my knowledge, there are three Golden Dawns in this region; in Hamilton, NJ and Levittown, PA, as well as this one. They are all good, and this may be the oldest in the clan, while Hamilton, the newest. Can't go wrong with any of them, especially if you enjoy diner desserts, which are baked in house, large portioned and generally delicious and inevitably fattening.

COVID-19 TAKEOUT REVIEW -  It was Saturday night and time for a break from extreme social distancing and constant home cooking.  We opted to go Italian with a family sized order from La Villa Pizza & Family Restaurant, Morrisville, PA. Housed in a former Pizza Hut in the parking lot of a small strip center, they are now open until 9 every night to care for the community. Although about 10 miles from home, their reputation for delicious tomato pie made the drive worthwhile.   It was eerie with the roads bereft of cars and seeing the occasional driver wearing a mask, but this is the way it is in the Days of Coronavirus.   We ordered in advance their Tradizionale Tomato Pie (dollops of chunky tomato sauce over mozza with plenty of Sweet Sausage), Chicken Parm, Sausage Pepper and Onion Sandwiches, and Steak Stromboli (basically a folded pizza loaded with Cheesesteak, Mozza and Red Sauce). I put on my newly designed and home constructed mask (formerly an old shirt), feeling vaguely like a bandito about to holdup the stagecoach, and went inside. My order was ready, so I completed the transaction with a credit card and plastic glove I carry around in my car for such purposes.   I always remind myself that carryout is almost never as good as eating at the source. This was so for this meal. While the tomato pie was still very good, it was no longer hot and needed more time in our oven to revive. Once reheated, it was fine. Same can't be said for the sammies, nor stromboli. There was far too much globby cheese atop the chicken parmigiana, and too little red sauce. The sausage was a motherload, but what happened to the pepper and onion? Sparse is the first word that comes to mind. And, the stomboli was huge, but again was mostly goo clumps of Mozza completely out of proportion to the meat component. We tossed out half the cheese just to make it edible.   This morning we got creative. We put the other half of the sausage sandwich sans bread into a frying wok, added fresh sliced red onion, green pepper and garlic and three eggs, to create a great hobo egg dish. It was far better than the dinner the night before.   Moral of this story: Stick to the tomato pie and disregard the rest.

FD Subs has been at this location in Ewing Plaza Shopping Strip for a few decades with different owners and levels of satisfaction. When I stopped in this week for late lunch of a turkey/swiss sub, the wall menu looked like it had been hung in the last century. Still, it was extensive and provided succor for the famished. It wasn't open for in house dining yet, but the husband wife team were well versed in their menu and demonstrated prodigious production skills.   Their strong suit was that everything for the sandwich contents was cut on demand, and thus as fresh as possible; and decent torpedo rolls (really the most important element of the creation) were pulled from a bag only as needed. My Honey Turkey and Swiss hoagie with shredded lettuce, mayo and hot/sweet peppers wasn't zoftig, but ample enough to warm and fill the belly of the beast. I enjoyed it.   I have been on a deli kick of late, and FD was about as rewarding as the other local family run shops in the region. Good to help keep all of them in business by chosing mom & pop businesses open and thriving, rather than those factory like places that offer gasoline as a side dish.

This new version of Ho Sai Gai (Prosperity), is so much nicer than the old one I visited several decades ago.  Small and cozy, it is clean, bright and friendly.  There is a full bar if that is the direction you want to go.  Their hours are long into the night to capture some of the after hours crowd, and their offerings compare well to the competition across the street.    There are both English and Chinese menus.  Their contents are somewhat different.  While the English version is similar to most Chinese/American offerings (read: non-authentic), the alternative book stays truer to what the Chinese diner looks for.  It should also be noted that this is a Taiwanese-styled kitchen, which brings it closer to Cantonese plates in taste, but also providing a few dishes that are more uniquely from Taipei.    The three of us were handed the English menus, which were quickly exchanged for Chinese when we explained that most of us only spoke English as a second language.  We ordered 3 dishes; two with Pork, Beef, Veggies and Rice or Tofu and Mushrooms in Brown Sauce, and a Crispy Pork Chop on top of a thick dark and flavorful sauce.  They were all decent, although none of us thought the meals exceptional.  The meats were well cooked on the first plate, but my other friend found her dish too salty.  My Pork Chop was a big, coated and fried slab with bone, but a bit passed prime, and seemingly dry.    Still, we consumed most of everything, enjoying our conversation.  The pot of hot tea was great to see delivered to our table as part of the presentation, and without added cost.  We are not fond of the Fried Noodles on the table for dipping in Duck Sauce, and had them removed to avoid caloric temptation.    The sweet spot for Ho Sai Gai appears to be its late night business.  Its mid-afternoon weekend lunch, not so much.

Pottstown, Pa., is an interesting old city.  We dropped into it late in the afternoon after a day in the heat of French Creek State Park and Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site.  I was feeling the effects of the 90F temp, and needed hydration and a little nourishment.    First choice was a tour of Yuengling Brewery, but I had confused Pottsville with Pottstown, and would have been too late anyway. (Should have looked further and found Sly Fox Brewery, but that will have to wait.)  Second choice was to find the nearest dairy bar and settle in for some fresh cool creamy ice cream and a burger.  Yelp Search found Coventry Parlor at Laurel Locks, not 10 minutes away from Main Street.  Not too many reviews, but a little more pioneering today wouldn't hurt.    Actually in Coventry Township, the Laurel Locks refer to both the canal built there to connect with the Schuylkill River canal system, and the large farm that took root there in the early 18th Century.  Another little remembered historic fact was that this area was the home of the a small religious sect called the Stubblebines, whose moral code allowed nudity and cohabitation; giving this locale the name, "Free Love Valley," in the early 19th Century.  It all got out of control, with murder and jealousy rampant.  The group died out by the mid 1800's, when self- proclaimed prophet, Hannah Williamson, caught the last wagon train out of town heading west.    So, we settled on a couple of burgers and split a Cashew Raspberry Shake.  The shake was thick with nuts and ice cream, and was quite refreshingly creamy sweet.  The burgers were something else.  Past well done, they were crunchy and almost beyond redemption.  I was too weary to bring it to the server's attention.  It came with store bought bun, cheap chips (not even Herr's), and a soft pickle.    If not for affording the opportunity to learn about the fascinating history of this community, I would have departed disappointed by the grub here.  I just won't look past the front retail ice cream shop next time, should that come to pass.

On a unusually balmy early November afternoon Café Alessio's outdoor patio is a great place to have lunch, enjoy the breeze and blue sky, and watch Doylestown go by.    The three of us stopped in after taking care of business in the courthouse.  The al fresco dining area was not crowded at 2:00 pm, and we settled in to review the lunch menu.  Our waitress was very helpful in pointing out the specials as well as those items she liked the most.  We ended up with two California Burgers (medium) and a Milano Sandwich.    The Burgers were half pounders and hand molded.  They arrived appropriately pink inside, one with Fries, the other, Chips.  The Lettuce, Tomato, Onion, Avocado and Cheese were loaded on top and encased in a brioche-style bun that held up well.  I was given a few bites and thought it was quite good - fresh tasting and nicely grilled.    My Milano Chicken Sandwich was served on the same bun and had interesting tomato based paste smeared on the bread, and more lettuce, garlic and sautéed spinach.  I liked it, but not quite as much as the burger.    The menu included salads, pizza and pasta dishes that all looked attractive as served to other patrons. Prices were reasonable for D'town and the price/quality value proposition made Alessio's a true deal, especially with all the autumn light glowing around us.    Definitely satisfying.

Another state of the art burger emporium from Five Guys.   If you like your sliders fresh, hot and greasy, this is your place.  For $10. you get the standard double with or without cheese and all the toppings you can imagine, on a crushed bun, and a cuppa hot fries that spills into the bag and is easily enough for three. Another few bucks for the bottomless drinks.  When the 13 year old we were with suggested McDonald's for lunch, I Yelped for an alternative and found this 5 Dudes even closer than the golden arches.  It was his first try and though he didn't say much, he ate the whole sandwich, plenty of fries, and washed everything down with Sprite.    Win-win for all of us.

I have been back regularly since my review.  Having overcome my hesitance about the quirky advertising with cows asking humans to eat more chickens (that's another dissertation about social morality), and eaten a few other things beyond the Sausage, Egg and Cheese Biscuit (5 Stars), I achieved the realization that I was too harsh in my evaluation before.   The sandwiches are good, the shakes superior, and the playroom for kids, unique.  I don't have to agree with corporate politics to appreciate the grub.   Okay. I am a fan. I am willing to admit it.

I came for a business lunch last week.  It is located in a sprawling commercial center parking lot, and is easy to see, but a bit harder to navigate to through the lot.   Like any mid-range casual dining franchise, there is a sameness to every plant.  While this may have been cozy and "intimate" at one time, today it feels tired, like an old home in need of new furniture and fresh paint.  The formula is dated.  The menu looked the same as when I visited other Applebees' a decade ago.  I guess I shouldn't argue with success, such as it is.  On this day, the customer profile seemed to primarily be grandparents and their grandkids.   In keeping with the "Oldies But Goodies" theme, I ordered the same Oriental Salad with Chicken as I had ten years ago.  My partner for the meal went with one of their burgers.  Not unexpectedly, my lunch looked and tasted the same as last time, although the bowl was now colorful rather than white.  While we were not there to discuss the food, I did learn that the burger was satisfying.   I don't feel as critical of this joint as many others here, although I am not enthusiastic about it, either.  It provided a decent meal, service and price in a reasonable time, and in a comfortable setting.    While this shop and its brethren will not make my short list of desirable dining, I will not turn up my nose if someone wants to go there.
Sweet, creamy, cold.   Orange Cream (twirl of vanilla and orange) tastes like childhood.

When the Viking Stovetop's downdraft exhaust fan went on the fritz, visions of very expensive repairs danced in my head. First, very few repair dudes handled Viking equipment, and those few who did wanted my first born as collateral before agreeing to come to the house to check it out.    I finally called Dave's Appliance Repair in Horsham after the local boys struck out. A real person answered the phone, listened to the symptoms, and seemed confident they could handle it.  Their only demand was that the first visit be paid for in advance. At $90, I knew why. My doctor visit costs less. Still, I paid it, and one of their service techs came for a visit within a few days.  He was a pleasant chap with an amiable sidekick.    He started taking apart the exhaust venting system to get to the root of the problem - the burned out motor. He had to dissemble the cabinet in front of it, remove the rear cabinet wall, and return to his truck several times to grab the right tools for this ever more difficult surgery.  He finally removed the dead metal, but didn't have the right one to replace it.  So began a series of visits (three and counting), as he ordered first one part, and then another, until the right one was obtained and installed.  I had to pay for the anticipated parts and labor before Dave would order them. At first, it annoyed me that a deposit wouldn't do, but I ultimately realized that this $900 one time bite was saving money, because of all the wrong parts and then extra pieces and effort necessary to get the job done.    Our kitchen contractor had installed this stove so tightly to the rear wall, that there was little space to maneuver to get the work done.  Each visit took longer than anticipated.  Our technician (who's name will go unmentioned out of respect for his impressive skills), had to freelance most of the way, because nothing seemed to fit as expected.  Ultimately, he succeeded in finishing the job, much to the relief of all of us.  The exhaust is literally up and sucking.   At this moment, we await replacement filters.  This has proved yet another saga, as the model number deemed appropriate does not fit in the frame. Dave is having the right size filters fabricated now.    Yes. The multiple visits have been frustrating, but Dave and his people have seen it through, and promise to make good on the entire operation.  I believe it. Not every job is a piece of cake, as this one turned out to be a real challenge.  Still, every step of the way, they have been honest with me about it, and attempted to create a workable solution.  They have been on time, and always courteous and even funny.  The stove and exhaust are working well for the first time in a few years, and once the filters are replaced (rather than just cleaned), everything will be good to go for many more.

Sorry folks.  This strictly take out joint on S. Broad Street, Trenton, is just not very good.  The family running it is nice, but the food leaves a lot to be desired.  I guess if you can't make the trip to a reasonably authentic or even a decent Americanized Chinois place, then this is what is left.  It's a shame because there are several good places not too far away.   The dishes were plentiful with abundant fried rice and a large pile of Sesame Chicken, but the quality just was not there.  The taste was generic sweet gloop on top of too long frozen chicken, and fried rice that was made either last night or early in the morning with a large dose of brown dyed beef bouillon.  I watched as a Bento Box was prepared for someone.  The fish came out of baggies and sat on the hot prep table as it was put together.  I was glad I was not the one who was going to eat it.  I could practically see the bacteria multiplying.    There are some relatively decent Chinese Take Out places in the area, but My Kitchen is not one of them.

Angelo's is a lovely local Italian establishment on 2nd Street Pike in the heart of the Southampton commercial district.  The reviews show they have the devotion of a lot of people living in the area.  After 30 years that is to be expected and it is well deserved.  The facility is fairly large, with ample privacy for the tables.  The staff is exceptionally friendly and attentive.  The menu is traditional Italian-American fare, with many pizza options, Parms, Alfredo's, Marsala's, etc.  Prices are very reasonable.  My son and I went there last night for the first time.  He had the Chicken Parm, with Minestone Soup; I the Pizza Rustica (small).  The accompanying Italian bread was very tasty, with enough thin crusty crispiness to be enjoyable in taste and bite.  I really enjoyed it with a smear of sweet butter.  It was served warm.   Son's Parm, was excellent.  The breast was pounded and breaded with a pleasant bread crumb mix, and covered in a heavy fresh tomato sauce.  He was rolling his eyes in delight.  If anything was off, perhaps, the spaghetti side was a bit mushy (he gave me a taste of everything so I could review it).   The Minestone was rich with veggies, pasta and a little beef.  Very good.  The Pizza Rustica was hand-pulled, with fresh Basil, Garlic, chunky Tomatoes, and a heavy Mozzarella finish.  It was good.  Now, pizza is a very personal and subjective taste.  We are all experts.  Some may love this style, but for me it left something to be desired.  I prefer my pizza to have a thin, but firm crust that does not bend or fold under the weight of the toppings.  This one suffered from cheese overload, and required a knife and fork.  It was tasty, but the cheese overwhelmed the other flavors and softened the firmness I prefer. I added crushed hot pepper and garlic powder, which was helpful.    We will certainly come again and see what else is cooking.  I will tell the waitress more about my pizza preferences, and perhaps, we can reach an accommodation. A good chef appreciates a customer's positive input.  Given all the other positives, Angelo's may yet become as special to me as it has been to so many long time patrons.

So, what do you order in a restaurant named, "Non Solo Pasta?"    Although it gave me a moment's pause, I went with the Rigatoni Aglio Olio with Spinach.  I did not see it on the menu, but that is what I had a craving for, and I suspected the kitchen knew how to make it.   I sat in the corner near the door and shared the attractive floor with three other occupied tables.  It was a cold and quiet night.  My server took a few minutes to find me, but she was courteous, efficient and prompt.  The Side Salad came out first.  It was small with a nice Spring Mix, if a bit light on the house Italian dressing.  Just greens. No cheese, nuts, dried fruit. Basic salad.   The two small dinner rolls were housemade and quite good with a crunchy crust and mildly salty flavor.    The wide brimmed white bowl of pasta was adequate, if not generous.  The spinach was cut into smaller pieces and fully sautéed into the oil and garlic.  Tasty.  The pool of oil at the bottom of the bowl was perhaps more than expected, but it did not detract from the al dente Rigatones that were bathing in it.  The garlic taste was strong although not a lot of the bulb was showing in the dish.    The meal was competent and filling, if not memorable.  There was a lack of energy emanating from the food. It did not visibly shine as many good meals do. Maybe it was the cold night, or the sparse occupancy, but the experience was flat.  Given the cost of this simple meal ($17), I guess I anticipated something more dynamic.   That I could not get an internet signal in the house compounded this impression.

Cone Heads Ice Cream is on the bottom (or top) of Mill Creek Parkway in Levittown, Pa.  It sits in a 4 shop strip commercial building with a pizza parlor, and dance studio.    Walking in, there is plenty of room in the brightly lit space.  Part of that is because there is no where to sit down to enjoy your creamies.  There are two benches out front, but it would be uncomfortable to hang there is cold or wet weather.  Don't know why they don't want people hanging around in the shop.  It would seem to be the best way to keep folks happy coming there.    I sampled a small cup with a scoop of Peanut Butter Ripple and Pumpkin (Pie).  At $2.85, the price was downright 1980! The service from the owner was friendly and efficient.  He told me he had been at this location for 6 years, and another nearby place, 9 years more.  That's a lot of ice cream cones and shakes.    Cone Heads doesn't make its own product, but uses several vendors depending on the flavors available.  That is both a strength and a weakness.  It certainly saves money not to invest in equipment, and provides flexibility in purchasing.  Yet, it reduces flavor and quality control by putting it in foreign hands.  I could taste the difference.  While the Peanut Butter Ripple was very good with a lot of peanut butter throughout its vanilla base, the Pumpkin had much less taste and creaminess, and was so subtle that I did not recognize it at first.  It was only when I came across pieces of pie crust in the mix that I realized that I was dealing with pumpkin pie ice cream, not merely the orange gourd.    This place could be so much more than it is, if it standardized its inventory to better manufacturers, and made the house more comfortable for folks to sit around and enjoy their sundaes and malts.

This Cheeburger Cheeburger franchise is right across the street from Red Robin, so there is a natural choice to make when making a burger run.  If you want a beer with that, than RR is your only option.  If great shakes are a priority, Chee Chee is the better way to go.    Here, the ambiance is all ersatz 1950's diner-esqueness.  Very similar to Nifty Fifty, Johnnie Rocket's, Jake's Wayback, and the like.  I forgive them the weak attempt at historical orientation, as the actual product is pretty good.    The burgers and fries are fresh, not frozen at the start, and the end result is a decent (not great) burger experience.  Compared to 5 Guys, it falls a little short in the taste department (not enough tasty grease), but it compensates with more menu variety (chicken, salads), and additional treats to put on the burger (banana chilies, shrooms, pickles, etc.).  The shakes are very good, and they will add malt powder for no additional charge if asked.  Really, creamy and tasty.   Bottom line - Worth the trip and money when you want a good nostalgia burger.

Cheeburger, Cheeburger is another 1950's throw back concept burger joint franchise.  It is similar to Jake's Wayback, Nifty Fifty, Johnnie Rocket's, etc.    The burgers are fresh beef, not frozen, and are quite good with tons of choices as to things you can add to customize your dining experience.  For me, I love the jalapeno chilies, sauteed onions, and sweet pickle, but there are a zillion combinations.  Last night, I had the Patty Melt, which comes on over sized rye bread, a pile of onions and American Cheese.  The Jalapenos added the kick I love.  The Fries are also fresh cut and not frozen, and come with some of the potato skin attached for extra taste and nutrition.  My son and I split a Vanilla Shake, which was very good - sweet and creamy.   There is certainly more on the menu here than at places like 5 Guys, the current standard bearer, which makes it a good option for those who do not want the beef, but prefer chicken or salads.  However, to my taste buds, the dining experience is slightly less satisfying than the more limited offerings at 5 Guys.    To each his own.  Certainly, the burgers at Chee Chee are worthy of your time, taste and money.  The cost for the burgers, fries, and shake came to $30, including tip and tax.  Not cheap, but not quite an indulgence, either.   Take a big bite.

Before getting on the Pa Turnpike early this morning, I made a short detour onto Horizon Boulevard to get some java and a small bite for breakfast.  When Chik-Fil-A was not yet open, I drove through the take out window at Starbucks next door.    I liked the convenience and time savings of a drive thru, but it seemed like the order taker was also the barista as well as the short order cook.  So, she looked rather busy, and in need of assistance.  Still, she kept her composure and got everything right.    As usual, the coffee had a burnt and bitter taste, but the extra milk requested helped to soften the harshness.  I asked for their Sausage, Egg and Cheese Sandwich on a croissant, but was told that all these meals are pre-packaged and microwaved just before sale.  I decided to go with the English Muffin as the only option.  I don't like what microwaves do to eggs and bread, so the meal was at best, average.  Nothing I would want a second time.    Hopefully, CFA will be open next time I find myself in a similar predicament.

Pho Xe Lua (Loosely translated as "long car special") is one of the older houses at the bottom of Race Street, and it shows its age.  The menu is extensive, particularly if you like Vietnamese dishes or Pho.  Portions are large.  Prices are low.  Very popular combination that keeps the two floors busy day and night.  Just don't spend time looking at the floor around your table, because cleanliness is an issue.  The house hasn't been inspected by L & I for a long time, and it shows.   Still, it is mind over matter.  If you don't mind the grit around you, it doesn't matter.  Just enjoy the plentitude so light on your wallet.    We were there for a late lunch and stayed with the soup.  My partner had the Pho Special that contained all the meats available in the kitchen, and I their Bun Bo Hue.  They label the sizes of their bowls as large and extra large, as if that was something everyone understood.  The former would be a large bowl in most establishments, and the later, a fish bowl.  We couldn't finish either.    The Pho broth was decent; full of noodles and a load of meat.  It was tasty, but lacked some of the more subtle flavors associated with the better noodle soups.  I did not taste Anise, although it could have been in there.  My Bun Bo was stocked with three big Pig's Feet (Glad they left him one on the hoof), plus slices of Beef and shreds of Pork.  It had ample Lemongrass for the strong spiciness that makes this so distinctive, Fermented Shrimp Paste for sourness,  plus Onions, Mint, and a few unidentified floating objects.  I did not detect Coriander, Rock Sugar, nor Congealed Pig Blood (thankfully), which are part of the totally authentic mix.  The side dish accompaniments had the usual Sprouts, Thai Basil, Jalapeno Slices and Lime Wedges, but was missing the Banana Blossom Slices, and/or Red Cabbage.    Still, it was pretty good; the first spoonful paralyzing my vocal cords so I could only whisper for about 15 minutes.  It wasn't the best BBH I have had in the City, but it wasn't the worst.  Given the complexity of the real deal, perhaps it was unfair of me to expect Pho Xe Lua to get it completely right.    Service was fine, and our server was multilingual, making my Mandarin speaking friend happy with his descriptions in her native tongue.   No need to run back here, but its broad non-Chinese menu makes it a reasonable alternative when in Chinatown, but not feeling like Chinese food.

Leave it to my 15 year old son to tell me he needs a haircut at 5:30 pm of the evening before he leaves on a trip with his church group. Arghhh!!!  Luckily, we knew of a couple of franchise hair shops that take walk ins and are open late.  We drove over to Hair Cuttery in the Village of Newtown Shopping Center, and found the "Open" sign lit, and people inside being served.    I sent him in ahead to get started while I parked the car, and then followed him inside.  He was already getting his hair washed when I came in.  I sat at the front window to watch and wait.  He has longish hair and only wanted a trim to help out with the heat that was coming while he was camping.  The conversation was animated, with him touching the back of his head and around his ears, and his stylist listening and asking questions.    Twenty minutes later, he was finished with a short blow dry and comb. He looked great, and seemed very satisfied with the result.  At $18 for the men's haircut (prices are higher than listed on Yelp), and a $5. gratuity, the price was still right, especially given the circumstances of our visit.  Son said he would go back there again.    That's a relief. Just give me more notice next time.

Great urban park with an amazing history. But, what makes it Philadelphia's gift to the world is the view from the Belmont Plateau overlooking Center City.  Go about 4 pm in Spring or Autumn when the light turns a golden hue, and it is... Simply.   Breathtaking.

Metro Diner on Street Road has the look of a cafe more than a traditional diner, with only a short counter with spinners overlooking the open kitchen, and a dining room to the other side. It is in a new building it shares with an as yet unleased commercial space. It is not the roadhouse a diner was designed to be.   Still, the menu looked diner. So, what the heck. I was ready for breakfast, and I was already there, and in the hunt for some good french toast. That they had in abundance, although not just the plain egg bread fried with the hint of vanilla and sugar I was hankering for. But, when I asked the friendly server if it was available, she assured me it was.   The coffee was strong, hot and free flowing. The main attraction was disappointing. It looked great on the plate, especially after melting some butter and running syrup over it. But, upon cutting and first bite, found its insides to be mushy and cooler than the surface. It wasn't eggy inside as you might expect, but almost watery, like the mix had been diluted to the point where it lacked the hen seed to thicken under heat. It just stayed wet. The flavor was about right, but texture counts, too.   I suppose I could have given it back to them for another try, but wasn't feeling like making that scene. I ate what I could and took my leave. Just glad I hadn't asked for the heavy hitters on the menu, which would have put a bigger dent in my wallet.  It was probably a mistake that wasn't caught before reaching its final destination, but first impressions were damaging.

Although designed primarily for take out, there are two tables in the front of the house for eating in.  Be forewarned that in cooler weather, the space is not heated, but for a small space heater that can be turned on near the tables.    Aside from that bit of discomfort, the fare from this Chinese/American shop is better than average.  My Orange Chicken, Fried Rice and Hot & Sour Soup were all superior to most of the other alternative takeaways in the Morrisville/Trenton region (except for the more authentically Chinese restos that don't fit in this category).  The chicken did not seem to have been frozen and the sauce was pleasantly thinner than the goop found in most places.  Too, it was a nice customer service to offer to make the Orange Chicken for a lunch special when it was not on the menu.    The Soup was loaded with tofu, sprouts and mushrooms, while not dosed heavily with MSG. The Fried Rice was dyed with the bouillon beef stock, but was otherwise full of veggies and chunks of pork.    The friendly, accommodating service made for an enjoyable, if chilly, meal.

I just had one of the best cheesesteaks of my life!  Steve's Prince of Steaks has a shop on Route 1 in Langhorne, and although not far from my home, I had never been there, always preferring my local pizza shop for my grease fix.  Friday night, while I waited to pick up my son at a Magic tournament at OVM, I had some hunger and time to kill.  Steve's came to mind.   I arrived about 30 minutes before closing.  There were only a few customers, and the staff was beginning to clean up.  I read the ordering directions a safe distance from the window, decided what I wanted and walked up to the young guy in the Steve T shirt and ballcap. The Cheesesteak wit Onions, Provolone and Roasted Peppers came out on the thin sheet of Steve paper.  When I attempted to pick it up with one hand I felt the heft of the sandwich and quickly put my other hand underneath to keep it from sliding off onto the floor. It was that heavy.  It was a work of art.  The peppers, onion and cheese glistened under the lights.  A small pool of oil began to collect once I placed it on the small stainless steel counter than runs around the shop.   I went back to the fixin's bar to get some Banana Peppers to add more heat.  I sat down on the bar stool and looked at this creation.  I took a photo to commemorate the moment.  I really thought there was no way I could eat the whole thing. Then I took the first bite...  Heaven. I'm in Heaven...Yes, the song danced in my head.  The roll was lightly crusted and extremely fresh.  Great taste in its own right.  The blending of the ingredients on chewing was an intense explosive release of flavors, textures, spice and heat.  I lost all control.  I couldn't hold back.  I had an orgasm in my mouth before the second bite.  The sweetness of the onions soothed the heat from the peppers, but did not overcome them.  The provolone provided a subtle undertone that played well with the roll and sliced beef.  My eyes rolled into the back of my head and when they returned, the sandwich was completely ingested.    The only thing I can say is, when can I go back for another?   Suggestions: 1. Cash only. There is an ATM inside the shop, but why pay the extra charge? 2. To keep cost down, go with the Cheesesteak with American or Wiz, as the other cheeses are extra.  3. Try the pepper fixin's bar before ordering extra peppers at the window.  There are plenty of choices there, and it is another buck or so to have them cooked with the steak.   4. The fries are very good. If you care at all about your heart, try them straight, w/o the extra cheese.  It looks great all melted over the fries, but when it cools it is just a coagulated yellow mess.  That is how your heart sees it.  5. Don't wait another day to have one.

Needing to paint the wood trim around my home the same color as the original, I took a chip of paint to The Paint Store in Newtown to see if they could match it.  They were able to match it as a Benjamin Moore paint called, "Steamed Spinach."  Who'd a thunk it would be that easy?   So, they mixed me a quart of it, low gloss, and I walked out a happy homeowner.  The experience was pleasant and completely no sweat.  The shop has all the material necessary for such jobs.  The prices are not as cheap as the highway box stores, but the convenience of being 5 minutes from home, and keeping our community businesses successful, is worth the small premium to me.    Now, all I need is a way to get 30 feet up to the gable to paint.

It seems all the service stations in Newtown are owned by the same extended family. Makes one wonder if that is one of the reason the price of gas in town is higher than anywhere else outside of New York City.  Maybe? Maybe not.  While I always attempt to fill up in Jersey where the prices are a good thirty cents a gallon cheaper, sometimes that is impossible.  When the good option is out of the question, I visit Kerrigan's to purchase enough fuel to get me around until I can cross the Delaware.    As Kimberly G. rightly notes, the cost here is the lowest in town. Too, Sunoco has the two grades of premium, and it is possible to go with the 90 Octane drink, rather than the 92, and save a few more shekels.   I can't speak to the mechanic's services.  I use a cousin's shop down on Sycamore for that, and find those folks totally reputable.

Apparently, at one time all the Palermo's in the area were under one ownership team.  These days, they have gone their separate ways and share only the name.  Having visited the Bordentown shop and been happy with their Tomato Pie, I wanted to try them all.    This Italian palace sits on the bottom of Klockner Road.  It is a nice space, if dated, but it definitely harkens to another time when these places were full of locals; the men around the bar, and families in the dining rooms eating home cooked Roman meals.  It certainly has its charm and could easily fit into Chambersburg, if Chambersburg was still Chambersburg.   I sat alone at the bar for a late lunch and ordered their Bar Tomato Pie with Sausage.  I was entertained by an array of large HDTVs above the back bar and the outer walls. It was a rectangular bar with seating on 4 sides.  I liked the lay out.  When the Pie arrived it looked beautiful - steaming with bright red chunky crushed Tomato and a nice spread of crumbled Sweet Sausage.  Rather than serving it on an aluminum pizza oven pan, it was presented on a large round white platter.    The outer crust was golden, cracker crisp and delicious.  Yet, the center of the pie had condensation between it and the cooler plate.  this caused dampening of the undercrust, and when I went to pick a slice up, the gravy, cheese and sausage slid off the base onto the plate, leaving just the white crust in my hand.  It still tasted good, but it did detract from the overall enjoyment of the pie.  I learned why most pizza shops serve their pies on the metal tray, to hold heat and reduce condensation.   I would certainly return to Palermo's if I found myself in that neighborhood, but there are so many other very good to excellent pie emporiums in Hamilton that there is no need to settle for less that total wonderful excellence when only a tomato pie will still the savage beast.

Bailey's sits in a small strip center on Emelie Road in Levittown, Pa, just off Five Points. It is a neighborhood bar and grill with a decent beer list and menu into wings, burgers, soups and salads. Prices are quite reasonable. Nothing fancy, but solid grub and suds. Family place. Loud music. Friendly staff, all of whom stopped by our table to see how we were doing.   We weren't feeling adventurous. Our thirst and hunger led us to a local brew IPA and Strongbow Cider, followed by roast beef panini and patty melt. Chips came as accompaniment, or for $1.50 more, a pile of fries.   The sandwiches were large and quite good. We brought half the panini home. We thought we were ready to go when our server asked if we had interest in dessert.   "Maybe. What ya got?"  Simple question. Profound answer.   The chef has a special gift for desserts. That day he had created a mango glazed cheesecake. The rest is history. We were given a big slice of this creamy orgasmic heartsweet forklicking beauty. It was a cool, dense, tastebud exploding chunk of the most extraordinary cheesecake I had ever experienced - better the Junior's, the Cheesecake Factory, and even your Aunt Betty.   Not even Bailey's knows what they have going on in their kitchen. This guy is the King of Cheesecake.   Check it out. Start with dessert.

Nice cold morning. Quiet breakfast with my son before camping. Sausage, egg & cheese biscuit quite tasty.  I am not really a fan of Chik Fil A.  I don't get the name, nor the advertising.  The chicken sandwiches do not move me. The only things I like are the breakfast sandwiches and the shakes, which are rich and creamy.

I was a regular breakfast patron at the Radcliffe Café for several years after discovering it was only a little off my route from Newtown to Mt. Holly on mornings I needed to be in court down there.  It is named for the street it is on, which runs along the Delaware River until reaching downtown Bristol.  It is easy to imagine how nice it was 100 years ago when the area more open and the river carried the commerce from Trenton to Philadelphia and all points in between.  The Café is a great spot for a hearty breakfast - traditional style. Eggs of all varieties, pancakes, sandwiches and bottomless cups of Joe predominate.  There are the regulars who are there daily, the semi-regulars who come routinely, but do not call the lunch counter seats their own, and the tourists who stop in because they stumbled onto it, or heard a good rumor about it (on Yelp?).  Dog eared copies of the Trentonian were available for reading accompaniment.   The staff is out of central casting for diner molls. You can't get out without being called, "Hon," or "Sugar," at least once.  You gotta like that cultural affect to be captivated by its charm.  When I was a semi-reg, there was a server who I wanted to call me that and more.  I always sat on the right hand of the counter to enjoy her intriguing smile and black jeans.  My choice was either a big breakfast sandwich, which always came with the Sunnyside Ups leaking out, or the French Toast.  Both tasty. Both completely satisfying.    Sadly, I could never linger for a long chat with her, as court beckoned.  Still, my imagination often ran wild with the possibilities.    Stop in and start your own daydreams.

Right on the Broad Street/Rt. 206 Circle in Hamilton, NJ, this Advance Auto Parts store used to be a Chinese Buffet back in the day.  There are similarities in the wide display of everything car/truck related being found on the aisles, the same way the multitude of chicken pieces were dressed up with many sauces, accompanied by veggie and rice alternatives.    I came in looking for a jack and lug wrench to replace the original equipment that had gone missing recently (one of the great mysteries of life).  Everything Advance had was for much heavier usage.  Even the smallest scissor jack was engineered to lift a panel truck, and much too heavy duty (and just plain heavy) for my needs.  I did remember to pick up a replacement wiper; finding myself studying the chart to determine which model and level of sophistication was required.  For $22 this better last forever.
