Service was of the DIY variety, which was okay after I located the area of the shop I wanted, but no one volunteered to assist.  I guess most customers have been there before.

Newtown Jewelers is a family run jewelry store on State Street, Newtown Borough.  It is a small shop, but it has a nice selection of affordable pieces, including watches, gold and silver rings, bracelets and necklaces, as well as a few nice gemstone articles. They are well connected and can find almost anything you want, and they enjoy the challenge.   I routinely bring my watches there for repair and batteries, and find the interaction with Cheryl and Bill to be warm and often entertaining.   This is certainly a shop locally winner!

I was looking for a place to hang out while a family member was in night class at Morrisville High School (English as a Second Language).  Yelp offered a few suggestions nearby, and I choose to discover the Morrisville Tavern on West Trenton Avenue, at the edge of the Big Oak Shopping Center.    It wasn't very busy at 7 pm when I walked in; just folks who looked to be regulars and family/friends of the attractive bartender.  No one bothered to look up, which is a good thing on a first visit.  I sat facing a multitude of HDTVs, and I was quickly approached by the lovely alchemist working the patrons.  She gave me a rundown of the beer on tap, and when I asked about hard cider she offered Angry Orchard Apple.  She also changed the channel on a few of the screens to bring up the Sixers basketball game (not that they would provide any real entertainment).    The Angry was cold with a sweet/tart bite.  Very good.  I took a look at the menu and specials board, and wished that I had not already had dinner.  The variety looked appealing, and the platters being served at the bar looked appetizing.  Will definitely make a point to come hungry in the future.    This is a nice dive bar.  The natives are friendly and seem to have a comfort with each other.  Personal conversations all around.  I could do without the smoking, but given the scarcity of tobacco-accepting taverns these days, I understand why those in the habit appreciate having a place to call their own.  I can deal with it now and then.    I will be back soon, perhaps, next time without my work suit, so I can join in the camaraderie with more enthusiasm.

Emei Shan is a holy Buddhist mountain in Szechuan Province, China. It is a difficult climb up steep trails and even steeper stairs. On the way, monkeys drop out of the trees seeking donations from the faithful, sometimes quite aggressively.  Still, once reaching the summit, you stand above the clouds and look out at a timeless world of sky and mountaintops.  Breathtaking.  E Mei Restaurant takes its name from this mountain.    When I made my first visit over the past weekend, I was impressed with the effort made to upgrade the floor with quality tables and chairs, as well as table clothes and an overall sense of wanting to treat the customer well.  It worked. The cuisine is slightly different than the better know superheat of most Szechuan style dishes.  The owner is from Chongqing, a major city in China, that was formerly part of Szechuan Province, but is now an Autonomous Zone, carved out of its former province.  Their food is spicy and often hot, but more subtle than the blast furnace approach found in better known Chengdu-ese molten flavors.   My companion and I started with apps of Dan Dan Noodles and Eggplant with Pepper. Both were well done, and only mildly hot.  The beef sauce on the noodles was plentiful. The eggplant more shredded than sliced, yet even with the ample peppers, did not raise a fire alarm.  Both were quite enjoyable.   Our main courses consisted of Fish Fillet in Hot Spicy Sauce, Diced Rabbit with Peanuts in Chili Sauce, and Saute Squash.  Here's were the thermometer began to rise.  The fish came in a deep dish with a ton of fillets.  The sheen from the chili oil in which the fish swam was very noticeable, and its red color contrasted nicely with the pale yellow of the odd shaped fish.  This dish was about 4 alarm, meaning my tongue instantly reacted to touching the sauce and began to numb a bit. Just the way I like it!   Rabbit is not my fave, but having had it in Chongqing I wanted to celebrate the opportunity.  The meat was on the bone, and cut into small pieces.  The peanuts were a strong presence, helping to control the overflowing chili and star peppers attempt at an insurrection. It was 5 alarm even with the peanuts holding the worst elements at bay.  For me, rabbit is a lot of work because of all the bones and small morsels of meat attained.  Still, it tasted very good, and all of it was gone by the time we called it quits on more eating.  The small green squash was a pleasantly sweet counterbalance to the rabbit's "hare" raising.   All in all a very enjoyable and authentic meal.  Definitely worth a return visit.  For those of us who love Szechuan heat, this place is worthy, even if not at the apex of the volcanic chili scale.  Climb E Mei and taste the view from the top.  All this for under $50. plus tip.

Jade Asian is a replacement for an earlier Chinese resto at this location. On approach it attempts to position itself as a "Fusion" place offering Chinese, Sushi and Thai cuisine.  While the space is clean and bright with a large HDTV on the wall playing NFL games on Sunday evening, and the servers are friendly and courteous, the reality is that this is primarily a Chinese restaurant that doesn't have a Japanese nor Thai chef to handle that end of the menu spectrum.    While I saw someone working the Sushi Bar who seemed to know what he was doing, it was obvious after ordering Tom Yum Soup (Vegetables) and Pad Se Yo Noodles (Chicken), that they have a ways to go before they should present themselves as offering a real Thai alternative.    The Soup was appropriately tart, but the Vegetables seem to have been thrown into the pot at the last minute.  While plentiful, they were large pieces that had not absorbed the flavor of the broth from slow simmering.  It just did not hang together as a true Tom Yum would.  I asked for a heavy spice infusion on my Pad Se Yo, but what I got was not a Thai dish at all.  It was Chinese Chicken Chow Fun, complete with the mild Cantonese brown sauce traditional to that dish.  When I asked for additional hot sauce to bring some of the taste I desired, I received only Sriracha in a small dish, but not any Hot Chili Oil, Sesame Oil or even a Curry Powder shaker to doctor it the right way.    For Chow Fun it wasn't bad, but for Pad Se Yo it was a major disappointment.    Jade Asian is really more about ConFusion, than Fusion.  For me, it is not worth a return visit as there are much better Thai places in the area.  While I can't comment on the sushi, I am left to believe it likely suffers from the same inauthenticity.

Chik Fil A in Newtown stands across the parking fields from Acme, and shares a parking lot with Appleby's.  They have both drive through and eat-in services.  I am not a fan of their chicken sandwiches and nuggets, although my young son loves them.  For me, they lack much taste and the roll and filet together are too soft for an enjoyable bite and chew. I will only eat them if I am very hungry. However, the breakfast sandwiches are superior products compared to other fast food variations.  The sausage, egg and cheese biscuit is super tasty and textured, so every bite is a pleasure.  The fresh biscuits are flakey and have a mild buttery flavor.   The best thing offered are the shakes.  They claim to be "hand spun," whatever that means.  The taste is wonderful with the right amount of sweetness and creaminess.  Their season special shakes are fun on St. Patrick's Day (green minty), late summer (peach), and fall (pumpkin).  They are a little expensive compared to the drink alternatives, but a palate pleaser.  I am not a regular here, but there is a time when it offers exactly what I want.

This Guatemalan house at the corner of Dayton and South Clinton Ave. in Trenton, NJ, is another of the fine casas Latinas in and around the capital city.  What used to be an Italian neighborhood with bars/restaurants on every block, have now become a league of nations of Central and South American culture and cuisine.    Stepping into the barroom the first impression is of a darkly lit, yet surprisingly clean and inviting space.  Nice back bar with lots of tequila and rum, an attractive friendly bar keeper who smoothly shifted between Spanish and English, and a pool table under bright lights for the real players.  There is a larger dining room in the back, but I was all about sitting on a spinner and grabbing lunch.    Symone was attentive and engaging; more than happy to provide some history for this place, while prepping for the evening crowd.  She's the daughter in law of the owner, and has been part of the scene for six years.  The menu offers traditional comidas Guatemalteca, which is similar to Mexican, but with a couple of pleasantly different flourishes.  The tortillas are thicker and chewier, and most side dishes offer more than rice and beans.  I ordered the Carne Adobada with Black Beans and Potato Salad.  The meat was well grilled and spiced with their secret recipe (I asked for it, but she claimed it was a secret even to her).  The Black Beans were rich and creamy, and the salad unlike any potato conglomerate I had ever tasted before.  Cool, chunky, slightly sweet, and mayo-ed with something else I couldn't define, that made it very good.  My Horchata drink was perfectly chilled for the heat of the afternoon.  Loved it.    All the while, Symore returned to be sure I was satisfied, and tell me more about the operation.  She even allowed a photo when I suggested it would be a boon to business.    Take a look.  You can see why.

Smart Park @ Philadelphia International Airport is currently the best choice for long term parking. If you reserve ahead online you are offered the best rates available ($6.95/day). With the obnoxious fees and taxes it is closer to $10.   The facility is south of the airport, so finding Smart on Yelp and using 'directions' is helpful to getting there, especially after dark. It is a bit out of the way. But once you arrive everything moves quickly. The shuttle van leads you to a parking spot. The driver takes your bags from the car and loads them into the van. He gives you a card with the location of your vehicle and the number to call for pick up upon return. Ten minutes later, you're at the terminal of choice.   It took about 15 minutes for the shuttle to arrive for pickup at 1 am. Not much conversation, but all of us were operating at half speed. Still, reached my car, loaded it and drove out quickly. I had to show my initial down payment email receipt to receive the right credit, and was given a sleeve of candy sours (perhaps to help me stay awake on the drive home).   I will be a 'Smart' parker at least until a better deal comes along.

Mercer Café at the corner of East Westmoreland and Mercer Streets in Port Richmond, Philadelphia, PA, is a classic neighborhood restaurant that helps give this section of the City of Brotherly Love its distinct character. It has a cozy, clubby atmosphere and a strong kitchen for classic and neo-classic menus focused on the morning and afternoon meal.  There is a small counter and a couple of dozen tables in the front of the house facing Westmoreland, and many more along the wall to the back of the house.. It is a very nice place to hang out with excellent La Colombe Coffee, and your favorite breakfast or lunch repast.   Our basic egg, hash browns and wheat toast, and Greek-style omelet (I edited the ingredients), were both solid meals, yet not the knockouts they could have been. We found the potatoes to lack crispness and be overly salted. Too, there are unusual upcharges on any bread accompaniment other than plain Jane white.  Their whole wheat option costs a few dimes more, looked good, but lacked any identifying flavor. It was just a good sponge for the runny over easy yolks. Similarly, my omelet which contained onions, spinach, tomato, feta and those taters, was pretty good (especially with a large dose of Cholula), but the premium rye toast was smallish and far from the freshest bread I have eaten for an additional half buck.  There must be a business reason for costing out the meals with add-ons for bread choice, but it is idiosyncratic to say the least, especially when the quality of the loaves denies that they could have cost so much more than the white.   Still, putting that aside, Mercer Café is a strong city breakfast and lunch nook, with superior Java, that can easily become a favorite stop on the Philadelphia breakfast train.

I stop in on occasion when in the area and feeling the "burger lust" hit me.  Red Robin offers a cool semi-roadhouse environment and sliders on the high side of the scale.  My preference was the Onion Burger with sauteed onions, red onion and onion roll for the bun.  Not sure it is still on the menu, but the First Bite Experience was so very pleasurable. Endless French Fries are also a plus for the hungry.   I know there are other things on the menu, but I have never gotten beyond the ground beef disks, fries or rings.   It compares well with Cheeburger Cheeburger, although it may lack a little something side by side with a 5 Guys.  As Grease Palaces go, Red Robin is a solid alternative, and scores well on the comfort scale and as a family activity destination.  08.12.13 - Returned after a movie at Neshaminy AMC. Same roadhouse atmosphere and friendly service. The special Berzerker Burger was nicely spicy and medium pink. Son was way happy with his basic Bacon Cheeseburger.  His thing is to put the fries inside the bun, and he relishes that first bite confirming his sound judgment. We split a Van Shake. It was pretty good, but not at the level of Nifty Fifty, or Chick Fil A.   Still a 4 Star experience. Very pleasant place for a above average burger.

Bigger than it looks from the outside, Mario & Frank have a good thing going at the tail end of Nottingham Way in Trenton/Hamilton, NJ.  Apparently, there are at least three other shops, as this one says it is number IV. I can understand why they have expanded.  Their food is very good as far as old school pizza parlors go.  Short menu with the usual suspects, but what they do, they do well.  This is a family operation, and during the course of my lunch, I received service from at least three of them.  All friendly, efficient, and happy to have one more customer in the house.    I ordered the Eggplant Parm Sandwich.  It arrived about 10 minutes later on a white oval plate (no paper here).  It was neatly transected amidship, with three layers of lightly breaded, twice sautéed eggplant, just enough mozza (not drowning in it), and dollops of homemade chunky tomato sauce with the right amount of garlic and pepper for a great aroma.    It is my habit lately, due to trying to reduce carbs, to eat almost every sandwich open face, to reduce the bread intake.  Thus, I was able to eat each layer of eggplant top to bottom, and enjoy each bite.  It was very good.  I couldn't resist a few bites of the roll.  The top was shiny and the bottom nicely showing flour and yeast remnants.  It was also enjoyable, and left me wanting to abandon my dietary resolution for another day.     The plan now is to find and try the other Mario & Franks locations and see how they measure up. If as good as #4, the discovery will be a great tasty adventure.

I am not sure I would have located a super Wawa in the center of Richboro, PA, but it is there, and takes its place as the crown jewel of this landlocked hamlet, gas islands and all.   The store itself is a good example of the new breed of roadside services that modernizes the convenience store with enlargement, attractive environment, and decent food and drink alternatives. And for the coffee crowd they have figured out that procuring better beans is a cheap way to grab the loyalty and favor of the java drinking public. Selling any size for a buck is a loss leader that everyone can appreciate, and leaves some jingle for something sweet to eat.   The gas prices are generally below the competition, and as it is self service in the Commonwealth, the efficiency pumping your own saves time and treasure.   The evolution of the reststop service oasis has come a long way in a short time. With plenty of choice in a reasonably clean cool space, there is something for almost everyone. Add a few tables for the sit and chat folks and it could become Richboro City Hall.

The Liberty Bell Diner on Frankford Avenue, Northeast Philly, is an urban diner.  It lacks the stretch stainless and glass look of the Jersey version of pure Americana roadside "stuff and go" restos.  Rather, it is more compact and hunkered down in what is now the parking lot of a strip commercial center that has seen better days.  The location certainly makes for easy parking, but I am sure the green field that was here first, was more attractive.    That doesn't stop it was being a very good representative of the genre.  The counter sits to one side just outside the kitchen. The dining room is a nice size with about two dozen tables, white and blue painted walls, dark carpet, and a couple of HDTVs up high.  Service is provided by young women and men in black, who are well trained and friendly, with the right amount of tats exposed on their arms.  Coffee arrives quickly, and they are patient with newbies scanning their menu and asking questions.     Our Blueberry Pancake short stack was fine, if not outstanding.  Fresh fruit in the mix was generous.  A noticeable shortcoming was the use of Kraft Syrup for the gooey sweetener, rather than something healthier and engaging. It is hard to get passed the heavy dose of corn syrup as its main ingredient.  I would gladly pay extra for a small pour of pure maple dark B grade.   The Sausage, Egg & Cheese on Kaiser was a crowd pleaser and customizable.  It was easy to swap out of a plain breakfast patty, and into a sliced/grilled Hot Italian Porker.  It made all the difference in creating an excellent sandwich designed for my taste.  The roll was also pleasantly fresh and strong enough to hold its contents to the last bite.  The Hash Browns were forgettable.   The staff seems to really enjoy the regulars.  There was a knot of ladies in black laughing and commenting on the photos one of the customers was sharing with them.  Even the owner allowed himself to enjoy the moment.  Very cool.   Overall, a superior breakfast stop.

BREAKFAST ONLY REVIEW -  Reno's is basically a pizza take out joint on very old (and nearly decrepit) business route one in Penndel, PA. There are two small tables in front, but upon talking with the one man on duty (owner?), it was apparent that their business plan had changed to a stripped down pizza-to-go operation. Even the sign offering breakfast was misleading, as they would still grill up a morning sandwich, but lacked a means to provide hot coffee to customers. So, my idea to sit down for a quick early bite was denied by the lack of the essential beverage.   Still, the sausage, egg and cheese on Kaiser roll was pretty good, with fried egg and white American cheese. The roll was more a potato roll than the described German loaf, but was actually better than the anticipated bake would have been. Just would have preferred not to eat it in the car.   Can't speak to Reno's pizza or other Italian plates, but the sammy itself was an enjoyable chew.

I am not a Star$$$ fan.   I love coffee that tastes good at its base and does not require extra processing (read, latte, capp, etc.) to make it palatable.  So, it is always somewhat surprising to see these little coffee caves sprout up in supermarkets and box stores and do moderately well.  I admit to having been a happy stockholder for a while, but that did not change my opinion of the underlying product.    So, I was skeptical when I walked into Target a few years ago, and several times since, to see this outpost hanging its shingle within.  It is still there, but seems to be scraping along with only one person running the operation.  Some people like to sip java as they push their shopping carts around the store.  A few actually stop in only for the coffee and depart.    It would be great if there were more coffee alternatives around here.  Until then, this place and the competing Dunkin Donuts and diners of the world will duke it out for my coffee dollar.

If you were blindfolded before walking into Julio's Famous Pizzeria, and saw it for the first time from inside, you would think you were in a 1950's burger and soda fountain emporium, with period photos of greats like James Dean and Marilyn Monroe, as well as the hot rods of that era plastered on the walls. Lots of paisley formica, too. Definitely not the expected décor for a pizza parlor. Yet, it is fun and it works as part of the entertainment offered in this unusual joint.   Their thing is the sandwich pouch. Looking like a half pita, but much thicker, it is an alternative to the standard torpedo roll. It is offered for all sandwiches. It does appear to hold greater volume than a hoagie roll, but the trade off is that it lacks flavor, density or any crustiness. It is basically plain white bread shaped like a sack. I chose to try this with the Italian sweet sausage, pepper and onion grinder I ordered. I also had them throw in a load of banana peppers to add some heat to the project. Service was personal and informative. The dude actually sat across from me to discuss my options in detail when he learned I was a first timer at Julio's.  Cool!  I quickly discovered that the ingredients in the sammich were great, with high quality sausage, and plenty of pepper, onion and red sauce. However, the pouch was tasteless and did little to add to the experience. It wasn't worth the empty calories, so I ended up leaving most of it in the basket.   My word to the wise is to stick with a regular long roll with a crust and a little sour dough flavor. It might not hold all the contents without overflow, but that is why forks were invented.

Chicken To Go has been around a long time on the point of South Broad and Chambers in the Trentony  part of Hamilton, NJ. It was Cluck - U Chicken before that.  So, this place knows from fried chicken, wings, and sammich, not to mention, ribs, burgers and milk shakes. Although painted yellow inside and out, the overall locale might be considered seedy.  Lunch is the time for a reasonably secure check out.   Inside, the order/waiting area was surprisingly clean; much nicer than the exterior.  The people working there were friendly, and more than happy to explain the facts of life to a newbie.  I decided on The Original Chicken Sandwich on fresh Kaiser Roll Special, with lettuce, tomato and mayo.  A side of  Wedge Fries came along for the ride, as well as a drink.   While waiting, I looked around and was curious to see a new patio area for al fresco dining on the side of the building.  Although 94 F was a bit warm for sitting under a large umbrella, it did seem a nice idea for a cooler day.    When I opened my lunch bag at my desk, I beheld a large chicken breast, pounded and stretched, and well breaded for frying.  It stuck out of the tasty roll on all sides, with the lettuce and tomato making it slick, but still manageable.  This was no ordinary fast food chicken sandwich.  The chicken had not been frozen, and retained its proper texture and moisture. It was excellent, far better than Chik Fil A, or Mickey D's.  It was a filling meal by itself, and I ended up giving away most of the wedge fries to an officemate.   Next time (and there will definitely be a next time), I will try some fried chicken and/or BBQ charcoal ribs.  And, for those dessert extremists out there, they offer sweets from milkshakes to hot apple pie, and fried Oreos, Twix and Reese's Peanut Butter Cups.  Haven't had those since my son was camping with the Boy Scouts, and I was providing adult supervision.   (Yeah. Right!)

Maggio's is down on 2nd Street Pike in the deep corner of a shopping center. From the outside it looks like just another Italian resto in Southampton, PA, where so many others exist. But, looks can be deceiving. Walk in and you find a large space with a high ceilinged dining room with glass roof, separate barroom and lots of tables and booths for a big crowd. Check out the two menus (one for breakfast and another for lunch and dinner), and you realize that Maggio's is more a universal American diner with just about something for everyone, but with Italian style.   We stopped in for lunch after a nearby endorsement meeting. Escorted to a table and promptly handed both menus, our server patiently waited as we dove into their long list of offerings. Eight pages take a few minutes to work through, but we chose an American burger and Italian sausage, onions, peppers and provolone sandwich. Both came with fries and slaw. Prices were on the high end of reasonable, and I would have been disappointed had the meal not met expectations set by the cost.   Luckily, our lunch was very good. The sausage was housemade - a mix of sweet and hot - at the bottom of a good torpedo roll, overloaded with sauteed onions, green frying and jalapeno peppers and blanketed in melted provolone. Half was enough for me, and I wish that choice had been suggested in the menu. Still, it was excellent. The textural and flavor profile was extremely entertaining. It was one of the best versions of this classic I have eaten in quite a while. The fries were good, but I wasn't there for extra carbs. The coleslaw was minimal, but a subtle sweet undertone to the spicy onslaught of the sandwich. My buddy enjoyed every last morsel of his burger.   Maggio's is a worthwhile stop for folks in the area. I will stick to the earlier meals, as the prices associated with dinner are a bit daunting. If they are able to serve half sandwiches or soup/sandwich/salad combos, the house could be even more popular.

South Philly is all about neighborhoods, and one of the best ways of bringing the community together is to have corner cafes in abundance that provide a warm safe place for people to congregate over excellent java and light comfort food. Whether studying or being contemplative, such atmosphere tends to bring to best out in us. So it is with Shot Tower Coffee.  Sitting on the southeast corner of S. 5th & Christian, the large plate glass windows filter the afternoon light into a mellow golden glow that quickly transforms the small room into a spiritual center whose ambiance is palpable. No wonder people come and hope to stay as long as possible; sometimes on their laptops, and often is simple chats or just meditating as they mindlessly stare out the windows to the street life on the other side of this gossamer screen.   Not to mention that the bean life is also excellent, with friendly service folk who engage so well with customers.   My chai latte was a large glass mug of well designed and prepared tea and milk that had great mellow taste and aroma. Likewise, the vanilla latte was bright with subtle vanilla flavor, and only needed a short shake of brownulated sugar to climb to the proper sweetness.  A sucker for lemon bars, theirs was wonderfully tart with crunchy base.  Loved it!   Why is it called, "Shot Tower?"  Damned if I know, with its double meaning.  I'll leave that to the coffee historians.  All I know is that I'm glad to have finally stopped in and realized the pleasure of its charismatic grace.

Cold Spring has moved uptown from its original digs in an blown out old industrial building in Yardley, to this modern warehouse just south of 5 Points on Rt. 413, Wrightstown, Pa.  While the 19th Century look of the old place was cool, having an air conditioned space large enough to hold and display a vast variety of American and international suds, is an improvement.  They even have room for the mid-sized shopping carts that can hold a couple of cases while you shop and make way to the cashier.    We were in a Mexican fiesta mood, so picked up a 12 bottle case of Corona, and another of Dos Equis (XX) Sampler.  Bought a supply of Lime at Tanner Bros.   True, the price of cerveza goes up all the time, especially for the imports, but there is something to be said for comfort and convenience in brew buying.   Cold Spring opens at 9 during the week, giving it a leg up on other local distributors who open later in the morning.  Never too early for fiesta!

Solid local family plumbing business in Newtown, Pa.  They take pride in their work and really attempt to diagnose and solve your problem in the most efficient and cost effective way possible.  All their techs are competent and friendly.  They give you value for your money.  Be sure to check their other Yelp listing at Lucas Ltd for more reviews.

Stumbled on Trent City Pizzeria on my way back from court. I had stopped to pick up fresh coffee at Trenton Coffee House, and continued down Cass Street until I turned onto Lamberton Street to head back to the office. I didn't remember a restaurant being there.  It looked new and shiny.  Decided the time was right for lunch, so I parked on the street in front of the shop and went in.    It was indeed a new store.  Four booths. Seven stools along the walls. A big kitchen in back, separated by glass counters and work space.  Everyone spoke Spanish, and Telemundo was on the tube, yet the menu was all Italian with Spanish specials behind the counter for the asking. I went with my old standby, eggplant parm sandwich.  I sat and waited.  A couple of local street dudes came in for a bite.  We all fiddled with our smart phones waiting for our food.    The nightshade was pretty good.  Plenty of thin sliced eggplant, breaded and sautéed in olive oil.  Tender and nice taste.  The red sauce was ample, as was the mozzarella melted on top.  The roll was crisp from the oven's warm embrace.  It was a big sandwich, and came with fries. Left most of those behind to concentrate on the star of the show.    With a Snapple, lunch was $9 and small change.  Thought it good enough to warrant a return visit to sample the pizza, and perhaps a cheesesteak or Italian Hot Dog.

Enid C. has it right.   Pork Soy Sauce Noodle, Shaved.   It was textured to the bite, lots of surface area to pick up and hold the wonderful sauce; a large bowled experience with Ground Pork, mild Chili Flavor, Cilantro cooked into the mix, and enough liquid to cover every nano of the free form Noodles.   Did it change my life as suggested by Enid?  The jury is still out, but the fact that they are taking so long to decide is definitely a good thing.    I am hooked!  Just added 5 or 6 spoons of Sesame/Chili Oil from the table container, and the taste exploded in my mouth.   When a joint has over 800 reviews there is little left to distinguish one from the rest.  Short and sweet (In this case more spicy) is the way to go.

If you like Polish food, beer, and atmosphere, Larry's Corner Tavern is your kind of place.    Sitting at the corner of New York Avenue and Mulberry Street in the bowels of Trenton, Larry's is a cool oasis where Polish is the primary language, and English is used only when absolutely necessary. Even the Blackboard Specials are in the mother tongue, and require translation by Daria, the amazing bartender and hostess of the dark barroom and back lounge that is called a "Euro" Bar.    Although I was there for Pierogies and a drink, I had the misfortune of coming on a day when there were no Potato and Cheese Pierogies, but only the Meat version.  No, thanks.  Still, the menu had other options and I had their Burger that was dressed with Onions, Peppers, Cheese and a side of Hot Sauce.  (Sorry. Can't remember its name.)    It was very good, along with fairly standard French Fries.  The best part of the experience was my exchange with Daria.  She is a natural friendly, warm and even flirty woman, who keeps the totally male customers in line with funny bilingual quips, and a sharp repartee.  All the guys watch her with active imaginations, and she plays her part well.  Quite entertaining.   I will return to Larry's some time soon, but call first for the pierogies I remember as being superlative with sautéed onions and cool sour cream.  Maybe, I'll consider their kielbasa or blood sausage if my yearning for my grandmother's cooking becomes very strong.   Parking in the rear, and an outdoor area with picnic tables also available.

Mission BBQ on Roosevelt Boulevard in Northeast Philadephia, does pretty good BBQ ribs and chicken, especially for a joint north of the Mason-Dixon Line.  The house looks the part, with lots of dark wood, picnic-like tables and photos of first responders on the walls.   We ordered the equivalent of half racks of baby backs and regular spare ribs, and a half chicken.  All had sides of some sort, but aside from the fries and corn bread, those were not memorable. The ribs on the other hand were very good.  Pull off the bone smoked, with tender meat and nice rub and bark.  Each table had 6 bottle rockets with various sauces to be squirted on to moisten and flavor the chew.  None of them really stood out, and for the most part, the "as is" ribs were fine without anything more.    Prices were reasonable. Service was all at the order counter with no table service.   The consensus was that this was a legit BBQ joint that we would return to when the mood for pork ribs or pulled meat overcame us again.

Approaching Rozmaryn (Rosemary) Restaurant on a rainy January night takes a bit of courage.  The store front is a rowhouse with a neon "Open" sign in the window and an old unlit sign beneath it.  The front door is open and all you see is a long hallway with dim yellow lighting.  Sketchy characters on the sidewalk make you involuntarily prepare your fight/flight responses.  Be ready for anything...  But, first walk across Olden Avenue to the liquor store to pick up authentic Polish beer to make the experience complete.  In the back of the store is the Polish section.  More sketchy guys standing around - these 'packin' employees watch your every move.  But, the Xywiec Beer is back there in bottles or cans. I pulled out a six pack of glass and brought it to the counter. $10. minimum for credit cards, so I had to pull out my wallet (I really didn't want to do it).  Done. Walked back across the street and up the front steps of 925.  On the first door to the left was the restaurant sign bidding we enter.  What was behind the door?   I went in first.  I was greeted by an apartment converted into a small eatery.  Yellow walls, stained wood trim. Wall sconces, but little other adornment.  No one else in the main dining area.  We stood a moment and waited to see if someone would come out to seat us.  A few long seconds later a woman appeared from the rear with a warm smile and firm voice welcoming us to her shop.  She was the owner, hostess, and chef.  Very big persona.  Lovely, and I immediately relaxed.  At 6:30 we expected other patrons, but we were the first and only folks there all night.  She sat us at a central table for 4, allowing us to spread out.  NFL Playoffs had depleted her clientele, but we were quite happy to have all her attention.    After getting the lay of the land from the gracious Madame, we ordered off the rather small menu, which is in both English and Polish.  The Polish Plate to share as our appetizer.  It consisted of Meat Pierogies, Potato Pancakes, Kielbasa in Yellow Mustard, and Apple Sauce.  The Pierogies were the least enjoyable part of the dish. While the dough was lightly fried and was a good consistency, the meat was too dense and organ-tasting for me. The Potato Pancakes were large and thin, not very oily, and a good mix of potato and flour (to hold them together).  They were crispy on the edges and tasty with a dollop of Apple Sauce to mix a little sweetness with the mild saltiness of the latke. The Kielbasa was excellent.  Scored before grilling to help the heat penetrate and to avoid splitting, the outer skin was just firm enough to hold the link together, but when bitten, it gave way nicely to allow the very tender innards to meet the tongue, disclosing its softness and interesting spice.  It was the surprise star of the plate.  The mustard kicked up the flavor, but did not overwhelm the essence of the sausage.    We had the Stuffed Cabbage and Breaded Chicken Cutlet as our entries.  The Cabbage dish came with Mashed Potato and Cucumber Salad.  The Cabbage was tender and the mix of beef and something else was good, but perhaps a little bland.  It needed something to sweeten it, or at least that was how my Polish-Jewish grandmother prepared them. The potatoes were not hot enough, and seemed to have been plated before visiting the oven. Mild disappointment.  The Cucumber Salad was a cream base and decent.    My Chicken dish was excellent.  The breast was large, with a pleasantly hand dipped breading coating it.  I opted for Mushrooms rather than Tomato Sauce, and was very pleased with the freshness and amount piled on the chicken.  Very tasty and definitely something I would order again.  The mashed were again cool and I left most of them alone.  The Red Beet Salad finished the plate.  Served appropriately cold, it was a nice fit, bringing mild sweetness to the mix of flavors in the breading, chicken, and shrooms.  I was happy.  To complete the repast, we ordered the Blintzes stuffed with Farmer's Cheese, and dusted with Powdered Sugar.  These babies were wonderful.  Perfect crepe wrap, and a whipped sweet cheesy filling.  Light, and a perfect end to the meal with freshly brewed coffee.    This is a one of a kind richly local ethnic urban place that is easy to love.  The entire experience from the sidewalk scene, to the liquor store, to the special charm of the owner/chef, make Rozmaryn worth a visit or two.  When a meal becomes the food for a short story you have found something remarkable.   This was definitely that, and more.

Full disclosure - I am not a Walmart fan, nor do I enter their warehouse-sized stores very often.  Given the alternatives available for discount shopping, the guys from Arkansas are on the bottom of my list.   Still, when I needed to pick up a quick pair of glasses to replace the expensive ones my stepson lost somewhere, Walmart was the place to go, as their vision centers offer inexpensive prescription glasses and relatively fast turn around time.  In fact, we walked in shortly before they were to close their in house nook, and were taken care of promptly by one of the white coat people.  We were able to shop for frames, take eye measurements, and pay for the pair in about 20 minutes.  Lens to be ground and framed within a week.  Under $100, compared to the boutique price the first time around when I was willing to be generous, thinking the glasses would not be misplaced within a month of purchase.  My bad!   While in the store we walked over to the electronics department to check out phone chargers (another lost item by stepson), plus another for the office.  Found the prices to be about the same as online, but surprisingly few options for our Apple and Motorola mobiles. There was only one sales associate in the department, and she was helping another customer find something, while a queue formed at her register.  We were not the only customers to decide not to wait.    I felt a little unclean and hypocritical spending money in Walmart, but this was a semi-emergency.  To be fair, the vision center handled us well, and seemed dedicated to customer service.

Until checking Yelp, I always thought of The Brick Hotel in Newtown, Pa., as both the first floor restaurant/bar and upstairs bed & breakfast.  Apparently, it is separated by function on this site.  Still, for more than 200 years it has been known in the community only as The Brick Hotel; the hotel made of bricks. Historically famous for its existence during the Revolutionary War (Yes. George Washington was there for many meetings and meals during his wintering in the area after being expelled from New York by the British, and before decisively crossing the Delaware River and surprising the Hessians in Trenton on Christmas Day, 1776.)    Although somewhat modernized with large enclosed dining space on what was a wrap around porch, the structure is very well preserved inside and out, and it is easy to imagine what it was like 250 years ago.  That is also the main problem here.  Most of the upstairs bedrooms seem to have remained unchanged since the 18th or 19th Century, and it is looking pretty worn out in the 21st. It was recently the focus of an episode of Hotel Hell, but despite the free publicity and promises, little has changed since that exposure.  So, unless you enjoy such ambiance and reported ghost sightings, this may not be the place you want to rest your head.   On the other hand, the large first floor dining room makes a very nice place for a gathering for up to 100 people.  I have attended several public meetings and fundraisers there, and have enjoyed them all.  The barroom is small, but beautifully appointed.  You can pick up your open bar wine or beer there, and stroll into the meeting room to chat with folks before the speakers take the floor.  Too, there are usually a few tables with oer d'oeuvres to quiet those stomach rumblings so often associated with rubber chicken experiences (speaking of the politics, not the food).    So, if you find yourself in the area, and enjoy American history and pleasant surroundings, you might consider stopping in for a drink.  There are several other very strong bars/taverns/restaurants on State Street for you to visit and indulge.  The Brick Hotel is not a bad place to begin or end your adventure.    Tell them "George" sent you.

59 Almshouse is the address of an attractive roadhouse in Richboro, PA. It is all light wood and stone, with a cathedral ceilinged barroom that echoes with the sound of a full house at happy hour and a more sedate rear dining room for families and more intimate conversation.   We stopped in for dinner on a Friday evening, just in time to catch the last five minutes of HH. My watermelon-tini and the bourbon barrel aged ale were both nice to get our appetites revved for what was to come. Blackened fish tacos and Southwest burger got top billing. We found both fairly well constructed and tasty, although my try at creativity, asking that the side of fries be poutine-ized was somewhat less than hoped.   The cod in the tacos was fresh and well blackened in a frypan. The semi-authentic Mexican fixings (avocado, lettuce, aoili crema) we're on target. An enjoyable dish for sharing, although the tiny cup of black beans was cool and not flavorful. The burger was delivered partially medium (as requested), but partially rare, making for a hand packed patty that was partially quite good, and also half less than hot enough. Must have been grilled on the outskirts of the steel. Still, it was okay. The brown gravy that covered the fries was flavorful, but too heavy for the potatoes and turned them soggy, sacrificing texture and crispiness for something closed to chunky mashed. Didn't work for me, but it was my idea so I don't put that on the kitchen. Won't do it again.  We sat at a small booth in the barroom. Tight fit. The house was full of happy timers of mixed age, all having fun. It was obvious that '59' was a well known local hangout where everyone was welcome. We enjoyed the atmosphere.   Nice place.   3.5 Stars, rounded up.

Donuts seem to be making a comeback after years of suffering through the likes of Dunkin and other over extended chains turning out mimeographic fry dough, that are little more than a standard platform for applying a variety of colored sugar. Yawn!  Places like Factory Donuts have the right idea.  Make the donuts just in time for the customer to receive them hot from the oil bath and customized on the spot to suit their taste.  It works for burgers and pizza, why not for other fun comfort food? It is an idea whose time has come.   Of course, it really helps if the overall experience contributes to the enjoyment of the finished product.  Here, that is not quite the case. I noticed that the rounders were smaller than found in most other outlets; and more expensive. If you are going to charge over a buck for one of these babies, shouldn't each one be magnificent in taste, texture and size?  Not only were they diminutive compared to the competition, but the apparent variety of flavors was not quite real. To my tongue several varieties had different colors, but more or less the same taste.  That pretty red one was no different than that pretty purple one with sprinkles.   Hocus pocus.   I don't know about you, but I love a good cup of Joe with my glazed sugar fix. The java at the factory doesn't stand up. It is a bland commercial blend that does not contribute to the enjoyment of the moment. For a premium price, there should also be a premium bean.   Finally, when I buy a box of six donuts, I don't expect to eat them all immediately.  I will sample one to taste it warm, and wait a bit for the rest, sometimes until the next day to consume them all with help of friends and family.  The first one eaten while I was still in their parking lot was terrific.  Fresh cake out of the kitchen, glaze barely set to hardening - a pleasant jolt on the tongue. Teased and almost seduced. Yet, by that evening the thrill was gone, even with a short burst in the microwave. Come the next morning, there was little to enjoy beyond scraping the excess icing from the bottom of the box for the mouth rush hardened sugar provides.   It wasn't a complete fiasco, as watching the donuts being made and customized was fun, and they were truly very good right off the assembly line.  If they would up their game on the coffee, I would return knowing that I should only buy what could be eaten within an hour or so. Under those conditions, Factory Donuts would be a hit.

This H Mart is in a very congested part of Upper Darby, and parking is at a premium. Still, if Asian groceries are your game this is one of the best places to play, short of going down to Chinatown or Washington Avenue to load up.   Our goal was the purchase of a variety of excellent noodles to allow us to prepare our home version of Dan Dan Mien, a regular dish in our kitchen. H Mart has an aisle full of all kinds of them, thick to thin and made from all types of veggie flour. We scored both Japanese Style Alimentary Paste Udon and Somen long noodles, made in Japan with "unbreached" wheat flour. Distributed by Daiei Trading Co., Inc. of College Point, N.Y.   We walked around a few minutes to see if there was anything else we needed, but the store really isn't conducive to easy cruising down the aisles, with some product boxes piled up, shopping carts and two way traffic with bad drivers. So, we cashed out and returned to the car. Once there we only had to wait 10 minutes for the street to clear enough for us to back out from our parking spot and get back on our way.

The upper reaches of Washington Avenue are rather bleak with warehouses and abandoned buildings all around.  The only ray of light in the area of 15th Street is the corner Dunkin Donuts.  On a dark night, it is like seeing Las Vegas as you drive in from the desert.    This particular shop seems to be a hang out for a certain taxi company, where at any time of the day, the parking lot and surround curbs are parked up with off duty cabs.  The drivers stand around outside or sit within, chatting in their native tongues, and sipping the local brew.  All this adds to the color of the joint.    The coffee is pretty much standard issue DD.  Never great. Always adequate. The bakery offerings are below average, as if they are being made by people who don't really get the donut concept.  Maybe that's the way the cabbies like them.   It's hard to get excited about any Dunkin, and this one is no different.    Any caffeine in a storm.

The word, "Mega," normally suggests something very large, but in the case of Mega Quality Pizza it can't be related to the size of their shop, as it is quite small, with only four booths shoehorned into a tiny storefront in the 9800 block of Bustleton Avenue, Northeast Philly. So, maybe they are talking about the immense quality of their pies. Some people seem to like them a lot, but they have never been nominated as among the best pizza in this city. After grabbing a quick dinner there last week of their Steak Royal sandwich, Caesar Salad and Quesadilla at very reasonable prices, I can only conclude that the value offered by the quantity and quality vectors from the kitchen makes dining there a pretty big deal if your fortunate enough to find an empty table.   My Steak Royal was enough for two people with ordinary appetites, with a load of chopped ribeye, onions, sweet & hot peppers and a splash of red sauce. Of course, the bread makes the sandwich, and their bakery provider has taken good care of them with a premium crunchy torpedo that really came back to life with a few moments in the oven to turn the package into a crispy grinder. It was very good. The cheese Quesadilla was decent, too, but the need for simplicity kept it from being a standout. There is only so much you can do with a single ingredient grilled cheese, even when found in a hot tortilla. Such is the effect of dietary restrictions. The Caesar was mega large in a big bowl, but little more than romaine, tomato, feta, red onion shavings, a sprinkle of parmesan and a plastic cup of Caesar dressing. It wasn't so much that we couldn't finish it, but more that we not motivated to do so. It was fresh, but fairly generic.  With a third mouth to fill, we would have ordered a small pizza, too, but we did not need it for the two of us. That will have to wait for another visit. As Mega is right down the street from my favorite Chinese foot massage center, that may not be very long.   Is Mega Quality Pizza deserving of that name? Check it out and let us know.

Bon Appetit has a South State Street, Newtown, PA, address, but if you look for it along that historic main street you will not find it. In fact, it is in the same building as the new State Store, but in the back without signage on the primary boulevard. So, drive down the driveway that is the extension of Penn Street, toward the creek, and you will find it on the northwest corner of the liquor store edifice. There is parking along the building, and a larger lot a bit further away, but still well within walking distance.   The space is bright and airy, with glass exterior walls on two sides, and a twelve foot ceiling. There are a half dozen tables inside, and three more outside. The waterway is overgrown and can't be seen, but on a quiet morning, it can be heard gurgling its way toward the wild Neshaminy. Service this morning was provided by Joann, who was chief, chef and busser. She was friendly, and easily answered my questions about this new café in Newtown (there are shops in Princeton and Plainsboro, NJ, too).   Breakfast offerings are limited, but I jumped at the bacon, egg and cheese (gruyere) on croissant sandwich.  It was excellent. The large croissant was flaky and had a fresh, buttery taste. The combo of bacon, nutty cheese, and flat grilled scrambled egg, had a happy Friday party in my mouth. I ate slowly to savor the moment. The coffee from Shady Brook Roasters in North Jersey was an enjoyably strong washdown and pick me up.  Bon Appetit Newtown is a welcome addition to the community. Open at 7:30 am, it is ready for breakfast when you are. The lunch possibilities also looked interesting. Will make my way back for that soon enough.

Mavis Discount Tire on Jaymor Road, Southampton, PA, took me by surprise. When my regular tire place was closed early over the weekend, I found Mavis not far away by researching on Yelp. I knew Mavis existed, but had no clue whether they were reputable or rip off like some other rubber joints that hold customers up in services performed. No need to worry. These guys were not only straight ahead honorable, but had very competitive prices and were open on Sunday. A phone call led to a discussion of available options, set the price and secured an appointment with the tires put aside for me.   I arrived Sunday morning and was greeted professionally, yet personably. The manager went over the agreement, and had my car up on a lift within 10 minutes of arrival. I was allowed into the garage to oversee the removal and replacement of the four bad boys. They discovered something loose in the wheel, pointed it out to me, and repaired it easily without extra charge. They bagged two of the old tires for me in case I needed a spare in the future.   I learned that Kelly Tire was part of Goodyear, and carried a solid 55,000 mile warranty for their all weather version. On an AWD wagon that was important for all the things we used it for. I was also told to return soon for a final check on how the tires and wheels were acclimating. Will take care of that tomorrow.   I was impressed with how smooth the operation ran, as much as I was with the very reasonable price given without the need to hondle. Mavis was as good as my regular tire folks, if not a bit better with follow up.   Literally, one door closes early, and another opens to accept a happy new customer.

Salerno's III on Lower Ferry Road, Ewing, NJ, recently changed hands, but has not lost its verve.    I stopped in for lunch earlier this week thinking I would have two slices of pie and be on my way. Those plans quickly evaporated when I was handed their lunch menu by the friendly server wearing a wonderful Italian accent.  Available were many downsized dinner dishes at very attractive sub-$10. Okay. I gave it a try.   I ordered cavatelli aglio olio.  It came with a nice side salad, and a basket of garlic knots/rollups. It was a substantial meal that would easily last through dinner.  The salad was romaine based, with sliced tomato, cucumber and red onion, with a standard balsamic dressing. The bread was right out of the oven and very tasty, especially as sops for the garlic/oil bath of the pasta bowl.  The cavatelli was cooked well, with amply browned garlic throughout.  There may have been a bit too much broth on the bottom of the bowl, but it was easy to adjust to avoid drippage.    This was a very pleasing and substantial lunch.  It was certainly bigger than I have encountered in other Italian houses in the area, and the taste was very good.  Certainly, dinner would have been enough for two.    I came for pizza, but ended up with something much better - a complete meal that was as pleasurable as it was surprising.

First thing - You gotta know what you are dealing with here.   JC Fish Market & Soul Food is a Chinese house that does a very good fried fish.  I walked in expecting something else entirely.  But, with the proprietress shouting into the phone in Cantonese, and the two male workers answering her similarly, it was plain the soul food had a very eastern orientation.    There is only one 4 seat table in the joint, so this is fundamentally a take out shop - something these folks do very well. The menu is set up primarily for sandwiches, platters, fried chicken and dessert.  Prices are downright cheap, with the range for sandwiches between $3.75 - $6.95; regular platters (fries & cole slaw), $4.65 - $10.65; and the dinners (two sides, corn bread), $6.60 - $12.75.  The quantities are large, easily enough for 2.    Still, to make it work, you need to understand how the deal is constructed.  As a newbie, I ordered the Whiting Sandwich.  I watched as the three fish fillets were taken from the fridge, hand dipped in the breading, and placed into the deep fryer.  Five minutes later they were removed from the hot oil with tongs, and placed into a styro take away, with holes in the top.  A pile of pre-packaged plastic wrapped 2 slices of bread were placed on top of the container, and everything placed in a plastic bag.  Plastic forks and napkins were to the side for the taking.  I picked up a square of corn bread to taste @ .85.  The price was under six bucks.   Returning to my office, I opened the package and prepared to eat.  I took out the bread, slapped 2 of the 3 fillets on the first slice and closed the preparation with the top slice.  The bread was soft and fresh.  The Whiting Fillets were great! The breading was light with a pleasant spice mix.  The fish itself was thin and tasted as if it had never been frozen. The cooking oil was clean and added nothing to the flavor of the meal.  The corn bread was likewise fresh and mildly sweet.  No complaints. Impressive.   Knowing what I know now, I would probably head for the platters in the future, to grab a little greenery for my diet.  Too, if the fish was this good, I can imagine what they might do with the chicken.    If there is a downside to all this, it is that the meal certainly smelled like fish.  Now, my car smells of it, and my office smells of it, too.  People walking by my door were loudly sniffing and asking;   "Fish?"

I have visited several past incarnations of restaurants at this location on a gentle rise along the Delaware River and Delaware & Raritan Canal.  No wonder successive owners have tried to make a go of a comfortable retreat here.  It is really quite lovely, especially before dusk when the western orientation raises a curtain on some magnificent sunsets. This was my first meal at Erini and I looked forward to the opportunity to enjoy a repast in the large and well appointed dining rooms of the past.   Walking in past the well fed cats, I soon saw that little had changed within. Same bar crowded at happy hour, and same spacious dining area.  Although we were early, the hostess easily sat us at a nice table, and the server brought us menus and took our drink order.  Seemless. We ordered the Grilled Salmon and Chicken Marsala, foregoing apps and sides in the expectation that we would have a substantial dinner.   And, substantial they were.  Both plates were large - steamy, colorful  and textural  in presentation. We dug in.  Not to bring you down too quickly, but nothing was quite as good as it at first appeared. The Salmon, although a nice size steak, was not first quality according to my companion.  She found it too "fatty," and less than the tight morsel she desired.  Good sauce, nice Roasted Potatoes, but still disappointing. My Marsala has a similar story.  The chicken was slightly overcooked in the fry pan and lacked moistness. The sauce, though plentiful, was monotonal and lacking finesse.   It was all good, but not good enough to make me a fan. Kudos to the staff that was professional and engaging. The Happy Hour trade is a success, and perhaps that is where the sweet spot is at Erini.

Tikal Restaurant & Lounge is the successor to the venerable Rossi's Bar at the corner of Morris and Franklin in the Chambersburg section of Trenton, NJ.  At one time, Rossi's was considered to grill the best burgers in the city. When they moved out to Quakerbridge Road in Hamilton, there was a big void left behind.    That emptiness has now been replaced with this well appointed  casa Guatemalteca. I stopped by for lunch recently and was impressed with the quality of the finished space.  The old square bar had been replaced with a wall unit with attractive wooden back bar.  There was new furniture in the barroom as well as the rear dining room.  New windows on the world were stenciled with the new name and its Mayan pyramid logo. Tikal is a famous historic site in northern Guatemala where the Mayan Civilization build a large city and temple complex before the arrival of Europeans, or even the Chinese before them.    The menu is a bit of a fusion exercise, with a large national delicacies list, and a few Americano dishes like hamburgers and cheesesteaks with a definite Central American flair.  They also blend up excellent shakes and fresh fruit bedidas, using your choice of water or milk base.  I took a stool on a hightop in the barroom, and was served by bartender, Ana.  She had the right temperament for the job, and was friendly and prompt with menu, order taking and food delivery.  She was also patient as I worked my way through the menu looking for the right combination for lunch. She finally recommended the Tikal Wrap, with came with papas fritas.  I also ordered a mango smoothie as a washdown.    The drink arrived in a tall frosted glass.  The mango mix with water was cool, semi-sweet, tasty and very refreshing.  The wrap was a monster, full of grilled chicken, lettuce, black beans, avocado, tomato and an interesting piquant sauce. I ate as much as I could, knowing that I would be skipping dinner that night.  It was excellent. The ample pile of fries was more than I could handle, but they tasted great with the spicy mayo that came in a bottle rocket on request. The app chips and homemade salsa were overkill, but I did dip a couple of the triangular chips, and thought the salsa nicely spiced.   Tikal is one of the higher end Guatemalan houses in the Trenton area, and definitely worth a visit for lunch or dinner.  Prices are very reasonable.  I am particularly curious about their burgers, given the gloried history of the joint.  As I am not a fan of the new Rossi's, it would be ironic and poetic justice if the new Latin take on this American classic was better than the "new" original.    Sometimes the city is the secret sauce that make for magical dishes.

Diana Vincent and Vincent Polisano are the principals of Diana Vincent Jewelry Designs in Washington Crossing, Pa., and now also Lambertville, New Jersey. If you have had the pleasure of visiting their well appointed, yet comfortable shop on General Greene Road, you have seen beautiful pieces of gem and high end metals in unique and very attractive design.   I am particularly attracted to the exquisitely cut colored gems; peridot, tourmaline, aquamarine, topaz, and similar stones.  Each is a marvel of contemporary cutting techniques that capture the inner light and project it directly to the brain, where it explodes with intense pure color. Surrounding each is a gold, platinum, silver or steel setting that support the stone in ways that allow the central star to shine while offering their own gracefulness. There are many other stones there, each carefully selected for their intrinsic value.  If they don't love the stones they see, they don't buy them. It is simple. Only work with what your feel an emotional connection.   I recently brought in a beautiful peach tourmaline and asked Vincent to design a ring around it.  We discussed my ideas, and he offered his with a few simple sketches.   I was excited by the opportunity to work with him.  He had a rough setting in his workshop that he brought up to show me.  He described how he could do something like that in any metal.  It would be one of a kind, and would be ample enough to house the stone without detracting from its inner light.  I had to use my imagination to see the finished product, but I liked what he was saying.  The suggested price range seemed reasonable, and I told him to go ahead.  The final result was a silver shaft four prong base gently gripping the tourmaline in its four fingered embrace with small diamonds at the end of each prong like a period at the end of a poetic verse. It was beautiful.   Give yourself the chance to visit Diana Vincent and fall in love with their work.

PIZZA BY THE SLICE REVIEW  Nova Trattoria recently moved to this location, replacing the Mexican casa that was there before. It is a smallish space with a row of tables along the wall, with kitchen on the opposite side behind another wall that gives the appearance of being a very narrow dining room.   I ordered a slice of Brooklyn pie and another tradition regular triangle. The Brooklyn slice was pretty good - thin crust, Marzano sauce and dollops of mozza in a square pan. It was firm, crisp and pleasantly chewy.  The regular slice was not as good.  The crust was limp despite requesting it be reheated well done, and there was ample oil drip onto the paper plate. Just not a strong presentation.  The price was good at around $5 for the slices and bottle of water. Service was pleasant from start to finish.   There is much better pizza and tomato pie right nearby.

If you are a Spaetzle lover, Barbara's Hungarian Restaurant is your Nirvana.  Ask for a side of the East European doughy pasta, and it will arrive covering the entire plate. To its credit, it is pretty good, especially with the sour cream mixed into it.    The rest of our meals were not up to its signature dish.  We ordered the Mushroom Stew and Breaded Chicken Cutlet (Schnitzel).  The Mushrooms were canned, and the sauce the same weak reddish liquid that was at the bottom of the chicken dish.  Little imagination. Less taste.   Canned mushrooms? Really?   The Chicken Breast was large, thick and nicely breaded.  It was juicy, and would have been the winner but for the saltiness of the coating.  It was obvious no one had bothered to taste the ingredients and preparations in the kitchen.    Both dishes came with Spaetzle overload.  The Mushroom Stew was really canned shrooms and spaetzle, with nothing else to make it a "stew."  The chicken lay naked on another thick bed of the same thing.  Nary a garnish or side dish to break the monotony.  It must have been obvious, because we were offered a Cucumber Salad by Barbara when she saw how forlorn our meals appeared.  That salad was the best part of the meal, although it would have been nice to know we were being charged $5 for that small bowl with sweet vinegar and thin sliced cukes.    Maybe, they were having a bad night, but based on our experience I wouldn't consider going back.  There are far better East European restaurants in the area where the cuisine really shines.

We ordered the Soy and Sweet Chili Wings, as well as an attractive plate of Kimbap on a late Sunday afternoon in September.   The house was dressed up in red and black lacquer, and KPOP blasted from the audio system.  Service was spotless.  We had the side room to ourselves.  So, while Soho may be SRO by night, if you want the great food without all the hustle, hassle and wait, try earlier in the day.   From the look of most reviews, everyone already knows how awesome the Korean Fried Chicken (KFC) wings are. Double fried, and heavily dipped and basted, they arrive plump, crisp, loaded with flavor and plenty of juicy meat.  At a buck a wing, you are paying more than in the standard Buffalo wing joints, but there is really no comparison to the quality of the experience.  I was blown away.   The Kimbap looked like sushi roll, but my server was adamant that they were very different.  Very good in their own right, but to my untrained palate, they were quite similar.    Café Soho is on Cheltenham Avenue, in the town by that name.  It is not the most convenient place to transport to, except for the locals who discovered it years ago.  It is 30 minutes from mi casa in Bucks County, and likely even farther from Center City, Philly.  The travel adds to the excitement, so when it is finally seen on the near horizon, the heart quickens, and the saliva flows, in anticipation.  Walking in is entry to an alternate Korean universe.  Don't worry. Everyone is bilingual and very friendly.  The music is cool and hot (like the wings), but loud enough to interfere at times with conversation and appetite.   Don't let that stop you.  The Wings are the Thing!

Walking into Pete's Steakhouse on North Olden Avenue, Ewing, NJ., is like falling down the rabbit hole in Alice in Wonderland.  From the outside, the place is nothing special, but on the inside, the joint is as bright and shiny as a new penny. Clearly, these folks put a lot of effort into polishing the place to a loud red and silver hue. That, and the old bicycle hanging from the ceiling, and the James Dean, "Devil Without a Cause," poster, tell you what is going on.    Welcome back to the 1950's!   I was there for breakfast this week, although a lot of the menu deals in burgers, cheesesteaks and other grilled dishes.  Still, the breakfast possibilities were not a short list, and I was able to chose from pancakes, omelets, and morning sandwiches.  I opted for the french toast, which was a full plate (6 half slices) of vanilla and sugared egg dipped decent bread.  Melted butter and a nice pour of syrup (not maple), and it was ready to eat.    It was a decent version of one of my favorite breakfasts.  Caramelized enough to enjoy the light crunch along the edges, and thick enough to absorb a lot of the egg and the follow on butter and syrup.  It wasn't the best of breed, but I was not complaining. Tasty and filling. The mugga joe was hot and strong, just as I like it.  At $10 and change for the meal, it was about what I expected from the outlets in the area.   But, the atmosphere was what really sets the place apart from other diners and cafes.  It is different enough to be refreshing.  Will return for the burgers and revisit the rating, but for now, three and a half stars is about right. Round up to 4.  NOTE: The name, "steakhouse," is a misnomer, as the only steaks available here come on a long role with cheese and onions.

Two Slices & and Drink Review Only -   The image in mind from the name was of an Italian shop anchored by the culture and cuisine of the eastern shore of the boot.  Not quite.  In fact, the reference is to the other side of the Adriatic Sea.    I went in for a quick dinner of their pizza.  The dining room was attractive with marble walls and tile floors.  The counter zone housed the ovens and the shelved display of pizzas already made and waiting for reheating. Wanting to sample the wares, I asked for one regular and another sausage.  They were about the largest slices of pizza I had ever seen, and in truth, one would have been enough.  Eyes bigger than stomach, I retreated to a table to await delivery.  All the while, the phone rang off the hook with take out orders, which were all fielded smoothly by the young woman dealing with this.  She asked good questions, and kept her poise and easy manner.    There is always a risk in consuming pie that has been sitting around for a while.  Sometimes, even when requesting "well done," it is not left in the oven long enough to revive the underlying taste of the pizza when first constructed, or they have been out so long that no amount of fire resuscitation will bring them back to life.  Such was the case this night.  The copious cheese topside was hot, but not enough to allow the flavor to come to the fore.  The undercarriage dough was amply scorched, and better than what was supported above.  Just not much life there.  The sausage triangle was similar.  The pellet shaped meat was cooler than the cheese around it, and lacked any real taste at all.  It left me wondering where they found this sausage vendor, because it neither looked, nor tasted, Italian.    No doubt Adriatic Pizza is a popular spot for fresh pies and platters judging from the orders calling in, and the other reviews.  It is just not a good place for reheat jobs, even with an incredible price of under $5. for everything.

Decent D & D on West Trenton Avenue, Morrisville, right next to Italian Peoples Bakery.  Run by an efficient and friendly crew.   The coffee is okay, but not outstanding.  The baked goods are also right down the middle of the road.  My Everything Bagel with Light Veggie Cream Cheese filled the need to quiet my stomach until after court.   Plenty of parking at a mildly difficult intersection.

My second visit to Bristol in one week after a few years absence. Mill Street is coming back to life, and the area close to the Delaware River seems to be spearheading the revival. It is great to see a renaissance in this old river city.  It has suffered hard times through some neglectful governments and perhaps not so fatherly town elders. Yet, it is hard to keep a good old ville down when it has natural beauty and a real purpose over the centuries.  So it is with the King George II Inn. Originally built to be close to the ferry to Burlington, New Jersey, the only way across this water course for more that 250 years AFTER the ferry was started, the KGII evolved into a restaurant and subsequently an inn. Sitting in the oldest part of the building, the tavern, it is easy to imagine what it was like to be living and traveling in colonial America.  The various farmers, businessmen, hucksters, cons, grifters, and cutthroats gathered here to do their business, and wait for the ferry to take them to the colony of West Jersey.   Even today, that historic atmosphere permeates the Inn. Certainly there are ghosts stories aplenty.  I stopped into the Tavern for late lunch, sitting at a small table at the window overlooking the bottom of Mill Street, and the river just beyond.  The server (who was as gracious as an owner) greeted me warmly, took my order, and left me to my mental wandering.  The Pierogies appeared on a long thin white dish, covered in sautéed onions and fresh chives. A dollop of sour cream occupied one corner.  They were lightly fried, potato and cheese. They were pretty good at 6 for $9. I knew I was paying for the privilege of location.  No complaints.  The Tavern itself was excellently preserved and rehabbed to feel very original. All dark woods, heavy oak tables, and mirrored bar.  A perfect place to reenact debates between Patriots and Tories over lagers and locally distilled whiskey.    It is certainly worth a visit and a meal if you are into American history.  It is not quite Williamsburg, Va., where the entire community is a historic park and everyone is in costume.  Still, with a little imagination it is capable of taking you on quite a trip.

In my search for the best bagel in the Trenton/Hamilton matrix, I stumbled upon Tina's Bagel Factory.  It is attached to Tina's Italian resto; and they no doubt share their pizza oven.    While I did not expect much, it turned out to be the best bagel I have tried so far in the area.  Not too dense as most of the other purveyors are; Tina does not over knead the dough, leaving air pockets throughout to keep the heart of the bagel light and the skin crunchy. Kudos!  I will be back as time allows to see if I just got lucky or she really knows what she is doing. But, for now, Tina goes to the head of the bagel class.    Nosh on!

Pho Ha is a utilitarian furnished soup shop in the heart of Philly's Little Ho Chi Minh City on Washington.  The tables and chairs are built for speed, not comfort, but given how fast they turn out a large bowl of Pho and Bun Bo Hue (weekends only), it is understandable that you will not be there very long.   We came in around six on a Saturday evening, and the place was nearly empty.  We were warmly greeted, directed to a table, and asked for drink preferences within 60 seconds.  After ordering Pho Tai and Bun Bo Hue, we barely had time to start a conversation before the steamy aromatic pots of soup were placed before us.  Don't ask why I went with the large option because I couldn't finish even half of it.  Even the small bowl was big enough to be a goldfish pond.   The soup was loaded with a variety of meats, veggies and noodles, floating in a richly spiced broth that tasted of secret recipe. Even my protégé, a restaurant owner in her own right, could not identify all the subtle flavors overlapping and melding with each other.  While she might attempt to concoct the Pho, she was at a loss with the Bun. Guess I'll have to return to Pho Ha if I want to be blown away by that mystical brew again, although rumor has it that it can be found in other hidden springs in the area.    I enjoyed Pho Ha both for it authenticity and its location in the midst of the Asian community that is growing in South Philly.  It is convenient to shop, eat and even massage within a small walking area and dream that I am back in HCMC enjoying the exotic culture that is Vietnam.  Cash only. ATM in house.

Old Friends Pizza, way down on Hulmeville Road, Bensalem, PA, has just enough table space for a few old friends to join you to mange Italiano. Four tables. Four chairs per. If you want to invite more than 16, well, that just can't happen.   You also need to be sure the air conditioning is working, otherwise the party will be a little uncomfortable dealing with the heat and humidity, as I was.   Not in the mood for pizza, I ordered an eggplant parmijiana sandwich on torpedo roll. I passed on the suggestion to add fries to that. Saw no need for the extra calories. I found a chair in the empty dining room and watched the Thursday afternoon rain through the storefront window.   One of the kitchen guys served my lunch on ceramic plate. So much better than paper. It was a large production, with thick slices of breaded and browned melanzone, layered with chunky red sauce and overlain with melted provolone by a turn in the oven. It was really too zoftig to pick up by hand and jam into my mouth. So, I asked for knife and fork - the table tools associated with proper dining. In reply, I was handed two thin plastic utensils.   They both failed the strength test, as they bowed and cracked attempting to cut through the sammy. The knife gave up from the density of the bread, and snapped in half. I decided to eat the eggplant, sauce and cheese with the fork used to pull things apart before spearing. Not the funnest way to go.   The taste was pretty good, but needed more sauce and less oil. It would also have benefited from thinner slicing and hotter pan to sear the copious coating, rather than the oil being absorbed into it.   This was not Old Friends finest hour. Pizza would have been a better way to go.

Another fairly typical urban Chinese/American house on Broad Street in Trenton.  They have all the classics on the menu from General Tso's Chicken to anything with Broccoli, and Steamed/Pan Fried Dumplings.    Nothing is outstanding, but neither is it beyond the pall.  My Egg Foo Young was thick and loaded with Veggie and Pork.  The Brown Sauce seemed identical to all the others I have tried in such joints.  The Pork Fried Rice had the brown tint of beef stock base, and the Egg Roll was mostly cabbage with a bit of something else - perhaps, pork.   At least, China Garden seemed cleaner than many of the others.  Too, it is obviously a family place because the owner's son was on site and helping out, though he seemed no more than 12.    The people are friendly, are fully bilingual, and the prices seem like from the 1990's, perhaps because they have been there so long and making a go of it in part because of the low rent on that strip of Broad Street.    It's not the place to take a date, but it is certainly decent enough for a combo lunch or cheap and filling dinner.    Garden? Can't see the connection from out front or inside.  But, maybe they all fly away to a secret place at night, or have a small cultivated plot out back.

Bagel Barrel on West State Street, Doylestown, PA, has been around for a while, and aside from the Manhattan Bagel shop a few blocks away, is the only game in town for boil and bake rounders. The joint is cozy with small dining area, self serve coffee and very reasonable prices. It's a nice place to hang out with friends and family (if you can find a table).   Downside is that their bagel style is not my fave. They are on the small side and more densely textured than I prefer.
