To my buds, they taste like sour dough loaf with thin shell and lots of sprinkles (onion being my primary choice). The quality is there, but I jump for a lighter, air-pocketed inside, crisper shell and less sour flavor. It comes down to the base flour used and the amount of kneading before forming the ring of dough that becomes the bagel. Like pie crust, less is more when it comes to great texture.   Everyone behind the counter was pleasant and having a good time when I was there. That's always a good sign for a positive atmosphere. If they made the kind of bagels I loved, I would stop in regularly. As it is, Bagel Train in Yardley will continue to be my station for awesome bagels in Bucks County.

If excellently crafted chocolate wasn't sexy enough, calling it, "Naked," is completely over the top.   Housed in a small shop in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center, this outfit is a one trick pony of creamy, succulent candies that have your taste buds working overtime to cope with the sensory load. It all looks fantastic, and the samples at the counter make certain you try enough to bring you back for more.   The one downside is the expense of self indulgence. The bonbons are $2.50 apiece, so a medium size box assortment hits $30 before you can take a breath. You really have to love someone (or yourself) to make that commitment. Well, I did and I do, so I won't be too disappointed in myself.   Yes, my friends were duly impressed. The little balls of intense flavor wrapped in excessive opulent cacao were all that. With a good red wine chaser it was a near orgasmic experience. I watched as they bit their first bonbon and began to chew. Their eyes rolled to the back of their heads and a involuntary gasp escaped their lips.   No doubt the best way to enjoy these delights from Naked Chocolate is to be naked yourself with someone you love.   Soon.

GuatePan Latin American Bakery is a local chain of three bakeries serving the greater Guatemalan and Latin American community of Trenton, NJ.  This particular location is the original shop, and it is large enough to have tables for breakfast and lunch.  The long display cases are a visual treat with colorful cakes, cookies, rolls and pastries under bright lights that make each come alive with sweets temptation.   My Desayuno Tipico Guatepan was a large plate with double fried eggs over tortilla, black beans, platanos, sausage, queso fresa, and salty goat cheese.  A choice of toast or tortilla completed the deal.  Everything was fresh and tasty, with the combination of flavors and textures competing for attention.  It was a fun solid meal to start the day.  Too, the coffee was strong and came in a large insulated carafe that never seemed to empty.    I left quite full, and unable to consider picking up a few of the beauties behind the counter (speaking of the pastries).  The house was full of families enjoying themselves, as well as regular walk in customers picking up their daily dough.    It is no wonder that GuatePan has been so successful.  They have a large constituency that appreciates the quality of the products the backroom bakery turns out, as well as the clean and friendly atmosphere created for their families to enjoy a repast together.   Too bad its sibling stores don't have room for dining, because there is no doubt they would draw like iron to magnets.

If this is the "Old Neshaminy Inn," I really want to see the new one!   This local tavern is new and modern, with large barroom, long bar, multiple HDTVs, and a better than average menu that will keep people coming back for an inexpensive pint and decent grub. It was refreshing to be able to pay a reasonable price for Angry Orchard apple cider, a personal size Old Trenton square tomato pie, chicken parmesan dinner, bowl of chili, and 10 blazing buffalo wings, and get change for my $50. That doesn't happen every day.  The atmosphere is noisy with high ceiling in the main room that amplifies sound. Upside, you know your conversation is private; downside, you can't always hear what your table mates are saying. The music is a mix of 70's through contemporary rock, which fits my groove well. Service is fine with women who seem to like people and have a sense of humor. Always appreciated.   The food? Solid bar offerings that can surprise you with it's taste and quality, but may not be consistently so. Big pluses on the chili, tomato pie, and hot wings; a little off on the chicken parmesan dinner. To be clear, the pizza was very good with crunchy crusty edges, tart marzano tomatoes and decent cheese. Not what you get at the new DeLorenzos', but a pleasant alternative. Chili was mildly sweet beneath the heat, and the wings brought tears to my eyes just sitting on the table. The dinner parmesan needed more flavorful sauce, especially with the load of penne it came with. Even dry pepper flakes could not compensate for the lack of spice in the pot. At $20, that was disappointing.   Next time, we will stick with the sandwiches, pizza and burgers - more traditional barfood - rather than treating Old Neshaminy Inn as an Italian restaurant, which it really isn't (yet?).   3.5 Stars

Manny's Restaurant & Delicatessen is the new name of the former Steve Stein's Deli on Buck Road in Holland, PA. It has been open for a few weeks, and it appears many of the old customers remain as regulars to enjoy the kosher style smoked meats, soups and salads for which the former management was renowned. The floorplan is attractive with large ceramic tiles on walls and ceiling and the dining room separated from the deli by a semi wall that still allows you to glimpse the operation and smell its delights.   The menu is small compared to its predecessor, so you may not find every ethnic dish hoped for. Still, there was enough for me to find something I liked for lunch. I went with a soup/sandwich combo of split pea and chicken salad on rye for $9.50. Service was friendly and attractive.   I wasn't overwhelmed by what arrived at my table a few minutes later. The split pea soup was thick and hot, but was salty and lacked any extras like croutons or other textural enhancements to add interest. The chicken salad was okay, but again monotonal in taste and lacking in chunkiness. Overall, a ho-hum lunch. Not bad, but lacking a spark to draw me back. Prices high for what they offer.

This was my first visit to Bonefish Grill. I guess I was always put off by their logo of a fish skeleton. Kinda spooky. But, we were nearby, and it was lunchtime, so for a moment I wasn't drawn to thinking about death when I saw the restaurant on Oxford Valley Road just near the mall.   The atmosphere and decor was quite nice, with lots of dark wood, large bar and servers wearing white chef coats. We were taken to a booth in the barroom. It was comfortable, with last century rock & roll playing on their sound system. We were brought menus that included both light lunch options and more substantial dinner choices. We went with Fish Tacos (Blackened Cod) and Fish & Chips.   Both were good, especially the tacos which included mango pieces for sweet juiciness to interact with the spicy salsa. Two were enough. The F&C was also good, but I wished that the outer breaded shell was less oily, as it didn't work as well with the lightness of the fish within. Still tasty, but the inconsistency was palpable. Service was excellent with our friendly white coat attentive and suggestive.   We agreed that we would certainly give Bonefish another try when the mood for seafood struck us.

TAPS Sports Bar on Veterans Highway, Levittown, PA, is a small tavern in the same old strip center as New Madison Restaurant. It is a large step up from the former dive dump bar that occupied this space for many years. Simple basic decor is true, but the clean up makes it show off its better attributes. The old adage that a thick coat of paint hides a multitude of sins, is very much in play here. The staff is friendly and the kitchen competently handles the menu.   It wasn't busy when I walked in to watch the second half of the Sixers game against OKC ( they lost by 2 in an exciting finish). There was a pod of millennials doing jello shots at the pool table and a dude manging a pizza a few stools away from me. I checked the menu while swallowing a cool Sam Adams Winter Lager. The pierogis were tempting, but I asked if they were homemade or frozen, and being the later, I opted for the Italian Sweet Sausage, Pepper and Onion Sandwich.   The sammy looked great on the plate. It was large, stuffed and in a fresh tasty absorbent roll which held it's own first bite to last, even with dipping into the red sauce. The sausage was on the grill too long and a tad dry, but still a satisfying chomp and chew. Plenty of peppers and 'yuns to nicely influence flavor. I had to ask for a fork, but there seemed to be a shift change going on and I could see how that oversight could happen.   TAPS is a family owned and operated watering hole in the heart of Levittown. It is a comfortable clubhouse for hanging out with friends, having a few while cuing balls on green velvet. Its grill and oven are capable for comfort food. That's okay because it doesn't pretend to be more than it is.

Surburban Diner has the misfortune of sitting at one of the ugliest intersections on the East Coast - Street Road X Bustleton Pike.  Man, where were the urban planners when we needed them? Recently with all the bad weather drivers have been too busy dodging potholes to notice that the entire zone is really one Grand Canyon sized pothole. Once safely in the parking lot the challenge becomes finding a slot for your wheels.  The lot is undersized for the capacity of the facility, but if you drive behind the building and turn right, you might get lucky.    Once inside, the familiarity of Diner World takes control and you know what needs be done.  Wait to be seated at booth or table, or slide past the throng at the door, turn right, and take a spinning stool at the counter - no waiting. So moved.  I was promptly greeted by a kind waitress in black and white who deposited a multi paged breakfast menu and inquired about a drink.  Coffee, please.  She turned and poured mine into a white mug from the antique Cecilware Auto Coffee Urn.  Can't get those any more, but back in the day they were the best way to make large volumes of java. Still great Joe. She returned often to refill.    I ordered the Whole Wheat French Toast.  It arrived on white oval industrial ceramic, dusted with powdered sugar.  The middle slice of bread stood on edge mid-plate, like a mainsail mast in a sea of Maple Syrup.   The bread was fresh and a thick cut.  It was super absorbent.  No matter how much syrup I pour on it, there was nothing at the bottom of the plate to sop up with the FT.  Three additional pours and still not a drop.  Oh, but the meal got sweeter.  I was impressed.    In years of French Toast sampling, I have come to prefer a thinner sliced bread over the thicker version, because the egg absorbs more completely, and with a hot grill carmelization takes place where hot metal cauterizes the egg/bread surfaces, creating a mild crispiness.  Still, this stuff was pretty good for thick cut, and I had no complaints.    Clearly, Suburban Diner has its loyal followers.  A look around the dining room disclosed a predominance of seniors, some with children and grandkids.  The place seemed wholesome. The bakery turned out some pretty cakes and pies.  Maybe next time for that.    With "I Love Lucy" playing in black and white on the TV, it was easy to slip into a time warp and imagine myself in a Back to The Future moment.    I enjoyed the experience on several levels, but I am not sure I would put Suburban Diner on my short list of fandom.

Lucas Plumbing and Lucas Ltd. are one in the same.   Had Brandon back to the house today to repair a balky toilet in the downstairs powder room.    Yes. He was a few hours later than originally scheduled, but that was beyond his control.  He ran into a one hour job that required four hours of work.  At least, the office called me twice with a heads up, and offer to reschedule.    Our job was truly one hour, and he was handing me the invoice in 50 minutes.  Not cheap by any stretch, but done right and with a positive attitude.    These guys have my loyalty.

We have the original Piccolo Trattoria in Newtown, PA, and watched with satisfaction as it succeeded to the extent of opening a second restaurant in Pennington, NJ., and now creating a new concept in Italian dining - fast casual, build your own pizza/pasta/salad.  Fahmi is a great guy, and deserves his good fortune.    I stopped in this afternoon to finally sample something from this new venture.  Not in the mood for designing my own personal pizza on this 90+ degree day, I decided to try a simple pasta dish - Penne Aglio Olio w/ Sauteed Spinach.  That combination was put together in the mostly open kitchen as I waited at the cashier to pay for lunch.  Yelp had a check in gift of a free soft drink, which was easily negotiated in exchange for a 16 ounce paper cup (regular price, $2.50).   The store is very bright with a wall of windows, high ceiling, and plenty of lighting. There are large sign on every wall with menus, instructions for building your meal, and goodwill sayings and quotes. A serious effort is made to be friendly, informational, and efficient.  I received salutations from most of the employees by the time I left the building. The company also is involved in the community, and makes generous contributions to many local charities. A big check for $6,000+, payable to the Trenton Soup Kitchen, sat in one corner of the dining room.   Impressive and heartwarming!   My pasta was served in an orange bowl on a metal tray.  Drinks and silverware were available farther down the assembly line beyond the cashier.  It was a good size portion for lunch, with ample olive oil and mashed garlic cloves.  A sprinkle of crushed dried hot and black pepper, and I was looking for a seat near a window. I am obliged to disclose that it was far from the best oglio olio I've ever had, with the garlic not sautéed long enough to turn it golden, and thus having a raw flavor rather than the mellowness of well cooked garlic in extra virgin oil.  Too, the spinach was in two large soft clumps, rather than spread throughout the dish.  It was next to impossible to separate the leaves, and the garlic taste did not penetrate to maximize flavor. A little more training in the kitchen would correct this preparation issue.  Overall, I like what Piccolo Pronto is about -  making traditional Italian dishes, pizzas, sandwiches, etc., available at lower cost with good ingredients and friendly service.  A little tinkering with small details could easily bring the final result up a few notches. Certainly the folks around the College of New Jersey have a good place to eat, but I hope for something more enticing to bring me back as a regular customer.

China Gourmet is a very pleasant surprise if you, like me, love a traditional dim sum Chinese brunch every once and a while.   Situated on St. Vincent Street in Northeast Philly between Brous Avenue and Roosevelt Boulevard in Mayfair, it is a large house in a developing Asian neighborhood that puts out trolley carts loaded with small dish treats both savory and sweet, at reasonable prices and with the expected hussle and flow that this dining style uniquely delivers. Admittedly, the aggressive nature of the cart ladies hawking their delicacies takes some getting used to. You have to be able to say "no" when you feel overwhelmed by the surrounding din. But, know that slowing down the onslaught is proper, and multiple opportunities will present themselves. Just take what you want in the moment and let the trolley women return when you are ready for more.   The most important thing at China Gourmet is that they know from dim sum. There are dozens of choices and most of them are good to great. Shrimp and pork shumai, shrimp hargow, beef rice rolls w vinegar, fried stuffed buns, various dumplings, fish filled chili peppers, egg tarts and many others are well prepared and served hot or cold as appropriate. My bowl of congee was also decent with plenty of ground pork and fresh cut scallion on top. There is plenty more, but you get the picture.   What's even better is the availability of FREE PARKING right in front of the restaurant, and the large Asian supermarket and Vietnamese kitchen right next door. The money saved is like getting a 25% discount off your check! Hard to beat!   Now that we've experienced the fun and convenience of a strong dim sum morning with grocery shopping for dessert, Chinatown has lost some of its cultural luster for us (not completely).   Gotta love it!

The best place I stayed in Tucson.  The rooms were renovated and comfortable. They overlooked the golf course and Santa Catalina Mountains. They had a small balcony, a perfect place for first coffee as the course was being watered and the mountains glowed in the morning sun.    Because I was working during the day, the family was happy to have so many entertainment options right on campus.  The swimming area kept my young son happy. He is a young seal in the water.  The location is at the end of North Campbell and there are plenty of restaurants and shops in the vicinity.  If I was spending the day in one stone area, I would be dropped off and they had the rental car to cruise town and explore.    It all worked well from La Paloma.

Richboro, PA, is experiencing a big growth spurt with the closing of the Davis Auto Group facility in the center of town and the new businesses being developed in that large space. The cranes and construction workers are still there, but a couple of buildings are finished and the new look downtown is taking shape. Dairy Queen leased the space at the rear of the new office/retail structure at Second Street Pike just off the Bustleton Pike intersection. It is a little hard to find hidden way in back.  The store itself is fairly small, with two rows of about a dozen booths and tables in front, cashier and kitchen in back and soda service area against the rear wall. Service is young, friendly and accommodating. The order taker was kind enough to point out that as I was there before 2, their $5 and $6 lunch specials were still in play. Cheeseburger, fries, soft drink and small sundae for a fin was good deal, so I went for it, except I knew I couldn't handle the dessert, so he gave me a coupon for a free one instead. Much appreciated. He even permitted me to swap the carbonated beverage for a small blizzard without upcharge.   The package was okay when delivered to my booth, but not really inspiring. Fries were hot and crisp. The bun was not grilled, nor heated and could have used something to improve its plain white bread texture and taste. The 3 oz. burger was decent with onion, lettuce and tomato topping. The shake was a shallow imitation of the thick, rich and creamy 'Zzard of my childhood. Too watery. Not much flavor. A disappointment. Maybe something was missed in the downsizing for lunch. The whipped cream on top was more dominant that the mix beneath.   So, while I might return, I would skip the cheap deal and go for their full bore burgers and blizzards to see if those were true to the DQ Brazier creed.   Life is too short for boring burgers.

It was the Red Door in the middle of the building that I wanted, but it took three tries to discover it.    The whole layout was confusing.  First, I walked into Levittown Lanes, the near-historic bowling alley at the east end.  I didn't want to bowl, but in my mind, the bar and bowling were in the same space, making for a lot of potential fun.  But, the man at the shoe counter, perhaps not understanding what I was looking for, sent me outside and to the last door on the right.  What did I know?   I went into this plain wooden door without much of a sign, and found myself in a tiny dining area full of restaurant supplies and no customers.  To the right was the small takeout area with high half wall protecting the cashier and pizza ovens.  Ok. I ordered a Chicken Cheesesteak and inquired where the BAR was.  I was again sent outside and advised to take a left and enter the next door I came to.  Would my sandwich find me?  Sure. No problem.    I followed directions, and finally entered the actual barroom.  It was of the dive bar genre.  Dim, smoky, rock & rolly, and full of fatigued workers who where here for a few brews on their way home after another tough day.  Def my kind of place.  I bellied up to see what the back bar looked like, and met Angela, the mistress of ceremonies and bartender fatale.  I explained the strange circumstance that brought me to her lair.  She laughed and said that I must really need a cold one.  The Pabst Blue Ribbon pint was $2 all night.  Solid unpretentious American suds, just like the Band Box.    It went down so smooth and cool and tasted so comforting.  The guys around the bar accepted me as they saw the pint pour down my gullet without more than a swallow.  Thank you, Milwaukee.  They confirmed that I had found the best bar in Levittown - best food; best drinks; best prices. The Steak Sandy found me a few minutes later.    It was large, with a cut transecting the midline.  The bread was nicely toasted and crisp.  It had a good yeasty flavor all by itself.  The shredded and grilled Chicken was mixed with Onion and Mushrooms, with American Cheese holding the innards together.  It was hot, steamy and delicious.  A squirt of Ketchup and I was in business.  Maybe it was the combination of Pabst, people and the deft touch of the kitchen hands, but that was the most enjoyable cheesesteak I had eaten in a long time (at least since my last visit to Steve's).    Angela and I exchanged a few bar stories before I left.  Seemed we might know some of the same people in the biz.  I drove away thinking that of all the cool and curious old taverns in this part of the world, Band Box might be the best of breed.    Next week. Same time. Same stool.

The Langhorne Hotel has anchored the corner of Maple and Bellevue for a couple of centuries.  The world around it may have changed, but this establishment has not, except for a few architectural modifications to accommodate the uses to which it was being put.    This is both good and not so. Walking into the tavern area throws you into the Eighteenth Century, where the local Sons of Liberty gathered to plot the Revolution. Downside, the beer selection is from the same era.  The dining area is also dated to about 1890.  The menu is solid for a 1960's kitchen.  Everything is well prepared and tasty, but if you want something in the way of vegetarian, vegan, or even contemporary cuisine, it will be hard to find. The burgers, traditional Italian, and usual suspects are present.  As long as that is what you want, you will be satisfied.    Today I tried the Italian Sausage with Peppers and Onions in red sauce over Linguini for a lunch special. At $7.99 the price was right.  I enjoyed the meal, but there was nothing memorable about it. We turned lunch into a work meeting and remained for  more than an hour after we finished eating. The room was practically deserted on a August Friday afternoon.  We were not rushed, and the room was comfortable, if somewhat brown in tone.   A new menu, broader beer options, fresh coat of paint and new carpets would go a long way to bring the Langhorne Hotel a new clientele. But, if they did that, the Sons of Liberty in the tavern might go elsewhere to plot our way to independence.   Maybe we are wise to leave well enough alone.

Sometimes first impressions are deceiving. So it was with Non Solo Pasta.   Returning to the Italian shop after a few years, this time for lunch, I had a completely different experience. This time rather than order a pasta bowl that was off menu, I went with their standard melanzon parmesan, which came with choice of soup or salad.    It was excellent.   First, the large bowl of escarole soup was steamy and full of flavor, with white beans simmered to softness for added texture and subtle flavor.  Very glad I went with that over a side salad. The eggplant was thin sliced and sautéed in extra virgin olive oil, without breading, and then ladled full of red gravy over the top.  It was tender, light and delicious.  So much better than the breaded/fried variety that adds more calories than taste. Easily cut with a fork.  The side of spaghetti was generous, but truly unnecessary in light of the quality of the star attraction. I left most of that behind.   My companion selected the caprese salad and the Caesar. The red and yellow tomatoes were ripe and mildly tart to offset the fresh buffalo mozzarella, which was soft and semi-sweet. Very well done and about the best I've sampled of this simple dish.   Everything was well presented and a delight to indulge. After my earlier visit, the quality of this meal took me by very pleasant surprise.  I will return sooner next time.   Only downside is the lack of WiFi in the house, given how poor reception is in this part of Morrisville. Made it impossible to check in or put photos directly through Yelp. Still, managed to deal with that upon returning to the office.

Located in a tightly designed old commercial strip on Bustleton Avenue in the far Northeast, Philadelphia, Little Istanbul is a small Turkish restaurant with pleasant atmosphere, good service, and a fairly broad menu of Mediterranean and Ottoman style cuisine. With about a dozen tables, it pays to know what you want to order coming in because the room turns over quickly. This part of the city has a strong East European, Silk Road community, and this place fits right in.  We ordered Red Lentil Soup, Sauced Eggplant, Ground Beef/Lamb Pide and the Baked Salmon dinner. Based on our experience we would stick with the gyros and appetizers next visit, and shy away from the more elaborate dinners and Pide. Here's why:  The soup and eggplant were excellent, with fresh flavor, plenty of spice and wonderful bread and pita to help it down the gullet. The lentil soup was creamy and steaming hot, and more yellow than red. Apparently, it had a chicken broth base, which surprised my companion. The eggplant came in a tomato and olive oil base, and was served cold. Loved it.   However, the salmon, while a thick steak, was delivered past its peak from the oven. It was a little dry and the sauce it came in was not able to revive it. Otherwise, the taste was okay, but it could have been so much more. The Pide is very similar to a dish found in Georgian bakeries. The shape of a boat, it is basically thin dough with cheese and ground beef and lamb spread thinly across parts of the dish, much like pizza in taste, but with more interesting crust. It would have been great with more meat topping, but as it was it was a simple pleasure.   The lamb and chicken gyros we saw served nearby looked like absolute winners, and we would definitely try them next time.   Too, enjoyed sitting across the dining room from the large photo mural of the Bosporus waterway that transects the city of Istanbul (not Constantinople), and separates eastern Europe from western Asia. A fantastic old fortress city now part of a modern Turkey.  3.5 STARS

This IHOP on Roosevelt Blvd in the Great Northeast, is an older version of this historic franchise. There are only two narrow rows of double and quad booths with open kitchen in the middle where the crash and drum of the cooks and server shouted orders offer a momentary throwback to an earlier time when a family trip to the local pancake house was a very special occasion.   I guess those memories led me there this morning, when I suddenly saw it in front of me as I drove south down the Boulevard. The parking lot is likewise a small footprint, but I found the last available in the row. The greeter sat me at a quad and brought me menu and thermos pitcher of Java. Thanks for the extra leg room, my dear. Your tip just rose a few bucks.   I ordered the Original French Toast Combo (2 slices w powdered sugar, 2 Scrambled Eggs, Home Fries and 2 Sausage Links). No. I didn't finish all of it, but I was pleasantly surprised how good each element was; especially the eggs, potatoes and coffee. The Frenchie was okay, but really need a touch of vanilla and cinnamon to bring up the flavor profile. Caramelization of the edges would have brought a nice crisp to the texture.   Still, all in all, it was a very satisfying meal that allowed a short dalliance in my childhood along with room to stretch my legs.

This may be the largest Starbucks I have seen east of Ohio!   At least 5,000 square feet, it feels like a small theater, more than a cafe. Plenty a seating with tables, chairs and more relaxed furniture in the corner. Easily 15 foot ceiling which does impact the acoustics, but almost feels like being outside. A 50 foot wall long black and white panel that pulls the room together.   Yet, when I was there at 4:30 on a recent afternoon, the operation was being run by only 3 baristas, including drive through service. Impressive that they managed to sweep and clean up the place during their shifts.   Menu was standard for the Green Mermaid, although the display case was somewhat depleted given the time of day. I snared the final slice of lemon pound cake - my endulgance for the week. It was as tart and sweet as always.   While still not a true fan of Starbucks, this place isn't bad.

We stopped by Nina's Waffles & Ice Cream as we cruised Doylestown after the March for Science. It was a first visit, and the instant impression was one of an old time, wood floor, bright walled, musical, ice cream parlor.  A small space for a popular destination, the room had less than a half dozen tables to sit and enjoy their interesting take on hot waffles and cold creams. The high glass refrigeration unit held about a dozen and a half flavors, with the industrial waffle iron right next to it.  As we took it all in, one of the women behind the counter let us know we could sample any of their creamies with tiny spoons.  We demurred, and went directly to ordering a waffle with two scoops of their offerings, Berry Berry and Banana Walnut.    It was served in a heavy weight paper boat (like for fried chicken and fries), with plastic utensils, including a knife for cutting the underlying thick waffle.  The cost of $10+ for what seemed to be two large scoops of ice cream and a thick waffle, took me aback for a second, but I decided to consume this dessert before deciding if it was overpriced.    Nina makes her own ice cream in her store in New Hope, Pa.  It is high quality, creamy, and invested in local sourced ingredients (where available), and subtle flavors that demand your attention for full enjoyment.  The Berry Berry was very good, and the Banana Walnut was a pleasant surprise in not having that unpleasant banana extract taste, but a gentle real ripe Chiquita lick.  Big chunky walnuts, too.  Nina knows from ice cream.    The waffle did require knife to cut into bite size pieces, and possessed a heavy texture that held up well to the melting above.  Yet, in the overall scheme of things, the ice cream was far superior to the doughy base.  The interplay between the solid and the liquid was pleasing for a moment, with the waffle offering a slight saltiness that magnified the sweetness topside. Still, if pressed to save a few calories, I would opt for all ice cream, and take a pass on the iron cakes.   A few more tables within, and some benches without, would help make Nina's into a true ice cream hangout, particularly on cooler or rainy days, when walking around town with an ice cream cone is not the funnest thing to do.  Hard to lick and hold an umbrella.   Still, if ice cream is your thing, Nina's has something waiting for you that will definitely make you smile. Maybe a tad overpriced the way I ordered it, but next time I would skip the waffle and go straight to the cool delicious prize.

This will be a somber review, and perhaps the ecstatic shouting should be tempered out of respect for the purpose of the National Cemetery located off Washington Crossing Road in Upper Makefield, Pa.   No words could ever be as poignant as those of the first reviewer, and all subsequent reviews will pay homage to the sense of deep personal loss expressed there.   Just down the road along the Delaware River in a more remote portion of Washington Crossing National Historic Site, is the original Revolutionary War burial ground for the soldiers/revolutionaries who fought for a freedom that was only a dream in the hearts of men/women in the 18th Century. What we take for granted now, was once only an abstract ideal, written in books, and discussed in taverns and around wood burning fires.    The new Washington Crossing National Cemetery rests on hallowed ground. All who visit there, either out of respect for a loved one for whom this earth is their final resting place, or for those of us who honor our warriors and the history they have forged with their blood, it is impossible not to dwell on the road we have taken to arrive in this place. It calls out a solemnity and deep appreciation, and brings us to the realization that all of us are called to continue and contribute to the experiment that is the American experience.

As chain Italian restaurants go, Macaroni Grill is a step above Olive Garden when it comes to atmosphere, and about equal in terms of food taste and quality.  It isn't bad, but just can't compare with the local mom and pop kitchens anywhere in eastern Pennsylvania, that give you cuisine right from momma's oven.    I like the Tuscany-esque high ceiling and heavy timber, as well as the open kitchen.  Service was excellent from "Big Sean." He was on top of all our needs.    My lunch special Chicken Parm Sandwich was pretty good, with fresh bird and enjoyable variation of an Italian loaf.  The chicken tasted deep fried rather than pan fried, but the sauce was okay and there was the right proportion of mozza/sauce.  My partner's Italian Pulled Pork was more unusual, but had a mildly sweet taste, and a lot of greens on top as a substitute for the American cole slaw.  I had never heard of BBQ on an Italian menu, and this was no doubt an attempt to capture more diners looking for something not strictly from the Boot.    The price for these lunches @ $7, was very good, and allowed us to eat a full and tasty meal at a reasonable price, rather than jumping to the dinner options.    Bottom Line - Not a bad choice for a road stop if you don't know the local haunts with genuine home cooking.

Ristorante Denicola has been around for more than a decade, but I just found out about it last week. Two Yelp friends introduced me to this fine Italian house when we met for dinner a few nights ago, and but for their detailing its location in the Mallard Creek Shopping Center I would never have seen it.  Intentionally or not, it is a well kept (hidden) secret.    The front door is inconspicuous, like a secondary entrance near green/white awnings that feel like the porch in the back of a home.  Walking in, it is surprisingly large with rough hewn wood horizontal panels, dark tones, carpet, and nicely spaced tables. We sat is the corner in an otherwise empty dining room.    Our server was well known to my friends, and she took very good care of us all night.  This family business' signature style is to deliver much more than expected in the form of non-ordered extra dishes that are a surprising addition to the meal.  For us, they dropped off Grilled Veggie Antipasto, Tomato Bisque, Homemade Sausage Pizza, Chicken Breast Joey (a piccata/marsala feel)  and Cannoli, on top of our main courses.  All this was a meal unto itself.  When they then deliver a large plate of Penne A'glio Olio with Sautéed heavily Garliced Spinach, the result was taking most of it home.  I'm not complaining, but it again brought to the forefront my discomfort with intentional excess in a world full of hunger.    Here's the ironic part of the experience - my pasta was very good; al dente with well browned Garlic Chips mixed into the Spinach and Red Pepper dusted Penne.  It was the best of my samplings, but the one I ate the least of because I was already full from everything that came surrounding it.  The gratis accompaniments were also good, but a step down from the main course.  The Antipasto had fresh cut tomato, onion and cilantro on top of the Grilled Zucchini and Eggplant.  The "bruschetta" was cold while the nicely grill-ribbed large veggies were warm.  It was an inconsistency that detracted from the cohesion of the dish.  The Homemade Sausage was excellent and plentiful, but the tomato sauce was thin and runny.  The Tomato Bisque had a pleasant creamy texture and taste, but was a little lumpy. The Chicken Joey was fine, but I was beginning to feel overwhelmed and mildly compelled to take a share. The Cannoli were perfect.   The overall effect was that each additional offering both added and detracted from the meal.  I don't think that was the intention in the kitchen, but that was how it felt.  The generosity of the house also opened the door to mild disappointment.    After this review my friends may regret inviting me, and I am sorry for that.  I will definitely return and ask for a more limited approach to my next meal.  I would rather be totally impressed with the food I desire, and have fewer filling distractions.   Less is More.

The sign on the front door points to the left where the entry of its sibling House of Pho is located. That tip alone alerts you to the fact that Taiko Bistro and its neighbor are closely related.  In fact, they are family; owned by the same people, and put in place after the success of House of Pho led to expansion to cover the bubble tea explosion around the country. They share a kitchen, while House handles traditional Vietnamese fare and Taiko addresses the taste for Asian snacks and tapioca ball drinks.   Following directions, I walked into the elder to order Roast Pork Banh Mi, Ribeye Pho and a Mango Smoothie "to go." I returned to my car for the suggested 20 minute wait, as the business wasn't really set up for in house dining.   Ten minutes later, the manager/owner/cashier was coming over to my vehicle with a nearly wrapped package. I opened my door to accept the bag and thank her for going the extra mile to find me when everything was ready, rather than waiting for me to re-enter ten minutes later.   That kind of courtesy is memorable.   The Banh Mi was excellent. Tasty load of thin sliced roast pork with pleasant hoisin flavor, daikon, carrot, cilantro in a fresh demi baguette. Liked it a lot. I assembled the Pho in a large bowl while it was still warm, but with the large next of noodles, generous beef and desire to add copious sprouts and Thai basil, I chose to microwave the broth to better cook everything else and bring the dish back to optimum. It was still good; the taste was there, but there was no doubt it had lost something in transportation.   The Mango Smoothie was more a slurpie, with too much freeze and little smooth. It was clearly made from a mix without a hint of fruit pulp. Disappointing. Maybe bubble tea was the way to go.   Lesson learned. Banh Mi travels well, and Pho can be resurrected by focuses reheating at home, but a poorly conceived smoothie is impossible to revive.   3.5 STARS

The Newtown Farmer's Market is not really a farmers' market at all.  It is a space where various food vendors sell their homemade (or not) products from Thursday thru Saturday.  The overall gestalt is Amish, but many of the retailers are local people selling non-Pa. Dutch things.  Go if you like fresh food options in meat, produce, dairy, bread, and Middle Eastern/Mediterranean food,  or Amish-style pickled stuff, sushi, fresh fish, or my favorite BBQ'd everything.  There is a small eating area if you love to snack or have a noisy meal, but otherwise take out is the name of the game.   The prices are more or LESS competitive with local grocers, but the freshness is what they score with. Also, the Pa Dutch folks who are there, provide a quaintness that makes the exploration a pleasant experience.    Overall, whether you like it or not depends on your expectations.  Don't think: Reading Terminal, because it is not even close to that in scope.  Think: small time alternative to megamarkets with some local color and fresh food.  With a little creativity and space, it could be so much more.   If you have the time and enjoy this kind of thing, the Trenton Farmers' Market is much larger and more diverse.  Worth a hungry visit.

This is a new drive thru Starbucks on RT. 541 (Burlington-Mt. Holly Road), is one of their smaller designs, yet with ample comfortable seating for those who prefer to sip in or work, and a tight bar area with two cashiers and snack offerings. The staff is skilled and friendly, and keep the joint humming and clean.   I stopped in after court in Mt. Holly, in need of a caffeine jolt to keep me sharp through the rest of a dreary Thursday. My grande low fat latte did the trick as I watched the laptops burying their noses in daily labor.   Wish I liked nitro cold brew, because that was very popular with the peeps there. There must be something to it, but I just don't like the bitterness.   Regardless, in the land of Dunkin it is nice to have an upgrade available.

I don't know who John Lucas is, nor how he learned to cook Italian food, but his small casa Italiana has it going on in the cheffing department. Bailey's Center now has a bona fide first rate pizza joint on the premises.  We visited for the first time Friday night. The dining room is small (3 booths, 6 tables), so the reservation made sense. Our booth had been set aside and prepped for our arrival. The house is cozy, and feels a lot more comfortable than it appeared from the outside. The menu is lengthy, with choices from pizza to full dinners and everything in between.   We began with bowls of pasta fagiole soup that arrived just after a basket of hot bread knots.  Both were excellent. The soup was full of short pasta tubes and white beans in a smooth veggie stock. The bread was out of the oven reheat, yet crisp on the outside and tender soft within. It was mildly salty with great texture. Perfect for dipping in the soup and the platter sauces that followed when unwound and pulled apart. Entrees were chicken francaise and veal marsala, both over penne aglio olio.   The francaise was wonderful. Egg dipped, pan sauteed in lemon and white wine. Delicious!  Three medallions turned golden brown and tender enough to be  cut by my fork. The penne beneath was also very good with the melding of the juices. Lemon and garlic are a great combo. The only disappointment was the veal. It was too thickly cut, not tenderized, and a little tough to chew. Too, the marsala sauce was off, more like the wine was turning to vinegar, making for a sourness that was not appealing.   Service was friendly and accommodating.   Overall, we were very satisfied with our experience at John Lucas. Far better than expected. Still, it wasn't perfect because of the marsala issue. Definitely worth a try.   4 Stars.

I must have gotten lucky judging by all the naysayers' reviews of this Mickey D's on Cottman Avenue at Roosevelt Blvd., in N.E. Philly. But, rather than being disappointed by its performance, we were actually pleasantly surprised by how good their food and service were.   We were in a rush to return home after a large shopping excursion to the Asian supermarket nearby, and opted for rapid food from the only drive through in sight. We ordered a quarter pounder w cheese, chicken nuggets, fries and drink, took possession within minutes, and continued our drive home to Bucks County.   We immediately noticed the heat coming off the fries In the open top paper sack. First sampling was of perfectly done Frenchies - hot, crisp and addicting. The burger was also just off the steel and settling nicely onto the bun. It reached my mouth in optimal condition, with even the onions soft and translucent and the pickle stuck to the cheese so it couldn't fall out. It was like the dream burger from the adverts, except this baby was for real.   Once in a lifetime!   Naturally, it wasn't all ideal, as the nuggets had a processed food texture. I knew I was awake. Still, this was as close to amazing as McDonalds ever gets, and the moment required recognition.   Now that we know it can be done, why should anyone settle for any less?

The Korean double fried chicken wings were excellent with their Secret Spice Sauce. Crisp, hot spicy and a little sweet. Made from scratch upon ordering so it took 20 minutes for them to be prepared. Next time I'll call ahead to save time. Great to have these near best of breed wings so close at hand, rather than having to travel to another county to get a fix.  Yet, that "Homemade Hamburger" needs to be reconsidered and hopefully reinvented. It was awful. The ground beef was a poor quality with pieces of fat and other nasties that fell apart upon biting into the sandwich. The slice of red onion was tough and bitter. Their signature burger sauce was okay, but really added nothing positive to the taste. A Sriracha mayo would have been a better option, or something like Russian dressing. The potato wedges were quite good, but it would take alot of convincing to get me to try that thing again.   So, it was the best of times and the worst of times at CHKN & BBQ. Stick with what you do well and move away from what you don't if you want to succeed.

B-Uno's still has its, "Grand Opening" sign up on the window, and it seems it has not been discovered on this out of the way corner of Jacksonville Road, just off Rt. 130 North, in Burlington, NJ.  It is really a Latino Casa that does breakfast and lunch.  The menu is on a large blackboard on the wall.  The gist is mostly burgers named after the automotive universe, with burritos a strong option.    I was there for a late breakfast around 10:30 am, and went with a Sausage, Egg & Cheese Sandwich on a Kaiser Roll.  At $6 for the sandwich with a small side of Tator Tots and a large Coffee, I thought the price proposition to be very attractive.  I sat at one of the 4 small tables along the front window, facing the wall menu, with the counter to my left and the short order grill just on the other side.    Standing up to look for the coffee (it was being fresh brewed for me in the back of the kitchen), I observed the cook putting my meal together.  Link sausage was being deep fried before slicing and grilling and lay the groundwork on the base of the roll.  I didn't need the extra oil from using that approach to preparation, but it did not affect the taste.  The same was true for the Tator Tots.  Deep fried and crunchy.  The eggs were fresh and folded flat on the hot steel before being slipped into place on top of the meat.  The cheese went on last and helped seal the fresh roll top to the contents of the creation.    All in all, a pretty good sandwich, and better cup of brewed java.    Next time, I will ask for one of their well-named burgers, as that seems to be their sweet spot.    These guys should make it.  They are friendly and play good music with a strong nod to Carlos Santana.   Oye Como Va!

Last Christmas Eve when General Washington crossed the Delaware River and marched on Trenton overnight to surprise the Hessian mercenaries in their barracks, he stopped in Patriot's Crossing for a cold one with his officers after the successful encounter. A very cold night, he chose to stay inside at the bar after the long ride on horseback.   While there he was greeted by fellow rebels and militiamen celebrating their victory.  Service was exceptional at the bar, with ample choices on tap or bottles. He particularly liked the Victory Summer Ale brewed down in Philadelphia, although the Dogfish Head dark was the favorite of most of his officers. Hungry, he ordered a southwest cheeseburger, loaded with onion, jalapeno chips and spicy aioli mayo smeared on the textured bun.  His charge de camp ordered the mushroom swiss burger. Both came with fries or onion rings. The General always demanded "Liberty Fries," as the French had not yet done enough as allies to warrant naming rights to those potatoes.   Their burgers were quite good. The beef recently slaughtered and ground by a local farmer, with no opportunity for freezing unless left out in the cold. Although camped along the Pennsylvania side of the river, this Jersey tavern had been off limits to all but the long boatmen who traversed the treacherous currents to trade in farm goods and military rumors. George Washington knew this, and counted on intelligence from these patriots to keep him informed about what they heard about enemy movement. This watering hole was an excellent place to carefully exchange information because although there were few Red Coats brave enough to be out of their encampments at night, there were still loyalists like Abraham Doan around and about, who would happily steal your horse and sell it to the British or trade in military secrets. In other words, it was a den of thieves and spies who bargained in hidden code and dastardly deeds for the right price. Perfect for the surreptitious exchange of information when the fate of the war remained unknown.  The crowd has not changed much since the day the General stopped in to have a round with his men.  The easy success in Trenton gave him the idea and the courage to attack again near Princeton the next day, to keep the Reds off balance and in retreat.   Little did anyone know that they were witnessing an important turning point of the Revolution, when the dream of freedom became the possibility of true independence.   Legend has it that General George stops in every Christmas Eve to carry on the tradition. The tavern owner keeps his barstool empty awaiting his arrival. A pewter pint of brown ale sits on the bar near that spot waiting for the anniversary party to begin.

Well, not exactly like Trenton Tomato Pie, but close enough to use the sacred name of the best pizzas in the Universe (Pardon me, Brooklyn).   These guys make excellent chunky red sauce for their red over white creations. Truth is, they may pour it on a bit on the heavy side, so that the thicker crust becomes moist from the tomato slurry. Makes for a base that can't support the topside, unlike the Trenton pie that uses both thinner crust and less nightshade, yet manages to hold its point beginning to end. Despite this engineering, the taste was superlative. The added mushrooms provided subtle flavor and more texture. So, I am not complaining at all; just pointing out the cultural difference. Both ways work, it just depends which you prefer.   The chicken parmesan sandwich was also quite good, with enough chicken tenders, great sauce and melted mozzarella for a pleasing full mouth bite. The weak link was the torpedo roll, which lacked crispness and sourdough flavor to enhance the finished mix.   There was kitchen artistry in both pie and sub, and a better baker would make the difference in reaching my fifth star.  Note to Alex - Thanks for the excellent comment to the review. I still have family on Anderson Street, and totally appreciate what Trenton brings to the (pizza) table. While all the Italian kitchens may have moved to the burbs, the heart remains in Chambersburg (perhaps at Italian People's Bakery on Butler).

Quintessential working person's dive bar, with a laid back atmosphere, decent kitchen, and friendly barkeeps.    Fair beer selection on tap, but not a craft beer haven. A great place for a Burger or Cheesesteak, especially on the days that they are a special low price. Open for breakfast for the early birds.  See their website for updates and events.    The outdoor patio is a great addition.  Enough TV screens to satisfy the most diverse taste in entertainment.  Last night, World Cup, Yankees, and Mexican soap opera played their unique games.  If you prefer live entertainment, it is available certain nights with local bands, or a customer acting out his comedic fantasy.  I enjoyed a guy in a Rod Stewart wig hitting on the lovely bartender with one pick up line after another, until we were all listening and shouting suggestions.  It was a kick! The dude was funny.   Puss N Boots. Definitely a great place for a hot plate, a cold brew, and a hearty laugh; all at great prices.

They say good things are worth waiting for.   Perhaps that wise person had plumbers in mind when he wrote this. Perhaps, not.  But, even with waiting a long time past the original window promised by the scheduler, ultimately, it was the quality of the work that counted most in the service industry.  Lucas had arranged with me to have someone at the house to fix a broken toilet between 8 and 10.  There was no way to know in advance that a one hour job would become a four hour slog.  They were courteous enough to call me twice to alert me to the circumstances, and offer to reschedule for next week.  The thought of going through the long weekend down a flusher with guests in the house was an unpleasant image.  I opted to wait it out.    Brandon arrived with apologies and explanations, and a positive demeanor.  He got right to work diagnosing the problem and prescribing the cure.  He had the necessary parts, and even had to change one when the first did not satisfy him.  Soup to nuts, he was finished in just under an hour.  He had to replace all the parts inside the tank to make the system work properly.    Plumbers aren't cheap.  This job came in just under two bills.  But, after I tried and failed to fix the problem last week, I considered the money well spent.  Truth be told, I should have called Lucas sooner and saved everyone a lot of stairs while this facility was down.  Lesson learned.

Sputino's has a great location in The Marketplace in Doylestown, but it is divided between it's kitchen up front and the dining room further back in this attractive indoor mall. There are a few stools right at the entrance to watch the maestros at work on their 90 second Napolitan pizzas, but a lot more room in back.   After standing in the misting rain during the March for Science at the old courthouse, we had quite an appetite, and wanted to give our business to a local shop in appreciation for the town being so inviting to our people. We weren't the only ones with this idea.   We ordered a pepperoni pie and two Sanpelligrinos - Limonata and Blood Orange to quench our thirsts.  The pie came out in about 7 minutes, looking hot and steaming. These Nappis are always small, and just enough for a snack for two. The edges were scorched with burnt dough and the thin 'ronis sweating out their oil.    The thing about this type of tomato pie is that because it is super thin and baked so fast, it also cools quickly causing condensation and a damp crust with minutes. It is imperative to eat it quickly to maximize the enjoyment. Few of us like damp, limp pizza, which these become by the time you get it home. So, eat it while it burns your palate to get the most flavor.  Too, unlike the traditional pizza, these Nappis are all about the crusty dough, not the toppings.  The quality of the undercarriage is what matters most.  So, a great pie maker will use the freshest flour and water, and add the right spices to make the crust taste dramatically superior to the other forms of this art.  The toppings are there to influence the taste of the dough, but not dominate it.   Sputino understands this concept and produces a very good crusty dough that hardens and blisters in 90 seconds in the wood burning hive oven.  It is not the best I have ever tried, but it is very solidly delicious.  If you are curious about other versions of these pies, come to Newtown and visit Acqua e Farina, another Napolitan house. There, for about twice the price you will experience a bit more taste in a new Italian stone and stucco villa. The Vault in Bordentown, NJ, also turns out a nice pie in a converted bank.   After trying these and more, I find them a nice alternative to my first love, Jersey Tomato Pie. Always good to have a change of pace comfort food close at hand.

When you walk into a pizza joint for lunch at 2:30 and the chef is gone and nothing can be prepared, the first impression cannot be good.    So it was today when I dropped by BellItalia of Trenton (not Bella Italia according to the sign and menu), a shoe box take out dive that had absolutely nothing to offer but its menu and the advice that I could order in the future and they would deliver.    'Fraid not, gentlemen.    There is nothing "Bella", nor even "Italia" about this place.  So many better options in town it would be a shame to waste even one meal on this outfit.

Still a great cheesesteak after several more visits over the past couple of years.    The BIG STORY is the availability of a credit card processor that saves the time and expense of bringing enough cash or using the captive ATM.    The sandwiches come to ten bucks with a drink, so it pays to be ready for the splurge.

Pat's King of Steaks reminds of the fable, The Emperor's New Clothes.  After picking up my California friend at 30th Street Station, we wove our way down to  South 9th Street for a taste of Philadelphia - the renowned, Pat's.  My 12 year old son came along when he heard we would go for cheesesteaks.    The environment around Pat's is terrific.  People all over the place.  The queue to order.  The Rules for Ordering.  The smack in the puss aroma of burning grease and onions.  The whole migila.  I felt my own excitement rise the closer I came to the ordering window.  I felt the vicarious thrill as my son ordered his first Cheesesteak Witout and Provolone, and a Birch Beer.  Truly, a right of passage.   Yet, when we sat down at a red metal grate table and began to devour our sandwiches, I noted my son's displeasure with the amount of fat and gristle he had to  spit out.  I, too, was surprised to find red meat in my tumultuous pile of steak, onions, mushrooms and cheese.  Uncooked.  It felt careless. I did not mind that each time I picked up the load to have a bite, and equal amount fell out the back end of the 'wich. That was to be expected from an unfortunate roll incapable of holding its load.  Still, I did not feel like picking up the canned shrooms  and steak pieces to eat them.    5 Stars for the institution and historic icon that is Pat's King of Steaks.  2 Stars for the actual product generated from this amazing operation.    3 Stars for the King who needs to look in the mirror and realize he may be wearing only his reputation.

Walking over to Viet Tofu to check out their Banh Mi and Spicy Tofu, I found the storefront empty.   The sign on the front door said they were temporarily closed for renovations and would reopen soon.   I'll try again in a few months.

I seem to remember this prefab diner being delivered and installed a few years ago.  Nice job making new look retro. It is not as big as I was expecting, but well maintained and definitely creates its own unique carnival-like atmospherics.    Stopped in for breakfast recently and took a seat at the counter.  Big breakfast menu, and a cup of coffee were placed in front of me before I had a chance to squirm to a comfortable position on the spinner.  Impressive attentiveness.  The servers wore smiles and were warmly engaging.    I opted for a breakfast sandwich on a Kaiser roll.  I thought that was all I would get for the reasonable price.  However, my waitperson then asked if I wanted Home Fries or Fresh Fruit with it.  Potatoes or fruit on top of what was already a big bite.  Thinking quickly for that time of day, I suppressed my surprise and inquired if it was possible to have half of each.  I wanted to sample more.  She nodded in appreciation.    Now, most Sausage, Egg and Cheese 'wiches come with a single sausage patty, one fried egg, and a slice or two of American cheese.  Not this baby.  It came with two patties, one egg, and a load of melted cheese that had to be three or four slices.  The Home Fries took up a third of the large plate, and the Fruit Cup was a nice mix of Cantelope, Watermelon, Pineapple, Grapes, Blackberries and Strawberries.    Needless to say, this was more than a single meal, and much more than I wanted to consume early in the morning, so I tasted a bit of everything, but could not finish anything.  I had a momentary qualm about the over the top quantity of food, the obesity epidemic in the US, and starvation elsewhere.  It felt excessive and indulgent.    While everything tasted good, if I return I will make a conscious effort to ask them to give me less.

Hinge Cafe on East Somerset Street in Port Richmond, Philly, is another great corner cafe in this part of the City of Brotherly Love. The atmosphere is urban casual, with wood upholstered furniture, step up side dining room, and lots of local artwork for sale on the walls. The menu is fairly traditional American fare. Breakfast and lunch are the focus.   During the week there is ample street parking, although it may be necessary to walk a block or two. There is a small storm room entry at the corner front door, but once inside the full effect of this turn of the twentieth century retail space takes effect. It could just as easily be 1930 and 2018. I love that kind of time warping.   Service is offered by friendly neighborhood women, who move efficiently through the shop loaded with coffee mugs, and large breakfast plates. The java was strong and refilled as needed. My request for milk rather than creamer was met with a small stainless pitcher of cow juice. My short stack french toast was well saturated with egg, vanilla and cinnamon mix and grilled up with a good caramelized surface. Tasted so good with melted butter and lots of syrup.   The combination of old city streets, repurposed space and quality food made for a strong morning impression. Could have hung out a while longer with another mugga joe, but an appointment back in the 21st century beckoned. Still, Hinge Cafe is another of those exceptional cafes, luncheonettes, and pocket restaurants that make these historic hoods so interesting and worthy of repeat visits.

This site attempts to do too many things.   In addition to housing a Dunkin' Donuts, it is also a Getty Gas Station, mini-deli, and lottery dispenser.  As a result, the place feels disorganized like it has a bad case of Attention Deficit Disorder.  Parking is limited and a bit dangerous with all the different uses bringing vehicles in from all directions.    The DD coffee is average.  The Bagel with Lite Veggie spread was toasted automatically, although I prefer it not, causing a cream cheese melt and a small mess in my car.  The taste was decent for a mass produced bakery product, but these rounders will never be mistaken for quality bagels.    It will do when time is very short and an injection of caffeine and a few calories are needed to survive through the first court appearance of the morning. Other than that, this is not a shop I would select for a morning munch nor java stop.

This is a tough spot to survive for a pizza shop due to its awkward location at the intersection of Buck and Holland Roads. Too many odd angles to negotiate unless your heading south on Holland. Still, it is worth your patience and driving skills to go to Giovanni's if you want a hot lunch or dinner to bring home.   I picked up a Sweet Italian Sausage Sandwich with sauteed onions and green peppers (sauce on the side) today. I called ahead and when I arrived 15 minutes later it was being kept hot on top of the pizza oven, wrapped and ready. It was a jumbo sammy, jammed with enough for at least two people, it's contents cut into bite size pieces of sausage and smaller virginized pepper & onion. The roll was a little soft due to being housed in one sided aluminum paper which trapped all the moisture inside, but even so it was an enjoyable lunch experience.   I managed to consume half before my warning lights alerted me to reaching overfull capacity. Repackaged the rest for home delivery.   Overall, a very good submarine @ just under $10 for a zoftig belly buster.

Fairless Hills is a little beyond my normal range for breakfast, but the reviews for Café Ferraro raised my curiosity, and on this morning without a 9 o'clock call I decided to check it out.   Good move, Mr. S.!  The Café is in another of those endless aging shopping strips that line Oxford Valley Road, but Ferraro's stood out from the rest of the concrete with a bright hand lettered sign on their front window artfully proclaiming its presence.  I walked in and saw the counter to the right with about 9 spinners, and several tables to the left.  The space seemed well occupied for 8:00 am, but what was obvious was the amount of conversation going on.  Everyone was engaged, not just with their own table, but with the rest of the house.  This was a very friendly joint.    I sat at an empty stood next to a woman who I had never met.  My coffee arrived before I could ask for it. The server took my order of French Toast and Country Sausage and immediately suggested the morning special which included two Eggs and Coffee for less than I would pay for my spoken desires.  I always appreciate getting more and paying less.  I was hooked.    Turned out that the French Toast was excellent, with a touch of Vanilla in the mix and nicely caramelized edges. The Sausage Patty was exceptionally fresh and tasty without being greasy.  The Scrambled needed a touch of Louisiana Hot Sauce to make it sing, but the well used bottle was quickly brought to me when I asked if it was available.    I had a long chat with my stoolmate and learned about her family, work, and plans for life.  She told me: "This place is like family.  Everyone knows your stuff and wants to help, if needed."  There is even a doctor who shows up almost daily and hangs his shingle while eating breakfast.  That's amazing!  No extra charge for a diagnosis with your pancakes.   Café Ferraro is a great little place.  If it was closer to home, it would quickly join my breakfast rotation, but given geographic realities, it will remain a treat for those rare mornings when I don't have to be standing in front of a judge at 9.

This was one of the more bizarre shops I have visited in the USA.  Clearly a take out dive with only one table with 5 chairs for those unlucky enough to need to eat in house (Moi), these folks clearly make food as a secondary enterprise to the antique business they run in the same space.  I was able to peruse some attractive Chinese and Western vases and curios while waiting for my meal to reach me in its polystyrene container.  Not an expert, but having spent enough time in China to know how these things are done, most of what I saw were copies of older pieces.  Of course, they insist they are the original Ming Dynasty pots, but no way they would leave them out in the open of a tiny resto if that were so.  The real McCoy's are under lock and key because of their large valuations.    Anyway, I know they do better with the pottery than the slop served, because the old man drove up in a Hummer full of more ceramics as I walked back to my car.  Which leads me back to the food.  I don't mind that there was no washing of hands between touching old pots and cooking pots.  I didn't mind that the menu I was forced to look at was smeared with sauce and whatever, rather than thrown away before I arrived.  I don't even mind that there was no air conditioning and the door was left wide open to allow me the pleasure of sharing my meal with flies.    But, I did mind that the Chicken had been frozen too long and lost its tenderness, and that the Fried Rice was a copper color from being dyed by the bouillon it had been cooked in yesterday.  What surprised me in all this were the actual veggies that found their way into the dish.  Not just Broccoli, but Water Chestnuts, Fresh Mushrooms, Carrots, Snap Peas and even Black Fungus (the good stuff) were all mixed in.  I didn't expect to see that in an otherwise lackluster presentation in styro.   No. Someone around there knew something about cooking, and took the time to get authentic ingredients for this slovenly meal.  The General's sauce was also near amazing, because it actually had the Hot/Sweet balance generally considered the proper taste for this dish.    Why they were able to develop the right sauce with the high end veggies, while throwing in old Chicken and rerun rice, is beyond me.  But, in retrospect it was no more unusual than the store itself.    I don't think I'll be back to Ying Hui unless I am looking for an attractive ersatz vase for a gift for someone I don't care too much about.  PS. Don't be too impressed with that Top 100 Award.  Whether than is legit or not, it certainly wasn't given for this operation.  Those awards are for sale on the internet.

If I had to guess, I would think that Chalfont Family Restaurant/Diner had changed hands somewhere in the not too distant past, and been taken over by Spanish speaking owners who were trying hard to duplicate traditional American cuisine, but not quite there yet. Nothing wrong with that, and I wish them success.   I found the large dining room clean, but somewhat dreary in worn yellow and brown tones. The menu hadn't been modernized in some time. Only one server handled the several parties there for breakfast, keeping him extremely busy and unable to check up on everyone often enough to keep coffee mugs full and timely remove old plates. He kept his smile and aplomb, but always running to catch up.   My County Style Omelet (onion, green pepper, potato mixed inside the egg shell), was ample, but a tad too dried out from over cooking. Too, I splashed on Tabasco to liven up the flavor when black pepper wasn't enough. It would have been so much better had a choice of cheese been part of the deal, rather than a steep upcharge. A little feta would have been a great place to start. Coffee was industrial; Rye Toast, standard.   Overall, it was an acceptable breakfast, but could have been a contender with more attention to detail, and perhaps another set of hands in the kitchen.

I stopped in this Ruby Tuesday's restaurant last night in the mood for a burger and beer. I sat at the small square bar, ordered a Sam's Winter Lager, but allowed myself to be distracted by the specials menu. So, rather than a burger I went with the Shepherd's Pie @ $11.99.   Big mistake.  While it included a reasonable salad bar, the "pie" itself was smaller than its photograph on the menu. It came in a cast iron skillet, perhaps 6" in diameter at the top, and smaller at the base. It was primarily instant mashed potatoes above a ground beef gruel. I counted 5 peas. There was little beef and mostly a gravy-like substance beneath the top layer. Pathetic.   I made the best of it, and did not request a better meal. I don't like being that guy. Still, it showed that Tuby Ruesday was willing to sell overpriced garbage dishes without qualms for quality nor their reputation.   If they don't care what they offer their customers, neither will we care to find out what comes next. In this business, one strike is all you get.  Complete ripoff.

FresCafe Food Company is a new Lahaska breakfast/brunch/lunch cottage in the Earl's Restaurant complex. It is in Nancy's old place, but with fresh coat of paint to bring out the country shine. It is a little hard to find, but if you use Earl's as a guide you will find it by parking there and walking into the courtyard. First you will see the blue umbrella outdoor seating, with the main doors to FresCafe just beyond.   Like most of Lahaska, it is an attractive countrified touristy house made to appear 18th Century village, with plenty of large trees, exposed beams, period artistry and wagonloads of charm. It is well done, and somewhat representative of the history of the area. Big windows and low ceilings with views of brick and aged board contributing to the comfortable atmosphere. Coming midweek avoids the crowds and allows for a leisurely morning cuppa joe and traditional repast. Service was attentive and friendly, but left me alone except to ask if I wanted more coffee or needed anything. Just the way I wanted it.  The Brioche French Toast was fine, topped with sliced straw and blueberries. A bit more vanilla extract in the egg mix would have enhanced the flavor, and an option for real maple syrup would have taken the dish to another level altogether. For a farm to table kind of place that would have been a strong move. Still, the coffee was decent and the overall experience quite positive.   There is a premium paid at all Lahaska establishments and FresCafe is no different. Still, the quality/price proposition is not out of line with the rest of town, and if you like these type of destinations, you will be pleased with this one.

China Chef in the Richboro Shopping Center is an average Chinese/American house that caters mostly to the take away crowd.  There are a half dozen or so tables, but the atmosphere is rather dreary, and not conducive to a comfortable meal.  The management is friendly and helpful.  My recent experience had me opening my bag of goodies at home for a first look.  My order of Fried Dumplings was not the crisp, browned dough pocket I envisioned, but rather a soggy, fried only on one side, unattractive package.  I had to refry them to bring them back to life. I also remixed the dipping sauce to add more heat as the one that came with the dumplings was mostly vinegar with little taste of ginger or chili pepper.    The Egg Foo Young was thick and loaded with veggies, pork and egg, but left too long in the wok.  The surface was too dark brown, but the taste wasn't as bad as the look. The Brown Sauce was good, and there was more than needed to cover the 3 pancakes.    Orange Chicken was plentiful; enough for at least 3 helpings.  The breading was a bit soggy; again not the crunch I was looking for.  The taste was about right, but the texture was off in the same way the dumplings were.    Overall, this was an average meal with too many shortcomings to have China Chef join my short list of China joints recommended for a fast meal.    The search continues.

Those who know and love tomato pie are aware that Trenton, NJ, has some of the best around. So, when a tiny take out shop in Penndel, PA, calls itself, "Trenton Tomato Pies" it has a lot to live up to. It has to be damn good to justify its name. Yet, because the pie can't be immediately consumed, it has an inherent disadvantage to those restaurants that allow you to eat it right out of the oven when the molten disk is nearest perfection and at its most dangerous.   So, I knew it was a challenge for these folks to succeed. I admired their courage and willingness to make the effort. I decided to stop in without advanced ordering to avoid any possibility the pie and sandwiches would be sitting around any longer than necessary for me to grab everything and get home as quickly as possible.   I ordered a small Tomato Pie, Cheesesteak w Hot Peppers and Hot/Sweet Sausage, Pepper & Onion, w Hot Pickled Pepper sandwiches. I waited in my car about 25 minutes until everything was done, and drove the 15 minutes home. In the car I opened the pizza box to let steam escape to preserve crispness, and partially unwrapped the  cheesesteak for the same reason. The aroma was terrific and set off my glands' anticipatory reaction.   Squirt...!!!  How was everything?  Glad you asked.   Well, despite my best effort to protect the crunch, the pie had lost some of its bite and much of its heat. It was still good, but I had to use my imagination as to how much better it would have been if eaten sooner. The thin crust had good flavor, the under layer of mozzarella was light and not overpowering, and the crushed tomato top spread across its body was mildly sweet and acidic. These guys knew the secret recipe, just too bad they didn't have an adjoining dining room.   The Cheesesteak was decent, but not upper echelon, and the Mixed Sausage Pepper & Onion was actually pretty good, and more tasty than the steak. They seemed to be made from different rolls, with the later superior to the former in texture and taste. Can't explain that.   Bottom line - Trenton Tomato Pies is a very good choice for your Italian menu, depending in large part on the travel distance until consumption, or your ability to reheat in your oven prior to first chomp. I suspect they are waiting for the vape shop next door to close so they can expand and have the dining space they so sorely need to jump up in rank and play with the tomato pie big boys.

When friends called unexpectedly and told me they were at Karla's for dinner and drinks, and invited me to join them, it was very easy to drop what I was doing and make the 20 minute drive from Newtown to New Hope.  I hadn't seen one of my old friends for some time, and Karla's has been a very nice institution in New Hope for more than a decade.   Parking is always an issue in this river town, but in winter it becomes possible to find a spot off Main Street and a reasonable (and healthy) walk to whatever destination you have in mind.  It was a cold Friday night, and while the streets were empty of most pedestrians, Karla's was packed with customers in each of their historic and well appointed rooms on its multi-leveled layout.  I found my friends sitting in a far corner at a deuce, and the staff was kind enough to find an extra chair, fit me in, and provide me with a menu, although my friends were far along in their meals.  Even the neighboring diners were accommodating to my squeezing in next to them, and we all were able to enjoy the post-Christmas spirits.    I ordered a Lemon Drop Martini and the Mahi Mahi Sliders - a light repast. Five minutes later the drink arrived, properly mixed and very refreshing.  Normally, I would take a pre-sip photo for Yelp, but on this night I didn't feel like waiting for the phone cam.  I took a long sip, and then another. Very nice.    The sliders arrived about 10 minutes later.  Three mini-burger bun sized sandwiches, with a nice chunk of Mahi, Lettuce, Red Onion shavings, and slightly spiced orange sauce, each complemented with a mini pickle lanced by a long wooden pick.  They were delicious.  Each component added subtly to the others.  The fish was fresh, and everything hung together and did not fall apart even after picking each up and holding it as I ate due to my distance from the table.  Thoroughly enjoyed them. My friends took bites and agreed.    Karla's is a place where the architecture, history, and ambiance of the space invites you to spend a long time savoring the experience.  Looking around it was obvious that everyone was having a good time with mostly larger groups of diners, and no one really wanted to leave.  Best of all, no one felt rushed.    Just a wonderful winter night.

Lunch Review  Bamboo Kitchen (Why do I want to say, "Bamboo Curtain?"), Sits in the space of the former Peng Yuan Chinese house. New owners. New look. Very similar menu.   I went down Buck Road to the Pleasant Valley Center to pick up my order for General Tso Chicken from their lunch list. It came with choice of rice (fried), but without soup or egg roll. Although I hadn't asked for it in advance, they were happy to add a Hot & Sour Soup for another $1.   Good decision.  Turned out that the soup was very good and the best part of the meal.
