It had fresh mushrooms, lots of sprouts and tofu, and  strong tart vinegar base. Liked it alot.   The rest was pretty much forgettable. The chicken was okay, but somewhat dried out, and the sauce sweet, but not the least bit spicy. The rice was dyed yellow from the bouillon it was cooked in, but did have a fair share of veggies and small pieces of pork. Given the quality of the soup compared to the rest, it would seem that lunch is a loss leader for them, priced too low to justify a really satisfying meal.  The dinner menu is likely better.

The SS United States is the third American vessel of that name (1864, 1903), this one the first ocean liner build entirely stateside, the largest of the American breed and the fastest to cross the Atlantic Ocean between New York and England, beginning in 1952. Its 990 feet was only ten feet shorter than the Queen Mary that was its main competition for bragging rights in the maritime world.   That rusting bucket at Pier 70 on the Delaware River in Philadelphia, was once the pride of our country, with people willingly paying a premium to book passage for the experience of a lifetime. One of its largest investors, the Department of Defense, saw it as a troop transport as it game planned World War III, although it was never used for that.   Sadly, where the Queen has found a successful retirement in the Port of Long Beach, California, as a major tourist attraction with hotel, restaurants, boutiques and bicycle rental out front, the SSUS has bottomed out in its latest home for two decades unable to find the right combination of capital and brilliance to attain metamorphosis as an attractive destination.  Several developers have tried and failed to move the project forward. One was sallow enough to sell off all the fixtures and furnishings just to pay the dockage fees. Finally, it was taken over by a non profit conservancy, with the mission of saving the ship, raising donations and ultimately finding a beneficial purpose. To date, very little has happened to improve its dire circumstance.   How the mighty have fallen. What was the epitome of the "Can Do" Golden Age of the American Century, has become a different kind of symbol; much less grand, and more deeply pitiful.   Where is that indomitable American spirit now? What would it take to bring this hulking giant back to life? Like a sleeping Buddha it rests with the murky Delaware lapping at its rusting hull.

Needed a fast bite between afternoon and evening meetings and decided to hit up the McDonald's on Horizon Boulevard, Bensalem, PA. I seem to prefer Mickey D's recently when in this "no time to sit and eat" mode. Starting with their surprisingly tasty crisp fries, to their less compelling, but still decent Quarter Pounders, this oldest of national burger franchises has really upped its game in the last few years.  I enjoyed my repast, even while slumming in the car as I drove to the next destination. Hot taters, oniony beef pucks, soft bun and cold chill drink, we're just about what I wanted and needed.   Not that I want this to become a habit (bad one), but I have to admit I felt a childlike sense of happy abandon in chowing down on this almost forbidden micro pleasure.

I just checked the Village Bagel website to confirm what I had read before; "...You will not be disappointed...Stop by..."  Well, when I arrived at their shop after a 30 minute drive from home to sample their product, I followed the directions posted on their windows to call in an order. No problem. Happy to comply.   Unfortunately, the friendly sounding woman on the line advised me that they were not conducting any retail business for the day, but only filling orders for Christmas. I could not walk in, nor order a breakfast bagel (onion w garden veggie & coffee), but would have to leave empty handed. Not even explaining my long drive, nor the absence of any notice on their website, let alone, Yelp, nor sign on their front door, could persuade her to extend a humanitarian exception and slice/smear a bagel for me.   Nope. I would have to drive away without satisfaction.   Ho hum...  Merry Christmas to you, too!   There wasn't any room at the inn, either. At least I am in good company.

One of the food things that comes out of dining solo in a diner-like restaurant is the opportunity to sit at the counter and engage in conversation with the people working there. Although this Denny's was busy this Saturday morning, I was the only customer by myself, so when the cashier asked if I would mind sitting at the empty 5 stool lunch counter, I jumped at the chance. He took a few seconds clearing space for me, and nodded toward it directing me to take a seat. A mug of fresh bracing coffee was placed before me a minute later.  I drove to this old school grubhouse for one thing - the need to satisfy an urge for Chicken Fried Steak. Where it came from I didn't know, as I hadn't had this dish very often in life, but I saw no point in denying myself even if I couldn't explain its etiology.   While waiting for my meal to be prepared and served I struck up a conversation with that cashier. He was all Jersey, growing up down the road from this place. Still, he had been around, and knew quite a bit about hunting, fishing and outdoor life. Covid also came up, and he was an early adapter to the vaccines, so early that he was observed in hospital. Impressive and brave on all counts. It was a good exchange in several pieces during my stool time.  Yup. The CFS was just what the doctor ordered - crunchy on the outside, tender ground steak within, and a white gravy over top that added a slightly sweet and peppery flavor. Sides of Red Potato Mashed and Sauteed Green and Yellow Zucchini completed the ensemble. Each was very good separately, and terrific together. It was a simple meal, and perhaps not the healthiest, but it rang every note of my expectations, and left a contented smile on my face.   Denny's is not a regular stop for me, but sure delivered for me this day. From good talk through al dente seasoned squash and brown gravy tinted mashed, it was better than imagined.   How often does that happen?

Great Made On Demand (MOD) Pizza that was actually much better than I expected from an assembly line restaurant concept.   My Jasper pie was an 11" round crust loaded with spicy chicken sausage, mushrooms, red sauce and mozzarella with my addition of roasted garlic and balsamic fig finish that I dripped directly on to the pie when I got to my table at the back of the post industrially decorated shop.   It was a thin crust that maintained crispness throughout. The taste was excellent with the three main ingredients able to project their flavors without the messy overlap of too many things going on to confuse the tastebuds. The garlic provided a touch of savory moodiness while the sweet/tart thick fig extract added a bit of gooey fun to the equation. It was darn good all thrown together.   Then, I completely overindulged with their No Name Cake, which came wrapped in thin foil. It was in fact a giant house made Ring Ding, complete with light chocolate cake and a flush injection of butter cream hidden within. As a kid who grew up on Ring Dings and Yodels as snacks with milk, this was a giddy blast from the past that brought a not quiet sugar smile.  Mod Pizza moves to the top of the Newtown pizza scene. As a brand new business in town, I wish them great success.

Old Navy in Fairless Hills, Pa., is an accurate representation of the bottom rung of the Gap Empire.  Not quite the quality of Gap stores.  Not quite the attractiveness of the consumer experience.  Yet, certainly not the price range, either.  So, if you generally like Gap's line of clothing, but prefer it at steep discounts to the going price upstream, then Old Navy will float your boat.   Of course, there is a price to pay for shopping in an outlet world where the products are made to be inferior to those of the mothership.  More shlock.  More returns.  More unkempt piles of clothing that don't get put back on the right shelves or racks by the understaffed, overworked employees.    Patience and a keen eye will uncover a few gems worth finding, and the rotating discounts that perpetually run through the store make each visit potentially rewarding.  There is always a line waiting to use the dressing rooms, and a longer queue for the cashiers.  It is all part of the gestalt imbued in Old Navy.    If you like TJ Maxx, Ross or Marshall's, you probably already know that Old Navy sails the same seas.  Some days I can enjoy the lost hour spent in this rummage sale. Other days, my mood resists.    Take Old Navy for what it is worth, and for how much coin you can save, if not how much time you may waste.

Asian Chopsticks is now just a takeout joint dispensing primarily Chinese American fare to the masses in lower Bucks County. There are two tables in the house, but they don't turn the heat on in the shop on cold days, so the message of inhospitality is evident. The staff behind the plexiglass are bundled up, too. So order, wait, pay and go, is the true order of business.  I only go with basics at a new place for me like this. After all, I might get lucky and have hit on a kitchen that can really cook despite the apparent slovenliness of the operation, but in all likelihood this is a poor to middling' wok room that is in it to survive and save enough dough to maybe launch a second store somewhere. So, I ordered roast pork egg foo young and wonton soup to size up the potential.   The soup was about average with a few more wontons than expected, and the three pancakes were also in the middle of the pack, although the brown sauce was better than most (just made, not lumpy and decent flavor).  Service through the glass was cordial but remote, with no effort at interaction.   Bottom line - You could do worse that Asian Chopsticks, but unless you are otherwise in the area, it doesn't pay to go out of your way to buy your Chinese victuals here. There are far better choices not very far away.

Happy China is the third in a series of Asian takeout at this location in Levittown, PA. The previous tenants lasted as long as their leases and succumbed to the poor location at the ass end of a run down strip, it's nearly invisible from the main roads and a tiny floor space that had little room for dining in.   Still, this iteration has a chance, if they maintain reasonable standards of taste and cleanliness and do a little advertising. I found the interaction with the woman owner to be pleasant. She took my phone order of Crispy Orange Chicken (extra spicy, with fried rice and Wonton Soup) graciously and had it ready moments after my arrival as discussed.   Here's my rundown of the this lunch special -  Crispy Orange Chicken had a pretty good sauce, and the cut chicken was plentiful, as was the rice. Problem was that the crispiness was gone by the time I opened the plastic container because both were mixed together, rather than keeping bird and sauce separate until consumed at final destination. Too, but for this premature exposure, the chicken could have been left dry with a little ventilation to allow excess moisture to escape as the food cooled. Still a tasty dish, but could have been so much better without the soggies.   Wonton Soup was less redeeming. The wontons were thick skinned and filled with mystery meat. The beef stock in which they swam was aging rapidly and lacked much to applaud. It was hot, so I'll give it that.   Fried Rice was the largest part of the combo. It was okay, with enough pork and veggies to warrant some merit, but I left most of it behind as unwanted starch.   There was nothing unusual about the meal, although the price was inexpensive. Happy China falls into the overall Average range of Chinese American takeout. It would be hard to find much better in similar joints, and much easier to find worse.

COVID-19 TAKEOUT REVIEW  Out on York Road just before it enters Montgomery County from Bucks, sits Rey Azteca (King of the Aztecs), a decent Casa Mexicana located in what looks to have been formerly a Pizza Hut. Adequate parking and nicely remodeled interior with those colorful carved chair backs and murals depicting the bright life made famous in all the pastel paintings sold on the streets of almost every small villa in Mexico.  Looking for a place to pick up a good meal, I picked this one because of strong reviews and relative proximity.   Bottom line - It lost something in-between house and store, as many carry-outs do. Sitting in aluminum containers and covered to keep in all the moisture, it was no longer as fresh and crisp as they would have been if eaten right there.   The Steak Fajitas were plentiful, but overcooked and too chewy when eaten at our kitchen table. Far too well-done and dried out. The side salad, guac and crema tasted good, but couldn't revive what was already deceased. Luckily, the Los Coco's Special (two beef/chicken quesadillas with red rice) was much better, especially with salsa roja generously applied over top. Very satisfied.   Neither dish came with the promised side tortillas.   The Chip & Salsa was a hefty bag of corn crunchies and fresh tomato, jalapeno, cilantro in a large plastic bowl. They were a strong compliment.   No doubt this meal would have been better if we had spoken with a server about how to finish the steak (medium), and done without the grillman scorch them to well done. It's hard to get it right when the only dialogue is over the phone, and all you see is a packed up brown paper sack with your name on it upon arrival. The dining room, though closed, looked inviting.

It's convenient to have a local parcel place to take care of shipping issues.   The shop is big for its purpose, and seems a bit sparsely inventoried.  When I worked for a big firm, our mail room looked more stacked and ready to wage a mailing barrage around the world. Still, everything here is computerized. Give them your phone number to find your account (or make one), and give them a name and city where you want to send your package, and in a second they have all the known names/addresses there, and you select the right one.    Small world and getting smaller by the minute.   The only real downside is the expense of using their services.  I just spend $70 to send a very small package to California overnight.  Makes me think I should set up an account directly with FedEx or UPS.    This charge felt like I had just been held up on the stage coach from Bisbee to Tombstone. These robbers didn't even bother to wear masks.  But, I sure felt someone's hand in my pocket.

On the same square as 1st Asian Supermarket in Mayfair, Philadelphia, in a corner brick two story, stands Marinucci's Deli. Those of you familiar, already know that it is a high volume higher quality Italian hoagie gold mine that creates stuffed sandwiches loaded with Dietz & Watson meats and cheeses, and a few signature pieces. Those of us who haven't been there before yesterday now know that this place is a legendary Philly landmark (30 years in this location) that turns out among the best Sammies in the city.   I stopped in after a heavy afternoon of food shopping next door, and ordered two "small" 12" torpedos with Rare Roast Beef & Provolone and Roast Turkey & Swiss, both dressed with lettuce, tomato, mayo, oregano, hot & sweet peppers. Both To Go.   Weighing in at about one pound each, we tore into the roast beef on the drive home. It was spectacular! The meat was fresh and tender, the provolone mildly tart and dry, that combined with all the accessories for a dynamic and delicious bite and chew. The best way to attack this zoftig big boy was with two hands and aggressive squeeze and stuff into the mouth, just like with a cheesesteak. We tag teamed it, my partner holding it in front of my face, while I grabbed with one hand and directed it into my mouth. It only worked at stoplights, but a couple of large bites did the trick. No fuss, no muss. Only a sesame seed from the roll jumping off the bread onto my lap before slipping to the floor.   The Turkey & Swiss was just as good. Top flight ingredients and delightful eye opening taste. Both were good for two meals apiece, so we finished them later that evening with good brew and jalapeño chips.   Marinucci's is one of those Philly joints that leave a lasting impression and a strong desire to return whenever in the neighborhood, which fortunately is about once a month.   The corner of Brous and St. Vincent is a true destination for everyone seeking variety in their low budget culinary exploits. Vietnamese, Chinese, Boba and Marinucci's all in one square of Mayfair is a foodie's dream come true.

Yummy Asian (no relation to Yummy Sushi) is a surprisingly decent Chinese restaurant.  Their menu has a large Japanese Roll offering, but little actual sushi, nor Thai cuisine.  If you stick with the Chinese dishes, you should be quite satisfied.    We came in for a Friday dinner.  The house was nicely appointed.  The service was attentive.  We ordered the Walnut Shrimp, Beef & Chicken Hunan and a Dragon Roll.  The shrimp dish consisted of 8 or 9 Jumbos, Tempura breaded, with a sweet mayo sauce covering the entire pile of crustaceans.  It wasn't the best I ever had, but was still quite enjoyable.    The Hunan style beef and chicken was also well done.  This approach uses less straight ahead red chilis, and substitutes a mix of chili and black beans. It retains a lot of heat, but not the fire breathing kind.  The meat was tender and did not seem to have been frozen.    The Dragon Roll was only okay.  The small amount of fish within the construct of rice, avo, seaweed, etc., was not the freshest.  The ginger was colored orange, rather than the natural white, and the wasabi was likewise artificially dyed green.  Clearly, the sushi guy had gone to Sushi College and finished the basic course in slicing and rolling, but was not working with top ingredients.    My friends enjoyed the chance to speak with management in Mandarin, and that seemed reciprocal.  Probably don't get many organically grown Chinese stopping in.

The Vault is housed inside an old bank building that has been renovated except for the remaining 'vault' complete with heavy duty safe door.  The high ceilings and windows easily remind of the days when banks testified to their success by using their depositors money to build grand edifices to their capitalist acumen.  These days our financial institutions are more often viewed with distain and mistrust, resulting in a more modest approach to their architecture, in which they all fundamentally look like fast food restaurants without the large menus in the drive thru.  Fortunately, the pizza created inside this now comfortable house is anything but what you find in most pie shops in the area.  This is a different animal.  Neapolitan style, meaning the focus is on wood burning ovens that reach over 900 degrees Fahrenheit, that completely bake and sear the dough inside of 90 seconds.  I stood and watched my Pie being made and then placed in the oven.  The crust turned brown and then scorched before my eyes.    The upside of this is incredibly fresh crust that becomes an accompaniment to the toppings (Margharita), rather than the firm platform for them to rest upon.  The experience is more like eating a hot pita dipped in spicy tomato sauce, mozza cheese, and basil leaf.  It sort of turns the meal on its head, but once I understood what was going on, I really enjoyed this variant approach to pizza.    The downside (such as it is) is only that if you have a firm belief that pizza should only be made one way-with a firm tasty crust upon which are placed fine ingredients to be eaten as one entity-you may be disappointed that The Vault's ingenuity takes tomato pie in a different direction.  You can actually tear off part of the crust and dip it into the toppings on the pie as you would salsa & chips.   I'm not suggesting that Napolitan Pie can replace that better known approach to pizza making.  It just that when you feel like something just as good but a little different, The Vault is waiting for you.

Massimo's Café sits at the point where Hamilton Ave. and Liberty Street merge in Hamilton Township.  Sitting in this primo location, Massimo's is a solid Italian lunch and dinner restaurant where you can sit down, fill up, and depart sated on a fairly small budget.  The food is what you would expect from one of the better Italian-influenced cities - Trenton, which sits a few blocks away.  The facility was recently renovated and the inside is attractive is a basic sort of way.  This is not a tablecloth joint, but the tables and chairs are spread sufficiently, and the atmosphere is casual. Nonna sits by the register most days, and adds to the Mange mentality here.   My lunch this week with a friend consisted of Eggplant Parm sandwich, fries, and ice tea.  My lunch mate had the Chicken Parm variant.  The torpedo rolls were fresh and crusty, made crunchy by a turn in the oven before serving.  The Eggplant was plentiful and tasty.  The gravy slightly sweet, which I prefer.  We were both happy with our choices.  The fries were...fries.  Service was good, but I did feel sorry for our wait person who had to cover the floor by herself with more than 8 tables occupied. Still, she provided service with a smile. Tipped her well for her effort.   When in the area I would certainly consider dinner here, but until I do and have a few more things on the menu, Massimo's gets Three Stars with a bullet.

It's unanimous!  Cheese Dawgs is a great joint for Hot Dawgs, Grilled Cheese, and multiple combinations thereof.  Unassumingly sitting in a old Bustleton Pike strip, just south of Street Road, Rick Tyrrell has created a little bit of nostalgia for those of us who grew up loving hot dogs (frankfurters if you are from the New York area).    While the décor is minimalist, it has everything needed for a legitimate happy meal.  With Bonanza playing on the TV, Rick introduced me to his shop and menu; recommending one of his newer items, the Grilled Cheese Dawg.  It is what is sounds like; a Grill Hot Dog wrapped inside a Grilled Cheese Sandwich.  All beef and well spiced (but not as much as Hebrew National garlicy meat tubes), it was an obvious "next step" in the evolution of two beloved American food groups. Symbiosis.  Tasty and fun.  With a side of Corn Chowder (perhaps, a little too thick, but still good), and a Stewart's Black Cherry Wishniak washdown, this was a fast lunch that had me smiling throughout.    I hated to leave my childhood again, but knew it had to be.  To make it easier, Rick gave me a $5 off coupon for ordering my next meal online in advance of arrival, and made a last recommendation of his new Bacon Buttercup.  What's that?  Close your eyes...Imagine the best homemade Peanut Butter Cup - way better than Reece's...then add bacon.  Peanut Butter, Chocolate and Bacon.    Stop drooling!  If that alone does not get you into your car and driving toward Bustleton, then go for the Dawgs and Grilled Cheese.  Either way, you can't lose.

"....with a name like Smucker's...  Couldn't resist, but the slogan does hold true.  If their food isn't good, they will hear about it in a bad way.    Fortunately, most of the salads and side dishes found in the display are very good.  The service is friendly and prompt, and you can even taste a sample of anything that interests you.  My favorites are the Baked Lima Beans, Chicken Salad, and Rice Pudding; all of which I can eat in one meal either in the tiny sitdown areas, or as take home.  Also, the jarred goods on the right hand side of the shop are worth a look for some esoteric Pennsylvania Dutch/Amish treats.  Their Corn Relish is great!   Still only open Thursday through Saturday, it is best to get there early for the freshest selection.  Eat it quickly to enjoy its peak flavors.

Shumai Wok is a new entry to the "Asian Fusion" takeout wars in Penndel, Pa. It is one of those places that really only does "to go" food, although there is a solitary table sitting there for those like me who want to eat before returning to the office.  It is also one of those pseudo-fusion joints that offers Chinese, Japanese, and Thai dishes on their menu, but are really just a low budget Chinese house that makes cheap inauthentic versions of Japanese and Thai food, and does a sushi business in an attempt to be all things to all people.    While I cannot speak to the sushi, I did recently have a dish of Pad Thai with Chicken, which as a lunch special came with a choice of Soup and Rice.  As Thai soups were not offered, I accepted Wonton and Pork Fried Rice as the complements to the meal. Strange combo.    Of course, although I was eating there, everything came to the table in take out containers.  Okay. I can deal with that.  The Wonton Soup was overly salty (MSG?), and the wontons themselves, thick and without much filling.  The Fried Rice was dyed yellow from the chicken broth it was cook in that morning, was al dente and not worth the calories.  Finally, the Pad Thai used the wrong thin noodles, and a sauce that tasted like the topping for General Tso's Chicken, not the traditional gravy that a Thai kitchen would produce.  The weird orange color gave it away.    This was a one time only visit.  Although the people who work there (owners) are friendly and the prices are low, the food was a major downer, and it seems impossible for it to get to neutral ground where it would be tolerable.

When I leased a storage unit at this Public Storage about 9 years ago, it was with the intention that I would only have it for a short time, and then be done with it.  Such are the empty intentions of this good man.   I finally ended my relationship with these folks yesterday.  What had been a reasonable $80 dollar a month rental had become more than $230 a month, and was taking a bite out of my budget.  No one to blame but me, yet there is a lesson to be learned about procrastination and the cost of delay.  I learned it!   The office people were always great to deal with.  They even suggested ways to reduce costs.  In fact, it was their positive attitude that finally woke me up to the need to be done with their services.   This operation demonstrates that there is a business available for any need.  Not so in every country, but in the USA, if you need a place to hold a generation of furniture you will likely never use, but to which you have an emotional attachment, free enterprise will provide you with the means to accomplish that end.    All we need now is another business to wake us up and remind us to be rid of useless junk.  Oh, wait...That business already exists, too.  1.800. GOT JUNK.   God bless America!

King Market is a traditional green grocer, the same as can be found on almost every street in every city and village in China and around the rest of Asia. Everything is fresh, well presented, and out on the sidewalk where the natural light lets you see exactly what you are buying.  It is also a great marketing tool to make you walk past the display on 10th Street.  It is impossible not to slow down or stop the take a closer look at some unusual veggies and fruit not seen routinely in the larger supermarkets outside of Asian neighborhoods.  Be it baby bok choy or the more exotic Fire Dragon Fruit, you are going to find something you are curious about and want to try.  Those lucky enough to have a long term experience with such wonderful healthy choices still appreciate the ability to secure their cultural comfort foods in such an authentic locale.     Inside are found what doesn't fit on the sidewalk, as well as packaged goods, food staples, and refrigeration units with things that require it.  The two aisles are narrow, with boxes under the display shelves and in the corners, making passage a bit of a challenge, but that is part of the fun.   If you are coming to Chinatown for a meal consider a stop at King Market for fresh produce, rice, home brewed soy sauce, vinegar, and a few sweets that you will not find at your local Giant or Super Fresh.   You will be glad you thought of it.

Slowly, but surely, Bagel Train has become my primary bagel source.  While I still miss Bagel Junction in Newtown, the B Train has found a way into my heart and stomach with regularity.  My son and I stop in once a week before school to grab a breakfast of Onion Bagel, Butter and Swiss. He goes for Yoohoo, while I pour my first coffee of the day.    The bite, texture and taste are exactly what we love (and kvell over).  This has become our routine. Bonding is a wonderful side dish with the bagels.    Given the importance it has taken on in our lives, and the high quality and exceptional taste sensations generated, a bump to 5 Stars is overdue.

Misleading advertising is a turn off.   This Original Dominick's Pizza joint on W. Trenton Avenue in Morrisville, Pa., has no relationship with the true "Original Dominick's" other than they owned/operated this restaurant until a few years ago when it was sold to the current people.  I guess the contract didn't require that the brand be protected, or perhaps the price included continuing the signage.  Regardless, if you click on the website listed here there is a straight up disclaimer that this store is not part of the family.    And, they really should care about their image, as the pizza and tomato pie prepared here are a few steps down from what you can eat at the Richboro and Washington Crossing outlets.  The Brooklyn and Tomato Pie slices I consumed the other evening were okay, but lacked the flavor of quality sauce and cheese.  Even the dough was less appealing.    Some may think that hanging a sign on the side of the building exclaiming new management is enough to alert the public that everything within had changed, but the name.  But, truth in advertising (even passive signs left over from the old regime) is important, and tells a lot about what is happening now.    Perhaps, that explains why the house is nearly empty whenever I drive by.  I won't be going back.

I work about half a mile from Ivy Tavern on South Broad Street in Hamilton.  It has been anchoring this area for a very long time. I remember hanging out here in the 80's when I was bartending downtown and had a night off.  They always had live bands, cheap drinks, and hot skirted bar mistresses.  Unbeatable combination.   Then, I moved on and didn't return until last week.  30-odd years and it still looked exactly the same!  Still pumping the standard label suds, and baking a very good bar pie.  The crowd seemed older than I remembered, but then again, so was I.  Those guys cemented to the barstools were likely the same as had been the young dudes the last time I was there. Funny how we find our place in the world.   Anyway, I was catching a late lunch and had less than an hour to shut the growl in the pit of my stomach, and get back for the next interview.  The servers were still muy attractiva, so I took a spinner at the end of the bar, ordered a pie and Redd's, while chatting up my collegial barkeep.  The pie arrived about 10 minutes later, cheese a bubbling, and the aroma of ripe tomato, garlic and sausage steaming into my face.  Tears came to my eyes.  Some things are just timeless.     The Bar Pie is an interesting creation.  Larger than the "personal size pizza," often found in the Nuevo-rias of the world, but smaller than the usual "small pie."  This is a "tweener,"- big enough for two for a late night comfort food raid, but also small enough for a hungry person to consume solo.  It is about 3 regular slices from a large pie.  This one was very good.  Scorched bottom from the superhot oven, and almost molten topping when it arrived.  It cooled slowly, and while the first sliced required fork and knife to handle, the last couple of slices could be handled manually without insulated gloves.  It was crunchy, feisty, and delicious.  Plenty of Sweet Italian Sausage to sate the savage beast.    While perhaps, a step down from its brothers at JoJo's Tavern, Ivy still bakes a very good bar pie. Well worth the trip from a wider radius.  Knowing that it is so close at hand, and offering good grub, good prices, and good reveries, makes it a priceless and prized stop on the Trenton Pizza Train.

A certain political party in Bucks County had its annual Jefferson Dinner at Pen Ryn Mansion last week.    The entire locale is incredibly pretty for Bensalem, Pa., but the Delaware River still has its charm, and the building and landscaping there are very nice.  There is plenty of parking and if you have time you can stroll down to the banks of the river and watch the dusk settle in and the lights of Burlington, NJ come up across the river.      The dining facility is ornate with heavy curtains and chandeliers, but although dated, it does give off an air of historical pretense.  If there is an issue it is with the HVAC.  On this relatively warm October night, the bar area was downright hot, and the large banquet room only a little more comfortable.  Of course, all the hot air from the podium may have had something to do with that.    Pen Ryn would be a nice place for a traditional wedding or other large format celebration.  This is my third of fourth visit, and it is always an attractive, if not completely comfortable place to spend the evening with a few hundred of my closest friends.

I sat down at the bar in the middle of Jester's Café and looked around.  A couple sat at a table separated by a low wood/glass wall from my vantage point.  The space had a 1920's feel to it with lots of windows on the street at this corner of Farnsworth and Crosswicks Ave.   With a little Art Deco it might touch magical.    Adam the bartender took good care of me; well versed in the menu and the beer on tap.  My Merry Monks was a rich reddish amber with a good flavor.  It went perfectly with my Fire Burger (medium), which had a few grilled Longhot Peppers and Aoili Mayo on top of the juicy and tasty ground beef to give the entire sandwich a spicy lift.    This was one of the better burgers I had eaten in the past six months, and after having tried the Rossi Burger just the week before I was surprised how much better this one was - and at a lower price.  The Fries were ample and decent.    Jester's Café is the best place I have lunched at in Bordentown so far on my rediscovery tour of this historic river town.  While I have enjoyed all my meals there, this one combines ambiance, personality and taste in ways that most please me.    It took me by surprise.  I became its happy captive, and will return.

The South Street Bridge literally connects two parts of my life - my law school days in West Philly, and my early professional life living at 26th and Delancy. The distance from 48th and Baltimore and my first home purchase may have been less than a mile distance, but the existential shift was immeasurable.  Regardless of on which side of the river I resided, the South Street Bridge stood as the connection between past and present, student and worker, freebird and taxpayer,  dreamer and doer.   So, when I return to the area for any reason, I feel compelled to reflect upon the passages in my life.  I drive by the old townhouse in Center City and consider my great fortune in being able to buy a home across the street from a warehouse and brownfield that soon became a beautiful park.  I cruise into West Philly to see what's new on campus on my way to the outer reaches of Balto Ave., and see how much better everything is now.  Even the Bridge itself has been renovated, and is no longer the rusty derelict I walked across so many times.  Like many things in life, its better days are now.  Hopefully, that is an indication of what lies ahead for all of us.    There are times when the span may have saved my life after leaving a great concert at Irvine Auditorium, and running into some folks who did not take kindly to the company I kept.  There were other times that it offered warm greetings to a returning prodigal son after too long away from the cozy confines of my piece of West Philly. And, yes, there were times it felt like a prison gate or pirate ship plank I had to walk while suffering the anxieties of final exams, or broken hearts.   I have said elsewhere that bridges hold a special significance for me. The South Street Bridge is one of the inner sanctum of spans between one life and another that enables me to feel life intensely as a continual passage on the roads (and bridges) of life.

Strong first impression of East Sushi.    Located in the shopping center at the corner of Scotch Road and Parkway in Ewing, that also houses Five Guys, and immediately next to Villa Rosa, East Sushi was a surprise find for me.  I had driven down this way many times and never seen it.  Very glad I finally did with Yelp help.     The space is attractive with hushed lighting, dark tones, the sushi bar to the left rear, and booths and tables along both walls.  A half wall divides the shop and provides a modicum of privacy.  This is a "fusion" house in the best sense of the word.  They really do succeed at being equally adept at fish sculpting/rice molding, and Chinese cuisine.  Although I was alone and ordered a Cantonese dish (Beef Chow Fun), I could see and hear my neighbors enjoying their sushi rolls and sashimi.    Not that I wanted to eavesdrop, but although it was lightly attended when I arrived around 8 pm, they sat the three tables of customers right next to each other, making it impossible to ignore my neighbors.  It would be a plus should management recognize that spacing out the customers when possible would enhance to overall experience of the diners.  My meal was very good.  The broad Rice Noodles, thin strips of Beef, abundant Vegetables and quality Brown Sauce, made for a quite enjoyable repast.  I could only finish half of the large plate in house, and took the rest home for a second round.  The Green Tea served singly in a ceramic mug was also tasty and promptly refilled without charge.    Service was professional.   I'll be back to check out the Japanese side of the operation and trust it to be as good as my neighbors made it seem.  There is also a short Thai menu for those who favor those flavors.

Another variation of the endless fastfood burger joints, this one a Wendy's.    Plenty of parking around the free standing building, but designed to have the only entrance door right near the drive through line.  Dangerous. Why not have them separated on opposite sides of the building to protect folks going in?    The dining room was empty at 2:30 in the afternoon.  Clean.  Plenty of tables, with seats all facing north and south.  I was looking for something easy for a late lunch and opted for the 4 for $4.  Fine print - you get a single sandwich of your choice, and must accept the 4 count chicken tenders, flies and a drink.  Want 2 burgers?  Tough luck. That's not how this deal is played.  Ridiculous!  Can't remember what I ate, other than it was hot and forgettable.  The tenders were average, and the French fries pretty good.  Large lemonade washdown.  Guess that's the point.  When the fries are the best part of the meal, there is a serious creativity problem at Chez Wendy.  Ho - hum.

At least once or twice while in town for the gem shows in late January, the family demands a dinner more in line with what we consider comfort food.  I may prefer to gorge on Indian, Mexican and Vietnamese cuisine, and my family goes along willingly. Still, I know with me working most of the day and leaving them at the hotel to play, they need something that is fun to eat.  BJ's Restaurant & Brewhouse fills the bill.  The place is large and bustling.  Mixed group of people at dinner time, with the happy hour folks mingling around the bar, and those of us in for a meal scattered around either along the bright windows, or deeper inside where it feels cool and dark.  While fairly typical of the latest variant of the modern roadhouse, it does it very well.  I get to drink a few interesting local craft beers, and my son gets his favorite drink of all time - root beer.  Once he tasted it he was mellow the rest of the night.  I took a sip. Smooth, light, sweet, and chill.  It was okay that he had nearly a pitcher of it.  He would remember it for a lifetime.  BJ's seemed to be about pizza and beer, and we saw no reason to stray far from their wheelhouse on the first visit.  2010 was our first sit down, and I still remember the deep dish pies as overwhelmingly thick and overloaded with terrific flavor and texture.  The BBQ Chicken Pizza was enough for 6 people, and the Flatbread Roasted Veggie and Goat Cheese a crispy, glorious treat.  We ordered both of these for the 3 of us, and ended up taking most of it back to the hotel for the next day. The following visit, we had a simpler design; one Flatbread Pizza, One Crispy Jalapeno Burger, Wedge Salad and Gourmet Mac & Cheese for the young man.  All very good, and less to take back with us.  We were a happy clan, especially after trying a Pizookie, their signature dessert.  If you love cookie dough, this is for you - baked cookie dough topped with Vanilla Bean Ice Cream and a square of Dark Chocolate.  It is one delicious hot mess.    Sitting back here on the East Coast as I write this, I can still recall the total satisfaction from the experiences at BJ's.  It makes me dream of returning next year for more of the same pleasures.

Ray's Deli Café is a throw back kind of place.   It sits at the bottom of High Street where it butts into Mill Street in Mount Holly, NJ.  Ray is the chief cook and bottle washer, and his better half runs the front of the house.  She is a stitch, with a load of funnies to crack, followed by a horse (hoarse) laugh that is infectious.    The house itself feels rather dark, with a small counter toward the back where I settled in earlier this week for breakfast.  Perhaps more lighting would dispel the sense that the back area needs a thorough cleaning. Still, the coffee was strong and plentiful, and the French Toast available as a Short Stack, which was all I wanted.  Ray came out to the grill to prepare the meal.  The dish was decent, if a little "eggy," around the edges. My compliment to the chef was met with a smile before he retreated back to his enclave.    Ray's is a place with some old world charm, but a bit disheveled.  The prices are in line with the atmosphere, so there is definitely a deal to be made on an inexpensive meal.  Still, Mt. Holly is a happening place this century, and there are more than a few better stops for a memorable morning meal.   I would return, but not anytime soon.

Coming here directly from Farmers' Best Supermarket on Adams is probably not fair to Farmers'.  But, we needed a few things in the way of kitchenware that Kobawoo had in large amounts.  It was impossible not to notice how clean and organized this place was compared to where we had just been.  Better lighting.  Broader aisles.  Smaller space, yet nicely laid out.    Strong display of serving vessels and cooking utensils for both the home and professional kitchen.  Only thing it lacked was plastic chopsticks for restaurant use, so bamboo would not have to be wasted on a single use.    Overall, a good place for Asian cooking needs, and one to which I would gladly return.
This is where the deliciously creamy Goodnoe Ice Cream is made.  You have to go to the Goodnoe Ice Cream shop on Sycamore Street to actually buy it.  Very worth the trip.

Still a great place for lunch or dinner in Newtown.   My son loves the Buffalo Chicken Cheese Steak and it is one of the first things he wants when he returns for a visit.   I had Penne Aglio Olio with Spinach tonight, and it was very good.  The side salad needs a little work to bring it up to par, but that is a small nit in an otherwise enjoyable dinner.

Broad Street Diner (formerly Manetas) is aptly named for the street where it is located. Of course, there are other diners on Broad Street, so don't be confused.  This place has been well renovated to match its new moniker, and although smaller than the better known places like Mastoris and Town and County a few miles away, it is still comfortable, although the tables are fairly close together.   I was there for a late lunch last week, and the floor was mostly empty.  I was greeted with a smile by a waitress and the cashier, and led to a deuce in the side dining room. A second waitress brought me a menu and informed me where to look for specials. She promptly brought water and lemon, and returned again moments later to take my order of Greek Turkey Burger on Pita.  The platter came out with the grilled pita on the bottom of the plate, and the burger on top of it. It was up to me to make it a sandwich, which I opted not to do.  There was a small plastic cup of fresh feta cheese, and tachini sauce in another, so I could use what I wanted. Lettuce and Jersey Tomato sat on the edge of the plate.  At first, I was a little put off that the finished product was not constructed in the kitchen, but as I got into my own preparation I began to appreciate leaving the raw materials for me to combine.  That way I had it just the way I wanted it. There were also a side of fries, but aside from being hot and crisp, I don't recall the taste two days later.   My server was very friendly and efficient, and obviously well trained.  She appeared to offer more water or ask if I needed anything, and I knew she really meant it, as opposed to the monotone I often get when the job is just routine.  I tipped her well for her pleasant professionalism.   The meal was good. Everything fresh, quality ingredients.  While I would not rush back for another meal, I certainly will remember I enjoyed my lunch and not hesitate to return to the Broad Street Diner when in the area.  January 4, 2016 - Stopped in for a late night dessert, coffee and conversation.  All three played their part well in making an enjoyable evening.  The Rice Pudding was excellent.

First rate gelati with an abundance of fruity flavors to mix with the heavy creaminess of the custard. Darkest Cherry, or Green Apple, or Mango Tango, or something like that are all treats.   Word on the street is that this Rita's is the most successful in their national franchise. For a little barn that is closed between Thanksgiving and May Day that is quite a feat.   Come to Newtown for ice cream and other sweet creamies. So many choices in a small area, and a great town to walk around while ice creams drips from your chin.

At the intersection of Stoopville Road and Washington Crossing Road in Lower Makefield, Village Market has been dishing out good breakfast and lunch sandwiches for decades.  Their recent upgrade adds to its luster, and the newly engineered intersection makes it easier to get in and out with risk of bodily harm.  It is easy to miss the deli section in the white building next to the Exxon station, but try to stop in.  VM has a deserved reputation among locals for hearty breakfast sandys and over-stuffed burritos, way above average lunch options (especially Cheesesteaks and Chicken Salad subs and wraps, and even decent fresh coffee. It is primarily a take out joint, and the parking is adequate.  The staff moves efficiently and knows what the regulars want.    There is a bit of confusion as to who has jurisdiction over Village Market.  Although much closer to the center of Newtown, it is actually in Lower Make.  Don't let that squabble deter you from sampling their homemade menu.  But, if you have the misfortune of being pulled over for speeding on Rt. 513, the police who will be stopping you and issuing the summons are from Lower Makefield, so don't blame Newtown.

A dozen or so visits to Bagel Train has led me to the opinion that it deserves an upgrade to four stars.  Perhaps, my taste bud memories have waned, allowing me to create new images of my childhood in the City.  Maybe, I am feeling more at home standing in line and interacting with the good folks working there.  Too, it could be the realization that BT's "baagels" are less expensive than the recently departed Bagel Junction (of blessed memory).  Regardless, I now look forward to the first bite of these creations, and that deserves recognition via promotion.

Originals Pizza sits to the side of the Giant Shopping Center on West Trenton Avenue in Morrisville, Pa.  It is in a small commercial strip next to a Wells Fargo office and a Dominos Pizza.  It has been here for a long time and has settled into its space nicely.  Although long and narrow, the furnishings create the sense of sitting on picnic tables under a striped awning along the outside walls of the building.  Nice, if gitchy, touch.   The moustachioed men behind the counter look like brothers, but they assured me they were not.  They were both friendly and ready to serve.  As I came in after 7 pm on a midweek evening, the pizza offerings were not vast for a guy in need of only a slice.  That is always the risk taken late in the day of any pizza shop.  You never know how long the pies on display have been waiting for your attention.  Their "Tomato Pie" seemed to have the most energy as it sat there, so I asked for it to be reheated to "well done" for me.    It was that.  When it arrived I could see that the heavy tomato pasty topping had been reawakened.  Picking it up gingerly, it held its point well with only the slightest quiver from the weight above.  The scorch marks on the chassis were well established from the oven.  That is what I wanted.  First bite revealed a thicker than expected crust that resisted my clenching incisors just enough to let me know it would not yield its secrets willingly.  Solid chew.    The slice was more than enough for an evening snack.  Two slices would have been way too much.  The top sauce was thicker and saltier than I prefer, and the few chunks of garlic not enough to demand serious attention.  I overheard the chef say to a customer that this was "Brooklyn Style" Tomato Pie.  Not sure what he meant, as it surely wasn't the T.Pie created and made famous across the Delaware in Jersey.  There, the mozza goes on before the sauce, and the tomato mix is applied more sparingly to achieve balance in texture and taste between the two main food groups.  Originals had little or no cheese that I could discern, but just the overpowering sauce.    It was okay for what it was, but not close to what I was accustomed to in a Tomato Pie.

When a hotel/bed & breakfast/restaurant has been around as long as The Brick, it gets some cred from its history and deep roots in the community.  While George Washington may not have slept here, he certainly ate here - and that is amazing. Through the centuries The Brick has seen its share of historic moments, as well as its share of scandal.  It has prospered and suffered at the hands of various owners, some of whom took great pride in the establishment, while others did not.    It went through such a change a few years ago, and the trail of reviews shows this plainly.  Through it all, the first floor bar and dining areas have retained their charm and well accented colonial airs.  For that alone, The Brick is worthy of Fandom.  The cuisine may not always keep pace with the aura of the old stone, brick and wood.    Today, I attended a special function for a community group honoring (and roasting) some of the more ancient sportspeople in town.  For the first time in the long history of the organization, the silver cup was engraved with the name of a woman.  Very happy to be part of the moment.  Buffet dinner was served before the award ceremony.  It was spread out in the bar room; a perfect setting.  Spring Mix Salad, Chicken Piccata, Penne Vodka, Roasted Potatoes sat waiting for our walk through.  The salad dressing was a pale yellow cheesy creamy Italian and the croutons from a box.  The Chicken was slightly above room temperature with the lemony gravy semi-solid on top.  The Roasted Potatoes somewhere between well done and dry.  The pasta was good, but also not hot enough.  It wasn't that the ingredients were lacking, but that the preparation and presentation were not quite right.   If not for the great camaraderie in a grand old room, the food would have been a near fail.  We were not there for the food, so to some extent I can overlook the issues.  I was happy to be there today, and it was very cool to be part of this small piece of history being made.    Go for the atmosphere, and perhaps a drink.  Go for a brunch when you can sit on the glassed-in porch and view downtown Newtown. Don't go for more, or risk disappointment.

A+ for this authentic "Hole In The Wall" Mexican café, The Tropical Rooster.    Right off South Broad Street at the corner of Park Avenue, El Gallo is a clean shop with about a dozen tables.  Sombreros line the walls, and Mexican soap operas play non-stop on the TV hanging from the ceiling.  The family owners are very friendly and bilingual, although I was the only Gringo having lunch.  I practiced my rusty Spanish, and received a few extra smiles for the effort.    The menu offers a broad range of lunch and dinner options, and the kitchen is sufficiently visible to be able to see and hear the meals being made complete with the banter and laughter of the gifted husband and wife team.    The Torta Al Pastor is a fat sandwich full of Grilled Pork, Onion, Pineapple, Cheese, Lettuce and a touch of Mayo, all stuffed into a oversized round roll.  It tasted great!  The Pork was lean with a touch of BBQ flavor, and the Pineapple added a distinct juicy undertone that really set off my taste buds. The mild Cheese hid beneath the two stars of the show, but provided a subtle ending to each bite.  This was large enough to be my dinner. I was not hungry again until morning.   Jarritos Mandarin, a favorite carbonated beverage, accompanied the feast, and a side of well tanned Fries completed the ensemble.  Apparently, they also concoct some tropical smoothies. I noticed them too late, but next time I will unlock that secret.   El Gallo Tropical is now on my short list for lunch, and will be a regular stop as one my favorite lunch spots now that I am working in the area.

When my son's bike went down, and he suddenly needed it for a scout trip in 2 days, I stuffed his wheels into the back of my car and drove over to Harry at the Newtown Bicycle Shop. As usual, Harry Betz was elbow deep in some repair and had to disengage before coming out to greet us and find out what we needed. His triage took about 10 seconds and he diagnosed both the obvious and hidden problems clearly to us.  Could he do the repair? Sans doubt.  Could he do it before tomorrow night, as son was leaving crack of dawn for New York State?  Oh, ye of little faith... Mais bien sur.   My son and I were relieved, and were out of the shop within 5 minutes ready for a stop at Rita's for a guilt free stress release celebration.    Returned the following evening before closing, and the bike was good as new, and much cleaner than when it entered.    I hear what the others are saying about "service with a smile." That may not always come with the expert repairs and knowledge that a local biz is watching our backs in a crunch. Still, I am a fan of having a confident expectation of getting the job done right and on time. Besides, Harry is  way cool when you spend any time with him.

If I need to hit an Asian grocery, butcher, fish monger, rice shop, or soy distributor, and can't get out of town to a H Mart, Hung Vuong Super Market in the Wing Phat Center will have to do.  It has all I need in so many varieties that I start to lose perspective and wonder if there really is one special soy sauce for the specific dish I want to prepare, rather than one of many that would do quite nicely.  Of course, I then search for a store employee to ask this question and he/she inevitably walks me down the aisle like a curator in a museum and pulls out a bottle and hands it to me with a look between bemusement and contempt that I didn't know what I was looking for.  Mea culpa!  Having spent a long time in Asia I know that this and other "super" markets exist there in much better condition and organization than Hung Vuong and the other big stores in the city.  There, they don't smell, they are kept clean, offer better packaging and more refrigeration, and actually sell a wide variety of western products you don't find here. I generally avoid those modern conveniences and shop the outdoor markets to find the specific item I want at the vendors who specialize in those things.  After all, I am a foreign traveler because I like the traditional ways of doing business.    Those outdoor or night markets are not to be found regularly around here, so I accept that Hung Vuong and its siblings down the street and in Chinatown, are as good as it gets.  Luckily, I enjoy the experience enough to make it all worthwhile.   These days I am working my way through all the bottled chili sauces to find the few I like best.  I should complete my research sometime around 2018.

Upon approaching the front door of Wrightstown Country Store there is a large sign advertising their Homemade Chicken Salad and recommending their Bacon Hoagie. Sad for me, they were out of the former, and I would never consider the later, when I arrived shortly after 1:00 on Wednesday afternoon.  Still, there were other choices.  I asked the women behind the counter in the rear of the store what was the best thing they made and was told that aside from the Chicken Salad and Breakfast Sandwiches, the Cheesesteak was high on the list.  They were cordial and chatty, so I ordered a Chicken Cheesesteak with Sautéed Onions and Mushrooms while I continued to question them about the Store and menu.  One lady retreated to the back room where the grill was located to made my lunch, and the other told me that her father had worked there 40 years ago, and she was creating a family tradition. Cool.   While waiting I took a stroll around the small shop that had been standing on this site for at least 80 years.  The front half shelves were mostly empty, except for an ATM machine and small groupings of soft drinks.  The rest of the space was sparsely inventories with cookies, chips, snacks and other lunch accessories.  It was all rather Spartan. The refrigeration unit had the best provisions with the meats and cheeses for lunch making. While I normally enjoy the historical/cultural ethos that permeates an old commercial building that has withstood the passage of time, I found myself in a more somber mood within this building.  I don't know what it was but I felt a pall that made the air feel heavy and brooding.  Perhaps, it was just my low blood sugar crying out for something to eat.  On reflection, I think that somehow the depression era around 1930 was trapped inside the building.   Only take out here, so I went back to my office to eat at my desk.  The Chicken Cheesesteak was presented in white wrapping paper only.  It was still warm, but no longer hot when I sat down 10 minutes later.  The Chicken, Onions and Mushrooms had been chopped and mixed well.  The roll was fresh, but had a soft exterior without any appreciable crustiness.  The overall taste was decent, but not really satisfying.  It was a bit too salty.  Given the nearby alternatives, I would not get it again.    Wrightstown Country Store has seen better days.  If walls could talk, they would certainly have tales to tell about life in these parts in the first half of the 20th Century, when Route 413 was still only Route 113.  But, the story for the second decade of the 21st Century is that the walls need a fresh coat of paint, and more imagination in the kitchen if it is going to attract business and continue to operate prosperously.   I will return soon for a breakfast sandwich and provide an update.  I want to see if the vibe is more upbeat in the morning.   Stay tuned.

Paige H. from Morrisville has it right.  This place is a mixed bag (of bagels).  When Bagel Junction in Newtown closed its doors unexpectedly a few months ago I was heartsick.  My favorite bagel joint for many years was gone. What was I going to do? I checked on Google and Yelp for a substitute for my addiction.  I tried several places in the area before going to Bagel Train. Their bagels are almost as good as Bagel Junction, and I found they satisfied my craving better than the others.  Many of us are bagel experts, and I consider myself one, being raised in New York, and having strong opinions about such important things.  So, this is now my local bagel place.  But, there is a reason for only 3 stars.  The bagels are 4 star (everything is relative), but the interaction with the owner is stiff and unwelcoming (1.5 stars).  The coffee is so-so.  The help is very good, and compensate in part for their boss's personality, and the lack of physical comfort as I stand in a long line waiting my turn.  Even that has its benefits, as there are many nice people to talk with. Cash or check only.

The third generation of Goodnoes are now in the ice cream business, carrying on the rich and creamy family tradition. While no longer occupying the history corner restaurant (great loss), they have the same ice cream that made the name synonymous with excellent ice cream, sundaes, malts, etc.  The dairy still turns out the same delicious flavors that your grandparents loved and waited for on Saturday nights.  Newtown has an embarrassment of ice cream riches.  Sweet Pea, Owowcow, Zebra Striped Whale and Goodnoes.  All are good in different ways. But, for my ice cream dollar, Goodnoes is still first in my heart and stomach.   It is worth a visit to Newtown to try all four places and decide for yourself.

Saw the movie, About Time, last night.  This isn't a movie review site, but if you are looking for theaters it does not hurt to get an idea about what is playing.   This was a feel good movie with enough suspension of disbelief required to last for weeks.  If you enjoy time travel (who doesn't like going back in time), then this one is for you.  It is light, funny, and endearingly idiosyncratic.  Yes, it leaves many questions unanswered, but that is not the point of romantic comedies.    The acting is believable, and the London and Cornwall locales attractive.    Looking for something to do next Sunday night, check this one out if you want a movie that leaves you with a smile, rather than a grimace.  If you want dinner with that, do what we did and go to Misto Diner for an above average Chinese meal first.

I was lucky enough to stumble into the Grand Opening of Café 128 one morning earlier this week.  The new coffee house is located at the prime location directly across from the State House on West State Street, and situated in a walk down basement space that has been very nicely renovated into a subterranean cozy space. Plenty of exposed brick, wood and granite all around.   It was obvious they were still getting set up when I walked down the steps, but I was greeted warmly and welcomed to their new enterprise.  They do breakfast and lunch and appear to have state of the art equipment, including point of service payment system that allows the customer to use the latest technology to cover expenses without the staff touching a credit card.   My order was a simple Everything Bagel with Butter and Swiss.  While I did not ask for it toasted, it came out that way.  No problem, as it appeared to have been pressed by a Panini iron that flattened the bagel, but also slightly melted the cheese and butter, but not enough to create a leakage issue.  It tasted very good as I drove back to the office.  The coffee was from the Small World Coffee people, and was a satisfying brew. The bagel was a good bite.     If this house can manage the flow of lunch customers in that small space, they have a great opportunity to do very well there.  This stretch of West State Street in Trenton is very attractive these days, inviting people to walk and take their pleasures as they stroll.    The proprietors are accomplished in the food trade, with other shops in Pennington and the sushi bar at Trenton Social.  They know "...Renton."   Best of luck!

Horsham Donuts just hit the big time.  It is joining up with Donut Connection, the national round hole franchiser, to take advantage of the marketing clout that name provides.    From the donut lovers perspective you gotta hope that this in no way interferes with the excellence of the current fare.  Horsham bakes up some high quality dough rings, with a broad variety that has captured the affection of the masses.    As long as their hard earned reputation for great donuts doesn't suffer, who could complain about a name change?  My last taste of their Glazed babies, Cherry, and Chocolate rounders, left me in a trance-like state.    Or was that just a wonderful sugar rush?

I don't quite get the Bubble Tea craze, but I did stop in to this one tonight to pick up something warm and stimulating for the drive north.   I took out a Bubble Green Tea, and discovered from the friendlies that the shop was under new ownership and had changed its name to, "Tea Chat."  The joint was a narrow corner store, but clean and inviting.  The prices for the various teas and smoothies were quite reasonable at between $3 and $5.    Good luck to the new enterprise.  May your Boba always snap when you chew them!

Miller's Ale House is a chain out of Florida with outlets from Nevada/Arizona, to right here in River City.  It sits on Rt. 1 (Southbound side) in Langhorne right up against Oxford Valley Mall.  It is easy to miss.    Perhaps, it should be.  It is basically a sports bar with televisions abounding, large beer offerings (the usual suspects in national brands, plus some better known smaller breweries.  The food is what we have come to expect from similar houses - lots of fried food, burgers, wings, salads, even an occasional lobster has been seen sitting at the bar.  It is all basically okay, but nothing worth going back for a second time, unless you find the bartenders or waitresses to your liking (then you are not going for the food).   Given a choice, I prefer the genuine local establishments, which in Newtown are The Clubhouse, Isaac's, Friends, and even The Green Parrot for either a comfortable place to drink and smooze, or watch the Olympics.  We all know our favorite dives.    Miller's is an adequate alternative, but never feels like home.

As an attorney who has appeared here on behalf of clients seeking to become United States citizens, I have witnessed both the good and bad of this important service of the US government.   The entire process takes too long from application to final examination and Citizenship ceremony, but that is not the fault of the good people who work here (except when furloughed because of a government shutdown). Most do their best to make the experience as positive as possible given that there are too few employees to cover the number of applicants.  The wait is generally under an hour to get into an interview or exam, and the actual face time with an examiner is under 30 minutes.  The questions are reasonable if the applicant has studied a little in advance, and the examiners tend to be patient and understanding of language and cultural differences.   The most important thing is to be prepared.  Be sure you have all your official documents in your possession, and have responded to all correspondence seeking more information.  You may need updated tax returns, or employment letters, etc., and be sure you have them.  Otherwise, there may be a need for a return visit. Review the information brochures provided for the form and content of questions.  It is very helpful to talk with those who have successfully completed the process because often the same questions are asked.  There is no shortcut to knowing basic American history and government structure.  Just memorize as much as possible, and be able to talk a little about some of the topics.   Most examiners are sympathetic to your goals, and want your to succeed.  A few may be having a bad day, and when that happens you have no choice but to roll with the punches.   Being represented by counsel is not required, but is often a good idea as it helps greatly with preparation of documents and reviewing possible questions, and can provide a sense of security while waiting in the large waiting room, as well as when with the examiners.

Jay's Steak & Hoagie Joint on Highland Avenue, Parkland, PA, turns out very good cheesesteaks and related grub and fair prices. Their style is heavy on chopped steak, with plenty of whatever you want on it. They do not skimp.   I walked in yesterday to discover a small building, recently renovated into the 21st Century, with a small order counter, one table, and a back kitchen behind a half wall that bisects the room. Easy to hear the banging and clanging on the grill as the beef is torn asunder and plied with cheese, onions, peppers and hot sauce for constructing a Jay's Special. The roll was decent and able to hold most of the overload as long as it is wrapped tight and held on the horizontal until you get to where you intend to consume it.   That was my kitchen table. There was a little leakage on one end, but it did not escape past the outer white paper. The taste was strong, spicy and very satisfying. I could only eat half.   Jay's is definitely a strong choice if you know you want steaks, wings, wraps or hoagies. A pizza parlor it is not. They do a great job in the quantity/quality department, and offer prices that do not offend. It is a bit hard to locate in an older residential neighborhood, that clearly lacked zoning when it was built. Winding streets are fun to navigate, and when you arrive there is a special sense of accomplishment.   Don't miss their food truck in the side yard, nor the outdoor seating on the rear patio.

The Saloon is housed in one of the most historic buildings in Newtown Township, although the interior has been so well redesigned that you would never know it once you get passed the old buggy out on the side porch.  Rest assured that you are dining where travelers and locals have chowed down for more than 200 years.  Yes. The food is much fresher than that.   I stop in occasionally for lunch or a late evening refresher with friends.  The bar is where I accomplish both.  As a former tender, I enjoy the tight confines of the long narrow room and excellent old bar.  Yesterday, I came in for a late lunch and sat at a high top along the wall.  A couple of old dudes sat at the bar chatting up the bartendress, so I basically had the room to myself.  I ordered their 10 oz. Saloon Burger with American, Red Onion, Lettuce on a Roll; Medium please.  It came out slightly beyond the midpoint, but still quite good.  The grill marks were pronounced, as was the taste of the hot steel.  The accompanying Fries were crisp, with a mix of those small overdone pieces that I love to crunch.  My attempt to reduce calories has me eating only half the roll, so the larger than usual burger was more than enough for a satisfying lunch.    The price points on most dishes offered in the afternoon are between $8 and $12, with their burger coming in at $9.    Really a nice spot for a quiet lunch, and a good night spot for a drink and conversation. In good weather, the deck outside awaits.

Still @ 4 Stars.  Returned to try a little Sushi in the form of Salmon Skin Roll.  It was well presented, tightly wrapped, and tasty.  Very happy for the low salt soy sauce option on the table.    Also ordered Chicken Pad Thai, and while amply plated with plenty of fresh ingredients, the taste was not what I expected from this Thai dish.  Wrong spice mix to my palate.   And, my pet peeve again presented itself.  Although there were only 3 tables occupied in the house, we were all seated on top of each other, disturbing the tranquility of the well crafted environment.  I just don't want to eavesdrop on what the next booth has ordered before as they show off for their guest, nor how many sushi roll orders should be eaten in vs. taken home to the kids.   Give us all a little space and we can enjoy our East Sushi in peace.

American menu with a Mexican twist, B-Unos sits where an old mom and pop luncheonette once filled the belly and entertained the troops in downtown Mt. Holly, NJ. They've done a nice redo of the place, with new furniture, walls and floors. The original six spinner lunch counter still sits in back for those who prefer taking a load off in the 60s, before returning to the teen years of the twenty first.   The menu offers BYO omelets, quesadillas and loaded french toast in equal measure, but it pays to keep it simple because each additional item has an upcharge that quickly runs over $10 for even a basic sounding plate. Clever, but not exactly consumer friendly. I chose the naked Frenchie with three slices of thick white bread, melted butter and table syrup.   It looked great with all the caramelized edges, but was a bit dry as the profile showed the egg mix had barely penetrated the wider bread and the middle remained uninvolved in the cooking process. It wasn't all bad, but could have been so much more. The java was hot and strong, as was the service by the young woman who also worked as the cashier and busser.   Maybe staying south of the Rio Grande is the way to happiness at B-Unos.

Sirtaky is the Greek restaurant on High Street in the middle of Mt. Holly, NJ, that replaced the Mugshot Diner.  It looks about the same as before, but the menu is now far more oriented toward the Aegean than the previous occupant. They are open for three squares a day, but I was there just for breakfast (Opens @ 8).  There is a nice counter with about half a dozen spinners, and three booths and a couple of tables.  The joint is pretty cozy.   I sat at the counter and ordered corned beef hash, two over easy eggs and rye toast. It came with a truckload of homefries, which I could not finish. It was a solid and tasty brekkie. Their java is strong and hot.   I had the pleasure of chatting with Paul, the chef (and owner?) of the house.  He was charming and very interested in what I thought of his cooking. It was not difficult to tell him what he already knew - that he knows his way around a Greek kitchen.  We ate breakfast together while we talked. That doesn't happen every day!   Sirtaky is a great addition to the scene in Mt. Holly. Now there are breweries, cafes and a few real good places for the morning repast within blocks of each other.  If Mt. Holly isn't careful, it could become a legit destination for foodies and crafties in the region.   That would be a good thing.

Most Applebee's, like almost any national restaurant chain, are interchangeable. Eaten in one, eaten in them all. That reliability is a good thing if the basic experience is positive anywhere in the Applebee's Universe. While not a favorite, I find that when it comes to dining with family, this name can normally be counted on to deliver a reasonably good quality/value proposition, that satisfies the greatest number for a decent price.   To be precise, my sons like their BBQ ribs, burgers and sides, while we adults can nicely make due with house salads as well as the beef offerings.   Usually.  But, not the other night.   For some reason, things started going sideways as soon as we sat down. First, my plastic water glass sprang a leak and left a pond on the table before we could catch anyone's attention for a towel. Then, when we did, a towel seemed beyond their ability to produce, and they brought a pile of napkins instead. Lacking much absorbency, they were quickly soaked to the max, leaving a large pile of sopping paper and smaller puddles on the table. At least the water was no longer spilling onto our laps, but the wet naps remained on our table through ordering and food delivery, untiI I asked for them to be removed.   My son enjoyed the ribs/chicken breast platter. Devoured all of it. My Whiskey Bacon burger was okay, but beyond the medium finish requested by a few time zones, and crumbly. Not their best effort.   Perhaps it was the exception that proves the rule, but this Applebee's night was all wet.   2.5 Stars

A business lunch brought 7 of us to Miller's late last week.  The house looks a lot better in daylight. Plenty of room, and large windows that open wide on beautiful days to give the feel of eating out on the spring porch.  Small choice of draft beers, but enough to keep most people happy. Service was fine, especially the fact that they have some extra large booths that fit all of us comfortably.  Most of us chose from the salad menu, but there was a burger in the group, too.  When served, although 5 different names, they all looked basically the same with each having been accessorized slightly differently. It was funny, and they were okay, but not particularly memorable. We talked more than we ate, so it didn't make much difference.  If we end up working a project together it will be all worthwhile.

This corner banh mi shop is not much to look at.  Maybe 150 square feet with only 2 tables for eating in, and the rest of the space totally utilitarian for the production of Vietnamese fast food.  There is a wall menu with photos of their offerings and a cooler full of fruit for their various smoothies.  The ladies of the house are pleasant, courteous and very deferential.  I love that they bowed when they delivered my food.   My Spring Roll arrived after the Banh Mi, but that was of no concern.  They were 5 lightly fried, tightly wrapped, logs full of ground shrimp and pork with veggie filler.  The dipping sauce was clear with a sweet vinegar taste. Very nice.    The Banh Mi was loaded with BBQed Pork, Cucumber, Carrot, Cilantro and a good Peanut Dipping Sauce.  The Roll was not quite a crusty baguette, but was fresh and complementarily soft and chewy as the palette on which the other flavors were painted.  Quite good.   Banh Mi Cali is primarily a take out joint for those wanting a good sandwich or one of their many handspun smoothies or bubble teas.  Still, as a solo traveler this night, it suited me perfectly as the place to relax with a good light meal in a small corner of Vietnam.

La Stalla Market on Sycamore Street, Newtown, Pa, does a very good job creating a traditional Italian deli in the heart of this old town. Plenty of cheese wheels, dried sausage, breads, sweets and takeout meals for the asking; all in a small shop that smells as great as it looks.   I was there to grab a sandwich for lunch. They have a long list of choices that can be wrapped, rolled or sliced-breaded. I went with their turkey BLT on a 12" crusty roll. It was huge. Stuffed with enough ingredients for two meals and smeared with aoili mayo that pulled the various tastes and textures together. The roll was excellent, with hard crusty exterior and well aerated sourdough flavor within. Definitely, best of breed master baker. Chomp and chew required strong jaw and teeth, and boy was it a worthwhile challenge.   It was a great sandwich experience.   Ate half, and rewrapped the remainder for later consumption (son devoured it as soon as I got home). $10 for two meals makes the price very reasonable.   In a land full of mediocre pizza shops, it is so nice to have another vision of Italian cuisine so well represented.

Jake's Eatery on Cambridge Lane replaces several Indian Restaurants that occupied this tiny strip mall about a quarter mile west of Sycamore Street in Newtown.   I have had lunch there several times, often choosing to sit at the bar rather than wait for a table.
