As I am usually eating alone, the stool is a good option, however, there always seems to be some confusion in the staff as to who will provide service to me.  Everyone is friendly, but as with many wait people, they avoid eye contact as much as possible and thus are not always attentive to their customers.  This happens repeatedly at Jake's, and thus the time until my order is taken, served, and the bill arrives, adds unnecessarily to the time in-house.   The food is all decent to good.  Most is fresh and tasty.  I enjoy their burgers, which are simple and can be customized to taste (sauteed onions, mushrooms, and jalapeno chilies, please).  The fish sandwich is also good.  The place is clean and bright, and always has a nice crowd.  Many business meals, and post-workout meet ups.   I do miss the Chicken Tikka Masala and Garlic Naan, but it has not turned up on the menu yet.

It is hard to get too excited about a multiplex cinema unless the IMAX seats vibrate and massage me during the show.  Otherwise, "seen one ya seen 'em all."   While IMAX is an improvement over the standard movie experience, I find the 3-D versions of movies to offer little beyond the regular mode.  After a few minutes my mind adjusts to the distorted perception that things are flying at me, and I forget that I am supposed to be having a different reaction.  Too, the cockamamie glasses are always dirty, requiring me to clean them, or suffer through  smudgy vision.  Just not worth the extra couple of bucks for me.   Otherwise, Neshaminy AMC has comfortable seats and convenient drink holders, which is a plus, but aside from the old Newtown Theater, almost all movie houses have similar conveniences.    Parking is fairly good, but a short walk is needed, and the snack bar is loaded with everything a movie goer generally wants, unless something healthy is what they seek.

Café Diem on South 8th Street, just north of Washington, may as well be located in Hue, the former royal capital of Vietnam.  Its version of Bun Bo would certainly satisfy the tastebuds of the Emperor and his retinue.    I admit to limited exposure to this Rice Vermicelli Beef Noodle Soup, but now that I have had it a couple of times, how will I ever go back to regular noodle soup?  It is so vastly superior to American slurp, that it is something of a cultural misnomer to label it "soup" at all.  It is much, much better.    The Café is a small 8 table house that closes at 7 pm daily.  My first attempt to enter was time barred because I arrived too late.  This time I planned around closing, and arrived at 6:30 to an almost empty room.  As I was solo, the hostess pointed to a deuce in the corner, which was perfect for a full view of the proceedings.  I ordered the small bowl of BBH and a Salty Lemonade to offset the 102F broil on the street.  That was gone in a flash.  The soup arrived two minutes later, so overfull with Thin Sliced Beef, Rice Noodles, Cilantro, Mint and a chunk of Oxtail, that it was difficult to add the fresh Thai Basil, Coriander, Sprouts and Squeeze of Lime.  I snapped off the smaller leaves, a handful of sprouts, and a full lime wedge, and managed to push everything into the hot broth with spoon and chopsticks. I think there was even a Banana Blossom on the plate that I tossed in.  With the room created on the side plate, I extruded copious amounts of Hoisin and Sriracha for dipping the beef.    The final product was about the best "soup" I had ever eaten.  Its Lemongrass base was dominant and strident.  The undertone of Fermented Shrimp Sauce added a sour note to the spiciness that really played well together.  Although I asked for "mild," that only applied to how much Hot Chili Oil they put in at the end, because the other condiments were already in the pot.  Finally, as I slowed down and reached the bottom of the bowl, the hint of sweetness came through.  Definitely a spoonful of sugar to make this medicine go down.    This was a great liquid celebration.  It cleared my sinuses and had me envisioning exotic nights in Hoi An and Da Nang.   I love Pho, but a well crafted Bun Bo is superior to that due to the many more ingredients, and the interplay of the four spice groups.  It is easy to see why this was the sup of the royals.

The coolest thing about Sloc's Bar & Grille is that it is attached to Slocum's Bowl-O-Drome, on Pennington Road, Ewing, N.J. If old school bowling is your thing, then this is a wonderful place to indulge yourself. The lanes are old, but full of families and leagues throwing strikes and spares, while the small tavern down the hall, pours suds from mostly well known national brands, and uses the kitchen in back for better than your average bear's bar grub. The dining area was full of groups playing cards on St. Patrick's Day, with most folks garbed in green.  I sipped on my Coor's draft, watching the NBA as I waited for my order of pierogi to be served. The friendly barkeeper was more than happy to change the channel to the game, as nobody else seemed to be interested in the NASCAR race showing on all the screens. Not even the grumpy dude sitting next to me at the bar seemed to mind. I guess there was enough green in my Eagles Super Bowl LII hat to satisfy him.  And, those pierogi were as good as advertised. Moderately chewy doughy dumplings stuffed with mashed potatoes and topped with a motherload of sautéed onions. They appeared to have been boiled and then fried in a pan, as the surface was browned and crisp on the surface, and tender within. The plate was heavy on the crude oil, but that added to the overall homestyle flavor. Delicious.   Best of all, the prices were reasonable. 8 ounce draft plus decent snack for just over $10., is quite the deal.   Although rather old, there did not appear to be any access issues, as everything was on the ground floor with sufficient space for assisted walking or even the private medical chariot.

I am new to Maryanne's Homestyle Cooking, although I know they had another location in the past.  I am glad I finally made it, and that it is now closer to home.    This is a modern version of the old style small town luncheonette that was prevalent across the USA in the early and middle part of the last century.  It is more than a simple place to have a good meal, but also the unofficial town center, where people meet to discuss their lives, community and nation.  It has a warm and comfortable Americana feel to it.  I enjoyed my first visit sitting in a booth behind two senior gentlemen who were doing movie reviews and political analysis at a fairly sophisticated level.  At least 75 each, they gave nothing away to younger minds.    The service was solid with timely walk bys asking if I wanted more coffee.  My French Toast was above average, but not among the best I have had.  The java was hot and tasty.    If there is a weak link in Maryanne's armor it might be the way they approach providing the accompaniments to the dishes served.  Their syrup came in a small plastic cup.  It seemed to be watered down to be just maple sweetwater, rather than anything close to authentic commercial grade maple syrup.  It was completely soaked up by the bread because it lacked the viscosity to sit atop the short stack long enough to allow for cutting and consumption.  It made for soggy French Toast half way through the meal.  I would gladly pay extra for the choice of syrups.  The butter was likewise very thin and airy and had little buttery taste.    Maryanne's could be a real HOME run if they decided to provided an upgrade to these items, or at least the choice to patrons.  Their prices are very reasonable for the clientele, but even folks on Social Security enjoy a little pampering now and then.

Walking into Ted's Montana Grill in Warrington, Pa., (its only location in the Commonwealth), reminded me of my first visit to the Short Branch Saloon in Steamboat Springs, Colorado. A very long bar backed by mirrors and multi-leveled bottles of liquor, tiled barroom floor, small dining areas spaced around the rest of the building.  Tight booths for couples and foursomes with high back benches to maximize privacy. Cowboy and Rocky Mountain accents. Wood beams, floors and paneling everywhere. The only thing missing were the spittoons on the floor at the ends of the bar. With fond memories of those western days, I immediately felt nostalgic, while my expectations rose quickly.   We were seated toward the rear of the house, in a booth out of sight of the bar.  We were about the first to dinner. The table top was covered with a paper map of the Bitterroot Mountains.  It was an early rendition and suitable for framing. We were in the mood for burgers and sandwiches.  We realized that we were in luck because Ted's specialized in beef and bison burgers, along with a few interesting chicken options.  Steak was also on the menu, but this was more an exploration of the lower ridges without the urge to climb to Trapper Peak.    We went with a Naked Bison Burger, Red Rock Chicken Sandwich, and The Z Bar Chicken Sandy.  All in the $13-14 range.  When the platters arrived our eyes widened at the sight of three well stacked dishes housed in interesting Rolls, Cheese, Onions, Shoestrings, and a sideload of French Fries.  The set up contained steak knives - a reasonable concession to the reality that there was no way to put these big brazen Buffalos in our mouths full bite.   All three meals were really good; the Bison being the most anticipated and enjoyable.  I knew that buffalo meat was more tender, leaner and sweeter than its bovine cousin, and this held true for this humdinger. It was large, loud, juicy and delicious. The Red Rock and The Z were also solid cluckwichs and very enjoyable, but much more in line with past experiences.  No knock on them, but Billy Bison stole the show, naked and proud.   Warrington isn't in our hood, but we do get to Doylestown with infrequent regularity.  Ted's Montana Grill will go on the short list of worthy stops on the way down from the mountains.

When it comes to old line fast food burgers like Wendy's, everything has to be graded on a curve. No one gets an "A," so to make everyone look better, the best of the worst gets the highest grade and all others climb a few steps. Yes. They are better than they used to be. But, no. They are not as good as the weakest of the newer fast casual competitors.   So, very late from court, and famished, I saw the polkadot dress and drove in.  My Doublestack came preloaded with ketchup, mustard, pickle, red onion and lettuce. When undressed, the bun looked as it had been compressed in wrapping.  The taste was reminiscent of a burger I used to know, but the saltiness detracted from the possibility of true enjoyment.   The fries were fine.   This "4 for 4" deal comes with mandatory processed chicken pieces (scrappled chicken), that was oily and nearly inedible. One was enough. They must have manufactured a billion of them, and be trying to get rid of them 4 at a time through this marketing gimmick. Bad idea. Better just to throw them away, and make it a "3 for 3" special.   The service was decent. The folks behind the counter were doing their best to keep everyone moving forward. This small store had plenty of seats and parking, so there's that.

While Aya Kitchen in the Oxford Valley Mall broadens the selection of food available in their somewhat bereft food court, it has had to make concessions to the reality of the market at the cost of faithfulness to its identity as a "Mediterranean" fast food dispensary.  Can't blame them for offering Afghani dishes (Kofta), Indian options (Samosas, Tikkas) and Central American snacks (Empanadas), in addition to the expected gyros and falafels in pita, but to say they fit into the geographic culture of the Mediterranean is inaccurate.   Still, even lacking the grill and spit for real lamb/beef gyro preparation, they do a decent job with what they have.  My lamb gyro in pita was overflowing with meat, tomato, onion, cucumber, yogurt and tahini sauce inside their somewhat thick skinned pita. It wasn't wrapped properly inside the aluminum foil, and was impossible to eat handheld once the paper and foil were opened enough to permit a big bite, thus making the use of a fork mandatory. The lamb was in small chunks rather than being carved in slivers from the mother as it slowly spun vertically on a grill. I found it tasty and filling despite missing the traditional cooking method.  No one will mistake Aya Kitchen for the real deal in Mediterranean dining, but it wasn't bad overall for a mall food court. I would easily chose it again if I found myself hungry and alone in Oxford Valley Mall.

Victoria's Bagel Bistro is really more of a tie dye T-shirt, hippie dippy kind of place out on Rt. 38 in Mt. Laurel, NJ.  The place has a nice sized room with about a dozen tables, Rock & Roll Classic Hits for sound, and photos/sketches of Presley, Marley and a few other music heavyweights on the walls.  Definitely, a chill place.    Victoria, herself, served me.  Very friendly and accommodating owner that puts herself into the environment she created.  She gave me the two bit tour of what was available for breakfast, and I opted for an Onion Bagel with a smear of Butter and a few slices of Swiss, not toasted. I took a seat at the table nearest the front window, and settled down to check in on Yelp.    The bagel arrived looking quite good.  There weren't a lot of toasted onion flakes on the surface, but enough to hold the flavor.  In profile, the transection was a nice layering of bread and cheese.  First bite announced that the surface of the bagel was not crisp, nor crunchy, but rather more like the regular crust of a bread loaf.  I really prefer a more distinct outer texture with a softer airy middle.  So, while the taste was decent, it was not an optimal bagel for me. We all have our own opinions about bagels, and this must be what the strong enthusiasts here like most.  For me, is was really only Okay.    Still, the java was hot and strong, the price very competitive, and the overall experience, positive.  I liked what Victoria was doing there.   And, wish her continued success.

This is a new listing for Original's Italian Pizzeria, a/k/a, Original's Pizza, in the Morrisville Shopping Center.  I returned for lunch last week and found a packed house full of luncheon moms and summer break kids enjoying their freedom sharing a pie without adult supervision. Good for them!  I found an empty booth under the "roof," and ordered an eggplant parm sandwich.  It arrived about ten minutes later, steaming hot.  My approach with scalding sandwiches is to attack with knife and fork, rather than attempt to pick it up and take a dangerous bite.   The eggplant was nicely breaded and sautéed in olive oil prior to being loaded into the Italian loaf and finished in the oven to melt the cheese and toast the outer edges.  There was enough tomato sauce on top to keep everything moist and tasty.  The gravy was a little salty, but that was not a big deal. The eggplant was soft and tender and mixed well with the sauce and cheese.  Saving the bread for last, it was very good - crunchy and tasting of all the elements that had been within. The surprise of the show!   I can see why people enjoy Originals and keep it jumping. The atmosphere is communal and neighborly.  My lunch was far better than average. Fair prices. Good service.  Great for kids to ride to on their bikes.    A keeper.

Stewart's is part of the small food court in Neshaminy Mall, Bensalem, PA. What it can't duplicate due to lack of being a stand alone drive up roadside dog, burger and root beer joint, it tries to make up for with friendly service and a menu straight from 1975.   A hot dog lover, when the mood strikes and there aren't many local frankfurter havens nearby, even this neutered version of the iconic Stewart's Root Beer emporium, will do. Although there are a few better dog shops around (Cheese Dogs on Bustleton being an excellent alternative). I ordered their special with fries and black cherry beverage and a skinny beefer buried under chili, relish, onions, mustard and ketchup. It came in a plain white bread bun that had a hard time holding up under the damp weight of all the condiments.  Lucky I grabbed a handful of napkins.   It was okay, but the doggie was lost in all the flavors above. The texture came through, but not much of the taste. The fries were decent because freshly made, and the carbonated drink stronger in flavor than the original root beer.   Stewart's would do well to investigate the competition, especially the more creative houses like Tower Dogs and Destination Dogs, that produce a far superior product and gastronomic experience. They should up their game to capture a more discerning crowd, while holding on to their simpler pleasures as well.   Why not appeal to everyone?

Duck Sauce pioneered Asian Fusion (Chinese foundation) in the Newtown area.  The facility is dark and comfortable, and the staff is friendly and attentive without being overbearing.  Management is stellar, with the proprietress, Amy, warmly greeting everyone with a warm smile and sparkling eyes.   The food is a few notches above standard Chinese fare, while also providing a taste of Thai cuisine for the more adventurous.  The dishes are nicely plated and presented individually to satisfy both your visual and aromatic sensibilities.  The tastes are unique and you always feel the extra thought put into the creation of your meal.    Lunch comes in at about $10 per, while dinner moves up to about $15.  Not bad for the quality and ambiance of the overall experience.    Everyone's taste buds are different, but I just had the Beef with Chinese Eggplant in a Basil Soy Sauce that was very good.  The Wonton Soup came with thin skinny wontons as well as spinach leaves, making for a mildly sweet sensation. White, brown or fresh made fried rice are all available with every meal.    Funny, I just returned from China and this was my first Chinese meal at home.  I found myself wondering why I was given a glass of ice water and western utensils when my Chinese eating companion had no water nor fork and knife.  I had to ask for chop sticks. This is only a small peeve, but perhaps it would be better to ask the patron if they want ice water or hot water and chop sticks or knife and fork rather than assuming from appearance what those answers will be, especially when the other diner is automatically given the Asian settings.

This International House of Pancakes on Mt. Holly Road, Burlington, NJ, sits in a renovated former fast food structure, and is small compared to the more recent versions of this franchise around the country. All the cues are there to prepare you for a hearty breakfast.   I walked in before court last week for a light bite and coffee, and to kill some time before my workday began. I took a seat at the 5 stool counter and was served by Tim, a young dude who seemed diligent and engaging. After a short look at the long menu, I opted for their traditional french toast and strong java. All the other choices seemed like they would be way too sweet with berries and whipped cream. Didn't want those calories.   My plate arrived ten minutes later looking attractive and tempting. I spread the cup of butter across the egg pocked surface, and poured on the old fashioned syrup (maple not on the counter).  First bite was very good, but a realized that their signature approach to this dish was to add pancake mix to the beaten eggs.  This was visible in the unusual shine on the surface of the toast, as well as the distinct mild taste of buttermilk with each forkful. I had not tasted this before, but I enjoyed this take on a historic platter.  Nice for a change of pace, but not something I would specifically request, as I prefer the traditional approach to french toast.   The carafe of hot coffee in front of me is another thing they do well. They realize that coffee is an inexpensive way to appear generous.   I have never been a IHOP regular, as I normally prefer a mom and pop shop to a chain or franchise for breakfast, or any meal. Still, I appreciate what they do, and their effort to find a new approach to their business. They even are doing burgers now. Haven't tried them, but they do look good on the menu.

The Courthouse Cafe is the closest restaurant to my new office, directly across the street from the red brick Church of the Redeemer and catercorner from both the new & old Mercer County courthouses. I have stopped in for a quick meal now and then when going to/departing these halls of justice over many years. Although the name used to be Gus's, it still looks and feels the same.  It is old school. It slings traditional breakfasts and lunches for the courthouse and state worker crowds, and keeps quality, creativity and price in balance for the limited time and budget restraints of their market. It does this well, as can be seen by the full house at lunch and the empty seats after about 1:30.  My Chicken Salad on Rye Toast was a decent sandwich. Fresh ingredients. Good bread. The side of fries was okay and the thimble cup of sweet slaw pretty tasty. At around $8 with tax, it was a fair deal.  The Turkey & Swiss was likewise a solid lunch, as was the Chicken Salad & Bacon Melt I had last week.   Ownership is in the house and involved in everything. They keep the house friendly and  check in with customers.    It's good to have a reasonable and reliable luncheonette as a neighbor.

The Bowl inspired Grill (sic) is a relatively new entry in the luncheon wars in beautiful downtown Trenton, NJ. It is located on South Warren Street, the cobblestoned lane that manages to look good despite all the degradation around it. It is an Americanized Mexi house that does it's best to imitate Chipotle, with bowls, burritos or wraps made to order as you select the rice, beans, meat, salsa and drink of choice being constructed behind the counter. All this for around ten bucks.  We walked down last week. The room was empty, but for one table when we arrived at 1:00. The two women working the assembly line were friendly and knew their craft. I ordered a bowl with brown rice, red beans, shredded beef, corn salsa and cilantro. It felt hefty on the plastic tray.   The result was tasty and filling, but far from special. Then again, I don't frequent Chipotle for the same reason. I prefer the authentic version of Central American cuisine so prevalent and delicious around this capital city. Yet, for a downtown foodery it certainly carries it's weight and contributes some variety to the lunch scene in these parts.

Kam Buffet sits deep in the heart of Trenton off Clinton Avenue.  It is a fairly large space and seems to have an active lunch trade.  Service is minimal as in most buffets, with the two women in black directing seating and delivering drinks.  They are friendly enough.  The food spread is a combination of hybrid Chinese American, Latin and variations of fried chicken for everyone.  I sampled a cross section of their offerings, including, General's Chicken, Sesame Chicken, Egg Foo Young, String Beans, Pepper Beef, Boneless BBQ Ribs, and Dumplings.  All were average to below, and some were cool from too much time out of the sun.  Edible fare, but far from inspiring.    The biggest problem is price.  When such low quality victuals cost $10, there is something wrong with the proposition.  Even Flaming Grill out on White Horse offers much more for substantially less.  And, they use bigger plates without the notice everywhere that if you leave food on your plate there will be a 15% extra charge for waste. Plus, an extra buck for hot tea!  Not a fan of buffet police.   Hard to recommend Kam unless you are in the immediate area without means of getting to another Chez Chinois.  Almost every China shop around here has lunch specials for $6 to $8, where the quality is better, and the portions ample.    Kam Buffet. Once was enough.

Las Margaritas on 2nd Street Pike, Southampton, PA, isn't bad for a casa Mexicana that serves mainly an American audience not necessarily familiar with the deep choices available in a kitchen that caters to its own nationals. The space is large and dimly lit, with plenty of colorful cues of its South of the Border cultural heritage. It is very popular as witnessed by the long wait for people walking in looking for a table. Luckily, as a solo diner, I was able to grab a barstool and take my liquid and solid choices right there.  I have been somewhat spoiled by the wide variety and authenticity of all the casas Latinas in and around Trenton, which has become a very ciudad Centro Americano. All those formerly Italian corner restaurants now speak Espanol, and they put out amazing cuisine.   Still, Las Margaritas is a good place for a reasonably priced cocktail by the same name, and the well known dishes found in most Mexican houses catering to gringos. Lots to choose from in terms of nachos, tacos, burritos, chimis, and tortas, and even a few decent dinner platters, like the chili rellenos ordered by me.  I found the two large breaded and fried poblano peppers to be nicely loaded with melted cheese and queso fresco, and topped with a thin, but well spiced, ranchero sauce. I tossed on the salsa from the chips to add texture and heat, and enjoyed the refried beans and dirty rice accompaniments.   Not a bad meal at all. Bartender service was fine and muy amable. The only hiccup was being tendered the wrong cuenta for a couple of bucks more than what I ordered. El hombre tried to tell me it was the same price as what I got, but I knew that was not the case. Still, it wasn't worth a challenge to his manhood, so I let it roll, and adjusted the tip accordingly.   Honesty is always the best policy when it comes to restaurant tabs.

Just returned to Duck Sauce after an absence of more than a year.  It remains the dark wooded small dining room with booths around the walls. The teapots are still heavy metal with better than standard tea.  The menu does not appear to have changed at all, and that was a small disappointment.    However, the Pan Seared Pork Dumplings were well made, held together, and were very tasty.  I asked for a side of Hot Sesame Oil to bring up the burn, and poured it directly into the Soy/Vinegar Mix they dispense with this dish.  With that, it was very enjoyable.  Too, the Teriyaki Salmon was a nice size steak and was grilled just enough to leave it thick and juicy with a glowing glaze.  The golden yellow Mango surrounding the salmon was both ripe and sweet and a great color combination.  I was happy with both dishes.  Duck Sauce is still a solid "Fusion" house, and the best Newtown currently has to offer.  It does feel a bit stuck in the 90s, and could use a makeover in terms of ambiance and offerings.  It will not satisfy the more sophisticated pallets accustomed to authentic Chinese, Japanese or Thai cuisine, but it does turn out tasty plates that are enjoyable for what they are.    I know where to go when I desire serious Asian food.  But, when I am not in the mood for a longer ride, and the comfort of home is appealing, Duck Sauce still provides the mood and flavor that keeps me satisfied.

It seems that Café con Leche has been in Newtown forever.  It is a place I used to go to with some frequency, but over the years it fell off my radar as a "go to" place for good Latin/Italian styled cuisine.  When a friend recommended it for lunch I jumped at the chance to revisit an old friend.   Daniel Lucci is the owner/chef in this walkout basement of a restaurant on the Newtown Creek side of State Street.  It is best approached from the parking lot next to Isaac Newtown's, where it must compete for parking.  It is accurate to describe the dining area as small and dark, but for some that adds to the ambiance and charm.  The menu seemed smaller than I remembered it, but it still had Mexican, Italian, and Continental flourishes.    Lunch was from the Sandwiches Menu.  All are prepared on French Bread with a side salad.  The bread is fresh with a moderately crunchy crusty ingratiating bite, and my accompanying salad was potato with celery and a mayo-mustard creamy connector.  The Yellow Fin Tuna Salad was good, layered with lettuce and tomato slices.  It was satisfying and filling.  The Cajun Salmon was nicely blackened with a Pesto Mayo dressing and side garden salad with Daniel's special Balsamic Vinegrette, he calls, "Balsamico." I tasted this and thought it was better than the tuna.    I could not escape the thought that perhaps, Café con Leche had remained too long in the same space, and thus cramped its growth in both tables and adventurous gourmet meals.  A little more sunshine might open this accomplished chef to brand new and exciting possibilities.  In some way it seemed that the rest of the local restaurant world had caught up to CCL, and even passed it by.

The anti-Starbucks. In sight of its backdoor. Pour your own and no waiting. Decent coffee and snacks. Inferior view, but no seating required. I'm not saying 7/11 is a true alternative to the Green Mermaid, but if you strip away the atmospherics and even the pretension, and the antisocial, illegal, parking in front so some can get their daily grind going without the trouble of finding a safe place to stash their wheels, what you are left with are taste and price.  On both counts, the Lucky Numbers win - with parking to spare.

Whether you're a fan or not of Golden Nugget Antique Flea Market depends on your feelings about junque, you know, that stuff packed away in your basement, attic or garage that you can't find a use for, but can't let go of.  Well, Golden Nugget is where you go if you want to be rid of it, or to get more of it.  Either way, this outdoor market along River Road south of Lambertville, NJ., is a cultural trip down memory lanes and forgotten trails.     When I stopped in this week it was after heavy rain and the gravel  trading area was pretty muddy.  Still, I was able to drive in and park behind the market and take the steps down to the action.  At 8:30 am, the place was busy with the gypsies, mountain men, pickers, and collectors who are addicted to finding obscure gems in a mountain of trashy throwaways.  It must work for most regulars, because many are there three times a week to search, bargain and barter for those old tools, keys, buttons, knick-knacks and the most esoteric tchotchkes that are precious baubles to them. Why was I there?  My hunt involves old pocket knives.  They don't need to be sharp, but they do need to open and close, and have all their blades.  I found several around, but only purchased one that was fairly valued after friendly haggling.  The others were nice, but too dearly priced for my blood.  Amazing what excellent handicraft attaches to American steel.  Secondly, I look for beautiful beads to use in making jewelry that has been a small business for many years. Strung with pearls and other natural stone stringable pieces, make for interesting and attractive neck or wrist ware.    I'm not in love with Golden Nugget, nor the other similar flea markets in the area, but every now and then I have an urge to explore these backwaters of the American economy to see what I can find on the worn out tables in the park.    Who knows?  Maybe I'll get lucky again.

I returned this morning for a breakfast sandwich after the mild disappointment from the Chicken Cheesesteak of the other day. To be honest, had this meal been at the same level as lunch, I would have lowered the ranking down to 2 Stars.   But, it wasn't the same.  The Sausage, Egg and Cheese sandwich was a totally different animal.  It was loaded and it exploded.  Where the run of the mill sandwich has one sausage patty, this one had two.  When most put in a single sunny side up egg on top, WCS cooked up two flat omelet style huevos and wrapped the sausage within it.  Most will not cut the sandwich before packing it up to go, but these folks cut the Kaiser Roll before enclosing it in white paper with a heavy tape sealer.  The only weak link was the roll, which was fresh, but lifeless.    The first bite released the mix of meat and cheese flavors strongly.  The textures worked well, especially the double patty which required more chewing, and thus more release of the undertones.  It was an imperfect pleasure to eat.   I would certainly go back to the Store to pick up breakfast on occasion. If we were just talking about breakfast sandwiches, 4 Stars might be attainable, but given the condition of the facility and the sadness it evokes, and the less than satisfactory lunch sandwich, 3 Stars is where the ranking belongs.    Breakfast saved the bacon.

City Market on Main Street, Lambertville, NJ, has all the charm of this river city, with a 1910 look and feel. High tin type ceiling, large blackboard menu, wooden counter for eating in back, and a window bar in front for sipping coffee. It is definitely a place you feel comfortable and timeless.   They are open for breakfast, and I was there to sample it. I asked the friendly server what they were about, and she replied that breakfast sandwiches were one of their claims to fame. Okay. Let's do a sausage, egg and cheese on Kaiser roll, please. I settled in with a mug of joe and waited for delivery. It arrived minutes later on a real plate, cut in half, and meekly smiling at me.   It wasn't all that good. Frozen sausage patty, single fried egg a little too dry, and melted white American cheese, on a tasteless, industrial strength roll that looked to have been crushed in transport. Not much effort, nor creativity put into it. Average at best. Not at all what I expected from a Lambertville institution, where the city itself is all about surpassing culinary expectations.   With all that atmosphere, City Market could and should have been so much more than a boring, unimaginative sandwich.

Marcos Pizzeria has reopened! The fire that closed Marcos and its neighbor put a serious dent in my pizza diet, and I can imagine others felt similarly.  It is located in the Village of Newtown Shopping Center, just behind the Wendy's. Once a week I go for a couple of slices (tomato pie and traditional eggplant), and never fail to run into someone I knew in the same frame of mind needing a pizza to brighten our day. The few times I was there for dinner, I had a parmigiana or aglio olio pasta dish. Satisfying. The downside has been that the shop is small and not comfortable enough for extended dining.  Too, in winter when the door opens, everyone is greeted with a cold blast, which chills both the patron and the food. There are other pizza options in Newtown, and I frequent most of them.  They are all decent, if not attaining the Trenton nor Brooklyn pizza pantheon. But, who can travel to those places every time you crave a T.pie?  Right now, Marcos offers me the most positive "Pizzaxperience" in town.

BREAKFAST REVIEW ONLY  Peter's Pizza & Deli is on the bottom floor of the corner highrise apartment building at Cooper & Market Streets, Trenton, NJ, right across the streets from the Hughes Justice Complex and the Mercer County Criminal Courts.  As "Location is Everything," these guys should have it made.  In fact, they do a good business for breakfast and lunch during the workweek.  I stopped in for a late brekkie earlier this week.    The shop was empty but for me around 11.  It is small with only a few tables.  Ordering is done at the counter, where you return to pick up your meal.  I went with a sausage, egg and cheese sandwich on a Kaiser roll, plus coffee.  I watched as the eggs were cooked in the microwave (don't like what this process does to eggs), and the sausage done the same way. The cheese was added at the end and melted by the heat of the other ingredients.  The roll came out of a plastic bag.  I can't say that I really enjoyed this sandwich.  The roll was soft; without much flavor and little texture.  The eggs were fluffy, but with almost no taste.  The sausage was okay, but would have really come to life if grilled on steel.  The coffee was decent.    Looking around, the pizzas on display looked better than the sandwich I was eating.  I might return to check out a few slices, but the breakfast sandwich was one and done.

There are more reviews for this PennDot Licensing Center to be found on a separate page labeled, PennDot.    Not sure why two pages are needed, but perhaps it adds to the chances of being found here.    The Commonwealth is really making an effort to make these places more consumer friendly.  I was able to renew my driver's license in less than ten minutes.  However, their interworking with other agencies remains problematic.  When Social Security and Homeland Security are required to be involved in securing a new license, the process is awkward, delayed, and guaranteed to frustrate.   Can't blame the Governor for the issues raised by the Feds, but there ought to be an easier way.

Newtown Book & Record Exchange has a prime location on State Street, Newtown, right next door to Starbucks.  If this isn't a gold mine just based on overflow from the S.$$$, I don't know what is.    First impressions walking through the front door is one of narrow aisles and stacks of used books and Cd's (also some tapes, etc), with hand written labels to direct you and creaky wooden floors that have been tread on for more than a century.  Yes, there is also a dustiness and slight scent of decaying paper, as would be expected where thousands of old books are stored.  It all adds to the overall gestalt of entering a literary and musical time warp.  It is quite enjoyable if you like this sort of thing.  I do.  Likely due to the rent paid for this location, the prices on the books and music are higher than seems reasonable, and the trade in policy is not designed to provide value to the trader.  Over the years, I have purchased a few things here on impulse, but overall aside from wanting the old place to survive, the selection is generally not what I am looking for, and the cost offsets the cultural and historic imperatives.   Definitely worth a long browse while sipping caffeine from next door, but if you have visited the Princeton Record Exchange you know what a dedicated used music emporium is all about.  This one is not that.  As to the books, you might find something you like, but if you don't, the Newtown Library Company is about 2 blocks away.  You can join and likely find what you seek and be able to return it after reading. Recycling at its earliest and best.

If you can't get to DiBruno's in South Philly, you should give La Stalla Italian Market a visit for your Italian delicatessen and specialty requirements.  While not packing the huge inventory of cheeses, smoked meats, salads, and bakery goods of its distant cousin to the south, the Newtown store sure is a reasonable facsimile.  This new place looks and smells like 9th Street, and goes overboard when asked to create a sandwich or other takeaway meal.    Their loaves are about the best Italian bread you can find anywhere in the area.  Certainly as good as Italian Peoples' Bakery and the dearly departed Barbero's in Chambersburg, Trenton, NJ.  It is so excellent that it can easily be enjoyed without anything more, or a little olive oil with black pepper, or a smear of butter.  But, if an incredible lunch is what you desire, just pick a few of your favorite sandwich ingredients, the size roll your want, and let the deli folk go to work.  You will receive an immense tower of wonderful meats, cheeses and accessories that will last at least two meals. If you prefer not to create your own combo, just select one of their house sammies.  You won't be disappointed.   Newtown has been undergoing a renaissance for the past several years, with improved restaurants and boutiques merchandising everything from designer clothing, great smoothies, to tasty tidbits. La Stalla Italian Market joins the fun and is built to scratch that impossible culinary itch.   Parking in the rear and on the street nearby.

Jersey hyper market comes to Bucks and shows up the local talent Acmes and Giants with huge selection and cutthroat pricing.  It has everything those other guys have, and so much more in a shelf by shelf comparison.   More labels.  More variety.  More choice.    It may not have been the wisest thing to make a first visit on a Saturday afternoon when the place was full of Sunday pushcart drivers, as the number of near misses with the granny class kept me on edge and hoping my auto insurance comprehensive would cover any property damage.  Too, the cost of things was not always clear on their price cards below the items, especially the discounted products.  A bit more clarity would be a big help.    Other than those nits, Shop Rite - Yardley is a great place to stock up.  We came in needing a few things, and walked out with a large cart full of everything else we would use in the months ahead.    Next time, a weekday evening will be explored to see if the overall experience will feel less risky.

This will be as much a testimonial as a review.    Driving out of Bordentown the other morning I heard my tire sensor start to beep.  Checking my maintenance screen I saw that one of my tires had a sudden and severe pressure drop.  Damn!  I had picked up a nail.    Unfamiliar with the auto shops and gas stations in the area, I was at a loss where to go to do the repair.  A minute later I was passing RW Tire on Rt. 206 northbound.  Serendipity?   I made it into the crowded parking lot and went inside with my lug lock in hand.  The man behind the counter finished with a customer and turned to me.  I explained the situation.  No sweat.  They'd get to it in a few minutes.  He took down my particulars and I handed over my keys and lug lock.    About 15 minutes later I watched as one of their mechanics went out to find my wheels and drive it into the shop.  I walked over to watch him work and see what he found.  The guy was fast getting the car up, and even faster getting the offending tire off the car.  He rolled the tire looking closely for the cause of the flat.  He found it in a minute, got his nail extractor, yanked a cotter pin out of the tread and had the hole plugged, sealed and snipped in under 5 minutes.  This dude knew his tire repair!  Twenty five minutes from pulling in, I was pulling out.  Impressive!  And, the cost for this service was under $20.    I complimented the tire jockey for his excellent work, and after paying the bill, asked the cashier what other work they did.    They were so unexpectedly good at fixing my flat tire, they had made me a loyal customer in mere minutes.  I was pleased as punch!

Lakernick Health & Wellness is a chiropractic office that also offers massage and other related services in a compact facility in Feasterville, PA. It can be found on East Mrytle Avenue, a side street off Brownsville Road. A converted private residence it has a small parking lot in front, large enough for four cars.   Walking in, the first impression is that the office is well worn with small treatment rooms to both sides down a central carpeted hall. Front desk staff is friendly and efficient, asking first time patients to fill out a two page questionnaire before seeing the doctor or masseuse. Prices are very reasonable.   I was there primarily for a deep tissue/sports massage from Marla Solarski, who sees customers at several places around lower Bucks County. I was also curious about Stuart Lakernick, the owner of the business and bone cracker in residence. I had used a few chiros in the past and wanted to see how he worked on my back and neck. Stu is a very communicative guy, who nicely explains what he sees in examination (diagnosis), as well as what he intends to do for treatment. His equipment is excellent, with an adjustment table that allows you to stand up on the vertical inclined padded board, before it is slowly lowered into horizontal position via motorized swivel.  A first time for me.  His adjustment of my lumbar/sciatic spine was a traditional heavy torque as I lay on my side with legs bent and overlapping my knee, as he both pushed on my upper hip/pelvis and pulled on my upper torso with his body weight. My left hip was "frozen," so that required a double move to get it done. But, done they were, and when finished, both back and neck felt looser and mobilized.  Thereafter, Marla's massage was great with her excellent stretching and probing style. I could see that doing both an adjustment and massage enhanced the effect of each on my body. They were symbiotic. I always felt wonderful, if a little lightheaded, after her handiwork, but this time it was more intense and the after effects lasted longer than usual. I took a short walk once outside to feel more grounded before driving home.   Suggestion - The purpose of chiropractic and massage is to lessen a stressed body and mind. I was a little put off seeing a political sign in front of the office, and it actually resulted in a shift in attitude going in. Regardless of affiliation, I prefer a health and wellness center to be apolitical, as I get enough of that everywhere else, all day long. I want to be able to relax in a sanctuary setting, not be reminded of harsh realities.  It is counterproductive to the goal I seek. Maybe others feel similarly.

Although Metro Diner doesn't originate around here, it fits right in with all the other dinners that have been in Bucks County for decades. It doesn't mimic the stainless facsades of yesteryear, but has its own style and comfort. More brick and glass with paint on glass stenciled sign windows proclaiming their most popular items (Chicken & Waffles, Chicken Pot Pie, Fish & Chips, etc.), and only a short counter with fewer than ten stools, the booths and tables are where most eating takes place.   On this weekend I was in the mood for something different for me, and asked for their chicken pot pie. I sat at the counter overlooking the kitchen and enjoyed the small talk among the cooks and servers.   I watched as my dinner was removed from the oven, put on a large plate, passed from the kitchen to the dining room though a window with shelves to facilitate transfer from one to the other. The wait person placed before me a huge biscuit crust covered oval dish, browned on top and steaming at its edges. How attack this enormous package?   I cracked open an end with my fork, lifted the corner of the crust and folded it back on itself. The aroma of the creamy thick sauce, full of vegetables and chunks of chicken wafted up to greet me. Seductive. I tasted a bit of crust. It was a fresh biscuit flavor, not too flaky, with a slight saltiness. The veggies were firm, the chicken, tender. It was all together terrific. Not that I am a pot pie maven, but this was the best I've had. In another house without the name "diner" attached, and with a good bottle of Pinot, this meal would be a star of the show and cost much more than the $10 it demands here.  The fried chicken looked appetizing, too. If as engaging as its potted cousin, Metro could become a habit.

I must confess.  I don't like malls. They seem dinosaurs in the 21st Century.   Perhaps, part of the problem are the anchor tenants; those big department stores that try to be all things to all people, and end up being quite the opposite - offering a sad retail experience that feels lifeless.  So it was when I decided to go to Sears to purchase a replacement for my dearly departed 12 year old Hoover canister. I knew I was risking a bout of depression, but throughout my life Sears was the place where appliances were plentiful.  My grandfather shopped there for refrigerators and washing machines with me in tow, and I would continue the custom with my son.   Not much to report beyond the fact that our saleswoman was knowledgeable and honest enough to point me in the right direction even when the price was lower.  Ended up with a Hoover Whirlwind in light blue. Good price.    After putting it together at home, and running it in the family room and a bedroom, I can candidly say that it sucks.  That is a good thing.

First time visiting the Gloucester Premium Outlets in Blackwood, NJ, but it likely won't be the last. I am usually averse to "outlet world" experiences, as being over the top gross commercialism, that no longer reflects the factory overrun and slightly defective merchandise where the concept began; but is now part of the corporate master plan to produce specifically for sale in this setting. Too, so often there is no real saving going on, but only the false perception of discount.   Certainly, I saw some of that in the Michael Kors Armani universe. But, surprisingly, other shops provided some true value. Calvin Klein had many casual shirts available at good prices, as did Banana Republic with their slightly eccentric styles. My biggest score was in Columbia Outdoors, where their outerwear was discounted up to 60% from the real online catalogue prices I had seen the day before. Picked up a really nice water resistant green vest and some camping gear.   The quasi-village look of the the center was attractive. Plenty of surrounding parking, wide walkways throughout, enough directories to keep from getting lost, and a few food outlets for when shopping no longer overcame hunger.   Yelp-wise, not every store was listed separately, making check ins and reviews impossible for we addicts who need to record our every move. That will hopefully take care of itself eventually.   Nonetheless, Gloucester Premium Outlets proved worth the drive and a pleasant consumption experience.

Tropical Family Restaurant at the western end of Lalor Street, Trenton, is one of the many converted corner bars that in their heyday were packed with the people who toiled the heavy industries of Trenton's steelworks and watered their weary souls here.  Those folks are mostly gone now; replaced by the next wave of immigrants who prefer their corners to provide spicy sustenance along with the cervesa. Tropical Family fills that need for the Puerto Rican pallet.   I stopped here for lunch last week.  I was pleasantly surprised by several things. First, they have a nice size parking lot surrounding the premises. So much easier than searching for street space.  Second, the house is very well renovated with brilliant color and murals and new buffet table, making it one of the nicer Latin places in the city.  Third, the service was first rate and came with sincere smiles from the bilingual staff.  Finally, the lunch menu while small, offers enough comida authentica to still the savage beast.    My Pernil Sandwich was loaded with Pork, Lettuce, Red Onion, and Mayo on a fresh roll.  The meat was tender and everything together was a fun munch.  I did find it a little lacking in the heat department, but the table Tabasco took care of that.  I also ordered a Refresco Mango - a blended ripe Mango with water and ice.  It was very good, but next time I would go without the ice to avoid the brain chill the came along with it.    Tropical Family seems like a solid choice for dinner, too.  And, as the name implies, it is a family joint where spouse and chachos would be comfortable and have plenty of great options for a meal.

Blooming Grove Inn occupies the space of what was Lieggi's on Upper Ferry Road in Ewing, NJ. It is a pleasant converted mansion on the slopes of the eastern side of the Delaware River Basin.  My visits have always been at the bar for after work meetings and light socializing.  The crowd is forty and fifty-somethings; all well behaved.  The bartenders are excellent.  Noah remembered my face, if not my name, after an absence of at least six months.  Impressive.    Last night, my margarita had the right touch of Padron and Cointreau, and my friend and fellow court gladiator enjoyed his aged malt whiskey.  Behind us at the end of the bar, a mellow guitar vocalist played gently and sang from a decent list of soft rock standards. It was just enough to fill the gaps in our conversation, but seemed to disappear when we spoke again.    We decided to have a bite at the bar, rather than score a table.  I asked for the Meatballs I had seen brought out earlier, and Sam went for the Tapas plate. My dish was excellent.  Tender, airy meatballs in a tart, garlic tomato sauce, sprinkled with dry Italian grated cheese.  I only skewered a few pieces of cheese, greens, mushrooms off his plate, but thought everything was fine, if not enthralling.   So, why four stars?  It has nothing to do with the quality of the house, the kitchen, nor the bar.  They were all fine.  Blooming Grove just isn't my cup of tequila.  I prefer a less well kempt, more outside the box, more diverse, kind of place.  It felt too tame.  More a place to take your aunt and uncle, or business associates, when you don't want them to know who you really are.

Joe's Mill Hill Saloon has been holding up the southeast corner of Broad & Market Streets in Trenton, NJ for decades, and aside from some refurbishing it continues to be an attractive barroom and dining venue as authentic as the day is long.  Large rectangular dark mahogany bar with stools for more than twenty. High tin type ceiling that show its age. Large beveled mirror with the Joe's logo etched in. On a late winter afternoon with the western sun blindingly pouring through the windows, the setting is good enough to be part of a Raymond Chandler novel.   I took a seat on a stool facing the Christmas adorned mirror. The barkeep must have been behind the well for twenty years; older but none the worse for wear. The menu still offered soups, salads, sandwiches, burgers and cheesesteaks, but the beer selection was way better than I remembered. Old Brown Dog Smutty Nose Draft. Yeah! Why not? It went down cold and biting, just as its name suggested.   The house Build Your Own Burger was constructed with American, fried onions & mushrooms, and sliced jalapeño. Medium rare, and delicious.  Fresh cut fries slightly undercooked, but still thickly good.   Very glad it's right down the street from my new office for the next time I'm feeling like Dashiell Hammett.

This is a newer Chick-fil-A in the footprint of the dearly departed Krispy Kreme.  They have done a nice job renovating the shop, and setting up dual take out drive up lanes.  The actual restaurant is also well laid out, and has very well trained staff running the place.    I ordered a late lunch there earlier this week, and was surprised by the level of friendliness and care coming from behind the counter.  They even brought my meal to the table so I did not have to wait off to the side while it was being prepared.  That was only the second time a fast food joint had risen to that level of service, and the other occurred right down the road.  Must be something good in the water.   My Spicy Chicken Sandwich was good.  The breast was soft and tender as if never frozen.  Somehow, CFA chicken is always the most flavorful and chewable of all fast food cluckers. The waffle fries were crisp and plentiful.  Their dipping sauces are pretty unique, and my sriracha packets were a mix of that well known chili heat and a subtle Thai-like sweetness.  Tasted great on both the chicken and the taters. Of course, the hand spun shake was as cool and creamy as always. Went the way of plain vanilla, as the cookies and cream option would have clogged the straw.    Generally, I like the breakfast sandwiches offered by Chick-fil-A more than their chicken, but I have to say the improved service here and the high quality of their menu is slowly making me a believer that they have something special going on.

While down in this neck of the woods we decided to check out this Home Depot's garden department to pick up a few more bags of mulch. It is basically the same layout as every other HAD, with their planting inventory primarily outside, and the soil, fertilizer and mulch stacked high in the adjacent parking lot.   I went over to the cashier to pay for what we wanted, and picked up a tray of petunas on sale nearby. Receipt in hand I went back to the wagon and drove it over to the mulch. The dude with the weight lifting vest met me there and helped load the bags in back. At $3 per bag, it was the regular price. (Note: It is on sale now for $2.)  The home garden is looking good with this dress up. Will go back this afternoon for another load at the discount price. Maybe look at more annual color on the borders.   I'm still not a HD lover, but do admit that they are hard to beat on many things.

Big Bear is a small local chain of health food stores in and around Bucks County, Pa., and Mercer County, NJ.  They have grown over the decades due to staying true to their mission of providing quality organics and nutritional supplements at reasonable prices.  Unlike the pharmacies and general merchandise stores than offer some of these things, Big Bear provides expertise along with multiple alternatives for staying on top of your life game.  If you can't find what you are looking for, just ask the people in the aprons, and they will take you to your destination.  If they don't have it, your probably don't need it.  I was in the Morrisville shop on Old Lincoln Highway (the local Rt. 1 and Rt. 13) over the weekend.  Only a few customers were there, along with the 72 year old manager, who was holding down the cashier's position, too.  Couldn't find the lecithin amidst the rows of bottles and cans of pills and powders.  He pointed me in the right direction, and when free, came over to talk about the options.  He inquired about other possible health issues that his products could address, and made intelligent suggestions.  Much appreciated.    I am not vegan, nor gluten averse, so I did not spend any time looking in their deli cases, fresh produce, nor bakery sections.  Still, good to know they cover those concerns.    Very glad they carry top quality merchandise, are knowledgeable and take time with their customers to listen and inform.    This is how Big Bear separates itself from most of the competition.

I understand why so many people enjoy dining at Café Michaelangelo on Bustleton Avenue in the Far Northeast, Philadelphia. While most customers are local to the area, we were coming down from Bucks County, and this Italian haven was just a few miles over the county line.   It doesn't look like much on the outside. A narrow parking lot separating the building from heavily trafficked Bustleton. The façade a worn brown wood with narrow doors and confusing signs.  Still, we found our way in through the side entrance and walked into a small lobby, followed by a large glass-walled dining room with high exposed beam ceiling and vistas overlooking a back yard that was treed and green - more like a tree house feel, than a structure anchored to the ground. Although aging, it was very attractive. Positive first impressions.   We were seated at the first table in the dining room.  Although closest to the door, there was a half wall with trellis protecting us, and we soon forgot we were sitting on the edge. The menus were brought out quickly and we settled in to scour it for that evening's delights. While reading, we ordered a Stone IPA and River Horse Raspberry Tripel Horse Belgian-Style Ale. (You're wrong! I had the fruity beer, and my beautiful companion the very stout IPA.) We decided to go light. Fried calamari as a shared appetizer, and roast pork and Italian sausage sandwiches as our mains. Alina was our excellent server. She took very good care of us first timers.   Although the calamari was almost exclusively cut into bands, with only one set of tentacles, it was quite good; especially the dipping red sauce which was spicily chunky and required a second helping. While I might not get it again, it was a fine vehicle for sauce delivery.   The sandwiches were both first rate. They were served on decent Italian rolls which supported their passengers from plate to mouth without hesitation or flopping. The meat was tender and flavorful, with dipping sauce to enhance the experience. The sausage was cut into smaller slices for ease of ripping off chunks of the sandwich, and had ample onions and green frying peppers mixed throughout and more of that wonderful red sauce.  Really liked both plates. And, there was a plentitude of stuffing in each - so much so that we could only eat half of each sandwich and brought the rest home for stepson to enjoy.  We had planned to order something separately for him, but we had so much that it wasn't necessary. Alina brought us the takeout containers and bags with an easy smile, despite the loss of the extra sale to the house. No doubt, she had seen this happen before.   We thoroughly and zestfully partook of our Café Michelangelo meal, and commented as we ate how good it was. In warmer weather, eating on the back patio would be a worthy addition to the program.   An exceptional find on the wild streets of Bustleton. And, the prices didn't hurt either.

Although this pizza shop calls itself, "The Original Dominick's," there is nothing of the that organization here beyond the name. The only Dom's these days are in Richboro and Washington Crossing, Pa. The family sold off the other locations several years ago, allowing the buyers to keep the name.   The space has seen better days when it was a convenience store, "Mr. Milk." Yes. I used to live on Riverside Drive on the Delaware and this was my local shop. Still, it is a survivor, and puts out decent pies at reasonable prices, as long as you are willing to overlook the worn out feel of a now run down store.    I am about the pizza and can ignore almost anything when in the presence of good T Pie. Pizza is at its apex right from the oven (even when reheated), so I prefer to mange right at its peak, and damn the torpedoes. We took a table and settled in.  The slices were served on the metal pans used for personal size pies. Nice touch that helps keep them warm,. Much better than the paper plates used by so many joints. I did not mind going to the high counter to retrieve them.   Although I seldom order a "fancy" slice, she asked for a chicken parm wedge. It came loaded with chunks of clucker, sauce and cheese. The chassis held the heavy topside with minimal assistance. My sample bite was okay. She devoured it. Mine were sausage and traditional Trenton tomato pie. They had a firm thin crunchy crust that held up well. Not too oily. The gravy was a little salty, but nice and thick with clumps of Tomato on top of the mozza on the TP. They used sliced sausage rather than free form which exuded less flavor than preferred.   They weren't perfect, nor even exceptional, but still pretty good. Clearly, they were given the recipes by Dominick, but had taken some creative liberties over the years.  A little elbow grease and TLC could bring this pizza parlor up a notch.

Fireside Smokehouse is the current incarnation of this old tavern down on Elmwood Avenue in Trevose, Pa. It has been run by one family since 1978, and they certainly know what they are doing adapting to changing tastes and fads to remain a solid choice for a hearty meal and a load of suds options.   First impressions are that Fireside has three personalities - a front room dive bar full of locals enjoying the broad beer list and a few eating something meaty from the grill; a simple dining room with a dozen tables, and outside patio enclosed in canvas and plastic for cold weather, with a few picnic tables and service bar. The front bar was the most crowded  and with the most attitude.  Our server told us to sit anywhere and came back to us quickly for drink orders. Menus were already on every table.  Two pages of beer options took a few, but we settled on Limbo IPA and Weyerbacher Imperial Pumpkin Ale drafts. Cool and smooth going down.   Son opted for a pulled pork sandwich with chips. He liked it, but has had better flavor. Too, there was no sauce on the table for added moisture and taste. The grilled salmon was a small steak, but fresh and nicely done. The spinach and slaw sides were forgettable.  My chicken & rib combo put a heavy plate with 6 ribs and quarter bird before me. They were both covered with the house BBQ sauce, a deep amber red.  The meat easily pulled from the bone and tasted of a good rub, long smoke and twangy sauce. Really liked it, and they were so loaded that I ate three, gave two away and brought one home along with the untouched clucker. The baked beanz were great and the mashed would have been too with a spoon of gravy or sauce on top.   Fireside is a solid choice for basic BBQ in a down home environment.  It's nothing fancy, just serious meat overload and strong fermentation possibilities. Put a few table rockets of Memphis, St.Louis, Carolina,  along with the house slather in front of me, bring the ribs out dry for me to doctor the way I want, polish up the sides a bit, and this smokehouse would be seeing stars.

Two Slices and a Drink Review  Stopped into Peppi's Pizza & Pasta after shopping at the Giant Supermarket in the same Shoppes at Flowers Mill commercial center.  Narrow in front, with dining room in back, this is a typical pizza parlor with booths, and a vast array of pies for examination, temptation and ordering.  I asked that my two regulars be "well done," in order to reawaken the taste slumbering within after extended time under hot lamps and hungry eyes.    The slices were as requested and picking each aloft showed the crust to be firm and able to supports its load.  The tomato sauce was on the salty side, as was the mozza.  Would have preferred a sweeter bite. Still, that's just a matter of taste, and many people like it that way.   Service was friendly and prompt, and the free refill of the soft drink, a nice touch.   Certainly worthy of a pizza snack when out and about.

We originally came to Kohl's to visit their Lee's Jeans collection. It was on the first floor in the back with large signs on the walls. Yet, it was frustrating to explore because of disorganization and a complete absence of smaller sizes. With Levis mixed in and Black Friday hordes making it impossible to maintain any order to the displays, we soon tired of the effort.   On our way out we did find a nice leather jacket sitting in a small group on a rack with outerwear sweaters. There was only one in the right size, and the price was very good with all the discounts applied.  We went for it, but quickly discovered that the queue to the cashiers wound through the store like a hungry giant Python.   Man! I dislike this insanity. But, there I was knee deep in this Big Muddy. I rode it out, and the line actually moved quickly with the help of a few workers who directed people to the next available register. All in all, we survived, but I will leave this shopping mania to those with a more accepting constitution.   Couldn't do a thing with the jeans, but the leather jacket was a nice consolation prize.

When I arrived around 2 for a late lunch there was one other table occupied and conducting business over lunch.  They left about 30 minutes later, and I was the only patron there. I don't know what it is like when crowded, but on a quiet late April afternoon it was quite peaceful, especially sitting in what seems to have been a porch, now enclosed.  Plenty of windows and the sunlight was pleasantly warming.    The overall impression is that it feels small inside, perhaps because of the dark wood and cut up design.  The bar has 9 or 10 stools on two levels, and the rest of the barroom seconds as the main dining area.  It feels somewhat rustic.    I ordered the Patty Melt, and it was quite good.  It was tasty and the combination of Sautéed Onions, Cheese, and Thousand Island Dressing had carmelized into a dark brown oozy sauce that was unusual and enjoyable.  This was a knife and fork job as my attempt to bite into it resulted in a Newtonian Principle being demonstrated - the equal and opposite reaction, as the backend began jetting out.  The rest of the menu seemed to offer plenty of comfort food that would be worth a try.    I remember when this was the Wycombe Inn back in the day.  It had a feel of faded elegance and charm that seems missing now.  Publick House is more of a frontier space, a bit rough and ready.  I will have to see it full of people to overcome the sense that it has seen better days.

As circumstances would have it, a single visit to a nearby Home Depot in West Windsor, NJ, has become a series of trips to three (possibly four) of their warehouse distribution stores in and around Mercer and Bucks Counties, NJ and PA.  I picked up a bag of black mulch while buying sand last week just to see how it would look in the flowerbeds and under trees.  At $3 per large 50 pound bag, it was worth the investment.  Turned out that the quality and coverage was very good, so I went to the location nearest where we were having dinner the other night, and purchased six more bags.    Can't have enough of a good thing, so I stopped in to the HD on Oxford Valley Road in Langhorne, PA, last night to haul away eight more sacks of the black moist blanket to spread this weekend.  What is obvious is that I'm not the only one getting this stuff, because the pile of bags in their nursery was depleted when I arrived last night.  Plenty of brown and red available, but the black was almost exhausted.  Too, I realized that if I am to attempt all my garden beds, I am going to need a lot more mulch!  The fifteen already stacked around my beds will likely double or triple before I am done.   So, while checking out, I inquired of the gardening lady cashier whether more would be brought out.  She assured me they had many more pallets where that came from, which would be moved into place before the store opened today.  Further, taking pity on my dirty work in lifting, stacking, hand trucking and car loading while in my suit, she informed me that they had people around who could do all that for me, and all I had to do was drive up and open the back gate of the wagon.    Nice to know I won't have to include a dry cleaning bill in the expense of freshening up my garden. Too late for these slacks, but I can deal with that.  PS. I'm now at 25 bags and no where near done. Luckily, they started a sale @ $2 per bag! I'm going to need a bigger truck!

Elmwood Park Zoo is a 16 acre community zoological garden on the outskirts of Norristown, PA. As small zoos go, this one is pretty cool. It has maximized its diminutive size with a 24 hour a day schedule and state of the arts events that can make everyone from 3 to 93 entertained, at least for a while.   From zip line through the treetops, to daily face to face animal feedings, to overnight camping with informative guide, Elmwood has it going on!  The late morning I was there to wait for my next meeting nearby, there were dozens of families with young kids walking around, interacting with the animals, and taking tours through this attractive, hilly landscape. Whether greeting Noah the Bald Eagle, or Stella the Horned Owl, the children were enthralled, and their parents happy to provide the family with an extraordinary experience.   The zoo is available for private parties, including weddings. Educational programs abound addressing conservation projects and endangered species. Cub Scouts to seniors have something to events geared to their age and ability to learn and engage.   Founded in 1924 when the private owner donated the original land to the Borough of Norristown, and managed by the government until it became too expensive to maintain on taxpayer funds, and was reorganized as a non-profit in 1977 known as the Norristown Zoological Society. Through the 21st Century it continued to expand its size and services, including a master plan that built several pavilions  and large scale permanent exhibits, including the Kimmel Conservation Kingdom in 2001, its interactive playground where human and other species met to learn from each other.   More than 500,000 visitors come annually, most of them families participating in all the activities. It may be small in stature compared to the more famous Philadelphia Zoo, but pound for pound it provides more alternative activities than its older, Ben Franklin founded, sibling.  Definitely worth a visit or two.

Back in the day when I lived in the Fairmount neighborhood at 26th and Brown Streets, shops as good as Rybread didn't yet exist, and we walked to the local corner taverns for suds and a meal.  Now, this neighborhood has experienced a modest renaissance and has a good variety of kitchen alternatives within a few blocks radius.  Makes me think about what it would be like to live here again in the shadow of the Museum of Art and take advantage of all the improvements.    We were showing out of town guests the beauty and grace of Philadelphia from the steps of the museum (so nice that on the weekend we could stop for a while right in front of the PMA and let our friends run up the stairs and enjoy the view without hassle).  When we agreed we were hungry, I searched Yelp for local restaurants, and saw Rybread in my bookmarks.  We drove there in about 3 minutes. Plenty of street parking.   There were no other customers when we arrived and we settled into the three small tables in the front of the shop.  One of the friendly servers explained that we should order at the cashier and we would be called when our lunches were ready.  Simple enough. There were five of us, and we wanted to sample everything that was selected.  They agreed to cut the sandwiches in quarters to accommodate.    There were good looking scones in the display, and we impulsively asked for a blueberry and cranberry. Baked in house, both were excellent; slightly moist and mildly sweet.  Nothing wrong with starting with dessert.  We then went with the Savannah (turkey, brie, cranberry sauce and mayo on multi-grain bread), Lake Tahoe (tuna salad, cheddar, tomato on ciabatta-panini style), Napa (fresh mozza, roma tomatoes, pesto, balsamic glaze on grilled baguette), and Tucson (oven roasted turkey, swiss, red onion, chipotle mayo and tomato; ciabatta panini style).  A large size soup of the day (sweet potato, chicken) was thrown in for good measure.   Each of the sandwiches was very good to excellent.  The bread fresh and brought to life through the panini press or just out of the bag.  The ingredients were fresh and ample.  No skimping on these works of art.  The soup was wholesome, hot and tasty.  We congratulated ourselves on our wise choices, and the good fortune of finding this charming, yet cramped, restaurant converted out of this block of row houses.     People came and went as we sat and ate.  Some came in, saw the indoor tables were occupied and walked out again. On this rainy day, the outdoor seating both front and rear was not a real option.  Still others, got their meals to go.    The bill for the indulgent five of us was less than $50, with a few shared Joe's Iced Teas.  At that cost, the priceless chalkboard atmosphere was free.    Would love to return for breakfast, which is available before noon.

This US Post Office in Morrisville, PA is about par for the course for an aging government facility. Parking in front. PO boxes to the right and services to the left upon entry. Queue of patrons longer than it should be at 1:30 in the afternoon, but only one guy working the counter until another co-worker got off lunch, an no postmaster in sight to address the service shortage.   Still, when my turn, the dude was friendly and attentive. He helped me out with the request for commemorative stamps for the office mail. Even made suggestions to be sure I saw everything. All the stamps were the forever variety; a big plus. Purple Heart, military service metals, team sport balls and Janis Joplin peaked my fancy. Janis?! Somebody in the institution really appreciates rock history. Thinking of framing those.  The place needs better lighting and a way to bring help to bear when it is busy, yet no major complaints given I was in and out in under 10 minutes.

Viet Tokyo Cuisine is a new restaurant on Haines Road, Bristol, PA.  Its doors have been open about ten days, offering Pho (Noodle Soups) and Com (Rice Dishes) from the southern part of Vietnam as well as Sushi.  It is owned and operated by a lovely Vietnamese woman and gentleman who are anxious to please customers with authentic beef broth noodle soups with a variety of thin sliced beef,  meatballs, or chicken.  The environment is utilitarian with about six booths and a few tables around the single dining room.  Decorations are sparse, but the house is clean and the service is solid.    I ordered a bowl of their Pho Bo Tai (Round Steak).  For $8.95 I was served in a large square bowl of a decent beef stock, nest of noodles, and 8 - 10 thin slices of the rare steak that I separated with my chopsticks to allow each to finish cooking in the heat of the soup.  I added Thai basil, sprouts, jalapeno slices and lime juice to taste, and set out to work my lunch.  The noodles needed to be pulled apart, but that was easily done. The beef was very good, especially when dipped in a mix of sriracha and hoisin sauces. I could not finish the pho.   Finding a pho shop in this part of Bucks County was a pleasant surprise.  While there are a few others around, they remain few and far between.  I found that the broth, while good, needed more time in the pot to simmer and reduce to a more complex spicy finish.  This is normally at least a 24 hour process, and this one was not quite mature. Still, I enjoyed it, as well as the labor of working the noodles, beef and consommé.  That is one of the best parts of slurping pho. It can be such a hands-on experience.   I will likely check Viet Tokyo out again to sample the rice options. It would be great if they also made Banh Mi sandwiches, but they were not on the menu.  Still, maybe they could do them as a special once in a while. If good it would guarantee my faithfulness.   3.5 Stars.   Can't speak to the sushi.

I enjoy the occasional lunch at the Broad Street Diner because in addition to being close to the office, they put together specials for the midday meal that are solid and filling.    Yesterday's Chicken Salad Sandwich on Rye was a fatty, and I had the option of several sides rather than fries.  Opted for Apple Sauce on a hot day, and the cup of Split Pea Soup that was placed before me was a complementary part of the deal.    At under $8, I felt well cared for.

Hit another Farnsworth Avenue hotspot yesterday with a late lunch in Under The Moon.  Have to say that Bordentown is turning into Lambertville.  That is a very good thing. Bonaparte would feel right at home.  Under The Moon dresses up like an old antique store that specializes in kitchen furniture and tableware.  It is wall to wall tubular steel tables and chairs and trundle tables.  The glassware and coffee mugs are a mix of various decades. The painted wood panel ceiling was attractive and interesting.  It was all so very charming and cozy.   I was alone when I entered around 2:30 looking for a late lunch.  Kim greeted me with a big smile and told me to sit anywhere.  I picked a double mid-shop to have equal views forward and aft.  A run through the menu had me narrow my selection to an appetizer ($9), as the prices were above my self imposed lunchtime limit.  The Corn Souffle with Leaks sounded about right.    It came with a few slices of home baked Garlic Bread, which itself had a small amount of Garlic Butter at the ready.
