The Souffle was not large, but it was filling.  The consistency was appropriately like whipped egg, and the Fried Leek topping looked like gray straw left by a miniature farmer.  The taste was remarkable for the sweetness of the corn and the crispy onion salute of the Leeks.  I liked this ensemble very much.  The price no longer felt so cher.  All the while, Kim returned periodically to check on me and keep me company.    When done I was asked if dessert was a consideration.  I saw the options in the display near my table.  Everything looked over the top!  Still, sweets would have to await another visit as I had plans at night.    The owners obviously take great pride in their establishment, and they have made an exceptional effort to stylize their house.  The food seemed to have a continental and mildly Spanish orientation.  No problem there.  The empanadas tapas were on my short list.  They were made in house by the mamacita or abuela.   Under The Moon is a great date.

It is hard to believe that prior to 1926 there were no bridges across the Delaware River south of Trenton, NJ. Despite the growing American love affair with the automobile, the only way to get across that body of water anywhere near Philadelphia was to swim or take one of the two ferries that operated from bank to bank at Camden and Burlington. There wasn't a car ferry until 1922, when a private business started a service that was wildly successful, but not nearly capable of meeting the growing demand.   So, the same entrepreneurs seeing the success of the new Benjamin Franklin Bridge just to the south that opened in 1926 as the longest suspension bridge in the world, organized their consortium to construct a span between Palmyra, NJ and the Tacony river ward in Philadelphia. Eighteen months and $4 million later, they had their toll bridge open for business. Rudolph Modjeski, the designer of the Ben Franklin and Manhattan Bridge in New York, did the work.   The first year the average volume was 3,500 cars per day. These days it is over 70,000. The original $.35 toll has gone up to match inflation and is now four bucks. Keeping things local, the steel components were fabricated by the American Bridge Company of Trenton, NJ, an offshoot of the older Roebling Steel Works, where the Brooklyn Bridge was cast.   This isn't a particularly efficient bridge these days, as it remains a drawbridge that raises up to allow ships to pass beneath, causing traffic to stop for 20 minutes with each opening. Too, the access on the Philly side it a problem as it has not been redesigned in nearly 100 years, except for modest improvement recently. Of course, it still is useful if your reliance on the trolley service hasn't changed since your great grandparents used them.   Otherwise, better to plan for the nearby Betsy Ross or Ben Franklin, both of which are easier to use than the venerable but outdated TPB.

Murphy's is a local bar down on Bristol Emilie Road, Levittown, PA. For a small dive bar it has some really good things going for it. Along with an interesting clientele who seem to all know each other, it possesses a beautiful classic wood shuffleboard along one wall, similarly well appointed bar runners whose friendly manner and fun loving personalities make them entertainers as much as mixologists, as they dance to the jukebox 'zak.   Although the kitchen was slammed when I ordered a cheeseburger off their limited menu and I had a bit of a wait until it reached me, it was well worth the delay. Served by the cook himself taking a walk from the grill to clear his head, it was the best half pounder I've had for quite a while. It was a perfect medium finish as requested. With lettuce, fat tomato slice and thin fresh red onion ringlets, the juicy flavor/texture was a masticating joy. Quality brioche roll, too. Crisp fries showed the small details were not taken for granted.   But for the fact that smoking is allowed, Murphy's was five star all the way. Have to add the expense of laundering the smell out of my clothes to the otherwise top drawer experience.  Maybe, "Beef & Ale" really means it!

I'm not sure what to make of the fact that there were no Indians in the kitchen of Cross Culture Indian Restaurant in Buckingham, PA. The menu was more limited than many I've seen, and the dishes themselves while decent, lacked some of the dynamism I associate with quality curry and other colorfully spiced South Asian cuisine.  We ordered their Veggie Samosa and Tomato Soup appetizers, Chicken Cashmere, Veggie Navaratan Korma as entrees and Garlic Naan for sopping up the anticipated creamy reductions. They were a mixed bag.   The Tomato Soup was disappointingly bland, and we decided to bring it all home to doctor it to a better place. The Samosas had a good crunchy shell, but the potato/pea contents was dry with little tongue tickle. The Cashmere was the best of the bunch - pleasantly creamy sauce sweetened by the cashew and raisins and tender dark chicken. The Korma was also quite good, but the sauce was too similar to the Cashmere and needed a bit more curry heat to make it distinguishable from its sibling. Where was the tumeric and chili? Finally, the Naan was hot and oily as it should be, and quickly gone as we enjoyed spooning up the sauces as our dessert.   Service was warm and efficient by one of the owners. She seemed to appreciate our presence in the days before restaurants were closed to protect from the COVID-19 crisis. We all suspected that moment to arrive soon, so in some ways we expected and acknowledged that this might well be our last meal out for the foreseeable future. Just wish the entire meal was as memorable as the societal moment we all were enduring.   Be safe everyone.

I have a love/hate relationship with Wawa. It applies more or less equally to all of them, but especially the super hyper Wawas that are currently being developed on the East Coast.   I certainly see the value buying their gasoline which is always a few cents cheaper than the regular gas stations in the area. Yet, I hesitate to buy it because I don't know who refines it for them, and thus can't trust its quality and ingredients. Too, I will sometimes stop in for coffee or a hoagie, but know that by doing so I am helping weaken the older mom and pop shops that rely on passing drivers for their survival. So, I usually feel conflicted visiting these 21st Century phenomena and avoid them more often than not.  It's not about whether they present a real monetary value to customers, nor offer the convenience of being able to fill up both your tank and stomach in the same place. Obviously, there are benefits in time and money being able to do so. But, do we want this to become normative behavior if the cost is really enforced conformity, universal standardization of our diets, and the end of all the variety that existed earlier in our cultural evolution?   I have concerns about this piece of progress, and wonder (perhaps, too often outloud) whether we would be better off if we spent more time doing little things like buying gas or eating lunch. Ultimately, I have no problem if I end up at a charging station to power my vehicle rather than slaving to the internal combustion engine, because that's good for the environment. But, on actions where convenience and not ecology is as stake, I vote for a little less time saving, and much more consideration of the existential quality of our lives.   It may not be fair to make Wawa the symbol of that degradation, rather than just another symptom of something bigger, but I came to that realization naturally, and it seems to capture my internal conflict as well as anything else.   Feel free to ignore these rantings of a peaceful lunatic, but sometimes you just have to ask the questions.

Decent enough bagel and friendly service, but it is somewhat amazing that there is so much disparity between one Manhattan Bagel shop and another; this one on Bustleton Avenue in the Russian part of Northeast Philly landing on the lower end of the spectrum.   Crust not as firm/crisp as others nearby, and far fewer roasted onion flakes attached. Still, more than adequate veggie cream cheese coverage within to help offset the shortcomings.   Their coffee is strong and holds its own for a breakfast blend. Been sipping it for several hours and it hasn't turned bitter.   Will certainly do until a real bakery shows up and turns out a Real McCoy bagel, that knows how to bathe well before baking.

Nino's Trattoria & Pizzeria sits just off the Brunswick Circle in Trenton, NJ.  It is easy to see how it is a pizzeria, but it does not look nor feel like a trattoria. Rather, there is a long narrow area to the left of the restaurant with the ovens and prep zone, and a larger dining room to the left as you enter.  There are a dozen or so tables and booths in this typical Italian shop.  It would look a lot nicer if the chairs had been taken down off the tables during business hours. It felt like they weren't quite ready for prime time.   However, my lunch was of considerably higher quality than the atmosphere.  My eggplant parm sandwich was made of thin sliced nightshade, dipped in breadcrumbs, and pan fried in olive oil before being placed in a submarine roll, topped with red sauce and slices of mozza cheese and thrown in the oven to melt the cheese and toast the bread.  The coating was thin enough to allow the flavor of the veggie to come through loud and clear.  Not too much gravy nor cheese to obscure the main ingredient, but enough to enhance it.    My companion went with penne with their house red gravy, in a child size portion. Just right for lunch.  I sampled the pencil points and found their sauce to be very good.  It had lots of minced garlic, salt, pepper and a touch of basil; creating a lightly chunky tasty crushed tomato texture and rich taste.  Although I usually eat the eggplant without the roll, I found myself sopping up the delicious mash with pieces of the hoagie roll, it was so good. When I asked for the second half of the sandwich to be packed up for home, the server put in two extra small containers of the sauce, because she had seen me going after it with gusto at the table. Gratitude!   Nino's has some strong kitchen skills with their pasta and baked specialties. Can't speak to their pizza.  A little attention to the impression created in their customers would allow them to make the dining room more presentable, and create the sense of a polished dining facility.

Fu Wah (Happy Children) is a small Chinese shop in an old strip center on Olden Avenue Extension, Ewing, NJ. It has the advantage of 8 booths/tables for the eat in crowd, in addition to a brisk take out business. The whole family pitches in during summer. Mom took my order at the front counter. Dad woked it up in the kitchen, and young son served me with a spirited, "Enjoy your lunch."  I would have if the hot and sour soup did not have a large lump of pork fat below the surface, and the sesame chicken wasn't all dark meat with little sauce to stir into the yellow dyed fried rice.   Get the picture? Not the greatest effort by these happy children.

Bagel Train remains my favorite bagel vendor in the area.   Always a curiosity why people from Bagel City (born and raised there myself) think they know rounders better than anyone else, or that there is any uniformity among Big Apple bagels. There really isn't. I've had great ones on the Westside, and crappy ones in Soho. I've bitten into rock hard dense losers in Canarsie, and lovely light crunchers in Elmwood.   So, don't listen to anyone who says they know what's best for anyone but themselves. If you love them, that's all that matters. Even if you never spent a day of your life in the City That Never Sleeps!

Ruben's Pizza sits in a tiny strip of stores that is easy to drive passed without even noticing. If not for the fact that I was on Spruce Street in Ewing for other reasons, I would never have stopped to settle my later afternoon hunger. But, there it was, with new sign out front just in the right place to catch my eye and safely pull into the miniscule parking area in front of their building.   They have both personal sized and small pies selling for $5 and $7.50 for 12" and 15" diameter wheels, which seemed perfectly designed for my pleasure - the equivalent of the bar pies famous throughout Trenton, but without the bar. Sized and priced right to move. So, I ordered the small 15"er with Sweet Italian Sausage.   The shop is too tiny for tables, and I planned to take it home, knowing that it would be past its prime by the time I opened the box. To my surprise, although no longer hot enough to burn my tongue, it retained its point when lifted, and folded nicely between my lips and into my mouth. Nice char on the undercarriage, too.   The taste was good with slightly salty tomato slurry top, hint of basil and correct amount of melted mozza proportional to the sauce. It left a very good first impression.   Def worth remembering the next time I'm in the Trenton Farmers Market zone.

Past time for an updated review to reflect all the positive changes that this bagel emporium has gone through over the last few years.   Biggest visible change was the expansion of their footprint and reorientation of the shop to permit side of building access which greatly enhances the size and feel of the space. Now Keystone is a for real cafe, with table and wall seating all around which gives a spaciousness to the operation.  Most important, they have built a bagel bakery right into the shop, with windows allowing customers to see the bagelmeisters at work. Not having to transport them from a more distant location means that the bagels are apex quality right from the oven to the bins. Nothing is lost in taste nor texture when the overall distance is about 20 feet. The difference in chewability is immediately apparent. Crisp firm outer skin and soft tender inner bagel, and full load of toppings (onion flakes for me), that stay affixed to the rounder, and don't fall off with normal handling.   Service was excellent all around, with ordering at the counter and delivery to the table when done. Take out seemed just as smooth as I watched people come and go quickly.   Keystone is planning an expansion into other shops and considering franchising the business. From what I saw and experienced on my last visit, they have a thoughtful plan and the means to execute. They listen to customers and are flexible enough to adapt to changing conditions. Personally, I would love to see them open up a little farther north in Bucks, and look into cross marketing with local coffee roasters where the best local Java and rounders were available in the same places and advertised together.   The current situation is impressive, I suspect it will only get better from here!   My candidate for Bucks Bagels of the Year!

Lai Lai Garden on Dekalb Pike, Blue Bell, PA, is one of the most attractive Asian houses I have seen in the Commonwealth. It is richly appointed with dark mahogany and fabrics, tables & chairs, and soft gold and amber tones. The male staff is in shirts and ties. The entire ambiance is of an upscale restaurant, with a menu that generally covers the broad range of Chinese cuisine and a more limited Japanese list of sushi, and popular offerings. Ownership is Chinese and I was there for a lunch of their American/Chinese dishes. Expectedly, prices were also significantly higher for their afternoon specials, which came with cups of soup and white rice.   It was Friday after court in Norristown, so I didn't mind spending more to send me serenely into the weekend. I opted for their Orange Beef and Wonton Soup @ $11.   The soup was excellent. Fresh, flavorful consomme with two goldfish wontons and small slices of scallion for extra taste. Enjoyed every hot steaming slurp. The beef platter was not as good. Rather than using lean beef textured to hold a crisp finish out of the wok, they appeared to use a different cut of beef more akin to beef for stew or roast. It was stringy on the inside and far more chewy than it should have been. With mastication pieces of each morsel became lodged in my teeth; not a pleasant sensation. The sauce was well designed, and mildly tart, which helped convince me that completing the meal was worthwhile, although a floss challenge thereafter.   Given that a much better version of this dish costs $2.50 less at my local dragon den, I see no point to spending more for lesser satisfaction, nor to exploring more of the menu when I have seen they don't handle the basics any better than less pretentious kitchens.

Hunan Wok (identified as only, "Hunan" on the sign above the shop), is a fairly typical Chinese/American suburban restaurant in the Fairgrounds Shopping Plaza just outside downtown Mt. Holly.  The menu is what you expect to find in such places.  It is set up primarily for takeout, but offers a few tables for those who prefer to eat in, as I did.    My lunch consisted of Sesame Chicken, Fried Rice, & Wonton Soup.  It was served to me in the takeout containers, with plastic utensils.  The soup was straight up chicken bouillon and the wontons were thick skinned and of average quality.  The Chicken itself was plentiful with a mix of white and dark meat, breaded, and drowned in dark amber goopy sauce, with sesame seeds sprinkled on top.  It was not bad, but undistinguishable from most other such joints.  The rice had been prepared in the same soup mix as the wonton, and carried the same yellow color.  More than enough, but not worth carbing out on.   Service was fine.  The proprietress was engaged and efficient.  The price was under $7 with a soft drink.

I guess it means something that it took four years for a return visit to Duck Sauce, despite the fact that it is the closest restaurant to my Newtown office, and I love Chinese food.   The reasons are what you'd expect. It just isn't the exceptional Asian fusion it once was, and the competition in that niche has grown in the interim. It seems there has been a change in ownership, with the old kitchen creativity having lost its edge. While it remains better than average as a Chinese/American house, it really doesn't overtly compete in that space. Rather, it's claim to fame has always been that it is a different kind of Asian place - a fusion experience that suggests traditional dishes, but does them in a unique way to make their menu special.   While the menu looks the same for the most part, the separation from standard offerings elsewhere is now less distinct; the distance between Duck Sauce and the average Chinois, smaller.   The Wonton Soup is still very good, but the wonton skin a bit thicker. The Calamari appetizer had a coarse breading that detracted from the softness and flavor of the tender crustacean beneath, while the dipping sauce was fine. The Orange Beef was soft rather than crispy, and the dark amber semi sweet sauce, thick and more gloopy than remembered. Yet, there were the potato sticks sprinkled on top, still a nice touch. The Shrimp and Cashew platter was very good, but not dissimilar to what you can find almost everywhere.   I finished my lunch satisfied, but not in love with the meal, as I once was. It is still a good place for quality ingredients and presentations, but I left with no urge to return within the next four years.   3.5 STARS

The Warrington town fathers & mothers showed their vision of the future when they approved The Shops at Valley Square commercial development on Route 611.  They did not see the big shopping malls of the 20th Century as enhancing the land values that surround them, but were open to the concept in modern urban planning that recognizes that people prefer to have consumer experiences on a more human scale.    Capture the essentials of small town America in an attractive village-like setting, and they will come to spend money.  They got that right.   The Shops at Valley Square found the sweet spot for commercial enterprise for this era.  Buildings designed to look like a country town, with sidewalks, narrow streets, street parking,  buildings no taller than three stories, and attractive shops and restaurants that are as inviting on the outside, as they are within.  Include the brands that people want and the eateries that beckon their hunger for relief, and success is almost assured.    The facility is very attractive and inviting.  We were there for dinner, and the choices were pretty good; Panera, Ted's Montana Grill, P.F. Chang's, Chipotle, and even a Wegman's if we wanted to take home.  It was easy to park near our destination, and fun to walk a few blocks to see what was going on.    Not every municipality shows the foresight to bring in such a sparkling center that has become a destination for the surrounding communities, and beyond.    Have a visit and enjoy the future.

Asian House sits in the Mallard Shopping Centre on northbound Route 130.  It is pretty far south of Bordentown, so don't give up hope if you don't see it right way if you are travelling south.    The space is very nicely appointed for a Chinese/American shop trying to be all things Asian for the hungry public.  There are Sushi, Thai and Chinese options on the menu.  I went Chinese for my first visit as I knew it was owned/operated by Fujianese folks from the Mainland.   I opted for Szechuan Chicken (extra spicy), which came with Wonton Soup and Pork Fried Rice.  The soup was not good.  It was a mass produced beef stock tinted brown from the dye in the can it came from.  The wontons were thick and not very tasty.  The Chicken dish was better.  The meat was fresh and the veggies colorful.  The sauce lacked much in the way of red Szechuan chilies, and was not hot enough despite asking for extra heat.  I think the kitchen was on autopilot and just turned out what they normally do and ignored my request.  At least it was decent, even lacking the spice.  The Fried Rice was better than average with the grains still distinct and veggies firm.     The best thing Asian House has going for it is Misty, the woman running the front of the house.  She was friendly, engaging, helpful, and prompt with service.  She singlehandedly made my lunch a memorable one, and provided the motivation to return to try other features of their menu.

Viet Thai Cuisine is a well designed Asian house just off the Pa Pike in Horsham.  Lots of stone and metal, and even a wall of pussy willow branches. A semi-private dining room was off to the side.  Service is warm and precise, and the menu offers a fairly broad cross section of dishes from Vietnam and Thailand.  In such "fusion" locales, the question always is whether it is really "fusion," or more confusion?    The staff we saw was Thai, and we took that as a suggestion to stay close to the menu from their homeland, just to be safe.  Besides, we have been to many very good Vietnamese shops in and around Philly, and our Thai options were always more limited.    We ordered Coconut Soup (w/ Tofu), Summer Rolls (Veggie), and Salmon in Red Curry Sauce for sharing.  The soup had the sweetness from the coconut and the hot bite of lemongrass, with plenty of veggies.  It was quite good, and was slurped away quickly.  The summer rolls were also top notch, with a thin strip of tofu holding the rest of the contents together.  The peanut dipping sauce was excellent with thin chili shavings and ground nuts sitting on top, looking like calligraphy (see photo).  If there was anything that missed the mark, it was the salmon, which was slightly overcooked, and was drier than desired.  Still, the presentation was lovely, and the surrounding elements on the plate along with the red curry, redeemed the fish to some extent.    We were enjoying our time here, and decided to extend it with a fried banana dessert.  It came in the guise of spring rolls with a large scoop of Bassett's Vanilla Ice Cream melting on top.  It was a creamy sweet ending to our evening at Viet Thai.    3.5 Stars

I just needed a light bite for the drive back from UDel to Bucks, and this McDonald's flashed on the Route 2 horizon. This was to be a drive through encounter, so I never saw the interior of the small footprint burger emporium.   It has been a long while since my last McBurger, and I faltered at the order stand, not remembering what the latest deals were. I asked for a quarter pounder, and was immediately asked by the speaker voice if I wanted a second one for a dollar.  Sure. Why not? Did I also want a value meal? I didn't want fries, but a bottle of water made sense. The voice was patient with me. I knew most customers were more familiar with Mickey's menu than me, although I was aware they were test marketing a new fried chicken sandwich at the behest of their franchisees, who were trying to compete with Popeyes and Chick-fil-A.   The burger tasted fresh, with nice flavor addition from thin red onion ringlets and pickles. The beef was a little salty for me, but not overly so. The bun held together well.   I was satisfied as I munched on the way north, and reminisced on my summer working at McDonald's in River Edge, NJ, the year I graduated from high school and prepared for college. I imagine it is still a great job for a teenager.

Rosario's is that turquoise colored 1940's tiny food shack that sits on Rt. 130 South, just past the 206 split in Bordentown, NJ. It has been spinning pizza for a couple of generations.  Grandpop still runs the show, but son is deeply involved.   Surprisingly ample parking lot for the 7 or 8 tables within, but with takeout and delivery options, the shop can get busy.  The afternoon I stopped in, there were four kids not yet in their teens who had ridden there on bikes, enjoying summer with slices and fries.  Perfect place for nostalgia. It was so easy to remember doing the same with my buds as we celebrated our nascent independence.   My two slices and a coke contributed to the reveries.  Yet, on their own, the pizza was solid, with good tasting mozza and fresh tomato sauce.  The crust could have been firmer, but I was in a forgiving mood.  At slightly more than $5 for lunch, this was a worthy pizza stop.  Too, Rosario's did not make a dozen pizzas in advance for display.  Their old style approach was appreciated, as I knew that whatever pie I was eating had not been made long before.  Just in time production works best for fresh food.  Those houses that leave pizza around all day for people to see and chose could learn from Rosario.  Stale warmed over pizza is never prime.   Next time I want a quick lunch with a dose of childhood, I will be back.  Probably sooner than later.

The good news is that this part of Street Road, Bensalem,PA, has a large Indian population and alot of commerce dedicated to meeting the needs of the community. The bad news is that Indian Hut is still the equivalent of a fast casual food outlet - better than fast food, but far short of haute subcontinental cuisine. So, unless your expectations are properly calibrated, you are probably going to be somewhat disappointed by the size of each entree, the roughness of the main ingredients, or the non-subtlety of the various sauces into which everything is thrown and mixed.   Our Malai Kofta (veggie balls in mild red curry), Chicken Korma and Makhani (boneless chunky chicken in spicy red/lightly sweet mild yellow curry), Chili Gobhi (fried cauliflower florets in Manchurian red chili/tumeric heat) and Veggie Biryani (long grain basmati rice mixed with chopped greens, like fried rice, but not as captivating), were strong on spice, pretty in color, but perhaps too monotonal in texture and heavy handed Indian spices.   Not that everything was bad, it wasn't. It's more that everything was too much alike, so that the dishes blended together indistinguishably from each other after a few bites.   At $11-12 per choice, it wasn't too expensive, but would have been so much better with a deft curry hand at the controls. Then again, if you can taste the difference between fast casual and superior tasting North or South Indian kitchens, you don't really belong at such inferior joints.

Was a time Dunkin Donuts was about the best coffee/cake sweets house in the nation because of their consistency. No matter where your caffeine bug bit, there was a DD nearby that could be counted on to offer java and fried dough that was similar from place to place.   Maybe it's because there are so many coffee houses and high quality roast cafes around these days, but it has been a long while since I truly enjoyed a cuppa joe from Dunkin. Could be the quality of water has declined, or that the beans have suffered from lax quality control or increased competition from all the new java outlets, but even the sweet dough lacks the enjoyability of the old days.   Hence, I was not surprised when I stopped in to this DD/Baskin Robbins joint to give me a boost the other night, and the small coffee and sour cream rounder were both hopelessly ordinary and lacking in life energy. In a word, they sucked.   Saving grace? The shop was large and had ample seating. The people working there were pleasant and engaged well with customers.   Ho Hum.

One of those old fashioned stainless steel and glass diners from the 1950's, that is still pumping out excellent breakfast fare for road warriors. Pulled in driving my late model Zipmobile, and when I returned, it had transformed into a 1958 Packard.  Just what I always wanted!  The staff was perfect for this stage.  Friendly, gregarious, and full of "Honey."    The French Toast was very good, too.  Enough egg, soaked through and through, and a caramelized texture where the super hot range had cauterized the surface of the bread.  If they had used real maple syrup rather than the mass produced prepackaged variety, it would have attained all star (5 Star) status.  Also needed a Cecilware coffee urn, rather than the newer Bunn for the best coffee.   I don't mind cutting corners to make ends meet, but in my fantasy the syrup comes straight from a Vermont Sugar Maple to my plate.

Metro Grill in the Glen Roc Shopping Center is another very good Italian restaurant with a clubby feel and full house for dinner nearly every weekend. The space is small, adding to the sense that its bar and dining room are popular in the hood. Service is in the traditional black and white mode - all first rate. Our reservation options were for either 5:30 (too early due to work) or 7:45. We grabbed that table for three.   The menu had everything expected from apps to dessert. We opted to share the calamari frita with a Thai chili dipping sauce, followed by chicken franchais, chicken marsala and their pork chop plate. All were very good to excellent. The squid had a strong crunchy breading that was enhanced by the Asian style sweet/hot spice. It was a legit alternative to the red sauce that normally accompanies this dish. The two chicken platters were tender fillets with with custom made sauces. The mushrooms in marsala wine and the artichoke in lemon and white wine renditions were a joy. The pasta sides were a nice counterbalance in red dress to the subtleties of the mains. The pork chop was at least a two inch cut with demiglaze, string beans and mashed. That heavy serrated blade came in very handy. If there was any weakness at all, it was the chop was a bit tougher than it should have been. Still, the juicy taste was there, it just required more mastication than desired.   We had no room for sweets at the end.   Metro Grill is an excellent representation of the Trenton Italian cuisinary tradition. It is proof that you can take the restaurant out of the Burg, while maintaining the Burg within the heart of the restaurant.

Jersey Bagel Cafe & Pizza on Rt. 130 Northbound, Willingboro, NJ, is a little hard to find, even when standing at their front door. It sits far off the highway in a multi building commercial center that is currently undergoing construction in their drives, and with retail shops all around each pod.   I was at the right place, but it took a few minutes due to poor signage to find the only open door to the premises on the side. The main doors were locked and a hand made arrow pointed to the second door, which was also bolted closed. I was too near to just give up, especially when I saw someone inside who didn't respond to my knocking on the glass. So, I walked around the corner, and lo and behold, there was another single door entrance inviting me in.   Very glad I hadn't given up, because despite the rough introduction to JBC&P, the bagels within were really very good. Service was friendly and Covid appropriate. For pennies over a 5 spot, I enjoyed a fairly large Onion Bagel smeared with a liberal amount of Veggie Cream Cheese spread, and large self-serve java.   The baker had the right touch and had left the bagel with a crisp skin, yet light inner texture. Just the way I prefer them, with nice mild sourdough flavor under the soft innards and crunchy dark brown toasted onion flakes (perhaps a bit burnt, but still quite good). The Joe was hot and strong.   While there I saw a tray of homemade baklava under display glass. Made it tempting to return sometime soon for their Italian offerings, and get a taste of that delicious looking honey drenched pistachio pastry.

Lemon Grass Thai Restaurant on Huntingdon Pike is a legit Thai kitchen that doesn't pretend to be what it is not. This is no erstaz fusion joint putting out sushi, Chinese and a little Bangkok cuisine. No. It is strictly what it claims to be - all Thai all the time. And, that's the way I like it.   The dining room is dark and small with a bamboo grove potted by the door and soft wood and cool orange tints throughout. Management is Siamese and the chef was likely raised there, too. So, it is as authentic as it can be, while making understandable concessions to American taste buds. I was very pleased with lunch the other day, as it all seemed deliciously consistently Phuket.   The lunch deal consisted of an appetizer, soup/salad and entree, for $9.95. I was attracted to the Buddha Dumplings (veggie), Coconut Soup (veggie) and Drunken Noodles (chicken and hot). It was a combination that came at me in waves. First, the fried dumplings were full of ground veggies and a good dipping sauce. Pleasantly chewy with mild flavor. The soup was steaming and loaded with thin sliced carrots, string beans, mushrooms, tofu, with a slightly stronger spice bite than the B. Balls. Finally, the drunk pasta, while not the jumbo noodles expected, was still strong enough to use it surface to hold on to the heavy brown sauce tenaciously. It had a larger quotient of hot chili powder, and thus the strongest taste and plenty more veggie and sliced chicken. It was perfectly sized at less than a dinner portion, but more than enough to fill me up after all that came before.   Service was attractive, friendly and invisible except when delivering the dishes to the table.   It was great to be back in an authentic Thai house after recent exposure to "fusion" huts that couldn't deliver on the promise of real Pattayan cuisine. If their duck is up to the standards of the rest of the menu, 5 stars won't be far behind.

Pho Ben City (clever ref to Franklin City), sits on Rt 611 in Abington, Pa. It is a nicely reused former fast food outpost, that is now a well designed, modern Vietnamese house with a full menu from pho to com to full plate dinners.  Service is friendly and prompt. Prices are competitive with other local pho shops, but higher than found in cities north and south by a couple of bucks.  Higher rents in the burbs lead to higher prices.  My Phone Tai was good. The broth was clear and could have simmered longer before serving to bring out the flavor. The accompanying Thai basil, sprouts, jalapeno and lime were freshly bright green. Plenty of lean beef and needles lurking beneath the calm surface.   The roast pork Banh Mi was tasty, with nice crusty baguette holding it together. Spring Rolls were average for content and taste, while the dipping sauce was a little thin.   Complimentary scoops of ice cream was a nice closer.   Pho Ben City is quite good, but it does give away some of the strongest elements of Viet cuisine, perhaps due to location and clientele. I have no problem with that, but admit to liking the style used where most visitors to Saigon houses seek the full Monty of taste.  To my tongue, it is superior to Pho & Beyond (less MSG), and about on par with Pho Palace, if a little behind House of Pho in overall richness of experience.

It's one thing to be almost out of donuts late on a Saturday night, quite another to leave the shop like it was hit by a cyclone.   There were very few choice by the time we arrived around 8:00 p.m., but enough for our limited sweet tooth and caffeine needs. I grabbed the last toasted coconut, and my sidekick the double chocolate. It was difficult to see what was in the bins because the paper liners were pulled out far enough to block the view, but not removed all together. The same was true around the trash receptacle, where many of the used napkins were scattered around, and the thin waxy sheets used to pick up and bag the donuts were crumpled and tossed haphazardly on the floor and counter.   Dude in the sloppy outfit and bedraggled white apron seemed to be working alone. Tidiness had gotten away from him, but he did have time to talk on his mobile, and with a bud who was hanging out at a corner hightop.   Dunkin or DD, there are certain basic requirements for doing the job correctly, and keeping the joint clean is one of them. He must have skipped that class. Made Steve's Prince of Steaks right next door look like a shining palace by comparison.   Oh, yeah... The donuts and coffee were fine.

Giovanni's Pizza is a Italian shop on York Road in Jamison, Pa. They do a big pizza business as suggested by the wall of pizza boxes awaiting use in the entrance hall. When I asked one of the guys behind the counter how many pies they do a day, I was told anywhere from 50 to 300! Quite a range, but they were getting ready for the high end when we were there by cutting up the dough and placing them in small aluminum canisters.   The house itself has two dining rooms and can accommodate quite a crowd. It is clean, and service is prompt and friendly. We ordered a single plain slice to see how they do with their most basic commodity, an eggplant parmesan sandwich and a burger with onions and mushrooms.  Nothing stood out as exceptional, and some things need work.   The plain pizza is average in size and taste. Mine was a reheat job, well done. They got that right, and the crust was nice and firm with a mild scorch on the undercarriage. There was too much cheese for me, and not enough sauce. Really could not get the flavor of the tomatoes due to cheesy dominance. Pizza requires the right balance on top to make it stand out. This did not do it. The eggplant parm sandwich was in a large torpedo roll, again covered in copious melted mozzarella. The nightshade itself had a heavy breading that absorbed a lot of oil in the frying.  Would have been better if just sautéed in olive oil without the extra breading, but was still okay. The burger was disappointing. A frozen puck, cooked to well done when medium was requested. Dry and tasteless, despite the additional sautéed onions and mushrooms. Even the ketchup couldn't save it.   This was a late lunch, and we didn't explore the dinner and pasta options, which may be as good as the other reviewers report. Still, I can only write about my experience, which was not quite middle of the road.  2.5 Stars.

Sad to say, the other reviewers are correct.  This is an example of how a bad business can continue to thrive in the absence of competition.  It is obvious the workers reflect the attitude of the management.  They make half hearted attempts to do the job, although they appear to be swarming over the car with sprays and rags.  There is always something left undone, and nary a smile or "thank you for coming."

Newtown Cleaners has opened a shop in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center, right next to Acme. The owners are the same as the good people who operated Top Cleaners on South State Street for many years. Minah continues as the face of the business, daughter of the founders, who help out with dry cleaning moving in and out, and tailoring garments with nimble thimble, needle and thread. The old place was far too small for all their customers, and moving to the commercial center while a risk because of the larger nut carried, is also a great opportunity to increase their hold as the best professional cleaners in Newtown.   I have been using them to launder my shirts and put cuffs on my pants for close to seven years after trying all the other places in and around town. While not the cheapest, the quality of services is undeniable, and Minah's personality outshines the pleasantries offered by the other store owners. Too, they run occasional specials that bring everything into line and makes them very competitive for the area.   While it's hard to get too worked up about dry cleaning establishments, I have the feeling that with the extra space and sitting room, Newtown Cleaners could become a center of hot stove conversations in our community.   Just provide great coffee and they will come.

Don't know about the salon in New York (although born and raised there), nor reputations well earned or not. But, I know what a good cut looks like, and how staff treats people. Most importantly, I know what makes my wife happy and what doesn't.   After parking the car, I arrived at Room 209 about 20 minutes after she went in for her appointment. There were a row of barber chairs on the right, and a statue of a black horse rearing on its hind legs on the left in front of the high cashier counter. Lao po was in the rear having her hair washed, so I took a seat in the front waiting area.   Eventually, she moved to her chair, where several assistants had their hands on her head combing and asking questions about her desired results. Sam came over to assess the situation, ran his hands through her hair for a minute or so, seemingly to contemplate the proper approach. He walked away a few times to supervise the other customers, but ultimately returned, shears in hand to put the finishing touches on the cut.   A bit of blow drying and final shaping and trimming, and they were done. She was clearly happy with her look in the mirror, and I have to admit with her face framed with straight black hair and falling easily on her shoulders, she was a sight to behold. Her classic facial structure, deep eyes and high cheekbones gave her the image of an empress.   Took my breath away.

Bonnet Lane Family Restaurant is a long standing urban diner on Old York Road, Abington, PA. The space is separated into two rooms; a dining room and another with counter service and a few booths. I chose a spinner at the counter nearest the kitchen swinging door where I could see the work area within when the door opened. Service was provided by a crew of dear ladies who addressed me as, "Dear," throughout my stay. Lovely, efficient and culturally affected. I didn't mind as long as they filled my coffee mug as needed.   Their menu was most the usual suspects, with daily specials on a separate A-frame in thick plastic on the counter and tables. I went with the Greek Omelette, with the home fries inside the egg shell (That's just the way I like it.) Rye toast finished the platter.   Loved the way all the flavors ran together, with the feta cheese offering the sharpest retort and the potatoes the most texture. The tomato, onion and spinach nicely occupied the middle ground between these two edges, while the crisp rye complimented the eggs with its mild savoriness.   I was in a groove with the meal feeling content and nourished. As I sat finishing my coffee, the kitchen door swung open and I saw two kitchen people prepping food without gloves. I didn't know if this was standard practice or just a solitary slip of their more rigorous cleanliness routine, but in the Age of Coronavirus such oversight is not just unacceptable, it's downright dangerous.   Please guys, caution and public health requires constant vigilance.  Minus 1 Star for unsanitary conditions.

Stopped by for breakfast this week, and was treated to excellent service, meal and ambiance all rolled into one sunny, cool autumnal morn.   I couldn't ask for better weather for sitting at a deuce in the front window and having the sun through the glass warm my shoulders. Even with the diaphanous shades drawn to reduce the glare, the room was bright, white, and clearstory cheery. The dining area walls were all glass, letting in the beautiful bucolic 360 degree panoramas. I was warmly greeted and had hot strong Ellis Coffee on my table when I return from the WC.    The menu had creative breakfasts on one side, and lunches on the other.  They change their signature quiche and frittata daily as described by my lovely server.  In addition, they offer pancakes, french toast, omelets and Caleb's Breakfast Sandwiches; with each coming in tempting varieties, like French Toast Bananas Foster, and seasonal specialties. I could have gone in any direction with all the sweet temptation, but chose their take on a sandwich made of chicken sage sausage, cheddar and two fried eggs on a soft fresh brioche roll.  It came with home fried potatoes on the side.   Everything was great!  The sandwich arrived leaking melted cheddar onto the plate that ran into the taters. It was overloaded, and could not be contained in my hands. With each bite one of the split sausage links fell out and had to be replaced.  Ultimately, I gave up on that and used knife and fork to handle what the challenged roll could not.  No problem.  It allowed each element to be savored separately and in combination.  Although the brioche could have been stronger, I have no complaints when the result is a veritable cornucopia of delicious pieces falling to the plate and being forked up in harmony with the home fries.  Those chunky tubers were excellent, too.  Just enough big pieces to hold the spices tossed onto them on the grill, and small enough for well done nibs to provide a tasty crunch. They were super fine, deserving recognition via their own photo. Let's not forget the Ellis brew that was free flowing and a strong wake up/washdown for this superlative breaking of the fast.   Can't speak for the other meals, but Caleb's does a might fine midweek morning repast.  Maybe a few bucks more cher than non-Lahaska cafes, but so very worth the experience.

More a cafe and less a bakery at the intersection of Holland and Buck Roads in Southampton, PA, this Eastern European house is well decorated with a large dining room and four private rooms for group breakfast and lunch. The menu is very interesting with the use of standard ingredients prepared by hands trained in formerly socialist republics.   I ordered the Tomato Feta Omelet. It was cooked in a personal sized polished steel pan and served to me still burning hot in that instrument, on an oval wooden insulating plank. The outer egg was almost a souffle texture and the taste was great. It came with two chunks of bread and a small dish of sweet butter. The bread had a crisp crust warm enough to melt the spread. It was also excellent and left me wishing for more.   The final surprise was the brewing of La Colombe coffee; strong enough to take immediate notice, and a pitcher of milk for mixing to my preferred shade of auburn. It was so good!  Service was efficient and beautifully accented.   This was a surprising and awesome meal at a very reasonable price. It was good to visit Kiev for a few minutes.

So many of the good Mexican houses are across the Bucks County line in Montco, and Don Chile Mexican Restaurant is yet another of them.   I called in my order of Chicken Cheese Flautas and Tacos al Pastor, and it was ready 15 minutes later. The space was attractive, and I can see eating in when the Covid coast is clear. The woman handling the front of the house was friendly, efficient and attractive. She made me feel appreciated for giving them my business.   When I returned home, I found nice sized portions of everything, including bags/containers of chips & salsa, red rice, silky refried beans and crema fresca. The three Flautas were six inches long and overstuffed with chunky semi- ground roast chicken and white cheese wrapped in a large wheat tortilla and fried to a pleasant crisp. I topped that with their gaucamole, lettuce and tomato. A final drizzle of queso fresca over everything, and I was a contented man.   My beautiful opposite number went after the Al Pastor with the same gusto, and described succulent roast pork surrounded by pieces of grilled pineapple, lettuce, tomato, guac and cheese; crammed into 3 smaller tortillas she could barely pinch and roll closed to get into her boca pequena bonita. She was hungry and didn't give me a chance to take photos before she demolished them. They sure had great aroma.   Even the rice and beans were exceptional and worthy of mention. The grains were freshly made and not clumpy nor tasting of reheating, and the refried mashed kidney beans surprisingly smooth and delicious. All without the heartburn normally associated with heavy application of lard. No Tums necessary.   Don Chile isn't in or near my neighborhood, but certainly is worth a drive in the country when the Mexican mood strikes.   Mucho gusto!

"Anything worth doing is worth overdoing." - Albert Einstein  And so it is with bubble tea shops in Philly Chinatown.  You can't cross the street without seeing bobba signs on every corner. Tapioca is definitely having an amazing resurgence. I don't get why gummy sweet goobers are so popular, but I'm obviously in the minority.   Still, I enjoy good milk tea as much as the next guy, and Vivi Bubble Tea has it's fair share of that. The space is larger than expected, with a large room with group tables in back for all your friends. Service is efficient and friendly. I had my almond milk tea in hand in under a minute. Impressive.   The tea was good and exactly what I needed to continue with my shopping list and Artiva haircut. Steamy hot, mildly sweet, sufficiently nutty. $4.   Noticed that Vivi offered fried chicken wings. Piquing my curiousity, I made a mental note to give them a try next time I needed a nosh while in Ctown.

Keystone Bagels on Mill Creek Parkway just off Route 13 South, sits in a small commercial strip with a pizza parlor and ice cream shop, so it is possible to have breakfast, lunch, dinner and dessert without leaving the premises. I was there for the first meal of the day, although I have previously sampled the creamies next door.   The store is fairly small, with half dozen tables and high tops, in addition to the kitchen area.  The bagels don't appear to be baked on site, but my onion bagel & swiss sandwich was certainly fresh and loaded with large crisp onion flakes.   The downside was that it was more dense than I prefer in a bagel. I like the ones that have crisp skins and lighter dough within. That's just a matter of taste.  However, I was disappointed that there was no real milk in the small refrigerator next to the self-serve coffee counter. Liquid CoffeeMate was available in various flavors, but none are as healthy as 2% or even whole milk.  They do have longer shelf life due to the lack of any dairy component, so I get it.  It's just not what I want in my java. My black coffee itself was adequate, but it was obvious that Joe is a secondary consideration there.    Upgrade the coffee operation and Keystone could be a real sweet spot for breakfast and lunch.

Covid Takeout Review  Did a GrubHub takeout from Shagun Palace yesterday, and was very satisfied with the result. The restaurant is in the rear of a shopping center on Street Road, Bensalem, where there is a significant cluster of South Asian kitchens. Competition being severe, the quality is higher than in many more isolated Indian houses.   Our order: Veggie Samosa for an appetizer; Chicken Korma, Chili Chicken - Dry, as entrees; and Baingan Bartha (curry eggplant), for a veggie side; and Garlic Naan to soak up the sauces. The foods were all very good to excellent, with kudos to the korma and dry chili chicken, which displayed spice skill with the sauces. The bird was perfectly cooked, and not at all dried out.   If there was a weakness, it was the Naan, which appeared premade and merely heated in the oven before wrapping in foil. It was thicker and drier than normal, and not the least bit flakey, nor with expected air pockets. There was practically no garlic flavor. Next time, skip the naan.   There are talented hands at Shagun Palace where they are allowed to perform their magic. They are masters of curry cream reductions, but make a mistake in not carrying the expertise through to their breads. If they lack a tandoor for BBQ and Indian oven breads, they really should invest in one. It would make Shagun a more complete 5 Star experience.

This 230 acre park was given to the people of Montgomery County by the estate of George Horace Lorimer, the editor of the Saturday Evening Post and president of Curtis Publishing Co., both headquartered in Philadelphia from the late 19th Century to the present. His mausoleum is in Laurel Hill Cemetery, so although originally from North Carolina, his true impact was on the cultural life of our city.   Fairly small, it feels considerably larger due to its connection to Pennypack Park covering a large area in Northeast Philadelphia to the border with Montco. The creek by the same name flows through both parks, tying them together geologically. The watercourse meanders through Lorimer where it has cut a deep ravine over the millennia. There are multiple scenic overlooks worth exploring, even in winter when the absence of foliage allows you to see through the trees to the actual contours of the steep rocky hills across the creek.   If power walking or family bike riding is your jam, Pennypack Trail runs along the northern boundary of the park and beyond for several miles, and it is flat, wide and dirt/gravel packed for smooth ambulation or cross country biking, allowing excellent views of the topography and creek vale.   Plenty of parking in a big lot across the road from the main entrance.

Returned today for lunch after an absence of almost a year.  There are so many Mexican or Guatemalan restos in the area now, that it took me 12 months to return with trying a new place several times a month.   The space is basically as before, although the tables have been moved around and the sombreros have been taken down.  South of the Border music playing a touch too loud, and the Mexican soaps on the HDTV muted, leaving a lot of facial expression without voices.   My Torta Carnitas (Grilled Pork Sandwich) was stuffed with shredded pork, lettuce, tomato, queso fresca and mayo.  The Roll was for this "small" sandy was larger than a typical Kaiser, with smooth skin and soft, fresh textured body.  It held together well, although it required considerable squeezing to compress it sufficiently to fit in mi boca grande.  I also saw a fruit drink at another table that looked very tempting.  I inquired about it and discovered that they make fresh fruit smoothies and shakes for a few bucks.  I got the strawberry shake and it was cool smooth sweet berry addicting succulence.   I skipped dinner tonight because this meal was so satisfying.   So good to be back.  Turns out the first place visited when I arrived in Hamilton was perhaps the best.

Santorini is one of the most beautiful Greek islands in the Agean Sea. Shaped like a crescent, it is the geologic remains of an extinct volcano, creating a large harbor where the central vents were before collapsing beneath the sea. Houses are all whitewashed in the towns that cling to the cliffs above the sunken caldera. These days it is best known for its blue domed churches, and excellent cuisine.   So, naming a gyro house after Santorini makes sense, as it suggests a rugged land with equally tough people capable of great artistry in the kitchen. This new small Greek place is well appointed to feel like you are sitting in a café in Kamari or Oia, the two main villages there. They have a limited menu, but their focus is on the traditional fare - gyros (the derivation of Heros), or sandwiches made with hot pita stuffed with well spiced meat, or veggies, i.e., falafel.   The shop has three vertical roasters for pork, lamb and chicken. A large electric shaver is used to slice off the meat from the central spit, before being loaded into the pita with tahini sauce, yogurt, onion, tomato, fries and paprika. The whole pita is then rolled snuggly around these contents, and wrapped in paper and again in aluminum foil, so it is served like a cornucopia on a plate.   The result - a delicious sandwich, requiring help from a fork to consume, because it is so filled to overflowing that each bite has some of it falling out onto the plate. Not that I'm complaining.   The gyro with a bottle of water was about $10 plus tax. The lamb is another buck or so.   Very worth a stop if you like Greek street food in an attractive setting overlooking Santorini Bay.

If you don't mind paying $23 for a four pack of local suds, Newtown Brewery is a worthwhile destination for the yeast heads in the crowd. The facility is very attractive with plenty of wood and stone, and the beer is excellent for the most part.   We stopped in last weekend and the room was hopping. Tables full of folks escaping Covid captivity. But, we weren't ready for a space packed with over a hundred people without masks, nor social separation, so we bought our "I lost My Marbles" Belgian Tripel four can and headed home. Just didn't feel safe (and thus the one star deduction for lack of public awareness by management).  Under better circumstances, Newtown Brewing would be a big hit in these parts, and in fact, it appears it already is.   The beer was quite strong at 11% alcohol content, but the taste was great, and the color a robust rusty slurry. Liked it a lot. I'm no expert, but these guys seem to have the right recipes.   They do have a food truck in the parking lot most weekends, and we were fortunate to approach the window of Stuff'd Bunns and grab two sliders to partake with the ale at home. They were great and a perfect partner to the cold fermentation. More on them in a separate review coming soon to these Yelp pages.   I hate to have to take out a loan to support my occasional beer addiction, but aside from that, and the insensitivity to the CDC guidelines, Newtown Brewery really enhances the neighborhood. Just hope no one gets exposed to the virus. That is a price far to high to pay for a momentary pleasure.

Bowman's Hill Tower sits in Washington Crossing Historic Park at a high point along the Delaware River where a most important part of the American Revolution was played out.  Construction was part of the Civilian Conservation Corp that put Americans to work during the Depression, and was completed in 1931.   The view from the deck 320 feet above river level is awesome.  Especially on a clear fall day, it is possible to see more than 12 miles up and down river, as far as Trenton to the south. The flowing river and changing foliage make for a strong memory. Certainly, Washington would have appreciated having such a tower to use to observe British activities approaching this location.     But, it was not just patriots occupying these fields after the Continental Army was defeated by the British in New York, and Washington beat a hasty retreat through New Jersey into Bucks County to save his remaining troops.  Not everyone believed in the cause, and many of the locals actually supported England and did its bidding, including spying and behind the lines mayhem.  The infamous Moses Doan was in this vicinity as the plan for the Christmas raid on Trenton was put into operation.  He is believed to have crossed the Delaware just ahead of his hunters, and rode to Trenton to warn the Hessians of the coming attack.  But, for the fact that the German commander Rahl did not bother to listen to Doan, we might still be speaking with British accents.   So, Bowman's Tower is worth a visit, and while you are at it, spend a few hours searching the old homes and cemeteries in the Park.  From New Hope to Morrisville there is plenty of history to be seen.    The ride along Rt. 32 is worth the price of admission alone.

I was last here when it was known as the Old Neshaminy Tavern about a year ago. Since then it has adopted the "Brewery" tag, and taken advantage of the Pennsylvania law that allows local breweries to manufacture their own suds, and sell the products of other Pennsylvania breweries (only) with special dispensation in taxing and licensing. Smart move, as the name is attractive, the kitchen remains solid, and they now have many beers, ales, IPAs, and other interesting fermentations for your drinking pleasure.   There is a large chalk board on one wall with a listing by number of what is available. Those numbers correlate to taps behind the bar with numbers above each. Call out what you want by name or number, and the gracious bartender will pour it for you. About half come from their own stainless vats, while the remainder are what management thinks is noteworthy from around the Commonwealth. Of course, if you want a national brand, some of those are available in bottles or other taps. I chose the Neshaminy Creek Churchville Lager, a well made semi-dark pilsner from right down the road in Penndel. Loved its dark amber color, and the corresponding flavors of black coffee and chocolate.   I also ordered their Trenton Pie and side of Brussel Sprouts. They were both very good. The pizza was true to its name, with thin crust, Marazano tomato chunks on top and mozzarella underneath. The Brussels were plentiful, and would have been better with a tossing of vinaigrette in addition to the bacon pieces to give them more bite. Took most of both home after sampling some at the bar as I enjoyed my lager.   Langhorne isn't known for its local attractions, but it does have a few interesting points to visit. Langhorne Brewing Company adds to that list of worthwhile destinations in this part of Bucks County.

Be Well Bakery & Cafe does it right.  Not only is the house cozy and spacious, the java very good and the bakery products excellent, but it is all wrapped into a business philosophy that promotes community, creativity, healthy living and complete genuineness.   All very noble, right? But, let's get back to their house goodies for a second. I was tempted by their lemon tart in the display case. I love lemon bars, so I figured, why not? It was awesome! Creamy tart/sweet lemon filling, thin, flakey crust, plump, cool blueberries sitting on top. An orgy in my mouth.   There are a lot of good bakeries and coffee houses these days; not as many in combination. Be Well is certainly one of the best of the genre in the region.   All this in a beautiful part of Montgomery County, just down the road from Bryn Athyn Cathedral and Historic District. Worthwhile drive with Be Well as the final destination.

I like what they've done with this place at the bottom of High Street, Mt. Holly, NJ.   What was a mom and pop dive restaurant for decades has been renovated into a clean, utiliitarian modern kitchen with small counter near the back and fairly large dining room upfront. It is the third B-Uno in the area, focusing on American cuisine with a overlay of Mexican flair. They have breakfast and lunch hours, except for Friday through Sunday when they are open until 9 for dinner. I stopped in after court this week to check them out for a morning bite and mugga joltin' joe.   Their menu has a lot of "Build Your Own" dishes from omelets to pancakes, meat, tater tots and quesadillas. That approach gets pricey and belly stuffed quickly, so I opted for an order of French Toast neat - with just melted butter and syrup. I drank their java and read the news while waiting for delivery to my table.  It was pretty good. Thick cut slices, well caramelized with decent mix of sugar and cinnamon in the eggs. The only shortcoming was that the egg hadn't penetrated past the outer layer of the bread, and as a result the thickness of the loaf became a detriment, making for a semi dry morning meal that required a copious pour from the syrup squeezem to keep it lubricated for consumption.    Service was fine. No problems with accessibility as far as I could see, although I didn't visit the bathrooms.   Still, I liked the joint and recognized its possibilities. It is a nice addition to downtown Mt. Holly and will certainly contribute to local commerce. It just need to soak the bread a bit more.

The Perk has successfully turned their parking lot into an outdoor dining garden complete with beautiful Japanese bonsai specimens from Bucks Bonsai landscapers. With large umbrellas and heating towers, it is a pleasant place to have a late lunch on a chill Saturday afternoon with the sun casting it's golden hue.  This is a great place to enjoy the Borough of Perkasie, a tight community in northwest Bucks.   I sat with the sun at my back and ordered a Blue Moon draft, French Onion Soup and Sauteed Pierogi from their appetizer menu. I also asked for takeout of Crab Cake and Chicken Parm sandwiches for my working family.   The beer was served in a soft plastic glass with orange slice split over the rim. Cool and refreshing. The beef broth and translucent onions were very good once I pierced the thick layer of melted provolone that sealed the steaming contents of the of the potage d'oignon gratinee. Liked it alot. The pierogi arrived in a styro container. There were four homemade potato pasta pockets that had been sauteed in butter and thin sliced browned onions. These were excellent, and I would have loved if there were one or two more in the box. Still, it was an appetizer, not an entree, so I understood they were designed more as a delicious tease than main course.   Last night, my wife and stepson came home to the crab cake and chicken parm. After a short reheat I sampled both and found them to be superior sandwiches. The crab cake was fresh, sweet and housed in a brioche roll. The parmigiana was a thick chicken breast, well breaded, with a decent red gravy and melted cheese. Very good. Both came with house deep fried potato chips. Nicely done.   The Perk is an anchor establishment in Perkasie, and well worth the travel from home to stop in now and then. If we lived closer, I would no doubt be a regular.

Simply Delicious by Tina is the star of the culinary show on this stretch of York Road, Jamison, PA. Plenty of parking alongside the stand alone building, with a long ramp up to the main door, you walk into a small deli/cashier area. There you can scan some of the home cooked meals offered by Proprietress Tina and her crew, as well as a sampling of her tasty baked goods.   The dining room is to the left, and bathed in bright sunlight on this Saturday morn. Only one table was occupied by a grandfather/granddaughter team, so I gamboled to the other side near the bar for my seat. Orders are taken at the register, so I returned there after perusing the two sided laminate menu.   Lots of healthy choices, and I selected the Hungry Person Breakfast Sandwich (3 eggs, 3 small homemade sausages, American cheese, tomato, greens on toasted thick sliced brioche). It was so large upon delivery to me that I asked that it be cut in half so I would have a chance to pick it up and take a bite without it falling apart in my hands.   Well, it sort of fell to pieces under pressure from the kitchen knife anyway, but it still looked great when it came back to me. It still wasn't possible to secure it by hand with all the slippery ingredients, so I went after it with knife and fork. I combined different elements on the tines of my fork and jammed each into my mouth, my jaws as wide open as possible.   It was totally worth the effort.  The parts were as good as the whole.   I took home a square of Tina's Key Lime Strawberry bar for later enjoyment. Just devoured that four hours later. Loved it! From moist graham cracker crust through tart creamy lime/cheese body, and hint of sweet strawberry, it was a pleasure all the way down. Hot coffee chaser to finish my excellent weekend early day repast.

As federal agencies go, USCIS sets the standard for how to treat people right.   The new facility on North 41st Street in West Philly is a vast improvement over Callowhill Avenue. Not only is the space well renovated for more comfort during the inevitable security screening and wait for your appointment, but the guards and staff are trained to treat people with respect and assistance. They patiently repeat instructions and never lose their cool.   The meetings are conducted across a counter and thick glass wall, but the interaction remains low key and humane. They intend to answer questions fully, and will make formal inquiry when they do not have a reasonable answer on their computer screen. Don't forget that most visa files are not in Philadelphia, and they cannot see everything in them.  Street parking, metered or not, is usually available if you are driving, and the subway is not far away. Too, this part of town, just beyond the universities and at the edge of Powelton Village, offers many tasty distractions before or after conducting your business.

Sulimay's Restaurant down on lower Girard Avenue, Philadelphia, is another of the many neighborhood corner luncheonettes that help define the incredible communities they help anchor. Fishtown has plenty of them, full of local charm and generally excellent grub. We have breakfasted at many of them and looked forward to checking out Sulimay's.   Walking in, the space was larger/deeper than expected, with nice counter up front and substantial dining room with booths and tables back to the kitchen and restrooms. It was clean and bright with interesting antiques and curios hanging on the walls. We were escorted to the last booth in back where the crash and din of the busy kitchen was easily and entertainingly heard. Our server promptly brought a carafe of coffee and side of milk for me, more than enough for the entire meal.   I was curious about the PBC (Philadelphia Brewing Company) Kinsinger corned beef hash, which came with 2 eggs, hash browns and toast. What effect did beer have on it? Soon found out. DT had a simple scrambled eggs, house made sausage, hash browns and toast.   The beer added a touch of savory to the well ground corned beef hash, while the over easy eggs mixed well to moisten the somewhat dry hash. Unfortunately, the potatoes on both plates were on the grill too long and were blackened carbon, although hidden from view by placing it face down at the bottom of the food pile. It was obvious that the cook saw it, as he had to fold them over to show only the unburned side. First bite told the bitter truth. The rest was left uneaten. The sausage was also grilled to excess and not enjoyable to eat.   We considered returning everything for a second try, but didn't see our server and given how busy it was, and our schedule, we decided to eat what we could and move on for the rest of our day.   Had there been more quality control and perhaps more caring in what was exiting the kitchen these plates would not have gone out the door. They did, and gave us a poor first impression. Too bad, because Sulimay's has alot going for it otherwise.

This Puerto Rican bakery is a tiny shop on Brownsville Road, Trevose, PA. Primarily takeout, it has a few tables for those of us who prefer to sit, sip and eat while the iron is hot. The business opens at 8:00 AM, not the 10:00 reflected on its Yelp page. As we were there for breakfast, the earlier time is important to know.   We ordered two egg platter breakfasts. Both had two fried eggs (ordered over easy, but delivered sunnyside up), five slices of small loaf toasted sweet bread, and bacon/sausage.  In addition, we had excellent coffee and shared a marble donut made for us after ordering. Service was friendly, informative and nicely paced.   Turned out that the egg/meat/toast part of the meal was pretty ordinary, with the only remarkable piece the pleasant taste of the bread. Much more interesting and rewarding was the strong java brewed through an expresso machine, and the donut.  Expresso coffee was used, which made for a rich, aromatic joe. The donut was still warm from the oven and covered in a thick icing of vanilla and chocolate. Delicious, but not too sweet. A super pleasant chew.   I would return to enjoy more baked goods and coffee, and likely pass on the breakfast offerings. Lo Le Lai has the feel of a café, and would be a great one just based on the quality of its flour products.    Definitely, a treasure to explore.

There are things to like about Brick House Tavern & Tap, and a few other things that detract from the overall experience.   The space is generally very nice, with an open floorplan, and brick wall along the back of the house. There are booths, high top large tables, sofas, and a bar - each offering a different comfort level. I was there as a solitary traveler, and chose to sit at the bar. This may have been a poor choice, as the design leaves a lot to be desired.   Although square with barstools along each side, lines of sight are obstructed on each side by the beer tap hardware that extends down from the ceiling and spreads out it large apparatus just above eye level so it is impossible to see the HDTVs behind the bar. Also, after a pour (I had a Summer Shandy), the individual tap continues to drip onto the metal splash guard above the drain, spraying droplets of beer in all directions - especially toward me, the customer. While it didn't make me wet, it did reach the wooden bar top, making it damp and causing damage to the finish. There must be a better, cleaner, more sanitary way to deal with drippy taps.   The bar ladies were clearly selected for their fit in jeans, more than their tending skills. While I am not complaining about the view, the dropped and broken glasses, cut fingers, and spillage was not the most fun to observe. And, it happened twice during my hour there.   The Brick House Cheeseburger seemed a safe bet.  It looked good on arrival. Yet, the medium grill requested was much closer to well done. The fries were fine. It was an average burger, at best.   The overall sense of this joint is that management does not run a tight ship, and should spend more time training staff to be sure the customer is the center of attention, rather than the interaction between the workers. The menu is pricy for this level of roadhouse experience, and the quality of the menu and service should reflect that. Otherwise, what you get is a dive bar trying to pass itself off as elite.

Round sugar cakes.  Sweeter than they should be, but fresh baked white cake base is tender and moist at least for a few hours. Many choices for dipped toppings in pretty colors, but all taste more or less the same. Really a confectionery more than a bakery.   To be avoided if sugar is a health issue for you. Best suited for kids whining for a candy fix, and other folks cheating on their diets.   Their Covid protocol should be improved a bit, because they allow you to come in to order and then wait outside for a staff person to bring your order out to you in 10 or more minutes. In hot or cold weather it gets a bit uncomfortable. Perhaps, a few folding chairs set up in the shade would alleviate the problem;  outdoor umbrellas, if necessary.   If you are into Ducks, don't forget your insulin.

This official arboretum of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and an extension of the University, began as the summer residence of John and Lydia Morris, the children of I. P. Morris, a wealthy Quaker who made his riches in the iron business. It was originally called Compton, a mansion built on the promontory of the 92 areas above Wissahiken Creek.   The soil was poor when they arrived, but over the years, they improved it until it supported the beautiful landscaping and exemplar botanicals found today. Sadly, the mansion was torn down about 100 years ago upon the death of Lydia, and it was bequeathed to the University in 1932. It is now an integral part of its sustainability efforts for the 21st Century.   There are 12,000 labeled specimens in the preserve, as well as a Fernery (currently closed due to Covid), Rose Garden, and Horticultural Center within the expanded 167 acres. The walkabout for healthy outdoor folks is about 2 hours, although it can take considerably longer with a slow pace and lots of bench sitting to enjoy the surroundings. The Visitor's Center is closed temporarily, but restrooms are well maintained beneath the building.   There are courses available throughout the year for all ages and skill levels. It is also a great place for a wedding or other occasion.   Wear decent walking shoes as there are several miles of trails and significant elevation change from the top near the parking lot, down to the creek and back again. Water for a hot summer day and a hat are also recommended.

This Rancocas Woods section of Mount Laurel, NJ, has a out of Jersey feel to it.  Semi-pine barrens, small cabin stores along every rural byway, and an almost eerie 19th Century feel.  So, when I found myself on these back roads looking for a way back to the present, and came across an old roadside stand with a small parking area and a sign that said, "coffee and breakfast," I was curious enough to stop and check it out.    Inside I found a 1950's shop, with a couple of tables up front, and a counter and grill in the far corner.  There was a woman in back putting together a large lunch order, and a younger guy working the hotspot.  He turned, smiled, and asked how he could be of assistance.  He recommended a breakfast sandwich by reputation.  I was down with that, and ordered a sausage, egg & cheese on Kaiser roll, with coffee, for immediate consumption.  I grabbed a take out menu and a seat at the table closest to the door.  Couldn't find them on Yelp, and decided to put them into the system.  He didn't mind.    Maybe it was all the surrounding country that played with my head, or just the quality of the air inside this old wooden structure, but there was a definite drift pulling me backward in time.  Kind of pleasant, and not strong enough to stop me from returning to today.  When the sandwich arrived on a green plastic plate covered in sandwich paper, I had been looking out the window at an old pickup parked under BJ's rusted and distended sign creaking in the breeze.     The aroma brought me out of reveries, and back to the quiet hunger in my pit.  It looked good; all steamy and melty.  Single sausage patty, two slices, and a nice egg scramble.  Tasted good, too., although their bakery provider could make crustier rolls. This one was soft and had the taste of white bread in roll form. The Joe was hot medium roast.  Only one size for coffee.  Fill it up as much as I liked, according to the chef/manager.  So, I did, about half way.   Not sure I will find myself in this neighborhood again, because I'm not exactly sure how I got there.  But, if I am, I will certainly stop in for one of their burgers or cheesesteaks, for which they won an award according to www.cheesesteaks.com.   Didn't realize they had internet back then.

Well, maybe that's just marketing.   Teddy says that the first ingredient in their recipe for success is quality.
