If that's the case, then corn syrup is really good for you, because that's the first ingredient in the ersatz breakfast syrup served with pancakes and french toast. We all know that the opposite is true, and that such sweeteners should be eliminated from your diet as much as possible. The same is true for butter. Monosaturated fats should be kept to a minimum, yet Teddy served a paper cup with a soft yellow substance in it, rather than real pats of individually wrapped butter.   Yes. I confess I ate my breakfast, although with less spread and sweet liquids, because I didn't want to be that guy, but decided before my first bite that Teddy would be a one time thing.   I ordered a short stack when told the french toast was thick. Turned out that it really wasn't so thick, but I didn't mind putting less of the bad stuff in my body. It doesn't pay to describe the taste and texture of the meal, because it doesn't matter - it was based on artificial ingredients anyway.   The coffee was okay, and I was given real milk when I requested it. So, there's that. It also may explain why the roadhouse was almost empty when I walked in.

Pho Le Lai is a Vietnamese restaurant located on St. Vincent Street in the Mayfair neighborhood of Northeast Philadelphia. It is found in the same building as 1st Asian Supermarket, making it convenient to eat and shop for our Southeast Asian grocery needs. Both are closer to our Bucks County home, saving time compared to either Chinatown (traffic & parking) or Washington Avenue (traffic).   I was the sole customer when I walked in around 3 P.M. The cordial manager got up from reading the newspaper and seated me at the table next to her and handed me their multi page menu. Another friendly woman came out of the kitchen with a pitcher of cold water, to answer questions and take my order. That was simple - Pho Tai and Roast Pork Banh Mi (This is a pho house, after all.)   Ten minutes later she was back with the "Small" bowl of steaming beef noodle soup requested, and a side plate of exceptionally fresh standard accoutrement (sprouts, sliced jalapeno, Thai basil sprigs and lime wedge). I took a pair of new wood chopsticks and flat bottomed spoon from the table holder and doctored the pho to my taste, paying attention to pull apart the nest of noodles lying beneath the surface of the dark broth (Northern Vietnamese style).   The flavor profile displayed some depth and had been simmering in a large pot for a long time. It wasn't quite as rich as Pho 75 or Pho Ha, but it was very good and didn't require help from the Sriracha bottle rocket on the table. It was plenty spicy with the addition of the jalapeno.   I was content to slurp away and patiently lift noodles out of the caldron and fold them onto the spoon before shoveling them into my mouth.   The Banh Mi arrived minutes later. It was a full sized sandwich on decent French baguette, cut in half. Like the pho, it was larger than anticipated, especially for $6!  It was loaded with dark roast pork, daikon radish, carrot, aioli and cilantro. I added a long squirt of Hoisin to bring up the savoriness of that combo, and took a bite. From crusty roll through crisp daikon and ultimately tender pork, it was delicious and captivating. It was a complete oral and tactile experience. One of the best sammys I've enjoyed since Ocean Grove, California, the capital of Vietnamese America.   Along with China Gourmet, the excellent dim sum emporium also in that building, the presence of Pho Le Lai make St. Vincent Street a strong destination for your Asian taste buds and culinary needs.

We just enjoyed a very satisfying Good Friday breakfast at Jake's in Newtown. Plenty to eat, tasty and quite fairly priced.   It seems time to revisit the old review and adjust the ranking to 4 stars. I've eaten here often enough to become a fan.

LUNCH REVIEW -   Cross Culture is a new Indian restaurant in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center where International Noodles used to be. I was there recently for lunch.   It was renovated beautifully with new furniture and large fabric wall hangings that remind of Indian rugs. I was the sole customer when I arrived about 1:45 p.m. I was led to a table along a wall by the man working the floor. He handed me a menu and brought me a glass of water when I declined the bottle of Pellegrino sitting there. He promptly removed it. The afternoon menu offered quite a bit from thali combo metal containers/trays, to individual dishes, all of which came with fresh tandoori baked naan and bowl of basmati rice.   Chicken Cashmere was my choice. It is a milk based curry dish, fairly mild, with almonds and raisins adding  a touch of sweetness. It was excellent. The four quartered naan was hot with oil sheen and the perfect scoop for carrying the extra sauce from bowl to mouth. It was thin and crisp, and baked expertly. The very long grain basmati was a great bed to lay the creamy chicken upon.   Yes. I really enjoyed my Indian lunch at Cross Culture. Gotta hope that they have a lot more business for dinner, because they certainly deserve to attract a wide audience given the quality of their kitchen.

White Elephant Thai Restaurant has served Huntington Valley, PA, for many years from it's location in a commercial center strip. Their menu is elaborate with separate lunch listings between 11:30 and 2:00. I was there to partake of midday meal and was greeted warmly by the gentleman who served me.   The room is attractively appointed with elephant totems and warm curry tangerine colors. I was seated at a table behind the jungle growth of tropical plants separating the waiting/seating areas. On a long term addictive run with Thai broad noodles and elaborate sauces, I ordered their $10.95 lunch of Coconut Soup, Fried Thai Dumplings and Drunken Noodles with Chicken, 'Thai spicy.'   The house began to fill as the hour approached 12, and more help appeared from the back. The soup arrived first in small cup. The lovely aroma of coconut smiled seductively. It was excellent, with a few slices of tender chicken, carrot, onion. It was semi sweet and steaming hot. Suspicious beginning.   The dumplings were round with ground pork and spicy dipping sauce. They were plump and quite tasty as well. Two for two!   Last came the noodles, and unfortunately, the letdown. Plentiful on the large plate, they appeared to have been sitting out too long after wokking, because the top was dry while the bottom of the dish showed sauce. Too, the chicken slices were extremely dry and dessicated. Likely yesterday's bird, reanimated. Disappointing, to say the least. Given that the chicken in the soup was right, the comparison was inevitable and suggested lack of concern.  A budding five star experience descended to three and a customer lost.   Sometimes the last impression is more powerful than the first.

This is just a great place to have a terrific burger that satisfies your Burger Lust for at least a few days.  With the evolution of Burger Culture throughout the planet, it is only a matter of time that the first wave of fast food meat patty institutions, like Mikey D's, BK, and Wendy's either adapt to the second wave epitomized by 5 Guys, Red Robin, Cheeburger, Jake's Wayburger, etc., by upgrading both the menu and the facilities, or go the way of the Doo Doo Bird, and face extinction.    This new breed of puck slingers is simply too good not to supplant their predecessors. Once the new Burger Meisters figure out how to drop their price points into the range of the old joints, their fate will be sealed, and as with the dinosaurs, they will become a distant memory, a story grandparents tell their grand kids about when they were young and went to a place with golden arches to get their burger needs met. As with all such tall tales, the kids won't believe anyone ever had to settle for something so ordinary.   Luckily, we don't have to.  The future is here and hiding is a grease-streaked brown paper bag.  Go get it!

General Deck, Bar & Grill on Street Road, Southampton, PA, is a deceptively attractive sports bar with decent kitchen and large outdoor rear deck for nicer weather. The barroom in front contains a rectangular bar, recently refurbished along with the rest of the house, with TVs everywhere you look. Behind the bar are two smallish dining rooms, redone to look rustic with stone and rough hewn wood. The deck comes last, and is approachable directly from the parking lot.   I stopped in to catch the 76ers game against the Lakers, and was lucky enough to watch the locals demolish the LeBrons by 23 points! The menu was sitting on the bar, and I heard their California Burger calling my name. Got it finished medium, with a side order of Brussel Sprouts fit onto the large plate right next door. Service was friendly, and young enough to need to show their IDs.   The burger was very good - done as requested, with fresh avo, lettuce, sliced sweet red onion, tomato and ranch dressing, on an above average bun that held together to the very end despite significant drippage from the puck and its playmates. The Brussels were excellently soft and savory with bacon, feta and a tart balsamic glaze overcoat.    NOTE: The only recognizable defect in the entire show was the steep staircase to the second floor restrooms, which were inaccessible to anyone with a disability. I know that rehabilitated old buildings present challenges to compliance with ADA requirements, but given the amount of work done on the structure, and the addition of the large deck, a unisex handicap outfitted restroom should have been designed into the first floor, and a ramp installed for wheelchairs and walkers for entry into The General.

Mallu Cafe on Verree just off Bustleton in far Northeast Philly is really a take out Indian joint, with a few tables for those who don't mind the run down decor or aren't aware of the business model employed (like me). Their website was interesting, and showed nice photos of many of their Kerala dishes. Perhaps, I should have been deterred by the sketchy dudes hanging by the front door (even more of them when we left), but they smiled when we approached and invited us in.   Strange, but no big deal.  We ordered Chicken 65 (spicy chili fried), Avial (mixed veggie coconut curry) and Appam (rice flour fry bread). They arrived in take out containers with plastic forks (?!). The chicken had been deep fried to a very dark brown and delivered without any sauce. Obviously, overcooked by someone who didn't know their own recipe, or hadn't looked at their website, as I had. I returned it to the kitchen. I wanted it done the right way, but that wasn't offered. Rather, they wanted to give us Kerala Chicken Curry.   Okay. Whatever.  While we waited we sampled the veggie dish. It was cool on top and hot at the base. Microwaved, and no one bothered to see if it was fully recooked. Nope. Further, it didn't look like the pics on the website, either. Rather than having distinct veggies, it was all mashed together. Didn't change the decent taste, but the presentation was lacking.   When the replacement curry arrived we quickly saw that it was bone in small pieces. Hard to deal with only a plastic fork. The flavor was fine, but with the morsels to contend with it was not worth the effort. It was hard to understand why they would give us the bones, when boneless was only a buck more. Besides, they never asked which we would prefer. No. My sense was they were annoyed about their earlier mistake with the 65, knew they could not charge us for that, and decided to throw some shade at us by literally boning us.   We surrendered, asked for the check, and definitely did not want to take anything home.   When we left there were more dudes just hanging around outside. Maybe they were waiting for us to leave so they could start their pinochle game.   Mallu Cafe just didn't seem to be a restaurant anymore. There are plenty of good Indian houses in this part of the city. This place just isn't one of them.   1 Star - Avoid

Ray Nudy is a second generation restauranteur whose 12 comfortable breakfast/lunch locations are perfect for satisfying meals. His Nudy's Cafes have been open and expanding in southeastern PA since 1979. Almost embarrassed to admit that yesterday was my first visit to any of them. I stopped in their Conshohocken Lafayette Street kitchen for a late breakfast.   They operate in a large high ceiling room with half wall divided spaces for tables, and booths against one outer wall, if that is your preference. The menu has most of the usual suspects, with particular attention to several varieties of french toast. That's where I was heading, and went with their traditional three slice offering, with maple syrup upgrade and fresh brewed coffee.   It was excellent. It arrived with plenty of caramelization for crisp edges, and a delicious mix of egg, sugar and vanilla extract that enhanced the flavor and texture, and a dusting of powdered sugar/cinnamon. A mini bottle of pure light amber maple syrup accompanied the large white ceramic plate. After spreading the melting butter, followed by the pouring of rich brown syrup, it was ready for sampling.  It was the best french toast I have had in a long time.   Service was also above expectations. Friendly, interactive and professional, with prompt coffee refills and timely bussing.   Too bad Nudy's isn't in Bucks County yet, because all locations are worth exploring. Given the quality of their product, it shouldn't be long before they secure kitchens closer to home.

Maido! has seen better days.  The "Marketplace of Japan," was our destination after an hour drive from Bucks. We were looking for quality Japanese noodles, ceramic bowls and vinegar unavailable at the Asian supermarket where we normally shop. To our surprise and disappointment there was little of anything on the shelves, and it looked like their inventory had not been replenished in weeks or longer. Same was true of fresh produce, where most bins were bare. What was going on here?!  They literally had nothing we came for. So, we decided to make lemonade from this sour experience, and went over to their restaurant operation in the same space and ordered a few things at the cashier before sitting on stools at a high eating counter facing onto Lancaster Avenue. The Karaage (fried chicken) and Okonomiyaki (veggie omelet) were prepared in their open kitchen and I picked them up when the buzzer alerted me everything was ready.   The chicken was deep fried from frozen plastic bag. It was not crisp, nor crunchy, but quite oily. The taste of the Karaage powder was there, but the combo of white and dark pieces left much to be desired. They need to improve the quality of those prefab chicken tenders. The Okonomiyaki was better with cabbage, scallion, pickled ginger, yam, bonito and a decent sauce, but the veggie option had little taste despite the ingredients. We finished about half and took the rest home. Its fate has not been determined. At $28+ with two tea bags and hot water, we expected better.   Not sure what the future holds for Maido!, but its continued presence in Ardmore does not appear assured.

My first time visiting HG Bucks Bagels in Warminster, PA. It was recently remodeled, and it looks quite nice and clean, with room for both a bagel and pizza operations. When it comes to dual production, you have to hope that they maintain adequate separation of ingredients and recipes, so the pizza doesn't start tasting like bagel, nor the bagel too much like tomato pie, particularly in the crust and toppings departments.   Luckily, that doesn't seem to be an issue, as, while I only tried an onion bagel (w Veggie Spread), it did not remind me of a slice O' pie.   Yet, perhaps there was some leakage in style. I found my bagel to be large, freshly baked and loaded with hard toasted onion bits, but the shell lacking in crispness to differentiate it from the inner bread. I much prefer a harder skin from boiling with lye for about 40 seconds. When that doesn't happen, the outer coat is more like ordinary loaf bread, and not the tougher exterior that epitomizes the true rounder. So, while I liked the chomp, it would have been so much better if it had required a stronger, sharper bite from my incisors.   It wasn't a bad bagel, but done right, it could have been a real contender.   3.5 STARS.

Copa on South Street was my mainstay for several years after tai chi classes at The Painted Bride.  Those days are only for reminiscing now, but the taste and zest of Copabanana remains a trigger to my salivary glands. I have returned on occasion, and still loved the dirty ambiance, lusty margaritas, incredible Copaburgers (extra jalapenos, please), and the earthshaking Spanish flies...er...fries.  My son, now 12, has gone with me, so another generation is preparing to take its place where Friday night legends are made (and oft forgotten by Saturday morning).   What others Yelpers say about the conditions in the joint is true, but the best Tex-Mex food is always found in the dingiest hole-in-the-wall places.  Am I right? At least you know there are no cleaning agent molecules in the air to settle on your food.  These days I try to stop in before or after a 76'er game.  Copa still possesses that "in your face" attitude that I have loved, lo these many years. May it always be so. Amen!

After an afternoon of legalized public inebriation at the Winetoberfest, I needed a cup of java to bring me back to Earth before returning to my car for the winding journey home.  After striking out at two cafes that seemed disenchanted with the day's events and were keeping a very low profile, someone suggested we check out Mal's.    It was open and almost empty, but the counter looked inviting.  We sat on a couple of old spinners and ordered the Joe large and hot.  That is what we got. Fresh and it a supersized styro take away cup.  It was what just what the doctor ordered. Helped straighten me out.  The restroom was also a big help after the amount of liquids consumed in a short time.    We sat where we could see into the kitchen and watched as a Cheesesteak was prepared and sent out.  Looked okay, but I was not tempted.    For being my personal oasis yesterday early evening, Mal's gets my undying appreciation, and 3 Stars.  The staff gets 4 because they definitely came through for me.

With the advent of coffee houses on every block around this piece of the Delaware Valley, there are now plenty of very good java outlets where you can order locally roasted bean drinks, settle in, and have a pleasant caffeinated interlude. Rojo Roasters is one of the early movers, and found a great old industrial site on far North Union Street in Lambertville, NJ, to set up shop. The place is cozy with strong Joe, laid back jazzy sound, and a reputation for well respected coffees. Half the shop is given to java mavens, and the other to making the beans morph from green to dark brown. The aroma can be overpowering. The regular customers seem well entrenched.  Yet, this inherent strength can also be a hidden weakness. A bit of sampling from the nearby competition leads to the realization that Rojo is strong in some areas, but weak in others. Because they are limited to their sources, equipment and process, there is a sameness to their products. When in the mood for powerful coffee, it is top of the mountain. All their beans and drinks are on the harsh side and lack subtlety. Reminds of Starbucks, and that is not necessarily a good thing.   The other houses offer Rojo and other local, regional and national companies. It allows them to select the best of breed from across a broad spectrum of styles and technical processes. Thus, when you want something milder, or perhaps, nuttier or fruitier, you can get it alongside the stronger Rojo label.   Yet, Rojo does what it does very well, and has a large following. Too, their bakery goods are first class. Loved the blueberry lemon pound cake this morning. Moist, dense, dark blue delicious.   We are in a buyers' coffee world these days. It pays to sip around and discover what you like most on any day of the week. Chances are you will find it close at hand.

On the second visit I opted to eat breakfast in house, and found it enjoyable with the smell of the baking bagels in the air, and the bucolic ambiance.  The Onion Bagel was as the first one - not quite crunchy enough.  Still, it was fresh and tasty, and at a great price of under $4. for the bagel and decent Jamaican Blue Mountain style java.    Easy to become a fan of this comfy chill.

Donuts Plus (exactly what the "Plus" is, is a secret), in the 4300 block of Chestnut Street, West Philly, sits in a rather inappropriately placed strip center in the middle of a heavy urbanscape. To look at it passing by you wouldn't think that this tiny shop cold possibly compete with the better known fry-dough emporiums around town.  But, the truth is that although it doesn't "cock-a-doodle-doo," its own rooster, it has the magic recipe for excellently addictive donuts.  We stopped four people along the way to ask directions, because the walking GPS seemed confused. Everyone thought we wanted a Dunkin, and hadn't heard of this joint, until we encountered a security guard who knew exactly where we were looking to go, and provided solid directions.  The space was tiny upfront where you place your order through heavy plexiglass and small defensive windows, but the folks behind the barrier possessed winning smiles, and the assurance of knowing they were very good at what they do.    We walked in after a meeting at USCIS nearby, looking for some sweet cheer and caffeine.  The cast of characters hanging around inside was loud and maybe even slightly bizarre, but they stepped away from the window and allowed us to do our business.  We ordered an apple fritter, a couple of old fashioned honey dipped donuts and two javas. A small handwritten sign said, "Donuts $.95 each." We paid cash and returned outside to enjoy the beautiful spring day in February, and stroll back to the car a few blocks away.  The dough boys were simple and delectable. Firm outside. Soft inside. Sweet layer of skin. These were yeasties, not the cake d-nuts found elsewhere.  The fritter was huge, but too oily for complete enjoyment.  The other two were simply a pleasure. The coffee was a mild brew, and easy going down.  Now that I know how close Donuts Plus is to USCIS, it will be a regular stop before or after immigration proceedings.

Seems this place is hard to find if you are not from the area. Here is the secret. Follow the signs to the Hampton Inn, and make a left just before you reach the front entrance. The DD is across the parking fields from the hotel.   There are two Dunkins within a couple of miles of each other. There is one on Swamp Road in Newtown, and this one just off 95 in Lower Makefield.  I prefer this one because the coffee just tastes better.  How is that possible?  It all comes down to the quality of the water going in if it is not being strongly filtered before it touches bean. Two different water companies service each shop.  Newtown's water is hard and does not play well with coffee.  The Lower Make water is softer, and is a better companion in the brew. Thus, the taste in Newtown tends toward bitterness, while the L.Make drink is smoother going down.   The donuts are about the same for each, with perhaps a slight edge to Ntown for available variety. Sandwiches and B and R ice cream seem identical.   So, given the choice, I go to this place. Secondarily, it is also larger, and friendlier than its sibling.   Lying just over the border with Ntown, this is the place the Newtown Zealots meet to plot their next move.   Also, the best place to caffeine-up before starting a long drive north or south.

After completing my nuclear stress test this morning, I think it fair to say that the entire staff of Jefferson Cardiology is first rate/5 Star.  I arrived at 7:15 am for a 7:30 appointment, and they had me signed in, consented, and parking validated before I could sit down in the waiting room.  The tech had me prepped and IVed a few minutes later, and I was in the cardio-camera room strapped into my seat by 7:35.    The entire process went smoothly, and I had ample time to talk with the two doctors participating in the test.  They showed real interest in me as a person, and were willing to offer some insight into themselves.  I appreciated the warmth and openness.  I was told the entire test would take from 3.5 to 4 hours, but I was out on 10th Street in 3.  Not only that, but I was given a cup of coffee on the way out because I said I had not had one this morning, and a gift card to Au Bon Pain for having to wait 5 minutes before they came to get me.  How often has that happened?    While I won't know the results until I call tomorrow, I can tell you that I was very pleased today.  My continued confidence in the docs and staff here was once again validated, along with my parking stub.    BTW. Valet parking $12. for the entire time I was there, including my stroll to Au Bon Pain to exercise my gift card.

You know those infinitesimal screws that are used to put eyeglasses together? The ones the size of baby gnats?   On a few occasions one of those poppy seed screws escaped and I returned to Steve for repair and consolation.  Each time he has graciously taken the pair into his repair shop and emerged a few minutes later with everything back in working order, cleaned and readjusted.  Yesterday, when a nose cushion fell off after about 5 years of wear, he replaced both free of charge and with a smile.    I have been very happy with the Prodesign frames from Denmark, and most of all with Steve Robbins for continuing to stand behind his product.    Does it get any better than that in the optometry world?    I think not.  5 Stars!

Steven Robbins has been providing my glasses (progressives and sunglasses) for over 15 years.  He has been in business in Newtown for three decades. His current location is next to Jake's Eatery and Domino Pizza, but don't let that deter you.  The shop is first class, and he and his staff make you feel comfortable right from jump.  Most important, he has a large collection of designer frames, at reasonable prices.  His turn around time is at the longest a few days.    Take a look around by yourself, or get the relaxed guided tour from Steve.  Kuerig Coffee Maker available with snacks while your stroll around the shop.  Definitely, worth a look before or after you have exhausted the alternatives.  Steven Robbins Eyewear is a winner.

First time down in the Cambodian neighborhood along south 7th Street. A bit sketchy, but plenty of street life with cafes, food stores, fruit mongers, and a lot of action down in the park at 6th and Wolf.   I Heart Cambodia has been in operation since December last.  It is bright and cheery, if a bit noisy due to constant drone of homegrown music videos and poor acoustics.  The folks operating the joint are friendly and amenable to longer discussions about their plans (a bar) and their kitchen (broadening the menu).  As a first timer, I had more than the usual questions about ingredients and spiciness.  When it was time to order we found out there were no Summer Rolls available.  Small disappointment. But, we moved on to select Papaya Salad, Stir Fried Flat Rice Noodles with Chicken, and Prahok Ktis (the "s" is silent).  They were all okay, but nothing was exceptional.  The Papaya Salad was spiced by something that tasted like radish.  It didn't work for us, especially compared to similar dishes in Thai houses. Even allowing for cultural differences, it just wasn't a pleasant flavor.  The Stir Fried Noodles was the best dish; well prepared, but still not as good as others I have had in Philly and in Asia. The sauce for the Prahok Ktis was tasty with a mix of Pork, Coconut Milk, Lemongrass, Kaffir, Fermented Fish Sauce and Peanuts, but the slices veggies to be used as scoops were very small, making it awkward to use as intended. Everything was fresh, but perhaps measured for smaller fingers.    It became clear looking around the room that the most exciting dish was the Ginger Fried Fish.  It looked great.  Next time that is where we start.   I would also skip the Thai Iced Tea and the extra bowls of rice as unnecessary for the meal at hand.

This was my standard 2 slice lunch at a new place for me, Palermo's on Rt. 206 South in Bordentown, NJ.   The joint has been at this location for a few decades it seems, and it shows its wear and tear both inside and out.  The booth I sat in was in need of new padding to compensate for the sag in the bench.    On the other hand, service was attractive, lively and prompt. Ingrid was an excellent salesperson for the menu and seemed passionate about the Tomato Pie.  I ordered two slices well done, and Iced Tea.  When the slices arrived on their aluminum tray they were darkly brooding and steaming.  The chunky crushed tomato sauce was mildly sweet, while the cheese carried the slight overtone of salt.  The crust was thin, but not as micro as other shops, yet was definitely bending under the weight of the topside when lifted from the outer crust.  It didn't collapse and fold, but I did have to lift the point from its downward trajectory to get it into my mouth.  On the other hand, these were big slices.   This is a very good Tomato Pie, and I was glad Ingrid double checked with me between the TP and the Pizza.  She encouraged me to get a fresh small pie for optimal results, but I knew I wouldn't eat that much at lunch today.  Management has put a lot of effort into the right ingredients, and for the most part they have succeeded with a superior Trenton style Pie.    Everyone is a pizza expert, and I am, too.  While I will try the fresh out of the oven pie before a final judgment, my preliminary observations were positive, with the exception of thinking there might actually be too much cheese on these babies causing the weight and serious bending going on at lift off.   Still with really superior taste and a strong biting crunch, Palermo's is worth another look or three.  SEPTEMBER 9, 2015 - UPDATE: Returned today and sampled an Italian Sweet Sausage Sandwich with Sautéed Onions, Peppers and Potatoes.  The sausage was butterflied and grilled thoroughly, and then placed at the bottom of a decent soft Italian long roll and overloaded with olive oil grilled peppers, onions and crispy cubed potato.  Very enjoyable.

Sakura Mandarin has become a regular stop when in Philly for any reason (do have an office there, but prefer to be in Princeton or Newtown).  Working through the menu I have discovered my favorites and tend to repeat them on most visits.  The Xiao Long Bao (Shanghai Steamed Pork Soup Dumplings or Juicy Buns) are the Best of Breed to my taste in Philly.  Six steaming top knot dumplings that require skill and care to eat without squirting the soup onto your date.  The waitresses love to offer a lesson in proper technique.  Be sure to pour some of the vinegar with ginger into the dumpling after it is opened to enhance the flavor of the soup and pork ball inside.   The Shanghai Pan Fried Pork Dumplings are also very good for those who prefer that preparation.  While not quite the experience of  XLB, they are quite good with a vinegar chili sauce mix accompaniment.    All the Vegetable and Tofu dishes are also good; the spicier the better. The Americanized dishes are okay, but clearly not as inspired, nor hot, as the more traditional Chinese styles.  When I go with my young son who is not acclimated to serious HEAT, he prefers the General Tso's Chicken, Orange Chicken, and Dan Dan Noodles.  They are all pleasing to him, but I find them a bit too sweet and thickly sauced, although the Dan Dan's are not bad at all when more Chili is mixed in.   The staff is very courteous and helpful.  No problem with attentiveness which can be an issue in some places.    Can't speak to the Japanese side of the menu, other than the take out menu is much prettier than the Chinese side.  Wonder what that means???

Pho Palace is a bit of a misnomer.    The facility is minimalist in décor, and a bit dreary in furniture and lighting.  Hardly a palace.  Still, there is a reasonable trade off to be made if your goal is good Pho, Banh Mi, Com or Bun dishes.  There are Thai and Chinese offerings on the menu, but I have not gone there even though management and staff appears to be primarily Chinese.    I ordered Banh Mi Thit Nuong (BBQ Pork Hoagie) and Pho Ga (Chicken Pho).  The Banh Mi was delivered on an oval plate over a strip of aluminum foil.  The torpedo roll was more Italian than French, with a thinner crust than a baguette, but toasted well.  The makings filled the bread with a nice quantity of tasty BBQ Pork, Daikon Radish, Cilantro, Carrots and Cucumber.  The mix crunched well and was quite satisfying.  My server assured me that the Banh Mi and a Medium Pho would not be too much for a meal.  He was right.  The sandwich was somewhat filling, but not so large as to be sufficient in and of itself.  I liked it and would definitely order it again.    The Pho bowl was large enough to hold what seemed to be a liter of clear, well developed broth, loads of Chicken Slices, Onions, Scallions and a nest of Noodles. I spent a minute lifting and separating the clumped Noodles. After throwing in Bean Sprouts, Basil Leaves, Jalapenos, and Squeezed Lime Wedges, the bowl was overflowing and the aroma rich and comforting.  I loaded the side sauce dish with a Hoisin/Sriracha mix to dip the chicken, and settled in for a slurpy meal.    Everything was pretty good, and the service was friendly and efficient.    Adequate parking in front. Cash only with in house ATM.  So, how does this compare to the nearest other Vietnamese restaurant, House of Pho in Southampton?  I find them both good, perhaps appealing to different customers.  Where House of Pho offers a much nicer environment, Pho Palace is more basic and less comfortable.  The Banh Mi is House of Pho is higher quality; using real French Baguette, and more Pork.  The Pho in both locales are very close in quality and freshness of accessories.  To my palate, they are a draw.  Where Pho Palace has a distinct advantage is price.  The Banh Mi was only $3.75 - a (pardon me, I can't resist) PHOnominal price.  The Pho at $6.75/7.75 (Med/Lrg) is also lower than at the House.    So, it comes down to what you need and want.  For a date or lux feel, House of Pho is the obvious choice.  You pay for it, but it may be worth it.  If only needing a solid tasty soup and sandwich, etc.,  without much environment, but saving a few bucks per person, Pho Palace is a very good alternative.  No doubt the rent each pays and the neighborhoods, have a lot to do with the prices on the menus.   Only separated by a few miles, the differences between Southampton and the Far Northeast Philly are considerable.  If I had to chose, House of Pho would be my first choice based on the overall experience from facility through food and ability to use credit cards.

A regular stop when in Tucson for the gem show, India Oven on North Campbell has always provided me with enough fresh, authentic cuisine of the sub continent to keep me happy and coming back for more.  The curry sauces are creamy and well spiced, with fresh chicken and veggies.  It is the place my then young son first tasted and began to appreciate Indian food.  He loved the Mango Lassis and Naans, and slowly tasted his way into a broader enjoyment of all the flavors, textures, and colors created in the kitchen.  Sometimes it is a bit hectic during the dinner rush, and the service while always friendly, can be spotty bordering on uncomfortable, but never having had a bad meal here over the many years of visiting, it has become a favorite while in town.    Many other gem show vendors come here after closing shop for the day.  On one occasion I sat next to a diamond merchant and his wife from India.  We started a conversation about business, and we ended up showing each other some of the stones we had with us right there on the tables, and finished a transaction the next day that resulted in some very happy gem folk buying/selling/trading stones that may never have transpired but for a common love of Indian food. Now, these good people are friends, and we plan to catch a meal together when in town.     Glad the resto didn't ask for a commission or finder's fee!   India Oven gives a whole new meaning to the concept of, "hidden gem."

When I was a kid, my father would take me with him when he went to the car wash. In those days, we could sit in the car as it went through the line of sprays, spinning brushes, waxing and drying.  It was like being eaten by a dragon, going through the entire digestive tract, and exiting the other end.  For a kid that was about as much fun as I could have without going on a family vacation.   Car washes have evolved over time, and the drive through variety has been mostly replaced with the "brushless" system that removes the passengers from the car, and pulls the vehicle through the wash on a conveyor chain. We are left to watch from the windows of the hall alongside the washing system.    I still enjoy watching the process, and can't help imagining being inside the car.   The Broad Street Car Wash has been around for a long while, although I never used it before.  It is the same mechanism as in my hometown, but this one seems better run, is definitely cheaper, and comes across with a better finished product.  At under $12 for the "Silver" Inside and Out service, it is a great deal.  There is even a $2 Off coupon for the Diamond Service, which provides foot massage while you wait (NOT - but wouldn't that be great!).  That it is less than 10 minutes from my office, making it a lunch date.

I just encountered a relatively unpleasant experience with Town & Country, but as the facts are uncertain, I can only fairly address the circumstances and attitudes confronted by this event.  Recently I had a sports coat's lining repaired there.  When I returned to pick it up, the work was done well, but there was an ink stain on the front of the coat that had not been present when I brought it in.  I brought it back to inquire about it, and of course they denied causing it, and further could not fix it.  So, bye-bye jacket.   It is possible that there was a pen in a pocket somewhere when I brought it to them, and that the pen leaked while in their possession.  I cannot dispute that.  However, why wasn't this problem pointed out to me when I picked it up and paid the cost of the repair?  It was quite obvious when I finally took it out of the plastic to wear it.  Regardless of the time the leak occurred (before, during  or after the repair), it was certainly there when they finished their work.    It would have been more honorable to point this out to me, rather than have me find it once at home.  I am a reasonable guy, and I recognize the ownership of the ink and time of leakage is in doubt.  Still, it was visible to me, and likely visible to them before the transaction was completed.  But, rather than be upfront about it, and explain it was not their fault and only saw the stain at the conclusion of their work, they chose to not inform me, and make me return to them to talk about it.  And, of course, they were defensive and unwilling to see any way they could have handled it differently.    Not a good business move, as I cannot continue to use their services in good conscience, and I am writing this review to warn off other people who might encounter a problem in the future.  These seem to be nice people, but a bit shortsighted.  All they had to do was deal with me directly, and as if they were sorry this happened even without any admission of responsibility, and I would have been unhappy, but satisfied with their deportment.  As it was, they failed on the human interaction scale, and lost a customer.
A worthy successor to the Clemons Supermarket that was here for many years. Bigger store. Better prices. Good people.

Towne & Country Cleaners sits right behind The Brick Hotel and next door to Grapevine Natural Foods on North State Street.  It is one of those places I never noticed until I asked around for a place that could repair the lining of my winter coat that had separated at its seam and needed to be reattached.  I was told that "Lucy" was very talented and could take care of it.    Walking in for the first time, the place is a bit dark and dreary; needing better lighting and a fresh coat of paint to really make it appear more appealing.  There is a small changing area in the front of the shop, and a large mirror where the recommended alternations are pinned.    Lucy greeted me with a warm smile and listened and observed as I opened the old coat to show her the problem.  She took a close look and realized that the wool and silk had separated and could be replaced or repaired.  She gave me the cost differential, and I went for the repair @ $25.  Two weeks later I picked up the finished job, and have been happily wearing the coat since.  After that, I have returned to T & C every time I need tailoring or repair.  I have always been happy with the work.    While the work is first in class, the shop environment needs the same TLC that Lucy puts into the clothes she touches.  Some lights, brighter colors, living plants, a nice area rug, would go a long way to making T & C an even better place to get this excellent work done.

I had not visited Slack's for a few years.  I guess their hoagies were just not that impressive to garner my loyalty.   With the arrival of Primos in the Village of Newtown Shopping Center, my interest in torpedo sandwiches has been rekindled, and after visiting another shop in the Slack's strip mall, I went in on impulse and ordered a Chicken Salad Hoagie with Provolone. The first thing I noticed was that they now offered their hoagies with a sesame seed roll option, just like Primos.  Who said competition doesn't improve all competitors?   The sandwich with hots and sweets was very good. About the equivalent of Primos, with a similar price.  If anything detracts from the Slack's experience it is that their facility has not changed in years and looks a bit dingy and dated. Also, the employees seem to lack the customer service polish of Primos.  These are not big things, but if the food is basically equivalent, then the decision comes down to atmosphere and price. Price is close. So, atmosphere carries the day, and Slack's is not on the same level as Primos.   I will stop in now and then to see if things are changing, but it will not win me over until it sees the need to offer a new image, and takes steps to meet it.

What a difference new ownership makes!  Last time I was in this shop it was a different pizzeria that touted its alleged New York City ties. In fact, the pizza had no resemblance to something from the Big Apple.  One visit was more than enough.  That place is now history.   What replaced it is another animal all together!  Jersey's Tomato Pies (and Bistro) actually knows what it is doing.  It turns out a very reasonable facsimile of authentic Trenton Tomato Pie, complete with super thin crust, quality Mozza base and chunky/sweet Tomato Sauce.  It was quite good, and my newly arrived foreign guests were treated to their first pizza that required no apologies.  They were very impressed and devoured our Sweet Italian Sausage Pie without much comment beyond satisfying grunts and big amazement eyes.    Thank you, JTP&B for a cultural experience my Chinese guests will remember for a lifetime.    Now, to reach the 5 star apex achievement, only a little tweeking is needed.  The center of the pie was a little damp, making the lifting of a slice problematic as the cheese/tomato/sausage mix could not be picked up by the crust, but needed to be slid onto our plates and folded back onto the drier part of each wedge.  Removing more of the water from the tomato and slightly longer time in the oven to harden the doughy center, might solve this.    Small nit is true, but when you come so close to perfection why not work to move the needle as far as it can go?

Jinrong Li, Master Massage Therapist, LMT, runs this clean, state of the art spa on the north end of State Street in Newtown Borough.  She previously was the massage master at the Newtown Athletic Club.    Jin does an excellent job relieving neck and back pain in a comfortable setting.  She is also a Skin Care Specialist, although I have never utilized those services.

The Weekday Café sits in the rear of the first floor of the Doylestown Commerce Center. There is no road sign to alert you to its presence, and even if you use Yelp directions you find yourself driving past the modern office complex without a clue the resto is in there someplace. It was only by driving around the parking lot to the rear of the building on the left that I spied the outdoor seating, parked and went inside to recon.   It was worth the effort.   The café is run by a lovely woman.  She was busy with a catering order when I arrived, but still greeted me warmly and took the time to explain the layout and breakfast menu.  Ordering a Bacon, Egg and Cheddar on Croissant, I found the coffee shelf and poured some excellent brew.    The sandwich was fresh and tasty and I took a few extra minutes to have a second cup while reading the morning news. People working in the building came in and out, and all had a pleasant repartee with the owner.    At under $5 for the breakfast, I knew The Weekday Café would become one of my stops when heading for D'town.

The price was great, but the bagel was way below average.   There was no differentiation between the crust and the meat of the bagel.  Just tasted like decent bread, but without any zest from a firm to crunchy crust, nor air pockets within to make the innards light and airy.  Clearly, RJ's has lost the recipe and won't admit it.   I appreciated the extra cheese in the sandwich and the coffee club pricing that brought my breakfast in at a skinny $3.  But, still, if it doesn't provide the bagel experience, what am I paying for?    New York Bagel around the corner on Parkway is a much better bagel option.

If you want an evening of All American Fun in the Central Jersey, Bucks County, Pa. area you can't do much better than catching a Trenton Thunder Minor League Baseball game at the newly renamed, Arm & Hammer Park on the riverfront in the state capital.  Although it is now 20 years old, the park still packs in the fans with a ton of concessions, decent and fairly priced food (I caught a $2 beer night), and a party festive atmosphere. Where it can easily cost a family of four a couple of hundred bucks to attend a Yankee or Phillie game to the north or south, here you can easily get away with less than a couple of Franklins.   Last Thursday night my son, his buddy, and I attended the park but faced a prolonged rain delay of over two hours.  We were in and out of our seats and into the shelter of the main concession area a few times.  No one complained as they were having too much fun, and the ball club was absolutely raking in the dough as people loaded up on food and drink while we waited.    I definitely had the impression that management loved these rain delays for the increased profits from the captured audience.  Pretty smart move.   They did not want to spoil the party by declaring a Rain Out too soon. They let us stay so we could all sate ourselves and continue to hope the game would get underway.  It never did as the mid-June storm soaked the outfield and puddled up on the infield tarp.   No harm done.  The ticket stubs will be honored at a future game.

The old saying, "You can't eat the atmosphere," is turned on its head at Po-Po No 1 Chinese Restaurant just off the intersection of East State Street and North Broad Street in Trenton, NJ.  At Po-Po, the atmosphere can eat you!   I walked in around 2 for lunch today, after easing my way around the throng of folks hanging on the corner waiting for the bus or other transaction.  Once inside, I walked to the counter to order a lunch size General Tso's Chicken for consuming on the premises.  Some of those nice people outside seemed to follow me in, and sat/stood around the dining area in various conversations laced with cursing and undisguised hostility toward the world.  Not one to give in to the anxiety I began to feel, I sat at the table waiting for my meal to be ready, and then returning to the counter to pick it up.    The food was about average for a cheap Chinese fast food lunch.  A pile of chicken chunks, breaded, fried and covered in goop, on top of yellow dyed fried rice with almost no veggies or meat in the load.  The taste of the bird was okay, but the rice was nothing more than filler on the plate. No effort to give it any real taste.    No. I won't return, nor would I recommend anyone that wants to dine in relative comfort and security do so.  This joint is just too close to a bad street scene that uses this place as part of its sordid sorrowful reality.

Newtown Chocolatier is a venerable and sweet institution in Newtown.  They recently moved from their old digs on State Street to Newtown Richboro Road (Swamp Road).  The new location is very well designed with plenty of display area to drool over.   The chocolate remains among the best home made sweets I have ever tasted.  The prices are higher than I like for a chocoholic, but I never complain about the quality.  Their arrangement with Whole Foods testifies to their dedication to their craft.   I am crazy for their peanut butter cups (Reeces), as well as their turtles and creams. But, to save a few bucks I usually go to the half price baskets to see what they are letting go at a discount. Yesterday, it was chocolate covered pretzels, cashew in milk chocolate, and solid milks, as well as a mix of darks.  Walked out with a bag at almost $10, that will satisfy my sweet tooth for a week or so.    Newtown Chocolatier is not a place I can frequent, but every now and then when I need a lift, it becomes my oasis.

Like most of us, Crowne Plaza Philadelphia-Bucks County looked better when it was younger.  What was once smooth, soft and supple, becomes lined, cracked and brittle.  This hotel is no different.   While it is still capable of putting heads on beds as it did 20 years ago, it no longer looks the part of a beauty queen.  The hair is streaked gray, the laugh lines more pronounced, and the plumbing often in need of repair.  Feel too hot?  Too cold?    Join the club.

Just discovered this place down State Street from my office. Full menu of massage alternatives. Chinese owner/practitioner.  First deep tissue massage was excellent for a long enduring herniated disk.   Prices higher than the cities, but the convenience and absence of driving, tolls, and gasoline costs, make this quite reasonable. Very comfortable environment and dedicated owner. Will definitely go again.  8.27.13 I have been back twice since the first visit/review.  Jinrong, the Master Massage Therapist, knows where the problem lies, and her hands find the pressure and trigger points to work.  An hour of a little discomfort when she digs in, but weeks of relief when she is finished opened the facet joints and calming the nerve roots.

Brownsville Road in Feasterville is a testament to poor planning.  It is an unredeeming stretch of blacktop more suited to driving in a 1955 Bel Air Chevy than a late model vehicle.  Still, if there is any one feature that is above the rest, D & W Brownsville Café and Deli, is it.  Within its walls time stands still.    The grub is pretty good, if not earthshaking.  Although most of the rumble is about breakfast, I arrived in time for late lunch.  I sat alone in the side dining room, and the gracious Cathy was my server.  First visit, I went with a Cecelia Burger - consisting of Provolone Cheese and Sautéed Mushrooms on a soft Kaiser.  The puck came to me Pink/Medium as requested, and the shrooms were larger and tastier than anticipated.  Provolone was okay as the sealant for the topping, but was too mild to really effect the flavor of the beef.  The only real weakness was the roll, which was soft and felt flimsy when trying to hold the weight of the burger with all its juices.    While I would not rush back for another lunch, on speaking with Cathy about breakfast, she lit up with enthusiasm for the French Toast, Sandies, and Egg combos.   I will make it back down Brownsville on a morning soon to see what the rave is all about.

Happy Hour Tavern is in a small commercial strip on Veteran's Highway, and quite easy to miss. Effort should be made to find it if a friendly working man's bar is what you like.    They have a fairly broad beer list, both tap and glass. The kitchen isn't exciting, but it does a decent job with the basics.  The important aspect is the atmosphere.  It is a cozy, unassuming place, where you can sit at the bar over a good crafty, shoot the breeze with some great storytellers, and walk out with change.    Most significantly, they have one of the rare shuffle board games - complete with sawdust needed to keep the oak surface slick.  Love that game. It ought to be an Olympic sport. Way more exciting than curling.    No. I wouldn't bring a date here, but when I want a hidden place to sit, think, smooze, and feel the cool weight of shuffle disks in my hand, Happy Hour Tavern does the trick.

While the drive thru moved well, the actual meal was not worth the wait.   It had been a while since I was this hungry and rushed enough to consider a BK stop.  This was one of those rare afternoons where I would eat at my desk.   The Mushroom Swiss Burger was a tasteless and textureless mush.  No wonder you can get 2 for $5.  They want to get rid of them. And, what about the Strawberry Lemonade?  The medium was about a half gallon of overly sweet, strawberry syruped, lemon wash ice water.    The condensation puddle on my desk slowly spread as I wondered what had possessed me to go for this meal.  Hunger makes for some bad choices.

This is a typical Chinese/American shop with the standard menu and lunch specials.  The effort at offering Thai dishes really doesn't work as everyone here is Chinese.    My General's Chicken was average, with dark amber gloopy sauce, but a nice portion of bird and rice.  As always, the ubiquitous sprigs of broccoli provided contrasting colors and a third food group.  The Wonton Soup had been prepared earlier and was dyed from whatever bouillon they were using.  Similarly, the Fried Rice had become dark from the same beef coloration.  Too thick wonton skins, and very dense filling of some kind of meat-food.    The taste was lackluster, but acceptable given the known parameters of such joints. At least, the room was well decorated and provided decent seating for eat in customers.  Service was fine.

It was a quiet Sunday night at Basil Leaf, the Vietnam/Asian Fusion restaurant in the Village of Newtown Shopping Center.  I had the place all to myself.  Looking around, I had the sense of being in the antechamber of an Asian palace. Dark tones, bamboo, the sound of a flowing stream.  Very comforting.  But, why was the place empty but for me?  Honestly, I don't know after eating some very good Southeast Asian cuisine tonight.  Vegetable Soup (Chicken Broth, but Veggie broth available) was piping hot and very tasty with lots of snow pea pods, broccoli and carrots.  Spicy Lemongrass with Chicken (nicely presented wok-fried dish with a really good tangy hot sauce and plenty of tender pieces of thin cut white meat), and Jasmine White Rice (softer than regular white rice); Ginseng Tea for a healthy chaser.    I know they were closed for lunch for a while, but I was advised lunch resumes this week.  Still closed on Tuesdays.   Bottom Line - I was totally satisfied, and will return. The cost of the meal as described, $20.  Maybe, the tea ($4) should be gratis in a nice place like this.  That would bring the cost down to a very reasonable dinner expense.  I don't want to forget to mention the service was friendly, knowledgeable and timely. Thanks, Jackie.

Brothers Pizza has been a cornerstone in Langhorne for years, and the new shop in the converted Shell/Texaco station at the corner of Pine and Maple makes it into an institution.    The restaurant is well designed with ample booths with high backs providing much more privacy than the old place.  There is a nice dining room that is separated by wood and glass doors from the take out/cashier area.  There is a level of comfort now that was missing in the earlier iteration.    The pizza and tomato pie are good, but not exceptional.  The crust is firm and crunchy and holds the weight of the toppings securely. The sauce and cheese are above average, but are not homemade with chunky tomatoes, nor likely shredded in house.  The Eggplant Parm Grinder is one of the best in the area, with fresh Italian loaf, nicely pan fried Eggplant and the same pizza sauce and cheese as on the pizza.  The sandwich is returned to the oven before serving, toasting the top edge of the meal, melting the cheese, and exciting the entire mix to a higher level that tastes great with wonderful texture when eaten.  I really like it.    Service is attentive.  I recognize one waitress as being with Brothers for many years.  She and her compatriots do a good job.  The prices are reasonable, and cheaper than the same meal down the hill in Newtown.    The joint is busy at lunch and dinner. The new space is barely adequate for the crowd.  Glad that their business has responded well to their new digs.
There are two listings for this supermarket, with this one containing the store number. Be sure to look for both to find all reviews.

Operating out of the old 1908 New Hope Eagle Fire Co. building and former Borough Hall on North Main Street, New Hope, PA., The Café @ The Four Crows has created a great space for the things they do best - brew excellent java (Rojo's Roastery, Princeton), and display electric guitars.  In fact, if you love rock music, you could come just for the strings and call this place a museum or guitar gallery.   The owner, an Australian rocker who can no longer finger the frets, ended up in New Hope and has the entire collection for sale.  Here's hoping he never sells them all, as they are a wonderful attraction to an otherwise well appointed coffee house. It would be way cool if there was an amp and a few speakers hooked up so those with skills can riff on the wide variety of sound created by all of these works of musical art.   But, back to the café.    The space is deep and runs the length of the narrow building. It is full of leather couches and easy chairs, as well as several stools and shelves for resting beverages. It is about the most comfortable java joint I have hung out in in the past few years. My latte was decent, but I am not a big fan of Rojo's as a bean outfitter.  Better choices are available locally.  Still, the drink was hot, strong, and warmed my hands on this cooler morn.    Everything here is made "to go."  The prices are very reasonable given the address.  So, overall, there is no reason not to stop by to service your caffeinated needs. It is a bit north of the center of New Hope, but there is plenty of street parking and a lot around the corner and behind Main Street.  Given the alternatives are the green mermaid and Dunkin, The Four Crows should be your first choice for coffee and comfort.

Ho Choi Chinese Restaurant is located in a small strip center, right next to a 7/11 convenience store. It is within the standard deviation for take out Chinois joints, with a tip of the hat to folks who want to eat in (4 tables).  The menu is the same one you have memorized from going to any other chopstick house in the USA.  It is perhaps cleaner than average, and the woman working the front is friendly and has a sense of humor.    The Roast Pork Egg Foo Young was also what I expected.  Two omelet/pancakes full of pork, sprouts, onion, on top of a massive pile of prefab yellow dyed fried rice.  The brown sauce tasted identical to all the others, with a slightly lighter color.  The meal was served in styro packaging with a mini fork for consumption.  The taste was fine.    It always seems strange when a Chinese place doesn't have hot tea for guests.  Can of soda or water bottle are part of the meal deal, but how nice it would be if they provided a 2 cent tea bag and a small pot of hot water!  Alas, it is seen as unnecessary because so few Americans drink tea in these circumstances.    Ho Choi did nothing to distinguish itself, but neither did it suck.

Gluten is not a problem for me, but I am always happy to find a new bakery in town. Whether cupcakes, breads, donuts or other pastries, I am game to give them a try.   The Happy Mixer in the Summit Square Shopping Center pays a steep rent to bake and sell their sweet delights. Hope they can appeal to enough people to make them successful, although a shop as limited as they are in this area is going to be challenged. Still, I stopped in to sample a few donuts and mini cakes to see what the hubbub was all about.   I took a few bites of their apple cider donut with maple glaze frosting, the coconut crunchy donut, and the mini lemon pound cake.  My impression was that they did a very good job on the cake part of each of them, but that the icing was still a work in progress. The base of each had a good moist texture that tasted as fresh as today.  Liked it a lot.   The glazing on each was stronger in flavor than expected, so much so that I found it was distracting from the overall enjoyment of each piece. It was thick, and easily flaked away from the underlying cake. The maple and lemon in particular felt like they were not really part of the donut or loaf, and the intensity of the flavors felt somewhat contrived to dominate the creation, rather than integrate with it. The lemon was very unusual and did not taste natural. Perhaps, too much extract was used. In any event, two bites were enough of that. Hopefully, a more mellow version will become available.   The shop is small and cute, with young assistants to take your order and ring it up. $13 and change for six pieces.  Everyone wants local business to succeed, and hopefully The Happy Mixer will find its niche in the community, with high quality baked goods that are far superior to the well known chains.

Langhorne Coffee House sits in the old Hicks House at the corner of Bellevue and Maple in the heart of Langhorne.  Edward Hicks was the artist who painted, "The Peaceable Kingdom," and other works that have some notoriety, so the name is well known by locals with a sense of history.  The café is cozy (some might say a tight squeeze), with tables in close proximity and a community seating sensibility.    The coffee is quite good and bottomless, with several daily options, including the organic blend I drank today.  The room is colorful with large windows and local artists' works for sale on the walls.  The staff is warm and cheerful.  The displays show varieties of attractive pastries.   My breakfast was a Sausage, Egg & Cheese in a Spinach Wrap.  It came quickly, but did look a little lost on the large white platter with a single slice of Orange.  It was fine, but the egg seemed to have been cooked in a microwave, which I do not prefer as it changes the consistency of the egg into something soft and airy, as opposed to how an egg is prepared in a fry pan giving it more substance.  I should have asked about that before ordering.    All in all, an adequate meal, but not one I will yearn to repeat.  Yet, the atmosphere, service and coffee were all nice enough to make it a positive experience.  I would definitely return for my morning coffee when in the area.  Not on my short list of noteworthy breakfast stops, but a worthy community-centric shop that has a loyal following for good reason.

Who am I kidding?  I just went into Newtown Chocolatier to pick up some Peanut Butter Cups and Pecan Turtles for my son to bring to his grandparents for Easter.  While I was at it I asked the kind woman behind the counter if they had any broken pieces available.  She went into the back room and came out with a box of Milk Chocolate Strips.  I took every last nibble, and just tasted a bit before writing this update.    Daaaahhhhmmmm!  So good.  Sweet, smooth, instantly addicting.   5 Aces, and should have been so all along.

Basil Leaf appears to be closed or out of business.  The blinds are drawn closed, and there is poster board covering the glass door. A business card from the Health Department attached to the door asked for a phone call.  Hopefully, this is a temporary situation. Will keep Yelp advised...

Why does Star$$$ coffee always taste burnt? This is always my problem with Green Mermaid coffee.  The house coffee, without the benefit of heavy doctoring into lattes, capps, etc., is close to awful - harsh, bitter, skin peeling.  After being reformulated into the expensive brew, they are good drinks.  But, should you have to forgo the basics and rely on alchemy to be able to drink their stuff? Just asking.  The bakery goods are very nice, and the oatmeal breakfast is way above average.   The former Rexall never looked this good.  This is a great place to meet someone, and sit for a while. The bench sitters out front may take that idea to an extreme.  So, how to rate when there is so much going on and such extreme divergence of quality and experience?  "Meh," doesn't really reflect the gestalt. "Yay!" is really going too far. "OK," is just about right.

It may be stating the obvious, but Monty's Sandwich Shop is all about what goes between two slices of bread. One glance at the full wall menu lets you know that you can spend your entire lunch hour reading the list and run out of time to eat anything. The list is that daunting.   Once getting past the Rosetta Stone wall by selecting the first thing I liked, rather than trying to absorb it all, and ordering an Italian Hot Dog at the counter, I looked around the rest of the room. There were tables and booths spread around, and on the opposite wall, the house slogan in large colorful letters, "Now That's A Sandwich!"   Which begs the question; is it?   They called my name when lunch was ready, and I went back to the counter separating the dining room from the kitchen, to pick it up. First impression was eye opening. A foot long torpedo roll spread open to hold a foot long frankfurter, split and grilled, on top of crisp fries and under a load of fried onions and peppers, and finished with heavy squiggles of yellow mustard. The shock effect was tremendous. I realized there was no way to squeeze all that together and fit it in my mouth. I found the basket with cheap plastic forks and knives, grabbed them and went to work.   The dog, onions, peppers and potatoes were very good. Garlic was the primary note of the dog, and the accompaniment went great together. I was proud to eat it all. But, I did leave the entire roll behind. It was in part strategic in that I could not consume all that bread. It was part choice. The loaf just wasn't worth the calories due to lack of flavor, absence of real crust, and a doughy, dense, dry texture without taste overall.  At nearly $11 for the sandwich and cold drink, it would have been consistent with real value to have a quality bakery provide a roll equivalent to its impressive  passengers.   Thus, "Now that's almost a (great) sandwich," is the answer.

When you hang a sign touting one of your special offerings, you really have to deliver the goods. When you don't do so it just compounds the failure.   As we approached Marhaba on foot at the bottom of Mt. Hope Street, Lambertville, NJ, we observed and commented on the smaller sign suspended beneath the painted wooden restaurant scripted plank.  "Falafel."  The dining room was heavily atmospheric, with exposed red brick, hanging metal/glass lights, and attractive Middle Eastern wall art. The small candles in colorful glass holders added to the flickering ambiance.   We ordered the falafel/hummus combo plate based on their advertisement outside, and the chicken shawarma platter. Both large plates arrived about 15 minutes later. A hot pillowy pita came along for the ride.   Needless to say we were disappointed when we attempted to pick up a falafel ball with a fork. The surface was impenetrable and the tines bounced off as if striking a rock. Plan B was picking the sphere up with my fingers and locking down with my bicuspids. My jaw forced the hard shell to collapse, only to find that the ground chickpeas within were chokingly dry and almost tasteless. A hard case disaster.   Made us wonder who was doing quality control in the kitchen? Why would the chef, manager or server who saw what was being served allow them to reach our table? These hardballs should have been trashed. But, it was actually worse than that.   The kitchen lacked vertical rotisserie grills for the proper preparation of gyros and shawarmas. Thus, the chicken which should have been sliced thin and constantly basted in a complex marinade was instead cut in small chunks and heated on hot steel. It was also far too dry and poorly spiced. If there was a marinade, it was weak or had only a passing acquaintance with the chicken. It was dry, lifeless and barely edible. O for 2.  On the other hand, the hummus was excellent and eating it with torn pieces of pita, great finger food. A wise person once said that life is short; eat dessert first. The baklava at Marhaba was unbelievably wonderful. Baked in-house, the phylo, honey and pistachio concoction was about the best I'd ever eaten. If that had been all we tried, this would have been a 5 star review, and we would have been very happy campers.   We only wish that we had followed that sage advice. It would have saved us time, money, dissatisfaction and many questions.

I understand why people love Casnova's Kitchen for breakfast. It sure doesn't look like much driving up, but once inside things start to come into focus. The dining room is a tight squeeze with only a handful of booths. But, if you go to the left and look around the back wall, you will find the infamous kitchen and a short luncheonette counter with a half dozen stools. If you enjoy watching the chef do his thing on the grill, and the entertaining talk between him, customers and his staff, then this is the joint for you.   Grab a spinner, check out the large menu and go for something good. Anything with eggs and coffee is the right idea. I went with a sausage, egg and cheese on kaiser roll, but those omelets being prepared on the hot steel looked real appealing, too. All the while, the second gen Casanova (Tim?) exchanged information with me and had funny dialogues with the guys coming to this backroom man cave grill. They all knew each other well, and the comradery was patent. Even as a stranger I felt I was almost part of their clique.   And, the sandwich was very good, too. Sausage logs (not links) a little crisp, with folded fried eggs and a couple slices of cheese, all on a  superior fresh roll brought in from a bakery in Jersey. Java refills as needed.   This was a three ring, holy roller circus. It didn't look like a winner, but much like the other special places around Bucks, the ones that are hardest to find or hidden in plain site, are usually the best.  One of the best breakfasts of the year!

Good Mood Restaurant sits in the back of the large commercial center on North Olden Avenue, Ewing, New Jersey.  Although there is a very large parking area around it, the proximity of a Planet Fitness and nursing school in session, makes finding a spot somewhat problematic on school days.  Still, after cruising for a few minutes, something opened up fairly nearby.    Good Mood has been open since February.  It has a fairly large footprint, with plenty of tables for a large crowd.  It only serves breakfast, brunch and lunch.  Service is friendly, and they do a brisk takeout trade. The menu is traditional American egg oriented dishes, with a nod to wraps and Mexican options, as well as burgers available at all times. The space is bright and clean, and when you order coffee, they give you a half full thermal pitcher with java, so you don't have to ask for refills.  Nice touch.   My breakfast wrap consisted of a large tortilla filled with scrambled eggs, green chili, chorizo sausage, onion and cheese.  It came with a large side of home fries that were crisp and tasty. The wrap was filling and satisfying, especially after a few drops of Tabasco were added.  Definitely enough to allow me to skip lunch today. Always a good thing.   Everything about Good Mood is solid. For the price, a little more pepper and chorizo would have been a positive. Nonetheless, it is a strong addition to the locale where it can be hard to find a decent meal first thing in the morning.   Wish them luck.

Although hard to find sitting on the second floor of the mostly Vietnamese shopping center at 11th and Washington, if you are into strong handed traditional Chinese massage, this place is worth the hunt.    After an exceptional meal nearby, we retreated to V & V for a foot massage.  This normally includes a brief full body massage while your feet soak in very hot herbed water to soften them up, while reclining comfortably in a large adjustable easy chair.  It has taken me several years to be able to put my sensitive feet into the near-scalding soup, but I finally can do it and actually enjoy it.    The first squeeze of my trapezius let me know my masseuse meant business.  Ouch! She knew the pressure points, meridians, and even a few pleasure points along the way.  Her English was just good enough to say, "relax."  Easy for her to say...  The foot portion of the hour was equally intense.  She triggered the deep sole points as she attempted to explain her concept of reflexology.  She would show me a place on my foot, and then say the body part of correspondence.  All the while her skilled and amazing strong hands prodded and dug, releasing the pain and tension I live with most days   It was an excellent massage.   At $50 for the hour, the price was decent, but no where near the $25 paid in New York's Chinatown or Flushing for the same work.  Still, there is a lot to be said for saving time, tolls and gas, so the cost was probably a savings, even with the expected $20 per first hour tip.

Girard, a breakfast/brunch/lunch house on the avenue by the same name on the southeastern corner with Marlborough Street in Fishtown has a lot of things going for it.   It uses locally sourced provisions to the greatest extent possible, and it tastes it. They bake their own muffins and coffee cakes, and even their milk and burgers pump and grind from nearby cows. Taste and texture are from the hands of neighbors.   They have a fair wage policy for all employees. That means everyone earns a reasonable living income ($14./hr now). This encourages long term commitment from workers and ownership, and shows great respect for people. As a result a 20 % tip is included in every check. Nothing more required unless you feel it warranted. Yes, this makes it difficult to express dissatisfaction with service or food quality through tipping, but on balance there is far more good from this approach, than negative.   Their Elixr Coffee is hot and strong. Cold brew is also available at a small premium. In exchange for their smallish cups, refills are attentively prompt. In truth, the tables are smallish, too, so saving space makes sense.   The room itself is tight, but brightly yellow. An odd angled ceiling helps with acoustics and gives a slight unreality to the space. Big windows overlook Fishtown, a corner of Philly undergoing a distinct renaissance.   Finally, our breakfast ( I don't do brunch ) was excellent. The Breakfast Burger was a double patty, thick bacon and sunnyside up egg on brioche bun that was juicy and fun. The side of fries was crisp and plentiful. Their homemade hot sauce, a kick in the pants when poured on generously. We shared a square of their peach/basil coffee cake. Both ingredients were easily palatable, and to our delight, it was not overly sweet, but allowed to make it's own quiet statement. Delicious.   Girard checked all the boxes that matter, and a few not normally considered.   Impressive!

Dessert Review  We stopped in Adonio's Diner as the last stop after foot massage and Afghani dinner. Just wanted some java and something sweet to finish the night's run. They advertise that they had a bakery, so they had to have some nice stuff. Right?  Not quite.   Perhaps, because it was a long holiday weekend, and they gave the Baker's the day off, but all they had was cheesecake and apple crumb pie, neither of which looked to be made in house.  Ordered the apple slice anyway. I have never seen a smaller excuse for a diner dessert. Where most diners go out of their way to be excessive in these situations, Adonio's fit on a small saucer, practically flat and with little apple.The taste was industrial. The accompanying cuppa joe was also small and not very good.  The dinner customers were scoring large platters of whatever, and seemed satisfied. So, this was all about apres diner offerings. For unknown reasons, mine sucked. My friend's rice pudding was okay, but also miniscule compared to what most diners provide.   First and last impression.

If fried chicken is one of your favorite comfort foods, then a visit to Lovebird on East Ashland Avenue, Doylestown, PA, is very worthwhile. At least, I know that was why I was there.   Brought to us by the folks who created the successful Jules Thin Crust Pizza, Lovebird is the brainchild of that same crew with equal parts great recipe, locally sourced, cage free, vegetarian raised Amish poultry, and simple gray toned shop with one collective table and five sunny bright window stools. As a newbie, I ordered the aptly named "Lovebird Sandwich," which came with a perfectly deep fried battered breast, cole slaw, pickles, lettuce and special sauce mayo, on a freshly baked local bakery brioche roll.   It was one of those meals where the enjoyment began with the first bite through the thick layers of crisp crusty bird, through the tender sweet roll. It was as textural as it was flavorful. It was delicious and fun to eat. And, if you prefer roasted chicken over fried, go for it! They have that, too, and although I didn't taste it, it looked awesome.  Tasted a few fries, and they were quite good, but I'm trying to be good to myself by some modification of diet, so I passed on getting my own. The Lovebird was so great on its own that I really didn't miss them. Also, begged off the Boylan Soda, one of my past faves.   Now for the News Extra! Lovebird is coming to Newtown soon, across Sycamore Street from its sibling, Jules. That is something to get excited about! Not just another knock off franchise, but a true original.

There is nothing nasty about this Han house of szechuan cuisine at Second & Chestnut in Philadelphia. This Chinese palace deserves all the praise it receives.  Housed in a former bank from the Golden Age, the high ceiling and neo-classical architecture are a fitting backdrop for the high quality and superior platters conceived and executed in the kitchen woks.   We had a 15 minute wait for our table to be ready, but the time was well spent at the bar sipping an excellent Malbec and adjusting to the bustle of a busy Friday night.
