Really liked our table in the back under the dramatic staircase. More private and romantic.   We ordered four dishes prepared in different styles, and moderately to seriously spiced. Cumin lamb, dry fry beef, dry pepper fish and string beans with minced pork, arrived seven minutes after our excellent server accepted our requests. The quickness surprised us. Yet, each dish was perfectly plated and at their peak flavor. None were overly oily, and each distinct in their texture and taste, despite the use of similar Szechuan red and black peppers. Everything was delicious, and we were glad for over-ordering so we had plenty to bring home.   The size of the room was unusual for an American Chinese restaurant, and reminded us of the large banquet showrooms popular in China. It added to the authenticity of the overall experience.   I didn't remember Han D. being such a complete and satisfying night when across the street. Whatever it is, they have it going on now. In spades!   Five Stars!

The Cake Box on Farnsworth Avenue in historic Bordentown, NJ, is a mellow country town cupcake house that also offers great La Colombe coffee, and a chill place to stop for dessert and java after a good meal down the street. The cuppies are small, with the head of buttercream frosting at least as high as it cake base. So, you have room for one after dinner.   I stopped by after court in Mt. Holly on my way to the Trenton office. The room has aged well, with white tile and old wood all around. The glass display is big enough to show the dozen or so alternatives cupcakes available that day. I was more interested in coffee renewal, but still wanted to sample one these beauties. The blueberry lemon sounded good. I took a seat at a small table up front to enjoy the streetview on a perfect autumn day.   The icing was a sugary blonde bouffant hairdo. It wasn't overly sweet, which allowed it's creaminess to shine through. The cake bottom was moist and firm like a solid white cake. I liked it, but a little bigger biteage would have pleased me more. The coffee was excellent, and the La Colombe beans were available for purchase.  $2.75 per cupcake. A great addition to the awakening that is happening in the Town  Borden.

Another great night for baseball at Arm & Hammer Park!   We watched a slow game through five innings, when no one seemed capable of mounting any offense, become a slug fest for the home town Thunder, who scored ten runs in two innings to put the game away.    All this under pink sunset clouds and Dollar Dog Night!    The adversary?  The Richmond Flying Squirrels.  Hard to imagine them even wearing pants.

Even with rain delays, Double AA Minor League Baseball as personified by the Trenton Thunder and the multi-named Waterfront Park/Arm&Hammer Park/Samuel Plumeri Park, offers a great all American experience that is great for family, friends, clubs, offices, and just solitary "Field of Dreams" lovers.    So, it is with a strong sense of having a beautiful and unique cultural experience that we return regularly to this Temple of Timeless Baseball to pay our respect and appreciation for the Great American Pastime.   It was so much fun to be back again.

I admit to not understanding the word order of this dental office in Holland, PA. Holland Family Dental makes alot more sense in English, but perhaps the point is that it is the correct linguistics in other cultures. Or, it could just be a mistake.   This office is on the lower level of this professional office building, and difficult to see from parking lot level. Once inside, there is a small waiting area with 6 chairs, a reception area with 2 women managing the intake and insurance operation, and three examination/treatment rooms with three hygienists and one dentist.   The expected first visit paperwork took a long while, but once that was accomplished, the wait to see the dentist, have x-rays, be examined and have a cleaning was fairly prompt. It ended up being an almost two hour visit.   Staff was efficient, friendly and explained the process well. They were patient with my questions, and made intelligent adjustments when I realized I did not have a necessary document.   My son seemed satisfied with his dental care. Hopefully, he won't need to return until next year's maintenance.

A fun and challenging course, especially for a public facility. Reminds of the wild rough and smallish greens of the British Open courses like St. Andrews in Scotland.    Apres golf in the cozy clubhouse is also a pleasure with a small bar and room for a small dinner party.   Also can't complain that it is the club nearest home.

Lexi Lu's Café is a strange setup.    Up front it is a well designed, attractive take out shop.  Walk past their kitchen and it is Amoroso's Flower Shop, where you can still buy a bouquet of roses for your anniversary.  Love the adaptive reuse of this old storefront on S. Broad Street, Trenton; right across from the very old courthouse.  It is hard to find driving by, and there are seldom parking spaces within the surrounding area.  But, if you work or live in the neighborhood, or go to the new civil or criminal courts, you can walk over and pick up soup, sandwich, breakfast muffin, etc., on your way to the office.  It closes at 2:00 pm.    Service is exemplary given how small the space is.  The two friendlies who helped me out were attractive and efficient.  One made up my grilled chicken chipotle wrap, while the other provided the history of the business and worked the register.  Both were happy to pose for photos when I pulled out my Yelp screen after ordering.  You can see the results.    The lunch was very good.  Fresh, quality ingredients and TLC.  Plenty of stuffing for a large wrap.  It was enough for two meals.  @ $8.50, it was a spectacular deal.    Too bad there is no place to sit, because the room is comfy in a cramped way, and it would be nice to absorb more atmosphere from the winsome workers.

After a pleasant exchange of messages with the owner of Langhorne Coffee House, I learned that the eggs are bathed in Italian Sparkling Water to create the light texture I described in my earlier review. Apparently, a family secret from the Old Country (the best kind of cooking secrets).    Knowing the truth of the matter, my impression has changed for the better.  An extra star is warranted, not only for the discovery of how the meal was made, but also for the wonderful extra step that continues a family tradition to be shared with the world.

Every once and a while you enter a world so unusual that the experience is just as much anthropological as a chance to eat unexpectedly connected cuisines. This happened last night when we ventured into Asian Mix Restaurant just off Haldeman Avenue in far Northeast Philadelphia. This little piece of urban heaven has a fair share of Chinese, Korean, Russian Georgian and Uzbek kitchens, but this was my first time sitting down for a dinner of Korean/Uzbek/Ukrainian dishes springing naturally from the life of one family.   Imagine leaving Korea as a child with parents and siblings for a new home in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, on the western fringe of Asia along the ancient Silk Road. Assimilating what you could in that crossroads city, and then moving further east to Kiev, Ukraine, and ultimately a generation after first departure, arriving in the City of Brotherly Love. More adaptation. More Integration.   Your grown children don't speak Korean, but are fluent in Uzbek, Russian and English. They open a restaurant offering what they learned to cook along the way; a menu equal shares spicy kimchee, soups, salads stuffed pastas and exotically prepared meats, chicken and fish. From these offerings, we selected potato Pierogi, kimchee, Ukrainian borscht and schnitzel made from ground chicken, turkey and beef ("A Family Feast") with a tomato/cabbage side salad with excellent balsamic vinaigrette.   It was all a little strange, but also very good. The pierogi looked like Chinese dumplings, with thin skin and a bit too watery mashed potatoes filling. Still very enjoyable. A dollop of sour cream implied eastern European sensibilities. Similarly, the borscht was a rich deep red served hot with mushrooms, beans and chunks of meat for flavoring. Very different than my grandmother's interpretation from Galacia that served this cold with a simple hot boiled potato and sour cream. Liked it alot. The kimchee was excellent and very spicy, the way it is done in the northern peninsula. The schnitzel had a nice walnut cream sauce, but was really more sliced meatloaf lightly fried, than a breaded fillet. Very good, but perhaps misnamed. The accompanying salad was a strong contributor to the plate.   As we ate, we saw that part of the owner's family was sitting in back with young children. They looked to be Korean, but as I walked by they were speaking Russian and English. I had the urge to sit with them and ask about their lives and long immigration story.   I knew it was the stuff of family legend.

Out of town friends chose to stay at the Radisson Hotel Philadelphia Northeast for a few nights while visiting the area.  I tried to tell them in advance that the hotel was not really in Philadelphia at all, but just beyond the city limits in Bucks County.  I also described the neighborhood as groaty old Route 1, auto dealers, by the hour motels, and garish liquor stores. They didn't care. The price was right, and they wanted to shop in the surrounding malls.    I went to see them there a couple of times. Parking was easy with a big lot.  The building looked a bit dated, but still highly functional.  Nice atrium in the lobby.  Cool black and whites of historic buildings in Philly.  A decent bar and free breakfast.  Clean, comfortable rooms.  Small bathrooms.   They managed to eat at several interesting places within a short distance (Steve's Prince of Steaks, Andy's Diner, Mission BBQ, Starbucks, to name a few).  They had nothing but good things to say about the place, other than they wished they had stayed in Center City, and could just put their horses in the stable and walk around town.    Maybe next time.

When Macy's does an after-sale sale, and the prices are up to 80% off the original, I can find useful, quality merchandise in the Men's Department.  The area is clean, organized and fairly relaxed for finding a style and quality I like.    At those discounts the value is greatly enhanced and it can compete with the deep dive price warehouses like TJ Maxx and Target.   Just picked up a couple of very nice sweaters at very attractive prices.  You don't even need to bring all those coupons that arrive in the mail or online.  The cashier will willingly give every discount available as you check out.

October 15, 2015 - Finally ordered their small, personal sized tomato pie as Ingrid had suggested months ago. Boy, was she right! The super thin crisp crust was a firm delight, and the mozza, chunky tomato pieces and spices exactly what was required. Simply stated, I loved it!

It is a testament to the American melting pot that bagels have become an American dish sold by people from the Middle East who have no cultural connection to the ethnic source.   A & S Bagel sits in a nondescript commercial strip at the bottom of Galloway Road.  It is clean and bright, even if uninspired in its décor, with yellow walls and lights, and white booths along one side.  The workers/owners are friendly enough and know how to slice and spread efficiently.  They don't have the broadest selection of bagels, but they are made in the back of the shop and are certainly fresh.    My Onion Bagel, Butter and Swiss was ordered and delivered to my table within 5 minutes.  This being a Boar's Head operation, the option on the cheese was eliminated in favor of only their own brand; always a disappointment as the taste and texture of the Swiss is not as good as Finlandia, Jarlesburg, or other Euro-based names.    The only major issue with the bagel was that it lacked a crusty skin, and had a weak yeast taste.  It was more like sourdough loaf in the shape of a bagel, and not the authentic crunchy outside and airy inside that notes a proper bagel.  Still, it was quite big, and obviously satisfying to many.  I suggest a visit to Bagel Train in Yardley if they aspire to a closer approximation of the real McCoy.

Bagel Board is a tiny corner bagel shop right next to the Croyden Train Station on Bristol Pike (Rt. 13). Location for commuters is perfect coming or going.  It is family owned/operated by a nice couple who seem to handle the rush efficiently and without loss of cool.    My Onion Bagel with Butter and Cheese was solid.  Firm crisp outer crust and light insides.  Wish they had Swiss Cheese, but the American was okay.  The sandwich was ready just as I capped my coffee.  Couldn't find milk, but had the choice of half & half or powdered creamer.    There is only one small table and a bench inside, so take away is the name of the game.  Given its proximity to the choo-choo, most wouldn't want to mange in the house in any event.  Not to mention that Dog & Bull is right down the street, where you can sit at the bar and have a cool one with your round one from the neighbor.  All aboard for Bagel Board! (Couldn't resist.)

I hadn't been to the Kopper Kettle Tavern for at least twenty years, perhaps indicating that I didn't feel an urge to visit this fish oriented restaurant on Bridgetown Pike in Trevose, PA. It was as remembered - cozy, slightly past its prime, with small bar and side dining room. Lots of old Formica tables and rolled stainless steel chairs. I took a stool at the bar and ordered a domestic light draft and the flounder dinner with pepper hash and baked potato.   Everything was pretty much average. No surprises in the brew. The fish was probably frozen, nicely breaded and fried in oil clean enough to have no secondary taste. The potato was not of a baking variety and remained dry no matter how much butter was melted into it. I liked the pepper hash, which was basically a spicy slaw. I mixed the tartar and shrimp cocktail sauces together on the plate from the two table rockets given me by the friendly bartender. They made for decent dipping of the fillets.   Maybe the sandwiches are the way to go at the Kettle, because the platter was twice the price, yet far less than double the value.

When it's 96 in the shade, it is okay to give yourself permission to cool down and chill out with some quality ice cream.  Finding myself in the northern wilds of Bucks County on a visit to Ockanickon Boy Scout Reservation on an unforgiving day under the broiling sun, I  wove my way down twisting two lanes into the oasis town of Plumsteadville. The blacktop mirage rippled its shimmer view, making the buildings appear to float.    I spied the Plumsteadville Inn, and right next to it, Chubby's.  Normally, I don't like ice cream before 5, and prefer not to eat it alone. But, this was an exception.  I needed to lower my body temp before I started to act on my hallucinations.  I walked in, and the AC hit me hard.  Two angels came to my aid, offering to provide me with cool scoops of any flavor I could imagine.  Because it was my first time in heaven they handled me a Golden Ruler as a gift (see photo).  They said it would help me stay "measured."   It was up to me to design the proper elixir to counteract the heat.  Intuition led me to Salted Caramel and Black Cherry. It was lovingly served me in a styro cup, for under $5.  The angelic smiles as I tossed the change into their prayer jar will not be forgotten.    By the time I walked the short distance to my car the ice cream was already melting.  I tasted both before I would be required to drink from the cup.  Sheer excellence.  Cool, creamy, sweet, salty, chunky, chewy - Ambrosia of the Gods.  What else do angels serve on a sweltering day?  ArcAngel Chubby does not make his own ice cream.  It is Nelson's Ice Cream, made in Royersford, Pa.  It may not be the bestest ice cream I have ever tasted, but on a day like today when shoes stick to pavement, it came straight from Valhalla.

I guess I picked the wrong night to see all the hubbub at the Buck Hotel.  No cougars. Not even a stray pussycat. The barroom feels like a hunting lodge with a large angular bar, large TV's and curiosities hanging on the walls. Most pronounced; a 12' nutcracker standing guard over the operation.  This was a quiet Sunday night. No complaint.   I had a Chicken Salad sandwich and a glass of red.  Both were fine, but certainly I was not in search of the sweet spots on the food nor liquor menus.  They were enough for the moment.    It had been many years since my last visit, and but for the suggestion of meeting someone there for a conversation, I would not have chosen it this time.  Still, I was curious to see what had changed, and I could not detect much alternation.    Not a bad place for a Sunday evening, but to taste the full flavor it would likely require a return on a busier night.

What a difference 18 months makes!   Returning to Pho Palace with a group of 6 to introduce neighbors to Vietnamese cuisine, and have another run at the menu, there were several new things going on in the house that all were all nice improvements.    First, walking in, the redesigned dining room was striking.  A large wooden pergola dominated the new front room, standing over the majority of the tables that were now separated by half walls.  Nice structure and lots more privacy.  New smaller dining rooms in the back for parties.  Second, credit cards were now accepted for orders over $20.  This was a big convenience for most customers, allowing the avoidance of the ATM monster in the lobby.  They were even willing to split our checks and allow us to use separate credit cards.  Friendly and seamless transactions.   Third, Service was more efficient and professional.  The mostly male staff was all in black, and  was attentive throughout the meal - refilling water glasses, removing plates, asking if we needed anything more.  All good flourishes from where the level of service was on last visit.    Most importantly, the food was still good, although the prices were up fractionally, no doubt to cover the cost of renovations.  The Pho was comforting and fun.  The Summer Rolls stuffed with Shrimp, Pork and fresh cabbage; and the Peanut Dipping Sauce cool and tasty. The Grilled Chicken and Pork Banh Mis were loaded with meat, Diakon Radish, Carrot in a crunchy Baguette-styled torpedo roll.  Everything was passed around with enthusiasm.  Even our neighbors who also ordered a Chinese dish to play it safe, were satisfied.    The improvements at Pho Palace were well conceived and executed.    Kudos!

This Popeye's Chicken shack sits in a long commercial strip on Trenton Road, Morrisville, Pa.  It is a standard franchise for the company.  The space is clean and attractive, with a well hidden drive thru component around to the back.    I went in the other evening for a light dinner and to help nourish my life long Southern Fried Chicken addiction. I just can't seem to get enough.  Love the crunch and the hot oil burning my fingers. Love the spicy coat.  Love the way it pulls away from the bone with a little coaxing.   These days, fried chicken is offered on the more sophisticated menus, and even for breakfast with waffles for those who just want max carb load.  (I'm not there yet.)  But, just because someone with a chef's hat and culinary school degree puts a batch together doesn't mean it is any better than the cheaper, faster, mass produced variety.  In fact, there is a school of thought that fried chicken is like singing the blues.  You know; "You have to suffer if you want to sing the blues..." Those hands playing six string acoustic or even Lucille, bring something to the experience that can be felt deep in the soul.    Chicken be that way, too.  The true fried chicken artists, like the best Delta or Hills Blues guitarists and singers, are rooted in a culture and existential angst that generates the creative instinct leading to emotionally charged performances.  Those same forces are at work with fried chicken.  In the hands of a master, the chicken becomes an extension of his life, the same way a great song emerges from that primordial place deep in the heart.  This 2 piece box o' chicken may not have been epic, but it was solid and even inspired this review.  So, even though we weren't sitting in Muscle Shoals, Alabama in a roadside chicken house, there was enough there to let the imagination run wild.  Just wish they actually played that music at Popeye's, rather than the current soundtrack.

I realize that I sometimes live in a fantasy world, but there are times when reality presents itself as phantasm.   So it was when I opened the old wooden door and entered The Hob Tavern.  Yes. They say the letters stand for "Heart of Bordentown," but there is another deeper meaning.  Bordentown has a rich if mysterious history of being the place where Napoleon Bonaparte was spirited away from Elba by French royalists who wanted to protect him from the republican elements at work in France, and hide him until the time was right for the 3rd Empire.  What better place than a tiny hamlet in the New World where his family owned a vacation home on a rise overlooking a wild Delaware River? Who would notice a small man speaking French walking around the village?    Too, it is easy to imagine entering Middle Earth and sitting in a Hobbit home while here. It is dark and glowing with friendly inhabitants that are inviting and have an open kitchen for all who visit.  So, if you give yourself time to consider the possibilities, and settle in, you could have quite an adventure.   The HOB is a dive in the best sense of the word.  It is a locals bar one block off of the main Farnsworth Avenue.  The streets back there are narrow, and the homes are small.  There is plenty of beer, and the kitchen remains "grill on" until 1:00 am on weekends.  Prices are ridiculously low.  The homemade soups are great.  The menu options for sandwiches, burgers, salads, etc., remarkably diverse.  The quality is several steps above bar food.    Try to go on an off hour to enjoy the environment before the crowd hides that from you.  Weekday lunch until 5 is a good window.    Let us know what you think.

Lion Dog in the Campus Town commercial zone on the campus of The College of New Jersey, is a take out only hot dog shop. It offers an extensive menu of frankfurters and sausage varieties, fries and soft drinks for the "dog" lovers in your world. Being one of them, I looked forward to stopping by to taste their merchandise. Took care of business today.  It took a circling of the block to spy Lion Dog, and around again to locate parking. Walking in I realized I would not be dining there as there were no tables, nor counters. Okay, I'll bring something home. I ordered the Italian Hot Dog with Sabrett Kosher beef woofer, and watched as the owner prepared the sandwich at the grill. I saw pieces of green pepper, potato wedges and the frank grilling up and packed into a torpedo sized roll, followed by a long squiggled squirt of brown mustard. I asked for Lenny's World Famous Pepper Hash on the side for application at home.   Turned out the hash was a nice addition with a vinegar sweetness and carrot chips, onion and maybe a little celery. I also added some ketchup for extra zing.   It was a good rendition of the Trenton originated hot dog creation, the Casino Dog. The Sabrett kept it's strong garlicy character, and allowed the rest of the pieces to harmonize with each jaw clenching bite. It would have been even better had there been double dogs and green frying peppers within a fresher roll from Italian People's Bakery, as the original did.   Bring that to life and Lion Dog would have a true special.   PRO QUESTION - What is the name of The College of New Jersey mascot?   ANSWER - Roscoe the Lion.

Makhani ("Buttery") is a small, dark, North Indian house on historic S. 3rd Street, Philadelphia, PA. Service is individually prepared, so you receive a large plate with your order and a side of Basmati rice, rather than the bowl approach used by most Indian shops. It is still easy to share with a companion, so it is really no big deal.   What they do very well, is make sauces/gravies for their dishes that are better than most. Uber creamy (perhaps from all the butter from which it takes its name), such that regardless of the solid part of the meal, the succulent sauce completely overwhelms it. Our paneer and lamb bases were very good, but the Tikka Masala and Muglai suspensions in which they swam were simply stupendous. With a little heat from the curries, and a spoon, not a drop was wasted. The garlic naan made the perfect tool for dipping/scooping as much rich gravy as possible.   This was really one of the best Indian sups I had enjoyed for a while. Even the Samosa Chaat appetizer was distinct enough with its ground potato/chickpea samosa and smaller crunchies and excellent tamarind flavoring to make us slow down and enjoy every morsel.   The only disappointment was the supposedly extravagant mango cheesecake. When it arrived, it was far smaller than expected, both in terms of length, width, volume, as well as taste. It was underwhelming to say the least. Maybe our expectations were too New York, but this job was not worth the $10 by half. Makhani does itself no favor by accentuating it as a popular delicious treat. It is not. Save your money for the real deal at better known cheesecake outlets.

Quick stop for a couple of slices and a drink on the way to a meeting.   The shop was nice in a slightly dated sort of way, and the kitchen was out front where everyone could see what was happening.  The service was friendly and prompt, as I told my waitperson I had a short time to get to my destination.  She complied.   The plain pizza slices were decent, but no better than what would pass for average in my part of the world.  Crust was firm enough to hold up its weight, but not overly crisp.  The sauce and cheese were okay, but not distinct.  Certainly a reasonable place to have lunch in the Far Northeast.  The dinner menu would be worth a try if in the area.    Thanks for lunch!

This Wendy's is freestanding in the parking lot of the shopping plaza that also contains Maryanne's Homestyle Restaurant.  It has not been completely modernized yet, but it is basically clean and ready for the effort Dave Thomas' ghost is making to upgrade their facilities. They do have that super soda dispenser that allows the customer to pour their own from a multitude of options.    We ordered the basic Dave's Single and Double, French Fries, and a drink.  Not bad, but both of our burgers were only slightly above room temperature.  They had obviously been cooked at some time before serving, and taken from a warming drawer to make the sandwich without a thought to reheating, or even putting the patty back on the grill for a couple of minutes before laying on the cold lettuce, tomato, cheese and onion.  Thus, while the veggies were cool and fresh, the main attraction suffered greatly by comparison, as the meat needed more heat to make it a full player.    Edible, but why couldn't they check on the patty and serve it at optimal temperature?    The soda machine was fun, though.  We probably should have gone to Maryanne's.

Grab-N-Go Bagel & Deli sits in the same commercial strip as Le Soleil Bakery and China Boys Restaurant. It is a neighborhood convenience store with a strong deli and grill department for good breakfasts and lunches.  Their inventory includes fresh bagels, muffins, and the right breads for making a superior Boar's Head sandwich.  They also offer Eight O'clock Coffee, the old A&P brand.  I have never seen it brewed for sale before.    My simple Onion Bagel, Butter and Swiss was prepared smartly, wrapped in foil and bagged in a minute.  With medium coffee, the $3.50 price was a true bargain.  Even better, the bagel was plump and freshly crisp on the outside and softly chewy within.  Can't be sure, but they may have gotten these babies from Bagel Stop over on Hamilton Ave.  I enjoyed the sandwich and the coffee cup sits on my desk as I write this review.  Still tastes good.   While this is not primarily a bagel shop, they can be forgiven because the rounders they do have are good, and the rest of their products are first rate, as long as you like Boar's Head.   Fast, friendly service.  Management on site.  Oh, Yeah....they also sell hookahs!

It is best to be a bit contrary to enjoy The Franklin Fountain.  Long and narrow shop with authentic antique early Americana, and the oldest working soda fountain in the USA, the place is worth a visit or two for that alone.  Servers in costume make it feel a bit touristy, but considering the entire facility is OLD, I can excuse the attempt at the Williamsburg effect.    But, in ice cream season the place is packed, often with lines onto the sidewalk.  So, if you don't mind eating ice cream in somewhat cooler weather, go anytime between October and April, or later in the evening, and the lines are gone.    The overall gestalt is very pleasant and it is obvious why TFF is a known destination. The ice cream is good, but not among the pantheon of ice cream greats.  The prices are high and not related to the quality nor quantity of the prime product. Too, it is CASH ONLY, something that is rather annoying given the expense of the product and the obvious fact that they can afford the extra bank card fees.    Bottom Line - Worth a visit for the experience and extra time in this oldest section of Philadelphia. But, they do themselves a disservice by not having credit card access, and failing to have air conditioning.

This tiny Spanish pizza joint is tucked in between a vape shop and an organic dry cleaner, and is very easy to miss, but AJ's is worth finding.  It is a family run business with the kids doing their homework at the back booth while mom and dad cook up a very good facsimile of authentic Italian food.    I stopped in last evening to see what it was all about and to satisfy my hunger.  Warmly greeted, I perused the menu and ordered the Eggplant Parm Sandwich and a drink.  While waiting, I observed the daughter working on a book report, while her infant brother was being entertained by an older sibling.  Mom worked as the chief chef and cashier, while a couple of other guys helped out, all the while keeping up a lively conversation en Espanol.    The food arrived with the mozza melted over the top of the eggplant and filing the valley made by the open torpedo roll.  First bite, very hot, but tender nightshade nicely contrasted by the well toasted and crunchy roll.  Surprisingly, the thin slices of eggplant were not breaded, but were allowed to stand for themselves.  Gratitude for the calorie saving.  The overall consumption was a pleasure, with even the olive oil adding to the experience.    AJ Pizza could use some elbow grease in the corners to avoid being a dive, but the dining was fine.  I will return to explore further.  And, at $6.50 for the big sandy, they well matched the local gentry and the jingle in my pocket.  UPDATE : APRIL 4, 2018  Stopped in this afternoon for a late lunch, and in a pasta aglio olio mood. The menu offered it with broccoli, but chef was happy to make it with spinach. For $7.95 it came with a small side salad and three of their garlic knots.    I should have further asked for penne, because what arrived on a large square plate was spaghetti with plenty of sauteed spinach and thin sliced garlic. Not a biggie, but I laughed at myself for missing that detail. Laughed again when I had to ask for a soup spoon in order to be able to spin it onto the fork for neat consumption. Details.   When I finally got down to it, the taste was very good and enjoyable. The biggest surprise on the upside was  the garlic knots that were hand delivered wrapped in aluminum foil a few minutes later. They were amazingly excellent! Great texture, perfectly baked and brought to life by the oven flame. Spiced and crunchy with strong garlicy flavor, and designed to sponge all the aglio olio swimming in the bottom of the platter. Best of breed.   AJ's doesn't look like much, and could use some TLC, but if you can look beyond that, you can find some decent grub and even some awesome details.

Taste King Restaurant is a generic Chinese restaurant established to satisfy the American palate. The house has been at this location for decades and has changed ownership at least once.  Of late, the neighborhood has taken on a distinct East European flavor, and Taste King certainly caters to it.  The night we were there a birthday party was in full swing with toasts and song in both Russian and English.    The menu is what you would expect from experience in most other Chinese/American shops, with a few specials designed by the chef that still tend to be variations on the established theme.  Pick a protein and the desired flavor; surround with rice or noodles; add on wonton or hot & sour soup, and those broad fried noodles for dipping in duck sauce and/or hot mustard. Voila! Your platter appears ready to consume.    We ordered lightly.  Hot & sour soup and chicken corn soup. Grandpa's chicken and a bowl of white rice.  We had just come from great foot massage down the road, and weren't overly hungry.    The soups were good, but not exceptional.  The hot and sour should have been warmed up more. The taste was about right.  The chicken corn was better. Certainly hot enough, but the surface was covered with tiny bubbles suggesting some chemical process was at work under the surface.  The Grandpa Chicken was made up of large chunks of white meat bird, wokked and covered in a dark red amber glaze sauce that was mildly spicy and enjoyable to eat. Only downside was that the chicken needed cutting before eating, making use of chopsticks problematic.  We found a work around.   Service was spotty.  Our waiter was attentive at times, and AWOL at others.  He delivered the soup and chicken with style, and then dropped the silverware on the table when he brought us ice cream after we received the check.  Whaaat?  There are more authentic Chinese restaurants a few miles farther down Bustleton, which compare favorably to Taste King. Try them all and decide for yourself which is preferable.

Most people who take the train north or south from the Trenton Transit Center would rather be someplace else. Although rebuilt and modernized in the fairly recent past, it is still an unpleasant place to visit even for five minutes.   Yet, I was surprised to find Pizza-Grill.com in the back of the station near the exit doors.  It actually has a café feel to it, with a few tables and chairs (and umbrellas) for sitting while eating their grub. The food offerings were far more extensive than expected; with sandwiches, wraps, breakfasts and pizza all on the menu, and hours starting from 4 AM to midnight. Friday and Saturday they are full tilt for 24.   It's not that the pizza I sampled was great - it was fair, at best. Even after requesting a well done reheat, it was still heavy with cheese than was warmed at its core, but far from hot.  The taste was okay, but in this capital city of tomato pie, that is not really good enough. There is so much awesome pizza around these parts that mediocre is just mediocre.  So, what it is, is, a pleasant surprise for Trenton train station, but beyond that, not a place atop your "Must Try" list. Nice enough if hungry while waiting for a train. Otherwise, not really worth the trip.  ART NOTE - There are some beautiful ceramic tiles placed around the Center (see photos) and a few right next to Pizza-Grill.  Really like the work, and would purchase a few of the local scenes if I knew where to find them. In fact, even Pizza Grill has murals painted on the walls of the shop that show talent.

Manny Brown's is in the Summit Square Shopping Center, down the strip from Giant Supermarket, and close by Moishe & Itzy's Deli.    How much more interesting both places would be if they knocked down the wall and served each other's customers.  Pastrami and beer, and 13 TVs would be a boon to both.  Maybe, this will start them talking.  I know they are not directly next to each other, but why should that stop the integration of interests?  Manny's is a friendly place with a game plan of serving a good mix of draft crafty beer, and a decent bar menu.  It does not have the room to offer the alternatives of Isaac Newton's, nor the diveyness of The Clubhouse to be a buffalo wing sports bar, but falls somewhere between the two.  Neither is the clientele the same as those mentioned.  It is not as yuppified as Isaac's, nor as dank and noisy as Clubhouse.  It servers those who are somewhere in the middle on the day they choose to go there.  It provides a reasonable alcohol component, satisfying grub and sports with the sound turned down.  A good compromise on the right occasion.   I was there on a Saturday afternoon during the World Cup.  The bar was mostly empty except for a few couples as tables awaiting lunch.  I was looking for a quick bite as I selected which TV monitor to watch.  I went with their Burger and Fries - a juicy half pounder with Sautéed Onions, Melted Swiss, and a large pile of Fries, and the Columbia v. Greece match.  I relaxed with a Domestic Draft awaiting service of my lunch, and chatted with the bartender trainee and her manager.  They were friendly, and clearly into their jobs.    The Burger was quite satisfying and would qualify as comfort food on those nights when necessary.  The price at under $10. for the meal was an excellent deal.    I wondered why I did not go there more often, and resolved to remedy that oversight in the near future.

1742.  Old enough for you?   The Washington House has anchored the heart of Sellersville, PA, since before the Revolution. Now, teamed with the Sellersville Theater next door, it offers a great destination in northern Bucks County to eat, drink, sleep and be entertained.   We drove up late Friday afternoon to buy tickets for the upcoming Indigenous rock/blues concert. It was a beautiful drive. Parking was right across the street, and the box office was open for business. This will be covered in more detail in a subsequent review.   The Washington House beckoned next door, so we walked down the street and entered through the bar. It was dim with long bar to the left and dining room to the right. We arrived at the right moment as there were several stools open. We grabbed two and we're immediately greeted by a tender who informed us that they were doing an Octoberfest Beer Tasting event, and we were just in time to join in.   Yes, we will. Thank you.  We chose Flight One, consisting of three 6 ounce pours of Paulaner Hefe Weissbier, Hardwood Park Pills and River Horse Cherry Berliner Weisse. They all came from freshly opened bottles. They were each distinct and very good. The Hefe was mildly bitter and peppery with a hint of clove and a surprising ripe banana-like end note. The Park Pils tasted of grass and grains and was cloudy like cider. The Cherry Berliner was sour and tart with a soft ruddy red tint. If we had more time we definitely would have saddled up for dinner and a second and third flight. Others had joined us at the bar and the dishes they were served were mighty appealing.   Our impressions were so positive of Washington House that we decided we would come back for a full night of revelry with music, food, drink and room upstairs so as to extend the celebration to breakfast the next morning.   If only the theater next door had bruncheon concerts!

Not sure how this one got passed the filters, but Broad St Car Wash and Broad Street Car Wash are one in the same.    They both do a very good job cleaning my vehicle of all the ashiness that covers the sheet metal (polymer) after snow and salt get finished turning the wheels into a ghost.   If I had to choose between one or the other, I would probably choose Street, as St implies sainthood, and I doubt that this "Shine On Line" operation is on the short list for canonization.   Although, there are times I thank the Almighty for creating this automated wonder of the world.

Those of us who remember and enjoyed the heyday of the Chambersburg section of Trenton, NJ, with Italian restaurants on practically every corner, felt a special sadness as one after another they began to close or move out of town to the suburbs. Over the last two decades as the neighborhood changed and the original families moved to greener lawns and better schools, they took most of their traditions and cultural institutions with them. When Amici's closed it's doors recently, the Italian era of this capital city was officially over.   Yet, there is another casa Siciliana still going strong after 30 years at the same location. It might not be in the "Burg," but sure feels like it once you step inside. Enzo's sits almost invisibly on the northern end of Princeton Avenue in Lawrenceville, west of the Brunswick Circle. It is a small, cozy, darkly lit, romantic hideaway, where the Scozzari family has been running a pure Italian kitchen for two generations. I sure hope there is a third.  Park in back and walk past the outdoor dining area, through the front door and then a second one on the right. Step down into the small dining room and be greeted by Anna, daughter of the namesake Enzo, who will seat you at one of only dozen or so tables, and hand you the menu. Moments later, the head waiter approaches with water and description of the available specials. There is a small lunch menu with soups, sandwiches, and pasta plates.   They didn't have the Italian Hot Dog I desired (being removed from the menu), but the suggested alternative, their "World Famous Meatball Sandwich," sounded about right.   And, it was. Excellently garlicked, crusty toasty Italian loaf, stuffed with hand-rolled meatballs,  sauteed broccoli rabe, spinach and roasted red peppers, with a side a sweet tater fries, all on a large white round plate. Delicious! I like to deconstruction a sandwich and eat its elements separately to savor each ingredient. I did that for half and had a mouthful of flavor with each bite. It was unforgettable. The second half I attacked​ en masse. Cleaving through it and enjoying the texture and taste of each bite as they melded in my mouth. No red gravy here. Just each part doing its job to make me happy. Quite a total experience for a lunch.   Got to go back for a romantic dinner soon with the woman of my dreams and a couple bottles of Chianti.  Enzo's is the real thing.

Carrabba's Italian Grill on Street Road across from Parx Casino, is a roadhouse with large bar, and substantial dining room. Although claiming to be authentic Italiano cuisine, it is really more of a hybrid with modern Americano thrown in to keep things interesting. We showed up on Super Bowl Sunday evening, suspecting that the game might suck, and we should be prepared with Plan B - a meal we could enjoy without need of huge HDTVs on the walls that demanded to be watched.   Well, we were half right. The game was not worth watching. The food was somewhat more entertaining, but definitely not Italiano robusto. We ordered the calamari and minestrone apps/sides, and entrees of chicken marsala and lasagna. There was a side salad in there somewhere, too. Have to say, that while everything was okay, none of it was kickass.   The calamari had an unusual breading that made it quite salty, despite the better than decent dipping sauce. No complaints about the soup, but the salad with house dressing, was, well, dull. Not worth finishing. My lasagna was middle of the road, with decent gravy, but the mozza and added Romano-grate were salty. There was not enough heft in the sauce, nor the pasta to give it any tasty substance. Finally, the marsala mushrooms were pretty good, but although we appreciated the large grilled chicken breast, it was not designed to be balanced with the sauce and mushrooms. The chicken was the dominant feature, rather than a melding with thin medallions, tender enough to mix perfectly with the marsala reduction. It was all about the chicken, not the dish.   We ate in the barroom. It was cozy and our server was a quality dude with excellent skills. I sort of felt sorry for him working beneath his rank at this not quite good enough and salty restaurant.

Munchie's Café was recommended to me by the phlebotomist who drew my blood for pre-op testing at Penn Med last week. I asked for a place to have a quick breakfast after fasting since midnight. She advised that Munchie's was popular with the staff because of a broad menu and reasonable prices. As she had just been expert in hitting an artery on the first attempt, I figured she'd be accurate on food choices as well.   This long/deep shop sits just off the southeast corner of 7th and Chestnut. Ordering is done at the counter, and delivered to the table. I really felt the need for coffee stronger than for sustenance, so I ordered a breakfast wrap and large java. I got to pour the joe myself at the coffee service table, and sipped while waiting for the food. The drink was decent industrial strength drip that lost its joy of living as it cooled. Became more bitter the longer it sat. The wrap of bacon, egg and cheese in wheat, was just okay.  The bacon was unrecognizable, and had a odd taste. Perhaps, it was beef or turkey bacon without designation.   So, while the grub served to abate my caffeine and hunger gnawings, it was not something I would return for. It was average at best, although the prices were about right for what was provided. There are far superior places in the neighborhood to bring mind, body and soul up to speed.

The best place to stop before a long drive north or south coming from Newtown, this DD is hidden in the office/hotel complex next to the Hampton Inn, right of Rt. 95.    The coffee is decent (far better than the coffee @ the other DD in Newtown), and the staff organized and efficient.  While I am not a fan of their baked goods, push come to shove, I can be found with breakfast sandy or toasted bagel in my possession.  My 13 year old goes for milk and a couple of glazed rounders.    All in all, a reasonably tasty coffee at a good price, with a smiling face.  I don't need more than that at a caffeine oasis.

Great to spend the morning in Fishtown having breakfast at the Milkcrate Cafe at the corner of E. Columbia and Girard. Interesting enviro with a huge record collection spanning music of the late 20th/early 21st Centuries. I didn't make it down to the vinyl shop in the basement (just read about it in their Yelp page), but as a holder of old wax, I wish I had. Next time.   Still, the cafe is part of the gentrification of this part of Philly and is in the perfect location to take advantage of it. It is a bit dusty around the edges, but with La Colombe coffee holding court and a good kitchen, it offers a mellow sitdown and strong java flow, with comfort food designed for the pioneering spirit of the surrounding neighborhood. Easy to spend hours there sipping joe and doing light sledding on your screen.   Loved the caffeine and found the well stuffed "Flying Breakfast Burrito Brother" a large tasty bite and chew. It was hot and moist and almost more than I could eat; but I managed to slay that dragon, and spend a few extra minutes watching the street life on Girard Avenue on a cold sunny morn.   It would be great to have a home on one of the narrow streets of this old revivalist corner of P.delph, but until that day arrives, Milkcrate will just have to be that place I can feel at home.

While Jamison Pour House is a comfortable roadside stop for beer and light meals. I have the impression that it is fighting out of its weight class trying to be more than it is. I stopped in to catch the Sunday afternoon NFL games on the multiple HDTVs on the walls surrounding the square bar. Plenty of stools available and a friendly crowd.   I selected Downeast Cider and their Jamison Patty Melt (medium), as the accompaniment to my entertainment. Service was prompt, efficient and friendly. I liked the tart apple taste of the hard cider, but $6.50 for a pint seemed hazardous to my health. One was enough at that price.   Too, the burger, though large and the right finish, was not the most flavorful I've ever had, and it crumbled as it cooled. Needed knife and fork due to the slickness of the Russian dressing, gruyere and natural greasiness of the puck. It was slip 'n slide all the way from plate to mouth. The heavier gauge friction of real rye would have helped over the lighter loaf used. It was still okay, but could have been a contender with more faithfulness to the concept. For $13, more was reasonably expected.   These folks should consider a weekend happy hour slot to draw people in with lower prices, just like during the week. It wasn't crowded this Sunday mid afternoon, and a little marketing might do the trick. No one minds saving a few bucks, even on the weekend.

Great Valley Diner on Route 30 in Malvern, PA, sits in a former fast food structure, but aside from the general boxy nature of the space, it has escaped its past, and now looks something like what it is - a kitchen for three squares a day. It has a small counter with three or four spinners, and a dining room with a dozen or so booths and tables. The menu has all the usual suspects, especially breakfast, with a full list of egg/omelet, pancake/french toast possibilities and decent coffee served in red mugs.   I went with their Italian Omelet, but subbed feta cheese for their regular provolone.  No sweat.  It was served less than ten minutes later and was quite good, with crispy home fries and rye toast.  There were plenty of sweet sausage, onion and pepper in addition to the fresh feta.  Service was provided by a family member, who was pleasant and attentive.  My red mug was refilled twice without request.   Adequate parking. Exiting from the connecting shopping plaza onto Route 30, a bit confusing.   3.5 STARS

Cheesecake Factory may be the quintessential modern American diner. Huge diverse menu and awesome desserts. Yeah, it doesn't exactly look like a stainless roadside palace; designed to appear more like a massive adobe warehouse on the outside and something out of the fantasiful Arabian Nights, within. While not a regular visitor, sometimes it is exactly what I am looking for, especially when the answer to every existential question is, "cheesecake!"  It certainly filled that bill last night. We weren't sure what we wanted for dinner, but knew what we didn't. Tired of checking off all the ethnic styles available within driving distance and eliminating most of them, we came to Cheesecake Factory. It had dishes from all continents, a bar, and those awesome creamy sweet cool desserts. Perfect cure for indecisiveness. We drove to Willow Grove in about 30. The expansive hall was busy but not full. We were seated immediately near the bar.  We caught the final minutes of happy hour and celebrated with half price glasses of an excellent cabernet. We selected the Crispy Brussel Sprouts for an appetizer (wonderfully done with bacon and maple syrup), and their Southwest Chicken Sandwich (strong contender in a crunchy baguette and spicy aioli), and Shepherd's Pie (savory ground beef and veggies in mushroom gravy topped with a load of mashed potatoes and melted cheese). Toasting our way through the meal, we completed with a flourish of a thick slice of shared almond cheesecake (they bake them right).   This was a full and fun dinner that permitted us to chose cravings that we didn't know we had. We couldn't finish any of it, and brought enough home for another meal. Cheesecake Factory may not see us again for a while, but it's good to know it's there when we need the modern American diner to help us decide what to eat.

Another great early summer night along the Mighty Delaware watching Trenton Thunder baseball.    We dined exclusively from Chickie's and Pete's this time.  Italian Sausage with Pepper and Onions, Trenton Hot Dogs (stuffed with Potato, Pepper and Pickle), and Crab Fries. I was surprised at the quality of the Sausage, and how well it was grilled just before being slapped into the fresh Italian Roll.  Even the P & O were sautéed correctly.  The Fries were dosed in Old Bay Seasoning and came with a side of Creamy Cheese Dressing for dipping.  All that for under $23.    We were all smiles despite a loss by the home team to New Hampshire.

El Changarro ( "small shop") in Mexican Spanish slang,  is exactly that - a small grocery/variety store with a Mexican Guatamaltecan kitchen and dining room in the rear. Like most of the other Latina cocinas in and around Bucks County, it caters to the growing population from south of that border so much in the news lately. (Have to say from observation that there are many more good cooks and entrepreneurs entering the USA, than undesirables. I guess the wall is to limit the number of Mexican restaurants setting up businesses around the country.) Please excuse the editorial.   So, I was there for a weekend dinner recently having learned about the joint on Yelp. As directed, I walked through the store to the dining area in back. It was pretty big. About a dozen tables nicely spaced,  colorful mural on the walls and wood carved people with amusing faces and traditional costume all around. The gestalt back there was definitely a little reality altering. It almost became a Mexican town square.   Food was ordered at the kitchen window and delivered to the table. My order was taken by a bilingual young guy. It was prepared by three women who were not. The menu had most of the usual suspects and house made bebidas and liquidas frescas. I went with an al pastor quesadilla rather than three tacos, to increase the contents and reduce the amount of tortilla. It was served about 10 minutes later. It was plump from all the spicy roast pork, beans, lettuce, tomato, pineapple and queso. It required knife and fork to avoid spillage.   Liked it a lot. Plenty of flavor and texture. Moist, too. I spread red salsa on top to ensure adequate burn. Filled me completely and left a pleasant belch at the finish. Ahh.   Right down Street Road from Parx Casino, in a shopping center with plenty of parking. Worth a trip.

"...'Cause I want to be there Wanna go back down and get high by the sea there  With a tin cup for a chalice Fill it up with good red wine And I'm a chewin' on a honeysuckle vine..." (Tin Cup Chalice - Jimmy Buffet - Highway A1A)   Turns out that you don't have to go all the way to Key West, FLA, to enjoy the benefits of its easy living ways. These days you can detour to Bristol, PA, and stop in to Cindy's Café on old Mill Street, and have breakfast or lunch within its sunny clime. The local family running the show loves both Bristol and Key West, and lives in both. They come by their passion for Trop Rock and old downtowns on the river naturally.   The former Station Stop has been transformed into a bright, cheerful beachside retreat, where good coffee and delicious meals abide. The walls are covered with their personal artifacts, from post cards to family photos to clothing worn to protect them from the Tropic of Cancer sun. Steve, Patty and Kelly are excited and proud of what they have created out of personal tragedy, and they all work with heart, soul and mind fully invested.   My sausage, egg and cheddar breakfast sandwich was one of the better renditions I have had the pleasure to devour.  There is a real chef in the kitchen who knows that runny fried eggs are much better than a hard finish, and the use of a fresh, quality roll or bun is the best way to contain the dynamic ingredients, and absorb the drippage for delectable texture and flavor. The side of home fries was a nice extra touch, although I am partial to skin-on red bliss potatoes for my morning fries. The java was hot and strong, too.   Mill Street is really coming on with many new restaurants and shops. What was once a main drag to avoid, has become a place of entertaining choices, with international cuisine and loads of local talent. Cindy's Café also does its own Key Lime Pie @ $3.50 a slice. Very tempting for later in the day.   "...Big straw hat, banana drink I can't remember what it is I think And my, my, my - Key Lime Pie... Not too tart, not too sweet My baby loves to watch me eat Her Key Lime Pie Her Key Lime Pie!...  (Key Lime Pie - Kenny Chesney - Be As You Are; Songs from an Old Blue Chair)  Will be back for that KLP, KLP.

The main entrance and bar of Baker's American Bar & Grille is around the back, so best to drive behind the building on Street Road in Southampton. Big parking lot back there. Ready access up the stairs and into the semicircular barroom, but not ADA compliant.  Place was nearly empty when I arrived around 6:30 to watch the Steelers-Patriots game. Sat at the bar, with HDTVs all around and a friendly barkeep happy for some company. Ordered an Amstel Light draft and asked for a menu. Went with the American Burger with pepper jack cheese. After the order was in I was shown the separate bar menu with light bar food from $5, including sliders and pizza. Just wish he brought it to my attention earlier, so I could have ordered more or less the same thing at less than half the price.   Just saying, it would have been nice to know.   The burger was 8 oz., with average taste and a nice load of crisp fries. It was served on wax paper on a plastic tray. Not appealing given I could only put the sandwich down on top of its dripped grease. I guess they we're saving on dish washing.   The Amstel was cold and refreshing.   Also ordered the spicy sausage pizza to go. Ate it later with the family when they got home. It was also okay, but not something I would return for. Far better bar pies in the area.   I enjoyed the game.

Tu's Tea & Banh Mi is the second Vietnamese sandwich and bubble tea shop opened by Tu's-day group (Couldn't resist). Although there are a few other places along Washington selling the traditional sammy, including a bakery west of Broad with excellent baguettes, Tu's uses better ingredients, wraps the work tightly in faux newsprint, and presents it in a red plastic basket. The loaf is not quite French, but is plenty good enough with the roast pork I had. Each bite left crusty crumbs on the table.    My bubble tea special was refreshing with large mango and coconut pieces swimming with tapioca balls that jammed the straw with every draw. I confess to not "getting" the bubble tea thing, but this one was cool, sweet and chewy. Not my favorite textures, but enjoyable nonetheless.   The only shortcoming was the Salt & Pepper Wings advertised as a new thing.  I love the Chinese version of salt & pepper cuisine found in the spicier houses, but these were not that.  Rather, the wings were thickly coated in breading that included a load of sodium chloride and black pepper.  They were overly deep fried to a dark brown, and as a result were encased in the breading rather than simply dressed in it.  Wouldn't order them again.    The shop itself is small, with 4-5 tables along one wall, and very high counter separation between dining and work area.  Felt defensive, not utilitarian.   Tu's is a worthwhile stop for Banh Mi and a drink, but wouldn't venture far beyond that on their menu.

All the usual suspects on the breakfast and lunch menu at Hatboro TNT Diner, and surprisingly good prices, too. That explains the dominance of the social security crowd. They know a good deal when they see one.   True, this is formerly a Wendy's burger house, and the outlines of the old small version franchise from the 1980s shows. Still, it is clean, well run and has a friendly serving staff capable of keeping you coffee cup full and quality small talk. This is an adaptive reuse that still works in the 21st.   My french toast was a well made two slice platter which was enough for me, decent sausage patties and a bottomless cup of java. I've had worse at twice the price.   What it lacks in local color, it makes up for in solid deliverables and stirling repartee with staff.   Thanks, Debbie.

What a great place for a rock concert!   300 seat theater. All unobstructed views. "Cafe" up front for members who love their music up close, personal and full of sprayed sweat. Even we peons in Row O were just above the heads of the band and had perfect location for the sound and fury. Comfortable seats and room enough to stand and boogie when the proper riffs blew us out of our chairs.   Indigenous was fantastic! The opening act, Greg Soder Band played bluesy rock for 20 minutes and then gracefully moved aside for Mato Nanji and his mates to take off the roof. This Native American group from North Dakota has been rocking since the late 1990s. The members have changed, but the raw talent and energy has not. Mato is a complete original heavy guitarist. He sounds like a cross between Stevie Ray Vaughn, Jimi Hendrix and Carlos Santana with Warren Haynes thrown in. His own songs are very good, and when he segues into Voodoo Child, Little Wing and I'm a Man instrumental, he amplifies and projects a towering presence that just sends the house into orbit.   And, when all is sung and done, and they have played their last encore, they come to the lobby for a meet & greet. No rush. Just hanging with their fans, signing autographs and selling their latest CD. Friendly, grateful and totally engaged.   Sellersville Theater is a gift from the rock and blues gods. How I wish the folks running the old Newtown Theater would take a chance and run some hot music through it's stage.

You can tell that folks in the Newtown, Bucks County, PA, area were hungry for great pizza, because Vince's Pizzeria and Taproom was absolutely jammed at 4:30 on the weekday afternoon I stopped in to check it out. There was hardly an empty parking space to be found.   And, I understand why. Our region has a load of pizza shops, but extremely few that really know the pizza business (read, none). The people behind Vince's have several generations invested in making superlative dough and sauce, and using quality cheeses to create exceptional pies. Only the sainted DeLorenzo's transplanted from Jersey compares.   Luckily for me, there was room at one of the large community tables in the back of the house. Everyone was friendly and welcoming. We ended up in extended conversations as we chowed down. There was a couple from Yardley, and another from Trenton, NJ. We were all there to sample the wares, and drink from the fountain of beers along the rear wall. It worked fairly well, although it was obvious that they were still on their shakedown cruise, this being their first week in operation.   The taproom concept is still new and not readily available. It requires the purchase of a RFID chipped card that attaches above the tap to the beer selected, releasing the brew into 12 oz. glasses which are filled by the customer. The available inventory is pictured above each tap, with brief description to help you choose. The beer card is good for 32 oz., after which you must pay for a reinfusion of funds. It all gets a bit complicated, as it seemed that the staff was repeated asking for a credit card for that, and again at check out. I handed mine over three times - there should be a better system in place.   Yet, all is forgiven because the tomato pie/pizza is so damn good! The crust is thin, but stays firm from first munch to last. No drooping points here. The taste is like a first rate cracker, with a little saltiness that offsets the mild sweetness of the sauce above. There is just the right ratio of red to white, so there is no excess run off from cheese oils, nor watery tomatoes. From first steaming bite to last cool belly filler, the consistency is constant with crunchy crust and easily distinguishable ingredients. These are high quality pies.   All  I can say is that the other pizza joints in and around Newtown are in trouble now. The competition just jumped up a few notches. Once word gets out that Vince's is the new sheriff in town, the old boys will find themselves out of luck, and will have to improve their game if they want to stay in business.   It's about time!  Thank you, Vince's!

Generally speaking, the Chinese restaurants in the far Northeast Philadelphia have been disappointing. Most seem to have settled into a "good enough" attitude when it comes to their kitchens, with little effort for excellence, nor originality. It is regrettable that the locals have few decent choices until they are prepared to travel farther down Bustleton, or all the way to Chinatown for a good meal.    One of the few exceptions to such poor performances is Taste Queen on Krewstown Road, just off Grant Avenue.  We settled in there for dinner late last week, and found it to be refreshingly concerned about quality cooking and satisfied knowledgeable customers. While it is accurate to called the "Queen" a study in pink as others mention, that eye-irritant is soon forgotten when dinner is brought to the table.  We were able to request a higher heat quotient than normal from our Hunan Chicken and Orange Beef, and actually have it prepared as we wished.  Both were large platters, with extra spicy black bean sauce on the chicken, and real Szechuan peppers mixed in with the tender beef.  They were so satisfying that we did not need to ask for more sesame oil or chili sauce. Very good job!  What was even more surprising was their rendition of Pumpkin Soup, on their Specials Board.  It was rich, creamy and very fresh.  Someone in the kitchen knows a thing or two about non-Chinese cuisine.   Service was friendly and prompt, and the server didn't mind me practicing my baby Chinese.  She was quite amused.   Finally an above average Chinois joint within range of home that meets our expectations for good Middle Kingdom dishes.    Return guaranteed.

Chili's has refurbished many of its stores, but basically maintained the same approach to fast casual cuisine and comfort.  Burgers, salads, ribs are the mainstays, with a reasonable bar.    This one just off Oxford Valley Road across from the mall of the same name is no different.  We stopped in for lunch last Saturday, and found the space full of HDTVs on mute, and enjoyable rock & roll soundtracks.  Service was friendly and prompt.  Our server was a bit of a character, and had a fun shtick with running repartee.    We ordered the Baked Potato Soup and the 4 Sliders app to share.  The Soup was fine, but we did not expect it to be more cheesy than creamy.  It actually detracted from the anticipated potato flavor.  The Sliders were the Medium finish requested, with long wooden spikes spearing them together.  They had sautéed onion and ein bissel cheese melted over the top.  They were pretty good, and exactly the right amount for light lunch and two stomachs to enjoy.    The Sam Adams Rebel IPA draft was appropriately hoppy and cold.  Not my fave, but okay.    Overall, this Chili's was about average for the genre.  No big complaints about the grub and drinks, but nothing to get wild about.   PRO TIP - Be careful choosing your table, as they are not aligned with the low hanging light fixtures.  So easy to stand up and klonk your head on the heavy glass.  I was warned by our comedic waiter, but still gave myself a klep en vant.

Once upon a time, Vince's Pizza in Yardley was a regular stop on the underground pizza railway running from Bristol up to Riegelsville.   It seems that somewhere along the way Vince's recipe or his touch for making good tomato pie got lost.  Today, my slices were doughy rather than crisp, not well reheated in the oven, and had a slightly bitter taste.  Too, it failed the most crucial pizza test - when lifted off the paper plate the point sagged like an old dog ear and immediately began to drip oil.  This was not the experience I was anticipating when I stopped in to renew acquaintances with one of my old haunts.    The price for the slices and small drink was just slightly above 5 bucks, which was great, but I would have gladly paid more for quality pizza.   Oh, woe is me.  How the mighty have fallen.

Palantes Italian Deli is a first rate small shop loaded to the gills with specialties from the Boot. They offer house made meats and pasta trays, as well as smoked meats from the old country. Think of it as a mini DiBruno's, and you get an idea of what is going on in there. Just too bad it isn't larger so that it could show more delectables. Too, it would be great to have a seating area and mange what they turn out right on the premises.   We stopped in for lunch earlier in the week. I ordered an eggplant parm sandwich, which was excellent from crusty sesame loaf down to the well double fried nightshade and mildly tart red sauce. My companion ordered a personal size pizza with sausage. That disc left my car with a pleasant aroma for days afterwards. Will be returning for one of those babies.   Staff was pleasant and very knowledgeable. Prices were fair, but it is hard to walk away with just a sandwich when the shelves are full of interesting and tasty snacks and side dish possibilities.   Palantes is almost too good for the neighborhood, yet with Richboro Coffee right next door, the opportunity to trade off each other presents several excellent choices for nosh and java combos. Wonder if the coffee vendor would permit someone to enjoy a tasty repast at their small sitting area and make the world a better place for everyone?   I would definitely sign up for that!

One door closes. Another door opens.    I drove to Glenside for breakfast at a well known diner close by the Keswick Theater. The doors were locked and lights off on a midweek morning, and no notice posted that it was closed for vacation, or for good? Having come that far, I checked Yelp for an alternative kitchen in the neighborhood. It showed me Welcome Home, a cafe about two miles away in Jenkintown.   I arrived there and found meter parking around the corner for $.50 for an hour.   This is a small cubby hole of a breakfast/lunch joint. 8 deuce tables at most. Walking in, I was greeted warmly by a lovely woman, who exclaimed, "Welcome Home." She immediately warmed my heart with her salutation. I sat in the back of the dining room, right in front of the glass partition with the kitchen. I was handed their small menu, followed quickly by a mugga joe. It was hot and brisk. I inquired about the French Toast Casserole. Learning that it was very sweet, and asked that it be less so. She said that could be done, and a few moments later, I had a three inch high stack of Texas Toast that had been well dipped in a egg/sugar/cinnamon/vanilla slurry and pan fried/assembled into one united structure. Strawberries and cream on top.   Yes. It was delicious from top to bottom, and even the accompanying sausage links played their second fiddle role well. I came in joneszing for sweet fried bread, and was completely satisfied.   Welcome Home is Black Woman owned and operated by Stephanie, who is the guiding light and creative force. Her personality dominates the proceedings in a great way. The combination of character and kitchen magic makes this place a keeper and highly worthy of your exploration. Be sure to bring hungry taste buds.  But for living in Bucks County, I would make Welcome Home a true and regular stop on my breakfast trail. It is that unique and appealing.

In the never ending search for good joints to hang out in while waiting for court to start, Yelp directed me to Jersey Bagel Café on Woodlane Road, which is right around the corner from the vicinage I was to appear in on a wet Tuesday morning.  It sits in the forlorn Tarnsfield Plaza, along with a few other lost souls and a store front law firm.    Walking in, I was pleasantly surprised by the décor.  It was dressed up as a country back porch with trellis and picnic sentimentality.  The women behind the counter were pleasant and prompt in their attention.  My order was quickly taken and prepared, and the price reflected the probable rent on the shop.  Cheap!  My Onion Bagel with Butter and Swiss was pretty good.  The rounder's crust could have been crisper, but the innards were light and airy as I prefer.  Given the precip outside, expecting a crunch might have been a pipedream. The coffee was decent, but not a premium bean.    I was comfortable sitting there, eating and reading the digital Washington Post.  It was quiet with only one other eat-in customer and a few take outs.  I will return on a dry day to sample their wares again, and if the crunch presents, I will have found a cool place to chill while I await an appearance before the bar.

Nonno's (Grandfather's) Bakery on South York Street, Hatboro, PA, is an old school Italian artisanal bake shop where everything you behold is made on site, and generally produces high quality cookies, pastries, donuts, fruit tarts, pies and an extraordinary number of marzipan fruit miniatures.   I stopped in after lunch down the street at Gallo Tropical, looking for interesting desserts for me and to take home for the fam. Upon entry I quickly realized that I had entered an unexpected time machine that would carry me back to childhood adventures with my parents and grandparents shopping the small ethnic stores in the Upper West Side of Manhattan, where Jewish and Italian delis, butchers, fish mongers and fruit stalls kept us fed and connected to our heritage.   Nonno's display cases were full of beautiful cakes and the like that required time to explore and difficult choices to be made among the incredible bounty of colorful, luxuriously tempting items. There is a health limit to the quantity of sugar anyone should consume, and this bakery would push that to the max. So, I let my camera do the tempting while I selected only a few things that were turning me on. A slice of carrot cake to cover the pastries, two donut twists to sample their coffee companions, and a marzipan banana to tease on the fruit bowl of choices created by the creative hand of their talented almond paste sculptors. Sure, it wasn't enough, but now I know where these artists are, and can return at will.  The carrot cake was not what I imagined would be a heavy cake base with uber sweet cream cheese icing; but instead a light gingery cake and a mildly sweet layer of butternut-like topping. It was excellent in this format. More subtle taste than the diner version. The donuts were a yeasty twist, still moist and chewy, with a delicious thin layer of icing that was a slow pleasure to eat. Better than anticipated. The marzipan banana (as were all the trayed fruit) was a softly firm almond paste that was best taken in small bites and masticated with attention to the release of that unique and seductive almond flavor that expanded as chewed. Ummm...  It wasn't a complete Roman heaven. I skipped the cookies covered with jimmies, and the cannoli prefilled with vanilla sweet ricotta (I'm not a jimmies guy, and prefer my cannoli filled when ordered). Nonetheless, Nonno's Bakery is a worthy destination to satisfy that part of your sweet tooth that can only be satisfied by high quality old world goodies.

Their Mission Statement: "Using creativity and improvisation to maximize human potential."   Even sitting in the audience of the Newtown Theater, it was apparent how effective Unscripted Productions in general, and The Teachers' Lounge troupe in particular, was in bringing parts of human personality to the fore and holding everyone involved in the light, both spiritually and klieg.   Will Dennis and his three companions were a high energy team involving the audience in their skits and even calling them up to the stage to join in the spontaneous merriment. Give them three unusual objects, moments in history or dialogue from Neil Simon plays, and they return with an hilarious sketch called out if their interactive imagination. It was all great!   Although the evening began as a fundraiser for local candidates a week before the election, it quickly became an exercise in team building and support for the final get out the vote push, while it also showed another side of all of us who were ready for some fun after so many month of all too serious campaigning. Didn't know how funny those guys were!   So, we raised some money, ate some good food provided by local restaurants and delis, and enjoyed an unexpectedly wonderful evening.   Thanks so much Unscripted Productions.   Creative Improv = Creative Improve

This may now be La Parrilla Steakhouse, but for me it will always also be DeLorenzo's on Hamilton Avenue, Trenton, NJ.  I was there too many times eating excellent pizza to be able to forget what came before.   Ho Hum.  But, that is not to say that this new Guatemaltecan meat house is not a very worthy successor.  It certainly is.  Where most Latino restaurants in and around the capital city are geared to feeding the neighborhood in a very down-country homey and comfortable dive (in a good way), La Parrilla has higher aspirations.  It is a degree or two fancier than most other casas, and the focus is primarily on meat in all forms, as opposed to handling the desires of the larger populous.  It offers 3 squares a day, like many others do, but does it in a somewhat more upscale environment.  The HDTVs and air conditioning were all working well, so there was no need to feel like I was living in Central America in order to enjoy their cuisine (although, I admit to liking that authenticity by necessity, too).  Although I really enjoy Central American kitchens, something on their menu caught my eye - the Guayo Burger.  I decided to check out this crossover dish to see how they would interpret this North American standard.  In addition to the expected Chips & Salsa (good), the large plate arrived with a 1/3 pound burger, done to my requested medium, with Lettuce, Onion, Spicy Mayo and broken Potato Chips inside.  Along side was a massive pile of French Fries, nice and crisp.  The roll had sesame seeds and reminded of a Whopper.  The real stand out was the mixture of taste and texture with each chomp.  It was very good, but not so foreign as to lose sight of its origination.  If they had stuffed some of the fries inside the sandwich, it would have been a dead ringer for an Animalized In N Out Burger.  A few grilled Jalapenos would have been totally over the top.  Still, it was very satisfying just as it was.    The homemade Horchata was excellently made; the rice and cinnamon blended drink, cold and so refreshing.  The whole meal came to under $12.   Def want to come back to try some of their BBQ grilled meats.    PRO TIP - Street parking only, so try to come early or late as parking around there on Hamilton Avenue can be challenging.  Side streets offer more opportunities.

For the sake of comparison, I decided to visit the Giant Supermarket in the Flowers Mill Shopping Center, Langhorne, Pa., just to see how it stacked up against my local market in Newtown/Middletown.    Not very well, I'm afraid.   While as large or larger than my local Giant, the layout was inferior, and the space felt dark from poor lighting.  It was difficult to find certain items that were not where they logically belonged (i.e., Bubba Burgers). So, I found myself wandering down aisles thinking that there was something wrong with my vision.  No. It wasn't me.    Service was fine, and the cashier very friendly.    Still, my neighborhood store retains my loyalty.

Birthday Flowers in the Age of COVID-19 -   Somethings in life must be celebrated on time regardless of surrounding risks.
