So it was that a bouquet of fresh cut flowers were required to honor my wife's birthday in the middle of a quarantine stay at home order. Roses didn't feel spontaneous enough, nor as crazy ebullient as the moment needed. No, the creative hand of a true florist and flora lover was the way to go.   I used the third party online vendor I had worked with before, but to my good fortune they subbed out to Penny's in Glenside for execution. They were on time and on my wavelength. We left the package on the porch for a day out of an abundance of caution to allow any Covid cooties to be rendered inert. When we brought it inside to the kitchen, and unbound its wrapping, we beheld a riot of daisies, sunflowers, zinnias, red carnations, a few gorgeous coral roses and dried sinuatum. They were soft to touch and scented like the dawn of Spring.   Most importantly, they generated the emotional response I was hoping for from the object of my affections. She kvelled like a purring kitten, and treated me like I was the celebrant, not her.   Just as it should be. Penny's had it exactly right. I now have a new florist.

(We) Miss Philly Grill is a stainless steel façade food emporium on Philmont Avenue in Huntingdon Valley, Montgomery County, PA.  If first impressions are important, this joint needs some help because the parking lot is a minefield of potholes to be avoided before even considering walking inside.  Not worth a tire or rim just to check out their breakfast, but if you are careful, you can make it without damaging your wheels.   Once inside, the décor and ambiance take you to another time and place somewhere in South Philadelphia in the middle of the last century. The walls are hung with Marilyn, James Dean, Connie Mack Stadium, etc., and the upholstery of the booths is red and white leatherette. Attractive and gitchy. Most of the patrons appear to be regulars from the first-naming going on with the staff. Almost all of them were bilingual and seemed interested in attending to everyone's needs.  The breakfast menu was extensive, with many specials and combo plates for those desiring a thimble of juice and mug of Joe with their egg dishes.  I certainly did.  I went with the french toast, orange juice and java. In reverse order, the coffee was decent, but served with those coffee creamer things. As that is all corn syrup and chemicals, I requested some milk as an alternative. I got it, but it took a while. The main course was okay, but it was presented sloppily, looking like the cook had just tossed it on the plate with no attempt to make it look attractive.  There were even little pieces of eggy bread detached from the slices on the dish.  I had to reorganize it before putting on the butter and syrup.  The "butter" was all prepackaged in tiny plastic tubs, and had the consistency of soft margarine.  Syrup? It came out of a label-less plastic squeeze bottle that had been refilled a million time with an industrial strength amber sweet goo. The OJ was poured from a large plastic pitcher of unknown age and origin.   You get the picture.   Every corner that could be cut to save a penny, was sliced thin. The result was a breakfast that could not be traced to the source, nor offered with pride of ownership. It wasn't that it was a bad meal, it's just that it lacked care and quality control.  The taste was close to being good, but fell short in various ways.  Miss Philly Grill? It takes more than a chill environment to make me miss it enough to want a return visit with all the potholes inside and out.

This was my first visit to Chili Szechuan since its relocation from Baltimore Avenue in West Philly.  It is certainly larger than before, and its booths and dark tones, more cozy than before. It has always offered authentic Szechuan spicy cuisine from Chongqing, China, but now it even adds the reality of many restaurants especially in the northern climes, of being chilly temperature-wise in winter.  We appreciated the cultural use of cold weather and wore our coats during the meal in honor of the reminiscent freeze in the house. Brrrr....  The food was as good as before. Spicy Lamb Chops, Szechuan Chili Sauce Fish Fillets, Eggplant in Garlic Sauce and Crispy Shrimp - Sweet & Sour, were our choices. They were all good to great, although our waiter admitted that even on the non-Americanized menu, they cut the heat for a western customer. So, even though we were mostly Chinese at the table, we all suffered through reduced burn and numbness. Next time, we will insist on the full monty fire treatment. We can all handle it!  The dishes arrived as prepared by the kitchen, and not all at once. Thus, the spicy lamb chops made the first impression of the night. They were excellent; with enough cumin and pepper to heat the tongue and gums, but not anesthetize them. Fun finger food.  Next came the eggplant in garlic sauce.  It, too, was a strong contender, with plenty of Chinese nightshade and a thick, rich dark amber coat. It could have been hotter, as the innate sweetness of the veggie dominated the other flavors, and needed more competition from Szechuan chilies. The shrimp was delivered next.  It was good, with 10 jumbos in an orange glaze. However, it was far more sweet than sour, and suffered most from Americanization syndrome. It really needed a blast from the smelter to bring out its hidden attributes. Finally, the Szechuan chili sauce fish fillets arrived in a deep dish to accommodate the soupy red hot bath it cooked in.  This dish was excellent and packed the most punch.  Tender pieces of boneless flounder is a beautiful orange/red conglomerated hot liquid.  Finally, a little numbness!  We passed on their dessert options, as they were not Chinese, and all came from an outside vendor.  The hot tea was from a non-descript bag, rather than loose pack.  Not so good.   Overall, Chili Szechuan was a worthwhile trip on a cold winter night, yet it would do itself a favor by fixing the heating equipment, not making assumptions about "round eyes," and upgrading their tea choices. While these are mostly secondary considerations, they do detract from the experience.  As such, it really can't compare holistically to Han Dynasty or the other Hot Houses in Philly, where those details mean something.

Very good Cantonese house on Race Street near 9th, with front of the house glassed in roasting kitchen and regular food preparation room in back for the rest of the menu. Our server advised that the chef was Fuzhounese. Regardless of his beginnings, he knew his way around a South Chinese chopchop.   The dining room was small, even by Ctown standards. Maybe 7 tables altogether. The food list was extensive, and we settled on Hong Kong Wonton Vegetable Soup (very good), Salt & Pepper Spare Ribs (excellent) and Beef Chow Fun (excellent). All dishes were substantial and we had plenty more than the two of us could handle, and a large amount to take home. On top of that, before leaving we picked up a pound of sliced roast pork because it looked so good hanging in the window. It was delicious and we worked through it for the next week. It was lean with thin layer of fat under the crispy brown dermis.   Lau Kee reminded of Ting Wong, a worthy place for a solid meal across the traditional food groups of Cantonese cuisine, with a comfort level that was inviting to regular visits for families or octogenarians on a date. Prices quite reasonable, too.

Stopped by for breakfast this week and sat at an otherwise empty counter.  The place looked refreshed since the last time I was here several years ago.  My server was friendly, courteous and prompt with the large red coffee mug, keeping it full throughout my meal.    The Sausage, Egg & Cheese on Croissant was a special this morning, and included a side of Hash Browns for a price under $6.  I was pleased that my waitperson pointed that out to me when she heard I was heading in that direction.    The sandwich was constructed with double Sausage Patties, American Cheese, and a nicely Fried Egg.  The Croissant was fresh, and had a pleasant sweetness with every bite.  It was very good.  Yet, the half plate of Home Fries were room temperature at best.  They were overcooked and dry.  Add cool temperature to that, and I found them inedible.  Not sure why the grill chef didn't know that those taters were left in the corner of the iron for too long.  Just as well, as I didn't need the extra calories turning into sugars.    The coffee came from a Bunn Double Drip.  It was a good bean, and I enjoyed having a large, heavy mug to sip from, rather than a smaller vessel to be constantly refilled.    Overall, the environment was attractive and comfortable.  A little more attention to detail would certainly make Blue Fountain a more positively memorable experience.

Wings To Go in the Queen Anne Plaza, Fairless Hills, PA, is part of a regional chain of wing, burger, rib, wrap houses in the Bucks/Mercer area. They are clean, friendly, and reasonably priced for what they offer, and tend to be better than many of the other franchised wing-a-do shops around.   I was there to grab a chicken sandwich and order two dozen wings for home consumption by the boys. I ordered at the counter, and walked into the dining area to await my light lunch. It arrived in a plastic basket, open faced, with a lightly coated breading on a large breast. A squirt from the ketchup table rocket and I was in business. It was a tasty chew, and I was pleasantly surprised by the thin coat and clean taste. Old oil was not used, and it was prepared just in time for me. Even the roll held up well to my gnawing assault.   I brought the Asian Zing and Suicide wings home, and sat with my guys as they attacked the flaming appendages. Average sized wings, but with decent distinctive sauces that pointed out their relative advantages. The Asian Zing were hot, but with a Thai sauce sweetness to offset the conflagration. Liked them a lot. The Suicide were less forgiving, and stung all the soft membranes of the mouth and lips. They were okay, although number one son seemed to be more enthusiastic about them. To each his own.   Both came with small containers of "sour cream." It wasn't, but they did chill the burn a bit as meat was scraped from bone by our incisors. Word to the wise, have your own sour cream in the fridge for such occasions to avoid unnecessary burn and blister.

Aside from the high price found across the board at Trenton Farmers Market, the baby back ribs offered by Smoke Chef Jeff of Hambone Opera are terrific. Meaty, tender, pull off the bone and barky, this hole in the wall is considered the best Q in New Jersey by those who know.   The main man himself learned the wood science while in Texas and brought his experience and original notions with him when he came here. The sauce is Kansas City red tart, but the secret lies in the wild cherry wood logs with which the meats are smoked for 12-13 hours in the huge closed steel smoker out back of the market.   The wood is the thing in the hands of a well trained smoke chef, and Jeff has developed it to the height of culinary arts it was meant to be. You can taste it in the mild sweetness in the heart of each rib before it is overcome by the spicy Kansas City rub and sauce, and yet again by the more tangy squirt squeezed on as the final step before eating.   This was great BBQ. At $14/lb, it was not cheap, but what you would pay for eat in platters, not takeout. Nonetheless, sometimes the splurge is worthwhile. It certainly was this time. The brisket looked just as good, as did their smoked beans.   Next time for those.

There are dive bars.  There are dumpy dive bars.  And, then there are hell holes.    Penn Tavern sits at the borderline between the last two, as well as on a dark strip of West Bridge Street in Morrisville, Pa.  The evening I was there the crowd was sparse with no more than 6 people on stools around the worn out bar.  The friendly/attractive bartender was just back from surgery and was obviously uncomfortable moving around.  The folks on one side of me were in a conversation laced with F-bombs.  The person on the other side was singing along with the music coming from the jukebox in the basement (I was amazed she could hear it).    The floor was in need of reinforcement, as only the underflooring was visible behind the bar.  The draft beer handles were all off to one side at the edge of the bar zone, attached to the freezer where the kegs were housed.  It had been a very long time since I saw a set up like that. All the pulls looked to be domestic.  My Yuengling mug was only $2, and I read elsewhere that a $.75 draft was available.    I needed a place to spend an hour while waiting for a local class to let out, and Penn Tavern was the next on the list for a visit.  Compared to the other neighborhood drinking halls, this is at the bottom of the (beer) barrel.

We stopped in last weekend as the COVID crisis tightened its chokehold on small food outlets in Bucks and our governor was about to order most closed to enforce social distancing but for takeout. We were looking for dessert choices and coffee after a decent last supper down the road in Buckingham.   Peddlers Village in Lahaska is a cutesy tourist center just outside New Hope, but where New Hope has a real community integrated among the beauty of an historic but tourist centric riverside town, Peddlers Village is all ersatz artificiality that looks dated and pretty, but lacks a human heart. So, it is not surprising to see all the poor reviews interspersed with a few positive ones.   If you get there on or near a baking day when most of the inventory is still new and moist, you are going to be happy. If you pick things that are a bit older and approaching their invisible sell by date, you're out of luck. Your purchase will be dry and disappointing. Problem is you can't tell them apart. Management hasn't figured out how to (or decided not to) inform the public which is which. There is no "Day Old" shelf.   Our experience appears to be somewhat typical. Their La Colombe java (a Philadelphia treasure) was hot and strong, although not at the peak of perfection at that hour, while the Lemon Cheesecake Cupcake we shared was pretty good, although plainly just a small cheesecake with a dollop of lemon buttercream swirled on top. It really stretched the meaning of "cupcake." Had it been creamier/softer it would have been fully satisfying, but as it was with the right taste yet wrong texture, it was just okay.   There were many other choices possible in the substantial display cases, so another selection might have made us happier, but we'll never know because as it was, our experience was just mediocre.

1/3/2016 - Finally made it here for dinner. The Tomato Pie (w. mushrooms) was excellent.  The Caesar Salad, not so much. Better to stick with what Palermo's does best and leave the greens to a garden master.

This is not part if the Villa Rosa empire from Yardley PA, as it changed hands sometime in the past few years, although the name and design are the same.   There are two operations here sharing a common kitchen. On the right is a pizza parlor with booths and small tables doing a slice, sandwich and takeout business, while on the left is a more formal dining room with similar menu and more comfort. Service is easily bilingual, and muy amable.   I stopped in for a light dinner and opted for the parlor side as I know I didn't want a full meal, nor the attendant cost of table service. An eggplant parmesan on torpedo roll would do nicely, thank you. And it did. Very thin sliced melanzone sauteed to a soft textured in an olive oiled pan and lowered into the valley of a cut roll, with mozza and red gravy on top, and a final melt down in the pizza oven.   The taste was right, but it would have been better if the cheese and sauce had been layered in with the eggplant. Without that, much of the middle was somewhat dry and monotonal, lacking the mix of tomato, garlic, salt and basil throughout to bring up the flavor. I tend to deconstruct these beauties and eat the contents with knife and fork to reduce carb intake. If the bread is exceptional, I will eat some of it as well. In this case I consumed half of it, meaning it was pretty good.   Based on my experience, I think the chef knows the recipes and techniques, but may lack the savior faire to realize that the ingredients need to interact more.

The Five Four Bar & Grill takes its moniker from the local zip code for this part of Levittown, Pa.  It is a fairly new house with large rooms for the bar, dining and even two pool tables for those so inclined.  Friday and Saturday nights starting around 9:30 local bands rock the casbah. The crowd is a mix of ages and interests, but have found a neighborhood spot where everyone is welcome, the drinks are not expensive, and the kitchen turns out reasonable good bar food and a few higher end dinner specials.  It is a non-smoking establishment.   We sat in a booth near the green felt tables, a little distance from the bar, but close by the stage.  We didn't mind when the pool cues invaded our space. We just moved the beer bottles and pint glasses to the other side.  Sharing is caring.  The Labatt Blue Draft was cold and refreshing, and the Coney Island Orange Vanilla Cider tasted like Brooklyn summer on the beach.  The prices from the multi-paged beer list were surprisingly low, especially after patronizing some other bars up county.    Dinner consisted of a Burger, Chicken Tender Wrap and Chicken Parm Sandwich.  All came with crisped French Fries.  They were all good, if not outstanding.  The Plain Burger with Cheese, Lettuce, Onion and Tomato was on a decent fresh roll, and came out slightly beyond the Medium requested.  Still good, but not memorable.  The Wrap disappeared quietly without complaint, and my Parmesan was also tasty on another good roll and enough red gravy.  None of these dishes were large, but given the price range, were more than enough for a light bite. Service was very friendly and prompt.  We were satisfied, but did not understand why silverware was not provided for the meals without request.  No biggie, but seemed odd.     Unfortunately, we had to depart before the band came on, but Five Four is worth a return visit later on a weekend evening to catch the show.

You would not be surprised by the total "shackiness" of Smoke 'n Dudes if their cabin was surrounded by forest rather than parking lot.  Outside was a large trailered-up grill/smoker ready to be hitched and taken on the road.  Step inside, and the knotty pine paneling and wood plank tables with red checkered cloths put you in a mind of a backcountry store where BBQ and moonshine are a way of life up there in the Smokey Mountains outside Ashville or Gatlinburg.  The menu is small reflecting the size of the joint.  In for lunch, the friendly server showed me the specials menu, and I opted for the Pulled Pork Sandwich with Cheddar and Sautéed Onions on a fresh oversized smooth topped Roll.  It came with chips, but for a buck extra, fries could be subbed in.  While I waited I sipped on my Lemonade and listened to the banter between the employees.  This might be Bensalem, but the accents and topics of conversation were straight from the southern Appalachians. I was right there with 'em.   The sandwich arrive full-plate, and I opened it up to have a look-see, and taste a small sample.  First impression was of a fully smoked meaty lean pork; good texture, but perhaps cooked with a milder marinade and BBQ sauce that left the meat juicy, yet not as flavorful as I like.  The Dudes were ready for that as the table had 3 bottle rockets of sauce ready for squirting.  Spicy, Hickory and Apple were the flavors.  I tasted each and found the Apple to be the most intriguing and tasty.  It had a nice fruity sweetness that was distinct from the other undertones of vinegar, molasses and brown sugar.  A long squirt dousing the pile of pork quickly resolved that issue.    From that point on the entire experience was pleasurable and satisfying.  I liked the Apple BBQ Sauce so much I added some to the chips, and if I had ordered the fries, would have used it rather than ketchup.  These sauces are for sale at the counter.    While great BBQ is hard to come by in this neck of the woods, Smoke 'n Dudes provides something very close to what I love - fall off the bone, spicy, tangy well grilled and smoked meat that assault the salivary glands and squeeze them dry.   What I would have given for the right beer and shot of Dickel at that moment! Alas, this was lunchtime in Bensalem, and that fantasy would have to await another time or place.    BYOB for dinner???

Curiosity finally got the best of me after going by Sophie's Kitchen several times to and from our monthly visit to First Oriental Supermarket to stock up on Asian groceries. The earlier Viet cafe at that corner was not all that good, so it was with a pleasant sense of change that this new operation caught my attention.   We walked over after shopping and found our way up to the second floor dining room. It looked basically the same as before with modern simple decor and large windowed walls overlooking Washington Avenue. There was a family at the middle table, so we grabbed one against the inner wall where we all could maintain some privacy. The guy overseeing things came over with menus, took our drink order (water) and placed white curved plates and flatware wrapped in black cloth napkins at the head of the table. Classy for lunch.   We ordered beef skewers and mee katang, a fat noodle dish with veggies. Both arrived with color and energy glistening from them. The beef was a thin sliced, well marinaded BBQ, and grilled just enough to be tender, moist, lightly crisp and delicious. Really good. The flat noods had a wonderful sauce, subtly savory and sweet with plenty of greens mixed in. A little sriracha on the edge of the plate for dipping and we had an excellent dish. Loved it.   While the menu was somewhat limited, we thoroughly enjoyed the food and bright atmosphere on an overcast day. Prices were reasonable ($24 w tip). Given it's convenience to the market next door, we could become regulars of this appetizing Cambodian house.

MUFFIN & COFFEE BREAKFAST REVIEW ONLY  Stopped in the Vincentown Diner after court in Mt. Holly this morning for a late light breakfast. It has been at least a decade since my last visit, and aside from the new sign out front, the inside looked basically the same with two main dining areas, a long counter with spinners, and servers in black.  It also has signs referring to local sourced foods, craft beer, and french press coffee.  The lighting seemed a bit dim which felt more somber than comforting.   I sat at the counter and was promptly approached by a woman in black offering a menu and asking if I wanted something to drink.  Coffee, please.  It arrived in a larger cup, about twice the size of the normal diner serving.  Nice touch. Felt generous.   I inquired about muffins, and was advised they had corn and blueberry.  A toasted corn muffin was exactly what I wanted.  The menu called them, "The Real Deal!"  It arrived cut in thirds and well grilled on top and bottom.  I small cup of butter and two jelly containers came along for the ride. I spread some butter on the heated surfaces, but pushed the sweets aside.    First bite was a small surprise.  Rather than having that expected corn muffin flavor, the mix included Lemon Zest, making the taste more a lemon corn muffin, than the traditional rich corn flavor and texture.  Disappointing, but certainly an acceptable variant if notified beforehand.  That was not the case here.    All the above would have resulted in a three star review, but for the heartburn I have been suffering since leaving the diner.  Whether the coffee or the muffin were the "Real Deal," or not, that was an aftertaste I could live without.

Standard pizzeria on Mill Creek Road, Levittown, PA. This place is in a tiny commercial strip, a double wide storefront with kitchen/counter to the right and dining room to the left. Strictly a slice, pie and steak joint. Management is friendly and clearly happy for your business.   The food is what you'd expect from a traditional northeastern Mexitalian pizza parlor. The pies are competently made and the cheesesteaks are loaded with chopped beef, cheese and whatever else you desire in terms of onions, peppers, mushrooms, etc. The roll is decent, too, but not particularly crispy. Prices are definitely on the low end of the scale, making for a good meal on a budget. My two slice lunch (mushroom and plain) were requested well done, and that was what I got. Firm points. Scorched undercarriage. Well remelted mozzarella. Quite solid with a sprinkle of crushed hot pepper.   Not sure if Luigi is in the house anymore, but as a place to grab a couple of slices and a drink for lunch, this place is worthy of consideration.

This old diner located at the intersection of Limekiln Pike and Mt. Carmel Avenue in Glenside, PA, is a miniature of today's full monte diner experience. The counter has only 6 spinners, and the main dining rooms together, less than a dozen tables. But, size does not tell the story of Moonlight Diner. This place has been running since the middle of the last century feeding this neighborhood with solid victuals and homemade desserts. That I was the only customer by the time I finished breakfast does not reflect on the quality of the experience.  I sat on the last stool on the right overlooking the refrigerator full of juice and milk and the kitchen door. The friendly server approached with a menu and inquiry about drinks. Coffee with a small glass of milk arrived in front of me two minutes later. I order their Farmers Omelet (onion, tomato, mushroom, bacon, feta cheese extra with home fries folded in) and rye toast, and took a phone call as I waited. The platter was placed before me before the call ended.   First bite alerted me to the need for a shake of black pepper and squirt of Frank's Hot Sauce, which I promptly applied. Those adjustments did the trick and it was smooth sailing from there. The taste and texture were excellent and it was a completely filling breakfast. Everything blended well together and seemed in perfect harmony. Coffee mug refills were forthcoming when required. Service was timely and cordial. They treated this stranger well.   Much appreciated.

As a first timer, I was pleasantly surprised by Steam, the railroad car-looking restaurant/pub on 2nd Street Pike in Southampton, Pa.    The Friday night crowd was loud, but friendly.  The bar was long and packed.  The dining tables seemed to turn over quickly enough without a reservation.  We waited about 20 minutes for a deuce hightop mid-floor.  The service dudes were all "can do!"   My burger was very good and required knife and fork as I could never open my jaws wide enough to capture it in a bite.  My companion's sliders were also tasty.  The French Onion Soup was decent, but not the strongest entry of the evening.    Steam (suggestive of the locomotive steam engine), appears to have a successful formula.  Space, fairly priced drinks($5 margaritas, beer specials), a long happy hour, and an above average bar menu.  Live music, too.    I will likely be back.

Giovanni's is an Italian house along Woodbourne Road in Levittown, Pa.  It has been around for a long time and the layout and décor show how restaurants were put together twenty years ago.  Two small dining rooms with kitchen in the rear.  Comfortable booths and pleasant aromas, but in need of a little refreshing.    Service was fine for most of the meal, except when our lone server was put to work elsewhere in the shop, and couldn't get back to us often enough to see we were finished eating and waiting for a box for the remaining pizza and our check.    The food is decent.  The Tomato Pie comes with just spicy tomato gravy and no cheese, unlike across the Delaware where the mozza is spread across the top of the chunky sauce.  The different style requires a much heavier hand ladling out the sauce to compensate for the lack of balancing cheese.  The result is a wet pie whose middle crust cannot hold the weight and moisture from above.  If a crisp cracker-like dough is your hope, you won't get that here.  Even picking up the slices caused runoff.  On the other hand, the half pepperoni showed generosity, as half the pie was covered in quarter-sized coins of nicely sliced p-roni.    The Caesar Salad was nice, with plenty of Romaine, Onions, Crutons, Tomatoes, but the small plastic container of dressing would have been so much nicer had it been presented in a small dish with a spoon.  No real complaints beyond style points.    The Chicken Cheesesteak/Fries combo was hefty, and devoured without complaint.  Fries were average.    Giovanni's is a nice family place with low cost menu.  Nothing stands out as exceptional, but everything we had was okay to pretty good.  It definitely has a place in the Italian restaurant continuum.

Hungry after a meeting with my lawyer, I wandered around Doylestown Borough to clear my head and find a place to eat. I was open to what the Universe would provide. Crossing through a parking lot I saw Artistic Pizza in front of me.  I thanked the great spirit that sent me in that direction, and went in.    The shop is very small, but the ovens are surrounded with a large variety of pies, and the owner/chef who was in the middle of making a new creation as I approached to make a choice.  I asked him for a recommendation for a first timer who loved great pizza.  He smiled at the challenge to satisfy me, and said his favorite was the Arugula Pie with a bit of Balsamic Dressing replacing the tomato sauce.  It was there in front of him, and I accepted that was what I should have.    I sat on one of the few tables in the front of the parlor and took in the street sights and sounds.  Tubby Olive was having its Grand Opening right next door, and there was a celebration going on.  People were walking around with samples of vinegars and oils.  Cool.  The slice arrived shortly on a paper plate.  It was a nice size, and the Arugula was plentiful and looked fresh, even after baking.  I found it quite tasty, especially the Balsamic.  A few cherry tomatoes dotted the landscape.  The only slightly odd thing to report is that although the presentation was more a flatbread "pizza" than a traditional one, the crust was not quite baked to completion.  Rather than being a dry, snappy crust, the middle of the crust still had some dough that was not completely hard.  The taste was there, but the texture not quite right.    Other than that, the meal was satisfying at one slice and a SanPelegrino Blood Orange drink.  I will stop in and try again.  I think this place is on to something good, and another visit may discover it fully.    Sometimes the Universe gets it totally right, and sometimes it is off a little.  Still, I accept what comes, and look for the deeper meaning. In this case, it's just to be sure the pizza stays in the oven long enough.

I've had a light addiction for tuna hoagies of late, and this Friday afternoon I found myself thinking about satisfying it again. Yelp alerted me to a Jersey Mike's down on Street Road in the Giant shopping center in Feasterville, about seven miles away. I found their app and ordered a standard sized sub with sesame seed roll, and added tomato, mayo, black pepper, lettuce, banana hot and sweet peppers. I drove down and arrived as the staff was finishing my order. It was right on time.  Back at the office I opened the twisted end wrapper and beheld a beautiful sandwich, if shorter than expected. First bite disclosed that the roll was superlative with bakery freshness, great texture and ideal flavor. On the other hand, the tuna tasted "thin," and lacking substance - not really all that good. The banana peppers and sweets were no where to be found. The actual eating experience was satisfactory despite these drawbacks, but could have been so much better had there been more quality control on the tuna salad and double checking the desired ingredients.   Overall, Jersey Mike's is somewhere in the middle of the pack of chain sub shop tuna hoagies available locally. Generally, mom and pop delis do them better, but there is wider diversity in how the tuna is prepared and more inquiry is needed to be sure each recipe has what you want in your sandwich.   3.5 STARS

Bukhara Restaurant & Tandoori Grill sits on southbound Route 130 in Burlington City, NJ, in a worn out mini strip center at the intersection with Wood Street. From the outside you might decide not to go in, but that would be a case of judging a good book by it's rummy cover.   Within is a small and attractive dining room with white clothed tables and large buffet along the wall. For lunch the buffet provides eight hot curry-oriented choices, a few sweet desserts, basmati rice, with naan coming from the kitchen oven, for $9.99. I tend to avoid buffets due to incentive to over indulge, but the only other dishes available on the menu seemed to be a personal portion of one of the entrees on the buffet table, @ $7.99, plus naan. So, the cost was the same whether I ate too much or just enough. Alas, the cost of principled consumption.   No matter, my buttered chicken was quite good in its mild yellow creamy sauce. The bird was a little dry, but I enjoyed it nonetheless. The naan arrived at the table hot, steaming and absorbtive. In the absence of rice it did excellent work as the spongy spoon lifting the extra curry to my mouth so as to leave nothing but crumbs behind. My lunch mate had nothing but praise for the buffet, and all the rice and naan desired.   There are better Indian kitchens, but none in the immediate vicinity. So, when the urge tugs this is not a bad option for scratching your itch.   3.5 Big Ones!

It has been awhile since my last visit to V & V Foot Massage because I found a place closer to home on Bustleton Avenue that made the drive to Washington Avenue less necessary. But, today with a sudden opening in my schedule and finding myself already in Philly, I decided on a return stop to get my tootsies, neck, shoulders and back some quality attention.   The place hasn't changed much. Maybe some new neon out front and new hands on deck, but it looked and felt as remembered. I opted for the 90 minute combo foot and body Chinese style massage. Judy was cleaning up the shop when I arrived and immediately directed me to one of the large recliner chairs and foot rests while she went to fill the wooden bucket with very hot water and herbal bags.   She dug and squeezed for half an hour, putting me immediately to sleep.  Felt great waking up and walking on air to the massage table in one of the back rooms. She found the knots in my back and shoulders and applied strong pressure to make them relax and allow blood and Qi to flow freely. Nice release and relief.   When she finished she cleaned the room and brought me a glass of cool water. She was friendly, but quiet as she worked. Very satisfying session.   Pro Tip - Although the sign says "Cash Only," in fact they do accept some credit cards, but prefer their tips in cash. Makes sense to me and I was happy with that arrangement.   It was nice to be back @ V&V.

Waterside Cafe & Diner sits in the street front building of the Waterside apartment complex in Bensalem, PA. There are only 5 parking spaces for customers who aren't disabled, so they must expect that most people eating there will live in that small neighborhood. The quality of their food suggests that they will soon outgrow their restrictive environment and need to expand their parking facilities to accommodate their anticipated success.  The dining room offers about a dozen tables and a counter with six stools. I sat on one of them as a sole diner, facing the work area. A server walked over with menu and inquiry about something to drink. At that time of morning, coffee was the only thing on my mind. It was strong and bracing. The breakfast choices were extensive, and I selected the Veggie Omelet & Home Fries with Rye Toast.   It was all quite good, with a load of fresh greens and melted cheddar. Including the half plate of potatoes and two slices of buttered bread, it was too much for me to consume, but a strong tasty breakfast all the way down. Service was first rate.   While this stretch of Bensalem is off my beaten path, I look forward to the occasion that leads me back there so I can sample more morning suggestions @ Waterfront.

Sitting in the long shadow of Bowman's Tower, the Conservation Corps public works project in the 1930s putting people back to work during the Depression, the tavern on beautiful River Road approaching New Hope, PA, is a well executed colonial style pub. It has a dark paneled dining room, and revolutionary edged barroom that capture what it may have been like to be part of the independence effort in the 18th Century around here. It really feels good to be part of that, even if just for lunch.   I was there for the first time in at least a decade, and the new ownership can be proud of what it has maintained, and created in terms of atmosphere and ethos. Their menu is wholesome with wide choice of apps, sandwiches, soup, salad, burgers, and trop cher entrees. When I spied a brussel sprouts side dish and potato bisque, I knew where I was going. Two of my favorite ingredients in any dish - cream based potato soup and kale/brussels side salad were too special to pass up. Even better, my lunchmate went with the scallops main course and slid a couple onto my plate for the tasting. Yes!  Everything was very good to amazing. The bisque seemed to have mushroom puree mixed with the pomme de terre, making for a savory rendition. Delicious. The balance between the slightly bitter kale, and the more subtle brussel sprouts was a bit off to my taste. It needed more petit choux and less kale to really make me happy (in fact, the kale was not in the a la carte sides description, but was definitely in the dish). The seared scallops was true to their word, and just mildly grilled, with sweet potato puree, caramelized apples, pancetta, almonds and cider brown butter drizzle. It was a real treat, but a heavy lift for lunch @ $27.   Bowman's Tavern is deep with atmosphere, and successfully carries out its promise of colonial charm, local produce where possible, and skilled hands in the kitchen. It is easy to imagine the General and his officers discussing plans for the next battles around the bar, or at the dinner table in the back room.

Fill A Bagel & Bread is a locally owned/operated bagel shop on Pennsylvania Avenue, Oreland, PA. It is their second store, and they have been a success baking and selling their goods to the surrounding communities for decades now. I was in the area after an appointment and hungry enough for breakfast as I drove back to my Bucks County office. A cuppa hot java and an onion bagel smeared with veggie cream cheese punched my ticket.   What about the bagel?   Well, it wasn't the best I've had, but far from the worst. Although fresh, I found its texture too dense, like perhaps the dough was kneaded too long before boiling/baking. The circumference of the rolled and twisted dough was smaller than ideal, and lacking air pockets that help lighten the bite and chew and allow the veggie cream cheese to afford more balance with the slightly sourdough flavor. The taste was alright, but the texture was not what I prefer. Plenty of roasted onion flakes all around. Service, friendly and efficient.  I agree with the comments that the cost/benefit is somewhat askew for the nature of the business, location and overall quality. I have paid less for better bagels and coffee in bigger towns and cities. Yet, I don't know their running costs, and no doubt the shop reflects its financial need to pay the bills and make a reasonable profit.   So, I find myself at the borderline between three and four stars attempt to find the right equipoise. I land at  3.5 Stars, and allow the app to round it up to 4.   I would certainly return given the opportunity.

Red Lion Diner in Horsham gives the impression of having had better days. The decor is somewhat worn with torn vinyl seats and dirty wall to walls. The menu attempts to cover the traditional bases, but only in a limited way by offering expected categories with only a few options in each. For example, their breakfast menu fits on half a page of a four sided laminate, rather than running on forever with combinations of possibilities.   My morning choices were a cup of Chicken Pastina Soup, which was quite good loaded with well cooked veggies, strips of chicken and tiny pastina pasta. Second, came a Sausage, Egg and Cheese on Kaiser, which while filling with two sausage patties, 2 eggs and lots of white gooey, came packaged in the sorriest looking ragged roll I've seen in years. Guess the budget didn't allow for decent bread provisions. It was crushed, dry and lifeless, and took most of the joy out of the substance of the meal.   Service was fine, bit not exemplary, and managed to pick one of my nits - Asked for milk for my coffee, but got those mini moos, with unwanted and non-nutritious fat and empty calories.   The soup was definitely the star of this show, leading to the reasonable conclusion that Red Lion was oriented toward lunch, much more than breakfast.

Chinatown Café is an refugee from Race Street, Philadelphia.  Owner Cary is a Bucks County pioneer, coming to this frontier lacking in quality Chinese cuisine, and opening his shop several years ago because he saw an opportunity to be one of the first quality chefs to start a business. He knew there was a great need, and the socio/economic means to support it.    He has succeeded.  Chinatown Café stand above most of the rest of the Chinese restos in Central Bucks, if not the entire domain.  The quality, taste, and overall gestalt of his shop are exceptional.  From soup through fortune cookie, the dining experience feels wholesome and well suited to the Chinese/American palate.  Cary knows what people like, and provides it at a high level.  When inside his world, you feel you will be exiting onto 11th Street.    This week I went in for lunch.  Although there is a lunch special menu, after my recent experience with an awful lunch at another place, I did not want to go that way.  So, I ordered off the main menu - Duck Fried Rice.  I knew that Cary was a duck wizard.  Out came a huge steaming platter loaded with well seasoned rice and big pieces of roast duck.  It was enough for 6 people.  It was moist, flavorful, and exactly what I wanted.  Just Ducky!   Cary and I chatted a bit about our businesses, and when he realized I spent time in China, he brought out a bowl of Wonton Soup for me to sample.  Very nice of him to do so.  The broth was rich, golden and as good as my Jewish grandmother made. Swimming easily in the bowl were several fancy goldfish wontons, with nearly translucent skin, and silky tails.  Stirring the mix gave the impression that the wontons were alive and enjoying themselves peacefully in a koi pond.  I think this style wonton is actually called, "Butterfly Wonton," but they look like goldfish to me.   The last remains of the Duck Fried Rice sits in my refrigerator awaiting consumption.  I have enjoyed it daily since the visit.  I have to finish it before I can go back for more.   Four Stars with a Bullet.  I have to see what Chinatown Café does not the spicy end of the spectrum to be completely in love.

BREAKFAST @ TIFFANY (Diner on the Boulevard)  Happy New Year (2022) Everyone!  My last Yelp of the old year was at this fine establishment in the Great Northeast, Philadelphia. It had been closed an extended period of time for renovations, and the effort appears to have been worthwhile. The facility has a new outer shell and the main dining hall is bright, attractively utilitarian and very clean. Staff from management to servers are courteous and helpful. The menu is a diner's long list of nearly infinite possibilities.   But, I was there for a New Year's Eve Day breakfast, and while prepared to be tempted, knew what I wanted - French Toast & crisp bacon. There is a long counter along the back wall, and when I arrived it was unoccupied. I sidled down to the third from last spinner, past the last booth, and found myself in the perfect Covidly socially distance spot. No one with ten feet of me. I ordered coffee and my Frenchie. and perused my phone for the latest news while I waited. These days that is always a risky thing to do and expect to keep a good mood, but old habits die hard. (Good riddance 2021!)  So, my plate was delivered with a warm smile. I beheld two slices of thickish bread well grilled and sided by four slices of heat curled bacon. Both good to the naked eye. First bites told the tale.   Although described as "Challah" bread, the texture was more a yellowish thick slice with extra sugar baked in. It lacked the rougher consistency and swirl of true Challah. Okay. I'm being picky, but the mental image of the real deal had excited my tastebuds and I was a little disappointed. Too, it came with those industrial corn syrup sweeteners, that are just empty calories and not conducive to good health. No Log Cabin nor Mrs. Butterworth in the house. True, it was edible and the bacon was fine, but these days I have reservations about putting such ersatz materials in my body, and would gladly pay extra for pure Grade B maple syrup.   I get that corners must be cut to stay ahead of the game, but I would prefer the choice.   But, that's just me.   Let's have a better 2022! Lord knows we need and deserve it.

If you are ever curious about what goes on in Roebling, NJ, the former company town owned by the steel company by that name, Kalman Bakery offers another tasty reason to satisfy your history bug.   The row houses down near the river are interesting, although this burg has definitely seen happier days. But, plan to stop at Kalman's for a sweet treat on your way out of town. This family operation bakes up very good cookies, cakes and donuts at low budget prices to meet the needs of the community. The coffee is decent, too.   When I visited last week in the late morning, I was the only customer. I was greeted by a woman behind a high refrigeration display case. She explained that everything was made there, and that Tuesday was the start of their week and all was freshly baked. The traditional Old Fashioned donut looked like a blooming flower, while the Glazed was a pillow of sweetness and light. So good with the java washdown.   Now that I know where it is hidden, I will be back to Kalman's as time and sweet tooth allow.

While Peace Valley Park is a beautiful oasis of field, forest and water, when I visited last weekend there was nary a parking space. People were packed in on the trails and along the waterfront with little concern for social distancing, nor masks. It looked so unsafe to be there despite the perfect weather, that we decided not to search for parking, but to leave the park for another less overcrowded day.   We are all feeling rammy about the too long quarantine and have chronic cabin fever, but to ignore the advice of health experts that precautions remain essential to avoid infection, is to not only risk my own life, but the lives of those I love.   The North Branch of Neshaminy Creek and the reservoir from its damming (Lake Galena) will still be there when it is safer to explore.

From the look of the dog eared, battered menus of the "Legendary" Dew Inn Diner @ the corner of 5th & Girard Avenue, Northern Liberties, they had been in use for the more than 50 years this awesome joint had been in business. The low 20th century prices didn't lead me to think differently. Sure, the furnishings were likewise dated, but it all came together to create the perfect environment for a traditional Philadelphia brekkie, sans all the hoopla of the nouveau brunch scene.   From our perch on two spinners at the counter, we sipped the Bunn java and watched the full house deep in convos and good winter Saturday morning feast-ivities. When our Spanish Omelet and A Hot Mess 'kitchen sink' omelet arrived, we were very ready to chow down with gusto.   And gusto was what we got. Each was a 3 egger, so full of ingredients that it was surprising that everything got tucked in. The ham, peppers, onions, cheese and salsa in the Spanish melded wonderfully and the taste/texture was great. The home fries were crisp, yet buttery, and all we needed were splashes of Crystal Hot Sauce to complete the excellent profile. The Hot Mess threw everything in the kitchen including the potatoes into the egg shell. How they zipped it up without leakage remained a secret. It was filling and delicious, and the rye toast added a touch of subtle sour savoriness that was good to the last bite.   Dew Inn is another awesome corner breakfast joint that the City of Brotherly Love is so rightly famous for. Loved every forkful.

We stopped for Saturday lunch after car hunting nearby.  Mirim Japanese and Korean Restaurant was the most interesting choice in the area, so we drove over to their location in a small commercial strip that also housed fried chicken, pizza and Chinese massage parlors for future exploration.   We quickly discovered that lunch menu was not available on weekends, so we ordered two dishes at dinner prices.  We went with Dolsot Bulgogi and Pork Katsu, which came with the traditional Banshan small dishes that accompany most Korean meals.  They were all well spiced pickled veggies, cabbage and sprouts that went well alone and with the spicy boiling beef bulgogi and the nicely breaded and pan fried katsu.  Everything was done well, and service was adequate, if lacking personality.   The room was divided into three areas; front dining room with booths, rear dining room with tables and a sushi bar.  Mirim had been there for a long time, and the water stained ceiling and the floor had seen better days.  Still, the kitchen knew what it was doing, and we were satisfied with our meals.  We took home what we couldn't finish, and enjoyed it with dinner.   I had visited Mirim many years ago and remember it as being in better shape than it was yesterday.  In the interim many more purely Korean houses have opened between there and Center City Philadelphia.  These newer places have the advantage of youth and the growing appreciation for Korean cuisine - especially their awesome fried chicken.  Mirim could get its groove back if it took a look at what was going on around them, made some needed upgrades in facility and menu choices, and considered being a purely Korean shop.

Pie'd Piper in the Trenton Farmers Market is a hybrid shop, equal parts traditional deli and bakery. There are sandwiches galore and plenty of kielbasi and other stuffed derma to chose from, and in the vein of filling skins, excellent jelly and cream donuts. Homemade pierogi, too.  Friendly staff filled out order, but the cost across the board took us by surprise. As with most of TFM, prices were far from the expected wholesale plus, and much more premium, take it or leave it. The bill came in at nearly $50. We shelled it out, realizing this place would have to be an acquired taste.

Before you get to the excellent restaurant in back, you pass through a small but packed with merchandise mercado general. It is worth the exploration in its own right before sitting down for almuertzo o diner. The collection of chilies alone is a botanist's wet dream.   It is not every day that you can walk through a museum quality exhibit of colorful peppers, followed by shelves full of Madonna and Child statuary, on the way to a delicious and culturally absorbing meal.   Although the market/kitchen concept is standard issue in Mexico and their outposts around the world, this one is a typical sample with outstanding chef at the back of the joint.

As soon as we walked in to Greystone it was obvious the new owners put alot of money into renovating the old Lavender Hall. Although mostly black and grey, the front bar/ lounge was beautifully sedate, and the dining room spacious with room between tables and large windows bringing in late afternoon light before the coming of dusk. It was impressive, and on this Tuesday evening, not crowded at all, which enhanced the sense that we had chosen well.   We were seated at a table mid floor, but asked to be moved near an electric outlet in order to charge a cell phone. They graciously obliged. Our server quickly introduced himself and brought drink and food menus. The wine and beer lists were broad enough without necessitating a trip to the wine cellar. My old friend selected a glass of zinfandel, while my beautiful date picked a light small brewery pilsner, and I a pineapple cider (delicious). We settled in with the drinks and caught up while perusing the menu.   We kept dinner on the lighter side, with a Chopped Greek Salad, Mushroom Burger and Fig Jam Burger for yours truly. At $15 per slider, the price was high, but still much more in line with our appetites than the entrees which were double the cost. So, we felt that management was smart to offer smaller options that allowed for drinks and/apps and a reasonable bottom line. Besides, we thoroughly enjoyed our meals. The burgers were half pounders with brioche rolls and homemade potato chips or fries. The fig jam added a nice sweet dimension to my burger. My friend asked for grilled scallops added to the salad, but when the kitchen lacked them, they inquired if he would be satisfied with shrimp instead. He was.   We were happy with our experience at Greystone. It was qualitatively superior to the previous tenants who tried to make a go of it in the old mansion on the road between Newtown and Washington Crossing. The outdoor patio looked appealing, but with the steam heat unrelenting even into the evening, now was not the time to try it out.   This was an interlude even George himself would enjoy.

Sun Yu Si Kao is now my favorite Szechuan restaurant in Philadelphia Chinatown. Not only is the food superlative, but the house is beautifully designed with high ceilings, stone accented walls, unusual rope lighting and attractive serving dishes. It's great to see Ctown dress up and show its more sophisticated side in the hot, spicy and numbing world of Chengdu cuisine.   We ordered seven dishes for the two of us, with enough to take home for the rest of the family. Allow me to enumerate:  * Sliced Beef & Tripe w Chili Sauce - Served cold but loaded with high temperature chilis, it was a great starting point. The textures of thin firm beef and loose tripe and the prickly feel of chili beginning the night of hotter and hotter choices;  * Takoyaki - Try to imagine whipped squid shaped into large marble sized balls. Creamy, yet definitely crustacean; slightly sweet, but also mildly fishy and sticky on the teeth. Very unusual, but surprisingly tasty;  * Spicy Shredded Beef - Tender mixed with pepper, onion, sprout,  Szechuan reds and a smattering of black  peppercorn and light film of chili oil, all of which continued to raise the Celsius in our mouths;  * Cumin Lamb Chops - The star of the show. Eight baby chops grilled and covered in more hot peppers, with bone wrapped in foil for ease of handling. Absolutely delicious enough to allow us to ignore the growing conflagration in the quest to strip every morsel of lamb from the finger width bone. Simply amazing;   * Pan Seared Green Shishito Pepper - Beautiful rich shiny green. An explosive pleasure to consume. These boys appeared to have an inner glow, and were as burning hot as they were gorgeous to behold. They may be an acquired taste, but thankfully I have acquired it;  * Spicy Sliced Fish - White fish fillets is a large sculpted iron cauldron full of multiple peppers, including black peppercorns for numbing anesthetic effect on the tongue and gums, black fungus and sprouts in a deeply fired near molten liquid that both punished and delighted.   Sure, there is a degree of masochism to loving Szechuanese food, but once the burn subsides as it always does, the full capsaicin rush can be fully appreciated as a successful challenge to the senses that grows on you.   Overcome and carry on.

No doubt, Green Eggs Café on South 13th Street is someone's idea of paradise.  Full up at 3 in the afternoon, with a 30 minute wait for a table (or, restrooms), there was nary an empty seat in the house.  The sidewalk was crowded with more people waiting their entry into Valhalla. It's not that the staff wasn't friendly and accommodating, it was just that unless you were totally committed to having brunch on this corner, and had the rest of the day to make your way inside, you might have considered the practical and humane limits of participating in this exercise in mass impulse run amok. Rather than the gates of green heaven, it felt more like Dante's purgatory on an empty stomach.   The promised thirty soon became 45, without realistic estimate of when a table would be available.  We were welcome to wait with name on list, and add to the aura of the last ship to sail before the invasion, but to do so meant that the rest of the day was shot, and the cost of parking would become exponentially higher; making this a very expensive meal indeed.  It just wasn't worth it.   So, we ordered a couple of joes to go, and once received, took our leave.  They were very good, and I imagine that used as a washdown for red velvet pancakes or some other overwrought sweet platter, would do quite nicely.    Can't hold success against the establishment, but neither do we have to suffer its consequences without reservation.

Iron Hill Brewery & Restaurant is a new entree among the many eating establishments in the expanded Village @ Newtown Shopping Center, focusing on mostly traditional tavern fare to go with their house brews from the stainless works in the rear of their premises. As a local outfit headquartered in Wilmington, Delaware, it is good to see how attractive their plant is and how successful their business model has been.   We used Yelp to get on their wait-list on a Sunday evening, and when we arrived they had us on the screen and we were seated immediately at a high top quad against a wall. The building was beautifully appointed with lots of wood and leather, high ceiling, and huge glass wall in the back to show off the brewery operation. The space was well thought out for the comfort and interest of the customer. Our server was friendly and knowledgeable, and aimed to please.  Son & I were thinking burgers and sandwiches, but I was also tempted by the seasonal Butternut Apple Soup on the appetizer menu. So, the young one went for a Grilled Chicken Sandwich w Fries, and the old man jumped at the Pub Burger w Fries (medium). First, the soup was really good with a cream base. The flavors of the squash and apple both came through. So nice! The burger was as requested - juicy, with gouda and jack cheese, bacon and aioli smear on the brioche style roll. Delicious, even if the bottom of the roll gave up the ghost halfway through the meal due to the dampness of the load. I had to finish with knife & fork. Son 'O Mine was happy with his meal, but didn't think it was exceptional. Fries were hot and crisp.   I sampled their Little Red Wagon suds. Maybe it was a kid's drink, but I liked the subtle strawberry rhubarb sour taste. Good complement to the rest of my meal.   Iron Hill is a big improvement to the restaurant scene in Newtown, along with several other eateries in the Village @ Newtown. It contributes to establishing our community as a legitimate destination for the hungry and parched. So many quality choices now available to us.   Check it out.

This Einstein Bagel shop in the Big Oak Shopping Center, Lower Makefield, PA, (No. It's not in Yardley), is well set up for Covid Protocols. It is clean, prepared for ordering and takeaway transactions, and even prebags the tops and stirrers for coffee cups. First time I've seen that. The service was prompt and friendly, and I saw no sign of the negativity referenced in other reviews.   Unfortunately, unlike their namesake Albert E., the bagels themselves are not as intelligently conceptualized. Their skin is soft rather than offering a crispness found in more traditional NY style bagels. This suggests the boiling in lye or brine was skipped or inadequate to foster the differing texture signature of the better bagels in the Universe. The overall taste is decent, and they do cover the surface with plenty of toppings (roasted onion flakes for me). Yet, missing a key step in the process relegates their product to strictly second tier status, when it would have been so easy to get it right.   They do have plenty of options and can throw together a reasonably good sandwich. So, if you don't mind the lack of textural differentiation, you will find the grab, bite and chew satisfying. Otherwise, you will discover yourself wishing for a more complete effort.   Their coffee is actually better than the bagels.

When you find street parking with time on the meter located directly across from your destination in Lambertville, you suspect that grace and parking angels are smiling down on you. So, expectations rise and you prepare for more magic moments.   I chose Tacos Cancun because I desired good Mexican cuisine in a safe space respecting Covid Protocol. Just so happened that the back patio had been recently renovated - replacing beach umbrellas with a large lime green tarpaulin over all the tables and a 6' bamboo screen all around. It made the backyard feel private and someplace more tropical than New Jersey. That I was the only paying customer late Sunday afternoon, certainly helped with the vibe. I took a table along the southern wall about halfway back and had all the attention I could ever want.   The menu had most of the usual suspects, plus a few house specialties. Although I was considering Flautas, Chili Rellenos, or Torta Milanese, when I arrived, I changed my mind for a walk on the wild side and ordered La Gringa, one of their specials that seemed to cover a lot of bases (sauteed veggies, ham, chorizo, melted cheese and crema drizzle). It was well reviewed, so I rolled with the optimistic sense I came in with.   Within 10 minutes a large white ceramic plate arrived, with Red Rice & Black Beans and hot Tortillas. It was all delicious, even though I didn't understand why the dish was called "Gringa," (North American Girl). No doubt there was a story there, but the servers didn't seem to know it. Even without the additional local color, it was a fine filling meal. It wasn't overly spicy, but not everything has to be a conflagration for me to be happy.   While not as intensely authentic as the kitchens found in the Hispanic neighborhoods of Trenton or Norristown, it was plenty good enough for me. No hesitation coming again.

This sports bar in Richboro, PA, is a fun place to watch Eagles football. It is a large space with a long U-shaped bar, surrounded by HDTVs high on the walls. The bartenders are so busy they don't have a moment to follow the action, but they are friendly and don't lose their cool.   Prices are reasonable for a bar that makes it bones primarily around sporting events. Most bar food (burgers, quesadillas, soups, salads, sandwiches) can be had for $10 or less. Beer selection is not focused on crafties, but there are a few in the house, while most of the usual suspects are on tap.  My pint of Miller Lite was $3 and change.   The house erupted each time the Eagles made a play, and went berserk when they pulled out the win of the Rams. There was a collective groan when Carson Wentz was injured. Of course, there were a couple of people in too deep with drink, who were obnoxious, but they were led outside by the firm arm of house security.   My chicken quesadilla was pretty good. Loaded with chicken and cheese, it was a solid app to get me through the game. It was exactly what I expected from the neighborhood sports bar.  I was particularly pleased that the lovely barkeeps made no attempt to refill my beer glass after I let them know I only wanted one. They were cool with someone who did not want more to drink, but only was there to enjoy the game with fellow fans.  I tipped them accordingly.

These new fangled Wawa stores are a great improvement over the last generation small box iteration with too small parking areas, and limited prepared food options. The 21st Century variation are at least 2,500 square feet, with gas pumps outside and elaborate food kitchen and computer aided ordering system able to please even the most picky pallette. The coffee hasn't changed much, but then again, it was darn good back in the day, and remains so.   But, despite the impressive modernization, these roadside way stations are far from perfect, and actually create some problems that didn't exist before. This facility on Parkway Avenue in Ewing, NJ, offers obvious examples of this evolution.   Access is only through a side street and a too narrow long driveway off to the side in front. At a significant intersection, it makes for challenging traffic entering from Parkway or exiting from the rear of the property. Too, there isn't enough parking around the building to accommodate all the folks going inside for food and drink. Two things therefore happen; first, people are encouraged to leave their vehicles at the gas pumps while they shop within, and second, others park illegally wherever they can, hoping not to cause a park rage incident. I've seen one such confrontation, and it wasn't pretty.   This friction point is exacerbated within by understaffed kitchen help causing back up in food prep and lots of people milling about with receipts waiting for their numbers to be called. It's a beautiful industrial kitchen, but whenever I am there, several food stations are without preparers, while one or two areas over backed up to the max. So, people wait, while many cars are interfering with traffic flow outside, and people can't get gasoline because abandoned looking vehicles clog the gas islands.  Bottom line, the store is too big for the lot it occupies, leaving too few parking spots. Greedy developers clearly oversold their prowess as designers of business flow, and the undermanned planning commissions approved the plan without adequate analysis. The internals should work, but if management fails to adapt to reality, there will never be enough workers on site to handle the crush inhouse caused by poor planning on the outside and shift manpower shortages.   This is how old problems reemerge in the new world. Poor planning and management is timeless, and in some cases, inevitable.  PS. The chicken salad on wheat torpedo was quite good.

Osaka Japanese/Chinese Restaurant has been around for a while. It is operated by a friendly Chinese couple who have degrees from Sushi University. Their shop is dimly lit with subtle Asian decor, with small fish bar and large dining room. Staff wears black T shirts and slacks and have been working there for a long time, indicating that it is probably a decent place to work.  Given the cultural orientation of management, I opted to try the Chinese side of the menu first. Although the lunch offerings were limited, I ordered General Tso's Chicken, which came with cup of wonton soup, small fried egg roll (surprisingly) and pork fried rice.   It arrived on a large white ceramic plate. This was much more than normally seen for a lunch special. I could only eat half, and they packaged the rest for me to take home. The volume of food was the most memorable part of the meal. The chicken was all dark meat, although the sauce was nicely spiced. The wontons were thick skinned and the consomme was also darker and more savory than usual. The rice wasn't bad, but had been sitting around for a while.   Overall, I might return to sample the Japanese side of the menu, but the Chinese elements were no better than average.

Found a nail embedded in the edge of the tread in a Run Flat Michelin. Drove over to Mavis on Route 1 across from Oxford Valley Mall because I had had a good experience at a different one of their tire havens in Richboro, PA. This one was closer to home.   The place was moderately busy with four bays with cars in varying degrees of repair or tire changes. Good sign I thought. Walking in, a manager approached to ask if I had an appointment. Didn't know I needed one, but he was cool about it. A few minutes later we went to look at my tire problem, saw the nail sticking out, advised me it had to be replaced due to where it was, and returned to the front desk to see if it was in stock.   It wasn't. But, he would order it and have it by Saturday sometime. He said he would call me when it came in and we would switch out the bad for the new. Sounded like a reasonable plan. I left there satisfied. What was one day?  The call never came and I ended up visiting a different tire center that also had to call for the Run Flat to be delivered to them the same day, for a few bucks less. They did call on arrival and the swap out was accomplished later the same afternoon.   Really appreciated their effort and friendly professionalism, even if their name wasn't Mavis.

This review reflects only the lunch buffet and service surrounding it.   In a sequence of odd/violative behavior from the moment we walked in:   ~ Although the place was almost empty, the greeter walked us to a booth right next to the only other occupants of the restaurant.  We relocated ourselves so all of us could have some privacy, but new customers were continually brought to the same area and seated too close to each other. The remainder of the floor remained unoccupied. I realize this is a Chinese custom, but here it is not cool.  VIOLATION.  ~ The buffet looks great, yet although we were making our choices shortly after 12, everything placed on my plate was at best warm, and at worst, room temperature. Nothing I tried was heated to the right temperature range. VIOLATION  ~ One of the managers came out of the kitchen to check what was needed. She was not dressed for kitchen work, nor did she wear gloves as she handled the food and utensils, pushing the contents of the chaffing dishes around to make room for more.  VIOLATION  ~ As we were eating our first round of food, and long before we were finished, a wait person dropped off the bill in the plastic billfold.  Not only was it "served" way too early, but it was placed right next to our plates full of food.  The table was otherwise empty, and there was plenty of space for it to be laid an appropriate distance from our plates. Not a word was said, and the male server seemed almost hostile.  We relocated it to the opposite corner of the table away from us.  VIOLATION   I hesitate to consider what goes on with the sushi.   No seconds today, thanks.

That Johnny Longhots has a great name for an Italian sandwich shop is beyond doubt. Reminds of Robert Louis Stevenson's Long John Silver in the great novel classic, Treasure Island. Capturing an image of pirate treasure and devious scalliwags as part of your business image has gotta be a strong beginning for this new enterprise on Oxford Valley Road in Fairless Hills, PA.   That they also turn out fantastic sandwiches, steaks and the like, means they can back up the talk (advertising) with action. My Italian Hot Dog was amazing. Three quality frankfurters in a sesame torpedo roll topped with a load of roast potato, Italian frying pepper, sauteed sweet onion, mustard and ketchup, and doctored with hot banana peppers from the fixings bar, makes for a memorable chomp down. It was the best I've enjoyed in many years.   At nearly $9 it wasn't cheap, but when you realize there is really enough there for two people or to take home half for later consumption, the value proposition comes into focus. Come with your favorite +1, or pack and carry for your later pleasure.   Johnny Longhots is good for eat in or carry out, or both, as I just discovered.   Totally impressive. Definitely a Treasure Island!

I've been kicking myself for several days now for not dining at The Churchville Inn before last Friday night. Living in central Bucks County for decades, someone should have alerted me to how good it was; and after joining Yelp I should have scouted it out myself long before. Mea Culpa!   Now that the boys and I have have broken the ice, we are in accord that we just had one of the best Bucks sups we can remember.  We mixed and matched the Whole Chicken Wings with Reaper (extremely hot) Sauce, Red Buds, Half Rack of Baby Backs, and the Maple-Bacon BBQ Grilled Salmon.   The wings were about the biggest I'd ever seen; plump, juicy and scalding to near numbness. Big hit!  The Red Buds were an app, but enough for a meal, with a mix of braised bacon, pulled pork and melted cheddar. Nice take on traditional twice baked potatoes.  The salmon wasn't a large steak, but with the maple bacon thickened to a fire glaze, it was great. The mashed sweets were a mellow counterpoint.  The star of the show were the ribs. Meaty, tangy and suck off the bone awesome. There was no choice of finishes, but no one complained.  They were a great gnaw. We had no though of dessert.    The inn facility is large and country comfortable, with downstairs and upstairs dining rooms and upside bar. No doubt we will have many happy returns.

The concept is a good one. Visit any Costco and you will see it done extremely well. Warehouse size store and warehouse prices. At this Aldi's on Woodbourne Road in Langhorne, Pa., they get the pricing part right, but the size and functionality of the space totally wrong.   This is a shop about the size of a large Wawa, but designed in the 1990's with completely inefficient layout, and snail paced cashier check outs.  The products are stacked onto shelves in their original boxes, with the discount prices listed above or below.  If you see something you need/want, it is easy enough to grab it and put it in the broken down supermarket carts that cost a quarter to unshackle out front. They are rusty and in need of maintenance.   The fresh produce is hit or miss. The bakery items limited.  There are plenty of canned and boxed goods, mostly from labels I never heard of.  Plenty of cold cereals. The check out line is long and slow, made worse by the absence of bags.  You have to bring your own or use the boxes in the store. That's okay, but the people loading them on the shelf beyond the two cashiers make for more congestion and confusion.    The shop has seen better days.  It is disheveled like a permanent bad hair day. It looks like it hasn't been thoroughly cleaned nor painted in the past decade.    For me, it is not worth the small savings to experience the depression I feel walking around the store.    This Aldi's needs an extreme makeover in the worst way.  It is the sister of one of my favorite stores, Trader Joe's. How they can be siblings is beyond me.  It sure needs more love and attention.

Just so happens that Momma D's Soul Food 2 is down Broad Street from my Trenton office. I don't know why I hadn't tried it before now, but the good news is that I'm off the schnied.   I ordered through the Yelp GrubHub connection, which was easy to do, and when I received the message that my Meatloaf, Yams, Fried Cabbage and Corn Bread meal was ready, I walked over to get it. The chef/manager/owner mistook me for the GrubHub delivery guy and addressed me as such a bit dismissively. An understandable mistake that we cleared up when we both realized that while I used that service, I was not of that agency. I was just the neighbor down the street come to pick up my food. Introductions completed, we parted on a first name basis.   I want to remain on good terms with Momma D, because that first meal made a lasting first impression. It was fantastic. The meatloaf was loose, rather than dense, just the way my mother used to make from the recipe she found on an old Quaker Oats round box. Mixed with the rich dark brown gravy, it was a glorious romp down memory lane, complete with all the excess calories. The yams were soft and sweet, and the cabbage tender and nicely spiced. The cornbread was as good as a fresh squared corn muffin. There was more than enough in the carry out styro for at least two filling meals. Given that quantity, the value proposition was outstanding.  This kitchen also turns out other favorites; fried chicken, whiting and BBQ beef ribs, not to mention several other sides and desserts (peach cobbler, anyone?!) So, I will be back when I find myself working late and getting hungry. The choices are rich and fattening, so I will have to watch the urge to splurge.   Only suggestion - Improve the takeout containers to a grade that doesn't leak. I hated to lose all that gravy that I found in the bottom of the large plastic bag I carried it back to the office in. Otherwise, it was a home run.

Gino runs his shop, Mamma Rosa's Restaurant, like he was inviting each customer into his home for a meal.  The space is a converted/expanded residence from a time before zoning made such mixed uses impossible in most places.  It is cozy, warm, and bright, sort of like a old summer home in Ortley Beach or Lavalette.   I sat at a kitchen table and ordered what Gino suggested was one of the better things on the menu, a Chicken Parm Sandwich.  It arrived about 10 minutes later; a fat breast, butterflied, with rich tomato gravy, grated cheese, on a very good oven toasted half torpedo.  It was excellent and required knife and fork to be eaten without losing the back end.    Gino introduced himself and we chatted about his bio and how he came to be a restauranteur. The entire experience was very personal, and it was easy to slip and stay in the embrace of your Italian grandfather's kitchen.

Stopped in for a late afternoon slice to hold off hunger for a few hours. Nice shop with a half dozen booths and broad Italian menu. HDTVs playing Mexican talk shows.  I asked for a slice of sausage pie "well done," from those under the display glass.   It arrived hot and steaming, and certainly what I asked for.  Sadly, all the heat had not helped rigidify the chassis. It still collapsed under its own weight. The crust was soggy from an approach that put too much on top and didn't allow enough moisture to escape in the oven. The taste was there, but the texture was AWOL.   There aren't many pizza joint in this area that understand the right balance between ingredients and strong crust that results in a pie that is crisp, tasty and light on its feet. Loading up on cheese at the expense of sauce and other toppings just misses the mark.    The secret is that when it comes to great pizza, less is more.

Time to upgrade Ms. Philly Grill after a return breakfast visit this week.   The place looks about the same as when last here several years ago. Still clean and full of red and white leatherette booths with chrome around the trim. This time staff was more attentive, bringing orders from the kitchen promptly and offering to refill the coffee mug as they passed around the dining room.   My Hercules Omelet was a three egger variant of a Greek, but with Gyro meat (beef/lamb) in place of sausage, and spinach, onion, tomato and feta. Large half plate of home fries alongside. I liked it a lot, especially with a squirt of hot sauce all around. Coffee was strong, too, with the requested milk rather than creamers.   It is quite possible that the same regulars I saw last time where still hanging out. My server looked like the woman who helped me before.
